# Patrologia Latina, volume 81 — English translation

# Patrologia Latina, Vol. 81

## The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal Library

The complete, uniform, convenient, economical library of all the holy Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reprinting of all the surviving monuments of Catholic tradition throughout the first twelve centuries of the Church, based on the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously illustrated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by the discovery of all works completed after the extensive editions owed to the last three centuries; furnished with particular analytical indexes following each volume or author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself and with titles distinguishing the upper margin of each page and indicating its subject matter; expanded by works both doubtful and apocryphal, as well as by works possessing some authority and influence with respect to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever any one of the Fathers has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it may readily be learned which Fathers, and in what places of their works, have commented on the individual books of Scripture.

A most accurate edition, and easily preferable to all others if one considers the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, the variety and number of the reprinted works, the very convenient form of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the whole work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, systematic, and chronological—which for the first time in our library gathers together six hundred fragments and minor works previously scattered here and there, drawn from works concerning every age, place, language, and form.

## Second Series

In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and ecclesiastical writers of the Latin Church from Gregory the Great to Innocent III.

Published by J.-P. Migne, editor of the Universal Library of the Clergy, or of complete series in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.

# [Isidorian Works]

[Col. 0009]

## To His Eminence and Most Reverend Lord, Don Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana y Buitrón

Priest of the Holy Roman Church, Cardinal, Archbishop of Toledo, Primate of Spain, and Grand Inquisitor; Chancellor Major of Castile; Royal Councillor of State; decorated with the Grand Cross of the illustrious Royal Spanish Order of Charles III, etc.

Faustino Arévalo.

What the most learned men had long and earnestly desired—that the works of Isidore, the most holy bishop of Seville, should once again come to light in a form and arrangement worthy of our age—I have undertaken to accomplish after so many unsuccessful efforts by others. I shall perhaps therefore incur various criticisms. Yet, undeterred by this, and with you as author and auspice, Most Eminent Prince, in whom alone all the hope and purpose of my studies are placed, I have dared to undertake something even greater than might satisfy the wishes of others.

For although many men distinguished by learning and talent, both in the memory of our fathers and ancestors and in our own time, have devoted diligent effort either to polishing and completing the complete works of Saint Isidore or merely to preparing this or that edition of them—and although some of their studies have indeed been submitted to the press but are scattered and rarely encountered, while others still lay hidden in manuscript—I did not think I would be showing sufficient love and devotion toward the Doctor of our Spain, or sufficient gratitude toward those who have illuminated his deeds and writings, unless I gathered all such writings of others into a single body, each suitably arranged in its proper place, and restored them to the standard of truth wherever this seemed necessary.

Thus, by adding what I have judged should be added to the best of my ability, this edition of mine alone may be regarded as equivalent to all the others. If this plan of mine meets with your approval, Most Eminent Prince—or rather, since I have already learned that it does please you—I do not doubt that all the rest will also approve it willingly, either compelled by the same considerations that moved me or encouraged by the authority of your judgment.

Indeed, I foresee and desire that this new edition of Isidore will be added as a kind of crowning achievement to your other immortal services to the study of the liberal arts. Your name, to which you seem to have left nothing that could be added to its distinction and greatness, will nevertheless become somewhat more illustrious—not only among those who have fostered sacred learning by their patronage and have made others mindful of them through their benefactions, but also among those who have cultivated the study of that same learning for the enduring remembrance and renown of their name.

May God preserve you, Most Eminent Cardinal and most illustrious prelate, for as long as possible, safe and unharmed, for the learned men of the Christian commonwealth and especially of our Spain, whose great light you are.

This was my prayer.

From Rome, on the Kalends of January, 1796.

[Col. 0009]

# Isidorian Works, or Prolegomena to the Edition of the Works of Saint Isidore of Seville

## Part One

### On the Life, Deeds, and Teaching of Saint Isidore, and on the Editions Containing All His Works

## Chapter One

### The Extreme Difficulty of Preparing an Accurate Edition of Saint Isidore’s Works. The Method Used in These Prolegomena

[Col. 0009]

### 1

I am undertaking a work full of peril. Let me preface it by saying what I could already have said when I first applied myself to comparing the works of ancient writers with manuscript copies; but now, certainly for still weightier reasons, I dare to declare that in this kind of study there is more labor and difficulty, and a greater store of learning is required, than is commonly thought by those who have either never tried it themselves or are incapable even of judging true scholarly excellence.

Franciscus Robertellus, who published a discussion of the art or method of correcting ancient books, says:

> “Many persons who may be seen in our age are extremely dangerous. Although they possess no knowledge of anything, they dare to claim that they are correctors of books, when they ought rather to be called corrupters. Would that some law had forbidden everyone to do this.”

Let us therefore establish first that our discipline requires a kind of boundless learning in anyone who wishes to be called a corrector of books. He must have read much, heard much, and gained much through practice; he must also have examined more recent works.

### 2

For although the writings of the ancients must be rigorously tested against ancient books, so that it would be wrong to depart from them rashly, nevertheless, since the copies themselves usually differ among one another and are often plainly corrupt, it is necessary to employ those methods and rules of conjectural criticism prescribed by masters skilled in this discipline.

Since conjectures are ordinarily made by addition, omission, transposition, expansion, contraction, punctuation, combination, or alteration, who could be so blind as not to see that this cannot possibly be done without precise knowledge of ancient writing, ancient words and expressions, antiquity itself, and finally the subject that the ancient writer undertook to treat or explain?

### 3

If this sort of difficulty is evident in reviewing any other ancient writers, what are we to think of our Isidore of Seville? One might rightly call him a second Varro, whether alongside Bishop Braulio of Zaragoza or, with others, a Christian Pliny—indeed, in large part richer than Pliny.

For Isidore left no field untouched. He approached every discipline, treated both human and divine sciences, read ancient pagan and sacred writers, and copied them for his own use. Nor was he content merely to contain an encyclopedia of the sciences in his etymological work. He also discussed many matters individually in his interpretation of Sacred Scripture, many in every other branch of theology, many in philosophical and astronomical subjects, and many in literary, chronological, and historical matters.

### 4

Just as Isidore drew outstandingly from earlier writers and preserved for us many monuments of antiquity that one would seek elsewhere in vain, so, conversely, those who flourished after Isidore—especially ecclesiastical writers—very frequently irrigated their own little gardens from Isidore’s springs.

This makes the revision of his works more laborious and complicated. It is not enough to have the ancient copies of Isidore before one’s hands and eyes; one must also repeatedly turn either to those writers who preceded Isidore as torchbearers or to those for whom Isidore himself provided the light. When all these sources are compared with one another, it often happens that Isidore is illuminated by other writers and sometimes that other writers are corrected from Isidore.

### 5

Since the abundance and selection of ancient manuscript books are especially important for this undertaking, and since Isidore was once examined and published at Madrid from many ancient Spanish copies and later at Paris from other Gallic ones, it happened very conveniently for me that, while many further collations of other people came into my hands, my principal task became the examination of the Roman libraries, which others had overlooked, and the careful review of the innumerable ancient manuscript codices preserved there.

I shall call this, if you wish, the Roman Spicilegium, so that no part of the glory may seem to have been taken away from those distinguished men who first labored in this field.

Yet, as far as the abundance of Isidore’s manuscript copies is concerned, I alone have been able to see and examine in the Vatican and other Roman libraries more copies than all the editors of Isidore’s works have listed—not even excluding those copies which the distinguished Francis Anthony Zaccaria had himself long ago collated for his projected edition of Isidore or had arranged for others to collate. Their collations have come into my hands, as I indicated above and shall explain more distinctly later.

### 6

Peter Lazerus, a man endowed with outstanding learning and talent, truly praised the glories of Rome in this respect in his preface to Saint Bruno of Asti’s commentary on the four Gospels:

> “This city, the foremost of all, which by the common judgment of mankind surpasses the others in many distinguished and excellent respects, I believe yields to no city, however extensive or splendid, in this one matter: it possesses very numerous and thoroughly equipped libraries, especially abounding in manuscript codices. Thus, from this kind of literary treasury, many works of Greeks, Latins, and foreign peoples, and especially many writings of the most learned Fathers of the Church, have either been brought forth into the light and sight of men, rescued from destruction, or, after the stains with which they had appeared defiled were wiped away, restored through the work of learned men to the splendor they had received from their authors and to their native elegance.”

I think this may be inferred not only from the larger and more distinguished libraries of the same city, which foreigners themselves—men highly skilled in these matters, such as Mabillon, Montfaucon, and others—have praised, and whose excellence in the magnificence of their buildings, the abundance of their books, and the quality of their manuscript codices no moderately learned person is unaware of, but especially from certain other smaller libraries whose fame and reputation have scarcely reached the knowledge of men. There is hardly one that could not display something rare and outstanding for the benefit of men of letters and the advancement of learning.

### 7

Thus Lazerus spoke when he was bringing the commentary I mentioned by Bruno into public view from the ancient parchments of the library of the Roman College.

It is almost astonishing how many extremely ancient codices of Isidore have appeared to me in the libraries of Rome, especially in the Vatican. Would that I had been permitted to hope so much from myself that I might have had leisure to compare all of them with the works already printed.

But since, as that writer said, “the sum of life is brief and prevents us from beginning a long hope,” I had to hasten, lest what happened to others laboring to illuminate Isidore should happen to me also: while they tried to pursue and embrace everything, they disentangled nothing.

I had to hasten all the more because there was a danger that, if I ceased working, not only my own little studies on Isidore but also the labors of others, which I had undertaken to rescue from destruction, would completely disappear.

### 8

Accordingly, after carefully examining the oldest and best copies in reviewing each of Isidore’s works, consulting the others in obscure and difficult passages, diligently investigating, transcribing, and collecting all writings not yet printed that attribute their authorship to Isidore in manuscript codices, and supplementing the works already published with additions of no little importance; after carefully reading countless authors of critical conjectures, probabilities, adversaria, commentaries, and annotations who have treated ancient sacred and profane writers with distinction and often cite Isidore as a witness, I judged that the time had come to arrange in an orderly fashion this immense forest—or almost, I might say, this confused heap—of materials, distributing my own and others’ contributions each in its proper place.

For I hold that all the materials pertaining to the explanation and correction of Isidore can scarcely, if indeed they can, be gathered by one person, however learned; and that they cannot be gathered by many unless someone brings his private resources openly to light, so that others may add their own when opportunity permits.

### 9

To make this more convenient, I am undertaking to prepare an edition of all Isidore’s works in which, although much will be new, nothing found in previous editions will be lacking.

But what suitable order can be adopted amid such a variety of materials? By what bonds can such disparate members be joined together? At the end of the *Prolegomena* I shall explain what should be observed in arranging the edition of Isidore’s works and the accompanying annotations. For now I shall briefly explain what must be done in the *Prolegomena*.

### 10

I shall present accurately transcribed the ancient monuments most closely connected with Isidore and which speak about his life, deeds, and death; these will be checked against manuscript codices and illustrated with observations.

They will provide the foundation for weaving together the sequence of Saint Isidore’s life. I shall then undertake separate investigations into many matters that have long been disputed. I shall discuss Isidore’s learning, authority, and praises.

I shall record the editions of his works more fully, adding the prefaces of the editors and even their dedicatory letters. I shall set out individually the attempts of others to prepare a new edition, as well as the collections they had assembled for that purpose.

### 11

I shall then proceed to enumerate Isidore’s works and distinguish the genuine from the spurious, after first presenting ancient catalogues of such works. I shall discuss each separately and indicate which works, separated from the others, appeared in print. I shall also take care that nothing from these individual editions be absent from the present one.

Finally, I shall prepare a substantial—not superficial—review of the ancient manuscript books with whose help I have worked, a review that may perhaps be useful in certain respects for illuminating literary history.

# Chapter Two

## The Final Chapter of Saint Leander’s Rules to His Sister Florentina, Concerning the Homeland, Parents, and Siblings of Saint Isidore, Collated with Printed Copies and Gothic Manuscripts

### 1

> “Now we are steering the ship of our speech toward harbor, and, having crossed the sea of our words, we cast anchor on the shore where we may rest. Yet, under the breath of your charity, I return once more amid the waves of words.
>
> “I beg you, sister Florentina, and adjure you by the blessed Trinity of the one Godhead: since you have departed from your homeland and your kin, together with Abraham, do not look back with Lot’s wife (Genesis 19), lest you become an example of evil, a lesson to others toward good; lest other women see in you what they should avoid in themselves. She became a seasoning of wisdom for others but, for herself, an image of folly: her evil deed harmed herself, while the contrary example benefited others.
>
> “May the thought of returning to your native soil never trouble you—the place where, if God had wished you to dwell, he would not have expelled you from it. But because he foresaw that this would be useful for your purpose, he drew you away from Sodom, as he drew Abraham from the Chaldeans and Lot from Sodom.
>
> “Indeed, I myself confess my error: I often addressed our common mother, wishing to know whether she wanted to return to her homeland. But she, knowing that she had left it by God’s will as the cause of her salvation, said under divine adjuration: ‘I neither wish to see that homeland nor shall I ever see it again.’ And with great tears she said: ‘Exile made me recognize God; I shall die an exile and be buried there where I received the knowledge of God.’
>
> “With Jesus as my witness, I remember having found this true in her desires: even if she lived for a long time, she would not revisit that homeland. Take care, therefore, sister Florentina, lest what our mother feared happen to you; prudently avoid the evil from which she fled.

### 2

> “Wretched me! I grieve that I sent our common brother Fulgentius there, whose dangers I fear with continual dread. Yet he will be safer if you are more secure and, although absent, pray for him.
>
> “You have been drawn away from there in such a manner that, even if you had been born there, you would not remember it. There is no memory that moves your soul with longing; and blessed are you who do not know what you might grieve.
>
> “Yet I speak from experience: that homeland has so lost its condition and appearance that no free person remains in it, nor is the land itself fertile with its accustomed abundance—and not without God’s judgment. For the land whose citizens have been removed and given over to a stranger, as soon as it lost its dignity, also lost its fertility.
>
> “See, sister Florentina, how I approach you trembling and grieving, lest the serpent snatch you from paradise and place you in that land which produces thorns and thistles; and lest, if you should again wish to stretch out your hand from there and take the tree of life to eat, you be forbidden to touch it.
>
> “For I testify to you with the prophet, and, with Jesus Christ as my witness, I admonish you, saying: ‘Hear, O daughter, and see, and incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house, because the king has desired your beauty, and he himself is your Lord God’ (Psalm 44:11–12).
>
> “‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God’” (Luke 9:62).

### 3

> “Do not fly away from the nest where the turtledove found a place to shelter her young (Psalm 83). You are the daughter of Simplicity, born of Mother Turtledove.
>
> “In the same person you make use of the office of several relationships. Regard Turtledove as your mother; attend to Turtledove as your teacher; and consider as a dearer mother the woman who gives birth to you for Christ every day through her affections than the mother from whom you were born.
>
> “Hide yourself in her bosom from every storm and every worldly whirlwind. May it be sweet for you to cling to her side; may it be dear to you to rest upon the lap of one advanced in years, which was so pleasing to you when you were an infant.”

### 4

> “Finally, I beg you, my dearest sister, to remember me in your prayers and not to forget our younger brother Isidore. Since our parents left him under God’s protection, with three siblings surviving, they departed joyfully to the Lord, fearing nothing concerning his infancy.
>
> “Since I regard him as truly my son, place nothing temporal before my affection for him, and recline upon him with devoted love, love him all the more dearly and entreat Jesus for him all the more earnestly, the more you know that he was tenderly loved by our parents.
>
> “I am certain that your virginal prayer bends the divine ears toward us. If you preserve the covenant you have made with Christ, a crown is owed to you for acting well, and pardon will be granted to Leander for his exhortation. If you persevere to the end, you will be saved. Amen.”

### 5

Flórez added these various readings in volume 9 of *España Sagrada*, appendix 5, from two Gothic manuscript copies: one belonging to the Royal Library of Madrid, the other to Saint Emiliano of Cucullatus, or La Cogolla, as it is called; and from the editions of Sandoval, Tamayo, and Holstenius.

Sandoval and Tamayo: *et immenso dietorum* (“and of an immense [number] of sayings”). Tamayo: *verborum revertor* (“I return to the words”). Tamayo: *inde ejecisset* (“had cast [you] out from there”). The Gothic manuscripts: *velit reverti* (“she may wish to return”). Sandoval and Tamayo: *experta fugit* (“having experienced it, she fled”).

### 6

Holstenius and Nicolás Antonio, in the eulogy of Saint Fulgentius, no. 12, *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispanica*: *ea inde aetate* (“at that age from there”). The manuscripts: *ea inde arte* (“by that means from there”). Sandoval: *si perdidisse* (“if [I] had lost”). Sandoval and Tamayo: *vitae ad edendum* (“of life for eating”). Sandoval and Tamayo: *in ejus pronus* (“inclined toward him”). Sandoval and Tamayo: *parentibus terrenis* (“earthly parents”).

### 7

If you wish, add to these some observations of my own.

Holstenius, no. 1, has *per beatam quoque* (“also by the blessed [Trinity]”). In the same place Holstenius has *te abstraxit* (“drew you away”), whereas Flórez printed *te adtraxit* (“drew you toward [himself]”). In the same place Holstenius has *sepulcrum habeam* (“that I may have a tomb”).

In no. 2 Holstenius has *ut vel si ibidem* (“so that, even if [you were] there”). In the same place I conjectured *de qua sursum si velis* (“from which above, if you wish”), etc. In the same place Holstenius has *in aratrum* (“onto the plow”).

In no. 3 Flórez has *te sinibus concede* (“entrust yourself to her bosoms”) and *jam profecto* (“indeed now”) instead of *jam provectae* (“now advanced [in age]”). The latter is better, or something with the same meaning: *jam profectae* (“now having advanced”).

I pass over other grammatical errors, which, although they may perhaps belong to Leander’s period, are better attributed to the copyists—for example, *ut nido* (“that in the nest”) instead of *nido quem* (“the nest which”), and so forth.

# Chapter Three

## The Preliminary Notice of the Books of Saint Isidore by Saint Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza

### 1

> “Isidore, an outstanding man and bishop of the Church of Seville, successor to and brother of Bishop Leander, flourished from the time of the Emperor Maurice and King Reccared. In him antiquity claimed something for itself—or rather, our own age imagined in him a knowledge of antiquity. He was formed in every kind of expression, so that, according to the quality of his speech, he was suitable both for the unlearned and for the learned, and, with appropriate fitness to the place and occasion, renowned for incomparable eloquence.
>
> “How great he was in wisdom, a prudent reader will very easily understand from his various studies and carefully composed works. I have therefore recorded here what has come to my knowledge.
>
> “He published two books of *Differentiae*, in which, with subtle discrimination, he distinguished in meaning things that are commonly expressed confusedly in usage.
>
> “One book of *Prefaces*, in which he briefly indicated what each book of Sacred Scripture contains.
>
> “One book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, in which he noted, with concise statements, their deeds, dignity, death, and burial.
>
> “Two books of *Ecclesiastical Offices* addressed to his own brother Fulgentius, bishop of Écija, in which he drew out, in his own explanatory style and not without the authority of his predecessors, the origin of the offices and why each one is performed in the Church of God.
>
> “Two books of *Synonyms*, by which, through the intervention of rational exhortation, he raised the soul toward consolation and the hope of obtaining pardon.
>
> “One book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to King Sisebut, in which, drawing both on the inquiry of ecclesiastical teachers and on that of philosophers, he clarified certain obscure matters concerning the elements.
>
> “One book *On Numbers*, in which he touched in part upon the discipline of arithmetic because of the numbers inserted into ecclesiastical Scripture.
>
> “One book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, in which he showed what the persons mentioned signify mystically.
>
> “One book *On Heresies*, in which, following the examples of his predecessors, he collected at the greatest brevity he could matters spread widely.
>
> “Three books of *Sentences*, which he adorned with flowers from the moral books of Pope Gregory.
>
> “One book of *Chronicles*, from the beginning of the world to his own time, compiled with excessive brevity.
>
> “Two books *Against the Jews*, written at the request of his sister Florentina, a vowed virgin, in which he proved from testimonies of the Law and the Prophets everything that the Catholic faith believes.
>
> “One book *On Illustrious Men*, to which we have added these materials.
>
> “One book of a *Monastic Rule*, which he most suitably adapted for the use of his homeland and for the minds of the weak.
>
> “One book containing the history of the origin of the Goths, the kingdom of the Suebi, and also the Vandals.
>
> “Two books of *Questions*, in which anyone who reads them will recognize a great abundance of material from ancient interpreters.
>
> “A book of *Etymologies*, distinguished by its immense size and divided by headings rather than by books. Since he composed it at my request, although he left it unfinished, I divided it into twenty books.
>
> “Whoever reads this work, which is altogether suited to philosophy, with frequent meditation, will rightly be no stranger to knowledge of divine and human affairs. In it there is a profusion of the elegance of various arts, since he gathered together, in compressed form, almost everything that ought to be known.
>
> “There are also many other minor works by this man, inscribed in the Church of God with much distinction.
>
> “After so many disasters in Spain, God raised him up in the final times, I believe, to restore the monuments of the ancients, lest we grow utterly antiquated through rustic ignorance; he set him before us, as it were, as a kind of destiny (*destina*).
>
> “To him we may rightly apply this philosophical saying:
>
> > ‘We, wandering and straying like guests and strangers in our own city, were brought back home by your books, so that at last we might recognize who and where we were. You opened up the age of our homeland; you, the accounts of the times; you, the laws of sacred things; you, those of priests; you, domestic and public discipline; you, the names, kinds, duties, and causes of dwellings, regions, and places; you opened up the names, kinds, duties, and causes of all divine and human things.’  
> > —Cicero, *First Academic Questions*
>
> “The stream of his eloquence, and the number of the darts from divine Scripture and the testimonies of the Fathers with which he pierced the heresy of the Acephalites, are revealed by the synodal acts held before him at Seville. In that assembly he asserted the truth against Gregory, the bishop of the aforesaid heresy.
>
> “He died during the reign of the Emperor Heraclius and of the most Christian King Chintila, superior to all in sound doctrine and richer than all in works of charity.”

### 2

This preliminary notice of Isidore’s books was added by John Baptist Pérez to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, as chapter 47 of that work, and was illustrated by the notes that I append.

## Notes of John Baptist Pérez on the Preliminary Notice of the Books of Saint Isidore

> “Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, whom Ildefonsus mentions, is the author of this life of Isidore, as is evident from ancient books and from those letters of Braulio that are customarily placed before Isidore’s *Etymologies*. For here too he testifies that Isidore composed the book of the *Etymologies* at his request.
>
> “*Quasi quamdam apposuit destinam*, etc. Thus it stands entirely in an ancient codex. Others, not understanding the passage, altered it by conjecture to: *Quamdam apposuit lucem destinare*. The African poet Corippus uses this word in his book *On the Praises of Justin the Younger*, recently published by the very learned Ruyz Azagrio:
>
> > *Et Thomas Libycae nutantis destina terrae* (“And Thomas, the destiny of wavering Libyan land”).
>
> “Braulio says that Isidore died under Chintila, king of the Goths. From this the errors of many of our countrymen concerning the year of Isidore’s death are refuted; it is astonishing how much the Spanish historians differ among themselves on this point.
>
> “Therefore, in honor of our author Isidore, whom we have undertaken above all to illuminate, let us determine the day and year on which he died. I assert that he died most certainly in the year of Christ 636.
>
> “First, because his disciple Redemptus, who had been present and saw Isidore’s death, says in describing it that he died in the Spanish Era 664—a date which no one doubts is the year of Christ 636.
>
> “Redemptus likewise represents Isidore as addressing the people four days before his death in these words: ‘Thus,’ he says, ‘may the water of the sacred font, which the devout people are to receive today, be for you unto the remission of sins.’
>
> “Since it is established from all the martyrologies that Isidore died on the day before the Nones of April, if one consults the Paschal cycles one will find clearly that in this year, 636, Easter fell on the day before the Kalends of April, and that the solemn baptism of the catechumens therefore preceded Isidore’s death by four days.
>
> “Moreover, if he died under Chintila, as Braulio says, he must have died in the first year of Chintila, since it is known from the Fifth Council of Toledo that Chintila began his reign in Era 674, that is, in the year of Christ 636. In the second year of Chintila we see the Sixth Council of Toledo being held, in which not Isidore—for he was already dead—but Honoratus, Isidore’s successor, took part.
>
> “Thus we recognize the truth of what Ildefonsus said: that Isidore flourished until the reign of King Sisenand, with no mention at all of Chintila, who followed Sisenand—namely because Isidore died in Chintila’s very first year.
>
> “We also recognize the truth of what the same Ildefonsus said: that Isidore presided over the Church of Seville for almost forty years. In fact, there were thirty-seven years altogether, from the year 600 to 636, as we calculated shortly before in the case of Leander and now in that of Isidore.”

[Col. 0018B]

### 3

In the excellent edition of the Toledo Fathers, the same book of Isidore *On Illustrious Men* was placed before Ildefonsus’s work of the same title. But in Braulio’s—or Braulion’s, for the name is pronounced both ways, as with *Taio*, *Taius*, and similar forms—preliminary notice of Isidore’s books, no variation in the text was recorded.

Constantine Cajetanus once published it in his work *The Lives and Deeds of the Three Bishops, Lights of the Benedictine Order: Isidore of Seville, Ildefonsus of Toledo, and Cardinal Gregory of Ostia*. Rome, 1606. I shall not omit his observations.

## Notes and Variant Readings of Abbot Constantine Cajetanus on the Life of Isidore Written by Saint Braulio

### 4

> “This testimony concerning Saint Isidore, composed by Saint Braulio, is marked with the title *Life* at the end of Isidore’s own work *On Illustrious Men*. Laurence Surius, Franciscus Haraeus, Zacharias Lippelous, and others likewise entitled it *Life* in their books on the lives of the saints.
>
> “In some copies, however, it is read as follows: ‘The Preliminary Notice of the Books of the Lord Isidore, Published by Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza.’
>
> “All who mention Braulio testify that the author of this life was distinguished in learning and holiness; some add that he was related by blood to Isidore.
>
> “Certainly the holy Church of God solemnly venerates his glorious memory every year on the twenty-sixth day of March. Saint Ildefonsus also speaks of him in chapter 11 of his book *On Illustrious Men*, as do the other writers of Spanish history.
>
> “At Braulio’s urging, Isidore composed the volume of the *Etymologies* through unremitting reading: a diffuse and varied work, and a marvel to be compared with that age.
>
> “The various readings that we have gathered and recorded from other codices, whether manuscripts or printed editions, are as follows.”

“In which antiquity itself [supplied] something to him. In which, indeed, antiquity [supplied something]. Unskilled. Imperial power. At an opportune time. Inopportunely. I have commemorated. I shall commemorate. With exhortation. With entreaty. In the elements. In the choice. Whom. Which. Of excessive size. Of excessive magnitude. Entirely suited to philosophy. Filled with every kind of philosophy. Not unknown. He will not be ignorant. Deservedly. Not deservedly. There. Where. Inscribed with adornment. Whom God [sent]. With adornment, the instruments that I have collected here. Whom the Lord [sent].

[Col. 0019A] “He set up, as it were, a certain *destina* [support].” Thus it stands altogether in the old codex. Since others failed to notice this passage, they emended it conjecturally: ‘He appointed a certain light to be destined.’ Others, however: ‘He set up certain things, appointing them.’ I would rather judge that it should read: ‘He set up a certain *destina*,’ masculine rather than feminine, if *destina* is understood as ‘one sent’ or ‘angel’; for when God sent Isidore as a teacher to Spain, which had until then grown old in rusticity, he was shaping it.

The African poet Corippus certainly uses this word (*On the Praise of Justin the Younger*, book I):

> And Thomas, the support of the wavering Libyan land.

Besides him, Arnobius also uses it (*Against the Nations*, book II): ‘Not after Theutin [variant: Theutates], the Egyptian, or after Atlas—as some relate him—the bearer, carrier, flute-player, and support of heaven?’ Finally, Saint Isidore himself (*Toledan Breviary*):

> Now the white toga of the Romulean city  
> Shines forth as the mission of seven pontiffs,  
> Whom an ancient report assigns to Hesperia  
> As messengers of the faith from the apostles.

See Johannes Meursius, *In the Arnobian Critic*, book II, chapter 13. To this, not unreasonably, we adapt that philosophical statement of ours: ‘We,’ he says, and so forth. This sentence is Cicero’s, concerning Marcus Varro, in book I of the *Academica*, not far from the beginning.

“‘You [know] the age of the fatherland,’ and so forth. Saint Augustine also quoted this from Cicero in book II of *The City of God*.

“‘And public discipline, you [know] the seats of regions.’ But in Cicero we read: ‘You [know] military discipline, you [know] the seat of regions.’ More copious. Copious.”

[Col. 0019C] 13 5. What Cajetan says—that, according to the testimony of certain persons, Braulio was related by blood to Isidore—rests on no ancient foundation. The same Cajetan also labors in vain to make *destina* masculine. Many think that Vitruvius too used this word in its proper sense, as a tie or chain by which something is bound and held together, in book V, at the end of the chapter; yet others read that passage differently. Compare Loaisa’s note on book II of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences*, chapter 40. Niccolò Antonio, book V, chapter 3, no. 85, thinks that Braulio expressed this from Fulgentius’s first letter, chapter 2; but he interprets *destina* as a support or substructure, not as a bond, which was Philander’s interpretation and was rejected by Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XV, chapter 13. The enlarged *Dictionary of Ducange* by the Maurists gives further material about this word.

[Col. 0019D] Braulio appears to have been imitated by Alvarus of Córdoba in the letter addressed to Abbot Speraindeus, volume II of the *Toledan Fathers*, page 637: ‘The all-knowing and almighty God, foreseeing these times into which we have fallen and the severe hunger for the word of God that we suffer, has set you before us as a strong *destina* [bulwark].’ I would read: ‘The all-knowing and almighty God, foreseeing these times into which we have fallen …’

6. Cajetan also praises Isidore as the author of the hymn *The White Toga of the Romulean City*, apparently for no other reason than that it occurs in the Isidorian breviary. I have shown this to be mistaken in the *Hymnody of Spain* under 15 May, where I discussed such a hymn in praise of the seven apostolic men. Cajetan correctly observes that Cicero’s words, in the source itself, read: ‘you [know] the seat of regions’; these words should apparently be restored in Braulio, for otherwise the sentence does not proceed properly. Likewise, one should read *and the names of human affairs*, as Grialius has it, not *of the names*, as it appears in Cajetan.

7. Among Zaccaria’s papers concerning Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, I find a collation of Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* with three manuscript codices: namely, one Roman codex belonging to the library of the Most Illustrious House of Albani, formerly Cardinal Sirlet’s, a paper quarto, with which the three Vatican codices that I collated agree—the Regio-Vaticanus, Urbinas, and Ottobonianus 1720; a second from the library of San Salvatore in Bologna; and a third which, I think, came either from that same library of San Salvatore or from the Florentine library of San Marco, since the title of this collation is missing. I shall indicate the variant readings of these three manuscripts.

[Col. 0020A] 14 The Albani Codex, Ottobonianus 1720, Regio-Vaticanus 349, and Urbinas 382 appear to have been copied from the same exemplar. *Concerning Isidore the bishop.*

8. ‘In which he was something—indeed, very much—[so that] in every kind of expression he existed both skilled and learned, and open in the quality of his speech.’ Albani: ‘formed in expression, and skilled,’ etc.; ‘incomparably eloquent’; ‘the prudent person can understand’; ‘to our knowledge.’

9. ‘For he published books—containing Sacred Scripture—of the Fathers, in which deeds [are recorded]—and dignity and death—bishop of offices—[so that the matter] may be treated in its own time, not without—among which, for the consolation of the soul.’

10. ‘Which [he drew] from the philosophers—certain things from the chosen—inserted and partly—Florentia, his sister—believes, and reads, and of the prophets—to which we append these things—a codex of excessive size—I divided it into twenty books. Whoever entirely—in every respect—will not be ignorant of the knowledge of divine and human affairs, deservedly will be.’ It should probably be written approximately as follows.

11. ‘There are, moreover, many little works of this man in the church, with adornment [and] instruments—he appointed as it were a certain light to be destined—we appropriate to ourselves—as a guest, as though [it were] a house—there we were.’

12. ‘But you, [know] the fatherland in the description of times, in the sacred life of priests—public discipline—But with what a stream—he confounded heresy—they clearly declare by a special act. Which—they assert.’

**Bolognese Codex**

[Col. 0020D] 13. ‘So that he might exist skilled and learned, and open in the quality of his speech—to our knowledge they came down—in a brief notation—[so that the matter] may be treated in its proper style.’

14. ‘Also through the investigation of philosophers—he will not be ignorant—of knowledge. “Deservedly” is redundant there—in descriptions of times, in the sacred life of priests—in his presence by a spiritual act.’

**The other Codex, perhaps Bolognese**

15. ‘In which, whatever—so that he might exist skilled and learned, and open in the quality of his speech—But with what a stream—’

16. There are many readings in which these manuscript codices agree among themselves and differ from Grialius’s edition. It should be especially noted that they omit *Astigitanum* after *Fulgentium episcopum*. For Florez, volume V of *Sacred Spain*, dissertation 4, presses the reading of the Madrid edition, *Fulgentium episcopum Astigitanum*, against Cardinal Belluga, who follows the wording of our codices in order to defend the view that Fulgentius, after governing the see of Astigi, also governed Carthage in Spain.

Grialius’s reading, which most people alter—namely, *non ignotus divinarum humanarumque rerum scientia* (‘not unknown in the knowledge of divine and human affairs’)—is preferable to the others. For Braulio and others of his period use *ignotus* in the sense of *ignarus* (‘ignorant’), just as *cognitus* is used for *gnarus* (‘knowledgeable’). See Isidore’s letter to Braulio himself, then archdeacon, which begins: ‘Since I am unable to enjoy you.’

17. Since Bignaeus was the first to publish Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* in his edition of Isidore, I shall not hesitate to indicate some of the variants found there. His title is: *The Life of Blessed Isidore, Bishop of Seville, Described by Blessed Braulio, Bishop of Zaragoza*. A marginal note says that this life of Isidore is found at the end of Braulio’s work—correct this to ‘Isidore’s work’—*On Illustrious Men*.

**Variant readings from Bignaeus**

18. ‘He imagined, so that in every kind of expression he might be renowned, and, existing skilled and learned in the quality of his speech, open—“I divided it into twenty books.” Whoever finds them all filled with every kind of philosophy, and so forth, “will not be ignorant of the knowledge of divine and human affairs. And deservedly.” For there is an abundance there,’ and so forth.

‘But you, [know] the fatherland in the description of times, and the sacred lives of priests; you [know] domestic and public discipline; you [know] the seats, regions, and places; you [know] all things,’ and so forth. ‘They declare by a special act what, on the contrary, they assert as truth—superior in the highest learning.’

19. Fabricius, in his *Ecclesiastical Bibliotheca*, gave a place to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* from Loaisa’s edition of the Hispanic Councils, and prefixed Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice*. He agrees for the most part with the others. These readings, however, are more particularly his own: ‘he explained by authority’; ‘On the Names of the Law and the Gospels,’ in which, following the examples of his predecessors, he collected in as expansive a manner as he could, with brevity; ‘that philosophical bishop, he asserted the truth.’

Perhaps the words ‘in which he shows what the persons mentioned signify mystically’ fell out of Fabricius’s printer. *On Heresies.* 16 ‘For it was easy, from the words of the Gospels, to move on to one book about other matters’—*one book On Heresies*. I do not approve *explicuit* (‘explained’) instead of *elicuit* (‘drew out’), for Braulio adapted Isidore’s word *elicui* from the letter to Fulgentius to the description of the work. I approve even less *of the philosopher* than *the philosophical*. Thus Eulogius of Córdoba, at the beginning of the *Memorial of the Saints*, says of a certain verse of Juvencus: ‘As that philosophical [verse] has it: “This work,”’ and so forth. I noted this in my note on Juvencus, book I, verse 30.

20. Although Ottobonianus 1720 agrees with the Albani codex, it is nevertheless more correct in some places, as at the beginning: ‘formed and skilled in every kind of expression.’ Ottobonianus 849 differs from the Albani codex in both the number and order of the chapters. In it the *Preliminary Notice* is entitled *The Life of Isidore*, with the author’s name omitted. Its wording generally agrees with Grialius’s edition. Its peculiar readings are: ‘so that he might exist skilled and learned, and open in the quality of his speech’; ‘Fulgentius, bishop of the Offices’; ‘at the request of Florentia’; ‘I divided [it] into twenty books,’ and so forth.

[Col. 0022A] 21. Bayer, in his notes on *Bibliotheca Hispana*, book V, chapter 4, no. 93, produces from ancient exemplars the following variant, which he attempts to defend: ‘I divided [it] into fifteen books,’ instead of ‘into twenty,’ or ‘into twenty books,’ as the printed editions have it. This controversy will be discussed in chapter 48. All our codices indicate twenty books in the *Preliminary Notice*.

## CHAPTER IV

**The *Preliminary Notice* of Isidore’s books is ascribed to Braulio and published under his name. Another, more extensive *Preliminary Notice*, found in certain manuscripts, is discussed.**

1. Since there are so many ancient exemplars that attribute Isidore’s *Preliminary Notice* to Braulio, what reason can I give for the fact that someone in both the preceding and the present century has wished to raise a dispute about it? Niccolò Antonio, in his *Old Hispanic Bibliotheca*, when he reviews Isidore’s works, repeatedly praises Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* without the slightest hesitation.

Moreover, in book V, chapter 5, no. 245, he mentions it as follows: ‘We have already spoken, in connection with Isidore, of the labor of this great bishop—Braulio—expended upon the work of his master Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies*. He says: “A codex distinguished by excessive size, divided by him into sections—not books—by titles. Because he produced it at my request, although he himself left it unfinished, I divided it into twenty books.”’ (In the preface to the works of the holy pontiff.)

Besides these works, not only Ildefonsus but also Isidore of Beja, and Rodrigo of Toledo after him, report that Braulio left other little works.

2. In the recent Madrid edition of the *Hispanic Bibliotheca*, the highly learned Bayer appended the following note to these words: ‘Our author seems here not to mention Isidore’s *Preliminary Notice of his Works*, which bibliographers, with almost one voice, ascribe to Braulio.’

Yet why did it seem to Bayer that Niccolò Antonio did not mention the *Preliminary Notice*? For he both quotes several words from it and calls it the preface to the works of Saint Isidore—either because Grialius prefixed it to the works of Saint Isidore, or because Braulio himself perhaps composed it so that it could serve as a preface to Isidore’s works, as the designation *preliminary notice* suggests. Otherwise, Braulio states that he appended his *Preliminary Notice* to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*: ‘Of illustrious men,’ he says, ‘we have appended these things to it.’

3. But what shall I say about the dispute raised by Mayans? In the *Life of Niccolò Antonio*, prefixed to the latter’s *Censure of Fictitious Histories*, no. 125, he asserts that the *Preliminary Notice* is falsely attributed to Braulio, and promises that he will prove this at greater length wherever the place or occasion permits.

Bayer rightly demands the reasons that led Mayans to this opinion. ‘For,’ he says, ‘it should not be thought that what we reported from him was thrown out without grounds or merely at his pleasure.’ Meanwhile, he continues, ‘until time brings those reasons to light, I consider the agreement of one of the ancient codices—of all those I have seen—and of nearly all bibliographers, for whom Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice*, the subject of our discussion, has always been like a torch and a pole star for distinguishing Isidore’s genuine works, quite sufficient to prevent us from removing it in any way from the position it has hitherto held among critics.’

4. I hold Mayans’s learning and judgment in the highest regard, but I fear that, excessively provoked by the frauds of forgers, he may at times have inclined toward the opposite side and asserted fraud where none exists. As for the recent architects of chronicles, 18 there is certainly no reason for suspicion, since Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* is found in manuscripts unquestionably older than they are.

Bayer does not state how many manuscript codices he saw in which this work is attributed to Braulio. Shortly before, in a note on no. 243, he reports that in a recent Escorial codex, copied from an older one, there is a *digramm.* and *plut. 4, no. 23*, the addition of Braulio of Zaragoza to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*—which is precisely the *Preliminary Notice*, although Bayer seems to list it as something different from that notice.

5. Nor did Bayer remember that this very question concerning Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* had been debated by Niccolò Antonio, and that Pellizer’s arguments against it had been refuted with Bayer himself supporting the refutation in his notes. Let us hear Niccolò Antonio, book V, chapter 4, no. 125:

‘For we have Braulio, listing both works among the other works of our Isidore. How shall we approve the claim that he did not write this *Preliminary Notice* of Saint Isidore’s books, when Pellizer first brandished it as a weapon against possession of the see of Seville, after he had already persuaded himself of the contrary?

‘First—for this is how it stands—this *Preliminary Notice* saw the light in the Madrid edition, but from ancient books consulted by those of the highest reputation who undertook the preparation of the edition among us. The style too reveals an author of the age in which Braulio lived; nor is it unlike the style of the works we possess from Braulio himself: his *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, the hymn in praise of the same saint—which is read, perhaps “which is inserted,” in the Gothic or Isidorian breviary—and the letters published with those of Isidore.’

6. I wish Niccolò Antonio had not been so generous as to grant that Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* first appeared in the Madrid edition—that is, in 1599. For Margarino de la Bigne prefixed it to his edition of Isidore’s works, prepared in Paris in 1580. Indeed, the *Preliminary Notice* had already appeared in Italian in the Italian translation of the *Synonyms* in 1570, which will be discussed again in chapter 70.

Bayer adds in a note: ‘If all others were lacking, the single Escorial codex, shelfmark Q, shelf II, no. 24, written in the year 781, or A.D. 743, in which Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* and its attribution to Isidore of Seville of the Chronicle under discussion are found in exactly as many words and in precisely the same wording as in Grialius, would settle the matter completely.’

Elsewhere he says that he saw several other codices in which this *Preliminary Notice* is found, written before the year 1000 of the Christian era, 19 namely in his note on chapter 4, book V, no. 93. He then copies Oudinus’s words from his special dissertation *On the Writings of Saint Isidore of Seville in the Seventh Century*, volume I, column 1583:

‘In order to judge correctly concerning the genuine and indisputable works of Saint Isidore of Seville, archbishop, I considered it necessary to place here first the *Preliminary Notice* of his books, edited by Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.’

He adds several passages from Johannes Vossius, *On Latin History*, book II, chapter 25, including the following concerning the *Preliminary Notice*: ‘Braulio, to whom more than to anyone else credence must be given.’

7. ‘But what kind of argument is that?’ Niccolò Antonio continues against Pellizer. ‘Braulio, if he were the author of the *Preliminary Notice*, would hardly have applied to Saint Isidore that pagan—or, as he calls it, philosophical—eulogy which Cicero uses of Marcus Terentius Varro in the first book of the *Academica*, and which we brought forward in the preceding chapter.

‘Braulio’s own studies and character plainly prove that he could make use of testimonies from secular disciplines, which he modestly acknowledges in part to have touched upon in the preface to the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*. Nor was he less accustomed to do so: in that same preface to the life he uses this verse of a certain ancient poet, as he says:

> This work—for perhaps it will rescue me from the fire.

‘It is particularly appropriate, moreover, and entirely worthy of being applied to Isidore, the holiest of Christians’ Varros, that old saying once spoken of Varro by Cicero: “The same zeal in investigating origins, and the same learning displayed in treating the same subject.”’

8. Niccolò Antonio argues this wisely; nevertheless, among testimonies from secular disciplines he should not have included the verse ‘This work,’ and so forth. It is a verse of the most holy poet Juvencus, in the prologue to his poem on evangelical history, later used by other Christian writers in the prefaces to their works, including Alcuin and Eulogius of Córdoba. I discussed them in my note on Juvencus, book I, verse 30, and have already mentioned them above.

Perhaps Braulio took Isidore’s eulogy of Varro from Augustine rather than from Cicero himself, since Augustine used Cicero’s words in book VI of *The City of God*, chapter 2, in support of his own argument, adapting the eulogy of Varro to Isidore.

It should also be noted that in some editions Augustine reads ‘you [know] the seats,’ but in most manuscripts, as in Cicero, ‘you [know] the seat.’ Some of the passages that I shall report in no. 10, I think Braulio likewise took from Saint Jerome.

20 9. To confirm Niccolò Antonio’s response, Bayer adds in a note that far superior to Cicero’s eulogy of Varro is the praise which, as we read, nearly a hundred fathers and nobles of Spain unanimously and deservedly bestowed upon the same holy doctor in the Eighth Council of Toledo, title 2, no. 32:

‘What of the fact,’ he adds, ‘that Cicero addresses Varro in person in the *Academica*? Braulio mourns Isidore, who had only recently died and whom he had loved beyond all others while he lived. What shame, or what limit, could there be in longing for so dear a person?

‘But,’ you say, ‘that expression came from a pagan.’ Granted. But why do we not make the same criticism of Basil, Gregory of Nazianzus, Jerome, and even Paul?

> The gods too have dwelt in the forests,  
> And Dardanian Paris.

Augustine could have been named with the others, since, as I said, before Braulio he brought Cicero’s very words about Varro into his own argument. It could also be asserted, according to the opinion of many, that Braulio was Isidore’s disciple and therefore willingly exaggerated his praises.

Risco, indeed, volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, chapter 7, no. 6, treatise 66, infers from Isidore’s letters to Braulio that Isidore was Braulio’s teacher. Yet neither in Isidore’s letters to Braulio nor in Braulio’s other letters to Isidore is there any mention of such a teacherly relationship. This silence rather leads us toward the opposite conclusion. From these letters alone it is certain only that Braulio and Isidore at some time lived together.

Risco is more successful in rejecting Martín Carrillo, who had asserted that Braulio had used Ildefonsus as his teacher, for the chronology does not establish this. Braulio himself, in the dedicatory letter of the *Life of Saint Aemilianus*, says that his brother John, his predecessor in a holy life and instruction, had been his teacher; he nowhere mentions other teachers. Compare what will be said in chapter 20.

10. That Braulio was imbued with secular disciplines, or at least learned in the writings of the ancients, is demonstrated by his works, and especially by his letter to the priest Tajon, volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, page 331 and following:

‘You should keep firmly in mind that I can bite back, if I wish, and, when wounded, drive in a genuine tooth—for we too, in accordance with Horace, have learned our letters and have often withdrawn our hand from the schoolmaster’s rod. It may also be said of us: “He has hay on his horn; flee far away”; or rather, that Virgilian line:

> And we too, father, scatter weapons and iron  
> Not weak in the right hand,  
> And blood follows from our wound.

21 And shortly afterward:

‘Let our story not have ungrateful jokes, according to Ovid, and, in accordance with Appius, let us not seem to exercise a doglike eloquence.’ Earlier he had prefaced this:

‘Let our story not cause long delays.’

11. It is therefore exceedingly difficult to believe that Mayans found any plausible arguments by which Braulio’s authorship of the *Preliminary Notice* of Isidore’s works could be denied, since it is found inscribed with Braulio’s name in manuscripts not far removed from Braulio’s own age.

We wish these statements about Isidore’s *Preliminary Notice of the Works* to be understood as referring to the notice that was long ago published and prefixed to editions of Isidore. For it is clear that another, more extensive notice exists in manuscript codices. What it is like must now be investigated more carefully.

12. Grialius reports in his prologue to the reader that Cyprian Suárez, who reviewed some of Isidore’s works for the Madrid edition, found the following words in an old *Preliminary Notice of Isidore’s Works*, words generally omitted:

‘He abridged the books of Saint Gregory the pope at the latter’s request. He elucidated the *Song of Songs* in a fluent exposition. He published a fourth edition of the Psalter. He devoted no small labor to the exposition of the books of Moses, the Psalter, and the four Gospels. In canon law and civil law as well he composed very extensive instruments.’

Mariana also brought this same fuller *Preliminary Notice* to light from two ancient codices, in his note on book I, chapter 2, *Against the Jews*: ‘In his life, written by Braulio,’ he says, ‘I find it written in two certainly ancient codices that he published a fourth translation of the Psalter.’ Compare Burriel’s letter below, chapter 40.

13. In his note on no. 160 of book V of the *Old Hispanic Bibliotheca*, Bayer testifies that he had long before seen this sort of expanded *Preliminary Notice* of Braulio, of uncertain origin. Yet by chance he encountered it in the royal Madrid codex of Rodrigo of Toledo’s *Variant Readings*, compiled by Juan López de León in 1566, folio 114, page 2. It contains exactly the same words as Grialius in the prologue to Isidore’s works, except that where the printed Grialius has ‘a fourth edition of the Psalter,’ the royal Madrid codex reads ‘a fourth translation.’ Mariana too had read ‘a fourth translation of the Psalter,’ as we saw in his words.

Rodríguez de Castro, volume II of the *Hispanic Bibliotheca*, page 294, produced the same fuller *Preliminary Notice* from an Escorial codex containing a fifteenth-century Spanish translation of the *Etymologies*, rendering it in the old Spanish language. It begins: ‘Isidore, a noble man,’ and so forth.

[Col. 0026B] 22 14. The following words belong to this same *Life of Isidore*, written by Braulio. Constantine Cajetanus, in the place cited, page 4, presented them as though repeated from some sermon of Braulio:

‘Meanwhile, dearest brothers, it is fitting that the whole Church should raise this most holy confessor Isidore on high with praises, but especially the Church of Spain, which, more than others, shone forth through his particularly salutary teaching. For just as Gregory the teacher succeeded Peter at Rome, so blessed Isidore succeeded the apostle James in the regions of Spain.

‘For the seeds of eternal life which the most blessed James sowed, this most blessed teacher Isidore sufficiently watered by the word of preaching, as though he were one of the four rivers of paradise; and he illumined all Spain both by the example of good works and by the fame of his holiness, like the most brilliant ray of the sun.’

15. Although Cajetan introduces this eulogy as taken from a sermon of Braulio, he reports in a note as follows:

‘I would judge that this eulogy, inscribed to Saint Isidore by Saint Braulio, was rather excerpted from some sermon composed in his praise than, as others claim, from the *Life of Isidore* that Braulio labored over. For what Braulio explains there did not contribute a single word to this passage, as we have seen.

‘Moreover, this entire sermon, which we have not yet been able to obtain, exists in an ancient, handwritten copy of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, preserved by the Carthusian monks of the monastery of Aula Dei, situated in the countryside of Zaragoza.

‘This passage should also be considered worthy of notice because Braulio, a man both exceedingly learned and exceedingly holy, wished to testify nearly a thousand years ago that the apostle James was the teacher of Spain and that he had sown the seeds of eternal life which Saint Isidore later watered. It is unfortunate, however, that Cajetan attempted to persuade us of this by appealing to the authority of the *Chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter*.’

16. The continuators of the Bollandist work, under 4 April, observed that at the beginning of the *Life of Saint Isidore*, whose author many believe to be Luke of Tuy, and which they published with notes by Niccolò Antonio and themselves, the same material is reported that Cajetan presented from Braulio’s sermon.

Among the works of Saint Martin of León, who flourished before Luke of Tuy, there is, according to a copy transcribed from the autograph by order of His Eminence the Lord Cardinal Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, archbishop of Toledo, and published at Segovia, volume IV, page 3, a sermon on the death of Saint Isidore. In it much is taken from Braulio’s already-published *Preliminary Notice*, 23 and certain passages also seem to have been drawn from Isidore’s *Life* or from Braulio’s sermon about him, which Cajetan mentions.

For Martin says:

‘For just as Gregory the teacher was the successor of the apostle Peter, so blessed Isidore succeeded the apostle James, because the seed of eternal life which the most blessed James sowed, this outstanding teacher sufficiently watered by the word of preaching, as though he were one of the four rivers of paradise; and he illumined all Spain both by the example of good works and by the fame of his holiness, like a most brilliant lamp.’

17. The most learned editor observed in a note on this passage that among the Bollandists these very words are found from a manuscript Toledan codex, no. 44, near the end, as are other portions of the same sermon under other numbers.

Although the Bollandists printed ‘the most brilliant ray of the sun’ instead of ‘the most brilliant lamp,’ the autograph of Martin correctly retains *splendidissima lampada*. For Plautus, Pollio, Fulgentius, and others used *lampada* for *lampas* in manuscript codices, as Salmasius and Ducange observed.

18. Florez, in the preface to Appendix 5 of volume V, does not doubt that the *Preliminary Notice* of Braulio appended to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* is genuine. He asserts, however, that the fuller one was interpolated by Luke of Tuy, whom he considers the author of the *Life of Isidore* published by the Bollandists.

Risco, volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, treatise 66, chapter 7, no. 65, thinks that Braulio’s sermon on Isidore, praised by Cajetan, is not distinct from chapter 11 of the same *Life* among the Bollandist Acts. That chapter is entitled: ‘Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, abbreviated account of the life of Saint Isidore, teacher of Spain.’

I shall certainly not object. But since many words taken from this abbreviation are found in the sermon of Saint Martin, who preceded Luke of Tuy in time, it necessarily follows that the *Life of Saint Isidore* published by the Bollandists—or at least Braulio’s abbreviation—is older than Luke of Tuy. I shall discuss this matter more fully in chapter 13.

For the present, it is enough to observe, lest ambiguity arise, that the same idea occurs in Braulio’s fuller *Preliminary Notice*, in the sermon called by Cajetan, at the beginning of the *Life of Isidore*, and in the sermon of Saint Martin. Yet the fuller *Preliminary Notice* and the sermon called by Cajetan agree entirely even in their wording, whereas the beginning of the *Life of Isidore* and Saint Martin’s sermon differ from one another and from Braulio’s fuller *Preliminary Notice* in many words.

## CHAPTER V 24

**Isidore’s eulogy from Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*, revised against ancient exemplars**

1. ‘After his brother Leander, Isidore held the chair of the see of Seville in the province of Baetica. He was a man distinguished alike by dignity and talent. For he displayed such an abundant wealth of delight in speaking that the admirable fullness of his discourse turned his hearers to astonishment; so that whoever had heard what had been heard twice praised it only when it had been repeated more often.

‘He wrote works both excellent and considerable in number, namely, a book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*; a book of *Lamentation*, which he himself called *Synonyms*; two little books addressed to his sister Florentina against the wickedness of the Jews; a book *On the Nature of Things* addressed to Prince Sisebut; a book of *Differences*; and a book of *Sentences*.

‘He also collected from various authors what he himself calls *Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments*. When these were gathered into one, the same book is called *Questions*.

‘Finally, at the request of Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, he wrote the book *Etymologies*. Although he tried for many years to complete it, he appeared to have brought his final day to a close while still engaged upon the work.

‘He flourished during the reigns of Kings Reccared, Liuvanis, Witteric, Gundemar, Sisebut, Suinthila, and Sisenand. He held the honor of the episcopate for approximately forty years and displayed at once the distinguished glory and beauty of holy learning.’

2. This is chapter 9 of Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*, which Constantine Cajetanus also included among Isidore’s eulogies, adding the following observations.

**Notes of Constantine Cajetanus**

3. ‘From what we shall shortly below consider worth noting about Saint Ildefonsus, it may already become clear that he drew from Saint Isidore the highest virtue and the highest learning.

‘Moreover, concerning Saint Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*, it was published by Juan Grial, a genuinely learned man, at Madrid in 1599, and by Jacques Breul, a French Benedictine, in Paris in 1601, among the works of Saint Isidore. It is also found in volume II 25 of *Illustrated Spain*, printed at Frankfurt in 1603.

‘We corrected it in several places, where it abounded in errors, from a very old manuscript codex of the library of Monte Cassino. But more about that same codex below.

‘For the Frankfurt edition has *illam*, [whereas] the Isidorian [manuscript reads] *ita*. Thus the Cassino manuscript, but “twice” is read in the Madrid and Breul editions. The Frankfurt [edition has] *his*. “Of the Origin and Death of the Fathers,” or “of the Death of the Prophets,” is found in the Frankfurt and Cassino [codices]. “What he himself calls the mysteries”: Frankfurt, “what he himself names secret [things] …” “In his work”: Frankfurt, “in the unfinished work.” “He flourished”: Frankfurt, “he became renowned.”’

4. Loaisa reads as follows in the *Hispanic Councils* from his own codex:

‘After Leander of the see of Seville … distinguished … he [displayed] such … from it … hearers. He wrote excellent and numerous works, namely … *On the Origin*, or *Death of the Prophets* … *The Book of Lamentations*, which he called *Synonyms* … to Florentina … which he himself calls … the same book … also finally … to complete, with the work unfinished … He became renowned during the reigns of Kings Reccared, Gundemar, Sisebut, Suinthila, and Sisenand,’ and so forth.

5. In the Albani codex, already mentioned, the variant readings are as follows:

‘A man distinguished alike by learning … the one who had heard … excellent works … a book *On the Death and Origin of the Fathers* … he himself called [it] *Synonyms* … his sister against … he called [them] *Expositions of the Sacraments*.’

It omits *secretorum* (‘of mysteries’), in place of which *sacratorum* (‘of sacred things’) is perhaps read in one place through a typographical error. *Secretorum* must be retained, for the hidden mysteries of the sacraments are so called in the prologue to the work.

6. Not many Vatican exemplars transmit Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*. Ottobonianus 1720 and Urbinas 382 agree with the Albani codex in Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, and likewise in Ildefonsus’s book.

Other codices that transmit Isidore’s book omit Ildefonsus’s book. Vatican Codex 4877, in which Ildefonsus’s book appears after Isidore’s book has been omitted, agrees with these three in the readings: ‘a man distinguished alike by learning … the one who had heard,’ and so forth.

7. In volume I of the edition of the Toledan Fathers, page 288, the following marginal note is attached to the words ‘what had been heard twice, whoever had heard’:

‘*BIS* (“twice”) is read in all editions. In the Toledo manuscript we read *HIS* (“these”), which does not fit unless we say that *HIS* was written for *IS* in the nominative case. This reading would be acceptable to everyone unless one preferred to conjecture *VIX* (“scarcely”) for *BIS*. In fact, it is quite common for *his* to be written for *is* in parchment manuscripts. Indeed, Cajetan published *is* from the Cassino manuscript; this reading was accepted by Niccolò Antonio, *Old Bibliotheca*, book V, no. 85, chapter 3. 26 Nor should I fail to observe that Loaisa, in the *Hispanic Councils*, and Fabricius, in the *Ecclesiastical Bibliotheca*, entirely omitted these words: “so that whoever had heard what had been heard twice praised it only when it had been repeated more often.” Thus the entire difficulty is avoided.’

8. For whether it is read *bis* (“twice”), *his* (“these”), *is* (“he”), or *vix* (“scarcely”), the sense is not sufficiently clear. Padilla, *Centuria* VII, chapter 22 of his *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, rendered Ildefonsus’s words into Spanish as follows: “He amazed those who heard him, and they desired to hear from him what they had already heard on other occasions; and, hearing it again, what he said was sweeter and more pleasing to them.” Florez, volume IX, page 195, gives nearly the same sense: “He astonished all who heard him, for everyone desired to hear him repeatedly, because of the delight produced by the fluency and sweetness of his speech.” Cellier, volume XVII, explains it in a similar way: those who had heard him twice did not grow weary even when the matter was repeated more often. The author of the French *Life of Saint Isidore*, of whom I shall speak in chapter 84, likewise understands the passage to mean that Isidore was especially pleasing when he repeated the same matter several times—contrary to what ordinarily happens, when listeners are chiefly delighted by the novelty of subjects. I myself, however, do not grasp this sense in Ildefonsus’s words. Retaining the more usual reading, *audita bis*, I would think it could be explained by reference to that remarkable fluency and abundance of Isidore’s speech which Ildefonsus praises: namely, that while speaking Isidore explained so many things, and so rapidly, that it was not enough to hear him once or twice on the same subjects; rather, the discourse one wished to commit to memory had to be repeated several times.

9. Perhaps the matter is also connected with the fact that among writers of that age, to “commend” an antiphon meant to sing its opening words first, so that another person could continue singing from there. On the art of rhetoric Isidore says this in book II, chapter 2:

> Translated into Latin by Cicero, of course, and Quintilian, but so copiously and variously that it is easy for the reader to admire it, while impossible to comprehend it. For, when the parchment is retained, the sequence of the discourse seems to cling to the memory; but as soon as it is put aside, all recollection slips away.

Ildefonsus therefore appears to have expressed Isidore’s praise in these words, especially if, instead of *commendaret*, we read *comprehenderet* (“comprehended” or “grasped”). The same sense can conveniently be obtained if, instead of *bis qui audisset*, we restore *is qui audisset* (“he who had heard”).

10. It should further be noted that Grialius, in the prologue to the first Madrid edition, transcribed Isidore’s encomium from Ildefonsus in such a way that, through carelessness, the words *librum de Genere officiorum, librum Prooemiorum* (“the book *On the Kinds of Offices*, the book of *Prefaces*”) were omitted; the same defect likewise appears in the second, recent [27] Madrid edition. This typographical omission gave Niccolò Antonio occasion for error, since he read Ildefonsus’s words about Isidore not in Ildefonsus’s own book *On Illustrious Men*, but in Grialius’s prolegomena. In book V of the *Bibliotheca Vetus*, no. 126, he asserts that Ildefonsus did not mention Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, nor two other books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; and again, in numbers 146 and 147, he maintains that Ildefonsus made no mention of Isidore’s work *Prefaces* or of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. “It is strange,” Bayerius says in a note, “that our author should have failed to remember these books of Isidore.” But, as I have said, Niccolò Antonio had before his eyes a copy corrupted—or mutilated—through the printer’s negligence, and therefore he may appear worthy of excuse.

As for his further statement that Ildefonsus did not mention Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, that is indeed true if the reference is to the encomium of Isidore, that is, to chapter 9 of Ildefonsus’s book. Otherwise, in the preface to his own book *On Illustrious Men*, after Jerome and Gennadius, the writers on illustrious men, Ildefonsus praises Isidore as follows:

> Then the most prudent man, Isidore, bishop of the see of Hispalis, following the same course, added to the record whatever excellent men he found.

## CHAPTER VI

### The Death of Blessed Isidore, Reported by Redemptus the Cleric; Various Readings from Manuscript Codices

1. “It seemed good to me briefly to explain to Your Holiness how my lord Isidore, of blessed memory, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Hispalis, received penitence and made his confession before God and men; and how he migrated from this world to heaven, so that I might make it known to Your Love in the faithful style of my written account. This matter first compelled me to give thanks to Your Charity for the concern which, out of love for him, you display; then, because I cannot suppress the truth, and because I am compelled, at your request, to speak of the little that I have been able to gather from the many things concerning him.

“While, by I know not what destiny, he was already foreseeing his end, and while the nature of his soul subtly perceived that his body was exhausted by continual illness, he distributed so much alms to the poor every day for nearly six months, or even longer—more than had been his custom—that from sunrise until evening he remained occupied in distributing a considerable substance. After this he was struck by a wound, so that, while the fever grew stronger in his body and his weakened stomach rejected food, he grew stronger for penitence. He immediately summoned his fellow bishops, namely the most blessed John and Epartius, to be present.

“And while he was being brought from his cell to the basilica of Saint Vincent the martyr, all the crowds of the poor, the clergy, all the religious, and all the people of this city received him with cries and great wailing, so that, if anyone possessed a breast of iron, it would instantly be melted into tears and lamentation. And while he was being placed in the aforesaid martyr’s basilica, in the middle of the choir near the altar rail, he ordered the crowds of women to stand farther away, so that, when he himself received penitence, only men—and not women—would be seen present around him.

“And while he was asking the aforesaid priests for one to place a hair shirt upon him and the other to sprinkle ashes over him, he stretched out his hands toward heaven and began to speak as follows:

“‘You, God, who know the hearts of men, and who deigned to forgive the sins of the publican standing far away while he struck his breast (Luke 18); who deigned to raise Lazarus, sleeping in the tomb, on the fourth day after the dissolution of the flesh (John 11), and willed that Abraham the patriarch should receive him into his bosom: receive my confession at this hour, and remove from Your sight the sins which I have contracted beyond number; do not remember my evils, and do not recall the offenses of my youth.

“‘You, Lord, did not impose penitence upon the righteous, who have not sinned against You, but upon me, a sinner who have sinned beyond the number of the sands of the sea (Luke 15). May the ancient enemy find nothing in me to punish. You know that, after I, unhappy man, had arrived unworthily in this holy church—more for this burden than for honor—I never ceased to sin; rather, I labored to act wickedly. And because You said, “At whatever hour the sinner turns back from his ways” (Ezekiel 18), You would consign all his iniquities to oblivion, I remember this command of Yours.

“‘Indeed, I cry out to You with hope and confidence, though I am not worthy to look upon Your heavens because of the multitude of sins that dwell within me. Be present, receive my prayer, and grant me, a sinner, the forgiveness I ask. But if the heavens are not clean in Your sight, how much less am I, a man who have drunk iniquity like water (Job 15), and taken sin as though it were colostrum?’

“When these things had been completed, he received the body and blood of the Lord from the bishops themselves, with profound contrition of heart, judging himself unworthy. Then he begged forgiveness from those same priests and from all who belonged to the clergy, from the citizens, and from all the people, saying:

“‘I implore you, my most holy lords the priests, and the holy assembly of the clergy and people, to offer your prayer to the Lord for me, unhappy and full of every filth of sin; so that, though I am not worthy by my own merits to obtain God’s mercy, I may deserve through your intercession to receive forgiveness for my sins.
