Forgive me, I beg you, unworthy as I am, for what I have done against each one of you: if I have despised anyone through hatred; if I have wickedly rejected anyone from the fellowship of charity; if I have stained anyone by counsel; if I have injured anyone through anger. Forgive me now, who ask—and indeed repent.’

“And when all had with one voice sought indulgence for him, and had cancelled for each person the bonds or written obligations owed to him, he again admonished those standing around, saying:

“‘My most holy lords the bishops, and all who are present, I ask and beseech you to show charity to one another, not returning evil for evil, nor wishing to be whisperers among the people. May the ancient enemy find nothing in you to punish; may the ravening wolf not find anything abandoned by you from which he may snatch prey. Rather, may the shepherd, rejoicing, carry back on his shoulders to this fold the sheep rescued from the wolf’s mouth.’

“After this confession and prayer, he immediately ordered the remaining money to be given to the needy and the poor. What believer, however, could doubt that, after he had immediately put aside every sin, he was joined to the companies of angels?

“Meanwhile he took care to be kissed by everyone, saying:

“‘If you forgive with your whole heart the adversities or wrongs that I have inflicted upon you until now, the almighty Creator will forgive you all your sins; so that the water of the sacred font, which the devout people will receive today, may be for you unto the remission of sins. And let this kiss between you and me remain as a testimony for the future.’

“When all these things had been completed, he was taken back to his cell. On the fourth day after the day of his confession and penitence, he completed his pastoral care and brought his life to its end in peace. Amen. On the day before the Nones of April, on the twenty-second day of the moon, in the year 674 of the Spanish Era.”

### Notes and Various Readings of Constantine Cajetanus on the Account of Saint Isidore’s Death Above

2. “We first read this distinguished testimony concerning Saint Isidore’s death prefixed to his works, published first at Madrid and then at Paris. What should I say about its author, Redemptus? I have nothing to add except that his words show him to have been familiar with Isidore, or at least his disciple; and that he addressed this very composition to some bishop. For he says: ‘It seemed good to me briefly to explain to Your Holiness how my lord Isidore, of blessed memory, etc.’ But no one, I think, will deny that this Redemptus was the same man to whom Isidore replied, solving certain sacred questions proposed by him. ‘To his beloved son in Christ, Redemptus, archdeacon, Isidore.’ This letter exists among Isidore’s works. If Isidore calls him an archdeacon while he calls himself only a cleric, this should be understood as reflecting the custom of those times.

“*Habuerit*: Breulius; *habuit*: Madrid manuscript. *Tanta eleemosyna*: but the Madrid edition incorrectly has *tantam eleemosynam*. *Ab oriente*: Madrid, *oriente*. *Convalesceret*: Madrid, *convaluit*. *Faceret*: Madrid, *fecit*. *Basilica*: Madrid, *basilicam*. *Cilicium, ab altero super se mitti exposceret cinerem*: the Madrid edition corruptly has *cilicio, ab alt. sup. se mitti exponere cin.* *Et ut*: Madrid, *et*. *Aufer*: Madrid, *differ*. *Finivi*: *sinivi*. Madrid. *Susurrones*: Madrid, *susurro*. *Tamen*: Breulius, *tandem*. *Amen. Sub die pridie Nonas Aprilis*: Breulius, *pridie Nonas Aprilis*. But the Madrid manuscript corruptly has *pridie Kalendas Aprilis*.”

3. Cajetanus also added the following notes in the margin:

To the words “he began to speak”: “The prayer of Saint Isidore dying.”

To the words “the publican,” etc.: he cites Luke, chapter 18.

To the words “who deigned to raise Lazarus”: John, chapter 11.

To the words “You, Lord, did not impose penitence”: Luke, chapter 15.

To the words “At whatever hour”: Ezekiel, chapter 18.

To the words “But if the heavens”: Job, chapter 15.

To the words “the body and blood”: “He devoutly receives the Lord’s body. He asks forgiveness from everyone and asks that they pray for him.”

To the words “he admonished them, saying”: “He exhorts everyone to charity.”

To the words “he took care to be kissed”: “He receives everyone with a kiss as a sign of charity, which never fails.”

I was entirely unwilling to omit these observations.

4. The account of Isidore’s death was preserved in a codex of the College of Ildefonsus at Alcalá, as Niccolò Antonio reports in book V, chapter 5, number 219 of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*, citing Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 2. That codex was then believed to be seven hundred years old and is now held in the Escorial Library, section *digr.*, shelf 1, according to Bayerius’s note. He likewise asserts that the same account is preserved in the collection of the minor works of John Baptist Pérez at Toledo.

Florez published it in volume IX of *España Sagrada*, page 366, from a royal Madrid codex entitled *Scintillae* of Álvaro of Córdoba, where the following title is found:

> Here begins the book concerning the passing of the most blessed Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, published for Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, by Redemptus, a cleric of that same Church of Hispalis.

The Acts of the translation follow.

5. I think the parchment codex in large folio in the Royal Library of Madrid, mentioned by Christopher Rodríguez in his *Polygraphia Hispanica* under the year 1047, is different from all these. It displays a specimen of writing from Saint Leander’s book to his sister Florentina, *On the Formation of Virgins*. It then adds the title: “Book concerning the passing of Isidore, published by Braulio.” But in the engraved specimen of the script the reading is:

> “Published for Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, by Redemptus, a cleric of that same Church of Hispalis.”

In *Braulione* the small overline customarily placed above the word is absent, perhaps erased by age; it should be read *Braulionem*. Other materials occur in the same codex, such as “The book of the genealogy of Jesus Christ, son of David, son of Abraham,” and “An exposition of the prophet Daniel,” etc. The author of the exposition is not named. The age and scribe of the codex are given as follows:

> “Facundus wrote it; may his memory be eternal. In the year 1085 of the Era, while our lord and glorious prince, lord Ferdinand, son of lord Sancho, and his glorious wife, lady Sancha, queen, daughter of prince Alfonso, were reigning, in the year of his reign this book was written.”

The year of Ferdinand’s reign was omitted by the person who copied the codex, at least in this subscription as I saw it published; but the Christian year was 1047.

6. Among Zaccaria’s papers I find a collation of Redemptus’s account from Breulius’s 1602 edition, made—I do not know by whom—with a tenth-century Lombard manuscript exemplar from Vallicella, number 22, folio 135 verso. The title in the codex is:

> “The death of Blessed Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, reported by Redemptus the cleric. The day before the Kalends of April.”

The following are the manuscript codex’s variant readings:

- *ad coelum migrasset* — “had migrated to heaven”;
- *ad poenitentiam convaluit* — “grew strong for penitence”;
- *scilicet et Huparcium* — “namely Huparcius also”;
- *adesse faceret* — “caused [them] to be present”;
- *et cum magno* — “and with great [wailing]”;
- *tantum ac non illarum* — “men only, and not women”;
- *die quarto* — “on the fourth day.”

7. *Ab oculis differ tuis* — “remove from Your sight.”

*Non inveniat … potius quam honorem in sanctam … laboravi* — “May he not find … rather than honor, in the holy … I labored.”

*Non reminiscaris mala mea, et juventutis delicta ne memineris* — “Do not remember my evils, and do not recall the offenses of my youth.”

*Tu, Domine, non posuisti*, etc. — “You, Lord, did not impose [penitence],” etc.

*arenae maris* — “the sands of the sea.”

*Et quia tu dixisti* — “And because You said.”

*ut claustra* — “as cloisters” [a corrupt reading].

*peccatum* — “sin.”

*dum magna voce indulgentiam cum lacrymis postulassent* — “when they had sought indulgence with a loud voice and with tears.”

*Amen: sub die pridie Kalendas Aprilis* — “Amen: on the day before the Kalends of April.”

8. The codex omits *luna*, etc., and “Era 574.” It is an obvious error to read *ut claustra* (“as cloisters”) instead of *ut colostra* (“as colostrum”), for *colostra* are the first milk, which formerly was regarded as a great delicacy.

Since the codex agrees with Grialius’s edition in the words *pridie Kalendas Aprilis* (“the day before the Kalends of April”), and since the Gothic manuscript exemplar used by Florez likewise designates the same day, the reason why Breulius and Cajetanus changed the reading—especially since they cite none of the ancient monuments, some of which I shall soon mention—is to be sought in the day on which Saint Isidore’s death is celebrated in the martyrologies, namely the day before the Nones of April.

Cajetanus adds, in the place cited, page 38, that in the year 636 Easter was celebrated on the day before the Kalends of April. Since, according to Redemptus’s account, Isidore died on the fourth day after his confession, on Easter itself, it follows that his death occurred on the day before the Nones of April.

9. Niccolò Antonio likewise adheres to this reasoning in book V of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*, no. 72, observing that it had been noted by the most learned John Grialius in a note to Redemptus’s account, before Constantine Cajetanus, who had forgotten that work. But since Grialius’s notes to Redemptus’s account do not exist, I think Niccolò Antonio intended to refer to the notes of John Baptist Pérez on Braulio’s prefatory notice. These are given above, in chapter 3; from them you will recognize that Cajetanus did not name Pérez’s notes, although he took his own reasoning from them—or, if he denies this, appropriated it.

My suspicion of an error on Niccolò Antonio’s part is increased by the fact that he also cites Breulius as preceding the edition of Isidore’s works. Breulius, however, introduces the matter as follows:

> “John Grialius confirms this opinion of Redemptus concerning the year of Blessed Isidore’s passing in the following note appended to Braulio’s prefatory notice,”

which I have already discussed. He then adds the note of John Baptist Pérez that I mentioned, but Breulius mistakenly attributes it to Grialius. In that note the editor Grialius incorrectly printed “died, Era 664” instead of 674.

10. In the *Acts of the Saints* of the Bollandists, under April 4, there is a *Life of Isidore* by a certain canon of León. It incorporates Redemptus’s account of Isidore’s death, but in an interpolated form, whether by the author of the *Life* himself or by someone else not much earlier. That *Life* will be published in the Appendices, and anyone who wishes can readily observe for himself the differences between Redemptus’s genuine account and this more expanded version. As for the year of Isidore’s death, the author of his *Life* differs greatly from Redemptus.

11. The Gothic exemplar of the Royal Library of Madrid, from which, as I said, Florez published Redemptus’s account in volume IX of *España Sagrada*, appendix 7, contains several differences from Grialius’s edition, which I shall record here.

*Habuerit* and *habuit* are both found.

*Migraverit* appears instead of *migrarit*.

The Gothic reading is:

> *Hoc vero primum compellor agere pro hac sollicitudine quam ex amore charitatis in eo offertis: deinde*

—“But this first compels me to act on account of the concern that, out of love of charity, you show toward him; then”—

instead of:

> *Quae res me primum compulit pro hac sollicitudine quam ex amore in eum offertis, vestrae charitati (gratias) agere: deinde*

—“This matter first compelled me to give thanks to Your Charity for the concern which, out of love for him, you display; then.”

Florez had thought that Grialius read *charitatis gratias agere* (“to give thanks for charity”), but he was deceived by the bracket with which Grialius enclosed the word *gratias* after *charitati*, thereby indicating that *gratias* was absent from the manuscript codex.

12. *Pauca* (“a few”) instead of *parva* (“little”).

*Igitur dum finem suum vir beatus nescio* (“Therefore, while the blessed man, I know not how, was foreseeing his end”) instead of *Dum finem suum nescio* (“While, I know not how, he was foreseeing his end”).

*Fatigato corpore* (“with his body exhausted”) instead of *aegritudine assidua* (“by continual illness”).

*Provideret* (“foresaw”) instead of *praevideret* (“foresaw”).

*Tanta eleemosyna* (“so great an alms”) instead of *tantam eleemosynam* (“so great an alms”).

*Ut ab ortu solis usque in vesperum multa in dispergendo occupatus maneret substantia* — “so that from sunrise until evening he remained occupied in distributing a considerable substance.” I have judged that *multam … substantiam* (“a considerable substance”) should be restored instead of *ut oriente sole usque in vesperum multis illis in accipiendam maneret substantiam* (“so that, from sunrise until evening, he remained with many of those things to be received as substance”).

*Et dum* (“and while”) instead of *ita ut dum* (“so that while”).

*Huparcium* instead of *Aparcium*.

*Tantum, et non* (“only, and not”) instead of *tantum non* (“only”).

*Mitti exposceret* (“he asked that [it] be placed upon him”), which is the correct reading, instead of *mitti exponere* (“to expose or place”), as Grialius’s edition has it.

13. *Sinu eum recipere voluisti* (“You wished to receive him into the bosom”) instead of *sinus eum reciperet, voluisti* (“the bosom should receive him; You wished”).

*Transfer tuis* (“remove to Your [sight]”) instead of *differ tuis* (“defer from Your [sight]”).

*Non destiti* (“I did not cease”) instead of *nunquam sinivi* (“I never permitted”).

*Peccator se a viis suis converterit* (“the sinner has turned back from his ways”) instead of *peccator a viis suis reverterit* (“the sinner has returned from his ways”).

*Ut claustra* (“as cloisters”) instead of *ut colostra* (“as colostrum”).

*Civium quoque, cunctarumque* (“of the citizens also, and of all”) instead of *civium, cunctarumque* (“of the citizens, and of all”).

*Impie a charitatis consortio* (“wickedly from the fellowship of charity”) instead of *impie charitatis consortio* (“wickedly [from] the fellowship of charity”).

*Dimittite mihi nunc* (“forgive me now”) instead of *dimittite nunc* (“forgive [me] now”).

*Magna voce* (“with a loud voice”) instead of *una voce* (“with one voice”).

*Indulgentiam cum lacrymis postulassent* (“when they had sought indulgence with tears”) instead of *indulgentiam postulassent* (“when they had sought indulgence”).

*Condonasset* (“had cancelled”) instead of *condonassent* (“had cancelled”).

*Susurrones* (“whisperers”) instead of *susurro* (“whispering”).

*Hanc aulam* (“this hall”) instead of *hanc caulam* (“this fold”).

*Dimissis omnibus facinoribus* (“with all crimes forgiven”) instead of *omni facinore dimisso* (“with every crime forgiven”).

*Coetibus angelorum* (“the assemblies of angels”) instead of *societatibus angelorum* (“the companies of angels”).

*Curam gerens, et* (“while tending the care, and”) instead of *curam, et* (“the care, and”).

14. “In peace, on the day before the Kalends of April, after he had administered pastoral care irreproachably for nearly forty years: Era 674,” instead of “in peace, amen, on the day before the Kalends of April,” etc., as has already been noted.

Florez observes that the lunar number XIX, given in Grialius’s edition, must be corrected to XXII, which corresponds to the fourth day of April in the year 636. That Isidore died in that year is confirmed by Redemptus, the author of the *Chronicle of the Burgos Calendar*, the *Compostellan Annals*, Roderic of Cerrato, and others.

In the *Compostellan Annals*, and likewise in a certain Gothic manuscript of the monastery of San Millán cited by Florez, the day is correctly written as the day before the Nones of April rather than the day before the Kalends of April, which is found corruptly in most manuscript copies of Redemptus’s account.

15. Florez further observes that Ambrosius Morales and others were mistaken in calling John and Epartius chorepiscopi, or rural bishops, when they were present at Isidore’s penitence. Redemptus calls them not chorepiscopi but *coepiscopi*, fellow bishops. Indeed, at the Fourth Council of Toledo in 633, which Isidore presided over, John, bishop of Iliplia, subscribed in the nineteenth place, and Eparius, bishop of Italica, in the fiftieth. These two dioceses had been established under the metropolitan of Hispalis.

16. As to whether Redemptus, the author of this account, was the same person to whom the letter bearing Isidore’s name is addressed—as Niccolò Antonio thought—Florez strongly doubts it. He considers it more probable that the letter was written to Redemptus, archdeacon of Emerita, who is discussed in chapter 9 of the *Fathers of Mérida*, while the author of the account was another Redemptus, a cleric of the Church of Hispalis, as the title of the Gothic manuscript exemplar prescribes.

## CHAPTER VII

### The Epitaph of Isidore Circulated from Ancient Parchments and Attributed to Saint Ildefonsus

1. Constantine Cajetanus, in the work frequently cited, page 10, published the epitaph of the blessed Leander, Isidore, and Florentina from a very ancient manuscript, as he says, written in Gothic letters and preserved in Paris by Nicolaus Faber, a truly learned man. It contains not only many other epitaphs of the ancient Spaniards, but also some writings of Dracontius, a Spanish presbyter, and of Eugenius III, bishop of Toledo, whose works are otherwise still lacking.

Perhaps this is the codex from which Sirmond printed, in types, the mutilated poems of Dracontius—although it is not certain that he was a presbyter—corrected by Eugenius III of Toledo. Yet Sirmond would not, in my opinion, have omitted Isidore’s epitaph. In Cajetanus, therefore, we read as follows:

#### Epitaph of the Blessed Leander, Isidore, and Florentina

> This nurturing cross holds the bodies of the holy brothers,  
> Leander and Isidore, foremost in the order of poets;  
> Third is their sister Florentina, eternally vowed to God,  
> And, thus placed, their companion … rests worthily.  
> Isidore in the middle separates the limbs of the two.  
> Learn from books, reader, what sort of men they were,  
> And you will learn that they spoke well on every subject.  
> See how the faithful grew through the doctrines of the saints,  
> And how those whom impious laws held were restored to the Lord.  
> And, that you may believe that sublime men live forever,  
> Looking upward, strive to see them painted there.

> Leander, bishop of blessed memory, died on the third day before the Kalends of March, in the year 641 of the Era.

> Isidore, bishop of holy memory, died on the second day before the Nones of April, in the year 674 of the Era.

> Florentina, of devout memory, vowed to God, died on the Kalends of September, in the year 671 of the Era.

2. In the fourth verse Cajetanus thinks that something such as *Christo digna* (“worthy of Christ”) should be supplied. In the ninth verse he conjectures *Dominio* instead of *Domino*. In Florentina’s death notice he corrects “the twelfth day before the Kalends of July” in place of “the Kalends of September,” for he admits that the codex contains errors in some places.

Perhaps these additions in verse concerning the saints’ dates of death are by another hand and author, since they are absent from other witnesses that transmit the same epitaph; moreover, Saint Leander’s death seems to have occurred before the year 641 of the Era, as I shall say in chapter 20.

3. The person who forged the work of the Pseudo-Julian the archpriest, published in 1628 in a collection of various poems falsely attributed to Julian, inserted an expanded epitaph of Isidore as though it had been composed by Ildefonsus. Since it differs in many respects, it must be reproduced here in full:

> This nurturing cross holds the bodies of twin brothers,  
> Leander and Isidore, likewise of the order of seers (*vatum*).  
> Third is their sister Florentina, eternally devoted.  
> O how harmoniously and worthily this consort rests!  
> Isidore in the middle separates the limbs of those before him.  
> Learn from books, reader, what sort of men they were.  
> You will learn that they spoke well on every subject.  
> Among whom Fulgentius lies here; behold these three,  
> Full of certain hope and faith, dear above all things.  
> You will see that the faithful grew through their doctrines,  
> And that those whom impious laws held were restored to the Lord.  
> And you will believe that sublime men live forever;  
> You will look upon the pure and strive to see them again.

4. The architect of the Pseudo-Julian took great pains to bring the verses which he had read in Cajetanus—or rather in others—back into conformity with meter. Nor, I think, did he conjecture badly when he restored *Ac reddi Domino quos* (“and that those should be restored to the Lord whom …”). Yet he should not have tampered with the final verses. The author of the ancient epitaph appears to be referring to images of the saints, which were customarily venerated on the very altar beneath which their bodies lay.

5. His insertion of Fulgentius was altogether inept, although he changed *disjungit membra duorum* (“separates the limbs of the two”) to *disjungit membra priorum* (“separates the limbs of the forefathers”) in order to accommodate that interpretation. Niccolò Antonio argues this at length in book V of the *Bibliotheca Vetus*, no. 32; he concludes that the entire epitaph reeks of centuries more barbarous than the seventh, the century of Ildefonsus.

Among the other poems falsely attributed to Ildefonsus by the Pseudo-Julian, this epitaph was included in the edition of the Toledan Fathers. Nevertheless, the most learned editor observes in a note that this epitaph is found under Ildefonsus’s name in the *Life of Saint Isidore*, believed to have been written by Lucas of Tuy. He nevertheless agrees with Niccolò Antonio, who does not consider it to belong either to Ildefonsus or to any other ancient author in the form in which it appeared in the compiler. As Niccolò Antonio explains, that form differs considerably from the form preserved in its proper state in the codex of Nicolaus Faber.

Niccolò Antonio makes no judgment concerning the form in which it appeared in the author of Saint Isidore’s *Life*; perhaps, when he wrote, he had not seen that version. In that *Life of Saint Isidore* we read, as in the Pseudo-Julian, with the following exceptions:

- *Leandri, Isidori, pariumque ex ordine vatum* — “of Leander, Isidore, and equals in the order of poets”;
- *O! quam composita consors! hic digna quiescit* — “O, how composed is the consort who rests worthily here.”

The mention of Fulgentius is omitted, as is the verse:

> *In quibus hic recubat Fulgentius: inspice tres hos*  
> “Among whom Fulgentius rests here; behold these three.”

The following variants also occur:

- *Spe certos, plenosque fide* — “certain in hope and full of faith”;
- *Dogmatibus cernas horum* — “you may see through their doctrines”;
- *Ac reddi Domino quod* — “and that [it] should be restored to the Lord”;
- *Utque viros credas sublimes vivere semper* — “and that you may believe sublime men to live forever”;
- *Aspiciens sursum pictos contende videre* — “looking upward, strive to see them painted there.”

6. Since, then, the author of Saint Isidore’s *Life*, who is believed to have lived in the thirteenth century, attributes Isidore’s epitaph to Ildefonsus, it must be asked whether verses of this kind, even if they are not Saint Ildefonsus’s, can nevertheless be considered earlier than the thirteenth century. Florez plainly denies this in volume X of *España Sagrada*, when he discusses Saint Fulgentius.

For my part, I cannot bring myself to believe that the writer of Saint Isidore’s *Life*—much less if he was Lucas of Tuy, an honorable man—composed Isidore’s epitaph in order to attribute it to Ildefonsus as its author. We must therefore judge that the epitaph had long before been circulated under Ildefonsus’s name, prior to the composition of Isidore’s *Life*, and that the author of the *Life of Isidore* adopted it in good faith.

As we have seen, Cajetanus praises a very ancient Gothic codex in which these verses were largely contained. If that is true, it indicates greater antiquity for the epitaph than Niccolò Antonio acknowledges. But Cajetanus’s reliability in citing ancient parchments appeared to Naudé and certain others to be weak and uncertain.

7. Otherwise, when I examine the verses themselves as they appear in the author of the ancient *Life of Saint Isidore* and in Cajetanus, I find nothing that would make me judge them unworthy of the seventh or eighth century—especially since, through the carelessness of copyists, as happens with almost all other texts, they could easily have come down to us in corrupt form.

Let them be compared with the verses certainly known to belong to Eugenius III of Toledo, and, in my opinion, no great difference will be found. In the second verse I prefer Cajetanus’s reading:

> *Leandri Isidorique, priorum ex ordine vatum*

—“of Leander and Isidore, foremost in the order of poets”—

unless one prefers, by conjecture:

> *Leandri, Isidori, primorum ex ordine vatum*  
> “of Leander and Isidore, foremost in the order of poets,”

or:

> *primori ex ordine vatum*  
> “foremost in the order of poets.”

At that time *vates* was used for a priest or bishop, as is demonstrated by many examples in the *Dictionary of Du Cange*, enlarged by the Maurists.

8. In the verses of Isidore’s Library, the following is said of Leander:

> You are not considered inferior to the teachers of ancient times,  
> Leander the poet; your words teach this.

Although, in a very ancient codex of the Vatican Archives, I found this title assigned to Isidore, not Leander; accordingly, it read *Isidore antistes* (“Isidore the bishop”), not *Leander vates* (“Leander the poet”).

9. In the fifteenth-century codex described by Rodríguez de Castro in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, page 286, which contains the *Etymologies* translated into the ancient Spanish language, the same epitaph exists both in Latin and in Spanish, nearly as it appears in Faber’s codex.

The readings are as follows:

- First verse: *geminorum corpora fratrum* — “the bodies of twin brothers.”
- Second: corruptly, *parumque ex ordine natum* — “and born little according to order.”
- Third: *soror devota* — “the devoted sister.”
- Fourth: *O quam composita concors hic digna quiescit* — “O, how composed and harmonious she rests worthily here.”
- Fifth: *Isidorus medius* — “Isidore in the middle.”
- Sixth: *Hi quales fuerunt* — “What sort of men these were.”
- Seventh: *Cognosces et eos* — “You will also learn of them.”
- Eighth, added: *Spe certos, plenosque fide, super omnia charos* — “certain in hope, full of faith, and dear above all things.”
- Ninth: *Dogmatibus cernes horum crevisse fideles* — “you will see that the faithful grew through their doctrines.”
- Tenth: *Ac rredi Domino* — “and [that they were] restored to the Lord,” for *Ac reddi*.

The two final verses, *Utque viros*, etc., are missing, but the Spanish translation proves that they were present.

10. Some sought not Ildefonsus but another author for Isidore’s epitaph, namely Braulio. Hear Niccolò Antonio, book V, chapter 5, number 67 of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*:

> “We have read somewhere that an epitaph of the holy Leander and Isidore was attributed to Braulio, bishop of Caesaraugusta, and that it is said to be written at the end of Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies* in the Gothic book of the monastery of Saint Dominic at Silos … Yet, from the letters of Don Antonio Zapata of Lupiana and Aragón to the Reverend Father Fray Luis de Mier, procurator in Rome of the Benedictine Congregation of Spain, dated February 11, 1657, and sent from the monastery of San Millán, we can establish that the following distich was read in the cited Exilian codex:

> This nurturing cross holds the bodies of the holy brothers,  
> Leander and Isidore, foremost in the order of poets.

> “Instead, it read:

> This nurturing cross holds … the bodies of the brothers,  
> Leander and Isidore, little according to the order of abbots.

> “I possess these letters written in Zapata’s own hand.”

Yet none of this removes us from sounder judgment, since so many unhealthy fabrications have come from that hand. Nor does the order of abbots deserve to be attributed to these most holy men by an utterly inept and rustic poet, especially in view of the pontifical dignity that both held; and Braulio certainly was not such a poet. Briefly, concerning these matters, etc.

11. He calls him the most inept and rustic poet, such as the notorious fabricator Zapata portrays him. In order to continue currying favor with the Benedictines, Zapata left no stone unturned and forged or corrupted every written source he could.

But if Niccolò Antonio persists in maintaining that Isidore’s epitaph—even without interpolation or corruption—is the work of a most inept and rustic poet, I openly declare that I adopt a different opinion.

Mabillon, volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, page 278, confirms that this epitaph is found appended to Leander’s rule in a certain codex. He thinks that perhaps, beneath a cross extending across the space, the three bodies of the holy brothers lay together; and that a painting on the adjoining wall represented their likenesses and merits.

He conjectures that Ildefonsus’s words in *On Illustrious Men*, “Leander flourished in the time of Reccared and brought his life to its close,” should not be understood too strictly so as to diminish the authority of the epitaph; and that Florentina was more probably buried at Hispalis than at Astigi, as others report.

I do not at all approve Mabillon’s opinion concerning the year of Saint Leander’s death. Compare chapter 20.

12. There is another epitaph of Isidore, likewise attributed to Ildefonsus in the Pseudo-Julian’s collection of poems. It is plainly apocryphal, both because no memory of it appears before the Pseudo-Julian and because it mentions Isidore’s exile, which is fictitious. It reads as follows:

> His mind penetrates the heavens; in this urn his body sleeps,  
> Sweet glory of your people, leader Isidore.  
> Receive what your disciple dedicates to you, master—  
> He who shared your exile and was your companion.  
> Gladly accept these poems, and the one whom you loved while alive,  
> Master, love him after your death, secure.  
> Pray for us wretched ones, most illustrious teacher,  
> Glory of Spain, honor of religion.  
> Grant, I beg you, that you be gracious; cease, I ask, to be entreated.  
> The peoples call you, and your disciple calls you.  
> He whom various cares surround and dense dangers assail—  
> Grant him to enjoy the station of heaven.

13. After the epitaph of Isidore, which he expressly asserts was composed by Ildefonsus—namely, “This nurturing cross holds …”—the author of Isidore’s *Life* adds another poem without naming its author. He therefore leaves the reader in doubt whether he attributes this second poem also to Ildefonsus.

Certainly, however, it does not belong to the age of the Gothic Fathers, since it contains interwoven fables and is composed in leonine verses, of which it is not established that such a form was then in use in Spain. At any rate, among the genuine poems of Eugenius and his contemporaries, no fairly long poem composed in this kind of common rhythm is found. It will therefore have its proper place when Isidore’s *Life* itself is published.

## CHAPTER VIII

### The Acts of the Translation of Saint Isidore’s Body, Revised from the Gothic Manuscript Codex of the Royal Library of Madrid; Another Copy of the Acts of the Translation; Observations on Both Accounts

1. “By divine providence his blessed body was translated from the city of Hispalis after 468 years [perhaps after 427 years] and buried with fitting honor in the city of León. Although it is written in an unpolished yet truthful style, we have nevertheless judged it worthy to insert into this work.

## Reading I

“Accordingly, in the seventy-fifth year after the passing of the most glorious bishop Isidore, the entire Gothic people was handed over, by the hidden judgment of God, to be slaughtered by a pagan sword. For the Saracens from overseas, crossing the sea that washes against the city of Seville, first captured that same city; then they occupied the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. King Roderic, having gathered an army of Goths, met them armed. But because the aforesaid king, neglecting divine religion, had enslaved himself to the dominion of vices, he was immediately turned to flight, and nearly the whole army was destroyed by the sword, even to annihilation. Thereafter the Saracens wandered far and wide, perpetrating innumerable and dreadful massacres. The overturned camps and the demolished walls of ancient cities bear witness to how many massacres and how great a slaughter they inflicted upon our people. At that time all Spain mourned: monasteries throughout it had been overthrown, bishoprics destroyed, books of sacred law burned by fire, the treasures of churches plundered, and all the inhabitants consumed by sword, flame, and famine. At last that mercy—which is not accustomed to destroy utterly those whom it chastises, but mercifully to correct them by scourging—strengthened the courage of a certain Pelagius, who was descended from royal stock. He rebelled against the Saracens at the place called the Cave of Saint Mary and declared war upon them. How the divine hand fought on behalf of our people in that conflict may be understood from this: the weapons’ missiles sent by the Saracens were turned back by divine power against the very men who had launched them; and a certain cliff, severed by God’s command, collapsed and, crushing a considerable multitude of Saracens, destroyed them. If anyone wishes to know the matter more fully, let him take care to read the mournful history of those times.” [Col. 0040A–C]

## 41. Reading II

“From that time onward, the glory and kingdom of the Gothic people gradually and little by little began to sprout again, like a shoot from a renewed root, and to increase from moment to moment through the diligence of kings who, born of royal lineage, nobly governed the summit of the kingdom. They were renowned in arms and strength, distinguished in counsel, outstanding in mercy and justice, devoted to religion; they renewed ancient bishoprics, founded basilicas and enriched them with treasures, adorned them with gold, gems, and books, and, to the best of their ability, extended the glory of the Christian name.

From this illustrious lineage emerged the most distinguished man Ferdinand, son of King Sancho. Once he had possessed the royal scepters, it is not our purpose to unfold how great and how frequent a disaster he inflicted upon the Saracens. Among the other works of piety that he religiously undertook, he asked Benabeth, king of Seville, to grant him the body of the most blessed virgin Justa, which rested in that same city, so that he might transfer it to the city of León. He granted his request as he wished and promised that he would give it to him.” [Col. 0040D–0041A]

## Reading III

“Having received this reply, the venerable bishop Alvitus addressed his companions privately in these words: ‘As you see, companions, unless divine mercy relieves the labor of our journey, we shall depart frustrated. It is therefore necessary, beloved ones, that we seek help from God and devote these three days to fasts and prayers, so that the divine majesty may deign to reveal to us the hidden treasure of the holy body.’

The bishop’s exhortation pleased everyone, and they spent those three days in fasting and prayer. On the third day, when the sun had set after the completion of its course, and the fourth night had come, the venerable bishop Alvitus remained wakeful in prayer. Meanwhile, as he sat on a small seat, turning over in his mind—I know not what—from the Psalms, he was overcome by sleep. A certain man appeared to him, adorned with venerable gray hair and clothed in a bishop’s fillet, and addressed him in these words:

‘Indeed, I know that you have come here with your companions in order to transfer the body of the most blessed virgin Justa and carry it away. Although it is not the divine will that this city be deserted through the departure of this virgin, divine goodness will nevertheless not send you back empty-handed. My body has been given to you; take it away and return safely to your own.’

When the reverend Alvitus asked who he was who imposed such instructions upon him, he replied: ‘I am Isidore, teacher of the Spains and bishop of this city.’ Having said this, he vanished from the eyes of the man who saw him.” [Col. 0041A–C]

## Reading IV

“But when the bishop awoke, he began to rejoice over the vision and to pray to God more earnestly, imploring that, if the vision were from God, it might be made known again, and a third time, more fully; but if not, that it might depart. While praying in this way, he fell asleep again. And behold, the same man appeared and delivered words no different from those spoken before; then he vanished again.

Awakening once more, the bishop more eagerly begged the Lord for a threefold confirmation of the vision. While he prayed to God with greater insistence, he was overcome by sleep a third time. The man mentioned above appeared to him as he had appeared once and twice before, and repeated for the third time what he had said earlier. Striking the ground three times with the pastoral staff that he held in his hand, he pointed out the place where the holy body lay hidden, saying: ‘Here, here, here you will find my body. And lest you think that you are being deceived by a phantom vision, this shall be a sign to you that it is true: as soon as you have brought my body out above the earth, you will be seized by a bodily illness, which death will immediately follow; and thus, stripped of this mortal body, you will come to us.’

Having said this, the vision disappeared. The bishop awoke, certain of so great a vision and rejoicing at his calling. When morning came, he said to his companions:

‘Beloved ones, we ought to adore the divine omnipotence with bowed heads, for he has deigned to go before us by his grace and has not allowed the reward of our journey to be frustrated. For by divine command we are forbidden to remove from here the limbs of the blessed virgin Justa, dedicated to God; but we shall carry away no lesser pledges, since we shall transfer the body of the most blessed Isidore, who held the episcopal office in this city and adorned Spain by his work and his word.’

He said this and disclosed to them, in order, the sequence of the vision.” [Col. 0041C–0042A]

## Reading V

“When they heard this, they gave thanks to God and went together to the king of the Saracens. They disclosed everything to him in due order. Although he was an unbeliever, he was nevertheless struck with fear when he recognized the power of God, and he replied:

‘If I grant you Isidore, with whom shall I remain here?’

But since it was not lawful for him to spurn men of such authority, he gave permission to search for the confessor’s remains.

I shall tell of something marvelous; nevertheless, I remember hearing it from those who were present. When the tomb of the blessed man’s body was being sought, the mark of the staff with which the holy confessor had pointed out the place of the monument by striking it three times was found on the very surface of the ground. When the place was uncovered, such a fragrance of scent poured forth that it covered the hair of the heads and beards of all who were present as if with a mist and dew of balsam.” [Col. 0042A–B]

## Reading VI

“The blessed body was covered by a wooden container made of juniper. As soon as it was opened, illness seized the reverend bishop Alvitus, and on the seventh day, having received penance, he surrendered his spirit to the angels, as we believe, in accordance with the command of the vision.

The Asturican bishop Ordoño and the entire army, having received the remains of blessed Isidore and the body of Alvitus, bishop of León, hastened to return to King Ferdinand. When the body of the most blessed Isidore was placed upon its bier, the aforesaid Saracen king, Benabeth, threw over his body a silk curtain woven with marvelous workmanship. Drawing deep sighs from the depths of his breast, he said:

‘Behold, venerable Isidore, you are departing from here; yet you yourself know how your affairs and mine stand. Therefore I beg you always to remember me.’

I recall hearing this from those who heard it.” [Col. 0042B–C]

## Reading VII

“When these things had been completed, they returned to their own country with the greatest joy. At their arrival, the most glorious King Ferdinand displayed great ceremony. Although he was saddened by the death of Alvitus, bishop of León, whom he had always revered with extraordinary affection, he nevertheless provided an elaborate procession for the arrival of the most glorious confessor Isidore. He placed his blessed body in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, which the same king had recently built. Having gathered all the noblemen and bishops of his kingdom, he had it consecrated in honor of the confessor. To this day, the tenth day before the Kalends of January is annually and solemnly celebrated as the day of the church’s dedication and of the translation of the blessed bishop.

The illustrious king is said to have devoted himself, together with his entire household, to humility with such devotion at that festival, out of reverence for the blessed confessor, that when the time came for the banquet, setting aside royal pride, he personally placed delicate foods before each religious man with his own hands, in the manner of a servant. The queen likewise, together with her sons and daughters, humbly rendered every service to the rest of the multitude as servants would.” [Col. 0042C–D]

## Reading VIII

“In that place where the relics of the holy body are venerated by the faithful people, our Lord Jesus Christ has deigned to display such numerous and such great miracles for the honor and glory of his name—restoring sight to the blind, hearing to the deaf, expelling unclean spirits from possessed bodies, and restoring the power of walking to the lame—that, if someone skilled in letters were to commit them to writing, he would produce volumes of books of no small size. But partly through ignorance and partly through negligence, they have been concealed in silence.

If the undoubting faith of those who ask requires it, our Lord Jesus Christ still deigns to perform similar works through his confessor even to this day. The relics of the blessed confessor were transferred from the city of Seville and brought to León in the year of the incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1063, in the first indiction, with the third concurrent.” [Col. 0043A–B]

## Reading IX

“That which follows also seems to belong to the praise of the gracious bishop. Although the city of Seville had never been accustomed to suffer the burning of frost because of the hot vapor of the sea, nevertheless in the year in which the blessed remains were taken from there, it was so scorched by burning frost that no fruit remained in the vineyards, olive groves, or fig orchards.

Let each person speak according to his own judgment. I, however, assert that the elements themselves felt the departure of the holy body; that, feeling it, they suffered; and that, by God’s command, they struck the inhabitants of the city, deprived of so great a patron, with the loss of their fruits. By such works and others of this kind, Jesus Christ glorifies his chosen ones in the sight of mortals, rewarding them with his vision in the presence of God the Father and the holy angels. He, with the same Father and the Holy Spirit, lives and reigns as one God through ages that shall never end. Amen.” [Col. 0043B–C]

## Editorial Observations

2. I restored several words to correct orthography, such as *urbem ceperunt* (“they captured the city”) instead of *coeperunt*, *internecionem* instead of *internicionem*, *idem* instead of *hisdem*, and so forth. Similar forms are found everywhere in monuments of the later period, whether introduced through the fault of scribes or through the abuse even of authors.

In Reading II I substituted *religioni dediti* (“devoted to religion”) for *religione dediti*, since in manuscripts *i* is easily changed into *e*. I consider it an error that in Reading III Florez printed *a socii* instead of *o socii*. It would also be preferable to read *talique eum voce* (“and addressing him with such a voice”) instead of *talique cum voce*.

It does not seem accidental that in Reading VI two hexameter verses are joined together:

> “Yet you yourself know how your affairs and mine stand.  
> Therefore I beg you always to remember me.” [Col. 0043C–D]

Perhaps the author intended to precede these words with: “Behold, venerable Isidore, you are departing from here.” The words that precede them also seem to be scattered fragments of a poet.

3. In the *Additions* for 4 April, p. 901, the Bollandists published these same Acts, which they call genuine and uninterpolated, from the manuscript of D. Juan Lucas Cortés of Seville. They omitted the opening words, “His blessed body,” and began with “Accordingly, in the seventy-fifth year.” They describe the manuscript as more than five or six hundred years old, written in letters already almost faded, with the title:

> “Acts of the translation of the body of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

Their notes are as follows:

### 4

“‘Accordingly, in the year.’ There seems to have been some prologue that is missing here.

“Reading II, ‘From that time onward.’ Here *quia et* is inserted in the manuscript; these words seem to be remnants omitted from some parenthesis during copying. Here, however, they already confused the sense and have therefore been omitted.

“Reading VII, ‘of Saint John the Baptist, which.’ Sandoval, p. 10, notes in the margin that the jawbone of Saint John the Baptist is preserved in this church. Since Baronius records the discovery of the head from the year 1025, he asserts, by conjecture, that it was given to Alfonso V by Count William of Aquitaine.” [Col. 0044A]

### 5

“Same Reading VII, ‘is celebrated annually.’ From this you may learn that this history was written for eight readings to be recited at Matins. But why is the tenth day before the Kalends of January indicated, when the feast is celebrated on the twelfth day before the Kalends?

“It is an error, but undoubtedly an ancient one, which the author of the longer Acts copied. The error, however, is supported not only by current usage but also by very ancient inscriptions from precisely that period, written in Gothic letters and intended to be read, above two pillars supporting small vaults that provide light for those entering from the cloister into the chapel. Sandoval recites these inscriptions on p. 16, and it is worth reproducing them here, since they illuminate the whole of the present history.

“The first is:

> ‘This hall, which you see …’

(See below, Chapter 28.)

“The other is:

> ‘Then, in the era 1103, on the sixth day before the Ides of May, they brought there from the city of Ávila the body of Saint Vincent, brother of Saint Sabina and of Christetes. In that year the aforesaid king, returning from war from the city of Valencia, came here on Saturday and died on Tuesday, the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the era 1103. Queen Sancha, dedicated to God, completed [this work].’

“To this may also be referred the epitaph of King Ferdinand, likewise carved in Gothic letters on his tomb and reported by Sandoval after the preceding inscriptions as follows:

> ‘Here lies buried Ferdinand the Great, king of all Spain, son of Sancho, king of the Pyrenees and of Toulouse. He transferred to León the bodies of the saints: of blessed Isidore the archbishop from Seville, and of Vincent the martyr from Ávila. He built this stone church, which had formerly been of clay. By fighting he made all the Saracens of Spain tributary to himself; he captured Coimbra, Lamego, Viseu, and other places. By force he seized the kingdoms of García and Vermudo. He died on the sixth day before the Kalends of January, in the era 1103.’” [Col. 0044B–C]

### 6

“Regarding Reading VIII, ‘In the year of Christ,’ and so forth: the Spaniards reckoned their years in public and private documents by the era customary among them. According to Loaysa, this practice was finally abolished only in the year 1383 by John I, king of Castile.

“How, then, are the years here reckoned from the incarnation of the Lord? From this we infer that the author was not Spanish, but probably a French monk from Cluny. Among the other points of reform introduced by them, they seem also to have taken care to recommend and spread among the Spaniards the method of reckoning the years of Christ, already commonly used elsewhere.” [Col. 0044D]

### 7

The Bollandists suspect that the author of this translation was the Cluniac monk Hebrelmus, who at the same time wrote a similar translation of Saint Indaletius from the kingdom of Granada into Aragon, published among the Bollandist Acts for 30 April. I shall speak of him shortly.

Nevertheless, one cannot help wondering how, in such ancient monuments—which were publicly recited in the Church—the year of the Lord’s incarnation came to be inserted in place of the Spanish era.

### 8

Florez, who published these same Acts in volume IX of *Hispania Sacra*, discusses the history of Saint Isidore’s translation in volume XXVII, p. 135. He considers it attributable to Lucas of Tuy; Risco, the continuator, disagrees in volume XXXIV, p. 198, because that history differs in several respects from the book of Saint Isidore’s miracles, certainly written by Lucas of Tuy. Accordingly, it appears to Risco to be later than Lucas of Tuy and not sufficiently reliable.

It is necessary, however, to distinguish the history of the translation—that is, the fuller Acts published by the Bollandists for 4 April—from the shorter and more authentic Acts, which the same Bollandists published in the appendix for 4 April and which Florez then published in volume IX, Appendix 7.

Florez corrected the Acts from a Gothic manuscript in which Redemptus’s narrative of Isidore’s death was also found, though in a different script, and expanded them with a brief prologue that the Bollandists had observed to be missing from their copy. [Col. 0045A–B]

### 9

These Acts were also included in the new Madrid edition, volume II, among the appendices, p. 61, from another manuscript copy, divided into nine readings for use in the ecclesiastical office. Although the editor notes at the bottom of the page that the readings were taken word for word from the Acts of Saint Isidore’s translation published by Florez, there is nevertheless considerable variation between the two copies in many places, so that it is necessary to reproduce those differences here.

### 10

But it should first be observed that in Florez’s copy the beginning of the Acts also appears mutilated: “His blessed body,” and so forth. Although Redemptus’s narrative precedes it, the Acts are written in a different script and must belong to a much later author.

I am of the opinion that the Acts themselves, as Florez presents them, were taken from the readings of the ecclesiastical office for the day of the translation. Since Isidore had already been mentioned in the office, it is not unreasonable that the readings should begin either, with Florez, “His blessed body,” or, with the Bollandists and the new Madrid edition, “Accordingly, in the year,” and so forth.

That these Acts were adapted to the form of readings for the ecclesiastical office is clearly demonstrated by the fact that in Reading VII one reads:

> “To this day, the tenth day before the Kalends of January is annually and solemnly celebrated as the day of the church’s dedication and of the translation of the blessed bishop.”

These words are absent from the copy in the new Madrid edition, although that copy otherwise names and distinguishes nine readings, as will soon become clear. The Bollandists divide the Acts into only eight readings. [Col. 0045C–D]

### 11

Regarding the author of the Acts, this much alone is clear from his own account. In Reading V he says:

> “I shall tell of something marvelous; nevertheless, I remember hearing it from those who were present”

—that is, at Seville, when Isidore’s body was being sought.

And in Reading VI, after reporting the words of the Saracen king of Seville when he handed over Isidore’s body, he says:

> “I recall hearing this from those who heard it.”

The author must therefore be considered a contemporary.

But should we regard these Acts as so genuine that nothing at all has been inserted from elsewhere? Certainly, since they were adapted for use as readings, as I have said, it should not seem surprising if some things were omitted or added. The Bollandists do indeed imply that something has been omitted, but they declare the Acts free from the leaven of interpolation.

Nevertheless, I would believe that the statements in Reading VIII concerning miracles that had been concealed in silence, partly through ignorance and partly through negligence, were added at a later time. The same applies to what follows:

> “If the undoubting faith of those who ask requires it, our Lord Jesus Christ still deigns to perform similar works through his confessor even to this day.” [Col. 0046A]

### 12

For, apart from the fact that it was the custom of the later period to interpolate genuine monuments, changes of this kind were quite frequent in ecclesiastical offices, especially when no certain author of the readings was identified.

Nor is there any other reason why the readings of the new Madrid edition differ in many respects from Florez’s Acts, as I have already noted.

There may be an error in the former where, in Reading IX, the year of the church’s consecration is given as 1081, on the Kalends of January. Florez’s Acts and the Bollandists’ Acts of the translation give the year of the translation and consecration as 1063, in the first indiction, with the third concurrent, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

From this Florez and the Bollandists argue that the author of the Acts was some Cluniac monk, because he did not express the era. Perhaps this too belongs among the interpolations.

In the Gothic manuscript of the Royal Library of Madrid, the era 1101—which is the year 1063—was written in the margin. In the old inscription that I shall cite in Chapter 28, this same era is recorded, together with the twelfth day before the Kalends of January. Florez proves that this date is preferable because, in the perpetual calendar published in 1578, 21 December is designated as the day of the church’s dedication and of Isidore’s bodily translation, although the church of León, as Tamayus observes in his *Martyrology*, chose the twentieth in order to avoid coincidence with the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle.

Florez adds that in the year 1063, 21 December fell on a Sunday, the day on which, according to the prescriptions of the canons, churches were to be consecrated. For this reason he says that *concurrente II* should be read in the Acts instead of *concurrente III*, and at the beginning that “after 427 years” should be read instead of “after 468 years.” [Col. 0046B–D]

### 13

Florez observed the following variants of the Bollandists’ copy from his own:

- Reading I: “How, then, in the conflict.”
- Reading II: “The glory and kingdom.”
- “With gold and gems.”
- “They adorned them, to the best of their ability.”
- “From the lineage emerged a distinguished man.”
- “The royal scepter.”
- “So that he might transfer her to the city.”
- “Nor any of them.”
- Reading III: “The labor and hardship of our journey.”
- “Unless mercy should reveal.”
- “The bishop’s prayer.”
- Reading IV: “To pray earnestly.”
- “The same man.”
- “Here you will find.”
- “Will follow.”
- “Having said this.”
- “Beloved ones, it is necessary.”
- Reading V: “With whom shall I remain?”
- “I shall tell of something marvelous.”
- “I remember hearing it from those who were present.”
- Reading VI: “Of Bishop Alvitus.”
- “From the depths of his body.”
- Reading VIII: “The faith of those who ask.”
- At the end: “the ages of ages that shall never end.”

### 14

There is some disagreement among the copies concerning the name of the Saracen king of Seville who granted Saint Isidore’s body.

In the readings of certain breviaries he is called Enetus. In the Bollandists’ Acts, in Florez’s, and in other fuller Acts among the Bollandists, he is called Benabeth. In the Acts of the new Madrid edition he is called Benabet and Benadab.

From the history of the Arabs by Rodrigo of Toledo, chapter 48, it may be inferred that the translation was carried out while Habeth was reigning at Seville.

The Acts of the new Madrid edition that I have mentioned, with certain errors corrected, are as follows:

## 15. Reading I

“Accordingly, in the seventy-fifth year after the passing of the most glorious bishop Isidore, the entire Gothic people was handed over, by the hidden judgment of God, to be slaughtered by a pagan sword. For the Saracens from overseas, crossing the sea that washes against the city of Seville, first captured that same city. Then they occupied the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. King Roderic, having gathered an army of Goths, met them armed. But because the aforesaid king, neglecting divine religion, had enslaved himself to the dominion of vices, he was immediately turned to flight, and nearly the whole army was destroyed by the sword, even to annihilation. Thereafter the Saracens wandered far and wide, perpetrating innumerable and dreadful massacres. The overturned camps and the demolished walls of ancient cities bear witness to how many massacres and how great a slaughter they inflicted upon our people.” [Col. 0047A–B]

## 16. Reading II

“At that time all Spain mourned: monasteries throughout it had been overthrown, bishoprics destroyed, books of sacred law burned, the treasures of churches plundered, and all the inhabitants consumed by sword, flame, and famine.

At last that mercy—which is not accustomed to destroy utterly those whom it chastises, but mercifully to correct them by scourging—strengthened the courage of a certain Pelagius, who was descended from royal stock. He rebelled against the Saracens at the place called the Cave of Saint Mary and declared war upon them.

How the divine hand fought on behalf of our people in that conflict may be understood from this: the missiles of weapons sent by the Saracens were turned back by divine power against the very men who had launched them. Therefore a certain cliff, severed by God’s command, collapsed and, crushing a considerable multitude of Saracens, destroyed them. If anyone wishes to know the matter more fully, let him take care to read the mournful history of those times.” [Col. 0047B–C]

## 17. Reading III

“From that time onward, the glory and kingdom of the Gothic people gradually and little by little began to sprout again, like a shoot from a renewed root, and to increase from moment to moment through the diligence of kings who, born of royal lineage, nobly governed the summit of the kingdom.

They were renowned in arms and strength, distinguished in counsel, outstanding in mercy and justice, devoted to religion. They also renewed bishoprics, founded basilicas and enriched them with treasures, adorned them with gold, gems, and books, and, to the best of their ability, extended the glory of the Christian name.

From this illustrious lineage emerged the most distinguished man Ferdinand, son of King Sancho. Once he had possessed the royal scepters, it is not our purpose to unfold how great [possibly: ‘how great a’] and how frequent a disaster he inflicted upon the Saracens.

Among the other works of piety that he religiously undertook, he asked Benadab, king of Seville, to grant him the body of the most blessed virgin Justa, which rested in that same city, so that he might transfer her to the city of León. He granted his request as he wished and promised that he would give her to him.” [Col. 0047C–0048A]

## 18. Reading IV

“Having received this promise, King Ferdinand summoned the venerable Albitus, bishop of León, and the reverend Ordoño, bishop of Astorga, together with Count Munio and a troop of soldiers, and sent them to Seville to carry away the body of the aforesaid virgin.

When they arrived, they explained the purpose of their mission to King Benadab. He said to them:

‘Clearly I promised your lord what you say; but neither I nor any of my people has shown you the body you seek. Search for it yourselves, take it when you have found it, and depart.’

Whether, however, by concealing the truth, the barbarian really said these things to our envoys, we have learned only imperfectly. But human desires are generally as changeable as they are vehement.

When the excellent Bishop Albitus heard this, he addressed his companions secretly, saying:

‘As we see, brothers, unless divine mercy comes to the aid of the labor of our journey, we shall depart frustrated. It therefore seems necessary that, seeking help from God, for whom nothing is impossible, we devote these three days to fasts and prayers, so that the divine majesty may deign to reveal to us the hidden treasure of the holy body.’

The bishop’s exhortation pleased everyone, and they spent those three days in prayer. On the third day, when the sun had set after completing its course, and night had properly arrived, the venerable Bishop Albitus remained wakeful in prayer.” [Col. 0048A–C]

## 19. Reading V

“Meanwhile, as he sat on a chair and supported his weary limbs for a little while, reciting to himself—I know not what—from the Psalms, he was overcome by sleep through excessive weariness from his vigils. A certain man appeared to him, adorned with venerable gray hair and clothed in a bishop’s fillet. Addressing him in these words, he said:

‘Indeed, I know that you have come here with your companions in order to transfer the body of the most blessed virgin Justa and carry it away with you. But since it is not the divine will that this city be deserted through the departure of this virgin, and since God’s immense mercy does not permit him to send you away empty-handed, my body has been given to you. Take it and return to your own.’

When the reverend man asked who he was who imposed such commands upon him, he replied:

‘I am Isidore, teacher of the Spains and bishop of this city.’

Having said this, he vanished from the eyes of the man who saw him.” [Col. 0048C–D]

## 20. Reading VI

“Awaking, the bishop began to rejoice over the vision and to pray to the Lord more earnestly, imploring that, if this vision were from God, it might be made known again and a third time more fully. While praying in this way, he fell asleep again. And behold, the same man, in the same attire, appeared and delivered words no different from those spoken before; then he vanished again.

Awakening once more, the bishop more eagerly begged the Lord for the confirmation of the vision. While he prayed to God with greater insistence, he was overcome by sleep a third time. Then the aforesaid man, appearing to him as he had appeared once and twice before, repeated for the third time what he had said earlier. Striking the ground three times with the staff he held in his hand, he pointed out the place where the holy treasure lay hidden, saying:

‘Here, here, here you will find my body.’

Therefore, lest you think that you are being deceived by a phantom, this shall be a sign of the truth of my words: as soon as my body has been brought out above the earth, you will be seized by a bodily illness, which the ensuing end of life will follow; and, stripped of this mortal body, you will come to us with the crown of righteousness [the Latin syntax is defective].”

After he had finished speaking, the vision disappeared.” [Col. 0048D–0049A]

## 21. Reading VII

“Therefore the bishop rose from sleep, certain of so great a vision and even more joyful at his calling. When morning had come, he encouraged his companions, saying:

‘Beloved ones, we ought to adore the divine omnipotence of the almighty Father with minds bowed down. He has deigned to go before us by his grace and has not allowed the reward of our journey to be frustrated. For by divine command we are forbidden to remove from here the limbs of the blessed virgin Justa, dedicated to God; but we shall carry away no lesser gift, since we shall transfer the body of the most blessed Isidore, who held the episcopal office in this city and adorned all Spain by his work and his word.’

Having said this, he disclosed to them the sequence of the vision in order.

When they heard this, they gave immense thanks to God and went together to the Saracen king, disclosing everything to him in due order. The barbarian was struck with fear and, although an unbeliever, admiring the power of the Lord, said to them:

‘If I grant you Isidore, with whom shall I remain here?’

Nevertheless, since he did not dare to spurn men of such authority, he gave permission to search for the confessor’s remains.

They tell of astonishing things, reported by those who were present: when the tomb of the blessed body was being sought, the mark of the staff with which the holy confessor had pointed out the place of the monument by striking it three times was found on the very surface of the ground. When the place was uncovered, such a fragrance poured forth that it covered the hair of the heads and beards of all who were present as if with a mist and dew of nectarous balsam.

The blessed body was covered by a wooden container made of juniper. As soon as it was opened, illness seized the venerable Bishop Albitus, and on the seventh day, having received penance, he surrendered his spirit into angelic hands, as true faith believes.” [Col. 0049A–C]

## 22. Reading VIII

“Bishop Ordoño of Astorga and the entire army, having received the remains of blessed Isidore and the body of the bishop of León, were already hastening to return to King Ferdinand.

Then behold, the aforesaid Saracen king Benabet threw a crown woven with marvelous workmanship over the sarcophagus of the blessed confessor and, breathing great sighs from the depths of his breast, said:

‘Behold, venerable Isidore, you are departing from here; yet you yourself know how your affairs and mine stand.’

This was reported by those who testified that they had heard it in person.

The envoys, setting out on their journey with so great a gift sent from heaven, returned to their own country. At their return, the most glorious King Ferdinand displayed great ceremony. Although he was saddened by the death of the bishop of León, he nevertheless provided an elaborate procession for the arrival of the most blessed confessor Isidore. He placed his holy body in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, which the same serene king, as I mentioned shortly before, had recently built at León.

The venerable Bishop Albitus, however, has a tomb, by God’s favor, in the church of blessed Mary, over which he had presided.” [Col. 0049C–0050A]

## 23. Reading IX

“Accordingly, four hundred years after his death, the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ Isidore was transferred from the city of Seville and buried in the city of León with due honor. For, having gathered the noble bishops and abbots of his entire kingdom, the king had the aforesaid church consecrated in honor of the blessed confessor in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1081, on the Kalends of January.

Moreover, the most glorious king is said to have devoted himself to humility with such devotion at that festival, out of reverence for the holy bishop, that when the time came for the banquet, setting aside royal pride, he personally placed delicate foods before each religious man with his own hands, in the manner of a servant. Queen Sancha likewise, together with her sons and daughters, humbly rendered every service to the rest of the multitude.

In that place where the relics of the blessed body are venerated by the faithful people, our Lord has deigned to display such numerous and such great miracles for the honor and glory of his name that, if someone skilled in letters were to commit them to parchment, he would produce volumes of books of no small size.” [Col. 0050A–B]

### 24

The Madrid editor, at the end of Reading IV, read *emesso olympo* and conjectured *e medio olympo*. I restored *emenso olympo* (“when the course had been completed”). I corrected several other orthographical errors, which it is not worthwhile to list.

The origin of these Acts of the translation will become clear from the following chapter.

# CHAPTER IX

## An account of the translation of the body of Saint Isidore, excerpted from the Chronicle of an anonymous monk of Silos
1. “King Ferdinand, having arranged matters along the frontiers, as soon as a suitable opportunity arose, gathered his army again and marched hostilely into the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. After devastating the barbarians’ lands and burning many villages, Abenhabet, king of Seville, met him with great gifts and entreated him, by friendship and by the honor of his kingdom, not to wish to pursue his own kingdom [Perhaps: ‘lest he himself wish to pursue’]. King Ferdinand, moved by human compassion [humanely], and softened by the old barbarian’s entreaties, ordered all suitable men to be summoned from Ireland, so that by their counsel he might decide what end to put to the Moorish king’s supplications. When the council had been held, in accordance with its decree he both accepted the gifts and ordered that the body of the martyr Saint Justa—who long ago had gone from Seville to Christ with the crown of martyrdom—be returned to him, so that he might transfer it to the city of León. The barbarian, immediately assenting to the royal commands, promised that he would give the body of the most blessed virgin.

2. “After this promise had been received, when that expedition had ended, King Ferdinand summoned to himself in León Alvito, the venerable bishop of that royal city, and Ordoño, the revered bishop of Astorga, together with Count Munio, and sent them with a troop of soldiers to bring the aforementioned virgin’s body from Seville. When they arrived, they reported King Abenhabet’s instructions. He said to them: ‘I know that I promised your lord what you seek. But neither I nor any of my men can show you the body you desire. Search for it yourselves, and when you have found it, take it away; depart in peace.’

“Whether, by concealing the truth, the barbarian really said these things to our embassy, we have learned only imperfectly. But human intentions are generally as changeable as they are passionate. When the distinguished Bishop Alvito heard this, he addressed his companions as follows: ‘As we see, brothers, unless divine mercy comes to the aid of the labor of our journey, we shall depart disappointed. It therefore seems necessary, beloved, that, seeking help from God, for whom nothing is impossible, we devote ourselves for three days to fasting and prayer, so that the divine majesty may deign to reveal to us the hidden treasure of the holy body.’

3. “All approved the bishop’s exhortation, so that they might spend those three days in prayer. On the third day, when the sun had set after the day had run its course, and the fourth night had arrived, the venerable Bishop Alvito continued in unceasing prayer. Meanwhile, while sitting on a chair and supporting his weary limbs for a little while, he was reciting something from the Psalms to himself and, overcome by sleep through excessive weariness from his vigils, a certain man appeared to him, adorned with venerable gray hair and clothed in a bishop’s mitre. He addressed him in these words:

“‘I know that you have come here with your companions to transfer the body of the most blessed virgin Justa and take it away with you. But since it is not the divine will that this city be left desolate by the departure of this virgin, and since God’s immense mercy does not permit him to send you away empty-handed, my body has been given to you. Take it and return to your own people.’

“When the venerable man asked who he was who imposed such a task upon him, he replied: ‘I am Isidore, teacher of the Spains and bishop of this city.’ Saying this, he vanished from the eyes of the one who saw him.

55. 4. “When the bishop awoke, he began to rejoice over the vision and to pray to God more earnestly, asking that, if the vision were from God, it might be made fully known to him a second and a third time. Praying in this way, he fell asleep again. And behold, the same man in the same appearance, uttering words no different from those spoken before, vanished again. The bishop awoke once more and more eagerly begged the Lord for a threefold confirmation of the vision. While he was entreating God more insistently [Perhaps: ‘more earnestly’], sleep seized him a third time.

“Then the aforementioned man appeared to him, as he had on the first and second occasions, and repeated for the third time what he had said earlier. Striking the ground three times with the staff he held in his hand, he pointed out the place where the holy treasure lay hidden, saying: ‘Here, here, here you will find my body. And lest you think that you are being deceived by a phantom, this will be the sign of the truth of my words: as soon as my body has been brought out of the earth, you will be seized by an illness of the body, and when the end of life follows, having cast off this mortal body, you will come to us with the crown of righteousness.’ After he had finished speaking, the vision disappeared.

5. “The bishop therefore rose from sleep, certain of the great vision but even happier at his own calling. When morning had come, he encouraged his companions, saying: ‘Beloved, we ought to adore with bowed minds the divine omnipotence of the supreme Father, who, with his grace going before us, has deigned to favor us and has not permitted the reward of our journey to be frustrated. For by divine will we are forbidden to carry away from here the remains of the blessed virgin Justa, dedicated to God; but we bear [Perhaps: ‘we shall bear’] no lesser gifts, since we shall carry the body of the most blessed Isidore, who held the episcopal dignity in this city and adorned all Spain by his work and word.’

“Saying this, he disclosed the course of the vision to them in sequence. When they heard it, they gave immense thanks to God and went together to the Saracen king, to whom they reported everything in order. The barbarian was terrified and, although an unbeliever, admiring the Lord’s power, said to them: ‘If I give you Isidore, with whom shall I remain here?’

“Nevertheless, not daring to reject men of such authority, he gave permission for them to search for the confessor’s remains. I report astonishing things, yet they were related by those who were present. When the tomb of the blessed body was being sought, the imprint of the staff with which the holy confessor had pointed out the place of the monument by striking it three times was found in the very ground. When the place was uncovered, such a fragrance of perfume poured forth that it covered the hair of the heads and beards of all who were present as though with a mist and dew of nectarous balsam.

“The blessed body was enclosed in a wooden vessel made of juniper. As soon as it was opened, illness seized the venerable Bishop Alvito, and on the seventh day, having received penance, he surrendered his spirit into angelic hands, as the true faith believes.

6. “Bishop Ordoño of Astorga and the whole army, having received the remains of blessed Isidore and the body of the bishop of León, were already hurrying back to King Ferdinand when, behold, the aforementioned Saracen king Abenhabet cast a curtain woven with marvelous workmanship over the sarcophagus of the blessed confessor. Sighing deeply from the bottom of his heart, he said: ‘Behold, Isidore, venerable man, from now on you are departing. Yet you yourself know what belongs to you and what belongs to me.’

“These things are known from those who testified that they had heard them in person. The envoys, setting out on their journey with this great gift sent from heaven, returned to their own people. On their return, the most glorious King Ferdinand made a great display. Although he grieved over the death of the bishop of León, he nevertheless put on an ambitious procession for the arrival of the most blessed confessor Isidore. He placed the saint’s body in the basilica of Saint John the Baptist, which, as I mentioned shortly before, that same serene king had newly built at León. The venerable Bishop Alvito, meanwhile, has a tomb in the church of Blessed Mary, over which he had presided, by God’s favor.

7. “Thus, four hundred years after his death, the body of the most blessed confessor of Christ, Isidore, was transferred from the city of Seville and buried with due honor in the city of León. Having gathered the nobles, bishops, and abbots of his entire kingdom, the king caused the aforementioned church to be consecrated in honor of the confessor in the year of the Lord’s incarnation 1052 [1062 should be read], on the eleventh day before the Kalends of January.

“Moreover, on that festival the most glorious king is said to have been so devoted to humility out of reverence for the holy bishop that, when they came to the banquet, he laid delicate foods before the religious men with his own hands, setting aside his royal pride and acting in place of servants. Queen Sancha likewise, together with her sons and daughters, humbly rendered every service to the rest of the company in the manner of servants.

[Col. 0053B] 8. “In that place where the relics of the blessed body are venerated by the faithful people, our Lord has deigned to display such numerous and such great miracles for the honor and glory of his name that, if someone skilled in writing were to commit them to parchment, he would produce no small volumes of books. But I, who have resolved merely to write the deeds of kings, do not presently intend to unfold how many and how frequent miracles have been accomplished through the merits of the confessor in the bodies of various sick persons who sought his help, by the divine Maker. To him be glory forever and ever. Amen.”

9. This Chronicle was published by Flórez in volume XVII of *España Sagrada*. In section 5 he supplied, after “Rising,” the words “after our journey,” although this may not be necessary, since “our reward” could be understood. I added “shortly before” after “after” in section 6, “Bishop Ordoño.” Others give the year of the church’s consecration as 1063.
