The author was writing not long afterward, namely at the beginning of the twelfth century, so that the truth of the event can hardly be called into question, although the Acts were later enlarged with certain additions. The author of the Chronicle is a Spaniard, indeed he plainly professes himself opposed to the Franks. Nevertheless, he mentions the year of the Lord’s incarnation, which seems strange to me unless we say that the Chronicle has been interpolated in this part. In any case, the fact that the Acts were drawn from this Chronicle is demonstrated by section 6, “as I mentioned shortly before,” words that also appear in the Acts. But the author of the Chronicle used them because he had in fact mentioned shortly before the basilica founded by the king.

# CHAPTER X. Sermon of Saint Martin of León on the Passing of Saint Isidore. Notes on This Sermon

[Col. 0053D]

1. “Isidore, a distinguished man, by nation a Carthaginian, born of Severianus, bishop of the Church of Seville, was the most holy brother and successor of Bishop Leander. From childhood this most blessed man was devoted to literary studies, instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, trained in every kind of speech, sweet in eloquence, outstanding in intellect, and likewise renowned in life and teaching [Note: Thus the Toledo manuscript, edited by Henschenius, sections 5 and 42].

“Thus progressing from virtue to virtue, the exceptional teacher shone forth, so that, according to the character of his speech, he was suitable for the instruction of all—Latin, Greek, and Hebrew speakers, the wise and the less learned alike—and vigorous in incomparable eloquence. This most glorious man possessed such wisdom, learning, and holiness that the following was rightly said of him: ‘Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous’ (Ecclesiasticus 44:16–17; 50:1).

2. “The word ‘priest’ is composed from Greek and Latin and is called *sacerdos*, as if meaning ‘one who gives sacred things.’ Just as a king is so called from ruling, so a priest is called from sanctifying and from giving what is sacred (Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VII, chapter 12). For a person becomes a great priest for two reasons: first, so that he may live well; second, so that he may teach well. Even if an ecclesiastical teacher lives well, nevertheless, if he does not teach well, he is not great. And even if he teaches well, nevertheless, if he does not live well, he will in no way be great.

“Teaching is therefore necessary together with a good life. For teaching without a good life makes a teacher arrogant, while life without teaching makes a teacher useless (Isidore, *Sentences*, book III, chapter 36). Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Whoever loosens one of these commandments and teaches people to do so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven; but whoever does them and teaches them will be called great in the kingdom of heaven’ (Matthew 5:19).

“In this passage, the kingdom of heaven is the assembly of the elect. Scripture often calls the Church of the faithful the kingdom of heaven because, since it longs for heavenly things, the Lord already reigns in it as though in heaven. Whoever therefore loosens one of the commandments of our Lord Jesus Christ—that is, whoever does not fulfill it in action but teaches people to fulfill it—will be called least in the kingdom of heaven, namely in the assembly of the faithful. It is as though he openly said: Whoever neglects to fulfill my commandments but teaches people to fulfill them will be called least; that is, he will be imperfect in the holy Church.

“Elsewhere also the Lord says of such people: ‘They say, and do not do.’ Then follows: ‘But whoever does them’—that is, whoever fulfills my commandments in action—and teaches people to fulfill them, will be great (Matthew 23:3), namely, suitable in the holy Church. The priest’s preaching must therefore be confirmed by works, so that what he teaches in word he may instill by example.

3. “The following passage from the Song of Songs also suitably confirms this testimony: ‘Behold, sixty mighty men surround Solomon’s couch, chosen from the strongest of Israel; all hold swords and are most skilled in battle. Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night’ (Song of Songs 3:7–8).

“Solomon is interpreted as ‘peaceful.’ Who, then, is understood by Solomon except Christ (Gregory, on this passage), of whom it is written: ‘He is our peace, who made both one’ (Ephesians 2:14)? Solomon’s couch, that is, Christ’s, is the holy Church. For when it withdraws from worldly anxieties, when it does not cease to cleanse its heart from every earthly pollution through repentance, and when with the whole desire of its mind it strives toward the heavenly homeland, it makes itself like a couch on which Christ rests with delight.

“Hence he himself says affectionately to his disciples: ‘Behold, I am with you all the days, until the consummation of the age’ (Matthew 28:20). Again, through the prophet he says: ‘I will walk among them and will be their God, and they will be my people’ (Leviticus 26:12).

“The sixty mighty men who surround Solomon’s couch signify the prelates of the Church, who fortify it by words and examples and drive away visible and invisible enemies from it by prayers and preaching. ‘All,’ he says, ‘hold swords and are most skilled in battle.’ What is signified by the sword except the word of God, and what by the hands that hold the swords except action? For, by fulfilling in works the word of God that they know in their hearts, they continually conquer the enemies of the Church more and more through wisdom and strength.

“They are most skilled in spiritual warfare because they know how to cut away vices first in themselves and then in those subject to them. They are most skilled in battle because they fulfill in action the commandments of God that they preach in word. They are prudent and highly skilled in battle because with the sword of discernment they cut away from themselves and from those subject to them what is superfluous and what is pleasing to this world.

“Of these it is rightly added: ‘Each man’s sword is upon his thigh because of the terrors of the night.’ What do we understand by the sword except the rigor of one’s manner of life, and by the thigh except the appetite of the flesh? The prelates of the Church, who have already reached perfection in virtue, always carry the sword upon their thigh, because by the rigor of their manner of life they continually break the appetite of the flesh. Thus the enemy whom they fear in the night of this world may not come suddenly and find them weak and slack in God’s work, and through the softness of pleasure and the delight of the flesh deceive them and those subject to them more easily and lead them into graver sins.

4. [Note: Toledo manuscript, in Henschenius, chapter 11, section 43, approximately midway.] “He, therefore, is called great in the kingdom of heaven, that is, in the Church, who fulfills in good works what he preaches in words. Let this therefore be said of blessed Isidore: ‘Behold the great priest, who in his days pleased God and was found righteous.’ Truly great, because he fulfilled in deeds the works of God that he preached in words.

“He is rightly called a great priest whom God raised up in Spain in the latter times, after so many declines, I believe, to restore the ancient wisdom of men, which through excessive antiquity had almost died out in human minds, lest the Christian people grow old any longer in ignorance and rusticity. Thus, full of charity and wisdom, he did not hide in the earth the talents entrusted to him; rather, he distributed them for the common benefit of all and, like a good merchant, returned them doubled to the Lord, while by preaching he stirred the minds of many to desire heavenly things.

“Just as Gregory the teacher succeeded the Apostle Peter, so blessed Isidore succeeded the Apostle James. For the seed of eternal life that the most blessed James sowed, this distinguished teacher sufficiently watered by the word of preaching, like one of the four rivers of Paradise, and illuminated all Spain by the example of good works and the reputation of holiness like a most brilliant [Note: The edition at the same place reads ‘most brilliant ray of the sun.’ Pollio says that *lampada* is used for *lampades*; Dufresne observed this from manuscript codices, and Salmasius noted it in Plautus: ‘Hold this lamp.’ Sermon 56, in the Appendix to Fulgentius, also uses this word: ‘O good lamp,’ says the author, ‘not one that loves the world, but one that loves heaven’; and below: ‘There are many who call the day a lamp.’ (Note of the editor of Saint Martin.)] lamp.”

5. “The prophet Ezekiel says among other things in his vision of the four living creatures: ‘And the likeness of the living creatures,’ he says, ‘was like burning coals of fire, and like the appearance of lamps’ (Ezekiel 1:13).

“By these four living creatures the multitude of the saints is signified. Their appearance is compared to fiery coals and burning lamps because whoever joins himself to holy men is kindled by their imitation and teaching in love of the Creator (from Gregory, *Homilies on Ezekiel*, book I, homily 5, section 6).

“Yet there is this difference between coals and lamps: coals burn, but they do not drive away the darkness from the place where they lie. Lamps, however, because they shine with the great brightness of flames, illuminate the darkness spread around them.

“From this it should be observed that many of the saints are so simple and hidden, and concealed in lesser places under profound silence, that their life can scarcely be recognized by others. What, then, are these people except coals? Although they possess the heat of the spirit through their ardor, they have no reputation for example and do not illuminate the darkness of sins in other hearts, because they entirely conceal their life from others. They are kindled for themselves, but they are not a light of example for others. Although they burn with the fire of divine charity, they do not kindle others by the reputation of holiness or by the word of preaching.

“Lamps, however, shine farther and, though they are in one place, gleam in another, because whoever shines by the example of good works and the word of preaching has a reputation that shines far and wide like a lamp. When those nearby hear of his good deeds, they rise through them to the love of heavenly goods. In displaying themselves through good works, they shine as though by the light of a lamp.

“When holy men kindle certain people placed near them, as though by contact, to the love of the heavenly homeland, they are coals. But when they shine upon people who are far away, lest they fall into the darkness of their sins, they become lamps for their journey. Those who provide examples of virtues and demonstrate to others, by their life and word, the light of good works are rightly called lamps.

“Truly they shine like lamps who, both through love of the Creator and through the flame of good preaching, drive away from sinners’ hearts the darkness of error. Whoever lives well in secret but benefits no one else is a coal. Whoever, placed in the Church as an example of holiness, provides the light of righteousness to many is a lamp, because he burns for himself and shines for others.”

[Col. 0057A] 6. “This most blessed man is therefore rightly compared to a shining lamp, because he illuminated both those present and those absent by the word of preaching and the reputation of holiness, and kindled them to love of the heavenly homeland. He is suitably compared to a burning lamp because he burned with love of God and neighbor and drove away the darkness of sins from the hearts of others. Whoever approached him received the light of truth through the constant sight of him, the practice of conversation, and the example of good works, and burned with desire for eternal light.

7. [Note: Toledo manuscript, no. 43, in Henschenius.] “For this most blessed man, in addition to the other works of holiness that he wisely performed in the Church of Christ, confounded and destroyed the wicked heresy of the Acephalites. They denied that Christ had two substances and proclaimed one nature in his person, asserting that he was not truly God and the Son of God, but merely a pure human being.

“After Gregory, the leader of the aforementioned heresy, had been overcome and convicted by the testimonies and authority of the holy Scriptures, Isidore taught that there were two natures in Christ, namely divine and human: divine, by which he is eternally coeternal and coequal with God the Father; human, by which, for our salvation, he deigned to become temporally the Son of Man, that is, of the Virgin.

“And what shall I say about his holiness and wisdom? Human speech is certainly not sufficient to relate fully how many benefits God bestowed through him upon his Church, and how useful he was to an ignorant people and an aging world, when in his *Chronicle* he disclosed the ages of the world and the sequence of times. In Greek, *chronica* is called, in Latin, ‘a sequence of times.’ For *chronos* in Greek means ‘time’ in Latin.

“He therefore disclosed to an ignorant people the sequence of times and the ages of the world; he displayed the laws of sacred things; he explained to priests the ecclesiastical offices and the ranks of every order; he established laws for kings and princes; he forbade avarice to judges; he instilled Christian religious discipline into citizens and all domestic peoples of the faith. Finally, by writing, he disclosed the names, kinds, functions, and causes of seats, regions, places, and all divine and human things, as well as everything obscure and almost removed from human minds.

[Note: The same place, section 44.] “He flourished in wisdom and holiness during the reigns of the emperors Maurice and Phocas, under Reccared, king of the Goths. He was generous in almsgiving, outstanding in hospitality, stern of heart, truthful in judgment, just in decision, constant in preaching, joyful in exhortation, diligent in winning souls for God, cautious in expounding the Scriptures, prudent in counsel, humble in dress, temperate at table, devoted in prayer, distinguished in honesty, and conspicuous in every goodness.

“Moreover, he was a father to clerics, a comforter of the sorrowful, a protection for orphans and widows, a relief to the oppressed, a defender of citizens, a persecutor of heretics, and a hammer against the proud. And what more shall I say? He became a mirror of every good thing to the world and therefore, as we believe, now reigns without end with Christ.

“He died in the time of the emperor Heraclius and of Suintila, king of Spain [Note: If the name of King Suintila was not added to our manuscript by an unreliable and more recent hand—and certainly after the Salamanca copy, which has ‘Suintila’—then the reign of the king and the year of Isidore’s death, 622, or era 660, would fit together correctly. But since the Toledo manuscript contains that error in assigning the era and later says that Isidore died under King Chintila, we have no doubt that our manuscript suffered from the same error, which the corrector attempted to remedy. We say that the author, or copyist, of the Toledo codex was mistaken when he asserted that the year of Saint Isidore’s death was 622; by now all have agreed on 636, unless this is supported by the authority of Redemptus, cleric or archdeacon of the same holy bishop, Saint Braulio, and Saint Ildephonsus. It is not surprising, however, that the aforementioned author or copyist fell into that error. For he was so confused in this matter that he first says Isidore died in the time of Chintila, then says that he flourished until Sisenand, and immediately afterward says that he died in the time of Suintila, in era 660—nine years before Sisenand began to reign and fourteen before Chintila. We are surprised that Henschenius did not note this. (Note of the editor of Saint Martin.)].

“That is, in the time of that Heraclius who restored and exalted in Jerusalem the Lord’s cross, which the impious King Khosrow had carried away. Blessed Isidore fell asleep with his fathers in era 660, superior to all in sound teaching and sound counsel and rich in works of charity, and he was buried in a good old age.

“In the meantime, dearest brothers, it is fitting that we pray more attentively to this most holy confessor, so that he may continually be an intercessor for us, miserable sinners who still stand amid dangers to our souls, before God, so that through his most sacred merits and prayers we may, after this life, reach the fellowship of God’s elect. Through him who, as perfect Trinity, lives and reigns as God forever and ever. Amen.”

8. This sermon appears in the extensive edition of the works of Saint Martin of León, volume IV, pages 3 and following, edited from a copy made from the autograph, like the other works of Saint Martin. The sermon is a cento, composed by stitching together passages taken here and there from various ancient sources; this was a practice of Martin of León and of other Fathers.

“As you see, some passages come from the shorter or genuine preliminary account of Braulio’s works on Isidore, some from the fuller or interpolated preliminary account, and some from the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, whose author Lucas of Tuy identified as Saint Ildephonsus. Martin nevertheless took nothing that smacked of fable, whether because it occurred in more carefully corrected or less interpolated works, or because, exercising the sharpness of a disciplined judgment, he selected only what had been most thoroughly tested.

“One thing can certainly be gathered: before Bishop Lucas of Tuy there existed certain records that were inserted into the Life of Saint Isidore, and that many believe were fabricated by Lucas himself. The old error concerning the year of Saint Isidore’s death is evident from the Life of Saint Isidore among the Bollandists; Martin seems to have followed that error. Compare the editor’s note.

64 [Note: It is not easy to guess why this and the following sermon are given by the author the title ‘On the Translation of Isidore,’ since they contain not a single word about it. The whole work turns [perhaps: ‘is concerned’ or ‘is turned’] on a matter altogether extraordinary, the credibility of which we leave to the reader. (Note of the editor of Saint Martin.)]

# CHAPTER XI. Sermon of Saint Martin of León on the Translation of Saint Isidore, with Notes. Doctrine Infused into Saint Martin of León from Heaven through the Aid of Isidore. Other Spaniards of the Thirteenth Century Celebrate Isidore’s Praises

[Col. 0059A]

1. “‘He will not fear for his house from the cold of snow, for all his household are clothed in double garments’ (Proverbs 31:21).

“In approximately the year 1147 from the Lord’s Incarnation, a messenger of the supreme King—namely, an angel whom the Lord sends around those who fear him (Psalm 33:8), one of those who always see the face of the Father who is in heaven (Matthew 18:10)—announced with joyful report in the court of the supreme Emperor, who commands the winds and the sea (Matthew 8:26), that the house of blessed Isidore, once metropolitan bishop of Seville, was being prepared, or rather restored, within the walls of the city of León for the order and residence of religious clerics.

“When venerable Father Augustine, the distinguished teacher of the Catholic Church, received this report, he rejoiced and exulted. Seeing Lord Isidore, foremost among confessors, pondering something to himself, he addressed him as follows: ‘What is it, reverend brother, that you are turning over in your mind? Are you perhaps considering the exposition of some passage of Scripture? But in this homeland of spirits, heaven—that is, Scripture—is not stretched out like a hide but folded like a book (Isaiah 34:4). Nor do you perceive that the peoples need instruction, because here is fulfilled what is written: “They shall not teach one another, nor each his brother, saying, Know the Lord, for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest” (Jeremiah 31:34).

“‘Since, as it seems, you are concerned with the governance and arrangement of the churches, you ought nevertheless to be concerned more spiritually [Perhaps: ‘more specially’] and more intimately with that which concerns you. I am speaking of the house within the walls of the city of León that contains the treasure of your body and is being prepared for residence by religious clerics.’

2. “To this Lord Isidore replied: ‘I am concerned about these matters, but especially about the clothing of those who serve God in that clerical house. For I have already provided a large part of what is necessary for their food, and I shall provide the remainder in sufficient measure; but that land does not abound in clothing. I want them, having food and clothing, to be content with these’ (1 Timothy 6:8).

“Father Augustine replied: ‘I too shall provide clothing for these sons of yours. It is written in Solomon concerning a certain woman that “she will not fear for her house from the cold of snow” (Proverbs 31:21), and so forth. Of her it is also added in the same passage: “She has worked with flax and wool” (ibid., 13).

“‘In this manner I shall provide these sons and members of your household with a double garment woven from flax and wool [Perhaps: “I shall weave”], namely, a surplice and a cape. In the one I want cleanliness to be understood, and in the other humility; this can also be recognized from the color and appearance of the garments themselves. For bodily cleanliness has whiteness, while the blackness of the garment represents humility.

“‘You also know that the most blessed Virgin, the mother of the Lord, was specially clothed in both. Hence it is written of her: “The glory of Lebanon was given to her, the beauty of Carmel and Sharon” (Isaiah 35:2). And she herself says of herself: “Because the Lord has regarded the humility of his handmaid” (Luke 1:48).

“‘The same distinction is also observed in the making of these garments. For the linen garment is completed with much labor and difficulty; the woolen garment not so much. In the same way, bodily cleanliness is usefully acquired and preserved with much labor and effort, since it is resisted by the law of the members, the tinder and weakness of nature, the sting of the flesh—which the Apostle himself confesses that he suffered (2 Corinthians 12:7)—perverse and shifting habit, the enticing temptation of another’s outer skin, and the suggestive provocation of the inner enemy.’

[Col. 0060B] 3. “With regard to flax, it is clear that it is first pulled from the earth, then gathered into bundles, lowered into a pool, dried in the sun, cleansed of refuse and tow, drawn through a distaff into threads, wound into balls, stretched upon a loom and woven, finally cut and sewn, and thus made into a surplice.

“Flax arises from the earth, and by it the shining beauty of cleanliness and bodily and spiritual chastity is signified. Flax is therefore first pulled from the earth because whoever desires to possess the cleanliness of chastity for fear and love of God must first abandon earthly and worldly conduct and join himself to the community of religious men. It is also fitting that a person withdraw bodily from the place where he remembers having served vices. For often, when the place is changed, the disposition of the mind is changed as well.

“Next the flax is gathered into bundles, because one who previously flowed away through illicit acts while living carnally ought, once bound by the bond of divine charity, to gather himself back within the dwelling of his own heart.

“After this the flax is lowered into a pool. Since a pool is always at the bottom, it signifies compunction of heart. For just as flax is cleansed and washed in a pool [Perhaps: ‘in the pool’], so the sinner is cleansed and washed from sins and vices in tears of compunction, which arise with deep groaning of the breast.

“Then it is dried in the sun. God is the true sun of righteousness, from whose heat no one can hide, that is, from his knowledge. By the heat of the eternal sun, therefore, the unlawful moisture of lust is dried up in a person, because, kindled by knowledge of him and by the fervor of charity, he immediately withdraws from the intention of evil action.

“Flax is also cleansed of tow and refuse, because every convert is cleansed through repentance from unlawful and superfluous actions.

“Flax is then drawn through a distaff into threads. The distaff is carried in the left hand and the spindle in the right. Just as the threads descend from the distaff, so all the actions of God’s servant depend upon the judgment of his superior, so that he may do nothing without his counsel.

“Then it is wound into balls, because it is restrained under the authority of its superior. After this it is stretched upon a loom and woven, while, at the command of the superior, the servant moves about inside and outside, performing whatever good he can.

“Finally the cloth is cut and sewn, while the servant of God perfectly despises the world, scorns visible things, and gathers himself inwardly in contemplation of his Creator. It is as though he is cut away from the tumult of the present age and, in mind and desire, sewn into the citizens of the eternal homeland—that is, attached to them—so that, although he cannot yet fully possess the sweetness of the heavenly kingdom, he may at least taste it by sighing for it.

“Thus the surplice of complete cleanliness and honor is fitted, because he is already made suitable for the fellowship of the perfect.”

4. “Now, by God’s grace, brothers, you have a surplice; but you still need a woolen cloak. The woolen and black garment signifies the humility of religious conduct. Wool, therefore, is first shorn, then cleaned and washed; it is suspended from the distaff, drawn out into threads, woven, and sewn together—and thus the cloak is completed. In the wool are displayed God’s gifts, which are granted to us by God in the present life. Wool is shorn when earthly possessions are cast aside for God’s sake. Wool is, as it were, cleaned and washed when, through the giving of alms, man is cleansed from sins. Hence the saying: ‘Give alms, and behold, all things are clean for you’ (Luke 11:41). The wool is suspended from the distaff when it is carefully watched over lest anything be given for the sake of vainglory or out of love of empty praise. It is drawn out into threads when alms are distributed with discernment. The wool is woven when one diligently devotes oneself to works of mercy. The cloth is cut when the will to possess has already been completely excluded from the mind. Finally, it is sewn together when each convert, ascending from the active life, is inserted and joined into the contemplative life after abandoning everything; and thus the regular cloak is completed, while by good works he earns from God the garment of eternal glory.

5. “Again the most blessed Augustine addresses Saint Isidore, saying: ‘Reverend brother, behold, I have clothed all your household, as I promised, in double garments. Do not therefore fear any longer the wintry cold for your household, since all your household are clothed in double garments. First I fitted them with a surplice, by which purity of mind and body is signified; then with a cloak woven from sheep’s wool, in which innocence of life and humility of conduct are displayed. You, therefore, venerable brother Isidore, obtain sufficient food for them, so that, while they abound in clothing, they may serve God without want. It is also your task to admonish them, while you are present in spirit and body, to strive with all devotion to fulfill the rule instituted for them by me. Preach to them also that they cling diligently to spiritual offices, lest—God forbid—delighted by earthly goods, they be wholly deprived of eternal ones.’ To this our patron Saint Isidore replied: ‘O most reverend Father Augustine, it is fitting for you thus to exhort them to live well. We render acts of thanksgiving to almighty God, who appointed you teacher of the holy Churches.’”

6. “Behold, dearest brothers, by God’s grace you have been sufficiently instructed by blessed Augustine and have been doubly clothed in regular garments, namely, the surplice and the cloak. In the surplice, as has already been said, purity of mind and body is signified. Take care, therefore, brothers, lest damnable fornication lie hidden beneath the surplice. Believe me: no one who is defiled by fornication is clothed in a surplice. What benefit is it to display outwardly before human eyes a surplice washed with water, while inwardly before God one carries a body polluted by fornication? Or what benefit is it outwardly, in the sight of men, to display the purity of a garment while concealing within the impurity of fornication? Nothing is hidden before God: he who made hidden things sees what is concealed. ‘All things are naked and open to his eyes’ (Hebrews 4:13). I therefore warn you, beloved, not to be whitewashed tombs, which outwardly appear beautiful to men, but inwardly are full of the bones of the dead, of worms, and of every kind of filth (Matthew 23:27).

7. “The cloak is woven from the wool of sheep, and therefore signifies the humility of religious conduct. Accordingly, dearest brothers, diligently take care lest a wolf lie hidden beneath the sheep’s skin. Hence the Lord says in the Gospel: ‘Beware of false prophets, who come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly are ravenous wolves’ (Matthew 7:15). The wolf lies hidden beneath the sheep’s skin when simulation, discord, and envy lie hidden beneath the habit of regular life. The wolf also lies hidden beneath the sheep’s skin when a hypocrite, under the appearance of religion, harms his neighbors. He is a ravenous wolf inwardly who, while outwardly pretending innocence, does not cease secretly to devour the flesh of his neighbors by slandering, grumbling, and whispering.

“Therefore, brothers, fill with good works the religious habit which you display in appearance. Do not seek to be one thing in secret and another in public. Let the inner mind agree with the religious garments. Let life agree with speech. The habit is holy; let the mind be holy. The garments are holy; let your works be holy. Having food and clothing, therefore, dearest brothers, be content with these (1 Timothy 6:8), and retain no private possession among you. There is no doubt that he commits theft who has everything in common with the other brothers but keeps something hidden for himself. To possess everything in common with the other brothers and to hide something else for oneself—what is this other than handing oneself over to punishments after death? He who has food and clothing in common with the other brothers but retains something else hidden—what is this other than manifest theft?

“Therefore, dearest brothers, despise riches, love poverty, disdain earthly things, and desire heavenly things. Seek nothing superfluous; retain nothing for yourselves; hide nothing, if you desire to reach the common fellowship of God’s elect. May he lead you to it who, as perfect Trinity, lives and reigns, God, throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

8. What follows is in volume IV of the works of Saint Martin, page 52, the second sermon on the translation of Saint Isidore. But since it contains nothing else except the same colloquy between Saint Augustine and Saint Isidore, adorned with the same or similar allegories, it is not worth transcribing. Martin, however, does not touch upon the Acts of the translation, because, since at that time—as it is reasonable to believe—the genuine Acts themselves were being read in the Church of León, divided into lessons, it was superfluous to explain the same history in a sermon or homily. Nor is it necessary for us to believe that the colloquy which Martin relates between Saint Augustine and Saint Isidore actually took place in this way: for Martin may have devised this sort of apologue in order to find an agreeable subject for his sermon.

9. Before we leave Saint Martin, it is worthwhile to report how he suddenly became most learned from being rough and uneducated, with Isidore interceding for him. Lucas, a deacon of León and later bishop of Tuy, wrote the Life of Saint Martin in the work entitled *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore*. It is found in volume I of Saint Martin’s works; in its first chapter we read:

“At that time Martin, a priest of venerable life and a canon of the same monastery, whom I mentioned shortly before above, was almost an idiot in his inward understanding of the Scriptures, but he flourished conspicuously and most wisely in works of virtue. Although he was learned in ecclesiastical offices and, as has been said, did not grasp the inward meaning of the Scriptures, like one who had never at all attended the schools of grammarians, nevertheless there was [Ms.: *inhierat*] in him the greatest desire to understand the holy Scriptures, and he devoted himself to prayers and fasts, serving the Lord day and night in the spirit of truth.

“But while one night he was keeping watch and devoting himself to prayer, blessed Isidore the teacher appeared to him, carrying a little book in his hands, and said to him: ‘Take this, my beloved, and eat; and the Lord will give you knowledge of the holy Scriptures, because you have been found faithful and just in his house. I have also obtained from the Lord Jesus Christ that you may receive whatever you ask of God; and you shall be a companion of the miracles which the Lord works through me in this church. I am Isidore, the patron of this place, and you shall strive to offer for the glory of Christ’s name the things which the Holy Spirit teaches you.’”

10. Lucas of Tuy also relates in chapter 12 concerning the same Martin of León:

“When he could not bear the weight of his hands and arms while writing, he had ropes fastened to a certain beam above; drawing them across his shoulders and arms, he endured, suspended in a manner, the burden of his weak body more easily. Thus, writing on wax tablets, he handed them over to scribes, who transferred to parchment what he had dictated or compiled [Ms.: *copilata*].”

From this I infer that this copy, transcribed in this manner onto parchment, was called the autograph in the edition of the works. It is also clear from this that the use of wax tablets continued in Spain into the thirteenth century. In chapter 2 of the *Acts of the Academy of Barcelona*, page 305, it is suggested that mention of this use is not easily found after the tenth century.

11. The same Lucas of Tuy, in chapter 15, reports that Peter, a very learned and upright man, dean of León, who had been freed from quartan fever through the prayers of Saint Martin, with Saint Isidore interceding, and who later governed the Church of Compostela, composed a homily distinguished by rhetorical ornament, in which he gloriously extolled Isidore, the confessor of Christ, with celebrated praise. I was unable to obtain it so as to insert it here. Risco, volume XXXV of *Hispania sacra*, pages 277 ff., discusses this Peter Munionis, or Muñoz, whom he says was bishop of León from 1205 to 1207 and was then transferred to the see of Compostela. From the same Lucas of Tuy, Risco praises on page 279, in the preface, two other men outstanding in learning: Martin, dean of León, and Veremund, archdeacon, who wrote verses in praise of Saint Isidore and seem to have flourished in the same thirteenth century.

## CHAPTER XII

The Continuation of the Chronicles of Blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville, composed by Blessed Ildephonsus, archbishop of Toledo, as Lucas of Tuy asserts, in which certain fabulous matters concerning Saint Isidore have been inserted. Notes on this continuation. Notice from the edition of the Toledan Fathers.

1. “Since the distinguished teacher Isidore revealed, in an easily understood summary, the ages of the world and the histories of certain emperors and kings from the beginning of the world up to the time of Sisenand, king of the Goths, let us begin from the time at which he ceased, lest the memory of present heroes fade from the minds of those to come.

2. “Era 671, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Heraclius: after King Suinthila, Sisenand reigns for three years. He held this synod of bishops, was patient, and stood firm in the orthodox Catholic rules. He ended his life at Toledo.

3. “Era 674, in the twenty-first year of the reign of Heraclius, Chintila received the kingdom. He held several synods at Toledo with the bishops and strengthened the kingdom subject to him in the Catholic faith. He reigned five years and four months. In the sixth year of Chintila’s reign, Isidore, teacher and lawgiver of the Spains, standing in the church, after completing a sermon to the people, stretched out his hand toward heaven, blessed all, and commended to God the flock entrusted to him until that time; then he fell asleep in the Lord in a most blessed sleep, adorned with a most holy old age.

“For he was renowned in the spirit of prophecy, generous in almsgiving, outstanding in hospitality, serene in heart, truthful in judgment, just in his decisions, constant in preaching, joyful in exhortation, diligent in winning souls for God, cautious in explaining the Scriptures, prudent in counsel, humble in dress, temperate at table, devoted in prayer, distinguished in uprightness, always ready to die for the Church and the defense of truth, and conspicuous in every goodness. Moreover, he was a father to clerics, a teacher and supporter of monks and nuns, a comforter of the sorrowful, a protection for orphans and widows, a relief for the oppressed, a defender of citizens, a crusher of the proud, and a persecutor and hammer of heretics.

“He governed the archiepiscopate of the Church of Seville for forty years, shining with various signs of miracles, flourishing in the dignity of the primacy, and acting in Spain as the representative of the Roman pope. He taught priests, kings, and peoples divine and human laws, and commanded them humbly to obey the Roman bishop. He imposed a curse upon those unwilling to obey and separated them from the fellowship of the faithful. He instructed Christ’s Church through many volumes of books and rested in peace in Era 680. He summoned the bishops to Toledo for a synod and, with prophetic voice, foretold to them the day of his death and what would come upon Spain.

“Star of uprightness, light of morals, sun of probity,

“These things that holy man Isidore said in the synod of Toledo,

“Isidore, through whom the nourishing faith flourished:

“‘If you preserve what is commanded to you,

“Christ will preserve you in his love.

“He will give grain and oil, and will give every good thing,

“If with pure mind you please him.

“If you neglect these things, you will not suffer with impunity,

“For God rightly punishes evil deeds.

“Then the Goths will fall in wars, and the barbarian enemy

“Will oppress you with countless disaster, fear, and famine.

“Then turn back; then lament your crimes,

“And at once the Lord will be your helper.

“Your glory will be greater, and Christ’s grace

“Will exalt the Goths with more abundant blessing.’”

4. “We have recorded these matters concerning his deeds among the acts of the kings, because he himself was born from the distinguished stock of the Gothic kings, his father being Severianus, the Carthaginian commander. After his death, one month later, the Catholic king Chintila died at Toledo, having met a good end. The most blessed teacher Isidore was succeeded by Theodist, a Greek by birth, learned in a variety of languages, outwardly polished in speech, but inwardly, as his end revealed, a most ravenous wolf beneath a sheep’s skin.

“For he corrupted, out of hatred for the faith, certain books on the natures of things, the art of medicine, and even the *ars notoria* (the notory art), which Father Isidore had composed in eloquent style and which had not yet reached the public, cutting out what was true and inserting what was false; and through a certain Arab named Avicenna he translated them from Latin into Arabic. Found unfaithful in these and many other matters, and proved erroneous in the articles of faith, he was degraded from the archiepiscopal dignity by a synod. For he asserted that our Lord Jesus Christ, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, was not one God, but rather an adopted son. As has been said, after being deprived of the honor of the priesthood, he went over to the Arabs, adhered to the sect of the pseudo-prophet Muhammad, and taught many detestable things under the emperor Heraclius. At that time the dignity of the primacy was transferred to the Church of Toledo.”

5. Thus the spurious author or interpolator of this continuation proceeds, relating many things that are based not only on no ancient records but are also contrary to them. In a longer account he adds a history of Muhammad woven from falsehoods. Of him he invents the following:

“Nevertheless, as is said, the devil, transforming himself into an angel of light, foretold certain future things to him. Hence it came about that at the beginning of his deceptive preaching he went to Spain and taught the sect of his perdition at Córdoba. For he said that Jesus Christ the Lord had been born from a Virgin through the operation of the Holy Spirit, but nevertheless was not God. When this had been reported to the most blessed Father Isidore, who was then returning from the Roman court, he immediately sent ministers to seize him. But the devil appeared to Muhammad and ordered him to flee as quickly as possible. After his flight into Africa and Arabia, Muhammad seduced innumerable peoples, and so forth.”

6. Concerning Chindaswinth, king of Spain, it reports under Era 682:

“He diligently ordered the books of the holy Fathers to be sought out and the institutions of Blessed Isidore to be firmly observed. By synodal judgment he exiled the treacherous Theodist, bishop of Seville, and transferred the dignity of the primacy to the Church of Toledo.”

7. Lucas of Tuy attached this continuation to Isidore’s fuller Chronicle—which is more extensive than his genuine Chronicle—under the name of Ildephonsus: either he himself fabricated the additions to Isidore’s Chronicle and this entire continuation, as some think; or at least he added certain things to Isidore’s Chronicle and interpolated Ildephonsus’s continuation; or, what is more reasonable to believe, he carelessly accepted the Chronicle and continuation, already enlarged and interpolated by someone earlier, as genuine.

Bayerius, in his notes on Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Veteris Hispaniae*, book V, no. 325, testifies that in the Escorial Codex, shelfmark B, pluteus 1, no. 9, there is a work bearing this title: *The Continuation of the History of the Goths by Blessed Ildephonsus, Archbishop of Toledo, from the Time of Sisenand to Recceswinth*.

8. The antiquity of this codex ought to be examined, and it should be seen whether it agrees with the continuation published by Lucas of Tuy. Rodrigo of Toledo, who was a contemporary of Lucas of Tuy, reports that Ildephonsus wrote the history of the Goths from the fifth year of Suinthila to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth; I shall give his words in the following chapter. This certainly shows that Lucas of Tuy was not the author of the entire continuation which he published under the name of Ildephonsus, as Laurentius de Padilla asserts in the *Life of Saint Isidore* among the *Lives of the Saints of Spain*.

We should reproduce here the notice of the most distinguished editor of the Toledan Fathers, volume I, concerning the Continuation of Saint Ildephonsus, which was reprinted there from volume IV of *Hispania illustrata* among the spurious works of Saint Ildephonsus.

9. Lucas of Tuy, bishop, who in the thirteenth century undertook, at the command of Queen Berengaria, to write the *Chronicle of the World*, was the first who, as though laying the foundations of that work, thrust upon us the present continuation of the Chronicles after the Chronicle written by Isidore up to the reign of Sisebut, as though it had been composed by Ildephonsus, bishop of Toledo—although no earlier memory of this work existed. From where Lucas of Tuy obtained it is uncertain. Some, with Laurentius de Padilla, think that everything he marketed under the name of Ildephonsus was fabricated by him.

They will never persuade us to think rashly of an honorable man; nevertheless, we cannot sufficiently marvel at the man’s credulity, since he did not see the multitude of fabulous monstrosities with which this entire portion of the history is woven. Therefore there is now no historian who does not despise it as a foul fiction, utterly unworthy of having ever been attributed to Saint Ildephonsus.

10. Among many other things, the most mendacious compiler of trifles expressly asserts that Saint Isidore held the see of Seville as primate. He introduces a certain Theodist as Isidore’s successor, previously known to no one and entered in no catalogues of bishops, who was deposed from his dignity for crimes of apostasy and went into exile; on this occasion he invents the transfer of the primatial dignity to the Church of Toledo.

11. To this fable he attached another no less foolish one concerning the arrival in Spain of Muhammad, the impious prophet, and his preaching established at Córdoba. He pretends that, having been warned by the devil of the return of Saint Isidore from Rome, Muhammad fled and thus escaped the chains, prisons, and punishments which Isidore had already decreed against him.

12. Who could read these things, having observed the true history of the infamous prophet and the chronology of his life, without laughing at such monstrosities and wondering that there were people who delighted either in inventing or in recounting so many witless old-womanish tales?

13. These indications, however slight, are sufficient to establish the falsity of this monument and to remove from our Ildephonsus the odium attached to it. Whoever wants more should consult Nicolás Antonio on Saint Isidore and Ildephonsus, where he pursues these fables at length; and then Father Flórez in volume V of *Hispania sacra*, and elsewhere, where he discusses the dignity of the primate of the Holy Church of Toledo.

14. In the meantime, we reproduce its edition according to the copy published by Francisco Scotus in volume II of *Hispania illustrata*, who transcribed it from Lucas of Tuy with this same title that we place before it.

15. Saint Martin of León also transferred certain matters from this continuation into his sermon on the death of Saint Isidore, such as nearly the whole of that passage: “For he was renowned in the spirit of prophecy,” and so forth. He omits the words “supporter of monks and nuns”; perhaps he encountered a continuation that was less interpolated. Constantine Cajetanus also partly transcribed this eulogy of Isidore in the place cited, page 15, from the Chronicles of Lucas, deacon of Tuy, as he says; but he ought to have called him first a deacon of León and then bishop of Tuy.

16. Nicolás Antonio thoroughly demolishes the fabrications reported in the spurious Continuation of Ildephonsus in the *Bibliotheca veteris Hispaniae*, where he discusses Isidore and Ildephonsus. He refutes Muhammad’s journey to Spain at such length that, as Bayerius notes, it could weary even Fabius; we shall briefly demolish that fable in chapter 25. He also discusses at greater length the works of Saint Isidore supposedly corrupted by Avicenna and the apostasy of Theodist; we shall treat these matters below.

Flórez, volume IX, pages 212 ff., demonstrates that Honoratus succeeded Isidore from 12 May 636 to 12 November 641, as is shown by the funerary inscription of Honoratus, which he carefully describes. In the Emilian Catalogue, Antonius is placed after Honoratus, and the name of Theodist does not appear, although the name of the intruder Epiphanius is not absent. I shall present this catalogue in chapter 24.

Since Ildephonsus died in the eighteenth year of King Recceswinth, it is clear that he could not have carried the continuation of the Chronicle down to Recceswinth’s own death, as it is read in Lucas of Tuy. In this respect the account of Rodrigo of Toledo could stand: he affirmed that Ildephonsus wrote the history of the Goths from the fifth year of Suinthila to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth.

It is certainly not surprising that through so many centuries of wars and ignorance in Spain many fables should have crept into our history—for in what nation’s histories does this not happen? Yet it is not sufficiently intelligible how learned men such as Lucas of Tuy and others could have put faith in such old-womanish tales. Once such inventions, accepted by them, had been transmitted from their hands to others, the evil began more easily to spread, and room was given to these fictions not only in other books but also in liturgical works, which the architects of false chronicles eagerly seized upon at the end of the sixteenth century and in the following century.

## CHAPTER XIII

Whether the Life of Saint Isidore published by the Bollandists has Lucas of Tuy as its author. That Life relegated to the appendices and Lucas of Tuy defended against certain persons who contend that he fabricated many things in the Chronicles and in matters concerning Isidore. Who was the author of the book *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore*?

1. I had intended to reprint here the Life of Saint Isidore which the Bollandists, preceded by a most learned commentary, included among the *Acts of the Saints* under 4 April. But since its method would considerably disturb the order of our *Prolegomena*, and since the deeds narrated in it can suitably be supplied from another, shorter Life in the following chapter, it seemed more convenient to relegate the Life illustrated by the Bollandists, together with the fuller history of the translation and the account of certain miracles, to the appendices. Nor ought we wholly omit it, since Zaccaria appears to have placed great reliance on this Life and on the Bollandists’ commentary for the prolegomena to his proposed edition.

2. Meanwhile, two matters must be investigated by us: who the author of that Life was, and whether Lucas of Tuy, who is commonly regarded as its author, was the architect of the fables that crept into the Acts of Isidore. When Nicolás Antonio sent the Bollandists a copy of the Life of Saint Isidore, he judged that its author was not Lucas of Tuy and attempted to establish this by many arguments, as is read in the Bollandists’ preliminary commentary. They readily adopted Nicolás Antonio’s opinion; but since Nicolás Antonio’s arguments relied chiefly on the difference between the style of Lucas of Tuy’s Chronicle and that of the Life of Isidore, and since many mutually contradictory things were mentioned in the two works, the Bollandists observed that someone who maintained that both works had the same author could oppose the claim that the Life of Saint Isidore had been written by Lucas while he was still a deacon in the monastery of Saint Isidore at León, whereas the Chronicle and other works had been written by the same man later, as an older bishop of Tuy and with more mature judgment.

3. After considering these matters in book VIII of the *Bibliotheca veteris Hispaniae*, no. 68, Nicolás Antonio in some way restrained his judgment:

“Now I pause,” he says, “and I do not reject the opinion of very learned men: this difference could perhaps be excused by the variety of a more mature or advanced age; yet not so far as to say that Lucas, already bishop of Tuy, wrote the Chronicle which they attribute to him, since, when sending it to Berengaria, he called himself a deacon.”

Nicolás Antonio adds that he scarcely doubts that one and the same author wrote the Life of Saint Isidore and the *History of the Translation of Saint Isidore the Bishop*, which is appended to the Life in his Toledo codex—so much so that the praise of neither of these works, or of both together, should be assigned to Lucas of Tuy.

We discussed the history of the translation in chapter 8. It is certainly older than Lucas of Tuy and was written by an author nearly contemporary with the translation, although afterward, as commonly happens with monuments of this kind, it was interpolated—as it is in that Toledo manuscript—from written traditions or documents that were common to many and could therefore be copied or compiled by different writers in their works. Lucas, in the Chronicle which is certainly known to have been written by him, also mentions the translation and relates something different. For whereas the Acts report that Saint Isidore appeared only to Bishop Albitus and that Albitus then indicated the revelation to Bishop Ordoñius, Lucas instead says: “Then the confessor of Christ, Isidore, appeared to both bishops while they were praying and showed them the place of his body.”

4. Concerning the author of the Life, I reach a similar judgment: he was someone other than Lucas of Tuy and entirely different from the author of the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, collected by Lucas of Tuy under the name of Ildephonsus along with other chronicles. Those who have examined the manuscript codices containing the Life of Isidore agree that the author’s name is not given. The Bollandists entitle it: *The Life of Saint Isidore, by a Regular Canon of the Monastery of Saint Isidore at León*. No other author of that period is brought forward who testifies that any Life of Saint Isidore was composed by Lucas of Tuy. What, then, is the reason for believing Lucas to be the author of the Life?

I showed in chapter 4 that there are many words and sentences which are expressed in the same context in this Life and in the sermon of Martin of León, who was older than Lucas of Tuy; and Martin seems rather to have drawn them from the Life than the author of the Life from Martin.

5. Since certain matters are narrated differently by Lucas of Tuy in the preface to his collection of Chronicles and by the author of the Life of Isidore, the latter must be distinguished from him. Nor should the Bollandists’ argument move us, namely, that Lucas could have changed his opinion. For whether we suppose that Lucas wrote the Life of Saint Isidore before the Chronicle or after the Chronicle—a question on which those who attribute the Chronicle, the Life, and the Translation of Saint Isidore to the same Lucas are not at all consistent—if he doubted the truth of some event or adopted another opinion, he ought to have noted this when he came to retract his judgment.

In the preface to the Chronicles he called Saint Isidore’s mother Theodora; in the Life she is called Turtura. If the author of both works is the same, why does he call her by different names, or fail to indicate why he adopted a different opinion?

6. There is indeed a tale about Muhammad’s preaching in Spain both in the Life of Isidore and in the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, reported by Lucas under the name of Ildephonsus among other histories. But apart from the fact that far more is related about this matter in the Life of Isidore, which is not found in the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, it is by no means established that Lucas was the author of that continuation or interpolation.

I indicated above, in the appropriate chapter, that Ildephonsus added some supplement to Isidore’s Chronicle or *History of the Goths*. In the oldest parchment manuscripts containing Isidore’s *Etymologies*, I have often found a shorter Chronicle of Isidore, with a computation of time added from the beginning of the world up to King Recceswinth. Ildephonsus flourished at that time; and just as he continued Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, so he may readily be believed to have continued this Chronicle of Isidore, especially the *History of the Goths*.

The words of Rodrigo of Toledo persuade us of this altogether, according to the recent edition of the Toledan Fathers, volume III, in the preface or dedicatory epistle to the books *On the Affairs of Spain*:

“For during the time of the devastation by the Arabs, writings and books perished together with the perishing fatherland, except for the few that escaped through the diligent care of those who preserved them. Thus, from the books of the blessed Isidore, Ildephonsus, the younger Isidore, Idacius, bishop of Galicia, Sulpicius of Aquitaine, the councils of Toledo . . . and other writings, which I laboriously investigated from parchments and tablets and compiled still more laboriously, I have faithfully labored, as far as I could, to weave together a history of Spain from the time of Japheth, son of Noah, up to your own time, most glorious King Ferdinand, as you earnestly requested.”

7. What Rodrigo calls Sulpicius of Aquitaine, I believe should be understood as the Chronicle which Flórez was the first to publish from Spanish parchments in volume IV of *Hispania sacra*, under this title: *Epitome of the Chronicles of Severus Sulpicius*. It ends at Era 771, or the year 733. Flórez doubts whether such a chronicle can in any part be attributed to Severus Sulpicius.

I would readily believe that Severus wrote some chronicles which another person later, as commonly occurs in this kind of work, reduced to an epitome, interpolated, and continued. I also think that John of Gerona referred to this Chronicle, or to Rodrigo’s words, in the preface to the *Anacephalaeosis of Spain*, where he states that Ildephonsus and Sulpicius added something to Isidore’s *History of the Goths*. There is no reason to emend Gerona’s text with Nicolás Antonio, book V, chapter 6, no. 327, and read Julian or Isidore of Pacensis in place of Sulpicius.

8. It is nevertheless more surprising that Nicolás Antonio, in the same work, no. 325, asserts that the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle can be attributed to Ildephonsus solely on the authority of Lucas of Tuy, and immediately afterward, in no. 327, cites Rodrigo’s authority for the same purpose. Many such statements that are scarcely consistent with one another occur in the *Bibliotheca Veteris*, since it is a posthumous work which the author did not revise thoroughly, even after Bayerius’s learned recension.

Thus in no. 325 Nicolás Antonio says:

“But if it really belongs in part to Ildephonsus—the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicles—which we can affirm only on the authority of Lucas of Tuy, certainly many things are sewn onto the ancient material by a new and alien hand.”

Soon afterward, in no. 327, he transcribes these words of Rodrigo of Toledo, book II, chapter 22, *On the Affairs of Spain*:

“And when blessed Isidore had written the origin of the Goths up to the fifth year of King Suinthila, Saint Ildephonsus wrote the times of the Goths, Alans, Vandals, and Suebi from the fifth year of Suinthila to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth.”

Thus far the Toledo manuscript. In other copies the following is added corruptly:

“And the younger Isidore, who begins his chronicle from the beginning of the world, faithfully continued it up to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth, and himself wrote up to the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.”

Nicolás Antonio emends the passage and joins these words to the preceding:

“From the fifth year of Suinthila to the eighteenth year of Recceswinth. And the younger Isidore himself continued it up to the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.”

I would nevertheless prefer to believe that this is an interpolation or addition by someone. For this was not the place for Rodrigo to speak of the younger Isidore, especially since the younger Isidore, or Isidore of Pacensis, began his Chronicle with the times of Isidore of Seville and continued it for many years after the destruction of Spain by the Arabs.

9. Since Rodrigo of Toledo and Lucas of Tuy flourished in the same century, it is foolish to suspect that the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, which bears the name of Ildephonsus, was fabricated by Lucas. Indeed, Nicolás Antonio, book V, no. 215, conjectures that Lucas of Tuy derived from Rodrigo of Toledo what is reported in the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle concerning the transfer of the primacy from the see of Seville to Toledo on account of the apostasy of Theodist, bishop of Seville.

“From whom, then,” he says, “did Lucas of Tuy derive this? These things seem in some way suspicious to me as coming from Rodrigo’s pen, who always defended this perpetual prerogative of the Toledan primacy so vigorously that, even in the very brief chapter we praised, he expressed it twice, though there was no need.”

But Lucas of Tuy completed his Chronicle in 1236, whereas Rodrigo did so seven years later. From this Flórez argues, in volume XXII of *Hispania sacra*, page 123, that Rodrigo used the words of Lucas rather than Lucas those of Rodrigo. It is, however, much more reasonable to believe that before the lifetimes of both men there already existed a continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle, which Rodrigo had before his eyes when composing his history and which Lucas admitted into his collection of Chronicles.

10. Someone might say that Roderic used the genuine continuation, which Lucas interpolated. But this too cannot be maintained. For although Roderic did not speak of Muhammad’s preaching in Spain, nevertheless, as I was just saying, he adopted another story about Theodisc[l]us that is found in that continuation, in *De rebus Hispaniae*, book II, chapter 21, where he reproduced many other passages word for word from that continuation concerning King Chindaswinth, including this passage relevant to our argument:

“He had the books of the holy Fathers diligently sought out, and firmly ordered the institutions of blessed Isidore to be observed. He sent the perfidious Theodistus, bishop of Seville, into exile by synodal judgment, and, with the approval of the entire council, confirmed for the Church of Toledo the dignity of the primacy that it had possessed from ancient times.”

In the margin it is noted, from the Complutensian manuscript and another, that *exsulavit* (“he went into exile”) is read instead of *exsulare fecit* (“he sent into exile”). And *exsulavit* is indeed read in the continuation; nevertheless, some eighty-one words of Roderic are absent there. It continues as follows: “he went into exile, and transferred the dignity of the primacy to the Church of Toledo.”

11. It must therefore be held that Ildefonsus appended to Isidore’s *History of the Goths* a supplement extending to his own times, and that others later enlarged and interpolated it—as they did Isidore’s *Chronicle* itself—from other records or from false popular rumors, before the time of Roderic of Toledo and Lucas of Tuy. Perhaps Pelagius of Oviedo, called “the Fabulist,” had some part in these interpolations; for, as I shall say in chapter 77, a *Supplement of D. Ildefonsus* is also found in the collection of chronicles of Pelagius of Oviedo.

In the twelfth century, moreover, in which Pelagius lived, such license in disfiguring ancient books with apocryphal additions had become widespread, as Mariana confirms in his treatise *On the Preaching and Arrival of Saint James in Spain*, chapter 12:

“I am certainly unable to establish that the genuine book of Calixtus exists anywhere, but only one disfigured by additions and alien patchwork, in accordance with the common practice of that age, when, under the pretext of enriching the writings of the ancients with additions, they rather disfigured them in miserable fashion. There is more than one example of this license.”

Yet examples of corruptions of this kind also exist from long before the twelfth century.

12. But to prevent us from believing that Lucas of Tuy was the author of the fables that crept into those ancient chronicles, consideration of his piety encourages us; and this is rightly observed in the preface to the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicles*, attributed to Ildefonsus:

“There are,” says the most learned editor, “some who, with Lorenzo de Padilla, think that everything which Lucas passed off under the name of Ildefonsus was fabricated by him. They will never persuade us to think rashly of a good man.”

Alfonso García Matamoros, in *On the Academies and Learned Men of Spain*, judges that Lucas of Tuy and Roderic of Toledo wrote not for the pleasure of the ears, but for memory and for the judgment of posterity, and that they were as far from frivolity and folly as they were from falsehood.

13. There is a sufficiently well-grounded account of the illustrious deeds of Lucas of Tuy and of his piety; it is also held that, while he was alive, God performed certain miracles at his prayers. Flórez discusses these at length in volume XXII of *Hispania Sacra*. What bears most directly on our subject is that Lucas himself, in his books against the Albigensians, inveighs most vigorously against corrupters of the writings of the ancients.

Nor does it help to reply that Lucas might have censured those who inserted erroneous or heretical material into the books of the Fathers without condemning those who inserted certain falsehoods in order to advance the cause of religion. For in book II, chapter 11, he says plainly:

“But when they say that some things ought to be fabricated, even though they are not true, in order to extend the glory of Christ’s name, we answer them simply with blessed Job: ‘Does God need your lie, that you should speak deceitfully for him?’”

Hence the instrument of the Holy Spirit, Gregory the Great, says concerning these words of Job: “God has no need of a lie, because truth does not seek the support of falsehood.”

Therefore, even according to Lucas of Tuy’s own judgment, the man cannot be excused who passes off under the name of Isidore or Ildefonsus things that he knows they never wrote, even if such things might otherwise appear to contribute to the extension of the glory of Christ’s name.

14. Flórez readily acknowledges the love of truth that Lucas candidly professes, in the place cited, page 124; nevertheless, he maintains that Lucas himself was the author of the interpolations. He argues that, being a man of good and simple disposition, Lucas thought this permissible because in his preface he had already indicated that he intended to compose a history in which the ancient historians would be seen together.

With this explanation, Lucas presented those writers in the form that he believed more suited to the benefit of readers, adding many things, cutting some, and recounting others in his own style. This would be an excellent defense of Lucas, so far as his devotion to truth is concerned, if he had actually indicated in his prefaces that he was not going to reproduce the genuine chronicles of Isidore and the others, but works adapted to his own style and enriched from other records.

A similar example had already occurred in the first part of the history now called the *Miscella*. For the first eleven books are Eutropius’s ten books, to which Paul Warnefrid subsequently added certain material; Paul himself continues Eutropius, and Landulfus Sagax continues Paul. Others added or interpolated other things.

Concerning Paul, Leo of Marsica says in book I, chapter 15, of the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*:

“At the request of the same Adelperga, he added here and there many things from ecclesiastical histories to the Roman History that Eutropius had composed briefly.”

This is indicated in the very title of the work. Adelperga, or Aldeberga, was a duchess of Benevento and the daughter of King Desiderius.

15. The following passages can be produced from Lucas of Tuy’s preface:

“Bound by the commands of the most glorious and prudent lady Berengaria, queen of the Spains, who ordered me to write for her the books of chronicles published by blessed Isidore and by certain other learned men concerning the history of the kings of Spain and of certain others, I have placed this preface first.”

In the fourth volume of *Hispania Illustrata*, *Astrictis* is printed. But the sense requires *Astrictus*, and I find it written thus in Vatican Codex 7004, formerly belonging to Francisco Peña.

Lucas continues:

“But now we apply our hand to the books of chronicles published by Isidore, the teacher of the Spains, while also following certain others in continuing the succession of the kings of Spain and of certain others, and desiring with all our heart faithfully to satisfy the commands of the most glorious lady Berengaria, queen of the Spains. For she, whose Catholic commands neither may nor can be resisted, ordered me, Lucas, an unworthy deacon, to complete this work.”

16. The words used by Lucas—“We apply our hand to the books,” and so forth—seem to suggest that the chronicles were not merely to be copied by Lucas but recast into a new form. I wish, nevertheless, that he had explained this more clearly, for there are other considerations suggesting that Lucas’s sole purpose was to arrange the sequence and collection of the chronicles.

What is more, Lucas himself seems to indicate that he would change nothing except what he found corrupted through the error or fraud of copyists. In the prologue to Isidore’s *Chronicle of the Goths* he says:

“Now we apply our hand to the deeds of the Gothic kings, setting forth in this work the book of the Chronicles of Isidore, the teacher of the Spains. Yet it must be understood that, in the succession of the Gothic kings, and of the Roman emperors and other princes, an inconsistent numbering of the years is found almost everywhere through the fault of copyists or rivals. Therefore I have labored, as best I could, to bring the years of this work into agreement. Yet let Catholic truth correct me if it should see that I have strayed in these or in any other of my little works.”

Certainly, if a continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle* did not exist before Lucas of Tuy, how could he have fabricated it without being branded a forger, and not only fabricated it but also attributed it to Ildefonsus?

17. To return to the author of the *Life and Translation of Saint Isidore*: I do not believe that he was Lucas of Tuy. First, nothing concerning the author is established by any testimony of the ancients or by any manuscript. Second, although several passages are shared by Lucas’s *Chronicle*, the *Life*, and the *Translation*, this merely proves that different authors took the same words from older records. Finally, both in the *Life* and in the *Translation* there are certain points that Lucas contradicts in his *Chronicle*. Nor can this argument be weakened by supposing that Lucas wrote his different works at different times, since it rather appears that he composed all his works before becoming bishop, as Flórez concludes in volume XXII, page 133, and more clearly on page 145.

18. Nevertheless, Flórez contends that Lucas was the author of the *Life* and *Translation* because he was the author of the book *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore*, and because the author of the *Life and Translation* is not different from the author of the work *On the Miracles*.

We must now consider what this work *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore* was. Nicolás Antonio conjectured that the book *On the Miracles* was not different from the history of the translation, in book VIII, no. 71. For, after discussing the history of the translation, he added:

“It plainly seems to us that Juan de Robles translated this work into the vernacular in the book commonly attributed to him, entitled *History of the Miracles of Saint Isidore, Archbishop of Seville*, and published in 1525.”

In the *Bibliotheca nova*, under the entry “JOANNES DE ROBLES,” he remained uncertain. He says of him:

“He is said to have written *On the Translation and Miracles of the Glorious Saint Isidore, Archbishop of Seville*, at Salamanca, as I suspect . . . He seems to me to have translated, or written, the anonymous work on the *Life of Saint Isidore* and, if the celebrated *Life* is also his, the little book on the translation and miracles of the same holy teacher. I possess both works in manuscript, from a codex of the Church of Toledo, and, since they have not yet been published, I shall shortly send them to the illustrious Godefrid Henschenius, and so forth.”

Flórez describes the book, having seen it. The edition was completed at Salamanca on 2 January 1525, as is clear from the final folio. On the first folio there is an image of Saint Isidore, and another of Saint Martin, Canon of León. On the other folio is the following title of the book:

“Here begins the history of the most blessed Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, primate and most excellent teacher of our Spains, which is divided into three parts. The first contains his life and origin. The second, his glorious passing from this world to perpetual blessedness. The third contains the translation of his holy body from the city of Seville to the city of León. And after the whole of the said history follows the principal book of the miracles of the same Saint Isidore. All of this was copied word for word from the original and most authoritative histories written by the blessed Saint Alfonso, archbishop of Toledo, and Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, disciples of Saint Isidore, and by other ancient writers who wrote his history. It was thus copied and translated from Latin into the Romance language by a religious Canon Regular of the monastery of Saint Isidore of León, who was the same man who rendered the said principal book of his miracles into Romance, without removing or adding anything substantial, as will be found by comparing this vernacular translation with the said originals, which are written in good Latin.”

19. No author is indicated for the Latin work or works concerning the life, passing, translation, and especially the miracles of Saint Isidore. The translator is said to have been one and the same person, a certain canon of the monastery of Saint Isidore at León, whom Aegidius Gonzalez and Nicolás Antonio call Juan de Robles.

In the work *On the Miracles*, the translator reports that a parchment Latin codex containing that Latin work once existed in the monastery of Saint Isidore at León. From there, after various vicissitudes, it came into the Complutensian College founded by Cardinal Francisco Jiménez; a copy was made from it and brought to the monastery of Saint Isidore at León. From this copy the book was translated into the Spanish language.

20. The history of the life and translation prefixed to the book *On the Miracles* is shorter than the one published by the Bollandists, to which they appended a few miracles.

Flórez therefore recognizes two different works, but considers them composed by the same author, Lucas of Tuy: the earlier work, *On the Miracles*, prefaced by a brief history of the life and translation; and the later work, a longer history of the life and translation, followed by an account of certain miracles.

That Lucas of Tuy wrote the work *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore* is established by the prologue to his books against the Albigensians:

“Setting aside for a time the continuation of what I had begun to narrate concerning the miracles of Saint Isidore the Confessor.”

And at the end of the books:

“I believe it was divinely arranged that I, who had undertaken to declare the miracles of blessed Father Isidore to the praise of the Lord . . .”

Finally, since the book *On the Miracles* contains many things that are reported in the same manner in the *Chronicle* and in the *History of the Life and Translation*, Flórez concludes from this that Lucas of Tuy is the one and the same author of all these works.

21. But even if I grant that Lucas completed the work *On the Miracles*, which he had begun to narrate and proposed to make known; and even if I admit that Lucas’s work *On the Miracles* is not different from the work translated into the vernacular, my answer returns, and will always return: it is easier for several different authors to insert into their books many passages, even word for word, from older records—as was then the custom of writing—than for one and the same author to be inconsistent and insufficiently coherent with himself in certain matters.

This is especially so since Flórez teaches that all these works were completed by Lucas of Tuy between the year 1234 and the year 1239, when he was elevated to the see of Tuy, and that he died only in the year 1249.

As for Flórez’s claim that different accounts are sometimes given in these works because Lucas believed both accounts probable, or because he regarded what he wrote last as more credible: the first explanation cannot stand when the subject is events contradictory to one another; the second would be valid if Lucas had explained why he had earlier stated the opposite. An historian’s incorruptible fidelity in some manner requires this.

## CHAPTER XIV

### The Life of Saint Isidore, by Roderic of Cerrato. Notes on this Life

1. “Isidore, a Carthaginian by nation, son of Severianus, duke of that same province and son of Theodoric, king of the Goths, brother of the saints Leander, archbishop of Seville, and Fulgentius, bishop and teacher, and of the virgin Florentina, superior of virgins, archbishop of Seville and primate of the Spains, when he was still a little child, was taken by his nurse to a garden and there, through forgetfulness, was left among the vegetables.

“After several days, Severianus, mourning his son, was sitting opposite the garden when he saw a multitude of bees with an immense buzzing. Astonished, he hurried to the garden after calling the servants. When they approached, they saw some bees entering and leaving the boy’s mouth, while others covered his face and his entire body with coverings of honey and honeycomb. His father then embraced the boy with cries and tears, and the bees rose so high that they could no longer be seen.”

2. “The archbishop Leander loved the boy spiritually, keeping him as a consolation outside his homeland, and did not spare himself the effort of urging and teaching him. When, therefore, the boy Isidore had been entrusted to letters and seemed to himself to possess a less capable intellect, fearing the teacher’s beatings he fled not far from the city of Seville.

“When, exhausted, he had sat down beside the edge of a certain well, he saw a very large stone pierced with winding holes, and a piece of grooved wood placed beneath it [perhaps ‘channeled’]. While he was silently reflecting on these things, behold, a woman came to draw water. The boy said to her: ‘Please explain: who made the holes in this stone and the channels in that piece of wood, and for what purpose?’

“She replied: ‘This stone was pierced by the frequent dripping of drops, and the wood was grooved by the frequent pulling of cords.’

“Then the boy came to himself and said: ‘If water hollows out the hardest stone, and cords cut wood, how much more will I, a human being, by learning every day, be able to attain an increase of knowledge?’

“Therefore he returned to Seville and humbly submitted himself to the discipline of his teachers. Such grace was infused into him from heaven that he eagerly retained whatever he heard from his teachers.
