Thus instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters, he became accomplished in the trivium and quadrivium, distinguished in the teachings of the philosophers, learned in divine and human law, and renowned for his gracious conversation, life, and teaching.”

3. “When he was a young man and had made great progress in knowledge, having heard of Gregory’s reputation, after the first lesson had been read on the night of the Lord’s Nativity in the church of Seville, he went outside the church and reached Rome in a very short time. He found blessed Gregory at Matins. When he saw him, blessed Gregory rejoiced exceedingly, immediately recognized him, and, giving thanks to God, embraced him. After the Gospel reading, he took his leave and returned that same night to the church at Seville, where he found the clergy celebrating the Matins praises.”

4. “For the benefit of the faithful he composed many books and eradicated many heresies; he condemned Arius. While the wicked were raging in the madness of that Arius, Alexandrian presbyter—after Athanasius had been expelled, Eusebius banished, and Hilary proscribed—King Leovigild, persecuting the churches of the Spains, exiled Masona, bishop of Mérida, and Leander, archbishop of Seville.

“But Isidore, distinguished in knowledge, noble in birth, handsome in body, serious in character, and gracious in eloquence, was neither terrified by threats nor softened by flattery amid the repeated clamors of the Arians. Rather, inflamed with the fervor of charity, he hurled forth the fiery thunderbolts of divine eloquence, by which he darkened the sight of those who raged against him.

“[He also approached Recared, son of King Leovigild, and recalled him from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith.]

“When Leovigild died miserably at Toledo and the Catholic Recared was installed in the kingdom, Leander returned from Carthage. Peace was restored to the Church, the Arian heresy was eradicated, and the Suebi, who held Galicia, received baptism.”

5. “When Leander saw Isidore’s steadfastness, moved by some unknown foreboding lest, after being dismissed by him, Isidore should seek foreign regions for the sake of preaching or for some other reason, or lest he should stain the virginity that he had guarded from infancy by a slight lapse, he confined him in a cell, though the king and many others bore this with difficulty.

“King Recared and many others, however, attended the cell and drew Isidore’s wisdom from the fount of the gracious Savior.”

“When Leander recognized that his end was approaching, he begged that his brother Isidore be brought out of the cell and presented to him. When this was reported to Isidore, who already preferred his little cell to all temporal [possessions], he said: ‘Know that I shall not leave this cell at all so long as my brother survives, for he himself has bound me by the obligation of this resolve.’”

6. “When blessed Leander had been translated among the angels, King Recared, the nobles, bishops, and people unanimously chose Isidore as bishop and, although he was unwilling, brought him out of the cell.

“[When this was announced to blessed Pope Gregory, he most willingly confirmed the election, bestowed the pallium, and granted him authority to exercise the honor of the primacy in the Spains.]

“He was therefore adorned with the episcopal insignia. He was always prudent, always chaste, always steadfast, always just, always modest; useful everywhere, devoted everywhere, always keeping the Passion of Christ before his eyes; desiring to be loved rather than feared; preferring to benefit rather than to rule; devoted to fasts, prayers, and meditation on the Holy Scriptures; taking only a little of the meanest foods, not out of greed but from necessity; sparing toward himself and generous toward others; maintaining the same humility that he had had before.

“It was as though characteristic of him to rejoice with those who rejoiced and to weep with those who wept. He sympathized with the wretched and gave them alms most generously. In prosperity and adversity alike, his countenance always appeared more joyful to everyone.

“Raised to so great a height of dignity, he acknowledged by his deeds no less than by his words that he had been called to the episcopal dignity not to a seat but to care, not to honor but to a burden, not to command but to serve, not to empty the purses of his subjects but to eradicate crimes, not to rest but to labor.”

7. “He was so concerned for the scholars that he was regarded as the father of each one. To remove from them the opportunity for wandering, he built outside the city of Seville a monastery of marvelous beauty, from which he granted no scholar permission to depart before four years had passed.

“Some of the wealthier students who refused to remain in the monastery he bound with iron fetters, lest their wandering minds should be recalled from study. From their community emerged Ildefonsus and Braulius, bishop of Zaragoza.

“And because he could not always teach them in person, wherever he knew suitable teachers, he brought them by entreaty and payment, so that they might devote themselves effectively to teaching the scholars. For the source and occasion of heresy, and the cause of the collapse of morals among clerics and religious, is the sluggish contempt of knowledge of the Scriptures.

“He also watched over religious men with the greatest care, lest any of them be overwhelmed by poverty or perish from hunger for the word of God.

“Although, while caring for his own salvation and that of others, he avoided the presence of women, whenever he saw religious women persevering in the praises of God he nevertheless venerated them with extraordinary affection and provided for them with constant gifts. Throughout the region of Spain he also built very many beautiful monasteries.”

8. “Not content to benefit one province alone, since he believed that he had been born for the benefit of all the faithful, he went through cities and regions preaching the word of God.

“[From there he went to Rome, the supreme pontiff humbly requesting it. After settling his affairs there, he returned to Spain with honor. When the Gauls and Spaniards heard of his arrival, and were suffering from the dryness of the air, so that through lack of rain the crops, trees, and herbs were withering, and people were enduring severe bodily distress from the same disorder of the weather, they came out from each city with crosses and lamps to meet him, so that he might pray to the Lord for them.

“The people of Narbonne cried out to him, saying: ‘O pious teacher of the Spains, Isidore! By your prayers rescue us from the dangers that threaten.’

“But he raised his hands to heaven and prayed to the Lord that, for the glory of his name, he might deign to grant his people remission of sins, health of body, temperate weather, abundance of rain, and plentiful crops.

“O marvelous power of prayer! Although the weather had been excessively clear and everything was parched by the heat of the sun, a great abundance of rain followed, together with temperate weather, bodily health, and an abundance of crops. From that point onward, cures of illnesses, and likewise rain, accompanied him.]

9. “When he was approaching a place not far from Seville, it was announced to him that a certain Muhammad had infected his hearers with the viper’s tongue of unheard-of opinions, and that a dragon, exceeding the size of a great beam, had reduced the suburbs to a desert with its flame-spouting mouth [*pta*, sic].

“When he heard this, he sent messengers to bring Muhammad, bound in chains, before him at his arrival. But the enemy of the human race appeared and said to Muhammad: ‘Our adversary Isidore is here. Therefore depart quickly from Spain, for neither you nor the angels of God can endure his presence.’

“Muhammad said to him: ‘What novelty is this—that angels cannot endure the presence of a mortal man?’

“The devil replied: ‘Do not call it a novelty, but a very ancient occurrence. For the first man, to whose guardianship angels had been appointed, was expelled from paradise through the devil’s deception, and the angels of God were unable to help him in any way.’

“Muhammad said to him: ‘If you knew that I would be utterly unable to prevail because of Isidore’s intervention, why did you say that I would win all Spain for myself?’

“The devil replied: ‘By divine revelation I learned that he had remained in Rome; but the *proposita* (“things ordained”) of the divine will, *alt* [lacuna] *in* [lacuna], seemed [uncertain] because of human wickedness and because of repentance: because of wickedness, as in the case of the sons of Israel, the sons of the Promised Land—for Scripture says that the iniquities of the Amorites have not yet been completed; because of repentance, as in the case of the people of Nineveh, whom God pitied because of their repentance.

“‘Now therefore hurry away from here and go to Africa, where you will become the leader of a great nation; and teach my commandments there, for the iniquities of the Spaniards have not yet been completed.’

“Thus Muhammad summoned his followers and recounted everything to them in order, then hastened his flight. When he came to Africa, he led astray an innumerable nation of Ishmaelites.

“When Isidore’s messengers came to Córdoba and did not find Muhammad, they pursued him as far as the sea. After capturing some of his men, they returned to the holy teacher.”

10. “In the year 656 of the era Muhammad prophesied during the time of Sisebut of the Goths and of Heraclius, Roman emperor. He held his sect for ten years and died in the year 666 of the era, in the seventeenth year of Heraclius, while Isidore was teaching in Spain.”

11. “When Isidore was approaching the place called Saint Eulalia, a most monstrous beast of dreadful appearance appeared. From its mouth a sound was heard amid the din of flames. The saint urged his men to approach without fear.

“When they drew near, the dragon stood with its head lowered. The saint said to it: ‘In the name of Jesus Christ I command you to go to a place where you will harm no creature.’

“At this, the serpent withdrew with hissing and tumult and disappeared from sight.”

12. “When Isidore approached Seville, a multitude of clerics, scholars, monks, and laypeople met him with great joy. In the crush of the crowds rushing together to touch the fringes of the holy Father, a pregnant woman was suffocated and died.

“When the saint saw this, he prayed to the Lord in tears, and the woman arose, saying: ‘Blessed are you, Father, because through you both my son and I have been delivered from the hand of the enemy.’

“When the people asked her how this had happened, she replied: ‘As my soul and the soul of my son, who is in my womb, were departing, a crowd of demons was preparing to drag them with fiery bonds to punishment. But while the glorious Father was praying for us, a voice was heard saying: “Let the souls of these people return to their bodies, because God’s friend Isidore is praying for them.”’”

13. “Others came to him: some to hear another Solomon’s wisdom; some to see him perform miracles; others to test him. One of these was Gregory, a heretical bishop, who disputed with him before the judges at a synod held at Seville. Astonished at his learning, he did not await the judges’ sentence but proclaimed himself defeated, while the bishops and everyone else rejoiced together.

“[A blind man stood before him, asking Isidore to grant that he might receive sight through him. Gregory, observing that Isidore was pretending not to notice, asked him to hand over the glove that he was holding. Having obtained it, Gregory arose, touched the blind man’s eyes with it, and said: ‘May the Lord Jesus Christ, who through blessed Isidore has illuminated the eyes of my heart, illuminate the eyes of your body through his merits.’ After he had said this, blood burst from the blind man’s eyes, and he recovered his sight.]”

14. “He foretold the day of his death to his disciples. Concerned for the flock entrusted to him, he summoned all the bishops, abbots, and princes of Spain to a synod at Toledo, where he proclaimed his end, established peace, and condemned heresies.

“Returning to Seville, he gave generous alms. Weakened by a severe fever, he ordered himself to be carried to the church. After praying for forgiveness of sins, he received the Viaticum and ordered the remaining money to be distributed to the poor. He kissed everyone and had himself carried back to his cell.

“While everyone was silent and awaiting his death, on the fourth day after his confession, he stood in the church. After addressing the people, he stretched out his hands to heaven, blessed everyone, entrusted the flock to God, and surrendered his holy spirit to God.

“From his body there flowed such a fragrance, surpassing the scent of every kind of spice, that all who were present seemed to enjoy heavenly blessedness. The sick came suffering from various illnesses, and they were restored to their former health not only by touching his body but merely by its odor.

“Many saw his soul carried aloft by rejoicing angels, with Christ coming to meet him accompanied by an innumerable throng of saints. One of his close companions, saddened and carried away in ecstasy, saw him holding primacy among the innocent with the crown of virginity and confession, and saying to him: ‘Take comfort, for I am ready to bring help to those who implore my aid’ [perhaps ‘those who beseech it’].

“He died in the year 74 of the era [the number 600 is missing], in the fortieth year of his episcopate, on the Nones of April, during the reign of Cincilianus, king of Spain, and of Heraclius, emperor of the Romans—the Heraclius who restored and exalted at Jerusalem the Lord’s cross, brought back from Chosroes.

“He was buried at Seville between his brother Leander and his sister, the virgin Florentina. He made no will, because before he died he distributed among the poor everything he possessed.

“[He himself made two lamps by natural art that burned perpetually. One was placed at his head and the other at his feet, so that they might continually illuminate his most holy body.]”

15. “In the eightieth year after Isidore’s death, during the time of Roderic, Spain was captured by the Saracens as far as the cave called Saint Mary’s, where Pelagius, descended from royal stock, and others after him bravely defeated the Saracens.

“In the year of the Lord 1062, while King Ferdinand, son of King Sancho, was reigning with his wife Sancha, the body of blessed Isidore was translated to the city of León on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.”

16. This *Life*, written by Roderic of Cerrato, is a certain abridgment of another *Life* published by the Bollandists, whose author was a Canon of León and whom some believe to have been Lucas of Tuy. It contains many things that are either plainly false or at least doubtful and apocryphal, especially those that Flórez enclosed in brackets; he appended brief notes.

In number 2, the manuscript had *spal*, for which Flórez printed *spiritualiter* (“spiritually”) and conjectured *specialiter* (“specially”), or something of that kind. I conjectured: *diligebat puerum. Spali* (for *Hispali*), *extra patriam*, etc. (“he loved the boy. At Seville, outside his homeland,” etc.).

In number 5, in the Bollandists’ text I do not know whether the reading was *quo*; in Flórez’s manuscript it seems to have been *nescitur quo* (“it is not known where”). In the same passage, the Bollandists read *temporalibus divitiis* (“temporal riches”); Flórez’s manuscript omits *divitiis*, which was perhaps omitted from the abridged *Life* by Roderic himself.

In number 14, instead of *Nonis Aprilis* (“on the Nones of April”), Flórez orders that *Pridie Nonas Aprilis* (“the day before the Nones of April”) be read, since the common and almost certain opinion is that Isidore died on 4 April.

In number 15, the statement “in the eightieth year” must be corrected; in the acts of the translation, “the seventy-fifth” is read.

17. It may also be questioned whether there are other errors of the copyists, such as in number 13, *synodo Hispali celebrato* (“at a synod celebrated at Seville”) instead of *celebrata* (“celebrated”), and in number 14, *crucem Domini a Cosdroe allatam* (“the Lord’s cross brought by Chosroes”) instead of *ablatam* (“taken away by Chosroes”).

Roderic of Cerrato, of the Order of Preachers, flourished in the thirteenth century. He collected the lives of the saints from ancient breviaries of the churches and other records. These works have not yet been published, except for a few that were printed in *Hispania Sacra*. Neither Nicolás Antonio in *Bibliotheca Veteris Hispaniae* nor Bayer in his notes mentions him.

Flórez, in volume III of *Hispania Sacra*, Appendix, page 396, no. 4, gathered from Cerrato’s own work who this man was; he affirms that Roderic wrote near the middle of the thirteenth century.

18. In the old edition of Saint Isidore’s books *Against the Jews*, which is assigned to the year 1483, as I shall explain in chapter 66, there are certain excerpts from this *Life*, as it seems, or from the readings of some office of Saint Isidore.

Since those excerpts read *nescitur quo ductus spiritu* (“it is not known by what spirit he was led”), the reading *nescitur* in number 5 of the *Life* could be retained, instead of *nescio* (“I do not know”), which Flórez printed.

## CHAPTER XV

### Readings for the Feast of Saint Isidore from Ancient Breviaries: Hymns; His Commemoration in Other Liturgical Books
1. “Isidore, a Spaniard by nationality, from New Carthage, where his father Severianus held authority, was piously and liberally educated in literary studies by holy men: his brothers Leander, archbishop of Seville, and Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi. He attained immense learning in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, together with great renown. While still a young man, he openly and steadfastly opposed the Arian heresy, which had long since invaded the Gothic people, who dominated the greater part of Spain, [Col. 0082A] so that he very nearly was killed by the Arians. But Leander restrained him, foreseeing that Isidore would be his successor, and advised him to preserve himself for a more favorable time; thus he moderated his indignation. Accordingly, after Leander’s death, Isidore was appointed to the archbishopric of Seville with the great assent of King Reccared and the people. Pope Gregory confirmed this election and sent him the pallium in Spain.

“As for how steadfast and humble, patient and kind, compassionate toward the wretched and the poor, and distinguished in every virtue he was once made pontiff, no tongue could adequately recount. He built monasteries and established communities; devoting himself there to sacred studies and divine readings, he instructed many disciples [Col. 0082B] who flocked to him. Among them was Blessed Ildephonsus, later archbishop of the Church of Toledo. He wrote the book of the *Etymologies* and commented on many books of the sacred Canon; indeed, he wrote so many and such great volumes that human life scarcely seems sufficient for labors of such magnitude. But those who devote themselves to God find nothing difficult, attempt nothing in vain, and attain everything according to their desire.

“Finally, Isidore’s reputation for learning and holiness became so great that, when a general council had been convened, he was voluntarily summoned by the supreme pontiff. There it is remarkable how much weight and authority Isidore’s opinion possessed in each matter with the pontiff and all the prelates. Returning to Spain, after publicly foretelling his own death and the devastation of Spain by the Saracens, he departed [Col. 0082C] this life on the day before the Nones of April, in the year of the Lord 635, while Sisenand was reigning in Spain, and was buried at Seville. Later he was transferred to the city of León by Ferdinand I, king of Castile and León alike, who obtained this from Eneto the Saracen, then ruling at Seville, through great entreaties and rewards. A church was built at León in his honor; there, buried and renowned for miracles, he is venerated with great devotion by the people.”

*Notes of Constantine Cajetan, abbot.*

2. We obtained this account of the life of Saint Isidore from a little book separately printed at Antwerp in 1572. As its preliminary title indicates, it contains *The Feasts of the Saints and Their Proper Offices, Received by Apostolic Authority, Which Are Celebrated Especially in Spain in the Order of Saint James*. These same Offices of the Spanish saints were also confirmed by Pius V, Gregory XIII, and Sixtus V, by that same apostolic authority for the benefit of the whole Spanish Church, and permission was granted for their use, as I learned from the edition printed at Rome in 1609.

Finally, before the Council of Trent, on the feast of Isidore itself, the Roman Church recited this same account of his life, likewise divided into lessons, as can be seen in the Breviary prepared by Cardinal Francisco de Quiñones at the command of Pope Clement VII, and revised and published by Paul III. For this reason, in this little work we too have more than once made use of the sacred authority of these Offices.

3. Cajetan implies that these same lessons for the feast of Saint Isidore occur in the Quiñonian Breviary; this is partly true. The Quiñonian Breviary agrees with these lessons up to the words “sent him the pallium in Spain.” It then omits the passage beginning “As for how he was once made pontiff” and ending “attain everything according to their desire.” It assigns Saint Isidore’s death to the year 622 after the birth of Christ. It adds: “He was transferred to the city of León by Ferdinand, king of León.” The lessons quoted by Cajetan call him “king of Castile and León alike”; this is indeed correct, and the same wording appears in the lessons among the proper Offices of the saints celebrated in Spain, printed at Antwerp in 1716:

“In the year of the Lord 635, while Sisenand was reigning in Spain. His body, first buried at Seville, was afterward transferred to the city of León by Ferdinand I, king of Castile and León alike,” and so forth.

The remainder agrees in these new lessons and in the older ones printed by Cajetan, except that the new lessons read *sufficientura esse*—“would be sufficient”—where Cajetan has *suffecta esse*—“was sufficient.” The lessons as published by Cardinal Quiñones in his Breviary later appeared in a certain Roman Breviary called “of the Chamber,” printed at Venice in folio in 1550. It was then easy, before Pius V’s constitution on the reform of the Roman Breviary, for more extensive Breviaries of this kind to be issued at the discretion of editors or printers.

4. Cajetan also infers from the Quiñonian Breviary that the Roman Church recited this Life of Isidore divided into lessons, but his argument is less than adequate. For the Roman Church never adopted that new Breviary; it was merely prepared by apostolic authority [Col. 0083C] so that private persons who wished to do so might use it after first requesting and obtaining permission. I discussed this matter more fully in the second Appendix to the *Hispanic Hymnody*, which is devoted entirely to explaining the fate of the Quiñonian Breviary.

I am now using the Lyon edition of 1553, which I praised when it was then in the Imperial Library and later acquired for myself at the auction of that library. I have noted in my papers several other and different editions of the same Breviary; these may be added to those described in that appendix if the *Hispanic Hymnody* is ever again entrusted to the press in an expanded and corrected form.

Meanwhile, I shall describe another edition, which I most recently purchased from the duplicate books of the Angelica Library. This edition was formerly in the Passionei Library, as its bookplate shows. [Col. 0083D] Its title is:

*The Roman Breviary, Drawn Especially from Sacred Scripture and Approved Histories of the Saints, Recently Compiled and Again More Carefully Revised by the Same Author, and This Year Cleansed of Errors with Such Diligence That It Does Not Fear the Judgment of Momus. With a Privilege for Ten Years. Lyon, at the house of the heirs of Jacopo Giunta, 1556.*

It is a folio edition, and I had not previously seen the Quiñonian Breviary published in this format. Heretics boast that copies of this Breviary are exceedingly rare because Catholics sought to abolish it. But in addition to the two copies I have mentioned, I formerly acquired three others, which distinguished men accepted as gifts from me.

5. Among the very ancient Breviaries of Spain in which a commemoration of Isidore occurs, Tamayo, in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, lists the Sevillian, Toledan, Piacenzan, Segovian, Salamancan, Zamoran, Sigüenzan, Ávilan, Compostelan, Cordoban, Illiberitan, Burgos, Palencian, Pamplonan, Zaragozan, Asturican manuscript, Tarazonan, Dominican, and Benedictine Breviaries. He testifies—if he is worthy of belief—that all of them are in his possession.

When Urban II restored and confirmed the primacy of the Spains to the see of Toledo in 1088, he simultaneously sent the pallium to D. Bernard, archbishop of Toledo, for use on the principal feasts, among which he names the Nativity of Saints Isidore and Leander.

6. Since the Office of Saint Isidore to be recited throughout the whole Church was introduced into the Roman Breviary in this century, it is useful to set down the new lessons here, so that they may be compared with the old:

### Lessons for the Feast of Saint Isidore from the Revised Roman Breviary: 4 April

7. **Lesson IV.**—“Isidore, a Spaniard by nationality, an outstanding teacher, was born at New Carthage to Severianus, governor of the province. He was piously and liberally educated by his holy brothers, Leander of Seville and Fulgentius of Carthage, and, instructed in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew letters and in divine and human laws, he became pre-eminent in every kind of knowledge and Christian virtue.

“While still a young man, he openly opposed with such steadfastness the Arian heresy, which had long since invaded the Gothic people who dominated the greater part of Spain, that he very nearly was killed by the heretics. After Leander’s death, he was appointed to the see of Seville, although unwilling, chiefly because King Reccared pressed him, and also with the great consent of the clergy and people. Saint Gregory the Great is said not only to have confirmed his election by apostolic authority, but also to have honored the newly elected bishop by sending him the customary pallium and even to have appointed him his own vicar and that of the Apostolic See throughout Spain.

**Lesson V.**—“No tongue could adequately recount how steadfast, humble, patient, and merciful he was in the episcopate; how diligently he labored to restore Christian and ecclesiastical discipline and tirelessly to establish it by word and writing; and how he was finally adorned with every virtue. He was also an outstanding promoter and enlarger of the monastic institution throughout Spain. He built several monasteries and likewise established communities, where, devoting himself to sacred studies and readings, he instructed many disciples who flocked to him. Among these, Saints Ildephonsus of Toledo and Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, stood out.

“After a council had been convened at Seville, he defeated and crushed by sharp and eloquent argument the heresy of the Acephali, which was already threatening Spain. He acquired such a reputation for holiness and learning among all people that, scarcely sixteen years after his death, with the entire Toledan synod of more than fifty-two bishops applauding and Saint Ildephonsus himself giving his support, he deserved to be called an outstanding teacher, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, the most learned man at the end of the ages, and one to be named with reverence. Saint Braulio not only compared him with Gregory the Great but also judged that he had been given from heaven to instruct Spain in place of the apostle James.

**Lesson VI.**—“Isidore wrote the books of the *Etymologies* and *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as well as many other works so useful to Christian and ecclesiastical discipline that Pope Leo IV did not hesitate to write to the bishops of Britain that, just as the sayings of Jerome and Augustine, so also those of Isidore should be retained whenever an unusual matter arose that could not be defined by the canons. Many opinions from his writings are also seen to have been incorporated into the canonical laws of the Church.

“He presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo, the most celebrated of all the councils of Spain. Finally, after he had eliminated the Arian heresy from Spain and had publicly foretold his death and the devastation of the kingdom by Saracen arms, having governed his church for about forty years, he migrated to heaven at Seville in the year 636.

“His body was first buried between his brother Leander and his sister Florentina, as he himself had ordered. Ferdinand I, king of Castile and León, having redeemed it at great cost from Eneto the Saracen, who ruled at Seville, transferred it to León. A church was built in his honor, where he is venerated, renowned for miracles, with great devotion by the people.”

8. The Office of Saint Isidore, bishop, confessor, and doctor, with these lessons, was granted for the universal Church by Innocent XIII on 25 April 1722. On this matter one may consult Benedict XIV, *On Beatification*, book IV, part II, chapter 11, no. 15, who adds the following reason:

“For this saint was already venerated as a doctor in the kingdoms of Spain and in the churches of the islands and mainland of the Indies subject to the Catholic king, according to the apostolic letters of Gregory XIII, where the following is stated concerning the Office of Saint Isidore: ‘Likewise, the feast of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, for whom the Office of a doctor is to be celebrated and the Creed recited during the celebration of Mass,’ and so forth.”

9. These lessons contain certain statements that are not established by older sources closer to the age of Saint Isidore: namely, that Severianus, Saint Isidore’s father, was governor of the province of Carthage; that Fulgentius held the bishopric of Carthage; that Braulio advanced under Isidore’s instruction; [Col. 0085D] that Braulio himself originated the comparison between Gregory the Great, who succeeded Peter, and Isidore, who took the place of the apostle James in instructing Spain, as I explained in chapter 4; that Isidore publicly foretold the devastation of Spain by Saracen arms; that he ordered his body to be buried between his brother Leander and his sister Florentina—to omit other matters concerning his confirmation, the pallium, and the office of apostolic vicar.

Flórez discusses all these matters in volume IX of the *Hispania Sacra*, page 193. Benedict XIV, who at that time held the office of Promoter of the Faith, when this cause was being debated at Rome, commends the responses of the petitioners and of Cardinal Belluga against his own objections in book IV of *On Beatification*, part II, chapter 11, no. 15.

Finally, the petitioners did not fail in their duty: gathering testimonies from every side, they fully demonstrated the excellence of Saint Isidore’s learning. They also published these testimonies in print with the support of the most eminent Cardinal Belluga, the relator of the cause, who learnedly, as was his custom, refuted the objections I had made as Promoter of the Faith and added much in praise of Saint Isidore’s outstanding learning.

10. If the lessons of Saint Isidore were to be tested against the most ancient sources, it would be preferable to use those found in the proper Offices of the saints of the Church of Toledo, printed at Madrid by the Royal Press in 1618, namely:

In the second nocturn, from Braulio of Zaragoza and Ildephonsus, archbishop of Toledo, from Redemptus, Isidore’s disciple, and from Isidore himself and the Second Council of Seville, chapter 12.

11. **Lesson IV.**—“Isidore, a Spaniard by nationality, was born to Severianus, of the province of Carthage, and Turtura, his mother. He was piously and liberally educated by holy men, his brothers Leander, archbishop of Seville, and Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi. Learned in Latin, Greek, and Hebrew, he attained an outstanding reputation for learning in every branch of knowledge.

“While still a young man, he openly attacked with such freedom and steadfastness the Arian heresy, which the arms of the Goths had brought into Spain and which was spreading farther each day, that he very nearly was killed by the Arians. After they had tried his faith in vain by every art of persuasion, Leander died, and Isidore—by the will of King Reccared and amid the extraordinary joy of the people of Seville—was elected as his successor in the episcopate, although he resisted for a long time and with great determination.

**Lesson V.**—“Once made bishop, understanding that he had been called to a burden, not to an honor, he wonderfully enlightened all Spain by the excellence of every virtue and the distinction of his singular learning. He trained many disciples, among whom was Ildephonsus, later archbishop of the Church of Toledo. He possessed admirable eloquence. He moderated the stricter rule of the monks and made it gentler for the weakness of the sick.

“He presided over the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo, in which Isidore’s judgment always carried great weight in establishing the doctrines of the faith. At the very Council of Seville he gravely refuted and brought to a better mind a certain Gregory, a Syrian bishop infected with the heresy of the Acephalites.

“He venerated the Apostolic See with exceptional reverence. Writing to Eugenius, archbishop of Toledo, about its power and the obedience due to it, he said:

“‘Although the dignity of this power has been transferred to all Catholic bishops, it nevertheless remains eternally, by a certain singular privilege, more especially with the Roman bishop, as with the head exalted above the other members. Therefore whoever does not reverently render him the obedience that is due is severed from the head and makes himself liable to the schism of the Acephalites [sic].’”

**Lesson VI.**—“By many and distinguished monuments of his own genius in every branch of divine and human letters, he greatly increased and adorned Christian discipline. He governed his church with the utmost holiness for nearly forty years.

“Foreseeing his approaching death long beforehand, for six months he devoted himself more fervently to prayer, penance, and works of mercy. When death was near, he was carried to the basilica of Saint Vincent. There, clothed in sackcloth and sprinkled with ashes, he received the body and blood of the Lord from the hands of the bishops Eparchius and John, whom he had summoned to him for this purpose, prostrate on the ground.

“Publicly seeking pardon from the people and commending mutual charity to all, he distributed all his goods among the poor. Poor in spirit and rich in Christ, full of days and good works, on the fourth day afterward he departed to the Lord, on the day before the Nones of April, and was buried at Seville.

“When that city had been occupied by the barbarians, Ferdinand I, king of Castile and León, obtained Isidore’s body from Benabetus, its Saracen king, through great gifts, and transferred it to León. He honorably placed it in a church dedicated to God under Isidore’s name. Isidore was renowned for miracles both alive and dead, and he conferred many benefits upon all Spain. Often, when Christian kings implored his help against the barbarians, he was present to assist them.”

12. I do not see many hymns in praise of Saint Isidore celebrated in the ancient Breviaries. In the *Proper Offices of the Saints of the Church of Seville*, printed in 1659, the following hymns occur for Saint Isidore’s feast day.

## Chapter XV. Hymns of the Sevillian Office for the Feast of Saint Isidore

### Hymn

#### At Vespers

Father and teacher of the Spanish people,  
worthy offspring of illustrious Severus,  
worthy brother of Leander, and like him  
holy in character,

while your loving sister tended your cradle,  
a swarm of bees, coming from the shining air,  
saw the infant’s clear lips  
flowing with honey.

This was a sweet sign of eloquent charm,  
and of heavenly learning,  
by which you feed the godly  
and prick sinners with sharp goads.

You pierce the infected race of the Arian  
plague, which threatens avenging fires;  
nor does the fury of kings, while you are young,  
resist your courageous efforts.

As bishop, you restore the triumph of the faith;  
you drive its treacherous enemies,  
terrified, from the shores of Spain  
by the thunderbolt of your tongue.

O father of the clergy and shepherd of the people,  
guardian of orphans, relief of widows,  
protector of virgins, for monks  
a strict rule of life,

now seated in the lofty heaven,  
O star and summit of our people,  
you shine with light equal to that  
of the ancient teachers of the faith.

Remember your beloved flock,  
and, we pray, be its patron  
before the eternal Trinity,  
to whom all ages throughout the world  
should resound with worthy praises.

#### At Matins

Sun from the setting toward rosy risings,  
you who, traversing the earth  
with better light, scatter the mists  
and dark shadows of the Spanish night,

at whose rising dark error,  
deceit, fickle fury, profane luxury,  
and greed thirsting for the breath  
of empty things flee away.

Right conduct returns, and piety revives;  
faith, crowned with chaste worship,  
and peace with holy integrity,  
and virtue conscious of justice, return.

O Isidore, bright radiance of Seville,  
restore the virtues after driving away vices;  
cause decaying ages to return  
to the morals of our forefathers.

Your people ask this at your sacred altars,  
while they pour forth pious vows  
to the true God,  
as the children of the Baetis  
celebrate your feast with rejoicing.

May everlasting praise, honor, and virtue  
be yours, O lofty Majesty,  
creator of humankind,  
whom the faithful rightly celebrate  
as the triune and one God.

#### At Lauds

You, Father, who leave your beloved peoples,  
sent to the lofty city of León,  
which has erected royal temples  
for you as its faithful patron?

Do you fear the enemy rebelling against the faith?  
The barbarian has fled; may you be permitted to return,  
or at least may the light sent from there  
help you to cherish your own.

The happy city, enriched by the precious relics  
of your sacred body, reviews your wondrous deeds  
depicted on painted panels, and the gifts  
of kings on its domes.

The triumphs you won by your merit  
they gratefully recounted in more than one war,  
for ancient report says  
that you are present in our armies.

Come here to us in our weariness, loving Father,  
and commend us to the powerful Trinity,  
whose everlasting glory resounds  
among all nations.

14. I too formerly presented these same hymns, not without due praise for their elegance, in the *Hispanic Hymnody* under 4 April. To adapt them to ecclesiastical chant, I altered four verses as follows:

1. “A swarm of light, coming from the air,” instead of “A shining swarm, coming from the ether.”
2. “Be before the eternal Trinity, we pray,” instead of “Be toward the eternal Trinity, we pray.”
3. “Peace, modesty, moral integrity, and justice,” instead of “Peace with holy integrity, and justice.”
4. “Report was telling,” instead of “Ancient report is.”

I think these hymns are recent. In the fifth stanza—“As bishop, you restore …”—their author seems to assent to the fables concerning Muhammad’s arrival in Spain and flight from it, unless perhaps he means the heresy of the Acephalites, which was overthrown by Isidore.

15. The following hymns, which Tamayo transcribes in the *Hispanic Martyrology* from ancient Breviaries of Spain, seem older:

#### At Vespers

Let the Church rejoice together,  
and celebrate with solemn honor  
the feast of Isidore,  
the renowned confessor,

who, like a ray of sunlight,  
after heresies had been utterly removed,  
and devoted to martyrdom,  
shone with varied doctrine.

He watched diligently over the peoples  
of the Spains through the rules  
of divine law  
and the customs of the Romans.

In the interests of the clergy  
and the support of the poor,  
he, the most illustrious giver of laws,  
clung more closely to his task.

#### At Lauds

Great teacher Isidore,  
cause us to be restored from this dreadful prison  
to the heavenly throne,  
with the Son of God appeased.

Through you, illustrious confessor,  
the rejoicing choir of the Church  
and the throng of the faithful  
praise Christ the Lord together.

Jesus Christ, King of glory,  
receive the vows of your servants;  
through the prayers of this teacher,  
look favorably upon us.

Grant forgiveness of sins;  
grant the glory of the saints,  
so that through the merits  
of so great a Father  
we may enjoy the joys of heaven.

16. Tamayo calls the Breviaries from which he derives these hymns “very ancient.” But since there were no hymns in praise of Isidore in the Gothic Office, and the Breviaries praised by Tamayo conform to the rite of the Roman Church, their antiquity must not be extended over too long a period. I do not consider these hymns older than the thirteenth century, although, since they are concerned only with commemorating Isidore’s praises, they contain nothing contrary to the ancient history.

The rules of verse are entirely neglected. The second stanza of the Vespers hymn seems to have been taken from Braulio’s fuller preliminary account [Col. 0089C] or from the prologue to the Life of Isidore by a certain Leonese canon, in the Bollandists.

17. Henschenius discusses the Martyrologies that celebrate the memory of Saint Isidore in his preliminary commentary on the Life of Saint Isidore. Saint Isidore is also mentioned in the *Martyrology of the Canons Regular*, at the end of the new edition of the Roman Martyrology issued by order of Benedict XIV, under 4 April:

“At Seville in Spain, Saint Isidore the Confessor, who, enrolled among the Canons Regular and consecrated bishop of that city, distinguished for holiness and learning, enlightened the Spains by his zeal for the Catholic faith and his observance of ecclesiastical discipline.”

A sign is placed before this entry indicating that the feast of Saint Isidore is celebrated on the same day by all Canons Regular.

In the same place, in the *Martyrology for all monks of the Cistercian Order*, under 4 April:

“At Seville in Spain, Saint Isidore, formerly a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict and bishop of that city, distinguished for holiness and learning, who by his zeal for the Catholic faith …”

This controversy concerning Saint Isidore’s monastic order will be discussed in chapter 19, where I shall quote several words from the Breviary of the Lateran Canons Regular.

18. I also found Isidore’s name in the litanies of ancient codices, to say nothing of the litanies of the Mozarabic Office. Thus, Vatican Codex 84, parchment, in folio, dating from approximately the tenth century, contains a Psalter revised by Jerome, with canticles. On folio 274 it presents prayers for the adoration of the cross, or for requesting the intercession of all the saints. An image of Christ affixed to the cross is painted [Col. 0090A] with four nails and with the right side of his chest pierced.

On folio 307 follow the Rogations, or litany of the saints, in which Saint Isidore is named and invoked. I think this is the codex that Blanchinus describes as Codex 82 in volume II of the *Fourfold Gospel*, page 604; a specimen of its script is printed there on plate 6, no. 1, after page 600.

Vatican Ottobonian Codex 576, written in Lombard or Beneventan script around the tenth century, contains a monastic Missal. Its litanies include Saints Gregory, Isidore, Germanus, Benedict, Maurus, Severinus, and others.

In another parchment codex of the fifteenth century from the town of Assergi in the diocese of L’Aquila, brought to Rome to request a proper Office for Saint Francis and apparently written for the use of some monastery, the litanies of the saints include, among others, Saint Francis, Macarius, Basil, Leonard, and Ysidorus, as the parchment writes the name.

I have no doubt that our Isidore is meant, although perhaps others may suspect that the reference is to another Isidore who was a monk.

# Chapter XVI. An Ordered Account of the Life and Deeds of Saint Isidore, Based on Ancient Sources and Writers

First, the question is raised concerning the different Isidores, in comparison with whom our Isidore of Seville is sometimes called the Younger and sometimes the Elder.

1. To begin with the name Isidore: in ancient parchment manuscripts and documents it is found written in various and differing ways, namely *Ysidorus, Hisidorus, Hysidorus, Hisydorus, Isydorus, Esidorus, Isodorus, Ysydorus,* and *Eisidorus*, as well as *Isidorus*, which is preferable to all the others. This discrepancy arises for the most part from differing methods of writing in different periods, to say nothing of the carelessness of antiquarians. For it often became customary to use *y* for *i*, and an aspirate was easily prefixed to a word at the beginning. Sometimes *e* was also used for *i*.

The name Isidore seems to be of Greek origin, from Isis; certainly many distinguished Greeks bore that name. Yet in the century in which Isidore flourished, the form *Esidorus* was in use, as is proved by the testimony of Saint Julian of Toledo in a manuscript work *On Grammar*, which I shall transcribe in chapter 103, no. 46 and following. He says there, in no. 324:

“Give another name composed of several parts. ESIDORUS: *E* is a preposition, *SI* is a conjunction, *DO* is a verb, and *RUS* is a noun.”

2. Fabricius, in volume IX of the *Greek Library*, page 256 and following, book V, chapter 34, no. 3, after discussing Isidore of Pelusium, with his customary painstaking curiosity compiled a catalogue of more than thirty other notable Isidores.

Among the Spaniards, besides Saint Isidore Agricola, he lists Isidore of Astorga, who signed the Council of Braga in 675; Isidore, by origin a Sevillian but bishop of Zaragoza, invented by Pellizerius; two Isidores of Córdoba, likewise invented by Pseudo-Dexter, one assigned to the year 384 and the other to the years 423 and 430; our Isidore of Seville; Isidore Mercator, or Peccator, compiler of the spurious decretals; Isidore of Pax, and Isidore of Setabis, or Setabitanus, who attended the Councils of Toledo in 681 and 688.

3. Of these, only six are genuine Spanish Isidores: Isidore of Seville; Isidore of Astorga; Isidore of Setabis, who attended the Twelfth Council of Toledo in 681; another distinct Isidore, who signed the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688 and again the Sixteenth Council in 693; Isidore of Pax; and Isidore Agricola.

To these may be added Isidore Juvenis, a monk and martyr of Córdoba, praised by Saint Eulogius in 853, book III of the *Memorial of the Saints*, chapter 15.

The others were discovered or fabricated so that the various works of Isidore might be distributed among several persons and so that the distinction found in ancient copies between Isidore the Elder and the Younger might be explained according to each person’s preference.

4. Sigebert does indeed praise, in chapter 51 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, an Isidore of Córdoba to whom he attributes a commentary on the Books of Kings. [Col. 0091B] From this the architects of spurious chronicles took their cue to fabricate two Isidores of Córdoba and invent many things about them.

But Nicolás Antonio, for substantial reasons, suspects that no such Isidore of Córdoba ever existed. Rather, Sigebert, a writer of the twelfth century, was deceived because he read, in a certain sermon published among the works of Saint Augustine, *On the Assumption of the Virgin Mary*, that the words of a certain Isidore were cited. Since Isidore’s work *On Allegories* was dedicated to Orosius, these circumstances may have prompted Sigebert to devise an Isidore older than our Isidore of Seville and contemporary with Augustine and Paul Orosius.

See *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book III, chapter 2, no. 52 and following.

There is no adequate conjecture as to why Sigebert chose to call that Isidore of his, to whom he attributed certain works of the true Isidore of Seville, a Cordoban. Flórez, who in volume X of the *Hispania Sacra* considers the Isidore of Córdoba fabricated by Sigebert, suspects that Sigebert was deceived by the name of Chartres and thus made that older Isidore a bishop of Córdoba. For the sermon *On the Assumption of the Virgin Mary*, which was formerly number 85 *On the Saints* among Augustine’s works, later number 83 in the appendix, and number 208 in the Maurist edition, is attributed by the theologians of Leuven to Fulbert of Chartres.

Yet this would be a very remote occasion for error, since the author of the sermon is not called Isidore; rather, the sermon merely mentions Isidore.

5. Mariana’s judgment on this matter, first published by Flórez in volume VIII of the *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 27, appendix 2, page 275, is as follows. It has been accepted as the opinion of scholars that there were three especially distinguished Isidores in Spain: the **Cordoban**, whom Trithemius says lived under Honorius, around the year 420 of salvation; the **Sevillian**, a contemporary of Gregory the Great; and the **Pacensian**, whose period of life is uncertain.

The Cordoban is called the **Elder**. The designation **Younger** is commonly given to the two later figures in comparison with the older one, and more frequently to the Sevillian. The Cordoban wrote nothing that survives, although Trithemius attributes certain works to him. The Sevillian wrote much, including a very brief chronicle from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of Suinthila, king of the Goths.

6. The judgment of this most learned man is approved and confirmed by Pérez Bayer in his notes to the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book V, no. 109. For in the Escorial codices of the tenth century and the beginning of the eleventh, shelfmark Q, pluteus 3, no. 7, and, in another [uncertain: *digramm.*] codex, pluteus 1, no. 3, as well as in others long before Sigebert, Isidore of Seville is distinguished from another, older author by the title “Younger.” He would not be called Younger unless another, older Isidore the writer had preceded him.

That none of the works written by the older Isidore survives is clear from the fact that the works which Sigebert and Trithemius attribute to Isidore the Elder or the Cordoban are certainly those of our Isidore of Seville. Pérez develops this point at greater length; he had prefaced it by saying that Mariana’s argument exhausted the matter.

7. The opinion of John Aegidius should also be mentioned. Nicolás Antonio writes the following about him in book V of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, no. 109:

“Concerning Isidore of Córdoba, whom Sigebert of Gembloux was the first to praise, while Dexter—the spurious author—fabricated him as the author of a Chronicle, a matter already discussed above in a more suitable place and not repeated here: I am content merely to note and add here that, long ago, concerning the statements about the Cordoban and, as he is called, the Elder Isidore, I learned that John Aegidius Zamorensis, a Franciscan who saw and recorded innumerable things about Spanish affairs and committed them to his still unpublished notes, acknowledged and praised only two Isidores in the sixth treatise of his *Adversaria*: namely, our Sevillian, whom he calls the Elder, and another whom he calls the Younger, who is the Pacensian and who continued the record of events throughout the world down to the Arab invasion of Spain.”

8. To place the distinction between Isidore the Elder and the Younger in a proper light, I shall briefly indicate the ancient copies and works of our Isidore of Seville in which he is called sometimes Elder and sometimes Younger.

John Vasaeus, who thinks that Isidore of Seville is called Younger because of Isidore of Córdoba, who flourished in the time of Orosius, asserts in chapter 4 of the *Annals of Spain* that the following is read at the beginning of Isidore’s *Etymologies*:

“Here begins the letter of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.”

Vasaeus does not explain from which manuscript he extracted this title.

9. Our Isidore is called “the Younger” in Vatican Codex 202, which I shall discuss in chapter 93, where passages from his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* are cited. The codex appears to have been written in Gaul around the tenth century. By contrast, in Vatican Codex 641, written in the ninth or tenth century and discussed in chapter 94, he is called “the Elder” in the title of the *Prefaces*, although the books *On Offices* and *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* are attributed to this same Elder Isidore.

In the Escorial Etymologies codex of the eleventh century, discussed in chapter 55, he is called “the Younger.” The same epithet is assigned to Isidore in thirteenth-century or later codices containing the continued and interpolated chronicle, discussed in chapter 78. Isidore is likewise called “the Younger” in the very ancient Vatican Codex 3321, discussed in chapter 96, which contains the *Differences of Words Arranged Alphabetically*; in the later Vatican Codex 4327, containing the two books *Against the Jews*, discussed in chapter 97; and in Vatican-Regio Codex 294, discussed in chapter 100 and apparently dating from the eleventh century, which contains the books of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0092D]

In Vatican-Regio Codex 310, in the same place, the following is written: “Here begin the *Spiritual Differences* of Isidore, the Younger, Spanish bishop.” And again: “Here begins the *Soliloquies* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, the Younger.” Isidore is also called “the Younger” in Vatican-Regio Codex 846, in the same place, where excerpts from the *Etymologies* are copied; this codex does not appear to be later than the eighth century. He is likewise called “the Younger” in the title of the chronicle in Palatine Codex 239, discussed in chapter 102 and apparently written in Gaul around the tenth century.

At the end of the *Etymologies* in the paper Urbino Codex 479, discussed in chapter 104, stands: “Of Isidore the Younger,” etc. In Ottobonian Codex 336, an *Etymologies* manuscript dating approximately from the fourteenth century and discussed in chapter 105, we find: “Of Isidore the Younger,” etc.

Other codices outside the Vatican Library similarly assign the title “the Younger” to our Isidore: for example, the Lucca codex of the books *Against the Jews*, discussed in chapter 43, no. 48; the Chisianus *Etymologies* codex, discussed in chapter 45, no. 2; and the very ancient Cesena Malatesta *Etymologies* codex, discussed in chapter 45, no. 6. In Codex 2 of the Vatican Archives, discussed in chapter 107, we read: “The *Etymologies* of Isidore the Younger,” etc. In the Roman College Codex, in the same place: “The Chronicle of Isidore the Younger.”

In chapter 55, numbers 18 and 19, there are two Florentine copies of Isidore the Younger’s *Etymologies*. In the same chapter, no. 24, there is the Florentine codex of Santa Croce, containing “the *Etymologies* of Isidore the Ancient” and “Isidore the Younger, *On Computation*.” Labbe lists the *Synonyms of Isidore the Younger*, as I shall say in chapter 70, no. 3. The letter to Leudefredus in the Vigilian Codex, discussed in chapter 73, no. 7, is inscribed in the name of Isidore the Younger. In the Florentine codex of Santa Croce, discussed in chapter 76, no. 9, the book *On the Nature of Things* bears the title “of Isidore the Younger, the Illustrious.”

The *Chronography*, or chronicle, of Isidore the Younger is indicated from the Medicean Codex in chapter 77, no. 7. In the Ovetus Codex of the twelfth century, discussed in the same chapter, no. 13, we find “the *Chorography*, or more correctly the *Chronography*, of Isidore the Younger.” In the Escorial Codex of the fourteenth century, discussed in chapter 78, no. 18, there is “the Chronicle of Isidore the Younger.”

### 10.

I readily agree with Mariana and Bayer that some Isidore older than Isidore of Seville must be recognized, in comparison with whom the Isidore of Seville is called “the Younger.” But since no mention of Isidore of Córdoba appears in the catalogues of Jerome, Gennadius, Isidore, Ildefonsus, or the other ancient writers on ecclesiastical authors, and since Sigebertus is the first to mention him—and even does so while plainly in error, assigning certain works of Isidore of Seville to the Cordoban—I am easily led to believe that Isidore of Seville was called “the Younger” because, before his time, Isidore of Pelusium had flourished in the fourth century. Isidore of Pelusium was renowned throughout the whole Church for his writings, virtues, and deeds, and was revered even by bishops themselves, as Bishop Ephraem of Antioch says in a letter to the scholasticus Zenobius, preserved by Photius in the *Bibliotheca*. Evagrius likewise writes in book 4 of his *Ecclesiastical History*: “During the reign of this same Theodosius, Isidore flourished, whose glory is exceedingly widespread and who is everywhere celebrated both for his deeds and for his eloquence.”

### 11.

Isidore of Pelusium was indeed an Egyptian, Alexandrian by birth, and a monk near Pelusium, a city of Egypt. Nevertheless, his reputation was no less strong among the Latins. Facundus of Hermiane, whom Isidore of Seville lists in his book *On Illustrious Men*, commends him as follows:

> “For Isidore the presbyter, an Egyptian of Pelusium, a most holy man and one of great glory in the Church—whom many know to have written two thousand letters for the edification of the Church—was, on account of the merits of his life and wisdom, both honored and called a father by Cyril himself,” etc.

See Natalis Alexander, *Ecclesiastical History*, fourth century, article 9, chapter 4. In 1737 a dissertation by Christoph August Heumann, *On Isidore of Pelusium and His Letters*, was published at Göttingen. It demonstrates that most of those letters are fictitious and is worthy, as the learned Zaccaria observes in his *Select Library*, of being refuted by a learned man.

Since the name of Isidore of Pelusium was already highly celebrated in the Church when Isidore of Seville was writing, it is not surprising that the inscription “the Younger” began to be attached to the works of the latter, especially where the title “bishop of Seville” was not prefixed. Later, copyists easily combined the two titles and called Isidore “the Younger, bishop of Seville,” although no other Isidore who was bishop of Seville had preceded our Isidore.

### 12.

Who, then, is Isidore the Younger, in comparison with whom Isidore of Seville is called “the Elder”? Mariana, Nicolás Antonio, and Bayer assert that Isidore of Pacensis is meant by Isidore the Younger of Seville. Isidore of Pacensis lived during the advancing eighth century, as Nicolás Antonio proves in book 6, chapter 3, and he continued the chronicle of Isidore of Seville down to the Arab destruction of Spain. This certainly is a writer who is later than Isidore of Seville, and many in fact call him “the Younger.”

[Col. 0094C]

Some, however, maintain that there were other Isidores later than Isidore of Seville, in comparison with whom the latter too might be called “the Elder.” They produce Isidore, bishop of Setabis, to whom Pellizerius attributes the book *On the Meaning of Names*, and they mention Luitprandus, who published a spurious collection of canons under the name of Isidore the Sinner, or Merchant. Nicolás Antonio refutes these fables in book 6 of the *Bibliotheca vetus*, chapter 3.

The book *On the Meaning of Names* is Isidore of Seville’s book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, as Braulio calls it; it is commonly known as the *Allegories*. We maintain that the author of the apocryphal collection of decretals was neither Isidore, bishop of Setabis, nor any other Spaniard.

There were, however, two bishops of Setabis, as I have said: the first attended the Twelfth Council of Toledo in 681; the second signed the acts of the Fifteenth Council of Toledo in 688 and of the Sixteenth in 693. Neither is known to have written anything, much less a false collection of canons fabricated only in the ninth century.

### 13.

Besides Isidore of Pacensis, Pellizerius recognized another distinct Isidore, whom he calls “of Beja,” the author of a certain chronicle beginning: “In six days God formed the creation of all things.” Perhaps Pellizerius thought that Isidore of Pacensis was so called from the city of Badajoz, for some have persuaded themselves of this. Most, however, understand *Pax* or *Pax Julia* to be the town of Beja.

Thus Isidore of Beja and Isidore of Pacensis are the same person, and the chronicle is the same work, which Pellizerius wrongly divided into two, as Nicolás Antonio demonstrates in the passage cited. Pellizerius appears far too liberal in multiplying both works and Isidores: he fabricated two Isidores of Seville, one of whom was supposedly bishop of Zaragoza, two Isidores of Córdoba, and two of Pacensis.

### 14.

Why did neither Pellizerius nor any other Spaniard instead invent something about Isidore of Astorga, who signed the acts of the Council of Braga in 675, when listing the writers? He could have been called “the Younger” in comparison with Isidore of Seville. Indeed, Fabricius places him among the medieval writers in his *Bibliotheca*. But what he contributed to literature, Fabricius adds, I do not know, although Cangius includes him among the writers.

S. Valerius reports that he died an unfortunate death in volume 16 of *Hispania sacra*, no. 36. The *Order of Lamentation* states:

> “While he was coming in this way, sent by the enemy so that he might cast me into destruction through agitation and cause the worst scandal to the other brothers, then—by the just judgment of the almighty Lord—he himself suddenly entered the pit that he had opened for us.”

He calls him the same “most pestilential man.” Others are silent about him.

### 15.

Since the name of Isidore of Pacensis was by no means obscure among the Spaniards, I have no doubt that the Spaniards designated him by the name “Isidore the Younger” in order to distinguish him from Isidore of Seville. Foreigners, however, may have had something else in mind, since they thought little or nothing of Isidore of Pacensis.

The author of the spurious collection of canons and decretals, toward the end of the eighth century, pretended not only to be a Spaniard but also appropriated the most famous name among the Spaniards, calling himself Isidore the Sinner, or Merchant. The collection immediately began to circulate in everyone’s hands. Although people believed our Isidore of Seville to be its author, others observed that councils and other documents later than Isidore of Seville had been inserted into it. They therefore inferred that another Isidore was the compiler; to distinguish him from the Sevillian, they called him “the Younger,” and by the same reasoning called Isidore of Seville “the Elder.”

We must therefore conclude that Isidore of Seville is called at one time “the Younger” and at another “the Elder”: “the Younger” when he is compared with Isidore of Pelusium, or even, if one wishes, with Isidore of Córdoba praised by Sigebertus; but “the Elder” when he is compared with Isidore of Pacensis, and then with the fictitious Isidore the Sinner, or Merchant.

## CHAPTER XVII. The homeland, parents, and birth of Saint Isidore of Seville

### 1.

I do not know why Johannes Eisengreinius dreamed in his *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth* that Isidore was German by nationality; the Centuriators of Magdeburg almost give him credence, century 7, chapter 18, section 8. Nicolás Antonio suspects that Eisengreinius thought Isidore was a Goth and that, for this reason, he wished to confuse his own eyes.

Since the Goths had already settled in Spain long before, even if one wishes to make Isidore a Goth, one cannot on that account call him German by nationality, unless one understands “German” to mean a Goth who had already become an inhabitant and citizen of Spain. Nor is there any reason to suspect that Isidore was Gothic by origin. On the contrary, the names of his parents, brothers, and sister argue against this: they are drawn from Latin and Greek, not from Gothic. This indicates that Isidore’s parents were Spanish by birth but Roman citizens—or, as Nicolás Antonio calls them, Hispano-Romans.

### 2.

There are nevertheless Spaniards who maintain that Severianus, Isidore’s father, was Gothic by origin. Apart from the pseudo-historians already universally discredited, Roderic Sánchez de Arévalo, Lorenzo Padilla, Beuter, and Sandoval nearly share this view; Andreas Resende does not oppose it in his letter to Ambrosio Morales.

In the continuation, or supplement, of Isidore’s chronicle, produced under the name of Ildefonsus by Lucas of Tuy and presented by us above in chapter 12, it is said that Isidore was descended from the royal Gothic blood. We have already noted that this continuation is falsely attributed to Ildefonsus and was written—or interpolated with fictions—long after the times of Isidore and Ildefonsus.

Roderic of Toledo and Lucas of Tuy add another detail: Theodoric the Amal, king of the Ostrogoths, who ruled in Italy and for several years held the Gothic kingdom in Spain on behalf of Amalaric, was the parent of Severianus, Isidore’s father.

### 3.

Others, including Ambrosio Morales, Antonio López, Mariana, Francisco Padilla, Pellizerius, and Nicolás Antonio, refuse to believe this account. Why, they ask, did Theodoric leave Amalaric, his grandson through his daughter Amalasuntha, as successor to the kingdom, rather than Severianus?

As for Ambrosio Morales’s claim that Theodoric never even went to Spain, Bivarius certainly refutes it with adequate arguments in his notes to Maximus, year 109. Isidore’s words in the *History of the Goths*, at the Spanish era 549, are sufficiently clear:

> “Theodoric, after King Gisaleic of the Goths of Spain had been killed, held the kingdom of Spain for fifteen years; he left it to his surviving grandson Amalaric. Returning from there to Italy, he ruled for some time with complete success.”

### 4.

Lucas of Tuy—or rather another interpolator of Isidore’s *History of the Goths*—who asserted that Theodoric was Severianus’s father, also said that Theodoric’s wife was a certain most noble woman from Toledo. Other ancient writers are silent about Severianus’s mother.

The pseudo-historians gave this woman the names Santina, Sanctina, Sanctiva, or Sancia. They also invented the story that she built the Benedictine monastery of Saint Peter at Cardeña. Nicolás Antonio explodes such fictions in book 4, chapter 4 of the *Bibliotheca vetus*. He ridicules the affectation of the pseudo-Haubertus in his chronicle under the year 534: “Leander, the first son of Severianus the duke,” etc.

### 5.

Perhaps, however, although Severianus was not the son of King Theodoric, his children were descended from Theodoric’s royal line—namely, if Severianus’s wife was Theodoric’s daughter. Quintanadueñas asserted this in his *Life of Saint Fulgentius*, Isidore’s brother; the Bollandists cite him in their note on the *Life of Saint Isidore*, chapter 1.

This certainly removes the difficulty that Severianus does not appear to have been Theodoric’s son, since Amalaric, Theodoric’s grandson through Amalasuntha, succeeded Theodoric in the kingdom, not Severianus. Otherwise, since it is not established that the documents from which the royal origin of Isidore and his brothers is inferred are earlier than the twelfth century, this opinion may in some measure be maintained as a tradition. It should not, however, be advertised as certain, whether we suppose Isidore’s mother to have been Theodoric’s daughter, Severianus to have been Theodoric’s son, or Severianus to have been Theodoric’s brother. The Bollandists, in the passage cited, indicate that some question exists on this matter.

### 6.

From the ancient documents we can affirm only this: the father of Leander, Isidore, Fulgentius, and Florentina was Severianus of the province of Carthaginiensis.

Isidore writes in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41:

> “Leander, born to Severianus, a man of the province of Carthaginiensis, was by profession a monk,” etc.

Everyone agrees on the name Severianus. The fact that he is called Severus in the hymns of the proper Sevillian Office, discussed above in chapter 15, is clearly due to metrical considerations.

Why is it necessary to point out that the province of Carthaginiensis was in Spain, not in Africa? Yet, understanding these words in a foreign sense, Johannes Trithemius, *On Illustrious Men of the Benedictine Order*, book 2, chapter 9, and Sixtus of Siena, *Bibliotheca*, book 4, declared Leander to have been an African.

### 7.

The more appropriate question is whether Severianus was the duke of the province of Carthaginiensis, in the same way that, according to the custom of that age and people, Claudius was duke of Lusitania and Paulus duke of the province of Narbonensis. That was the title given to those who administered provinces.

Joannes Baptista Pérez observes in his notes on Isidore that Lucas of Tuy and others falsely add the word “duke” to Isidore’s words. Roderic of Toledo, a contemporary of Lucas of Tuy, and the author of the continuation of Isidore’s chronicle under the name of Ildefonsus, plainly call Severianus duke of the province of Carthaginiensis.

In the ancient Spanish breviaries, either this very fact is transmitted or it is asserted that Severianus then ruled Carthago Nova. The revised Roman Breviary likewise calls Severianus duke of the province in the lessons for Saint Isidore. Nevertheless, in the proper Offices of the Church of Toledo, discussed above in chapter 15, Isidore’s words are retained without adding that Severianus was a duke.

Breulius, trusting the idle inventions of commentators in his dedicatory letter to Isidore’s works, asserts that Severianus, Isidore’s father, was the son of King Theodoric, and that Isidore’s mother, whom he calls Theodora, was descended from the royal Gothic blood.

### 8.

Roderic Sánchez de Arévalo, bishop of Palencia, left it written in part 2 of his *History of Spain*, chapter 9, that Severianus’s wife was called Theodora. Nicolás Antonio did not know from where he had taken this. But the Bollandists had already observed in their note on chapter 1 of the *Life of Saint Isidore* that Lucas of Tuy called Severianus’s wife by this name in his preface to the *Chronicles*. Indeed, Nicolás Antonio himself had noticed the same thing in his letter to the Bollandists, which they mention in their preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint Isidore*.

The pseudo-historians eagerly seized the name and added other details from their own store: they called her Flavia Theodora Cervella, or Cervilia, daughter of Paula, of the most illustrious Gothic lineage. The pseudo-Luitprandus, however, calls her Theodosia Cervela.

Nicolás Antonio refutes these dreams at length, in his customary manner, when discussing Saint Leander. There he also produces two inscriptions from Ambrosio Morales, one concerning a certain most illustrious woman named Paula, the other concerning a most illustrious woman named Cervella.

The pseudo-historians had these inscriptions before their eyes when they invented Flavia Theodora Cervella, daughter of Paula, as the wife of Severianus; others adapted the same inscriptions to their own purposes. It should also be noted that some people do not regard Ambrosio Morales’s reliability in producing ancient inscriptions as sufficiently secure.

### 9.

Rejecting the name Theodora, Nicolás Antonio maintains that Severianus’s wife was called Turtura. He cites both the words of Leander, which will shortly be given, and several Spanish breviaries that Bivarius had seen.

Flórez, volume 9 of *Hispania sacra*, says that Nicolás Antonio, along with others and the Sevillian Breviary, held this view. Above all, we must name the Leonese canon who wrote the *Life of Saint Isidore*: “The mother, however, was called Turtura.”

Saint Leander, in the final chapter of his rule for his sister Florentina, which was quoted above in chapter 2, mentions their common mother and writes, among other things:

> “You are the daughter of Simplicity, born of Turtura your mother; in one and the same person you enjoy the service of several relationships. Look upon Turtura as your mother; attend to Turtura as your teacher,” etc.

“Nothing could be clearer,” says Nicolás Antonio, “so much so that even Bivarius, moved by this authority, judged that the reading ‘Theodora, surnamed Cervella,’ in the pseudo-Maximus should be changed to ‘Turtura, surnamed Cerula.’”

### 10.

In our own time, however, Nicolás Antonio has found a stronger opponent in this matter, namely Flórez, volume 9 of *Hispania sacra*. Since Flórez did not find the name Turtura assigned to Severianus’s wife among writers close to the seventh century, he considers that it cannot be supported by any foundation. Leander’s words, he argues, do not suggest that Turtura was called Florentina’s mother, but rather that she was another woman placed over the monastery in which Florentina lived.

Leander is encouraging Florentina to regard her superior Turtura as a teacher and mother, and to consider her a mother even dearer than the mother from whom she was born.

### 11.

I admit that Leander’s words—“consider as mother the one who is dearer than the mother from whom you were born”—are somewhat obscure. But since the same Leander says, “You were born of Turtura your mother. In one and the same person you enjoy the service of several relationships …,” and later, “May her bosom be sweet to you now that you are grown, the bosom that was most pleasing to you as an infant,” these statements can scarcely be understood unless they concern Florentina’s true mother. She would at the same time have been her teacher on the way to perfection and should therefore have been dearer to Florentina because she had brought her forth for Christ by her affections than because she had brought her into the light of this world.

A greater difficulty arises because Flórez insists that Leander is speaking of a woman named Turtura who was still alive at that time, whereas shortly afterward he says that Florentina’s parents had departed to the Lord.

### 12.

Leander says:

> “Attend to Turtura as your teacher; and regard as a mother the one who daily gives birth to you for Christ by her affections, dearer than the mother from whom you were born.”

Nevertheless, I understand this to refer to Florentina’s mother, who, having already been received into heaven, was daily giving birth to Florentina for Christ through her affections.

Leander continues:

> “Hide yourself in her bosom from every storm and every worldly tempest. May it be pleasant for you to cling to her side; may the embrace of one advanced in years be sweet to you—[some copies read: ‘of one already established’]—the embrace that was most pleasing to you as an infant.”

Since Leander begins this entire exhortation as follows—

> “Do not fly away from the nest that the turtledove found in which to place her young. You are the daughter of Simplicity, born of Turtura your mother,” etc.—

there is still reason to doubt whether Turtur is a proper name in Leander, or whether he calls the mother “turtledove” because she is being compared with a turtledove.

### 13.

As for Isidore’s brothers and sister, we must plainly reject what Breulius reports from the Sevillian Breviary in his dedicatory letter: that Justina, the abbess, was Isidore’s sister and Braulio of Zaragoza his brother. He adds, on the authority of Vasaeus’s chronicle under the year 567, that this Justina was the same person as Florentina, and that Braulio should by no means be counted among Isidore’s brothers.

Riscus, volume 30 of *Hispania sacra*, page 143, refutes the error of Lucius Marineus Siculus, who gives Isidore not only Braulio as a brother but also Saint Hermenegild and King Reccared. The first bishop of Chalon, in the entry “Hispalis” in his *Topography*, and Maurolycus under April 13, foolishly asserted that Braulio—whose true lineage is by no means established among the ancients—was the brother of Hermenegild and King Reccared.

### 14.

The tradition has also been accepted among the Spaniards that Severianus had a daughter named Theodora, married to Leovigild, from whom Saint Hermenegild the martyr and Reccared, the first Catholic king of the Goths, were born.

Nicolás Antonio, who examined with acute judgment the alleged Gothic origin of Severianus and his offspring, states this as certain. “We believe,” he adds, “that this kinship, and no other, existed between the descendants of Severianus and the Gothic kings.”

But if one asks on what authorities it is established that there ever was a Theodora, daughter of Severianus and wife of King Leovigild, no one, I think, will produce any others than those same writers whose claims concerning Severianus’s Gothic descent, the name Theodora for Severianus’s wife, and many other matters are not deserving of belief, since the earlier sources are silent.

Yet those sources are equally silent about such a kinship between Leander, Isidore, and the Gothic kings—something they certainly ought not to have omitted. Flórez discusses at length the force of this negative argument in the passage cited, especially because Leander, in the final chapter of his rule for his sister Florentina, lists no brothers other than Fulgentius and Isidore, and no sister other than Florentina.

He adds that Leovigild had two wives, as is established from the ancient historians: one named Rinchild, the other Goswintha. Nor was it then customary for Gothic kings to marry women of Roman descent. John of Biclaro writes under the year 573 in his chronicle concerning Leovigild:

> “He makes his two sons, Hermenegild and Reccared, by his deceased wife, partners in the kingdom.”

This wife was Rinchild.

### 15.

Concerning Isidore’s brothers and sister, therefore, we have this certainty: Leander and Fulgentius were his brothers, and Florentina his sister, so that Isidore himself was the youngest of them all, as is shown by the final chapter of Saint Leander’s rule.

Isidore also mentions his sister Florentina in his eulogy of Leander, where he relates that Leander published a short work *On the Instruction of Virgins* for his sister Florentina. Isidore himself dedicated two books *Against the Jews* to the same sister Florentina, as he testifies in the prologue:

> “To the holy sister Florentina, Isidore, etc. These books, holy sister, I have dedicated to you at your request for the building up of your study, so that you, with whom I share blood, might also become a co-heir of my labor.”

Braulio likewise mentions Florentina in his preliminary list of Isidore’s books:
