> “Two books *Against the Jews*, requested by Florentina, his sister, superior of virgins,” etc.

Ildefonsus does the same in chapter 9 of *On Illustrious Men*. That Florentina was buried in the same tomb as her brothers Leander and Isidore is related in the epitaph quoted above in chapter 7. But it is not established that the epitaph belongs to Saint Ildefonsus, to whom it is attributed, and Flórez vigorously disputes it in volume 10 of *Hispania sacra*. He reports that Florentina was buried at Écija and lay there until, when the Moors invaded Spain, she was transferred to the Aquilupian, or Guadalupian, mountains.

For Florentina’s various names, see chapter 66.

### 16.

Isidore also sent two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* to Fulgentius, his brother. Although the inscription says only:

> “To my lord and servant of God, Fulgentius the bishop, Isidore,”

Braulio plainly says:

> “Two books of the *Offices* to his brother Fulgentius the bishop.”

The printed editions add “bishop of Écija.” This is also expressed in the Italian version of Alcuin’s preliminary list of 1570, chapter 70, no. 17, which will be described: “Bishop of Écija.” On this matter, see the notes above in chapter 3.

Fulgentius was bishop of Écija in 610, when he signed the decree of Gundemar together with Isidore, as I shall say in chapter 21, and in 618 or 619, when he attended the Second Council of Seville, as I shall relate in the same chapter.

Nicolás Antonio, book 5, chapter 1, no. 16 of the *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, asserts that Fulgentius attended two councils with Isidore, the Sevillian and the Toledan—namely, the Toledan Council of 610. For in no. 13 he had taught that Fulgentius died before the year 623—correct this to 633—when Bishop Habentius of Écija is recorded as having signed the Fourth Council of Toledo.

Whether Fulgentius, Isidore’s brother, wrote anything is discussed by Nicolás Antonio and, after him, by Flórez in volume 10 of *Hispania sacra*. Flórez maintains that the title of doctor, which Fulgentius is said to have attained among the Spaniards, rests on no ancient evidence.

### 17.

An old seventh-century document preserved by Flórez in volume 3 of *Hispania sacra*, appendix, no. 3, page 390, testifies to Fulgentius’s considerable learning:

> “And so the Catholic faith in Spain gradually grew, until it was illumined by orthodox and Catholic men, namely Fulgentius, Peter, Leander, Isidore, Ildefonsus, Fructuosus, and Julian.”

The testimony of Roderic of Toledo concerning Fulgentius’s learning belongs to the thirteenth century. Lucas of Tuy, who flourished in the same century, offered similar testimony in Isidore’s chronicle.

This controversy was treated in the Sacred Congregation of Rites in 1723, as Benedict XIV explains in *On the Beatification*, book 4, part 2, chapter 11. At that time he was serving as Promoter of the Faith. He concludes the account as follows:

> “When new petitions had been presented to the Sacred Congregation, based especially on the fact that from ancient times he had possessed the title of doctor in certain dioceses of Spain, the response given on April 17, 1723, was that the customary practice should be observed in the Office of Saint Fulgentius with respect to the rite of doctor.”

[Col. 0101B]

### 18.

The matter is clearer in the case of Saint Leander, whom Isidore praised in his book *On Illustrious Men*. In a letter to the duke Claudius, Isidore called him “our common teacher,” and in the verses of the library he called him not inferior to the ancient teachers. Whether that letter and those verses are genuine works of Isidore will, however, be judged in their proper place.

Benedict XIV, who adduces other evidence in the same passage, concludes as follows concerning Leander:

> “In the churches and dioceses of Seville and Carthaginiensis, however, an Office is celebrated for him as a doctor; and this Office was extended on April 25, 1722, to the whole of Spain and to the regions subject to the Catholic King.”

Before Isidore, Saint Gregory the Great celebrated Leander’s praises in letters addressed to him. Gregory also sent Leander the pallium and dedicated his books *Moralia on Job* to him.

### 19.

Having discussed matters concerning Isidore’s parents and brothers, we must now consider his birthplace.

Isidore himself left it written that Severianus came from the province of Carthaginiensis in Spain. The Spanish breviaries state that Leander and Florentina were born at Carthage in Spain. Many assert the same concerning Fulgentius, although Nicolás Antonio does not dare to affirm it.

There is greater controversy concerning Isidore. The tradition is that he was born at Seville, where his parents had gone into exile from New Carthage. What the Spanish Breviaries, the Quignon Breviary, and the revised Roman Breviary say—that Isidore was Spanish by nationality, from New Carthage—suggests that Isidore came from that city, not that he was born there.

Roderic of Cerrato and certain ancient breviaries call him Carthaginian by nationality. An old Sevillian Breviary says:

> “He derived his origin from the city of Carthage in the province of Spain.”

In two Florentine codices of the books *Against the Jews*, which I shall discuss in chapter 43, Isidore is called either “bishop of Toledo” or “bishop of Toledo and Seville.” No one will doubt that this must be attributed to a copyist’s error. The same error occurs in certain manuscript copies in the Vatican Library and in other codices containing the same work *Against the Jews*.

### 20.

Since it is inferred from the exile of his parents that Isidore was not born in their homeland, let us first examine what kind of exile this was.

Leander speaks of this exile and homeland in the final chapter of his rule for his sister Florentina, discussed above in chapter 2. He warns his sister not to think of returning to the homeland from which God had once driven her. He sets before her the example of their mother, who repeatedly protested that she would never see again the homeland from which she had departed for the sake of salvation and who wished to be buried in the place of exile where she had begun to recognize God.

Nicolás Antonio suspected that Severianus’s wife might once have been entangled in the Arian error, which she had detested during her exile. He rightly observes, however, that Leander’s words may be understood to mean that in exile she had acquired a greater sense of piety than she had previously possessed.

### 21.

Indeed, since she departed from her homeland for the sake of salvation, this is a strong indication that the calamity inflicted upon the household of Severianus, because it was devoted to the Catholic faith, was brought about by the Arian Goths.

Isidore recalls the fervor with which Leander attacked the Arian heresy in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41:

> “For during his journey through the exile imposed upon him, he composed two books against the doctrines of the heretics, exceedingly rich in learning drawn from the sacred Scriptures. In them, with vehement style, he pierced and exposed the depravity of Arian impiety, showing what the Catholic Church holds against them, how far it differs from them in religion, and how far in the sacraments of faith. There is also another praiseworthy short work of his against the practices of the Arians, in which, after setting out their statements, he opposes his own responses. Moreover, he published one work for his sister Florentina, *On the Instruction of Virgins*,” etc.

### 22.

The journey of exile, as Isidore calls it, may be understood to have been shared by the parents and to have been the same exile that Leander mentions in the final chapter of his rule, or *On the Instruction of Virgins*.

Leander, however, not only records the exile of his household in that passage but also describes the destruction of their homeland:

> “I speak from experience: it has lost its former condition and appearance so completely that no free person remains in it, nor is the land itself fertile with its customary abundance—and not without God’s judgment. For when a land has been deprived of its citizens and surrendered to a stranger, as soon as it loses its dignity it also loses its fertility.”

Since it is scarcely doubtful that Leander is speaking of Carthage Spartaria, or New Carthage, we must investigate when the destruction of Carthage occurred.

### 23.

Isidore writes in book 15 of the *Etymologies*, chapter 1:

> “The Africans, occupying the maritime regions of Spain under Hannibal”—more correctly, under Hasdrubal—“built Carthage Spartaria, which was soon captured by the Romans and made a colony, and gave its name to the province. But now it has been destroyed by the Goths and reduced to desolation.”

Flórez, book 5 of *Hispania sacra*, treatise 4, chapter 2, asserts that Carthage was first destroyed by the Vandals and then by the Goths, at the time when Isidore was writing. He assigns this meaning to Isidore’s words: “It has just now been destroyed by the Goths.”

I understand Isidore’s words instead to indicate three states of the city: first under the Africans, second under the Romans, and third the state in which it was then found, already reduced to desolation. It cannot be inferred that this desolation was recent.

### 24.

Some have thought that this destruction of Carthage was the one Isidore attributes to the Vandals in his *History of the Vandals*, under the Spanish era 459, in the year 421:

> “Gunderic, the first king of the Vandals in Spain, etc., plundered the Balearic islands of the province of Tarraconensis. Then, after Carthage Spartaria had been destroyed, he crossed into Baetica with all the Vandals, destroyed Seville, and, after committing slaughter, gave it over to plunder.”

But since Leander suggests that the plundering of Carthage was a different event, one on account of which his parents moved to Baetica, Isidore too must be understood in book 15 of the *Etymologies* to be speaking of this very plundering mentioned by Leander. This is all the more likely because, in his *History of the Vandals*, he attributes the destruction of Carthage to them, whereas in book 15 of the *Etymologies* he attributes it to the Goths. Nor is it likely that he took “Goths” for “Vandals.”

25. [Col. 0103B] Bivarius, in his commentary on Maximus under the year 509, considers Carthage Spartaria to have been destroyed by Agila in the year of Christ 552. He proves with adequate arguments that a twofold destruction of New Carthage must be distinguished: one, of which Isidore speaks in Book XV of the *Etymologies*: “Now destroyed by the Goths, etc.”; the other, earlier, of which Hydatius speaks in his *Chronicle* under the first year of Theodosius, that is, the year of Christ 423: “The Vandals plunder the Balearic Islands; then, after Carthage Spartaria and Hispalis have been destroyed and the Spanish provinces plundered, they invade Mauretania.” Isidore’s words cannot refer to this ancient destruction by the Vandals, since he not only explicitly names the Goths but also clearly suggests that the event took place in his own time.

26. Agila was an extremely hostile enemy of the Catholic religion, as is clear from Isidore’s *History of the Goths* under the era 587 [Col. 0103C]: “Agila is made king and reigns for five years. When he was waging war against the city of Cordoba, and, in contempt of the Catholic religion, had inflicted an insult upon the most blessed martyr Acisclus, and, as a profaner, had polluted the sacred place of his tomb with the blood of enemies and beasts of burden, he entered into battle against the citizens of Cordoba and deserved fitting punishments, inflicted by the saints.”

27. If, therefore, we maintain that Agila destroyed Carthage Spartaria, it will have to be concluded that Leander’s and Florentina’s parents, steadfast in the Catholic religion, were shaken by this calamity suffered by their homeland and went into exile around the year 552. I would suppose that Fulgentius and Isidore were born after that time; but no certain judgment can be made either about the year [Col. 0103D] or about the place, except that tradition holds Hispalis to have been Isidore’s birthplace. His birth may conjecturally be assigned to about the year 560, since he was elected bishop around the year 600, as I shall say shortly [123]; and it is credible that he did not receive the episcopate before his fortieth year, as prescribed in the letter sent by Pope Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona in 385. I do not see why Florez, Book X of *Hispania sacra*, p. 120, should treat it as certain that Isidore was born at Carthage. Dupin, by contrast, in Volume V of the *Ecclesiastical Library*, asserts that he was born at Hispalis.

## CHAPTER XVIII. Isidore’s childhood; the portent concerning the swarm of bees; his formation in virtues and letters. He was not a disciple of Gregory the Great. Isidore’s Roman journey on the very night of the Nativity of the Lord is fictitious. Whether Isidore acted in Leander’s place while the latter was in exile. Discussion of Leander’s embassy and exile, and of Hermenegild’s martyrdom.

[Col. 0104A]

1. Nic. Antonius infers from the words of Ildefonsus, chapter IX of *On Illustrious Men*, that Isidore was commended from childhood for the beauty of his appearance: “A man distinguished alike in appearance and in intelligence,” as the author of the *Life of Saint Isidore*, the Leonese Canon, explicitly states. In this same historian, as also in Roderic of Cerrato, above, chapter 14, one may read of the miracle, or portent, concerning the swarm of bees that appeared to the infant Isidore. Berneggerus confirms in *Miscellaneous Observations*, chapter V, that this happened to others as well, as an omen of their future learning or their agreeable eloquence [Col. 0104B]. The author of the *Life of Saint Isidore* relates that the swarm of bees was seen by Isidore’s father. In the proper lessons of Saint Florentina among the Spaniards, this account differs somewhat:

“She proved worthy to undertake the care of educating her younger brother Isidore, and, together with Leander, diligently nourished him with the milk of the spirit and instructed him in every doctrine of the faith. She considered him worthy of being formed with all the more eager care because she was more strongly impelled to this by what happened when he was still in the cradle: seeing a swarm of bees enter his mouth, then emerge from it, and fly up into heaven, she was terrified and, turning to prayer, understood what this sign meant—that he would become a great teacher of the Church who would drive heretics from the borders of Spain.”

[Col. 0104C] 2. According to the authors of the *Life*, the Leonese Canon and Roderic of Cerrato, Isidore’s father saw the portent, and saw it in a garden; in the lessons of Saint Florentina it is said that she observed the swarm of bees in his cradle [124], unless one wishes to explain this as meaning “while he was in the cradle,” that is, while he was still an infant. It could therefore have happened that both Isidore’s father and his sister saw the portent of the bees in the garden; for there is no reason to believe that such a miracle occurred twice. Tamayus, in the *Spanish Martyrology*, collected Isidore’s acts from various sources, as he says; there Florentina is described as follows:

“Recognizing the infant’s spirit and discerning in him a sign beyond nature—for at one time she saw Isidore rise from his cradle and fly through the transparent air, and at another extinguish monstrous and deformed apparitions with his hands—she, prescient of the future, [Col. 0104D] devoted all her care to his education.”

I have not been able to find these details in other sources.

3. Florez, Volume IX, p. 194, relates the matter from the Leonese Canon, the author of the *Life of Saint Isidore*, and Roderic of Cerrato. Although he relegates many things reported by these writers to the realm of fables, he does not dare to pass a similar judgment on this portent, since nothing is found in the ancient records that appears to contradict it. He takes the same view of the story that the boy Isidore, at the edge of a well hollowed out by constant drops of water, drew from it the lesson that the difficulty of acquiring knowledge must be overcome by labor and persevering study—a story likewise reported by those writers and by others of approximately the same period. The same Florez [Col. 0105A], Volume X, p. 120, asserts that, if it is assumed—as he thinks it must be—that Isidore was born at Carthage, it cannot be reconciled with the account that Florentina saw the swarm of bees and, having recourse to prayer, understood that Isidore would become a great teacher of the Church, as the old Breviary of Hispalis and other sources relate. For Leander addresses Florentina in the final chapter of the Rule:

“You were taken away from there—that is, from your homeland—at such an age that, even if you had been born there, you would not remember it. There is no recollection that could stir your soul with longing.”

But even if we wish to take Leander’s words as referring to Florentina’s infancy—which is by no means necessary—there is no other evidence that Isidore was born at Carthage rather than at Hispalis, as I said at the end of chapter 17.

4. That Isidore was instructed in the first rudiments of letters at Hispalis is clear from the frequently cited *Life*. At that time, as the same work relates, there occurred what I have just mentioned: by the example of a stone hollowed out by frequent drops and of a piece of wood worn by the repeated passage of ropes into the shape of a channel, the boy Isidore learned that he too, despite arduous labor, could overcome the difficulties that commonly arise in the course of literary study. These things are indeed transmitted by later sources. But [125] Joannes Mariana, in *History of Spain*, Book VI, chapter 7, testifies that traces of this account were still displayed at Hispalis:

“A section of a marble well is preserved in the church of Saint Isidore at Hispalis; the boy Isidore observed that it had been hollowed out by the use and friction of a rope.”

The following is certain concerning Isidore’s education, as Leander states in the final chapter of the Rule [Col. 0105C]:

“Finally, dearest sister, I ask you to remember me in your prayers and not to forget our younger brother Isidore. Because our parents left him under God’s protection, with three of his siblings surviving, they departed joyfully to the Lord, fearing nothing concerning his infancy. Since I truly regard him as a son, I place no temporal thing before my affection for him and am wholly inclined toward him in love; love him all the more dearly and pray to Jesus for him all the more earnestly, the more you know that he was loved by his earthly parents.”

5. Isidore’s parents therefore died while he was still in infancy, and for that reason entrusted his education to their three surviving older children: Leander, Fulgentius, and Florentina. But since Leander managed the household, apparently as the firstborn, [Col. 0105D] he sent Fulgentius to the homeland. He himself reports this in the passage cited:

“Please, sister Florentina, take care to avoid what our mother feared and prudently flee the evil from which she escaped. Wretched that I am! I grieve that I sent our brother Fulgentius there, for I am terrified by the continual fear of the danger threatening him. Yet he will be safer if you are more secure and, though absent, pray for him.”

Perhaps certain affairs had arisen in the homeland from which they had gone into exile, and Leander wished Fulgentius to attend to them, while Isidore was still young and Florentina was living among virgins devoted to God. The principal responsibility for Isidore’s education therefore remained with Leander, who carried it out with a love more paternal than fraternal.

[Col. 0106A] 6. Florentina nevertheless had some share in Isidore’s education, as the lessons of hers that I cited shortly before relate. Her lessons concerning Fulgentius likewise contain the following:

“Another proof of this is that the same distinguished teacher Isidore, who had been brought up by him and instructed in pious teachings, etc.”

There is no reason to deny that this was true to some extent, but it must nevertheless be asserted that Leander was Isidore’s principal teacher—not only because Leander implies this, but also because Isidore himself declares as much in his letter to Duke Claudius:

“Remember our common teacher [126] Leander, and imitate his faith and teaching to the best of your ability.”

Many, however, consider this letter from Isidore to Claudius spurious; I shall discuss it elsewhere.

The statement of the pseudo-Maximus under the year 568, number 8, that Isidore had used David of Hispalis as his teacher is a fabrication. [Col. 0106B] Bivarius attempted to clarify this passage by first expressing doubt whether this David was different from David, bishop of Hispalis; then he observed that, while living in a monastery, Leander would have been less suited to educate Isidore personally in letters. The Leonese Canon, author of the *Life*, reports that Isidore used other teachers besides Leander, evidently so that he might acquire that encyclopedia of learning which is greatly exaggerated.

Nevertheless, it must be admitted that, judged by the capacity of those times, Isidore was a kind of prodigy in the study of secular letters—not because he excelled in every language or every discipline, but because he was so richly furnished with knowledge of many different subjects and writers [Col. 0106C] that he inspires admiration even in our own age.

7. It is asked whether Isidore was a student of Gregory the Great. Lucius Marinaeus Siculus, Book V of *On Spanish Affairs*, Arnoldus Wion, Book II of the *Tree of Life*, Eisengrein in the *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, and Constantinus Cajetanus, p. 45, assert that he was. Joannes Andreas Quenstedt, in *On Illustrious Fathers*, p. 4, says confidently:

“Hispalis venerates Saint Isidore, its bishop and its foster-son, as a disciple of Gregory the Great from his earliest age.”

Nic. Antonius suspects that this claim originated in the fact that Isidore agrees with Gregory not only in his opinions but also in his wording. Lucas of Tuy, Book II, chapter 4, did not hesitate to attribute this to a special inspiration of the Holy Spirit in his work against the Albigensians [Col. 0106D]. Prudentius of Troyes may perhaps also have alluded to it in his work against Erigena, *On Predestination*, in the edition of the authors who wrote on predestination in the ninth century, Volume II, p. 215, and Volume XV of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 474:

“Following him [Gregory] in faith, thought, and words, Saint Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, inserted almost the same opinion into his own statements. Whoever wishes to compare them will find that they spoke with one spirit and one mouth, so that he will have no doubt that the same Holy Spirit was present in both and spoke unanimously through both. Isidore: ‘There is a twofold predestination,’ etc.”

He quotes the words from Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 6. Lucas of Tuy tries to prove the point more fully, adducing arguments as well, in the passage cited, where he concludes [127] [Col. 0107A]:

“Let us therefore admit that their writings agree through the Holy Spirit, as has been said, and that such eminent philosophers of the Church of God did not agree through borrowed attestations.”

Lucas was moved to this conclusion because not all Gregory’s books had reached Isidore, as is evident from the book *On Illustrious Men*. But this hardly proves that those books of Gregory had not reached Isidore which contain the sentences that Isidore used in the same words. In this respect, therefore, the charge of plagiarism could not be excused.

8. Nic. Antonius rightly responds, following Theophilus Raynaudus, *On Good and Evil Books*, Part I, question 10, number 275, that one should not be considered a plagiarist who likes to pluck flowers from another’s work, as Isidore did from Gregory and others. Isidore himself makes this clear when he says that he took his commentaries on the Old Testament [Col. 0107B] from Origen, etc., and from Gregory, who was outstandingly eloquent in our own times. The title of the *Book of Sentences* sufficiently indicates that ancient sentences have been collected there; for this reason Braulio says in his preface that Isidore collected three books of sentences, which he adorned with flowers from the moral books of Pope Gregory.

None of this, although other Fathers likewise customarily did such things, proves that Isidore was either Gregory’s student or his plagiarist. Indeed, Margarinus de la Bigne, in the dedicatory letter of his edition of Isidore, argues that Isidore was not Gregory’s disciple, since otherwise he would not have commended Gregory without mentioning the discipline he had gratefully received from him.

9. Perhaps, too, because another Isidore of Sicily is said to have been a disciple of Saint Gregory—a man discussed by Constantius Felix in his *Calendar*, Ferrarius in the notes to his *Catalogue of the Saints*, and Arnoldus Wion in Book III of the *Tree of Life*—the similarity of names led people to believe that Isidore of Hispalis was also a student of Saint Gregory.

The Leonese Canon, author of the *Life*, merely reports that Isidore was known to Gregory, on the basis of a letter concerning blessedness that Isidore sent to him; but the reliability of this claim must rest with the author himself. There is no mention of this letter among earlier writers.

Much more astonishing is what the same historian goes on to relate: that one night during the Nativity of the Lord Isidore was miraculously transported to Rome to meet Gregory, and returned home that same night. The Bollandists have made various observations about this portent. Tamayus, in the *Spanish Martyrology*, lists this Roman journey of Isidore on the Nativity of the Lord among uncertain or incredible events, drawing it from Lucas of Tuy’s *Miracles of Saint Isidore*, from which the very ancient Segovian Breviary also relates the same story in lesson 2 [128] [Col. 0107D]. Whether Isidore ever came to Rome will be discussed in chapter 23.

10. When Isidore, now a young man, was fit to take up arms against heretics, the author of the *Life* says that he attacked the Arian heretics with the utmost vigor. This is sufficiently plausible and is confirmed by the proper Hispanic offices. But the Breviaries relate that Isidore was restrained by Leander and admonished to reserve himself for a more suitable time.

The author of the *Life*, after reporting that Leander had been expelled from Spain by the heretics, adds that Isidore acted in his brother’s place at Hispalis [Col. 0108A] and was encouraged by him through letters to prosecute the cause of the faith energetically. But what exile of Leander is this? Perhaps it is the very one that the author of the *Life* had mentioned earlier, when he related that Leander formed a bond of friendship with Gregory the Great at Constantinople, at the time when he had gone there, under Leovigild, to confirm the articles of the holy and immaculate Trinity.

11. The same writer of the *Life* nevertheless seems to suggest something else here, when he reports that, after Leovigild’s death, Leander returned triumphantly from Carthage to Spain. Since he first mentions the friendship established between Gregory the Great and Leander at Constantinople, and Isidore’s marvelous journey to Rome, and then explains Leander’s exile and Isidore’s steadfastness in acting on Leander’s behalf [Col. 0108B] in defending the faith, he implies that this exile of Leander was different from his journey to the imperial city of Constantinople.

Let us gather from the historical records what is probable in this matter. Leander, as Isidore says in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41, was made bishop after having been a monk of the Church of Hispalis in the province of Baetica. He was renowned for his learning, so that through his faith and diligence the people of the Gothic nation might return from Arian madness to the Catholic faith.

“For during his journey in exile he composed two books against the doctrines of the heretics,” and so forth.

12. Furthermore, we have the following from Book III of Gregory the Great’s *Dialogues*, chapter 31 [Col. 0108C]:

“As we have recently learned from the report of many who come from the regions of Spain, King Hermenegild, son of Leovigild, king of the Visigoths, was converted from the Arian heresy to the Catholic faith through the preaching of the most reverend man Leander, bishop of Hispalis, who had long before become closely bound to me in friendship.”

I would punctuate it better as follows: “We have recently learned that King Hermenegild,” and so forth. Saint Gregory was writing the *Dialogues* around the year 594. Hermenegild’s conversion and Gregory’s friendship [129] with Leander had taken place some time earlier; but shortly before Gregory wrote this—hence his use of “recently”—he had received the account of the martyrdom, the miracles that followed, and the veneration shown at the martyr’s tomb.

After relating Hermenegild’s martyrdom, he continues:

“But the obstinate and parricidal father, moved to repentance, regretted having done this; yet he did not repent so far as to obtain salvation. For he recognized that the Catholic faith was true, but, terrified by fear of his nation, [Col. 0108D] he did not deserve to reach it. When illness arose and brought him to his end, he took care to commend to Bishop Leander, whom he had previously afflicted most severely, his son King Reccared, whom he was leaving in his heresy, so that Leander might do for him what he had done for his brother through his exhortations.”

Hermenegild’s conversion is therefore attributed to Leander’s exhortations.

13. Gregory of Tours gives a different account in Book V of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 38. He says that Leovigild gave Hermenegild and his wife Ingund one of the cities, where they were to reside and reign. When they had gone there, Ingund began urging her husband to abandon the deceit of heresy and recognize the truth of the Catholic faith [Col. 0109A]. After resisting her preaching for a long time, he was finally moved by it and converted to the Catholic religion.

This can nevertheless be explained in such a way that, in addition to Ingund’s preaching, a more learned persuasion and exhortation by Leander also intervened, so that the principal role in Hermenegild’s conversion may be assigned to him. Gregory the Great, Leander’s closest friend, must certainly be believed when he asserts this. The city that Gregory of Tours says was granted to Hermenegild may perhaps have been Hispalis, where Leander was bishop. Florez, Volume IX of *Hispania sacra*, p. 162, asserts that Hermenegild established his seat at Hispalis in the year 579.

14. As for the time when these events occurred, Isidore should be consulted. In his *Chronicle*, under the year 5780 from the creation of the world, he says:

“Tiberius reigns for seven years. [Col. 0109B] The Lombards, having driven out the Romans, enter Italy. The Goths, divided into two factions through Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild, are ravaged by mutual slaughter.”

And again, under the year 5801 from the creation of the world:

“Mauricius reigns for twenty-one years. … At this time Leander, bishop in Spain, became renowned among the Gothic people for his teaching of the faith and of the sciences, leading to their conversion.”

In the *History of the Goths*, under era 624, that is, the year of Christ 586, in the third year of the emperor Mauricius, he says:

“After Leovigild’s death, his son Reccared was crowned king. … At the very beginning of his reign he embraced the Catholic faith and, abandoning the stain of the long-standing error, recalled the peoples of the entire Gothic nation to the worship of the true faith.”

Add the words of the abbot of Biclaro:

“In the third year of Mauricius—which was the seventeenth year of Leovigild—Hermenegild was killed at Tarragona by Sisbert.”

[Col. 0109C] 15. Petavius, in *Rationarium temporum*, Part I, Book VIII, chapter 12, and Pagius in his notes on Baronius under the year 584, conclude that Hermenegild’s martyrdom occurred in the year 585. This will readily persuade anyone, although some have assigned the year 583, 584, 586, 588, or 589 for the death of the martyr Hermenegild.

Baronius assigned Leovigild’s death to the year 585, and, later retracting this, postponed it less satisfactorily to the year 591. Bollandus, in his commentary on the *Life of Saint Leander*, assigns it to the year 587; Pagius, more probably following the abbot of Biclaro, assigns it to 585. Florez agrees with Pagius concerning the year of Hermenegild’s and Leovigild’s deaths in Volume IX of *Hispania sacra*, p. 163; earlier, in Volume VI, p. 409, he had assigned the year 585 to that death.

[Col. 0109D] It must therefore now be investigated when Leander met Gregory the Great at Constantinople. Baronius, under the year 583, number 11, proves that Saint Gregory was sent to Constantinople that same year, 583, by Pope Pelagius II as *apocrisiarius*, or legate. At the end of 584, or at the beginning of 585, Saint Gregory left Constantinople and came to Rome, as Pagius confirms.

16. Thus, in 583 or the following year, Leander was staying at Constantinople. Saint Gregory says of him in the preface to the *Moralia*:

“Knowing you long ago, most blessed brother, in the city of Constantinople, when the responses of the Apostolic See bound me there, and the embassy entrusted to you for the causes of the faith of the king of the Visigoths had brought you there [Col. 0110A], I disclosed to your ears everything that displeased you about me.”

But by what other king could Leander have been sent for the causes of the faith except Hermenegild? Hermenegild was seeking the emperor’s assistance for the Catholic cause against the Arians, and he chose Leander to send as his legate to Constantinople concerning this matter.

Florez, Volume IX, p. 182, rejects the opinion of the Bollandists, who think that Leander went to Constantinople before Hermenegild embraced the Catholic faith. They are moved by the consideration that Gregory the Great, in Book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31, calls Hermenegild’s conversion recent, but describes his friendship with Leander as having occurred long before.

Florez replies that Hermenegild could not have sent Leander to Constantinople for the causes of the faith unless he was already a Catholic [131] [Col. 0110B]. This is a plausible argument, but not entirely conclusive. Hermenegild, although not yet a Catholic, could have decided upon that embassy because he favored the Catholics, while the Catholics in turn supported his cause.

I would favor the Bollandists’ opinion if it were certain that Gregory consistently observed the precise force of adverbs; but this is by no means certain. Nic. Antonius, number 85, holds that Leander’s journey to Constantinople occurred after Hermenegild’s conversion; but in number 87 he denies that it is certain that Leander returned to Spain before Leovigild’s death.

If the sentence is punctuated differently—“We have recently learned that King Hermenegild,” as I explained above—the Bollandists’ difficulty disappears. Many think that Leander was sent into exile after Hermenegild’s martyrdom, for Ado of Vienne relates that, after Hermenegild’s murder, his father Leovigild launched a harsher persecution against the Catholics, [Col. 0110C] banishing orthodox bishops to various places.

17. I myself believe that Leander, having completed his embassy, returned from Constantinople to Spain and even obtained auxiliary troops from the emperor for Hermenegild. Gregory of Tours relates in Book V of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 38, that Leovigild gave the emperor’s prefect thirty thousand solidi to withdraw him from his son’s support, which was done.

Hermenegild, the same historian continues, summoned the Greeks and marched against his father, leaving his wife in the city. When Leovigild came against him from the opposite direction, Hermenegild, abandoned by the support of the Greeks, saw that he could accomplish nothing, and so forth.

He adds that Ingund, Hermenegild’s wife, was seized by the Greeks, who intended to take her to the emperor, and died in Africa. I would suppose that this was the time when, after Hermenegild had been captured and his army destroyed, Leander went into exile in Africa [Col. 0110D], perhaps following Ingund, in the year 584. Thus the report of the Leonese Canon, the author of Isidore’s *Life*, that Leander returned from Carthage to Spain after Leovigild’s death may be true.

18. The account of the same historian is also consistent with this reasoning: while his brother Leander was absent, Isidore vigorously pursued the cause of religion, not only without Leander’s restraint but rather at his urging. When the revered teacher Leander heard of the steadfastness of the courageous young Isidore, he rejoiced in the Lord, and so forth.

He therefore sent him a letter in which he warned him that death for the Catholic faith was not to be feared. This is the letter that Isidore mentions concerning Leander in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41 [132] [Col. 0111A]:

“He also wrote many letters: one to Pope Gregory concerning baptism, and another to his brother, in which he warned him that death was not to be feared.”

The same author of the *Life* relates Isidore’s steadfastness in the face of the flatteries, threats, and tortures inflicted by the Arian heretics.

19. When the records we have produced are carefully compared and weighed against one another, the error of Ambrosius Morales in Book X, chapter 5, becomes clear. He says that Leander attended the fifth ecumenical council at Constantinople with Gregory the Great. [Col. 0111B] Florez, Volume IX, pp. 185 ff., refutes him at length.

Morales inferred from this that Leander had held the see of Hispalis for a long period, since he places the second Council of Constantinople, the fifth general council, in the year 554, and says that Leander was already bishop of Hispalis at that time and attended that council. From this he derives the beginning of the friendship formed between Leander and Gregory the Great.

But he cites no other authorities for the matter, nor does the chronology in any way permit it to be maintained.

## CHAPTER XIX. Whether Isidore professed some monastic institute, or that of the Regular Canons or of the Carmelites.

1. After the peace granted to the Church of Spain by Reccared around the year 586, Leander arranged for his brother Isidore to live enclosed in a cell, not unwillingly, if the author of the *Life* is telling the truth. The old Breviaries indeed agree that Leander took care that Isidore not appear in public [Col. 0111C], but they say that this happened at the time when the Arians were raging against the Catholics, since Leander was trying to preserve Isidore from the fury of the heretics.

The author of the *Life* gives other reasons for his confinement. The more ancient records are entirely silent. Since at that time it was customary for some people, fleeing human company, to shut themselves up in a cell, perhaps Isidore, with Leander’s approval, adopted this way of life. For I consider it less consistent with reason that Leander himself was the first author of this decision.

2. Nic. Antonius suspects that some people were persuaded by this confinement in a cell that Isidore had lived in some monastic order. The Bollandists dealt with this argument in their preliminary commentary.

Among those who assert that Isidore belonged to the Benedictine order are [133] [Col. 0111D] Sandoval; Leander of Saint Thomas in his *Benedictine Lusitanian Additions*, chapter 3; Quintanaduenas in *The Saints of Hispalis*; Joannes Cisneros in his manuscript *Life of Isidore*; Tamayus in the *Spanish Martyrology*; and above all Constantinus Cajetanus, who rebukes Petrus Ricordatus, *History of Monasticism*, day 4; Hieronymus Platus, *On the Good of the Religious State*, Book I, chapter 31; and Arnoldus Wion, because, although they assign Isidore to the Benedictines, they touch upon the matter, as he says, so superficially and casually that it would have been better had they passed over it in silence.

Arnoldus Wion had reported that, approximately 140 years earlier, an image of Isidore had been painted among several others of illustrious Benedictines in monastic dress:

“And I too,” Cajetanus adds, “do not hesitate to affirm this.”

[Col. 0112A] 3. Cajetanus nevertheless considers the stronger argument to be the one he draws from the Rule of Saint Isidore, which he claims to be Benedictine. Others, following the Benedictine Iepes, more correctly adopt the opposite view and infer from Isidore’s own Rule that he was not a Benedictine.

I shall not discuss here the opinion of the most learned Hernandez in his notes to chapter 42 of the *Synopsis of the Edition of Saint Isidore by Zaccaria*, which I shall produce elsewhere. He suspects that the Rule of Monks published under Isidore’s name has another author, because the author presents himself as a monk. “But no one,” he adds, “will say that Isidore wore the monastic hood without being both completely blinded and actually blind.”

Compare chapter 71, where I shall observe that, in an Escorial manuscript of the ninth or early tenth century, some incompetent copyist added the following heading [Col. 0112B]:

“Here begins the Rule of Saint Father Isidore, abbot.”

Cajetanus insists that Isidore wrote not only the extant Rule of Monks but also lost, fuller commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict. He adduces certain fragments from Petrus the Casinensian deacon, who says in his manuscript epitome on the Rule of Saint Benedict:

“But we shall explain this briefly for that reason: in this matter Paul the Casinensian deacon, Rabanus Maurus, the teacher Isidore, Stephen, and Paul the abbots have applied their efforts.”

I pass over the suspicion of Naudé and others, who do not place sufficient trust in Cajetanus when he cites old manuscript copies.

[Col. 0112C] 4. Nic. Antonius responds to this argument that most fragments of this kind are found in Isidore’s own Rule, while others are taken from other works of Isidore. He also observes, in number 158, following Benedictus Haeftenus, Book X of *Monastic Investigations*, treatise VI, investigation 3, that the Rule of Monks of Saint Isidore is not similar to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

He explains the words of Petrus Casinensis from the manuscript work in such a way that Petrus means that he is adducing several passages from Isidore’s Rule to elucidate the Rule of Saint Benedict—not that Isidore had the Benedictine Rule in view, but because monastic rules have many things in common. Unless one prefers to admit that Petrus Casinensis too could have been deceived, if he inferred from Isidore’s published Rule that Isidore intended to expound the Benedictine Rule.

5. But Cajetanus, impelled by that vehement desire of his to attach every saint to the Benedictine order, goes further still. “To all these considerations,” he says, [Col. 0112D] “let us also add an irrefutable argument. It is beyond dispute that in those times no one who was not a monk served as a teacher of monks; indeed, it was considered almost a sacrilege if a monk presumed in any way to listen to an outsider.”

Is that really so? In the councils of Spain we find something else decreed. The Council of Huesca, in the year 598, canon 1:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, when we had all assembled together in the Council of Huesca, this holy synod decreed that, each year in turn, every one of us should order all the abbots of the monasteries, as well as the priests and deacons of his diocese, to assemble at the place chosen by the bishop, and should set forth the Rule to all for the conduct of their lives, warning all to remain under ecclesiastical rules, [Col. 0113A] and commending them also to the example of honorable men in thrift, sobriety, and truthful chastity.”

Shortly afterward Isidore was made bishop. What, then, is surprising if he prescribed a rule to monks although he was not himself a monk?

6. Still less tolerable is what Cajetanus adds: that it was universally acknowledged that the chairs of the most celebrated schools were held only by Benedictines, most of which they themselves had founded … and that the Roman pontiffs had taken care that, while the heresies of Arius, Pelagius, and other monsters of that kind were spreading throughout the Christian world at that time, the sacred Scriptures should be taught nowhere except in monasteries and by monks.

He asserts the last point as certain for the kingdom of England, while saying that it is above all probable in the other regions. “Hence,” he immediately concludes [Col. 0113B], “it follows that Isidore, who at that very time publicly professed the interpretation of the sacred Scriptures, must necessarily have been a monk and could not have performed this task outside a monastery.”

What is one to do with this ingenious disputant? I suppose he would have liked all the bishops and all the priests flourishing at that time to have been Benedictines.

Certainly, in the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633 and presided over by our Isidore, we read that the following was established [135] in canon 25 [Col. 0113C]:

“Ignorance, the mother of all errors, must especially be avoided by the priests of God, who have undertaken the duty of teaching the peoples. Priests are admonished to read the sacred Scriptures, as the Apostle Paul says to Timothy: ‘Attend to reading, exhortation, and teaching; remain always in these things.’ Therefore priests must know the sacred Scriptures and the canons, so that all their work may consist in preaching and teaching, and so that they may edify everyone both by knowledge of the faith and by the discipline of their works.”

7. In support of Saint Isidore’s Benedictine monasticism, one might cite the Martyrology for the Cistercians appended to the Roman Martyrology by order of Benedict XIV, whose words I quoted in chapter 15. But since a similar Martyrology for the Regular Canons asserts that Saint Isidore had been enrolled among the Regular Canons, the authority of that Martyrology in this matter becomes doubtful, since it favors both orders equally.

Among the *Proper Offices of the Saints of the Regular Canons*, to be recited by the Lateran Congregation under a special concession of Saint Pius V, published at Milan in 1751, the feast of Saint Isidore, bishop and confessor, occurs on April 4 [Col. 0113D], with the designation “Regular Canon.” In the first lesson of the second nocturn the following is found:

“Saint Isidore, descended from the Gothic race, was the son of Severianus, duke of Carthage, and the brother of that great saint Leander, formerly bishop of Hispalis. Having professed the institute of the Regular Canons and being endowed with the highest virtues, he was consecrated prelate of the Church of Hispalis …”

The words “descended from the Gothic race” and “duke” rest upon records of a later age.

8. Nic. Antonius inclines to the view that Isidore should be reckoned among the Regular Canons. For when he had observed that, in the eulogy of St. Fructuosus, abbot and bishop of Braga, whom we shall discuss in chapter 33, no. 3, Fructuosus and Isidore are compared with one another in such a way that the intention of religious life is attributed to Fructuosus, not to Isidore, he added that the same point is confirmed by Lucas of Tuy in these words, *Chronicle*, book III, at the beginning:

> Moreover, he was the father of clerics, teacher and supporter of monks and nuns.

These words, he says, clearly indicate that Isidore taught and nourished monks, but presided over clerics. For the title “father” is customarily applied to a superior, as it is to abbots in canon 10 of the Second Council of Seville, likewise in canon 11, and elsewhere. Nor, he continues, should the term “cell” be confined within monastic enclosures, since it is clear from the account of Redemptus that, already dying, Isidore had himself carried from his cell—that is, from a room of the episcopal house—to the church; and canon 23 of the Fourth Council of Toledo mentions the cells of priests and deacons.

He also observes that, in Isidore’s epitaph, discussed above in chapter 7, Antonius Lupian Zapata either found somewhere or invented *parum ex ordine abbatum*—“scarcely from the order of abbots”—in place of *priorum ex ordine vatum*—“of the foremost from the order of prophets”—in order to establish Isidore’s monastic profession; yet the adverb *parum* rather argues against a monastic profession. Perhaps Zapata intended someone to conjecture the reading *patrum ex ordine abbatum*—“of the fathers from the order of abbots.” But the true reading, as I showed in that place, is *priorum ex ordine vatum*, so that Isidore is understood to have been a priest of the first rank.

9. At that time a certain form of common life flourished in Spain in the residences of bishops, which may be compared with the order of the Regular Canons. Thus the Fourth Council of Toledo, under the presidency of Isidore, decrees in canons 22 and 23:

> Bishops ought to have in their chamber the testimony of persons of proven character, so that they may please God by a pure conscience and the Church by an excellent reputation. It has likewise seemed good that, as bishops do, priests and deacons—whom illness or the burden of age may perhaps prevent from remaining in the bishop’s chamber—should have witnesses of their life in their own cells, and should maintain their life not only in name but also in merits.

The institution of the Canons, moreover, proposed at the Council of Aachen in the year 816, was composed also from the opinions of other Fathers, but especially from Isidore’s works, as I shall show in chapter 31. Hence some have come to think that Isidore wrote the rule of the Canons. Pennottus, in *History of the Regular Canons*, book II, chapter 31, no. 5, reckons the metropolitan church of Seville among the churches of the Regular Canons, together with John of Nigravalle:

> And rightly so, for its archbishop was Blessed Isidore, who undoubtedly wished, in restoring the canonical order in the churches of Spain, to begin this undertaking with the church of which he himself was bishop.

Since, however, some, along with Thomassinus, *Ecclesiastical Discipline*, part I, book I, chapter 40 and following, trace the origin of the Regular Canons back to St. Augustine, certain people have consequently wished to number St. Isidore among the Augustinians.

10. Another argument for Isidore’s monastic profession is drawn from the fact that his brother Leander was a monk and instructed Isidore. But this conjecture is quite weak, since it is entirely compatible with the facts that Leander, either before becoming a monk or already as a monk, partly instructed Isidore and partly arranged for him to be instructed, without Isidore ever professing the monastic order.

Nor are Cajetan’s other conjectures any more substantial. First, without citing any authority, he asserts that Leander had put on the monastic hood from the beginning of his life. Then, concerning the location of the monastery, he says that it is more probable that Leander, already a monk at Seville for some time, subsequently caused Isidore to be initiated there through his own association and example; but that, when the Goths, followers of the Arian depravity, soon began to rage, Leander withdrew to León. He says that the same judgment must be made concerning St. Fulgentius, bishop of Écija.

These are mere fantasies. For among the ancient writers—I mean those who are not fictitious—neither Leander nor Isidore is ever said to have come to León. Isidore’s body was transferred there only many centuries later, and this perhaps furnished some people with an occasion for inventing or conjecturing that they had gone there.

11. Leander himself, whom Isidore reports to have been a monk, is considered by most sensible men, free from partisan zeal, not to be reckoned among the Benedictines. Although monks and monasteries are frequently mentioned in the councils and other monuments of the Gothic Church, not a word appears concerning Benedict or his Rule.

Cennius, *Dissertation 6*, chapter 3, *On the Antiquity of the Church of Spain*, devotes considerable effort to refuting the opinion of the Benedictines, who maintain that the Rule of St. Benedict had already been received in Spain in the seventh century. He argues that the Rule was not older in Spain than the ninth century; that St. Isidore’s rule agrees with the rule of the monastery of Servitanus proposed in Eutropius’s letter, but differs entirely from the Benedictine Rule in many chapters; and that St. Leander’s intimacy with St. Gregory the Great by no means proves that Benedictine monks were summoned from Italy to introduce some new rule, much less that they came to spread more widely an already established Benedictine order, as some suppose.

Joseph Perez, a learned Benedictine, placed this title in his *Ecclesiastical Dissertations*, p. 109: “Even while the Gothic kingdom stood, the Benedictine institution flourished greatly in Spain.” He attempted to prove this with considerable labor, but made little progress. In a certain sense he was more successful in another paradox of his, no less absurd: that the famous charter concerning the vow made by Ramiro I in favor of St. James during the battle of Clavijo was a forgery. Certain legalists in Spain embraced this claim with both arms, and went even further, as freedom to form opinions about sacred or pious matters commonly drives people into reckless audacity.

12. Henschenius also discusses the reasons that moved Lezana to assign Isidore to his Carmelite order—a claim also maintained by Casanate in *The Paradise of Carmelite Glory* and by others. Nic. Antonius dispatched the controversy in a few words:

> The Benedictines, and indeed the Carmelites as well, claim Isidore for their institution. The latter have no basis; the former at least have some semblance of one.

P. Daniel of the Virgin Mary, in *The Carmelite Vineyard*, no. 475, advances Lezana’s arguments on behalf of the Carmelite order. He mentions, on the authority of his sources, that an ascetic house of Carmel was built at Seville by St. Elmidus, in which Leander and Isidore professed the prophetic institution of Elijah. There is neither the faintest trace nor the slightest evidence of this among ancient writers.

In support of the same view he adduces an epitaph which he thinks was composed by Ildefonsus:

> Of Leander and Isidore, the foremost from the order of prophets.

We shall discuss the age and interpretation of this epitaph more fully in chapter 7. He adds the authority of Isidore, who in book II of *The Offices*, chapter 15, says that Elijah was the founder of the monastic institution. But this certainly gives no indication whatever that Isidore’s profession was either monastic or Carmelite.

The Carmelites argued at length for the antiquity of their order against Papebrochius, and Papebrochius replied at length in his *Response to the Displayed Errors*. On pp. 564 and following of the *Apologies*, he discusses a certain statue of the Mother of God found at Seville, at whose feet a figure had been represented in such a manner that many inferred from its habit that it was a Carmelite. Morgadus, who relates the story, at the same time asserts that it is certain that the Carmelite order was not received in Spain before Seville was finally recovered—that is, before the year 1248.

## CHAPTER XX

**Isidore is appointed bishop of Seville after Leander: the year in which this occurred. Whether he established at Seville a college adapted to the ecclesiastical education of young men. St. Ildefonsus, Isidore’s disciple; and whether Braulio and the cleric Redemptus were also his disciples**

1. St. Leander, who devoted the greatest effort to the conversion of the Gothic nation and subscribed to the Third Council of Toledo in the year 589, presided over the First Council of Seville in the following year, 590.

In the epitaph discussed in chapter 7, Leander is said to have died in the era 641, that is, in the year 603. But although that epitaph may be ancient, at least in this respect it scarcely deserves any credence. Apart from the evidence I cited in the place mentioned, the antiquity of the epitaph may be established from the codex of the Rules of St. Benedict of Aniane, from which Holstenius apparently published it after the Rule of St. Leander. Perhaps Mabillonius had this codex in mind when he asserts, in volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 278, that it is found appended to the Rule of St. Leander in a certain codex.

In Holstenius’s copy the epitaph consists of twelve hexameters, as it does in Fabri’s codex, discussed above in chapter 7, no. 1, with the following differences in reading: in verse 2 Holstenius has *piorum* rather than *priorum*; in verse 3, *devota* rather than *Deo vota*; in verse 4, *Et posita amborum consors sic digna quiescit* rather than *Et posita consors sic . . . digna quiescit*; in verse 7, *Et cognosce illos* rather than *Et cognoces eos*; in verse 8, *Dogmate sanctorum cernens* rather than *Dogmatibus sanctorum cerne*; and in verse 9, *Aeterno Domino* rather than *Ac re Domino*—both readings being corrupt in place of *Ac reddi Domino*.

Holstenius omits the day of St. Isidore’s and St. Florentina’s deaths. But these are the words expressed concerning St. Leander:

> Leander, bishop of blessed memory, died on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the era 641.

This same era is recorded by Rodericus Carus in *The Maximum*, p. 212, and by Tamayus de Salazar in the *Hispanic Martyrology* under February 27. Baronius, Breulius, Mabillonius, and others continue to accept it.

Yet its falsity is disproved by other monuments. Three letters of St. Gregory the Great to Leander survive: book I of the *Registers*, letter 41; book IV, letter 46; and book VII, letter 126. The last is assigned to the year 599, as is another letter in the same book to Reccared, no. 127, congratulating him on his conversion.

In the Maurist edition these two letters are numbered 121 and 122 of book IX, under indiction 2—that is, the year 599—although indiction 2 begins in September of the year 598. From these letters it could be inferred that Leander was still alive at least in the year 599.

Nic. Antonius, however, thinks that these two letters have not been placed in their proper order. For it is not very probable that Gregory delayed for so long—indeed, for a decade—his congratulations on Reccared’s conversion and the transmission of the pallium to Leander. In letter 126 of book VII, Gregory says that he is sending the pallium to Leander.

2. Nic. Antonius therefore takes another route in determining the year of Leander’s death. It is established from Redemptus that Isidore died in the year 636, while Ildefonsus says that he held the see of Seville for nearly forty years. It follows that Isidore was raised to the episcopate in 596 or shortly afterward, and consequently that Leander exchanged life for death shortly beforehand.

He further conjectures that in the year 597, when another Council of Toledo was held under Reccared, the church of Seville was still vacant. For the signature of the bishop of Seville is absent, although among the metropolitans there were Massona of Mérida, Migetius of Narbonne, and Adelphius of Toledo. From this it may be inferred that the council comprised all Spain and Gothic Gaul, although the acts state that only sixteen bishops assembled for it. The architect of the pseudo-Julian seems to have inclined to this same view.

3. Joan. Baptista Perez, however, thinks otherwise in his notes on Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41. He argues from the following conjectures that Leander died in the year 600.

First, Isidore says that Leander died during the lifetime of King Reccared, who died in the year 600. That Leander did not die before this year is clear from the fact that Pope Gregory wrote to him in 599. Thus the total period of Isidore’s episcopate will amount to nearly forty years, as Ildefonsus says. For when someone says “nearly forty years,” this may reasonably be understood as thirty-six years.

I strongly doubt, however, that Ildefonsus, who certainly ought to have known the number of years, intended to speak in this way. For concerning Eugenius II he says, “He lived in the priesthood for almost eleven years,” and concerning Eugenius III, “Holding the dignity for almost twelve years.” Likewise, in the case of Isidore, he seems to imply that Isidore came close to completing forty years of episcopate, but did not actually complete them.

4. Florezius, volume IX of *Sacred Spain*, p. 182, noticed an error in the number in the ancient Calendar published by Muratorius, part II, volume II of *Writers on Italian Affairs*, column 1024:

> In the era 640 Leander, bishop, died,

that is, in the year 602. Florezius himself thinks it more probable that Leander died in 599 and that Isidore was consecrated bishop of Seville in that same year.

I shall not linger over refuting the error of a certain Florentine codex of Isidore’s books *Against the Jews*, which I shall describe in chapter 43: namely, that Isidore was bishop of Toledo—whether this means that he was a native of Toledo and bishop of Seville, or that he held the episcopate of Toledo.

5. The distinguished deeds Isidore performed in administering the episcopate are narrated more fully and explicitly by the Canon of León and Rodericus of Cerrato in his *Life*. Although these deeds are not attested individually in the older monuments, they are certainly probable, and I am willing to believe that they are true in large part.

The first matter that seems worthy of investigation is whether he really built a monastery—or college—at Seville in which he might imbue young men with ecclesiastical disciplines. Not only do the authors just mentioned record this, but other more recent writers confirm it, saying that the Fathers of the Council of Trent took it as a model when establishing seminaries for the clergy.

Two considerations draw me toward this opinion: canon 24 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided, and the account of Cixila in the *Life of St. Ildefonsus*.

6. The Fourth Council of Toledo prescribes as follows in canon 24:

> Every age, from adolescence onward, is inclined toward evil; for nothing is more uncertain than the life of adolescents. Therefore it ought to be established that, if there are in the clergy any adults (another reading: minors) or adolescents, they should all live together in one chamber of the atrium, so that they may spend the years of slippery youth not in luxury but in ecclesiastical disciplines, assigned to a most approved elder whom they may have as a teacher of doctrine and witness of life . . . . Those, however, who resist these precepts are to be assigned to monasteries, so that their wandering and proud spirits may be restrained by a stricter rule.

Who, then, would not persuade himself that Isidore, even before this council had been held, had observed so useful an admonition?

7. Cixila adds this beginning to the *Life of St. Ildefonsus*:

> Behold the honey-sweet fare of that illustrious lord Ildefonsus, which, snatching from the Paradise of God and scattering throughout all Hesperia, satisfied our hunger with mighty eloquence. He was not unequal in merit to that most holy lord Isidore, from whose fountain he, while still a dependent, drank the purest waters. For when he had been sent by the holy and venerable Father Eugenius, metropolitan bishop of the see of Toledo, to the aforesaid teacher, the metropolitan bishop of Seville, although he already seemed learned to himself, he was so retained and polished by him—and, as they say, bound with temporal iron—that, if anything was lacking in his knowledge, he was more fully instructed. When he returned to his teacher, Lord Eugenius, after not many days, while he was still performing the office of deacon, he was appointed abbot in the church of Saints Cosmas and Damian, which is situated in the suburb of Toledo.

8. Writers of the thirteenth century and other more recent authors report that Braulio also emerged from that college at Seville, in which Ildefonsus was educated in ecclesiastical disciplines.

The Spanish offices of the saints celebrated on March 18, the feast of St. Braulio, agree with this:

> Having been entrusted to St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, to be instructed in letters, he first achieved this: that Isidore regarded him in the place of a most beloved son. Thereafter he valued him so highly that he entrusted his books to him for correction and arrangement.

But, as I indicated in chapter 4, this is not clearly established from ancient monuments. A more probable conjecture concerns Redemptus, who wrote the account of St. Isidore’s death. Since he is called a cleric of the church of Seville in very ancient parchment manuscripts, and calls Isidore his lord, it is reasonable to believe that he was educated among the other young clerics in the college at Seville.

## CHAPTER XXI

**Isidore subscribed the decree of Gundemar in the year 610. He then presided over the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo. Whether he also took part in other councils**

1. When, at the Council of Toledo held under Gundemar in the year 610, the bishops of the province of Carthage had declared that, according to the synodal judgment of the ancient Fathers, the authority of the metropolitan title over all the bishops of that province belonged to the bishop of Toledo, King Gundemar issued a decree in the same year by which he wished this declaration to be confirmed. After Gundemar, twenty-six bishops subscribed it who did not belong to the province of Carthage.

The first of these was Isidore, as follows:

> I, Isidore, metropolitan bishop of the province of the Baetican Church of Seville, having come to the city of Toledo for the royal assembly, after recognizing these constitutions, gave my assent and subscribed.

The metropolitan of Mérida follows, along with other bishops, among whom was Fulgentius of Écija, Isidore’s brother.

Those who invoke Gundemar’s decree in support of the primacy of the Church of Toledo over all the churches of Spain act with little prudence.

2. The following mention of Isidore occurs in the councils of Spain.

He presided over the Second Council of Seville, under King Sisebut, in the year 619—or 618, as Pagius and Mansius prefer in their notes on Baronius under the year 619. Rodericus of Toledo, book II, chapter 17, incorrectly extended the year of this council to the era 661, or A.D. 623.

Florezius, volume IX, p. 258, establishes the year 619, since all the manuscript codices cited by Perez and Loaisa agree in assigning it to the era 657. Accordingly, he concludes that the council was convened in the seventh year of Sisebut, not the ninth, as some copies have it.

In Dupin, volume V of the *Ecclesiastical Library*, the year 614 appears to be a typographical error for 618 or 619. Here is the opening:

> In the name of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ: We, Isidore, Bisinus, Ruffinus, Cambra, Fidentius, Theodulfus, and Honorius, bishops, who have assembled together in the city of Seville for certain ecclesiastical affairs, while we were seated in the sacristy of the holy church of Jerusalem of Seville, with the illustrious men Sisisclus, administrator of public affairs, and Suanila, administrator of the fiscal affairs, present, together with the most devout gathering of clerics.

The church of Seville is called Jerusalem, clearly after that city of Jerusalem which John describes in the Apocalypse.

3. The church of Mérida is likewise called Jerusalem in the Council of Mérida and in Paul of Mérida, chapter 12:

> Of the elder church, which is called Holy Jerusalem.

A similar expression occurs in the Gothic-Hispanic prayer book from the Veronese Codex published by Blanchinus, p. 65:

> Likewise, the concluding prayer after the completed praises, which they proceed by chanting as far as Holy Jerusalem, is to be said in honor of St. Fructuosus.

The reference is to the church of Tarragona, which was dedicated to St. Fructuosus. Florezius, volume IX, p. 100, demonstrates from Redemptus’s account of Isidore’s death and from other ancient monuments that the principal church of Seville was dedicated to St. Vincent.

As for interpreting the word *secretarium* as a hall of the church in which the council was held privately, with the doors closed, and explaining the matter of the Syrian bishop—which is said at the end to have been settled in three *secretaria*—as having been decided in three private sessions, and as for asserting that this meaning of *secretarium* is absent from Ducange’s dictionary and could be added, this misses the point entirely.

For a *secretarium* was the sanctuary of churches, now called the sacristy. Ducange demonstrates with many examples that councils were accustomed to assemble in the *secretarium*. He adds:

> Hence the sessions themselves of councils are almost always called *secretaria*,

and he produces further evidence. I pass over the highly learned work of Cancellierius, *On the Secretariums of the Ancients*.

Sisisclus, administrator of public affairs—or administrator of the public grain supply—and Suanila, or Suinthila, curator of the royal patrimony, were present. The latter was the son of Reccared, later appointed commander of the army by Sisebut, subsequently raised to the kingship, and finally deposed by Sisenand and the Fourth Council of Toledo, as Pueyus notes.

4. This Second Council of Seville is learned and scholarly, rich in the wisdom of civil and canon law, as Loaisa rightly says in his notes. Among other matters, chapter 2 dealt with the dispute between Fulgentius, bishop of Écija and Isidore’s brother, and Honorius, bishop of Córdoba, concerning a parish church which one of them asserted was Coelesticense and the other Reginense.

5. In his preliminary notice to Isidore’s works, Braulio reports the following concerning Isidore’s actions at this council:

> The synodal acts held before him at Seville declare with what flood of eloquence, and with how many darts drawn from divine Scripture or the testimonies of the Fathers, he pierced the heresy of the Acephalites. In this matter, against Gregory, the bishop of the aforesaid heresy, he asserted the truth.

Braulio attributes to Isidore at least that portion of the acts in which the Acephalian heresy is discussed.

Isidore of Pacensis, in his *Chronicle* under the era 650, says:

> Spain celebrates Isidore, metropolitan pontiff of Seville, a distinguished teacher, who in the seventh year of the aforementioned ruler Sisebut, with great authority, conducted a council at Seville in the sacristy of Holy Jerusalem against the heresy of the Acephali.

Florezius, volume IX, p. 258, thinks that this was not the principal reason for convening the synod, but rather other ecclesiastical affairs, and that, once the council had begun, this new contest against the Acephali arose. I consider this less probable. Although some lesser matters were decided first, the dispute against the Syrian bishop could nevertheless have been postponed because it required a more careful examination.

Florezius further thinks, p. 261, that the entire council should be attributed to Isidore’s teaching. Cellierius likewise says, in volume XVII, that the canons of the Second Council of Seville reveal a zeal for the discipline of the ancient Church, and that they should be regarded as Isidore’s work.

This council will therefore rightly be placed among the appendices, especially since Isidore of Pacensis continues at the place cited:

> And by the truthful testimonies of the teachers he overcomes a certain Syrian bishop of the Acephali, who defended the aforementioned heresy; he confirms the true assertions of the council, condemns him by his eloquence, and, by pursuing him for a long time, finally frees the aforesaid pontiff from his former error.

6. The eight bishops named in the opening subscribe, with Isidore in the first place:

> Isidore, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Seville, have subscribed.

In the fourth place:

> Fulgentius, in the name of Christ, bishop of the Church of Écija, have subscribed.

Loaisa notes several matters concerning the heresy of the Acephali from Isidore, book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, and from Nicephorus, book XVIII of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 45.

7. From the Sixth Council of Toledo, convened in the year 638, it is demonstrated that, after this Second Council of Seville and before the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633, there was another Council of Seville.

Among the acts of this Sixth Council of Toledo there is a copy of the judgment between the bishops Martianus and Habentius, in which we read:

> Formerly, at the Council of Seville, Martianus, bishop of the Church of Écija, was deprived of office on the basis of false accusations. He then fled to the remedy of the present universal council to be purged, and with an unworthy plea begged that the judgment of his condemnation be reconsidered. For at the preceding universal council he had been heard in part and restored only to his rank, not to his see, because lack of time had prevented his case from being fully examined.

Some think that this refers to the Fifth Council of Toledo, which the bishop of Écija did not attend, and at which they believe Martianus’s case began to be reconsidered. But since the preceding council, at which Martianus had been heard in part, is called universal—that is, national—it cannot be understood as the Fifth Council, which was attended by only twenty-four bishops, together with episcopal vicars, and one metropolitan, namely Eugenius, bishop of Toledo.

It is indeed said that priests from various provinces of Spain assembled; but when the council was national, the priests of Spain and Gaul assembled, among whom there were three, four, or five metropolitans. We must therefore understand this to refer to the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided and which Habentius, bishop of Écija, attended.

8. After Fulgentius’s death, Martianus succeeded him following the Second Council of Seville. Martianus was deprived of office at a certain Council of Seville, and Habentius was substituted for him; as I have just said, Habentius subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo.

Martianus must therefore have been condemned at a Council of Seville over which Isidore, then metropolitan of the Church of Seville, necessarily presided. At the Fourth Council of Toledo, as I interpret the matter, Martianus was restored to his rank but not to his see. For this reason Habentius subscribed as bishop of the Church of Écija.

No bishop of Écija attended the Fifth Council of Toledo, since it was not a universal, or national, council. At the Fifth Council of Toledo, when the judgment was reconsidered, Habentius was removed from the see of the Church of Écija and Martianus was restored, while Habentius, under the obligation of penitential satisfaction, was placed under Martianus but retained his honor. False accusations had been gathered against Martianus through Habentius’s counsel and assistance.

9. Concerning the judges in whose presence Martianus was cast down or deposed, it is decreed that they judged not through cunning or by corrupting the judgment, but that the deceit of the witnesses deceived them. Therefore the right of appeal against them was denied both to the bishops Habentius and Martianus.

Isidore, already dead, seems to be included among these judges. For the text begins:

> Although the greater part of the judges had already departed from the present life, etc.

But it cannot be established with certainty that Martianus was condemned with Isidore’s vote. For the acts continue their account of Martianus as follows:

> Nor did he receive a unanimous sentence from those judges, since some of them, as they themselves confessed, declared him innocent at that time, while others proclaimed him guilty.

10. It is difficult to determine in what year Martianus was deposed at the Council of Seville. But since, in the year 638, most of Martianus’s judges had already died, we may infer that Fulgentius, bishop of Écija, did not long survive the Second Council of Seville, to which he subscribed. His successor Martianus was deprived of office after a few years, perhaps around the year 624.

Neither Martianus nor Habentius subscribed the Sixth Council of Toledo. The judgment between them was first published by Florezius and later reprinted in the *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, arranged by Silvester Pueyo after the model of the body of canon law.

Habentius subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo in thirty-eighth place, after which another twenty-four bishops subscribed. This suggests that Habentius had occupied the see of Écija for many years after Martianus’s expulsion. For in subscriptions the order of seniority was generally preserved.

11. Isidore also presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo in the year 633. This was a national council, the most famous of all the councils of Spain, and one of great authority throughout the universal Church.

Baronius says concerning it under the year 633, no. 68:

> St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, presided; he was listed first in order and placed before the others in the bishops’ subscriptions. From this there can be no doubt that this council was a noble offspring of Isidore himself, properly formed and adorned by the judgments of the other bishops.

Florezius adopts nearly the same view in volume IX, p. 196. He says that Isidore presided because he was older than the other metropolitans, not because—as Cellierius maintains—he surpassed the others in learning and holiness.

Isidore of Pacensis merely reports that Sisenand celebrated this council while Isidore of Seville was still bishop, “shining brilliantly in many books.” Mabillonius, volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 361, adds that St. Isidore was the author of the canons of this Fourth Council of Toledo.

12. Sisenand, who succeeded Suinthila after depriving him of his kingdom, summoned a synod of the entire nation and all the provinces in order to consolidate his power.

The final chapter, chapter 75, begins as follows:

> After certain provisions of ecclesiastical order, or decrees relating to the discipline of particular persons, our final judgment as a body of priests is that, for the strength of our kings and the stability of the Gothic nation, we should issue a final pontifical decree under the judgment of God.

Sixty-nine men subscribed, partly bishops and partly episcopal vicars. In the first place:

> I, Isidore, in the name of Christ, metropolitan bishop of the Church of Seville, have subscribed.

In the fifth place:

> Justus, metropolitan of the Church of Toledo, have subscribed.

In the fifty-fourth place:

> Braulio, bishop of the Church of Zaragoza, have subscribed.
