13. This is the council at which, according to the authors of the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle* under the name of Ildefonsus and of the *Life of St. Isidore*, Isidore is said to have predicted the destruction of Spain.

The same prophecy is explained at greater length in the fuller acts of the translation of St. Isidore’s body among the Bollandists. The more ancient writers are silent.

Tamayus, in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, thinks that this was not a true prophecy but the prudent conjecture of a wise man.

Loaisa, in his dissertation on the primacy of the Church of Toledo, which he inserted into the *Councils of Spain* after Gundemar’s decree of the year 610, asserts in section 3 that Justus, metropolitan of Toledo, presided over this council. But he adds:

> Some maintain that Isidore carried out a legation of the Apostolic See at this council and presided over it.

Yet Loaisa himself assigns Isidore the first place in the subscriptions. How, then, could he have inferred that Justus presided?

14. From Braulio’s letters I infer that Isidore attended, or even presided over, a certain synod at which the case of a certain Sintharius was discussed.

In the letter beginning “O pious Lord,” Braulio addresses Isidore as follows:

> I earnestly suggest and beg with every kind of supplication that, remembering your promise to your servant, you order the book of the *Etymologies*, which, by the Lord’s favor, we have heard to be completed, to be sent to me. For, as I am conscious, you have labored greatly there at the request of your servant. Therefore be generous toward me first, so that in the heavenly dwellings of the saints you may be considered both blessed and first.
>
> I also beg that, at your urging, the acts of the synod in which Sintharius is found to have been, though not purified, nevertheless melted down in the fire of your examination, be sent to us quickly by your son, our lord the king. For our own petition likewise sought his glory, since there is great need in the council to investigate the truth.

In the copy of the Bignaean edition in the Vatican Library, beside the words *Sintharius examinis vestri*—or, as it is corruptly printed there, *Sintaurius exanimis vestri*—this manuscript note is written:

> in which there is a treasury, *examinis vestri*, etc.

But the proper name Sintharius must be retained, as most copies confirm it; and that the name was not unknown among the Spaniards is clear from the Spanish councils.

15. This council, in which Isidore’s learning and virtue shone forth so greatly against Sintharius, was certainly not the Fourth Council of Toledo, held in the year 633. This is clear not only because nothing about Sintharius is read in its acts, but also because Braulio’s letter had been written long before that time, as I shall now explain.

Braulio asked Isidore for the book of the *Etymologies*, which he had heard was completed. After several years, apparently, Braulio again requested the book in another letter, which has been lost, as may be gathered from Isidore’s reply:

> Since I found you safe and well, etc.

There Isidore says:

> I was not worthy to read through your words. As soon as I received your little letter, a royal servant came to me. I gave your little letter to my chamberlain and immediately went to the prince, intending afterward to read it and write back. When I returned from the royal palace, I found not only your writing missing but also everything else that had been on the papers; it had all perished.

16. Braulio then wrote a longer letter in reply, in which he says:

> It is, if I am not mistaken, the seventh year that has revolved since I remember asking you for the books entitled *Origins*. In various and different ways, both when I was present you have frustrated me, and when I was absent you have written me nothing about them. At one time you alleged that they were not yet finished, at another that they were not yet written, at another that my letters had been lost, together with many other excuses. We have reached this day, and remain without the result of our request.

Braulio wrote this before the year 633. For in that year Audax, bishop of Tarragona, subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo, while Braulio wrote his letters when the see of Tarragona was vacant through the death of its predecessor, Eusebius.

Thus the synod against Sintharius appears to have been held in the year 625, or earlier.

17. But who is this Sintharius, and what was his case? I find nothing about the matter except that, at the Council of Egara in 614, Sintharius the bishop signed in eleventh place. Some suspect that this Sintharius who signed at the Council of Egara was Sisaldus, bishop of Emporiae, who took part in the Fourth Council of Toledo. But since the name Sintharius occurs in Braulio’s letter, there is no reason why we should not read Sintharius in the subscriptions of the Council of Egara in the same way.

18. Cellier, volume XVII, observes that the subject cannot be the Syrian bishop who was converted to the Catholic faith at the Second Council of Seville, nor is there reason to suspect that Gregory was called Sintharius. For Braulio speaks of Sintharius, who, although he had been boiled down—or convicted—had nevertheless not been purified, that is, converted to a better way of life. “If Sintharius,” he adds, “is Suinthila, the Gothic king, the acts must be understood to be those of the Fourth Council of Toledo, at which Suinthila was struck with anathema.” This suspicion is excluded, among other considerations, by the chronology.

It is more credible that Sintharius was the name of that bishop of Córdoba concerning whom Isidore wrote to Helladius of Toledo and the other bishops assembled with him:

> We beseech your holiness that, once this same fallen man has been presented to your holy assembly and you have recognized the language of his confession, he be deposed from the rank of the priesthood by synodal judgment.

Although Padilla, *Ecclesiastical History*, century VII, chapter 32, and Gómez Bravo, *On the Bishops of Córdoba*, p. 72, strongly doubt whether that letter is genuinely Isidore’s, Flórez, volume IX, p. 254, refutes them on the grounds that, being ignorant of the ecclesiastical discipline of those times, they thought that the letter could in some way be used to impugn the primacy of the Church of Toledo. Hernández later undertook to attack the same letter with stronger arguments; we shall discuss them in chapter 74.

Risco, volume XXX of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 154, believes that Braulio’s letter was written shortly before the Fourth Council of Toledo, to which Braulio intended to come, prepared by his reading of the acts of the Second Council of Seville against Gregory. But, as I said, this cannot be maintained, nor is it plausible that Braulio, after so many years, was ignorant of the proceedings of the Second Council of Seville, or that he ought to have sought permission from the king.

Finally, someone might suspect that by that name Braulio meant Martianus, mentioned above, who had been deprived of office. In that case one might conjecture that *Centaurus* should be read instead of *Sintharius*: for that is what clerics who involved themselves excessively in worldly affairs were accustomed to be called.

19. In the letter in which Isidore replies to Braulio and says that he has sent him the *Codex of the Etymologies*—that is, while the see of Tarragona was vacant—there is mention of another council to which Isidore had been summoned. Isidore reports it as follows:

> Your Holiness’s letter found me in the city of Toledo; for I had been stirred on account of a council. Although the ruler’s command, once I was already on the road, had instructed me to return, nevertheless, since I was nearer to his presence than to turning back, I preferred not to interrupt the course of my journey.

It appears that this council had been summoned and soon afterward suspended. Perhaps it was the council that was subsequently held in 633, namely the Fourth Council of Toledo, which the king had wished to celebrate before that time but postponed to another occasion for certain reasons. Braulio ought to have attended that council; but when the king changed his mind, Isidore—who had brought the *Codex of the Etymologies* to present to Braulio—sent it to him from the road.

20. For Isidore says:

> I sent the *Codex of the Etymologies*, together with other books, from the road. Although it was uncorrected because of my illness, I had nevertheless intended to offer it to you for correction, if I had reached the appointed place of the council.

I would more readily read “if you had reached” than “if I had reached”; for Isidore, who did not interrupt the course of his journey, seems to have arrived at the appointed place, even though the council was not held. This journey of Isidore to the city of Toledo may be assigned approximately to the year 631.

Braulio had recommended his deacon for the bishopric of Tarragona, which was then vacant. Isidore replies:

> As for appointing the bishop of Tarragona, I did not perceive in the king the opinion you requested; yet it remains uncertain even to him where he will more firmly direct his mind.

Flórez, volume XXV of *Hispania Sacra*, conjectures that Eusebius was bishop of Tarragona around the year 632; Audax had succeeded him by 633.

## CHAPTER XXII. Whether a pallium was sent to Isidore by the Roman pontiff; whether Isidore held the primacy of Spain, or exercised the functions of the Roman pontiff in Spain

[Col. 0125D]

1. In the ancient readings of the Office of the Saints of Spain it is asserted that Saint Gregory the Great confirmed Isidore’s election as bishop of Seville and sent him a pallium to Spain. In the readings of the Roman Breviary this is expressed as follows:

> His election is said to have been confirmed by Saint Gregory the Great not only with apostolic authority, but also to have been adorned, after the customary fashion, by the pallium sent to him after his election; indeed, he is said to have been appointed his own vicar and the vicar of the Apostolic See throughout all Spain.

The author of the *Life* confirms that Gregory granted Isidore both the pallium and the honor of primacy. The author of the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle*, in book III of the *Chronicles* of Lucas of Tuy, puts it briefly:

> Flourishing in the dignity of primacy and exercising the functions of the Roman pope in Spain.

He then relates that, under Theodisclus the apostate, Isidore’s successor, the dignity of primacy was transferred to the Church of Toledo.

2. We have no authors of any of these matters earlier than the thirteenth century. As for the pallium, certainly we must not measure ancient times by our own customs. In our time the pallium is sent to all archbishops; formerly the matter was different. Saint Gregory the Great writes in book VII, letter 5:

> An ancient custom has prevailed that the honor of the pallium should not be granted unless the merits of the circumstances require it and the person concerned makes a vigorous request.

That honor was especially obtained by those who came to the threshold of the Apostles. Later the pallium began to be sent through legates of the Apostolic See, and finally through agents, as is now done: these agents earnestly, more earnestly, and most earnestly request the pallium from the supreme pontiff in the consistory on behalf of archbishops, as is now customary for all archbishops.

There are innumerable authors who discuss the pallium. Among more recent writers one may consult the dissertation of Father Giovanni Lorenzo Berti in his vernacular prose works, p. 273, reprinted in Zaccaria’s collection of dissertations in the Italian language, volume IX, p. 223: “On the prescribed subject of the antiquity of the pallium, and whether it was once granted only to metropolitans.”

3. Although Isidore was a metropolitan and, on account of his exceptional merits, most worthy of the honor of the pallium, it cannot immediately be inferred with certainty that he received a pallium either from Saint Gregory or from another pontiff. Nevertheless, I consider it highly probable that Isidore was not deprived of the honor of the pallium.

For at times the Roman pontiffs appear to have sent the pallium even to those who had not requested it, if they otherwise excelled through extraordinary virtue and learning. When Gregory the Great sent the pallium to Leander, he makes no mention of a request. In book VII, letter 126, he writes:

> Moreover, from the blessing of blessed Peter, prince of the Apostles, we have sent you the pallium, to be used only for the solemn celebrations of Mass. After sending it, I ought to have admonished you at length concerning how you should live; but I suppress my words, because you surpass words by your conduct.

And in the following letter to Reccared, king of Spain:

> To our most reverend brother and fellow bishop Leander we have sent the pallium from the see of blessed Peter the Apostle; we owe this both to the ancient custom, to our practices, and to his goodness and dignity.

These statements sufficiently suggest that no request for the pallium had previously been made in Leander’s name. It is therefore credible that Isidore, whose learning and holiness of life had aroused everyone’s admiration, possessed a pallium sent by some Roman pontiff, even if he had not requested it.

4. The fact that Isidore presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo may also be relevant here. Five other metropolitans took part in it: Selva of Narbonne, Stephen of Mérida, Julian of Braga, Justus of Toledo, and Audax of Tarragona. This itself may indicate that he held the primacy of the Church of Spain and exercised the functions of the Roman pontiff.

The story of Theodiscus, or Theodistus, bishop of Seville, is certainly fabulous. He is said to have succeeded Saint Isidore—or, as others maintain, Honoratus, bishop of Seville, after Saint Isidore—and, after he was sent into exile, the dignity of primacy is said to have been transferred from Seville to the Church of Toledo. Besides Pseudo-Ildefonsus, in the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle*, this is also related by Rodrigo of Toledo, book II, chapter 21.

Nicholas Antonius, speaking of Saint Isidore in book V, chapter 3, no. 70, writes:

> I fear that the assertion that Pope Gregory confirmed his election as bishop and created him legate of the Apostolic See and primate was written without sufficient foundation in a certain breviary at Cajetanus, p. 14, in Gonzales, *Theatrum Hispaniae*, in Tamayo on 14 April, and by Lucas of Tuy at the beginning of book III of the *Chronicle* and in the *Life of Isidore*.

Nevertheless, he adds:

> Let us grant this last point to our breviaries and to Seville as his birthplace—something which Baronius also admitted under the year 636.

When Nicholas Antonius discusses Isidore’s letter to Helladius and the other bishops gathered with him, so that they might investigate the case of the bishop of Córdoba who had fallen into a charge involving sexual misconduct, he adds that from this it may in some way be inferred that an apostolic delegation, or the rights of primacy, had been granted to Isidore.

5. Nicholas Antonius had nothing else to offer in support of Seville, his native city. But Baronius took from Pseudo-Ildefonsus, in the *Chronicles* of Lucas of Tuy, the account both of the primatial dignity and of the vicariate of the Roman pontiff in Spain, as well as of Theodiscus’s succession and heresy, and of the transfer of the primatial dignity from the Church of Seville to that of Toledo, although Nicholas Antonius considers the entire history of Theodiscus fabricated.

“This is the account of Tuy,” says Baronius, “which Francis Pegna, my most devoted auditor of the Rota, granted us as copied from the original.” Baronius calls him Theodiscus and transcribes the words concerning Isidore’s primacy as follows:

> Flourishing in primatial dignity and exercising the functions of the Roman pope in Spain.

And afterward:

> At that time the dignity of primacy was transferred to the Church of Toledo.

Aguirre dismisses this same tale of Theodiscus with a hiss in *Collectio conciliorum Hispaniae*, volume I, pp. 85 ff., dissertation 4, excursus 7, whose title is: “Who was the interpolator and corrupter of those same letters—the False Decretals of Pseudo-Isidore—or perhaps Theodiscus, successor of Saint Isidore in the bishopric of Seville?” The testimony published by Lucas of Tuy under the name of Saint Ildefonsus of Toledo is presented and examined. It is shown, however, to be either spurious or highly suspect.

6. Some maintain that the primacy of the churches of Spain had long rested with the metropolitan of Seville. They support this by pointing out that Simplicius, the Roman pontiff, appointed Zeno, bishop of Seville, as his vicar, and that Hormisdas entrusted his functions to Sallustius, bishop of Seville, in the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania.

These facts, however, do not at all prove that the primacy of the Spains and the honor of a pontifical vicariate were attached to the see of Seville either by ancient custom or by some papal privilege.

As for what they add specifically in Isidore’s favor—that Braulio calls him “the highest of the bishops” in the title of the letter beginning “O pious lord”—this should rather be referred to Isidore’s supreme virtue and learning than to any dignity by which he is understood to have ranked above the other bishops.

Braulio may also have hinted that Isidore already customarily presided over councils. For in that very letter he writes:

> Therefore, be generous first toward me; thus in the assemblies of the saints you may be regarded as both blessed and first. I ask that, at your prompting, the proceedings of the synod in which Sintharius is found to have been boiled down, though not purified, by the fire of your examination be sent to us quickly by your son, our lord the king.

There is little difference in the wording of another letter beginning “So it is accustomed to be filled,” where Braulio speaks of Isidore as follows:

> Relying also on a special grace toward a special lord, in whom the strength of the Church resides, I submit, etc.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Whether Isidore ever came to Rome, to the pontiff or to a council; whether the book *On the Order of Created Things* is Isidore’s

1. The first extraordinary story of Isidore’s arrival in the city of Rome, which some relate or invent, was indicated in chapter 18. We must now discuss his journey, as they say, to a general council convened at Rome.

In the old breviaries of Spain we read:

> Finally, such was the reputation for Isidore’s learning and holiness that, when a general council had been convened, he was voluntarily summoned by the supreme pontiff.

There it is remarkable how much weight and authority Isidore’s opinion possessed with the pontiff and all the prelates in individual matters.

This account is given more fully in the *Life of Isidore* by the Leonese canon. The Bollandists observe there that it may have been some non-public or solemn council, such as the two councils held at Rome in 601. In fact, the author of the *Life* by no means indicates that it was a general council; rather, he suggests that Isidore was not summoned from Spain to the council, but that, while Isidore was already present in Rome, consideration was given to summoning him so that the synodal proceedings might be guided by his counsel.

2. Nicholas Antonius seems to have read in some breviary that Gregory the Great was the pontiff who summoned Isidore to attend the Roman council. He concludes, however, that this probably cannot be true, since during the last years of Saint Gregory, when Isidore was his contemporary, and likewise during the pontificates of Gregory’s successors Sabinian, Boniface III, Boniface IV, Deusdedit, Boniface V, and Honorius I—under whom this light of Spain was extinguished—no general council was held in the city to which the bishop of Seville ought to have been summoned.

These considerations may indeed prove that the detail concerning a general council, found in the ancient readings, is false; but they do not weaken the Bollandists’ interpretation that the synod was non-public or solemn.

3. Tamayo, in the *Martyrology of Spain*, cites very ancient Spanish breviaries—the breviaries of Ávila, Compostela, Sigüenza, Tarazona, Huesca, Zaragoza, and others—which relate that Isidore was summoned by Gregory the Great to Rome for a general council and that the proceedings were successfully completed through Isidore’s counsels.

Tamayo adds that this is not certain. As for the cause of Isidore’s Roman journey, he refers to Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 21; Mariana, book VI, chapter 7; and Padilla, *Seventh Century*, chapter 22.

4. Since this Roman journey of Isidore rests only on monuments no earlier than the twelfth century, we must inquire whether the account can be supported by any conjecture.

5. I pass over for the moment what I shall discuss elsewhere: that some believed Isidore died at Bologna on his return from Rome to Spain, and that his body still rests in the church of the Celestines in that city. For our writers who relate Isidore’s Roman journey affirm that he returned to Spain and exchanged life for death at Seville.

Some trace of such a journey, however, appears in the book *On the Order of Created Things*, which bears the name of Saint Isidore. Acherius—or, if you prefer, Dacherius or D’Acherius—published it in his *Spicilegium* from a manuscript copied not far from Isidore’s age in the Benedictine monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims.

The book is dedicated to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome. Henschenius, in his preliminary commentary on the *Life of Isidore*, conjectures that “Braulio” should be read as “Boniface, bishop of the city of Rome.” Since the author of the work seems to address the person to whom he dedicates it as present, and says that he is hastening to his homeland, it is inferred from this that Isidore had at some time been in Rome under one of the Bonifaces who held the Roman see at the beginning of the seventh century.

6. Three matters must nevertheless be disentangled here. First, whether the book *On the Order of Created Things* should be assigned to Isidore; next, whether the name Braulio should be retained in the title or the name Boniface restored; and finally, whether it is correctly inferred that Isidore was physically present in Rome, if it is established that the book was written by him and addressed to Boniface, the Roman pontiff.

Bellarmin, Cave, Placcius, and other chiefly early bibliographers say nothing at all about such a book. Others, such as Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca media*, reach no conclusion. Acherius, Henschenius, Du Pin, and Cellier recognize Isidorian style in the work. Nicholas Antonius calls it the style of Isidore’s age, but notes certain statements about purgatorial fire that do not entirely please him.

In the latest Madrid edition of the works of Saint Isidore, the book *On the Order of Created Things* was omitted because, as the author of the prologue says, it is either a spurious work or excessively suspect. Bayer, however, writes in a note to the *Ancient Library of Spain*:

> We do not hesitate to ascribe this work to Isidore, even though the prologue of the latest Madrid edition objects.

Zaccaria remained uncertain, in the prospectus of the edition of Isidore’s works that he was planning, whether the work could be attributed to Isidore. A very learned man who had prepared a preface to Isidore’s works, chapter 38, for transcription, demonstrates at length that the book appears to be a genuine offspring of Isidore and argues that the passages in it concerning the origin of souls and purgatorial fire present no obstacle.

7. Let us examine the old copies. The manuscript indicated by Acherius, in which the book *On the Order of Created Things* is attributed to Isidore, was old and not far removed from Isidore’s age. Bayer testifies that, in a very ancient Escorial manuscript from the beginning of the eighth century, shelfmark R, pluteus 2, no. 18, there is a single book of Isidore *On the Order of Created Things*. He does not explain whether the heading adds “to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome.”

The same Bayer saw another copy of the work in an Escorial manuscript, shelfmark E, pluteus 4, no. 13, apparently written in the thirteenth century but copied from an older and distinctly Gothic manuscript, as is clear from the frequent Gothicisms scattered throughout it.

It gives no heading, but Bayer notes that the peroration, or dedication, of the work is somewhat fuller than the one published by Acherius and concludes as follows:

> Blessed be God, who brought the labor to an end. Isidore’s *On the Order of Created Things* ends.

Rodriguez, volume II of the *Spanish Library*, p. 326, believes that the manuscript was written in the fourteenth century. He adds that it is on parchment, in octavo, with the chapter titles, initial letters, and index in red, and with a more recent inscription:

> Blessed Isidore, *On the Order of Created Things*. And homilies on “The angel Gabriel was sent.”

The work begins:

> The ordering of the universe must be understood in a twofold manner.

The homilies begin:

> Devotion also commands me to write something, etc.

They end:

> the eighth age of the blessed resurrection, in which they will reign perpetually with the Lord . . .

They are imperfect and mutilated, and, in my opinion, they are not attributed to Isidore in the manuscript.

8. Bandini, volume III of the *Latin Manuscripts of the Florentine Gaddian Library*, pluteus 89, manuscript 31, a parchment manuscript of the twelfth century, no. 1, contains:

> Isidore’s book *On the Order of Created Things*.

It begins:

> The ordering of the universe:

and ends:

> Let us reserve it for the knowledge of the Creator.

Bandini observes that this book *On the Order of Created Things*, addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome, was published by Dacherius and is thirty-nine verses longer there. At the bottom of the page he notes that Jacopo Gaddi, *On Non-Ecclesiastical Writers*, volume I, p. 263, mentions the manuscripts of Isidore’s works existing in the Gaddian Library.

But the fact that this book was addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome, was learned by Bandini not, as I believe, from the Gaddian manuscript, but from Acherius or Dacherius. For my friend Rochus Menchaca, when I asked him to inspect the title of the work carefully and report to me about it, replied that the rubric at the beginning reads:

> Here begins Isidore’s book *On the Order of Created Things*;

and at the end:

> Isidore’s book *On the Order of Created Things* ends.

In the old catalogue of the monastery of Bobbio, apparently written in the tenth century and published by Muratori, volume III of *Italian Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, p. 818, the *Book on the Order of Created Things* is listed among the books of Isidore in the older library. I do not know whether the Book of Canons I, mentioned immediately afterward, belongs here, in which there is a work entitled *Isidore’s On the Order of Things*.

Likewise, among the old books of the monastery of Fulda and of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch there was a *Book of Isidore on the Order of Created Things* in a single manuscript, as I shall say in chapter 46 from the oldest catalogues.

9. Saint Martin of León, sermon 2 *On the Advent of the Lord*, p. 27, volume I, assigns the book *On the Order of Created Things* to Isidore. He reports:

> Therefore Isidore, the teacher of the Spains, explaining that passage of Isaiah, says: “After judgment, or as the reward for his labor, he will receive [it].” Hence the prophet says: “The sun will shine sevenfold,” etc.

The very learned editor observes that Saint Martin constructed this from the *Master of the Sentences*, book IV, distinction 48, section “Some think,” which argues from chapter 5 of the book *On the Order of Created Things* that Isidore explained the passage from Isaiah in this way.

He adds that it is reasonably doubtful whether such a book *On the Order of Created Things* is Isidore’s, and that elsewhere one reads only this statement:

> When . . . the saints shine with the reward of their labor . . . like the sun of righteousness . . . then, as the reward of their ministry, the radiance of this corporeal sun itself will also be restored sevenfold.

Again Martin of León cites the same fifth chapter of the book *On the Order of Created Things* in sermon 2 *On the Resurrection of the Lord*, p. 411, volume II, in these words:

> Hence the distinguished teacher Isidore says: “On that day the sun will not set, nor the moon, but they will remain in the order in which they were created, lest the wicked, placed beneath the earth in torments, enjoy their light.”

The editor again observes that these words were extracted from the *Master of the Sentences*, book IV, distinction 45. Let us therefore conclude that the *Master of the Sentences* regarded the book *On the Order of Created Things* as Isidorian, with Martin of León either approving or not dissenting.

10. Acherius, who, as we said, published this book from a manuscript at Reims, noted in the margin that he had found it cited by Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in his treatise *Against the Greeks*, but under another title, namely: “Isidore, *On the Catholic Faith*.”

Nicholas Antonius fears that this should instead be referred to the books *On the Catholic Faith against the Jews*, addressed to his sister Florentina.

The work *Against the Greeks* by Aeneas of Paris, who flourished in the ninth century, was published by Dacherius himself in volume VII of the *Spicilegium*. In it I find Isidore praised from the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, from the book of *Differences*, and from the books of *Etymologies* and *Sentences*. But I do not find him cited from the book *On the Order of Created Things* under the title *On the Catholic Faith*, as Dacherius asserted in the preface to this book, nor from the book *On the Catholic Faith against the Jews*, as Nicholas Antonius suspected.

11. Since the style of the work *On the Order of Created Things* bears the stamp of Isidore, as the most authoritative scholars agree, and the oldest manuscripts clearly attribute it to Isidore, it must be held to have proceeded from Isidore’s hand unless something else stands in the way.

The only objection is that in the manuscript at Reims the book is said to have been addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome. I do not know whether this is expressed in the same way in other manuscripts. In the Florentine Gaddian manuscript those words concerning Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome, are entirely absent, as they are also in the Escorial manuscript.

But even if other manuscripts agree in this dedication, it by no means proves that the work is not Saint Isidore’s. It may have been added by someone else without any foundation, or with some foundation. Since the titles of works in manuscripts are generally extremely corrupt, the work should not be taken away from Isidore because of the difficulty posed by this title, when it is clearly attributed to him in many places.

In Ottobonian manuscript 404, the work *Etymologies* is said to be dedicated to Ambrose; for I find “Ambrose” written where “Braulio” should be. In Ottobonian manuscript 477, Braulio’s name is indicated more than once only by its first letter, B, although in this manuscript Braulio’s full name is written out in some places.

12. The heading published by Acherius can be explained in two ways: either all its words may be retained, or “Boniface” may be read in place of “Braulio.”

If the name Braulio is retained, we must then determine how Caesaraugusta, the city of which Braulio was bishop, can be called Rome, since Acherius added “of the city of Rome” by way of explanation—that is, Caesaraugusta.

Nicholas Antonius devotes considerable space to explaining this controversy. The substance of the matter is as follows. The *Forum of Judges*, or book of Gothic laws, in its preface, volume III of *Hispania Illustrata*, mentions a city of Rome in Spain. It seems to be called this because it was the royal court. Cixila, in the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*, called Toledo the Romulean see.

Just as, in ecclesiastical writings, the Spaniards called any metropolitan church Jerusalem, as was observed in chapter 21, so in secular writings any royal city was, by antonomasia or excellence, called Rome.

13. But since Caesaraugusta was never a royal city in the time of the Goths, Nicholas Antonius reasonably says in the preface to the reader of the first volume of the *Spicilegium* that the inscription addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome, should be regarded as suspect by Dacherius—unless one says that those cities also which had at some time enjoyed some prerogative of the city of Rome, sacred or secular, earned the name “second Rome” or “another Rome.”

Thus, in the epitaph of Cardinal Ivo, buried at Trier:

> Rome, the second Rome, granted me venerable funeral rites.

This appears in Brower, book XIV of the *Annals of Trier*. Likewise Gerard, chapter 6 *On the Miracles of Saint Adelhard*:

> From then on the fame of this matter began to spread so far and wide that Corbie—the monastery of Corbie—was rightly regarded as deserving to be called another Rome.

Mabillon gives another example concerning the city of Tours, the second see of the Roman city, in his *Analecta*, p. 16. Flórez, volume V of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 512, no. 15, defends this same interpretation of “the city of Rome,” that is, Caesaraugusta.

14. Bayer, in a note to the *Ancient Library of Spain*, replies that these are mere divinations and, if one may philosophize freely, “the most inept of ineptitudes.”

Risco, the continuator of *Hispania Sacra*, volume XXX, treatise 66, chapter 3, no. 21, proves in a similar way that Caesaraugusta was never called Rome and that the work *On the Order of Created Things* was addressed not to Braulio but to Boniface, the Roman pontiff. He adds that it is not Isidore’s work, apparently following the judgment of the Bollandists and, I think, Flórez, who in volume IX, p. 197, abandoning the position he had embraced in volume V, said that the judgment of the Bollandists should be preferred, since they do not agree that the work is Isidore’s.

The Bollandists, however, conjecture that “Boniface” should be read in place of “Braulio,” and add:

> We determine nothing here by our own conjecture,

since they did not have time to read the whole little work more attentively. For my part, I am entirely unwilling to apply to Braulio—and still less to Saint Isidore—the title “bishop of the city of Rome,” which is everywhere assigned as proper to the Roman pontiff.

15. Moreover, Bayer sets out other arguments against believing that the work *On the Order of Created Things* was dedicated by Isidore to Braulio. Braulio was not a man of such authority that Isidore would dedicate a little work to him with such reverence and humility: calling him “Venerable Father,” saying that his fear would keep the envious and talkative in line, commending his authority, and repeatedly professing his own obedience, submission, and veneration toward him.

Isidore customarily addressed Braulio in an entirely different style—as an old man addresses a young man, as a teacher addresses a disciple, although perhaps Braulio did not live under Isidore’s discipline.

Henschenius’ conjecture is therefore exceedingly probable and almost necessary: “Boniface” should be restored in place of “Braulio” in the title of the work. Of the three Bonifaces who were Roman pontiffs at the beginning of the seventh century, the most likely is Boniface V, to whom Isidore may have dedicated his work after being consulted by him. Boniface V held the pontificate from 617 to 625, at which time Isidore’s name and teaching had already spread everywhere.

16. Let us therefore establish that the book *On the Order of Created Things* is Isidore’s work and that it was dedicated to Boniface, the Roman pontiff. Will this make Isidore’s journey to the city of Rome certain?

Bayer concludes that scarcely any room for doubt remains concerning Isidore’s Roman journey. For these words are clear:

> With the Lord’s support as my armor, I shall make sure to hasten safely to my homeland, protected on both sides.

He infers that Isidore remained for a long time in the City from the work involved in composing the little book, which was neither improvised nor ordinary—unless we say that he undertook it in his homeland.

For my part, I incline to this very opinion, since this appears to have been an ancient tradition in Spain, repeated in the *Life of Isidore* and in the old breviaries. Yet I fear that the words of the dedication may be twisted into another meaning.

The author speaks allegorically:

> Do not disdain to receive the obedience of my smallness in the calm harbor of your heart, and do not be unwilling to steer the little vessel of this work against the unstable waves of the talkative by the fear—or perhaps the helm—of your present authority.

He adds that he does not care about the complaints of the envious:

> Against them, protected by the shield of your prayer and armed with the Lord’s support, I shall make sure to hasten safely to my homeland, protected on both sides.

Thus he takes “homeland” to mean “harbor,” unless here too one prefers to read “to hasten to the harbor,” etc.

In the Escorial manuscript we read:

> of the Lord, by whose support I am armed;

in Dacherius:

> of the Lord, I shall proceed armed with support.

I prefer “armed with the Lord’s support.”

In the Florentine manuscript, which is believed to date from the twelfth century, the entire concluding dedication of the work is absent; perhaps it was added by a later hand in other manuscripts. I possess very carefully collected variant readings from that manuscript, supplied by the distinguished Thomas de Andrade, or Dendrade, a priest of the College of the Most Sacred Heart of Jesus at Marseille, which I shall publish in their proper place.

The work ends as follows:

> Let us reserve it for the knowledge of the Creator. Isidore’s book *On the Order of Created Things* ends.

17. As for Nicholas Antonius’s opinion, mentioned above, that certain statements at the end of the work concerning the state of souls after death and purgatorial fire are not entirely acceptable, Bayer amply refutes this scruple in his notes.

> Our author shows himself here excessively cautious; for, unless I am greatly mistaken, everything is plain and free of difficulty.

Chapter 13 is entitled “On the Diversity of Sinners.” It discusses unbelievers, fornicators, adulterers, the avaricious, and others. Chapter 14 is “On Purgatorial Fire.” It discusses those who, while alive, became poor for Christ and persevered in labor and weariness, and those who suffered persecution from human beings on account of righteousness.

Isidore says that the former have already been judged and will not rise for judgment; but that to the latter not only is the kingdom of heaven promised in the life to come, it is also granted in the present.

The meaning is evidently this: people endowed with the praise of perfect holiness in a certain sense seize the kingdom of God in advance even in this life; whereas wicked and impenitent people are tormented even while alive by the goads of conscience.

This manner of speaking is found among other Fathers as well: those who are neither pious nor impious are to be judged, for judgment is unnecessary in the case of the pious, while in the case of the impious it has already been carried out in this life.

18. Hear Saint Hilary, *Exposition on Psalm I*:

> For there are some between the impious and the pious . . . Many indeed are held within the Church by fear of God, yet the allurements of the world entice these same people toward worldly vices . . . They do not stand among the impious, because God’s name is held in honor among them; they are not pious, because they pursue what is foreign to piety . . . Judgment therefore concerns them: it has already been carried out against unbelievers, and it is unnecessary for believers.

Compare my notes in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, no. 179, and Constantius’ preface to Saint Hilary, section 7, p. 69.

Moreover, Isidore’s teaching on purgatorial fire in chapter 14 of the book *On the Order of Created Things* is entirely consistent with Catholic doctrine and with what Isidore himself teaches in book I, chapter 18, of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, as Cellier observes in his discussion of Isidore, no. 38. Cellier says that the Bollandists’ conjecture concerning the name Braulio, in place of Boniface, is supported by the first letter B, which was supplied by some copyist, and by the style of this work, which agrees with Isidore’s other works.

In the cited chapter 18, Isidore shows that the Catholic Church holds that, in the other world, sins are to be remitted to certain deceased believers and cleansed by a kind of purgatorial fire. The same doctrine appears in chapters 27 and 28 of book II *On Offices*, although these two chapters are absent from some manuscripts and printed editions.

The final sentence of book III of the *Sentences*, which is absent from certain printed editions and manuscripts, also belongs here:

> This is the disposition of Christian compassion: that a sacrifice be offered to God for each deceased person, etc.

But the words of chapter 18 of book I of *Offices* are perfectly clear and certainly taken by Isidore from Augustine’s *Enchiridion to Laurentius*, chapter 110.

## CHAPTER XXIV. The fiction concerning Isidore the exiled bishop and Gordianus intruded into his place; catalogue of the ancient bishops of Seville

[Col. 0135A]

1. Aegidius Gonzalez, in *Theatrum of the Church of Seville*, p. 27, Tamayus, in the *Hispanic Martyrology* under 4 April, and others relate that Isidore lived for some time in exile at Málaga; they derive this from the Pseudo-Luitprand. In chapter 9 we transcribed the epitaph of Isidore that is attributed to Ildefonsus by the Pseudo-Julian, where Ildefonsus, addressing Isidore, says of himself:

> Who was both a part and a companion of your exile.

Such fabulously embroidered narratives would have to be disregarded, were it not that pseudo-historians took the occasion for inventing them from some probable foundation, which must be brought under examination.

[Col. 0135B]

2. The Roman pontiff Deusdedit held the chair of Peter from the year 614 to the year 617; a letter of his to Gordian, bishop of Seville, is in circulation. Gordian, therefore, was then bishop of Seville—a fact that cannot be understood unless he had been intruded into the place of Isidore, who was still alive and had been sent into exile. Nicholas Antonius objects that it is wholly implausible that both Isidore and the Church of Seville could have suffered so great a calamity under the most Catholic kings, or that the Roman pontiff could have exchanged letters so courteously with Gordian, the usurper of the See of Seville. At that time, to be sure, the king of the Goths was Sisebut, of whom we can suspect nothing sinister. Indeed, Isidore pursued his praises most brilliantly in his *History of the Goths*.

[Col. 0135C]

3. What, then, shall we reply concerning the decretal letter of Pope Deusdedit? Nicholas Antonius considers the inscription false, and notes in the margin that, in Anselm, Burchard, and Luitprand, *Hispaniensem* should be read instead of *Hispalensem*. On this, see Thomas Tamayus in his note to Luitprand, p. 37. In the collection of canons of Vatican Codex 1348, arranged in five books and compiled around the eleventh century, Book IV, title 5, the letter is likewise addressed “to Gordian, bishop of Hispania.” In reviewing manuscript codices, we shall often find *Hispaniensem* used for *Hispalensem*, since the alteration of these two words is easy. Similarly, Flórez, vol. IX of *Sacred Spain*, p. 156, observes that *Hispalensis* is sometimes found for *Hispellensis*, and *Spolitanus* for *Spalitanus* or *Hispalitanus*. Conversely, [Col. 0135D] Augustine is in some places called *Hispalensis* instead of *Hipponensis*, as I shall say in chapter 83.

In Labbe’s *Councils*, this note is attached to the margin: “That the letter is false is shown both by other considerations and by Isidore himself, who sat at Seville from the year 600 to the year 636 and had no colleague imposed upon him from 614 to 617.” In D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 410, there is a letter of Arnulf, or Ernulf, *On Uncertain Marriages*, in which the letter of Pope Deusdedit to Gordian, bishop of Seville, is praised. But since Arnulf flourished in the twelfth century, his authority is not so great that it can free Pope Deusdedit’s letter to Gordian from suspicion of forgery.

4. Cardinal Aguirre, although otherwise not hostile to apocryphal decretals, demonstrates that this letter is either spurious [Col. 0136A] or corrupt, in vol. II of the *Hispanic Councils*, p. 461. See also Nicholas Antonius, Book IV, chapter 5, §124 and following, who likewise rejects another fictitious letter said to have been written to Isidore in exile in the name of a certain Artuagi, a Goth and Augustinian monk of Toledo.

It will not be superfluous to append a catalogue of the ancient bishops of Seville from the Aemilian Manuscript, written in the year 962, so that it may be clear that neither this Gordian nor another Theodiscus, whom some have invented as Isidore’s successor, held a place in the See of Seville. This catalogue appears in Flórez, vol. IX of *Sacred Spain*, p. 124.

> Here begin the names of the deceased bishops of the See of Seville:
>
> 1. Marcellus.  
> 2. Sabinus.  
> 3. Evidius.  
> 4. Deocletus [perhaps Deodatus].  
> 5. Sampronianus [perhaps Sempronianus].  
> 6. Geminus.  
> 7. Glaucus.  
> 8. Marcianus.  
> 9. Sabinus.  
> 10. Epiphanius.  
> 11. Orontius.  
> 12. Zeno.  
> 13. Asfalus.  
> 14. Maximianus.  
> 15. Sallustius.  
> 16. Crispinus.  
> 17. Pigasius.  
> 18. Stephanus.  
> 19. Theodulus.  
> 20. Hyacinthus.  
> 21. Reparatus.  
> 22. Stephanus.  
> 23. Leander.  
> 24. Isidore.  
> 25. Honoratus.  
> 26. Antonius.  
> 27. Fugitivus.  
> 28. Bracarius.  
> 29. Florentius.  
> 30. Florentinus.  
> 31. Floresindus.  
> 32. Faustinus.  
> 33. Gabriel.  
> 34. Sisivertus.  
> 35. Oppas.  
> 36. Nonnitus.  
> 37. Elias.  
> 38. Teudulfus.  
> 39. Aspidius.  
> 40. Humelianus.  
> 41. Meudulanus.  
> 42. David.  
> 43. Julianus.

Here the catalogue ends. The last eight bishops are later than the Moorish invasion, but their memory is preserved nowhere else.

165. **CHAPTER XXV. Fabulous accounts of Muhammad, expelled from Spain by Isidore; of two lamps burning perpetually; of the prediction of Spain’s overthrow. Other spurious or doubtful deeds of Isidore.**

[Col. 0136C]

1. The Pseudo-Ildefonsus, in the *Continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle*, and the Leonese Canon, in the *Life of Saint Isidore*, relate Muhammad’s—or Machomet’s—journey into Spain and his expulsion from there by Isidore. Henschenius conjectures that some propagator of the Muhammadan sect may have come to Spain and then been compelled to leave it soon afterward, from which this narrative may have originated.

We find the following in the pseudo-historians. Maximus, under the year 606, §2: “Machumetus, an impious and criminal man, ravages through the Spanish lands.” Luitprand, under the year 607: “Machumetus, who, spreading the poison of his error through Spain, began to sow it at Córdoba, Seville, and Toledo, was driven out by Aurasio, archbishop at Toledo (*Toleti archiepiscopo Toletano*; perhaps *Toleto*). Catholic teachers persecute the nefarious error by word and writing.” Again, under the year 615: “Machumetus, the pseudo-prophet, preaches at Córdoba.” Finally, under the year 619, he asserts that Muhammad published the books of his error in Arabia.

This appears to have been taken from the Pseudo-Ildefonsus, in the *Continuation of the Isidorian Chronicle*, under the era 653: “Muhammad, shamefully driven from Spain, preached the wickedness of his evil law to foolish peoples in Africa.”

2. Not only have many more recent writers embraced this fabulous history—Alfonso de Espina, Werner of Rolevinck, Quintanadueñas, Bleda, Vasaeus, and the old Spanish Breviaries of Évora and Zamora, in Tamayus’s *Hispanic Martyrology* under 4 [Col. 0137A] April—but also certain earlier writers, such as the author of the *General History of Spain* under Alfonso X, which was composed under his patronage or even through his labor, and Saint Antoninus, *History*, title 13, chapter 2, §6.

The latter relates that when Muhammad encountered Isidore, Isidore, from his countenance, made a prediction concerning him: that this man would someday become a plague to the Church. By this example jurists also confirm that judgment concerning a crime may be formed from the ugliness of a face, as Mascardus states in *On Proofs*, vol. II, conclusion 831, §29.

Ambrosius Morales, Franciscus Padilla, Mariana, Rodericus Carus in his notes to Maximus, Joannes Tamayus in the *Hispanic Martyrology*—otherwise one of the most vigorous defenders of such fables and inventions—and most other recent writers reject the whole story [Col. 0137B] of Muhammad’s preaching in Spain.

3. Nicholas Antonius refutes this fabricated account of Muhammad’s arrival in Spain at great length. From Arab, Greek, and Latin historians he proves that Muhammad never came to Spain, much less could have remained there for a long period. He also adds conjectures, although these would carry less weight if the matter rested on a stronger historical foundation.

He nevertheless passed over one outstanding testimony, which we must not omit. Saint Eulogius of Córdoba, the glorious martyr of Christ in the ninth century, wishing in his *Apology of the Martyrs*, §§14 and following, to produce the testimony, as he calls it, of earlier teachers concerning Muhammad’s crimes, relates as follows:

> When I was formerly staying in the town of Pamplona and residing at the monastery of Leyre, and was turning over, for the sake of examining them, all the volumes that were there, I suddenly found in a certain part of a little work this brief history of the wicked prophet, without the author’s name.

4. “For Muhammad, the arch-heresiarch, arose in the time of the emperor Heraclius, in the seventh year of his reign, while the era 656 was running. At that time Isidore, bishop of Seville, shone in Catholic doctrine, and Sisebut held the royal summit at Toledo . . . . . And the aforesaid wicked prophet Muhammad held the principate for ten years,” and so forth.

Thus that ancient author continues to describe Muhammad’s life, without saying a single word about a journey to Spain. John of Seville sent a similar narrative to Alvarus of Córdoba, in Flórez, vol. XI, p. 146, where *regale culmen* (“royal summit”) is incorrectly written *regulae culmen* (“summit of rule”).

Since Muhammad’s journey to Spain is reported only by historians of approximately the thirteenth century [Col. 0137D]—among whom many other false things about Isidore are also found—and by ancient pseudo-historians, while the deeds of Muhammad as related by Elmacin, Abulfaraige, and Muhammad himself contradict such an invention, it must absolutely be concluded that there is no probable basis for maintaining that Muhammad came to Spain and was driven and expelled by Isidore.

5. It is truly remarkable that the Leonese canon, the author of Isidore’s *Life*, relates near its end that Isidore made two lamps burn almost perpetually, and nearly impossible to extinguish, by natural art. One was placed at the head and the other at the feet in Isidore’s tomb, so that his most holy body might enjoy an almost continuous light. Roderic of Cerrato gives nearly the same account at the end of Isidore’s *Life*.

In the age in which Isidore lived, his contemporaries revered him as a marvel of learning; this opinion was greatly strengthened in subsequent centuries under Moorish rule. Yet I find no trace of these lamps—not only among those writers who lived with Isidore, but not even in the ancient Acts of the translation of his body, which we have published in chapter 8. If they had been placed in Isidore’s tomb, some mention of the two lamps ought to have been made there.

Tamayus, in his *Martyrology*, drawing on Peter Crinitus, *On Honest Learning*, Book VII, chapter 13, says that such lamps have something of the chemical about them, and therefore, together with Ambrosius Morales, concludes that they are unworthy of Isidore.

[Col. 0138B]

6. Many call into question the perpetual light of such lamps, which are said sometimes to have been discovered; some openly attack it, others have regarded them as a kind of phosphorus and a light without heat, while certain persons attribute everything that is seen as a flame when tombs are opened to the ventilation of the air.

See the authors cited by Fabricius in *Ancient Bibliography*, chapter 23, §10. Fabricius opposes to them the experience of those who excavated these lamps and testified that, once air had entered, the light indeed went out, but that they still detected heat coming from them.

“Certainly,” he says, “it was known to the ancients that lamps which are not consumed by fire could be prepared from Carystian stone and Carpasian flax-asbestos . . . . . Yet what that substance may be which can feed so constant and enduring a flame and heat still seems less fully known. Nevertheless, I would by no means judge the matter to be denied on that account, against so many αὐτόπται [*autoptai*, eyewitnesses],” and so forth.

Licetus, Robert Plot, Franciscus Carolus, Joannes Baptista Ursatus, Jacob Ozanam, and others discuss the matter more extensively; Fabricius lists their works.

7. Some discussion has already taken place in chapter 21 concerning the prediction by which Isidore is said to have foretold Spain’s overthrow. Tamayus, in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, drawing on certain writers and Breviaries, relates that Isidore, already near death, admonished the people in the basilica of Saint Vincent in a prepared address and, among other things, predicted the destruction of Spain.

He takes this from Luke of Tuy’s *Chronicles*, Book III; Baronius, under the year 636, §7, and Don Laurentius Ramirez, in his notes to Luitprand, [168] §188, fol. 390, took it from the same source. Ramirez testifies that he received the following words of Isidore from Aegidius Gonzalez Dávila, copied from a very ancient parchment:

> Woe to you, Spain, twice lost, to be lost a third time because of evil marriages!

Tamayus contradicts this. He also asks, concerning the words that Isidore is said to have uttered at the Council of Toledo—“If you preserve . . .”—whether they proceeded from a prophetic spirit or from prudent conjecture. Although he appears to adhere to the common opinion concerning Isidore’s prophecy, he adds that certain verses in a Gothic manuscript come closer to a prediction. In his copy they were added in the margin of the preface to Rodrigo Jiménez’s *Roman History*:

> To you I turn, Spain, harlot of the world, and so forth.

Rodrigo’s actual words are so harsh against princes, powerful men, and judges that, under Saint Ferdinand, they could refer only to the tyrannical abuses of certain nobles against their subjects, while the laws were silent amid the wars, as Nicholas Antonius judges in Book VIII, §46:

> Unless, he adds, this tragic lament is an appendix of a later age written in the margin of the book . . . , a kind of crime for which examples are not lacking . . .

But the ancient manuscript copies contradict this, and Nicholas Antonius himself praises them; it was to these copies that Rodrigo of Toledo’s *History* was recently compared in the exact edition of the Toledan Fathers.

8. Isidore’s miraculous journey to Rome on the very night of the Nativity of the Lord was treated in chapter 18; his other journey to the Roman council, or for whatever other reason, in chapter 23. Other matters concerning Isidore’s parents and brothers were discussed in chapter 17.

One may also consult the *Life of Isidore* by Roderic of Cerrato, described in chapter 14, where material enclosed in brackets appears—material that is either certainly false in its account of Isidore or at least seems doubtful and apocryphal.

9. Among the false or doubtful accounts concerning Isidore may be placed his friendship with Cyriacus, bishop of Zaragoza, whom Isidore is said to have urged to travel to Rome in order to obtain certain relics of the Apostle Peter.

This is related in the document called the canonical charter of the monastery of Saint Peter of Taberna, transcribed in 1415, under the following title:

> From the very ancient Codex of Saint John of Pinna, written on parchment in ancient letters, there is here found the Canonical Charter of Saint Peter of Taberna.

The author of this *Canonical Charter* is said to have been Balastutus, a monk of the eighth century, who, when near death, recounted to monks who asked him the history of the foundation of his monastery of Saint Peter of Taberna; the narrative was taken down from his mouth.

“After this,” Balastutus said, “there was Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, and Cyriacus in the city of Zaragoza. Suintila was king in Córdoba, and Reccared held the kingdom in the regions of Iberia. Thus the two bishops were joined in one charity and rejoiced; they came together and found this salutary counsel,” and so forth.

There follows the account of Cyriacus’s journey to Rome. Risco, vol. XXX of *Sacred Spain*, pp. 132 and 199 and following, demonstrates with substantial arguments that this canonical document is spurious, and that there is no other evidence for a bishop of Zaragoza named Cyriacus. Pellizerius inserted the *Canonical Charter* at the beginning of the *Annals of the Spanish Monarchy*, after its overthrow.

**CHAPTER XXVI. It is shown that Saint Isidore died in the year 636.**

[Col. 0139D]

1. Everything that happened during Isidore’s final illness and death is related by Redemptus the Cleric, in chapter 6, which we have reproduced. Although Redemptus testifies that Isidore died on the day before the Nones of April [4 April], in the era 674, which falls in the year 636, there is nevertheless great disagreement among writers concerning the year of Isidore’s death. This is either because they did not have Redemptus’s narrative before their eyes, because they did not trust it, or because they believed that an error had entered the numbers.

Labbe, in his note to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says: “Let the most foolish Patrologist, together with his Pelargus, who teaches that Isidore flourished in the year 650, go to ruin.”

The Regiomontan compilers of Eucharistic readings observe that the day of Isidore’s death was changed from 4 April to 14 April, unless this is a typographical error. Isidore died on the fifth weekday after Easter, which in the leap year 636, with the Sunday letters G and F, fell on 31 March, era 674.

2. The Pseudo-Ildefonsus, in the continuation of the Isidorian Chronicle, and the Zaragoza Breviary cited by Nicholas Antonius indicate the year 632 for Isidore’s death. Some old Breviaries of Spain give the year 635, as does the Zaragoza Breviary cited by Breulius, who refers to the *Proper Office of the Spanish Saints*, printed at Zaragoza in 1597, for that same year 635. Arnoldus Wion gives 642; the Leonese canon, author of the *Life of Saint Isidore*, gives 622; Baronius, under the year 626; Padilla, century 7, chapter 22; Ribadeneira [Col. 0140B] in the *Flower of the Saints* under 4 April; the author of the catalogue of the Gothic kings in Loaysa’s edition of the Spanish Councils; and most recent writers, together with Redemptus, give 636 as the year of Saint Isidore’s death.

The author of the fuller Acts of the translation of Saint Isidore also implies that he died in 636, when he relates that the Saracens crossed into Spain seventy-five years after Isidore’s death. Henschenius notes that this occurred in the year 711.

In an old Spanish monastic calendar, a fragment of which Muratori published in vol. II, part II of *Writers of Italian Affairs*, column 1023, we read: “In the era 674, Isidore the bishop died”—that is, in the year 636.

Nicholas Antonius attributes to the Pseudo-Ildefonsus the claim that the final year of Isidore’s life was 632, or era 670. But, as I said, the continuation of the Isidorian Chronicle indicates the year 642, for it gives the era as 680. And lest anyone suppose that this is a numerical error, the author had prefaced it by saying that Isidore fell asleep in the Lord in the sixth year of Chintila’s reign.

3. Braulio, in his preliminary notice to Isidore’s works, indeed states that Isidore died in the times of Heraclius and Chintila, or Chintilanus. Ildefonsus, however, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, says that Isidore flourished in the times of Reccared, Liuba, Witteric, Gundemar, Suinthila, and Sisenand; he does not mention Chintila, who succeeded Sisenand.

These statements fit together correctly if the year 636 designated by Redemptus is retained. That was the first year of Chintila’s reign, so Braulio could rightly say that Isidore died in the time of Chintila. Since he died at the very beginning of Chintila’s reign, Ildefonsus also rightly omitted Chintila from the list of kings under whom Isidore flourished.

4. The Acts of the councils establish that Isidore was still alive in the year 633, when he presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo, and had already died by the year 638, when Honoratus, bishop of the See of Seville, attended the Sixth Council of Toledo. Ambrosius Morales disagrees, less accurately, believing that the Sixth Council of Toledo was held in 636 and therefore assigning Isidore’s death to 635.

Pagius, in his note to Baronius under the year 636, asserts that certain Spaniards infer that Saint Isidore had already died in 636, on the day before the Kalends of July, when the Fifth Council of Toledo was held, because he did not attend that council. But since that council was provincial and no successor of Isidore signed its acts, this is certainly a weak argument.

5. The effective reason for not departing from the year 636 is therefore drawn from Redemptus himself. He not only designates era 674, in whose numerals someone might suspect an error, but also relates that Isidore’s death occurred on the day before the Nones of April and on the fourth day after the baptism of the catechumens.

The fourth day of April is commonly assigned as the feast day of Saint Isidore. It follows that Redemptus’s reading should be retained as the day before the Nones of April, not the day before the Kalends of April.

Trithemius, as I shall say in chapter 47, §10 and following, went far astray when he asserted that our Isidore was the one celebrated on 15 January in the Roman calendar.

In the additions to Usuard’s martyrology under 7 January we read:

> On this same day, Saint Isidore the bishop, a man of great holiness.

Sollerius notes: “This Isidore is known nowhere.” Yet in Palatine Codex 1448, which will be discussed in chapter 103, there is an ancient calendar in which the memory of Isidore the bishop is commemorated on 7 January.

But this Isidore too must be distinguished from ours, whose feast—or at least the day of whose death—must be assigned to 4 April. In fact, from the Paschal cycles it is calculated that in the year 636 Easter, or the day on which the baptism of the catechumens took place, fell on the last day of March, that is, the day before the Kalends of April. Isidore, therefore, who is said by Redemptus to have died on the fourth day afterward, died on the fifth weekday of Easter week, which in that year was the day before the Nones of April.

6. Constantine Cajetanus would like to confirm this with what he calls an “indissoluble argument,” because Isidore could not have died in April of the year 637, since in that year the Sixth Council of Toledo was held in January, in the second year of Chintila’s reign.

But he is mistaken in designating the year of the council. It was held in the second year of Chintila, but in the year 638. Since Chintila began to reign in 636, at the beginning of 638 his second regnal year was still in progress.

Thus certain compilers of the councils of Spain ineptly conjecture that “the second year of Chintila, on the fifth day before the Ides of January, era 676,” should be understood as the second completed year and the beginning of the third.

The note in which Joannes Baptista Pérez discusses this argument has already been set out in chapter 3, §2. It should be observed there that the era in which Isidore died is named twice: first, he is said to have died in era 664, which is a numerical error; then it is correctly stated that Chintila began his reign in era 674.

That numerical error in the Grialian edition also entered other editions and must be corrected more clearly by us when Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, followed by Braulio’s preliminary notice with Pérez’s note, is reprinted.

172. **CHAPTER XXVII. The life of Saint Isidore arranged according to its periods.**

1. Although it is difficult to attach the deeds of Saint Isidore to their precise years, we shall nevertheless gather from what has so far been discussed those things that are more probable and closer to the truth, and distribute each according to its year.

2. It may be believed from chapter 17, near the end, that Isidore was born around the year 560.

[Col. 0142A]

3. In the year 583 or the following year, when Leander, Isidore’s brother, was living at Constantinople, Isidore vigorously defended the cause of religion against the Arians and, as some relate, was acting in Leander’s place in the bishopric of Seville. This is inferred from chapter 18, near the end.

4. In the year 586 or the years following, when peace had already been restored to the Church of Spain, Isidore is said, not unwillingly, to have been enclosed by Leander in a cell so that he might devote himself to God, to himself, and to letters.

5. Around the year 590 or in the following years, Isidore’s miraculous journey to the city of Rome is supposed to have occurred, so that he might visit Gregory the Great—on the night of the Nativity of the Lord, on which same night he is said to have returned to Seville. See above, chapter 18.

6. Around the year 600, Isidore was appointed bishop of Seville, as follows from chapter 20.

[Col. 0142B]

7. In the year 606, Isidore’s letter to Massona was written, as will be established when we discuss Isidore’s letters.

8. In the year 610, Isidore subscribed to the decree of King Gundemar at the assembly of the bishops of Toledo, as follows from chapter 21.

9. From the year 612 or thereafter until the year 619, during the reign of Sisebut, Isidore wrote the book *On the Nature of Things*, which he dedicated to King Sisebut, unless the inscription is misleading. The dedicatory letter does not prove that Sisebut was already king at that time.

10. From the year 615 and thereafter until 633, Helladius was bishop of Toledo, to whom a letter of Isidore is extant. In the year 616, Isidore completed his *Chronicle*, namely in the fifth year of Sisebut. Compare the notes on the *Chronicle* and the words of Hermannus Contractus concerning Isidore below, chapter 33.

173. 11. In the year 618 or thereafter, Isidore presided over the Second Council of Seville, as follows from chapter 21.

12. In the year 619 or thereafter until 625, Isidore is conjectured to have come to Rome to Boniface V. At that time he may perhaps have composed the work *On the Order of Created Things*, as follows from chapter 23.

13. Around the year 620, Fulgentius, Isidore’s brother, is believed to have died; consequently, before that time Isidore dedicated his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* to Fulgentius.

14. Around the year 623, Isidore attended or presided over a certain council against Sintharius. See chapter 21, near the end.

15. Around the year 624, we believe that a certain Council of Seville was held under Isidore’s presidency, at which Marcianus, bishop of Écija, was deposed.

16. In the year 625, Isidore completed his *History of the Goths*, namely in the fifth year of the reign of King Suinthila, which fell in the year 625, as Pagius demonstrates in his note to Baronius under the year 625, §18. Although Pagius names the *Chronicle*, it is clear from the words cited that he means the *History of the Goths*, which Isidore completed in Suinthila’s fifth year.

17. Around the year 630, Isidore went to the city of Toledo on account of a certain council, although that council does not appear to have been held at that time. He sent the book of the *Etymologies* to Braulio. He dealt with the king concerning the appointment of a bishop of Tarragona, as follows from chapter 21.

[Col. 0143A]

18. In the year 633, or era 671, Florentina, Isidore’s sister, is said to have died, according to the epitaph reviewed in chapter 7. Therefore Isidore must have written his books *Against the Jews*, addressed to his sister Florentina, before that year.

19. In the year 633, Isidore presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo, as follows from chapter 21.

20. Isidore died in the year 636, as was shown in chapter 26.

**CHAPTER XXVIII. The false report that the body of Saint Isidore of Seville is preserved at Bologna. Miracles at the altar of the church of León, where his body rests.**

1. Most writers who deal with the affairs of Bologna assert that Isidore of Seville, while returning from Rome to Spain, died at Bologna on 14 April, in the year 615, 616, 640, 670, or some other year; for they do not agree among themselves about the year.

They add that the body of Saint Isidore was buried in the church of Saint Stephen, formerly belonging to the Black Monks and now to the Celestines. Around the year 1141, under Henry, bishop of Bologna, it was discovered, identified, and exposed for veneration on 16 September, the day on which his memory is celebrated at Bologna.

Sigonius, under the year 616, writes:

> At this time Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, is said to have died at Bologna while traveling through Emilia.

Even today, certainly, his tomb is shown in the basilica of Saints Peter and Paul behind the high altar, which is commonly called the chapel of Saints Peter and Paul. This is the Basilica of Saint Stephen and the church of the Celestine Fathers.

Arnoldus Wion reports of Isidore:

> He died in the year 642, or thereabouts, on the day before the Nones of April; his body rests at Bologna in the church of the Reverend Fathers, the Celestines.

2. The occasion for this fable was provided by an anonymous Benedictine author of the chronicle of that church and monastery, written around the year 1180. Henschenius gives his words in the preliminary commentary to the *Life of Saint Isidore*. Antonius Casalis, a Celestine, addresses the Basilica of Saint Stephen in the following terms, taken from a manuscript chronicle:

> Likewise, the body of the most blessed Isidore, confessor of Christ and illustrious teacher, rests in you. When he was returning from Rome, he lodged near this city and was detained by a serious illness of the body, and so forth.

If anyone insists that this must be understood of Isidore of Seville, we shall maintain that this is an intolerable fiction of that chronicle, which Redemptus, Isidore’s cleric, clearly refutes in his account of Isidore’s death, to say nothing of all the other Spanish writers and martyrologies.

It is equally certain that Isidore’s body was buried at Seville and was transferred from there to León, as we related from the authentic Acts of the translation in chapter 8.

3. To these may be added an ancient testimony from an outsider. Breulius, in the preface to the works of Saint Isidore, reports that in the Victorine Library at Paris there is an extremely ancient book written on parchment describing the itinerary to Saint James of Galicia. It contains the following:

> Near the city of León one must visit the body of Blessed Isidore, bishop and confessor, or teacher. He established a most holy rule for the clergy of the churches, imbued the Spanish people with his teachings, and adorned the entire holy Church with books rich in flowers.

Constantine Cajetanus rightly noted the error of William of Malmesbury, who took *Toledo* instead of *León*, and of Johannes Nauclerus, who took *Seville* instead of *León*, in this account of the translation of Saint Isidore’s body. He discussed at length both the place where Isidore died and the place where his bones rest.

William of Malmesbury’s words, in Book II, chapter 10 of *Deeds of the Kings of England*, are these:

> Isidore, distinguished in learning and holiness, succeeded Leander; in our own age King Alfonso of Galicia transferred his body to Toledo, having purchased it for its weight in gold.

Nauclerus, *Chronography*, vol. II, generation 9, says:

> To this Ferdinand, too—the king who transferred him to Seville—Blessed Isidore revealed the day of his death.

William of Malmesbury also erred in the king’s name: he ought to have called him Ferdinand, king of Castile and León, not Alfonso, king of Galicia. Nevertheless, both writers sufficiently refute by their account the opinion that places Isidore’s tomb at Bologna.

4. Cajetanus likewise conjectures that the bishop Isidore of Sicily—of whom Constantius Felix speaks in his Calendar on 15 Kalends of February [18 January], and Arnoldus Wion in *Lignum Vitae*, Book III, on 18 Kalends of February [15 January]—is the saint whose bones the people of Bologna venerate; deceived by the similarity of names, they called him Isidore of Seville.

The Bollandists also present this conjecture in the preliminary commentary to the *Life of Saint Isidore*. Ughellus, in *Sacred Italy*, vol. 11, under Bishop Peter of Bologna, calls Constantine Cajetanus’s account of Isidore of Sicily’s death at Bologna true, but does not confirm it.

The Bollandists raised the question again on 18 December in their catalogue of omitted saints:

> Saint Isidore of Bologna, they say, is announced in Castellanus’s universal Martyrology in Italy as the bishop of another city. On this day the people of Bologna celebrate Saint Isidore, whom they believe to be Isidore of Seville, through the error that he died at Bologna . . .

Certainly, I have not found arguments so solid for the possession by the people of Bologna of the body of any Isidore that I must immediately infer another Isidore from their manifest error concerning the body of Isidore of Seville.

Masini, in *Bologna Surveyed*, discusses the cult of Saint Isidore on 4 April and 16 September.

5. Although no further proof is needed concerning the place where the body of our Isidore lies, since an appropriate opportunity now presents itself, we shall produce an ancient inscription visible in the cloister of the Leonese monastery of Saint Isidore.

Antonius Ponzius transcribed it in his *Itinerary of Spain*, published at Madrid in 1783, vol. XI, p. 218. It appears to have been made at the beginning of the twelfth century or the end of the eleventh; at any rate, it is composed in a barbarous style.

176. 6. “This hall of Saint John the Baptist, which you see, was once made of mud; recently the most excellent King Ferdinand and Queen Sancha built it of stone. At that time they brought here from the city of Seville the body of Saint Isidore, bishop, on the dedication of this temple, on 12 Kalends of January, era 1101 [21 December 1063].

“Then, in era 1103 [1065], on 6 Kalends of May [26 April], they brought here from the city of Ávila the body of Saint Vincent, brother of Sabina and Cristeta (the text reads *S. Vincentii FR Sabinae, Cristetisque ipsius*); and in that same year the aforesaid king, returning from the enemy territory of the city of Valencia, came here thence on Saturday and died on the third day, Friday, six days before the Kalends of January, era 1103. Queen Sancha, devoted to God, completed [it].”

[Col. 0145A]

7. The same inscription appears in Flórez, vol. IX, p. 211, taken from Sandoval’s *History of King Ferdinand*, fol. 16, but only as far as the words “era 1101.” There it reads: *olim fuit* (“was once”) . . . *excellentissimus Fredinandus* (“the most excellent Fredinandus”) . . . *edificaverunt* (“they built”) . . . *episcopi* (“bishop”).

8. From this inscription it is inferred that the translation of Saint Isidore’s body was celebrated in the year 1063, on 20 December. The feast of this translation was observed in the Toledan Breviary on 22 December, but among the people of León on the 20th, as Cajetanus reports, p. 44.

Mariana, Book IX of his *History of Spain*, chapter 13, shows that the temple subsequently became known by Isidore’s name:

> The body of Alvito was buried in the great temple, while that of Isidore was placed in the lofty and distinguished site of John the Baptist. Hence, in later times, it came about that that ancient church of John the Baptist exchanged its name for the name of Isidore.

9. To this may be referred the claim that the architect Peter of God is said to have built over the church of Saint Isidore, according to the epitaph transcribed by Risco, vol. XXXV of *Sacred Spain*, p. 356:

> Here rests Peter of God, who built above this church. He also founded the bridge called “of God” (*de Deus tamben*); and because he was a man of extraordinary abstinence and flourished through many miracles, everyone proclaimed him with praises. He was buried here by the emperor Alfonso and Queen Sancha.

The word *tamben* means “also,” in modern Spanish *también*, from the Latin *tam bene* (“so well” or “likewise”).

10. Nor is the following irrelevant to this subject, which Mariana, Book IX of his *History of Spain*, chapter 3, records concerning Elisabeth, the wife of Alfonso VI, formerly called Zaida:

> Following the example of Casilda, or moved by her own inclination, Zaida, cleansed by Christian baptism according to our custom, entered into the marriage of King Alfonso after several years. The miracles that, as was said shortly before, occurred through divine agency when Isidore’s body was being carried away seem to have contributed greatly to her becoming intensely eager to embrace the Christian religion. A dream also occurred, in which she had seen Saint Isidore in majestic form, warning her in a gentle voice to hasten the matter, and so forth.

She was the daughter of Benabet, king of Seville, who permitted Saint Isidore’s body to be carried away.

11. Several ancient documents also pertain to confirming this same matter and to establishing Isidore’s posthumous glory. They mention the transfer of Isidore’s body to León, or its burial in that city. In volume XXXVI of *Hispania Sacra*, after other appendices, documents relating to the distinguished monastery of St. Isidore at León are described. The first bears this title: “King Ferdinand and Queen Sancha, after transferring the body of St. Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, to León, magnificently adorn and endow the monastery of St. John the Baptist before many bishops and nobles who had come to celebrate the translation.” From it I excerpt the following:
