“We, the unworthy and insignificant servants of Christ, King Ferdinand and Queen Sancha, caused the body of blessed Isidore to be transferred from metropolitan Seville by the hands of bishops, or priests, within the walls of León, our city, into the church of St. [Col. 0146A] John the Baptist.”

Among other provisions, the church, or monastery, of St. John the Baptist is granted a church with three altars in the Goths’ fields at Rioseco, near Villa Verde, “because there the body of the most blessed Isidore rested when it was carried away from metropolitan Seville.” At the end we read:

“This testamentary instrument, or confirmation, was drawn up on the twelfth Kalends of January, at the dedication of that basilica; but on the following day, the eleventh Kalends of January, we celebrated the translation of the body of St. Isidore, in the year 1101 of the era.”

12. This was the year of Christ 1063. Thus formerly—or certainly in that first year—the dedication of the church of St. John the Baptist was celebrated on 21 December, and the translation of St. Isidore’s body on 22 December. As time went on, the dedication and translation were celebrated on one and the same day. From this arose the differing opinions of authors on the matter; see chapters 8 and 9, where we presented the Acts of the translation.

Pagi, in his notes on Baronius for the year 1053, no. 47, mentions this very document from Sandoval, and there corrects Baronius’s error in assigning the translation to the year 1053. Pagi himself, however, calls Albitus, or Alvitus, who was bishop of León, bishop of Seville. In the words that he quotes from Pelagius of Oviedo concerning the same matter:

“This man transferred the body of St. Isidore, bishop, from metropolitan Seville to León through the hands of the bishops Aloytus of León and Ordoñus of Astorga”—

this should be corrected to: “Albitus of León, who died at Seville before the translation, and Ordoñus of Astorga, or Asturias.”

[Col. 0146C] 13. The second document contains other donations made to the Leonese monastery of St. Isidore in 1148 by Alfonso, emperor of Spain. The third records a donation by which, in 1159, King Ferdinand of León, after the body of his aunt, Lady Sancha, had been buried in the monastery of St. Isidore, donated the monastery of St. Julian to its abbot and the other canons.

Risco, in the same volume XXXVI of *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 72, chapter 2, reports an edict of the Catholic monarchs Ferdinand and Isabella, by which they order observance of a command issued under penalty of excommunication by the abbot of the Leonese monastery of St. Isidore: that oaths intended to establish the truth should not be sworn over the chest in which Isidore’s body was enclosed. For this custom and belief had become widespread: those who perjured themselves in this way were thought to be taken from life within a year of their perjury.

Nor should we pass over the diploma of Gregory IX to the abbot and community of St. Isidore of León, preserved by Raynaldus under the year 1233, no. 69:

“Since, as we have learned, the body of blessed Isidore rests in your monastery, we, considering the holiness of that place and the uprightness of the brothers residing there, trusting in the authority of the blessed Peter and Paul, grant forty days’ remission of the penance imposed upon all who devoutly come to that monastery on the feast of blessed Isidore, out of reverence for that saint. Given at the Lateran, on the fourteenth Kalends of June, in the seventh year of our pontificate.”

14. When Bishop Ordoñus of Astorga had transferred the body of St. Isidore to León, King Ferdinand, in that same year 1063, on 22 December—that is, the day after the translation had been celebrated—gave him, as a reward, the monastery of St. Martha of Tera and the land called Noceta:

“For this reason,” says the king, “because you, most holy father, Bishop Ordoñus, rendered us a worthy service when we took you from the expedition against the city of Mérida to Seville—recently called the city of Sibilia—with Bishop Alvitus, where he himself departed to the Lord, while you, with the Lord’s consent, caused us to carry from there the most holy and glorious body of blessed Isidore, our teacher, Archbishop and confessor of Christ, whom we, through your hands and those of the other prelates, caused to be placed in the city of León, in the church of St. John. There, through you, is preserved the honor and glory of our doctrine, the teacher of all Spain. Therefore, etc.”

15. In their preliminary commentary the Bollandists report several miracles obtained through St. Isidore’s assistance after his body had already been exposed for veneration at León. Others may be added from their shorter *Life of St. Ferdinand the King*, no. 8, and especially from Lucas of Tuy’s work *On the Miracles of St. Isidore*.

Pelagius of Oviedo, an eyewitness, relates in his *Chronicle*, near the end of the *Life of Alfonso VI*, that water flowed from the altar stones of St. Isidore, where the priest places his feet while celebrating Mass; this was understood to foretell the calamities that would occur after the king’s death.

Rodrigo of Toledo also reports, in book VI of *The History of Spain*, chapter 13, that Isidore appeared to Ferdinand I and foretold the day of his death. The most devout king prayed before Isidore’s sarcophagus, received penance and the grace of extreme unction from the bishops, put on sackcloth, and, sprinkled with ashes, survived for two days in penitence and tears. [Col. 0147C] He was buried beside his father in the same church of St. Isidore.

Lucas of Tuy reports another apparition of St. Isidore in his *Chronicle*: in the year 1230, Isidore was seen bringing aid, together with St. James, to the Christians against the Saracens. He further relates that Count Diego, who had rebelled against King St. Ferdinand and occupied the tower and church of St. Isidore, was afflicted with a severe illness until he restored the tower and church, swearing that thereafter he would be St. Isidore’s soldier and vassal.

16. Mabillon, volume IV of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 671, reports that King Ferdinand died in 1065 after being warned beforehand by St. Isidore, and was buried in the church of St. Isidore, which he had founded together with the adjoining Benedictine monastery. Concerning this monastery, he had stated earlier, on p. 649, that it later passed from the Benedictines to Benedictine nuns, and then, at the beginning of the thirteenth century, to the Canons Regular, who possess it today.

In the same place Mabillon records King Ferdinand’s donation from Iepesio: “This document was drawn up on the very day of the basilica’s dedication, the twelfth Kalends of January, the day after the translation of his relics had taken place.” Perhaps *pridie quam*—“the day before”—should be read, as in document no. 11.

180

## CHAPTER XXIX  
## Isidore, Doctor of the Church  
### Whether formerly there was discussion of numbering him among the four Fathers of the Latin Church in place of St. Ambrose

1. The title of distinguished doctor was bestowed upon Isidore in the most ample terms by the Eighth Council of Toledo, celebrated in 653—that is, seventeen years after his death—canon 2:

“Also the distinguished doctor of our age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him, not inferior in comparison of doctrine, and, what is more, the most learned at the end of the ages and to be named with reverence, Isidore, etc.”

Some read less correctly: “and, what is more, the most learned already at the end of the completed ages.”

Fifty-two bishops, twelve abbots, ten representatives of bishops, and sixteen illustrious Palatine officials attended and subscribed this council. At the Fifteenth Council of Toledo, also, which was subscribed by sixty-one bishops, eleven abbots, five representatives of bishops, and seventeen illustrious officials of the Palatine office, and which was celebrated in 688, [Col. 0148B] the same title of distinguished doctor was confirmed for Isidore:

“Honoring, therefore, and following the opinion of the distinguished doctor, Isidore, bishop of the see of Seville, which he discussed in his books *On the Difference of the Nature of Christ and Our Nature*, where he says, etc.”

John Baptist Perez, in his *Various Readings of Manuscripts for the Councils of Spain*, suspects that Isidore’s name is missing here after “distinguished doctor.” Thus ancient Spanish writers commonly call Isidore “the great doctor of Spain” or “of the Spains,” as do Isidore of Pacensis, St. Martin of León, and others.

2. Pope Benedict XIV, *On the Beatification of the Saints*, book III, part II, chapter 11, no. 15, reports that on 25 April 1722 apostolic authority granted that the Office of St. Isidore should be recited throughout the universal Church as obligatory, with the antiphon “O most excellent doctor” and the Gospel “You are the salt of the earth.”

He was already venerated as a doctor in the kingdoms of Spain and in the churches of the Indies subject to the Catholic king, according to the apostolic letters of Gregory XIII, by which he approved the Offices of the saints of the kingdom of Spain. Concerning the Office of St. Isidore they contain the following:

“Likewise, the feast of St. Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, for whom the Office of a doctor is to be celebrated, and the Creed is to be recited during the celebration of Mass.”

181

3. Benedict XIV further adds the authority of St. Leo IV in the canon *De libellis*, distinction 20, where Leo numbered St. Isidore among the doctors of the Church. After setting out rules whose use was to be required in ecclesiastical judgments, and after mentioning certain councils and decrees of the Roman pontiffs, he says:

“These, then, are altogether the authorities by which bishops judge, and by which bishops and clergy are themselves judged. For if some unusual matter should arise or occur that cannot at all be decided by these authorities, then, if statements of those whom you have mentioned—Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, or other holy doctors likewise—are found, they must be retained and promulgated with courage.”

These same words, with some alterations but with precisely the same meaning retained, are transcribed by Berard in the *Genuine Canons of Gratian*, part II, chapter 76, from the published complete copies of the letter, with the readings of other manuscripts also added.

After explaining the opinion of certain persons who had thought that Isidore should either be added to the other four doctors of the Latin Church or preferred to Ambrose, Pope Benedict XIV adds:

“Finally, there was no lack of petitioners who, having gathered testimonies from every quarter, demonstrated most fully the excellence of St. Isidore’s doctrine. They even published in print the supporting opinion of the most eminent Lord Cardinal Belluga, the relator of the cause, who learnedly and, as usual, refuted the observations I had made as promoter of the faith and added further arguments in commendation of the outstanding doctrine of that same St. Isidore.”

4. The words of Hadrian I, who flourished in the eighth century, may be joined to, or placed before, the authority of Leo IV. Hadrian wrote to Egila, bishop in the regions of Spain, in letter 95 of the *Carolingian Code*, volume III of Duchesne’s *Gallic Writers*:

“Do not at all follow the sluggishness of heretical men, their impious and perverse madness, or their empty and deceitful tales. Rather, as they have instructed us, attach yourself to the divine words of our holy doctors and Fathers—namely, of the blessed popes Silvester and Innocent, and likewise of the venerable Jerome and Isidore—and, holding firmly and beyond doubt to the Saturday fast according to our apostolic ancient [*olitana*, i.e. *vetere*] rule, may your holiness not cease.”

In the Ottobonian Codex 336, discussed in chapter 105, the title is:

“Here begin the chapters of the book of the *Sentences* of St. Isidore, doctor of the Church.”

Other titles, not greatly different and amounting to the same thing, occur in other manuscripts.

182

5. The Bollandists report in their preliminary commentary on the *Life of St. Isidore*, quoting Mariana’s words from his *History of Spain*, that under Boniface VIII there was discussion of numbering Isidore among the four Fathers of the Latin Church. The question is who originated this account.

In his Latin *History*, Mariana says only:

“There are some who write that, when Pope Boniface VIII was deliberating about those who were to be honored with the name and number of doctors of the Church, etc.”

But in the same history, freely rendered by Mariana himself into the Spanish language, he asserts that Martin of Poland was the source of the account:

“Martin of Poland says in his *Chronicon* that, when Pope Boniface VIII was undertaking to name the four doctors of the Church, etc.”

Nicolaus Antonius denies that Mariana cites Martin of Poland as the witness to this account, because he did not consult the *History of Spain* in the vernacular Spanish version translated by Mariana at this point.

He observes that this testimony is absent from the Antwerp edition of Martin of Poland’s *Chronicle* of 1574, and that it is not unusual for many spurious additions to have crept into that *Chronicle*, such as the tale of Pope John the Englishman, or Pope Joan, refuted by so many arguments and documents from ancient manuscripts.

6. Since Martin of Poland states that he continued his *Chronicle* to the year 1277 and died not long afterward, as Fabricius reports in his *Bibliotheca of the Middle and Lower Ages*, he could certainly not have written about events that occurred under Boniface VIII, Roman pontiff, since Boniface did not occupy the apostolic chair of Peter until 1294.

Accordingly, Mariana seems to have encountered the *Chronicle of Martin of Poland* as continued by someone else, although perhaps the entire work was attributed to Martin himself in its title. Copies of the *Chronicle* are indeed found extended to the year 1320, from which some have supposed that Martin of Poland lived until that time.

Fabricius, in the place cited, asserts that what follows in Martin’s *Chronicle* after 1277 was added by Ptolemy of Lucca to 1294 and by Bernard Gui to 1316. Schoettgen, in volume VI of the same *Bibliotheca of the Middle and Lower Ages*, under the entry “Ptolemy of Lucca,” observes that in the two editions of the *Chronicle* available to him the continuation did not appear under the name of Ptolemy of Lucca, nor had he found that information in any other writer.

7. I myself have examined several published copies of Martin of Poland’s *Chronicle*, as well as some manuscripts, in which a continuation after the time of Boniface VIII was appended without the author’s name. Yet I nowhere found what Mariana reports concerning the honoring of Isidore among the other doctors of the Church.

Nevertheless, I am willing to believe Mariana when he asserts it, since the additions to Martin of Poland’s *Chronicle* may be numerous and varied. Raynaldus, under the year 1295, no. 55, produces a diploma in which Boniface VIII, in 1295, decreed that the feasts of the apostles, evangelists, and the four doctors of the Church—Gregory the Great, Augustine, Ambrose, and Jerome—were to be celebrated with a double office throughout all the churches of the world. In 1297 this decree was largely inserted by the same Roman pontiff into book six of the *Decretals* (chapter *Gloriosus*, *On the Relics and Veneration of the Saints*).

8. Pseudo-Luitprand, *Adversaria* 169, p. 860, in the Madrid edition of Thomas Tamayo, relates the very story that Mariana derived from Martin of Poland’s *Chronicle*. But how reckless and stupid was the architect of that spurious work—as Nicolaus Antonius aptly notes—to attribute to Luitprand, a tenth-century writer, an account of events said to have occurred under Boniface VIII, who became Roman pontiff at the end of the thirteenth century!

Laurentius Ramirez de Prado omitted that *Adversaria* 169 from the Plantin edition of the same work, perhaps because he had noticed the anachronism. He would nevertheless have acted more wisely had he condemned the entire work to darkness rather than attempted to illuminate it with a new edition.

## CHAPTER XXX  
## Isidore’s Doctrine of Predestination Defended against Hincmar of Reims, and of the Sacraments of the Holy Eucharist and Confirmation against Bingham and Others

[Col. 0150D]

1. Although Isidore engaged with nearly every theological controversy, his doctrine was everywhere received with great approval, and scarcely anything can be found in it that would incur the criticism even of the strictest theologians. Let us therefore examine here whether Isidore ever favored the Predestinarians, as Hincmar of Reims seems to imply.

Thus he says in chapter 9, *On Predestination*:

“They also bring forward Isidore, bishop of Seville, as a witness—a learned man and one who is profitable to readers in many respects—who says in his book of the *Sentences* that there is a twofold predestination: of the elect to rest and of the reprobate to death. He compiled this opinion in the second book, chapter 6, as though from the words of St. Gregory in book XXIV or XXV of the *Moralia*, or, as it seems to readers, from statements of St. Augustine, or from some other source. But he did not extract it in such a way as anyone can clearly recognize from reading that same book, according to the meaning of blessed Gregory. Hence one may suppose that this Isidore, learned in other matters, in this opinion retained something of the remnants of the Gauls in Spain.”

2. Hincmar adds that Augustine wrote the books *On Predestination* and *On the Gift of Perseverance* against the Gauls, who held an incorrect view of predestination. He concludes that Gregory demonstrated the modes of the heavenly judgments concerning the elect and the reprobate in a sense different from that which Isidore gathers in the passage cited above.

The words he cites from Isidore are:

“Predestination is twofold: of the elect to rest and of the reprobate to death. Both are governed by divine judgment: he always causes the elect to follow heavenly and interior things, while he always permits the reprobate, by abandoning them, to delight in lowly and exterior things. Just as a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be, so, etc.”

But in Hincmar we read *aguntur*—“are governed”—instead of *agitur*—“is governed”—and immediately afterward: “he permits the reprobate, by abandoning them, to delight in lowly and exterior things.” Thus also: “so that a human being does not know the boundary between light and darkness, or what the end of either may be.”

These variants, however, do not introduce any difference in the substance of the matter under discussion. The reading “to delight in lowly and exterior things” is extremely common in our manuscript codices; from this others suspect the reading “to pursue lowly and exterior things.”

Loaisa identifies Gregory’s passage as book XXXIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 20, alternatively 21 and 25, where Gregory says:

“No one, therefore, anticipates God by merits, so that he might hold Him as though He were a debtor. Rather, in a wonderful way, the just Creator both chooses some beforehand and justly abandons others in their wicked ways.”

I find no other passage that could be fitted to Isidore’s twofold predestination from Gregory the Great. What follows in Isidore concerning God’s hidden judgments is drawn more clearly from the same Gregory, book XXIX, chapter 33, alternatively 32 and 18. Prudentius of Troyes identifies this passage, as I shall now explain.

Nevertheless, I believe that in distinguishing a twofold predestination Isidore had before his eyes the view of Augustine and of his disciples Fulgentius and Prosper rather than Gregory’s. I shall cite their words more distinctly later, when I explain Isidore’s meaning and show that the sense of his words is entirely free from any suspicion of error.

3. The monk Ratramnus of Corbie, in book II of *On Predestination to Charles the Bald*, and Prudentius of Troyes—or Tricassinus—in chapter 2 of *On Predestination against John Scotus Eriugena*, defended Isidore’s cause.

Ratramnus, or Bertramus, begins his defense as follows:

“Thus St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, distinguished for the merits of his life and the brilliance of his wisdom, following the teaching of the Catholic masters, teaches in the second book of the *Sentences*, with the testimony both of his meaning and of his words, that predestination is twofold.”

Our Prudentius Galindo, in the place cited, argues that Isidore plainly agrees with Gregory the Great, because what Isidore calls “twofold predestination,” Gregory, in the cited book XXIX, calls “predestinations” in the plural. He prefaces Gregory’s words with these:

“To know the order of heaven is to behold the hidden predestinations of the heavenly dispositions.”

4. To understand Isidore’s opinion and reasoning more clearly, we must explain the error of the Gauls that Hincmar believed he detected in it.

When many monks of Hadrumetum read St. Augustine’s Letter 105, to Sixtus, they understood the holy doctor’s words in a sense foreign to his intention. From this arose the disagreement among the monks that Augustine explains in his letter to Valentinus:

“Two young men, Cresconius and Felix, came to us, saying that they belonged to your community. They reported to us that your monastery was disturbed by some disagreement, because certain among you preach grace in such a way as to deny that the human being possesses free will and, what is more serious, say that on the day of judgment God will not render to each person according to his works. They also indicated that many among you do not hold this view, but acknowledge that free will is assisted by God’s grace, so that we may think and do what is right.”

5. Augustine sent this letter to Valentinus, prefect of the Hadrumetum monastery, together with his book *On Grace and Free Will*, in which he explained to the monks the harmony between grace and free will.

After reading that book, a certain monk of Hadrumetum collected its statements and wanted to maintain that no one should be rebuked, but that one should pray only for the person who is evil, since all good works, as Augustine repeatedly teaches in that work, are gifts of God.

Augustine refuted this error by publishing his book *On Rebuke and Grace*, in which he showed that rebuke is useful and necessary, even though all good works are gifts of God.

Sirmond and others therefore assert that the Predestinarian heresy arose in the Hadrumetum monastery, which was situated in Africa, from books of St. Augustine that had been wrongly understood. Natalis Alexander, in dissertation 5 *On the Predestinarian Heresy* for the fifth century, maintains with others that there were no Predestinarians in the Hadrumetum monastery. For Augustine wrote the book *On Grace and Free Will* on behalf of those who, when God’s grace is defended, think that free will is being denied and therefore defend free will in such a way as to deny God’s grace, asserting that grace is given according to our merits, as Augustine himself says in book II of the *Retractions*, chapter 66.

6. Regarding Augustine’s words quoted above—“certain among you preach grace in such a way as to deny that the human being possesses free will”—Natalis Alexander replies that Cresconius and Felix, through simplicity and lack of knowledge, could not have properly explained the state of the controversy that was disturbing Hadrumetum. He supposes that St. Augustine himself suspected this, since in chapter 1 of *On Grace and Free Will* he speaks disjunctively and hypothetically:

“But since there are some who defend God’s grace in such a way as to deny human free will, or who think that free will is denied when grace is defended, I have therefore taken care to write something . . .”

But how absurd it is to believe that Cresconius and Felix, Hadrumetum monks who came to Augustine at the expense of their abbot Valentinus and with a letter from him, in order to seek his judgment concerning the disagreement that had arisen in their monastery, were unable properly to explain the state of the question, and openly said that there were certain monks who preached God’s grace in such a way as to deny that human free will existed—when none of them had fallen into such an error!

Let us nevertheless imagine that those monks were so foolish, as was their abbot Valentinus, who would then have sent others rather than them to Augustine. Certainly Augustine ought to have trusted their account and therefore to have written against those who denied that human beings possess free will.

“But,” you say, “he suspected that their account was untrue.”

Why would he have suspected this? You will reply that he suspected it because he speaks disjunctively and hypothetically.

First, in his letter to Valentinus he does not speak disjunctively or hypothetically:

“They reported to us that your monastery was disturbed by some disagreement because certain among you **preach grace in such a way as to deny that the human being possesses free will**, and, what is more serious, say that on the day of judgment God will not render to each person according to his works.”

187

7. The fact that Augustine therefore speaks disjunctively in chapter 1 of the book *On Grace and Free Will* does not show that he doubted whether the account of Cresconius and Felix was false. Rather, he wished in the same work to refute both those who preached God’s grace in such a way as to deny human free will and those who thought that free will was denied when God’s grace was defended, whether they approved or disapproved of the way Augustine defended it.

Moreover, even if we are willing to admit that Augustine doubted whether the Hadrumetum monks denied free will or merely thought that free will was denied when God’s grace was defended, we must nevertheless acknowledge that Augustine wrote *On Grace and Free Will* so as to encompass both sides of his doubt: both against those who preached God’s grace in such a way as to deny human free will and against those who thought that human free will was denied when God’s grace was defended.

What argument, then, do you produce for persistently denying that there were Predestinarians in the Hadrumetum monastery? Cresconius and Felix, Hadrumetum monks, frankly admit that there were Predestinarians in their monastery. You strive to infer from Augustine only that he doubted whether those two monks knew how to explain the state of the question.

8. Thus, in Augustine’s writings, the Pelagians and Semipelagians criticized his doctrine of grace because they denied that it could coexist with free will, which they themselves defended.

Others, on the contrary, interpreted and retained Augustine’s doctrine of grace in such a way that they simultaneously denied free will. For although they regarded Augustine’s opinion as Catholic—as indeed it truly is Catholic—they nevertheless erred in thinking that, once it was accepted, freedom of the will collapsed. They defended this position against Augustine’s own intention, and were called Predestinarians by Gennadius, Hincmar, and others.

Finally, others defended the harmony of grace and free will from Augustine’s books and teaching.

Hincmarus testifies in his letter to Pope Nicholas that the Predestinarian heresy arose in Gaul not long afterward:

“From the ancient Predestinarian heresy, which first arose in Africa and afterward in Gaul at the same time as the Nestorian heresy arose, and which, in the time of Pope Celestine, was restrained by his authority and initiative.”

Natalis Alexander argues that the Predestinarian heresy did not arise in Gaul during the time of Celestine I, Roman pontiff. But he extricates himself from the difficulties raised only by denying credibility at one point to Hincmar and at another to the author of the *Predestinatus* published by Sirmond.

He nevertheless concedes that the Predestinarian heresy was not imaginary, although it did not have many adherents, and that the presbyter Lucidus adhered to Predestinarian errors, which were condemned in the Council of Arles III and in the Council of Lyon in the fifth century.

He concludes that the wandering, turbulent, and innovative monk Gottschalk revived the Predestinarian heresy in the ninth century.

9. Setting aside, then, the quibbles of the Jansenists, who contend that Hincmar and others called the true disciples of St. Augustine Predestinarians, we must maintain both that some—although perhaps not many—in Gaul taught the Predestinarian heresy in the fifth century and that Gottschalk renewed the same heresy in the ninth century.

The first Predestinarian doctrine was this, as Hincmar reports in his letter to Pope Nicholas:

“That just as God predestined some to eternal life, so He predestined others to death.”

When, therefore, Hincmar, attacking the Predestinarians, was confronted with Isidore’s statement—“Predestination is twofold: of the elect to rest and of the reprobate to death”—he could apply no other interpretation except that perhaps Isidore, in this opinion, had retained remnants of the Gauls in Spain.

10. But since no other traces of the Predestinarian heresy appear in Spain, whether introduced through the succession of the Gauls or by some other means, it was necessary to examine Isidore’s intention more carefully and to compare his statement here with other statements of his, so that its true meaning might be recovered.

It is well known that the Semipelagians objected to St. Augustine that a similar opinion was defended, as it were, in his writings. In St. Prosper, the first chapter among the objections of the Gauls is:

“That, through God’s predestination, as though through a fatal necessity, human beings are compelled and forced into sins and thus into death.”

The ninth chapter of the Gauls is:

“That by His power God compels human beings to sin.”

St. Fulgentius, in his letter to Monimus, chapter 30, reproduces the same objection, which the Massilians had brought against Augustine, and at the same time explains Augustine’s intention:

“You are not unaware that, even in an earlier period, certain Gauls objected to that brilliant work of St. Augustine *On the Predestination of the Saints*: they claimed that, in asserting divine predestination, blessed Augustine said that sinners were predestined not only to judgment but also to sin. Since Augustine was overtaken by a premature death, Prosper, that learned and holy man, rightly defended his statements with sound faith and abundant eloquence.”

189

11. The Predestinarian Lucidus was condemned because he defended the predestination of the reprobate to death in such a way that he believed the reprobate were predestined by God and driven into sin.

Natalis Alexander, dissertation *On the Predestinarian Heresy*, fifth century, proposition 4, reports as follows:

“The sixth proposition, by which some are said to be assigned to death and others predestined to life, is Catholic when understood in the sense that some are predestined to eternal damnation on account of evil merits, while others are so predestined to life that, in their election, the mercy of God precedes good merits. This doctrine was asserted by the Council of Valence according to the teaching of St. Augustine and St. Fulgentius and defended by the Church of Lyon.

“But when understood in the sense that God drives the reprobate into sin, or that, by the general intention and goodness of the Creator, not all were created so as to attain eternal life but some were created so as to be condemned, it is heretical.”

The presbyter Lucidus, moreover, defended those propositions in the erroneous sense that we have indicated in each case.

12. Predestination, however, may be understood in two senses. For God is said, in a certain true sense, to predestine all those things which he himself is going to do, although, in the more proper and customary sense, God’s predestination is said to occur only when God, out of his benevolence, orders someone to some end beneficial to that person. In this more proper sense God does not predestine a reprobate human being to eternal punishment; yet he may be said to predestine him to eternal punishment in a less proper sense, because, moved by his foreknowledge of the sin, he decrees to punish him with eternal punishment.

It will be useful to explain this more fully in the words of Suárez, volume I, treatise 2, book I, chapter 5, where he also indicates the passage of our Isidore:

> Secondly, it must be said that although God may be said, in some true sense, to predestine certain human beings to the evil of punishment, nevertheless this is not in the most proper and rigorous sense in which we are now speaking.

The first part is posited on account of Augustine, who sometimes says absolutely that certain persons were predestined by God to Gehenna, as is evident in the *Enchiridion*, chapter 100, and in book XV of *The City of God*, chapter 1, and book XXI, chapter 24. Thus he is to be understood if he should anywhere have said absolutely that certain persons were predestined to destruction, as in the book *On the Perfection of Justice*—as Fulgentius explains him in the aforementioned book I addressed to Monimus. Isidore speaks in the same way in book II of *On the Supreme Good*, chapter 6, and he indicates the Council of Valence under Lothair, chapter 3.

But in this kind of expression it should be noted that the particle *prae-* (“before”) signifies the priority of eternity over time, not the priority of the divine will over his foreknowledge. For in this way it is true that God did not predestine anyone to evil by his own power, as the Council of Orange and the Council of Trent defined. I understand this also of the evil of punishment and of eternal misery, as I shall show more fully in the second part of this matter. I nevertheless consider that word, **BY HIS OWN POWER**, by which it is signified that God, by mere power and will, ordered no one to the evil of eternal misery. This does not exclude that he may have decreed, in justice, to punish certain persons eternally.

That decree, however, presupposes foreknowledge of sin, on account of which a human being is worthy of such punishment. Therefore such a decree cannot be called predestination in relation to foreknowledge, but rather in relation to the eternity compared with such an effect; and the Fathers mentioned above speak in this way, for they expressly declare that this predestination presupposes the foreknowledge in question.

From these points, then, the first part of the assertion is clear. For the expression just mentioned is true in the first sense. Its basis is that God is truly said to predestine those things which, by his absolute and efficacious will, he has ordained and decreed to bring about from eternity—at least in the sense that the particle *PRAE* signifies the priority of eternity over time. But God decreed by an absolute will to punish those whom he foreknew would sin and remain in their sins to the end. Therefore he is rightly said to have predestined them, as wicked persons, to punishment.

The second part of the assertion is likewise explained by the same doctrine, because God is said most properly to predestine a human being when, from himself and from his benevolence and affection—not merely moved by foreknowledge of some work of that human being—he efficaciously orders him to some end or goal suitable and beneficial to the human being, and so forth.

13. Suárez makes several further observations to the same effect. That Isidore in no way understood reprobates to be predestined by God to the evil of guilt, or to the death of the soul, is clear from the preceding chapter 5 of the same book, where, speaking of the hardening and blindness of human beings, he reasons as follows:

> God is said to harden a human being, not by making his hardness, but by not taking away the hardness which he himself has nourished. In the same way God is said to blind certain persons, not because he himself creates that blindness in them, but because, on account of their unprofitable merits, he does not take their blindness away from them.

On human free will, and on the reprobation of the wicked—that is, on the predestination of reprobates to punishment on account of their sins—Isidore himself speaks more clearly in book II of the *Differences*, no. 32:

> The good that we do belongs to God, on account of prevenient and subsequent grace. What belongs to us is the will of free choice that obeys . . . . Therefore, in that we are preceded by grace, it belongs to God; but in that, by acting well, we follow prevenient grace, it belongs to us. Yet no one precedes God by merits, so as to be able to hold him as though he were a debtor. Nevertheless, in a wondrous manner the equitable Creator chooses some in advance by predestining them, while by a just judgment he abandons others in their wicked ways . . . . For some are saved by the gift of his exceedingly gracious prevenient mercy, having been made vessels of mercy; but others, regarded as reprobates and predestined to punishment, are condemned, having been made vessels of wrath.

There are theologians who defend predestination after foreseen merits and maintain that this does not conflict with Augustine; some even do not hesitate to abandon Augustine on this point. Perhaps this is the purpose of a work in Codex Vaticanus Ottobonianus 392, entitled *A Christian Dialogue on Predestination against Saint Augustine*. At the end of the codex there is a list of authorities supporting the position, beginning in Italian: “Felice e beato” (“Happy and blessed”).

Predestination before foreseen merits, however, is not only more consistent with Augustine; it is also more common among theologians and more suited to the words of Isidore quoted above.

14. From these and similar passages Hincmar could have concluded that Isidore taught the predestination of reprobates to punishment not from the remnants of the Gallic Predestinarians, but from the books of Augustine and Gregory the Great, taking the word “predestination” in a certain true sense, though not in the more proper and customary sense.

Honorius of Autun approves both the opinion and Isidore’s very words in *On Free Choice*, volume II of Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, where he collects several opinions of the Fathers, especially those of Isidore. The first opinion is: “Free choice is the will of free power,” and so forth, from book II of the *Differences*, no. 32, elsewhere 27. The second is: “Let the defenders of free choice know,” and so forth, from book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 5. The third is: “Predestination is twofold,” continuing through the words “to weigh the order,” from the passage noted by Hincmar. The fourth is: “God predestined certain persons,” and so forth.

But concerning this entire controversy, as well as other matters relating to grace, my friend Franciscus Xaverius Perotes will deal extensively and learnedly. He has long had ready for publication a complete history of all controversies in any way relating to divine providence, contained in many volumes, filled with refined learning, and composed through immense labor. It is greatly to be hoped that, so that he may carry this work through, some generous Maecenas equal to so great an undertaking may be found.

[Col. 0157C] 15. The heterodox raise another controversy for us by denying the true presence of the body of our Lord Jesus Christ, or transubstantiation, in the Eucharist, and attempting to draw Isidore over to their position.

Joseph Bingham, *Ecclesiastical Origins*, book XV, chapter 5, adduces the following passage from Isidore, book I, chapter 18, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, in support of his heresy:

> For the bread which we break is the body of Christ, who said: “I am the living bread which came down from heaven.” The wine, however, is his blood, and this is what is written: “I am the true vine.” But the bread, because it strengthens the body, is therefore called the body of Christ; while the wine, because it produces blood in the flesh, is therefore referred to Christ’s blood. Although these things are visible, once sanctified by the Holy Spirit they pass over into the sacrament of the divine body.

[Col. 0157D] 16. Bingham adduces another passage from book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, in these words:

> Bread and wine are therefore compared with the body and blood of the Lord because, just as the visible substance of this bread and wine nourishes and intoxicates the outward human being, so the word of God, which is the living bread, refreshes the minds of the faithful through participation in it.

He observes that these words are cited by Bertram *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* in Flaccus’s *Catalogue of Witnesses to the Truth*, book X, but that they are now, through some fraud, not found in their proper place.

17. It must now be asked whether the words attributed to Isidore in the second passage should be considered genuine—words which are said to have been moved from their proper place through some fraud.

Bertram, or Ratramnus, by which second name he is better known, flourished in the ninth century. Since the words about the Eucharist which he himself attributes to Isidore not only do not appear in printed editions today but are entirely absent from manuscript codices, including those older than Bertram, why does Bingham confidently assert that, through some fraud, those words cannot be found in their proper place?

I carefully compared numerous manuscript copies of the *Etymologies*, to see whether I could find those words in the cited location; some of these copies predate the ninth century and the age of Bertram. Yet nowhere was I able to find what Ratramnus attributes to Isidore. All the copies, including the oldest, the Queen of Sweden’s codex, no. 1953, agree with the printed editions at book VI, chapter 19, where the sacrament of the Eucharist is discussed as follows:

[Col. 0158B]

> The sacrifice is so called as if it were a sacred act, because it is consecrated by mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s Passion undertaken for us. Hence, at his command, we call it the body and blood of Christ; although it is made from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament, through the invisible working of the Spirit of God. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *eucharistia*, which is interpreted in Latin as “good grace.” And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

After these words of Isidore, quoted from the books of the *Etymologies*, Ratramnus immediately says: “But bread and wine, and so forth,” as I reported above from Bingham. The marginal note reads:

> The words “Bread,” and so forth, are not found in Isidore at the cited place, *Etymologies* VI, chapter 19; but in book I *On Offices*, chapter 18, these words are found: “The bread, because it strengthens the body,” and so forth.

Ratramnus continues: “And this Catholic teacher,” and so forth, “when he says that bread and wine are therefore compared with the body and blood of the Lord,” and so forth.

18. Why, then, should we not conclude either that Ratramnus came upon an interpolated copy of Isidore, or that the words attributed to Isidore, together with the subsequent argument, were inserted into Ratramnus’s work by some forger?

Certainly Ratramnus’s work is not such that we ought to place complete reliance upon it. It was prohibited in the Roman Tridentine Index and in the Spanish Index of Cardinal Quiroga. Natalis Alexander, in dissertation 13 on the ninth century, although he maintains that Ratramnus agrees concerning the real presence of Christ’s body and blood in the Eucharist and concerning transubstantiation, nevertheless concedes that his book was rejected in the index published by order of Clement VIII, Supreme Pontiff, among books containing unsound or suspect doctrine, on account of certain harsher and more obscure propositions that required some softening by explanation.

Theophilus Raynaudus, volume XI, part I, *Erotémata* 10, *On Good and Bad Books*, page 276, lists several writers who judged that Ratramnus’s book on the Eucharist had been wholly or largely forged by Oecolampadius. Yet it cannot be denied that the book was written by Ratramnus; I would more readily believe that it was interpolated by someone, although many, together with Natalis Alexander, think that nothing contrary to Catholic doctrine itself is found in it.

In the Paris edition of Ratramnus, in French and Latin, published in 1686, there is a reasonably learned preface in which Ratramnus is asserted to be the true author of the work. Notes are added in which Ratramnus’s words are explained in a Catholic sense.

[Col. 0159A] 19. If Ratramnus in that work of his contains nothing contrary to Catholic doctrine concerning transubstantiation, Isidore—whom Ratramnus cites in his support—should be considered even less contrary to the true faith.

In reality, the passage cited by Ratramnus under Isidore’s name proves nothing except that Christ’s body is presented in the sacrament of the Eucharist under the appearance of bread, and Christ’s blood under the appearance of wine, because just as bread nourishes a human being and wine intoxicates, so the word of God—or Christ himself, who is the true bread—refreshes the minds of those who partake of it.

Who, however, would on that account deny the conversion of bread into the body and of wine into the blood of our Lord Jesus Christ? Isidore clearly intimates this conversion—which the Catholic Church aptly calls transubstantiation—in the same chapter 19 of book VI, in the genuine words which we quoted:

> Hence, at his command, we call it the body and blood of Christ; although it is made from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament, through the invisible working of the Spirit of God . . . . And what is better than the body and blood of Christ?

[Col. 0159B] 20. Let us now explain the earlier passage, which certainly belongs to Isidore, from book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 18.

There can be no doubt that in that chapter he asserts the real presence of Christ’s body:

> The sacrifice, then, which is offered to God by Christians, was first instituted by Christ our Lord and teacher when, before he was handed over, he entrusted his body and blood to the apostles, and so forth. For it pleased the Holy Spirit, through the apostles, that in honor of so great a sacrament the Lord’s body should first enter the mouth of a Christian before any other food; and therefore this custom is observed throughout the whole world. For the bread which we break is the body of Christ, and so forth.

From this someone might conclude that Isidore recognizes the substance of bread together with Christ’s body in the Eucharist, and therefore denies transubstantiation. Certainly not.

For after Isidore explained that the bread is called Christ’s body because it strengthens the body, and that the wine is referred to Christ’s blood because it produces blood in the flesh, he immediately indicated, in unmistakable words, the conversion of bread into the body and of wine into Christ’s blood:

> Although these things are visible, once sanctified by the Holy Spirit they **PASS OVER** into the sacrament of the divine body.

This passage cannot be understood without transubstantiation.

[Col. 0159D] 21. Nor does it matter that Isidore says, “The bread which we break is the body of Christ.” For he speaks in accordance with the Apostle, 1 Corinthians, chapter 10, verse 16:

> The cup of blessing which we bless, is it not a participation in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?

To explain this statement, Isidore said that the bread which we break is Christ’s body; and this cannot be understood in any true sense unless the bread has been converted into Christ’s body.

Gregory of Valencia, book II *On the Eucharist*, chapter 6, responds to heretics who deny transubstantiation because the Apostle calls the Eucharist bread even after the blessing. He observes that the Apostle declares the bread to be Christ’s very body when he says:

> The bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of Christ?

It is as though he said that the distribution and participation of this bread is not, in substance, participation in some other thing, but participation in Christ’s very body.

To this should be referred the many statements of the Fathers in which, as he says, they affirm that the Eucharistic bread is truly Christ’s very body.

The Eucharist is called bread for three reasons: first, because it refreshes, like bread; second, because it appears to be bread; third, because it was made from bread.

This passage would require me to refute the opinion defended by certain recent theologians in Germany. They indeed admit that Christ’s body and blood are present in the Eucharist and that the substance of bread and wine is absent, but they deny that it is necessary to assert the word “conversion.”

This argument, however, has been taken up and exhausted by a man of the highest distinction in both learning and dignity, whom I wish to name out of respect: Cardinal Gerdil, in an anonymous work entitled *Observations on the Notes Which the Distinguished Feller Judged Should Be Added, for Greater Clarity, to Certain Propositions of the Synod of Pistoia Condemned in the Dogmatic Constitution of Our Most Holy Lord Pius VI, Beginning “Auctorem Fidei”*. Rome, 1795, at the Lazarists’.

What theological censure that opinion deserves had already been clearly explained by Suárez, volume XVIII, question 75, disputation 50, article 8, section 1, at the end:

> Secondly, I infer that if someone confesses the presence of Christ’s body and the absence of bread, yet denies the true conversion of one into the other, he falls into heresy, because the Catholic Church not only defines and teaches the first two points but also this third one. Thus, in the miracle performed by Christ at Cana in John II, it is not only a matter of faith that water was first placed in those jars and that wine was later found there; it is also a matter of faith that the water was converted into wine.

> Nevertheless, if someone, while confessing the whole reality, were to reject the word **TRANSUBSTANTIATION** as inept and barbarous, I do not think that he would thereby be a heretic, because the use of the word in itself does not belong to the object of faith. He would nevertheless be extremely rash and scandalous, would offend pious ears, and finally would have to be regarded in the external forum as strongly suspected of heresy.

[Col. 0160D] 22. Bingham attempts to confirm another error from the same chapter 19 of Isidore’s book VI of the *Etymologies*, in book XII of *Ecclesiastical Origins*, chapter 1.

He gathers that baptism and chrism are one and the same sacrament from these words of Isidore at the cited place:

> The sacraments are baptism and chrism, body and blood. Therefore, just as body and blood constitute one sacrament, so baptism and chrism do likewise.

This is Bingham’s argument, based on the conjunction *et* (“and”) after *baptismus* (“baptism”). This is indeed how the passage is presented not only in the printed editions but also in most manuscript codices.

In Codex 2 of the Vatican Archives, however—for I consulted two codices from that archive, which I shall describe later—it is read differently:

> The sacraments are baptism, the body and blood of Christ.

Other manuscript copies and printed editions add the word *Christi* (“of Christ”); the Madrid Royal Edition omits it.

In the Queen of Sweden’s codex, no. 1850, it reads as follows:

> The sacraments are baptism, chrism, body and blood.

Whichever of these readings we prefer, Bingham’s argument collapses.

23. But let us retain the common reading, if you please. Who would think that it can rightly be inferred from that conjunction alone that Isidore did not distinguish the sacrament of confirmation from the sacrament of baptism?

He expresses the one sacrament of the Eucharist in the same way: “body and blood.” I add that the conjunction is also omitted after *chrism*, which may indicate that only two sacraments are listed there: one by the words “baptism and chrism,” the other by the words “body and blood.”

But when a matter of such importance is being established, these are too slight indications to demonstrate the author’s mind plainly. The other words that follow rather demonstrate the contrary.

For after explaining the sacrament of the Eucharist shortly before through both Christ’s body and blood, Isidore, after defining the sacrament in general, treats baptism separately:

> *Baptismus* is Greek; in Latin it is interpreted as “dipping,” and so forth.

Then he explains the sacrament of chrism as plainly distinct from baptism:

> *Chrisma* is called in Greek, and in Latin *unctio* (“anointing”). From this name Christ is also called, and after the washing the human being is sanctified. For just as the remission of sins is granted in baptism, so through anointing the sanctification of the Spirit is applied.

Thus, in explaining the sacrament of chrism, or confirmation, he proceeds with words taken almost verbatim from Tertullian, chapter 7 *On Baptism*, in which the doctrine of the sacrament of confirmation is admirably conveyed.

24. Likewise, in book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, the same Isidore treats the sacrament of baptism in chapter 25, then chrism in chapter 26, and finally confirmation, or the imposition of hands, in chapter 27:

> Since, however, after baptism the Holy Spirit is given by bishops together with the imposition of hands, we remember that the apostles did this in the Acts of the Apostles, and so forth.

Gregory of Valencia indicates this passage in his book *On the Number of the Sacraments of the New Law*, where he confirms the Catholic doctrine concerning the sevenfold number of the sacraments and refutes the almost universal opinion of the sectarians, who teach that there are only two sacraments of the New Law, namely baptism and the Eucharist.

Natalis Alexander, in dissertation 10 on the second century, defends the sacrament of confirmation against Dallaeus and other heretics, and specifically explains Isidore’s doctrine from Isidore’s words in chapter 26 of book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> Since after baptism the Holy Spirit is given by bishops together with the imposition of hands, and so forth.

Dallaeus inferred from this that the anointing with chrism, which preceded the imposition of hands, belonged to baptism. But Dallaeus argues this absurdly, for Isidore plainly teaches that both the anointing with chrism and the imposition of hands occur after baptism. Thus, after baptism, chrism is given first, and then the imposition of hands by the bishops.

25. What is stated in the work published under Isidore’s name, *On the Order of Creation*, concerning purgatorial fire and the state of souls after death was not entirely accepted by Nicolás Antonio. Nevertheless, this matter was discussed sufficiently in chapter 23.

Some other statements of Isidore have been noted by certain writers concerning the defenders of what are called the Three Chapters. Grialius briefly explains these in his preface to Isidore’s works. He also believes that the statements concerning the determination of the final day, which occur in some copies of the exposition on Genesis, chapter 6, but are absent from others, were maliciously and impiously added. These matters will be discussed in their proper places.

## CHAPTER XXXI. Isidore Praised by the Roman Pontiffs and in Many Councils

1. I have quoted outstanding words in praise of Isidore by Adrian I, who lived in the eighth century, in chapter 29.

Leo IV, Roman pontiff, flourished in the ninth century. At the Roman synod of the year 853 he promulgated several canons concerning ecclesiastical discipline, and on account of his heroic virtues he was numbered among the saints. I stated in the cited chapter 29 what eulogy he bestowed upon Isidore.

Gregory IX entrusted Saint Raymond of Peñafort with the task of bringing together into one body the replies of the Roman pontiffs and the decrees of the general councils held in more recent times. Accordingly, the pontiff himself published the five books of the *Decretals* under his own name around the year 1230 and confirmed them by his authority.

In these books of the *Decretals*, statements are often drawn from Isidore. Thus, in book IV, title 2, chapter 3:

> Isidore, in Baetica in the year 630: “Adults (*puberes*) are so called from puberty (*pubes*),” and so forth.

Bignaeus indicates other similar passages in the preface to Isidore’s works, which will soon be transcribed.

2. Isidore was praised with great distinction in two Toledan councils, the Eighth and the Fifteenth, held in the seventh century, as was already explained in chapter 29.

Between these two councils another Council of Toledo ought to be placed, at which the division of the provinces of Spain is said to have been carried out in the time of King Wamba under Quiriacus, or Quiricus, bishop of Toledo—unless it were established that this division is fictitious.

Quiricus actually presided over the Eleventh Council of Toledo in the year 675. The spurious division appears in Labbe, volume V of the *Councils*, column 878, from manuscripts of the Church of Toledo and of Oviedo. Near the end we read:

> It was further decreed in the said council that all clerics should live according to the rule of the most holy Father Isidore, as contained in his book *On the Honor of Clerics*.

The reference is to the second book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

Certainly, numerous Gallican [Col. 0162D] and German councils followed Isidore’s doctrine. Bignaeus, at the cited place, adduces as witnesses the Council of Frankfurt on the Main, both Councils of Aachen, the Council of Mainz, the Council of Tribur, and the Council of Paris. These councils confirmed Catholic doctrine through Isidore’s authority and words and established exceedingly wise canons. We shall say something about each.

3. The Council of Frankfurt, at which the Felician, or Adoptionist, heresy was condemned in the year 794 by the bishops of the entire Frankish kingdom, of Italy, Gaul, and Germany, in the presence of King Charlemagne and the legates of Pope Adrian—Bishops Theophylact and Stephen—mentions Isidore in its synodal letter to the bishops of Spain as follows:

> Isidore likewise, in the book of the *Etymologies*, says: “Human nature was so joined to the Son of God that from two substances there came to be one person.”

These words are found in book VII, chapter 2, near the end.

4. In the year 816 the Council of Aachen was held, at which the form of the institution of canons was excerpted from the sacred canons and the sayings of the holy Fathers, at the urging of King and Emperor Louis the Pious.

Book I is *On the Institution of Canons*; book II is *On the Institution of Nuns*. Book I contains 145 chapters, most of which have been composed from the books of Saint Isidore:

- Chapter 1, on the tonsure of clerics, from book II, chapter 4, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.
- Chapter 2, on doorkeepers, from chapter 14 of the same work.
- Chapter 3, on readers, from chapter 11 of the same work.
- Chapter 4, on exorcists, from chapter 13 of the same work.
- Chapter 5, on acolytes, from book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 12.
- Chapter 6, on subdeacons, from book II *On Offices*, chapter 10.
- Chapter 7, on deacons, from chapter 8 of the same work.
- Chapter 8, on presbyters, from chapter 7 of the same work.
- Chapter 9, on priests, from chapter 5 of the same work.

5. After other material drawn from other Fathers, chapter 15, on unworthy superiors, is again taken from Isidore’s book III *Sentences*, chapter 34. Chapter 16, on unlearned superiors, is from chapter 35 of the same work. Chapter 18, on ecclesiastical superiors, is from chapter 33. Chapter 20, on the instruction and examples of superiors, is from chapter 36. Chapter 22, on the humility of superiors, is from chapter 42. Chapter 29, on those who teach well and live badly, is from chapter 37. Chapter 30, on examples of wicked priests, is from chapter 38. Chapter 31, on carnal superiors, is from chapter 39. Chapter 33, on irascible teachers, is from chapter 40. Chapter 36, on the discipline of priests in the case of those who sin, is from chapter 46. Chapter 99, on clerics, is from book II of the *Offices*, chapter 1. Chapter 100, on the rules of clerics, is from chapter 2 of the same work. Chapter 101, on the kinds of clerics, is from chapter 3 of the same work. Chapter 104, on subjects, is from book III *Sentences*, chapter 17.

6. It should be noted that after chapter 113, which belongs to Saint Augustine’s *On the Life and Morals of the Clergy*, this admonition is added:

> Finished. Since, therefore, it is established that the holy Church ought to follow the examples of the preaching Fathers, whose teachings are known to make it shine abundantly after the apostolic institutions, not only prelates by imitating them but also subjects by obeying them ought everywhere to strive that, following their examples and teachings, they may be able to reach the joys of happiness to which those Fathers have gone before them, and so forth.

7. Other chapters follow. Chapter 126 is entitled:

> By what authority the canonical hours are celebrated, which canons ought to know and observe religiously.

It is excerpted from Isidore’s book II *Offices*, chapter 19. Chapter 127, on vespers, is from chapter 20 of the same work. Chapter 128, on compline, is from chapter 21. Chapter 129, on the antiquity of vigils, is from chapter 22. Chapter 130, on matins, is from chapter 23.

8. Isidore’s authority is therefore praised in this council far more frequently than that of any other Father—Jerome, Augustine, Gregory, Prosper, or rather Julianus Pomerius, Pope Leo, and Pope Gelasius—who are also cited in the same council.

The chapters attributed to Isidore in Codex 1351 of the Vatican Library’s inventory were taken from this Council of Aachen: “On the tonsure,” “On doorkeepers,” and so forth.

Nor do I think that the work *On the Rules of Canons*, which Nicolás Antonio says is preserved in the Ambrosian Library, is anything other than this, although he himself suspects that it should be understood of book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

Amalarius, deacon of Metz, is said to have devoted the principal labor to that council. He composed the entire work from the various opinions of learned men, and it was approved by the council’s judgment and authority.

There is also a rule of canons arranged by Chrodegang, bishop of Metz, enlarged and interpolated by some anonymous writer with several chapters from the aforementioned Council of Aachen and with material from elsewhere. Several passages of Isidore already indicated are repeated there.

I also find—and I wished to note this in passing—in chapter 62 certain verses from poem 5, part I, of Eugenius of Toledo, against drunkenness, quoted without the author’s name.

Nor should I omit that the Vatican Library’s inventory lists a parchment codex of the Council of Aachen under Emperor Louis I. It adds that the Rule of Canons placed in it is stricter than the one found in print and also inserted into this council.

9. The Council of Paris was held in the year 829 by the bishops of the four provinces of Rheims, Sens, Tours, and Rouen.

In chapter 19 of book I of this council, Isidore’s words are quoted from chapter 28 of book III *Sentences*:

> For, as Isidore writes in the book of the *Sentences*, rulers are to be judged by God alone, not by their subjects, and so forth.

The same Isidore is praised in book II, chapter 1, from chapters 28 and 29 of book III *Sentences*, where he discusses the probity and justice of kings.

Again, in chapter 3 of the same book, without Isidore’s location being indicated, there is material from book III *Sentences*, chapter 21:

> Isidore: Secular princes sometimes hold within the Church the heights of the power they have acquired, and so forth.

And in chapter 3:

> That when wicked judges are set over the people of God, this belongs to the offense of the one by whom they are appointed, is shown by Isidore’s words, in which he says: “It belongs to the offense of princes who, against the will of God, set wicked judges over faithful peoples,” and so forth.

These words are taken from the same book III *Sentences*, chapter 52.

Likewise, chapter 5, from book III *Sentences*, chapter 28:

> As Isidore explains, when God is angry, the people receive such a ruler as they deserve on account of their sin.

At the beginning of book II, chapter 1, although Isidore’s name is not expressed, his doctrine is presented from book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3, where the distinction between kings and tyrants is explained.

10. The same statements of Isidore are celebrated in the Second Council of Aachen, held in the year 836, chapter 2, canon 1, where the book of the *Etymologies* is expressly cited:

> The ancients, as the same Isidore writes in the book of the *Etymologies*, called all kings tyrants; but later those who ruled piously, justly, and mercifully acquired the name of king, whereas for those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly, the appropriate name is not “king” but “tyrant.”

These are not Isidore’s words, although, as I said, the sentiment is found in book IX, chapter 3 of the *Etymologies*.

The books of the *Sentences* are cited in this council as follows:

> To explain why he is called a king, Isidore writes in the book of the *Sentences*: “For a king is so called from ruling.”

11. The Council of Tribur was convened in the year 895 to reform ecclesiastical discipline. The archbishops of Mainz, Cologne, and Trier, together with many other bishops, attended.

Canon 27 deals with clerics who return to the secular world and concludes as follows:

> Saint Isidore says that such men are like hippocentaurs, who are neither horses nor human beings, and who are carried about like brute animals by their freedom and desire.

This is an excerpted statement from Isidore, book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 3.

12. To the five councils indicated by Bignaeus, others may be added that commended Isidore’s doctrine.

The Second Council of Douzy was held in the year 874. In the synodal letter of this council to the bishops of Aquitaine, Isidore is cited from book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6:

> Isidore therefore speaks as follows concerning consanguinity: “Its sequence is separated into seven degrees in this way,” and so forth.

13. The General Council of Florence for the union of the Greeks was held in the year 1439.

In the second part of this council, conference 21, Johannes de Monte Nigro, of the Order of Preachers and provincial of Lombardy, confirmed against the Greeks the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son by Isidore’s words.

Isidore also flourished in Spain in the time of the blessed Gregory the Dialogist. I shall give one testimony concerning him. He composed a book of the *Etymologies* divided into twenty-two books. In the twelfth book, chapter 3, he says:

> There is this difference between the Son who is born and the Spirit who proceeds: the Son is born from one, whereas the Spirit proceeds from both. Therefore it is said: “If anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, he does not belong to him” . . . .

> And because after this teacher the entire Spanish nation, together with King Reccared, who had been an Arian, and with his predecessors, rejected the Arian heresy and anathematized it, they received the faith. It was necessary that many things be done in their proper place, so that this people might be instructed in the faith through the frequent celebration of councils. These councils were of great authority, and in them certain matters of faith were stated against the heretics. The entire Greek and Latin Church received those councils with great veneration, and there the rule of faith was established in this manner: “The rule of the Catholic faith, which the bishops of Carthage,” and so forth: “We believe in one true God,” and so forth.

14. Some points require notice here. The manuscripts do not agree among themselves concerning the number of books of the *Etymologies*, as I shall explain elsewhere. John the Provincial—for that is how he is ordinarily called in the acts of the council—recognized twenty-two books, and chapter 3 of Book XII is indicated when Isidore’s cited words actually occur in Book VII, chapter 3. In Isidore they are read somewhat differently: “and the Holy Spirit who proceeds, because the Son is born from one, while the Holy Spirit proceeds from both; and therefore the Apostle says: ‘Whoever does not have the Spirit of Christ,’ etc.” But the statement that Spain renounced the Arian heresy after Isidore is inconsistent with the chronology and with historical truth; I think one should read *per istum doctiorem* (“through this learned man”), not *post ipsum doctorem* (“after this learned man”), especially since the Provincial himself observes that Isidore flourished in the time of Gregory the Great, who is commonly called “the Dialogist” from his books of the *Dialogues*.

15. For this same reason, the variant reading indicated in the margin of Labbe’s collection—namely, “with King Thorismund” instead of “with King Reccared”—must be rejected, not merely as false but also as contrary to what precedes. Thorismund, son of Theodoric, was alive in the year 447, a time very far removed from the periods of Isidore and Gregory the Great. Otherwise the Provincial seriously confuses the chronology: for he implies that, in the Spanish councils celebrated after the abjuration of the Arian heresy, the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was added to the Creed. He asserts that this was first done in the time of Pope Leo, in the *Rule of Catholic Faith* which the bishops of Tarragona, Carthage, Lusitania, and Baetica composed and sent, at the command of Pope Leo of Rome, to Balconius, bishop of Galicia.

16. The facts are as follows. In the year 400 the First Council of Toledo was convened, at which a Rule of Faith was presented and the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was expressed in explicit words. This same Rule of Faith was sent, by order of Pope Leo, from a Spanish council held in the time of Theodoric and Thorismund, in the year 447, to Balconius—not Baleonius—bishop of Galicia. It is certain that all these events long preceded the time of King Reccared, under whom the Goths, after abjuring the Arian heresy, embraced the Catholic faith. In the index of the old Collection of the Canons of Spain, published by Aguirre and Censius, Book IV, title 4, the Rule of Faith enacted at the First Council of Toledo is explicitly cited. Flórez demonstrates in treatise 6, dissertation 1 of *Hispania sacra*, against some who without adequate reason believe that the phrase was interpolated here, that the word *Filioque* was already read in this Rule from the beginning.

# CHAPTER XXXII. Isidore’s Authority among the Collectors of Sacred Canons. The Canons of Gratian Identified and Corrected by Carlo Sebastiano Berardo

[Col. 0166C]

1. Saint Leo IV, Roman pontiff, judged that ecclesiastical matters which could not be clearly decided from the decrees of councils or Roman pontiffs—because, evidently, nothing certain had previously been defined concerning them—were to be settled from the statements of Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, and similar doctors of the Church. I presented his words in chapter 29. I showed above how weighty Isidore’s authority was in many councils, where I also discussed the collection of the Decretals of Gregory IX, in which Isidore’s words are frequently produced. I shall now speak of those who gathered ecclesiastical canons into some unified body through private scholarly effort and enriched their collections with passages from Isidore.

2. A Collection of Canons, divided into seven books and compiled at the beginning of the twelfth century, is preserved in Vatican Codex 1346; the Ballerini also discuss it in Part IV, chapter 18, *On the Antiquity of Collections of Canons*. Isidore’s authority is cited throughout this collection, and on folio 15 verso a catalogue of heretics is taken from Isidore’s books of the *Etymologies*. The title, or chapter, 183 of the Collection of Canons preserved in a parchment codex in the episcopal library of Pistoia—“On the Resurrection of the Dead, the Joy of the Good, the Punishment of the Wicked, and Punitive Purification”—is composed in several places from Gregory, Isidore, Ambrose, and especially Augustine. Bandini reports that Pluteus 19 of the Library of Santa Croce, Codex 5 of the eleventh century, contains, among certain canonical constitutions, in chapter 15, Isidore’s statement concerning those who make God their heir.

3. Burchard of Worms flourished toward the end of the tenth century. He compiled twelve volumes of decretals from many sources, including Isidore’s works, and Gratian derived very much from him. In the eleventh century Anselm of Lucca became prominent; from his *Decree*, or the thirteen books of his Collection of Canons, Gratian likewise took much, as Latinus Latinius noted in *Bibliotheca selecta sacra et profana*, p. 81. A manuscript of Anselm of Lucca’s collection exists in many libraries. The entry in the inventory of the Vatican Library, Codex 3531, which identifies “Extracts from Isidore’s *Etymologies*,” refers to this collection; the same extracts recur in Codex 3551. The former paper codex contains Anselm of Lucca’s *Decree*; the latter parchment codex contains certain miscellanies.

4. Above all, the *Decree of Gratian* must be mentioned, or, as Gratian himself titled it, the *Concordance of Discordant Canons*. Gratian flourished in the twelfth century. Nicholas Antonius writes of him as follows:

“Gratian, compiler of the decretals, intending to set forth in orderly fashion the rules of ecclesiastical discipline and to place before the Christian people, as it were, a tablet of holy laws, was not an author but merely a collector of the most select documents and statements of the ancient Fathers. Diligent scholars have discovered that he gathered more flowers from no other writer than from our Isidore.”

This may nevertheless appear somewhat exaggerated if Isidore is compared with Augustine, Jerome, and several others. Certainly there is no doubt that Gratian took much from Isidore. An index of Isidore’s passages incorporated by Gratian into his *Decree* is printed in the Paris editions of Bignaeus and Breul, in the old and the more recent Madrid editions, and in Cajetan’s *Eulogy of Saint Isidore*, p. 35; but it is presented most accurately by Berardo in Part III, chapter 27 of *Gratian’s Genuine Canons Distinguished from the Apocryphal*, a chapter devoted entirely to Isidore of Seville.

Cajetan considered the following points worth noting: in Distinction 2, canon “Plebiscita,” Isidore reads *scita* (“enactments”) rather than *plebiscita* (“plebiscites”); in the canon “Responsa prudentum,” Isidore lacks the word *prudentum* (“of the prudent”); and in Distinction 16, the canon “Canones qui dicuntur” is believed to belong to another Isidore, since Isidore wrote excellently concerning the canons of the Apostles. But Cajetan is mistaken: the Isidore who accepted the Apostolic Canons is not Isidore of Seville but the fictitious Isidore Mercator. The words of the canon are drawn from the preface to the genuine Collection of the Canons of the Church of Spain, whose author Gratian believed Isidore to have been—and many still believe this. Cajetan adds that the canon “Whoever consents to sinners,” Cause XI, Question 3, agrees with Isidore’s rule of life: “Not only the perpetrator but also the accomplice is held liable for the sin.”

I now present the chapter I mentioned, or Berardo’s dissertation, in smaller type in order to save space, using the first Turin edition of 1535 for comparison, since the Venetian edition is more corrupt.

209. 6. After Isidore of Córdoba, also called the Elder, who was celebrated among the Spaniards with the highest reputation for learning and holiness, another Isidore flourished among them toward the end of the sixth and the beginning of the seventh century. He was therefore called the Younger, and was bishop of Seville, from approximately the year 595 to the year 636. His outstanding praise is recorded in chapter 2 of the Eighth Council of Toledo, held in 653, in these words, etc. Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, who presided from the year 658 to 667, enumerated many distinguished works of this holy man in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9, writing as follows, etc.

Would that the complete works of so great a man had survived to our own time! It is certainly lamentable that a certain Theodiscus, who succeeded Isidore in the episcopal see, corrupted the works of his predecessor by cutting away the best material and inserting worthless matter; and then, through the Arab Avicenna, had everything so corrupted translated from Latin into Arabic. Let no one wonder at Theodiscus’s monstrous crime. He was a depraved man, condemned in ecclesiastical councils and deposed from his episcopal see as a heretic, because he said that Christ was a man, not God, and that he should be called the Son of God only by a kind of adoption. Nor did he withdraw from the heresy after his condemnation; rather, he defected entirely to Muhammad, whose sect he joined, and under the emperor Heraclius taught many detestable and abominable doctrines. From this everyone can infer how carefully one must examine the books attributed to Isidore. If anything objectionable is found in them, it will not necessarily be attributable to Isidore, but perhaps to Theodiscus or Avicenna.

## On the Book *On the Difference between the Old and the New Testament*

7. No book bearing the title *On the Difference between the Old and the New Testament* exists among Isidore’s works, such as the one cited by Gratian in Canon 5, Distinction 34. When Ivo of Chartres transcribed the same words in Part VIII of his *Decree*, chapter 66, he gave them the title: “Isidore, *On the Harmony of the Old and the New Testament*, chapter 3.” The authors of this title were the collectors of the canons themselves. When explaining certain statements of Isidore—statements made by the holy bishop as he compared the Old Testament with the New—they described Isidore as discussing the difference or harmony of the two Testaments.

In any case, neither Ivo’s chapter nor Gratian’s is found in the teaching of Isidore of Seville; only certain passages appear which agree very closely with that chapter. First, in Book II of *On Spiritual Differences*, no. 28, we read:

“Between the Law and the Gospel there is this difference: in the Law there is the letter, in the Gospel grace . . . . The former, granting permission for marriage, commands people to increase and beget children; the latter commends continence.”
