Moreover, in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, much is said concerning marriages. Among these passages are the following, which agree very closely with Gratian’s canon:

“That one man, and not one man with many women, but one man and one woman are joined together is demonstrated by the very first union divinely instituted as an example. For when the Lord had fashioned the man and saw that he needed a companion equal to him, he took one of his ribs and fashioned one woman for him. Thus Adam and the woman Eve, joined to one another in marriage, established for human beings, by the authority of their origin and by God’s first will, the form of marriage.

“Likewise, in spiritual marriage, just as there is one Christ and one Church, so there is one husband and one wife, both according to the testimony of nature and according to the sacrament of Christ. The number of marriages, however, began with the accursed man Lamech, who, married to two women, made three persons one flesh.

“But someone may say that the patriarchs also used several wives at the same time; therefore it will be lawful for us as well to marry or possess several wives. Certainly it will be lawful—if there still remain types of some future sacrament by which several marriages are symbolized. But the Apostle commands second marriages on account of incontinence; for it is better to marry one man again than to fornicate with several in order to satisfy lust. The permission to marry repeatedly is now more a matter of crime than of religion.

“For the fact that women are blessed by a priest in the very union of marriage was accomplished by God in the first union of man. Thus it is written: ‘God made man in his own image; male and female he made them, and he blessed them, saying: Increase and multiply.’ By this likeness, therefore, what was then done in paradise is now done in the Church.

“Finally, in Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 20, entitled ‘On the Difference of the Testaments,’ we read:

> ‘Some people do not accept the Old Testament because one thing was done in ancient times and another in the New Testament, not understanding that God, in a great dispensation, granted to each age whatever was suited to it. Thus in the Law he commands marriage, while in the Gospel he commends virginity . . . . For there fornication and the requital of injury were permitted and did not bring harm; but in the New Testament they are condemned with severe punishment if committed.’”

From these passages it may easily be inferred that those who first elaborated Gratian’s canon intended to touch upon the subject briefly, adding certain points and omitting others, which are found scattered throughout Isidore.

## On the Commentaries on Exodus

8. Isidore wrote commentaries on several books of the Old Testament, using a shorter style so that what the sacred author had explained at length he might place before readers briefly, thereby relieving the tedium of the indolent. In his preface the holy bishop declared that, in this work, he had followed the earlier Fathers—Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and Gregory the Great.

In his *Commentary on Exodus*, chapter 29, Isidore, considering the commandments of the Decalogue, says:

“Fifth: ‘You shall not commit adultery’; that is, no one may associate with women other than his wife outside the marriage covenant in order to satisfy lust. A person commits adultery specifically when he approaches another woman apart from his own.”

These words appear in Canon 15, Cause 32, Question 5. It should be observed, however, that Isidore lists this commandment in fifth place and places the other commandment, “You shall not kill,” in sixth place, without preserving the order of the commandments as it appears in chapter 20 of Exodus.

## On the Books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*

9. John Cochlaeus was the first among modern editors to publish two small books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* under Isidore’s name. He wrote that he had found them in an ancient codex among the books of Amalarius, formerly archbishop of Trier, in the time of Charlemagne. Isidore sent these books to Fulgentius, bishop, with the following brief letter prefixed. From it the work’s purpose and method may be understood:

“To my lord and servant of God, Fulgentius, bishop: Isidore, bishop.

“You ask me about the origin of the offices by whose instruction we are educated in the Churches, so that you may learn briefly by whose authorship they were instituted. Therefore, as you requested, I have sent an arranged little book on the kinds of offices, commenting on the writings of the most ancient authors wherever the subject required. In it I have drawn out many things in my own style; others, however, I have incorporated just as they stood in their authors, so that the reading might more readily preserve the authority of the faith concerning each matter. If any of these things should displease you, forgiveness will more readily be granted for my errors, since those matters for which the testimony of authors is cited should not be charged to my account as faults.”

The first book presents various ecclesiastical matters, namely, various institutions concerning churches, psalmody, sacred readings, prayers, solemnities, and fasts. The second concerns the distinctions among the ranks of the clergy and likewise the classes of monks and laypeople. Some have doubted the authenticity of these books; but, in my judgment, either arguments establishing a reasonable doubt are lacking or those proposed are insufficiently strong.

In Book II, chapter 1, Isidore begins by interpreting the name “clergy,” writing that they are so called because they have been called into the Lord’s lot. The same holy man taught this elsewhere, namely in the books of the *Etymologies*, from which Canon 1, Distinction 21, was drawn.

After this, in chapter 2, he proceeds to examine the rules of the clergy, writing as follows:

“By the law of the Fathers it is therefore provided that, separated from ordinary life, they abstain from the pleasures of the world; that they take no part in spectacles or pageants; that they avoid public banquets and pursue private ones not only chastely but also soberly. They must by no means engage in usury, nor seek shameful occupations for profit or pursue any kind of fraud; they must flee the love of money as the source of all [read: all crimes]; they must reject secular offices and business and not enter upon ranks of honor through ambition.

“They must not accept fees for medical services; they must beware of deceit and conspiracies; they must flee hatred, rivalry, slander, and envy. They must not walk with wandering eyes, an unrestrained tongue, or an insolent and arrogant gait, but must display modesty and shamefacedness of mind through simple dress and bearing. They must utterly abhor obscenity of speech, just as they abhor obscenity of conduct.

“They must avoid overly frequent visits to widows and virgins and in no way desire companionship with foreign women. They must also strive continually to preserve the chastity of an inviolate body, or at least bind themselves by the bond of a single marriage. They must show due obedience to their elders and must not exalt themselves through any desire for ostentation.

“Finally, they must devote themselves unceasingly to instruction, readings, psalms, hymns, and songs. For such must those be who strive to dedicate themselves to divine worship: namely, that while they apply themselves to knowledge, they may administer the grace of teaching to the people.”

I have transcribed Isidore’s words in full; Canon 3, Distinction 23, is to be compared with them.

10. Canon 20, Distinction 63, was cited as though it should be referred to Isidore’s books *On Offices*. But not even a similar statement is found there, in which the exceptional authority of archdeacons in choosing parish rectors and administering vacant parish churches is discussed. Rather, several passages are read which appear to contradict that same Canon 20.

Isidore says in Book II, chapter 6:

“Chorepiscopi—that is, vicars of bishops—were instituted, as the canons themselves testify, after the example of the seventy elders, as priests on account of their care for the poor. Instituted in villages and rural districts, they govern the churches entrusted to them, having permission to appoint readers, subdeacons, and exorcists. But they must not presume to ordain presbyters or deacons without the knowledge of the bishop in whose territory they are known to preside; for these are ordained only by the bishop of the city to which they belong.”

Why, according to Isidore’s statement, was the jurisdiction of these lower prelates restricted, especially in ordaining priests, with this authority reserved to bishops alone, if Isidore had likewise assigned to archdeacons the election of parish priests?

I admit that archdeacons were vicars of bishops. But Isidore also taught that chorepiscopi performed vicarious service for the bishop. Why would he grant to one kind of vicar what he denied to the others? This observation seems to me all the more solid because it is more clearly established from ancient records that archdeacons assisted the bishops in the temporal affairs of the churches, while chorepiscopi assisted them in spiritual affairs.

I further admit that, in the seventh century of the Church and in subsequent centuries, archdeacons exercised very great authority in the parishes. But this arose from the actions of those same archdeacons, who exceeded the limits of the jurisdiction entrusted to them. Hence, at the Council of Chalon-sur-Saône, from which Canon 3, Distinction 94, was drawn, it was worthwhile to restrict their authority. Hincmar of Rheims, in the capitularies he issued for archdeacons, chapter 5, section 7, warned them not to confuse the parishes by going around them, to divide one from another, or to subject one to another.

But such authority was not confirmed by the general testimony of holy men; it would have been, if we were genuinely to make Isidore the author of that Canon 20. In light of this observation, it is useful to suspect that the editor of the canon wished to follow, in composing his text, what is transmitted under Isidore’s name in Canon 1, Distinction 25, where certain matters are presented concerning the authority of archdeacons in the affairs of parish churches. What should be said about that canon will be explained below.

11. In Book I, chapter 42, the words of Canon 10, Distinction 76, are found; that passage concerns the various times appointed for ecclesiastical fasts.

12. The material found in Canon 7, Cause 30, Question 5, is read in Book II, chapter 19, where the whole passage is Isidore’s and demonstrates that only one wife is to be joined to a husband. The holy man proves this in several ways, as is clear from what I noted shortly before concerning Canon 5, Distinction 34. After that he continues as follows:

“That the same women, when they marry, are veiled is specifically so that they may know that by this they are subject and humble toward their husbands. Hence the veil itself is commonly called *Mavortem*, that is, Mars, because it is a sign of marital dignity and authority. For the head of a woman is the man. They are therefore veiled when they marry so that they may recognize the woman’s modesty, since what follows from this is already a matter of shame.

“Thus Rebecca, when she was being led to her bridegroom, as soon as she saw him, received greeting or kisses; but immediately, realizing what she was about to become, she veiled her head with a cloak. For *obnubere* means ‘to veil’; hence married women are also called *nuptae*, because they veil their faces. Hence clouds are called *nubes*, because they cover the earth or the ether.

“That brides are joined together after the blessing by a band tied around them signifies that they must not dissolve the bond of marital unity. But the fact that this same band is mixed with white and purple colors signifies that the white is applied to purity of life and the purple to the succession of blood, so that by this sign both parties may be reminded for a time to observe the law of continence, while afterward they are not forbidden to render the marital debt.

“For what the Apostle says to married people—‘Abstain for a time, so that you may devote yourselves to prayer’—the white of the band signifies; but what he adds—‘Return again to the same’—the purple color demonstrates.

“The fact that at first the bridegroom gives a ring to the bride is done either as a sign of mutual fidelity or, rather, so that their hearts may be joined by the same pledge. The ring is therefore placed on the fourth finger because, as is said, a certain vein of blood passes through it all the way to the heart. In ancient times, however, no more than one ring was given, lest plurality divide a single love.”

13. Whether Canon 19 or Canon 74, *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, is intended, the material is found in Book II, chapter 24, where baptism and those who receive or administer that sacrament are discussed. When the subject is the baptism of children, the words of Canon 74 are presented, and they agree entirely with the complete manuscripts of Isidore. But the words of Canon 19, in which the minister of the sacrament is discussed, require correction.

The holy bishop was demonstrating that the ministry of baptism had been entrusted by Christ to priests alone. For Christ said to the Apostles, whose successors are priests: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing,” etc. Likewise, the sacrament of Penance is reserved for administration by priests alone, since divine power to remit sins was given to the Apostles. After this he concludes:

“Thus it is clear that baptism has been entrusted to priests alone. Even deacons are not permitted to complete its mystery without bishops or presbyters, unless, when those ministers are far away, extreme necessity caused by the final illness compels it; and this is often permitted even to faithful laypeople, so that no one may be summoned from this world without the saving remedy.”

Gratian adds certain material under the name of Gelasius. These words are in fact the same as those of Canon 13, Distinction 93. Since I omitted them in their proper place, I shall transcribe them here. They are found in Letter 1 of Gelasius to the bishops of Lucania, chapters 7 and 8:

“We have also established that deacons must preserve their proper measure, and we do not permit them to attempt anything beyond the scope assigned by the canons of the Fathers. They must apply to their ministry absolutely none of those things which antiquity decreed to belong properly to the higher orders. They must not presume to baptize without a bishop or presbyter, unless, when the aforesaid ministers are perhaps situated at a considerable distance, extreme necessity compels it. This is often permitted also to Christian laypeople.

“They must not sit in the presbytery while divine rites are being celebrated or any ecclesiastical discussion is being held. They have no right to exercise the privilege of distributing the sacred Body in the presence of the bishop or presbyter, except when these are absent.”

## On the Letter to Ludifred
### 14. On the Letter to Ludifred

After the two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in the Breulian edition of Isidore’s works, there follows a letter to Ludifred, bishop of Córdoba. The editor had reproduced it there, as he himself states, in the form in which he had found it in Gratian, canon 1, Distinction 25; in Ivo, Part VI of the *Decretum*, chapter 20; and also in manuscript codices. [Col. 0173C] Then, after the *Books of Sentences*, he added the final part of the same letter, previously omitted, which, as he says, he had very recently obtained.

There are certain points at which Breul’s text differs. Thus, where Gratian reads in canon 1, Distinction 25:

> “What follows . . . the psalmist’s office is to sing, to pronounce blessings . . . what the prophets foretold . . . to hold the towel, and to the bishop, presbyter, and levites . . . to arrange upon the altar . . . are divided through the care of the first-chanter and treasurer . . . let him read the Epistle and Gospel . . . and disputes belong to his care . . . and by him it is publicly preached in the church”—

(the word “preached” was added by the Roman Correctors, since formerly the reading was “they preach”)—

> “above all the presbyters . . . and, with careful attention to the office of considering and carrying out the readings, blessings, psalm, praises, offertory, and responsories, [to determine] which of the clergy ought to recite them. Also the order and manner of psalmody in the choir according to the solemnity of the seasons . . . To the treasurer belongs the appointment of the basilicaries and doorkeeper, etc.”

[Col. 0173D] Breul wished the text to be printed as follows:

> “What follows . . . The psalmist’s office is to sing, namely, to pronounce blessings . . . what the prophets have foretold . . . to hold the towel for the bishop, presbyters, and levites . . . to arrange upon the altar . . . are divided through the care of the first-chanter and treasurer . . . let him read the Apostle and Gospel . . . and disputes belong to his care . . . and by him they are publicly preached in the church . . . over all the presbyters . . . and [to determine] which of the clergy ought carefully to consider and carry out the office of singing, the readings, psalm, praises, responsories of the offices. Also the order and manner of singing in the choir according to solemnity and season . . . To the treasurer belongs the appointment of the doorkeeper of the basilicas, etc.”

It will not be useless to add the final part of the letter, omitted by Gratian and, as we noted above, edited by Breul; for the complete letter, once published, will make the distribution of ecclesiastical offices clearer. The author of the letter continues after Gratian’s words: [Col. 0174A]

> “To him”—that is, to the treasurer—“they will come from the parishes for chrism. He himself receives from the people the candles and offerings of the altar. He himself collects candles throughout the churches on feast days. The ornaments and vestments of the altar belong to him, and whatever is used in the temple exists under his direction. He himself guards the veils and ornaments of the basilicas located in the city that do not have a presbyter. As for the daily candles and small candles, whatever remains in the basilicas, the basilicary carries to him each month. From these the treasurer gives one quarter to the basilicary. They divide the remaining three parts equally among themselves with the first-chanter and the presbyter who celebrates Mass in that basilica.

> “To the steward belongs the repair”—perhaps *reparatio* should be read instead of *separatio*, “separation”—“of the basilicas and their construction; the church’s actions in lawsuits, whether in bringing proceedings or responding; also the collection of tribute and the accounts of what is brought in. The care of the fields and the cultivation of the vineyards, [215] cases concerning possessions, and the stipends of the clergy’s servants, widows, and devoted poor; the distribution of clothing and food to the household servants of the clergy, as well as to servants and craftsmen—all these duties are fulfilled by him according to the command and judgment of his bishop.

[Col. 0174B] “These are the things that have either been distributed by our predecessors according to the ranks of the offices, or preserved for each office by the custom of the churches. You should attribute none of these matters to our own judgment, except what reason has taught or the antiquity of tradition has decreed.

> “As for the father of the monastery about whom you have informed us, the man who should be placed first is he whom holy life and uprightness of conduct commend, and in whom, while he was subject to authority, there was no fraud. Grace is justly heaped upon such a man, as the Lord says: ‘Because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much.’

> “But he who, while still under authority, lived wickedly and did not hesitate to defraud the brothers will, when appointed superior and once he sees himself in power and freedom, freely and without restraint commit greater and worse offenses. For concerning such men the Apostle says: ‘But you do wrong, and this to your brothers. Do you not know that the unrighteous will not possess the kingdom of God?’

> “But let it suffice for us to say this to you: Fulfill what you judge worthy of God.

> “After this I do not cease to pray for your holiness, that you may stand as an intercessor for me before the Lord, so that, because I have fallen through my own fault, I may obtain remission of sins through you.”

[Col. 0174C] Thus the complete letter has been transcribed from the Breulian codex. It must now be considered whether it was rightly attributed to Isidore of Seville. I do not deny that Ludifred was subject, by metropolitan right, to Isidore of Seville. He is shown to have held the bishopric of Córdoba as early as the year 633, since in that year he subscribed the Fourth Council of Toledo—although under the name Leodeficus in Labbe—and in 638, at the Sixth Council of Toledo, under the name Laufredus in the same author.

But whatever his name—Ludifred, Laodeficus, or Laufredus—I very much doubt that he asked Isidore to enumerate the individual offices of the clergy. Indeed, once the complete letter is considered, since it has the character of a written reply, arguments immediately emerge from which one may infer that it is apocryphal, unless someone should maintain that the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* are not genuinely Isidore’s.

It is certain that Ludifred came to the bishopric of Córdoba at a time when Isidore was already worn out by old age; for Isidore died scarcely two or three years after Ludifred obtained the episcopate, as can be gathered by comparing the episcopal subscriptions in the Spanish councils. [Col. 0174D] Thus Isidore could have composed the letter when already elderly, and consequently at a time when the two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* mentioned above had already been published.

Who could readily say that, after complete and indeed more extensive books on ecclesiastical offices had been published, Ludifred asked Isidore about the same subject, as though those books were insufficient for Ludifred’s instruction? Who could readily say that Isidore, in his reply, made no mention at all of those little books on offices, nor urged Ludifred to read them in that section?

Add to this that the method of this letter differs from that preserved by Isidore in the book *On Offices*. In the books *On Offices*, where he deliberately enumerated the individual ranks of the clergy, he entirely passed over those whom he enumerated in the letter; and conversely, in the letter he passed over all the ranks that he enumerated in the books *On Offices*.

[Col. 0175A] [216] To give examples: much is said in the books *On Offices* about chorepiscopi, and much about minor clerics initiated by tonsure. Where is there any discussion of these in the letter to Ludifred? In this letter, almost everything concerns the authority of archpresbyters, archdeacons, first-chanters, basilicaries, and similar persons. Where is any mention of these in the books *On Offices*?

Finally, the great variety of codices in which the letter appears copied in different forms—here more expansive, there more abbreviated—seems to increase the suspicion. The Roman Correctors have already noted several matters concerning this variation among the codices in the Gratianic canon: verses that appear in one place are missing elsewhere, while in yet other places they are written in reverse order.

Garzias Loaisa published another copy of the letter in Labbe, volume VII of the Venetian edition, page 434, stating that he had received it from a very ancient manuscript codex of the library of St. Lawrence, called the *Vigilano*—“the admirable work of King Philip the Catholic.” [Col. 0175B] I shall reproduce the wording of this copy, which may be very useful for correcting the Gratianic canon and even, if it seems appropriate, the Breulian edition. It reads as follows:

> “Having read through the letter of your holiness, I rejoiced because, through the report of others, I learned of your desired health. Concerning those matters which the discourse of your speech has sought to disclose in what follows, I give thanks to God that you are devoting yourself to the care of pastoral office and inquiring how ecclesiastical offices are to be ordered. Although everything is known to your prudence, nevertheless, because you consult me with fatherly affection, I shall explain, insofar as I am able, and shall declare what belongs to each of all the grades of the Church.

> “To the doorkeeper belong the keys of the church, so that he may close and open the temple of God and guard everything that is inside and outside; he is to receive the faithful and cast out the excommunicated and unbelieving.

> “To the acolyte belongs the preparation of the lights in the sacristy. He carries the candle and prepares the stands for the Eucharistic chalice.

> “To the exorcist belongs the duty of memorizing the exorcisms and laying his hands upon the possessed and catechumens during exorcism.

[Col. 0175C] “To the psalmist belongs the office of singing: to pronounce blessings, praises, the sacrifice, responsories, and everything that pertains to skill in singing.

> “To the reader belongs the duty of proclaiming the readings and preaching to the people what the prophets foretold.

> “To the subdeacon belongs the duty of carrying the chalice and paten to the altar of Christ and handing them to the levites, and ministering to them; also of holding the pitcher and water, the basin and towel; and of providing water to the bishop, presbyter, and levites for washing their hands before the altar.

> “To the deacon belongs the duty of assisting the priests and ministering in everything performed in the sacraments of Christ—in baptism, that is, and in chrism; of bringing the offerings in the paten and chalice and arranging them upon the altar; also of preparing and clothing the Lord’s table; of carrying the cross; and of preaching the Gospel and the Apostle. For just as the Old Testament is entrusted to the readers, so the New Testament is commanded to be preached by the deacons.

[Col. 0175D] “To him also belongs the office of prayers and the recitation of the names. He himself warns that ears should be attentive to God; he himself exhorts the people to pray; he himself cries out, and he himself announces peace.

> “To the presbyter belongs the duty of consecrating the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood upon God’s altar, saying the prayers, and blessing God’s gifts.

> “To the bishop belongs the consecration of basilicas, the anointing of the altar, and the preparation of chrism. He establishes the aforesaid offices [217] and ecclesiastical orders; he blesses holy virgins; and although each person presides over his own individual office, he himself is nevertheless the organizer of all.

> “These are the orders and ministries of the clergy; yet, by pontifical authority, they are distributed under the care of the archdeacon and through the supervision of the first-chanter and treasurer.

> “For the archdeacon commands the subdeacons and levites. To him belong these ministries: the arrangement by the levites of the clothing of the altar; the care of carrying incense and the sacrifice to the altar; and the care that the subdeacons bring to the altar, for the sacrifice, the things that are necessary.

[Col. 0176A] “He is responsible for determining which of the levites shall read the Apostle and Gospel, which shall say the prayers or the responsory on Sundays or feast days. The care of the parish churches, their ordering, and disputes belong to him. For the repair of the diocesan basilicas he makes recommendations to the priest; with the bishop’s authorization he himself investigates the parishes and the ornaments or property of the parish basilicas. He likewise brings to the bishop the records of ecclesiastical freedoms; he himself receives the money collected from Communion and brings it to the bishop, and he distributes the proper shares to the clergy.

> “The offenses of the deacons are reported to the bishop by the archdeacon. He himself announces to the priest in the sacristy the days of fasting and the feast days, and he himself preaches publicly in the church. When the archdeacon is absent, the deacon next in rank fulfills his office.

> “To the first-chanter belong the acolytes, exorcists, psalmists, and readers; also the giving of the signal for the clergy’s office, for honorable conduct of life, and the duty of considering and carrying out the office; and the responsibility for determining which of the clergy should say the readings, blessings, psalm, praises, offertory, and responsories.

[Col. 0176B] “Also the order and manner of psalmody in the choir according to solemnity and season. Also the arrangement for carrying the lights. If anything is needed for repairing the basilicas located in the city, he announces it to the priest. He himself sends the bishop’s letters concerning the days of fasting to the parish churches through the doorkeepers. He disciplines the clerics whom he knows to be offending. Those whom he does not wish to correct, he reports to the bishop’s attention. He himself appoints the basilicaries and arranges the registers (*matriculae*).

> “When the first-chanter is absent, the matters mentioned above are carried out by the man who is either next to him in rank or devoted by his learning to the careful administration of these things.

> “To the treasurer belong the basilicaries and doorkeepers; the arrangement for preparing the incense; the care of making the chrism; the care of organizing the baptistery; the preparation of the lights in the sacristy; the preparation of the sacrifice from the things to be offered, etc.”

Some matters concerning the office of the basilicaries and stewards follow at this point, but I shall not discuss them here, since that part of the letter does not appear in Gratian. [Col. 0176C]

Meanwhile, from what has been said it is useful to conclude that the celebrated Gratianic canon can have little force for establishing the discipline of the clergy, either because the authenticity of the letter is not sufficiently certain or because the manuscripts differ so greatly.

### On the Rule of Monks

#### 15.

The rule that Isidore published for the instruction of monks has always been held in the highest esteem by ecclesiastical men and by the monks themselves. It is found among the other works of the holy bishop and was published [218] through the care of Lucas Holstenius, together with the other rules, in almost the same wording, though with some variation in individual words that does not alter the meaning.

From it was drawn canon 18, Cause 11, Question 3, which Gratian, in his usual manner, presented as a general monument of ecclesiastical discipline, adding several things that he extracted from elsewhere.

[Col. 0176D] In chapter 18 of Isidore’s rule, the following is read concerning a monk excluded from communion with the other monks:

> “No one may pray or speak with an excommunicated person. No one at all may eat with an excommunicated person, not even the man who supplies him with food for his sustenance.”

The Collectors, who were earlier than Gratian, added the words “except those things that pertain to the same excommunication.” Gratian further added what follows in the section beginning “For if anyone,” which has nothing to do with Isidore.

Ivo gave Gratian an opportunity for error. Having copied Isidore’s words in Part XIV of the *Decretum*, chapter 95, he added the following in chapter 96:

> “Hence, above: If any brother, either openly or secretly, has spoken with an excommunicated person, he immediately incurs with him the common penalty of excommunication.”

He understood the words “hence, above” as though he thought that the following fragment referred [perhaps read *referri*, “to be referred”] to the same Isidore, the author of the preceding chapter. This is false, however; rather, it should have been referred to the author of chapters 93 and 94, namely, the Council of Mainz of the year 888, where the canon against robbers is worded as follows: [Col. 0177A]

> “But if anyone, after this sentence has been pronounced by us, knowingly communicates with them, let him know that he has been struck by us with the same sword as they.”

Ivo had set down this judgment of the Fathers of Mainz in different words in the aforementioned chapter 96, and our collector transferred it, in that form, into his own codex.

Therefore, anyone who wishes to interpret Gratian’s canon correctly will first understand that among monks it had been established that, on account of certain crimes, monks were to be separated from the fellowship of the others. He will then understand that those who had communicated with robbers were, by the decree of the Fathers of Mainz, to be condemned to a similar penalty.

We read this very decree under the name of the Eighth Synod in canon 28 of the same cause and question, although it is found in no council called the Eighth. These are Gratian’s interpolations: using corrupt codices, he more than once cited under the name of the Eighth Synod things that were thought to belong to Isidore, as I had to point out in the first part of chapter 56, at the beginning, and in this same [Col. 0177B] Part III, chapter 9.

### On the Books of Sentences, or On the Highest Good

#### 16.

The books of Isidore called the *Sentences* are also called *On the Highest Good*, because the work begins with these words: “God is the highest good,” and so forth. It is divided into three little books, a truly beautiful work and one well suited to directing human affections rightly.

From the end of book III, chapter 6, canon 3, Distinction 6, was extracted the following:

> “It is not a sin when we are unwillingly deceived by nocturnal images; but it is a sin if, before we are deceived, we are anticipated by the affections of our thoughts. For the images of lust,” and so forth.

The remainder agrees with Gratian’s canon.

#### 17.

In the same book III, chapter 51, canon 2, Distinction 9, is found. In place of the words *nec in se convenit posse damnare jura*—“nor is it fitting that laws be able to condemn in themselves”—[219] some codices of Isidore read *nec in se convenit frustrari jura*—“nor is it fitting that laws be frustrated in themselves.” In the Breulian edition, however, the reading is: “nor can laws condemn in themselves.”

#### 18.

Likewise, in book III, chapter 13, the words of canon [Col. 0177C] 15, Distinction 37, are found. The opening words should be read, according to the Breulian edition: “Therefore Christians are forbidden,” and so forth.

There Isidore was discussing those who took pleasure in the fables of the poets for two reasons: first, because certain obscene matters were placed before the mind in them and readers were thereby aroused to lust; second, because some Christians made these writings their delight to such an extent that they grew weary of meditating on the divine Scriptures.

Thus Isidore continues after the words reported by Gratian:

> “Some take greater pleasure in meditating upon the sayings of the pagans because of their swelling and ornate style than upon Holy Scripture because of its humble eloquence. But what benefit is there in *perficere* [read *proficere*, ‘make progress’] in worldly teachings and becoming empty in divine ones? In pursuing perishable fictions and scorning heavenly mysteries? Such books must therefore be avoided, and shunned for the love of the holy Scriptures.”

#### 19.

What is read in canon 10, Distinction 45, is found in full in book II, chapter 52, where the holy [Col. 0177D] bishop discussed at length the duties of judges.

Canon 9, Distinction 81, is found at the end of chapter 10 of book II. In place of the words “what he often thought or did there,” Breul published: “what he always thought or did there.”

#### 20.

In book III, chapter 54, Isidore turns his speech against those judges who allow themselves to be corrupted by gifts from the wealthy and consequently oppress the poor. Among other things he writes:

> “The rich man quickly corrupts the judge with gifts. But the poor man, since he does not have what he can offer,” and so forth.

These words, together with what follows, are reported in canon 72, Cause 11, Question 3.

#### 21.

Isidore said much about oaths in book II, chapter 31. He begins there as follows:

> “Just as one who does not speak cannot lie, so one who does not desire to swear cannot commit perjury. An oath must therefore be avoided, and should not be used except in absolute necessity. It is not contrary to God’s command to swear; but when we make a practice of swearing, we incur the crime of perjury.”

These words are found in canon 13, Cause 22, Question 1.

Then, after some intervening material, he continues: [Col. 0178A]

> “Whatever art of words a person may use in swearing, God, who is the witness of the conscience, receives it in the way understood by the person to whom the oath is sworn. A person becomes guilty in two ways: by taking God’s name in vain and by deceitfully ensnaring his neighbor.

> “An oath by which evil is rashly promised is not to be kept—for example, if someone should promise an adulterous woman his faith that he would remain with her permanently. It is more tolerable not to fulfill such an oath than to remain in the disgrace of fornication.”

Gratian copied these words in canon 13, Cause 22, Question 4, and in canon 9, Cause 22, Question 5. Anyone who carefully considers them will immediately understand that they overturn the opinion of those who do not hesitate to foster lies by means of what they call mental reservations.

#### 22.

In book III, chapter 51, shortly after the words cited above in canon 2, Distinction 9, the words of canon 20, Cause 23, Question 5, are found. In place of the Gratianic text, the following should be substituted:

> “The princes of the world . . . But within the Church . . . let authority command this through the fear of discipline . . . and, so that it may deserve veneration, let it confer this by the power of authority, etc.”

[Col. 0178B] [220] #### 23.

Canon 15, Cause 32, Question 7, must be referred to book II, chapter 39. There Isidore indicated, in the following words, when a person is still stained by the slippery condition of sin:

> “If the pleasure of fornication delights the mind more than the love of chastity, sin still reigns in the person. Certainly, if the beauty of inward chastity delights him more, sin no longer reigns, but justice reigns. For sin does not reign in a person only on account of fornication committed; if he still takes delight in it and it holds his spirit, without doubt it reigns.

> “Fornication of the flesh is adultery; fornication of the soul is slavery to idols. There is also spiritual fornication, according to what the Lord says: ‘Whoever looks upon a woman in order to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart.’ Every unclean pollution is called fornication, although each person gives himself over to a different pleasure of disgrace.

[Col. 0178C] “For from the pleasure of fornication various crimes are born, by which the kingdom of God is closed and a person is separated from God. Among the seven vices, fornication is the gravest crime, because through the uncleanness of the flesh it violates the temple of God and, taking away the members of Christ, makes them members of a prostitute.”

What follows in Gratian beginning “Now there are certain things” does not belong to Isidore, but rather to Origen, who writes in Homily 5 on Genesis, concerning chapters 19 and 20:

> “There are indeed certain women—for we do not condemn all women indiscriminately—who, like animals without any discernment, serve lust incessantly. I would not even compare them with dumb beasts. For beasts themselves know that, once they have conceived, they should no longer grant males access to themselves.”

#### 24.

Canon 9 *On Penance*, Distinction 3, is presented by Gratian under the name of Smaragdus. Smaragdus, who flourished among monks at the beginning of the ninth century and wrote commentaries on the rule of Saint Benedict, collected many sayings of the ancient Fathers, especially those of Isidore of Seville.

But since the statement of canon 9 is found in full in Isidore, we need be less concerned with the later writer, whom I would rather call a compiler. Isidore says in book II, chapter [Col. 0178D] 13:

> “That man performs penance worthily who laments his guilt through legitimate satisfaction, condemning and grieving over what he has done, and grieving all the more abundantly the more readily he was inclined to sin.

> “That man performs penance worthily who so laments past evils that he does not commit them again in the future. For he who laments sin and again commits sin is like someone washing an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.”

I have transcribed more from Isidore than Gratian published, so that I might clearly explain the twofold character of penance according to Isidore’s judgment: the first part concerns past crimes, while the second looks toward the future.

#### 25.

Canon 11 *On Penance*, Distinction 3, must be tested against book II, chapter 16, and should be set out in these words:

> “He is a mocker, not a penitent, who still does what he regrets; nor does he seem, as a submissive man, to be asking God, but rather, as a proud man, to be mocking him. The penitent who returns to sin is a dog returning to its vomit.

> “For many shed tears without ceasing [Col. 0179A] and do not stop sinning. [221] It is clear that some receive tears for penance but do not attain the effect of penance, because through instability of mind they now shed tears at the recollection of sin, but then, when their former habit revives, they repeat and commit again the things over which they had wept.

> “He who wishes both to lament the past and to devote himself to worldly actions does not possess cleansing, since he still does what he could lament in penance. Isaiah says to sinners: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean.’ Therefore he is washed and clean who both laments the past and does not again commit things that ought to be lamented.

> “He is washed but not clean who laments what he has done but does not abandon it, and after his tears repeats the things over which he had wept.”

#### 26.

Canon 24 *On Consecration*, Distinction 2, and canon 115 *On Consecration*, Distinction 4, should be joined together, for both were extracted from book I, chapter 22, where Isidore was discussing baptism and Eucharistic communion. Indeed, the words read at the end of canon 115 are the same as those copied in canon 24.

I shall reproduce Isidore’s entire passage here. He says:

> “Those who are in their mother’s [Col. 0179B] womb cannot be baptized together with their mother, because one who has not yet been born according to Adam cannot be reborn according to Christ. For regeneration cannot be spoken of in one whom generation has not preceded.

> “Those who do not live within the Church according to the dignity of the Church, but destroy by their deeds the faith that they hold in word, are spoken of in the following passage: ‘They have been multiplied beyond number’—understand, ‘in the kingdom of the predestined.’

> “Those who live wickedly in the Church and do not cease to receive Communion, thinking that they are cleansed by such communion, should learn that it profits them nothing for cleansing, as the prophet says: ‘What is it that my beloved has done many wicked things in my house? Will holy flesh take away your evils from you?’ And the Apostle says: ‘Let a person examine himself, and then let him eat of that bread and drink from the cup.’”

### On the Books of the Etymologies

#### 27.

[Col. 0179C] That Isidore was a man of universal learning can easily be demonstrated by the twenty books of the *Etymologies*, also called the *Origins*. In them the holy man ranged so widely across all the sciences that he briefly touched upon the subject matter of each and upon all things in general, especially noting the meanings and distinctions of the terms used by those who cultivate the disciplines.

If only Isidore had completed those books! We should then have been profoundly amazed at the great elegance joined with exceptional learning. Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, knew that Isidore was being exhausted by the kind of labor in which he investigated the origins and powers of all things and words. For this reason he asked nothing more insistently of him than that the same little books should be published as quickly as possible for the common good.

Before the work was entirely finished, the holy man of Seville nevertheless complied with his friend Braulio and sent him the little books, still rough and far from complete. When the bishop of Zaragoza received them, he arranged them in a definite order and published them under Isidore’s name. Braulio himself testifies to this in a letter to Isidore, writing: [Col. 0179D]

> “Unless I am mistaken, seven years have now revolved since I remember asking you for the books of the *Origins* that you had composed. In various and different ways you frustrated me when I was present, and when I was absent you wrote nothing back to me about them. Instead, by subtle delay, you offered now that they were not yet finished, now that they had not yet been written, now that my letters had been lost, and many other excuses. Thus we have reached the present day, and I remain without the result of my request.

> “[222] For this reason I shall turn my prayers into complaint, so that what I could not obtain by entreaty I may perhaps achieve by provoking you with reproach,” and so forth.

Isidore replied to him as follows:

> “I sent the codex of the *Etymologies* along with other codices while traveling. Although it is uncorrected because of my illness, I had nevertheless intended to offer it to you for correction when I reached the appointed place of the council.”

Thus, although Isidore was the author of the books, Braulio was free to arrange and correct them, since the final hand had not yet been laid upon them.

[Col. 0180A] Here is a brief outline of the division of the little books. In the first, grammar is treated; in the second, rhetoric and dialectic; in the third, arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy; in the fourth, medicine; in the fifth, laws and times; in the sixth, books and ecclesiastical offices; in the seventh, God, angels, and the orders of the faithful; in the eighth, the Church and various sects; in the ninth, languages and societies; in the tenth, letters and their alphabet; in the eleventh, humanity and prodigies; in the twelfth, animals; in the thirteenth, the world and its parts; in the fourteenth, the earth and its parts; in the fifteenth, buildings and fields; in the sixteenth, stones and metals; in the seventeenth, rural matters; in the eighteenth, war and games; in the nineteenth, ships, buildings, and clothing; and finally, in the twentieth, provisions and rural and domestic implements.

## 28.

Gratian could not have chosen a better beginning for his collection than to start from the general principles of law which Isidore set forth in Book V of the *Etymologies*, where—as we have said—the subject matter of laws was treated. [Col. 0180B] To this book, therefore, canon 1 and the following canons of the whole of Distinction 1, canon 1 and the following canons of the whole of Distinction 2, canons 3 and 4 of Distinction 3, canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 4, and canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 7 must be referred.

In order to explain this matter systematically, Isidore, in chapter 1, examines the origin of laws in general and briefly states who the more distinguished authors of laws were. Thus he says in chapter 1:

“Moses first of all explained the divine laws to the Hebrew people in sacred writings,” and so forth.

This is canon 1 of Distinction 7. There, in place of the words, “Lycurgus first devised laws for the Lacedaemonians on the authority of Apollo,” one should read, in accordance with the commonly circulated Isidorian manuscripts: “Lycurgus first devised the legal rights/laws of Lacedaemon on the authority of Apollo.”

Immediately after canon 1, canon 2 of the same Distinction 7 should be connected with it. Its wording is displayed somewhat differently in the commonly circulated Isidorian manuscripts:

“These were Appius Claudius, Genutius, Veturius, Julius, Manilius, Sulpicius, Sextius, Curiatius, Romilius, Postumius . . . through neglect they fell out of use, of which,” and so forth.

[Col. 0180C] Here it should be noted that Isidore maintains a profound silence concerning the compilation of laws made under Justinian’s authority, although he mentions the Theodosian Code. This is a most serious indication, from which it is inferred that Justinian’s Codes were then unknown among the Spaniards, because they had not been subject to the empire of Justinian or of the emperors who followed him.

Isidore continues in chapter 2:

“All laws are either divine or human. Divine laws are based on nature, human laws on customs; and for that reason these differ, since some laws please one people and others another. *Fas* is the divine law, *ius* the human law. It is permitted by divine law to pass through another’s field, but it is not permitted by human law.”

This is canon 1 of Distinction 1.

Perhaps someone might find difficulty with the statement made there that divine laws are based on nature, as though Isidore recognized no distinction between natural and divine laws. I, however, although I could say that Isidore was speaking of the author, origin, and cause of laws—a category in which divine laws differ in no way from natural laws, since the author of all natural and divine laws is the same—nevertheless [Col. 0180D] believe that Isidore’s statement should be referred to the force and validity of laws. In this respect divine laws are rightly said to be based on nature, just as human laws are based on customs. Since nature, according to the philosophical maxim, is an everlasting cause, divine law is for that reason perpetual—that is, such as remains valid everywhere and at every time. Human laws, by contrast, because they rest upon human customs, may vary according to the variety of customs.

Nor should one object that certain divine laws of the Old Testament were superseded by the Gospel. For it is not implausible that Isidore was speaking only of the divine laws of the Gospel, which are truly perpetual. Unless one prefers to say that even all the laws of the Old Testament can still be called perpetual in this sense: either because they could be superseded only at a divinely appointed time, or because they have continued, if not in their specific form, at least in their general character. In fact, all ceremonial [Col. 0181A] precepts, whether old or new, refer to Christ: those that prefigured Christ who was to come before Christ’s advent changed their form when he came, but not their category, since other precepts succeeded them that likewise referred to Christ—not to Christ who was to come, but to Christ who had been born, suffered, been glorified, and sits at the right hand of God.

In chapter 3 are found canons 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Distinction 1, in these words:

“*Ius* is a general term, whereas law is a species of *ius*. *Ius* is so called because it is just; and all *ius* consists of laws and customs. Law is a written enactment. Custom is a practice approved by age, or unwritten law. For *lex* is derived from *legere*—‘to read’—because it is written. Custom, however, is a long-standing practice derived merely from conduct. Custom is a kind of *ius* established by practice and accepted in place of law when the law is lacking. Nor does it matter whether it consists in writing or in reason, since reason also commends law. Therefore, if law consists in reason, everything that has been established by reason will be law, provided only that it accords with religion, conforms to discipline, and contributes to salvation. It is called custom because it is in common use.”

[Col. 0181B] In chapters 4, 5, and 6 the common division of *ius* into natural law, the law of nations, and civil law is set forth, in these words.

In chapter 4:

“Natural law is either civil law or the law of nations. Natural law is common to all nations, because it is held everywhere by the instinct of nature and not by any enactment: for example, the union of man and woman; the succession of children [the Roman Correctors note that in some manuscripts *susceptio*—‘taking up’ or ‘receiving’—is read. Both readings seem excellent, provided that by *successio* one does not understand hereditary succession but personal succession, by which a son naturally succeeds his father by virtue of generation]; the upbringing of children; the common possession of all things; the one liberty of all; the acquisition of things taken from heaven, earth, and sea. Likewise, the restoration of a deposited object or entrusted money, and the repulsion of violence by force. For this, or anything similar, is never considered unjust, but is regarded as natural and equitable.”

In chapter 5:

“Civil law is what each people or state establishes for itself for human or divine reasons.”

In chapter 6:

“The law of nations includes the occupation of places, building, fortification, 224 wars, captivities, slavery, the right of return, treaties of peace, truces, the religious obligation not to violate ambassadors, and the prohibition of marriages between foreigners. It is called the law of nations because nearly all peoples make use of this law.”

To these passages canons 6, 7, 8, and 9 of Distinction 1 must be referred.

Isidore did not stop here. He went on to examine what military law is, what public law is, and what the special law of the Quirites is. Thus, in chapter 7, to which canon 10 of Distinction 1 must be referred, he says:

“Military law is the formal declaration of war, the binding of an alliance, the attack upon the enemy after the signal has been given, or the engagement itself. It also includes retreat after the signal has been given; military discipline concerning misconduct if a position is abandoned; the scale of pay; the ranks of honors; the distinction of rewards, as when a crown or neck-chain is bestowed; the division of booty; its equitable distribution according to the rank and labors of the persons involved; and the prince’s share.”

In chapter 8, which is identical with canon 11 of Distinction 1:

“Public law [Col. 0181D] consists in sacred matters and priests, and in magistrates.”

In chapter 9, which is identical with canon 12 of Distinction 1:

“The law of the Quirites is specifically Roman law, which no one except the Quirites—that is, the Romans—possesses. It concerns legitimate inheritances, formal acceptances of inheritances, guardianships, usucaption, and other laws found among no other people, but belonging specifically to the Romans and established among them alone. The law of the Quirites consists”—these words are identical with Gratian’s, where the compiler begins Distinction 2—“of laws and plebiscites, decrees of the emperors and edicts, and the opinions of jurisconsults.”

After this, the individual species of the law of the Quirites mentioned above are explained in chapters 10, 11, 12, 13, and 14. From these chapters Gratian extracted canons 1, 2, 3, 4, and 5 of Distinction 2.

In chapter 10:

“Law is an enactment of the people, by which the elders, together with the plebs, establish something.”

In chapter 11:

“Plebiscites are what the plebs alone establish. They are called *scita* because the plebs knows them, or because it inquires and requests that they be made.”

[Col. 0182A] John Grial notes here that a corruption has entered the common Isidorian manuscripts and that one should instead read: “because the plebs knows it, or because it inquires,” as it appears in certain ancient manuscripts. This certainly agrees better with the ancient formulas of plebiscites, according to which the plebs did not ask but was asked.

In chapter 12:

“A decree of the Senate is what the senators alone decide after consulting the people.”

In chapter 13:

“A constitution or edict is what a king or emperor establishes or orders.”

In chapter 14:

“*Responsa* are the answers which jurists are said to give to those who consult them; hence the answers of Paulus are also so called. For there were certain learned men and arbiters of equity who published composed treatises on civil law, by which they might settle the lawsuits and disputes of litigants.”

Isidore examines other special laws as well—namely, consular, tribunician, and the others named after their authors, as well as the *satyrical* and Rhodian laws—in chapters 15, 16, and 17. Their words should be read in canons 6, 7, and 8 of Distinction 2, taken from chapter 15:

[Col. 0182B] “Certain laws are also called after those who enacted them, such as consular, tribunician, Julian, and Cornelian laws. Under Octavian Caesar, the suffect consuls Papius and Pompeius also enacted a law which, from their names, is called the Papian and Pompeian law. It initially contained rewards for having children. Under the same emperor, the tribune of the plebs Falcidius enacted a law that no one might leave more by testament to outsiders than would leave one fourth for the heirs. From his name the Falcidian law 225 was so called. Aquilius too enacted a law that is still called the Aquilian law.”

From chapter 16:

“*Satyra* is a law that speaks about several matters at once. It is so called from the abundance of matters and, as it were, from their association. Hence to write a *satyra* is to compose varied poems, as in the case of Horace, Juvenal, and Persius.”

From chapter 17:

“The Rhodian laws are laws concerning maritime commerce, named after the island of Rhodes, where the practice of merchants existed in ancient times.”

What Isidore continues in chapters 18 and 19 Gratian published [Col. 0182C] in canons 3 and 4 of Distinction 3.

In chapter 18 we read:

“Privileges are laws for private persons, as it were private laws. For *privilegium* is so called because it is enacted for a private person.”

And in chapter 19:

“Every law either permits something—for example, that a brave man may seek a reward—or prohibits something—for example, that no one may seek marriage with consecrated virgins—or punishes something—for example, that one who has committed murder should be punished by death. Human life is governed either by reward or by punishment.”

In two further chapters, chapters 20 and 21, Isidore explained the general precepts of laws, which are listed in canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 4.

In chapter 20:

“Laws were made so that human boldness might be restrained by fear of them, that innocence might be safe among the wicked, and that, among the wicked themselves, the ability to do harm might be curbed by fear of the punishment held in dread.”

In chapter 21:

[Col. 0182D] “A law, however, must be honorable, just, possible, in accordance with nature, in accordance with the custom of the country, suitable to place and time, necessary, useful, and also clear, so that it may not contain anything entrapping through obscurity. It must be written not for any private advantage but for the common benefit of the citizens.”

## 29.

Having thus transmitted a general account of laws, the holy prelate proceeded to the various matters in which legal discipline is concerned—namely, inheritances, contracts, and the restraint of crimes.

Hence, in chapter 26 of the same Book V, distinguishing many kinds of crimes, he says among other things:

“*Stuprum*, that is, abduction, is properly illicit intercourse; it is called so from *corrumpere*, ‘to corrupt,’ and hence the one who obtains something by abduction enjoys *stuprum*.”

Gratian reported this in two places, not only differently from Isidore but also differently from himself, as anyone may see in canon 48, Cause 27, Question 2, and canon 1, Cause 36, Question 1.

Anyone wishing to use these canons must always bear in mind that Isidore merely noted the origin of the term and did not intend to explain the nature either of abduction or of *stuprum*.

## 30.

[Col. 0183A] In the sixth book of the *Etymologies*, which deals with books and ecclesiastical offices, some material concerning the canons of ecclesiastical councils is transmitted in chapter 15. To this chapter canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 3 and canon 1 of Distinction 15 must be referred.

At the beginning we read:

“*Canon* in Greek is called *regula* in Latin. It is called a rule because it leads straight and never turns elsewhere. Others have said that it is called a rule either because it governs, or because it provides a norm for living rightly, or because it corrects what is distorted and crooked.”

These are the words of canons 1 and 2 of Distinction 3. After them Isidore continues:

“The canons of general councils began in the time of Constantine,” and so forth.

This material is presented in canon 1 of Distinction 15. There, in place of the words, “to meet together . . . one judgment of the Fathers condemned . . . the things established in this work are contained . . . the name of council,” and so forth, one should read, according to the Breulian edition:

“To come together as one . . . one judgment of the Fathers condemned beforehand . . . the things established in this work are contained . . . The name *council* is taken from Roman custom. For at the time 226 when cases were being heard, everyone came together in one place and deliberated with a common purpose. [Col. 0183B] Hence *council* was also named from a common purpose. For the eyelids are called *cilia*; hence *considium*, that is, counsel, with the *d* passing into the letter *l*. A gathering is a meeting or assembly, from *coire*, that is, from coming together in one place. Hence it was called a *conventus*, just as a gathering is named from coming together, or a council from the association of many into one.”

## 31.

In Book VII of the *Etymologies* we noted above that, among other things, various orders of ecclesiastical persons are discussed. To this belongs canon 1 of Distinction 21, drawn from chapter 12.

[Col. 0183C] There, in place of Gratian’s words—“we believe that *cleros* and *clerici* are so called because . . . ‘supreme of the Fathers’ was interpreted . . . *archbishop* is said in Greek because he is the supreme of bishops . . . it was entrusted to them . . . the chief, hence archbishop . . . the term *bishopric* is derived from the fact that the one who is made bishop watches over . . . in Greek ‘to watch over’ is said . . . previously those who were kings were also priests and pontiffs, for this was the custom of the ancestors, that the king should also be priest and pontiff . . . for he consecrates and sacrifices, while the priests of the pagans . . . when they could not bear the heat . . . not only on account of age . . . but also on account of honor . . . the same bishops . . . the name is one of dignity and not of age . . . just as bishops . . . which belongs to bishops alone . . . the ministries of the mystical sacrament were performed . . . and the offices of the Levites. For the offerings in the temple of God . . . let them pronounce so pitifully . . . they are also called pronouncers . . . in Latin they may be called *praecentor* and *succentor*. The *praecentor* is the one who . . . the *concentor* is so called because he harmonizes . . . he will be neither singer nor *consentor* . . . adjuring or rebuking . . . the doorkeepers are also gatekeepers, who in the Old Testament . . . so that the unclean might not enter it . . . having judgment, they receive the faithful and receive the unbelievers”—one should read, according to the Breulian edition:

“*Clerus* and *clericus* are so called because . . . ‘supreme father’ is interpreted . . . *archbishop* in Greek is called ‘supreme of bishops’ . . . it was entrusted to the bishops themselves [Col. 0183D] . . . the chief. Archbishop . . . the term *bishopric* is so called from the fact that the one who is placed above watches over those beneath him . . . in Greek, ‘to watch over’ is said in Latin *intendere* . . . formerly there were pontiffs and kings; for this was the custom of the ancestors, that the king should also be priest and pontiff [Breulius noted in the margin that some manuscripts read ‘or pontiff’] . . . for he consecrates and sanctifies. The priests of the pagans . . . when they could not bear it because of the heat [the Breulian editions read in the margin: ‘otherwise, through the heat’] . . . not on account of age . . . but on account of honor . . . the same bishops . . . a name of dignity, that is, of age . . . just as bishops also . . . which belongs to bishops alone . . . the mysteries of the mystical sacrament were performed [Breulius notes in the margin: ‘otherwise, ministries’] . . . and the offices of the Levites, who in Ezra are called Nathinim, that is, serving the Lord in humility. For the offerings in the temple of God . . . let them pronounce so miserably . . . they are also called pronouncers . . . in Latin they may be called *praecentor* and [Col. 0184A] *succentor*. The *praecentor* is the one who . . . the *concentor* is the one who harmonizes . . . he will be neither singer nor *succentor* . . . those who adjure or rebuke . . . the doorkeepers, 227 that is, the gatekeepers, who in Ezra are called guardians of the temple, the sons of the servants of Solomon [Breulius notes that the words ‘who in Ezra,’ and so forth, through the word ‘sons,’ are not found in the manuscript] . . . who in the Old Testament . . . so that the unclean might not enter it . . . possessing judgment [Breulius notes in the margin: ‘otherwise, holding it’], they receive the faithful and reject the unbelievers.”

## 32.

In Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, which deals with the Church and various sects, chapter 5 contains canon 39 of Cause 24, Question 3. There the succession of heretics is clearly woven together in chronological order.

The Roman Correctors have already emended some passages. To align the canon with the Breulian edition, in place of Gratian’s words—“Certain heretics . . . skilled in magic . . . of the followers of Menander . . . they assert that it happened . . . marriages might be exchanged . . . ‘that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans’ . . . in Latin they are called Millenarians . . . he was called Nazarene . . . the Appellitae, whose author was Apelles . . . affirming him to be fire, he said that Christ was not truly God . . . hence they are called Cainites . . . from the son of Adam . . . the Apostolics assumed this name for themselves for this reason . . . who make use of something in this world . . . asserted principles. The Marcionists, from Marcion . . . of creation and goodness. The Artotyrites . . . saying that this derived from the first human beings . . . and from the fruits of sheep . . . the province of Phrygia gave the Cataphrygians their name, because they arose there. Their authors were Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. They said that the coming of the Holy Spirit was not upon the apostles . . . this man asserted two natures . . . he asserted that it came from some source . . . received it in part. The Anthropomorphites . . . the Hierarchites, from Hierarchus . . . the Novatians, from Novatian . . . the priestly chair . . . receiving apostates and rebaptizing the baptized . . . through progress alone the just man . . . they were called by the name of understanding. For these are semi-Jews . . . of Gallo-Greek Sirmium . . . the Aeriani, from Aerius . . . the Aetians, from Aetius, and likewise . . . from a disciple of Aetius . . . different bodies of sins from heaven to earth . . . and that the world was made for this reason. The Noetians . . . who said that Christ . . . because they say that the Father suffered . . . ‘I and the Father are one,’ which the Lord said . . . the Antidicomaritae . . . that she had intercourse with her husband . . . for they assert that this is so . . . within the larger vessel . . . the Colluthians, from a certain Colluthus . . . not to do evil . . . ‘the Lord who creates evils,’ as it is written. The Floriani, from Florianus . . . against this, that . . . they are called Circumcellions . . . whom they call Scototopici . . . arose from Lucifer, bishop of Sardinia, who separated from the Catholic Church the Catholic bishops who, during the persecution of Constantius, had consented to the perfidy of the Arians and later, having corrected their error, chose to return to the Catholic Church . . . withdrew from communion with the Church . . . no married women or virgins . . . that she gave birth by her own Joseph . . . those who arose [said] the lower parts of the body . . . and at the last both would rise again . . . asserted only the mother . . . neither one Christ . . . one the Son of God and the other the son of man . . . to exist in two natures, but asserted that in him there was only a divine nature . . . that is, without a head, for none of them is found to have been the author . . . the Agnoitae . . . from whom the Agnoitae . . . because toward perversity . . . which are written below . . . they assert that there are three Gods . . . there are other heresies . . . they do not believe in Christ’s descent . . . and whatever animals . . . understands Holy Scripture,” and so forth—one should read:

“Certain heretics also . . . skilled in magical discipline . . . the Menandrians . . . asserted that it had happened . . . that marriages should be changed . . . because you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans . . . in Latin they are called Milliastae . . . he was called Nazarene . . . the Appellitae, whose leader was Apelles . . . affirming him to be fiery. The Appellitae, whose author was Apelles, said that Christ was not God in truth . . . hence they were called Cainites, from the son of Adam . . . the Apostolics assumed this name for themselves for this reason . . . who make use of something in this world . . . assert principles. The Marcionists, from Marcion . . . of the Creator and goodness. The Artoteritae . . . saying that it came from the first human beings . . . and from the fruits of sheep . . . The province of Cataphrygia [Col. 0185A] gave the Cataphrygians their name, because their authors Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla arose there [Breulius notes in the margin: ‘otherwise, Phrygia’]. They said that the coming of the Holy Spirit was not upon the apostles . . . This Manes asserted two natures . . . asserted that it flowed from some source . . . receives it in part. The Anomians, that is, in Latin ‘the lawless,’ are so called. The Anthropomorphites . . . the Heraclites, from Heraclius . . . the Novatians, from Novatus . . . the pontifical chair . . . receiving apostates and rebaptizing the baptized . . . through the prophet [Breulius notes in the margin: ‘otherwise, *prophetata*; otherwise, *profectum*, which is the more correct reading’] the only truly just man . . . they were called by the name of understanding. These are semi-Jews . . . of Gallo-Greek Sirmium . . . the Aetians, from Aetius . . . the Aetians were so called from a certain Aetius, and likewise . . . from a disciple of Aetius . . . diverse bodies of sinners fallen [Col. 0184C] from heaven to earth . . . and that for this reason the world was made. The Noetians . . . who said that Christ . . . because they say that the Father suffered . . . as the Lord says: ‘I and the Father’ . . . the Antidicomaritae . . . that she had intercourse with her husband . . . for they assert that this is so . . . within the larger vessel . . . [Col. 0185B] the Colluthians, from a certain Colluthus . . . not to do evil . . . as it is written: ‘I am the Lord, creating evil.’ The Floriani, from Florinus . . . against that which . . . called Circumcellions . . . whom they call Cotopites . . . from Lucifer, bishop of Sirmium, who opposed the Catholic bishops who, during the persecution of Constantius [Breulius notes that elsewhere one reads: ‘when Constantius was persecuting’], had consented to the perfidy of the Arians and later, having corrected their error, chose to return to the Catholic Church . . . they withdrew from communion . . . no marriages or virgins . . . that she gave birth from the man Joseph . . . those arose who said that the lower parts of the body . . . and that on the last day both would rise again . . . asserted only the mother as progenitor . . . neither one Christ . . . one the Son of God and the other the son of man . . . to exist from two natures, but asserted that only the divine nature existed in him . . . [Col. 0184D] that is, without a head, whom the heretics follow; for no author of any of them is found . . . the Gnoitae . . . because of perversity . . . which are written . . . they assert that there are three gods . . . there are also other heresies . . . they do not believe in Christ’s descent . . . and [Col. 0185C] into whatever animals . . . understands Holy Scripture,” and so forth.

## 33.

In chapter 9 of the same book Isidore enumerates various kinds of magicians and writes, among other things:

“Sortilegi are those who, under the name of a fictitious religion, profess the knowledge of divination through certain practices which they call the lots of the saints, or who promise the future by examining any sort of writings.”

This is canon 1 of Cause 26, Question 1.

229 ## 34.

As we have said, Book IX of the *Etymologies* deals with languages and societies; in its final chapters it treats the relationship of spouses and relatives. To this belongs chapter 8, and canon 6 of Cause 26, Question 2, where Isidore writes:

“Spouses are so called because of the yoke imposed upon those joined in marriage. For newly married persons are accustomed to be placed under a yoke, on account of the harmony that is to come, so that they may not be separated. They are more truly called spouses because of the first faith of betrothal, although marital [Col. 0185D] intercourse is still unknown between them, just as Mary is called Joseph’s spouse, although there had been—and was to be—no bodily intercourse between them.”

To chapter 5 of the same book must be referred canon 15 of Cause 32, Question 4, where Isidore writes:

“Children are also called *liberi* because they are born from a free marriage. For children born of a free man and a slave woman are of servile condition; for whoever is born always assumes the inferior status of the parent. Those born of freeborn concubines are called natural children, whom nature alone has generated, not the honor of marriage.”

A little farther on, after discussing [perhaps, having discussed] bastards—who have a certain mother but an uncertain father—he says:

“Hence those who are not born from a legitimate marriage follow the mother rather than the father.”

## 35.

The material read under Isidore’s name in canon 1 of Cause 35, Question 4 is not found in all Isidore’s manuscripts, as Breulius testified at the end of chapter 6 of Book IX, adding that it was found “in certain copies,” as he himself says.

[Col. 0186A] There, in place of Gratian’s words, “Consanguinity . . . to the sixth degree of generation,” one reads: “This consanguinity extends to the sixth degree of kindred.”

I readily agree with the Roman Correctors that this was added from the works of Saint Augustine, specifically from Book XV, chapter 16, of *The City of God*, where we read:

“Among the ancient Fathers there was a religious concern that kinship, gradually separating itself through successive generations and going farther away, should cease to be kinship; therefore, while it was still not far removed, they sought to bind it again by the bond of marriage and, as it were, call back what was fleeing.”

As for what follows concerning the restriction of degrees of kinship within the sixth degree, on the analogy of the six ages of the world, learned men are far from approving it, since I find nowhere that this analogy was approved by the ancient Fathers of the Church. Hence Van Espen says in his brief commentary on Gratian concerning this same canon:

“Concerning this restriction to the sixth degree, I do not remember having read it elsewhere; still less do I know of anyone who has approved the reason [Col. 0186B] given for it.”

## 36.

We noted above that Isidore treated war and games in Book XVIII of the *Etymologies*. To this belongs canon 1 of Cause 23, Question 2.

230 In chapter 1, after the holy prelate had stated that wars originated with Ninus, king of the Assyrians, he continues:

“There are four kinds of war: just, unjust, civil, and more than civil. A just war is one waged after formal declaration for the recovery of things claimed, or for the purpose of repelling enemies. An unjust war is one begun out of rage and not on the basis of legitimate reason.”

And shortly afterward:

“No war is considered just unless it has been announced, unless it has been formally declared, unless it concerns things claimed for recovery.”

What is added in Gratian under the word “Judge” does not seem suited to Gratian’s purpose. It is found instead in chapter 15 of the same book, where Isidore transmitted some material concerning disputes in court. After teaching that six persons constitute a legal proceeding—a judge, an accuser, [Col. 0186C] a defendant, and three witnesses—he says:

“A judge is so called as though he were one who speaks the law to the people, or because he deliberates according to law. To deliberate according to law is to judge justly. But he is not a judge if there is no justice in him.”

## On the Books of the *Synonyms*

## 37.

The two books called by the name of Isidore of Seville, *Synonyms*, are also—and more correctly—called *Soliloquies*. In them a man, oppressed and broken by various hardships, is introduced lamenting and brought almost to despair; reason, in response, consoles him through the mercy of God.

It is certainly an ascetic work, one that almost drives the human mind toward contemplation of divine things, as toward the state in which true happiness is situated.

Breulius appended to this work a letter of Isidore directing the book to Braulio, under the following heading:

“In the name of the Lord. To the most beloved and dearest brother in Christ, Braulio, archdeacon: Isidore.”

In the letter itself he is introduced as writing:

“We send you the little book of the *Synonyms*, not because it is of any usefulness, [Col. 0186D] but because you wished to have it.”

They commonly think that the book is called *Synonyms* because many words there converge upon a single meaning.

For my part, I can scarcely persuade myself that it is genuinely the work of Isidore of Seville, although it contains much that is useful. First of all, I observe that in the letter Braulio is called not a bishop but an archdeacon; he is also called simply “brother,” although bishops customarily called their fellow bishops “brothers.”
