Furthermore, in the same letter Isidore is introduced as awaiting from Braulio the *decade* of Saint Augustine, adding:

“I ask you also to make me known to him in whatever way you can.”

These words more readily refer to a man still living than to one who had long been dead.

I add that two other books are circulated under the same name of Isidore. The first is entitled *On Contempt of the World*, the second *On the Rule of Living*. In all of them, however, almost the same words—and not merely the same ideas—are repeatedly found throughout, so that it is extremely unlikely that the holy man pursued the same subject several times. [Col. 0187A]

If this consideration carried so much weight with learned men that some of them thought the books *On Contempt of the World* and *On the Rule of Living* apocryphal, I do not know why it could not likewise lead someone to regard the book of the *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*, as spurious.

Having prefaced the discussion with these few remarks concerning the work’s authenticity, I turn to the canons of Gratian that were drawn from it. All of them must be referred to Book II, except canon 12 of *On Penance*, Distinction 3, which Gratian wrongly attributes to Augustine.

That canon is read at the end of Book I, where, after the dialogue between the man and reason has been completed, reason finally concludes:

“Having lamented your offenses, do not do again what you will once more lament; do not presume to repeat the fault for which you ask pardon. Repentance is empty when frequent fault defiles it. A repeated wound is healed more slowly, and the frequent sinner who mourns scarcely merits pardon. Lamentation is of no benefit if sins are repeated; it is useless to ask pardon for evil and then commit evil again.

“Therefore, persevere in confession; stand firmly established in repentance [Col. 0187B]. Do not abandon the good life you have begun to maintain; preserve continually your resolve to live well. You will be blessed if you remain; blessed if you persevere. Salvation is promised to those who persevere, and reward is given to those who persevere. Blessed are those who keep judgment and do justice at all times. He is not blessed who does good, but he who does it continually. For whoever perseveres to the end will be saved.”

## 38.

In chapter 16 of Book II is found canon 1 of Distinction 11. There the author lamented that human actions had been corrupted by a long habit of sinning, and he laid down this rule:

“Many things have been corrupted by custom; many have been presumed upon through evil practice; many have been illicitly appropriated against modest conduct. Remove the custom; preserve the law. Let custom yield to authority, evil practice to law, and reason prevail.”

From these words it is clear that the discussion there does not concern just any custom, but a custom by which someone acts privately against [Col. 0187C] public laws.

To put it briefly, he wished to condemn the custom that leads toward evil; by contrast, he praised in chapter 12 the habit that makes a person inclined toward good, writing:

“Often nature is changed by customs; often nature is overcome by habit. For constant repetition creates character, and continual practice turns into nature. Everything yields to practice; everything obeys practice; the matter itself proceeds as practice dictates. What you begin with difficulty, you will complete through practice and willingness.”

At the beginning of chapter 10 of the same book is found canon 16 of Cause 22, Question 2:

“Flee every kind of lie with the greatest care, and do not speak falsely either by accident or deliberately. Do not seek to lie through witnesses, nor defend anyone’s fault by any kind of deception. Beware of lying in everything, for through lying faith is removed, error is introduced, and truth is abolished.”

And at the end of the same chapter we read:

[Col. 0187D] “In evil promises, however, let faith be rescinded; in a disgraceful vow, change your decision. Do not do what you rashly vowed. An impious promise is one that is fulfilled through crime.”

This is canon 5 of Cause 22, Question 4.

## 39.

In chapter 1 of the same book canon 8 of Cause 32, Question 5 is presented. It should be read in these words:

“The body cannot be corrupted unless the soul has first been corrupted. While the soul is present, the flesh is immediately ready to sin. For the soul precedes the flesh in crime, and the flesh can do nothing except what the soul has willed. Therefore cleanse the soul by your thoughts, and the flesh will not sin; for if you wish to be conquered, you will by no means be able [the transmitted reading appears corrupt].”

## On the Letter to Bishop Massanus
### 40.

It appeared almost intact in Gratian, both as canon 28, distinction 50, and as canon 11, cause 33, question 2: an epistle under the name of Isidore to a certain bishop whom he called at one time Massanus and at another Massio. Others likewise called him Mason and others Massenus. I do not hesitate to transcribe it here in full, so that Gratian’s canons may thereby be more conveniently examined. It was printed in the Breulian edition, p. 352, from a manuscript codex of the library of the monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés:

> “To the truly holy lord, and in merits blessed brother Massanus, bishop, Isidore, bishop. Your religious servant Nicetius came to us and brought us a letter from your honored self, in which assurance of your well-being was no less evident—especially through the bearer, whose tongue was the living letter. Therefore, having offered thanks to our God for your salvation, our modest ability has endeavored, insofar as it could, to respond to your inquiry, asking you to commend us to the divine presence through the support of your merits.
>
> “But what your fraternity subsequently made known to us in your letter—namely, that in chapter 19 of the Council of Ancyra it is read that after a bodily fall the degree of honor is to be restored after penance, whereas elsewhere it is read that after such a crime the merit of the ancient rank is by no means to be restored—this difference is distinguished in the following manner. The canon commands those to return to their former ranks who have been preceded by the satisfaction of penance or by a fitting confession of their sins. On the other hand, those who, though seized by vice, do not amend themselves, and who even attempt, with a certain superstitious boldness, to justify the very carnal offense they have committed, receive neither the rank of honor nor the grace of communion.
>
> “Therefore the two statements must be reconciled in such a way that those who have merited reconciliation through penance must be restored to the place of honor by divine mercy. For these men not undeservedly regain the status of the dignity taken from them, since through the amendment of penance they are known to have recovered the remedy of life.
>
> “So that this may not perhaps remain more ambiguous, let it be confirmed by the judgment of divine authority. For the prophet Ezekiel, under the figure of unfaithful Jerusalem, shows that through the satisfaction of penance former honor is restored. ‘Be ashamed,’ he says, ‘and bear your disgrace, O Judah.’ And shortly afterward: ‘You and your daughters,’ he says, ‘shall return to your former condition.’
>
> “By saying ‘Be ashamed,’ he shows that after the deed of sin everyone ought to blush, and after confession, for the crimes committed, to lower his shamefaced brow to the ground, because he has perpetrated a deed worthy of shame. Then he commands him to bear the disgrace of his deposition, mourning with humility. If he bears it, he can, according to the prophet, be recalled to his former state.
>
> “The evangelist John likewise writes something similar, among other things, to the angel of the church at Ephesus: ‘Remember from where you have fallen, and do penance, and perform your first works; otherwise I shall come to you and remove your lampstand from its place.’
>
> “By the angel of the church he clearly indicates the ruler, that is, the priest, in accordance with Malachi, who says: ‘The lips of the priest preserve knowledge, and they seek the law from his mouth, because he is the angel of the Lord.’ The ruler, therefore, having fallen into vice, is warned through the evangelist to remember from where he has fallen, to do penance, and to perform his first works, so that his lampstand may not be removed.
>
> “For the lampstand of the angel is understood as the priestly teaching or the honor of the authority that he bears. In accordance with what is written concerning the condemnation of Eli in Samuel: ‘His eyes grew dim, and he could not see the lamp of God before it was extinguished.’ He had been the lamp of God when, flourishing in priestly dignity, he shone with the brightness of justice. The prophet declares it extinguished when, because of the crimes of his sons, he lost the authority and light of his merits.
>
> “The priest’s lampstand or lamp—which signifies the gifts of honor—is therefore completely extinguished or removed, according to John, when, after the fall into sin, penance is neglected and the crimes committed are not mourned. For he did not say, ‘Because you have fallen, I shall remove your lampstand,’ but, ‘Unless you do penance, I shall remove your lampstand.’
>
> “If penance for the offense precedes in any sinful ruler, then restoration of merit necessarily follows. And in Proverbs: ‘Whoever hides his crimes will not prosper; but whoever confesses and abandons them obtains mercy.’
>
> “Moreover, the very provision by which the disciplinary judgment of the canons commands the penitent to return to his former state after seven years [this is canon 11, cause 33, question 2] was established by the Fathers not according to their own arbitrary choice, but rather according to the judgment of divine justice.
>
> “For we read that Mary, the prophetess and sister of Aaron, incurred the offense of slander against Moses [Breulius notes that some manuscripts read *detraction*, ‘detraction,’ instead]. Immediately she was covered with the mark of leprosy. When Moses asked that she be healed, the Lord commanded her to go outside the camp for seven days and, after her cleansing, to be admitted again into the camp.
>
> “Mary, therefore, the sister of Aaron, signifies the priestly flesh. When it is devoted to pride and stained by the filthiest contagions of corruption, it is cast outside the camp for seven days—that is, outside the fellowship of Holy Church for seven years—where, after the cleansing of its vices, it receives the merit of its position or former dignity.
>
> “Behold, insofar as I have been able, I have explained by sacred testimonies the ancient and wholly authoritative judgment of the Council of Ancyra [Gratian transcribed this again as canon 28, distinction 50], showing that the man who has learned to mourn his former offenses through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his own honor, whereas he cannot be restored who neither mourns what he has done nor, without any religious shame or fear of divine judgment, commits what ought to be mourned.
>
> “At the end of this letter I have thought it necessary to add the following [Gratian outlined this in both places]: whenever a contradictory judgment is found in the acts of councils, the judgment of that council whose authority is older or greater is to be followed.
>
> “Given on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our lord, the glorious king Victericus.”

From this Breulius wishes the letter to be assigned to the year 609, since the third year of Victericus’ reign fell in that year.

Now that Gratian’s canons have been restored from the complete letter, the observations of learned men must not be omitted. They judged that the same letter had falsely been attributed to Isidore, as Natalis Alexander related in *The History of the Seventh Century*, chapter 4, article 4. Certainly, substantial arguments for this position are not lacking.

First, many things in it are awkwardly arranged, contrary to Isidore’s custom, and the examples from sacred Scripture are poorly adapted to the subject, as in the case of Mary, who is said to signify the flesh of priests, so that just as Mary was restored after seven days of penance, priests might be restored after seven years of penance.

One may also add what is said at the end of the letter concerning the observance of the canons of councils whenever one set of canons happens to conflict with another. Although such an observation would have been useful where conflicting canons of several councils were before Isidore, it was pointless where only one canon of the Council of Ancyra was under consideration.

The strongest argument, however, is drawn from other statements of Isidore, who more than once taught that priests who had fallen into public crime could not, according to ordinary law, return to their dignity. Thus he writes in his letter to Helladius and the other bishops assembled with him concerning the bishop of Córdoba, who had miserably fallen into a grave crime:

> “With an outpouring of tears we beseech your holiness that, once this fallen man has been presented to your holy assembly and his confession has been acknowledged by you, he be deposed from the priestly rank by synodal judgment. It is better for him to be judged by you temporarily than to be condemned by eternal judgment. The disgrace of the present time is lighter for him than the future torments of Gehenna.
>
> “For he should know that the man who has lost the merit of holiness has lost the name and office of priest. Therefore, by the decree of your judgment, let him continually lament the crimes he has committed, with a sorrowful confession of penance; let him mourn the priestly dignity that he lost by living wickedly. Let him grieve over the condition of his soul, which he has polluted with so great a filth of corruption. Perhaps the Holy Spirit will one day extend a hand to him, so that through worthy satisfaction he may merit the remission of his sins.”

The same doctrine is transmitted by Isidore in book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5.

Finally, since the entire letter explains nothing other than the Ancyrene canon—which permanently removes from office priests polluted by a grave public crime—it does not seem worthy of Isidore to interpret the Ancyrene canon as referring only to priests who persist in sin. For what doubt could there have been that such men were not to be admitted to the duties of the priesthood? Indeed, the rigor of ecclesiastical discipline among the bishops of Ancyra demanded something more.

### On the other canons attributed to Isidore

### 41.

Several canons inscribed to the holy man under the name of Isidore in Gratian still remain to be tested against Isidore’s works. Among them are chiefly canon 1 and canon 4 of distinction 16, under the heading “Isidore.” When the two are compared with one another, they immediately appear to be the work of different authors, since in canon 1 the Apostolic Canons are rejected as apocryphal, whereas in canon 4 they are presented as venerable.

For a long time, however, after the Roman Correctors, numerous learned men knew how to distinguish one Isidore from another: the Isidore of Seville from the Mercator, attributing canon 1 to the former and canon 4 to the latter. Both wrote prefaces to the canons of the councils.

The Roman Correctors mentioned above saw the preface of Isidore of Seville, which had been sent to them from the library of the Church of Toledo, and in which they state that they had read the canon in question. Antonius Augustinus also saw the same preface placed before the Spanish Councils, as he himself testifies in book I of *On the Correction of Gratian*, dialogues 6 and 20. He laments that in the more recent edition of the Councils the preface of Mercator had been substituted for the preface of Isidore of Seville.

Isidore of Seville, moreover, never wished the origin of ecclesiastical canons to be traced back to the Apostolic Canons, but rather to the time of the Council of Nicaea, or to the settlement of the affairs of the Church under the rule of Constantine. This is demonstrated most clearly by book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 16, which is cited in canon 1, distinction 15, mentioned above.

As for canon 4, it is indeed found in Mercator’s preface. No one is unaware of what sort, and of what degree, its authority or credibility must be—namely, that which belongs to the distinguished deceiver, as everyone calls him.

It is unnecessary to explain here the controversy over the Apostolic Canons; it has already been discussed at greater length elsewhere. I shall merely note that this canon 4 is cited by Ivo in part IV of the *Decree*, chapter 106. Its author is expressly named as Isidore Mercator. Moreover, in place of the words “because many accept them,” which Gratian transcribed, Ivo’s text reads “because the common people accept them.”

If Ivo’s edition is to be accepted, it will have to be concluded that even Isidore Mercator did not believe the first canons he presented to be truly apostolic, but displayed them in order to indulge popular or common tradition, whatever its character may have been.

### 42.

In canon 1, distinction 29, I do not think that the very words of Isidore of Seville are transcribed, but rather a statement of the kind found in books attributed to that same Isidore.

For, first, in the book *On the Rule of Life* we read:

> “Consider what is suitable for you, and at what time, in what place, when, why, and for how long it ought to be done. Examine the causes and times of things, and carefully distinguish the particular requirements of each action.”

Likewise, in the book *On Contempt of the World* we find:

> “Before an action, think; before undertaking a task, deliberate for a long time about what you wish to do; acquire it slowly, test it slowly, and then act. When you have thought for a long time, do what you have approved . . . . The truth about persons must be received, and whoever you instruct in any manner must be treated accordingly. Speak common matters to everyone, more secret matters to the more advanced; announce what is open to all, what is hidden to few.”

All these statements are read in almost the same words in book II of the *Synonyms*, chapter 16 and those that follow. But since the authority of all these books is uncertain, as I mentioned above, these statements, like Gratian’s canon, cannot safely be attributed to Isidore.

### 43.

What is read under Isidore’s name in canon 8, distinction 40, is not only entirely absent from Isidore’s works, but also seems less worthy of any ecclesiastical man, let alone Isidore.

Who could approve those crude comparisons improperly heaped together between the union of man and woman, by which one body of the spouses is formed, and the election and consecration of bishops, from which a single episcopate emerges?

What could be more inept than to add that all these things form one body which will more quickly be corrupted and dragged down to the earth unless it is lawfully preserved and commended by righteous living?

I think that the author of this fragment attempted to imitate the formulas of Isidore Mercator, who in the letters he fabricated repeatedly pursues, to the point of nausea, those comparisons between bodily and spiritual marriage. A particularly clear example occurs in canon 11, cause 7, question 1. Through this imitation, the name of Isidore may have slipped into the aforementioned canon 8.

If Isidore of Seville at some point extended the comparison with marriage to sacred matters, I find that he did so more elegantly, as is clear from book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 19, where we read:

> “That not one man and many women, but one man and one woman, are joined together is itself an example of the first union made by God. For when the Lord had fashioned the man and saw that he required a partner equal to him, he took one of his ribs and fashioned for him one woman. Thus Adam and the woman Eve, joined to one another in marriage, established for human beings, by the authority of their origin and the first will of God, the proper form.
>
> “Likewise, according to spiritual marriage, just as there is one Christ and one Church, so there is one husband and one wife, both according to the teaching of nature and according to the sacrament of Christ.”

In these words the very doctrine of the apostle Paul shines forth, as it is found in chapter V of the Epistle to the Ephesians.

### 44.

Canon 23 of the consecration, distinction 4, must be joined with canon 59, cause 1, question 1, for in both places the same statement is described under Isidore’s name.

One must not remain confined to Gratian’s Codex, but must look back to the earlier Collectors whom Gratian followed, in order to investigate the author of the document.

Ivo of Chartres, in part I of the *Decree*, chapter 294, cites it from “the sayings of Isidore the bishop.” This inscription clearly indicates nothing more than that certain passages from Isidore had been transferred into that chapter.

Something clearer appears in the manuscript codex of the *Panormia* in the Royal Athenaeum. On p. 11, col. 1, the words of the aforementioned canon 23 are listed under this heading: “Augustine to Fortunatus, from the sayings of Isidore the bishop”; and in the margin, in another hand: “From the sayings of Isidore the bishop.”

From this I readily conclude that the author of the canon composed the statement in the form that prevailed in later centuries and attributed the statement so composed to the ancient Fathers Augustine and Isidore because certain passages could be found in Augustine and Isidore by which that discipline of the Church might be established.

To explain this more clearly, it must be observed that the ancient controversy which for a long time agitated the African Church against the Roman Church in the time of Pope Stephen and Cyprian of Carthage had already been settled in the third century: the controversy concerned the reception of the baptism of heretics, or whether those who had once been properly baptized by heretics should be rebaptized.

But whether those who had been baptized by persons who themselves had not been baptized should also be regarded as truly baptized had not yet been clearly handed down. Hence Augustine presented himself as doubtful on that question, although he inclined rather toward the opinion that the baptism was valid, as appears from canon 31 on the consecration, distinction 4.

In later centuries, as circumstances arose, the controversy began to be settled by individual rescripts of the supreme pontiffs. Thus we read in book V of the *Capitularies*, chapter 6:

> “If someone has been baptized by a priest who was not baptized, and the Holy Trinity was invoked in that baptism, he has been baptized, as Pope Sergius said; but he needs the imposition of hands. Bishop Gregory of Rome and John the Sacristan held the same opinion.”

Likewise, under Nicholas I, the Bulgarians consulted the Roman pontiff on this same controversy. It was determined by a rescript that baptism conferred even by an unbaptized person was valid when the legitimate form of baptism had been preserved, canon 24 on the consecration, distinction 4.

Thus, as occasion arose, the Roman pontiffs derived grounds for issuing rescripts from the writings of the ancient Fathers Augustine and Isidore.

Augustine repeatedly taught in his books that, in conferring the sacrament of baptism, one must take account neither of the minister’s moral character nor of his faith, since the efficacy of baptism depends entirely upon Christ’s institution and not upon the merit of the one who confers it.

As for Isidore, in chapter 24 of book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices* he wrote:

> “It is established that baptism has been entrusted only to priests, and that even deacons are not permitted to complete its mystery without bishops or priests, except when, in their absence at a distance, the final necessity of illness compels it. This is also commonly permitted to faithful laypeople, so that no one may be called from this world without the remedy of salvation.
>
> “Heretics, however, if they are found to have received baptism with the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit being invoked, are not to be baptized again, but are to be cleansed only by chrism and the imposition of hands. Baptism is not the merit of a human being, but of Christ; therefore it makes no difference whether a heretic or a believer baptizes.
>
> “This sacrament is so holy that it is not polluted even when administered by a murderer. A heretic indeed possesses Christ’s baptism; but because he is outside the unity of faith, it benefits him nothing. Once he has entered it, however, the baptism that he possessed outside, to his destruction, begins to benefit him for salvation.
>
> “What he receives I approve; but because he receives it outside, I disapprove. When he comes in, it is not changed but recognized: baptism is the character of my King, not sacrilegious error. I correct the deserter; I do not change the character.”

Accordingly, the statements of the Fathers Augustine and Isidore were clear in the respect in which they taught that baptism conferred by heretics was valid. In the other respect—whether the person performing the baptism had to be baptized—they seemed somewhat doubtful.

When they taught that the merit of the baptizer was not to be considered, but only the institution of Christ, the author of the sacrament, their general statement appeared easily applicable to the unbaptized. But when they spoke specifically of heretics, and therefore of baptized persons, that general definition seemed to be restricted to those who were already baptized.

The doubtful intention of the Fathers had to be clarified by the supreme pontiffs. Among those named is Sergius and Gregory; Nicholas I might also have been named. Thus the Collectors of the canons, in briefly summarizing the entire matter, explained that one opinion might perhaps be drawn from Augustine and Isidore, but that the definition of the Roman bishops prevailed over all the doubts of the ancients.

This, then, is the meaning of the aforementioned canon 59, explained briefly. At its beginning a doubt was proposed, such as arose from the sayings of Isidore or Augustine; at its conclusion the judgment of the supreme pontiffs was set forth.

I shall add a few remarks on the interpretation of chapter 6 of book V of the *Capitularies*, where it is said that one baptized by an unbaptized priest needs the imposition of hands.

Either “imposition of hands” means the ceremonial imposition of hands, which an unbaptized priest could not lawfully perform; or it means the imposition of hands to be performed by a bishop in the sacrament of confirmation.

Let us suppose that the case concerns an unbaptized priest who, according to an ancient custom of certain provinces, had administered both the sacrament of baptism and the sacrament of confirmation. Although the sacrament of baptism was not to be repeated, the sacrament of confirmation nevertheless had to be repeated; this is often called “the imposition of hands” by the ancients, as in canon 1, distinction 95, and in chapter 4 on custom.

The imposition of hands mentioned in the passage cited above must be understood differently, where Isidore stated that those baptized by heretics were to be received. That imposition of hands was reconciliatory, by which heretics returning to the Church were accustomed to be reconciled.

As for what is read in the same canon—that an unbaptized priest is to be baptized but not ordained again—this is found nowhere in the ancient Fathers, whether Augustine or Isidore. Nor do I think that the statement was inserted there to indicate that this practice had once been observed. Rather, it was inserted so that a possible matter for doubt might be proposed.

For what follows—“But the Roman pontiff,” and so on—was attached in order to signify that the preceding words of the canon had never been received into the discipline of the Church.

The author of the *Paleae* appears to have had this in mind when he transcribed the following canon, canon 60, in which it is established that an unbaptized priest must both be baptized and ordained again.

That canon was taken from book VI of the *Capitularies*, chapter 94:

> “If a man who has been ordained a priest discovers that he has not been baptized, let him be baptized and ordained again, together with all those whom he previously baptized.”

Burchard included the same canon under the name of the council at Compiègne—for he did not think it appropriate to name explicitly the Frankish *Capitularies* among the Germans, who at that time were hostile to the Franks—in chapter 74 of book I. From Burchard, Ivo included it in part I, chapter 268.

Baluze, however, had already observed in his notes on the *Capitularies* that this canon is not found in the Council of Compiègne. I find that document among the penitential canons of Theodore of Canterbury, which will be discussed below in its proper place.

Certainly, in the part establishing that an unbaptized priest must be baptized and ordained again, we recognize a correct statement, later included in chapter 1, *On the Unbaptized Priest*. In accordance with it, Innocent III rightly wished to issue a rescript in chapter 3 of the same title.

But in the part stating that those baptized by the same priest must be rebaptized, it may indeed be referred to the doubts of the ancients about which I have just spoken. Once the matter had been settled differently by the rescripts of the supreme pontiffs, however, it could not in any way be accepted.

For this reason that portion of the chapter was omitted from the aforementioned chapter 1, *On the Unbaptized Priest*, and the Roman Correctors rightly judged that it should be removed from Gratian’s Codices in the aforementioned canon 60.

### 45.

I have already observed elsewhere that Gratian composed canon 84, cause 1, question 1, from various statements of the ancient Fathers Jerome, Gregory the Great, and Isidore—namely, both in chapter 59 of part II and in chapter 3 of this part III, where I presented which passages belonged to Gregory and which to Jerome.

It remains now to transcribe what was taken from Isidore.

In Isidore’s book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 19, several passages are read against which the verse beginning “Therefore the mystery” and continuing to the verse “This concerning the body” must be tested. There we read:

> “Sacrifice is so called as though it were a sacred act, because it is consecrated by mystical prayer in memory of the Lord’s passion suffered for us. Hence, at his command, we call this the body and blood of Christ; although it is made from the fruits of the earth, it is sanctified and becomes a sacrament, while the Spirit of God works invisibly. The Greeks call the sacrament of this bread and cup *Eucharistia*, which is interpreted in Latin as ‘good grace.’
>
> “And what is better than the body and blood of Christ? A sacrament is something in a sacred celebration in which an event is so enacted that it is understood to signify something, and it must be received in a holy manner.
>
> “The sacraments are baptism, chrism, the body, and the blood of Christ. They are called sacraments because beneath the covering of bodily things the divine power secretly works the salvation of these same sacraments. Hence they are called sacraments either from secret powers or from sacred things.
>
> “They are performed fruitfully within the Church because the Holy Spirit, dwelling in it, secretly brings about the effect of these sacraments. Therefore, whether they are administered within God’s Church by good or bad ministers, since the Holy Spirit, who once appeared in apostolic times through visible works, mystically gives them life, these gifts are neither increased by the merits of good dispensers nor diminished by those of bad ones. For neither the one who plants is anything nor the one who waters, but God who gives the growth.
>
> “Hence in Greek it is called *mysterion*, because it contains a secret and hidden dispensation.”

The Roman Correctors have already observed that not only statements of Isidore but also those of several other founders of monastic life were gathered into canon 100, cause 11, question 3. The canon is found in its entirety in Smaragdus, the compiler of monastic rules.

Ivo described the canon somewhat differently in part 14 of the *Decree*, chapter 110, in these words:

> “Whoever consents to sinners and defends another who is delinquent will be accursed before God and human beings, and will be corrected with the severest rebuke. Hence a certain most holy Father also says: If anyone consents to another’s error, let him know that he is to be judged and excommunicated as guilty in the same manner.”

Ivo cites this from the sayings of Basil.

Indeed, in Basil’s rule as edited by Holstenius, question 26, several similar passages are found:

> “What judgment should be passed upon those who defend their brothers? In my opinion, a more severe one, according to what the Lord said: ‘It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea than that he should scandalize one of these little ones.’
>
> “For the delinquent no longer accepts correction and amendment, but undertakes a defense to confirm his sin, and also provokes others to a similar evil, so that what was said may fittingly be applied to him who defends sinners: ‘For if you do not show worthy fruits of penance, you will be cut off and cast into the fire.’”

Moreover, in the rule of Saint Pachomius, edited by the same Holstenius, chapter 176, the very first words of Gratian’s canon are presented:

> “Whoever consents to sinners and defends another who is delinquent will be accursed before God and human beings, and will be corrected with the severest rebuke.”

To bring together the corresponding statements of Isidore, from which this document appears not unjustly to have been attributed to that same holy man, I note first that Isidore wrote as follows at the end of book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 32:

> “Many wicked men defend those who are like themselves in evil and, through their patronage, support the depraved against the correction of the good, so that they may not amend the things by which they are displeasing. They add the sins of others to their own, so that they may be punished not only for their own evils but also for the crimes of those whose sins they defend.”

And at the end of chapter 50:

> “Whoever follows another’s sin must necessarily follow that person’s punishment. For he will not be unequal in punishment to the one whose error and vice he shares.”

Likewise, in the *Rule for Monks*, chapter 14:

> “No one should conceal a person who is sinning, for after a second warning it is complicity in crime to conceal anyone who is sinning.”

There are also similar passages in the little books attributed to Isidore.

Thus in *The Rule of Life*, chapter 12, we read:

> “For not only the perpetrator of deeds but also the accomplice in sin is held liable; nor is he free from crime who obeyed in order to do evil. The one who obeys is like the one who does evil; bind the doer and the obedient together with an equal punishment.”

And in book II of the *Synonyms*, chapter 16:

> “The one who obeys in evil is like the one who does evil.”

Everyone can see that nearly all these statements concern the institutions of monks; consequently, the aforementioned canon of Gratian must especially be tested against them.

### 46.

By a similar process, canon 101, cause 11, question 3, bears the name of Isidore. The Roman Correctors have already noted that its statement is found in the shorter rules of Saint Basil.

It also agrees very closely with what Basil teaches in the *Ascetica*, chapter 11, writing as follows:

> “If the master is evil, commanding unjust things and compelling the servant to transgress the commandment of our true Lord Jesus Christ, care must be taken that the name of the Lord not be blasphemed because of that servant, if he does something displeasing to God.”

Jerome likewise agrees in the words I cited above in connection with canon 93, cause 11, question 3.

But to turn to the statements of Isidore alone, whose name therefore appears on the canon, I read in his book *On Contempt of the World*:

> “Obey a human being in such a way that you do not offend the will of God.”

Likewise, in the book *On the Rule of Life*:

> “Obey everyone in such a way in all commands that, by obeying human wishes, you do not offend God.”

Finally, in book II of the *Synonyms*, chapter 16:

> “When commanded to do evil, do not comply; when commanded to do evil, do not consent. Do not consent to evil at the command of anyone, even if punishment compels you. It is better to suffer death than to fulfill destructive commands, and so forth.”

As for the reliability and authority of these books, we have already touched upon the matter above.

What we read under Isidore’s name in canon 4, cause 20, question 1, does not seem altogether to have pleased Isidore himself, if the *Rule for Monks* attributed to him is his. For in chapter 4 it reads, among other things:

> “No convert is to be received into the monastery unless he has first pledged in writing that he will remain.”

Nevertheless, under Isidore’s name, as the Roman Correctors testify, the passage is read in Smaragdus’ exposition of the rule of Saint Benedict.

I do not think that the words themselves belong to Isidore. Rather, Smaragdus briefly explained what practice prevailed in Isidore’s time concerning children being assigned to monasteries by the will of their parents.

This was drawn chiefly from canon 49 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided. I have therefore thought it appropriate to cite it here; it is found in canon 3 of the same cause and question:

> “A monk is made either by paternal devotion or by his own profession; whichever of these has been alleged [others read *allegatum*, ‘alleged’], that condition shall stand. Accordingly, we close the way for such persons to return to the world and forbid every return to the secular life.”

Baluze notes on this canon that this discipline was later renewed by King Chindaswinth in a constitution found in book III of the Visigothic Law, title 5, chapter 3.

Thus Smaragdus formed a rule from the Toledan canon under the name of the holy bishop of Seville, adding the example of Samuel. Smaragdus had also found several passages concerning Samuel in Isidore, both in his *Commentary on the First Book of Kings*, chapter 1, and in his allegories on Sacred Scripture, under the entries “Anna” and “Samuel.”

### 47.

From what has been said it may be inferred that Gratian sometimes cited Isidore in place of Basil. This could easily have arisen from the abbreviated notations used by ancient copyists.

Suppose, for example, that they wrote *Bsius* for the name *Basilius*. Those who read it might have taken the opportunity to read: “B. Isidore,” that is, “Blessed Isidore.”

I think this happened in canon 19, cause 22, question 4, whose words are found in Basil’s shorter rules, in the Latin translation of Rufinus, question 184:

> “If anyone has been induced to decide to do something among those things that do not please God, he ought to do penance . . . . Whatever has been established presumptuously against the commandment of God ought to be revoked as invalid.”

At present I add nothing concerning the verse beginning “Three”: I have already examined it above, where it was necessary to discuss the writings of Jerome.

48. In canon 18, Cause 33, Question 2, the actual words of Isidore are not reproduced; rather, the opinion that the holy man expresses in chapter 19 of Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices* is summarized briefly, as follows:

> “The Apostle says, ‘I command—not I, but the Lord—that a wife should not depart from her husband.’ For he forbids her to be dismissed for any reason whatever, lest she join herself to another, in accordance with the custom of the Jews, which the Lord prohibited when he said: ‘Whoever dismisses his wife, except on account of fornication, and marries another, commits adultery.’ As Jerome says, adultery alone overcomes the wife’s affection; indeed, when she has divided the one flesh shared with her husband into another and separated herself through fornication, she ought not to be retained by her husband, lest she make the husband also subject to a curse, since Scripture says: ‘He who keeps an adulteress is foolish and impious.’ Wherever, therefore, there is fornication or suspicion of fornication, the wife may freely be dismissed. What, then, if she is barren, deformed, elderly, foul-smelling, drunk, irritable, of bad character, wanton, gluttonous, foolish, wandering, quarrelsome, or abusive? Whether you wish it or not, she must be retained, and she must be regarded as she was received, whatever her condition.”

What is read in Hincmar of Reims, in his work *On the Divorce of Lothair*, in the response to the fifth question, is also not far removed from Gratian’s canon:

> “A marriage lawfully contracted cannot be dissolved for any reason, unless it is accompanied by a spiritual separation, or by an explicit confession or clear proof of bodily fornication.”

49. No one can deny that the heading of canon 14, Cause 35, Question 2, is corrupt. It reads: “Isidore, from the Council of Mantes,” or, as some editions have it, “from the Council of Macia.” Ivo of Chartres, in Part IX of the *Decree*, chapter 44, cited the same testimony, omitting Isidore’s name, as coming from the Council of Mantes. Hugh of Saint Victor, however, in Book II of *On the Sacraments*, Part XI, chapter 15, cites it as coming from the Council of Mâcon.

What more need we investigate? That canon is read in the Council of Worms of the year 868, number 78, in these words:

> “We likewise prohibit anyone from entering marriage in the fourth generation; but wherever anyone is found to have married after the prohibition had been issued, the marriage shall be separated. Certainly, the same rule of marriage law that is to be observed regarding the man’s kindred must also be observed regarding the wife’s kindred, since it is clear that the two are one flesh. Therefore their kindred on both sides must be regarded as common, just as it is written: ‘The two shall be one flesh.’”

The same words are read in the First Council of Mainz of the year 847, canon 30. A similar statement is found in the Council of Chalon of the year 813, canon 29:

> “Certainly, the same rule of marriage law that is to be observed regarding one’s own husband must also be observed regarding the wife’s kindred. Since, therefore, it is clear that the two are one flesh, their kindred on both sides must be regarded as common, just as it is written: ‘The two shall be one flesh.’”

Thus the Council of Worms began to be called “Macia” by the collectors, under a corrupted name, or “Manticum”; and from this it is evident that Gratian easily went astray in the heading of the canon.

But you may ask how it could have happened that Isidore’s name entered the heading. I think Gratian made his mistake from Ivo’s codex. For in Ivo the aforementioned canon is described in Part IX, chapter 44, under the name of the Council of Manticum. Then in chapter 45 the following heading occurs: “Likewise, from the sayings of Isidore.” Gratian, judging from the particle *item* (“likewise”), which seems to form a connection, thought that Isidore’s name could also be assigned to the preceding canon.

50. There remain canons 1 and 6 of Cause 35, Question [Col. 0196C] 5. In these Isidore’s words are not quoted; rather, Isidore’s name is praised because he transmitted much concerning this subject in Book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5 and following. Indeed, canon 6 is entirely taken from Julius Paulus’s Book IV of the *Sentences*, title 11, “On Degrees.”

Ivo copied this canon in Part IX of the *Decree*, chapter 64, without adding the author’s name. A note was nevertheless written in the margin that Isidore treated the matter extensively. I think this gave Gratian the occasion to suppose that Isidore was the author of the canon.

I shall therefore set forth Isidore’s words in the said chapter 5 and the following chapters, against which the Gratianic testimonies must be tested and corrected. He says:

> “A father is the one from whom the beginning of a lineage arises; therefore he is called the head of the household. A father is so called because, after the act of begetting has been completed, he produces a son . . . . A mother is so called because something is brought forth from her; for a mother is, as it were, matter, whereas the father is the cause . . . . A grandfather is the father of one’s father; he is called *avus* from *aevum*, that is, from antiquity. A great-grandfather is the father of one’s grandfather, as it were, near (*prope*) the grandfather. A great-great-grandfather is the father of one’s great-grandfather, already far removed from the grandfather. A great-great-great-grandfather is the father of one’s great-great-grandfather. A great-great-great-great-grandfather is the father of one’s great-great-great-grandfather, as it were *tretavus* [read: *tetravus*], that is, the fourth degree above the great-great-grandfather. But *tritavus* is the final name of kinship. A family begins with the father and ends with the *tritavus*. Son and daughter derive their names from the family, for they are the first in the order of those who are born . . . . A grandson is one who is born from a son; he is called *nepos*, as it were, ‘born afterward’ . . . . A great-grandson is one who has been conceived and born from a grandson; and he is called *pronepos*, as it were, ‘born farther afterward’ . . . . *Pronepos* is so called because he is near (*prope*) the grandson. *Abnepos* is so called because he is separated from the grandson. For there is a *pronepos* between him and the grandson. *Adnepos* is the son of a great-grandson; *trinepos* is the son of a great-great-grandson, because he is fourth in order after the grandson, as it were a *tetranepos*. We do not speak of ‘lesser descendants’ except when the name of the degrees fails us—for example, son, grandson, great-grandson, great-great-grandson, great-great-great-grandson, and *trinepos*. When these degrees have run out, we rightly speak of ‘lesser descendants’; likewise, after the names father, grandfather, great-grandfather, great-great-grandfather, great-great-great-grandfather, and *tritavus*, we speak of ‘greater ancestors.’”

After this, in the subsequent chapters, Isidore proceeds to explain the names of blood-relatives and agnatic relatives, whom we call collateral relatives:

> “Brothers are so called because they are born from the same fruit, that is, from the same seed . . . . A sister, like a brother, is so called because she is born from the same seed; she is said to be the only one who shares with her brothers in the lot of agnation. The sons of brothers are called *patrueles*, because their fathers were full brothers to one another. *Consobrini* are those born either from a sister and a brother or from two sisters, as it were *consororini*. *Fratrueles*, however, are the sons of a maternal aunt; *sobrini* are the sons of *consobrini*. *Tius* is a Greek name. A paternal uncle is one’s father’s brother, as it were another father; hence, when a father dies, the paternal uncle first takes charge of the orphan and protects him by law as though he were his son. A maternal uncle is one’s mother’s brother; his name appears to have the form of a diminutive, because he is shown to derive from *avus*. An aunt on the father’s side is one’s father’s sister, as it were another mother. An aunt on the mother’s side is one’s mother’s sister, as it were another mother. A father-in-law is one who gives his daughter in marriage. A son-in-law is one who marries a daughter; he is called *gener* because he is admitted for the enlargement of the family. A father-in-law and mother-in-law are so called because one has associated a son-in-law or daughter-in-law with oneself. A stepfather is one who marries a woman who has a son or daughter by another man; he is called *vitricus*, as it were *novitricius*, because a new husband is brought in by the mother. A stepson is one who was born from another father; he is thought to be called *privignus*, as it were *privigenus*, because he was begotten first, and is therefore also commonly called ‘born previously.’ These names appear to be derived from *gens*: *genitor*, *genitrix*, *agnati*, *agnatae*, *cognati*, *cognatae*, *progenitores*, *progenitrices*, *germani*, and *germanae*.”

After this, in some copies, as has already been noted above, the words of canon 1, Cause 35, Question 4, are read. Finally, in chapter 7 Isidore expands his discussion, explaining more clearly the degrees of ascendants and descendants, as well as of collateral relatives—that is, paternal uncles, paternal aunts, maternal uncles, and maternal aunts—in these words:

> “The author of my lineage is my father; I am his son or daughter. My father’s father is my grandfather; I am his grandson or granddaughter. My father’s grandfather is my great-grandfather; I am his great-grandson or great-granddaughter. My father’s great-grandfather is my great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-grandson or great-great-granddaughter. My father’s great-great-grandfather is my great-great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-great-grandson or great-great-great-granddaughter. My father’s great-great-great-grandfather is my great-great-great-great-grandfather; I am his great-great-great-great-grandson or great-great-great-great-granddaughter.

> “My father’s brother is my paternal uncle; I am his brother’s son or daughter. My paternal uncle’s father is my grand-paternal uncle; I am his brother’s son’s son or daughter. My paternal uncle’s grandfather is my great-paternal uncle; I am his son’s grandson or granddaughter. My paternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my great-great-paternal uncle; I am his grandson’s son or daughter.

> “My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt; I am her brother’s son or daughter. My maternal aunt’s mother is my grand-maternal aunt; I am her brother’s daughter’s son or daughter. My maternal aunt’s grandmother is my great-maternal aunt; I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter. My maternal aunt’s great-grandmother is my great-great-maternal aunt; I am her granddaughter’s grandson or granddaughter.

> “My mother’s brother is my maternal uncle; I am his sister’s son or daughter. My maternal uncle’s father is my grand-maternal uncle; I am his sister’s son’s son or daughter. My maternal uncle’s grandfather is my great-maternal uncle; I am his son’s grandson or granddaughter. My maternal uncle’s great-grandfather is my great-great-maternal uncle; I am his granddaughter’s son or daughter.

> “My mother’s sister is my maternal aunt; I am her sister’s son or daughter. My maternal aunt’s sister is my grand-maternal aunt; I am her sister’s grandson or granddaughter. My grandmother’s sister is my great-maternal aunt; I am her sister’s great-grandson or great-granddaughter. My great-grandmother’s sister is my great-great-maternal aunt; I am her granddaughter’s son or daughter.”

51. I think that even from this specimen concerning our Isidore it is sufficiently clear that Berardus performed a highly useful service by distinguishing genuine Gratianic canons from apocryphal ones, bringing corrupt texts into conformity with more accurate codices, and elucidating passages that were more difficult to interpret. I nevertheless approve less of his judgment concerning certain legitimate works of Isidore. I wish he had compared the Isidorian canons with the Grialian edition rather than with the Breulian edition. But apparently he did not have Grialius’s edition at hand, nor did he examine other manuscript copies by which he could have been assisted.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. Praise of Isidore Gathered from Certain Ancient Writers

1. Enough has already been brought forward from which it can clearly be inferred that Isidore’s learning was held in high esteem by ancient writers. It will nevertheless be useful to add some further material, so that it may be understood that Isidore was praised not only by those who deliberately set forth his deeds or composed his eulogy—such as Braulio, Ildefonsus, Redemptus, the anonymous historians of his *Life* or of the translation of his body, and Martin of León in his sermons on that translation—but also by those who, while engaged in other matters, nevertheless digressed into praise of Isidore and used his authority either to confirm the doctrines and institutions of our religion or to provide a wealth of every kind of learning.

Nor need I search anxiously for writers of this kind: what limit or end could there be to such labor and study? I shall mention only a few who readily presented themselves to me. I shall refer to more of them in the notes to the works themselves whenever the occasion arises, or bring them forward again.

2. Joseph Rodríguez de Castro, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, page 293, begins his chapter on Saint Isidore as follows. I render his Spanish words into Latin:

> “Of Saint Isidore—another Daniel, as Saint Gregory the Great judged; the teacher of Spain, according to Saint Braulio and the archbishop—indeed, the bishop—Don Lucas of Tuy; the mirror of bishops and priests, according to Saint Ildefonsus; the prelate of bishops and prince of priests, according to Saint Martin [of León, I think]; the apostle of Christ, as Don Pedro, archbishop of Compostela, judged; and so forth.”

It is regrettable that Rodríguez does not indicate the passages from which he drew these splendid praises of Isidore. But, I think, he took Gregory the Great’s, Braulio’s, and Ildefonsus’s words from apocryphal works.

That archbishop of Compostela may have been Pedro Monsoro, or, as others call him, Monsoncio. Some assign him to the tenth century, others to the twelfth; concerning him, see Nicolás Antonio. But since Rodríguez himself, on page 487, maintains that no bishop Pedro Monsoro, or Monsoncio, can have a place among Spanish writers, I remain uncertain and wish to know which Pedro, archbishop of Compostela, he called a praiser of Isidore.

3. Saint Valerius, abbot of the monastery of Montes and author of the *Life of Saint Fructuosus*, bishop of Braga, at the end of the seventh century, compares Saint Isidore with Fructuosus in these words:

> “After the ancient darkness of the world had been illumined by the new brightness of heavenly truth, and from the Roman See, the first chair of the holy Church, the immensity of the doctrines of the catholic faith shone forth in flashing brilliance; after the most excellent examples of sacred religion had radiated from Egypt, the eastern province, and the small extremity of this western region had shone through; divine mercy illumined two lamps of conspicuous brilliance: Isidore, that most reverend man, bishop of Seville, and the most blessed Fructuosus, immaculate and just from childhood.
>
> “The former, resplendent in the radiance of his speech, acquired the first fruits of the art of the distinguished sophist and set forth anew the doctrines of the Romans; the latter, kindled by the flame of the Holy Spirit in his most sacred religious vocation, shone forth so exercised in all spiritual matters and so perfect in every holy work that he easily equaled, in merit [perhaps: ‘in merits’], the ancient Thebans.
>
> “The former, through the industry of the active life, instructed all Spain externally; the latter, shining with flashing brilliance through his mastery of the contemplative life, illumined the inner secrets of hearts. The former, glowing with excellent eloquence, became famous in books of edification; the latter, flashing at the summit [perhaps: ‘from the summit’] of the virtues, left an example of holy religion and, with blameless step, followed the footprints of our Lord and Savior, and so forth.”

Thus it was published by Flórez in volume XV of *Sacred Spain*, from a new recension of manuscript codices following Sandoval, Tamayo, and Mabillon.

4. This same eulogy was published by Constantine Cajetanus, page 6, under the name of an anonymous Benedictine in the *Life of Saint Fructuosus, Abbot and Bishop of Braga*. But it is now established that the author of the *Life of Saint Fructuosus, Abbot of Dumio and Bishop of Braga*, who flourished shortly after Isidore, was Valerius, abbot of the monastery of Saint Peter of Montes, at the end of the seventh century.

That *Life* was published by Prudencio de Sandoval, Juan Tamayo de Salazar, Mabillon in volume II of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, page 581, and by the Bollandists under 16 April. Flórez, volume XV of *Sacred Spain*, page 139, and Bayer in his notes to the *Old Spanish Library*, Book V, chapter [as printed: “c”], number 263, observe that in the Oviedo, Carrazeda, Arlanza, Toledo, and other codices, the *Life of Saint Fructuosus* is listed among Valerius’s genuine works and that its style is unmistakably Valerius’s.

Fructuosus’s and Valerius’s Benedictine monasticism will, however, be more readily proved to Benedictines than to others. Consult Nicolás Antonio, in the place cited, in the *Old Spanish Library*.

5. It should be counted to Isidore’s credit that his name and authority are preserved in ancient collections of sayings taken from the holy Fathers. Many people in former times devoted themselves to extracting flowers from the holy Fathers. In John Egon’s *On Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Reichenau*, in Pez’s volume I of the *Anecdotes*, Part III, chapter 9, the monk Reginbert is praised. He presided over the library in the ninth century and copied many volumes with his own hand, usually placing before them an epigram beginning, “In great honor of God,” and extracted abridgments and little flowers from the holy Fathers.

The most famous work of this kind is entitled *The Book of Sparks, Collected from the Sayings of the Holy Fathers*—namely, Ambrose, Athanasius, Augustine, Basil, Caesarius, Clement, Cassian, Cyprian, Ephrem, Isaiah, Eusebius, Gregory, Jerome, Hilary, Isidore, Josephus, Origen, and the *Lives of the Fathers*. In volume VII of Bede’s works, the title of this work is *Questions of the Fathers*. At the beginning, Sedulius is included among the Fathers, perhaps the poet who composed the poem on evangelical history; yet I find nothing by him in the work itself.

I do not think the work entitled *Alcuin’s Book of Sparks*, preserved by Bandini, shelf 35, volume IV, codex 5 of Santa Croce, is different. In it Isidore is praised together with Ambrose and others. This book of sparks, which is attributed to Bede in some codices, is attributed in others to Paul Alvarus of Córdoba. Concerning him, see Nicolás Antonio in the *Old Spanish Library*, with Bayer’s notes, and Flórez, *Sacred Spain*, volume XI, pages 47 and following. In other codices it is attributed to Defensor, a monk of Ligugé among the Pictons, as Fabricius infers from the preface in the *Medieval Library*, under the entry “Defensor.” Others, less correctly, assert that Bishop Caesarius or Cassiodorus was the author of this collection. Certainly Bede, in his commentaries on Holy Scripture, gathers Isidore’s words together with those of other Fathers.

6. In Codex Vatican Regina of Sweden 254 there is a similar collection: “Here begin sayings excerpted from various books of the holy doctors.” It begins: “The Son of almighty God”; it ends: “he knows how to yearn more ardently.” The authors cited for the sayings are Isidore, Bede, Xystus, Gregory, Augustine, Seneca, and Jerome.

In the same codex there follows another work, whose first title is: “Here begin chapters on the snares of the crafty enemy.” In reality, however, it is a collection of sayings by Isidore, Cassiodorus, Hilary, Jerome, Gregory, and Xystus.

7. Among the Florentine manuscript codices of Santa Croce, Bandini lists, under shelf 10, a parchment Codex 10 from the beginning of the thirteenth century. He notes that after Peter of Riga’s *Aurora* there are certain sententious sayings attributed to the Apostle Peter, Seneca, Bernard, Augustine, and Isidore.

In the same place, under shelf 36, he lists parchment Codex 9 from the fourteenth century, entitled *The Book of Authorities of the Saints*, published by Brother Vincent of Beauvais of the Order of Preachers. The sayings are drawn from Isidore and others. Bandini observes that the book is mentioned neither by Echard nor by Fabricius.

8. In Codex 2951 of the Old Vatican Library, after Isidore’s book *On the World* and other works, on page 135 there begin sayings from several ancient authors on a variety of subjects, among whom Isidore is also named. This work, however, is not by a particularly ancient author.

Likewise, in the thirteenth century Thomas of Ireland wrote *Manipulus florum*, or *Flowers of All the Doctors Who Wrote on Sacred Scripture*. This work was very frequently reprinted.

An older collection is the collection of sayings by Megingotus addressed to Reginmar, bishop of Passau, in the twelfth century. Pez mentions it in his *Introductory Dissertation*, volume IV of the *Treasury of Anecdotes*, page 3. Megingotus collected sayings from Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Prosper of Aquitaine, Claudius Mamertus, Gregory the Great, Bede, Haymo of Halberstadt [printed: “Haeymone”], Abbot Smaragdus, and Bishop Severinus. Isidore is not named by Pez. Fabricius omitted this Megingotus, or Mengotus, from his *Medieval Library*, apart from a few other remarks.

9. Among the appendices to volume VI of Augustine’s works there is a work entitled *The Mirror*. The Maurist editors think it was compiled from sayings of Augustine, Gregory, and Isidore, and even of Alcuin. Mabillon, however, in the *Analecta*, page 492 of the Paris edition of 1723, asserts that it was excerpted from the *Confession of Faith*, which he attributes to Alcuin.

But, as Risco rightly observes in volume XXXI of *Sacred Spain*, page 162, when Taio in the seventh century—the same period in which Isidore flourished—undertook to collect sayings from Gregory the Great, adding some from Augustine, he extracted many passages from the *Mirror*, as from a work that Risco thinks was Augustinian, or was then considered to be so.

Therefore, the passages that the Maurists identify as having been taken by the author of the *Mirror* from Isidore’s books of *Sentences* were rather taken by Isidore from the *Mirror*.

10. When manuscript codices are examined, Isidore’s name will often occur in such ancient collections of sayings. Thus, in Vatican Codex 4250, there are Isidore’s *Collected Extracts from the Books on the Trinity*. In Ottobonian Codex 2524, concerning which see chapter 106, there are *Flowers from Isidore and Other Fathers*.

Among the autograph works of Saint Lawrence Justinian, donated to the Vatican Library by Innocent XI in the year 1684, there is Codex 6460, partly on paper and partly on parchment, in small octavo format. It contains *Flowers from Various Holy Fathers and from Book I of Saint Isidore’s On the Highest Good*: “Contrition of heart,” and so forth.

11. Isidore’s name is also prominent among those who composed chronicles from older sources, including Isidore himself and other earlier writers. Shortly after Isidore, Fredegarius Scholasticus flourished around the year 641. His *Chronicle* was published among the works of Gregory of Tours, edited by Thierry Ruinart, column 585. At the beginning he writes:

> “Thus, having diligently read through the chronicles of blessed Jerome, Hydatius, and a certain Wise Man, or also Isidore, and even Gregory, from the origin of the world to the end of the reign of Guntram, I inserted individually into this little book, in an appropriate style, whatever belonged to these five chronicles, omitting nothing further; for they composed their works with the greatest skill and without reproach.”

Ruinart notes that *nec plura praetermissa* (“omitting nothing further”) may perhaps stand in the sixth case, *nec pluribus praetermissis* (“with nothing further omitted”). I have often observed this manner of expression in Isidore and other writers of the same period, although foolish correctors of codices have sometimes corrupted it.

12. Nicolás Antonio, in the *Old Spanish Library*, Book V, chapter 4, number 111, considers it worthy of note that Fredegarius scarcely shows himself certain about the author of the Isidorian *Chronicle*. But, as I think, Fredegarius understands a chronicle by some anonymous author, distinct from the Isidorian one, since he praises the chronicle of “a certain Wise Man” and takes the particles *seu et* as a simple conjunction.

Nicolás Antonio also suspects that *Georgii*, that is, “of George the monk,” should be read instead of *Gregorii*. But why should we not understand the passage as referring to Gregory of Tours?

Many other writers have likewise praised Isidore as an authority in composing chronicles, especially Spaniards, such as Isidore Pacensis, Lucas of Tuy, the author of the *General History of Spain* under the name of Alfonso the Wise, and others.

Theodoric Engelhus, in the fifteenth century, wrote the *Chronicle of Chronicles* and drew upon Isidore’s books of *Etymologies*. Ranulf Higden, in the fourteenth century, used Pliny, Isidore, and others as authorities in his *Polychronicon*. John Fordun, in the fifteenth century, frequently praises and follows Isidore in his *Scotichronicon*—for that is the title he gave it.

13. Alcuin, besides inserting certain prayers from Isidore into the offices for the weekdays, expresses his praise of Isidore in Book II *Against Elipandus* as follows:

> “Be silent, brothers; be silent, and do not attribute the blasphemy of your error to your fathers. They had their own times, and they left us the splendid traces of their labor in holy conduct. We praise and love them. Thus, of blessed Isidore, that most illustrious teacher not only of Spain but also of all the Churches of Latin eloquence, we have read very many little works, and we hold them in great veneration. In them we have never found the word ‘adoption’ written concerning the humanity of our Redeemer.”

14. Bignaeus suggests in his preface to Saint Isidore’s works that Elipandus himself, whose errors Alcuin refuted, used Isidore’s authority in a letter to Charlemagne. This is also shown by Charlemagne’s letter to Elipandus and the other bishops of Spain:

> “You have set before me the example of the emperor Constantine, whose beginning, you say, blessed Isidore praised, and whose end he lamented; and you kindly advise me lest the same thing happen to me through a certain Beatus, whom you have called ‘Antiphrasius.’”

In Labbe’s collection of the councils, volume VII, column 1051, the text reads *per quemdam beatum* (“through a certain blessed man”). But it should be written *per quemdam Beatum* (“through a certain Beatus”), for Beatus was the name of a learned Spanish presbyter who refuted Elipandus’s heresy. Elipandus called him *Antiphrasius*, that is, “Beatus” by antiphrasis, as though he were unhappy.

The letter to Charlemagne was finally published by Flórez from a manuscript in the Toledo Codex, volume V of *Sacred History*. In connection with the proposed example of Constantine, it says:

> “Concerning him blessed Isidore says: ‘Alas, for sorrow! He made good use of his beginning, but his end was evil.’”

These words were taken from the *Chronicle*, which Elipandus repeatedly brought forward in his letter to Alcuin. In that letter he composed the following eulogy of Isidore:

> “Blessed Isidore also, the radiance of the Church, the star of the West, the teacher of Spain, says in the book of the *Etymologies*, and so forth.”

15. Regino, abbot of the monastery of Prüm, who flourished in the tenth century, writes in his *Chronicle* under the year 572:

> “Under these kings also Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, flourished. He should be placed behind none of the teachers of our own time; he discussed many matters concerning the faith, rules, and ecclesiastical disciplines.”

Other chroniclers speak in a similar way.

16. In Schelstrat’s volume I of *Ecclesiastical Antiquities* there is a chronicle written in the eleventh century from Vatican Codex 1358. Under Heraclius it says:

> “Isidore, bishop of Seville in Spain, was illustrious, an outstanding teacher, together with Eugenius of Toledo, Selva of Narbonne, and others.”

Earlier it had stated:

> “The councils of Spain, Toledo and Seville, where Leander and Euphemius were illustrious.”

17. Hermannus Contractus, under the year 616, in volume I of Canisius’s *Ancient Readings*, page 497:

> “At this time Isidore, bishop of Seville, was renowned in Spain. He carried the abbreviation of the history of the times down to this point, and he also published many excellent little works.”

18. Sigebert, under the year 627, in Aubert Miraeus’s edition, Antwerp, 1608, page 90:

> “In Spain Isidore of Seville was renowned both for holiness and for learning.”

It is noted that in manuscript codices *Spalensis* is read, just as Spain was formerly called *Spania*.

19. Martin of Poland, under the year 621:

> “At this time Isidore, bishop of Seville and successor of blessed Leander, flourished. This man composed the very learned book of the *Etymologies*, and so forth.”

20. William of Malmesbury, Book II of *The Deeds of the English*, chapter 10:

> “Through Leander, bishop of Spain [perhaps: of Seville], and through Richard [that is, Reccared], the Goths were united with the catholic choir. Isidore, distinguished in learning and holiness, succeeded Leander, and so forth.”

Compare chapter 28 concerning this passage of William.

21. Vincent of Beauvais, or Bellovacensis, *Historical Mirror*, Book XXIII, chapter 31:

> “This holy Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote many useful works, and so forth.”

He lists his works. He gives the commentary on the books of the Old Testament the title *Allegories*. He attributes to Isidore one treatise *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, and a book *On the Apostolic Decrees*, which, he says, Isidore was the first to compile and from which Ivo and Gratian profited.

22. Saint Antoninus, in his *Chronicle*, Part II, title 13, chapter 2, discusses Saint Isidore and his works at length:

> “Under the emperor Heraclius, mentioned above, blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, was illustrious in Spain around the year of the Lord 640, rich in holiness and learning, and so forth.”

In the *Chronicle of Liège*, in Labbe’s *Library of Manuscripts*, volume I, page 335, the statement is brief:

> “In the year 613, Isidore the bishop was illustrious.”

23. Petrus Equilinus, in the *Catalogue of the Saints*, Book IV, chapter 30:

> “Isidore, bishop of Seville, and so forth, who produced many volumes useful to the Church of God, and so forth. He died at Seville, resplendent in life and teaching, on the day before the Nones of April, and there he lies buried.”

Peter of Natalibus evidently did not know about the translation of Isidore’s body. In listing his books, he sometimes discusses the same book twice and makes many errors: he names four books of *Sentences* and twenty of the *Synonyms*, unless this is an error of the copyists. Other material seems to have been borrowed from Vincent of Beauvais, especially the account of the book *On the Apostolic Decrees of the Roman Pontiffs and the Canons of the Councils*.

It would be a long task to list all the authors of chronicles and catalogues who celebrate the praises of our Isidore.

24. The name Panormiuon is unknown to me, nor is it found in the *Spanish Library*. I shall nevertheless transcribe Constantine Cajetan’s words concerning him in the *Eulogy of Isidore*, page 34:

> “Finally, as the conclusion of our eulogy, let us be permitted to commend the profound learning of this most eminent man, also on the ground that he performed a most useful service for the catholic Church. This is evident from many other sources, but especially from the decrees, a considerable part of which was excerpted from his labors. At this point, therefore, the following observation must be made. A certain bishop Panormiuon—as it appears in Maurus Castella—an extremely ancient writer, in his book *On the Various Distinctions of the Scriptures*, when he mentions those books that in his time had been received by the catholic Church, also enumerates all the written works of Saint Isidore. This author’s work exists in the church of Braga, written by hand in Gothic letters.”

Did Maurus Castella, or someone else, fabricate from Ivo’s *Pannormia* the name Panormiuon, a bishop? That is what I conjectured.

25. Samson, abbot of Córdoba in the ninth century, Book I of the *Apologeticus*, chapter 3, volume XI of *Sacred History*, page 344:

> “As for the names of that same Son of God, which are proper names, and so forth, I do not think it necessary to insert anything concerning them in this work. It is nevertheless clear that blessed Isidore discussed them magnificently. By consulting his works, the reader will be able to ascertain clearly that he was filled with a heavenly gift.”

Samson frequently quotes Isidore’s words with praise, as does his contemporary Alvarus of Córdoba in his letters and in the *Luminous Index*, in the same volume XI of *Sacred Spain*, as well as later Spanish writers.

Lucas of Tuy’s books *Against the Albigensians* are full of praise for Isidore, whose sayings Lucas very frequently employs. “Isidore,” he says in Book II, chapter 7, “the most illustrious philosopher of the catholics, holds primacy among teachers in discussing both etymologies and the natures of things, and in the variety of sciences and languages.”

26. It has already happened several times in these *Prolegomena*, and it will occur more frequently hereafter, that ancient writers are cited who use Isidore’s words for their own purposes. Among these, to mention a few now, is Theodulf of Orléans. In his work *On the Holy Spirit*, in volume II of Sirmond’s works, he cites Isidore from Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 3; from Book II, or I, of the *Differences*, chapter 3; and from Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 17.

There is also the author of the rhythmic description of Verona, which Rather of Verona, bishop of that city, brought back from Italy and had attached to his autograph at Lanbi, when Pepin, son of Charlemagne, was ruling among the Lombards. It is preserved in Mabillon, volume I, page 371 of the Paris edition of 1675:

> “This great and splendid city in the regions of Venetia in Italy is powerful, as Isidore teaches; it is called Verona, formerly in ancient times.”

27. In Pez’s volume II of the *Treasury of Anecdotes*, Part II, column 41, Adhelerus, in his admonition to Nosuinda, chapter 13:

> “For Isidore says that we are cleansed by prayers and instructed by readings.”

This is from Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 8, at the beginning.

In the same work, column 91, Placidus of Nonantula, *On the Honor of the Church*, chapter 16:

> “From the sayings of Saint Isidore the bishop: ‘Under the discipline of government, the powers of the world,’ and so forth.”

Peter of Celle, Book IV, letter 2, in Sirmond’s volume III of the *Works*:

> “Hence God is said to be simple—not for any other reason, according to Isidore, than that he himself is not one thing and what is in him another.”

This is from Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 1.

To these may be added the Anonymous of Ravenna, whether he was Guido the presbyter, who praises Isidore on page 12 of his *Geography*, and the old scholiast on Horace, who uses Isidore’s authority on page 207 of Jacobus Cruquius’s edition.

28. In Blanchini’s *Fourfold Gospel Book*, page 603 verso, Royal-Vatican Codex 76 is listed. It was written in the eleventh century, and a specimen of its script is reproduced as plate 5, number 7, after page 60.

This codex contains Paul’s *Problems Concerning Riddles* and canonical books. Its beginning is as follows:

> “The Old Testament, says Isidore, is so called because, when the New came, it ceased.”

It is not explained which Paul this is. He may perhaps be the deacon Warnefrid, or, as others call him, Warnefridus.

I shall observe in passing that two authors of Roman history written in the old Italian language also derive their opening from Isidore’s authority. One is in Ottobonian Codex 2616:

> “The glorious holy lord Saint Isidore says . . .”

The other is in Ottobonian Codex 2658:

> “The glorious holy Saint Isidore says in the book of the *Etymologies*, and so forth.”

The author of the first work is called Lello Petroni; the other is anonymous.

In Royal-Vatican Codex 1573, which will shortly be described and which contains certain works of Isidore, there is a work entitled *On the Fourteen Divisions of Time*. It begins:

> “How many divisions of time are there? Fourteen: the atom, the moment, and so forth.”

Isidore is praised throughout:

> “Isidore defined it, saying . . .”

In volume I of Bede’s works there is a work bearing this title; Mabillon recommends its fuller manuscript codex in volume I of the *Italian Museum*, page 69.

In another Codex of Regina of Sweden, which will also be listed below, there is a work by a less ancient author, with this title: *Authorities That Constantine Was Baptized by Saint Sylvester at Rome*. Isidore is indicated among others as an authority for this subject. But, I think, this was taken from the apocryphal collection of Isidore Mercator.

29. Codex Vaticanus 1343 contains a certain collection of decretals and canons, together with several short works on ecclesiastical matters. The first work is mutilated at the beginning; it concerns priestly vestments, the sacraments, and other subjects, and Isidore is frequently cited in its rubrics—for example, on exorcisms, on the scrutiny, and so forth. [Col. 0205C] In the same place, on page 445, a short work on baptism and its entire order, according to the investigation of the Catholics, begins: “If I unfold the sacrament of baptism by returning to its first origin…”—from chapter 24 of book II of Isidore’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, who is explicitly named in the title: “On the Exorcism of Catechumens: Isidore”; that is, from book II, chapter 20, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

30. You may also see Isidore’s celebrated name in the Laurentian Codex of San Marco, which will be examined in chapter 44; it contains a certain homily under Isidore’s name. Bandini, in volume II of the *Latin Codices of the Medicean Library*, Pluteus 47, describes a codex from the beginning of the eleventh century containing scholia on Priscian, in which, besides others, Isidore and Bede are praised.

31. A curious work is entitled *A Singular Volume of Distinguished Authors, Both Greek and Latin, Collected from Various Libraries and Now for the First Time Ordered to Appear in Print and to Benefit the Public by Petrus Stevartius of Liège*, printed at Ingolstadt by the Fiderian press, in quarto.
