In some of these short pieces, words of Isidore are brought forward, as I shall say in chapters 69 and 73; Isidore is sometimes cited in his *Sentences*, for example on page 691—that is, in the books of the *Sentences*.

# CHAPTER XXXIV. Various Judgments of Certain More Recent Writers Concerning Isidore’s Works

1. Those who wish to pass judgment on Isidore’s works ought to approach him in the spirit with which he himself read earlier authors. “We ought not,” he says in book XV, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*, “to condemn historians or commentators who say different things as ignorant, because antiquity itself created the error.” Thus, amid the great variety of ancient matters that Isidore treated, if some error entered his works, it seems attributable to antiquity rather than to Isidore himself. Nor should one judge him so rashly, as some do, although most writers raise him up with deserved praise.

Nicolaus Antonius collected several judgments of more recent writers concerning Isidore in book V, chapter 4, no. 91 of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*. Thus Jacobus Gaddius, in volume I of the *Non-Ecclesiastical Writers*, calls Isidore “a model bishop, complete in every respect, a man of varied learning and immense erudition.” Xystus of Siena, in book IV of the *Bibliotheca Sancta*, calls him “a man of outstanding holiness and learning, most skilled in the divine Scriptures, possessing an insatiable desire and wholly inexhaustible strength in reading, collecting, arranging, and combining the sayings, opinions, and compilations of the ancient Fathers from their innumerable and immense volumes.” [Col. 0206B]

2. Resendius, in book II of the *Lusitanian Antiquities*, calls him “a great man” and “well versed in many matters,” and says that he was not so unfamiliar with more elegant letters that he should be dismissed from the testimony of eloquence with contemptuous disdain. Elsewhere he calls him “a man of much learning and diligence.”

Raphael Volaterranus, Nicolaus Antonius continues, judged him not so much a philosopher in learning as in life, and in expression not so much crude as unpracticed—yet not altogether correctly. For who would criticize in him the style of his age? Or to whom would a man seem not to be a philosopher in learning who prescribed rules of conduct and piety for all the ages of the Church, rules rightly to be embraced?

How greatly Joseph Scaliger favors him! “Isidore,” Scaliger says in the *Prima Scaligeriana*, page 65, “transcribed many things from ancient books that we lack today, and those of the highest quality. For that reason I should like to possess him. He is exceedingly useful to learned men.” [Col. 0206C]

255 3. This is more or less what Nicolaus Antonius says. Just as he defends Isidore against Raphael Volaterranus, so Julius Minutolus also prepares a similar defense against Alciatus and Polletus, who call Isidore “a man more good than learned.” Minutolus continues, dissertation 7:

“Isidore, in his *Etymological Work*, although it is sprinkled with certain blemishes, is nevertheless filled to overflowing with learning, and has lent antiquity a great light. Hence that prodigy of learning, Panvinius, candidly admits at the beginning of his work *On the Circensian Games*: ‘I was not a little helped by Isidore’s books of the *Etymologies*.’”

Baillet, in the *Judgments of the Learned*, title 99, observes that Vossius the Elder, in *On Philology*, page 26, agrees with Scaliger in favor of Isidore; that Junius du Verdier, in opposition to Isidore, agrees with Paulus Merula’s *Censure of Authors*, page 26; and that the anonymous author of the *Bibliographia historica curiosa*, page 36, considers it of little importance what Isidore added from his own resources.

Ludovicus Vives, in book III of *On the Transmission of Disciplines*, where he discusses philologists, says:

“I do not know whether grammarians will allow Isidore of Seville to be included among their number. He offers several things drawn from the ancients that are not wholly to be despised, especially since those sources have not survived to our age.”

4. If you please, let us add other critical writers who have praised Isidore. Lilius Gyraldus, in book II, dialogue 12, uses these words of Isidore: “the pontiff,” he says, “renowned for learning and holiness.” [Col. 0207A]

Gerardus Joannes Vossius, *On the Nature of the Arts*, book II, chapter 5, says:

“Useful also is the work that Isidore . . . performed in the twenty books of the *Origins*, which he compiled from the best writers, most of them ecclesiastical.”

5. Thomas Dempsterus, in the *Catalogue of Writers for the Supplement to Rosinus’s Roman Antiquities*, calls Isidore of Seville “an indispensable grammarian, in whom are found many things found nowhere else.”

Albert Dieterus Trekel, in his notes on Brissonius, book IV, chapter 20 of the *Selected Antiquities*, writes:

“Joannes Daniel Ritterus, in the preface to volume I of the *Theodosian Code*, dealt with cognitors and procurators more diligently than the others, but omitted the passage of Isidore in which no ancient writer explains better the difference between procurators and cognitors in the proper sense.”

[Col. 0207B] 6. Franciscus Floridus Sabinus, in book II, chapter 12 of the *Abridged Readings*, admits that Isidore was held in high esteem by Beroaldus, while addressing him as follows:

“You weave together tasteless and unattractive writings from Isidore and Albert the Great.”

Salmasius, in his commentary on Aelius Spartianus, page 5, line 35, after citing Pliny’s passage about the Samothracian rings, says:

“Lipsius was mistaken when he attempted to emend Pliny at that point.”

He then brings forward Isidore’s words from book XIX, chapter 31 of the *Etymologies*: “Samothracian, etc.,” and concludes:

“No one could explain Pliny’s passage better or more briefly.”

The same Salmasius, in his commentary on Flavius Vopiscus, page 225, line 33, writes:

“Isidore, in whom I have often found many things of good quality, and things found nowhere else, describes the *mullei* in this way, etc.”

7. Cellier, who in volume XVII of the *History of Ecclesiastical Authors* describes Isidore’s works with careful examination, reviews them, and praises them individually, concludes in general concerning Isidore’s learning on page 650:

“From Isidore’s works that have come down to us it is evident that he was endowed with immense learning and that he made skillful use of the ancient writers, both ecclesiastical and secular, whom he had read. His style is neither eloquent nor polished, but it is clear and easy. In his works on moral instruction, a certain flavor of piety and spiritual compunction stands out; it penetrates and softens the heart. His other works are commended by the astonishing variety of the matters they treat.”

This has been translated into Latin from Cellier’s French words.

8. The judgment of Jacob Brucker concerning Isidore’s learning, in volume III of the *Critical History of Philosophy*, pages 569 and following, should certainly not be passed over in silence. He says:

“That he was a man highly skilled not only in sacred but also in secular literature is shown by his writings, as they have been recounted by distinguished men and repeatedly listed by writers of ecclesiastical literary history. Although in them he acted as a compiler of the ancients and, like a patchwork garment, stitched his own work together from their writings, he nevertheless displayed judgment in selecting the best; and since he excerpted much from books that we now lack, he ought to be considered to have rendered a service of no little value to later ages.”

Then, concerning the *Etymologies*:

“For he does not pursue etymologies alone, nor trace a meager subject with a dry pen; rather, he extends across almost every kind of learning and contributes many things worth knowing, as well as many excellent matters scarcely found elsewhere . . . . He also published a book *On the Nature of Things*, or *On the World*, in which he presents a kind of cosmography. It is commendable for this reason alone: that it preserves many fragments of Nigidius, Varro, Suetonius Tranquillus, and others that had long since perished.”

“From these things one must judge both Isidore’s own philosophy and his merits in philosophy. It is clear from what has been said that the former consisted more in collections from the ancients than in setting forth some coherent system; accordingly, he does not occupy a prominent place among philosophers—a position he perhaps did not greatly seek. Yet his achievement was not insignificant, because he preserved numerous fragments and excerpts of the ancient philosophers who wrote in Latin. Although he did not always display sound judgment, and drew his material not from his own storehouses but from the resources of others, he nevertheless rendered the same service to philosophy and its history that we rightly praise in Diogenes Laertius, Suidas, Stobaeus, and other writers of philosophical collections. This deserves to be counted among his merits all the more because those ages neither had nor needed better resources, while there was a great scarcity of ancient writers.”

“Those therefore deal harshly with Isidore, and do not sufficiently remember the circumstances of the age in which he lived, who, by calling him a compiler and patcher of centos, accuse him of plagiarism and inept compilation. If writers of later ages had not possessed him, they would have stumbled much more seriously in many matters and would not have been able to draw forth the material with which they adorn their writings as with gems. Guilielmus of Malmesbury observed that Rabanus Maurus did this, despite Guilielmus Cave’s opposition (*Ecclesiastical Literary History*, page 456). Had Cave considered that it was the custom of almost all medieval writers to excerpt earlier authors and compile their own works from them, he would have understood that nothing was detracted from Rabanus’s learning—as it existed in the ninth century—by his having copied Isidore.”

9. Among the encomia of Isidore produced by more recent writers we may place a cento-panegyric, composed by Joannes de la Peña in praise of the Blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville, from various verses of poets and published at Seville in 1643, in quarto. We may also place here the book of Constantinus Cajetanus, entitled *The Lives and Deeds of the Three Holy Bishops, Lights of the Benedictine Order: Isidore of Seville, Ildefonsus of Toledo, and Gregorius, Cardinal-Bishop of Ostia*, etc. Several writings of Isidore himself, not previously published, were added; it was printed at Rome in 1606, in quarto, by Jacobus Mascardus.

Cajetanus gathers much in Isidore’s praise in his dedicatory letters, including the following:

“Among these men, just as Saint Isidore of Seville is most distinguished for holiness, so also, in the abundance of his books, the richness of his intellect, his eloquence, and the weight of his learning, he is pre-eminent—or certainly must be ranked among the foremost. In him youth, eager for learning, finds something to taste; curiosity finds something to admire,” etc.

# CHAPTER XXXV. The Edition of Isidore’s Works Undertaken by Bignaeus Is Described

1. To ensure that nothing is lacking from our edition, I intend to gather everything found in the other editions of Isidore. First I shall review those prepared to encompass all of Isidore’s works. Then I shall discuss the separate editions of certain particular works of the same holy teacher.

Joseph Rodriguez de Castro, in volume II of his *Hispanic Library*, page 334, praises an edition of all Isidore’s works printed at Basel in 1477, in folio, an edition entirely omitted by other writers. I fear that the Basel edition of the *Etymologies* reviewed by Maittaire, which will be discussed below in chapter 54, may through someone’s error have been regarded as an edition of all the works. Margarinus de la Bigne was, as I believe, the first of all to labor diligently to collect Isidore’s works into a single corpus. The title of his edition is as follows.

2. *The Complete Extant Works of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, Partly Published at Various Times through the Labors of Most Learned Men, Partly Now for the First Time Transcribed and Corrected. By Margarinus de la Bigne, Doctor of Theology of Paris. Paris, at the house of Michael Sonnius, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Basel shield, 1580, in folio.*

I shall now set forth the material prefixed to that edition.

## DEDICATORY LETTER

“To the Reverend Father in Christ and Most Distinguished Lord, Lord Franciscus Parcus, Apostolic Protonotary of the Holy See, Dean of the Church of Le Mans, and Lord of Chemiray, my most beloved maternal uncle: Margarinus de la Bigne, Doctor of Sacred Theology, sends grace and peace in Christ.”

3. When I had returned to this city on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of June, in order to attend, on behalf of our province of Rouen, the assembly that the Most Christian King had summoned for that time to settle the affairs of the Gallican Church—Reverend Lord and uncle—several friends came first to greet me, out of their goodwill and kindness toward me. They conversed with me at length and in various ways about the subject of our assemblies, the disasters of the Church, the dangers arising from the character of this most wretched age, the condition of the French state, and other matters.

Finally, after considering the outcome of the assembly of the three orders of this kingdom at Blois, and after carefully weighing all the circumstances of our affairs, they foresaw that either, if those arrangements were properly confirmed which otherwise perhaps could not stand, the Church would continue to groan forever under the burden of the agreements entered into long ago in the name of the clergy; or, after having labored long and painfully, like a woman in childbirth, we would give birth to nothing except something courtly—something revealed by the wisdom of this world, which is hostile to God, and which, although it pleases men, does not serve Christ—nothing worthy of the majesty of the ecclesiastical order.

For in truth, they could never endure that the most holy and ecumenical Council of Trent should be sincerely promulgated in this most religious kingdom; that the Gallican clergy should choose their pastors according to canonical order; that our property and all our rights should be preserved intact and secure—this being the substance of our petitions; or, finally, that the Most Christian King should everywhere emulate better gifts. They could never endure the idea that those who flourish and revel in another’s blood should be judged to seek profit rather than parricide.

Since I could not bring myself to accept this view—having recognized through many indications the openness and piety of our most merciful prince, by which he has already obtained from many people the reputation of being called not merely the Most Christian and the most Catholic of all the Gauls, but also the most devout—and since I saw that several Fathers, easily the leading men of the entire Gallican clergy, would attend our assembly, men whom I had plainly observed at the assemblies of the kingdom at Blois to be devoting faithful and energetic service to Christ and to his bride, the Church, and to be courageously setting themselves as a bronze wall before the house of God, I nevertheless preferred to devote my labor safely to the reading of some one of the ancient Fathers of the Church.

Thus, if our negotiation, because our sins were fighting and dividing us against ourselves and against God, should have a less desirable outcome, and should proceed otherwise than the poverty of our brothers, for whom we are undertaking this embassy, required, I might obtain in the storm a sacred anchor for the appropriate day of mourning and, amid uncertain circumstances, a sure consolation from the divine oracle. But if the Most Christian King should wish to pity our distress and relieve it by some august edict of his, I would thereby have opportunely provided myself with a most suitable governor of spiritual joy.

4. After the four lights of the Western Church—our lords Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and the thrice-greatest pontiff Gregory—Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, can, in my judgment, deservedly and rightfully carry off the palm from all others in piety and learning. He was not, as some think, Gregory’s disciple, but he was so near to him in age that, as a young man, he could have seen the supreme pontiff. This may be inferred from the fact that he himself states in the preface to his *Commentaries on the Old Testament* that he took them from the mystical treasures of the ancient sages and, as he says, from such authors as Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, and Gregory, who was distinguished for eloquence in his own time.

It is not likely that so great and distinguished a man could have been passed over by so devout a disciple without the most grateful acknowledgment of his instruction. There are indeed several indications of the very high esteem in which our Isidore was held many ages ago. Above all, there is Gratian himself, who drew scarcely any larger number of canons of the *Decretum* from another source than from Isidore, as the index that we have appended below on this subject shows clearly enough.

Nor was Gratian content to cite more from Isidore’s books than from those of anyone else. As though he wished, not obscurely, to place Isidore before the great Augustine, whenever he could have cited something from Augustine’s works, he nevertheless preferred more than once to transcribe it from Isidore—for example, the passage found in Gratian, *Decretum*, part II, question 24, canon 3.

Certain heretics also drew from book VIII, chapter 5 of Isidore’s *Origins* their lengthy treatment of heresies.

5. Nor did Gratian doubt that some majesty would be added to the constitutions of the Council of Seville by mentioning Isidore’s name. Almost every time he cites something from that council, he cites it only after naming Isidore: “From the Council of Seville, which Isidore attended,” in part II, question 7, canon 15; “without a synod,” in part II, question 3, canon 16; and in the first action, question 7, in the ninth action. Perhaps one would not find this practice observed elsewhere except in those councils at which the supreme pontiffs were present themselves, not merely through legates.

Nor should anyone who considers those Gallican and German synods—the Council of Frankfurt on the Main, both Councils of Aachen, the Council of Mainz, the Council of Tribur, and the Council of Paris—say that this was Gratian’s private judgment. Rather, it was the common and synodical judgment of the Gallican Church, indeed of the entire Christian world, which thought so magnificently of Saint Isidore.

At these councils, under the auspices of the Most Christian emperors Charlemagne, Louis the Pious, Arnulf, and others, ecclesiastical discipline was restored with such wisdom and prudence, and a rule of life was religiously prescribed for kings, nobles, the common people, and finally all the orders of this empire—not with any other legislator than Isidore, not with any other guide, not with any other teacher. Although they had taken scarcely one or two passages from the chief doctors of the Church, the lords Jerome and Augustine, they nevertheless transcribed many chapters everywhere, with one spirit and under one direction, from Isidore’s books.

6. Why should I mention how carefully the venerable Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt, together with all the bishops of Germany, Gaul, and Aquitaine, the entire clergy of Catholic peace, the prelates of Spain, and all the others who there bore the name of Christians, confirmed from book VII, chapter 2 of his *Etymologies* that the human nature was so joined to the Son of God that one person was formed from two substances?

Or that the Council of Tribur, in chapter 27, cites from book II, chapter 3 of his *Ecclesiastical Offices* that those who returned from the clergy to the secular world were like hippocentaurs—and innumerable other examples of the same kind?

Indeed, it will be much more useful to remember that splendid passage of the Council of Paris, book II, chapter 1, drawn from book III, chapters 48 and 49 of Isidore’s *Sentences*:

“He who rightly uses royal power ought to show himself superior to all, so that the more he shines in the height of honor, the more he humbles himself in mind, setting before himself the example of David’s humility. David did not become swollen with pride over his merits, but humbly abasing himself said: ‘I shall walk humbly, and I shall appear humble before the Lord, who chose me.’”

And also this:

“Those who exercise kingship wickedly descend, after their splendid clothing and the glitter of their jewels, naked and wretched to be tortured in hell.” [Col. 0211A]

“Kings are so called from acting rightly; therefore, just as the name of king is retained by acting rightly, so it is lost by sinning.”

7. After the Fathers of the Second Council of Aachen had repeated almost these very words under Louis the Pious, approximately four years after the Council of Paris, the Synod of Mainz under the emperor Arnulf, approximately fifty-five years after the Second Council of Aachen, added the following from book IX, chapter 3 of Isidore’s *Origins*:

“All kings were anciently called tyrants; but afterward those who ruled piously, justly, and mercifully acquired the name of king, whereas the name tyrant, not king, was applied to those who ruled impiously, unjustly, and cruelly.”

The Fathers of the Council of Paris judged that such rulers, when God is angry, are given to peoples as punishment for sin and therefore are not to be judged but endured: book I, chapter 19, and book II, chapter 5, from book III, chapter 28 of Isidore’s *Sentences*.

“Those are rightly called kings who know how to pacify both themselves and their subjects by ruling well, and who keep within the Church the heights of the authority they have acquired, so that through that same authority they may strengthen ecclesiastical discipline.”

Otherwise, as the Fathers of the same council wrote in book II, chapter 2, from book III, chapter 21 of Isidore’s *Sentences*:

“Powers would not be necessary in the Church unless, where the priest cannot accomplish something through the speech of teaching, authority might command it through the terror of discipline.”

It would not be easy to enumerate in a brief summary all that was transcribed from Isidore in the First Council of Aachen concerning the divine offices, ecclesiastical orders, and the authorities of the chapters. For the present, it is enough to say this: truly this apostolic man possessed the good testimony that the Apostle desired in a Christian bishop, even from those who were outside.

8. Since it would have been beyond all impudence to abuse the words of a man proven in every respect by the whole course of his learning and life in order to confirm error, Felix, bishop of Urgel, and Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, nevertheless wished to draw the emperor Charlemagne away from the Catholic faith into impiety. They pressed upon him the authority of Saint Isidore, as he himself recalls in the letter in which he answered them:

“You have set before me the example of the emperor Constantine,” he says, “whose beginning you say blessed Isidore praised, but whose end he lamented,” and so forth.

But since those who have departed from us and suffered shipwreck in the faith are not to be believed in anything whatsoever, Gregory IX, Supreme Pontiff, shall give the final judgment concerning Saint Isidore. How highly he regarded Isidore’s authority is evident even from the fact that he frequently makes him a witness and authority for the canons of the *Decretals*.

Thus, in book IV, title 2, *On the Betrothal of Minors*, chapter 3, “Puberes a pube,” he cites book XI, chapter 2 of the *Origins*; in book V, title 40, *On the Meaning of Words*, chapter 9, “Quamvis omnes,” he cites book V, chapter 10 of the *Origins*, “Forus is a place for conducting lawsuits”; in chapter 12, “Law derived from the right of possessing,” he cites book V, chapter 25 of the *Origins*; and perhaps elsewhere quite frequently.

A few years ago, F. Antonius Stella of Vercelli, a Minorite, dared to criticize some of these canons. Although he confessed that Saint Isidore was a man of great intellect and virtue, I do not know with what confidence he did so, since one may not rashly tear down what has once been received into a canon by the supreme pontiff. Nor is it perhaps established beyond doubt that *fora* and *foros* differ not only in gender but also in meaning. Indeed, one may oppose to Stella, Survius, and Martialis the authority of the ancients, who, if we believe Coelius Rhodiginus, generally pronounced the word in the masculine gender, as did the Greeks, with *phóros* [φόρος] as a paroxytone.

9. I do not dwell on the claim, reported by that writer, that Isidore wished *forum* also to be named from the king Foroneus, although nothing of the kind has ever appeared to me in the four manuscript copies that the very distinguished men Brissonius, advocate of the king and the state in the Parisian senate; Joannes of Saint-André, dean of Carcassonne; and Father Daniel, all of whom have rendered the literary world the greatest services, placed at my disposal for use in this edition of Isidore.

I return to Isidore. Seeing that the works of so great and distinguished a man, as though they were his limbs, had not yet, so far as I knew, been joined into a single body, to the great detriment of literary scholarship, I undertook this labor and completed it during the spare hours in which I was able to return from the extremely serious business of our assemblies to these studies.

Whatever small contribution this work may contain that can be called mine, I send to you, Reverend Lord and uncle, at the beginning of this new year as a little gift, Paris, on the Kalends of January, 1580.

“From the depths of my heart devoted and obedient to you,

M. DE LA BIGNE.”

10. In this preface, which Nicolaus Antonius calls sufficiently learned and elegant, Bignaeus denies that Isidore was a hearer of Saint Gregory the Great, as we likewise denied in chapter 18. Bignaeus’s judgment concerning the number of canons that Gratian collected from Isidore must be revised in light of what was said in chapter 53, no. 4. How highly the councils and collectors of canons valued Isidore’s authority has been shown at greater length in chapters 31 and 32. The defense of certain of Isidore’s etymologies hinted at by Bignaeus will be developed more carefully in their proper places.

Here, however, is the order of Isidore’s works that Bignaeus followed in his edition. [Col. 0212C]

## Index of the Works of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville

An asterisk placed in the margin indicates those works now published for the first time.

The first part of this work contains the following:

11. The twenty books of the *Origins* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, purged of errors and illustrated with various readings and brief scholia by Bonaventura Vulcanius of Bruges.

[asterisk] One book *On Differences*, from the library of the distinguished Petrus Daniel of Orléans.

[asterisk] One book *On the Proper Use of Words*, from the same library.

One book *On the Nature of Things*, addressed to King Sisebutus.

History, or *Chronicle, of the Goths*.

*History of the Vandals.*

*History of the Sueves.*

One book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

One book *On the Life or Death of the Saints Who Pleased God*.

One book addressed to his sister Florentina, *On the Nativity of the Lord, the Passion, Resurrection, Kingdom, and Judgment*.

One book addressed to the same sister Florentina, *On the Calling of the Nations*.

One book *On Certain Allegories of Sacred Scripture*.

One book of *Prologues to the Old and New Testaments*.

The second volume contains the following:

[asterisk] Commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, the book of Judges, the First, Second, Third, and Fourth Books of Kings, and Ezra.

On King Antiochus and the Completion of the Martyrdom of the Maccabees.

*A Rule for Living*, now transcribed for the first time from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris.

*Synonyms.*

*Letters.*

[asterisk] Three books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*, previously most faithfully purged through the study and labor of the highly learned Joannes Aleaume, doctor of the Sorbonne and penitentiary of Paris. We have added Isidore’s preface to these same books, from the library of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris.

*On Contempt of the World*, revised by Hubertus Scutteputeus, canon of Leuven.

Two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices.*

[asterisk] *On the Teaching and Faith of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, from the library of the distinguished Petrus Daniel of Orléans.

12. In this index, which I have augmented somewhat from the work itself by adding the book *On Numbers* and the *Letters*, the asterisk is marked in such a way as to indicate that Bignaeus was then publishing the books of the *Sentences* for the first time; although he perhaps means not those books but the *Synonyms* were appearing for the first time.

Both claims are false, as will become clear when the editions of the individual works are reviewed. Bignaeus says that he is adding Isidore’s preface to the books of the *Sentences*; but no other preface is added except a letter in Isidore’s name to Masson, which is prefixed to the books of the *Sentences* in certain codices, although it clearly seems in no way to belong to those books, as I shall explain more fully in chapter 73.

Although Bignaeus does not mention the letters in the index, he nevertheless publishes several of them in part I, pages 60 and following: namely, the letter to Masson, the letter to Leudifredus, fragments of the letter to Masson again, and the letter to Fulgentius, his brother. He also places the dedicatory letter of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in a less suitable position, before the books of the *Sentences*, which immediately follow.

After the index of the works, Bignaeus adds certain fragments attributed to Isidore in a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint-Denis. We shall append these to the books of the *Etymologies*, since they may perhaps represent a different reading from copies of the *Etymologies* that more than once circulated from Isidore’s own hand, as we shall shortly explain.

13. In Bignaeus’s edition, six letters precede the books of the *Etymologies*:

1. Isidore to Braulio: “With every desire.”
2. Braulio to Isidore: “O pious lord.”
3. Isidore to Braulio: “Because I find you safe and well.”
4. Braulio to Isidore: “It is customary for it to be fulfilled.”
5. Isidore to Braulio: “Of Your Holiness.”
6. The same writer to the same recipient: “Behold for you,” which is rather the preface to the *Etymologies*.

The edition is elegant and, as far as the matter permits, corrected. Since Bignaeus was the first of all to publish certain of Isidore’s works and, as often happens, encountered corrupt copies, it is not surprising that the diligence of more recent scholars has noticed many things in need of correction.

He added some textual variations in the margin, as well as occasional brief notes, especially in the *Etymologies*, from Vulcanius’s edition. At the beginning he appended a catalogue of the writers whom Isidore used in the books of the *Etymologies*; at the end, two indexes, one of subjects and the other of passages of Sacred Scripture.

Finally, it should be noted that there is considerable disorder in the page numbers, and sometimes also in the chapter numbers.

# CHAPTER XXXVI. The First Madrid Edition of Isidore’s Works, Prepared by Juan Grial, Is Described. His Dedicatory Letter to Philip III and Preface to the Reader Are Set Forth.

[Col. 0214A]

1. This edition is most accurate and highly celebrated because of the distinguished men who labored to prepare it. Here is its title-page: *The Works of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, Corrected from Ancient Copies by Order of Philip II, the Catholic King. Madrid, from the Royal Press, 1599, in folio.*

2. There follows the king’s privilege for the publisher Julio Junti de Modesti, subscribed on 28 November 1595. The king begins it as follows:

“Since I have learned that the works of the glorious Saint Isidore, doctor of the Spains, have been incorrectly transcribed and corrupted in many places, so that there was no slight danger that some might think ill of his sound and admirable teaching, which the holy Church of God has always held in great esteem, moved by the devotion which I bear toward the holy doctor and by the service rightly due to him in these kingdoms, and wishing to avert such great inconveniences, I ordered manuscript copies of the same works to be sought in the ancient libraries of Spain and in those of other kingdoms. When many copies of great antiquity and authority had been found, I ordered them distributed among learned men, who most carefully and diligently corrected and emended the works of Saint Isidore by those copies and endeavored to restore them to their ancient, original, and true text.”

3. These words have been translated from the beginning of the Spanish privilege just mentioned. There follows an index of the works in the first part; for Grial divided the works into two parts and prefixed an index of the works to each. I shall give both here together, so that the whole arrangement of the works may be grasped at a glance.

## FIRST PART OF THE WORKS OF SAINT ISIDORE, CONTAINING GRAMMATICAL AND HISTORICAL WRITINGS

—Twenty books of the *Etymologies.*—Two books of *Differences.*—One book *On the Nature of Things.*—*Chronicle.*—*On Illustrious Men*, with the little book of Saint Ildefonsus.—*On the Birth and Death of the Fathers.*—History of the Goths, Vandals, and Sueves, with a catalogue of Gothic kings and bishops of Toledo.

## SECOND PART

—Three books of *Sentences.*—Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments.—Allegories from the Old and New Testaments.—Two books *Against the Jews.*—Book of Prologues.—Two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices.*—Two books of *Synonyms.*—Several letters.—Rule for Monks.—*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues.*—Exposition of the Song of Solomon.

4. After the index of the works in the first part follow Grial’s dedication and preface to the reader, which I now present.

(The dedication and this preface may be read at the beginning of the following volume.)

273 31. Some falsely assert that Grial dedicated the edition to Philip II, deceived by the fact that it was begun at Philip II’s command. This is not surprising in others; but the error should be noted in Rodríguez de Castro, who otherwise described the entire edition rather carefully in volume II of his *Bibliotheca Hispanica*, page 298. Grial’s repeated assertion in the dedicatory letter that the Catholic kings derive their lineage from Isidore’s stock is now generally rejected or called into doubt. In chapter 17 we discussed the tradition once especially prevalent among Spaniards that Isidore had a full sister named Theodora, wife of Leovigild and mother of Saint Hermenegild and Reccared; we denied that this tradition rests on a solid foundation. Grial admits in his preface to the reader that he attributed too little—perhaps less than was fair—to the diligence which Pedro Chacón had applied in correcting Isidore’s *Etymologies.* It is greatly to be regretted that both Chacón’s conjectures and the very large body of Álvar Gómez’s annotations on all twenty books of the *Etymologies*, mentioned by Grial himself, have either entirely perished or are in a place from which they may perhaps never emerge.

32. I have no doubt at all about Grial’s integrity and diligence, and that he selected everything which seemed necessary or highly useful to him. But since the matter concerns the commentaries of very learned men, I would rather Grial had included too much than left us uncertain whether he had omitted anything that others might perhaps have considered relevant to correcting or elucidating Isidore’s writings.

Fabricius speaks rather inaccurately of these notes in *Bibliotheca vetus Latina*, book IV, chapter 6, section 6. He reports that the *Etymologies* appeared at Madrid in 1599 and finally adds that they were published more accurately at Paris in 1601, with various notes edited by Juan Grial and printed through the efforts of Jacques Breul. In fact, in the Madrid edition—which is far more correct and accurate than the Breulian edition—the notes of Grial had already appeared, appended by Breul to the end of his own edition. Fabricius is right, however, to say that Bar­thius aptly calls these notes “not ambitious, yet exceedingly learned” (*Ad Britonem*, p. 344).

33. Grial also added a catalogue of the writers either cited by Isidore or apparently used by him to the greatest extent, as well as a special preface to the books of the *Etymologies*. But we shall present below, in chapter 53, a more carefully prepared catalogue of the authors by Barthius, with the passages in which Isidore names them; likewise, in chapter 50, we shall reproduce Grial’s preface to the books of the *Etymologies*.

At the end of the first part one finds: “Madrid, at the press of Juan Flamenco, 1597.” At the end of the second part: “Madrid, at the press of Juan Flamenco, 1599.” Grial omitted an index of passages from Sacred Scripture, contenting himself with a single general index.

34. When Nicolás Antonio reviews this Madrid edition, he says that it was begun by order of Philip II and prepared in installments by the most learned and erudite men in all Spain. Of these, Grial alone eventually survived; with the assistance of the deceased and after completing his own labors, he brought the work into public circulation. Yet even then there were other survivors, such as Loaysa and Mariana, as can be sufficiently gathered from Grial’s own preface.

35. Andrés Burriel, who, as we shall soon relate, directed his plans toward printing Isidore’s writings, asserts in a letter to Don Pedro de Castro that both this edition, the royal edition, and the other edition of Breul which is now to be described are very defective. In a letter to Father Francisco de Rábago, however, he says that these same editions lack the finishing hand and the more polished treatment demanded by our age.

The learned Don Pedro Manuel Hernández, prefect of the archiepiscopal library of Toledo, in the notes which he intended to publish on chapter 42 of Zaccaria’s *Survey of the Isidorian Edition*, judged this royal Madrid edition preferable to all others, whether earlier or later. Nevertheless, he admitted that it teems with typographical errors and includes certain spurious or doubtful works among the genuine ones. Flórez also bears witness especially to its typographical errors in the *Chronicle*, volume VI, p. 478. He rightly observes that this edition was little known abroad, so that neither Baronius nor Pagius, and apparently not even our Cardinal Aguirre, seems to have had it at hand.

After Zaccaria’s death I acquired, from his books, a copy of this edition sprinkled with several manuscript notes in Zaccaria’s own hand.

## CHAPTER XXXVII  
### Edition of Isidore’s Works, Prepared by Breul at Paris in 1602 and Reprinted at Cologne in 1617

1. Not long after the Madrid edition of Isidore’s works, Jacques du Breul, a Benedictine monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, prepared another edition. Nicolás Antonio regards it as an exemplar of the Margarin edition, though more correct and clearer, and enriched with certain booklets newly published.

He is mistaken, however, when he adds that Breul had not seen our Spanish edition, as will soon become clear. Breul attached the following title to his edition:

2. *The Complete Extant Works of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville: partly previously published through the labors of very learned men, partly now transcribed for the first time, and corrected more accurately than before against manuscript exemplars. By Brother Jacques du Breul, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. Paris, at the shop of Michel Sonnius, on the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Basilisk sign, 1601.*

3. Breul’s dedicatory letter deserves to be reproduced here, although it mentions some false things about Isidore, as I shall note later, and although for the most part it does not even concern Isidore.

276. **To the Reverend Father in Christ and Lord, Don Mariano de Martimbos, abbot of Saint Michael in the Wilderness, his patron, Brother Jacques du Breul, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, offers respectful greetings.**

4. When, on a specified day in May of the year of Christian salvation 1579, Henry III, Most Christian King of France, had summoned the clergy of Gaul to an assembly at Paris, and our monastery had been selected for this purpose, about sixty ecclesiastical men gathered here: namely, the most reverend cardinal and most illustrious prince Charles of Bourbon, leader of them all; three archbishops; eight bishops; and the remaining abbots, or men distinguished by some dignity in their dioceses. All had been chosen from among the whole body with great discernment and without partiality, on account of their exceptional learning, experience in affairs, and—what is more important—integrity of life.

From their number, most worthy archimandrite, you were appointed, although absent, together with Master Margarin de la Bigne, doctor of theology at Paris, as delegates for the province of Rouen. This certainly brings you greater honor than if you had been present. For some ill-disposed person, measuring others by his own crooked foot and inexact standard, might have said either that those present had been intimidated, or that they had been corrupted in this matter by entreaty or money and, for your sake, had cast a white pebble into the urn.

But your colleague, thinking that the affairs of the Church could soon be concluded, or that they would leave him sufficient spare hours for study, was asked by the celebrated bookseller Michel Sonnius to undertake the correction of the works of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. He was entirely unable to complete it, being continually occupied with the affairs of the Church; the assembly nevertheless continued until the seventh day of February of the following year.

5. The bookseller’s son, however—retaining his father’s name, position, and blameless character, and no less desirous of the public good—often urged me, hiding in my cell, to finish what another had been unable to complete in his leisure, although he promises to do so on the title page and in the preliminary letter to his uncle, the dean of Le Mans.

With God’s favor, and with strength of mind and body sustained despite their decline under old age, I completed the work. I collated many handwritten codices, especially one belonging to the distinguished scholar Paul Petau, councillor of the Paris Senate; another belonging to Papirius Masson, an advocate in the same Senate and widely known from his published books; and a third belonging to the upright Sebastian Nivellius, dean—that is, the senior—of all booksellers.

The two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* were so corrupt and so full of errors and lacunae that nothing could be worse. We corrected them, however, from an old manuscript codex of our library and from another printed at Cologne in the year of Christ 1568 by Gervuinus Calenius and the heirs of Johann Quentel; we also added the complete chapters that had been missing.

The works newly recovered through our labor and published in this edition will be indicated in the catalogue of the works. In addition, we marked in the margin the books and chapters of Sacred Scripture quoted in the text, so that the diligent reader might return to the very sources, as though shown the route by a finger, and see whether the passage sought had been abridged more than was appropriate—whence its obscurity arose—or had been cited incorrectly.

This labor will never be valued as highly as it cost me—not only me, but also my brother Jerome Le Juge, the staff of my old age, whom I had summoned to assist me. For in certain passages the author uses not the common translation but that of the Seventy Interpreters; in such cases it would have been useless to consult biblical concordances.

6. It is now time briefly to report what we have learned from the historians of Spain concerning Saint Isidore’s parents, birth, holiness of life, learning, and death.

The region of Baetica in Spain, later called Wandalicia by the Vandals and now Andalusia, most of which it comprises, contains the city of Hispalis, now called Seville, so delightful, beautiful, and prosperous that there was an old proverb: “For people whom God loves, he grants a house and livelihood at Seville.”

In the oldest manuscript codices, and also frequently in other printed books, *Spalis* and *Spalensis* are read with the first syllable suppressed in place of *Hispalis* and *Hispalensis*. Thus the Greeks call Spain *Spania*. Childebert, the second Christian king of the Franks, imitated them in his charter of foundation for our basilica, issued a thousand years ago. Speaking of Saint Vincent the martyr, he says: “Whose relics we brought from Spania.”

Saint Isidore, therefore, was born at Seville. His father was Severianus, son of Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths and of Italy; his mother was Theodora, descended from the illustrious blood of the Gothic kings. The same story is told of him as is read concerning Saint Ambrose: namely, that a swarm of bees was seen entering the infant’s mouth, leaving it, and flying upward to heaven, a portent of his future eloquence. This eloquence later became so great that it often brought his listeners into a state of amazement.

He had as brothers Saint Leander, archbishop of Seville, and Saint Fulgentius, first bishop of Écija and afterward of Cartagena; and a sister, Florentina, who was placed in charge of monasteries of holy virgins. Cardinal Caesar Baronius, in the seventh volume of his *Annals*, under the year of Christ 569, adds Theodosia, wife of King Leovigild.

7. The *Hispalense Breviary* additionally names Justina, an abbess, and Braulio, or Braulion, bishop of Zaragoza. But Juan Vasaeus, in his *Chronicle* under the year of the Lord 567, thinks that Justina was the same person as Florentina; he denies, however, that Braulio was the brother of the others.

After Leander’s death on 27 February 603, as Baronius himself noted in the *Roman Martyrology*, Isidore was elected archbishop of Seville. He did not succeed by hereditary right, in the manner of those who say, “Let us possess the sanctuary of God as an inheritance,” and do not fear the curses of the royal poet which follow in that passage.

Saint Gregory the pope confirmed this election and sent him a pallium appropriate to his dignity—indeed necessary for the exercise of it—as stated in his particular office, printed among the proper offices of the Spanish saints at Zaragoza in the year of the Lord 1597.

Rodrigo of Toledo, Alfonso of Cartagena, Vasaeus, and Braulio all acknowledge that he was not merely an archbishop but also a metropolitan, primate, and chief of the bishops. Baronius supports them, saying: “He shone with various signs of miracles, flourishing in the foremost dignity and acting as the representative of the Roman pope in Spain.”

Lucas of Tuy extols him in the following encomium:

> He was adorned with holiness, renowned for the spirit of prophecy, generous in almsgiving, outstanding in hospitality, serene in heart, truthful in judgment, just in decision, joyful in preaching, zealous in winning souls for God, careful in expounding the Scriptures, provident in counsel, humble in conduct, temperate at table, devoted in prayer, distinguished for integrity, always ready to die in defense of the Church and of truth, and conspicuous in every goodness. Moreover, he was the father of clerics, the teacher and support of monks and nuns, the comforter of the sorrowful, the protector of orphans and widows, the chastiser of the proud, and the persecutor and hammer of heretics.

8. He displayed that last quality with great confidence from the beginning of his life. For, as stated in the lessons of his feast, while still a young man he publicly denounced the Arian heresy—which had long before completely invaded the Gothic people, then ruling most extensively throughout Spain—with such firmness that he narrowly escaped being killed by the Arians.

But when Leander warned him, foreseeing that Isidore would be his successor, he moderated his indignation. Against them, or against any other heretics, he wrote a book—now lost—according to Saint Braulio, archbishop of Toledo—or Zaragoza, as he is elsewhere called.

Moreover, in the Spanish era 661, that is, in the year of the Lord 623, the seventh year of the reign of King Sisebut, he held at Seville, in the secretarium of Saint Hierusalem, a council against the Acephali, that is, heretics whose original founder is unknown. He refuted a certain bishop Cyrus, who defended their heresy, by the truthful testimonies of learned men. Thus the saving faith flourished through him.

His successor, very unlike him, attempted to corrupt it, as Tuy declares in these words:

> Theodiscus, a Greek by nation, learned in a variety of languages and outwardly polished in speech, succeeded the most blessed Isidore; but in truth, as the outcome showed, he was a most voracious wolf beneath a sheep’s skin. For he corrupted certain books of Isidore, *On the Natures of Things*, *On the Art of Medicine*, and also *On the Notory Art* (*Arte notoria*), before they came into public circulation, cutting out what was true and inserting what was false; and through a certain Arab named Avicenna he translated them from Latin into Arabic. He was also found to be erroneous in matters of faith and was stripped of his archiepiscopal dignity by a synod. For this reason he went over to the Arabs and attached himself to the sect of the false prophet Muhammad, who had arisen in that century.

9. In detestation of this Theodiscus, the Church of Seville itself—which until then had possessed eleven suffragan bishops, named in the *Theatre of the World*—was deprived of the dignities of primacy, archbishopric, and metropolitan status, reduced to ordinary rank, and subjected to the Church of Toledo.

How long this degradation of its higher see lasted is not sufficiently clear. For now restored to its former status, it has only three suffragan prelates: Málaga, Cádiz, and the Fortunate Islands. So difficult is it to recover completely what has once been lost.

Saint Isidore built certain monasteries and colleges in which, devoting himself to sacred studies and the divine writings, he instructed many disciples who flocked to him. Among them was the blessed Ildefonsus, later archbishop of the Church of Toledo.

The cleric Redemptus was also among their number. He recorded the manner of Isidore’s death, which he witnessed, and asserted that it occurred on the day before the Kalends of April, in the era 674, that is, in the year of Christ 636. Let the contrary opinions of others therefore be disregarded, as Plautus says:

> One eyewitness is worth more than ten ear-witnesses.

You will find Redemptus’s account below. Thus far concerning Saint Isidore. I now turn to you, my lord, so that you may know what reasons moved me to dedicate this labor to your name.

10. The mellifluous and remarkably spiritual teacher Bernard, in order to make us grateful to God and to human beings for benefits received, and fit to merit greater ones, interprets these two passages of Sacred Scripture spiritually: “Consider carefully what is set before you,” and “Gather up the fragments, lest they perish.”

Learn, he says, not to be slow or sluggish in returning thanks. Learn to give thanks for each individual gift. “Consider carefully what is set before you,” so that no gifts of God may be frustrated through a fitting act of thanksgiving—not great gifts, not moderate gifts, not small ones. Finally, we are commanded to gather the fragments lest they perish: that is, not to forget even the smallest benefits. Does not what is given to an ungrateful person perish?

He then shows what evils ingratitude carries in its wake. Ingratitude is the enemy of the soul, the emptying of merits, the dispersal of virtues, and the destruction of benefits. Ingratitude is a burning wind, drying up for itself the fountain of piety, the dew of mercy, and the streams of grace.

But far be it from me to consign to oblivion the benefits I have received from you since I came to know you through the most reverend and illustrious Cardinal Bourbon, your senior archbishop and my first patron. Far be it from me to imitate the nine evangelical lepers who, though healed in body, carried away with them the worse leprosy of ingratitude. Far be it from me ever to imitate Pharaoh’s cupbearer, restored to his former position but meanwhile forgetful of his prophet Joseph.

“Let my tongue cleave to my jaws if I do not remember you,” especially among those—a very large company—who know you exceedingly well because of your noble birth, your accumulation of virtues, and the height of the dignities you have deserved.

But since gratitude must be expressed not only in words but also confirmed by some deed, here I offer you the labors I have spent in correcting Isidore and restoring him to his original purity. I earnestly beg you to act as a steadfast critic of them, and not, out of regard for me, to pass superficially over the errors you discover. Rather, strike them through with obelisks and restore the genuine reading.

At least I shall try to bring my new copy back to your anvil and reshape it; for who could do so with the others, which have already been distributed and sold? If you do this, I shall repeat of you what Saint Augustine, writing to Saint Jerome in a similar exhortation, takes from the royal poet:

> Let the righteous strike me in mercy and reprove me; but let not the oil of the sinner anoint my head.

11. The second reason that led me to what has been described was the memory of the aforementioned cardinal, who loved us both above all others and wished to make such use of his intimacy with us that he often kept us in conversation, back and forth, far into the night.

This seemed more remarkable in my case, namely, that so great an archbishop and prince should, lowering his exalted position, make himself equal to a very poor and ignorant monk, as Elisha did to the boy. It was not so in your case, since people knew that, on account of your prudence, wisdom, and experience in affairs, he had already appointed you—like Joseph by the ancient Pharaoh—as master of his household and prince over all his possessions.

You exercised this office so prudently and modestly until his death that there was no room for anyone’s complaint, but everything was carried out peacefully, quietly, and orderly, as in Solomon’s house.

12. Since, according to the Psalmist, “Our lots are in the hands of God,” and fall to us now happily, now sadly, as he himself permits, I may briefly recall how varied were the lots of my lord, the prince, cardinal, and abbot. I shall do so, however, without saying anything concerning his misfortunes except when they began and where they ended with his death, lest I stir up Camarina,

> and suffer wounds from weapons made by my own hands.

Our Charles was born in the castle of La Ferté-Jouarre on 22 December 1523, at the eleventh hour of the morning. His sponsors from the sacred font were his elder brother, Antoine de Bourbon, father of Henry IV, now reigning, and the lord of Hames. The women who stood as sponsors were the distinguished in virtue and nobility ladies of Pleumeson and Torsy. They gave him his father’s name, for his father was called Charles.

His mother was Françoise of Alençon, daughter of the excellent René, duke of Alençon, and of Marguerite of Lorraine, foundress of the Parthenon of Argentan in Normandy.

When he had grown up and seemed suited to liberal studies, he was sent to the royal college of Champagne, or Navarre, in Paris, where he had as a fellow student Charles of Lorraine, later archbishop of Reims and cardinal. After several years, in support of the latter, he moved to the archiepiscopal residence in Paris, where they studied jurisprudence and theology. Either of these sciences can scarcely be mastered in its entirety within the whole span of even a very long human life.

Nevertheless, after completing two years our Bourbon was summoned to the royal court. In addition to certain abbeys he already held, the bishopric of Nevers was added to help defray the expenses of court life. Leaving that position, he became bishop of Saintes; afterward, when George of Amboise, nephew of the legate, died, he became archbishop of Rouen, in August of the year of the Lord 1549. On the following 10 January, Pope Paul III ordained him a cardinal-deacon of the title of Saint Sixtus.

13. He was subsequently promoted by Pope Julius III to be a cardinal-priest. When the cardinal known as Cardinal of Meudon died, he assumed his title, that of Saint Chrysogonus, relinquishing the other. He never afterward changed it.

We have called him Cardinal Bourbon up to this point, although he did not use that surname before the death of his paternal uncle, Louis de Bourbon, cardinal and archbishop of Sens, which occurred in the year 1556. Before then he was called Cardinal of Vendôme.

The pious teacher Antoine Demochares adorns him with these praises in book II, chapter 20, *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*:

> If someone must be brought forward in our own times to stand in defense of the Mass, what nobler prince, what more energetic leader could be presented than Charles of Vendôme, the most reverend cardinal? Does not this one man surpass the entire host of his opponents in authority, nobility, learning, dignity, and good morals?

To prove this, I shall be satisfied with a single example worthy of everlasting memory, although other examples are not lacking. In the year of Christ 1575, on Saturday, 14 July, when evening was already approaching and he was at Rouen, he admonished the leaders of his citizens, with the pious feeling customary to him, not to allow the heretics any longer to hold meetings and deceive the unstable people, prone to fall, with poisonous sermons, transferring them from the way of salvation to the way of perdition.

Nevertheless, on the following Sunday nearly three thousand men, as was thought, gathered in a certain square of the city to hear a deceiver preaching. When the good shepherd learned of this, dressed in a pontifical linen garment like a coat of mail and carrying a cross before him, he went out at seven in the morning from the house of Saint-Ouen, where he was staying, taking with him only a few companions: namely, Don Claude de Sainctes, bishop of Évreux; three or four canons, one of whom we know with certainty was you; and from among the lay nobility, the lords of Rouge-Pré and Maineville, together with a few others.

14. Although it was thought that he was going to his own basilica, he turned aside and came to the place where the heretics and other curious adherents of the new doctrine had assembled. With his reverend appearance and his vestments he terrified them, just as Jaddua, the high priest of Jerusalem, terrified Alexander the Great with his violet stole and tiara. The false preacher immediately fell silent, while his listeners stood stunned, fearing armed force.

With great authority he restrained the use of force. He addressed them gently and urged them to remain in the Catholic, apostolic, and Roman faith, warning them not to believe false prophets who come in sheep’s clothing but inwardly are ravenous wolves.

As many words as he spoke, so many goads he drove into the hearts of those standing there. Struck and pierced with remorse, they each returned to his own house without any disturbance. From that time onward it was never heard that heresy had been publicly preached at Rouen.

Proud of so great a victory over souls, our Bourbon hastened to the church and gave thanks to God, its author. He often testified among his people that no day had ever dawned more joyfully for him.

Attend, I beg you, whoever will read this, and consider whether he does not resemble Jacob’s son Joseph in many respects. Joseph is called in Genesis “the growing son,” and others interpret the name as “the Lord’s increase.” How greatly this man grew for the advancement of the Church has been stated: from abbot he became bishop, from bishop archbishop, and finally cardinal, adorning whatever position he obtained.

The patriarch Joseph was prince of the fathers; this man was no less so, having under him six fathers, or suffragan bishops, signified by the individual elements of the word formed here: **SACBLE**.

Joseph, by command of his father, left home and sought his brothers at Dothan—that is, those who had gone forth for defense. This man likewise hurried to his brothers who had defected from the faith and were listening to an incantator with ears open, rather than stopped in the manner of an asp. In almost the same words as Joseph, he said to them: “Peace be with you; it is I; do not be afraid. For your salvation the Lord has sent me to you.”

As he said this, he could not restrain himself from wetting his cheeks with a few tears. Yet because they seemed less fitting to his authority and dignity, he secretly wiped them away.

15. Those who accompanied him shed far more tears, both because they had witnessed the piety and charity of so great a shepherd and because his wandering sheep had been brought back to the way of salvation. These were tears of delight and joy, not of pain or sorrow.

Alas, the changed circumstances of his life later wrung from all those sincerely devoted to him tears of another kind. For on 23 December of the year of the Lord 1588, he began to be filled with bitterness and saturated with wormwood, when he was detained at Blois by the angry command of the king and afterward led through various stations to Fontenay-le-Comte, a small town in Poitou.

In this man, as Alfonso of Cartagena puts it, those who saw him—and even those who did not see him but heard of him—could clearly recognize the worth of worldly prosperity, since Fortune’s wheel frequently and swiftly turns human success from the greatest prosperity to the greatest adversity.

Nevertheless, he never lost his steadfastness and patience amid adversity until the end of his life. Though he ought to have been consoled by his own people, he himself consoled them when they were sorrowful, often recalling these words: “The sufferings of this present time are not worthy of the future glory that shall be revealed in us.” And: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, why should we not endure evil things?” He also recalled the saying from the Maccabees: “The adverse events that occur are not for the destruction but for the correction of our race.” For not allowing sinners to act according to their own will for a long time, but immediately applying punishments, is a sign of great benevolence.

He died at the same place, Fontenay, in the year of Christ 1590, on Wednesday, 9 May, around the ninth hour of the day, in the sixty-seventh year of his age. He was overcome not by poison, as some suspected, but by strangury caused by a stone and by fever.

I had been summoned to Tours by the most reverend and illustrious Cardinal of Vendôme, his nephew, when the bearer of this evil news arrived. Then my eyes failed amid tears, and my innermost being was troubled. My liver was poured out upon the ground because of the crushing grief at the death of my patron.

16. It is impossible to report how many crowds of people flocked to see him throughout the day. Those who departed praised his goodness, clemency, and humanity, and were astonished that he appeared more beautiful in death.

He was brought out of that unhappy city on 19 July and, with you, his most faithful Achates, arranging everything and accompanying him and his household in sorrow, entered the castle of Gaillon on 8 August.

His soul now enjoys heaven, I believe, because of his past life, his sins expiated by confession, and his devout reception of the sacraments at the very end of life. Yet if anything remains that might hinder him, I beg you, good Jesus, to cleanse it through the merit of your most sacred Passion.

According to Demochares, he was the eighty-first in the succession of archbishops of Rouen; according to others, the eighty-second. He held that see for forty-one years.

Through his generosity, most of the library—not the common library, but our own cell, which many learned men praise for the number of its books and the excellence of its authors—came into existence. There is no doubt that it would have grown immensely had Atropos not taken him from us so quickly.

You, however, succeeding him, as it were, and showing me no less affection, have already enlarged it by several books beyond what I deserved. In gratitude for this benefit, I never cease daily to pray to God, the giver of all good things, that he may richly repay you with temporal and spiritual gifts and prolong your life for many years.

Remember me also before him, most upright abbot and most nobly adorned with the double whiteness of age, both in your prayers and in the unbloody sacrifice of the altar, so that he who taught me from my youth and whose wonders in the Church I daily proclaim with our brothers may not abandon me even in old age and gray hairs.

Farewell. From our monastery of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, erected beside the walls of Paris, in the year of Christ 1601, on 15 September.

**Your most obedient client,  
JACQUES DU BREUL**

17. Breul, along with many others, asserts that Baetica was called *Wandalicia* by the Vandals and is now called Andalusia. I, however, and others hold a different opinion.

We have never discovered that the ancients called Baetica *Wandalicia*. The term *Andalusia* first began to be heard among the Moors while they ruled Spain. By that name they called all Spain, and especially the provinces subject to their dominion, apparently from the Arabic word *andalos*, which some conjecture means “the western region.”

In later times the name *Andalusia* or *Andaluzia* became fixed, as though a proper name, around the regions of Baetica in which the Moors remained longer. If you please, compare my *Prolegomena* to Dracontius, chapter 12, section 116, and the writers cited there, Nicolás Antonio and Flórez.

18. Breul rashly asserts that Severianus, Isidore’s father, was the son of King Theodoric. Nor is there any certainty that Isidore’s mother was called Theodora, much less that she descended from the blood of the Gothic kings. Recall what I discussed concerning Isidore’s parents in chapter 17.

I noted in chapter 3 that Fulgentius’s bishopric of Cartagena should be regarded as fictitious. In chapter 17 I said that it is highly doubtful whether Isidore had a sister named Theodora or Theodosia who was the wife of King Leovigild. Nor can Leander’s year of death have been 603, for the reasons presented in chapter 20.

The question of the pallium said to have been sent to Isidore by Gregory the Great was discussed in chapter 22.

Breul first called Braulio a bishop of Zaragoza, but shortly afterward, through an error, named him archbishop of Toledo. He means Braulio when he reports from him that Isidore wrote a book against heretics. For in Ildefonsus’s eulogy of Isidore nothing at all similar is found, whereas Braulio writes: “One book on heresies, in which, following the examples of the ancients, he collected in the briefest manner he could the material that had been spread abroad.”

You should not, however, infer from this that Isidore refuted heresies in this book rather than narrating their history.

19. I discussed the year in which the Second Council of Seville was held in chapter 21. At that council Bishop Gregory was convicted.

Breul calls a certain bishop “Cyrus,” through what I think is a typographical error, instead of “a certain Syrian bishop.” For Gregory was Syrian by nation, as is clear from the council of Seville itself.

Finally, Breul recounts the fables that others had long ago fabricated concerning Theodiscus, Isidore’s successor; I refuted them in chapter 22.

20. After the dedicatory letter, the preliminary list of Isidore’s books edited by Braulio, the sections of Sigebert and John Trithemius concerning Isidore’s eulogy, and Redemptus’s account of Isidore’s death, Breul adds certain material concerning the year of Isidore’s death and the translation of his body. I have examined these matters in their proper places.

Breul appends a catalogue of the books under the following title:

**Index of the books of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville; among these, those now appearing for the first time are indicated in the margin by an asterisk.**
21. Twenty books of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*. One book of *Differences*, or *The Proper Meaning of Words*. A second book of *Spiritual Differences*. Two books of *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*. A short work *On Contempt of the World*. *The Rule of Living.* *An Exhortation to Repentance, with Consolation and the Mercy of God, addressed to a soul fearing the judgments to come.* [Col. 0223D] This was transcribed from a manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Maur-des-Fossés, formerly a regular monastery, at the direction of the distinguished scholar Nicolas Faber. *A Lament of Repentance, composed in verse and arranged according to two alphabets.* From the same library. *A lengthy prayer of Saint Isidore, for continual lamentation over sins and the amendment of life.* From the same library. *A short prayer by the same author, against the snares of the devil.* A letter to Massanus (also called Masson), bishop, concerning the fall and restoration of a priest. It was restored in full from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; previously only certain fragments had been printed. *A book on the nature of things, or on the world, addressed to King Sisebut.* *A chronicle from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of Suinthila, king of the Goths, corrected by García de Loaysa and furnished with scholia.* A Chronicle of the Goths; a History of the Vandals; a History of the Suevi. [Col. 0224A] A book of prefaces to the Old and New Testaments. Commentaries on Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, First, Second, Third, and Fourth Kings, and Ezra. 285 On King Antiochus and the martyrdom of the Maccabees. One book of various allegories of Sacred Scripture. One book on ecclesiastical writers. On the life or death of the saints who pleased God. One book addressed to his sister Florentina on the Lord’s Nativity, Passion, Resurrection, kingdom, and judgment. To the same woman, on the calling of the nations. Two books on ecclesiastical offices. Corrected from the manuscript codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. A letter to Ludifredus (also called Leudefredus), bishop of Córdoba, [Col. 0224B] concerning the office of a bishop and of the other clergy in the Church. The latter part of this letter, which was missing and which a Spanish copy from Madrid eventually supplied to us, is given below. Three books of *Sentences*, or *On the Highest Good*. *Several letters, besides those found before the *Etymologies* and the *Synonyms**.* *A Rule for Monks.* *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues.* *An Exposition of the Song of Songs.* *Saint Ildefonsus’s book on illustrious men.* *A book on differences, or the proper meaning of words.* It was found in the Madrid edition of 1599, in addition to the other two printed above, after the *Etymologies*. *A book by the divine Isidore on illustrious men,* which certainly ought to have been placed before Saint Ildefonsus’s book on the same subject, [Col. 0224C] but did not become known to us so quickly. *Notes by learned men on certain books of the Lord Isidore, collected and enlarged by Juan Grial.* *A glossary compiled from various works circulated under the name of Isidore, bishop of Seville.* An index of the authorities of Sacred Scripture cited and explained throughout this work. A very full index of the subjects and words contained in this work.

22. Breul’s edition places an asterisk before those works that were lacking in Bignaeus’s edition, although they had already appeared in print in Grial’s edition—for example, the *Chronicle from the Beginning of the World*, and all the works listed after the books of the *Sentences*. It seems that Breul had already brought his edition nearly to completion when the royal Madrid edition came into his hands. Hence he relegated to the end even those works that he found in the Madrid edition but had not himself noticed, together with Grial’s notes; meanwhile, the text of the works he had edited [Col. 0224D] remained without any correction from Grial, and could benefit from his notes only in some respects.

23. In Breul’s edition, Colomesius and others complain bitterly of the omission of the prefaces of the Madrid edition, as Fabricius noted in the *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae aetatis*. I presented the judgment of the very learned Andrea Burriel concerning both editions, Grial’s and Breul’s, in chapter 36, near the end. Otherwise, the Breulian edition is also handsome, accurate, and far superior to Bignaeus’s edition; it is fuller than the royal Madrid edition as well, although less carefully corrected. Yet in both the Grialian and Breulian editions there is lacking the book *On the Doctrine and Faith of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, produced by Bignaeus and attributed by many to Isidore. Although it is not truly Isidore’s, it can nevertheless be placed in an appendix of doubtful or spurious works with no less justification than the other works. [Col. 0225A]

24. Breul’s edition of the works of Saint Isidore was reprinted at Cologne in 1617, in typography that was not especially elegant. The Paris edition contains 975 pages, and the Cologne edition 631, apart from the indexes. In the Cologne edition, after the title supplied by Breul, there is added: “The latest, enlarged and corrected edition, Cologne, expenses borne by Antonius Hierat, 1617.” But it is neither enlarged nor corrected in comparison with Breul’s Paris edition, since it is merely a reprint by the printer, as I have said, with no one undertaking any correction of the earlier edition. Only the order of the notes in Grial’s edition was changed, and the notes on the work of the *Sentences* are presented book by book from the Turin edition. An elogium of Isidore from Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* was also added at the beginning. [Col. 0225B]

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. The More Recent Madrid Edition of the Works of Saint Isidore

An erudite preface that was being prepared to precede this edition, drawn from the distinguished author’s notebooks.

1. Bartholomew Ulloa, a Madrid bookseller of no little distinction in our time, having learned that a new edition of the works of Saint Isidore had long been desired, energetically undertook to produce one in elegant format. Here is its title:

*The Works of the Divine Isidore, Bishop of Seville, corrected by order of Philip II, Catholic king, and by ancient copies; now corrected again with the greatest diligence and enlarged by certain short works in the place of an Appendix. Madrid, printed and financed by Bartholomew Ulloa, [Col. 0225C] near the Hieronymite monastery of the Conception, in the year of Our Lord 1778.* Two large volumes in folio.

287

2. The order of the edition is as follows. All the works of Isidore published by Grial are reprinted in the same order and with exactly the same notes, with no other new notes. The dedicatory letter and Grial’s preface to the reader are also present—whose omission by Breul some people had regretted, as we have said. There is also a new preface by the editor, in this form:

### A Brief Preface by the Editor to the New Edition of the Works of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville

3. I wish to say only a few words to you, kindly reader. I gladly offer for your benefit and for the common benefit of all the complete works of Isidore, that most holy Father and illustrious teacher of Spain, insofar as they survive and insofar as learned men judge them to be the genuine offspring of that same author. Nor do I think that whatever labor I have devoted to preparing this edition will prove unwelcome to anyone. I am sufficiently persuaded of this even by the fact that, for nearly two centuries—namely, since the year 1617—as far as I know no one has undertaken to reprint them. The universal and distinguished learning of this most noble author surely demanded that, just as he is rightly praised by everyone, so his works should long be handled day and night by everyone. But how can this happen unless copies are abundant? Their scarcity, therefore, which increased the great renown of this teacher celebrated throughout the world, stirred and urged the minds of all learned men, especially Spaniards, [Col. 0225D] toward preparing a new and highly accurate edition. Yet no one came forward to satisfy the public desire by his work and industry. Observing all this, and at the same time fearing that some disgrace might thereby fall upon the Spanish people, I undertook this edition [Col. 0226A] and saw to its completion with as much diligence and zeal as I could muster.

4. Indeed, I greatly desired not merely to bring into public view the works of Isidore, long ago printed, once again furnished with the finest type and with other ornaments belonging to the printer’s art, but also, by gathering ancient manuscripts from every quarter, to publish them in a more corrected, fuller, and more distinguished form. But the magnitude of the undertaking, beyond my resources, restrained my resolve, as did the realization that the hope of my effort had either already been entirely fulfilled or could be fulfilled only with excessive difficulty. No one is unaware of the care and diligence with which, following the special command of Philip II, the most august prince of Spain, the most learned men from throughout Spain—having searched out ancient codices not only throughout Spain but also through almost the whole of Italy, and having each carefully examined his assigned portion—finally corrected all the writings of Saint Isidore that could be found and illustrated them with selected annotations. From this there appeared in 1599 [Col. 0226B] an edition distinguished by the royal name, which the very distinguished Juan Grial, taking advantage of the labors of others and adding his own, published for the general public, dedicating it to Philip III, then reigning. 288 Learned men declare this royal edition to be excellent and preferable even to the later editions, although they do not consider it complete in every respect. “There is still a contest,” they cry, “and new labor must be undertaken, so that Isidore may come forth publicly with the glory and honor that are his due.” But they speak and do not act; meanwhile Isidore remains almost hidden and is increasingly missed.

5.
