Therefore, I provide what lies within my power, and what both my respect for Isidore and my love of public utility demand: namely, I again bring into public view that same royal edition in its entirety, arranged in a more distinguished format, with more elegant type and bright paper—that is, with the finest printing, which belongs to the printer’s craft. Nor should you, kindly reader, expect anything else from me. But perhaps, [Col. 0226C] you will say, there are other short works bearing Isidore’s name that you will search for in vain in the royal edition. Some of these have been published here and there by various people; the rest still lie hidden in the archives or chartularies of churches. They certainly exist, and I now present them to you in the form of an Appendix. In this matter you have clear testimony that my conjecture has been confirmed by the event itself. For I spared neither labor nor expense in seeking out everything that might make the new edition fuller and richer. I therefore obtained various copies here and there, marked with the name of Saint Isidore. But after they had been examined by learned men, almost all were found to be apocryphal. Nevertheless, I published them both for the benefit of students and for the exercise of learned men. Accordingly, I shall set out the series of each, with a brief critical assessment.

6. The first place is occupied by Book Four of the *Sentences*, which until now some people, relying on the testimony of certain codices bearing Isidore’s name, had regarded as a genuine work of that holy teacher. [Col. 0226D] But no one who has carefully read the five books of the *Sentences* collected by Taio, bishop of Zaragoza, and most recently published by the continuator of *Sacred Spain* in volume 31, has hesitated to regard it as spurious. For this fourth book has been excerpted from that work, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. And so that this may easily be recognized, each chapter contains a note indicating from which book and chapter of Taio it has been taken. Various readings are also recorded, as are places where the continuous sequence of the *Sentences*, otherwise mutually connected, is interrupted. All this will be of considerable use in illuminating the works of the holy Fathers Augustine and Gregory, from whom Taio compiled his books.

7. Two other chapters of the *Sentences* follow. The first is taken word for word from Saint Gregory’s work on Ezekiel; the second from Book Three, chapters 3, 4, 9, and 10, of Julianus Pomerius’s *On the Contemplative Life*. This work is found among the writings of Saint Prosper of Aquitaine [Col. 0227A] and was attributed to him for a long time by very many writers. Now all assign it to Pomerius. On this matter see our Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 25, and the distinguished Ceillier, volume 15, in his *General History of Ecclesiastical Authors*, where he discusses Julianus Pomerius.

8. In third place I appended a short work entitled *An Exhortation to Humility*, which is attributed to Saint Martin, bishop of Braga, and was published among his works in volume 15 of *Sacred Spain* by the very learned Flórez. 289

9. The sermon that follows, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter*, must likewise be rejected as a work of our Isidore, since it is entirely identical with Homily 7 of Saint Caesarius of Arles, *On Easter*. See the *Library of the Fathers*, volume II, column 277, Paris edition, 1624.

10. Certain poems appended to the library of Saint Isidore are added; they were published in volume 9 of *Sacred Spain* under this heading: “Title of the Library published by Lord Isidore.” Some fragments are also included [Col. 0227B] to complete the chapters indicated there.

11. In sixth place I published an *Exposition of the Mass*. Although it may not seem unworthy of Isidore’s ability and learning, it must be excluded from his works for this reason alone: in Isidore’s time another order and rite of the Mass prevailed in the Spanish Church, different from the one expounded here, which is altogether identical with the modern Roman rite.

12. Next I appended nine readings, formerly recited on the feast of the translation of Saint Isidore. They are taken word for word from the acts of that translation, published in volume 9 of *Sacred Spain*.

13. Finally, I saw to the supplementation of Chapter 17 of the *Questions on Leviticus*, transcribed from the Albornoz Codex by Don Pedro de Castro. Its copy is preserved in the Flórez library of the convent of the royal Saint Philip in Madrid, belonging to the Order of Saint Augustine.

14. I did not add to this edition the *Lament of Repentance*, composed according to two alphabets, and so forth, which the distinguished Nicolás Antonio mentions in volume I of the *Old Library*, book V, chapter 4, page 265, [Col. 0227C] and which the *Acta Sanctorum* editors published from that same Nicolás in volume I for April, on the fourth day. I was informed of it too late—when the edition was already almost completed.

15. As for the book *On the Order of Creatures*, published by Dom D’Achery in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, page 225, and the short works that Abbot Constantine Cajetan published under Isidore’s name: since learned men classify them either as spurious or as excessively doubtful, they did not seem suitable for insertion here.

16. You therefore have, candid reader, the works of Isidore—not illustrated and restored to their native purity with that supreme diligence which only the most learned and scholarly men could provide, but nevertheless somewhat more purified and fuller than the royal edition presented them. Enjoy them, therefore; devote yourself diligently to their reading; and willingly embrace my labor, zeal, and effort. Farewell.

17. The editor states that manuscripts were sought for Grial’s royal edition [Col. 0227D] not only throughout Spain but also through almost the whole of Italy. I consider this less than accurate, as can be inferred from Grial’s own preface. Grial himself, as he declares in his dedicatory letter, hoped that other distinguished men, learned not only among us but also abroad, would strive together to continue investigating the painstaking excerpts of the Spanish teacher and would strengthen our resources with their own means.

290

18. I regret the situation of this excellent editor, who spared neither labor nor expense in seeking all the embellishments that might make the new edition fuller and richer, yet did not encounter [Col. 0228A] a learned man who could satisfy his wishes. First, he reproduced Grial’s old edition in such a way that nowhere did he restore an ancient reading, record a variant reading, or illuminate Isidore’s meaning with any annotation. A number of errors had crept into Grial’s edition; not one was corrected in this newer Madrid edition, and many errors, some of them far from trivial, were added.

19. It is a particularly strong indication of negligence that, although Grial at the end, as is customary, had indicated certain typographical errors for correction, the editor of the new Madrid edition left those same errors untouched in the text and proposed at the end neither their correction nor that of any other errors. What, then, becomes of the claim made on the title page and in the preface—[Col. 0228B] that Isidore’s works are now being published “corrected with the greatest care” and “somewhat more purified” than in the royal edition?

20. Furthermore, since the editor intended to make the new edition fuller and richer than the old royal edition, why did he not have Breul’s edition before him, from which the new edition could have become more complete? “I was informed too late,” he says, “about the *Lament of Repentance* published by the Bollandists.” Yet this very *Lament*, as well as other works missing from the new Madrid edition, had appeared in Breul’s edition. Indeed, the *Lament of Repentance* is much fuller in Breul than in the Bollandists. In the Appendix, chapter 47, *On the Parts of the Earth*, from the book *On the Nature of Things*, [Col. 0228C] is presented from manuscript codices as though it were unpublished. In fact, this chapter was omitted by Grial—I do not know through what cause or negligence—for it is found not only in Breul but also in Bignaeus, who preceded Grial in publishing an edition of Isidore’s works, and in many very ancient parchment manuscripts, though not in all the old copies of the book *On the Nature of Things*.

21. I shall examine elsewhere, at greater convenience, the editor’s judgment concerning several works circulated under Isidore’s name, which he considers either spurious or doubtful. I now append the list of works presented in the Appendix.

22. *Appendix to the Works of the Divine Isidore, Bishop of Seville, from Ancient Manuscript Codices Found in Various Archives and Libraries of the Churches of Spain, as Contained in This Second Volume.* Madrid, printed and financed by Bartholomew Ulloa, on Conception Street, in the year of Our Lord 1778.

[Col. 0228D]

*The Fourth Book of the Sentences of the Lord Isidore, contained in this second volume.* Here ends the third book.

Here begin the chapters of the fourth book.

[Col. 0229C]

Here end the four books of the *Sentences* of the Lord Isidore. Here begin other chapters of the *Sentences* of the same author.

On pride, desire, envy, and boasting. Here begins *An Exhortation to Humility*. A sermon of Isidore, bishop, on the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter. Here begins the *Title of the Library published by Lord Isidore*. Additions to the *Book on the Nature of Things*. On the Parts of the Earth, chapter 47, from the Oviedo Codex. From the Osma Codex: *On the Parts of the Earth*. Additions to the *Book on the Nature of Things* from the aforementioned Oviedo Codex. Additions to the mystical expositions of the sacraments, or *Questions on the Old Testament and on Judges*. An exposition of the Mass. Readings for the translation of Saint Isidore, bishop and confessor [Col. 0229D]. Chapter 17 of Saint Isidore’s *Questions on Leviticus*. Saint Isidore’s elogium in praise of Spain. Very ancient verses once read in the library of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. Here begins the *Title of the Library published by Lord Isidore*.

24. The title of the library is printed twice, as you see, but from different copies, which vary somewhat from one another. From the Oviedo Codex, a very elegant eclogue is added in the book *On the Nature of Things*, as it says there: “You perhaps in the lights”—a certain astrological poem, published long ago, as I shall explain below. Isidore’s elogium in praise of Spain, already published by Labbe, is to be placed before the *History of the Goths* as its preface. An index of subjects follows, exactly the same as in Grial’s edition.

25. [Col. 0230A] It is not very difficult to discern what my judgment of this entire edition is, both with respect to what it contains and with respect to what it lacks. Nor is it obscure what others think of it. Bayer notes this in chapter 4 of book V of the *Old Spanish Library*:

“Recently, namely in 1778, a fifth edition of Isidore’s works appeared at Madrid, with the complete notes of Grial’s 1599 edition, together with others certainly not worthy of cedar oil, in two folio volumes. To these is added, as though it were Isidore’s, a fourth book of the *Sentences*, although for the most part it has Taio of Zaragoza as its author . . . together with many other things from various, as is claimed, ancient codices, especially from the royal library of the Escorial, WITHOUT ANY WINNOWING OR SIEVING.”

26. Bayer perhaps calls the notes in the Appendix “new,” for in the other works only the notes of Grial’s edition were printed, as I have said. But his claim that the fourth book of the *Sentences* is added as though it were Isidore’s is certainly false, as is clear not only [Col. 0230B] from the editor’s preface but also from note 1 to the book itself, which reads as follows: “This book has been extracted word for word from Taio’s books of the *Sentences*. See volume 31 of *Sacred Spain*.” Taio’s passages are then indicated throughout. Nevertheless, Bayer repeats the same criticism in his note to number 137 of the same fifth book:

“In the new Madrid edition of 1778, a fourth book of the same subject and title is appended to the third book of the *Sentences*, as though it were Isidore’s, although for the most part it has Taio, or Taion, of Zaragoza, and Gregory the Great as its authors . . . a fact which the editor himself openly acknowledged when he realized that he had been miserably deceived.”

But how do these statements cohere? At the very moment when the editor admits that the book is not Isidore’s, he appends it as though it were Isidore’s. The editor therefore inserted such a book into the Appendix [Col. 0230C] because many had thought it was Isidore’s, and because, as Bayer himself reports, in an Escorial Codex of approximately the twelfth century this fourth book of the *Sentences* is appended, in a continuous line of writing, to Isidore’s three books on the same subject, although the editor simultaneously observed that the book was in reality not Isidore’s. Even if the Madrid editor, when he first decided to have the fourth book of the *Sentences* printed, may have been unaware that it was excerpted from Taio, it is nevertheless entirely clear that he began publishing it while by no means ignorant of the matter. Whether there is absolutely no reason to doubt the author or compiler of these sentences, so that the book must certainly be rejected as Isidore’s, will be discussed below at a more appropriate place.

294

27. [Col. 0230D] Joseph Rodríguez de Castro, in his *Spanish Library*, volume II, pages 333 and following, finds several things lacking in this edition: the diligence of the corrector, judgment in assessing doubtful works, and learning in examining manuscript copies. “I speak only briefly on this matter,” he says, “for an edition of the works of Saint Isidore completed in these times will bring both our own people and foreigners into the greatest admiration, since they understand very well how great a store of learning is required for the writings of so distinguished a teacher to be entrusted to the public light and the press with the dignity they deserve.”

28. I possess a copy of a letter by the distinguished Don Pedro Manuel Hernández, prefect of the archiepiscopal library of Toledo, to the archbishop of Toledo himself, now the most eminent cardinal Don Francisco [Col. 0231A] Lorenzana, dated 15 December 1782, in which he expresses his judgment concerning the prospectus of Zaccaria’s edition of the works of Saint Isidore. He frankly declares Ulloa’s labor in the Isidorian edition to have been entirely useless: “Ulloa ruined all the work he had done in printing the Saint.” He adds, however, that the works placed by Ulloa in the Appendix must not be omitted from the new edition that is to be prepared.

29. I also possess an autograph letter from the learned canon of Cádiz, Don Joseph Muñoz y Raso, to Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, written at Cádiz on 13 October 1778, in which he confirms that Ulloa took no care to secure, for his Isidorian edition, the work of learned men who could have illustrated it.

30. There was indeed a man of great distinction and learning who could have added honor and brilliance [Col. 0231B] to the edition and was preparing a most learned preface for it. But it remained among his notebooks; from these, however, I shall bring it to light, so that our Isidorian collection may not lack so notable an elogium of Isidore.

### Preface to a New Edition of Saint Isidore, from the Manuscript Papers of a Very Learned Man

31. After the great labors of the ancients have been exhausted, to reveal something new to posterity is the virtue of few. To present the torn archives of antiquity in a more vigorous and purer form, and to make the obscure centuries of the past clearer, may be undertaken only with some mark of temerity and boldness.

32. From the seventh century, in which our excellent teacher Isidore, bishop of Seville, flourished, down to the present time, the minds of both our own people and foreigners have labored greatly to investigate, establish, and clarify his works [Col. 0231C]: separating authentic writings from apocryphal ones, distinguishing spurious short works from legitimate ones, leaving other doubtful works in their own state of uncertainty, and entirely rejecting writings that were corrupted, enlarged, or most disgracefully attributed to our holy teacher.

33. Among our own scholars, Nicolás Antonio devoted himself to this undertaking in his *Old Spanish Library*, where he examines individually all the works that, rightly or wrongly, bear the name of the holy teacher. Ambrosius Morales and other most learned men did likewise; by order of King Philip II they published these works in Madrid in 1599. The Reverend Father Henry Flórez did so in volumes V and VI of *Sacred Spain*: in the fifth he committed to the press Saint Isidore’s treatise *On Illustrious Men*, and in the sixth his *Chronicle* and *History of the Vandals and Goths*. He added the notes of Grotius and Labbe, and also corrected the work with the greatest care and established its chronological order.

34. Foreign scholars labored no less to make [Col. 0231D] Saint Isidore, as though born in their own land alone, more illustrious, eagerly collecting his writings and competing for glory. Godefridus Henschenius and Daniel Papebrochius discuss Saint Isidore’s works at length under 4 April; Albert Fabricius undertook to elucidate the same field in volume IV of his *Library of Medieval and Late Latin Literature*.

35. Abbot Constantine Cajetan published short works of the holy teacher that were lacking in the earlier Paris editions produced through the efforts of Bignaeus and Jacques du Breul, and in the royal Madrid edition. Although the aforesaid abbot counted all the saints enrolled in the catalogue of his Benedictine family as sons of that family, to such an extent that it provoked laughter to read that Saint Francis of Assisi had been a Benedictine monk, and Cardinal Cobellucius therefore hesitated over whether Abbot Constantine had transformed the apostle Saint Peter into a monk of his order, sensible men nevertheless do not consider the aforementioned edition unimportant.

[Col. 0232A]

36. Cardinal Bona, Mabillon, Ceillier, Jean Daillé, Casimir Oudin, and Wilhelm Fentzel judge the letters of Saint Isidore of Seville to be spurious: the first, addressed to the archdeacon Redemptus—for it concerns the controversy between the Eastern and Western Churches over whether Christ used unleavened or leavened bread at the supper of the final night; yet this dispute is not recorded as having arisen until four centuries after the works of Saint Isidore—the second, addressed to Claudius, and the third, addressed to Eugenius, bishop, in which a controversy between Greeks and Latins is reported concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit, although it is otherwise sufficiently known that this Greek ambiguity grew only in the seventh century. Finally, they reject them because in these last two letters the power of the supreme pontiff is portrayed in a manner in which an author of the thirteenth century might have expressed it more forcefully.

37. Jean Morin, Zeger Bernard van Espen, and Ceillier reject as spurious Saint Isidore’s letter to Massona, bishop of Mérida, [Col. 0232B] although the Antwerp Fathers and Flórez defend it as genuine. The very learned Morin and Van Espen, supported by the authority of the councils and Fathers of the first six centuries of the Church, and by two testimonies from Saint Isidore himself—in Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5, and in the letter to Helladius—show by the strongest arguments that the aforementioned letter cannot in any way be attributed to Saint Isidore. For it mentions the question whether a cleric of sacred orders who has fallen into a grave sin may, according to the ancient discipline, be admitted to the exercise of his order after completing penance. The author of the letter attempts to reconcile decisions favorable to both sides, persuading himself that the men of that age had gone off in different directions in their opinions. But the leniency of restoration is wholly opposed to the mind of Saint Isidore and of the Fathers of the earlier centuries; nor is there found in the older collections any canon permitting a delinquent person to return to the functions of his sacred ministry.

38. Eugenius, the bishop to whom [Col. 0232C] Saint Isidore is presumed to have written, was, according to the distinguished Juan Bautista Pérez of Valencia, canon of Toledo and later bishop of Segorbe, Eugenius II, archbishop of Toledo. Henry Flórez, on the other hand, asserts that he was Eugenius, bishop of Egara, who attended the Fourth Council of Toledo together with Saint Isidore. From this arises a considerable suspicion against the aforementioned letter, in which the Church is said to have received a creed inscribed with the name of Saint Athanasius—yet you will not find it under this title until after the time of Saint Isidore.

39. Among the works of the saints Ambrose, Augustine, and Leo, there is counted a treatise *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, attributed to Saint Ambrose; it is likewise identified in the catalogue of the library of the Holy Primate Church of Toledo. But since Mabillon, Nicolás Antonio, Fabricius, and Ceillier judge that it was unjustly attributed to Ambrose, Augustine, or Leo, thereby overturning the opinion of those who eventually [Col. 0232D] assigned it to Saint Isidore of Seville, we incline toward the grounds on which its author is believed to be not Ambrose of Milan but another Ambrose, namely Ambrose Autpert, a Benedictine monk and writer of the eighth century.

40. We are entirely unable to determine whether the *Exposition of the Song of Songs* is a work of the holy teacher of Seville. Ceillier asserts that it can neither be denied to so great a teacher nor certainly attributed to him; and we leave the matter to the judgment of others.

41. Lucas Achery, of the Congregation of Saint-Maur, published in the seventeenth century, in his *Spicilegium of Certain Ancient Writers*, a book by Saint Isidore *On the Order of Creatures*. Nicolás Antonio says of it that it gives off the scent of Isidore’s age. But because in its final chapter it accumulates certain doubts about the state of souls after death and about purgatorial fire—doubts that seem to overturn the piety or teaching of the holy teacher—he in no way agrees with those who assert that the work belongs to our teacher.

[Col. 0233A] **42.** Since this matter is of such importance, permit us to linger over it somewhat in order to express our opinion. The order preserved in the aforementioned book *On the Order of Creatures*, its division into chapters, its concise style filled with proverbial sayings, its “lime without sand,” its “cement without the beauty of form,” and its clarity of expression without eloquence—when all these features are compared with one another—really agree with the method observed by St. Isidore in the book *On Etymologies*, and especially in the *Sentences*, works about which no one has hitherto entertained doubts. Although doubts [p. 297] concerning the state of souls after death and purgatory do not smell agreeable to a man of such keen discernment as Nicolaus Antonius, I nevertheless do not wonder that St. Isidore may have spoken more obscurely on this subject.

**43.** As they turn over the books of the ancient Fathers and diligently reflect upon their opinions, readers will not be alarmed when they discover that the bishop of Alexandria disputed rather sharply with Pope Victor concerning the date of Easter; that Justin, Irenaeus, and other Fathers of the same age slipped somewhat toward the opinion of the Millenarians; that Cyprian firmly opposed Pope Stephen concerning the rebaptism of heretics, so that Cyprian believed nothing from them could come to us for spiritual salvation, as from dead instruments cast out of the Church of God; and that Hilary of Arles was rebuked and his reputation diminished in letters by Pope Leo. They will not look upon these and similar matters with hostile eyes, first because, although the articles of faith have always been the same, they were not all revealed at the same time. For they are all contained in the Apostles’ Creed, just as grains of wheat are contained in an ear; but they do not all appear equally openly and plainly until they are brought to light after discussion.

[Col. 0233B]

**44.** Second, such disputes among the Fathers and teachers of the Church arose not from pride, arrogance, or a hostile disposition, but from a certain sincerity, a desire to learn, and a personal judgment concerning matters which they persuaded themselves did not pertain to the faith. And, if one wishes to add this, the holy Fathers, considered individually as human beings, could have been deceived or mistaken in some matter. Hear how Augustine, in his *Retractations*, did not disdain to retract certain words and opinions, thereby preparing for us a path of humility. God alone is wise by essence; he knows all things and understands everything completely, and can neither deceive nor be deceived in any respect. Nor has he yet sent into his Church a holy teacher who was perfectly enlightened in every matter and above all others; rather, he filled each with knowledge suited to the work for which he appointed him. Thus no one surpassed Tertullian and Justin in defending the Catholic religion in their *Apologies*; Origen and Jerome in understanding and translating the Old and New Testaments; Gregory and Ambrose in moral interpretation; Augustine in explaining the hidden matters of grace and human free will; and, in our own Spain, Isidore in the *Etymologies*, the *Sentences*, and the mastery of a diversity of arts.

**45.** If the reader wishes to examine Dionysius the Athenian Areopagite’s works *On the Divine Names* and *On the Celestial Hierarchy*, he needs the golden thread of the Angelic Doctor, St. Thomas, in order to grasp their meaning and avoid falling into an abyss. St. Augustine, when speaking of the substance of angels and of the human soul and its faculties, appears to readers to be enveloped in darkness; indeed, the holy Doctor himself admits the weakness of his understanding. What, then, is there to hinder our St. Isidore if, in chapter 15 on the future life of the book *On the Order of Creatures*, he does not speak of the rational soul with complete precision and eloquence? For, as he says at the end, addressing Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza:

> “For my part, agreeing with good and Catholic readers, I do not care about the complaints (or lamentations) of the envious, who, crawling upon the earth without wings, mock the nests of birds with the flight of frogs!”

Let anyone who wishes consult St. Augustine, book V of *Against Julian*, chapter 3; there he will find an even more obscure statement concerning the transmission of the soul with respect to original sin [p. 298], in these words: “As to which of these alternatives is true, I prefer to learn rather than to state it, lest I dare to teach what I do not know.”

**46.** Around the middle of the aforementioned chapter, the holy Doctor Isidore asserts that God did not make the soul either from God himself or from any underlying matter of bodily creatures. We believe it to be not a part of God, but God’s creature; nor does it have anything corporeal in its nature—neither heat from fire, breath from air, moisture from water, nor thickness and solidity from earth. Since it lacks all these, it is incorporeal; and through this incorporeality, mutability, and power of free will, it is known both to have the same substance as the angels and to have its origin in creation.

[Col. 0234A]

**47.** Whether God creates the soul individually for each body, or whether creation took place in Adam’s time or afterward, he refers this question to the knowledge of the Creator. Let the most devout reader not take offense at these words, for he will certainly find the same position in St. Augustine and in other teachers who flourished before him. It follows only that St. Isidore either fixed his position or was unable to state a definitive opinion, because theological language on this matter had not yet been settled and the question whether God created a soul for each individual body remained shrouded in great darkness.

[Col. 0234B]

**48.** Lucas Acherius suggests that *immutabilitatem* (“immutability”) should perhaps be read in the aforementioned passage of St. Isidore. But we do not need this correction, since in the present state of life the soul, insofar as it possesses the power of free will, is mutable toward good or evil in temporal matters: it is mutable through its affections and through changes of thought, while suffering the penalties of the first man’s just condemnation. The holy Doctor himself expresses this in clearer words in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12, *On the Soul*.

**49.** A more suitable authority for the matter is the following passage from St. Augustine, letter 157, to Optatus:

> “But there are considerations of things and causes which move me in such a way that my assent inclines to neither assertion, but I still dispute between the two.”

And in book I *On the Origin of the Soul*, chapter 16, speaking of the transmission of souls, he says:

> “I neither defend nor refute it.”

More explicitly, in book X of *On Genesis*, chapter 21, criticizing in his judgment Tertullian’s error—Tertullian had asserted that souls derived their origin from corporeal seeds—he says:

> “I am still uncertain and troubled between the two alternatives, at one time inclined this way, at another that.”

[Col. 0234C]

**50.** Augustine criticized Tertullian not because he posited the transmission of souls, but because he did not assert it correctly, thinking that the soul was corporeal and therefore transmitted through the corporeal seed of the procreator. This is what the most learned Cardinal Henry of Noris asserts in *Augustinian Vindications*, § III; we shall demonstrate it more fully in the notes to the chapter on the future life of St. Isidore’s *On the Order of Creatures*.

For the present, it is enough to say that St. Augustine, the African Fathers, and many others of the Western Church were completely certain of the soul’s incorporeality, eternity, spirituality, and immortality. Their only doubt concerned the manner of the soul’s transmission. Some believed that human souls were created at the same time as the angels, or afterward. Others believed that souls came from Adam—not by transmission from Adam’s body, but from Adam’s soul—as though the other souls of future human beings were contained potentially within Adam’s soul. For just as we now assert that [p. 299], with respect to original sin, all human beings were in Adam in headship, will, and seed, and that the bodies of those who are born derive from his material, so certain Western Fathers maintained that the souls of those born descended by transmission from Adam’s soul. They did not know how this occurred, and for this reason St. Augustine called it an insoluble question, using the same words as St. Isidore.

To leave no room for doubt, we close the argument with St. Isidore’s explicit testimony in book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 23, *On the Rule of Faith*. After confessing the mysteries of the most holy Trinity, the Incarnation, and the articles of faith, he adds these words:

> “And that the origin of souls is uncertain, and that the origin and nature of angels—or of souls—is not a part of the divine substance, but God’s creature created from nothing, and that it is evidently in the body.”

**51.** In the chapter on the fire of purgatory, the holy Doctor Isidore asserts that the more serious crimes which defile people—those whose perpetrators Paul excluded from the kingdom of God—are not purged by that fire, but rather those which do not do much harm, although they contribute less to edification:

> “These lesser sins, therefore, or venial sins, can be purged by fire, and this must not be denied; and their perpetrator, if he is not burdened by greater offenses, must nevertheless be thought to be saved as through fire.”

Let someone else inquire, and we shall quickly yield: one would scarcely find words any clearer in another holy Father of the same age speaking about the fire of purgatory, especially if he weighs St. Isidore’s final words:

> “But concerning that purgatorial fire, this must be observed: it is both longer and more severe than every kind of torment that a person can presently imagine.”

**52.** Aeneas of Paris, compiler of the sentences of the holy Fathers of both East and West against the Greeks who denied the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son, cites St. Isidore’s passage from *On the Order of Creatures* (Lucas Acherius, *Spicilegium*). From this a not insignificant judgment can be formed concerning the circulation of this treatise under St. Isidore’s name during the period when Aeneas flourished, and his testimony supports that conclusion.

[Col. 0235B]

**53.** We do not reject the book *On Illustrious Men*, because in chapters 5 and 14 the memory of Hosius, bishop of Córdoba, appears defiled and polluted. In the preface to the *Gothic Breviary* we already brought forward Athanasius’s testimony in defense of Hosius’s posthumous reputation. The origin of the fable directed against the honor of the great Hosius and against the final episode of his life was fabricated and invented by Marcellinus and Faustinus, Luciferian priests. They devised such a crime against Hosius in order to make their perverse doctrine more secure—namely, that one must not communicate with those who had fallen away from the faith, even after they had performed penance judged sufficient by the Church.

The Luciferians repeatedly circulated letters falsely attributed to themselves and to others, in order to inform the Fathers of Spain, Gaul, Italy, and Africa of the great Hosius’s lapse at the end of his life, his wealth and avarice, and his weakness and fear lest he displease the emperor. Since the frailty of the human mind and the desire of the flesh have long been known, and since the sacred writings teach, amid the Church’s great lamentation, that Solomon was corrupted and depraved toward the end of his life, and no one denies that Tertullian and Origen strayed from the path, it is not surprising that the holy Hilary and Isidore [p. 300] should have assented to Hosius’s lapse—especially since, at so advanced an age, under pressure from threatening imperial letters, it was to be feared that the decrepit old man, having returned to a childlike state, might have been deceived, or rather compelled by the heretics, to subscribe to the Arians’ deceptive formula.

What then, even if it had happened? We would say that, through an imperfect deliberation at such an advanced age, with a complete lack of freedom and examination of the formula, Hosius could have been deceived under force and fear, but that he had in no way departed from the true and right faith by a deliberate judgment of his mind.

**54.** We return again to the other works of St. Isidore. In the library of the House of Medici there is preserved a work of St. Isidore *On the Stars*, which may perhaps be the same as the work kept in the royal library of El Escorial.

[Col. 0235D]

**55.** The prayer *Hear, O Christ, the sorrowful lament* was published by Papebrochius in volume I of the April *Acta Sanctorum*. It was published by Papebrochius in volume I for April. It lacks nearly fifty *stantiae*, or stanzas; for it originally consisted of one hundred and ten, although the division of the text may perhaps have increased the number. This work is not unworthy of St. Isidore. Although he may not have corrected everything completely, his disciples nevertheless preserved for posterity his rough and unpolished little works.

**56.** In distinguishing the aforementioned books, we have other highly learned men as judges; but they provide us with no material for defending the manuscript of the fourth book of the *Sentences*, which has not hitherto been published. It is preserved in the royal library of El Escorial, written so neatly, clearly, and in Gothic characters that no room for doubt remains concerning it. The dignity of the subject it treats not only equals but surpasses that of the three earlier books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*. Sentences, or proverbial sayings, occur there throughout in great abundance, excerpted from the *Moralia* and *Pastoral Rule* of St. Gregory the Great. This accords with the testimony of St. Braulio, who states that St. Isidore adorned the three books of the *Sentences* with flowers gathered from the moral works of Pope Gregory.

[Col. 0236A]

**57.** It is not unusual for authors who have treated this subject to raise the question whether St. Isidore comprised the entire work of the *Sentences*—which was called *On the Supreme Good*—in a single book, beginning with the opening of its first chapter: “The supreme good is God.” But this opinion plainly contradicts the authority of St. Braulio, who counts three books of the *Sentences* and at the same time asserts that St. Isidore himself divided the *Etymologies* into twenty books, because the work had come from the holy Doctor unfinished through its excessive length, with headings rather than books. How, then, shall we untie the knots of this difficulty so that credence may be given to the fourth book *On the Supreme Good*?

**58.** Some may suspect that the fourth book was added by another teacher. Others will think it a fragment of St. Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Rule* or *Moralia*. Since we stand on this uncertain ground, we do not dare to pronounce judgment concerning the work’s parentage. It is better to say that the fourth book lay hidden for many years and escaped the eyes of the most discerning men, so that its autograph was published neither in the royal edition of Madrid nor in the Paris editions. And if it is not truly a copy of St. Isidore’s work, I praise the author’s skill: he has made the son resemble his father more than the father resembles himself. The choice of words, the clear sense of the *Sentences*, and the style redolent of the seventh century—all these features seem to belong not to an abortive offspring of St. Isidore, but [p. 301] to a natural one. Let others therefore examine the matter and constitute themselves judges; we shall gladly submit to their judgment.

**59.** The manuscript from which the fourth book of the *Sentences* was transcribed has the appearance and antiquity of the twelfth century. We are therefore seized with admiration when we consider that such a manuscript of the fourth book never came to the attention of St. Braulio, Sigebert of Gembloux, or John Trithemius, who wrote about St. Isidore’s little works, nor to that of others, although, with great diligence and by royal command, manuscripts had been sought throughout Spain, Italy, and Gaul.

[Col. 0236C]

**60.** In order to lend greater credibility to this edition, at the end of this preface we shall append a list of St. Isidore’s books that were printed in Paris by Sebastian Nivellius in 1601, through the study, work, and labor of Brother Jacques du Breul, monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, and of other distinguished men. By comparing this fuller edition with the aforementioned edition of du Breul, we shall note the books of St. Isidore that have hitherto remained unpublished, namely: the fourth book of the *Sentences*; the *Exposition of the Mass*, which may perhaps be the same treatise that John Trithemius, in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, calls *On the Office of the Mass*; one book *On the Stars*, which may perhaps be the same as the work Trithemius titles *On Astronomy*; and the sermon *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which Trithemius also mentions among St. Isidore’s works. Thus readers will have access to an examination of all his works, whether certain or doubtful, and will not be compelled to beg for editions from foreigners.

[Col. 0236D]

**61.** Concerning the treatise *On the Exposition of the Mass*, we dare not assume not only the role of judge but even that of arbitrator, until clearer arguments appear on one side or the other. Trithemius does mention a book of St. Isidore *On the Office of the Mass*, but since the superscription does not agree, and although the wording of the *Exposition* and the *Office* differs somewhat, this already introduces doubt into the mind. On the other hand, an even greater difficulty weighs against the aforementioned treatise: in it the Mass is explained with the same prayers and in precisely the same manner in which it is celebrated today after the correction of the Missal by St. Pius V and Clement VIII. Yet it is established, and clear from the ancient Roman Missal, that the earlier Roman liturgy differs in many respects, although not in essentials, from the corrected liturgy.

**62.** Since, therefore, such an order of prayers was observed neither in the time of Gregory the Great nor did St. Isidore recognize any other rite for celebrating the Mass than the one he himself explains in chapter 15 of book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as will be clear to readers and is explained more fully in our *Dissertation on the Gothic Breviary*, it is not likely that St. Isidore was its author, although we willingly admit that Gregory the Great transmitted that order of the Mass to him.

**63.** The Cistercians, Carthusians, Dominicans, and Shod Carmelites use their own rite and Missal from before the correction. To all who hear Mass, the order of prayers and ceremonies appears different, although it is neither the Gothic rite nor that of the Eastern Church, but only the ancient Roman rite that was in use after the century in which St. Gregory the Great lived.

**64.** The cardinals and prelates of Toledo, Brother Francisco Jiménez de Cisneros [p. 302] and Juan Martínez Silíceo, published the *Toledan Mixed Missal*. Cardinal Juan Tavera likewise ordered it to be printed again. It differs considerably not only in the rubrics of the Missal but also in the order of prayers from the Roman Missal after the correction of St. Pius V. In confirmation of this, it is known that Philip II, king of Spain, addressed prayers to St. Pius V asking him to preserve the praiseworthy customs of the Holy Church of Toledo, its chant, and its rubrics, as may be seen in the bull prefixed to St. Pius V’s Missal. Although the Supreme Pontiff ordered his Missal to be observed throughout the entire world, he nevertheless graciously granted the Catholic king an exception with respect to the praiseworthy customs and chant.

[Col. 0237B]

**65.** The *Toledan Mixed Missal* was in reality the ancient Roman Missal introduced into the Church of Toledo in the time of King Alfonso VI. Under his auspices, the Supreme Pontiff extended the Roman rite throughout Spain, while the Gothic or Mozarabic rite was confined to the enclosures of certain parishes in the city of Toledo and to the chapel of the Holy Church. As soon as Pius V sent Philip II the corrected Missal, the *Mixed Missal* fell into disuse. It was so called both because it combined the Roman and Gothic rites and because its rubrics were interwoven with those of the old and corrected Roman rites.

[Col. 0237C]

**66.** The Ambrosian Missal, printed in 1522, agrees in very many respects with the Mixed Missal used by the Church of Toledo before the Council of Trent. Yet the aforementioned Ambrosian Missal, according to the custom of St. Ambrose, as its title page declares, was ordered by the holy Doctor Ambrose not only before the correction of St. Pius V but even before the liturgical arrangement made by St. Gregory the Great. It cannot be called a Gothic Ambrosian rite, but rather the most ancient Roman rite.

**67.** We offer you, most gracious reader, whatever we have been able to find that is best. Add to it, if you can, and enrich your dissertations with the works of our Doctor. It is no less dangerous for us to doubt everything indiscriminately than to doubt nothing. Immediately after the death of the holy Doctor himself—whether Theodiscus, his successor, about whom we shall not linger, or others—the men most hostile to St. Isidore’s honor sought to obscure and almost extinguish Isidore, the brilliant light of our Spain. Others, especially monks, gathering his codices into safekeeping, endeavored with the greatest care to transcribe them. But not all were equally diligent in copying, and for that reason very many errors entered the manuscripts. Others, whether clerics or monks, wishing to adorn their own meager labor, stained themselves with the foulest crime of fraud and foxlike cunning: uttering their absurdities under St. Isidore’s name, they left to posterity works corrupted from the virginal and most pure works of St. Isidore, in order to exalt their own work through so great an author. They did not recognize that wolves should not be covered with sheep’s clothing, nor that the ravings of asses can any longer be contained under the appearance of piety.

[Col. 0237D]

**68.** Isidore, therefore, does not need our testimony. He is content with the simple authority of St. Braulio, his most intimate friend, and of St. Ildephonsus, his disciple, as well as with the account of his death given by Redemptus, his cleric, who saw him depart from this life to God in the greatest peace. We shall present all the testimonies, so as to perform for you, dearest reader, a pleasing service.

**69.** “Isidore,” says St. Braulio, “an outstanding man and bishop of the Church of Seville, successor and brother of Bishop Leander [p. 303], flourished from the time of the Emperor Maurice and King Reccared . . . a man trained in every kind of expression, renowned for incomparable eloquence . . . and how great he was in wisdom, the prudent reader will be able to understand very easily from his various studies and carefully composed little works . . . He died in the time of the Emperor Heraclius and the most Christian King Chintila, superior to all in sound doctrine and richer than all in works of charity.” St. Ildephonsus states that he wrote outstanding and considerable works.

**70.** John Trithemius calls St. Isidore a man second to none in his time in divine Scripture and secular literature; subtle in intellect, clear in understanding, polished in expression, excellent in poetry and prose, and distinguished no less for holiness than for learning.

[Col. 0238B]

**71.** Redemptus, the cleric who was present at St. Isidore’s death, reports in exact detail the holy Doctor’s prayer to God in the church of St. Vincent before his death and his address to his fellow bishops, clergy, and people. Clad in a hair shirt and sprinkled with ashes according to the rule of the ancient discipline, he stretched out his hands toward heaven; and, when all had been completed, after the fourth day from the day of his confession or penance, he brought his pastoral, continuous care and his life to an end in peace, on the day before the Nones of April, in the era 679, in the year of our Lord 686.

**72.** Be imbued with Isidore’s maxims, most eloquent reader; hold the work of the Fathers in reverence, even if spurious offspring have exposed it. Do not investigate the spots of the sun or the eclipses of the moon with a dimmed light or a blunted instrument; learn instead to defer to your elders, and attribute the evils to the vicissitudes of circumstances—to the pen, the press, so many calamities, disasters, devastations, plunderings, wars, and incursions of barbarians—if you wish to cross this age upon a favorable sea.

# CHAPTER XXXIX  
## The efforts of certain men to complete a new edition of Isidore’s works. Casimir Oudinus’s judgment concerning the method by which it should be produced.

[Col. 0238C]

**1.** Since many learned men had long desired a new edition of his works, not a few undertook to plan its completion, including Jacob Hommey, Andreas Burriel, Francisco Pérez Bayer, and Francisco Antonio Zaccaria. I shall soon speak separately of Burriel and Zaccaria. That Jacob Hommey, prevented by death, was unable to carry out what he had conceived concerning the printing of Isidore’s writings is attested by the aforementioned Zaccaria in the prospectus of his prepared Isidorian edition; Fabricius also reports it in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under the entry “Isidore.”

[p. 304]

**2.** Bayer’s efforts to prepare an edition of Isidore appear to have been more modest; perhaps he did not even intend to publish all of Isidore’s works. Bandini, in volume I of the *Codex Latinus Bibliothecae Mediceae Laurentianae*, shelf 19, codex 31, after reviewing the mystical expositions of the sacraments, or Isidore’s questions on the Old Testament, added this note:

> “Our codex was ordered to be collated in 1756 by the distinguished Father Zacharias, S.J., with the Spanish edition. In the Toledan library, however, there is preserved a parchment codex in a square format, of the most remote antiquity, written in the eighth century or at the beginning of the ninth. The aforementioned Zacharias ought to have consulted it, as the canon of Barcelona, Bayer Pérez, assured me at that time. He had collated that codex most diligently by order of Ferdinand VI, king of Spain, while he was planning to publish it.”

Andreas Petrus Julianellius, serving as royal librarian at the Laurentian Library, heard this very account from Bayer, as he himself testifies in the words to be cited in chapter 43, when I discuss that Florentine codex.

[Col. 0239A]

**3.** I nevertheless wonder that Bayer silently passed over this labor of his in the notes to the *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*. In the note to book V, chapter 4, no. 102, he does indeed mention that in the year 1752 he collated a Toledan codex of the *Etymologies* from the ninth or early tenth century, together with another ancient codex, against Grial’s printed edition. “From this labor,” he says, “a harvest of variant readings, not to be regretted, grew for me.” But when, in the note to no. 139, he discusses manuscript codices of the *Questions on the Old Testament*, he lists five Escorial codices and says not a word about the Toledan ones. Indeed, Andreas Burriel, who had investigated and consulted the manuscript copies of Isidore at Toledo with the greatest diligence, reports no codex containing the *Questions on the Old Testament*, as will become clear from his letter soon to be presented.

Rodríguez de Castro, volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 312, confirms in a note that Bayer collected various readings from the old Gothic Toledan book of the *Etymologies*.

**4.** Since, long before this, Casimir Oudinus published a special dissertation on the writings of St. Isidore of Seville in volume I of *De Scriptoribus ecclesiasticis*, col. 1583, in which he set out the order he himself wished to be observed in an edition of Isidore’s works, let us see what judgment this learned man—rather a heterodox or even apostate—held.

[p. 305]

**Order of the Works of St. Isidore, Bishop of Seville**

[Col. 0239C]

**5.** Twenty books of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*. Three books of the *Differences*, or *On the Proper Meaning of Language*, in the order stated above—namely, first the alphabetical book of words, then the book of words without alphabetical order, and finally the book of the *Differences of Things*. *On the Nature of Things*, or *On the World*, addressed to King Sisebut. The book of *Prologues* concerning the books of the Old and New Testaments. The book of *Allegories of Sacred Scripture* concerning the names of the Old and New Testaments. Brief commentaries on the historical books of the Old Testament, Genesis, and so forth. Three books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*. Two books *Against the Wickedness of the Jews*. Two books *On Divine or Ecclesiastical Offices*. A letter to Ludifred, bishop of Córdoba, concerning the same offices. Two books of the *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*, addressed to Braulio, archdeacon. A *Rule for Monks*, divided into twenty-four chapters, for the use of the country. *On the Life and Death of the Saints Who Pleased God*, or *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. The book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, with the supplement of St. Ildephonsus, archbishop of Toledo. A *Chronicle* from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of Suintila, king of the Goths, A.D. 626. A *History of the Goths, Suevi, and Vandals*, though according to the edition of Labbe, which we have indicated. A very few brief letters.

**Appendix of uncertain works.**

[Col. 0239D]

**6.** *An Exhortation to Repentance with Consolation and the Mercy of God*, addressed to a soul fearful of the future judgments. *A Lament of Repentance for the Forgiveness of Sins*, arranged in a double alphabet and in trochaic verse. A long prayer for continually lamenting sins and correcting one’s life. A brief prayer against the snares of the devil. *On the Order of Creatures*. A commentary on the *Song of Songs*.

**Appendix of spurious works.**

**7.** *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which belongs to Ambrose Autpertus. — *Letters*: — to Masso, concerning the fall of a priest and restoration after the fall; — to Claudius, the duke; — to Redemptus, the archdeacon; — to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo.

**8.** This is the order that Oudinus wished to be observed in the forthcoming edition of all Isidore’s works. In many respects it agrees with the order I prescribed for myself.

[p. 306]

**CHAPTER XL**  
## Andreas Burriel’s plans for preparing a new edition of St. Isidore’s works, and his learned letter. Another letter of the distinguished Peter de Castro to Francisco Antonio Zaccaria.

[Col. 0240B]

**1.** Francisco Rabago of the Society of Jesus, a remarkably learned man, as his writings testify, and exceedingly devoted to increasing learning among the Spaniards, while serving as confessor to Ferdinand VI, the Catholic king, arranged by royal authority for many other undertakings highly useful to Spanish scholarship. Among these, he especially saw to it that highly skilled men were ordered diligently to investigate the archives of the ancient cathedral churches, so that the oldest monuments—whatever might illuminate religion or history—could be brought from darkness into the light.

Andreas Burriel, of the same Society, an exceptionally eager and diligent cultivator of antiquity, was assigned to examine the archives of the Church of Toledo, the most celebrated of all the churches of Spain. Francisco Pérez Bayer, a man of no obscure reputation in the literary world, was added to him as a colleague.

[Col. 0240C]

**2.** Bayer himself mentions this undertaking in the note to book III, chapter 3, no. 69 of the *Bibliotheca Vetus Hispana*, where, concerning Dracontius’s manuscript codex, he reports:

> “The distinguished friend collated it and noted the variant readings. In collecting from the archive and library of the illustrious college of the Canons of Toledo the monuments that could contribute to the history of the homeland, my former colleague Andreas Marcus Burriel, a priest of the Society of Jesus, was carried off several years ago by a premature death, to the great loss of literary scholarship. I now possess at hand these materials, together with very many offspring of that truly astonishing labor and industry, which were later transferred to the royal library at Madrid, and whose autographs I have at hand.”

[Col. 0240D]

**3.** Accordingly, when Burriel was reporting the progress of his studies to Rabago, he spoke of St. Isidore in a letter written in Spanish at Toledo on 22 December 1752. I translate its substance into Latin.

**Excerpt from Burriel’s letter to Father Rabago**

**4.** “Since St. Isidore is the most celebrated Doctor of our Spain, and his works were printed in two editions, the edition of Breul and the royal edition of Madrid, without the final hand and more polished refinement demanded by our times [p. 307], certain of his works have been collated with the manuscript codices preserved here, especially the books of the *Etymologies* with two Gothic copies. One of these may perhaps have been written before the Moors invaded Spain; neither, however, was noticed by the Madrid editors of Isidore.

[Col. 0241A]

**5.** “In this library there is a Bible of the Vulgate edition, in a rather thick volume written in three columns. Mariana judged, in the dedicatory letter to his commentary on the New Testament and in the dedicatory letter to Cardinal Bellarmine prefixed to his commentary on the Old Testament, that it had been written before the Moors invaded Spain—that is, more than a thousand years ago. This invaluable codex was evidently arranged by St. Isidore for the use of the churches of Spain. Each book is preceded, apart from Jerome’s prologue, by another prologue of St. Isidore, and each prophet by a historical eulogy found in St. Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*.

[Col. 0241B]

“It is a widespread controversy whether such a work belongs to Isidore. For my part, moved by six hundred conjectures, I think that the holy Doctor composed those eulogies of the prophets in order to place them before the individual prophets in the Bible; I hold the same opinion concerning the prologues. Just as the prologues, when joined together, form a separate little work called the *Book of Prologues*, so too do the eulogies of the prophets. The other eulogies of the holy Virgin and the apostles, which constitute the other part of the little work *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, may perhaps have another author than Isidore.

“In the same codex, ten canons of Eusebius of Caesarea are placed before the Gospels for the harmony of the evangelists; Isidore explains their harmony in the books of the *Etymologies*. Before Paul’s letters are found the canons of the heretic Priscillian, corrected by Bishop Peregrinus. I do not know of their being mentioned by others, and so I transcribed them.”

[Col. 0241C]

**6.** Concerning the canons of Priscillian mentioned by Burriel, one may consult Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi* and Zaccaria, volume V of the *Literary History of Italy*, chapter 9, no. 4. Zaccaria admits that he does not know who that Bishop Peregrinus was who corrected Priscillian’s canons. Perhaps the author was a pseudonymist who, wishing to conceal his own name, assumed the name Peregrinus; it is known that others adopted such names for a similar reason.

In a letter to Don Peter de Castro dated 3 January 1754, to be presented shortly, Burriel still thought that these canons of Priscillian had not been printed. But Zaccaria had already published them in 1752 in the *Pistoria Library*, where he observed that the same Priscillianic [p. 308] canons corrected by Peregrinus are extant in the Vatican Library, codex 5729, folio 217—perhaps he means page 217 of the codex.

In the aforementioned Gothic Bible of the Church of Toledo, the first prologue, common to all the sacred books, was missing. Burriel arranged for it to be transcribed from another celebrated codex of the Collegium Maius of Alcalá.

### 7

Two years after the letters sent to Rabago, Burriel was consulted, in Zaccaria’s name—Zaccaria being then planning an edition of the works of Saint Isidore—about the manuscript copies of Isidore preserved at Toledo. From the Royal Spanish College at Bologna, called Saint Clement’s, there had come to Madrid the distinguished Pedro de Castro, an alumnus of that college and now a canon of the Church of Seville. He is the author of a learned [Col. 0242A] letter to the Benedictine monks of the Parisian Congregation of Saint Maur concerning certain passages in the life of Saint Gregory the Great, prepared by them, that were somewhat inconsistent, omitted, or improbable; this letter was published in volume IV of the *Opera*, printed at Madrid and Bologna in 1754.

Zaccaria therefore wrote to him, asking that he himself collate the Toledan manuscripts of Isidore, or arrange for them to be collated by someone else. Pedro referred the matter to Burriel. I have in my possession four informal letters from Burriel to Pedro, written in 1754, on 3, 6, and 13 December, and in 1755, on 3 January.

### 8

The sole subject of these brief letters is a discussion of how one might reply to Zaccaria. Burriel begins by saying that he intended to prepare an edition of Isidore, arranged according to a better method [Col. 0242B] than the Royal Madrid edition, on the basis of Spanish manuscript codices. He adds that he would readily entrust all his studies of Isidore to Zaccaria, if this could be done with the good will of those upon whose decision the matter depended. Otherwise, if Zaccaria requested nothing more, Burriel could provide him with a brief description of the manuscript codices.

Burriel would have liked the edition to be produced through combined assistance and advice, whether in Italy or in Spain; but he did not place sufficient confidence in fortune, which at that time was favoring him at the Spanish court. The outcome itself confirmed the prudent man’s fears. He also recognized the difficulties that sometimes arise in Spain when works of this kind are to be completed.

“I fear,” he says, “that some obstacle may perhaps be placed in the way of an edition outside Spain, [Col. 0242C] while meanwhile nothing is accomplished in Spain.”

Finally, he drafted a longer letter that could be sent to Zaccaria. It has already been published by José Rodríguez de Castro in the *Biblioteca Hispana*, under the entry “Isidorus.” But although Rodríguez de Castro perhaps placed it in a somewhat unsuitable location, we ought not to omit it from a place especially appropriate for it, particularly since it deserves to be communicated to foreigners. I therefore translated it into Latin from the Spanish autograph copy as follows.

> To Don Pedro de Castro, my dearest friend, Andreas Burriel sends greetings.

### 9

I read your letter, together with that which Father Francesco Antonio Zaccaria sent you from Bologna on 8 November, with the greatest pleasure. As it happened, at this very time Fathers Panigai and Bramieri, of the Venetian province of the Society of Jesus, were passing this way as they travelled from Lisbon to that royal [Col. 0242D] court. Since they had stayed five days at Toledo observing the antiquities of the city and its rarer monuments, I found a suitable opportunity to engage them in a long conversation about Father Zaccaria, whom they know extremely well. Indeed, we unanimously praised the prudence of the Duke of Modena, who appointed him to the direction of his library in succession to the illustrious Muratori. We also discussed among ourselves the best way in which I ought to answer your requests on behalf of Zaccaria.

### 10

First of all, I thank you from the heart for striving with such sincere and favorable goodwill to promote the studies and reputation of that learned Jesuit. I wish I could also use the united voice of our entire nation, so that I might offer Zaccaria the clearest evidence of our remembrance and gratitude, since he has resolved to pour forth the abundance of his knowledge and learning for the purpose of illuminating the writings of our teacher, Saint Isidore.

[Col. 0243A] ### 11

Next, I am convinced that a new edition of the works of this holy Spanish teacher is urgently necessary and would bring many advantages. It is necessary because the two editions produced at almost the same time—the Madrid and Paris editions, those of Grial and of De Breul—are very imperfect, as is evident both from the editions themselves and from the judgment passed upon them by Nicolás Antonio. A new edition is especially necessary because Isidore’s writings shed a splendid light in every direction upon the ecclesiastical and secular antiquities of Spain, so that they readily encompass every kind of learning.

### 12

Indeed, the Spanish nation could erect an incomparable monument to the Catholic religion and to tradition if, with the splendor and refinement required by our age, it were to bring into public view the foundations and pillars of its faith and monarchy, and then continuously extend the series of ecclesiastical and secular monuments down to our own times. I speak of the Gothic Bibles, of the Gothic collection of canons, of the martyrologies and the authentic acts of martyrs and confessors, and of whatever concerns the Gothic kingdom; of the works of the holy Spanish Fathers of the Gothic period [Col. 0243B] or of earlier times; and finally of chronicles, whether ancient secular or ecclesiastical historians. Upon these foundations and pillars the edifice of Spanish religion and monarchy rests. From their very beginnings the two have been joined by a fortunate bond, and, God willing, they will remain joined through the long span of the ages.

### 13

Moreover, all these things, individually and collectively, are most closely connected with Saint Isidore and his works. We possess copies of the Bible a thousand years old, containing Saint Jerome’s version but revised by Isidore, who added a new preface to each book; from this arose the *Book of Prefaces*. To each prophet he added an account of the prophet’s life and death; from this was formed the *Book on the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. To the Books of Kings he prefixed a chronological sequence of the kings of Judah and Israel [Col. 0243C], corresponding to his chronicle. He incorporated the Canons of Eusebius, whose use he explained in the *Etymologies*, into a harmony of the Gospels. For easier understanding of Paul’s Epistles, in addition to the verses of Saint Damasus, he added the canons of Priscillian, corrected by a certain Bishop Peregrinus and not yet published. He also supplied summaries, or chapter headings, for almost all the books that are divided in a different order from that of the Vulgate edition.

### 14

Finally, I incline to the view that it is truly asserted in some copies of Saint Braulio’s annotations that the holy teacher produced a fourth edition of the Psalter. Father Juan de Mariana holds this opinion in his note on chapter 2 of book I of *Against the Jews*. He believed that the Psalter of Saint Isidore was the very one used by the Mozarabs, which in fact differs from the Psalter found in our Gothic Bibles, based on Saint Jerome’s translation. Therefore, if we wish to make our Gothic Bibles publicly available, we shall find that they are intimately connected with Isidore’s writings.

[Col. 0243D] ### 15

I now omit the fact that those passages of Sacred Scripture which Isidore repeatedly quotes throughout all his works, in the form in which he himself read them, ought to be examined with careful attention, as Mariana observed in his notes on the works of the holy teacher that he illustrated. The same applies to the passages found in the Fourth Council of Toledo and the Second Council of Seville, which he presided over, as well as throughout the entire Mozarabic liturgy. Nor shall I mention what Isidore wrote in the *Etymologies* concerning the canonical books, their versions, and the explanations of the names of the Old and New Testaments. I shall say nothing either about his *Book of Allegories*, or about his questions and commentaries on almost all the sacred books.

However these matters may stand, we cannot bring into public view the most ancient witnesses to the foundation of our faith without Isidore accompanying them and preserving them in many ways.

### 16

We also possess a great number of genuine and legitimate copies of the Gothic collection of canons, [Col. 0244A] some written in the ninth century, others in the tenth, others in the eleventh, and some in the twelfth. The Spanish Church used this collection almost down to the present age. This work is entirely different from the one printed by Cardinal Aguirre and, after him, Cenni, both of whom were misled by many errors and prefixed the title *Code of the Ancient Canons of the Spanish Church*. The work edited by these authors is only a certain canonical treatise prefixed to the collection in the manuscript codices. Juan Bautista Pérez suspected that its author was Saint Julian of Toledo, though Antonio Agustín did not accept this.

### 17

This collection also differs from the collection of Eastern canons by Saint Martin of Dumium. For Saint Martin’s collection, which some have incorrectly considered the Council of Lugo, is small and is one of the parts of Saint Isidore’s canonical collection, placed among the synods of Braga.

Nor can our Code be that canonical Code of general and particular councils which was read at the First Council of Braga. For, to omit other arguments, that Code was certainly very short [Col. 0244B], whereas ours is extremely extensive.

Our collection is likewise distinct from the collection of conciliar canons and synodal letters of the Roman prelates, which Canon 1 of the Third Council of Toledo, presided over by Saint Leander, approved. For that canon certainly referred to the short, unadulterated collection of Dionysius Exiguus, without the additions of Hadrian I, as did many other canons of that celebrated council.

### 18

The Gothic collection differs still more from the collection published under the name of Isidore the Merchant, or the Sinner. Cardinal Aguirre vainly attempted to free this collection from the charge of forgery and invention, despite the unanimous agreement of the literary world. He also elaborately defended its apocryphal preface, argued that its documents were legitimate, and sought to prove that the work was the genuine and authentic work of Saint Isidore.

What astonishing obstinacy in so learned and diligent a man! He ought to have examined the two outstanding Gothic codices of the true Gothic collection preserved in this primatial Church of Toledo, the five in the library of Saint Lawrence at El Escorial, and the others that he could easily have found in Spain. Archbishop Marca found such a copy in Catalonia, from which he transcribed the true preface, although Aguirre nevertheless refuted him.

I do not know whether even a single old manuscript copy of that pseudo-Isidorian collection exists anywhere in the whole of Spain.

### 19

By contrast, apart from the most ancient Lucan Code, which was burned in the Escorial library—its indexes still survive, and a copy of it was sent to Rome to assist in correcting Gratian’s *Decree*—we possess not only the five Escorial Gothic copies that I mentioned and two Toledan ones, but also another Gothic copy that once belonged to Archbishop Loaysa and is now in my possession, having been designated by the king for the royal library.

We also possess two others in the Gallic character: one belonging to the Church of Urgell, renowned through Mendoza, who transcribed from it the subscriptions of the priests in his commentary on the Council of Elvira; and the other belonging to the Church of Gerona, at whose end are found the two Councils of Gerona that Tavernier of Ardenne sent to Father Hardouin, who in turn appended them after the indexes in volume XII.

There is another copy belonging to the Church of Córdoba; others belong to the monastery of Ripoll; another Gothic copy is in Vienna, Austria, having been brought there from Milan. Finally, there is part of an index from another copy at Celanova in Galicia, which contained the desired Eighteenth Council of Toledo.

I saw this autograph fragment in the possession of Father Sarmiento; Flórez later committed it to print. I omit the codices of the same collection preserved in France, since Father Constant lists them.

### 20

Our Gothic canonical collection is therefore the most extensive, purest, and best organized of all those that have ever existed in the Eastern or Western Catholic Church. It begins with the canonical treatise that I mentioned, published by Aguirre and Cenni, divided into ten books and entitled in the manuscript codices *Excerpts from the Canons*. This work is found arranged in two different ways and, in my opinion, is later than Isidore.

It is followed by the genuine preface, printed by Marca and reprinted by Aguirre. The Roman Correctors of Gratian’s *Decree* also had it before their eyes after it had been sent from Toledo by Álvaro Gómez de Castro.

### 21

Next comes an index of councils. After the index, with no mention of the Apostolic Canons—for in the preface they are rejected as apocryphal and fabricated by heretics, in the very words that Gratian transcribed, although those words are entirely contrary to others that he likewise drew from the spurious preface—comes the Council of Nicaea, consisting of only twenty canons.

These are precisely the canons later repeated at the Sixth Council of Carthage, extracted at that time from the authentic Constantinopolitan records, when controversy arose concerning the distinction between the Nicene and Sardican canons, because Dionysius Exiguus had gathered them together in confusion under the same numerical order and sequence.

The canons of the other Greek councils follow, not in the Latin translation of Dionysius Exiguus, but in another, different version, which the Pseudo-Isidore retained for the most part and which Hardouin, in his great Collection, placed in a separate column under the name of that same Pseudo-Isidore.

### 22

After the Greek synods come the African councils, arranged in order and without the confusion observed in Dionysius Exiguus. After the African councils come the Gallican, and after the Gallican, the Spanish.

Thus the first part of the collection is completed.

The second part, after a brief prologue and an index, presents 102 decretal letters. The first two letters are by Saint Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch; then come three by Siricius; twenty-two by Innocent I; two by Zosimus; four by Boniface; three by Celestine; thirty-nine by Leo the Great, including one from Flavian of Constantinople and another from Peter of Ravenna; three by Hilary; two by Simplicius, one being Simplicius’s letter to Zeno of Seville and the other Acacius of Constantinople’s letter [Col. 0245C] to Simplicius; three by Felix; two by Gelasius; one by Anastasius; one by Symmachus; ten by Hormisdas, among which are one by the emperor Justin and another by John of Constantinople to that same Hormisdas; one by Vigilius; and finally the four letters that Saint Gregory the Great sent to Spain—three to Saint Leander and one to King Reccared.

### 23

In almost all the manuscript copies there is added a decretal concerning books to be received and books not to be received, from which Gratian took the chapter beginning *Sancta Romana*. In all our manuscripts it is attributed to Hormisdas, not to Gelasius. It is also found in another Gothic codex of various treatises, which will be discussed below.

Such a letter, whether by Gelasius or by Hormisdas, was not inserted with the others in the original collection of canons; otherwise it would appear in its proper place. There can therefore be no doubt that it was added to the collection, indeed after the canonical treatise, or *Excerpts from the Canons*. No mention of it is made there, although such a mention ought to have been made if it had belonged to the original collection.

Of these decretals [313] not one is illegitimate or unauthentic, and not one suffers from falsification or interpolation. These alone are the ancient decretal letters known, observed, and read by the Spanish Church—apart from those joined to the Acts of the Sixth Synod—until other letters fabricated by the impersonator Isidore the Merchant came to its knowledge from foreign regions.

### 24

Although most of the documents contained in this collection have already been printed, it would nevertheless greatly benefit the welfare and glory of the Church and the confirmation of the faith of the Spanish nation to publish this second foundation and pillar of its religion and ecclesiastical discipline in the form in which it is found in the oldest copies of unquestioned authority, which agree remarkably with one another in substance, and according to the method, arrangement of chapters, division of titles, and so forth represented by the manuscript codices.

### 25

It would be necessary to make evident to the Christian world that, when a copy of this genuine Gothic canonical collection was brought from Spain to the Franco-Gallic empire—at a time when, in those regions, only the short collections published by Justellus and Quesnell, which Father Constant discusses at length, together with the collection of Dionysius Exiguus, enlarged by Hadrian I and presented to Charlemagne in acrostic verses, were known, at the end of the eighth or beginning of the ninth century—another detestable collection, filled with fabrications, was erected to everlasting disgrace from this Spanish copy as though from its sole soil and foundation.

Nevertheless, it was clearly and expressly attributed to Saint Isidore, under the assumed name of Isidore the Sinner or Merchant. This corrupt work prevailed because the forger wished to lend an appearance of authority to his most pernicious fictions by exploiting the public reputation that the holy Spanish teacher had already acquired throughout the Church through his widely disseminated writings.

[Col. 0246B] ### 26

It would also be necessary to make clear that not only was the most learned Father Turrianus deceived in defending the Apostolic Canons and the decretals preceding Siricius—although he deserves an adequate excuse for this—but that Beveregius too was deceived in defending those same canons. Above all, the learned Cardinal Aguirre obstinately maintained not only that the collection of Isidore the Sinner was legitimate, but also that its true author was the Spanish teacher Saint Isidore.

If the genuine Gothic canonical collection, as it is preserved in so many Spanish manuscript codices, were compared with the collection of Isidore the Sinner, as it was fabricated in the Franco-Gallic empire and from there spread into other regions, Spain excepted—for Spain was then occupied with other matters and oppressed under the Moorish yoke, and we have found no manuscript copy of it there at all—it would clearly appear what has been added, interpolated, corrupted, altered, or fabricated.

### 27

Yet none of this can be accomplished without Isidore and his works [Col. 0246C], for he is being considered as the author. It is therefore necessary to establish by strong conjectures that Isidore composed and arranged our genuine collection after the model of the Dionysian collection, but by a much better method and judgment and with greater abundance and variety of material.

It is equally necessary to show that neither Saint Isidore nor any other Spaniard was the author of the apocryphal collection [314]. Its author may have been the very person who fabricated the chapters, which some titles state were presented to Ingilrhamnus, or Ingelrannus, by Hadrian I, while others—as Sirmond observed—state that they were presented by Ingilrhamnus to Hadrian I.
