This is an entirely different claim. Perhaps both statements are false, and neither has any foundation except the addition by Hadrian I to the Dionysian collection that I have already mentioned.

### 28

Whatever the case may be, it is certain that Hadrian I did not insert those chapters into his addition, although that would have been the most appropriate place for them, as is clear from the two ancient codices of that addition at Ripoll, which I have seen [Col. 0246D].

Since, then, these chapters were fabricated, Aguirre’s chief argument collapses. The author of this spurious collection could also have been Archbishop Riculfus, who disseminated it throughout the regions of the Franco-Gallic empire. Perhaps, however, this prelate acted innocently, having been deceived by some obscure author who corrupted a genuine Spanish codex and foisted it upon Riculfus as something brought from Spain in that form.

### 29

Certainly the Franco-Gallic collection was neither fabricated in Spain nor could it in any way have been fabricated there at that time. The testimony of Hincmar of Reims therefore collapses; on the authority of Hincmar, Labbe and others, including Constant, believed Spain to be the mother of that aborted offspring.

Moreover, certain matters in the collection itself must be considered as pertaining to Isidore—for example, the words of the genuine preface found in the *Etymologies*, including the statement, “The Councils . . . whose proceedings are contained in this work.” These words are entirely inappropriate to the work of the *Etymologies* and ought to have been omitted, as Grial observed.

### 30

It must also be considered that the Fifth General Synod, which was earlier than Isidore, is omitted from the collection. This omission is consistent with the fact that both in the preface and in the *Etymologies* Isidore mentions only four general synods.

It should be investigated what his opinion was concerning the Fifth Synod and the question of the Three Chapters. This can be inferred from what he wrote about the Acephali, Justinian, Victor of Tunnuna, and others; from what he did at the Second Council of Seville with regard to that Eastern bishop; and from Braulio’s preliminary annotation.

### 31

It must also be explained why, in most of the manuscript copies of the collection, the Second Council of Constantinople, the Sixth General Synod, is found together with Pope Leo’s letters to the bishops of Spain, to Quiricus of Toledo, and to the comes Simplicius, as well as the letters of Benedict, the elected pontiff, to Peter, the regional notary, and to King Ervig—all of which are later than Isidore.

Cardinal Baronius did not regard such letters as genuine, because Archbishop Loaysa had produced them as found in only one manuscript copy, that of the royal convent of Saint John of the Kings at Toledo, which is now lost. But Loaysa could have cited the Gothic codex that he possessed and that is now in my possession; likewise two Gothic copies of the Church of Toledo, one of Urgell, one of Gerona, and one of Lugo then existing in the Escorial library, together with others in which these letters are contained after the Second Council of Constantinople.

### 32

Neither Loaysa nor Aguirre observed such letters in the codices mentioned [315], because their purpose and labor were directed exclusively toward the councils of Spain. They did not take the trouble to examine the codices in the section where the Greek councils are placed, not even suspecting that anything relevant to Spain might be hidden there.

Had it been established that these letters were found not only in the Code of Saint John of the Kings but also in all the other copies containing the Second Council of Constantinople [Col. 0247C], perhaps neither Baronius nor the writers who followed him would have doubted their legitimacy.

### 33

It will also be necessary to explain why some codices, such as those examined by Marca at the monastery of Ripoll, present only the councils of Spain up to the Fourth Council of Toledo, while others extend to the Eleventh Council of Toledo, others to the Fifteenth, others to the Seventeenth, and the aforementioned codex at Celanova extends to the Eighteenth and final council. All these councils took place after Isidore.

By what path and method, then, was the collection enlarged by additions, as is indicated by the Ninth, Fourteenth, and Sixteenth Councils of Toledo?

### 34

A sufficient explanation must be given for the fact that, although Pope Leo in his letters accepts and praises five general synods and calls the Second Council of Constantinople, which he sends to the Spaniards, the Sixth General Synod, the Spanish bishops at the Sixteenth Council of Toledo, when subscribing to the Second Council of Constantinople, do not call it the Sixth [Col. 0247D]. Instead, leaving aside the Fifth General Synod, they mention only the four earlier general synods that they imply are contained in their Code, or collection.

What, moreover, should be thought about the extra-collection councils—that is, certain provincial councils that appear out of order in one or another codex, especially in the Aemilianensis Codex of the Escorial library, in which the method of the canonical collection is not observed? Why, since those councils are older than Isidore, are they not found in the other codices in which the collection is properly arranged?

### 35

What, then, is the reason that the letters of Gregory the Great concerning the deposition of the bishop of Málaga were not inserted into the collection, although the event necessarily occurred in Isidore’s time and within the boundaries of the province of Baetica, of which Isidore was metropolitan?

What should also be said about another letter of Saint Leo the Great to the bishops of Baetica and Lusitania concerning the deposition of another bishop, Sabinus? It is found at the end of the Codex of the Church of Gerona, but added out of order, after the collection had already concluded with the decretal letter previously mentioned under the name of Hormisdas.

### 36

All these matters in some way concern Isidore, and all must be discussed if we wish to place our Gothic canonical collection in a proper light.

I omit the fact that, in order to complete the dissertations, one must have recourse to Isidore’s works for commentaries or notes on the history and councils of Spain, since the true understanding of many matters is explained there, especially those relating to the councils of Spain.

I also omit the fact that Spanish monastic discipline depends upon his Rule and the Second Council of Seville, just as the ecclesiastical discipline of the secular clergy depends upon his letters, books, and the Fourth Council of Toledo.

I have spoken at excessive length about our Gothic canonical collection, arranged by Isidore. But since Father Zaccaria asked about it point by point, it was necessary, when you replied, for you to treat this subject at length [Col. 0248B].

### 37

I shall speak more briefly about the Gothic liturgy, which is the third foundation and pillar of our faith, since its connection with Saint Isidore is evident from the very name “Isidorian.” It is called the Mozarabic liturgy because, when this city of Toledo was conquered by Alfonso VI in 1085, several Christian communities were found there that had been preserved from the time of the Goths through nearly four centuries of captivity. They were divided into seven parishes, to which they belonged perpetually by right—not by territory, but by blood and lineage.

These communities, whom the conqueror loaded with deserved honors and to whom he granted the supreme government of the city, were called by a Moorish term *Muzarabes*, or Mozarabs. By this name they were distinguished from the other Castilian and Frankish inhabitants, who were distributed among newly established territorial parishes according to territorial right.

### 38

The same King Alfonso VI took care to abolish throughout his entire dominion not only the Gothic rite, or liturgy, but also the Gothic script [Col. 0248C]. Yet although he could uproot Gothic writing and liturgy from the cathedral churches and monasteries, replacing them with Gallican or Roman script and liturgy, he either could not or did not wish to exact the same from the Mozarabs of Toledo. They preserved the ancient rite in their parishes and still preserve it.

Thus Gothic writing and liturgy remained exclusively with the Mozarabs. For that reason they came to be called Mozarabic writing and liturgy, and the Mozarabic rite and office; the name “Toledan” is added because the rite is retained only at Toledo.

### 39

It was also, and still is, called the Isidorian liturgy, or Isidorian office, because it is held as certain that Isidore was its principal author, at least with regard to the method and arrangement of the entire liturgy and office and to the many parts of which it consists.

When the incomparable Cardinal Ximénez de Cisneros saw the use of this office declining in the Mozarabic parishes, he erected an imposing chapel in this primatial church and founded fourteen chaplaincies, so that fourteen Mozarabic parish priests and beneficed clergy might sing the Mass and all the canonical hours daily according to their own rite.

To accomplish this, he collected all the manuscript books of the parishes and ordered that from them a Mozarabic-Isidorian missal and breviary be prepared and printed, although certain recent materials were added and some ancient ones omitted.

### 40

In the library of this holy church there are still preserved those eight manuscript parchment volumes, written in the Gothic character, which Father Juan Pinius mentions in his treatise on this liturgy, on the basis of the description by Don Pedro Caminus, my friend, who is still alive and now presides over the Mozarabic congregation.

Three others are also preserved, which Caminus did not see, in addition to certain fragments of other books.

Although Father Manuel Azevedo has now reprinted in Rome Cardinal Ximénez’s Mozarabic missal and breviary, furnished with notes, it would nevertheless be necessary for these Gothic manuscript volumes [Col. 0249A] to be published in the same manner as other writers of every nation have published their books, and as Muratori recently published, in 1748, the codices of the ancient Roman liturgy. In two volumes he printed the Sacramentaries of Saint Leo, Saint Gelasius, and Saint Gregory, along with other works, exactly as they are found transcribed in the ancient manuscript copies, with brief notes appended.

### 41

In the new edition of the works of Cardinal Thomasius, in the first volume—which our booksellers divided into two volumes and sold at times as two separate works, with distinct titles and dedicatory letters—Blanchinus inserted a codex of the Gothic liturgy found in the library of the chapter of the Church of Verona.

I have also seen a prospectus of the edition that the Assemani prelates are planning in Rome: fifteen volumes containing the liturgies of the whole world, printed as they lie in the ancient codices.

Our Gothic Mozarabic, or Isidorian, liturgy can, for many reasons, compete in dignity and extent with the liturgy of any other nation. The library of this primatial Church of Toledo alone, as I have already said, provides us with eleven volumes.

There is our Gothic missal printed by Mabillon and reprinted by Muratori; there is our aforementioned codex of the chapter of Verona; and there are our Gothic volumes from the monastery of Cardeña, from which Father Berganza placed certain excerpts at the end of his appendices.

I have no doubt that other Gothic manuscript liturgical volumes are also hidden in other Spanish monasteries, as in the monastery of Cardeña. From these a collection could be completed so extensive that no other nation would be able to produce its equal.

### 42

Martyrologies and their use in the divine office originated in the Church of Córdoba and from there spread to the other Churches, if we may trust the letter that circulates with additions to Ado of Vienne’s Martyrology.

There are some such martyrologies in Spain, and they are sufficiently ancient. This library of the Church of Toledo alone possesses two that differ from one another [Col. 0249C].

We also possess a great number of books of saints and books of the acts of martyrs, which were read in the churches. In this city there are very ancient codices of this kind; in other parts of Spain there are also copies written in the Gothic character and dating from the Gothic period.

Although such monuments were disfigured in Tamayo’s Martyrology, they have not thereby lost the inner foundation of their splendor. Any learned, faithful, and sincere scholar will be able to demonstrate this, provided that, with a prudent and incorrupt judgment free from partisan zeal, he brings their merits to light.

These ancient liturgical documents of Spain cannot be illuminated in any way without Isidore’s assistance: first, because he is their principal author, and second, because light must be sought from his various works. I say nothing meanwhile of the bond linking them with the Gothic Bibles and the Gothic canonical collection.

### 43

If we wish to gather into a single body the works of the ancient saints and ecclesiastical writers of Spain, which constitute the fourth foundation and pillar of our faith’s tradition, and to illustrate them with suitable notes, Saint Isidore must unquestionably be regarded as the foremost of them all, whether one considers the number of his works or their character.

Moreover, Isidore was the first among our people to compile a catalogue of illustrious men, following Jerome and Gennadius. From him we must derive the greater part of our knowledge of the history of our literature and of the lives and works of writers who preceded him.

Those who followed Isidore looked up to him as their common teacher.

### 44

Finally, the foundations of our monarchy, intimately connected with religion, are the Gothic laws and history. The Latin *Forum of the Judges* of the Goths has never been committed to print in Spain.

Editions produced outside Spain could be revised and corrected against the oldest codices that we possess. Three are found in the library of this Church of Toledo. One is Gothic, with Arabic notes of the kind also found in the codices of the canonical collection and of the Bibles [Col. 0250A]. Another is an old copy, six hundred years old, in the convent of Saint John of the Kings. The third is more recent and is in this college of the Society of Jesus.

The Escorial library also possesses other Gothic copies.

### 45

Our divine king, Saint Ferdinand, immediately after conquering Córdoba, and before sketching out the great work to which he gave the title *Partidas*, ordered, with the greatest prudence, that the laws be published in the language of the common people and that the same laws be observed throughout the kingdom, insofar as the nation’s devotion and love for its municipal laws permitted.

For this purpose he ordered the Latin *Forum of the Judges*, which prevailed at Toledo—although the Castilian *Forum* was also in use—to be translated into Castilian. The governor of the Mozarabs, among whom the Gothic laws had been preserved just as the Gothic liturgy had been preserved, was the chief judge of the city and its territory.

After it had been translated, he assigned it to Córdoba as its municipal law and ordered it to be called the *Forum of Córdoba*. He immediately gave the same *Forum of the Judges* in the vernacular to Seville, which he had conquered [Col. 0250B], and likewise to Murcia and Lorca, as soon as they submitted to his son Alfonso the Wise, then an infante and later king.

46. This Castilian translation of the *Forum Judicum* has been printed only once, and that edition very poorly and with innumerable errors, although on the title page of the edition a notary solemnly affirms in a legal attestation that it was conformed to a certain manuscript volume of the Church of Toledo. There are not one but three excellent manuscript copies of this translation in the library of that church; others are preserved in the Escorial library; Colmenares possessed another, as he testifies in his history of Segovia; the city of Murcia still preserves the autograph copy presented by its conqueror; and others are found elsewhere. It is reasonable to suppose that these laws—on which our Spanish monarchy rests as on foundations, which have been observed for so many centuries, confirmed by many kings, and repealed by none to date—should be published in both languages as accurately as possible. Besides innumerable other [Col. 0250C] benefits, one conspicuous advantage is that which accrues to religion, which these laws have confirmed in a remarkable manner.

47. However this matter may be brought to completion, we certainly cannot pass over Isidore in silence. For, if we give credence to Lucas of Tuy, he himself is the principal author of this kind of legal collection; and the collection itself was formed and published at the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided, if the headings and prologue of the Castilian version are reliable. Indeed, nothing prevents us from supposing that, even if the Gothic kings Ervig, Leovigild, and others compiled books of laws—as Alaric had earlier published the *Breviary* and the *Codex Anianus*—Sisenand nevertheless made use of Isidore to give the Code a new form and increase it; and that Chindaswinth and the other succeeding kings in turn altered, corrected, and enlarged it. Moreover, the interpretation of many matters in this same collection must likewise be sought in Isidore.

48. What need is there to speak of history, when it is clear that [Col. 0250D] the sources of our history consist chiefly in Isidore’s chronicles and histories? Finally, if we wish to know what learning our people possessed in those ancient times in every branch of knowledge and in the divine and human disciplines, Saint Isidore is at hand. In his books of the *Etymologies* he constructed an encyclopedia and reduced to a compendium all the arts then known both within and beyond Spain. Although this compendium is sprinkled with certain blemishes, it must nevertheless be regarded as the outstanding work among all those that those centuries produced among any other nations.

49. The bringing together of all these monuments of our venerable antiquity would undoubtedly be a most honorable achievement for our nation. It would provide, in every article of Catholic doctrine, an invincible argument for the reliability of the Spanish tradition from the earliest centuries of the Church; and at the same time, in chronological sequence, it would demonstrate that the supreme authority of the Roman Church and the Apostolic See had been consistently acknowledged in [Col. 0251A] Spain from the first splendors of the Gospel down to our own times. I could use an argument of excellent cumulative force in each of these matters, but it will suffice to indicate certain points relating to the Apostolic See, since the rest are necessarily included in the rightful submission to and communion of faith with that Apostolic See.

50. Whatever one may wish to maintain concerning the arrival and preaching in our peninsula of the holy apostles Peter, Paul, and James, this at least is absolutely certain: our Gothic Church celebrated as its apostles the holy bishops sent into Spain by the apostle Peter, and therefore called “Apostolic.” In the first Christian century they firmly established the Spanish Church in due submission and union with the Roman Church. In the third century, submission to Rome’s supreme authority is shown both by the appeal of the deposed *libellatici* and by the straits into which the commands of the Roman pontiff forced Sabinus and Felix, and the clergy and people who had elected them. They were driven to such desperate extremity that they were compelled to seek the advice of Saint Cyprian in Africa; [Col. 0251B] and they would not have done so had they not acknowledged the legitimate authority that was compelling them.

51. [Col. 0251B] The same thing is confirmed in the succeeding centuries by the appeals, consultations, decrees, legations, apostolic vicariates, and transmissions of relics and the pallium contained in the letters of Siricius to Himerius of Tarragona; of Saint Leo to Saint Turibius of Astorga; of Hilary to Ascanias of Tarragona; of Simplicius to Zeno of Seville; of Felix to that same man; of Hormisdas to John of Elche and to the other bishops of Spain generally, to Sallustius of Seville and the bishops of Baetica; of Vigilius to Profuturus of Braga; and of Saint Gregory to Saint Leander and to Reccared; finally, in the letters of Leo and Benedict already mentioned concerning the subscription to the Sixth General Council. No one presided over the Council of Nicaea other than the great Hosius, bishop of Córdoba. In the First Council of Toledo one may observe the obedience and veneration shown to Saint Leo’s letter concerning Priscillian, [Col. 0251C] which the bishops sent to Balconius together with their rule of faith. The same reverence is repeatedly evident in the First Council of Braga toward the decretal letters of Saints Leo and Vigilius and toward the authority of the Chair of Peter.

52. After the Arian heresy had been renounced, the first undertaking of the entire Spanish Church assembled at the Third Council of Toledo was to receive the authority of the councils and synodal letters of the Roman pontiffs, as is clear from the first canon. At the national Fourth Council of Toledo, under the presidency of Saint Isidore, a letter of Saint Gregory was produced in order to resolve the question of triple immersion. Finally, Saint Isidore himself solemnly professed this very point in the preface to his canonical collection:

> “We also submit the decrees of the Roman prelates, in which, because of the eminence of the Apostolic See, there exists an authority not inferior to that of the councils.”

53. A clear exposition of the antiquities of Spain, carried out by the method that I consider most appropriate, [Col. 0251D] will therefore bring great benefit and glory. But, as is evident from what has been said, none of these matters can be illuminated without Isidore continually before our minds and eyes. It is therefore of the greatest importance that a new edition of all the holy Doctor’s works be carefully prepared—an edition more extensive than those of Grial and Breul and proceeding by a better method. Besides, those two editions are now extremely rare and cannot be obtained by all who desire them.

54. Thirdly, I must inform you that the manuscript works of Saint Isidore existing here are those of which I am now about to speak.

55. In the library of the primatial church, shelf 15, nos. 8, 9, 10, and 11, there are four copies of the books of the *Etymologies*: two written in Gothic script and two in French script. They lack any indication of the time when they were copied. But the first, no. 8, appears [Col. 0252A] so ancient that it is reasonably suspected of having been written before the Moorish invasion. This copy is complete and written with great care. It is adorned with multicolored geometric figures and likewise with musical figures, which are absent from the printed editions; everywhere it is supplied with brief notes and with the corresponding meanings of Arabic words. It was not examined by Álvaro Gómez de Castro and the others who prepared the Madrid royal edition, for it did not pass to the library until 1727 from the more secluded archive of the Sacristy, where it had been hidden. Fathers Benedictines Mecolaeta and Sarmiento, who inspected the Codex, were the ones who urged this transfer.

56. [Col. 0252B] The second Gothic copy, no. 9, written in a clearer and larger script, is certainly no later than the eleventh century. The third, no. 10, written in smaller French script, belongs to the eleventh century; its bindings indicate that it once belonged to the monastery of Oña. The fourth, no. 11, was copied in larger French letters near the end of the thirteenth century or even later. For it is preceded by a preliminary notice of Braulio, which had been interpolated and corrupted by Lucas of Tuy, who flourished in the middle of that century. In this same volume, after the *Etymologies*, is found the book *On the Stars of Heaven*, addressed to King Sisebut.

57. On the same shelf, 15, no. 12, is preserved another Gothic Codex containing the three books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*. It is mutilated at the beginning 321, beginning at chapter 7 of Book I. At the end is written:

> “It ends on the second day before the Kalends of April, at the seventh hour, in the year 953 of the era. Theodemir wrote, although unworthy.”  
> *(Perhaps: “I wrote.”)*  
> “Pray for me.”

It was therefore completed in the year 915. This is the very Codex cited by Archbishop Loaysa in his notes.

58. Another parchment Codex, written in thirteenth-century French script, is preserved on shelf 21, no. 12. At the beginning it presents a Life of the holy Doctor, described in a lengthy account, together with an interpolated *Renotatio* of Braulio, an *Alphabet of Prayer*, certain letters of Isidore himself, an interpolated narrative by Redemptus, [Col. 0252C] some verses under the name of Ildefonsus, and another lengthy narrative concerning the translation of Saint Isidore and his miracles. The whole appears to be the work of Lucas of Tuy, filled with fables. These are followed, in smaller script, by the chronicles of Saint Isidore, Saint Ildefonsus, Saint Julian, and finally Lucas of Tuy himself, who interpolated the rest, as they were published in volume IV of *Hispania illustrata* under the editorship of Father Mariana. Several verses written in this Codex can be recognized as being in the hand of Mariana and likewise of Álvaro Gómez de Castro.

59. On shelf 2, no. 1, is found the celebrated copy of the Gothic Bible, which Mariana judged, on the strongest grounds, to have been written before the Moorish invasion. In their proper places it contains several prologues and eulogies of the prophets composed by Isidore, as well as other ornaments that I described when speaking of the Gothic Bible.

60. On shelf 31, nos. 18, 19, and 20, are found three volumes written in a recent script, which John Baptist [Col. 0252D] Pérez had prepared to be copied from ancient exemplars. They contain councils, works of the saints, and ancient histories of Spain. In this collection he inserted Saint Isidore’s letters to Leudefredus, Massona, Helladius, Claudius, Redemptus, and Eugenius; the *Rule of Monks*; the *Verses of the Library*, published by Tamayo, then by Muratori, and recently by Flórez; the *Alphabet of Prayer*; the *Chronicle*; the *Histories of the Goths, Vandals, and Suebi*; and finally the *Book of [Col. 0253A] Illustrious Men*, as it was printed in the Madrid edition, with sixteen doubtful eulogies added from the Galistean Codex.

61. On shelf 14, no. 23, there is a recent copy, written at Loaysa’s command, of the works of Beatus, Etherius, and Samson of Córdoba that are found in the Gothic Codex of the same library. It is followed by a recent copy of Saint Isidore’s books of the *Differences*, extending to chapter 38 of Book II; the *Rule of Monks*; and the *Book of Illustrious Men*, as it was published by Loaysa in his collection of councils and reproduced by Aguirre. There are certain notes in this book, perhaps by Archbishop Loaysa, though not in his hand, which I know very well.

62. In the royal convent of Saint John of the Kings I saw an old Codex written in French letters containing the books of the *Sentences*. I also saw another ancient parchment manuscript of *The Origin and Death of the Fathers*, which nevertheless contains only the Lives of the Fathers of the Old Testament, although its index promises the Lives of the Fathers of the New Testament as well.

63. I possess a small Gothic Codex of the books *Against the Jews*, formerly belonging to the library of Archbishop Don García de Loaysa and now destined for the royal library at Madrid.

64. I also have a Gothic Codex borrowed from a friend. It is extremely old, written on enormous parchment leaves, but in poor condition and torn to pieces. Among other works it contains the books of Jerome, Gennadius, and Isidore *On Illustrious Men*, together with additions by Braulio, Ildefonsus, [Col. 0253B] and Julian. It also contains the *Book of Allegories* and the *Book on the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, which differs considerably from the printed editions. I suspect that this Codex also once contained Isidore’s book *On Heresies*, which Braulio praises. Finally, I remain uncertain whether a certain acephalous book of brief questions concerning Sacred Scripture, arranged by questions and answers, belongs to Isidore.

65. Among the manuscript volumes of Father Juan de Mariana preserved in this college of the Society, where I am writing these letters, there is a copy of the commentaries on the *Song of Songs* as they appear in the Madrid royal edition; Braulio’s genuine *Renotatio*, together with another interpolated by Lucas of Tuy; the genuine narrative of Redemptus; and, most importantly, a copy of the books of the *Differences*, examined by Mariana against several manuscript Codices, whose variant readings he carefully entered in the margin, identifying the Codices by letter signs. This copy should be highly valued, for in the Grial edition Mariana’s work was entirely omitted.

[Col. 0253C] 66. Fourthly, I inform you that I have examined and collated nearly all the Toledo manuscripts of this kind with the purpose of gradually assembling, as carefully as possible and insofar as my other occupations permit, material for a new edition of the works of Saint Isidore, to be completed at some future time—a task which, as I have already explained, is of the greatest necessity.

67. All who know me know that I have been and remain more than sufficiently generous with whatever knowledge, notes, and curious documents I possess. I owe it to Father Zaccaria to show myself still more generous than to anyone else: first, because he is undertaking a work that I desire most ardently, and which, as I have explained, I regard as so useful and so glorious for the Spanish name; secondly, because Zaccaria, with the immense learning in which he excels, may advance the new edition toward a perfection that I could not attain, especially since he can easily do what I cannot—consult all the ancient [Col. 0253D] manuscript Codices of Italy and the rest of Europe; and finally, because in publishing the work Zaccaria will not encounter the terrible obstacles and innumerable difficulties against which I may perhaps stumble, even if after many years I should be able to complete my labor.

68. Yet in what I am now doing, I am subject not to my own discretion but to the authority of others, nor do I have the right to give away such scholarly labors at will. Therefore I cannot promise Zaccaria’s excellent endeavors whatever assistance and service I may be able to provide unless he obtains the gracious permission of those on whose decision I depend. This learned Jesuit, I think, will judge that my answer is not attributable to inhumanity but to the conditions by which I am bound—conditions that would compel Zaccaria himself to think and answer in the same way. Since I hope that [Col. 0254A] an opportunity will arise to discuss this subject with you again, I shall bring this letter to an end; and once more I declare my particular gratitude both for Zaccaria’s industry and for your own zeal. Farewell. Toledo, 30 December 1754.

69. In these most learned letters of Burriel, certain matters require notice so that they may be read without any offense. Saint Isidore is said to have published a fourth translation of the Psalter in the interpolated, or fuller, *Renotatio* of Braulio, of which I spoke in chapter 4. I have already discussed shortly beforehand the canons of Priscillian, which Burriel did not yet know had been published.

70. [Col. 0254B] Burriel had not specified at which Council of Carthage the twenty Nicene canons had been repeated, although he had left a blank for the number to be supplied. I added that it was the Sixth Council of Carthage, otherwise called the Fifth, under Boniface I, in the year 419. I believe this is the council Burriel meant. The matter itself, however, requires explanation and perhaps some correction. Long before Dionysius Exiguus, who flourished in the sixth century, the Sardican canons had been joined to the Nicene canons in copies of the Roman Church, and the Roman pontiffs called them Nicene, because the Sardican canons were, as it were, an explanation of the Nicene ones. Thus, when Faustinus, bishop and legate of the Roman Church, had presented at the Sixth Council of Carthage a memorandum from Pope Zosimus in which certain Sardican canons were cited under the name of the Nicene canons, and when the Fathers of that Council of Carthage failed to find them in the Greek copies of the Council of Nicaea, they sent a letter on the matter to Boniface, who had succeeded Zosimus, and arranged for authentic copies from Constantinople and Alexandria [Col. 0254C] to be compared. Consult Labbe, *Collection of the Councils*, vol. II, col. 1594, where the twenty Nicene canons are produced, translated from Greek into Latin by Teilo and Tharistus of Constantinople; and again cols. 1671 ff.

71. Burriel relates that, at the time when he was writing, the Gothic breviary and missal, furnished with notes by Emmanuel Azevedo, were being printed in Rome. The matter occurred as follows. Alexander Lesleus, of the Society of Jesus, provided the Mozarabic missal with most learned notes, and it was published in Rome in 1755. Zacharia states in volume I of the *Bibliotheca Liturgica*, p. 63, that Azevedo worked on preparing the edition. Lesleus’s premature death interrupted the publication of the Mozarabic breviary after it had already begun. There still exist in the possession of the most distinguished prelate Joseph [Col. 0254D] Dini, an expert in the sacred rites and ceremonies of the churches, sheets of the Mozarabic breviary that had already been printed under Lesleus’s supervision.

72. I already noted in the text that Sabinus and Felix should be substituted for Basilides and Martial. Basilides and Martial were heretical *libellatici* who, after being deposed, appealed to the Roman See. Sabinus and Felix had been substituted for them, and Cyprian approved their election.

73. As for the other controversies raised by Burriel, a more appropriate occasion will come for stating my final judgment. But now, to conclude this chapter concerning Burriel’s efforts to prepare an edition of Isidore, I shall append [Col. 0255A] a letter that Pedro de Castro wrote to Zaccaria when he sent him Burriel’s longer letter together with the other shorter personal letters mentioned earlier. Pedro de Castro’s letter, composed by him in Latin, is in my possession in autograph.

> To the Most Reverend Father Francisco Antonio Zaccaria, of the Society of Jesus,  
> Pedro de Castro sends greetings.

74. On the day before the Kalends of December, most learned Father, I received your letter, full of goodwill toward me. The reason why I took care, through the Reverend Father Andrea Burriel, to comply with your wishes in the matters concerning your edition of Isidore of Seville—a task which I could not carry out, being of great extent while I was wholly occupied with the weightiest affairs of the college—is shown more than sufficiently by the letters themselves, which I transmit to you: they show what kindness of this sort there has been toward us, what persistence on the same subject, and finally how much you need his assistance. Since, however, they do not indicate from whom you must obtain permission to communicate with him about these matters, I shall state it briefly.

For four years now this most learned man of your illustrious Society, supported by royal authority and a stipend, has been residing in Toledo [Col. 0255B] in order to investigate the archive of that primatial church. I therefore suspect that unless, through your Serene Duke of Modena, you obtain it from the royal ministers—the confessor and the minister of state—I have no confidence that you will be able to obtain it by any other means. I should certainly wish you not to let this opportunity escape. For if an edition is not completed by you, who have consulted nearly all the manuscript Codices, who will undertake it?

As for what you write—that you wish to be informed by some learned man about the books being published here—the wisest man of the Franciscan family, namely the Reverend Father Joseph Torrubia, has undertaken to do this. I enjoy his most agreeable company. But I see that he is so occupied with his writings and afflicted by gout that I am doubtful about his promise. [Col. 0255C] He will also send you a copy of his recently published work, entitled *Aparato para la historia natural de España* [*Materials for the Natural History of Spain*], which I have no doubt you will receive with the greatest favor. I warmly congratulate you on the prefecture of the library which the Duke of Modena rightly entrusted to you after Muratori’s death. Certainly so great a prince, under whose auspices Italian literary history has been and is being published, could not have rendered you a different or greater service. Farewell. Madrid, 11 January 1755.

75. After Zaccaria’s death, among the other letters written to him by distinguished men that I retain, I found three from Burriel: the first in Latin, from Madrid, 20 September 1755; the second in Spanish, from Toledo, 12 December 1755; and the third, also in Spanish, longer than the others and in autograph, from Madrid, 25 February 1759. Omitting other matters that do not concern me—or, if they do concern me, do not belong to this time or work—[Col. 0255D] Burriel says the following in the first letter, in precisely these words:

> “Isidore is a kind of fountain, center, and origin of Spanish wisdom, both ecclesiastical and secular. We do not yet possess all his works in published form, nor have they been illustrated by the method they deserve. A new edition and exposition of all his works, therefore, can bring nothing but great benefit to the republic of letters. I regret only that the teacher of Spain will be illustrated by a man who is not Spanish but foreign, and that the honor of our nation will receive a new distinction from men other than those of our nation, and not without some disgrace to us.”

76. In his Spanish letters Burriel explains that, as far as the studies to which he had devoted himself were concerned, [Col. 0256A] circumstances at the Madrid court had changed: Father Francisco Rábago, who had been the king’s confessor and had persuaded and promoted such literary undertakings, had been removed. Of what he had prepared for the Isidorian edition, he would send nothing at all to Zaccaria without the king’s gracious permission or command. He adds that the Gothic canonical collection, which he had examined against five manuscript Codices, was being kept in the Secretariat of State, as it is called; this too he would willingly grant to Zaccaria, if the king permitted it. In the meantime Burriel, withdrawn from scholarly studies, had devoted himself entirely to explaining scholastic theology and performing the other ministries of the Society, although even during that period he published certain learned works for the general public, suppressing his name.

[Col. 0256B] 77. Together with these letters there is a catalogue of Burriel’s works, compiled after his death. Some had been published, while others remained in manuscript. It is our purpose merely to record the following:

- A Gothic canonical collection, opposed to the collection of Isidore Mercator, in four folio volumes, completed in 1754.
- Manuscript dissertations on this Gothic canonical collection and against Cennio’s errors.
- A manuscript dissertation on the Bibles used in Spain in Isidore’s time, dated 1759.
- A manuscript letter to Don Juan de Amaya on the laws of Spain.
- A letter to Don Pedro de Castro on the canonical laws of Spain.
- The *Forum Judicum* of Spain, with notes and manuscript variant readings.

# CHAPTER XLI  
## Francisco Antonio Zaccaria Entrusts the Prospectus of His Isidorian Edition to the Press

[Col. 0256C]

1. I find nothing else in Zaccaria’s papers indicating that anything concerning the preparation of a new edition of Isidore had been discussed between him and Burriel. Burriel’s scholarly labors, as I already reported from Bayer, were all transferred to the royal library at Madrid and are preserved there. Meanwhile Zaccaria was diligently applying himself to his work. At last he revealed his plans to the republic of letters by publishing a *Prospectus*, of which no copy remained with the author at all except an autograph copy differing somewhat from the published version. But, through the gift of a most learned and distinguished prelate of Reggio—an eager investigator and fair evaluator of such literary materials—I obtained the printed *Prospectus* and judged that it should be inserted into the Isidorian [Col. 0256D] *Prolegomena*.

> *Prospectus of a New Edition of the Works of Saint Isidore of Seville, prepared by Francisco Antonio Zaccaria of the Society of Jesus, prefect of the library of the Serene Duke of Modena.*  
> Venice, 1758, from the Remondinian printing house.

2. Since there are altogether only three editions of all the works of Saint Isidore of Seville—one by Margarino de la Bigne, Paris, 1580; a second, and by far the best, the Madrid edition of Juan Grial, 1599; and finally a third, the Paris edition of the Benedictine monk Jacques Breul, 1601—for the edition printed at Cologne in 1617 is itself a reprint of Breul’s Paris edition and can scarcely be counted as a new edition—nevertheless all men devoted to sacred and secular learning complain that much is still lacking before we possess a complete edition of the books [Col. 0257A] of so great a doctor of the Spanish and indeed Catholic Church, worthy of him. Jacob Hommey had led us to hope for such an edition, but death intervened and he was unable to fulfill his promise. We have therefore considered preparing it, lest so great an adornment should henceforth be lacking to the republic of letters, and above all to the Christian republic. We wish to place before learned men, especially Spaniards, whose glory is particularly involved in this holy Doctor, what we have thus far accomplished and what we are additionally undertaking in order that this edition of ours may be as perfect as possible. We do this before its publication so that, if they judge anything ought to be changed, they may courteously inform us of it, and at the same time communicate to us whatever they believe would contribute to the excellence and usefulness of the long-desired work.

3. Oudinus, in the commentary on ecclesiastical writers and writings that he published at Leipzig (vol. I, p. 1595 ff.), sets out the order according to which a new edition of Isidore’s works, if anyone should prepare one, ought to be arranged. We prefer an entirely different order.

[Col. 0257B]

4. We therefore divide our edition into five volumes. In the first, which we divide into two parts, we shall publish the biblical and dogmatic works of the holy Doctor, first those that are certainly genuine and then those that have appeared to us spurious.

5. The biblical works are as follows:

I. The *Book of Prologues*, compared, in addition to the editions with which we have always collated it, with three Codices: the Veronese, the Cesena, and the Florentine of Santa Croce.

II. The *Questions* and mystical expositions of the sacraments of the Old Testament. We have collated these not only with those authors whom we know to have transferred many of these questions into their own commentaries—Bede and Claudius of Turin—I mean the latter, recently edited from the Pistoia Codex by the distinguished Giovanni Battista Trombellius—but also with two manuscript copies of the Laurentian Library, one more recent and the other extremely ancient. In addition, we have collated them with the distinguished Codex of the Alburnotian Library at Bologna, which Cardinal Alburnoti took pains to bring into conformity with the autograph of Isidore himself, then preserved at Toledo, although [Col. 0257C] damaged in many places by the ravages of time. Among other things, we have thereby discovered that the final chapter of the *Questions on Leviticus* is almost entirely missing from the printed copies.

III. The *Allegories*, collated with the manuscript books of the Veronese, Cesena, and Florentine Santa Croce libraries.

IV. The *Book on Numbers*, which Oudinus thought had perished, while Johann Albert Fabricius wrongly conjectured that it was perhaps not distinct from certain chapters of the *Etymologies*. We shall be the first to bring it forth from an excellent manuscript Codex of the royal library at Turin. It is divided into eighteen chapters, beginning as follows:

> “It is not superfluous to attend to the reasons for numbers in the Holy Scriptures. For they contain a certain teaching of knowledge and very many mystical sacraments. Therefore, as you wished, I have decided briefly to explain the principles of certain numbers. But at the beginning it must be defined what a number is.”

By way of an appendix, a spurious commentary on the *Song of Songs* will be published—not the longer one that the Maurists, its editors, vindicated in opposition to Gussanville, [Col. 0257D] but the shorter one published by Grial and Breul, which many considerations persuade me must be denied to Isidore.

6. The second part of the first volume will contain the dogmatic works of Saint Isidore, as I recently stated. Among these, the first place is claimed by the three books of the *Sentences*, also entitled *On the Supreme Good*. We shall reprint them after collating them with eleven manuscript Codices: the Veronese, Chisian, Barberinian, Pistoia, Lucca, two Florentine Codices of San Marco, three Florentine Codices of Santa Croce, and our own thirteenth-century Codex.

There will follow the two books addressed to his sister Florentina, collated with five manuscript Codices: two Malatesta Codices, two Florentine Codices, and a Lucca Codex. Then will come several letters: to Massona—this one we have collated with two copies, namely the Pistoia and Vienna exemplars—to Helladius, to Claudius the Duke, to Redemptus [Col. 0258A] the archdeacon, and to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo. Concerning the authenticity (*αὐθεντία*, *authentia*) of these we shall argue at length against certain hypercritics.

I mention only these letters here. Those sent by Isidore to Braulio concern, respectively, the books of the *Etymologies*, the *Synonyma*, and the *Rule of Monks*. Since they are, so to speak, dedicatory letters to those books, I do not see why, even though the manuscript Codices almost uniformly oppose it, they should be detached from their proper places.

The book *On the Order of Created Things*, edited by Dacherius, will follow the letters. Although, besides the arguments of Dacherius and Nicolás Antonio, an index from Bobbio, published by Muratori, also assigns it to Isidore, I fear that it cannot be attributed to the holy Doctor.

Finally, several sermons will close the volume—not those two spurious sermons *On the Nativity of the Lord* and *On the Holy Angels* published by Constantinus Cajetanus, for these, as the editor failed to notice, are excerpted from other books of Isidore, but three spurious sermons [Col. 0258B] wrongly attributed to Isidore, which we were the first to recover from libraries: one from the Malatesta Codex at Cesena, *Against the Arians*; another, mentioned by Nicolás Antonio, *On the Praises of Saint Emilianus*, from the archive of Vercelli; and a third from a Florentine manuscript of San Marco. A fourth will be added, published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*. In Martène’s work (*On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, vol. I, Milan edition, p. 410), the very old Codices of Rouen and Pratelli attribute this sermon to our Isidore.

7. At the beginning of this first part of the volume, besides a general preface, there will be two dissertations. The first will discuss the distinguished deeds of Saint Isidore; there we shall also debate his Benedictine monasticism and his body. Following Mabillon, we shall deny the monastic affiliation against Constantinus Cajetanus; but we shall assert that his body is in Spain, contrary to the opinion of certain writers on the history of Bologna. We shall also reprint the saint’s Life, written by Lucas of Tuy and published by the Bollandists, together with the notes of the distinguished Henschenius and our own. [Col. 0258C] We shall reprint the account of his death, narrated by Redemptus, according to the same Bollandist edition, which I collated with Constantinus Cajetanus’s copy, the edition in *Hispania sacra* (vol. IX), and the extremely ancient Vallicellian Codex.

The second dissertation will explain matters concerning Isidore’s teaching and writings. In it we shall therefore discuss the books written by him, both those that have come down to us and those whose loss we regret; the Catholic doctrines that he defended; the version of Scripture that he used; the great reputation for learning that he attained; and the more extensive editions of his works. We shall also illustrate his library by explaining the most ancient verses said to have been inscribed on the shelves of the Isidorian library, as may be seen in Muratori’s second volume of *Anecdota Latina* (p. 208 ff.) and in *Hispania sacra* (vol. IX, p. 376).

8. We likewise divide the second volume of Isidore’s works into two parts, assigning one to ascetic books and the other [Col. 0258D] to those relating to ecclesiastical discipline. The works of the first kind are:

1. The two books of the *Synonyma*, collated with two copies of the Laurentian Library.
2. *On Contempt of the World*.
3. *Exhortation to Repentance*.
4. *Lament of Repentance*.
5. *Prayer for the Correction of Life*.
6. *Prayer against the Snares of the Devil*.
7. *Prayer, or Confession*, published by Constantinus Cajetanus.
8. The *Rule of Monks*, to which will be added from the ninth volume of Martène’s collection the final chapter, or *Rule of Devout Women*; and from the first volume of the Benedictine annals, the *Pact* that the monks of the monastery of Honorias made with their abbot. For Isidore wrote his Rule for their benefit.

These works are genuine. We do not, however, include here the little book *On Converts*, first published by Heinrich Canisius and later reprinted by Cajetanus—not because it should be denied to Isidore, as Basnage foolishly claims, but because, as Cajetanus himself does not deny, it was excerpted from Isidore’s books of the *Sentences*. It will therefore be sufficient to note, in the observations on those books, the chapters from which the little book *On Converts* is composed.

The following will be counted among the spurious works:

1. Fragments of commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, which the recently named Constantinus Cajetanus collected from Peter the Deacon and Smaragdus with misplaced diligence.
2. The little book *On the Rule of Life*.
3. The short work *On the Conflict of the Vices*.
4. The book *On the Instruction of a Good Life*, mentioned by Nicolás Antonio and now published for the first time from the Veronese Codex.

9. The liturgical works occupy the first place among the books concerning ecclesiastical discipline. Accordingly, after the Ascetic works we shall reprint Isidore’s two books *On Offices*, which we have collated with four manuscript codices: one Bolognese, another from Pistoia, and the remaining ones from Lucca. Then we shall publish the letter to Leudefredus and two hymns from the older editions. Of greater scope, however, will be the Dissertation on the Isidorian Liturgy that we shall add as a kind of preliminary study to the little book of Prayers of the Isidorian rite. This book was printed at Rome by the distinguished Father Joseph Blanchini; here we shall publish it again, together with his and our annotations. The Isidorian collection of canons also belongs to the same field of ecclesiastical discipline, both the collection published by Cardinal Aguirre and that published by the learned priest Cennius. Both will be discussed here at some length, along with other collections of canons, from which we shall bring forth certain materials, perhaps hitherto unnoticed and by no means useless. Nor shall we omit the two councils over which Isidore presided, and whose canons he himself perhaps wrote—the Councils of Seville and Toledo—but we shall present them from Aguirre’s edition with the variant readings. Would that we might obtain the materials which the Most Illustrious Father Buriel of the Society of Jesus collected at Toledo for this purpose!

10. The third volume will comprise the Historical works. It will therefore consist entirely of three parts. The first will present sacred and secular history, namely:

1. The *Chronicle*. To free it from the errors and interpolating additions of its reworkers, we have used, besides the editions of Aguirre, Schelstrate, and others, five very ancient codices: the Vatican, the Lucchese, the Pistoian, the Florentine codex of San Marco, and the Cesena Malatesta codex. Since we found the *Chronicle* extended to the tenth century in three codices, we shall publish these continuations for the first time, not without, as we hope, benefit to learned men.

2. The *History of the Goths*, which we shall publish from Labbe’s edition, without omitting the variant readings of the other editions.

3. The book *On the Life and Death of the Fathers*, which, despite the opposition of many critics, we shall vindicate for its author, using three codices for the variant readings: the very ancient Veronese codex and two Florentine codices, one of San Marco and the other of the Medicean-Laurentian Library.

11. Nor did Saint Isidore neglect literary history. We do not think, therefore, that our fellow Jesuit Hardouin should be heeded when he counted among the spurious books the Isidorian little work *On Illustrious Men*. Relying on Dupin’s arguments (*Preface to the fifth volume of his Library*) and on the authority of ancient codices, we reject that paradox. I examined seven codices in all and compared them with the Fabrician edition, which is the latest edition of this book: the Barberini, the Este, three Florentine codices, and two Bolognese codices. The celebrated Father Abbot Trombellius most courteously made the last two available to me.

12. Among the Isidorian works there is also a little book that may be assigned to natural history, namely the *Book on the Nature of Things*. For this reason we shall have it printed in the third part of this volume, after revising it against four manuscript books: one from Lucca, another Florentine codex belonging to the richly endowed Medicean-Laurentian Library, and the remaining ones from the Florentine Library of San Marco.

13. This third part will be enlarged by an Appendix. In it we shall publish the Blessed Isidore’s *Image of the World*, a little book plainly alien to Saint Isidore, whose name it bears as its title, but outstanding in the abundance and usefulness of its subject matter. We shall be the first to publish it from a manuscript codex which the most courteous Father Gabriel Laget of the distinguished Augustinian order shared with us. Although it is in reality a work of Honorius of Autun, in our codex—where it is attributed to Isidore—it differs considerably from the printed copies. It will therefore not be useless to present it here as well.

14. The philological works remain. Accordingly, in the fourth volume we shall gather the first twelve books of the *Etymologies*.

15. In the fifth volume, however, we shall include the remaining eight books, together with the variant readings that we have drawn from eight manuscript codices: Vatican Codex 624, the Este codex, the Chisian codex, the Bolognese, the Lucchese, the Florentine codex of San Marco, and two Malatesta codices. The older of the latter two is assigned to the seventh century by the Most Illustrious Father Giovanni Domenico Mansi, in book IX of Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca Latina mediae et infimae aetatis*, p. 190.

We shall append to the books of the *Etymologies* the *Glossary*, together with the observations and emendations already published by the most celebrated scholars Giovanni Ludovico de la Cerda, S.J., Johann Georg Graevius, Theodor Jansson van Almeloveen, Barthius, Schurzfleischius, and Daumius, as well as the unpublished and very extensive observations of the learned Giovanni Salomon Semler, who sent them to me from Altdorf in 1752, with the greatest and truly commendable generosity. Finally, in this volume I shall include the three books of *Differences*, collated with two Lucchese codices and two others, one belonging to the chapter of Pistoia and the other to the Florentine Library of Santa Croce.

16. Four indexes will put the finishing touch to the work. The first will contain the scriptural testimonies used by Isidore. The second will contain the authors whom he cites. The third will contain the subjects contained in the books of the Saint. The fourth will contain the subjects explained in the annotations.

17. Thus far I have followed the order of the books and the various readings by which they will additionally be illuminated. I shall now explain briefly the method of the edition itself.

18. First: in the prefaces that will precede each of Isidore’s books, we shall:

1. Assert that the book in question belongs to the holy Doctor.

2. Report all, or at least the principal, editions of those books. In the Dissertation on Saint Isidore’s doctrine and books, we shall number only those editions that contain the complete Works.

3. Carefully review the codices against which we examined them, and discuss their antiquity.

19. Second: we wish the variant readings to be separated from the annotations.

20. Third: the annotations, both our own and those of others, shall not be relegated to the end of the volumes, as is customary; rather, we shall present each in its proper place, with the names of the authors attached.

Written at Modena, from the library of the Este princes, on the Kalends of January, in the year 1738 of the common era.

21. Before this printed overview of the Isidorian edition, I find in Zaccaria’s papers another and different plan for completing the edition, or rather a different distribution of the works devised by him. Five volumes are also designated in that earlier overview.

The first volume was to contain the prolegomena and the first twelve books of the *Etymologies*. The second was to contain the remaining eight books of the *Etymologies*, together with the variant readings, the *Glossary*, and the three books of *Differences*. The third was to contain the historical books of the holy Doctor, then the ascetic works, and finally the book *On the Nature of Things*. The fourth was to contain first the biblical works, then the dogmatic works, and finally the liturgical works. The fifth was to contain the doubtful works, or those certainly spurious.

22. Among these spurious works is listed a more extensive commentary on the *Song of Songs*, which the second overview is said to omit. Similarly, the earlier overview counts among the spurious works the *Scriptural Testimonies*, about which the other overview is entirely silent. The words of the earlier overview are:

“*Scriptural Testimonies*, an unpublished little book in the most ancient Veronese Codex, from which we shall be the first to bring it into public circulation.”

The Most Illustrious Maffei had once resolved to publish it. In Zaccaria’s papers there is no other mention of this little book. Evidently, unwilling to allow Zaccaria’s edition to be delayed any longer, he published it in the second volume of the *Literary Excursions through Italy*. We shall place it among the appendices, since it appeared to the Most Illustrious Maffei to be Isidorian. A fuller discussion of it will return in chapter 83, where we shall examine the opposing arguments of Zaccaria, who does not believe it to be a genuine work of Isidore, and Maffei, who attributes it to Isidore.

23. The passage of Dupin in which the book *On Illustrious Men* is defended against Hardouin is identified from the preface to volume V of his *Library*. In the edition that I examined, however, I found it not in the preface to volume V but in that to volume IV. Zaccaria’s judgment concerning Isidore’s writings will be assessed below in its proper place, when each work is discussed.

## CHAPTER XLII  
### Zaccaria’s New Efforts to Produce an Isidorian Edition: A New Overview of This Edition. Observations of Don Pedro Manuel Hernández, Prefect of the Archiepiscopal Library of Toledo, on This Overview

1. Although Zaccaria published an overview of the Isidorian edition at Venice in 1758, he nevertheless allowed several years to pass without seriously turning his attention to bringing it to completion. Perhaps he was occupied with other, more necessary duties; perhaps he was impeded by the misfortunes of the times that followed. After the suppression of the Society of Jesus, he began to consider how he might fulfill the promise he had made to the learned world.

Among his papers I possess a copy of a supplicatory memorial to His Holiness Pope Pius VI, either submitted or prepared for submission. In it Zaccaria begged the Supreme Pontiff to attempt, through the Nuncio to the Catholic King, to induce the Most Eminent Cardinal Francisco Xavier Delgado, Archbishop of Seville and Patriarch of the Indies, somehow to undertake the patronage of the Isidorian edition. At that time Zaccaria requested the following:

“Reserving the request that Your Holiness later grant some assistance for consulting at leisure and without expense certain codices of the Vatican Library, as I once obtained from His Holiness Benedict XIV.”

2. Delgado did not long enjoy the dignity of cardinal. He was admitted to the College of Cardinals in 1778 and exchanged life for death in 1781. For this reason, or for some other, Zaccaria’s hopes came to nothing. Perhaps even the letters that Zaccaria had written to the Most Eminent Delgado were never sent to Spain. I possess two copies of them, one entirely written in Zaccaria’s hand. Neither specifies the day or year on which they were sent or were to be sent. I do not wish them to be lost; they run as follows:

3. “Most Eminent and Most Reverend Lord, my Lord,

“You may perhaps wonder, most eminent prince, that I, who am unknown to you, should dare to write to you concerning a matter of great importance. Do not, however, attribute this to inconsiderate rashness; attribute it rather to the dignity that you sustain in the Church of Seville and to your exceptional virtues, whose reputation increases among us from day to day. I shall explain the matter itself at once.

4. “In 1758, when I was still librarian to the Most Serene Duke of Modena, out of my devotion to the illustrious Spanish nation I published an overview of the new edition that I had begun to prepare of the Works of your great predecessor and the most distinguished Doctor of Spain, Saint Isidore. Yet from that time onward, owing to many difficulties, I have so far been unable to fulfill what I promised.

“Many people, both among our own countrymen and abroad, regret that the labors I have expended in collating manuscript codices of Isidore’s Works throughout Italy have been fruitless. I myself regret this above all, since I understand that those labors will likewise be fruitless in the future unless I find a most munificent and beneficent patron who will both contribute the resources needed to complete the work and undertake, at his own expense, to have the edition produced in Rome under my direction and supervision, as splendidly as possible, so that it may fully answer to the name and dignity of so great a Doctor and of the Spanish Church.

“This would be done with the certain hope that the expenses of the entire undertaking—which could not, without doubt, be small and might reach two thousand gold pieces—would be generously reimbursed by the sale of the copies, which ought to number 750. But so be it. While I was often thinking of these matters, and not without sorrow of heart, it fortunately occurred to me that the See of Seville, whose immortal glory and protection Isidore is, is held by Your Eminence. To whom, then, should I flee? Whose patronage could I implore with greater right and with firmer confidence of obtaining what I seek than that of Your Eminence, who cherishes with singular devotion Isidore, your most holy and learned predecessor?

5. “I know, indeed, that a new edition of the Works of Isidore has recently appeared at Madrid. I have so far waited in vain to receive from Spain two copies of it, indispensable for completing my work more easily, together with volumes XVI and those that follow of Flórez’s *España Sagrada*. But if you have enough leisure to compare with that edition the overview of my edition which I submit to you, you will immediately understand that it will not only fail to hinder my efforts but that, in your wisdom, you will judge them still necessary for producing an excellent edition of so great a Father.

6. “Come, then, most eminent prince, embrace with your kindness one who is laboring for the glory of your predecessor and for the benefit of the universal Church, and do not allow this most desirable edition to be delayed any longer for lack of the necessary resources. If these are supplied, it can easily be begun within six months and completed within three years, perhaps even sooner. While the first volume is being published, the remaining two can be completed most conveniently.

7. “When you have read this, call your Isidore repeatedly to mind, and consider that he is making entreaty to you partly on my behalf, partly on his own behalf and for the dignity of his books. If Your Eminence reflects on this, I am certain that you will not refuse the role of the most generous Maecenas, of which I am in the greatest need. Farewell, most eminent prince, and pardon my boldness in addressing you in such a way, so that you may favor my love and devotion toward Isidore and my most obedient good will toward you. Rome.

“Your Eminence’s most humble and devoted servant.”

8. These letters show that Zaccaria had already conceived the plan of completing the edition of Isidore’s Works in three volumes, although he had formerly promised five volumes. What this new overview was like may be inferred from the one that Zaccaria soon afterward sent to the Most Excellent Archbishop of Toledo, now the Most Eminent Cardinal Francisco Antonio Lorenzana.

I possess two autograph letters from Zaccaria to the Most Eminent Cardinal Lorenzana. They are so covered with frequent erasures and corrections that one may reasonably doubt whether the copy sent to Spain agrees with them in every respect. In substance, however, I believe there was scarcely any difference. I suppose the first letter was written in 1782; it begins without any heading:

“Zaccaria’s letter to the Most Excellent Archbishop of Toledo, now the Most Eminent Cardinal Lorenzana.”

9. “The letters from Toledo revived me. From them I had learned with what generosity of spirit you had decided not only to present me with those magnificent editions of the Fathers of Toledo and of the Councils of Spain, but also to enrich the edition of all the Isidorian books that I have been laboring to prepare for many years with the addition of some remarkable work hitherto unpublished, and to assist this very undertaking with some financial support, difficult though the times are.

“Indeed, I could have expected nothing else, whether I considered the dignity of your most distinguished See, which boasts of having had Isidore as president of two councils held there, or your singular devotion to the ancient Fathers of Spain, of whom Isidore is unquestionably the foremost, or the exquisite learning in which you excel.

10. “But allow me, most excellent prelate, to open my mind to you with complete frankness: I was somewhat troubled when I later learned that you were considering having this edition of mine produced at Toledo. If I were to object, I feared that I might appear either ungrateful for the great kindness you had shown me or troublesome and importunate in my request. Nevertheless, I must disclose to you the very serious reasons why I greatly wish to dissuade you from this plan.

“The first and certainly the most weighty is the great distance that separates us. Most recently, after being exhausted by waiting for two or three years, I finally managed to obtain at Cádiz the last edition of Saint Isidore from Madrid that I needed. Yet the vessel carrying my Isidore was lost twenty-five miles from the port of Livorno. Could not the copy of my work that I sent you for publication be lost on the same journey—or even, as has happened more than once, there at the printer’s itself, or through some similar accident elsewhere?

“You will say: keep another copy with you. But no one understands better than you how difficult it would now be to have those three very large volumes copied and then reviewed with the utmost care, as would be absolutely necessary, amid such an abundance of variant readings and annotations. The edition would consequently be greatly prolonged, and the copyists would have to be paid a very large sum.”

11. “But what if I possess in my notebooks a great many things—almost innumerable things—relating to the edition, while very few are ready for the press? My intention has always been that, once I had found a Maecenas like you who would arrange for the edition to be printed at his own expense, with the costs properly reimbursed through the easy sale of the printed copies, I should then for the first time apply myself to it, committing at the same time to writing whatever was to be published and delivering what I had written to the printer for typesetting.

“You will not be surprised at this, most excellent prelate, since you understand well how tedious it would have been for me to correct the text, add variant readings, and explain obscure passages with suitable annotations of my own and of others, without any certain hope that such a laborious work would ever finally be brought into the light of day.

12. “You see, therefore, that I cannot think about the edition anywhere except in Rome, where I live. Let me have the money: it will be undertaken within a month or two, and it will never cease until it is completed.

13. “Moreover, frequent doubts are bound to arise, especially concerning the variant readings, which can scarcely be resolved except by a new and very easy consultation of the codices that are available here in great number. But what if my manuscript copy were there with you?

14. “These, so as not to be more lengthy than is proper, are the most serious reasons why I consider a Roman edition necessarily preferable to a Toledan one. If you weigh them in light of your experience in these matters, why should I not hope that you will judge them fair and reasonable? Nor do I fear that your assistance will fail me.

“I therefore ask you first of all to inform me what sort of unpublished work of Saint Isidore I understand to be hidden in your possession. Once you have communicated this to me, I shall immediately publish here a new overview of my edition and disseminate it widely throughout Italy, Spain, France, and other regions, inviting learned men to attach their names to the edition without paying anything in advance; they will pay the agreed price only when they have received the individual volumes.

15. “Next, I particularly ask that you not refuse to allow this Isidorian edition to be dedicated to your illustrious name. Since I have no doubt that the number of associates will be sufficient to provide the expenses of the second volume and subsequently of the third, it will be an act of your kindness and of your devotion to Isidore to provide at least as much money as you judge necessary for the first volume to be prepared by copyists and completed with the greatest magnificence by the printer. The condition, however, will be the one I mentioned above: you must know that whatever you spend will be reimbursed to you through the number and sale of the copies.

16. “See, most illustrious prelate, with what freedom I speak to you. Please do not take this amiss. Attribute it first to my frankness, and then to your own affability, which has enabled me to recognize in you a most loving Father. Meanwhile, I shall not cease to ask the most holy Bishop of Seville to preserve you safe and unharmed for the Spanish Church for as long as possible. From Rome.”

17. In these letters Zaccaria mentions the new overview that he was preparing to publish. But, as I believe, he had already arranged for a brief overview of the Isidorian edition to be conveyed to the Archbishop of Toledo through two distinguished members of the Order of the Most Holy Trinity: one, Father Antonio Quevedo, the Procurator General, then residing in Rome; the other, Father Martín Ortega, prefect of the Castilian province. They were extremely eager to advance the Isidorian edition to a successful conclusion.

This perhaps explains why Zaccaria believed that the Archbishop of Toledo wanted the Works of Isidore to be printed at Toledo, whereas the highly esteemed prelate had in fact designated the Madrid presses for the edition. I likewise refer to the report received by Zaccaria that some unpublished work of Isidore was hidden with the Bishop of Toledo. I find absolutely no mention of this either in the letters of that prelate or in the observations of Don Pedro Manuel Hernández, prefect of the archiepiscopal library, which I now begin to discuss.

18. The Archbishop of Toledo sent the new overview mentioned above to his librarian so that he might give his opinion of it. I possess a copy of the librarian’s Spanish letter to the Archbishop, dated 15 December 1782. Hernández briefly explains the overview of the edition that Zaccaria had published on 1 January 1758, which is also mentioned in the *Trivultian Memoirs* in December of the same year. He prefers the new overview and praises Zaccaria’s great zeal to the highest degree, in order to move the Archbishop to undertake the patronage of the work.

He observes that Zaccaria is already advanced in age, and that it is in any event necessary for the edition to be compared with the Spanish manuscript codices, especially those that escaped the diligence of the correctors of the royal Madrid edition. He therefore suggests that suitable men in Spain should be appointed to whom the collation of the manuscript copies could be entrusted, and that Zaccaria should select one or more persons to undertake the same work, should anything human happen to him.

19. Hernández considers Zaccaria’s new overview not yet complete. Although the bookseller Ulloa has recently wasted his effort and expense on the Madrid edition, the appendices to that edition must nevertheless have a place in the new edition being prepared. Moreover, the overview presents as legitimate certain works that are either spurious or at least doubtful. Hernández promises to deal with these at a more convenient time.

He kept his promise. The Archbishop of Toledo sent his Latin observations on the overview of the edition prepared by Zaccaria to Zaccaria himself, together with the following letter, which bears the Archbishop’s seal. Since it is especially worthy of being read by everyone, I append it here:

“To the Most Illustrious Lord Francisco Antonio Zaccaria, Francisco, Archbishop of Toledo, sends greetings.”

20. “Your letters were exceedingly welcome to me, full as they were of love and reverence toward our father Isidore—for we are joined by the same affection. You rightly prefer his Works to those of the other Fathers of Spain. For although Saint Julian may rightly be called a theologian in his presence, nevertheless, because of the all-encompassing learning of Isidore, I embrace your judgment with both arms.

21. “The Spaniards have nowhere consigned his remarkable writings to oblivion. The monks in particular have diligently cared for learning, preserving, copying, and committing them to the press, although not as much as would befit so great a teacher. You, however, as though born in this western land and imbued with its literature, have for many years devoted yourself to them with constant attention, examined and investigated his judgments, diligently searched out manuscripts, compared them most faithfully with others, and long meditated upon a complete edition of them all.

“I praise your zeal, I rival your hopes, and my own aims are directed toward the same end.

22. “Do not be surprised that I still persist in my view that the edition should be produced at Madrid and nowhere else. Very many private and public considerations compel me to this. Nor do I begrudge foreign printers their work, being content with the Madrid edition and relying on the labor of many years that you have undertaken. I hope that it will surpass the others.

23. “I had already understood the same difficulties with which you press me to accept your judgment, before Father Ortega wrote back to his fellow religious, Father Quevedo. If you wish, read the notes that my librarian added to the overview of your new edition, as well as the additional notes he will add. The edition will therefore be more exact—not because it is fuller, but because it is truer, more correct, and more consistent with the enumeration of the works of the holy Doctor made individually by his most beloved Braulius of Zaragoza.

24. “I shall disclose my mind in a single word. You yourself call Isidore the president of two councils held at Toledo; we testify that he presided only at the Fourth Council. As for the council called that of Gundemar, he was not present, but merely signed it at the king’s request. Moreover, the manuscript codices preserved in Italy, Gaul, and elsewhere, having been carried away from Spain, may perhaps not agree with those at Toledo and the Escorial. And while we wish to prepare a perfect edition, we may perhaps run onto even greater shoals.

25. “Therefore, most illustrious sir, do not delay in sending your scholarly labors as soon as possible. We shall not depart from them by even a hair’s breadth, and your name shall be heard throughout the edition, even if the edition is produced at my expense. We shall first copy them accurately; and if anything more obscure or difficult should arise that appears to require correction, nothing will be changed without your consultation and knowledge: I give you my word.

“Meanwhile I beseech Almighty God to preserve you for a long time in health and safety. Madrid, 20 March 1783.”

26. In Zaccaria’s Isidorian papers I found the following letters of the Most Eminent Cardinal Lorenzana.
