After Zaccaria’s death, among the other letters of distinguished men addressed to him that I retain, I came upon two from the same most learned cardinal: one dated 8 January 1786, the other 14 September 1789. In them he strongly urges Zaccaria to complete the edition of Isidore.

I do not believe that the supplementary notes of the archiepiscopal librarian, promised in the copied letter, were sent to Zaccaria in Rome. I possess the notes themselves, filled with exceptional learning, and I think they should be inserted here. I shall first give Zaccaria’s overview, marked with numbers and letters to which the notes correspond.

### Brief Overview of the New Edition of the Works of Saint Isidore of Seville, Which Francisco Antonio Zaccaria Has Been Preparing for Many Years

27. The complete edition will consist of three volumes, although the Works will be divided into seven classes, as it were.

The first part will contain the biblical works, namely:

1. The *Book of Prologues*.

2. *Questions and Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments on the Old Testament* +.

3. *Allegories*.

4. A book *On Numbers*, never before published, from the Royal Turin Codex.

A spurious commentary on the *Song of Songs* will be added (1).

The second part will present the dogmatic works. These are:

1. The three books of the *Sentences*.

2. The two books addressed to Florentina, his sister.

A doubtful book *On the Order of Creatures* will be added (2).

The third part will be ascetic, namely:

1. The book of *Synonyms*.

2. *On Contempt of the World* (3).

3. *Exhortation to Repentance* (4).

4. *Lament of Repentance* (5).

5. *Prayer for the Correction of Life* (6).

6. *Prayer against the Snares of the Devil* (7).

7. *Prayer, or Confession*, first published by Constantine Cajetanus (8).

8. The *Rule of Monks*, but complete (9).

Spurious works will be added in the customary manner, namely:

1. Certain fragments of commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

2. The little book *On the Rule of Life*.

3. The *Booklet on the Conflict of the Vices* +.

4. The book *On the Formation of Life*, now published for the first time from the very ancient Veronese chapter codex, where it is attributed to Saint Isidore.

All these works will be contained in the first volume.

28. The second volume will likewise have three parts.

The first part will contain a few letters and sermons attributed to Isidore in manuscripts (10).

The second part will contain matters pertaining to ecclesiastical discipline, namely:

1. The two books *On Offices*, together with the letter to Leudefredus and two hymns. There will be added the *Book of Prayers of the Isidorian Rite* (11), edited by the Most Illustrious Blanchini from a Veronese codex, preceded by a Dissertation on the Isidorian Liturgy.

2. The Isidorian collection of canons, both that published by Cardinal Aguirre and that published by Cennius, together with our judgment concerning both (12).

Two councils will be added, over which the holy Doctor presided and whose canons he himself perhaps wrote.

The third part will contain the Historical works, namely:

1. Works that present sacred and secular history, specifically:

   1. The *Chronicle*.

   2. The *History of the Goths* (13).

   3. The book *On the Life and Death of the Fathers*.

2. The work pertaining to literary history, namely the little book *On Illustrious Men*.

3. The work that can be assigned to natural history, such as the little book *On the Nature of Things* (14).

29. In the third volume we shall reprint the philological works. These are:

1. The twenty books of the *Etymologies*, to which we shall append the *Glossary*, together with the observations and emendations of the most distinguished scholars.

2. The three books of *Differences* (15).

Four indexes will close the volume:

1. The scriptural testimonies used by the holy Doctor.

2. The authors whom he cites.

3. The subjects contained in his books.

4. The subjects explained in the annotations.

Two dissertations will precede the entire work.

In the first we shall publish the life of the holy Doctor.

In the second we shall discuss his writings, doctrine, and editions.

All the works of the holy Doctor that we publish will be collated with the codices of approximately fifty of the most celebrated Italian libraries and illustrated with notes, both our own and those of others.

### Observations of Don Pedro Manuel Hernández, Prefect of the Archiepiscopal Library of Toledo, on the Brief Overview of the New Isidorian Edition

30. The Works of Saint Isidore were reprinted with insufficient care at Madrid in 1778, in two folio volumes, from the presses and at the expense of Bartholomew Ulloa. But in the edition that the Most Illustrious Zaccaria is preparing, he ought to add, from the appendix at the end of volume II, those little works that we shall mark in the notes to his overview with the letter A.

### Notes on the Overview of the Isidorian Edition Prepared by Francisco Antonio Zaccaria

31. With respect to the royal Madrid edition of 1599, in the preparation of which, for more than twenty years and by order of Philip II, the most distinguished scholars labored—as John Grial records in the preface—it is necessary for Zaccaria to follow it as the text, since it is far more complete than all other editions, whether earlier or later.

The variant readings should therefore be adapted to it, so that, unless the text can be restored to a better form by the authority of some codex, it should always be preferred to the others, whose wording should be relegated to the bottom of the page. This does not prevent the correction of the typographical errors with which it abounds, nor the relegation to the Appendix of doubtful or spurious works that it includes among the legitimate works.

Indeed, among the genuinely Isidorian works, if one excepts the book of *Numbers*, which we have not seen, scarcely any others can, in our judgment, be counted apart from those contained in the royal edition, as will appear from the observations appended below. I therefore thought that, retaining only those works, we should place the rest in the Appendices.

32. + Let fragments be added from pages 54 and 64 A.

33. (1, and so forth through 8.) Since the book *On Contempt of the World* has been assembled from the book of *Synonyms*, it will be the offspring of an unknown compiler rather than of Isidore, as Breulius himself now suspects.

The *Exhortation to Repentance*, the *Lament of Repentance*, and the prayers *for the Correction of Life* and *against the Snares of the Devil* also appear to us to be cut from the same cloth. The *Exhortation* is almost entirely metrical, a fact that no one has noted, and I consider its mention of Cyprian the Magus, later a priest and martyr, alien to Isidore. None of the Spanish calendars of saints mentions him.

Thus Cyprian is thought by the author of the *Exhortation* to be *Surius*—perhaps *Syrus*; otherwise the error is enormous. For the rest concerning this martyr, see the Antwerp records under 26 September.

In the *Prayer for the Correction of Life*, apart from the fact that its author makes abundant use of the Vulgate version of the Bible—which neither the holy Fathers nor the Spanish interpreters of the seventh century used in that period—he, whoever he may be, took from Isidore the material that he treats concerning repentance and satisfaction, namely from book VI of the *Etymologies*, final chapter, and book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 13.

The *Prayer against the Snares of the Devil* seems to have the same, though uncertain, author. The other prayer, published by Constantine Cajetanus, is literally a chapter, or the final section, of book I of the *Synonyms*. Therefore these little works, as well as the book *On Converts* published by Cajetanus himself, deserve to be relegated to the class of the apocrypha.

### 34. (9)

Whatever may be thought about Braulio’s *Praenotatio*, which mentions the *Rule of Monks* among Isidore’s works, we regard the *Rule* published under his name as altogether suspect, and believe it to be the offspring of some unknown monk—neither a Spaniard, however, but a later writer than Isidore—who cites Isidore’s words from book III, chapter 21 of the *Sentences*, under the name of a certain Father, in chapter 5 of Holstenius’s edition.

We call him a monk because, speaking here of monks, he says: “Therefore we too must be free from the affairs of the world,” and so forth. Yet no one would say that Isidore ever donned the monk’s cowl unless he were utterly blinded—and were regarded as such, and actually were so.

We judge the author to have been a foreigner because the monastery of Honoriacum, to which the *Rule* appears to have been written in the same edition, is wholly unknown among the Spaniards, whatever Ceillier may say about it. The days of fasting mentioned in chapters 11 and 12 of that *Rule* differ completely from those described by Isidore in book I, chapter 38 and following, of *Ecclesiastical Offices*. Moreover, the author of the *Rule* twice insists upon the feast of the Circumcision, of which there is not a word in Isidore. In Isidore’s time, in fact, a solemn fast had been prescribed for that day, as is clear from chapter 41 of the aforementioned book I and from canon 10 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. The Spanish Church began to celebrate the feast of the Circumcision a few years after Isidore’s death. Among us there is no older record of this matter than law 11, title 1, book II of the Visigothic laws, promulgated by Reccesuinthus around the year 650.

Finally, the order of the chapters differs greatly in Holstenius, Grialius, and Breulius; and Holstenius has duplicate chapters, some of them containing additions absent from the other two editions. All these things, I say, and several others that will occur to anyone who examines this *Rule* more closely, seem to us sufficient grounds for removing it from Isidore.

### 35. (10)

The letters published under Isidore’s name that are addressed to Redemptus, Duke Claudius, and Bishop Eugenius are spurious, as Bona, Mabillon, Nicolaus Antonius, Fabricius, Ceillier, and the Ballerini brothers of Verona have demonstrated.

At least doubtful, on account of the arguments of Morinus, Aguirre, Espenius, and Ceillier, is the letter addressed to Massona, although the Antwerp Fathers and Flórez argue the contrary.

The other letter, addressed to Helladius, will appear to be of dubious authenticity if the discipline it mentions is compared with canons 6 and 28 of the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo, and with title 13 of Martin of Braga’s collection. Those passages establish that a bishop, priest, or deacon entangled in a crime must, before approaching another tribunal, submit to the judgment of the synod of his own province. The priest of Córdoba suffered nothing of this sort.

Blessed Isidore, being thoroughly versed in the canons, would not have sent the guilty man to a synod so that he might be deposed from his rank, but so that the Fathers might confirm or revoke the sentence he had pronounced. Besides, there was no need here to lodge an appeal, since the accused confessed the crime of sexual misconduct and the canonical penalty of deposition imposed upon such offenders was questioned by no one.

Moreover, the author of the letter appears to have belonged to an order other than the episcopal. These words—“The pastoral care rests upon you, and divine judgment has ordained that the errors of offenders be examined by your judgment, saying: ‘The priests shall stand in my judgments, and shall judge between what is holy and what is polluted’”—these words, I say, who would acknowledge as spoken by a bishop, and by so eminent a bishop as Isidore?

I pass over the supine error found in the old Complutensian Codex, mentioned by Ambrosius Morales in book XII, chapter 20, of the *Spanish Chronicle*: namely, that Isidore wrote the letter to Helladius and that the Third Council of Toledo took place at that time. The council itself makes clear that Leander occupied the see of Seville and Euphemius that of Toledo.

For all these reasons, therefore, I judge that the letter should be removed from the number of Isidorian letters. As for the remaining letters, I should like them to be published with the notes of the author of volume XXX of *Hispania Sacra*.

### 36

We have seen no other sermons circulated under Isidore’s name apart from those published by Constantinus Cajetanus. The first of these is chapter 26 of book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*. The first part of the second is the whole of chapter 10 of book I of the *Sentences*; its second part, however, is composed from Gregory the Great, book XXVIII of the *Moralia*, section 3, except for the passage from Daniel inserted by the compiler.

The same, or a similar, judgment should be made concerning the sermon on the feast of Saint Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli, mentioned by Nicolaus Antonius, and concerning any others published or unpublished under Isidore’s name. But since, as we have said, they have not come to our notice, we shall await the judgment of learned men.

Add to these spurious works the sermon *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, page 45 A.

### 37

As for the hymns, I have no doubt that I should remove them from Isidore. Regarding the letter to Leudifredus, however, I sense some ill omen, though I cannot say precisely what it is.

Among the manuscript codices that contain a not entirely pure, disguised-Isidore collection, this letter appears under the title: “Letter of the Pope, bishop of Seville, to Laudefredus of Córdoba,” as the Ballerini brothers of Verona report in volume III of their edition of the works of Saint Leo, page CCXXXV.

What is read in some of the codices containing it concerning the office of the archpriest—as Breulius printed it in the text and John Baptist Perez in his notes—will seem entirely foreign to Isidore’s mind and to the discipline of the Catholic Church during its first eight centuries. I would therefore judge it to be the product of a patchwork writer, stuffed with material from book II of the *Offices* of the blessed bishop.

### 38. (11, 12)

I shall not object if this edition gives a place to the little book of *Prayers* published by Blanchini, to the collection of canons compiled by Aguirre and reprinted by Cennius, and to the two synods convened under Isidore’s presidency. In my judgment, however, we shall by no means approve Isidore as their author.

They should therefore be printed again as an appendix, as Quesnellus and the Ballerini brothers did in their edition of the works of Saint Leo, together with the *Sacramentary* and the *Code of Ecclesiastical Canons*.

It must be observed, however, that Blanchini greatly went astray in his notes, particularly in the note dealing with the beginning of the year among the Spaniards, where he was led by the authority of a codex that is manifestly corrupt at this point. Wherever it reads “the fourth day before the Kalends of January,” it must certainly read “the fourth day before the Nones,” so that the prayers are assigned to the second day of January, not to the twenty-ninth of December.

For this reason they are placed in the Codex immediately after the feast of the Circumcision, whereas at the fourth day before the Kalends of January mention is made of the feast of John the Evangelist, which we celebrated on that day at least until the eleventh century.

### 39

We shall reprint the collection of canons, excessively disfigured in the editions of Aguirre and Cennius, in its most correct form at the end of volume II of the *Collection of the Holy Fathers of Toledo*, where it properly belongs.

Although we do not agree with the very learned John Baptist Perez, who thought that Saint Julian composed it, we nevertheless have no doubt that it was arranged around his time.

Place the *Exposition of the Mass*, page 54 A, among the spurious works.

**(13)** According to some codices, a panegyric of Spain, page 66 A, may precede the *History of the Goths*.

**(14)** A fragment of this little book appears on page 51 A.

**(15)** Among the philological works, why should no place be given to the verses on pages 47 and 67 A?

### 40

I hold Hernandez’s distinctive learning and sharp judgment in the highest regard. Whether his opinions can be maintained in every respect, however, when I discuss the individual books of Isidore, I shall examine at length.

In Zaccaria’s new prospectus I note that he silently passes over the *Image of the World*, attributed in some places to Saint Isidore, although it has Honorius of Autun as its author. He had once promised to publish it from a manuscript codex that differs greatly from the printed editions. Yet in his *Adversaria* I find neither a leaf nor a trace of the *Image of the World*.

### 41

Who, then, would believe that Zaccaria, warmly invited by the archbishop of Toledo in the most flattering letters to send his scholarly labors to Spain, stubbornly refused, and did not understand that the Spaniards did not sufficiently trust that a foreigner, however learned, would embrace Spain’s own affairs with the understanding and caution required?

Yet he again offered reasons why he could not comply with the archbishop’s request. These reasons survive in an autograph copy of his letter, filled with deletions and corrections, which I present here:

> To the most excellent and most reverend lord, Don Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana, bishop of the Church of Toledo: Franciscus Antonius Zaccaria wishes happiness.

### 42

The letter which you, most illustrious archbishop, deigned to write to me—most devoted to Saint Isidore of Seville and most gracious toward me—I received on the fifth day before the Ides of April.

Would that I were able to satisfy your desire and send you the works of so great a doctor prepared for the press, so that they might be printed in the most elegant Madrid type. Nothing would be more pleasing or more honorable to me.

Yet, as I remember writing to you, although I have nearly arranged the various readings of the Italian codices and preserve in my papers much else relating to the notes, I scarcely have anything ready—not only to send there, but even to hand over immediately to a printer here.

For I had decided, once I had obtained the latest Madrid edition, to compare it with the older Madrid edition and gradually to enrich it with exact variants and notes at the very time when the printer would commit it to the press. This would have been much more convenient for me and would not have subjected me to the expenses which I could not bear, yet which would have been unavoidable if I had arranged for the whole work to be copied out by amanuenses.

### 43

Since, therefore, I cannot, even against my will, think about the Madrid edition that you desire, you will grant me permission, most excellent prelate, to take another route in preparing this edition here—one that, if less splendid, will at least be easier and more suitable for me.

I understand the straitened circumstances under which the printers here labor. I also regret that I am in serious financial difficulty, although the amanuenses must be paid for their work, and paid more generously in proportion as they must be more accurate.

Nevertheless, I hope that the Society’s assistance, which will be offered before the edition in a public announcement to learned men, and especially to Spaniards, will provide the printers with substantial support.

**[Note: “Huiates,” from the interjection *hui*, that is, “to be pitied.” EDIT.]**

### 44

As for me, relying upon your indulgence, I do not hesitate to undertake the matter, using the advice communicated to me by the most distinguished man who serves as your librarian. I do so all the more willingly because most of his suggestions agree entirely with my own views, even though I concealed them in the brief prospectus of my edition.

Come, therefore, illustrious archbishop, and permit me, in view of your singular kindness, to ask three things of you.

First, since you do not cease to undertake, at such enormous expense, a new and magnificent edition among you of the Mozarabic Breviary, the Fathers of Toledo, and the Councils of Spain, I ask that you not refuse to contribute some subsidy toward preparing my edition of Isidore. Although I should most eagerly wish to prepare it nearby in Madrid, so as to comply with your wishes, the plans adopted earlier in my life prevent this; the subsidy need only suffice for the initial expenses of the necessary apparatus.

### 45

Second, I ask that you send me, as soon as possible, the books which you had led me to hope for.

Finally, I earnestly beg you to grant this consolation to an old man of seventy who reveres you most deeply and greatly praises and values your labors for the glory and interests of Spain’s most noble Church: let the Roman edition of Isidore’s works appear under the protection of your illustrious name, as a witness to our own age and to posterity of my most humble devotion toward you.

If you make this one thing possible for me, I shall immediately publish a new and sufficiently extensive prospectus of the entire edition and devote all my efforts to beginning it as quickly as possible.

Farewell, most excellent bishop, and extend your favor to me, who kiss your sacred hands.

Rome, on the Ides of April, 1783.

### 46

What was discussed after these letters of Zaccaria—whether those sent to the archbishop of Toledo or those written with the intention of being sent to him—I do not know at all.

Yet from the matter itself, and from the two later letters of His Eminence Cardinal Lorenzana, which I mentioned in section 26, it is sufficiently clear that nothing was done afterward.

At that time the archbishop of Toledo, moved by many and very weighty reasons, had decided that an edition prepared by Zaccaria—certainly a most learned man, but perhaps not equally well acquainted with our affairs—should be undertaken in Spain.

Zaccaria could not accomplish this unless he assumed the arduous task of arranging exactly everything he had prepared and completing what he had promised, so that it might be sent to Spain already prepared for the press.

Already worn out by old age, impeded by various occupations of the greatest importance, and unaccustomed to the laborious comparison of the text with manuscript and printed copies, he had only one aim: with financial assistance, to try to bring the matter to completion in Rome, both by himself and through others, with the greatest convenience possible.

Certainly Zaccaria had promised many things in his public prospectuses which he intended to complete but had not yet begun, as I shall now explain more distinctly.

## CHAPTER XLIII  
### Zaccaria’s apparatus for an edition of the works of Saint Isidore reviewed. His papers for the first volume

### 1

Since the most learned man of our age, Zaccaria, had labored for forty years and more on preparing a new Isidorian edition, the expectation of learned men concerning such an apparatus ought surely to be extraordinary.

That expectation is somewhat diminished, however, among some people when they turn their attention to the countless works of every kind of learning which Zaccaria composed, elucidated, or arranged for publication at this very time—works which it is scarcely possible to understand as having proceeded from one man. I say nothing of the many other works, great in size or varied in subject, which he undertook and promised, and which at his death he left among his papers.

In recent years, when most people had already despaired of Zaccaria’s edition of Isidore, it also occurred to me that, although I was considerably occupied with printing other works, I might turn my attention to preparing a new edition of Isidore’s works. Yet it seemed wholly unworthy that Zaccaria’s labor should either perish or, if the Spaniards ceased their efforts, pass into the hands of others.

Accordingly, in July of the previous year, 1794, chiefly at the urging of His Eminence Cardinal Don Stefano Borgia, an outstanding cultivator of all branches of learning and patron of learned men, Zaccaria consented that all his papers concerning Isidore should be brought to me.

### 2

I shall describe them as I received them.

In addition to the letters already mentioned, there was a *Life of Saint Isidore* copied from the Bollandists with a preliminary commentary, as well as a handwritten history of the translation of Saint Isidore’s body, also from the Bollandists. Neither the *Life* nor the history of the translation was complete, and both had been copied incorrectly.

The notes that Zaccaria had promised were missing. There were only certain variant readings for Redemptus’s account of Saint Isidore’s death, taken from a Vallicellian codex.

Nicolaus Antonius had devoted two chapters—chapters 3 and 4 of book V of his work—to illustrating Isidore’s life and teaching. Zaccaria had therefore arranged for these two chapters to be copied in the same manner, that is, from the first edition and consequently without the annotations added by Bayer in the Madrid edition, which is fuller on this subject than on most others, since Bayer too had contemplated publishing the works of Saint Isidore.

Zaccaria had promised two dissertations: one on the life and deeds of Saint Isidore, the other on his teaching and writings. Neither had been begun, much less completed, unless perhaps he meant the *Life* extracted from the Bollandist Acts, which I have mentioned, and the two chapters of Nicolaus Antonius’s *Bibliotheca Hispana*.

He had also intended to discuss Isidore’s genuine letters, the Mozarabic liturgy, and the Spanish collection of canons, but he had not applied his hand to the work.

He had decided to preface each of Saint Isidore’s books with an introduction, but I find only a draft for the book of *Prooemia* and another for the book *On Illustrious Men*. I shall publish them when I discuss those books.

Since he had considered printing the *Prooemia* first, he had begun preparing a prologue for that work. He had decided to publish *On Illustrious Men* together with the whole of Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*; hence we possess a prologue to that book.

### 3

He had decided in certain places to add his own annotations to the older notes of others. I find no completed annotations of this kind, except a few for the book *On Illustrious Men*, together with references to passages of certain authors from which he might have drawn light if he ever undertook that labor.

After his death I acquired the Royal Madrid edition of Saint Isidore, in the margin of which he had similarly added the names and passages of certain authors.

He had collected, especially through others, variant readings from numerous codices, which he intended to place beneath the text in an ordered arrangement. But after undertaking this difficult labor, he stopped at the very threshold.

His plan had been to publish the book of *Prooemia* before all the others, as I recently said, and this is evident from the prospectus of his edition. Thus he had begun arranging the variant readings as follows:

**VARIANT READINGS**

**I. B. E.** *The book of the Prooemia, authored by blessed Isidore.*

**Br. E.** *In the name of the Holy Trinity begins the book of the Prooemia of Blessed Isidore, concerning the books of the Old and New Testament.*

**C. C.** *Here begins the book of the Prooemia concerning the books of the New and Old Testament, by Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.*

**V. C.** *In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Be my helper, Holy Trinity. The dialogue of Saint Jerome the priest begins the book of the “premiums” [sic].*

### 4

Only these materials, written in Zaccaria’s own hand, were found in a large bundle of blank sheets prepared for recording variant readings.

The sigla refer to the editions of Bigne and Breulius and to the Cesena and Verona codices, as Zaccaria himself had noted in the prologue to the book of *Prooemia* mentioned above.

You can see, therefore, that apart from having amassed a kind of forest of materials, Zaccaria had nothing else prepared for the edition. He openly admits this himself in his letters to His Eminence the cardinal and archbishop of Toledo.

It remains for us to enumerate the codices which Zaccaria claimed in his prospectus to have collated, preserving the order he himself established.

I should first point out, however—and I shall observe this more distinctly in the appropriate places—that Zaccaria collated few codices himself, while most were collated by others.

Although it would have been desirable for Zaccaria himself to compare Isidore’s published works with manuscript codices, we must nevertheless be content with the riches he left behind. I truly regard the large supply of collations as riches: some of them appear sufficiently accurate in themselves, and some were collected from very ancient manuscript copies.

### 5

The *Prooemia*, which Zaccaria intended to publish first, had been collated with three codices: the Veronese, the Cesena, and the Florentine of Santa Croce.

He described them in the preface, which I shall insert in its proper place.

I possess the variant readings of these three codices, but they are not in Zaccaria’s hand, except in the first chapters of the Cesena Codex.

### 6

The *Questions on the Old Testament* had been collated with two manuscripts of the Laurentian Medicean Library and with the notable Albornozian Codex, or, as Zaccaria calls it, the Alburnotian Bononian Codex.

The collation of these three codices was delivered to me together with a certification by Andrea Petri Julianelli, who was acting as deputy for the royal librarian of the Laurentian Library.

He states that the first codex, perhaps written in the eleventh century, is in quarto, plut. 19, no. 31, and that the second, a fifteenth-century parchment codex in folio, is plut. 21, no. 18. Both, he says, were collated by the most diligent students of the Florentine college of the Society of Jesus at the request of the most learned Francis Zaccaria, under Julianelli’s direction and, on occasion, with his assistance in interpreting the script.

He continues, particularly concerning Codex 31: it is of venerable antiquity and certainly holds second place after the parchment codex of the eighth century preserved in the Toledo library, written in square script.

The canon of Barcelona Bayer told me that he himself had collated this codex and intended to revise and illustrate Alvar Gómez’s edition of these commentaries.

### 7

For “Alvar Gómez” the name of John Grialius must be substituted. He prepared the Royal Madrid edition and illustrated this work with his notes.

I reviewed Bandini’s words, in which he related the same account about the Toledo Codex collated by Bayer, in chapter 39, and gave reasons why the account seems doubtful to me.

Bandini adds in volume I of the *Codices of the Laurentian Medicean Library* that Codex 31, plut. 19, parchment, in smaller quarto, supplemented at the end by a different but likewise ancient hand, consists of 193 written folios and appears once to have belonged to the Camaldolese hermitage.

After the title of the book *Questions on the Old Testament*, a table of its 31 chapters is provided.

After Isidore’s book, the same codex contains anonymous commentaries on Genesis, on Solomon’s Proverbs, and on Ecclesiastes; and on page 184, *Interpretations of the Sayings or Passages of the Old and New Testaments*.

It begins: “The names of the rivers that flow out of paradise.”

It ends: “and delights in the corruption of the ancient wickedness.”

### 8

The title of the Isidorian work is:

> In the name of the Lord. Here begins the Codex by Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, explained from the five books of Moses and the remaining books of the Old Testament, and collected from various authors into one work and expounded with clarity. Here begins the prologue.

In Zaccaria’s papers the wording is recorded as: “explained . . . collected . . . expounded.” Perhaps the Codex has precisely this reading.

### 9

Bandini describes Codex 18, plut. 21, as follows:

A parchment codex in folio from the beginning of the sixteenth century, extremely fine, with an image of the author, the coat of arms of Leo X, and a coin of the Emperor Antoninus on the first page, together with beautifully painted and illuminated initials.

In Zaccaria’s papers and in Julianelli’s certification, the Codex is said to belong to the fifteenth century.

Number 1 is the five books of the *Sentences* of Caius—“Taius” should be read—or of Taio, surnamed Saorohel, or Samuel.

*Letter to Quiricus . . . Table of the chapters of the five books.*

Book I begins: “God alone is unchangeable in himself.”

The final book ends: “we shall see him as he is.”

A letter of Quiricus to Taio follows: “Behold, most blessed of men,” and so forth.

At the end: “Here ends the book of the *Sentences* of Samuel, bishop.”

### 10

The most distinguished continuer of *Hispania Sacra*, Risco, published these five books of the *Sentences* in volume XXXI, although they are mutilated at the end, as I shall explain more fully in chapter 47.

Nicolaus Antonius discusses Taio in book V, chapter 7, of the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, as does Bayer in his notes. Both are entirely silent concerning Taio’s surname Saorohel, or Samuel. I shall make several observations about this in the cited chapter 47.

When Mabillon says in his *Analecta* that Taio seems to him to have been the first person after whom others, including Peter Lombard, formed collections of this kind, he may have forgotten that before Taio Isidore had composed three books of *Sentences*. Taio most certainly imitated him, as will be clear to anyone who reads both authors. The matter will arise again in the cited chapter 47.

### 11

Number 2 of this Codex contains Saint Isidore’s *Questions on the Old Testament*.

Bandini says that the distinguished Francis Antonius Zaccaria had this Codex collated with the printed editions in February 1756.

Its title is:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity begins the little book which Isidore, bishop of Seville, collected from various works of the Fathers. Concerning the exposition of the History.

### 12

I wish Bandini had noted whose image is painted at the beginning of the Codex: Taio’s, Isidore’s, or both.

This practice is observed in some ancient codices, in which images are provided of the author or authors whose works are being copied. I shall discuss this matter more fully in these *Prolegomena*, chapter 105.

### 13

The celebrated Albornozian Codex, no. 11 in the Bononian library of the Spanish College of Saint Clement, must now be described.

It is a parchment codex in folio from the thirteenth century.

An exposition of the psalms by an uncertain author is placed at the beginning.

It is followed by:

> A brief and most useful exposition of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the Heptateuch—that is, on the five books of Moses, Joshua, and Judges—and thereafter on Ruth, ending with Kings. Isidore, bishop of Seville, on Genesis.

The preface is omitted. The commentary on the books of Kings is also missing.

The final book is Ruth, which concludes as follows:

> With him be honor and glory forever and ever. Amen.

It was collated as well as possible.

### 14

Immediately afterward, in the same hand and the same ink, this fragment is added:

> The adamant stone—corrected from *adamans* to *adamas*—has a bronze-colored appearance. The priest wore it when he entered the Holy of Holies, but three times a year: at Passover, Pentecost, and the Feast of Tabernacles, that is, the erection of the tabernacle. For over the tunic the priest placed the breastpiece, in which this stone was situated before the chest. The breastpiece descended only a little below the chest: its length, from the right to the left over the breasts, was one and a half palms. [The passage is obscure.] In it were two *scota*—perhaps *scuta* or *scutula* should be read—each with its own emerald. Between the two [obscure] little shields was the adamant. Between the shoulders, on either side, were twelve precious stones.
>
> When the priest therefore prayed for the people, and his prayer was not acceptable to God, the color of the adamant sometimes changed to black, signifying mortality among the people; sometimes to blood-red, signifying a sword against the people, as in Jeremiah:
>
> “Let all the dwellings approach: those appointed to death, to death; those appointed to the sword, to the sword; those appointed to pestilence, to pestilence; those appointed to captivity, to captivity.”
>
> But if the color of the stone changed to white, the priest knew that the people were free from sin, and they celebrated solemnly with joy.
>
> Hence the prophet says:
>
> “Keep your solemn feast, Judah; fulfill your vows to God. The Lord has taken away your iniquities; he has delivered you from the hands of your enemies. The Lord will reign in your midst, and you shall not see evil.”
>
> Therefore, when Zachariah, the father of John the Baptist, had first assumed the priesthood according to the annual course, the stone became white; Saint Jo . . . was signified when . . . Zachariah stood in ecstasy in the Holy Place, and the people were greatly afraid. Another priest entered the Holy Place and displayed the breastpiece to the people. Thus everyone understood that Zachariah had seen an angelic vision.

The copyist of the Codex adds the following after the fragment:

> Let the one who wrote this write on, and live always with the Lord.  
> May the good man, happy in name, live in heaven.

### 15

Isidore discusses the priestly vestment prescribed in the law in book XIX, chapter 21, of the *Etymologies*, and in chapter 59 of the *Exposition of Exodus*. These passages may be compared with the fragment.

The words of Jeremiah appear to come from chapter XV, verse 2, where the Vulgate reads:

> Thus says the Lord: Those destined for death, to death; those destined for the sword, to the sword; those destined for famine, to famine; those destined for captivity, to captivity.

The stories about the priest displaying the breastpiece to the people are apocryphal. Epiphanius, in *On the Twelve Gems*, and Suidas under the word *Ephod* report that the adamant was joined to the gems of the breastpiece, and that God answered those who consulted him through its radiance.

Procopius, Arias Montanus, and others add two gems for this purpose; these may perhaps be the two little shields mentioned by this author. See Calmet under the heading “Urim and Thummim.”

The name of the person who copied the Codex is expressed in the final two verses: “the good man,” or “Homobonus.” Among us there is a famous Dominican named Alfonso Bonushomo, who flourished in the same fourteenth century as Albornoz and, as some believe, in the same city of Cuenca in which Albornoz was born. Many centuries later, his family, bearing that surname, remained in that city under the name Buenhombre.

Why should we not conjecture that this very Alfonso Bonushomo was the copyist of the Codex?

I see that the Codex is assigned to the thirteenth century. But is it certain that it should be assigned to the thirteenth rather than the following century? Rochus Menchaca, who inspected the Codex at my request, thinks it appears to belong more probably to the thirteenth than to the fourteenth century, but leaves the matter undecided.

### 16

It would be still more useful, if there were any hope of discovering it, to investigate the exemplar with which the copyist is said to have compared this Codex.

In his prospectus Zaccaria states that Albornoz arranged for this Codex to be compared with the Isidorian autograph itself, which was then preserved at Toledo.

Yet, as can be gathered from the variant readings, Albornoz himself performed the collation. For Zaccaria, as well as others who collated the Codex, observes that variant readings were written in Albornoz’s hand. He sometimes notes: “Isidore in the original,” or “Isidore says in the complete original.”

The value of this Codex is certainly greatly increased by the fact that so eminent a man compared its text with the autograph, or Isidorian original.

I should nevertheless like to know what proves that an autograph work was then preserved at Toledo.

### 17

On this matter too I sought the advice and judgment of my friend Rochus Menchaca.

After carefully examining the Codex and conferring with Don Simon Rodriguez, rector of the Spanish College at Bologna, who, with the learning for which he is distinguished, had most courteously offered the old copies of his college for the completion of the Isidorian edition, Menchaca wrote to me as follows:

> I have sometimes read in the parchment manuscripts “Isidore in the complete original,” and more often “Isidore in the original.” The characters of these annotations appear to be not much later than the age of the Codex and are not very different from the characters of Albornoz found in scholia to a certain book of Justinian, where it is noted that the hand is Albornoz’s. It is not at all clear, however, that the variant readings were written into the Isidorian Codex by Albornoz, or that an original existed at Toledo.

### 18

As for the variant readings extracted from that source, some are in Zaccaria’s hand, while others are in the hands of three or four people who appear to have divided the labor among themselves.

I also wonder whether the hand of Don Pietro de Castro appears anywhere. From the letters of the recently mentioned Rochus Menchaca, I certainly learned that a note now visible in the Codex indicates that it was collated in 1752 by Don Pietro de Castro, while he was a member of the Albornozian College.

In the recent Madrid edition, chapter 17 on Leviticus was supplied from the Albornozian Codex, using Don Pietro de Castro’s apograph as the exemplar.

Finally, I observe that this outstanding Codex appears to have been collated with uncommon diligence. Perhaps Father Giovanni Luigi Mingarelli and Don Pons, a student of the same college and later archdeacon of Tortosa, also contributed some portion to these variant readings. They assisted in collating this and other Isidorian copies in 1748, especially a fifteenth-century manuscript of the *Etymologies*, at the end of which are summaries of each of the twenty books.

### 19

**Allegories.** Zaccaria had promised a collation of three codices for this work: the Florentine of Santa Croce, the Veronese, and the Cesena. These are the same codices discussed above in connection with the *Prooemia*.

In the Florentine Codex of Santa Croce, after the *Prooemia*:

> Likewise, Isidore to Orosius.

At the end of the *Allegories*:

> Here ends the book of the first [*Prooemia*] of holy Isidore to Odorosius [sic].

This suggests that both works were dedicated to Orosius under the title of *Prooemia*.

In the Veronese Codex:

> Here begins the little works of Saint Isidore.

In the Cesena Codex:

> Here ends the life, or death, of the saints who have gone before us in the Lord. Here begins the letter of Saint Isidore to Orosius the priest.

### 20

**On Numbers.** I possess, to be published in its proper place, this little work divided into 27 chapters, not 28 as it is reported in the prospectus of Zaccaria’s edition. It was copied by an unknown hand.

I give the description of the Turin Codex from the *Catalogue of the Manuscript Codices of the Royal Turin Athenaeum*, by Antonio Rivautella and Francesco Berta, part II, page 12, Codex 53, d. 4, 30:

> A parchment codex of the eleventh century, consisting of 201 folios, containing the complete work of Saint Isidore of Seville, *Origins* or *Etymologies*, divided into seventeen books . . . Nothing is missing from our Codex. Only the order of the chapters has been altered, and so forth. There is, moreover, considerable variation in the readings, and so forth.

The authors of the *Catalogue* note that among the prefatory letters there is also a letter of Isidore beginning: “With every desire.” They provide a specimen of the variant readings.

[Col. 0278A] **21.** Folio 193 contains the book *On Numbers* by the same Isidore of Seville, preceded by a table of chapters. The compilers of the Catalogue observe that Dupin made no mention at all of this book, while Oudin and Cave thought that it had completely vanished from human hands. “We possess,” they continue, “the complete work in our Codex, by the favor of the gods above; [p. 354] and for that reason we have judged it worthwhile to provide here a complete analysis of it, until we either publish it among the *Anecdota* or prepare a new edition of St. Isidore’s works with the aid of this manuscript Codex.” They reproduce in an engraving a specimen of the script from the beginning of the book *On Numbers*. They appear to have contemplated publishing all Isidore’s works. Zaccaria, in *Italian Literary History*, vol. II, book II, chapter 5, states that Rivautella intended to commit the book *On Numbers* to print—[Col. 0278B] perhaps because he had received this information from some particular report; for in the passage I have quoted, the compilers of the Catalogue indicate that an edition of the book was to be prepared either among the *Anecdota* or in the projected new edition of St. Isidore’s works.

**22.** In the same Turin Codex, folio 20, page 2, there is a very brief treatise *On Alleluia and Amen*. *Alleluia* means in Latin, “Praise the Lord.” Folio 202 contains *Figures*, such as are generally found in the authors. *Endiadys* is a figure in which one thing is divided into two, with a conjunction inserted between them. The compilers of the Catalogue infer from the style that both these little works are by Isidore. The first little work appears among the fragments published by Breulius after the *Etymologies*. The second concerns schemes or figures, on which Isidore treats in Book I of the *Etymologies*. On the front of the Codex, Philibert Pingonius, [Col. 0278C] to whom it once belonged, left a written statement that he had received it as a gift from the celebrated Cujas in the year of human salvation 1367.

**23.** The last work of the first part was a brief commentary on the *Song of Songs*, spurious; nothing about it is recorded in Zaccaria’s *Adversaria*. We have it published in Grialius’s edition, reprinted by Breulius.

**24.** The three books of the *Sentences* belonged to the second part of the first volume. Zaccaria had promised various readings from eleven manuscripts. I found various readings from three Codices of Santa Croce in Florence. The first is a parchment volume in folio, perhaps of the tenth century or certainly of the eleventh, in which, besides these books, are the *Dialogues* of St. Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, no. 230.

[Col. 0278D] **25.** The second is a parchment in quarto of the fourteenth century, no. 233; see Zaccaria’s preface to the book of the *Prooemia* below, chapter 62. The third is at least a twelfth-century parchment in folio, no. 231, in which, after the books of the *Sentences*, follows a book of St. Augustine’s *Exhortations* to a certain count, his very dear friend. These three Codices belong [p. 355] to the same bookcase, namely case XX, on the church side. The letter to Massona, which precedes the books of the *Sentences* in Bignaeus’s edition, is absent from all of them. An amanuensis or friend of Zaccaria collated these Codices with that edition; the same hand is observed in other collations as well. He noted only those variant readings in which these three Codices either agree [Col. 0279A] with the Lucca Codex or at least differ from the printed edition.

**26.** Codex no. 230 ends: “The third book has happily been completed. Thanks be to God, amen.” Codex 233: “The third book of St. Isidore has happily been completed. Thanks be to God, amen.” There seems not to have been much diligence in recording the differences among the manuscripts.

**27.** The collations of the Lucca Codex mentioned above, made in the same hand, are with Bignaeus’s edition and with another, older edition of these books, namely that of 1483. The Codex belongs to the Chapter Library of Lucca; it is a parchment volume in folio of the eleventh century, bookcase 2, no. 56. It also contains the books *Against the Jews*, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and the book *Of Differences*; in addition, Alcuin’s books *On the Trinity*, with his letter to the emperor Charles, [Col. 0279B] and the epigram beginning, “O king,” etc.

The title of the Codex is: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the prologue of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, to Massona, bishop.” The prologue is absent from the edition of 1483. After the prologue and the table of chapters: “The first book of St. Isidore, bishop, begins.” At the end: “The book of the *Sentences* of St. Isidore, bishop of Hispania, has been completed. Thanks be to God, amen.” There are many remarkable variations of wording in this old Lucca Codex.

**28.** The books of the *Sentences* were apparently collated with two manuscript Codices of the Florentine Library of San Marco by the same hand. The first, an older Codex of the eleventh century, contains the following: the three books of Blessed Prosper *On the Contemplative Life* (the true author is Julianus Pomerius); St. Ambrose’s treatise *On Penance*, divided into two books; St. Augustine’s sermon *On Penance*: “Penitents, penitents, if indeed you are penitents and not mockers”; Isidore’s *On Penance*: “Each righteous person begins to be righteous from the moment he becomes his own accuser”; [Col. 0279C] Aurelius Augustine’s *Soliloquy*, “While I desired”; St. Augustine’s *Retractations*; Bishop Ambrose’s book *On the Paradise of God*, and likewise the book *On Cain and Abel*; and the books of St. Isidore, namely the *Sentences*. The Codex is a parchment volume in folio, arranged in two columns; the chapter titles [p. 356] are written in red. The work of Isidore indicated as though it were a distinct book *On Penance* is nothing else—as its opening words show—than an excerpt from Book II, chapter 13, of the *Sentences*.

**29.** The other Codex is a parchment in octavo, written toward the end of the twelfth century. It contains many works, namely [Col. 0279D] Isidore’s books of the *Sentences*; a letter whose subject is written in the margin: “What existed before the creation of the world, and what will exist after the judgment, and concerning the final judgment itself.” It begins: “To the most beloved brother Adam, the humble sinner-monk sends greeting in the Lord.” There follows a brief exposition of what is read in the Books of Kings: that David, fleeing from Saul, entered a cave to relieve his bowels.

Then follows a letter or book by Bruno, bishop of Segni, to his beloved brother G., bishop of Maguelonne, *On the Consecration of a Church, the Sacraments, and Priestly Vestments*. An excerpt from a letter of Pope Clement, *How the Ecclesiastical Order Ought to Be Perfected*. A brief fragment of Pope Gregory to Honoratus, deacon of Salona, *On the Archdeacon’s Pastoral Care*. [Col. 0280A] A sermon on the words of James, “Do not swear.” St. Augustine’s book *On Holy Virginity*. His book *On the Letter and the Spirit*. A collection of certain authorities of the holy Fathers and of laws.

**30.** In the older Codex: “The prologue of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, to Massona, bishop, begins.” The more recent Codex omits the prologue. In both, a table of chapters is placed first. In the older: “The chapters have been completed; the first book of St. Isidore, bishop, begins.” At the end of the older: “The book of the *Sentences* of St. Isidore, bishop of Hispania, has been completed. Thanks be to God, amen.” The more recent: “The book of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*, of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, has been completed.” The differences in wording, especially from the older exemplar, are carefully noted on slips.

[Col. 0280B] **31.** The Pistoia Codex generally agrees with the Lucca Codex described above. Zaccaria entered most of the variant readings from the Pistoia Codex in his own hand, but after the opening chapters of Book I he scarcely notes anything other than that the Pistoia Codex agrees with the Lucca Codex. The Pistoia Codex also contains the letter to Massona, prefixed to the books of the *Sentences* in place of a prologue, and after the books of the *Sentences*, the books *Of Differences* and *Of Offices* by St. Isidore, who is called Isidore, bishop of Hispania.

**32.** In Zaccaria’s prospectus, only one Verona Codex is mentioned. In his papers I find variant readings from two Codices [p. 357] under this heading: “The books of the *Sentences* of the Madrid edition collated with two Codices, one mutilated, whose beginning is at chapter 21 of the first book, perhaps of the ninth century, the other of the fifteenth century. We carefully collated the older one; from the other we excerpted only certain variant readings.” Since I was uncertain to which library these two Codices belonged, I came upon a letter from Giovanni Francesco Seguier, sent from Verona to Zaccaria on 6 March 1755, in which the manuscript copies of Isidore preserved at Verona are listed, together with a Latin description left by the most learned Maffei, who had already died. From this letter I conclude that both these Codices are Veronese. Maffei describes the older Codex, no. 23, as follows.

**33.** “Written partly in large letters, partly in smaller letters, and partly in rapid script, this book is distinctive for that reason and has often been mentioned by me, who am engaged in the study of ancient scripts. It contains the books of Isidore of Seville, the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*. Each book is preceded by its own table. Neither the title of the work [Col. 0280D] nor the author’s name survives. The first quires have flown away, and the present beginning is: ‘Exercise over the whole earth,’ Book I, chapter 21, in the distinguished edition produced at Madrid in 1599, vol. I, p. 26. The following chapter is brought to an end with the words ‘testimony is given,’ and the text proceeds to chapter 23. Thus the words ‘they are banished and suffer punishment in hell for original guilt alone,’ and what follows, are absent. Where the same error concerning predestination lies in the manuscript as in the printed editions—‘let them delight in external things’—one must read ‘let them pursue’ [*sectentur*]. In Book II, chapter 39 of the printed editions, the heading is ‘On Fornication’; in the manuscript, ‘On Luxury.’ The final words in the manuscript are: ‘not those whom the heavenly court closes in order to gladden them.’”

**34.** Canon Giovanni Giacomo Dionysius discusses this very Codex in a letter to Zaccaria dated 25 July [Col. 0281A] 1781 at Verona, and says that the Codex ends: “You who read, keep the scribes in mind, if you have them for God the giver.” Maffei had previously discussed the same Codex, as he himself indicates, in Part I, p. 88, of the *Verona Library’s Manuscripts*. Zaccaria had wished to insert Maffei’s words in the preface to the *Prooemia of the Old and New Testament*, which I shall later quote.

As for the error Maffei wished to correct—“let them delight in external things”—I do not know whether it may rather be a locution proper to Isidore’s period, meaning “let them delight in external things.” The Codices remarkably agree in that reading, *exteriora delectentur*. The passage occurs in Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 6.

[p. 358] **35.** The more recent Codex, no. 54, 2, which was still among Maffei’s books but had already been destined for the Chapter Library of Verona, is described by Maffei as follows: [Col. 0281B] “A new parchment volume in quarto has arrived. The chapters of the first book begin; afterward: ‘The first book of Blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville, *On the Supreme Good*, has been completed,’ named after the opening words according to Hebrew custom. After the third book: ‘Completed on the first day of December 1467.’ The first and only book of the same author *On the Formation of a Good Life* begins: ‘Dear son, love tears,’ etc. After a short work has been given: ‘The prologue of St. Isidore’s *Synonyms* begins.’”

Zaccaria had begun to record the variant readings of these Codices in his own hand; but from chapter 12 of Book I onward he entrusted their transcription to another person who, it seems, did not work with the diligence Zaccaria had desired. The letter to Massona is absent from the more recent Codex; the older one is mutilated at the beginning. I shall discuss what the little work *On the Formation of a Good Life* is in chapter 82.

[Col. 0281C] **36.** One *Sentences* Codex from the Chigi Library is mentioned in the prospectus. Several are mentioned in the papers, but only as having been collated generally with the printed editions. Thus, in the Chigi Library, A 6, 164, there is a parchment in quarto of the thirteenth century containing the books of the *Sentences*. A table of approximately thirty chapters of the first book follows, as in the printed editions. There is also a parchment in quarto of the fourteenth century, A 6, 159, containing Isidore’s books of the *Sentences*. The order of the first book is as in the preceding Codex. It is followed by a book of the martyr Cyprian—or rather of someone else—*On the Twelve Abuses of the World*. Another parchment Codex of the fifteenth century, A. 3, 74, contains the books of the *Sentences*, as in the preceding manuscripts. In all three Codices, Book I, chapter 3, reads as in the printed editions: “The humanity assumed by Christ, which is the third person in the Trinity.” See the notes on that passage.

**37.** At the beginning of this third Codex, Cardinal Bona described the list of the little works contained in it as follows:

“This Codex contains various little works pertaining to ascetic practice, collected together by a religious man. All have been printed except nos. 9, 19, and 20, which are of no importance.

1. There occur the three books of the *Sentences*, which St. Isidore excerpted for the most part from St. Gregory the Great, adding some material from St. Augustine. In the printed editions, the passages of the holy Fathers are noted in the margin.

2. Several sermons of St. Ephrem the Syrian, translated by Ambrose of Camaldoli. They were printed at Strasbourg in 1509 and at Cologne in 1547. Gerard Vossius of Tongeren first published all of Ephrem’s works at Rome in three folio volumes in 1593.

3. An abridgment [p. 359] of the life of St. Jerome, after which follow letters of Eusebius of Cremona and of Jerome himself; but they are false and spurious, full of errors, fables, and anachronisms, as learned men have observed.

4. St. Augustine’s *Soliloquies*, which appear in volume IX of his works, but have been relegated to the appendix because they were compiled from his *Confessions* and other little works.

5. The book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, attributed to the same Augustine, from the same appendix to volume IX; it is also ascribed to St. Leo. The true author is believed to be St. Isidore of Seville, among whose little works it is found.

6. St. Isidore’s *Soliloquies*, published among his other works.

7. St. Bernard the abbot’s *On the Contemplative Life*. In the printed editions it is entitled *Meditations for Understanding the Human Condition*. It wrongly bears Bernard’s name: it is the first book *On the Soul* among the works of Hugh of St. Victor.

8. Certain excerpts from Hugh’s books *On the Cloister of the Soul*, which have been published.

9. An abridged *Decree of Gratian*: it is an index of all the matters noted by Gratian, containing the subject of each chapter.

10. A pseudepigraphical book of St. Bernard *On Conscience*. [Col. 0282B] In the printed editions it is entitled Bernard’s *On the Interior House*. Among Hugh of St. Victor’s four books *On the Soul*, it is the third in order.

11. A letter of St. Bonaventure, found in volume II of his little works.

12. St. Anthony’s exposition of the Decalogue. It appears to be excerpted from his published book *On the Instruction of Confessors*.

13. Certain examples transcribed from various books, all of which have been published.

14. The four books *On the Imitation of Christ*, formerly attributed to John Gerson, now to Thomas à Kempis.

15. A treatise of St. Bernard called *The Ladder of Paradise*. It is also found in volume IX of St. Augustine, but is in fact by Guigo, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, who died in 1137.

16. Bernard’s *Formula of an Honest Life*. It belongs to Bernard Sylvester, a Cistercian monk, who also wrote the letter *On Properly Managing Household Affairs* found among the works of St. Bernard.

17. Peter Damian’s letter *On the Day of Death*.

18. Certain brief prayers before and after Communion.

19. A prayer to the guardian angel.

20. An epigram on the sacrament of the Eucharist.”

[Col. 0282C] **38.** Thus far Cardinal Bona’s list of the little works. The *Conflict of Vices and Virtues* and Isidore’s *Soliloquies* will be discussed in their proper places. The date of the Codex is inferred from the end of St. Ephrem’s sermons, where we read: “On 26 June 1481, written in my own hand by Brother Giovanni Gaius of the Order of St. Dominic.”

[p. 360] **39.** Of the Codices mentioned by Zaccaria in his prospectus, I alone lack the collations of the Barberini and Modena Codices—unless certain variant readings may have been excerpted from one of them—from a Codex unknown to me, described as follows: “The second Codex, bookcase 13, on the left as one enters, a parchment volume in small folio, is entitled *The Soliloquies of Isidore of Seville*, containing the books of the *Sentences*. The Codex is mutilated at the beginning, for it begins at chapter 12 of the first book. It is also mutilated near the end, for although the third book ought to consist of 65 chapters, it ends midway through chapter 22. A few extraneous works are also added: the lament of the Blessed Virgin Mary according to St. Bernard, ‘Let my Lady say, say,’ etc.; a letter of St. Dionysius *On Paul’s Death*; a short summary concerning comets; and finally a beautiful and devout prayer.”

**40.** Perhaps Isidore’s *Soliloquies* had preceded this Codex, which would explain the surviving title, since it is entirely unsuitable for the books of the *Sentences*. In the autograph prospectus of his edition, Zaccaria does not name the Modena Codex, but after ten others adds: “And finally, our thirteenth-century Codex, which we received as a gift from the learned Father Laget, a member of the Augustinian family.” We may suspect that this is the Modena Codex itself and that it is not different from the one whose variant readings I possess, written in the thirteenth century and perhaps brought by Zaccaria into the Modena Library.

**41.** From a letter sent to Father Domenico Troili, S.J., by an unnamed Jesuit friend, it can be inferred that a manuscript Codex of the books of the *Sentences* was preserved in the town of Montepulciano, and that Zaccaria had requested that it be collated for him. But the Codex appeared to be more recent, and only chapter 13—or perhaps 15—of Book I, *On the Senses of the Flesh*, is transcribed from it as a specimen. The published work *On the Sentences* of St. Isidore was not found in that town.

**42.** Among certain Pistoia manuscript Codices there is listed a fourteenth-century *Booklet on the Supreme Good*, which has nothing to do with our Isidore, as is clear from its beginning. Chapter 1: “How, under the guidance of natural reason, the human mind discovered the one God. God is the supreme principle of all things; to find him is as difficult as it is, once found, to proclaim him worthily.” It is believed to be the book of a scholastic writer.

**43.** Don Carlo Maria Orsini had raised hopes of collating another Codex of the *Sentences*. In a letter to V. C. Trombellius, written from the Carthusian monastery at Pisa on 22 September 1752, [p. 361] he states that there was, as he thought, in that monastery a Codex entitled *The Sentences of St. Isidore*, and also *The Monks’ Diadem*, as well as another, *Isidore’s Synonyms*. He was arranging for these to be conveyed to him under proper safeguards. Trombellius informed Zaccaria about these Codices, but I find no evidence that anything further was done.

**44.** The two books *Against the Jews*, addressed to his sister Florentina, are said in the prospectus of Zaccaria’s edition to have been checked against five manuscript Codices: two Malatesta Codices, two Florentine Codices, and one from Lucca. A parchment in quarto from the Malatesta Library at Cesena, bookcase 1 on the left as one enters, contains the Gospel of St. John, written with glosses in the twelfth century, although the glosses are later. It also contains: “Isidore to his sister Florentina. The book against the Jews concerning Christ begins.” Zaccaria entered a few variant readings; another person entered the remainder—though there were not many—up to chapter 9 of Book I, where he observes: “As you see, this Codex is rather an epitome of the books than the books themselves.” At the end of Book II, instead of chapter 28, there is the preface found on page 256 of the Madrid edition. From this I selected the following variants.

The other Malatesta Codex is the very one in which, as I said, the *Prooemia* and several other works of Isidore are contained. After the sermon against the Arians: “To the holy lady, his sister Florentina, Isidore, bishop of Toledo.” At the end: “The book of Isidore, bishop of Toledo, against the Jews has been completed: amen.” The matter of this error, by which Isidore is absurdly called bishop of Toledo, will be discussed shortly.

**45.** Of the two Florentine manuscript Codices, one is Laurentian and the other is from San Marco. The Laurentian Codex, briefly described in Zaccaria’s papers, will be listed more fully and distinctly from Bandini’s catalogue, vol. I, Latin Codices, bookcase 23, Codex 14. It is a parchment volume in small folio of the fifteenth century, extremely elegant, with the initial letters of the books in gold. On the front of the Codex, the titles of the works appear in four golden circles, decorated in various ways and distinguished by emblems; on the facing page is the Medici coat of arms. The works are as follows:

1. Blessed Prosper’s *On the Contemplative Life*, with the letter of Jacopo Becchetti, as found in the San Marco Library Codex. Zaccaria published this in *A Literary Journey through Italy*, p. 54.

2. Isidore’s book of the *Primora*—correct to *Prooemia*—“On Books,” etc.

3. *Allegories*, without a title: [p. 362] “To the holy and most reverend brother Orosius, Isidore,” etc. At the end this work is entitled *The Book of the Primora*, or *Prooemia*, but incorrectly.

4. The *Book of Differences*, consisting of 42 chapters, preceded by a table. This is Grialius’s second book of the *Differences*: “Between God and man,” etc.

5. A book of St. Augustine, bishop, *On the Four Virtues*, or *Properties, of Charity*: “The desire for your charity demands from us,” etc.; it ends, “not the leaves of praise.” It is not found among St. Augustine’s works.

6. The three books of Isidore’s *Sentences*, each preceded by a table of chapters. At the end: “The book of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*, of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, has been completed. Isidore flourished in the time of the emperor Heraclius, who began his reign in the year of the Lord 614 and reigned for thirty years, as Vincent says in Part III, chapter 31, of the *Speculum*.”

The two books of Isidore *Against the Jews* follow, each preceded by a table of chapters.

**46.** The title of the work is: “The preface, or recapitulation of the Catholic faith, or the superscription of the work of Isidore, bishop of Seville, to his sister Florentina, begins. To holy Florentina, Isidore, bishop of Toledo. Certain matters,” etc. Since Isidore is first called bishop of Seville and afterward bishop of Toledo, perhaps the interpolator of the Codex understood him to have been a native of Toledo. This is seen more clearly in Codex 10, bookcase 21, described by Bandini as follows: “A parchment Codex from the beginning of the thirteenth century, with rubricated titles and colored initials. Two books of St. Isidore of Toledo, bishop of Seville, *Against the Jews*.”

The Malatesta Codex I have just described likewise has the title *Against the Jews* under the name of Isidore, bishop of Toledo. Thus you can easily understand that these three Codices derive their origin from one and the same corrupted source. It must be regarded as certain that this error was introduced by some interpolating copyist, or through carelessness. Bandini notes concerning Codex 14, bookcase 23, [Col. 0284D] that he observed many variant readings in the manuscript exemplar differing from Isidore’s printed works; but he does not mention the variant readings that Zaccaria had obtained from the two books *Against the Jews*, with the aid and in the hand of someone unknown to me.

**47.** The other Florentine Codex is from San Marco, a small quarto parchment volume of the fifteenth century. It contains writings of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, to his sister Florentina *On the Passion of the Lord*, compiled from several sources and from the testimonies of the prophets. In addition, Augustine’s work addressed “to simple and uneducated hermits, concerning their governance, so that in their simplicity they may not fall into the snares of error”; other excerpts from Augustine; [p. 363] Blessed Augustine’s book *On True and False Penance*, divided into several chapters; Augustine’s book *On Purgatorial Fire*: “We have heard, most beloved brothers, the Apostle saying that another foundation,” [Col. 0285A] etc.; likewise *On the Praise of God and the Punishments of Purgatory*: “The resurrection and glorification of our Lord Jesus Christ”; his work *On the Grace of the New Testament* and *On Five Questions*; and Blessed Augustine’s book *On Faith in Invisible Things*. At the end: “The little work of Isidore of Seville to his sister Florentina *On the Passion of the Lord* has been completed.” This Codex was collated by the same person who collated the preceding Laurentian Codex, as is evident from the handwriting.

**48.** The variant readings of the Lucca Codex are also in the same hand. Its title is: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the letter of St. Isidore the Younger, bishop, to his sister Florentina, in the book of testimonies of the prophets concerning Christ.” A table of chapters follows the prologue. At the end these words are added:

“By these twelve vices justice is darkened on earth:

A young man without obedience.  
A woman without modesty.  
A wise man without works.  
A people without law.  
Old men without religion.  
A lord without virtue.  
A rich man who lies.  
A proud poor man.  
A contentious Christian.  
An unjust king.  
A negligent bishop.”

The same material is found in another Pistoia Codex. Compare the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World* among the spurious works of St. Cyprian, and below, chapter 85, no. 4.

**49.** Zaccaria’s prospectus does not mention the Codex of the Barberini Library, although I find its variant readings in his *Adversaria*. It is a parchment volume in quarto, perhaps of the eighth century; for it is written in the same script as the Orosius of the Laurentian Library, formerly designated no. 230, which once belonged to the Friars of St. Savior of Settimo of the Cistercian order and afterward to Carlo Strozza, son of Thomas. Its title is: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ and of Blessed Mary ever-virgin begins the preface, or superscription of the work, to his sister Florentina.” In the Laurentian Codex recently described, this preface is likewise called the “superscription of the work.” I shall make certain observations about this Codex in chapter 66.

**50.** Several homilies of St. Augustine follow; a homily of St. Faustinus *On the Epiphany*: “It is near”; then more homilies of Augustine; also a work *On the Passing of St. Martin*, from the letter that Sulpicius Severus wrote to Bassula, his mother-in-law; several homilies of St. Gregory; an admonition of St. Basil, bishop, to monks; St. Ephrem the deacon’s books *On the Day of Judgment*; [Col. 0285D] his work *On Compunction of Heart*; St. Augustine’s *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. An exposition of the Creed follows, beginning: “While we wish to discuss the Creed.” But one article is missing from this exposition: “eternal life.”

**51.** A booklet follows entitled *What Are the Instruments of Good Works?* “First, to love the Lord God,” etc. Sayings of St. Ephrem *On the End of the World*: “And the consummation of the age, and the disturbance of the nations.” Sayings of St. Methodius, bishop. The Codex is mutilated at the end. The *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, falsely attributed to Augustine, is also attributed to Isidore, as I shall explain in chapter 83. A learned person, apparently for Zaccaria’s use, noted certain variant readings from this Barberini Codex, prefacing them as follows: [Col. 0286A] “We excerpted some material from here by collating the books addressed to Florentina, from the Paris edition of 1601.”

**52.** Zaccaria calls the book *On the Order of Creatures* doubtful, and does not indicate that it was collated by himself or others for use in his edition. I find nothing about this book in his papers.

**53.** *Synonyms.* In his prospectus Zaccaria had indicated two Laurentian manuscripts for the collation of this work; but in the *Adversaria* I find three Laurentian Codices collated by the same hand that collated the other Florentine Codices. The first is a parchment in octavo, bookcase 20, no. 46, of the thirteenth or fourteenth century. Bandini assigns it to the fifteenth century and notes that it bears the Medici coat of arms. He also observes that the first prologue and something else in the body of the work are missing, and that Book II ends with “through the reward that is to come,” as in the Madrid edition, p. 390, col. 2, line 31. It is mutilated at the end. Its title is: “The book of the *Synonyms* of the Lord Isidore, bishop of Seville, begins.” It begins: “A certain little sheet of Cicero recently came into my hands,” etc.

**54.** The other Laurentian Codex is a parchment in quarto of the thirteenth century, bookcase 20, no. 49. Bandini says that the Codex is partly of the twelfth and partly of the thirteenth century. It has two prologues, as in the Madrid edition. The title appears to be: “Isidore of Seville’s *Synonyms*.” Several miscellaneous works follow, especially the book of Ecclesiastes, the seven Catholic Epistles, and the book of Job with glosses. The following annotation comes next:

“In the year 1215 from the Incarnation of the Lord, a holy universal synod was held at Rome in the church of St. Savior, which is called Constantina [perhaps *Constantiniana*], [Col. 0286C] in the month of November, under the presidency of Lord Innocent III, pope, in the eighteenth year of his pontificate. There were 412 bishops,” etc.

A booklet *On the Office of the Judge* follows.

**55.** The third Laurentian Codex is a parchment volume in folio, bookcase 23, no. 23, in small folio, of the century that Bandini believes to be the eleventh; it is very well preserved. It contains sayings of the holy Fathers, Martin of Braga’s book *On the Four Virtues*, and St. John Chrysostom’s sermon *On Patience*. Then follows: “In the name of the most high God begins the book of St. Isidore, bishop of Hispania”—thus written—namely, the *Synonyms*. At the end: “The second book of the *Synonyms* of Lord Isidore has been completed.” After other works there are three books of St. Julian of Toledo’s *Prognosticon*.

**56.** Zaccaria’s papers contain nothing concerning *On Contempt of the World*, *On the Exhortation to Repent*, *On the Lament of Repentance*, *On Prayer for the Correction of Life*, *Against the Devil’s Snares*, *On Confession*, *The Rule for Monks*, *Fragments on the Rule of St. Benedict*, or *On the Conflict of Vices*. The book *On the Formation of a Good Life* is likewise listed among the spurious works; I find it transcribed from the Verona Codex. I shall discuss the work separately. The Codex will be described in Zaccaria’s preface to the book of the *Prooemia*, to be referred to in its proper place.

# CHAPTER XLIV  
## Zaccaria’s Apparatus for the Second Volume of His Edition of St. Isidore

**1.** In the second volume Zaccaria had assigned the first place to the letters, and likewise to sermons attributed to Isidore in the manuscripts. The letter to Massona is said in the prospectus to have been collated with the Pistoia and Vienna manuscripts. From the Codex of the Vienna Library I find the entire letter transcribed; from the Pistoia Codex, however, I find variant readings in the margin of a copy of the Madrid edition. But the nature of the Vienna Codex is not stated. He had intended to reprint the remaining letters from the editions.

**2.** Besides the sermon *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, commonly published under the name of Emissenus and attributed to Isidore by Martene on the authority of two very ancient Codices, Zaccaria had promised three previously unpublished spurious works: the first, *Against the Arians*, from the Malatesta Codex; the second, *On St. Aemilian*, from the Vercelli Codex; and the third, without a title, from the Florentine Codex of San Marco.

The sermon *Against the Arians* exists in the Malatesta Codex, which also contains the *Prooemia of the Old and New Testament*, as was explained in the preceding [p. 366] chapter. In the catalogue of the Pomposa monastery, dating from the eleventh century, this sermon was already attributed to Isidore, as I shall say below in chapter 46. In both places it begins: “Come, Lord Jesus Christ, Redeemer.” I shall state my judgment concerning this sermon and the following two in chapter 72.

**3.** The sermon in praise of St. Aemilian was transcribed from a very ancient manuscript Codex of the archive of St. Eusebius at Vercelli, under this title: “Sermon of Blessed Isidore on the feast of St. Aemilian, bishop of Vercelli. The ecclesiastical man,” etc.

The third sermon is against gluttony, avarice, and pride, entitled “Homily of St. Isidore, bishop. Brothers, we ought to fear greatly,” etc. A fuller description of this Florentine Codex of San Marco is given as follows.

[Col. 0287C] **4.** “A parchment in octavo of the thirteenth century, containing several homilies. Then follows: ‘In the name of the Father begins the letter concerning the Lord’s Day, sent by God: The holy Lord’s Day,’ etc. ‘From the seventh throne a letter came into the city of Gaza, sent by the Lord, where St. Peter received the episcopate.’ Against this or a similar letter there exists a letter of Licinianus, bishop of Carthage in Spain at the end of the sixth century, to Vincentius, bishop of the island of Ibiza: ‘Among various matters,’ etc. At the beginning of that letter we read that the Lord’s Day should be honored, etc. It was published in volume V of *Hispania Sacra*, appendix 4.

“A brief explanation of the Lord’s Prayer. Other homilies. A certain treatise on the beasts mentioned in Scripture. An exposition of the Mass, with certain verses expressing this meaning:
