> There is a reason why the right side of the altar holds  
> the beginning and the end of the Mass, while the middle lies on the left:  
> the right signifies the Jews, the left the Gentiles.  
> From the former our faith began, is transferred to the latter,  
> and is returned to the former; and at the end of the world there will be believers.  
> Let your mind recall this; let your tongue utter this.

It seems that *referatur* and *sonet* should be read instead of *refertur* and *sonat*.”

**5.** The Introit of the Mass follows: “The Introit of the Mass is so called,” etc. A treatise *On Vestments*, *On the Praises of the Mass*, again *On Sacred Vestments*, and *On the Mass*. “The celebration of the Mass is performed in commemoration of Christ’s Passion.” In this chapter Isidore is cited; mention is also made of the deacon, who after the Gospel ought to say: “If there is any catechumen, let him go outside.” Other material follows concerning the Mass, the exposition of the Creed, and the passion of St. Margaret. A similar exposition of the Mass exists in Codex Vaticanus Palatinus 1578, as I shall say in chapter 84.

[p. 367] **6.** Thus much concerning the spurious sermons of Isidore mentioned by Zaccaria. Whether it must be regarded as certain that they are spurious will be investigated more distinctly in its proper place, as I have noted.

**7.** The two books *On Offices* were checked against four manuscript Codices: the Bolognese, the Pistoia Codex, and two Lucca Codices. The Bolognese is a Codex of the Albornoziana Library of the major college of St. Clement of the Spanish nation, a parchment volume in folio, no. 10, at least of the eleventh century. [Col. 0288B] It contains St. Jerome the presbyter’s book *Against Jovinianus the Heretic*; St. Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, *On the Origin of Offices*; St. Augustine, bishop, *On Christian Discipline*; and the disputation of Lanfranc and Berengar *On the Body and Blood of Christ*: “Lanfranc, by the mercy of God a Catholic, to Berengar, adversary of the Catholic Church. If divine mercy would deign to inspire your heart.” It is a dialogue between Lanfranc and Berengar. At the end: “The dispute of Lanfranc and Berengar concerning the Body and Blood of Christ has been completed.”

8. The two books *On the Origin of the Offices* are complete, with a preface and table of chapters. Bayer mentions this codex in his note on book V of the *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanica*, no. 147:

“I remember that I once saw at Bologna, in the distinguished college of S. Clement of the Spaniards, an outstanding codex of the Offices of the Church, which seemed somewhat fuller than the printed editions.”

But the variant readings collected by Zaccaria from this codex, when he compared it with the royal Madrid edition, by no means indicate that it is fuller than the printed editions. I have learned from the appended notes and from the report of others that this codex, like all the other Isidorian codices of the Spanish College at Bologna, was collated in 1748 by Mingarelli and Ponsio.

9. The Pistoia codex is that same one in which the books of the *Sentences* are found, as mentioned above. Its inscription reads: “Here begins the prologue to the book of the Offices published by blessed Isidore, bishop.” It also has a table of chapters. The first book appears to have been collated partly in Zaccaria’s hand and partly in that of another person. At its end Zaccaria wrote: “Thus far I collated in 1755. I noted the rest cursorily.” That is, a few passages from book II, at the end of which it reads: “Here end the two books of the Offices. Here begin the chapters of the book of the Differences.”

10. The two Lucca codices were carefully collated—I do not know by whom—for the hands of two different persons are visible. There is no note distinguishing the codices from one another. For one of them the following heading is given:

“Collation of S. Isidore of Seville, *On the Divine Offices*, with the parchment manuscript codex of the canons of the cathedral church of Lucca.”

The title of the manuscript codex is: “Here begins the prologue to the book of the Offices published by blessed Isidore, bishop.” This agrees completely with the prologue of the Pistoia codex just described. After the prologue comes a table of chapters.

[Col. 0289A] 11. For the other Lucca codex Zaccaria prefixed this title:

“Books on the ecclesiastical offices of the Paris edition of 1580, collated with the codex of the chapter of Lucca, concerning which Mansi writes in volume XLV of Calogerà.”

The variant readings follow, in the hand of another person, which Zaccaria very frequently used in such collations. In the cited volume XLV of Calogerà’s collection, page 73, there is a commentary by Giovanni Domenico Mansi on a distinguished codex written in the age of Charlemagne and preserved in the library of the canons of the cathedral church of Lucca.

The codex is a quarto parchment manuscript, written sometimes in an exceedingly small Italian hand, sometimes in a larger Italian hand, and sometimes in a square script; whether copied by one person or by several, it was copied inaccurately. It suffered many serious wounds from the practiced hand of some meddlesome physician. Moreover, some passages were written unclearly by the scribe of the codex and were confused and mixed together.

[Col. 0289B] The age of the codex is indicated by the following old notation:

“From the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ up to the present year of King Charles in Lombardy, in the month of September, when the sun displayed an eclipse, in the tenth indiction, there are 762 years, five months.”

The year of Christ 787 is indicated. Mansi concludes that several years were spent in writing this codex, since among other things it contains an excerpt from a letter of Leo III, who began to be pope in 795.

12. Someone might nevertheless doubt whether the notation concerning the year 787 was copied by the scribe from another codex, as often happens. Mabillon, who examined the codex, indicated that it belonged to the age of Charlemagne, as Mansi reports.

This codex contains:

1. Eusebius’s *Chronicle*, translated into Latin by S. Jerome and continued.

2. Several antiphons for the annual cycle.

3. Isidore’s *Chronicle*.

4. Isidore’s two books *On the Offices*, collated by Mansi with Cochlaeus’s edition. The final two chapters, *On Suffrages*, and so forth, are missing from the codex, just as they are missing from Cochlaeus’s edition, from the collection *On the Catholic Offices of the Church* (Cologne, 1568), and from others.

5. Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History*, in Rufinus’s translation.

6. A letter of S. Gregory the Great to Augustine, apostle of the English, fuller than the copies that have been printed.

7. Jerome’s and Gennadius’s books *On Illustrious Men*.

8. The *Lives of the Roman Pontiffs*, without the author’s name; elsewhere they are attributed to Anastasius the Librarian.

9. A fragment of Isidore *On Heresy and Schism*, from book VIII, chapter 3 of the *Etymologies*. It does not bear Isidore’s name and was formerly believed to be a fragment of some work by Jerome.

10. The *Ecclesiastical Rules of the Apostles*, or the well-known fifty canons.

11. The work *On Mosaics*, already edited from this codex by Muratori in volume II of *Dissertations on the Middle Ages*, page 668. Two other works in the same codex, written on a blank page, nevertheless escaped him: *On Construction in Water* and *On a Fine*.

12. Verses beginning “Gregory, prelate worthy in merit and name,” more numerous and more correct than those given by Vezzosius in his notes on the fourth volume of the works of Thomas of Jesus.

13. “Here begins *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, by Gennadius, bishop of Marseille” (the manuscript reads “Maxiliensis”).

14. Certain superstitious trifles concerning numbers.

15. A collection of canons.

16. The book of blessed Augustine *On the Mirror of the Soul*, falsely attributed to him.

In addition to several other materials, there follow excerpts from canons taken from certain codices of the churches of Spain, as well as fragments of books VII and VIII of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.

13. For the second volume Zaccaria had promised a book of prayers of the Isidorian rite, edited by Blanchini, preceded by a dissertation on the Isidorian liturgy; Aguirre’s and Cenni’s collection of Isidorian canons, together with his own judgment concerning both; and two councils over which the holy doctor presided, with variant readings. Of all these I find nothing begun by him, much less completed. In his papers I find only Scipione Maffei’s judgment concerning the Veronese codex of the sixth or seventh century, which contains the Gothic Breviary. I shall discuss it more fully below.

14. The *Chronicle* also belonged to the second volume. It was collated with five manuscript codices, namely the Vatican, Lucca, Pistoia, Florence S. Marco, and Cesena Malatesta codices, with an appendix drawn from three codices extending to the tenth century. The collations of the Vatican codex are missing. There are variant readings of Isidore’s *Chronicle* in the Breulian edition, collated with the manuscript codex of the chapter of Lucca, which is discussed in the cited volume XLV of Calogerà’s collection of pamphlets. The heading is in Zaccaria’s hand; the remainder is in another hand.

Mansi gives the title in the cited place as: “The Chronicles of Isidore, bishop.” He adds that he collated this chronicle with Loaisa’s edition, from which he gathered a rich harvest of variant readings. Among other things, he notes that in the printed editions Heraclius is assigned to the year 5814, whereas in the manuscript he is placed together with the year 5813. I nevertheless believe that the Zaccarian variant readings belong not to Mansi but to another person.

15. From the codex of the chapter of Pistoia there is transcribed a certain abridgment of Isidore’s *Chronicle*, which begins:

“David reigned forty years; Solomon, etc.”

It ends:

“Heraclius is thereafter in his fifth year of reign. Thus, from the beginning of the world up to the present era—that is, the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius and the fourth year of the ruler Sisebut—there are 5,813 years.”

After a blank page, an appendix follows:

“Adaloaldus, etc.”

It continues up to the year 1027.

16. The Florentine codex of S. Marco is a quarto parchment manuscript of the eleventh century. As is noted at the beginning, it came from the inheritance of the Florentine Niccolò Niccoli. Its title is:

“Here begins the book of the Chronicles of S. Isidore, bishop of Seville, from the beginning of the world up to the reign of Heraclius and the rule of Sisebut, king of the Goths, who reigned around the year of the Lord six thousand six hundred.”

The two Italian words “six thousand six hundred” were, I think, written by the person who collated the codex in place of Roman numerals, and perhaps he did not understand them. For Isidore’s *Chronicle* does not reach the year 6000 of the world.

The manuscript codex differs greatly from the published *Chronicle*. It ends:

“Here ends the book of the Chronicles, or *On Times*, of holy Isidore, archbishop of Seville.”

17. Another *Chronicle* continues as far as the reign of the emperor Leo, who succeeded Michael. It should be noted that when the author of this supplement speaks of the emperor Nicephorus, Leo’s predecessor, he has the following:

“Thus rebuked, Nicephorus ceased from his greed . . . and began to demand the repayments of the preceding eight years from the houses; and there was great lamentation. The Lord knows these things. I myself, the writer of this account, heard them by word of mouth from Theodosius.”

An appendix follows:

“Albuin, the tenth king of the Lombards, etc.”

It continues up to the year 1051.

18. After the prefaces and other works of Isidore, the Malatesta codex gives this title for the *Chronicle*:

“Here begins the *Chronicle of S. Isidore, bishop of Spalato*, presenting abridged histories from the beginning of the world.”

19. Zaccaria’s prospectus makes no mention of the Albani and Modena codices. Nevertheless, in his papers I find variant readings from them, written in another hand.

The Albani codex is a paper manuscript, no. 4, at whose beginning one reads:

“Isidore of Seville, *On Illustrious Men*. Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, *On Illustrious Men after Isidore*. *On the Origin and Death of the Holy Fathers*, without the author’s name being specified.”

At the beginning of this little work, however, another hand has written:

“By Isidore of Seville the Younger. A brief chronicle of Isidore of Seville, from the beginning of the world up to the emperor Heraclius. This book, transcribed in this manner, was given to me as a gift by my most illustrious and most reverend lord, D. Cardinal Sirletus, to whom I acknowledge that I owe very much. Rome, 22 June 1576. B. Cardinal Lomellinus.”

The inscription in the codex is:

“Here begins the book of the Chronicles of Isidore, bishop of Seville, from the beginning of the world up to the reign of Heraclius Augustus and the rule of Sisebut.”

A preface follows. The *Chronicle*, interpolated in many places by some French writer, appears to have been copied from an exemplar written in the fortieth year of Lothair, king of the Franks, and the fourteenth year of the emperor Heraclius, as can be inferred from the final words.

20. The Modena codex is mutilated in several places. Its title is:

“Here begins the book of the Chronicles of S. Isidore, bishop.”

At the end, the years are reckoned up to the twenty-seventh year of Charlemagne, at which time the codex appears to have been copied. A sample of the script, which I possess, also confirms this date.

The orthography of the codex is as follows: *Eusevius*, *condedit*, *adque*, *reperit*, *morvi*, *inlustris*, *Spanias*, and *nomi* for *numi*.

The final words of the work are:

“But from the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius up to the twenty-eighth year of Luiprand, king of the Lombards, and my age—[that] of unhappy John—. . . 124 years are reckoned. From then up to the twenty-seventh year of the most Christian and most pious lord Charles the Great, king of the Franks and Lombards in Italy, there are found . . . 62 years.

Thus all the years from Adam up to the present eighth indiction are added together: in that year the Passover of the Hebrews falls on the Ides of April, but our Passover on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of May; the beginning of the world on the fourth day before the Ides of April; the moon was created on the Ides of April; humanity was made in the image of God on the seventh day before the Kalends of May; the years are completed . . .

The remaining time of the age is therefore uncertain to human investigation.”

21. *History of the Goths*: Zaccaria made no notes concerning this work except that it was to be published with variant readings from Labbe’s edition.

22. *The Book on the Life and Death of the Fathers*: variant readings collected from the manuscript codices of Verona and Florence, which were promised in Zaccaria’s prospectus, also appear in his papers.

The Veronese codex contains several works of Isidore and is described as follows by Marquis Maffei in the letter of Seguier to Zaccaria, whom I mentioned earlier:

“The codex of the chapter of Verona, no. 54, written in old minuscule script, with rubricated titles and with the titles themselves and the opening verses of the works elegantly formed in larger letters: four compositions of the same Isidore are included.

“I. ‘The book of the rewards begins: a dialogue of the priest S. Jerome.’ It mentions neither rewards, nor is it a dialogue; rather, it is that work of Isidore of Seville about which Braulio writes, one book of *Prefaces*.

“Editions: *Prefaces to the Books of the Old and New Testament*: thus in the Madrid edition, volume II, page 310. After that comes a manuscript book of the Old Testament, followed by: ‘Also, prefaces to the books of the New Testament.’ The manuscript does not have ‘To the Evangelists: namely Matthew, namely Mark, namely Luke’; these words have slipped from the margins of the books into the text.

“Where the printed editions read *penetrat*, the manuscript reads *compenetrat*. After *digessit*, the printed editions add twenty verses, which are absent from the manuscript. It also lacks certain periods in the letters of S. Peter.”

23. Second in order:

“Here begins the life or death of the saints who have gone before in the Lord.”

Third:

“Here begins the little work of S. Isidore: Isidore to the most reverend Lord Orosius.”

A book follows which the second volume printed at Madrid presents under this title:

“Certain sacred allegories of Scripture.”

It is the same work as *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, which is wrongly attributed to Isidore of Córdoba by the spurious Flavius Dexter. I think Braulio gave it this title because it begins: “Certain very well-known names of the Law and the Gospels.”

William Cave listed it among lost works, indeed suspecting that it had never existed, since he wondered whether it might be the same as the book of the *Prefaces*. But he had not seen the Madrid edition.

Fourth in the manuscript, in very large letters:

“Here begin testimonies of divine Scripture”—and also of certain Fathers. This is an Isidorian and unpublished collection which, if leisure permits, may profitably be brought forth among the *Anecdota*.

24. The person who collated this Veronese codex with the Madrid edition gives its title as follows:

“Isidore: Here begins the life or death of the saints who have gone before in the Lord.”

At the end he appended this note:

“Since in this codex the first little book of the *Prefaces* is attributed to Jerome, while this work is prefaced by no author’s title, although the name Isidore has been written above the margin in a sufficiently ancient hand, whereas the words that follow bear this title—‘Here begins the little work of S. Isidore’—it seems that the first scribe denied this work to Isidore.

“But all that can be concluded is that the first scribe perhaps did not know whose work *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* was. This is of little consequence, especially since the same scribe foolishly called the book of the *Prefaces* a dialogue and attributed it to S. Jerome.”

In the manuscript codex the work ends after the praises of the Fathers of the New Testament:

“Here ends the life or death of the Saints who have gone before in the Lord.”

25. The first Florentine codex is Laurentianus, plut. 67, no. 12, a folio parchment manuscript of the fifteenth century. It contains Eusebius’s and Rufinus’s *Ecclesiastical History*, Bede’s *Chronicle*, and the works of Gennadius, Isidore, and Ildefonsus *On Illustrious Men*. The person who collected the variant readings from Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, which follows Gennadius’s book, testifies that he collated these three books *On Illustrious Men*.

Its inscription is:

“The book of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the origin, life, and death of the holy Fathers. Here begins the prologue.”

At the end:

“The book of Isidore on the origin, life, and death of the Fathers ends.”

26. From Bandini, volume II of the *Catalogue of the Latin Codices of the Laurentian Library*, we learn that this volume is extremely clean and ornate and bears the Medici device.

According to the same author, Isidore’s book consists of thirty-eight chapters, the first being on Sixtus and the last on Severus; several errors occur. Braulio’s addition, or prefatory notice of Isidore’s works, follows.

Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men* preserves a different order of chapters from the book edited by Fabricius. The first chapter in the manuscript is on Asterius, or Astyrius, as it is written in the manuscript. The work ends:

“S. Leocadia holds the tomb of her dwelling.”

An anonymous addition concerning S. Ildefonsus follows:

“Ildefonsus, in memory, etc.”

This is Julian of Toledo’s work, although in certain manuscripts it is attributed to Felix.

27. The other Florentine manuscript is a paper codex of the fifteenth century belonging to the library of S. Marco. At the beginning one reads:

“This book belongs to the convent of S. Marco of Florence, of the Order of Friars Preachers. It was written by Brother Leonardo Ser Uberti of Florence, a son of that convent, who died at Rome on 25 May 1481.”

The following works are contained in it:

“A treatise of blessed Bernard on spiritual exercise, namely reading, meditation, prayer, and contemplation.

“Words of S. Bernard on the Passion of the Lord: ‘From the beginning of my religious life, a bundle . . .’

“A letter of blessed Bernard to one of his devout followers on uprightness of life and religion: ‘You ask me, my dearest brother, for something that never and nowhere . . .’”

28. “A letter of blessed Bernard to someone on the exercise of religious life and the stages of perfection: ‘Since, my beloved brother, I am still set before you in the presence of the Lord . . .’”

At the end of this letter it is noted:

“Although it is good and useful, it nevertheless has less of the flavor of Bernard, because it seems to give off neither his thought nor his eloquence.”

“A letter of blessed Bernard to the parents of a certain novice, who grieved over him as though he were lost: ‘If your son . . .’

“Another of the same author to the same persons, written in the name of the said novice: ‘The sole reason, which does not permit . . .’

“Another to someone who had left and was delaying his return to the order: ‘I grieve over you, my son Gualfred . . .’”

29. “A letter of blessed Ambrose, bishop, to one of his disciples on conduct and uprightness of life: ‘Beloved son, love tears.’”

This appears to be the little work *On the Formation of a Good Life*, attributed to Isidore in certain manuscript books; we shall discuss it in chapter 83.

“The book of S. Augustine *On the Mirror of the Soul*.

“Hugh of Saint-Victor’s exposition of the rule of blessed Augustine, bishop.

“Hugh’s work *On the Cloister of the Soul*.”

30. “The book of S. Isidore of Seville, archbishop, *On Illustrious Men*, written after Jerome and Gennadius.

“The book of blessed Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, *On Illustrious Men*.

“The book of S. Isidore, bishop of Seville, *On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Holy Fathers Who Shone in Virtue in the Old and New Testament*.”

31. “Bede’s book of the *Chronicles*.

“The preface of Jacobus Antonius Marcellus to René, king of Sicily, concerning a certain history of the priesthood of Jesus Christ.

“That history follows; it does not agree with the sayings of the saints, and we shall discuss it elsewhere.

“Certain material concerning the Erythraean Sibyl.

“Letters of Lentulus and Pilate concerning Jesus Christ.

“Letters of S. Anastasia and S. Chrysogonus.

“The legend of S. Robert, bishop of Worms.

“The life of S. Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, by an uncertain author.

“Aristotle’s *Naval Astrology*.”

32. “A treatise of John Gerson *On the Celebration of Mass*.

“A treatise of Bartholomew Lapaicius, of the Order of Preachers, bishop of Coron, *On the Glorification of the Senses in Paradise*, with a eulogy of the author.

“A history of the destruction of Constantinople, written from Chios on 13 August 1453.

“A sermon delivered on Holy Thursday in the chapter of the convent of S. Marco at Florence.”

33. On the final page it is noted that the scribe of the codex, Brother Leonardo Ser Uberti, died of the plague at Rome, in the convent of S. Maria sopra Minerva, on 25 May 1481.

Bede’s *Chronicle* is fuller in this codex than in the printed edition. The inscription of Isidore’s work is:

“Here begins the book of S. Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the origin, life, and death of the holy Fathers who shone in virtue in the Old and New Testament.”

At the end:

“Amen. Praise be to God. 22 November 1472. The book of S. Isidore, etc., ends.”

[Col. 0294C] 34. Among Zaccaria’s notebooks there is a book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, reduced to an abridgment; his prospectus makes no mention of it. It is found in a folio parchment codex of the chapter of Verona, of the tenth century, no. 58, shelfmark Q, which contains seven books, perhaps by Bede or Rabanus.

Very similar to this is Codex Regio-Vaticanus 309, which I shall describe in chapter 10. Book I, no. 8, begins:

“Here begins *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*.”

As I have said, it is an abridgment of Isidore’s book, collated with another codex of the same chapter, no. 63, shelfmark P, which contains Bede’s Blanchinian *Martyrology*. Blanchinus published its variant readings in his prolegomena to volume IV of Anastasius.

In this codex 63, after the eulogy of Titus, the following is added:

“Also, the names of those whose tombs are unknown.

“Abel, son of Adam, etc., as in Isidore.

“Lot, son of Aram, etc., as in Isidore.

“Phinehas the priest, etc., as in Isidore.

“The seven Maccabee brothers, etc., as in Isidore.”

It is pleasant to believe that the words “as in Isidore” were read in the manuscript codex itself, not added by the person who transcribed the little work from an old codex.

35. I also possess, among Zaccaria’s papers, variant readings from the Albani codex, which contains Isidore’s *Chronicle*, as I explained shortly before. Its inscription is:

“Here begins the book of Isidore of Seville the Younger, *On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Holy Fathers Who Shone in Virtue in the Old and New Testament*.”

A preface follows.

When you hear “Isidore the Younger,” do not suppose that he is someone other than our most famous author of the *Etymologies*. For the same Isidore is called sometimes “elder” and sometimes “younger” in the codices, for the reasons I set out in chapter 16.

In the same papers there are also variant readings from the Malatesta codex, which contains the *Prefaces* and other works of Isidore:

“Here begin the chapters of the book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the life, origin, or death of the holy Fathers.”

After a table of chapters from the Old and New Testament:

“Here begins Isidore’s book on the life, origin, or death of the holy Fathers who are recorded in the praises of Scripture: first, on Adam.”

36. The book *On Illustrious Men*, for which Zaccaria had promised a collation of seven manuscript codices—the Barberini, Este, three Florentine, and two Bolognese codices—I do not find, except for the variant readings of two Bolognese codices, which the most learned man Giovanni Chrysostom Trombetti sent to Zaccaria.

I preserve these in autograph, together with Trombetti’s letters to Zaccaria, dated 3 July 1754, in which he also promises a report on differences in the text of Jerome’s and Gennadius’s books *On Illustrious Men*.

Nothing is recorded about these Bolognese codices except that both—or at least one of them—belonged to the common library of the monastery of S. Salvatore at Bologna.

37. When shortly before I described the Laurentian codex *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, I observed that the person who collated that work had also collated the book *On Illustrious Men*. Whatever that labor was, it has not reached us.

In its place I find a variant reading from the Albani codex described above, when I was discussing the *Chronicle*. This codex omits the prologue “Although above . . .” and begins as follows:

“Isidore of Seville, *On Illustrious Men*. On Pope Sixtus.”

And so it proceeds:

“On Macrobius the deacon, etc.”

It preserves the order of the Madrid edition.

38. I also find a preface prepared by Zaccaria for this book. But I think it was composed before he conceived the idea of an edition of all Isidore’s works. The preface appears to have been arranged for the reprinting of Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*.

Fabricius’s edition of Isidore’s book appears to have been revised against several other editions, not against manuscript copies; it is furnished with notes by various scholars and with some notes by Zaccaria as well.

I shall publish the preface in its proper place, when I discuss this book; and I shall review the notes when the book is printed. I learned after Zaccaria’s death, from his literary papers, that he had indeed thought of preparing a new edition of Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, as I already mentioned above.

39. The book *On the Nature of Things*, collated with four manuscript codices: one from Lucca, two from Florence S. Marco, and one Florentine Laurentian codex. Variant readings from these four copies are preserved.

The Lucca codex belongs to S. Maria Curtis Orlandingorum, or Orlandigorum. It is a quarto parchment manuscript of the twelfth or thirteenth century. It begins:

“Here begins the book of S. Isidore, bishop of Seville, *On the Stars of Heaven*. Here begins the prologue. To the lord brother, etc.”

40. Of the two Florentine codices of S. Marco, one belongs to the ninth century. It also contains S. Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. It begins:

“Of Isidore the priest, in a more polished style” (so the manuscript reads).

The prologue is omitted. Several chapters are also omitted in this same codex.

41. The other codex is more recent, belonging to the twelfth century. It presents the work of the *Etymologies* divided into twenty-three books, the last of which is this book *On the Nature of Things*. Its title is therefore:

“Here begin the chapters of book XXIII.”

After the prologue comes a table of chapters.

42. Codex 39 of the Laurentian Library, shelfmark plut. 29, is a quarto parchment manuscript of the thirteenth century. Besides Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*, it contains an excerpt from the histories of the Eastern Churches, concerning the great faith of Christians and the unchangeable words of our Lord Jesus Christ, who said: “Whatever you bind on earth will be bound also in heaven”; and concerning the fact that this power was given not only to the apostle Peter but also to all the apostles, and indeed to all priests who rightly believe and preach the word of truth.

It also contains an exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, penitential canons, material *On Concurrent Epacts*, and other works.

43. The inscription of the Isidorian book is:

“Here begins the book of S. Isidore, bishop of Seville, *On the Stars of Heaven*. Here begins the prologue. To the lord brother Sisebut, Isidore.”

It ends with “They judged five,” together with a circular diagram of the three parts of the world, as Bandini teaches us in volume II of the *Latin Codices of the Medicean Laurentian Library*.

# CHAPTER XLV. Variant readings from manuscript codices prepared for volume III of Zaccaria’s edition. The death and eulogy of Zaccaria.

[Col. 0296C] 1. Zaccaria had intended the first and principal work of the third volume of his edition to be the books of the *Etymologies*, corrected against eight manuscript copies: namely the Vatican codex, no. 624; the Este, Chisian, Bolognese, Lucca, Florence S. Marco, and two Malatesta codices.

The variant readings of the Vatican, Bolognese, and Este codices are missing. There is, however, the codex of the chapter of Modena, mutilated and half-burned, from the ninth century. It begins with the preface to book III and ends at chapter 3 of book IX. I possess a sample of this codex’s script.

2. The Chisian copy is a folio parchment manuscript, marked A. 3, 35, of the fourteenth century. It begins:

“Here begin the chapters of the books of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, written to Braulio Augustine” (so the manuscript reads), “or to Sisebutus, namely his lord and son.”

It differs greatly from the printed edition, both in the order and sequence of the books themselves and in the matters that appear to have been inserted elsewhere by some interpolator.

Book I: *On Grammar*.

Book II: *On Rhetoric*. There, from the word *Anadiplosis* in chapter 21 through the end of the chapter, the passage is omitted.

Book III: *On Dialectic*.

Book IV: *On Arithmetic*.

Book V: *On Geometry*.

Book VI: *On Music*.

Book VII: *On Astronomy*.

The following then appears:

“Here begins the book on medicine according to Isidore.”

In chapter 4, after the final words, the following is added:

“The reasoning of the logician, etc.”

We shall publish this fragment elsewhere among the appendices.

A book *On Laws* follows, preceded by a letter to Braulio. At the end of the book *On Laws*, after a brief *Chronicle*, the following is added:

“In Spain the Jews are baptized. Here ends the *Chronicle according to S. Isidore*. At this time S. Isidore lived.”

[Col. 0297A] 3. An appendix to the *Chronicle* follows:

“Theodosius in his fourth year, etc.”

It ends:

“Otto IV, seven years.”

“He was deposed by Innocent, and Frederick II was appointed, who now reigns.”

Thus, at the beginning of the thirteenth century, the exemplar of the *Etymologies* from which the Chisian codex appears to have been copied had been interpolated.

Book XIV is wholly altered and enlarged by two chapters, one on the Holy Land and the other on glorious Jerusalem, the metropolitan city. From that point to the end of the work everything has been altered at will. There follows material *On the Schism of Heretics*, a *Catalogue of Heretics* attributed to Jerome—“A certain Simon Magus, etc.”—a chapter on the philosophers of the nations, one on poets, and so forth.

We shall present the *Catalogue of Heretics* from other, older parchment manuscripts.

4. The Lucca codex is shelfmark plut. 2, no. 55, collated with the Bignaean edition and with the older edition of 1483. It is a folio parchment manuscript of the eleventh century. At the beginning of the codex the following has been written:

“This book belongs to the blessed episcopate of S. Martin of Lucca. Whoever steals it or fraudulently retains it shall, by the authority of this mother church, which is the head of all the churches of the diocese of Lucca, and with the consent of the canons, be anathema forever, unless he returns it. Amen, let it be done, let it be done, let it be done, let it be done, let it be done, let it be done.”

There is no title for the letters in the codex. After the letters comes a table of the chapters of book I. Then:

“Here begins the first book, *On Grammar and Its Parts*.”

At the end:

“Here ends the book of the *Etymologies* of our lord Isidore, bishop. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

A certain scribe, or one of Zaccaria’s associates, collected quite a substantial number of variant readings. As I have already observed, he frequently devoted his labor to collating manuscript copies of this kind.

5. Variant readings, not so plentiful, of the Florentine codex in the library of S. Marco were written in another hand. It is a folio parchment manuscript, perhaps of the eleventh century, in which the work of the *Etymologies* is distributed into twenty-two books, with the book *On the Nature of Things* appended as book XXIII.

Its inscription is:

“Here begin the texts of the letters of Isidore and Braulio to Isidore concerning the request for the book of the *Etymologies*.”

Many features peculiar to the Lucca codex are also found in this S. Marco codex.

6. The oldest Malatesta copy of the *Etymologies*, shelfmark plut. 21, no. 5, bears this title:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ: here begins the book of the *Etymologies*, etc.”

Then:

“Here begins the letter, etc.”

That is, Isidore’s letter beginning “With every desire, etc.,” and Braulio’s beginning “O pious lord, etc.”

Then follows:

“Here begin the books of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, written to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.”

“Here begins the prologue. Behold for you, etc.”

“Here begin the chapters of the first book.”

7. Mansi describes this outstanding codex as follows in his supplement to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca mediaevalis*, under the entry ISIDORE:

“I ask the indulgence of fair-minded readers if I here place before their eyes the oldest codex of S. Isidore’s *Etymologies* of all those I have ever heard of or read, preserved in the library of the Malatesta family at Cesena—a book which I believe was written in the seventh century.

“It contains twenty-five books, namely five more than the number presented by the printed editions. This difference does not arise from the addition of material beyond what is printed, but solely from a different arrangement of the work.

“It is distributed as follows. The first four books are as in the printed editions, except that book IV, chapter 13, *On the Beginning of Medicine*, is missing.

“In book V Isidore’s *Chronicle* differs somewhat; in this codex it begins *The Order of Times*.

“The remaining books proceed step by step with the printed editions up to chapter 26—one should read chapter 16 of book XVIII. But the beginning of chapter 27—one should read chapter 17—in the printed editions is, in the codex, the beginning of book XIX.

“Then chapter 20 of book XVIII in the printed editions is book XX there; book XXI begins with chapter 52 of book XVIII; book XXII is chapter 60 of book XVIII; book XXIII begins with chapter 7 of book XIX; and finally book XXV is joined to book XX of the printed editions.”

[Col. 0298B] 8. Those additions which are given separately in the Paris edition of 1601, page 269, also appear here, though not all of them, written in the margin: *talent*, etc.; *mina*, etc.; *obol*, etc.; *shekel*, etc.

These additions are in a hand different from, and somewhat more recent than, all the rest. Some not insignificant variant readings occur, which, because of the pressure of time, I was prevented from recording with greater care.

I did not neglect only this one point. Where the printed edition, book XIX, chapter 19, reads *canterium, gablaia, guvia*, the codex reads *cauteria lingulina*.

Finally, at the end of the book, in the same hand as the rest, these verses are found:

“As it is labor for farmers to cleave the lands with the plow,

so for me the reed pen is to furrow the fallow fields.

That man too rejoices to see the ripened harvests;

so I too, [lecto: uncertain], rejoice to bring the verse to its end.”

9. Zaccaria also transcribed these verses, but in the first he read better: “to cleave with the plow for the farmers.” The word *is* is redundant, so that the verse may stand. In the second verse one should restore “with a reed pen.” In the last verse Zaccaria more correctly reads *letor*—“I rejoice”—rather than *laetor*, for Mansi has nothing at *lecto*. In place of *versum* it would be preferable to read *versu*.

Zaccaria added the following from the same codex:

“I ask you, good readers, to pray for Peter the scribe, if you have God as your protector. The end. Thanks be always to God. Amen.”

I possess a sample of the script of this codex, which I readily believe to be extremely ancient. I would not so readily agree with Mansi that it belongs to the seventh century, that is, the century in which Isidore died.

10. In 1780 Joseph Maria Mucciolus published at Cesena a catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Malatesta Library at Cesena, entrusted to the custody and care of the Conventual Friars Minor.

In volume II, pages 141 and following, he describes this very codex, shelfmark plut. 20, no. 4:

“Twenty-five books of S. Isidore’s *Etymologies*.”

In large square letters, on the first page of the codex, there is this heading:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, here begins the book of the *Etymologies*, edited by Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, written to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.”

A parchment leaf is firmly attached to the inside of the first cover of the codex. It contains a table of the subjects treated in the codex:

“So that you may be able to find what you seek, etc.”

11. Then come the alternating letters of Isidore and Braulio. Mucciolus observes that the heading of the codex is:

“Here begins the book of the *Etymologies*,”

because, he says, Isidore himself did not arrange it into books. After Isidore’s death, however, Braulio gave the work its final form, divided it into twenty books, and added many highly useful things collected from various excellent authors—things worth knowing that could scarcely be found elsewhere.

12. It is indeed true that Isidore did not divide his work into books; it is also true that the division into books is Braulio’s. But that Braulio added or inserted anything into the work is reported neither by Braulio himself nor established from any other source. Mucciolus carefully sets out the individual contents of the Codex because, as he says, the Codex possesses such venerable antiquity that the most learned men who have traveled through many European libraries admit that they have neither heard of nor read any Codex older than this one. Since many are contemplating a new edition of Isidore’s Works, [Col. 0299B] it can contribute greatly to a complete and accurate reading. Lovers of learning eagerly await an edition of all the Works of Saint Isidore, either already prepared or soon to be prepared by the distinguished Abbot Francesco Zaccaria. Would that fate not forestall his plan!

13. He again makes the following observation concerning the Codex’s antiquity: “The Codex is the oldest of all those preserved by the distinguished Malatesta Library at Cesena. If, concerning the antiquity of such a Codex, we consult what has been printed in the additions of the distinguished Mansi to Fabricius’s Library, it is of the seventh century, [lacuna] although in the manuscript pages of our library we read, written by the copyist (Mansi), that the Codex is of the ninth century.” The most learned Abbot Zaccaria likewise considers the Codex to be of the ninth century; [Col. 0299C] his judgment was conveyed to me by letter by the learned young man Gaetano Marini. Mucciolus adds Zaccaria’s judgment, which is as follows:

“In the celebrated Malatesta Library at Cesena there are two membranaceous Codices of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, one from the eleventh century; the other, older, no. 5, is perhaps from the ninth century. Both deserve recommendation on many grounds, since they provide a very abundant harvest of readings differing from the printed copies. In both Codices Isidore’s Chronicle is especially noteworthy. It is placed as book V, chapter 37, and is entitled in the Madrid edition of 1599 *On the Distinction of Times*; nor does it differ slightly from the printed books of this Chronicle. In the more recent copy, however, there is this singular feature: books V, chapters 4 and 5, of Saint Isidore *On Heresies* are omitted, and in their place an equal number of chapters from Jerome’s *Index of Heresies* 382 is substituted, from which many corrections may be made to the exceedingly corrupt Paris edition of the same work, first prepared by Claudius Menardus.” [Col. 0299D]

14. Mucciolus reports these matters from Zaccaria’s letters. He further notes that many words have been added in the margins, either omitted by the scribe or indicating what particular matter is being treated there; that a preface concerning the four disciplines that follow is placed before book III, and another brief preface before book XIII. “These two prefaces,” he says, “do not, as far as we know, occur at all in the editions.” He had read the editions rather inattentively: for in the commonly circulated editions of the *Etymologies* such brief prefaces are readily found.

15. Mucciolus observes that Mansi was deceived when [Col. 0300A] he wrote in the additions to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca media* that book IV, chapter 13, *On the Beginning of Medicine*, was missing. For the title of this final chapter is present, and through a scribal error it is read, “On the Beginning of Medicine” (*de Initium medicinae*). Indeed, on the right and lower margin of the chapter itself, small annotations are visible, whose final words are: “Caruticum, Calasticum, Martiatu.” Nor can it so easily be judged that anything is missing.

16. After the *Etymologies*, the same Codex contains several homilies of Saint Augustine and certain questions on Sacred Scripture, arranged by questions and answers and mutilated at the end. The beginning is: “Because I see that you wish to contend about the Scriptures,” etc. Mucciolus published them among his *Anecdota*, p. 249 ff.

17. On p. 287 Mucciolus presents a catalogue of the manuscript Codices of the Malatesta Library, which Mansi had once compiled. Concerning this Codex it is noted that it contains certain works of Augustine, but apocryphal ones. [Col. 0300B] Mansi adds:

“This Codex is the most outstanding of all those in this library, since it displays a script characteristic of the ninth century [lacuna]. It has several annotations added in the margin by a somewhat later hand, especially in book V, where two imperial constitutions are read; the author takes the first of these from book I of the *Constitutions*. I have nowhere found these laws.”

Mucciolus affirms, p. 143, that all the additions which are printed separately in the Paris edition of 1601—whether in the margins or in the text of the Codex—are visible there, such as *talentum*, etc., *mina*, etc., *obolus*, etc.

18. Zaccaria noted the difference between the script of the celebrated Malatesta Codex and the Madrid edition in the first three books, [Col. 0300C] while also collating a second, more recent Malatesta Codex. “Up to this point,” he says at the end of book III, “I have collated the Madrid edition with both Cesena Codices. Since I had to leave Cesena, however, I left the remaining books to be collated with the Venetian edition of 1483 by Francesco Gualterius, a priest.”

19. Gualterius did in fact collate both Cesena Codices and copied from the more recent one the *Index of Heretics* attributed to Saint Jerome. At its end I find the following note: “Francesco Gualterius, priest, copied this at Cesena on the Ides of September in the year 1755 of the restoration of mankind.”

Now this more recent Malatesta Codex, shelf 21, no. 1, of the eleventh century, bears the following inscription:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the first book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, of the *Etymologies*.” [Col. 0300D]

The table of contents of the first book follows, with the Epistles commonly printed in the editions omitted.

20. *Glossary.* In addition to the observations already published by many scholars on the *Glossary* circulated under Isidore’s name, Zaccaria had promised the extensive notes of Johann Salomon Semler, which he testifies were sent to him by their author in 1752. Among Zaccaria’s papers I find these autograph observations of Semler, together with letters addressed to the Marquis Maffei in March 1752, by which he sent his annotations for printing. But when Semler learned from Maffei that Zaccaria was undertaking a new edition of all Isidore’s Works, he readily agreed that his notes on the *Glossary* should be delivered to Zaccaria; indeed, he promised some additional observations on the books of the *Etymologies*, as may be gathered from his letter to Maffei written in August of that same year, 1752.

In fact, [Col. 0301A] some observations of Semler on the books of the *Etymologies* are also present. But the notes on the *Glossary* and on the books of the *Etymologies* are written in such a difficult hand and are moreover so defaced by erasures that little benefit can be expected from them. “Lack of time,” he himself says in one of his letters to Maffei, “prevented me from having them copied again, although the multitude of erasures almost demanded it.”

21. Nevertheless, I shall strive, as far as I can, so that the republic of letters may not be entirely deprived of Semler’s learned labors on Isidore. He himself had ordered the following title to be placed on the work:

“Latin Glossary, published several times under the name of Isidore, illustrated with various corrections by the most learned men and with other new material, by Johann Salomon Semler, Professor of History and Poetry in the Altdorf Academy of the Free Imperial City of Nuremberg in the Holy Roman Empire, honorary member of the Latin Society of Jena.” [Col. 0301B]

He dedicated the work to the Marquis Maffei as follows:

“To the illustrious and most excellent lord, Lord Scipione Maffei, Marquis, most deserving of all literary pursuits, a man of the highest renown: this edition of the *Glossary*, which he himself most brilliantly assisted, is given, dedicated, and consecrated by Johann Salomon Semler.”

22. *The Three Books of the Differentiae*, with two Lucchese manuscripts, one belonging to the chapter of Pistoia and the other to the Florentine Library of Santa Croce. Thus the [Col. 0301C] *Prospectus* of Zaccaria’s edition reported it; but in his *Adversaria* there are only variant readings of one Lucchese Codex and of the Santa Croce Codex. Nor do these readings belong to the two books of the *Differentiae verborum*, or *On the Properties of Expressions*, but only to the book of the *Differentiae rerum*.

The Lucchese Codex is the very one in which I also said that the books *Against the Jews* are contained. Its title is:

“Here begin the chapters of the book of the *Differentiae* of Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

After the table of contents:

“Here begins the book of the *Differentiae* of Isidore, bishop.”

23. The Florentine Codex of Santa Croce, no. 233, shelf 20, also displays Isidore’s prefaces and will therefore be described in Zaccaria’s preface to the *Prooemia*. The title of the present work is:

“Here begins the book of the *Differentiae* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

These two [Col. 0301D] Codices were collated with the Breulian edition. But a serious inconvenience has arisen in this work and in certain other recensions by Zaccaria: the words of the edition are not copied out; only a number is recorded, corresponding to the variant word in the edition, which is distinguished by the same number. Since the copy of that Breulian edition to which such numbers were appended is not available, and indeed I have not ascertained where it is kept, it is absolutely necessary that the true reading of the Codices be investigated only through arduous labor—and often it may not be discovered at all.

24. There are some variant readings from the Malatesta Codex, which, as I have often noted, contains the *Prooemia* and other Isidorian books. Its title is:

“Here begins the book [Col. 0302A] of the *Differentiae* of Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

Then:

“These are the *Differentiae rerum*.”

It continues:

“The first book is complete. Here begins the second, concerning the *Differentiae verborum*.”

Only from the prologue is a divergence in the writing noted.

25. Although in his prospectus Zaccaria did not mention the variant readings of Vatican Codex 624, 385 I nevertheless find some from that Codex in his *Adversaria*, for the book of the *Differentiae nominum*, or *Differentiae verborum*. Perhaps some will wish to know why Zaccaria excerpted so few materials from the manuscript copies of the Vatican Library, since he himself relates in the volume of his literary journey through Italy that he was able, at leisure, to consult the Vatican manuscripts.

26. But if we examine the sequence of his account, we shall rather conclude that he had no leisure to examine the manuscript copies of the Vatican Library. He reports [Col. 0302B] in part I, chapter 6, of his *Literary Journey through Italy*, that in 1754, while staying at Florence, he was summoned by His Serene Highness Francesco III, Duke of Modena, to take charge of the Este Library. Then he adds the following:

27. “But before I departed for Modena, I realized that I had to go to Rome, so that I might consult the manuscript Codices of the Vatican and of the other libraries, which are present in great number in that foremost city of the world, for the edition of Isidore’s Works that I am preparing. Accordingly, having obtained permission from Father Ignatius Visconti, then Superior General of our Society, I undertook the journey to Rome in September.

“Most of our Roman associates, who were especially bound to me by friendship—Lagomarsini, Noceti, Contucci, Carpani, Mazzolari, Lazzaro, Boscovich, Cunich, Faurius, and many others, men who had rendered the greatest service to learning, whose names it would be altogether too long to enumerate—were all spending time in the country at Tusculum. [Col. 0302C] Yet, so that I would not leave Rome without visiting them, as soon as I entered the city I resolved at once to visit the libraries and seek out Isidorian Codices everywhere, so that, once that labor had been completed, I might go out to Tusculum to embrace them.

“Therefore, so that I might have easier access to the Vatican Library, whose Codices above all I intended to collate with the printed copies of Isidore, at the urging of Fabius Danzetta, a most learned and wise man of our Society, and under the guidance of Jerome Lombardus, himself also a highly learned priest of our Society, I humbly threw myself at the feet of Benedict XIV, the Supreme Pontiff. It is incredible to relate how kindly that most merciful pontiff received me, how carefully he inquired about the character and purpose of my studies, and how he promised and provided me with every assistance. To all the other services of such great kindness he added this: once each week, on Fridays, during the weeks I stayed in Rome, I was permitted to visit the pontiff himself and enjoy his most learned conversations.”

28. “Thus, by papal authority, I went to the [Col. 0302D] Vatican Library, that immense treasury of ancient learning. From its equally learned and humane prefect, Assemani, I easily obtained permission to consult all the Isidorian Codices at leisure. After examining the Vatican Library, I visited the Chigi and Barberini Libraries and also examined the Vallicelliana. The time available to me did not permit me to go beyond the Isidorian Codices in those libraries.

“Meanwhile, through the kindness of Peter Lazzaro, prefect of the library of our Roman college, he left Tusculum for a time and came to the city to show me that library, which had been wonderfully enlarged since my departure from Rome after my theological studies and adorned chiefly through the efforts and under the direction of its rector, Domenico Franchini. From it I could certainly have borrowed no small number of items for publication in this volume. But since only a few months earlier Lazzaro himself had brought to light the first book of miscellanies from its manuscript Codices, while the republic of letters applauded, [Col. 0303A] I did not wish, as they say, to put my sickle into another’s harvest.

“Thus it occurred to me instead to examine the library of our professed house and, if anything noteworthy lay hidden in its manuscripts, to record it in my notebooks, so that it might later be printed in this book in its public form. This plan of mine was strongly encouraged, apart from Father Ignatius Visconti, the Superior General of our Society whom I mentioned earlier, by Domenico Turanius, a Sicilian and an outstanding theologian of the Sacred Penitentiary, as they say.

“I nevertheless postponed this labor until I returned from Tusculum, where I was planning to go; for I was held by an extraordinary desire to see my associates. I therefore went to Tusculum, where Benedict Stay, the most elegant of poets, paid me a most courteous visit at the home of Lagomarsini, who was then suffering from gout. From there I turned aside to Castel Gandolfo and also to Albano; on my return I visited the most learned Abbot Rodolfinus Venuti, who was spending time in the country.

“After a few days of residence at Tusculum had passed, I reluctantly tore myself away from my friends, among whom was Prospero Buttarus, a nobleman of Auximum and a young man of outstanding character, and hastened to Rome.” [Col. 0303B]

29. “I was awaiting the most illustrious prelate, a man memorable to me for many reasons, Francesco Saverio Zelada, who was returning from some mission or other. He returned, in fact, sooner than I had expected. Accordingly, I divided the days that I subsequently spent in Rome between him and the library of the professors of our house. But the discussion must now turn to the manuscript Codices of this library. They are as follows, etc.”

30. Zaccaria compiled not only this catalogue of manuscript books during his stay in Rome; he also obtained information about several coins recently discovered at Rome and carefully described them. Yet, although, as we have seen, he undertook his Roman journey in September, by the beginning of November of that same year [Col. 0303C] he had already gone to Modena, as he continues to relate in the same chapter 6:

“But at last Rome had to be left, and Florence also, toward which city I proceeded by the direct route, so that, after gathering my belongings, I might depart for Modena. Thus I arrived at Modena at the beginning of November.”

It is therefore not surprising that, for the edition he was then especially preparing, he collected little from the Vatican Library.

The distinguished Aloysius Cuccagni, in the *Life of Zaccaria* which he recently published and which he commendably compiled from various documents with great diligence, thinks, no. 36, that it can be inferred from manuscript papers that as soon as Zaccaria had been appointed prefect of the Este Library, he went to Modena before undertaking his journey to Rome. But the contrary is clear even from the title of the cited chapter 6 of the *Literary Journey*: “In August the author was summoned to Modena by His Serene Highness Duke Francesco III, to take charge of the Este Library. Before moving there, he went to Rome in September,” etc. [Col. 0303D]

31. Since, therefore, Zaccaria published the *Prospectus* of his Isidorian edition in 1758, after inspecting the ancient copies of the Vatican Library, and since in it he promised that he would draw scarcely anything from the Vatican Library, we must conclude that he excerpted little from that library and did not arrange for anyone else to excerpt much for him.

Nevertheless, [Col. 0304A] among Zaccaria’s papers I find seven pages written in the hand of someone unknown to me, apparently delivered to him after the publication of the prospectus. On these pages the various readings of the *Differentiae sermonum* mentioned above are recorded, and some other Vatican Codices containing Isidorian works—nineteen in all—are briefly listed, with some variation in their script described in one or another of them, as a specimen.

So much for Zaccaria’s scholarly apparatus for the Isidorian edition. For this part of his industry and labors, we Spaniards in particular ought to be deeply grateful.

32. This would be the place, since we can now praise the most learned man without any charge of flattery, to compose his eulogy. But what a broad field of discourse would open before us! We are hastening on to other matters. As I suggested earlier, the distinguished Aloysius Cuccagni, who undertook that task, has commended his life to posterity.

I shall present [Col. 0304B] what Zaccaria himself wrote concerning his earliest studies in 1750 or the following year, for inclusion in the Jesuit Library, omitting the large catalogue of works that he had already published by then. In the manuscript papers relating to the Jesuit Library I find his surname written in more than one form: *Zaccarias*, *Zacharias*, *Zaccaria*. I retain the last form, which accords with the Italian language.

33. Francesco Antonio Zaccaria was born at Venice in 1714, on 27 March. He entered the Society at Vienna in Austria in 1731, in the month of October. After completing his novitiate, he was sent to Gorizia, where he taught the humanities for four years; then he was summoned to Rome to study theology. Subsequently, at Milan, he made (*misit*; perhaps *emisit*) his solemn profession of the four vows on 15 August 1747. He is now serving throughout Italy as a preacher.

The Most Eminent Quirinus, in a letter written to Father Jerome Lagomarsini on 13 August 1749, speaks of him as follows.

[Col. 0304C] 388

34. “Finally, I ask you, Jerome, to give my warmest greetings to Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, your associate, who is presently staying with you at Florence, and assure him that I esteem highly his learning, which is attested by the many scholarly works he has published.”

The most illustrious and equally learned Giovanni Battista Passeri dedicated to Father Zaccaria a dissertation on the bone-gathering of the ancients, published at Florence in 1747 in volume I of the *Monumenta of the Florentine Colombaria Society*. The very distinguished Antonio Francesco Gori, however, says in volume I of the *Literary Symbols*, p. 34:

“Also deserving of the highest praise are the most learned priests of the Society of Jesus, Emmanuel de Azevedo, a Portuguese, and his associates in the arduous work of publishing the *Liturgical Treasury*, namely Peter Lazzaro and Francesco Antonio Zaccaria.”

For his fame had spread that he was to be summoned to Rome as Father de Azevedo’s associate; and this had indeed been almost decided, but for certain reasons that plan was changed. [Col. 0304D]

35. These materials, as I said, are preserved in the manuscript papers of the Jesuit Library, which Francesco Oudin and Giovanni Ludovico Courtois collected with the greatest care while the Society of Jesus still existed. Many of these documents have sadly perished; but many are still preserved in my possession, and they could be useful for illuminating the literary history of nearly all sciences and nations. I shall undertake, if I can, to make them so at some time.

Now the funeral eulogy which I promised, engraved on Zaccaria’s tomb, is as follows:

“Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, a Venetian by birth, a priest of the Society of Jesus, which institution he candidly professed for as long as it existed, richly, learnedly, and orthodoxly published many books and rendered the greatest service to letters, sciences, and religion. He lived 82 years, 6 months, 14 days. He died on 10 October 1795. P. Q.”

36. I add another epitaph, composed by the distinguished and highly expert master of this faculty, Stefano Antonio Morcelli, which is circulated in printed form. But in both epitaphs *he lived 81 years* should be read instead of *82 years*.

[Col. 0306A]

“To the rest and memory of Francesco Antonio Zaccaria, a Venetian by birth, who fulfilled every office of learning, most illustrious in religion and doctrine, in whom zeal for the Church and love of right-thinking men shone forth, and in whom industry in writing, judgment, and discrimination are considered supreme. He lived piously for 82 years, 6 months, 14 days, surpassing the age of his works in number. From his friends, to the excellent and most gentle old man. F. C.”

## Part Two. On the Individual Works of Saint Isidore and Their Particular Editions

[Col. 0305]

389

## Chapter XLVI. The Works of Saint Isidore Listed from Ancient Library Catalogues

[Col. 0305B]

1. In the oldest library catalogues that have come down to us, the Works of Saint Isidore are occasionally indicated. It will be worthwhile to mention them, both so that we may better understand the esteem in which Isidore was formerly held, and especially so that we may judge more securely concerning his genuine works.

2. The name of the monastery of Fulda is famous. Its oldest library catalogue is preserved in Vatican-Palatine Codex 1877, approximately of the tenth century, and is entitled as follows:

“How many books there were, and whose, in the Fulda library.”

Although after the enumeration of certain books of Jerome there is a note written by another hand, “Catalogue of the Lorsch Library,” it is nevertheless clear that the Fulda catalogue continues. For the catalogue of the Lorsch Library has already preceded it in this volume and is different from this Fulda catalogue.

There one reads: “Twenty-one books of Isidore’s *Etymologies*,” etc., as in the catalogue of the Lorsch Library soon to be reported, from this same Codex. Here the reading is *de Nativitate*, “On the Nativity,” not *de civitate*, “On the city,” and book II addressed to Florentina is not indicated. It ends: “of the Apostles Peter and Paul.”

At the end of the catalogue:

“Arculf’s description of the site of Jerusalem and of the holy places around it, and Isidore’s work *On the Order of Created Things*, in one Codex.”

It appears to read *creatura* or *creaturae*.

3. Codex Vatican-Palatine 57, membranaceous, quarto, approximately from the beginning of the ninth century, presents the oldest catalogue of the books of the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch. From there several Codices, through various vicissitudes, passed into the Palatine Library and from there into the Vatican Library. [Col. 0305D]

In this catalogue are listed:

“Twenty-one books of Isidore’s *Etymologies* in one Codex. Three books of the same author, the *Sentences*. The first begins: ‘That God is supreme and unchangeable.’ The same author’s *On the Nature of Things*, and his book of the *Differentiae*. The same author’s work addressed to his sister Florentina, *On the Nativity*—read *On the Nativity*, not *On the City*—of the Lord. His *Prologues* and *Chronicle*. His *Breviary* on the books of sacred history. Isidore’s *On the Origin*—perhaps *On the Order*—of created things, in one gathering. The *Sentences* and the *Chronicle* in gatherings.”

In this catalogue, besides the biblical books, most Codices list works of the Holy Fathers, including Bede and Albinus. There is also noted a booklet of Quintus Julius Hilarion *On the Origin of the World* in one Codex; likewise, an exposition by Justus, bishop of Urgell, on the *Song of Songs*; likewise, the book of *Prognostics* by Julian, bishop—namely of Toledo. I believe the book called *Anti Cymenon* also belongs to him, for it should be read *Antikeimenōn* [ἀντικειμένων, “of things opposed”].

4. Another, fuller catalogue of the same library is described in the cited Vatican-Palatine Codex 1877. The listing of Saint Isidore’s Works agrees with the preceding one up to “is unchangeable”; it continues:

“The second, *On Wisdom*. The third, *On the Scourges of God*, in one Codex. The same author’s *On the Nature of Things*—above, that is, the book *On Wheels*—and book I of the *Differentiae*. Also two books *On the Origin of Offices*, and two books of his *Synonyma*, and *How the Saying ‘Do Not Judge’ Is to Be Understood*, and *On the Beam and the Speck*: all these in one Codex.

“The same author’s book addressed to his sister Florentina, *On the Nativity*—*On the City* is written, but read *On the Nativity*—of the Lord, his Passion, Resurrection, Kingdom, and Judgment, book I; and book II, *On the Calling of the Nations*, in one Codex.

“His *Prologues*, and *Chronicle*, and his *On the Meaning of Names* addressed to Orosius, in one Codex. His *Breviary* on the books of sacred history, and the verses composed by him that are written in his bookcase; and in the same book, a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint John the Baptist and on the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul.

“Isidore’s *On the Origin*—*Order*—of created things,” etc., as above.

Near the end:

“Likewise, a book of glosses, and Isidore’s *Chronicle*; and Seneca’s *Sentences* in one Codex.” [Col. 0306C]

5. In another Vatican-Palatine Codex, no. 233, paper, folio, p. 294, there are listed, apparently from the catalogue of some old library, three books of Isidore *On the Supreme Good*, twenty books of the *Etymologies*, and Isidore *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, whose ending is: “might be confirmed by sentences,” as in Grialius’s edition. Others add certain further items.

This Codex contains excerpts collected from the Works of Saint Augustine. Codex 226 of the same Vatican-Palatine Library, paper, quarto, of the fifteenth century, presents the same works of Isidore in a similar fashion, but omits the final words of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

6. Pez, volume III of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, part III, col. 609, reports the following from ancient records of the monastery of Benediktbeuern:

“The books which the nun Kisyla, born of the royal stock of the Franks, gave to the church of Saint Michael at Quochalum are described. Kisyla had these books written by her chaplains, namely by Engilhard, Chadold, Tracholf, bishop of the Church of Freising, Rudpert, and Racholf.” [Col. 0307A]

Among them is “the book of the *Synonyma*, namely Isidore’s.” For the books donated by Kisyla—also called Gisela or Gisala—the wife of Childeric, the last Merovingian king, who was deposed by his own people, were later transferred to the monastery of Benediktbeuern.

In the catalogue of the books of the monastery of Benediktbeuern from the thirteenth century, cited by Pez, the following are listed:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies* [lacuna]. Isidore’s *Sentences*; also another book of *Sentences* [lacuna]. Isidore’s *Synonyma*.”

It is noted that the Codex of the *Etymologies* is of good quality and was written in the tenth century.

7. Charles Meichelbeck, of the Benedictine Order, volume I of the *History of Freising*, part I, under Joseph, the third bishop of Freising, relates as follows:

“The wife of that deposed Childeric, Gisala, withdrew among the religious nuns of the Parthenon recently established at Cochel on the Bavarian lake and subject to the monastery of Benediktbeuern. [Col. 0307B] The very ancient Codices of that same Gisala are still displayed intact in the said monastery of Benediktbeuern. Among these, therefore, I believe Isidore’s *Synonyma* should be placed; consequently, it must be said that they were written in the eighth century.”

From this it may also be inferred how falsely some have reported that Childeric was celibate. Indeed, Mabillon, *Benedictine Annals*, book XII, p. 154, no. 55, reports from the Fontanella chronicle that Theodoric, the son of Childeric, who had been expelled from the kingdom, was made a cleric.

8. In the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, no. 43, Pez cites from the catalogue of the books of the monastery of Weihenstephan, approximately of the eleventh century:

“Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*.”

Again, no. 71, from the catalogue of the books of the thirteenth century that existed in the Canonry of Saint Nicholas at Passau, but were burned in 1395, he presents:

“Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*; Isidore’s letters.”

In the same place, no. 45, he says:

“In the library of the Canons of Freising there are certain Codices that approach one thousand years in age. We viewed, not without amazement, the Works of Gregory the Great, Jerome, Isidore, and others.” [Col. 0307C] “Orosius, approximately of the eighth century,” etc.

In the same volume I, part 3, it is established from the work of John Egon *On the Illustrious Men of the Monastery of Reichenau*, chapter 12, that the monk Kerard wrote the *Synonyma* contained in one volume in the tenth century. Anyone can easily convince himself that these are our Isidore’s *Synonyma*, for the discussion is about the scribe, not the author of the book.

In Pez’s introductory dissertation to volume II, p. 11, books given by Heinricus to the church of Göttweig are listed from a Codex of the twelfth century, including:

“Eucherius, *On Hebrew Names*. Isidore, briefly, on the entire library”—I understand, “on the whole of Sacred Scripture.” “Also Isidore’s *Sentences* on both Testaments,” etc.

9. Montfaucon, in the *Italian Journal*, chapter 6, gives the catalogue of the books of the monastery of Pomposa from the eleventh century. It includes:

“Isidore’s letter to Maston, bishop—alternatively, Masson, Massanus, or Massenus—*On the Fallen Priest’s Ability to Rise Again through Penance to His Former State of Grace*. It begins: ‘When a servant came to us.’ Isidore’s book of the *Etymologies*, bishop of Seville. The book of *Prologues* on the New and Old Testament.

“Also Saint Isidore’s book *On the Life, Origin, and Death of the Holy Fathers Who Are Mentioned in the Praises of Scripture*. This book begins as follows—the *Allegories*: ‘Here begin the names of the Holy Fathers of the Old Testament mystically explained by Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.’ This book begins: ‘Adam bore the figure of Christ.’

“Also the names of the saints of the New Testament. This work begins: ‘Four.’

“Saint Isidore’s *Chronicle*, a book describing a brief summary of histories, from the beginning of the world up to the time of Heraclius.

“Isidore’s book of the *Differentiae*, bishop of Seville. This book begins [lacuna].

“Also *On the Distinctions of the Four Vices*. This book begins: ‘Yet, however, against these [there are] four kinds of virtues.’” This is the end of book II of the *Differentiae*.

“Also the second book, *On the Differentiae of Words*. This book begins: ‘Isidore to the reader, greetings. Most of the ancients endeavored to distinguish the differences of expressions.’ [Col. 0308B]

“Isidore’s sermon against the Arians, which begins: ‘Come, Lord Jesus, our Redeemer.’”

10. I discussed the catalogue of the manuscript books preserved in the monastery of Bobbio in the tenth century in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 27, from Muratori, volume III of the *Antiquities of the Middle Ages in Italy*, col. 817 ff.

In the older part of its library I find:

“Book I, containing someone’s art, the *Synonyma*, and the *Chronicle of the Apostles*.” Isidore’s *Synonyma* may perhaps be intended.

More clearly concerning Isidore:

“Also concerning the books of Isidore: an exposition on Genesis, book I. On days and weeks, times, and signs, two books”—perhaps from the *Etymologies*, or from the book *On the Nature of Things*. “Five books of *Offices*, and in one of these are contained letters of various people, Cicero’s *Synonyma*, and glosses. Three books of the *Differentiae*. Two books of the *Prologues*. Four books of the *Homologaria*—that is, the *Etymologies*. Three books of the *Sentences*. One book *On the Order of Created Things*. One book of Isidore’s *Chronicle* [lacuna].”

The catalogue continues below:

“Also concerning the canons [lacuna]. One book of canons, in which Isidore’s *On the Order of Things* is contained [lacuna]. A *Rule of an Honorable Life* by a certain Martin”—Martin of Dume—“[lacuna]. Cicero’s *Synonyma* [lacuna]. One book of Isidore *On Vices*.”

11. All these items are in the older library, as I said. The books that Dungal donated to the monastery of Bobbio in the ninth century follow. Among them the catalogue lists:

“One book of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.”

Among the books of the priest Benedict:

“One book of Isidore’s *Offices*.” [Col. 0308D]

Among the books of the priest Theodore:

“Julianus Pomerius’s book of *Prognostics* [lacuna]. One book of Isidore’s *Chronicle* [lacuna]. One book of Isidore, Servius, etc.”—I believe this concerns what Isidore treats about grammar in the *Etymologies*—“[lacuna]. One book *On Dialectic* by Martianus, Augustine, Apuleius, and Isidore.”

It must be observed that the numbers I, II, III, etc., attached to the books do not indicate the parts into which a work was divided, but rather the number of volumes in the library that contained such a work.

It is also worth noting that even at that time the surname *Pomerius* had been attached to Julian, bishop of Toledo. This is appropriate only to Julianus Pomerius, a Moor by nationality and the author of the three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which circulate under the name of Prosper.

12. The Pistoia Library, published by Zaccaria in 1752, presents a catalogue of twelfth-century books with the following title:

“Brief record of the treasury of the church of Saint Zeno.” [Col. 0309A]

Among other items are:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies* [lacuna]; Isidore’s *Supreme Good*.”

This may perhaps be the copy indicated among the books that exist, p. 13:

“Three books of Saint Isidore of Seville,” namely, the *Sentences*.

13. In volume I of the *Monasticon Anglicanum* there is a charter concerning the lands, ornaments, vestments, and books of the church of Saint Peter of the monastery of Exeter, granted by Leofric, bishop of that place, who died in 1071. Among the books, p. 223, are listed:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies* and the passions of the Apostles [lacuna]. Isidore’s book *On the Miracles of Christ*.”

14. In volume XXXIV of *Sacred Spain*, p. 455, it is reported of Oveco, bishop of León, that about the year 951 he gave, among other things, to the monastery of Saint John of Vega, which he had founded, seven ecclesiastical books, namely an Antiphonary, etc. He also gave ten spiritual books, namely the *Lives of the Fathers* [lacuna], “the *Sentences* of blessed Isidore and his *Synonyma*; the *Sentences* of Lord Gregory,” etc.

Perhaps the work of Taio is meant by “the *Sentences* of Lord Gregory.”

15. At the Fontanelle monastery, as is reported in chapter 12 of its Chronicle, during the time of Abbot Wando, from the year 742 onward, the following books of Isidore are recorded among others as having been acquired:

“Likewise, in the same book, [there is] a work On the Spiritual and Bodily Differences by Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, in which there are forty-two chapters . . . Likewise, in the same [library there are] thirteen chapters from Isidore’s book of Sentences.”

Ansigisus, who was abbot from the year 823 onward, as is clear from chapter 16 of the same Chronicle, donated to the Fontanelle monastery one volume of Taio’s (Tagii, Taii, or Tajonis) Sentences. To the Flavigny monastery [he donated] the Apocalypse of Saint John, in which codex the Book of Saint Isidore’s Differences was also contained . . . one codex of Isidore’s Book of Testimonies concerning Christ and the Church; one codex of his Etymologies; and one codex of his Wheels (On the Nature of Things) addressed to King Sisebut.

16. The index of the manuscript codices of the Basilica of Saint Peter at Rome, surviving in paper in octavo in Codex Regio-Vaticanus 1598, should not be counted among the ancient catalogues, although it deserves mention either because the manuscript is otherwise concealed or because of the dignity of the archive. In it the following are listed:

Folio 7: “Isidore of Seville, on the book of Genesis through the book of Judges.”

Folio 8, from a lectionary written in the year [Col. 0309D] 998: “Testimonies of Bishop Isidore concerning the passion of Christ,” namely, from the books Against the Jews.

Folio 9: “Of Bishop Isidore, On the Incarnation,” from the same books.

On the same folio: “On the Divine Offices,” in an ancient script.^395

Folio 80: “Isidore, why virgins are veiled at the blessing,” from chapter 18, book II of On the Offices, near the end.

# CHAPTER XLVII. Catalogue of Isidore’s Works from Ancient Writers

1. We examined in chapters 3, 4, and 5 the statements about Isidore made by Braulio and Ildefonsus, who lived in his time. Some similar information about Isidore’s writings is also preserved by the author of Isidore’s Life, commonly believed to be Lucas of Tuy; other information we presented in chapter 14 from the author of the Cerratense account, who condensed the same Life. The books listed by Braulio number seventeen, although he says that other short works of Isidore also existed.

The monk who wrote the Silos Chronicle, in Flórez, volume XVII of *Hispania Sacra*, seems to have acknowledged only fourteen, or perhaps fifteen, books of Isidore. Speaking of the Gothic histories, he writes in section 6:
