“These things were written in the book of blessed Isidore, which, among fourteen others that he published, he carefully composed concerning the deeds of the Vandals, Sueves, and Goths.”

By these words, however, he may have meant Isidorian codices containing several works. This author flourished at the beginning of the twelfth century. We shall now bring forward those writers who specifically devoted themselves to cataloguing the books of distinguished men.

2. Notker Balbulus, who died at the beginning of the tenth century, published a book *On Interpreters of Sacred Scripture*. It was printed by Pez in volume I, part I of the *Anecdota*, p. 17, and reprinted by Fabricius at the end of volume V of the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*. Chapter 5 is entitled “On Those Who, Taking Occasion from Their Own Discussions, Explained Certain Sentences of Divine Authority.” There Balbulus proceeds as follows:

“The books of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, entitled *Etymologies*, perfect you in every kind of knowledge. Likewise, you will find his most useful book of *Sentences*. Likewise, another book On the Fathers of the Old and New Testament. Likewise, another On Ecclesiastical Offices and Orders, which are especially necessary for you, who by God’s grace will soon be a priest. In them you will find the entire system and the names of the individual festivals and fasts, so that you may be able to announce beforehand to God’s people the stations to come in the *Keriki* (that is, in the church). For if you do not announce it to the people, you who desire the office of a watchman, and the sword comes and takes him away (Ezekiel 33:6), he himself will die in his iniquity, but his blood will be required at your hand.”^396

3. Notker was writing to Solomon, his pupil, later bishop of the Church of Constance. Although his purpose especially required it, he does not mention Isidore’s commentaries on Sacred Scripture. Perhaps he had read only those commentaries that were mixed and confused under the name of Eucherius and sold as his works. Concerning these he reports in chapter 6:

“You have Eucherius—I do not know whether he is the same man whom the most blessed Augustine relates in the twenty-second book of *The City of God* to have been a priest from old Spain, suffering from the stone and cured through the holy Stephen; or whether he is another bishop or teacher who set forth and explained many very useful interpretations, tropologies, and anagogies of Sacred Scripture.”

Elsewhere we shall discuss this Eucherius and the commentaries bearing his name.

4. Sigebert of Gembloux, who died at a very advanced age in 1112 or shortly thereafter, praises our Isidore in chapter 55 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* as follows:

“Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, wrote much. He wrote twenty books of *Etymologies* to Braulio, bishop. He wrote a book of *Prologues*, concerning the books of the Old and New Testament that the Catholic Church receives into the canon. On Ecclesiastical Offices, to Fulgentius. On the Origin, Life, and Death of the holy Fathers who are praised in Scripture. To Orosius, a book On the Meanings of Names. To Sisebutus, a book On the Nature of Things. He also wrote a book On the Differences of Words, a book On the Properties of Things, a book of Sermons, and a book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas.

“He wrote the *Synonyms*, in which two persons are introduced, one a grieving human being, the other Reason offering admonition. He also wrote the *Lament of the Penitent*, arranged alphabetically, with a prayer added. He wrote one book On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices. One book On the Mysteries of the Savior. He traverses the whole Old Testament by expounding it in a straightforward manner. He also wrote other works belonging to secular literature, which it is not relevant for us to mention.”

5. Sigebert also briefly mentions Isidore of Córdoba in chapter 51:

“Isidore, bishop of Córdoba, wrote four books to Orosius on the books of Kings.”

Yet it is exceedingly likely that this very work also belongs to our Isidore of Seville, as can be inferred from chapter 65. Trithemius, however, seems to have heard nothing about Isidore of Córdoba except what he had read in Sigebert, although he praises him more fully in chapter 120 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*:

“Isidore the Elder, bishop of Córdoba, a man highly skilled in Sacred Scripture and not ignorant of secular literature, quick in intellect and sufficiently eloquent in speech, distinguished no less by his conduct than by his knowledge of Scripture, whose learning was held in great esteem among the ancients, wrote several short works on the divine books. Of these, however, I found one outstanding work that he published to the holy Orosius, a Spanish priest: four books on the four books of Kings. Of the rest I found nothing. He flourished under the emperors Theodosius and Honorius, in the year of the Lord 420.”^397

6. An anonymous twelfth-century writer of Melk, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, published by Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, after Bernard Pez in the Benedictine Library of the Maurists, again lists the following works of Isidore in chapter 26:

“Isidore, bishop of Seville, who succeeded blessed Leander in the episcopate, published many important short works. Among other things, he wrote the *Synonyms* and a chronology, which he brought down to Constantine, son of Heraclius; also a book of *Etymologies*, a book of *Offices*, and a book of *Illustrious Men*. In addition, he transmitted to posterity many sermons, delivered at various times and written in an excellent style.”

7. In the twelfth century Honorius of Autun composed his book *On the Luminaries of the Church*, or *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. In chapter 4 of book III he reports:

“Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote innumerable short works, among which are these: twenty-two books of *Etymologies*, a book of Glosses, a book of *Sentences*, the *Synonyms*, and a book On Difference. He expounded the entire Old Testament in two ways, historically and allegorically, and many other things. He flourished under Heraclius.”

8. In the fourteenth century William Pastrengus, or of Pastrengo, the teacher and friend of Petrarch, became distinguished. In his book *On the Origins of Things*, printed at Venice in 1547 by Nicolaus de Bascharinis, he discusses the writings of distinguished men in alphabetical order. On page 43 and following he writes the following about Isidore:

“Isidore, a Spaniard by nation, bishop of Seville, flourishing in the time of the emperor Heraclius, wrote two books of *Soliloquies* or *Synonyms*; three books of *Sentences*; two books On the Origin of Offices; two books To His Sister Florentina Against the Jews; two books To Orosius the Bishop On the Meaning of the Old and New Testament; one book of Allegories on Genesis; one book on Leviticus; one book on Numbers; one book on Deuteronomy; one book on Joshua; one book on Judges; one book on the book of Kings; one treatise On the Body and Blood of the Lord; and many other works.

“Likewise, a book On Differences; likewise, a book of *Etymologies*; likewise, a large volume of the Decretal Letters of the Roman pontiffs and the Canons of the Councils celebrated at different places throughout the world by Catholic bishops over the course of time. From this, it is clear that the decrees of John, provost of Beauvais, and of Gratian were for the most part excerpted. Likewise, a work On the Life and Death of the Saints who have gone before in the Lord. Likewise, On the Nature of Things. Likewise, a book of the Arts. Likewise, a book of Differences. Likewise, a book On the Supreme Good.”

9. In this edition of Pastrengus it is noted that the work was published under the care of Michael Angelo Blondi, purged of every error. Montfaucon, however, remarks in the *Diario Italico*, p. 48, that it is disfigured by countless faults, so that scarcely a coherent meaning can be extracted from it; it is full of gaps and mutilated in many places. This can already be understood sufficiently from the eulogy of Isidore.

Some details, nevertheless, belong to the author himself—for example, that the books of *Sentences* are listed twice under different titles—unless he ascribes to Isidore another work of *Sentences* from the work of Taio, who in certain manuscripts is mistakenly, I think, called Samuel, and which Risco published less fully than he supposed. See chapter 67.

10. I shall not omit Trithemius, although he had already reached the sixteenth century, for he devoted vigorous effort and the greatest diligence to examining ancient manuscript copies. In chapter 232 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* he composed the following catalogue of Isidore’s works:

“Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, a man most learned in Sacred Scripture and second to none of his time in secular literature, subtle in intellect, clear in understanding, composed in expression, excellent both in verse and prose, and distinguished no less by holiness than by learning, shone forth. He is called ‘the Younger’ to distinguish him from the elder bishop of Córdoba, whom we mentioned above (chapter 120), or from another bishop of Seville who preceded him.

“This Isidore the Younger wrote many distinguished short works, of which I found only the following:

“To Bishop Braulio, twenty books of *Etymologies*. ‘Discipline derives from learning.’

“Allegorically on Genesis, one book. ‘The history of the sacred law.’

“On Exodus, one book. ‘Certain mysteries.’

“On Numbers, one book. ‘Therefore this is one book.’

“On Leviticus, one book. ‘The following book is Leviticus.’

“On Deuteronomy, one book. ‘The book of Deuteronomy.’

“On Joshua, one book. ‘After the death of Moses.’

“On Judges, one book. ‘The history of the Judges.’

“On Kings, four books. ‘After the book of Judges comes . . .’

“On Ruth, one book.

“On Chronicles, two books.

“On Ezra and Nehemiah, three books.

“On Tobit, one book.

“On Judith, one book.

“On Esther, one book.

“On Job, one book.

“On the Psalter, one book.

“On the Proverbs of Solomon, one book.

“On Ecclesiastes, one book.

“On the Song of Songs, one book.

“On the book of Wisdom, one book.

“On Ecclesiasticus, one book.

“On the prophet Isaiah, one book.

“On Jeremiah, one book.

“On Ezekiel, one book.

“On the prophet Daniel, one book.

“On the twelve minor prophets, twelve books.

“On Maccabees, two books.

“On the four Gospels, one book. ‘The book of the genealogy.’

“On the Epistles of Paul, fourteen books.

“On the Acts of the Apostles, one book.

“On the Catholic Epistles, seven books.

“On the Apocalypse, one book.

“On the Interpretation of the Old and New Testament, two books. ‘To my lord and servant of God.’

“On Prologues, one book. ‘The five books of Moses.’

“On Differences, one book. ‘Between God and man.’

“On the Birth and Death of the Saints, one book. ‘Adam, the first-formed man.’

“To his sister Against the Jews, two books. ‘To the holy lady Florentina, my sister.’

“On Synonyms, or Soliloquies, two books. ‘It has recently come into my hands.’

“On Illustrious Men, one book. ‘Hosius of Córdoba.’

“On the Supreme Good, or *Sentences*, two books. ‘God is the supreme good.’

“On the Origin of Offices, two books. ‘Those things that concern Offices.’

“On the Holy Trinity, one book.

“On the Body and Blood of the Lord, one book.

“On the Office of the Mass, one book.

“A Decree of Canons, one book.

“On Computation and the Nature of Things, one book.

“On the Properties of Things, one book.

“On Sermons, one book.

“On Ecclesiastical Dogmas, one book.

“On the Lament of Penance, one book.

“On Astronomy, one book. ‘To my lord and most beloved son.’

“A History, or Chronicle, three books.

“On Cosmography, one book.

“On Grammar and Vocabulary, one book.

“Also one book of Allegories. ‘The mysteries of Sacred Scripture.’

“On Heresies, one book.

“Letters to Various Persons, one book.

“He is also said to have written many other works that have not come to my notice. He flourished under the emperor Heraclonas, son of Heraclius, in the year of the Lord 630, during the reign of Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain; and because of his most holy life and conduct he was entered in the catalogue of the saints. His feast is celebrated on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February.”^398

11. As it seems to me, Trithemius had seen only those works of Isidore whose opening words he records. Of these, the only works now missing are the four books of commentaries on the four Gospels, whose opening is recorded as “The book of the genealogy.”

In listing the other works, Trithemius sometimes divides one work into two or three on the basis of different titles of the same book. We shall explain all these matters more distinctly in their proper places.

The Isidore whom the Roman Martyrology, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of February—that is, 15 January—calls “Blessed Isidore, distinguished in holiness of life, faith, and miracles,” is a different person from our Isidore.

I have followed Fabricius’s edition in the *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*. Elsewhere the order of the books varies, and two separate books are listed: one book of Allegories and one book On the Mysteries of Sacred Scripture. In fact, no book of Allegories begins with the words “The mysteries of Sacred Scripture.”

# CHAPTER XLVIII. The Order in Which Isidore’s Works Should Be Arranged in Our Edition. The Books of the *Etymologies* Are Discussed First

1. As we have seen, different people preferred different orders when publishing Isidore’s works together. I judged that I should follow a different course from the others.

I wished to assign the first place to those works that are in some way universal and encompass almost every subject. Among works dealing with a particular matter, I shall follow the dignity of the subjects, so that biblical works come first, followed in their order by dogmatic, theological, liturgical, canonical, mystical, poetic, physical, and historical works.

Within each class I shall observe the same rule: I shall give precedence to works that are more general and range across several species of the same kind.

2. This order, while closer than any other to that of the royal Madrid edition, has above all the advantage that, in the more universal works, the more general concepts of things are set out; these readily lead to an understanding of particular subjects.

Whoever first reads Isidore’s *Etymologies*, the books On the Differences of Things and Words, and the Latin glossary—whether his own or at least excerpted for the most part from his works—and grasps them intellectually, will be able to proceed through his remaining works without great difficulty.

Likewise, in the biblical writings, if the Allegories on the Old and New Testament, the Eulogies of the Fathers of the Old and New Testament, and the Prologues to the Books of the Old and New Testament are placed first, the way to understanding the commentaries on the individual books will be opened more easily.

It remains, therefore, to discuss each work individually and accurately, in the order I shall follow in the edition.

3. Isidore’s *Etymologies* is the greatest and principal of all his other works.^401 Concerning it, one should consult Braulio and Ildefonsus in Isidore’s eulogy above, chapters 3 and 5, as well as the other authors of Isidore’s Life in chapters 13 and 14, and the reciprocal letters of Isidore and Braulio.

We cannot place sufficient reliance on the canonical writer of León who asserts in Isidore’s Life that the work of the *Etymologies* was begun by him while he was still young. I showed in chapters 21 and 27 that around the year 630 Isidore sent a copy of the *Etymologies* to Braulio.

4. Long before this, Braulio had requested in letters that the *Etymologies* be sent to him:

“I earnestly beg you,” he says, “to remember your promise and order the book of *Etymologies*, which, with the Lord’s favor, we have already heard to be completed, to be sent to your servant. For, as I am conscious in myself, you have labored there to a great extent at the request of your servant.”

Braulio sent Isidore another letter on the same matter, but it was lost before Isidore could read it. Braulio wrote in reply:

“Seven years, if I am not mistaken, have revolved since I remember requesting the books of *Origins* composed by you. In various and different ways you have frustrated me when I was present, and when I was absent you have written me nothing about the matter. By subtle delay—sometimes claiming that they were not yet finished, sometimes that my letters had been lost, and offering many other excuses—we have reached this day, and remain without the result of our request.”

5. From this it is clear that Isidore had been engaged in this kind of work long before the year 630, when the books of the *Etymologies* were sent to Braulio. We may infer that the letter in which Braulio says that he had heard the work was already complete was written seven years before the other letter in which he says, “Seven years, if I am not mistaken, have revolved,” and so forth.

A further point can be gathered from this second letter of Braulio’s, which must be kept before our eyes: some books or titles of the *Etymologies* had been published separately by Isidore and circulated among the public before Braulio received the complete work.

For after many other things he continues:

“Therefore I also make this known: the books of the *Etymologies* that I request from you, my lord, although mutilated and corroded, are already possessed by many. I therefore ask you to deign to send me copies of them that are complete, corrected, and properly fitted together, lest, carried away by eagerness, I be compelled to accept defects as virtues.”

I would think that *corrososque* should be read *corrasosque* rather than *corrososque* (“corroded”), for Braulio is indicating that certain parts of the work had been torn away from its body.^402

6. It is therefore not surprising if copies of the *Etymologies* differ in many places and are sometimes fuller than one another. Indeed, as I think, after the complete copy had been sent to Braulio, Isidore added or altered certain things in his own autograph. The work of the *Etymologies* is of such a kind that something can always be added anew or recast.

Certainly Ildefonsus says of Isidore:

“He also wrote, at the end, at the request of Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, the book of *Etymologies*. Although he had tried for many years to complete it, he appears to have brought his final day to a close in the midst of that work.”

Since, as I said, Isidore arranged for the *Etymologies* to be delivered to Braulio around the year 630, and afterward survived until the year 636, it follows that even after the copy sent to Braulio he continued laboring to perfect the same work more and more.

7. In the letter by which Isidore sends the *Etymologies* to Braulio, he says that the codex is *uncorrected*:

“I have sent the Codex of the *Etymologies* along with other codices on the journey; and although, because of my illness, it is uncorrected, I had nevertheless decided to offer it to you for correction, if I had reached the appointed place of the council.”

Perhaps *pervenisses* (“if you had reached”) should be read here, as I conjectured in chapter 21.

Braulio understood the matter in precisely this way when he said in his *Preliminary Notice of Isidore’s Books*:

“The Codex of the *Etymologies*, although he himself left it incomplete,” and so forth.

For since Isidore says that he had decided to offer the uncorrected codex to Braulio for correction, he appears already to have brought the work to completion and merely to have wished Braulio to correct a copy transcribed from Isidore’s autograph.

Braulio, on the contrary, had asked Isidore to send him books of the *Etymologies* that were complete, corrected, and properly fitted together.

8. Semler, moved by Braulio’s words in the preface to his notes on the manuscripts of Isidore’s Glossary, believes that Isidore did not leave a complete Codex of the *Etymologies*, but sent his autograph to Braulio, spread out with many spaces and intervals, which he ordinarily filled each day with supplements and in which he added and collected whatever occurred to him anew.

When Braulio says that the Codex was of excessive size, Semler interprets this as referring to such spaces and intervals, for the size in which the work exists today could not be called excessive.

This argument, however, is weak. The word “excessive” should not be pressed so strictly as to imply an immense codex. The Codex of the *Etymologies* is indeed very large, not only when compared with Isidore’s other works and with most other works of ancient writers, but also considered in itself, as can be seen in many enormous parchment manuscripts containing only the books of the *Etymologies*, especially when they are written in large characters.

Nicolaus Antonius does not hesitate to call it a work of immense bulk, although perhaps he wished to commend not so much the size as the labor and effort of the work.

But Braulio certainly should not have celebrated the excessive size of the Codex on account of all those spaces and intervals in which nothing had been written.

9. Since Isidore had composed the work of the *Etymologies* at his request and had left it either uncorrected or incomplete, Braulio thought it appropriate to divide the Codex into books distinguished only by titles supplied by Isidore.

Fabricius is less accurate in *Bibliotheca vetus Latina*, book IV, chapter 8, no. 14, when he says of the work of the *Etymologies*: “Isidore wrote it and left it incomplete; Braulio then completed it and arranged it into books.” I see that others also hold this view.

Braulio does not say that he completed or corrected the work, although we can readily believe that he saw to it that the work was copied, insofar as possible, without scribal errors.

It is wholly impossible to infer from Braulio’s words that he altered or added anything. Nor can I agree with otherwise learned men who, whenever something occurs in the *Etymologies* that they declare cannot be excused by any reasoning, immediately proclaim that such an error was inserted by Braulio.

They seem to be unaware what kind of man Braulio was. His eulogy from Ildefonsus will be reported in the book *On Illustrious Men*, and we have already presented some material in his commendation in chapter 4—not because he should be equated with Isidore, or because it would not have been easier for Braulio rather than Isidore to have erred, but because, since it is not established that the *Etymologies* were interpolated in any way by Braulio, fairness demands that if something should occur that is wholly unworthy of Isidore, the intolerable error be attributed not to Braulio but to any other interpolator.

10. It is entirely unknown into how many titles Isidore divided the work of the *Etymologies*. Nor is it sufficiently clear into how many books Braulio divided it.

The common belief is that he divided it into twenty books; this is the widely accepted division of the work, supported by Braulio’s published *Preliminary Notice*: “I divided it into twenty books.”

Bayer attempted to weaken this accepted opinion in his notes on book V, chapter 4, no. 93, of the *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*:

“Braulio,” he says, “divided Isidore’s work of the *Etymologies* not into twenty but into fifteen books, as is shown by the ancient codices, all those written before the year 1000 of the Christian era that I have seen. I have seen not a few. The royal library of El Escorial supplies two: one, marked Q, shelf 11, no. 24, from the Spanish era 781, that is, the year of Christ 743; the other, likewise extremely ancient, formerly belonging to the Church of Oviedo, marked b, shelf III, no. 14. In both, Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* concerning the work of the *Etymologies* reads: ‘divided by Isidore into titles, not books, which I,’ says Braulio, ‘divided into fifteen books.’

“A fourteenth-century Spanish version of the same work, preserved in the same Escorial library, marked b, shelf I, no. 13, agrees with this: ‘And because he made it at my request, although he did not finish it, nevertheless I divided it into fifteen books.’”

I shall present other words of Bayer in support of this position in chapter 67, when I bring forward his observations on the fourth book of the *Sentences*, attributed to Isidore in a certain codex.

11. Among the variant readings from our manuscript copies that I recorded in chapter 3 to illuminate Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice*, there is nothing that can confirm Bayer’s opinion. In the ancient parchments themselves, in which Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* displays the words “I divided it into fifteen books,” the *Etymologies* are divided into twenty books.

Bayer does not conceal this, but replies:

“Some more inquisitive person may have immediately, or not long after Braulio’s death, or scribes may have subdivided some of the fifteen books, or reshaped the original arrangement of the work, without adding anything to it.”

Fabricius—or rather Mansi, in the supplement to Fabricius—reports that this happened in the oldest of all, the seventh-century Codex of Cesena belonging to the Malatesta library, in *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae* under Isidore, no. 25; for although it consists altogether of twenty-five books, it contains nothing that is not found in the published codices.

12. Yet how much easier it was for some scribe to change the number twenty into fifteen, from which this error might have spread into several copies, than for someone to make twenty books out of fifteen in such a way that no copy of the original division into fifteen books remained!

The Spanish version of Braulio’s *Preliminary Notice* is the very one published by Rodríguez de Castro in volume II of the *Biblioteca Hispana*, p. 294. Nor is this the genuine *Preliminary Notice* of Braulio, but another interpolated version, as has already been said.

The Italian version of the genuine *Preliminary Notice*, however, with Alchain as translator, which will be discussed in chapter 70, section 17, expresses twenty books: “in twenty books.”

Therefore I judge that the *Etymologies* were divided by Braulio into twenty books. This is why most copies agree in this number of books, while scarcely any indicate a smaller number.

Why, then, is the work distributed into more than twenty books in some, even very ancient, copies? I think the reason for this sort of variation in division can be sought in the fact that Isidore himself divided the work into titles, as Braulio reports, and that there were more titles, in my judgment, than twenty.

It is also clear from Braulio’s letters to Isidore that several books of the *Etymologies*—or titles, if we prefer to call them that—had been separately published before the complete Codex was delivered to Braulio.

Moreover, as I recently argued, the autograph copy of the *Etymologies* remained with Isidore. It was therefore easy for others, although Braulio reduced the work to twenty books, to increase the number of books either from Isidore’s autograph, from the separately published books, or from the arrangement and division of certain titles, just as in some copies they also changed the order.

13. This will be explained more distinctly when the manuscript codices are discussed. For now, it is enough to observe that the order and division of the books commonly published in the royal Madrid edition is widespread.

Nevertheless, in many ancient manuscript copies in which the division into twenty books is visible, it still appears that the first hand had made a division into twenty-five books, as in the Malatesta Codex cited by Bayer and discussed by us in chapter 45, and as in Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive and others.

The Albanian Codex also offers the number of twenty-five books, but it is divided in such a way that it ought rather to report twenty-six. The numbers themselves have been corrupted and altered by many erasures, yet some trace remains that the book now numbered twenty was originally marked by the first hand with the number fifteen. This may support the division defended by Bayer.

14. In other manuscripts the books of the *Etymologies* number twenty-two, as in the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, discussed in chapter 45. Although twenty-three books are indicated, the last, or twenty-third, is the book On the Nature of Things.

Honorius of Autun also assigns twenty-two books. In the twenty-first session of the ecumenical Council of Florence, in Labbe, volume XIII, column 1113, we read:

“Also, during the time of blessed Gregory the Dialogist, Isidore by name flourished in Spain. I shall give one testimony from him. He made a book of *Etymologies* divided into twenty-two books. In the twelfth book, chapter 3, he says: ‘But this is the difference between the Son who is born and the Spirit who proceeds,’ and so forth.”

Here one should observe that a different order of books is also indicated, for the passage cited now occurs in chapter 3 of book VII.

Codex Vaticanus 623, to be described in chapter 93, divides the *Etymologies* into twenty books. But in the first hand of the manuscript it is noted that some people assign twenty-eight books, and the locations of the divisions are indicated individually. More examples of varying divisions of the books occur in chapter 55.

15. As for the order of the books, in some manuscripts the book On Laws precedes the book On Medicine, as in the Albanian Codex and in the less ancient Codex of Cesena.

The Chisian copy, discussed in chapter 45, varies extraordinarily in the order of the books and subjects. Codex Regio-Vaticanus 1850, mutilated at the beginning, contains a great mixture and confusion of the books and has been interpolated and expanded in many places, as I shall explain in chapter 101.

In several very old copies I also find book X of the *Etymologies* missing, the book in which certain words are explained alphabetically. In these copies book XI immediately follows book IX. Perhaps this is because, by that time, a glossary was already circulating under Isidore’s name, so that it could have seemed unnecessary to insert book X—which performs the function of a glossary—among the other books of the *Etymologies*.

16. Less commonly encountered is the division of the *Etymologies* into two parts, the first comprising the first ten books and the second the remaining ten, while the numbering continues in the same sequence through the twentieth book. This can be seen in Codex Vaticanus 623, which I shall discuss in chapter 93.

A similar arrangement is indicated, more or less, in two Florentine codices of Santa Croce, which will be discussed in chapter 55. There more information about the manuscript codices of the *Etymologies* is either given or indicated.

17. We need not labor greatly over the title. Manuscript books consistently bear the title *Etymologies*; some more recent ones have *Etymologicon of Isidore*. Others, following an old and frequent usage, have *Isidore of the Etymologies*, so that our holy teacher is in a manner surnamed “Isidore of the Etymologies.” This will readily occur to anyone in the examination of the manuscript codices.

In a later age many such titles were introduced, such as “Master of the Sentences,” “Valerius of the Histories,” and so forth.^407

18. Although ancient writers, when praising these books, call them the *Etymologies*, many later writers commonly call them the books of the *Origins*. Vulcanius, Bignaeus, and Breulius preferred this title in their editions.

Francisco Padilla was deceived by this. In the seventh century of his *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, folio 227, having seen Baronius praise the books of the *Origins*, he asserted that no such work was found among Isidore’s other writings.

Nicolaus Antonius suspects that Braulio attached the title *Etymologies* to the work when he prepared it for publication, and that, just as he separated its members, he adapted its heading, making it deviate slightly from the author, who left a written statement that he was sending the *Origins*, or supplied a title that Isidore had not yet added.

Isidore, indeed, thinking modestly and unpretentiously of his work, as Nicolaus Antonius says, dedicated it to Braulio in these words:

“Here you have, as I promised, the work concerning the origin of certain things, collected from the recollection of ancient reading, which I have sent,” and so forth.

But it should not be inferred from this that Isidore gave it the title *Origins* rather than *Etymologies*, since in the dedicatory letter to Braulio he apparently did not repeat the heading but set out the subject of the book.

19. It is certain from another source that the work of the *Etymologies* was called this not only by Braulio but also by Isidore before its publication, as is clear from their reciprocal letters.

Isidore calls it the Codex of the *Etymologies*; Braulio first calls it the first book of the *Etymologies*, and then the books of the *Etymologies*. In the second letter, however, in which he calls them the books of the *Etymologies*, he had previously called them the books of the *Origins*.

Therefore, although the title *Etymologies*, which Ildefonsus also used, is more common and more accurate, the other title, *Origins*, can be defended. Perhaps the author himself wrote the combined title *Etymologies, or On the Origin of Things*.

Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, wonders whether this work is called anywhere “The Book of All Sciences.” When describing Codex 92 in the library of the monastery of Saint-Martin of Tours, dated to the year 800, he writes: “The Book of All Sciences,” and adds, “Whether it belongs to Isidore of Seville remains to be seen.” Montfaucon could have been referring to no other work than the *Etymologies*.

20. We have said that the Etymological work was dedicated by Isidore to Braulio [Col. 0319D] 408, and everyone says so. But is it certain that it was dedicated to Braulio and not to someone else? I have no doubt that Isidore dedicated the Etymologies to Braulio, not only because the dedicatory letter, preserved in most manuscripts, suggests this, but also because the mutual letters of the two men make it entirely clear. Nevertheless, I find that in Codex Regio-Vaticanus 112, written at the beginning of the eleventh century, after the six alternating letters of Braulio and Isidore—including Isidore’s dedicatory letter to Braulio—and after the list of books that follows the letters, a preface to King Sisebutus is added, using exactly the same words as the letter to Braulio. The same is true of Palatinus 283. Ottobonianus 336, however, gives the title as follows: *The Books of Isidore to Braulio, or to Sisebutus.* [Col. 0320A] Ottobonianus 343 and 427 present the dedicatory letter to Sisebutus, not to Braulio. On these and other manuscripts, see chapter 55.

21. In the Chisian manuscript described in chapter 45, and in Codex 2 of the Vatican Archives, discussed in chapter 107, the disjunction is used in such a way that the *Etymologies* are said to have been written to Braulio, or to Sisebutus, his lord and son respectively. But why could it not have happened that the work was inscribed to both? The ancients were accustomed to prefix two prefaces to their works; they were accustomed to send the same work to two persons, with a dedicatory letter to each, as I have shown in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 16. The only obstacle may be that Sisebutus died in the year 621, whereas Isidore sent the codex of the *Etymologies* to Braulio only around the year 630. Therefore Isidore could have offered Sisebutus only certain books of the *Etymologies*, or sections published separately earlier, as is clear from Braulio’s letters. I am nevertheless more inclined to believe that Isidore’s dedicatory letter to Braulio was prefixed to the *Etymologies* with an inscription to Sisebutus by some incompetent copyist who had seen the book *On the Nature of Things*, dedicated to Sisebutus, placed in some manuscript as the twenty-third and final book.

22. What if someone should maintain that the author of the *Etymologies* was not our Isidore of Seville, but another Isidore of Córdoba? It would seem hardly possible that this could have occurred to anyone. Yet the otherwise most learned Martinus Roa held this opinion in his book *On the Principate of Córdoba*, as Nicolás Antonio observes. However, when I examined the Lyon edition of the Latin work of 1617, Roa’s words did not appear; nor does Nicolás Antonio cite any other edition when he praises Roa in his *Bibliotheca nova*. I also see that, in book II, *Singularia*, chapter 9, Roa repeatedly calls the *Etymologies* the work of “Saint Isidore.” By this title of sanctity he certainly means Isidore of Seville, since he did not name Isidore of Córdoba even among the saints of Córdoba. I should therefore like someone to show me where Nicolás Antonio found that Roa held so absurd an opinion. Fabricius likewise repeats this claim under “Isidore of Córdoba” in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, but plainly on the authority of Nicolás Antonio. The Spanish translation of the same work, translated by Roa himself, will have to be consulted; I have not seen it.

## CHAPTER XLIX. Judgments of Learned Men concerning Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Isidore’s Endeavor in the *Etymologies* to Explain Matters Peculiar to Spain

1. In chapter 34 we defended Isidore’s learning against the criticisms of certain critics by adducing the clearest testimony of more serious authorities. We now take up the particular case of the *Etymologies*. “As for the name *Etymologies* and the work as a whole,” says Nicolás Antonio, “the sons of the grammarians, whom this concern occupies, have long been shouting outrageously, attacking Isidore with many javelins of accusation.” For a complete refutation of them, however, he refers the reader to Grialius’s preface, which we shall present later. In the meantime he observes that certain of Isidore’s etymologies, condemned by some, are defended by others. Thus Johannes Kirchmannus turns up his nose at the etymology of *feretrum*, although Vossius does not reject it. Nicolás Rigaltius blames Isidore for saying that a scorpion is named from *sagitta*, “arrow,” whereas Stewechius defends him. Johannes Schefferus criticizes Isidore for believing that the Egyptian Pharos was named from Greek φῶς, “light,” and ὁρᾷν, “to see”; yet Martinius called this an etymology not to be despised.

2. This Martinius, in the preface to his *Lexicon*, distinguished two kinds of etymologies: one consisting of those which are such δυνάμει, that is, potentially, from which a name could have been derived; and another consisting of those which are such ἐνεργείᾳ, that is, actually, to which the authors of words probably had regard. Both kinds are found in Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Isidore himself teaches in book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 29, that not all names were imposed by the ancients according to nature, but that some were imposed according to convention: “For this reason the etymologies of all names are not found, since some words received their names not according to the quality from which they originated, but according to human choice.”

3. For this reason the origins of words are so difficult to discover that Aegidius Menagius, in the dedicatory letter of his *Origins of the French Language*, asserted that no one up to his own time, however distinguished his reputation among either ancient or modern writers, had touched the matter precisely. Nevertheless, Nicolás Antonio confirms that an etymological work such as the one produced by Isidore could not have been expected after the extinguishing of those lights of ancient and flourishing philology—not in Isidore’s age, nor in later ages, including Bede, who devoted himself to an encyclopedia. For this work does not seem to be the product of the Isidorian—that is, half-barbarous—age, but something comparable to a complete miracle, especially in a holy man so devoted to piety and so entirely intent upon carrying out his office with dignity. Although Barthius calls Isidore a perpetual copyist of Servius in his commentary on book VI of the *Thebaid*, verse 241, he nevertheless asserts, on book XII, verse 812, that Isidore embraced almost the whole encyclopedia of his age. By this he sufficiently indicates that Isidore included much of which Servius had not even thought.

4. Nicolás Antonio also observes that readers of every age seem to have thought themselves permitted more in this Isidorian work than in almost any other, and that they attached to the margins of the book—whose contents they scarcely allowed to leave their hands, regarding it as a cornucopia, or at least a compendium of all books—anything that came to hand here and there. Copyists were thereby misled into inserting foolish marginal notes into the text. Nor should Isidore be criticized if at times, looking by his own ingenuity toward what seemed probable, he invented certain etymologies, as many other ancient writers did. “Isidore explains certain matters differently from what anyone might suppose,” says Turnebus, *Adversaria* XXVI, chapter 22, “yet neither without learning nor without good sense.” Great value is also added to these books of the *Etymologies* because they illuminate many obscure passages of distinguished authors, as may be gathered from the same Turnebus, *Adversaria* VI, chapter 19; XI, chapter 5; and XX, chapter 5.

5. Christian Becmannus, who wrote sufficiently carefully on the origins of the Latin language and published his book in 1608, admits that there has been a certain abuse in this etymological art, but maintains that it should not therefore be despised. Thus, in the preface to *On the Proper Signification of Words*, p. 158, he writes:

> “Valla,” he says, “in book VII, chapter 37, of the *Elegantiae*, and others with him, says: ‘Nothing is more ridiculous in this science of which we are speaking than etymology. It should therefore not be valued so highly, as though proper meaning were thereby extracted.’ The answer is readily available by means of a distinction. Valla is not speaking of every etymology, nor of a sound and true etymology; otherwise he would contradict himself, for throughout the six books of the *Elegantiae*, and especially against Antonius Raudensis, he frequently relies upon etymologies. He is speaking rather of witty allusions, and likewise of ridiculous and often foolish alliterations, which arose chiefly from ignorance of languages and which we willingly leave to their authors, while avoiding them wherever seriousness is required. Such examples occur in Varro, when he unsuccessfully derives everything from Latin; in Isidore, bishop of Seville; Peter Lombard; Durandus; Zacharias of Chrysopolis; Jacobus de Voragine; Accursius among the jurists; and others of the same kind.”

6. Becmannus offers examples in *pascha*, from πάσχω, “to suffer”; *diabolus*, from “two boluses”; *locusta*, because it is long-legged, like a spear; *Donatus*, as if “born from God”; *Marcellus*, as if “warding off evil” or “striking the seas”; *Fabianus*, as if *fabricanus*, “fabricating,” that is, fabricating blessedness; *Sebastianus*, as if “pursuing blessedness,” and because *Astin* is a city and *aria* means “upward”; *Euphemia*, as if “good woman,” or “pleasant sound”; *Colossus*, as if “honoring bones”; and *examen*, from ἐξ and ἀμήν, an etymology which a certain Zachaeus Faber invented in order to correct a metrical fault he had committed by shortening the *a* in *examen*.

“But suppose,” Becmannus continues, “though it is not conceded, that Valla and some others call every etymology altogether ridiculous. What then? One, two, three, or even four swallows do not make a spring. Yet when the same Becmannus, on p. 146, sets Varro, Festus, and Isidore against one another, saying that Isidore sometimes does nothing but trifle and provoke the reader’s laughter, he fails to notice that the very trifles he attributes to Isidore were taken from Varro or from other ancient writers of great renown.” Fabricius defends him thus under “Isidore” in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*:

> “A grammarian indispensable even in the judgment of those who disparage him . . . In indicating the origins of words, he does not always hit the matter precisely—no more than Varro among the Latins, or Plato among the Greeks, or Philo among the Jews. Hence Christian Becmannus’s harsher criticism, that he does nothing but trifle and provoke laughter, as well as Salmasius’s disapproval in his commentary on the *Historia Augusta*, p. 28, where he condemns Isidore, in his customary fashion, as inept in presenting etymologies—although other learned men have shown that he must be defended on many points.”

7. Johannes Georgius Walchius, in his *Critical History of the Latin Language*, Cologne, 1734, chapter 5, no. 6, gathers much concerning Isidore and this entire etymological discipline:

> “The order of what must now be said requires us to turn to an account of the various kinds of Latin lexicons. First among these we place etymological lexicons, which are concerned with explaining the origins of Roman words. In both earlier and later ages the most learned men undertook this task: Marcus Terentius Varro, Marcus Verrius Flaccus, and Sextus Pompeius Festus, concerning whom we have already said something in the chapter on grammarians. Their prince is Isidore of Seville, whose twenty books of *Origins* or *Etymologies* survive and were published separately at Venice in 1483, at Paris in 1512, and elsewhere.
>
> “There are learned men who have held an unfavorable opinion of him. Jacobus Thomasius collected their judgments in §484 of *On Literary Plagiarism*, and, following Petrus Ciacconius, observed that Isidore copied most things word for word from Servius, the commentator on Virgil, from Festus, Nonius, Augustine, and other authors of better standing. Rhenanus likewise judged that Isidore’s rhapsody among the Latins was much like the *Suda* among the Greeks, which had been patched together from all directions by many contributors. Janus Dousa counted him among the half-ancient patchers and elsewhere called him a compiler of centos. Cornelius Rittershusius, in his commentary on Salvianus, p. 208, thought that he often introduced trifles into these books. Although this cannot be denied, nor can it be denied that he transcribed much from other authors, we nevertheless owe it to his industry—a thing altogether deserving of praise—that various monuments of ancient writers have been preserved through his efforts. Johannes Fabricius has more on this author in part III of his *History of the Library*, p. 273.”

8. Walchius then reviews certain more recent writers of *Etymologies*: Johannes Fungerus, Christian Becmannus, Matthias Martinius, Gerardus Johannes Vossius, and Christian Daumius. Concerning the usefulness of the *Etymologies*, he writes in § VII:

> “It must indeed not be denied that etymological study benefits those who cultivate languages and makes it possible, once the origins of words are known, to illuminate the true and native force of meaning that they possess. Nevertheless, even in this branch of study one ought to observe moderation, so that we neither devote more effort than is appropriate to investigating the origins of words nor assign greater importance to etymological science than the dignity of the subject itself requires. Most matters in this part of philology are doubtful and uncertain . . . The nature of the matter itself declares how the origins of the Latin language can be restored, when they have been hidden and buried for so many centuries. Varro himself, that most diligent investigator of the Latin language, admits this when he says in book IV of *On the Latin Language*: ‘Not every imposition of words survives, for antiquity has destroyed some; nor was every surviving word imposed without error; nor does every word correctly imposed remain. For many words have been altered by changes of letters.’”

9. Walchius adds further observations on this subject. He notes that Richard Simon, in part I, p. 113, of his French work *Nouvelle Bibliothèque choisie*, demonstrated through the example of the Greek word θεός, “god,” how uncertain etymological studies are, and that Christian Falster treated the same argument in his *Various Philological Reflections*, p. 179. Morhof had already observed in *Polyhistor* I, book VI, chapter 9, no. 2, that the ancient grammarians—Varro, Festus, Flaccus, and Isidore—had sought the origins of names, and that Isidore in particular was chastised for compiling earlier authors. Although, among more recent writers, Julius Caesar Scaliger undertook a great work, *The Origins of the Latin Language*, to be completed in twenty-four books, no printer was found who dared to publish it. Nevertheless, in his dedicatory letter of *The Origins of the French Language* to Puteanus, Menagius did not expect much benefit from it even if it had appeared, judging from the etymologies Scaliger inserted in his book *On the Causes of the Latin Language*. These are no better than those of earlier writers.

10. How highly Burriel thought of Isidore’s works, especially with regard to explaining matters peculiar to Spain, is clear from his letter quoted in chapter 40. I shall now review his observation concerning the *Etymologies* in a Spanish work entitled *Informe de Toledo sobre igualacion de pesos, y medidas* [Report from Toledo on the standardization of weights and measures], published at Madrid in 1758. It appeared without his name, but that it was prepared by him is established both by other evidence and by a note in his own hand in the copy I possess. Thus, on p. 219 and following, he observes that Saint Isidore, in his encyclopedic work *Etymologies*, took particular care to explain diligently those things that were then peculiar to Spain and by which Spain especially differed from other regions. He offers the following examples.

11. Isidore says in book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 38, elsewhere numbered 39, concerning *threni*:

> “They were used at funerals and for lamentations; and likewise they are used now.”

In book IV, chapter 8, concerning *impetigo*:

> “The common people call this *sarna*.”

The name *sarna* still remains. In book XII, chapter 7:

> “*Tucos*, which the Spaniards call *cuculos*,”

and so forth. Spaniards now say *cuclillos*. Grialius would prefer to read, with Chacon, “*Cuculos*, which the Spaniards call *cucos*.”

In book XIII, chapter 11, concerning the wind *Corus*, or *Caurus*:

> “Most people call it *Argestes*, not, as the ignorant common people do, *Agrestes*.”

In the same place, concerning the *Circius*:

> “The Spaniards call this *Gallecus*, because it blows upon them from the region of Galicia.”

Today *Galleco* is the Spanish name of the wind.

12. In book XV, chapter 9:

> “In Africa or Spain they call walls made of earth *formati* or *formatia*.”

We still say *hormigón*. In book XVI, chapter 2, concerning *chalcantum* and related matters, once found in the wells or pools of Spain, Isidore follows Pliny. In the same book, chapter 4, concerning *pyrites*:

> “The common people call this *focaris petra*, ‘fire-stone.’”

Concerning *haematites*:

> “It is found in the remotest Egypt, Babylonia, and Spain.”

In the same place:

> “*Schistos* is found in the remotest Spain.”

In chapter 21, concerning waters into which iron is immersed to make it more useful:

> “As at Bilbilis in Spain and at Tarazona, and at Como in Italy.”

In chapter 22, concerning lead:

> “For it is also produced in Lusitania and Galicia . . . Black lead abounds around Cantabria,”

and so forth.

13. In book XVII, chapter 7, concerning a certain kind of lamp called *Pausia*, as Burriel says, Isidore writes:

> “*Pausia*, which the country people corruptly call *Pusia*, is suitable for green and sweet oil.”

From this Burriel suspects that the Spanish names *pavesa* and *bujía* arose. But Isidore is not speaking of a lamp; he is speaking of a particularly pleasant olive, also called *posea*. In manuscripts, however, *v* is often changed into *o*, and *i* into *e*, as in *pusia* for *posea*.

In the same book, concerning *crustumina*, also called *volemis*:

> “Some understand *volemum*, in the Gallic language, to mean ‘good and large.’”

I do not know why Burriel brings this forward, since, besides being taken from Servius, it has nothing to do with Spain. In the same book:

> “The oil, however . . . which has been expressed from white olives, is called Spanish.”

This is taken from Galen and Aurelianus.

14. In the same book XVII, chapter 9:

> “*Toxic* poisons are so called because they are expressed from yew trees, especially in Cantabria.”

In book XVIII, chapter 6:

> “*Framea* . . . which the common people call *spatha*.”

In the same place:

> “Axes . . . which the Spaniards also call *franciscae*, by derivation from the use of the Franks.”

In chapter 9:

> “*Dolones* . . . These the common people call by the Greek name *oxos*, that is, ‘sharp.’”

In book XIX, chapter 10:

> “The *arenatius* stone . . . The same stone is found in Baetica, where it is called Gaditanus, after the island in the Ocean, where it is quarried in great abundance.”

In chapter 16:

> “*Minium* . . . Spain abounds in this pigment more than other regions; hence it also gave its name to a particular river.”

15. Chapter 22 of the same book XIX:

> “An exotic garment is foreign, coming from outside, as into Spain from the Greeks.”

In the same place:

> “*Armelansa*, as it is commonly called . . . We call them *camisae*, because we sleep in them, in *camae*, that is, in our beds.”

Spaniards still say *cama* and *camisa*. In the same place:

> “*Femoralia* . . . also called *braccae* . . . and called *tubruci*, because they cover the shins and breeches.”

Chapter 23:

> “Each people has its own distinctive garment: among the Parthians, the *sarabara* . . . among the Spaniards, the *stringes*.”

A little later:

> “We see the *cirri* of the Germans, the *grani*, and the *cinnabari* of the Goths.”

Chapter 24:

> “The Spaniards call it a *mantum*, because it covers only the hands.”

The Spaniards use the same word, but now with a broader meaning.

16. Chapter 25 of the same book XIX, concerning the *amicus*:

> “For among the ancients this was a sign of meretricious clothing; now in Spain it is a sign of respectability.”

In the same place:

> “An *anaboladium* is a linen covering for women, by which the shoulders are covered, which the Greeks and Latins call a *sindon*.”

From this Burriel argues that *anaboladium* is neither a Greek nor a Latin word and therefore must be Spanish, surviving to some extent in the word *pavana* with the same meaning. This criticism requires qualification. The Latins could have derived *anaboladium* from the Greek verb ἀναβάλλω, “to throw over,” and in fact did so. Long before Isidore, and outside Spain, Jerome and Ambrose used the word *anaboladium* with the same meaning.

17. Chapter 28 of the same book XIX:

> “*Ferrugo* is a purplish-black color produced in Spain, as in ‘bright with Iberian *ferrugo*.’”

Grialius believes in his notes that Isidore took this from corrupt copies of Servius. Chapter 33:

> “Women did not use rings . . . but now, because of gold, no limb of women is insignificant or exempt.”

This was taken from Tertullian. Also in chapter 33:

> “A *redimiculum* is what we call a *succinctory* or bracelet.”

This was taken from Cassianus. In the final chapter, 34:

> “*Socci*, whose diminutive is *soccelli*.”

Hence the old Spanish word *suchiellos*, approximately *zucquillos*. I note that the diminutive *socculus* was used by Seneca, Suetonius, and both Plinys.

18. In book XX, chapter 2:

> “*Caelia* is so called from *calefacere*, ‘to warm’ . . . It is made in those parts of Spain where the land is not suitable for wine.”

Burriel suspects that *cilla*, *cillero*, and *cillerizo* arose from this, although he also agrees that they could have arisen from *cella*, *cellarium*, or from *cillare*, which in Isidore means “to move grain.” In chapter 9:

> “*Mozicia*, as if *modicia*, whence also *modicum*: *z* for *d*, as Italians customarily say *ozie* for *hodie*.”

I do not see how this observation concerns the Spaniards. *Mozica* or *mozina* is said to be a kind of repository or small chest. In chapter 15:

> “Gardeners call it *telonem* . . .”

This instrument the Spaniards call a *ciconia*.

19. These are the examples Burriel offered, as I have said. But, as I have sometimes observed, not all of them achieve what he intends. Some, taken from foreign authors, reveal nothing peculiar to Spain; others do touch upon Spanish matters, but in the same way as matters belonging to other peoples, which are mentioned by ancient writers and, from them, by Isidore. Nevertheless, there is no doubt that Isidore sometimes made it sufficiently clear that he took pleasure in explaining those things which seemed more particularly characteristic of Spain.

## CHAPTER L. Vulcanius’s Edition of the *Etymologies*; His Preface

1. Since I intend to bring Vulcanius’s preface to Isidore’s *Etymologies* before the reader, it seemed appropriate first to describe the edition itself. Here is the title:

*The Twenty Books of Origins of Isidore, Bishop of Seville, Recovered from Antiquity; and the Nine Books of Martianus Capella on the Marriage of Philology and Mercury. Both works, together with Fulgentius and the ancient grammarians, illustrated with various readings and scholia through the work and industry of Bonaventura Vulcanius of Bruges.*

Basel, through Peter Perna. The year of publication is not indicated, but the dedicatory letter is dated 1577, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September. Vulcanius omits all the letters that others commonly place at the beginning, including the one that Isidore inserted in place of a preface, beginning “Behold for you,” and so forth. Various readings, and sometimes brief annotations, are attached in the margin.

2. After Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Vulcanius added Fulgentius’s little book *On Ancient Speech*, which he found attached at the end of a certain manuscript of Isidore in a very old copy under the following title: *Fabius Plantiades Fulgentius, Exposition of Virgil’s Ancient Expressions, with Testimonia.*

Vulcanius then includes booklets by ancient grammarians on the propriety and difference of language: those of Cornelius Fronto, Nonius Marcellus, Agroetius, Aelius Donatus, Arruntius Celsus, Flavius Sosipater Charisius, Quintus Asconius Pedianus, Marius Servius Honoratus, Sextus Pompeius Festus, Marcus Terentius Varro, Quintus Terentius Scaurus, and Agellius. Two indexes of Isidore follow, one containing common nouns, the other proper names of places, animals, plants, gems, and similar things. A brief index of the authors cited by Isidore in these books had appeared at the beginning of the volume; below, we shall present a fuller version based on Barthius. Finally, Vulcanius published the nine books of Martianus Felix Capella, an African of Carthage, *On the Marriage of Philology and Mercury*. Vulcanius certainly devoted useful labor to assembling and publishing this collection of such writers. If only the edition were more polished and more thoroughly purged of errors! Vulcanius, however, used the same excuse as many others: the urgency of the printer caused by the proximity of the Frankfurt fair. Let us now present his preface to Isidore’s *Etymologies*, or dedicatory letter.

> To the most illustrious prince and most reverend prelate Gerardus of Groesbeck, bishop of Liège, duke of Bouillon, marquis of Franchimont, count of Looz, prince of the Holy Roman Empire, my most gracious lord, Bonaventura Vulcanius of Bruges sends respectful greetings.

3. Since it is greatly to be desired, most illustrious and most reverend prince, that we possess complete and corrected editions of the ancient authors who wrote on individual arts and sciences, this is especially true of those who embrace not one particular art but the entire circle of the sciences, which the Greeks call ἐγκυκλοπαιδεία. Among these I find two leading figures: Isidore, bishop of Seville, and Martianus Capella the African. The latter, however, included only those seven disciplines which we call the liberal arts, in the nine books he wrote on the marriage of Philology and Mercury. The former, besides these, treated medicine, law, theology, both kinds of history—that is, natural history and the history concerned with time—and finally dealt with everything that falls within the common use of life. He called these books *Origins*, because in them he set forth not merely bare etymologies of words, as those imagine who try to diminish and tear down the dignity of these books, but the origins of things themselves, and laid the foundations of all the arts.

4. How highly the authority of these books has always been regarded can be clearly seen from the fact that all those who, for many centuries, have taught both civil and canon law, as well as medicine and even theology itself, have drawn many monuments of antiquity and learning from these books as from springs, and have relied upon Isidore’s testimony with the greatest willingness and frequency. Nor is this without good reason, since it is certain that in Isidore’s age many writings of the ancients, now lost through the injustice of time, still existed complete. From them he constructed this outstanding work, as can easily be seen from the many authors he cites, of whom today nothing survives except bare names—and even those are unknown to us.

Consequently, certain men, whether hindered by ignorance or seized by a mad desire to criticize, rashly dissent from this author and attack him; but when the ancient books from which he had borrowed those passages are later brought to light, they pay the most just penalty for their rash and precipitous judgment and their slander. I could offer many examples of this, if the brevity of this letter allowed it.

5. More correctly, Alciatus defended Isidore’s opinion when a certain jurist, otherwise of great reputation, criticized him because he thought that *cretio* was derived as though from *decretio*, that is, “to decide” or “to establish.” Why should *cretio* not be understood as something like *decretio*, since *cernere* is something like *decernere*, “to decide” that one is heir? Thus it is said in the law *Is qui haeres*, final paragraph, in the *Digest*, *On the Acquisition of Inheritance*: “Before the heir decides concerning the inheritance”; and in the law *pupillus*, under the same title: “An age such as this can neither know nor decide.”

Since these matters are so, and since I have been thoroughly persuaded—partly by experience, partly by the judgment and approval of the most learned men—that these books can contribute to the Christian commonwealth no less, and certainly a more varied and multifaceted, usefulness than Varro, Nonius Marcellus, Verrius Flaccus, and other writers of that kind, and that no one, whatever subject he may have devoted his mind to studying, will fail gladly to acknowledge that he has learned something previously unknown from their reading, I could not endure that they should remain any longer hidden in neglect and squalor.

Accordingly, when I had at last obtained a respite from my Latin translation of Cyril, enlarged by more than a third and awaiting better times for publication, and had a little more leisure, I took into my hands both printed and manuscript copies of Isidore, which I had collected over a long period from Spain and the Netherlands. I undertook to purge him of innumerable and exceedingly foul errors and, as far as possible, to restore him to his former brightness.

6. In this work I followed the principle of changing nothing rashly unless the agreement of ancient ἀντίγραφα, “manuscript copies,” supported the alteration, or unless an error arising from the ignorance of scribes or printers clearly revealed itself. I did not think I should imitate those who, boasting of a kind of religious diligence—which I would rather call empty superstition or foolish ostentation—prefer, when the agreement of several manuscripts permits the correction of a passage that the sense itself shows to be corrupt, nevertheless to retain the earlier and defective text and burden both the margins of books and their readers with variant readings. I have instead supplied variant readings only when both readings can be tolerated.

7. As for the *Etymologies* and several other matters in which Isidore either went astray through ignorance of Greek or pursued the origin of a word too far, I did not wish to be excessively fastidious. Varro and others who worked in this kind of writing each indulged his own judgment or conjecture, and Pliny himself was often mistaken through ignorance of Greek. Nevertheless, I corrected many Greek etymologies. They caused me a great deal of trouble, since in manuscript copies either no trace of Greek letters survived, or the traces were such that nothing certain could be gathered from them except by conjecture and by recollection of variant readings, or, where the characters were still intact and legible, they nevertheless transmitted a false origin of the name. I warned readers about these matters here and there by adding a note in the margin, although through the negligence of the printers quite a few such notes were omitted.

8. I also annotated very many passages, including passages by which Pliny can be corrected, especially in the section dealing with gems and marbles. Finally, I added two indexes to make it easier for students to find the etymologies. This is what I have done concerning Isidore; yet I openly acknowledge that much in him was necessarily left for ταῖς δευτέραις φροντίσιν, “second thoughts” or “later attention.”

9. In Martianus Capella I followed the same method. Since his text was no less corrupt than Isidore’s, I corrected it according to the authority of the most ancient manuscripts, some printed and some written by hand, which the distinguished man Basil Amerbachius, doctor of law and exceptionally devoted to the preservation of literature, supplied to me. I also illustrated it with scholia, partly ancient and partly my own, so that the roughness and obscurity of the language—which he seems to have cultivated especially in the first two books and at the beginnings and endings of the remaining books—would not deter many readers from reading him, as it has done until now.

10. These are the services I have rendered, out of my devotion to literary scholarship, in correcting these authors; and shortly, God willing, I shall render the same service to the letters of Cassiodorus and Symmachus and to the *Dictionary* of Julius Pollux.

When I was considering to whom I should offer and dedicate this little work, Your Highness, most illustrious prince, occurred to me above all. Your exceptional humanity, benevolence, and generosity, by which you embrace all those devoted to letters, are celebrated throughout the world. For who would not admire, who would not proclaim your outstanding praises, when, although the neighboring provinces are burning with the most disastrous fires of war, you maintain your diocese flourishing in peace and literary studies? From it so many distinguished and learned men emerge daily that the Greek and Latin Muses seem to have transferred their seat and dwelling from the Grudii to the Eburones.

11. Since you not only treat learned men who flee to you with singular kindness, but also attract with the greatest rewards all whom you recognize as distinguished by some rare excellence of learning, I have been raised to the firm hope that this Isidore, as a learned writer and prelate, will be especially welcome to you—not merely as a learned man and prelate, but as a most illustrious prince. In particular, if I have omitted anything that might contribute to his praise, I trust that Dominicus Lampsonius, my fellow countryman, whom long ago you appointed to your confidential affairs as secretary because of his exceptional learning, virtue, fidelity, and other outstanding qualities of mind, will easily compensate for the omission through the keenness of judgment he possesses and the singular favor he enjoys with you.

If, through his recommendation, Isidore and Martianus should at some time be handled and read in the presence and hands of Your Most Illustrious Highness, I shall judge that I have received the richest fruit of my labor. May the Lord God preserve you, most illustrious prince and most reverend prelate, safe and sound for as long as possible for the servants of the Christian commonwealth and for your dependents.

In the year of Our Lord 1677, on the fourth day before the Kalends of September.

## CHAPTER LI. Grialius’s Preface to Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Some Observations on This Preface. It Is Suspected That the Names of the Authors Cited by Isidore Have Often Perished through the Carelessness of Copyists

1. Grialius defended Isidore’s cause more fully than Vulcanius did. We reviewed his edition in chapter 36 and there transcribed the prologue to all of Isidore’s works. But since he illustrated the books of the *Etymologies* with a separate preface, it should be inserted here.

### To the Books of the *Etymologies*, by Johannes Grialius
2. Those who explain the origins of words—whether they confine themselves within the limits of grammar, range more widely in the pursuit of philosophy, or follow both approaches, as Saint Isidore did—undertake a task fraught with danger and full of hazard. Not only Plato, Varro, and the Stoics (whom we know from Cicero to have been especially devoted to this subject), but also nearly all the most serious writers among our own people, have learned this through excessive experience. Yet the fault was not theirs, but that of those who failed adequately to understand what they had in view. The principal point is this: as Varro says, each word has two natures—“from what” and “in relation to what” the word was imposed. To consider the former belongs to grammarians; 421 to consider the latter is more properly the philosopher’s task. Many who enter upon the former method and devote themselves to this discipline, which is called Ἑτυμολογική (*Etymologikē*, etymology), repeatedly show themselves difficult and captious: while reducing everything to syllables and letters, they cannot compel themselves to conceal any slight deviation from their rule.

[Col. 0329C]

3. But those who set before themselves the other class of explanation—which Varro likewise calls *περὶ σημαινομένων* (“concerning meanings”)—are intent on teaching and presenting the things themselves to the eyes. They seize upon words merely as an opportunity, and strive to shed light not so much upon words as upon things. Yet, while they neglect to appear very grammatical, they fall under the judgment of the less learned, although for the most part they are far more skillful in this very matter than those who profess this one art, provided only that they apply their minds to the method which they seriously pretend not to know.

Who could believe that matters obvious to the most insignificant grammarians escaped the parents and discoverers of all learning so completely that they so often offered themselves up to be ridiculed by the most frivolous men? Will anyone really believe that, for Cicero, *tumultus* was “much fear”; for Sulpicius, *testamentum* was “a testimony of the mind”; or for Tertullian, *limus* was “a rich liquid”? Or that Sylvester and the Fathers of the Roman synod thought that *curia* was named from blood? It would be superfluous to pile up examples from Plato, Varro, and Jerome. The first two had long since acquired a bad reputation among the common people on this subject; Jerome, however, acknowledges this fault—if it is a fault—in such a way that he excuses himself, for otherwise he would not so often admit it in his own work, assigning Hebrew explanations, to use his own expression, so violently to Greek and Latin names.

[Col. 0329D]

4. “You will say that the gravest men were merely playing.” I do not deny it. I say that they achieved this result: when they wished to be thought to have been playing, they appeared to less prudent men to have fallen disgracefully into error. But again, whether one calls these things play or absurdities, I maintain that they are not without fruit and usefulness. No fair-minded judge of such matters will deny that they either explain things previously obscure and tangled, bring dark matters into the open, or make things already known and manifest more sharply stimulate the mind.

Isidore wants *mantum*—which Suidas says is a Spanish garment—to have been so named because it covers only the hands. By this more expansive explanation he shows that we now use the garment in such a way that it covers not only the hands but the feet as well. From his Servius—for he had worn out no other book by reading it so thoroughly—he knew that a *lorica* was a covering made from leather. He preferred to call it “without thongs,” so that from *lorica*, which had long since fallen out of use, he might turn the reader’s mind and eyes toward a covering fastened together with iron rings. There are hundreds of examples of this kind.

[Col. 0330A]

5. Those who have written about definitions honor one definition as worthy of the name of a true definition, because it approaches most closely to the nature of the thing; yet they do not disdain the others so much as to investigate carefully their many varieties—for Victorinus and Boethius handed down fifteen or even more. If one asks why they are so hostile to the various conceptions of explanations, which are clarifications and descriptions of words, what reason do they give? Perhaps they are indignant because such deviations appear more conspicuously in wordplay than in play concerning things. But they appear with less danger, and sometimes with no less profit. Thus, if anywhere, it is certainly true in this matter what Flaccus says:

> [lacuna] Ridicule, sharper and more powerful,  
> Usually cuts through great matters more effectively and more successfully.

[Col. 0330B]

422

6. But let us return to Isidore. Since he had carefully worked through every kind of writing, he judged that the best course would be to open an easy and concise path to all the disciplines for the people of a poorly educated age, so that he might impart knowledge both of things and of words, and show, so far as possible, that everything adheres to the words themselves. Nothing seemed more suitable than that, in disentangling the meanings of words, he should show both their proper usage and, once their sound had been heard, bring before the eyes the things denoted by them, so that some sort of image and likeness might remain there.

In doing this, he certainly took many origins or explanations from ancient writers; but, following their example, he did not hesitate to put forward new ones of his own, and to engage in similar play—following, I say, the example of those whose negligence he desired to imitate, caring little for the obscure diligence of shallow critics. If such critics had paid attention to what they attacked in him, they would have raged against him less often and less boldly. For they themselves are plainly ridiculous when they frequently laugh at things which turn out, for the most part, to have belonged to the good works of those whom they themselves venerate and whom our author treated as authorities.

[Col. 0330C]

7. I hope they will now be more equitable when they see that many things which they greeted with laughter as though they were Isidore’s have been restored to older authors. If Saint Isidore had either completed this work himself, or readers had not greatly damaged it, we might perhaps not despair of freeing him from nearly every fault. For it bears witness that the work was collected from the recollection of old reading; and he himself expressly declares that he does not wish to claim the faults of others.

But now, since the author’s final hand was absent, and Braulio interpolated and arranged the work—as some think—and since readers, believing that they possessed in this volume a sufficiently large and sufficiently splendid supply of books for that age, gathered into it whatever they could obtain from elsewhere, while scribes, seeing anything written on the margin of the parchment, each eagerly inserted it into the text, why should they, through the offenses of so many others, exploit the odium directed against Isidore with such audacity—or rather, should I call it impiety?

[Col. 0330D]

8. But, to see what they blame in him, it will be worthwhile to set out the main points of the accusation. They say that he assigns Greek origins to Latin words and Latin origins to Greek words; that he wants earlier words to arise from later ones; that he pays no attention to orthography; that he counts vowel lengthenings among stems and roots; and that, in place of true origins, he arbitrarily substitutes other origins that serve the meanings. In my opinion, all the charges may be reduced to this summary. Unless I show that these practices are shared by him with the best authors, I do not plead his case, and he may bear whatever punishment he deserves. But I shall not use many examples, since anyone can easily bring together an immense forest from the passages indicated.

[Col. 0331A]

9. No one doubts that *ars* and *orator* are Latin words. Yet Donatus held *ars* to be ἀρετή (*aretē*, “virtue”), and Festus held *orator* to be ἀρατήρ (*aratēr*). How many things did Varro derive in the same way, even from those matters which, as he says, “do not creep in either field”? What of those among our own writers who said that *Jesus* was ἴασις (*iasis*, “healing”), and *Cephas* κεφαλή (*kephalē*, “head”), although they knew from the Gospel the true origins and interpretations of these names? But what men they were!

Isidore derived *quattuor* (“four”) from a square figure, although it seems straightforward and simple that *quadratum* (“square”) should arise from *quattuor*. Did not Ulpian likewise derive *ius* (“law”) from *iustitia* (“justice”)? What of the man who teaches that *hortus* (“garden”) comes from *oriri* (“to arise”), or *hedera* (“ivy”) from *edere* (“to eat”), or from *haerere* (“to cling”)? That man is Festus Pompeius. And who, I ask, among those who practiced this game ever lacked the derivation of vowel lengthenings in place of stems, as in Sulpicius’s *testamentum* and Aquillius’s *postliminium*? I believe there was no one at all.

423

10. What can one do with those who complain about the substitution of origins intended to make meanings clearer, except

> bid them lament amid the grammarians’ chairs?

For when Servius derives *sinister* (“left”), insofar as augury is concerned, from *sinere* (“to permit”), and *senator*, insofar as the ability to act is concerned, from the same verb, does he not knowingly and deliberately conceal another account of the word? What is one to say when the nature of the subject itself sometimes compels this procedure? Varro denies that *germanus* (“brother”) comes from the same *germen* (“germ”), but says that it flows from the same *genetrix* (“mother”).
