What when the derivations serve dignity or honor, or hint at something better than the words themselves display? Did the same Varro not know that *culina* (“kitchen”), which he said was situated in the rear part of the house, was named from the rear part of an animal? He preferred to derive it from *colere* (“to cultivate” or “tend the fire”). Was it obscure to Isidore that *medicina* (“medicine”) arose from *mederi* (“to heal”)? He bent it away from *modus* (“measure” or “manner”) in order to show what its use ought to be.

[Col. 0331B]

11. But they persist in their outcries and press the charge: etymologies and word-explanations which are neither etymologies nor word-explanations ought never to have been called such; and therefore the books ought not to have been entitled *Etymologies*. As though Galen had not called etymology ἀλάζων μάρτυς ἡ ἐτυμολογία—“etymology is a boastful witness.”

[Col. 0331C]

Yet the most holy man plainly seems to have labored to designate, in the briefest and, so to speak, thinnest manner, a work of the greatest usefulness and, for those times, of immense labor. Thus, he wished commentaries filled with the learning of many things to be called *Books of Etymologies*, as though they contained names alone; or at least, when he had proceeded farther, he writes to Braulio that he was sending him a work concerning the origin of certain things. What could have been devised under such a title more modest or restrained?

[Col. 0331D]

Thus he achieved this: that succeeding generations, down to our own time, have continually acknowledged and loudly proclaimed that from these books they acquired knowledge not merely of certain things, but—almost one might say—of all things and words.

12. I called this Grialius’s preface to the *Etymologies* because in my copy, and in others that I have seen, it is placed before the *Etymologies*. But since Rodriguez de Castro, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 299, asserts that after the *Etymologies* there is a long dissertation by Grialius on the same subject, I wonder whether in some copies such a dissertation, or preface, may have been bound or placed elsewhere.

[Col. 0332A]

Grialius admirably defends the work of the *Etymologies*, especially against those who wish to judge and condemn commentaries filled with the learning of many things on the basis of a few etymologies which they themselves consider foolish. I have already shown that I do not approve the claim made by some that Braulio so interpolated the work as to mix in absurdities and errors. I further agree that nothing Isidore adduces in deriving etymologies is so absurd that it does not have a closely similar example among the most distinguished ancient authors.

Whether Isidore in fact, following the example of others, invented such etymologies without the authority of older writers, I would not dare to determine. To me, Isidore seems in this work, as in most of his others, to be a patchwork writer (*centonarius*), so that I believe he almost always relies upon the words, or at least the opinions, of others. And just as many things have been found which are now known to have been certainly taken from ancient authors, so many more similar examples could be produced if the writings from which Isidore benefited had not largely perished.

424

[Col. 0332B]

13. It is ridiculous to bring a charge of plagiarism when Isidore himself frankly admits that he uses the words of his predecessors. Thus, in his preface to the *Etymologies*, he says that it is a work concerning the origin of certain things, collected from the recollection of ancient reading, and that in certain places it has been annotated as it stands written in the style of his predecessors.

In the preface to the book of *Differences*, or *On the Peculiarity of Expressions*, he says:

> Of these matters Cato was the first among the Latins to write; following his example, I have published only a very few of them, partly editing them myself and partly drawing them from the books of authors.

Similarly, in the dedicatory letter of the book *On the Nature of Things* to Sisebutus:

> Presenting all these matters according to what was written by ancient men, and especially as they are found in the writings of Catholic men, we have marked them in a brief table.

He speaks almost the same way in the preface to his commentaries on the Old Testament, and more clearly in Book I of the *Offices*:

> He sent a little book on the origin of offices, arranged from the writings of the most ancient authors and commented upon as the occasion required. In it I have mixed in many things in my own style, and some things exactly as they were found among those authors, so that the reading of each matter might more easily retain the authority of faith. If any of these things should nevertheless displease, forgiveness will be more readily granted for my errors, since matters for which the testimony of authors is supplied are not to be charged to the account of my own fault.

[Col. 0332C]

14. Isidore often does not expressly identify this testimony of the authors in the places where he uses it. Perhaps he thought it sufficient to warn the reader about the matter at the beginning; or, as I suppose, he sometimes placed the author’s name in the margin, which scribes later easily omitted.

I have encountered many copies of ancient writers in which the names of the authors whose words are being transcribed are placed in this way in the margin or at the beginning of a chapter, but in such a manner that in some places the name of the cited author has been omitted by the scribe.

I shall cite, in chapter 61, the manuscript codex of Sedulius Scottus’s explanations, in which Isidore’s words are quoted, with only the first letters of this name placed in the margin. Nevertheless, the other authors whose words they were copying were neglected and left unnamed.

425

[Col. 0333A]

Charles Burontius del Signore, in his preface to the works of Atto of Vercelli, observes that Atto himself did not indicate the passages from which he took his testimonies:

> Since Atto, being exceedingly well versed in divine and ecclesiastical matters, adorned his compositions with testimonies taken like pearls from Holy Scripture, from the Councils, and from the Fathers of the Church, yet did not indicate the passages, etc.

Burontius was publishing Atto’s works, prepared according to the authority of the Vercelli autograph; consequently, he was able to observe for himself that the author had not indicated the passages of the writings which he brought forward.

15. It follows that Atto sometimes also transcribes the words of others which seem poorly suited to his own argument, as in volume II, p. 140, in his exposition of the Epistle to Timothy:

[Col. 0333B]

> Although the whole world belongs to God, the Church is nevertheless called his house, whose ruler today is Damasus.

The editor writes in a note:

> What are we to say about these Epistles to the Thessalonians and to Timothy? We are very uncertain. The mention here of Damasus has the odor of a contemporary reference. Yet these words could belong to those interpolations which commentators were accustomed to make very frequently.

The same words are found in commentaries falsely attributed to Ambrose. See the Appendix, volume II of the Maurist edition, col. 296. Similar examples occasionally occur in Isidore, as when, in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 16, he adduces many things found in the preface to the Hispanic collection of canons, although some of them seem to have been placed outside their proper context.

[Col. 0333C]

16. Isidore is accustomed to weave together a longer discourse either from his own other works or from the works of others, as I shall show more fully in chapter 65. Accordingly, when he was about to discuss the origin of the canons, he inserted for the most part the preface that had been placed before the ancient Hispanic collection of canons, whether it had once been prepared by himself or by others. Among other things it contains these words:

[Col. 0333D]

> But if there are any councils which the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, have enacted, they remain established with complete force after the authority of these four; their acts are contained in this work.

What work or collection is this? For some manuscripts read “in this collection.” Certainly the collection of canons to which the preface and these words refer is not the *Etymologies*, in which the acts of the councils are by no means contained.

But if Isidore copied these words in such a way that he had noted either at the beginning of the chapter or in the margin the place from which they had been extracted, no difficulty would arise. Everyone would then easily understand that the work containing the acts of the councils was not Isidore’s *Etymologies*, but the collection of canons.

426

Thus these same words from the *Etymologies* are quoted in full by Gratian, *Distinction* 15, chapter 1; by Saint Antoninus, Part II of the *Chronicle*, title 13, chapter 2; and by others. Nevertheless, everyone understands that the work said to contain the acts of the canons is not the work of Gratian, Antoninus, or the others who cite the words, but another work about which Isidore is speaking.

Rabanus Maurus, who compiled his twenty-two books *On the Universe* chiefly from Isidore, without naming him, also gives the same words concerning the canons and councils in Book V, chapter 7:

[Col. 0334A]

> Their acts, he continues, are contained in this work.

17. If Isidore himself clearly directed the reader to the collection of canons, but that notation was omitted by the scribe, no fault or negligence should be attributed to him. I would nevertheless not strongly resist anyone who maintained that Isidore entrusted certain longer passages to a copyist, intending to remove the superfluous material when he corrected the work himself, but that he failed to do so because he was prevented by other occupations.

[Col. 0334B]

18. There are also certain statements in Isidore that contradict one another because they were taken from different authors. All contradiction would disappear if each opinion were assigned to its own author. Isidore either did this, but the authors’ names have been lost, as I have already said; or, amid such varied and numerous subjects, he sometimes failed to pay sufficient attention to contrary statements that he was excerpting from other writers; or he did not regard it as a serious inconvenience, since he professed to collect the opinions of others, to present the reader with two opinions that were not entirely consistent concerning some disputed matter.

19. My conjecture—that the names of the authors were indeed indicated by Isidore, but were not copied into the manuscripts through the carelessness or ignorance of scribes—is confirmed in a remarkable way by Bede’s example in the *Collectanea* drawn from the sayings of the ancient Fathers. Xystus of Siena says the following about it in Book IV of the *Bibliotheca sancta*:

[Col. 0334C]

> And lest he should seem to steal the sayings of his predecessors and assemble them as though they were his own, he had decided to insert the names of the teachers throughout and to indicate by name what had been said by which author. But when this appeared too laborious for him, he placed only the first syllables of the names in the margins opposite each saying; these later perished from all the copies through either the ignorance or the carelessness of the scribes.

427

20. There is also substantial evidence for the same conclusion in the fact that in the *Etymologies* and in Isidore’s other works infinitives often occur without a verb governing them, a feature especially observable in manuscript copies. Thus, in Book III, chapter 3 of the *Etymologies*:

[Col. 0334D]

> For one to be the seed of number, not itself a number.

Grialius notes that Greek *τὸ* has been added in printed editions; it is absent, he says, from the Gothic copies. He further remarks that such truncated expressions with infinitive verbs are frequent throughout this work.

But how could Isidore, so skilled in grammar, have written them in this form? Surely, as I suppose, he placed only the first letters of the name of the author who was reporting something, together with a verb such as *refert*, *tradit*, or *dicit*: for example, *Aug. d.*, *Gr. d.*, meaning “Augustine says” and “Gregory says.” Since the scribes did not understand these abbreviations, they did not copy them, and left the sense incomplete.

# CHAPTER LII

## On the Unfinished Manuscript Observations of Johann Salomon Semler on the Books of the *Etymologies*: His Preface and Observations on It

1. Semler had begun observations on Isidore’s *Etymologies*, but stopped at chapter 16 of Book I. Or, if he proceeded beyond that point, I have found none of his notes apart from those I mentioned among the Zaccarian papers. The prologue certainly ought not to be omitted.

## Observations and Notes of Johann Salomon Semler on the Books of the *Origins*

[Col. 0335A]

2. It is sufficiently well established, I think, that these books of the *Etymologies*, which almost contain the learning and instruction of earlier times, were once held in great esteem and are not despised today. In former times, when they were chiefly being composed and gathered from six hundred other writers, they were regarded not merely as a kind of abridgment, but as a substitute for the most useful instruction for lovers of letters, many of which were then perishing; certainly, they were written with great labor for the purpose of aiding study.

In our own age they are not wholly without the same usefulness, nor do they deserve less esteem, due to their celebrated author’s reputation for piety, learning, and diligence.

428

3. For there were certain men of roughly the preceding age who criticized this immense labor undertaken by Isidore, on the grounds that the fault of abridgments, once excessively widespread, had caused us to lack many distinguished and complete bodies of books. I do not know whether such an argument is sufficiently worthy of those who understand and judge matters properly, since it seems to deprive many excellent men of almost all the fruit of their most honorable labors—men who, insofar as it depended upon them, were almost the sole and wisest supports of declining letters.

Indeed, they deserved even greater praise because it is owing to their service that we can at least console ourselves through the proper use of the epitomes that survive, and bear the loss of the complete books with considerably less distress.

[Col. 0335B]

4. Their accusers seize upon this as an occasion for blame and complaint: the complete works themselves, they say, began to be neglected once abridgments could be used. Let us grant that there were some who, content with little, did not care for more. But should I transfer to these men the blame for a negligence that reduced larger works to smaller ones without abandoning the definite advantages they sought? Did not countless books perish for which no abridgment had been made?

[Col. 0335C]

I myself once held that mistaken opinion, which seemed to be confirmed by the authority of great men. But after calculating the matter more accurately, I now abandon it.

5. Trogus Pompeius would by now have perished altogether had Justin’s epitome not been available to us. Nor would we have Festus any more complete, even if the work of Paulus had been altogether absent. The grammatical writings of Varro and others would still not have reached us intact, even if certain grammarians of later ages had written nothing similar from them.

Thus, in the case of these books of Isidore, there is no reason to suppose that harm was inflicted upon other larger and similar works by their existence.

6. Others criticize the fact that the treasuries of many authors have been compiled here. These men seem either to be ignorant of, or to disregard, the whole purpose and rationale of this undertaking. Who would criticize Cassiodorus’s *Excerpt on Orthography*? Is the situation different because Isidore did not add the names of the writers? I do not think so.

[Col. 0335D]

How often would the same authors have had to be repeated, and why should a large book in itself—for we do not possess it complete, since it was never finished—be enlarged by several hundred names? It is enough that Isidore gathered material from the recollection of ancient reading and from many old books, as he himself writes to Braulio.

7. Isidore’s diligence was truly admirable and altogether remarkable, as was the supreme zeal of a man who acquired, read through, and excerpted so many books—and, most importantly for his praise, was moved to do so by requests and for the usefulness of others.

[Col. 0336A]

It is an excellent and most worthy example for others today to imitate, especially those who bear the solemn office of bishops and who can accomplish the same thing with less labor and greater benefit, since what was once more difficult and less widely accessible can now be done more easily and made available more broadly.

8. I need not enumerate here at length the writers whom Isidore used in these *Origins*, since they can be indicated more briefly in their proper places. At the same time, we shall gain this advantage: the variety of readings and the true text will be illuminated. For these books have not enjoyed better fortune than all the older works, whose integrity time, the pen, and ignorance have altered here and there.

429

9. I hastily collected brief observations—whatever from time to time occurred to me on this subject—whenever I was able to devote some labor and study to these humane letters. I read these very books carefully and profited greatly from them; the credit for that benefit belongs not to me but to their usefulness.

Meanwhile, I did not wish to neglect the opportunity to use an old edition of these *Origins*, whose title is as follows:

10.

> The most distinguished work of the divine Isidore of Seville, entitled *Etymologies*.  
>   
> Do not let an impression deceive you, diligent reader, when you see the title, as though this volume contained mention only of grammatical matters and the interpretations of words. For it contains such knowledge of so many great and lofty subjects that nowhere else can greater or worthier knowledge be found. Whatever knowledge of Greek and Latin history as a whole is found among other writers, you will find in this single book in a useful brevity. If you read it through, you will profit no less from the variety of its histories and the magnitude of its subjects than you will be entertained by them.  
>   
> It is for sale in the street of Saint James, under the sign of the golden lily.  
>   
> End: printed in Paris at the expense of Jean Petit, in the year of salvation 1520, on the twenty-fifth day of September.

[Col. 0336B]

11. This edition was printed from a good manuscript, as is apparent from certain readings that are not to be disregarded. But the book has another virtue as well. Corrections and variant readings were added by a learned man in an ancient hand; I hope some of them will prove useful.

Nor did I neglect other editions that were available, which I collated with the edition of Dionysius Gothofredus in the *Corpus of Latin Authors*, 1602, quarto.

[Col. 0336C]

12. Since these books of the *Origins* were once read with great care and were copied almost in full into other glossaries and lexica—as is shown by Papias, Huguitio, the *Catholicon*, Salomon of Constance, the *Breviloquus*, and others—I have also occasionally called them to my aid.

The same applies to the older grammarians, from whom Isidore excerpted much material. I called my observations brief because readers would easily have done without more verbose ones—or at least because I lacked the leisure while hastily writing even these.

13. I shall use the following signs to distinguish the books. *A* indicates a manuscript reading written in the margin of Petit’s edition. As I understand from the title page, this edition belonged among the books of Dionysius Duranti, who added not only his own name but also those of his friends. The codex now belongs to the celebrated ornament of the Altdorf Academy, Johann Heumann, who, with the greatest courtesy, willingly made it available to me.

[Col. 0336D]

*B* will designate the printed reading of this Petit edition.

14. Finally, I do not think it worthwhile to add anything about those features that seem to depart from the true nature of the Latin language. This was a fault of the age and of a few grammarians; Isidore therefore collected these features as well, since at that time they were not without importance. But most of the absurdities were inserted by the clumsy hand of later ages. Happy are we, to whom it has fallen to make full use of a purer light of letters.

430

15. This is Semler’s preface. He placed this title beneath his notes: *Brief Observations on the Books of the Origins*. He immediately observes that the index of all the books prefixed by Gothofredus is absent from the Petit edition and from the codex whose readings are written in the margin. In its place, that edition contains six letters of Isidore and Braulio.

[Col. 0337A]

He also observes that chapter 4 of Book I in Gothofredus’s edition corresponds to chapter 3 of the Petit edition, though he does not approve this arrangement.

16. Among the abridgments which many think caused the destruction of complete works, encyclopedic works such as Isidore’s *Etymologies* and similar writings are commonly included. Perhaps it sometimes happened that a work perished because an abridgment of it had been made.

But apart from the fact that the nature of epitomes seems different from that of Isidore’s etymological work and other works of this kind, I would rather think that some people, moved by the love of learning inspired by Isidore’s *Etymologies*, acquired complete copies of the authors whom he praises, than that the loss of certain ancient writers’ books arose from the existence of these abridgments.

[Col. 0337B]

For although Isidore’s *Etymologies* provide certain general notions of things that can be extremely useful, they sharpen the reader’s desire rather than satisfy it.

17. In the eulogy with which Semler honors Isidore, I observe that he commemorates not only Isidore’s learning, singular diligence, and supreme zeal, but also his piety. He calls it an excellent and most worthy example for others today to imitate, especially those who bear the solemn office of bishops.

I willingly and gratefully accept this praise from a man otherwise heterodox.

Semler says that we do not possess the complete work of the *Etymologies* because it was never finished, and that even what we possess was interpolated by a later hand. This is not so easy to prove. Isidore certainly left his codex uncorrected, but it was no longer lacking anything. Nor is there reason to deny that the material found in most corrected copies belongs to Isidore.

[Col. 0337C]

Indeed, it has already been established that many things which some attribute to an incompetent interpolator have authors far older than Isidore—authors whom antiquity admired as flourishing in the best age of Latin language and refined learning.

431

3. In compiling this index, Barthius appears to have followed the Breulian edition; consequently, some variation is observed in the names and chapter numbers. Thus, in the first place, it has “Achatesius of Miletus,” bk. I, ch. 38, whereas Grialius has ch. 39, where “Hecataeus of Miletus” is read, as Fabricius correctly amended it in his note. Other authors whom Isidore cites in his book *On the Nature of Things* and elsewhere could be added; but since this is to be done by us in the general Index, it will suffice for the present not to have neglected the labors of others in the general Index 435.

What Fabricius says in his note about the first and third books of the *Differentiae* will be explained more fully in ch. 56, where I shall show that there are only two books of the *Differentiae*: one concerning things, the other concerning language. The book of *Differentiae* concerning language, however, exists in two forms: one fuller and arranged alphabetically, edited by Grialius, which Fabricius calls the third book of the *Differentiae*; the other shorter and without alphabetical order, which Fabricius calls the first book.

## CHAPTER LIV. Editions of the *Etymologies* surveyed

1. Niccolò Antonio seems to have recognized no edition of Isidore’s *Etymologies* earlier than the Paris edition of 1520. He reports that D. Joseph Pellizerius regarded it as the first edition; Pellizerius possessed a copy and mentioned it in his book *Maximo obispo de Zaragoza* (“Maximus, Bishop of Zaragoza”) and in its preface. But several others had appeared much earlier, which I shall now survey. [Col. 0341D]

2. Maittaire indicates this in *Annales typographici*, vol. I, part 1 of the enlarged edition, p. 768:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies*: twenty-two books of Rabanus Maurus *On the Nature and Properties of Things*, folio.”

He notes that the edition is an old one and, apparently, primitive, without signatures, pagination, or catchwords. But I doubt whether these are the genuine *Etymologies* of Isidore, or those which Rabanus Maurus interpolated and published under Isidore’s name, suppressing his own. No place or year is specified.

[Col. 0342A] 3. Fabricius reports in the *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis* that the *Etymologies* appeared in Italy in an old edition, in an uncertain year and place, and he refers to Gesner’s library, p. 468. The epitome of Gesner’s edition, Zurich 1574, p. 435, says the following under Isidore: “The twenty books of the *Origins*, printed in Italy.” Bayerius doubts whether this is the edition said to have appeared around 1470, without indication of place, in the catalogue of the library of the Duke de La Vallière, vol. II, p. 12, no. 2185.

4. This is the edition which I shall now describe. Six letters are placed at the beginning:

“Here begins the letter of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Braulio, bishop of Caesar Augustus” [sic].

Then follows:

“Here begins the first book of the *Etymologies* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

In the first book, chapters 3 and 4 are included under a single chapter, whereas they are more correctly separated in other copies. After book XX comes an index, or repertory, of all the chapters in the books of the *Etymologies*, etc. The three books of the *Sentences* follow, as in another Venetian edition of 1483:

“In the name of Christ begins the first book,” etc., “on the highest good.”

In the third book, after the words “to be made joyful,” it includes what in other copies is the final passage, followed by this:

“For this is the affection of Christian compassion: that a sacrifice be offered to God for each dead person. Hence it is written: ‘And do not defraud the dead of mercy.’”

The books *On the Highest Good* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, “most recently revised and corrected of all errors,” come to an end. An index of chapters follows.

The type approaches what is called Gothic. The edition may be assigned approximately to the year 1470. Its place of publication appears to be in Italy, and, I think, Venice—unless perhaps the following presents an obstacle: Peter Delfinus of San Michele di Murano wrote to Jerome, the General, on 16 March 1480, letter 141, in Martène’s *Collectio veterum scriptorum*, vol. III:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies*, whose possession you indicated that you desired, is not found in print.”

On the title in the middle of the first page was written: “The work of Isidore’s *Etymologies.” The same applies to *On the Highest Good*.

5. Fabricius records an edition of the *Etymologies* for the year 1472 in both of his *Bibliothecae*. He says that it was in the possession of our venerable Wolfius; he likewise reports that certain copies were printed on parchment. This edition was completed at Augsburg, in folio, by Gonterius Zainer of Reutlingen, or, as others write, Ginther Zainer of Reutlingen. Maittaire also mentions it, from Caillio, in *Annales typographici*, vol. I, p. 100; and Philippus Jacobus Lambacher, author of the 1750 catalogue of the old Vienna library, mentions it in part I, p. 127, among others whom I omit.

In the enlarged edition of Maittaire, p. 317, vol. I, part 1, the following title is given:

“Twenty books of the *Etymologies* of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, printed by Ginther Zainer.”

At the end:

“The books end successfully, printed by Ginther Zainer, born at Reutlingen, with foreign letters, in the year from the incarnation of the Lord 1472, on the nineteenth day of November.”

The type is Roman.

6. For the year 1477, Maittaire’s enlarged Amsterdam edition of 1733, vol. I, part 1, p. 382, reports a folio edition at Basel:

“The works of Isidore of Seville, folio. Basel, 1477,” from the catalogue of John van Horne, p. 36, no. 54.

As I think, these are the *Etymologies* together with the books of the *Sentences*, and not other works of Isidore.

437 7. In the year 1483, at Venice, in folio, together with the books *On the Highest Good*, by Peter Loslein of Langenzenn. Maittaire, Fabricius in both of his Latin *Bibliothecae*, Fr. Peregrinus Antonius Orlandus in his Italian work *On the Origin and Progress of Printing*, and Bayerius, who had the book at hand, mention this edition.

It begins:

“Register of the books of the *Etymologies* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

After the index of chapters come six letters of Isidore and Braulio. After the twentieth book:

“The book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, ends.”

Then follows:

“Rubric of the first book *On the Highest Good* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

Then:

“In the name of Christ begins the first book of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, *On the Highest Good*.”

After the third book:

“The third and final book *On the Highest Good* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, ends. Printed at Venice by Peter Loslein of Langenzenn, 1483.”

Since Maittaire’s alphabetical appendix lists “the letters of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza,” Venice, folio, 1483, we may correctly infer that this is nothing other than the letters which, as stated above, precede the *Etymologies* in this edition.

8. In the year 1489, at Basel, in folio, according to Bayerius and Fabricius in both *Bibliothecae*. Maittaire, in the enlarged edition, p. 515, vol. I, part 1, gives it as follows:

“Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologicon*, folio. Basel, 1489.”

And in a note:

“Corrected from various manuscripts by the hand of Janus Gruterus, this copy, with Gruterus’s continuous commentary, was in the library of Gerhard John Vossius. It appears later to have passed into the library of Chancellor Weimann.”

9. In the year 1493, at Venice: Isidore’s *Etymologies* and *On the Highest Good*, by Bonetus Locatellus, at the expense of Octavianus Scotus, in folio. Maittaire cites Caillio. In the enlarged edition he notes that Orlandus reports it on p. 199:

“Isidore, *On the Highest Good*. Leipzig, 1493.”

Maittaire later writes:

“Isidore’s *Etymologies*, by Bonetus Locatellus, at the expense of Octavianus Scotus, folio. Venice, 1494.”

This may perhaps be the same edition. For he names no author, not even in the enlarged edition.

10. In the year 1499, at Paris, in folio, according to Maittaire and Bayerius, who possessed a copy. Maittaire gives the title:

“Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*, the work of Georgius Wolff and Thielmann Keruer. Paris, 1499, 25 May. J. P. Jehan Petit, for sale in the Rue Saint-Jacques, at the sign of the Silver Lion.”

438 11. In the year 1500, at Paris, quarto, according to Joseph Rodríguez de Castro in the *Bibliotheca Hispana* and Maittaire, p. 72, vol. I, part 1 of the enlarged edition, who says:

“Isidore of Hispalis [I correct this to ‘of Seville’], an etymological work, quarto. Paris, 1500.”

He notes that it is listed in the catalogue of Vander Meer.

12. In the year 1509, at Paris, according to Fabricius in both *Bibliothecae* and Dupin in *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*, vol. V.

13. In the year 1520, at Paris: Semler accurately describes this edition in the preface which I reproduced in chapter 52. I saw a copy of this edition in the library of the Roman College.

14. In the year 1529, at Haguenau, from Secerius, according to Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis* and Niccolò Antonio, who asserts that other books of Isidore were published together with the *Etymologies*. In the Vatican Library, no. 884, there is a collection of certain works of Saint Isidore published at Haguenau in that same year 1529; after Zaccaria’s death I acquired a copy of this edition from his books. [Col. 0344B] But the *Etymologies* were not published with it. I shall describe that edition later.

I did, however, see an edition in quarto or large octavo in the possession of the distinguished Gaspare de Segovia, which others do not mention. The *Etymologies*, together with the *Differentiae rerum* (“Differences of Things”) and *Differentiae sermonum* (“Differences of Language”), were published together; but since the first leaves are missing, neither the year nor the place of publication can be determined. At the end appears, as a device, Mercury with wings and the motto: “I carry learned writings throughout the world.” All the evidence indicates that the *Etymologies* and *Differentiae* were taken from the Bignaean edition.

15. In the year 1577, under the direction of Vulcanius, as was discussed more fully in chapter 50. I now omit repeating the editions of Bignaeus, Grialius, and Breulius. Nor shall I describe in detail the editions of the *Etymologies* from the years 1595, 1602, and 1622, included among Dionysius Gothofredus’s *Scriptores linguae Latinae*, since he followed Vulcanius and Bignaeus.

The title of the 1622 edition in my possession is:

“Authors of the Latin language brought together into one body; the following page will show the list of these ancient and modern authors. With notes by Dionysius Gothofredus, J.C., together with a general index to all the authors. The latest edition, more corrected and enlarged in some respects. Geneva: printed by Alexander Pernet, 1622, quarto.”

The *Etymologies* of Isidore occupy column 809; various readings in Isidore, from Vulcanius’s edition, occupy column 1905.

## CHAPTER LV. Manuscript codices of the *Etymologies*: excerpts, notes, and translations

1. Manuscript codices of the *Etymologies*, as Niccolò Antonio says, are found everywhere, in the corners of libraries. He mentions a codex nearly seven hundred years old in the College of Saint Ildefonsus at Alcalá; Bayerius reports that it was transferred to the Escorial library and that he himself examined it in 1762. Niccolò Antonio adds another in the Milanese library, written in large Lombard letters, and others in the library of Saint John at Padua, then belonging to the Lateran Canons; in the Paris library of the physician René Moreau; in the Venetian library of Saint Anthony; and in the Pincian monastery of Saint Benedict. For the Venetian library of Saint Anthony he cites Tomasinus, p. 13, who certainly more than once records *Etymologies* in the manuscript holdings of Padua, for example on pp. 30, 31, and elsewhere.

2. In addition to these, Bayerius says that he saw and examined more than forty old codices of the *Etymologies*, both among the Spanish collections at Toledo and Seville and in the royal monastery of the Escorial, and in the libraries of Italy: the Vatican, Laurentian-Medicean, Riccardian-Florentine, Ambrosian at Milan, San Salvatore at Bologna, Saint Mark’s at Venice, Padua, the Academy of Turin, and others. He observes that the Escorial possesses at least ten of them, some of which exceed the millennium of the Church, or the year 1000 of the Christian era, in antiquity. I shall examine what Bayerius adds concerning the legal notes found in codices older than a thousand years in chapter 93, when I describe Vatican Codex 623.

3. Rodríguez de Castro, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, pp. 314 ff., describes at length, and not without useful labor, the codices of the *Etymologies* and other works of Isidore preserved in the Escorial library. In shelfmarks 1 and 3 there is a parchment codex of the *Etymologies*, written in the year 781 of the era—that is, in A.D. 743, as Rodríguez infers from a certain note in the codex which I shall quote shortly. But he should have noticed that the codex he describes was not written in that era, but at a later time from another codex that had been written in the year 781, as is clear from Rodríguez’s own account.

On the first leaf, which is paper, the following note is read:

“This book was written in the era 1085 by Dominicus the priest, as is said at the end of the book. This is the year of Christ 1042. And perhaps it belonged to Sancho II, not yet king, who was born of Queen Sancha, the sister of Vermund III. Since all three are mentioned both at the beginning of this book, in the checkered panel where the name is often repeated, and in the first book, in the tables of poetic feet, and the chronology does not conflict.”

4. This note should have warned Rodríguez that the codex was copied not in the year 743 but only in 1042, since the era-year is perhaps 1080. On the same first leaf there is this note in Spanish:

“Este libro es de la Iglesia de nuestra Señora del Pilar de Zaragoza.”

That is:

“This book belongs to the church of Our Lady of the Pillar of Zaragoza.”

On the second leaf, which is parchment, as are the following leaves, it is noted:

“This script is called Mozarabic, or Toledan.”

The characters are Gothic, but skillfully and carefully written. At the beginning a multicolored cross is depicted, with these words in its upper part: “Peace, Light”; and in its lower part: “Law, King.” A labyrinth of words follows, decorated in various colors like the cross, in honor of the blessed Virgin Mary; and another similar one, in which is read: “To Sancho and Sancha the book.”

On the following leaf, in capital letters, is this notice:

“In the name of God, in simple, triple, divine form, the chapters of the book of the *Etymologies* begin. So that you may quickly find in this volume what you seek, this page, reader, shows you the subjects concerning which the founder of this codex will discuss [read: ‘discussed’] in the twelve books. Thanks be to God, amen, world without end.”

5. We find a similar notice in our Vatican codices. From it we may suspect that the Zaragoza exemplar was modeled on other external copies, especially since the author Isidore, as we shall soon see, is called “the Younger.” The statement that there are twelve books appears to be a scribal error. For, as Rodríguez observes, this codex agrees with Grialius’s edition in the distribution of its parts and chapters. After the notice there is an index of the books and chapters, executed with great artistry and divided by circles.

6. The title of the work is as follows:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the book of the *Etymologies* of the most blessed Esidor the Younger, bishop of the church of Seville, written to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.”

Before the letters of Isidore and Braulio, which precede the *Etymologies*, there are legal notes which Isidore reports as abolished in bk. I, ch. 28. In some of our manuscripts they are inserted at that place; in most they are absent.

Isidore’s letters to Braulio are five:

1. “In Christ the Lord, and to my beloved son Braulio the archdeacon” [correct: “archdeacon,” not “arcedianus”], “Isidore.”

2. “In Christ, most reverend and most honored brother Braulio, Isidore.”

The remaining three begin:

“To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio, Isidore.”

The first of these five letters begins: “While a friend’s letters”; the second: “Because I am unable.”

Braulio’s letters to Isidore are two, with this heading:

“To my lord, and truly lord, and chosen of Christ, Isidore, bishop supreme among bishops, Braulio, an unworthy servant of God’s saints.”

7. At the end of book V, where the *Chronicle* occurs, we read:

“After Maurice’s twenty-one years, the Goths become Catholic. After eight years of Phocas . . . In the year 808, the Romans are slaughtered by the Persians. Heraclius is now in his seventeenth year, in the year 826. The Jews of Spain become Christians. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone.”

Immediately afterward is added:

“We find that this *Chronicle* was collected in the era 666, as also in another [copy]. Then, from the following era 667 up to the present era, which is 781, 116 years have passed. Added to the preceding total of this *Chronicle*, these make altogether 5,942 years from the beginning of the world up to the aforesaid era 781. Since these matters have thus been stated—or rather arranged—we finally acknowledge that it is difficult for any human being, even after the time of the Lord’s incarnation, to calculate the total of the years through kings and princes, while also omitting the era that is the indicator of truth, and not fall into error. Therefore it is necessary to divide that era according to the custom which happened to prevail in its own time. Whatever one finds by dividing, one must add to the greater era [perhaps: ‘to the greater era’], which is known to run from Adam to Christ. Then it will surely be proved that one has reached the path of truth.”

8. From this badly written Latin note, Rodríguez wrongly inferred that the Zaragoza codex had been written in the era 781. But the only fact established by it is that the codex derives from another written in that era. This may frequently be observed in other codices, in which scribes of later times copied word for word everything that earlier scribes had inserted into the original works.

442 9. Another Escorial codex should not be separated from this discussion. It contains the *Etymologies* in Spanish, but in an order different from that of the printed editions. The *Etymologies* are divided into chapters, treatises, and books, and several passages found in the printed editions and other manuscripts are omitted.

It begins:

“First chapter: on discipline and art.”

The final chapter concerns history. Then, on folio 60, the third treatise begins, which is on rhetoric. But the beginning of the second treatise is not stated. On folio 77:

“Third book, and first chapter on dialectic.”

Other chapters follow in the same manner. Perhaps when the third treatise was mentioned earlier, it is a scribal error for “second treatise”; or perhaps “third book” should be read here. For on folio 93 there follows:

“Fifth chapter, first [chapter] of the four disciplines,” etc.

10. After three chapters, on folio 117:

“First chapter on the makers of the laws.”

On folio 131, again:

“Fifth chapter, first [chapter] of the word *Chronicle*.”

On folio 142:

“First chapter on the languages of the peoples.”

On folio 190:

“Here begins the eleventh book, the origin of certain names,” etc.

This is called the eleventh book, whereas in the other copies it is the tenth, namely, the book on Names arranged alphabetically. In this version the book ends with the word *seditiosus* (“seditious”).

11. Rodríguez immediately adds that chapter 7 of the *Life of Saint Isidore* concerns “the books which he left written,” etc. But since he did not state beforehand that this codex contains the *Life of Saint Isidore* divided into chapters, I suspect that a substantial typographical error has entered at this point, and that everything Rodríguez goes on to narrate should be understood as referring to another codex, which he describes on p. 320.

The codex, therefore, in which the *Etymologies* are represented in Spanish appears to contain only the first books of the *Etymologies*, in disordered sequence and with some omissions.

Rodríguez’s conjecture that these *Etymologies* were taken from the first exemplar which Isidore sent to Braulio, because they are divided, as he says, not by books but by treatises or chapters—just as he asserts that Isidore wrote them to Braulio—cannot be sustained. For Braulio says that Isidore divided the work not into books but into titles. The Spanish *Etymologies*, however, as Rodríguez should have observed, are divided into chapters, treatises, and books, not titles.

12. Rodríguez adds that much is missing from the Spanish *Etymologies* which is found in the printed editions. This could agree with the exemplar sent by Isidore to Braulio, since Braulio reports that Isidore did not complete the *Etymologies*. But, as I have shown elsewhere, Braulio added nothing to the *Etymologies*; he merely divided them into books.

The Spanish translator either found some mutilated and disordered exemplar, of which many are found everywhere; or he wished to translate only certain parts of the *Etymologies* into the vernacular; or perhaps he encountered separate portions of the *Etymologies* already divided into books by someone, among those portions which Isidore had published separately before sending the entire work, assembled into one body, to Braulio.

13. On p. 320 Rodríguez describes Escorial codex III.b.I, a paper codex containing several works translated into Spanish from an old Latin codex of the library of the church of Toledo. It was written in the year 1444. The works are the *Life of Saint Isidore*, the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*, the latter’s work *On the Perpetual Virginity of Saint Mary*, and Saint Augustine’s *Soliloquies*. All are in Spanish.

The title of the *Life of Saint Isidore* reads:

“Here begins the prologue of the Life of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, which, as may be gathered from it, is a homily written by some holy man of that same time.”

It consists of thirty-one chapters and includes several letters of Saint Isidore, as well as his treatise *On Prayer*, or *Lament of Repentance*, arranged alphabetically.

14. I think I should attach here what Rodríguez related on p. 318, when he was discussing the Spanish *Etymologies*: namely, that chapter 7 of this *Life of Saint Isidore* concerns the books written by Isidore himself, especially the [Col. 0348B] *Etymologies*, which it praises at length.

Chapter 20 is the *Lament of Repentance*; chapter 21 is Saint Isidore’s letter to Mausona, also called Massona. This is followed by Isidore’s letter inviting Braulio to come to him; then Braulio’s letter requesting the book of the *Etymologies*; Isidore’s reply; another letter of Isidore to Eugenius; and another to Leofredus, or Leudefredus.

15. Rodríguez considers this *Life of Isidore* different from the one generally attributed to Lucas of Tuy and published in the *Acta Sanctorum* by the Bollandists. The division into chapters is indeed different. But since the Bollandists did not publish everything that existed in the old Toledo manuscript from which their copy of the *Life* had been taken, and since it is observed elsewhere that the letters of Isidore mentioned above are also inserted in the *Life* published by the Bollandists, there is reason to suspect that the Spanish *Life* does not in reality differ from the Latin one written by the canon of León, or by Lucas of Tuy. Certainly, much is common to both *Lives*.

444 16. Burriel described the Toledo copies in his letters, above, in chapter 40. Fabricius testifies in the *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis* that excellent manuscript codices of the *Etymologies* exist at Leiden among the books formerly belonging to Isaac Vossius. It would take too long to list all the manuscript codices of the *Etymologies* indicated in Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca bibliothecarum manuscriptorum* and in catalogues of the same kind.

In the *Journal Encyclopédique*, published in French in January 1761, part I, pp. 18 and 20, the silver codex of Ulfilas is described; it contains the Gothic translation of the Gospels, which had by then been published in print by Junius. It is added that around the year 1757, Mr. Knitell found in the Wolfenbüttel library a parchment codex of Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies* among those called *rescripti*—that is, manuscripts in which new writing has been added over some earlier writing that was erased, though sometimes in such a way that the earlier text can still be read.

In this codex the overlying text, as it is called, is the work of the *Etymologies*. The earlier writing contained several ancient documents, among them part of the Gothic translation of Saint Paul’s Letter to the Romans. The script of the *Etymologies* is similar to that which Mabillon reproduces on p. 351 of *De re diplomatica*; the Gothic translation was written in the same letters as the famous silver codex of Ulfilas.

17. Bandini, in the *Catalogus Codicum Latinorum bibliothecae Mediceae Laurentianae Florentinae*, describes several codices of the *Etymologies* more distinctly. One is in vol. I, shelfmark 19, codex 32, paper, small quarto; it is extremely elegant, with painted initials for each book, and consists of 318 folios.

There are the *Etymologies* in twenty-two books, preceded by an index of the chapters of each book, together with six letters of Isidore and Braulio. The second book, as well as the third, is divided into two; hence there are twenty-two books, concerning which I spoke in chapter 48.

18. In the same place, vol. II, pluteus 52, codex 21, a small quarto parchment manuscript of the thirteenth century. At the top edge of its binding is written: “Isidore, Etymologies, five florins, 87 leaves, mark N.” It contains twenty-two books, preceded by a table of chapters for each book, and, before the first book, a letter of Isidore—called Junior—to Braulio, beginning “Your Holiness.” At the end: “Here end the books of Isidore’s Etymologies. Thanks be to God.” The codex closes with a table of the subjects treated in the chapters of the twenty books.

19. Among the books of the Gaddiana Library, vol. III, pluteus 98, is a parchment codex in small folio of the thirteenth century, with decorated initials and rubricated titles, 445 leaves, and furnished in the margins with many fairly good variant readings. Its former owner was Franciscus Maria Tartarinus of Modena, a cleric. Its title is: “The Etymological Work in twenty books of Isidore Junior, bishop of the church of Seville, addressed to Braulio, bishop.” It is preceded by a table of books and chapters and by seven letters, as in the Madrid edition, part II, p. 393. In the first two letters one reads *Braulioni archidiaconus Isidorus* (“Isidore, archdeacon, to Braulio”) instead of *Braulioni archidiacono Isidorus* (“Isidore to Braulio, archdeacon”). In most other copies only five letters are customarily prefixed to the Etymologies, apart from the one that serves as the preface. In this copy, and in some others, two additional letters addressed to Braulio are included; they were written while he was still an archdeacon. A very full index was added to the codex by a later hand.

20. Another copy of the Etymologies in the same Codex 17, no. 2, is entitled: “The twenty books of the Etymologies of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis.” The five customary letters precede it. It ends with: “*character* (Greek), in Latin *forma*,” as near the end of the edition. The codex is a parchment manuscript in folio from the eleventh century, with rubricated titles and a preliminary index of books and chapters added by a later hand. From certain documents inserted in it, one may infer that it formerly belonged to some monastery at Imola.

21. A third copy of the Etymologies in the same Codex 17, no. 3, is entitled: “The twenty books of the Etymological Work of Isidore of Seville.” It is a parchment manuscript in large quarto, without letters, from the thirteenth century, with a rough painting of the author at the beginning, in addition to three others. I shall provide further examples in chapter 105 of the custom of placing portraits of authors at the beginning of works. The name of the former owner is Giovanni Gaddi.

22. In the former library of Santa Croce, vol. IV, pluteus 27, Codex 7 contains the first part of Isidore’s Etymologies, preceded by letters. It ends at the close of the eleventh book—equivalent to the tenth in the edition—with the words: “winged things, pressers.” Codex 8 contains the second part of the Etymologies, from book XII—book XI in the edition—to the end of book XXII—book XX in the edition. These are parchment codices from the beginning of the thirteenth century, written in the same hand, with rubricated titles and several summaries in the margins. Appended are an excerpt on precious stones and an anonymous astronomical treatise beginning: “The heavens are divided by five circles”; it ends: “let us enjoy one thing and remain in one. Amen.”

23. From the same library of Santa Croce, pluteus 27, Codex 9 is a folio manuscript of the eleventh century, truly remarkable, with summaries in the margins and colored initials. Its first four pages of the Etymologies were supplied by a thirteenth-century hand; the letters are omitted. It is preceded by an alphabetical table of subjects and words. [446] At its end stands: “Here ends the table written concerning Isidore’s Etymologies by Brother Thedaldus of Mugello, at Florence, 20 October 1384.” This later table, which occupies the first eight leaves of the codex, is followed by another, older one, presenting the contents of the individual books, with the following notice attached:

> “After these books of the Etymologies, this volume contains a book of Saint Isidore addressed to Sisebutus, on astronomy; on days and nights; on the solstice; on the world and its parts; on the heavens and their parts and all their adornment; on the sun, moon, and stars; on thunder; on lightning; on the rainbow; on clouds and rains; on snow and hail; on winds and their names; on storm and calm; on pestilence; on the ocean and the saltiness of seawater; on the river Nile; on earthquakes; and on Mount Etna. It also contains a certain treatise on the nature of birds.”

24. Another inscription occurs on p. 10:

> “This book of the Etymologies of Isidore the Ancient, in which there is Isidore the Younger on computation and the world, and a catalogue of the supreme pontiffs down to the time of Hermes, and a catalogue of the ministers-general of the Order of Saint Francis down to Michael of Cesena, together with an excellent alphabetical table, belonged to Brother Thedaldus of Casa, who gave it to the convent in the year of the Lord 1410, on 4 December.”

On p. 11 the Etymologies begin, with a short prologue addressed to Braulio and a table of chapters. At the end: “Here ends the book of the Etymologies of Saint Isidore, bishop.”

25. There follows, no. 2, p. 69, an untitled book which the catalogue perhaps attributes to Isidore, concerning certain animals. Chapter 1 begins with the night-raven:

> “In Psalm 101 David says: ‘I have become like a night-raven in a dwelling.’ The *Physiologus* says: ‘The night-raven is an unclean bird,’ etc.”

The final chapter, on the pelican, ends:

> “Thus also our Lord Jesus Christ says through the prophet Isaiah: ‘I have begotten and exalted children; but they have despised me.’”

The book called the *Physiologus* is attributed by some to Florinus and by others to Theobaldus. But there are two *Physiologi* in manuscript codices: one in Florinus’s elegiac verses, the other in Theobaldus’s leonine verses, as may be gathered from Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*. It is uncertain in what period these authors lived; but they are certainly later than Isidore. Accordingly, the book on the nature of birds, or on certain animals, must be denied to Isidore.

26. The work *On the World*, or *On the Nature of Things*, which follows in the codex, together with certain additions from the Etymologies, will be explained [447] in its proper place. There follows a catalogue of the apostles and disciples of Christ, and of the ministers-general and protectors of the Order of Saint Francis. The following inscription is appended:

> “This book belongs for the use of Brother Thedaldus, son of Ser Octavianus of Mugello. He bought it from a certain layman for the price of six florins in the year of the Lord 1371, near the end of November.”

Thedaldus added in his own hand an account of the seven wonders of the world and a table of the books and chapters of the Etymologies. The codex closes with a certain document concerning the electors of the emperor.

27. A codex of the same library of Santa Croce, pluteus 27, no. 10, is a truly remarkable folio parchment manuscript of the tenth century, with rubricated letters and titles. It contains the Etymologies, preceded by summaries, letters, and a table of chapters. On the first folio is written:

> “This Isidore’s Etymologies is for the use of Brother Andrea Ursiti of Florence, of the Order of Friars Minor. After his death it must be placed in the book chest of the Florentine convent and remain there, since it was purchased principally for this purpose.”

28. In the catalogue of the manuscripts of the Royal Athenaeum of Turin, Rivautella and Berta, besides Codex 53—which contains the Etymologies and the Book of Numbers, discussed elsewhere—list three other codices of the Etymologies.

Codex LV, d. IV, 30, is a parchment manuscript of the eleventh century, consisting of 176 leaves. It contains the first sixteen books of the *Origins* of Saint Isidore of Seville. It supplies a specimen of variant readings. Innumerable diagrams relating to geometry, astronomy, and music are elegantly painted in red throughout the codex, especially on fols. 135 and following, where painted hands and figures of human beings indicate various methods of counting. Similar materials are found in the Vatican codices, in which there are books on computation, or on speech by the finger. At the end: “Here ends the sixteenth book. Here begin, successfully, the chapters of the seventeenth book of the Etymologies of Bishop Isidore.”

29. Codex LVI, d. IV, 33, of the same Turin Athenaeum, is a parchment manuscript of the tenth century containing the twenty books of the Etymologies. At the end: “Here ends the twentieth book. Amen.” Nearly the same variant readings occur as in the preceding Codices 53 and 55.

30. Codex LVII, d. IV, 34, of Turin, is a parchment manuscript of the fourteenth century. It contains the twenty books of the Etymologies, followed at the end by a table of subjects arranged alphabetically.

31. Muratori, vol. III of the *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, dissertation 43, col. 804, describes a certain codex of the Milanese library which we must not pass over in silence:

> “In my *Anecdotes* I published a little work by Gezonius, abbot, etc. All these materials were contained in a single Ambrosian codex, into which other things had also been gathered: glosses on Genesis, etc.; Etymologies by Virgilius, a Spanish presbyter; then others from the book of Lord Isidore. Finally, there are glosses on the Old and New Testament, on the book of the Offices, on a certain book called *Rotar*—I do not know what is meant here—on the book of the Lives of the Saints, on Cassian, on Eusebius, on Orosius, etc.”

The *Book of Rotar* mentioned here is Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*, called in the manuscripts the *Book of Wheels* because of the circles, or wheels, painted to explain the subjects. I also think that Isidore’s book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* is meant by the *Book of the Lives of the Saints*. The *Book of the Offices* and the glosses on the Old and New Testament may likewise belong to him.

The name of Virgilius, the Spanish presbyter whose Etymologies are praised, is still unknown in the Spanish library. Muratori, vol. II of the *Latin Anecdotes*, in the inquiry following the *Exposition of the Creed Quicumque*, observed that this codex had been written more than a thousand years ago. It also contains an anonymous book, *On the Dogma of Faith*—the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, attributed by most people to Gennadius—and another entitled *The Faith of Bacharius*, namely, an Apology.

32. Which manuscript copies of the Etymologies Zaccaria used for his variant readings I explained in chapter 45; likewise, in chapter 46, I listed other copies identified from old catalogues.

In the Vatican and other Roman codices that I consulted, and which I shall later review individually, the work of the Etymologies frequently occurs. Thus it appears in Vatican Codex 623, discussed in chapter 93; Vatican Codex 624, discussed in chapter 94; Vatican Codex 625, in the same place; and Vatican Codices 5763 and 5764, formerly belonging to the monastery of Bobbio, in chapter 98.

In Vatican Codex 5873 are interpolated Etymologies, arranged in a different order from the printed editions, but incomplete toward the end. See chapter 98.

In Royal Vatican Codex 61, discussed in chapter 99, several books of the Etymologies are excerpted here and there. In Royal Vatican Codex 84, in the same place, are other excerpts from the Etymologies. In Royal Vatican Codex 112, in the same place, is a beautiful copy of the Etymologies written at the beginning of the eleventh century. Another is in Royal Vatican Codex 137, in the same place, where Isidore is called “of Hispalis” at the beginning. Another occurs in Royal Vatican Codex 205, and another in 239, in the same place. [449] The final ten books are in Royal Vatican Codex 287, chapter 100.

The Etymologies, with the preliminary letters, incomplete at the end, are in Royal Vatican Codex 294, the same chapter, 109. The tenth book of the Etymologies is in Royal Vatican Codex 310, in the same place. The fifth book of the Etymologies of Isidore Junior is in Royal Vatican Codex 846, which also contains certain other fragments of the Etymologies written in ancient Tironian notes. Other fragments of the Etymologies are in Royal Vatican Codex 1048, chapter 101; others in Royal Vatican Codex 1315, in the same place; and in 1573, likewise. In Royal Vatican Codex 1824, chapter 101, are the twenty books of the Etymologies, but arranged differently from the printed editions and with many passages abridged.

In the same place, in Royal Vatican Codex 1850, is the work of the Etymologies, arranged differently from the printed copies and incomplete. In Royal Vatican Codex 1953, in the same place, is an old and beautiful copy of the twenty books of the Etymologies, with six letters identified as those of Isidore and Braulio.

In Palatine Codex 281, chapter 102, are the twenty books of the Etymologies, written in the eighth or ninth century and nearly corresponding to the printed editions. In the same place, in a Palatine Codex 281 of approximately the fourteenth century, stand: “Here begin the chapters in the book of the Etymologies of Isidore Junior, bishop of Seville.” There are twenty books, differing little from the printed copies.

In the same place, in Palatine Codex 283, of approximately the fourteenth century, stand: “The rubrics of the first book of Isidore’s Etymologies,” etc., together with the letters of Isidore and Braulio, who is sometimes indicated only by the letter B. The work is divided into twenty-two books and is addressed both to Braulio and to Sisebutus.

In Palatine Codex 1050, chapter 103, is a fragment from book V of the Etymologies, *On Divine and Human Laws*. In the same place are other fragments of the Etymologies in Palatine Codex 1357, and others in Palatine 1448.

In Urbinate Codex 100, chapter 104, the Etymologies are divided into twenty-two books, with a twenty-third book added, *On the Nature of Things*. In Urbinate 479, in the same place: “Isidore’s Etymologies. There are twenty books.” At the end: “Of Isidore Junior, bishop of Seville.”

In Ottobonian Codex 336, chapter 105, are the books of Isidore Junior, bishop of Seville, addressed to Braulio—or to Sisebutus. In Ottobonian 343, in the same place, the Etymologies are addressed to Sisebutus, not to Braulio. In Ottobonian 345, in the same place: “Etymologies. There are twenty books, but they differ in their titles; there are also certain old variant readings.” In Ottobonian 352 are the twenty books of the Etymologies addressed to Sisebutus, not to Braulio, in the same place. In Ottobonian 1100, in the same place, the Etymologies are divided into twenty-two books. In Ottobonian 427, in the same place, are twenty books of the Etymologies addressed to Sisebutus. In Ottobonian 477, in the same place, are twenty books of the Etymologies.

In Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive, discussed in chapter 107, the Etymologies are divided into twenty-five books. In Codex 2 of the same Archive, in the same place, are the Etymologies addressed either to Braulio or to Sisebutus. In the same chapter 107 I shall discuss the Albanian Codex of the Etymologies, in which much extraneous material has been mixed in, as well as the codices of the Angelica Library and of the Roman College.

33. Certain excerpts from the Etymologies, as Nicholas Antonius observes, are preserved in a codex of the Imperial Library, as may be read in book II, chapter 8, p. 934, of Peter Lambecius’s commentary on that library. We could add innumerable other examples of this kind.

Bandini, vol. IV of the *Latin Catalogue of the Laurentian Medicean Library*, indicates, from books formerly belonging to Santa Croce, pluteus 17, codex 10, of the eleventh century, an encomium of Saint Augustine from book X, chapter 6—or, in another numbering, book VII, chapter 6—of the Etymologies.

Isidore’s *Art of Rhetoric* occurs in the ancient rhetoricians of François Pithou, taken from book II of the Etymologies. A catalogue of heresies from book VIII of the Etymologies is repeated by Gratian in part II of the *Decree*, cause 24, question 3. It was also published by Hieronymus Gebuwler at Strasbourg in 1523, in quarto, together with Saint Augustine’s *On Faith and Works* and Saint Jerome’s works *Against Helvidius* and *Against Vigilantius*; and separately by Jean Quintin, J.C., at Paris in 1560, as Fabricius observes in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

In the old Lucchese codex that I described from Mansio in chapter 44 are excerpts on heresy and schism, and others from book VII, chapters 1, 2, and 3; from book VIII, chapters 1 and 2, on the Church and the Synagogue, etc. These two chapters are joined to the final chapter of book VII, as though the three chapters belonged to one and the same book.

A catalogue of heretics occurs in Vatican Codex 511; see chapter 93. Fragments on weights and measures occur in Urbinate 307, chapter 94. Other materials were indicated in the preceding number.

Fragments on the *Art of Rhetoric* and on grammar from the books of the Etymologies have also been published. On avoiding faults of speech, and on tropes and figures, see the Italian collection *Authors on Speaking Well*, part II, p. 237 onward, Venice, 1643. The book *On Rhetoric* is found in the appendix to *Authors of Rhetoric*, vol. II, after p. 30. The first part of the same book appears among the *Ancient Latin Rhetoricians* of Claudius Capperonnesius, Strasbourg, 1757, p. 387 onward. This is the art of rhetoric which, as I said, is found among the *Ancient Rhetoricians* of François Pithou, taken from book II of the Etymologies.

34. We reported further material on excerpts from Isidore’s books in chapter 33. In Vatican Codex 3906 and in another Vatican Codex, 4877, discussed in chapter 97, there is an excerpt from book XVI of the Etymologies, on weights and measures, etc. The same material occurs in Vatican Palatine Codex 1719 without the author’s name; appended to it is a chapter on how to compose a formal letter, as in Sirmond, at the end of vol. II of the *Gallican Councils*.

In Vatican Ottobonian Codex 56, a quarto parchment manuscript, there is Proba’s cento, preceded by Isidore’s words from the Etymologies, book I, chapter 39, on the nature of centos.

35. Among the ecclesiastical writers on sacred music edited by Martin Gerbert at the presses of Saint Blasien in 1784, vol. I, p. 19, are inserted Saint Isidore of Seville’s *Sentences on Music*. What these sentences are, Gerbert explains in the following notice, which he places before them:

> “In a thirteenth-century manuscript of the Imperial Library at Vienna, I found separately the following excerpts from book III of the Etymologies of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, under this title: ‘Here begin the Sentences of Bishop Isidore to Bishop Braulio on Music.’ We judged this heading should be retained, since, after comparing these excerpts with the printed editions, we thought them fit to be published with Cassiodorus; for later medieval writers on music frequently used the authority of both authors. Nor did we wish to separate the excerpt on Rhythmimachia, which is added immediately afterward in the aforementioned Viennese codex and which likewise concerns this subject, namely the calculation of musical numbers.”

Gerbert had observed in the preface to volume I that in Isidore’s time, at the beginning of the seventh century, theoretical music, together with practical music, had been flourishing increasingly, especially in Gaul.

The excerpt consists of nine chapters of Isidore’s material on music, beginning with chapter 15 and following of book III of the Etymologies. Gerbert records certain variant readings. The chapter he adds—namely, the excerpt on Rhythmimachia—may reasonably be placed among Isidore’s doubtful works, or among the fragments in appendix 5 to the Etymologies.

In the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under the entry “Berno,” Fabricius included a list of medieval Latin writers who dealt with music and ecclesiastical song; among them he lists Isidore, book III of the Etymologies, chapter 14, and so forth.

36. Nicholas Antonius reports, from various manuscript annotations of Alfonso Chacón preserved at Saint Isidore’s convent of the Irish Friars Minor, a certain commentary arranged according to the letters of the alphabet and covering the entire work of the Etymologies. This codex exists in the Vatican Library—Nicholas Antonius suspected it was no. 625—which I shall describe with its own features in chapter 94.

For now it is enough to observe that it is an old glossary compiled in full measure not only from the Etymologies but also from other works. Rodríguez, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 336 and following, failing to understand Nicholas Antonius’s meaning, asserted that the Vatican Library contained the alphabetical Etymologies themselves, copied in Alfonso Chacón’s hand.

The author of this, or of a similar, Alphabet is Jacobus Cina of Saint Andrew, of the Order of Preachers, who died in 1380. Apart from other writings of his, concerning which see Quétif, vol. I, p. 681, and Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, an *Alphabet of the Etymologies from Isidore of Seville addressed to Gregory XI* is preserved in the Bodleian Library.

The same Nicholas Antonius had read somewhere that Symphorianus Camperius had published another special commentary, or set of observations, on book IV of the Etymologies, which deals with medical matters.

37. It would serve no purpose to repeat Semler’s remarks on the notes of Bonaventura Vulcanius, Bignaeus, and Breutius, on Grialius’s most meticulous notes of all, and on other notes left unfinished. From a letter of the learned Andrea Gallandi to Zaccaria, dated 23 September 1758, I gather that the Venetian Library of the Fathers of the Oratory of Saint Philip Neri possesses a Breulian edition of Saint Isidore, adorned with certain manuscript notes and variant readings, partly also conjectures. At its beginning is written, apparently in the same hand as the notes: “Of Peter Thomas, John F., Simon N., John P., from the library.”

Gallandius considered some of these annotations valuable, but not others, since they are concerned with identifying the passages in the authors cited by Isidore.

38. In the Bignaean edition of Isidore preserved in the Vatican Library there are certain notes and variant readings on the books of the Etymologies which will be of some use to me. The rest of Isidore’s works lack observations of this kind. Sometimes a note is marked P., sometimes P. A., sometimes P. R. I am uncertain whether these letters refer to two codices of the Basilica of Saint Peter, the Ancient and the Recent, or to the name of some author.

39. Nicholas Antonius says that the following is worthy of notice: in a catalogue of Greek books belonging to Antonio Verderio, in the *Supplement to Gesner’s Library*, one finds listed an *Etymological Work of Isidore of Hispalis on Theology*. He thinks this must be understood as referring to that part in which theological origins are discussed.

“But of what use is it,” he says, “to teach Greeks Latin etymologies?” Yet has Nicholas Antonius forgotten himself? A little earlier he presented Isidore to us under that modest title, the Etymologies—not as one pursuing merely the derivations of words, but also as one demonstrating the origins of things themselves and laying the foundations of all the arts.

Indeed, in books VII and VIII, where Isidore discusses theological matters, he scarcely debates anything concerning the origins of Latin words. And besides, would it not be useful for a Greek wishing to learn Latin to investigate the etymologies of words, just as Latins who know Greek learn the origins of Greek words?

40. From Bayer I reported in chapter 48 a Spanish version of the Etymologies from the fourteenth century, concerning which Bayer professes to be treating elsewhere, at a place unknown to me. I think it is the same version that I described from Rodríguez in this chapter 55.

# CHAPTER LVI

## On the Books of Differences of Words and Things; whether Agraetius or someone else was the author of the *Synonyms*, or of the Differences of Words; and for what reasons errors formerly entered the titles of books

1. Ildefonsus called this work of Isidore the *Book of Differences*, while Braulio more precisely called it two books of Differences, in which, through subtle discrimination, he distinguished in meaning things that are expressed confusedly in ordinary usage. Nicholas Antonius observes that it is wrong to count three books; Bayer adds Grialius to those who do so. Bayer also thinks that Braulio made two books out of the single earlier book, according to the diversity of the things whose differences Isidore discusses; for Cellier, vol. XVII, no. 7, had already conjectured that the first two books in Isidore had originally been undivided.

2. Since, however, the order varies in descriptions of these books, we must first establish the place occupied by these three books in each edition.

Bignaeus published only two. He entitled the first *Book of Differences*; it concerns differences between things: “Between God and Lord,” etc. The second he entitled *Book II of Differences, or On the Property of Expressions*, without preserving alphabetical order: “Between to promise and to pledge,” etc. He also omitted the prologue, “Most of the ancients.”

John Grialius, together with this prologue, placed first a book entitled *Differences, or On the Property of Expressions*: “Between suitable and useful,” etc., preserving alphabetical order. After completing this first book, he added the following title: “The same book of Differences, or On the Property of Expressions, from the Paris edition,” namely, Bignaeus’s edition: “Between to pledge and to promise,” etc.

Therefore Grialius did not distinguish two supposedly different books, as Bayer claims; rather, he represented the same book in the different forms in which it had been edited by himself and by Bignaeus. Accordingly, he gave the following book the title: “The second book of Differences. Between God and Lord,” etc.—that is, the differences between things.

3. Breulius published the two books of Bignaeus’s edition, but in a different order: first, *On Differences, or the Property of Expressions*: “Between to pledge and to promise,” etc.; second, *On Spiritual Differences*—as he calls the differences between things, together with certain manuscripts: “Between God and Lord,” etc.

Later, when he came upon the Madrid edition, he added, near the end of p. 741, a book of Differences, or *On the Property of Expressions*, edited by Grialius in alphabetical order. Hence Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, when reviewing Isidore’s works from the Breulian edition, calls this a third book, which, he says, is much fuller than the first, arranged alphabetically, and enriched with learned notes from the Madrid edition of 1599.

This amounts to saying that the alphabetical book of Differences of Expressions edited by Grialius is fuller than the book of the same Differences of Words which Bignaeus called the second and Breulius the first book of Differences, without arranging it alphabetically.

4. Therefore Grialius should not be blamed for counting three books of Differences, nor should Bayer’s opinion be approved—that Braulio made two books out of the single earlier one. Although Ildefonsus calls it a book of Differences, he uses “book” in the sense of a codex, volume, or work.

In any event, the author himself must have distinguished two books: one is alphabetical and explains only differences of meaning between words; the other is principally concerned with explaining things and does not preserve alphabetical order, so that definitions may be understood—of God and Lord, of Trinity and unity, and so forth.

I would certainly not deny that Braulio’s words should rather be referred to the book of Differences of Expressions than to the other, concerning things: “In these,” he says, “he distinguished in meaning, through subtle discrimination, those things which are expressed confusedly in ordinary usage.”

But Braulio took from the prologue of the first book something that also agrees in part with the other book, as when Isidore explains the difference between *man* and *human being*, between *boy* and *infant*, between *mind* and *reason*, and so forth.

Dupin, vol. V of the *Bibliotheca Ecclesiastica*, stated that a treatise *On the Property of Words* had appeared separately at Madrid in 1529. But, unless I am mistaken, he was misled by the book *On the Property of Expressions* which Breulius extracted from the Madrid edition of all Isidore’s works, published in 1599.

I have indeed seen an edition mutilated at the beginning, containing the Differences of Things and of Expressions, as I said in chapter 54. But this edition, whether produced at Madrid or elsewhere, was entirely modeled on the Bignaean edition, including its marginal notes.

5. Many have observed that the book of Differences of Expressions—whether the fuller alphabetical version or the shorter unarranged version—was largely taken from Agraetius. Goldastus expressly noted this in his commentary on Valerianus’s *On the Benefit of Discipline*, p. 54, where he corrects the difference “between *herbosus* and *herbidus,” etc.

I observed in chapter 50 that very many similar little works on the differences and properties of the Latin language had been published by Vulcanius after Isidore’s Etymologies; these were also reprinted in Gothofred’s edition of the Latin authors.
