Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book IV, chapter 6, besides earlier writers on differences in the Latin language, lists the four books of Ausonius Popma on *The Differences of Latin Words* and the two books *On the Use of Ancient Expression*, reprinted with additions by Johann Friedrich Heckel at Leipzig in 1694, in octavo; and *Differences of the Latin Language*, collected and edited by Daniel Achrelius at Åbo in 1692, in octavo.

In Codex 624, which I shall describe in chapter 94, after the Etymologies there is a book of Differences of Words. It is neither clearly attributed to Isidore nor arranged alphabetically, nor does it begin with “Between to pledge,” etc., but with “Between fear,” etc., almost as in the already published little work to which we shall return below, *On Cicero’s Differences in Doubtful Matters*.

6. Which book of Differences of Words should be regarded as Isidore’s—the shorter one or the fuller alphabetical one—must be determined from ancient parchment manuscripts.

The shorter book, which begins “Between to pledge and to promise,” etc., was published after Gothofred’s Latin authors under the title: “Excerpts of Differences communicated by Jacques Bongars, royal ambassador, on the Property of Expressions or Things.”

The part of the title that mentions the property of things does not fit the book very well; it is more appropriate to book II, on differences between things.

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under Sigebert, chapter 55, notes that Sigebert wrongly called Isidore’s book of differences of words *On the Property of Things*. But Sigebert did not give that title to Isidore’s first book, but to the second; for he says: “He wrote a book on the Differences of Words and a book on the Property of Things.”

This is how it was printed in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca ecclesiastica*. Others report: “He also wrote two books on the Differences of Words, or on the Property of Things.” Here *or* may be taken as *and*, so that the sense is that the book on Differences of Words is distinct from the book on the Property of Things. In one codex, however, discussed in no. 8, the same book is called *On the Property of Expressions or Things*.

7. Of the two books on the Property of Expressions attributed to Isidore, the older may perhaps be considered the shorter one, which does not preserve alphabetical order. It is more likely that someone arranged and expanded a disorderly collection of verbal differences according to the alphabet than that he excerpted certain passages from a fuller, well-arranged book without any order at all.

Thus, if the correctly ordered book is said to be Isidore’s, the disordered and confused one must be allowed to be older. But why could Isidore himself not first have published differences of words without a fixed method, and then arranged and expanded the same material according to the letters of the alphabet?

From Isidore’s practice and that of other ancient authors, I regard as probable the view that some of their works appeared sometimes in shorter and sometimes in fuller forms, occasionally with certain alterations.

But when I compare these two commentaries with each other, I infer that they are rather the work of two different authors. For of the 253 differences contained in the shorter work, many are absent from the fuller one, though they would hardly have been omitted by someone wishing to enlarge the work. Accordingly, it cannot be determined which of these books was earlier in date.

8. A short commentary beginning “Between to pledge and to promise” occurs among Isidore’s other works in Royal Vatican Codex 310, dating approximately from the tenth century, after book X of the Etymologies and the book of Spiritual Differences, or Differences of Things. Its title is: “Here begins [the book] on the Property of Expressions or Things: Between to pledge,” etc.

Afterward stand the words: “Here begin Isidore’s Spiritual Differences.” At the end: “Here end Isidore’s Differences of Spiritual or Carnal Things.” Thus both books are attributed to Isidore.

In Ottobonian Codex 1261, discussed in chapter 106, the title of a similar work is: “The book of Marcus Tullius Cicero on the Differences of Words begins: Between to pledge,” etc. It ends: “Between *vesper* and *vespera*,” etc. The Isidorian book ends differently. For other similar manuscripts, compare numbers 10 and 19.

9. The fuller alphabetical book, beginning “Between suitable and useful,” etc., is attributed to Isidore by the very ancient Vatican Codex 3321, to be described in chapter 97, where it is called the work of Isidore Junior.

10. There are certain codices in which, without the author’s name, Isidorian or similar works on Differences of Words or on the Property of Expressions occur: Vatican 1471, discussed in chapter 96; Vatican 1558, in the same place; and Vatican 5120, discussed in chapter 97, where there is Isidore’s prologue, “Most of the ancients,” together with differences arranged in an order different from the printed editions and not alphabetically.

The same is true of Vatican 5134, in the same place, where there are two anonymous copies of the Differences: one arranged alphabetically and the other not. The same is true in Vatican 5203, in the same place.

11. I discussed the Malatesta Codex of the Differences of Expressions in chapter 45. Bayer testifies that many codices of Isidore’s Differences, or *On the Property of Expressions*, exist in the Royal Library of the Escorial, but he does not describe their contents.

Barthius, *Adversaria*, book XXXIX, chapter 6, writes:

> “I once purchased a manuscript of Isidore’s Differences, and I remember having already offered something from it. Its preface is as follows: ‘Most of the ancients,’ etc. This is the preface which, since it is Latin and elegant, while the little book itself contains very much that is foolish, I think suffered the fate that has befallen most works of this class, namely, that it is stuffed with the dreams of the monks who copied it. We shall note a few selected passages.”

The same Barthius, book XXXIX, chapter 14, calls his copy of Isidore *On the Property of Expressions* a very ancient parchment manuscript. He observes that this commentary contains not a few passages taken either from Cato, as the preface indicates, or from other eminent writers of antiquity, and that for this reason they should be rescued from the tyranny of the bookworms.

Barthius had considered publishing and illustrating the entire book, as he explains in book XXXII, chapter 1:

> “I intend at some point to publish and purge a manuscript commentary of Isidore, which is entitled *DIFFERENCES* on parchment, so that, if anyone can derive some benefit or pleasure from it, our work may be useful to them.”

He concludes the chapter as follows:

> “I wished to present here these passages worthy of notice, omitting many more foolish ones. The commentary itself is not insignificant in size, since the scribes inserted into it almost whatever they pleased, according to their whim.”

12. Nevertheless, Nicholas Antonius replies, if Barthius had seen the Madrid edition, he could have found sound and complete many of the passages that he intended to heal or supplement because they appeared defective or mutilated in his codex. It is generally a considerable undertaking to exercise one’s ingenuity on books of poor quality—or rather, to attempt to exhaust oneself in doing so.

Barthius should indeed be forgiven in this respect, since he had conjectured many such things in his *Adversaria* before Isidore’s works had been published at Madrid or could have reached him.

Even in our own century one may see certain scholars who, ignorant of or forgetful of the old Madrid edition, strive with immense labor and the greatest effort to restore various passages of Isidore that are corrupt in other editions, and at length scarcely do anything more than repeat work already completed.

### 13.

Since, however, certain books circulate under the titles *On the Proper Use of Language*, *On the Distinction of Words*, *Synonyms*, or some other title—some attributed to Cicero Victurius, some to Agroetius, while elsewhere they are also said to belong to Isidore—this controversy must likewise be examined by us.

I saw a book with this title: “The *Synonyms of Cicero Victurius*, most eloquent rhetorician, together with the *Synonyms of Stephanus Fliscus*, and also the *Differences* of that same Cicero Victurius and of Bartholomaeus Fatius. Golden little works, newly revised, corrected, enlarged, etc. Venice, at the press of Dominicus Nicolinus, 1564, octavo.”

The prologue runs as follows:

“Cicero Victurius greets the reader. I have collected those words which could be expressed in several ways, etc. Therefore let us begin in alphabetical order: *abditum*, hidden; *opertum*, covered; *obscurum*, obscure; *obumbratum*, overshadowed; etc.”

It ends: “*Videtur, apparet, lucet, exstat*: it is seen, it appears, it shines, it is manifest.”

This is followed by Cicero’s *Differences in Matters of Doubt*:

“Between *metus*, fear; *timor*, dread; and *pavor*, terror, there is this difference: *metus* looks ahead to future events; *timor* is a sudden consternation of the mind; *pavor* is fear of the spirit.”

A little later:

“*Pollicemur ultro, promittimus rogati*: we offer voluntarily, we promise when asked.”

It ends:

“*Nefarius* is understood from things already past; *nefandus* refers to one who was the beginning in the deed.”

### 14.

Fatius’s little work begins: “Between *ignavum* and *pigrum*,” followed by Fliscus’s *Synonyms arranged by classes*, beginning with “Prudence,” etc. Fliscus was writing at Venice in the year 1456.

In the same century, among the Spaniards, Alfonsus Palentinus composed three books of *Synonyms*, as reported by Nicolaus Antonius. Raymundus Diosdado, in his excellent work *On the First Age of Printing in Spain*, p. 34, listed the work *Synonyms of Lord Alfonsus Palentinus, historiographer*, printed at Seville by Meinardus Ungut of Germany and Ladislaus the Pole, partners, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1491, on 24 November.

On p. 87, after Maittaire and Nicolaus Antonius, he described *Differences of Words*, excerpted from Laurentius Valla, Nonius, Marcellus, and Servius, by the excerptor Antonius Nebrissensis.

Victurius’s *Synonyms and Differences* appeared together with Fatius’s little work at Venice in 1507, and without it in 1552.

I see the following listed in the Casanatense Library: *Vetruvius Cicero: Synonyms together with Differences in Matters of Doubt*, Milan, 1508, quarto.

Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book I, chapter 8, no. 8, reports *The Synonyms of Cicero Victurius*, published at Venice in 1587, octavo, and in 1515, quarto; the same work was first printed under Cicero’s name at Padua in 1482, quarto, by Matthaeus Cerdonis, and then without place of publication in 1483, quarto, under the title *On the Properties of Terms*.

He had at hand the Augsburg edition of 1488, bearing the title *Cicero’s On the Properties of Terms*. It begins:

“Between *polliceri*, to offer, and *promittere*, to promise, there is this difference: we promise when asked, but we offer voluntarily.”

This is the beginning of Isidore’s book *On the Proper Use of Language*, as published by Bignaeus and others.

### 15.

Fabricius had also seen another edition at Paris, at the press of Ascensius, without a date, prefaced by a letter:

“Cicero greets Lucius Venturius. I have collected those things which could be called synonyms in many ways, etc.”

In this edition the beginning of the work is omitted; it merely observes that, in Erasmus’s judgment, this book of *Synonyms* is a disorderly collection of not very many words, made somehow by one of Cicero’s students from his writings.

### 16.

In Vatican Codex 2930, discussed in chapter 96, among the manuscripts there is an old edition of Cicero’s *Synonyms*, with a prologue addressed to Vetur(i)us:

“I have collected, etc. *Abditum, opertum*, hidden, covered, etc.”

It ends:

“*Vela tetendit, moratur, opperitur, cunctatur, praestolatur, exspectat*: he spread the sails, lingers, waits, delays, awaits, expects.”

This is followed by *Cicero’s Differences in Matters of Doubt*:

“Between *metus*, *timor*, and *pavor*, etc.”

It ends:

“*Nefarius* is understood from things already past; *nefandus*, from one who was the beginning in the deed. The end.”

Then follow the *Differences of Bartholomaeus Fatius*, together with a letter from him to Joannes Jacobus, in which he says that he had also written *Synonyms*, but asserts that greater usefulness and benefit lie in recognizing *Differences*.

The letter begins:

“I remember, Joannes Jacobe, etc.”

The *Differences* begin:

“Between *ignavum* and *pigrum*.”

The final difference is:

“Between *latria* and *dulia*. *Latria* is the celebration or veneration owed to the saints and angels and to divine worship. *Dulia* is the worship owed to God alone.”

This is mistaken, for the matter is the reverse. *Latria* is the worship offered to God because of his uncreated and infinite excellence; *dulia* is the worship rendered to the saints because of their created supernatural excellence.

### 17.

There follows Fatius’s *Synonyms*, as can be inferred from the letter prefixed to the *Differences*. They begin:

“*Abesse, distare, remotum esse*: to be absent, to be distant, to be removed.”

They end:

“*Videtur, apparet, elucet, exstat*: it is seen, appears, shines forth, is manifest.”

Printed at Rome by the honorable Master Eucharius Silber, otherwise called Franck, in the year of the Lord 1490, on 3 October.

The following notice is added, which I have thought should be appended here.

### 18.

“Paulus Alexius Sulpitianus sends greetings to the reader.

You now have, boy, two most useful books on abundance and elegance of expression. If anything in them seems, according to the judgment of your proper teacher, worthy of disapproval, mark it with a dog’s-letter; if anything is corrupt, correct it; if anything seems to require addition, mark it in the margin, so that it may be clear that it belongs neither to Cicero nor to Fatius.

Although we certainly cannot determine whether these *Synonyms* that circulate were collected by Cicero, nevertheless the title found in ancient manuscripts, and Cicero’s youth—in which he also published rhetorical works unworthy of a mature age—provide a strong argument, so that I would not dare deny that they belong either to him or to one of the Ciceros. Farewell.”

This edition escaped the painstaking attention of the most learned Father Audiffredi in his examination of fifteenth-century Roman editions.

### 19.

In Royal-Vatican Codex 215, written in the ninth century, the work is entitled on p. 52:

“Cicero’s *Synonyms*. Cicero greets his Vetur(i)us. I have collected those things which could be expressed in many ways and which correspond in several meanings, beginning alphabetically: *abditum, opertum, absconsum*, hidden, covered, concealed, etc.”

It ends:

“*Vitare, declinare, cavere, subterfugere*: to avoid, turn aside, beware, escape.”

Vatican Codex 6265, discussed in chapter 98, is similar.

Codex Ottobonianus 604, discussed in chapter 106, ends differently; it contains *The Synonyms of Marcus Tullius Cicero*. “Cicero to Lucius Vecturius,” etc.

The ending in Ottobonianus 2992, discussed in the same chapter 106, is also different. See above, no. 8, concerning Ottobonianus 1261.

Pezius, in the preface to the *Anecdota*, vol. I, no. 65, mentions a parchment codex in folio, at least eight hundred years old, entitled *Cicero’s Book of Synonyms*. It begins:

“Cicero greets his Vetur(i)us. I have collected those things…”

Ambrosius Camaldulensis reports the following concerning a certain Lucius, in his letters preserved by Martenius in the *Thesaurus anecdotorum*, vol. II, col. 447:

“He transcribed and carried away with him a certain little work distinguished by Cicero’s name; but in my judgment it is not his. It contains first synonyms and then differences of words.”

It is therefore established that the little works attributed in many editions to Victurius, or to Cicero Victurius or Vetur(i)us, are found in the oldest parchment manuscripts under the name of Cicero addressed to Vetur(i)us. This may be confirmed by the wording of many codices in the preface to Isidore’s *Soliloquies*, or *Synonyms*:

“Recently a certain sheet of Cicero came into my hands, which they call *Synonyms…”

Some omit “of Cicero.”

### 20.

The work in Vatican Codex 6018, dating approximately from the tenth century, is nevertheless different from the printed editions. It is entitled:

“*The Distinction of Words. Cicero’s Synonyms*.”

It begins:

“*Tenebo, possidebo, obtinebo*: I shall hold, possess, obtain, etc.”

It ends:

“*Persecutor, emissarius, praedo*: persecutor, emissary, plunderer.”

We may suspect, not without some basis for conjecture, that it belongs to Isidore. For after the work, in the same codex, there is a work entitled *Glosses of Saint Isidore the Bishop on the Distinction of Words*, and before the Isidorian *Chronicle*.

The title *Glosses on the Distinction of Words* seems to comprise not only the immediately preceding little work—which is an alphabetical index of the orthography of certain words, together with chapter 21 of the *Etymologies*—but also this other work appended directly afterward:

“Here begins *The Distinction of Words: Cicero’s Synonyms*.”

These words seem to indicate that Cicero was not the compiler of those *Synonyms*, but that the synonymous words were extracted from Cicero’s works.

### 21.

But here we enter upon another question. After the title I mentioned, in Vatican Codex 6018, *Glosses of Saint Isidore the Bishop on the Distinction of Words*, the work begins as follows:

“*Acrocius* is written with *c* and *o*, not with *y*, as some think. ‘I go to him’ and ‘he came to me’ must be written with *d*.”

It should, however, be read *Agroetius*, with *o* and *e*, not with *y*, as some think. This is almost the beginning of the book published among the grammarians of Putsch, under the name of Agroetius; namely, *Agroetius* must be written with the Latin diphthong *ae* when one writes in Latin, not, as some think, *Agrytius* with *y*.

The title is *Agroetius on Orthography, the Proper Use of Language, and Difference of Language*.

“Agroetius to Lord Eucherius the Bishop. You sent me Caprus’s little book on orthography, etc.”

Without this preface the work exists in Vatican Codex 1491, discussed in chapter 96.

In Urbinate Codex 308, discussed in chapter 104, there is, without a title for the work, a dedicatory letter:

“To my lord Eucherius the Bishop, Agretius sends greetings. You sent me Caprus’s little book, etc.”

Which book, then, should be considered the earlier: the one attributed to Isidore, or the one attributed to Agroetius?

### 22.

The answer would be easy if it were established that the grammarian Agroetius flourished in the middle of the fifth century and supplemented Caprus’s *Orthography*, as Fabricius asserts in his *Bibliotheca mediae*. In the *Bibliotheca vetus*, to which he refers us, however, he makes no assertion about Agroetius’s date; he merely says that his work first appeared through Vulcanius’s efforts in an edition of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, and was later revised from the Bongarsian manuscript among Putsch’s grammarians.

I scarcely find any mention of an Agroetius, except that Sidonius wrote a letter to Pope Agroecius in book VII, letter 5. Perhaps this is the Agroetius of the fifth-century grammarian meant by Fabricius.

I would nevertheless like this to be confirmed from another source, especially since I find it easier to believe that the author’s name was fabricated from the first word of his book than that some author wished to begin a book by prescribing the orthography of his own name.

We also have a bishop of Barcelona named Agricius, who signed the Council of Tarragona in 516 and the Council of Gerunda in 517. This name could be related to the first word of the little book, since some called him *Agroetius* or *Agroecius*, while others called him *Agrycius* or *Agricius*. But, as I was suggesting, I have another thought.

### 23.

It has happened more than once that ancient scribes fabricated an author’s name from the opening words of an anonymous work or title.

Ludovicus Vives, *On the Corruption of the Disciplines*, book I, says:

“There were those who, in order to lend a book authority, attached to it the name of a great author. Others, when many anonymous books were once being published, assigned them to this or that author on the basis of some very slight conjecture. Others, if they did not recognize the name in the title, did not hesitate to alter it and transfer it to whomever they pleased. There were copyists who placed as the title whatever name first came to mind.”

I observed something similar in a note on Prudentius’s *Dittochaeum*: certain verses by an anonymous poet, who in ancient parchment manuscripts is described as *facet(us)* (“witty”), were later attributed to a poet named Facetus; likewise Prudentius himself was called *Amoenus*—indeed, “the poet Amoenus,” distinguished somewhere from Prudentius—because in old manuscripts verses are prefixed to the *Dittochaeum*, the first of which is:

“Here begin the titles of the pleasant manual book.”

Since Prudentius’s name was absent, some scribes thought that the author was a certain poet named Amaenus and that the title of the book was *The Manual Book*, or *Enchiridion*. The true author of those verses, who wished to praise the *Dittochaeum*, called the book “the pleasant manual.”

### 24.

In my *Prudentiana*, p. 44, I had also observed that the work itself, appropriately called *Dittochaeum*—that is, “double nourishment”—in the oldest copies is called in some more recent ones *On the Doves*, or *On the Dove*, for no other reason than that its first verse begins:

“Eve was a dove.”

Nevertheless the most learned Bayerius was deceived. In a note on book VIII, chapter 8, no. 283, of his *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, among other writers whom he refers, though hesitantly, to the thirteenth century, he listed the Spanish writer “Prudentius Columba,” who is none other than our sacred poet Prudentius of the fourth and fifth centuries.

“Just as hesitantly as I refer Manfredus to this period, so too I refer Joannes de Valentia, etc. Likewise Prudentius Columba—at Limoges, *Prudens Coloma*—of Valencia or Catalonia, whose various four-line epigrams are extant: on Adam and Eve, the Flood, the Ark, Abraham, Joseph the Chaste, Moses, Samson, David, and the ancient Fathers up to the coming of Christ. In the Escorial, shelf-mark S, shelf 3, no. 16, and at Monte Cassino in Montfaucon’s *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum*, p. 202, shelf-mark A.”

You can see that this is precisely Aurelius Clemens Prudentius’s *Dittochaeum*.

I am even more surprised that, in the same note, Bayerius wished to assign Joannes Davila de Roa, a famous seventeenth-century writer and one by no means cursorily mentioned by Nicolaus Antonius in the *Bibliotheca nova*, to the thirteenth century or the beginning of the following one.

“And finally,” he says, “to omit others who seem to have produced some works toward the end of this thirteenth century or at the beginning of the next, Joannes Davila de Roa, prior of Saint John of Chavero, Canon Regular of Saint Augustine, whose treatise *On the Personal Preaching of the Apostle Saint James in Spain* is preserved in the Vatican in the codex of Queen Christina of Sweden, no. 472.”

Not only this commentary but also many other manuscripts of this recent writer are preserved in the Vatican Library.

### 25.

But, to return to the point from which I digressed for a while: from the beginning of Isidore’s book *Glosses on the Distinction of Words*, the name of the writer Agroetius could have been fabricated.

The title of a comedy by Plautus, now lost, was *Agroicus*, that is, “rustic” or “country-dwelling.” Nonius cites it in chapter 3, no. 43, where some read less correctly *Abroico* or *Ambroico* in Plautus.

It ought to be written in Latin letters *Agroecus*, not *Agrycus*, as some thought, perhaps deceived by the pronunciation.

The author of the glosses had perhaps read this observation in some scholiast on Plautus and wished to begin from it his *Distinctions of Words*, which he was arranging in alphabetical order.

Whether, then, the Isidorian book was later or earlier than the other work attributed to Agroetius, we must equally conjecture that some scribe gave the anonymous work its name from the first word.

Someone else then easily added a prologue in the name of Agroetius to Eucherius, just as in similar commentaries a prologue by Cicero to Vetur(i)us is read.

Moreover, Didacus Rodriguez de Almella, in a work entitled *Valerio de las historias escolásticas*, which is elsewhere incorrectly attributed to Ferdinand Perez de Guzman, book VIII, title 6, chapter 6, relates that Isidore had dedicated a work entitled *The Book of Differences* to Fulgentius, Bishop and his brother. I have not, however, been able to find this in the copies of these books that I examined.

### 26.

Now concerning Pantinus, who revised and illustrated the *Differences of Words* in the Madrid edition—that is, the alphabetical book *On the Proper Use of Language*—you may read Grialius’s preface above, chapter 36.

I presented, in chapter 53, from Barthius, a catalogue of the authors whom Isidore cites in his book *Differences of Words*, or *On the Proper Use of Language*.

In the more recent Royal-Vatican Codex 1838 there is another book of Isidore’s *Differences*, beginning differently from the others:

“Between *abundare*, to abound, and *superfluere*, to overflow, there is this difference: a wave abounds, moisture overflows.”

It ends:

“Between *vesper*, *vespera*, *vespere*, and *vesperum* there is this difference: *vesper* and *vespere* are nouns of the third declension, whereas *vespera* is feminine of the second declension, and *vesperum* is neuter and of the second declension.”

It is occasionally marked:

“The *Differences* of the most distinguished Hesidorus.”

I shall discuss this codex again in chapter 101.

### 27.

We must deal more briefly with *The Differences of Things*.

This book was sometimes cited by the ancients simply under the name *Differences*. Thus Aeneas, Bishop of Paris, cites Isidore in his work against the Greeks, vol. VII of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, as having written in the book *Differences*, with words taken from book III of *The Differences of Things*.

In Royal-Vatican Codex 310, as I noted shortly before, the entire work is entitled *On the Proper Use of Words or Things*. After the first book, beginning “Between *polliceri*,” etc., a new title is added:

“Here begin the *Spiritual Differences* of Isidore, Bishop of Seville the Younger, between God, etc.”

At the end:

“Here end the *Differences of Spiritual or Carnal Things* of Isidore.”

The *Differences of Words* are therefore called carnal, and those of things spiritual, because the latter contain a greater number of passages concerning spiritual matters.

You can observe a similar title in chapter 46, in a certain codex of the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*.

### 28.

*The Differences of Things* are cited in an unusual way at the Fifteenth Council of Toledo. A statement is praised there which Isidore discussed in his books *On the Difference between Christ’s Nature and Ours*.

The words are taken from Difference 8 in Grialius and 6 in Breulius:

“Between Christ’s birth and ours there is this difference.”

Perhaps, however, at the Council of Toledo one ought to read: “On the Difference of Christ’s Birth, or of ours.”

Certainly Royal-Vatican Codex 1823, Lombardic or Gothic, as it is called, written in a corded script, contains, after several other works of Isidore, *The Differences of Things*, without a title, but beginning as follows:

“Between Christ’s birth and ours there is this difference.”

This book of *Differences* is shorter than the printed editions.

### 29.

Rolandus Vicelius corrected and furnished notes on the Madrid edition of *The Differences of Things*, as Grialius explained in the preface above, chapter 36.

I reviewed the codices of this work consulted for Zaccaria’s edition in chapter 45.

I shall also publish, among the doubtful works, from ancient parchment manuscripts, a certain little work *On the Difference between the Active and Contemplative Life*, which perhaps belongs to *The Differences of Things*.

### 30.

Here we must recall that, according to Burriel’s letter in chapter 40, a copy of the books of *The Differences*, revised by Mariana against several manuscript codices, was preserved in the Jesuit college at Toledo until Burriel’s time. He accurately recorded their various readings in the margin.

This copy deserves to be held in high esteem, since it was not used to correct Grialius’s edition.

### 31.

Certain excerpts from *The Differences of Things*, without any title, are extant in Royal-Vatican Codex 1823, discussed in chapter 101.

In Urbinate Codex 100, discussed in chapter 104, *The Book of Differences of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville*, begins:

“Between God and Lord, etc.”

The *Differences of Words* are absent from this codex.

In Urbinate Codex 1504, also discussed in chapter 104, there is *The Book of Differences of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Spain*:

“Between God, etc.”

The *Differences of Words* are absent.

In Ottobonianus 240, dating approximately from the twelfth century and discussed in chapter 105, there are only *The Differences of Things*, under this distinctive title:

“Isidore on the Differences of the Catholic Faith.”

### 32.

I believe that Joannes Baptista Marus mistakenly attributes Isidore’s *Differences* to the presbyter Auxilius, in a note on the book of Peter the Deacon’s *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 13.

There he reports that Authpert, abbot of Monte Cassino, bequeathed his library to the Cassinese monks from the year 834 onward, and that among the other books was “the *Etymologicon* of the presbyter Auxilius,” on shelf 5 to the left, codex 29; and, at no. 30 in the same place, various theological works by the same Auxilius, namely *Questions on the Hexaemeron*, and “chapter 36 of the *Differences*, on the distinction of the four virtues.”

Isidore’s *Differences* are usually divided into the same number of chapters, the last of which concerns the four virtues.

Perhaps that *Etymologicon* and the *Questions on the Hexaemeron* also belong to Isidore, although they formerly came under the ownership of the presbyter Auxilius. The name of the possessor has often deprived the author of the glory of his books.

The only known books of the presbyter Auxilius are two works *On Ordinations Performed by Formosus*, which Joannes Morinus brought to public light at the end of his work *On Sacred Ordinations*.

# CHAPTER LVII. On the Glossaries Circulating under Isidore’s Name. Ludovicus de la Cerda’s Prologue and Epilogue. Prologue to Barthius’s and Others’ Notes

### 1.

Barthius’s opinion, in book XVI, chapter 24, of his *Adversaria*, is that the glossary circulating under the name of Isidore, a teacher by no means uncultivated, is entirely necessary in order to clarify obscure or erroneous passages in many ancient writers.

He adds, however, that scarcely anyone except a person thoroughly skilled in the German language could explain it, since among what people do Gothic words survive together with the arrangement of their phrases, darkened by Latin usage?

Again, in book X, chapter 22:

“Whenever you examine closely the glosses contained under Isidore’s name, you learn many things each time—things less accessible elsewhere or things that would be sought in vain. It is a good work to make them as clear as possible.”

In book XXVI, chapter 14, he likewise calls it “the glossary of Isidore the Younger,” in which, he says, “many things are excellent, many are ludicrously corrupt, and nothing should be neglected by those who devote themselves especially to understanding declining Latin.”

Elsewhere, and especially in book XXXI, chapter 4, he asserts that such glosses belong to Isidore, “although they were enlarged by successive teachers until they reached the bundle, now full of good things, that we possess.”

More explicitly, in book LV, chapter 9:

“Countless such things can be noted in those glosses that are commonly attributed to Isidore. I, however, suppose that something of this kind was first instituted by him and then, as time passed, enlarged by other grammarians, so that countless additions were made which can in no way now be cited under his name.

“When I say ‘Isidore,’ I do not immediately mean the one person known exclusively and alone to those who have no concern for others, provided that they know what they cannot fail to know. Yet what prevents us from believing that such a writer also devised something of this kind—the same writer who gave us the *Origins* and those commentaries on the *Differences*—so that such labor should by no means be considered ignoble even if he himself were its author?

“We know, nevertheless, that after him others of the same name were active in the same places as he was; elsewhere I have discussed other Isidores, themselves famous in letters, each according to the capacity of his own age.”

### 2.

I explained the controversy concerning the various Spanish Isidores in chapter 16.

Nicolaus Antonius has a similar opinion concerning the author of the glossary: he thinks that the glosses are a compilation by several people, made neither once nor all at one time, though some part of it belongs to Isidore of Seville—that is, the first elements of the work, and what was most anciently inserted into the book and laid a foundation for later additions.

The opinion of Ludovicus de la Cerda was no different. In chapter 141 of his *Sacred Adversaria*, he illustrated Isidore’s *Glossary* with learned observations, prefacing it with a short notice to the *Glossary* and another to the notes that I shall now append.

### 3.

“It is my pleasure to transcribe a large part of Saint Isidore’s *Glossary*, which has been very badly deformed. Here I shall append only those entries that present particular difficulty and may be relevant to further investigations.

“Moreover, since Isidore is most holy, he properly belongs in these *Adversaria*. This glossary, which circulates under Isidore’s name, is not found among his books.

“Finally, and most importantly, I shall correct this glossary by bringing together the notes of the most learned men—Turnebus, Scaliger, Salmasius, Rutgersius, Gebhardus, and nearly countless others—which exist in Isidore’s interest, together with not a few of my own.

“For this purpose it is necessary to place the glossary first.”

### 4.

Here is his prologue to the notes on the glossary:

“I have completed the *Glossary*. It is now fitting to proceed to its correction, in which I shall ensure that I either correct or illustrate this glossary, which many reject as worthless, although the opposite is true. In it the profound learning of Isidore, a most holy man, shines forth; he excelled not only in divine but also in human literature.

“I shall also often bring forward Isidore’s manuscript glossary, which belonged to Peter and Francis Pithoeus. Thus you will quite often not encounter in this glossary the words that I shall discuss; I mention this from time to time.”

### 5.

I shall add his epilogue:

“These things I have thought worth noting in Isidore’s glosses, if I can succeed in giving them authority. I care nothing about the remainder, which has been deformed. For I believe that the additions were made by ignorant people, and that no learned person would approve them.

“Who would approve *coso* (‘I sew’) for *insuo* (‘I sew in’), *cordiscosio* for *agnosco* (‘I recognize’), *aequoro* (‘I sail’) for *navigo* (‘I sail’), *gignarus* (‘knowing’) for *ignarus* (‘ignorant’), *matrasta* (‘stepmother’) for *noverca* (‘stepmother’), *tius* for *avunculus* (‘maternal uncle’), *torno* (‘I return’) for *redeo* (‘I return’), and similar forms, which are truly foolish and contribute nothing to Isidore’s glory?”

### 6.

When Cerda prefaced his work by saying that Isidore’s *Glossary* is not found among his books, I think he meant the Paris edition of Bignaeus and the royal Madrid edition.

For in the Paris edition of Breulius, it was appended to the end of the works, apparently from the edition of Dionysius Gothofredus, after the Latin grammarians, Geneva, 1595; that edition was reprinted in 1602 and 1622.

The title is:

“*The Book of Glosses, collected from various glossaries circulating under Isidore’s name*.”

Gothofredus adds:

“Pithoean excerpts from ancient glosses.”

### 7.

Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book IV, chapter 6, section II, no. 13, observes that the *Book of Glosses*, taken from various Isidorian glossaries, was published together with other Greek-Latin and Latin-Greek glossaries by Bonaventura Vulcanius in 1600.

Among others who illustrated this glossary with observations, he lists Meursius in his *Critical Exercises*, Vossius in his *Etymological Dictionary*, and Cangius in his *Dictionary*.

He also observes, on the authority of Joannes Diecmannus, that the manuscript glosses of Isidore are plainly different and more worthy than the author whom the printed copies put forward. Savaro used those received from the library of Peter and Francis Pithoeus and transferred not a few of them into his notes on Sidonius Apollinaris.

### 8.

In volume III of the *Acts of the Latin Society of Jena*, published at Jena in 1754, p. 252, there are inserted *Notes and Corrections to Isidore’s Glosses*, collected and published from the manuscripts of Barthius, Schurzfleischius, and Daumius by Joannes Ernestus Immanuel Walchius, director of the society.

The prologue is as follows:

“In the very well-furnished library of the most serene Duke of Weimar there is preserved an edition of the Greek-Latin and Latin-Greek glossaries which Bonaventura Vulcanius first published at Leiden in 1600.

“After I asked the most learned librarian, J. C. Bartholomaeus, about several matters concerning these observations of Barthius and Schurzfleischius which seemed relevant for me to know, the most courteous man replied that Barthius had annotated his corrections in Bonaventura Vulcanius’s *Thesaurus of Both Languages*, first published at Leiden in 1600.

“After Barthius’s death, this copy came into the hands of Christian Friedrich Franckenstein, a professor at Leipzig, who added Daumian observations to the Barthian ones; these had been found in another copy of the same book.

“When Franckenstein died, the book passed into Schurtzfleischius’s library, then into that of his brother, and finally into the ducal library at Weimar.

“Conrad Samuel Schurtzfleischius also wrote many things concerning Carolus Labbe’s edition of the glossaries, by which several of the more difficult passages of these glosses might be restored to their original soundness.

“His brother, Henricus Leonardus, wished to publish these observations of Schurtzfleischius together with the Barthian observations, to add those of Bersmannus and Daumius, and to title the work:

“*The Observations and Glossaries of Caspar Barthius and Conrad Samuel Schurtzfleischius: Isidore’s Glosses, School Dialogues, and Other Glossographical Writings. With Certain Observations of Gregorius Bersmannus and Christian Daumius. All Now Published for the First Time from the Manuscripts of Heinrich Leonhard Schurtzfleischius.*

“For various reasons, however, this praiseworthy plan was frustrated.

“Those observations that came from Bersmannus were marked by Conrad Samuel Schurtzfleischius with the letter B in his copy. His brother Heinrich Leonhard suspected that he had also used another codex of Stephanus Le Moyne, from the following words of his found in the said glossaries:

“‘*Hercularis turba*: read *Hercularis herba*, or *porcularis faba*. Thus Stephanus Le Moyne corrected it. So it appears in the excerpts. *Erculus*, Ἡρακλῆς, is read.’

“It is clear from this at the same time that I have now given only part of these observations and that I shall give more of them later, if I discover that my plan has not displeased lovers of these studies.”

In the copy of the book, many extremely useful annotations by the most distinguished men Caspar Barthius and Conrad Samuel Schurzfleischius, as well as some by Daumius, are found beside those glosses collected from various glossaries circulating under Isidore’s name.

They were either entirely omitted or insufficiently explained by those who corrected and illustrated these glosses.

Among those, besides the aforementioned Graevius and Almeloveen, are Joannes Ludovicus de la Cerda, *Sacred Adversaria*, chapter 141; Adrianus Turnebus and Barthius themselves in their *Adversaria*; Thomas Reinesius in his various readings; Joannes Meursius in his *Critical Exercises*; Carolus du Fresne in his *Glossary of Medieval and Low Latin*; and others listed by Fabricius in the place cited.

I therefore thought I would perform a useful service if I brought into public view the learned observations of these three men on that glossary, which had been kindly communicated to me.

Those marked with an asterisk belong to Barthius; those marked with the letter D belong to Daumius; the remainder belong to Schurzfleischius.

# CHAPTER LVIII. Semler’s Preface to the Manuscript Notes on the Isidorian Glossary

### 1.

It has already been observed in chapter 45 that Semler sent his notes on Isidore’s *Glossary* to be published by the Marquis Scipione Maffei. It will by no means be superfluous to present his preface here.

**To the reader.**
2. My work, whatever its worth, now appears through the benevolent assistance of the most celebrated and illustrious Marquis Scipione Maffei [Note: [Col. 0369B] I may regard it as an honor that I have been fortunate enough to enjoy a certain literary exchange, which the most celebrated Bosius of Wittenberg, a professor fully worthy of this age of learning, obtained for me from the Marquis Maffei, whom he honorifically praised. He is an entirely excellent man, devoted to every kind of generous goodwill. For as regards this very excellent man, for whom it was no safe matter, indeed almost a dangerous one, to find supporters of his virtue and learning in Italy among the purple, and to win the favor of the supreme and most holy pontiff: no one should wonder or be afraid, since envy usually stands as far as possible from outstanding virtue. Certainly many very distinguished men could be brought into a similar danger, men who conduct themselves in this light of learning as they ought. Indeed, even if this kind of offense cannot be removed—if you please, let the charge of discourtesy fall upon others, or upon many others, because they do not live at Wittenberg, where alone it is incurred—nevertheless so many good and highly deserving men are involved in this cause that, if they are deprived of fire and water in the republic of letters, we and posterity must do without that remarkable benefit which they have learned to gather from their most humane intercourse, worthy of Christian men, with all foreigners; and much must also be taken away from the praise of their virtues and learning. I shall hope for better things, nor shall I fear this outcome, even if it should happen not only to become known to many sensible and outstanding men of other sacred orders [Col. 0369D], but also to be kissed, as a mark of honor, by Benedict, the supreme pontiff of sacred matters, most worthy both of that see and of our own age. But if I were to praise the illustrious Maffei even in a word, I know that the republic of letters—which, because of his merits, will transmit this name among the best to posterity—would resent it.], who here performs the office of Lucina, a brief Glossary commonly distinguished by the name of ISIDORE. It is endowed with such utility that it has the less need of my praise, since the usual rule of most similar little books and lexicons [Note: [Col. 0369D] I do not think it worth the trouble to copy out the honorable judgments of learned men concerning Greek and Latin glossaries. Some have commended them at greater length; most, by diligently consulting and citing them, have always praised them highly. They preserve, as it were, monuments of earlier times; they aid the study of languages; they teach or indicate the diversity of opinions and words; they illuminate ancient and more recent writers; and they increase either the knowledge or the adornment of the languages transmitted down to us. Their use and utility were certainly once greater; for this very reason they deserved not to be neglected by us. But the fault which the malice of later times imposed upon them—the multitude of absurdities that gradually insinuated itself—places before our eyes the unhappiness of an age in which officiously zealous men, driven by a blind impulse to teach Latin and Greek, increased the mass with material of their own and, by inventing, imitating, and energetically fabricating, helped by something like public law and authority to perpetuate the barbarous character of the language which they wished to avoid and expel by their own instruction. And for this very reason, because they collected so many unbeautiful things, they are necessary: for those who produced anything polished and excellent were accustomed to draw from these sources. On the origin of glosses, see the editions of Harpocration, Maussac’s dissertation, and du Cange’s prolegomena to the Glossary of Medieval Latin.] is that it should be commended to learned and discerning men. This Glossary, moreover, seems to enjoy a particular good fortune, since it has been handled and emended by the hands of very many learned men almost down to the present day. Nor is the work obscure by which Bonaventure Vulcanius [Note: [Col. 0370C] Vulcanius published, among other glossaries, one at Leiden in 1600, in folio. Gebhard touches upon it in his Crepundia; de la Cerda in his Sacred Adversaria; Matthias Martinius in his Etymological Lexicon; Rutgersius in his Various Readings; Barthius in the immense body of his Adversaria, and here and there elsewhere; Turnebus in his Adversaria; Reinesius in his Various Readings and their Defense; van Almeloveen in the appendix to the new edition of this Glossary, published by Graevius at the end of the aforementioned Lexicon of Martinius; du Fresne in his celebrated Glossary; Graevius in his edition of Martinius’s Etymological Lexicon, Amsterdam 1701, to which this Glossary is appended. Vossius also touches upon it lightly in his Etymological Dictionary, as does Meursius here and there.], Janus Gebhard, de la Cerda, Martinius, Rutgersius, Barthius, Reinesius, van Almeloveen, du Fresne, and most recently Johann Georg Graevius, each vying with the efforts of his predecessors, contributed to correcting and illustrating this little work. This fact alone ought to carry considerable weight in forming a favorable judgment of the book [Col. 0370A]. Nor does it defend itself by that single, external support: there are not lacking—indeed, there are many, and nearly all the features—that can easily prove its definite utility to fair-minded judges.

3. Certainly, if anyone thinks that he can easily do without this little work of ours because he possesses the great work of du Fresne, he is, in my judgment, considerably mistaken. For that massive work, an immortal memorial of the greatest labors, omitted many things [Note: [Col. 0370C] Vulcanius published, among other glossaries, one at Leiden in 1600, in folio. Gebhard touches upon it in his Crepundia; de la Cerda in his Sacred Adversaria; Matthias Martinius in his Etymological Lexicon; Rutgersius in his Various Readings; Barthius in the immense body of his Adversaria, and here and there elsewhere; Turnebus in his Adversaria; Reinesius in his Various Readings and their Defense; van Almeloveen in the appendix to the new edition of this Glossary, published by Graevius at the end of the aforementioned Lexicon of Martinius; du Fresne in his celebrated Glossary; Graevius in his edition of Martinius’s Etymological Lexicon, Amsterdam 1701, to which this Glossary is appended. Vossius also touches upon it lightly in his Etymological Dictionary, as does Meursius here and there.], which nevertheless are explained here and nowhere else, and which have not been supplied even in the more recent edition of the Reverend Fathers Benedictines and their associates of Saint-Maur [Note: [Col. 0370D] Those items could rightly be omitted, since they were taken from the best authors of the Latin language—Virgil, Cicero, Plautus, Terence, and others—for they cannot properly be assigned a place in a Glossary of Medieval Latin. Some of these, however, have also been omitted from that work, while other material has been collected there, including more of the same kind belonging to the medieval period, as we shall usually observe in the notes.]. I myself, moreover, am not accustomed to praise this greatly: that these most diligent editors enlarged the great work from this Glossary. I am still less tolerant of their intermingling Graevius’s conjectures, while preserving everything else, even though they cite the praised author. For the opinions of that most elegant and highly accomplished Latin scholar are so far from having all been happily conceived and discovered that, rather, he wrote a great many things more carelessly than he was accustomed to write when pursuing his distinguished reputation [Col. 0370B]. Nor can I approve the fact that they did not make an inventory or count the number of words collected here from the best authors. Such words cannot possibly be thrown into a Glossary of the Middle Ages, since they belong rather to the best lexicons, which are normally compiled from the principal authors of the Latin language. This Glossary had gathered good things from good sources [Note: [Col. 0370D] We hear—and with sufficient certainty—that new supplements to this work are being written by these same Benedictines, chiefly under the direction of a certain Father R., who had played a major role in the new edition of du Fresne. No doubt, therefore, this Glossary of ours will also be collated anew; perhaps our wishes will even be fulfilled, so that from all the Latin glossaries, lexicographers, and vocabularies—whatever their various names—better materials may be collected, while the insane and imitative fabrications are rejected.]; although later still worse material was mixed in, as happened in these times, and now nearly exceeds the quantity of the former.

[Note: [Col. 0372B] [ [Col. 0371] This note is printed at the foot of column 372, but its callout letter, d, does not appear in the text.] Concerning Saint Isidore of Seville, or the Younger, this is not the place for me to speak at length, since, besides the earlier writers who have discussed him in Aubertus Miraeus’s Ecclesiastical Library of the Society of Jesus, and Lucas of Tuy’s Life of Saint Isidore in the Acta Sanctorum, the very learned men of our own age, Cardinal Bellarmine, Du Pin, and Cave, have carefully explained his writings, to say nothing of what Cardinal Bona, Jean Mabillon, and Jean Launoy have observed here and there in passing. As for this Glossary, I shall shortly bring forward what learned men have thought about it.]]

[Col. 0371A] 4. For the rest, it is established, as I have already said, that among the glossaries of earlier times [Note: [Col. 0371B] That is, it was compiled for the most part from Saint Isidore’s *Etymologies* and other writings; but that most diligent author composed his books from the older grammarians—Varro, Verrius, Velius Longus, Aulus Gellius, Festus, Nonius, Macrobius, Priscian, Servius, Donatus, and the Latin scholiasts on poets other than Virgil, namely Horace, Persius, Statius, and others—a compendium most useful in those times and devised with the best judgment.], provided they are sufficiently emended and properly illustrated, there is much help and support not only for the whole Latin language and its true origins, but also for understanding the writers of the Middle Ages, to say nothing of the earlier writers, whether sacred—those of the Fathers of the Church—or secular and other religious authors. Therefore, if there are matters here that deserve discussion, I shall gather them very briefly, so as to bring forward a few observations both about the Glossary and about my own new work.

Here it may be permissible to pass over what certain highly learned men have explained at greater length concerning the origin of glossaries and glosses. The term γλῶσσαι (*glōssai*) was applied to words from foreign languages that seemed to have been introduced into Greek and Latin. There was a large number of writers who collected such glosses and explained foreign and more obscure words by means of others that were better known. Certainly, the scholiasts of poets very often refer to glossaries of this kind.

5. Later, the meaning of the word γλῶσσαι changed, so that everything that seemed somewhat difficult to understand was designated by that name and made clearer through other words. Glossaries now came to be collected and composed from explanations and interpretations of poets and other writers: the words of those writers, when appropriated, were called γλῶσσαι; that is, they were placed first, while in second place came the explanation itself, supplied by famous scholars or writers. At length the authority of glosses grew so great that the whole compass and ornament of the Latin—and often the Greek—language seemed to be contained in them.

As for the Latin language, Varro, Verrius, Festus, Servius, Donatus, and the other grammarians already named [Note: [Col. 0371C] I shall praise Johann Albert Fabricius without qualification. In Book IV, chapter 6, page 779, of his *Bibliotheca Latina*, using our Glossary as his occasion, he writes: “In these glosses many recondite words of both languages and meanings buried in oblivion are explained. Hence you may see the most learned everywhere turning to them as to an oracle, and devoting their efforts to examining and illuminating them.”], as well as unnamed grammarians, virtually paved the way for the glossographers who followed.

6. That celebrated bishop of Seville, Isidore, whom they usually call the Younger [Note: [Col. 0371C] It cannot be unknown that the works commonly bearing the names of Servius, Donatus, Acron, and Cornutus cannot be credited with sufficient certainty. Commentaries of considerable length on Virgil bear the name of Servius; they are certainly not without value and are extremely useful, especially the portion drawn from the older grammarians and interpreters of Virgil. But much was added and inserted in subsequent times, so that we cannot attribute solely to Servius either all the benefit that comes to us from them or all the faults now present in them.

The name of Donatus is more distinguished by his commentary on Terence than by that apparatus of trifles and frivolous matters which disgraces Virgil and must be assigned to worthless and most foolish little men who wished to imitate Donatus. Even the work concerning Terence is not by Donatus—at least not in the form in which we now possess it—and it did not proceed from a learned man of that name, since for the most part it consists of empty distinctions and prophecies rather than explanations, and is not free from internal contradictions. Certain good remains, not unworthy of that name, have been mixed with the ignorance of various minor scholars. The case is much the same with other scholiasts, whom one must rarely trust, although they can sometimes be useful and necessary. I could not bring myself even to mention the names of Eographius and other obscure men here; they are so utterly worthless.

Festus, or Sextus Pompeius, followed the alphabetical order in his compilation, and the same method later prevailed, so that the opinions or explanations of various authors were gathered under the same headings. Gradually Greek material was sprinkled in, expressing the matter more briefly and clearly, until at length the multitude of Greek words seemed to demand an alphabetical arrangement of its own. Thus Greek-Latin and Latin-Greek glossaries arose. Traces of this method of explanation are already found in the old authors of grammar and orthography, Charisius, Priscian, Eutyches, and others whose material Cassiodorus collected.], began, with remarkable labor and great effort, to assemble his work of the *Etymologies* from those whom I have named, although he did not complete it [Note: [Col. 0372C] That he did not complete it is made clear not only by the work itself but also by Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, who plainly affirms it in his eulogy of Saint Isidore. When he reaches these books, he writes as follows: “The book of the *Etymologies*, distinguished by excessive size, divided by headings rather than by books. Since he made it at my request, although he himself left it unfinished, I divided it into twenty books, and so forth.” Braulio is plainly speaking of that very codex which Isidore had written with his own hand. Since Isidore continually enlarged it and gathered more material under those headings, Braulio says that it was of excessive size—plainly because Isidore had left many spaces and intervals into which he could insert new supplements each day. For its actual size as it exists today cannot be called excessive.]. Nevertheless, it provided considerable assistance in later ages for learning the old Roman language.

Rabanus Maurus followed him in a similar undertaking [Note: [Col. 0372D] I remember reading many things of this kind in his works; his Latin-barbarian glosses also exist.]. Others followed, so that before the revival of literary studies after the capture of Constantinople, it seemed to almost all writers to be of the first importance and to possess great weight to devote special attention to etymologies [Note: [Col. 0372D] Durand’s *Rationale of the Divine Offices* is well known; so is the *History of the Lombards*. I shall not now mention the many commentaries that follow the same plan.]—and to word-origins, as Varro explains the term—and to derive from them some increase to the subject under discussion, both of ornament and of usefulness.

7. For later writers it had now become easy to display great resources in these matters, since Papias, Salomon of Constance, Ugutio or Huguitio, John of Genoa, the author of the *Breviloquus*, the *Gemma gemmarum*, and others who produced similar works had exhausted almost all the powers of human ingenuity in deriving, explaining, and expanding Greek, Hebrew, and Latin words [Note: [Col. 0372D] Commentators on the sacred books had proceeded along this path from Philo onward: they investigated the word-origins of Hebrew names and used them to support a mystical or allegorical meaning. They therefore excerpted the ancient writers and inserted either their explanations or their opinions into glossaries. In Martianay’s edition of the works of Saint Jerome there are many explanations of this kind, although the editor seems to have earned little praise in this part of the work, because he handles the matter here and there imperfectly—perhaps ineptly?—though it bears greatly upon the reputation of so great a scholar as Jerome and of other excellent men.]. For a large part of the glosses of the later centuries was drawn from the writings and commentaries on Holy Scripture of Blessed Jerome, Saint Augustine, and other holy Fathers, especially Latin ones. Isidore’s *Origins*, however, serve almost universally as their foundation, and they copy that book assiduously.

8. Nor do all of them follow the same method or have the same purpose. Some glossaries explain more sacred material, others less [Note: [Col. 0373B] *Mammothreptus*, a well-known vocabulary arranged according to the order of the Latin Bibles, explains more obscure words, although for that reason it is also useful for correcting other glossaries. It likewise collected certain grammatical and orthographical rules. It has many editions, which sometimes differ; all of them, however, often require correction. The name of this book varies remarkably. Recently there have even been those who insisted that it should be called *Mammotractum*, but the reasoning they impose is not established. For one must take into account both the most ancient practice of writing and a not unreasonable etymology. The oldest writers, however, write *Mammotreptus*, through an easy scribal error; Erasmus of Rotterdam, whose authority is all the greater because the book was well known to him and he criticized it somewhat, writes the correct form. See his letter in which he defends his *Colloquies* against the attacks of certain people, and the catalogues of the Halle library—which belongs to Siegmund Jakob Baumgarten, doctor of theology at Halle in Saxony and most celebrated professor—volume VI, where a certain observation in the Berlin journals (the publication entitled *Berlin Library*) is attacked; Erasmus’s evidence has already conclusively refuted it. We shall immediately illustrate Erasmus’s judgment.], others name the sources from which they derive their material, while others keep silent about them [Note: [Col. 0373C] It is entirely plausible that in former times it was carefully noted from where both a gloss and its explanation had been taken. Traces of this remain in our own Glossary, where Augustine, Plautus, and Donatus are named; but eventually, in order to find a shorter way of writing, scribes omitted such indications. Papias names Isidore; the *Breviloquus* names Papias, Hugutio, the legal interpreters, and others; the *Catholicon* does the same, though not everywhere. I do not remember that the Constance writer usually does so, but he often transcribes Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, Pliny, and others at considerable length, although he does not indicate them.]. Some add material of their own [Note: [Col. 0373D] The *Breviloquus* occasionally adds material of its own, but under extremely unfortunate auspices and most unsuccessfully, not to say worse. It is wholly unnecessary to gather examples of this.], while others merely repeat and collect what has already been written.

Some explain Greek and Latin words in Latin only [Note: [Col. 0373D] Our Glossary occasionally adds Greek material; much has been neglected and omitted. Other works derive their titles from this and are called Greek-Latin or Latin-Greek glossaries, according as the Greek or Latin words come first or second, as can be seen in certain ancient glossaries, including those of Cyril and Philoxenus, which are called, as I understand, onomastic. If God wills, I have resolved to publish them in a better and fuller form, using the observations or notes of various learned men, many of which have not yet been published.], while others interpret and explain them also in the old Frankish or German language [Note: [Col. 0373D] The glosses of Ælfric belong here, as do those of Rabanus Maurus, bishop of Mainz; likewise Salomon of Constance, who explains many Greek words in Latin, although the Greek words printed in Latin letters are insanely corrupt. He explains many Greek or Latin words in the Frankish-German language, and I do not know whether they have ever been used or even seen by the most learned men who have so brilliantly illuminated the Frankish-German language. They certainly contain some excellent material, which could shed extraordinary light on older documents and even on the medieval Latin language.].

If anyone knows these matters properly, he can correct one work from another with exceptional success and purge them of the many absurd, tasteless, inelegant, barbarous, and uncouth faults of speech and writing that are often falsely attributed by people too hasty in forming opinions to certain good, deserving, and not unlearned men [Note: [Col. 0374B] To excuse Saint Isidore on their account for what some, being too accustomed to Latin elegance, criticize in his books of the *Origins*, I ask: who nowadays would not readily tolerate such things? For how is it credible that this diligent man, who handled ancient commentaries so carefully, could have strayed so far and followed worse material while neglecting better material, as we see here and there today? The things he collected were placed before his eyes; he therefore could not himself have invented such absurdities. Rather, this is the fault of later minor scholars, who mixed their own material into the good and provided an opportunity for alteration and corruption.

In the same way I would excuse certain other authors whose not-bad glossaries were disfigured by various scribal servants with the refuse, blemishes, and ugliness of their own insertions. As for those who themselves did not invent and discuss the best material, that is the fault of the times, not of the men. They seemed to deserve well of students of the language if, by tracing and forming its origins in the smallest details, they opened up its principles; but who can justly demand the ancient, most elegant method of the language from those times? Today we know that those guides for forming youth are unnecessary, since, by the singular favor of God, the best path to both the elements and the beauties of literature lies open.

This is how we should understand what Erasmus of Rotterdam seems to criticize in the letter defending the cause of his *Colloquies*: “If boys learned nothing else from these works—*Hippoplanus*, *Ptochologia*, and *Fabularum Convivium*—than to speak Latin, how much more praise does my industry deserve, which accomplishes this through play and pleasure, than that of those who imposed *Mammotrepti*, *Brachylogi*, *Catholicons*, and modes of signification upon wretched youth?” He speaks of his own time, when the Latin language was already flourishing, and censures the fact that there were people who taught Latin speech through such books. For, through the fault of the age, at the end of the fifteenth and beginning of the sixteenth century those commentaries were held in the highest esteem, because better and shorter works did not exist, or could not be found because the ancient writers had been neglected. *Brachylogi* is an older form than *Breviloqui*; but why Erasmus used *Catholicons*, and why Ludovicus Vives likewise used this altered form of the name, I shall not explain, since he ought to have formed *Catholicon*, *catholici*, *catholico*, and so on. At any rate, they ought not to have supported the ignorance of others by their authority. These words of Erasmus appear on page 904 of the oldest edition of the *Colloquies*—the first edition prepared by Erasmus himself—in 1529.]: for all this disgrace belongs to minor scholars, affected critics, and foolish scribes.

9. I am firmly convinced that the learned man of earlier times, Salomon of Constance, if he returned to these lands and now saw his work, remarkable for such obscurity, would be unable to restrain himself equally from anger and laughter. He would rightly detest the deranged minds that rendered the excellent plan of this most diligent man useless and covered him himself with such disgrace, unless we offer a warning.

For I know with certainty, having examined it carefully, that this work was truly outstanding and excellent; above all, it is the one work of all others that helps in understanding and driving out the monstrosities of others, including those that subsequently crept in. Nor will the benefit be small or nonexistent that could come to the Latin language and to ancient writers from collating and comparing these lexicons with one another [Note: [Col. 0374D] For a long time I have wished that one comprehensive work might be made from the scholiasts of the Greek poets, and another from the Greek interpreters of Greek prose writers, because these works must be acquired at great expense and can scarcely be obtained even if one spends as much as possible—not to mention the loss of labor involved in examining them. I would desire the same above all for the twofold interpreters of Latin authors. In this way the authors themselves could be printed without great expense, since better aids to understanding would always be readily available to everyone once they had been acquired. Thus each new edition gives rise to new expenses, which the modest means of most people can never match, although the costs could have been smaller and bearable. There is no need to repeat everything that adds nothing new. I shall explain this plan more fully in due course, if the opportunity to publish arises, and I hope that competent judges will readily approve it.], provided that the secular material were separated from it, as well as the material belonging specifically to the sacred books.

10. Certainly, the important task of recording variant readings could derive considerable assistance from this, because the authors of the glosses transcribed them from ancient books, which rarely survive. In this way those enormous bodies of material—which are large by their own bulk and have grown still larger through the defects of the printing art, not yet mature and perfected—could finally lie hidden in bookcases without serious loss to us, since we should neither hope nor advise that new editions be prepared today.

These oldest editions, from the fifteenth century after the birth of Christ, properly belong among the κειμήλια (*keimēlia*), the treasures of libraries. Those who lacked them contributed little assistance toward correcting this Glossary.

11. Martinius, whose Etymological Lexicon is not without utility even today, although it has ceased to be distinguished, was the first to make reasonably good use of Papias, the *Catholicon*, the *Breviloquus*, the *Gemma gemmarum*, the *Mammothreptus*, and similar works; but he used the work of the Constance writer more rarely, as well as another lexicon that was published shortly after the invention of printing together with this one. Martinius, however, often indulged his own ingenuity too much and was altogether excessively abundant. He often invents rather than interprets things unworthy of a competent judge of languages, so that at times he seems to surpass and embellish the unfortunate craft of invention practiced by certain earlier writers.

Caspar Barthius and Almeloveen made little or no use of all these sources [Note: [Col. 0375D] Barthius will never lack the praise of immense reading and vast learning. But he often seems to heap up raw, insufficiently digested learning, and to rely more on ingenuity than on judgment. His great and monstrous work, the *Adversaria*, could have been much smaller while containing all the utility it possesses. Almost everything he says about these glosses he divines from the German language—uncertain, incredible, and unsupported by any appearance of truth.]. They engage in childish trifles with great effort. We must state the truth, and we shall not today defend such things, which tend at least to bring envy and disgrace upon good letters or upon men who are insufficiently or excessively learned.

12. There were also others who did not use these aids with the same sustained diligence with which they devoted themselves to conjectures; but they generally worked under more favorable auspices. I do not know whether Vulcanius deserves such praise for this particular virtue of ingenuity. Thomas Reinesius, however, almost always corrected successfully whatever he touched; Gebhard worked on the same subject without failure, and de la Cerda also deserved some praise. Rutgersius touched upon few matters, nor did he choose particularly bad ones. Du Fresne could work more successfully in this field, since almost all the treasures of the monasteries lay open to him.

Graevius did not handle this province badly, although not with exceptional brilliance. For the observations he made on these glosses seem to be αὐτοσχεδίαστα (*autoschediasta*), improvised work; he himself does not deny it. Such things will certainly not enhance the man’s outstanding reputation. He uses Papias, with fairly good success; he also uses John of Genoa. But he does not seem to have handled the latter with his own hands, since whenever need and usefulness require it, he cites an old vocabulary through Martinius [Col. 0376A]. Yet that very work is the *Catholicon*, a major book. He also wished to have the Constance writer in hand, but he used him less carefully and less consistently than was necessary; otherwise he would have seen more, and seen it more clearly.

13. But I must return to the point from which I digressed. This Glossary bears the name of Isidore, and for that reason it is cited and praised by everyone. Nor would I myself alter the name without serious cause, since it enables us to distinguish it from other glossaries compiled according to a similar method.

But I would seek another reason for this designation and name than the one commonly offered. Some people usually regard Isidore as its author as well; this is not a new opinion, but an ancient one. Thus Honorius of Autun names it among Isidore’s other works [Note: [Col. 0375D] In Aubertus Miraeus’s *Ecclesiastical Library*, page 127, Honorius’s chapter 40 reads as follows: “Isidore, bishop of Seville, wrote innumerable little works, among which are these: twenty-two books of the *Etymologies*, a book of Glosses, a book of *Sentences*, the *Synonyms*, and a book *On Difference*. He explained the whole Old Testament in two ways, historically and allegorically, and many other things.”].

But that explanation does not seem sufficiently certain to me. I think that it was not Honorius himself so much as the scribes who copied him who added and named the Glossary, since Ildefonsus of Toledo, Braulio, and other earlier writers do not list a Glossary among Isidore’s works.

I readily find two reasons for this opinion and designation. The first is that this Glossary was gathered and compiled largely from Isidore’s works, especially the *Origins*, whose very words it often retains and would always retain if it had not been altered from time to time during the following centuries. The second is that it was appended and attached to certain works of Isidore, since it consists of material similar in subject to the books of the *Etymologies* and was largely extracted from them.

14. Thus even today learned men commonly count or name it among Isidore’s works, as Cardinal Bellarmine, Cave, and others do [Note: [Col. 0376C] Thus R. Bellarmine, in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, Cologne 1684, in quarto, page 138, after listing Isidore’s other writings, says: “A Glossary collected from various works circulated under the name of Isidore of Seville.” Cave and others say likewise.].

Whatever may be thought, this little corpus, which we are now publishing, could in no way have proceeded from Isidore. But if he did indeed begin something like an index of certain explanations [Note: [Col. 0376C] This does not seem plausible to us; for what purpose would he have done it? But it is highly credible that after him there were people who excerpted the book of the *Etymologies*, which was of excessive size. Since Isidore himself was the author and collector of glosses, or explanations, in that work of the *Origins*, his name was also given to this Glossary.], he left behind something more incomplete and much smaller, but also better, than the work as it now exists.

Much material from Greek and later glossaries, much that was misunderstood or misread, has been introduced into it, so that I think additions and insertions began especially in the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries [Note: [Col. 0376D] I think this happened because, by the time of Honorius, the book of Glosses was already being counted among Isidore’s other works. I believe, however, that it was not Honorius himself but the cataloguers who copied him who added the new little book. It would itself be shorter and contain fewer folios if the ineptitude of scribes had not caused the same word to be repeated three or four times because of a slight change in one or several letters.

It was also through their fault that material belonging under other letters was entered under letters that could plainly no longer accommodate new words, as with *Bras* and *Brat*, which derive from *lucubro, -as, -at*. Who could think that Honorius considered these and other absurdities of the same kind worthy of Isidore’s name? Yet sleepy and inept scribes excerpted material from other glossaries and, if you please, enlarged the letters with new glosses.].

And this was done under very unfortunate auspices, by an ignorant and barbarous hand which, for some reason I know not what, forced corrupted or truncated syllables into alphabetical order [Col. 0376C]. Then an even worse evil followed: the scribes, following the strokes of the writing without understanding them, faithfully preserved the practice that whenever a letter changed they themselves would create new words from it. From this it may be inferred that scribes had already been using other glossaries, with which they compared this one, and that they had thereby, if you please, adorned it rather cleverly [Col. 0377A].

But what purpose is served by criticizing and reviling? Let us always give thanks to God by making proper use of this light of letters and, as far as we are able, enlarging and illuminating it.

### 15

I come now to the other matter I promised. Since I have loved good literature exceptionally from childhood, I diligently wore out such little books in my hands as I understood would bring me no small benefit. I used that edition of this Glossary which Dionysius Gothofredus added to the corpus of Latin authors: a muddy edition, certainly, and without aids, but for that very reason one that attracted me all the more to test my youthful abilities. I wrote in the margin what seemed capable of being corrected by me; I collected the opinions of the most learned men, compared them with my own, devised new ones from the comparison, or confirmed those opinions. At last, when I was able to compare my work with Graevius’s edition and with the new Glossary of du Fresne by the Benedictine Fathers, I seemed to have found not a few things better, and many that were new. The most celebrated Menken, most learned and most expert in law and in every refinement, inserted a specimen of this work in the *Leipzig Miscellanies* [Note: [Col. 0377D] It appears in the fourth part of the seventh volume, beginning at page 717 and extending to pages 730.]. Yet I was not able to find the goddess Lucina in our lands.

### 16

Finally, it happened—through the favor of the most illustrious Marquis Scipione Maffei—that I was brought to his attention. Since, from his widely known and generous goodwill toward all good men, I could understand that he would not take this amiss, I approached him by letter, which among other things briefly indicated that I was preparing glossaries. He assented most kindly, and embraced an unknown name with such humanity that he himself urged me to send the work to Verona as soon as I first could; there would be people who would publish it.
