I have now lightly reread what I had rashly collected many years earlier, and have enlarged it here and there, corrected it, and confirmed it from the *Catholicus*, the *Constantiensis*, another old lexicon, and the *Breviloquus*. From this there arose, for the most part, the *Spicilegium* which I appended [Note: [Col. 0377D] I could have used those works at greater length, but, except in obscure matters, I could not persuade myself to do so—not only lest this edition should grow too large, but also lest I should be too lavish a dispenser of time, since by now I have scarcely been able to devote a few hours to this new undertaking. I shall, however, take care that, if I am permitted to publish Latin-Greek and other glossaries, there may be a sort of place for a supplement [Col. 0378D] embracing both other Latin glosses and anything better that may occur to me.].

The public library of the Altdorf Academy at Nuremberg is furnished with all these very ancient books—a circumstance unusual elsewhere. The old lexicon, which I call by that name because I do not know what else to call it, appears to have been printed at the same time and in the same format and appearance, on a very large folio, as the *Constantiensis*; at any rate, it is one volume. It is much smaller in bulk than Salomo’s work and almost transcribes Festus, from which some good readings may consequently be extracted. It introduces many Hebrew and Greek names, so that Festus seems to have been enlarged by a learned man for private use.

### 17

With these aids, and with diligent and repeated reading of this Glossary [Note: [Col. 0378D] This is the greatest resource and aid enjoyed by these glosses—indeed, by a large part of the critical art, insofar as it rightly applies itself to correcting books. I still cannot cease wondering how it happened that the most learned men, neglecting this path, so often chose another that was less safe, when by this one they could have reached their goal so much more quickly.], as I myself commend it, I certainly restored not a few passages that all the greatest scholars had abandoned; I devised many things better and more securely than they had, and confirmed more besides. Although, taken in itself, this entire work is small when compared with the greater magnitude and importance of the other branches of divine and human knowledge, nevertheless fair-minded judges will readily pardon youthful labor devoted to students of the Latin language.

If God wills it, I shall from time to time, as opportunity teaches me, prepare other and more carefully corrected Latin-Greek or Greek-Latin glossaries.

Written at Altdorf in Nuremberg, in March of the year 1752.

**Joannes Salomo Semler, ordinary public professor of history and poetry**

### 18

Thus far Semler, whose opinion concerning the author of the Isidorian Glossary, together with his arguments, I shall examine in the following chapter. Although he was heterodox, I consider his essays on humane letters worthy of not remaining hidden any longer.

## CHAPTER LIX  
### What, finally, should be thought about the author of the Isidorian Glossary; manuscripts indicated

### 1

Others have already observed that the Isidorian Glossary could have acquired that name either because it is usually joined with the works of Isidore in manuscripts, or because a large part of it was composed from his *Etymologies*. It remains to investigate whether there is any plausible reason for believing that Isidore himself composed some glossary which others later enlarged, or in imitation of which other glossaries appeared.

Semler insists that Braulio and Ildefonsus do not count the Glossary among Isidore’s other works, and therefore concludes that the scribes of Honorius of Autun added the Glossary when cataloguing Isidore’s books. First, however, the silence of Braulio and Ildefonsus does not immediately prove that the work is not Isidore’s, especially since they acknowledge that other works were published by Isidore which they do not enumerate individually. Second, the suspicion that the passage of Honorius of Autun containing Isidore’s eulogy was interpolated is groundless. Since Honorius of Autun flourished in the twelfth century, while the parchments in which glossaries are attributed to Isidore were written much earlier, there is no reason why we should deny that Honorius mentioned the Glossary among Isidore’s other works.

### 2

Sigebertus indeed omitted the Glossary from his catalogue of Isidore’s books, but he added these words: “He also wrote other works belonging to secular literature, which it is of no concern to us to mention.” The Glossary could have had a place among these.

Trithemius does not use the name *Glossary*, but says that Isidore wrote on grammar and words. What prevents the second title from including a vocabulary, or Glossary? Indeed, what else is the tenth book of the *Etymologies* itself except a vocabulary, or Glossary? The title of that book is: “On certain words of names, arranged alphabetically,” or “An alphabet of particular words.” In this book Isidore chiefly investigates the origins of words alphabetically, but often adds an appropriate explanation.

### 3

Nor does it seem unreasonable to me to suppose that Isidore fashioned the tenth book of the *Etymologies* for the most part from some fuller Glossary of his own, almost in the same way as he reduced the *Chronicle* to an epitome in chapter 37 of Book V of the *Etymologies* and, as may be conjectured, compiled chapters 4 and 5 of Book VIII from the book *On Heresies*, which Braulio lists among Isidore’s works.

If we assume that Isidore was the author of some Glossary, it will nevertheless be difficult to determine which one was his genuine Glossary, since perhaps none exists that has not been either enlarged or abridged, and even then interpolated. For I do not approve the method of judging that a Glossary is older in proportion as it is shorter. Just as a Glossary could easily have been enlarged by someone, so it could have been abridged by another, with words selected that seemed more deserving of explanation.

Among those ancient glossaries, therefore, which bear Isidore’s name, the chief question should be which one is overloaded with the larger number of words belonging to a later age, so that we may conclude either that such a Glossary is not Isidore’s, or that it has been interpolated much more than the others. In manuscripts I have observed the following glossaries.

### 4

In Vatican Codex 1471, discussed in chapter 96, there is a Glossary without Isidore’s name, though it is entitled *The Book of Etymologies*. A similar one, but fuller, occurs in the very old Vatican Codex 3320, also discussed in chapter 96. Another, which is called Isidore’s by an external title, is found in Regio-Vatican Codex 227, discussed in chapter 99.

### 5

Since it cannot be denied that the words of the Isidorian Glossary are for the most part explained by genuine explanations of Isidore, and since it is otherwise sufficiently probable that he prepared the first form of a Glossary which others later enlarged, the order prescribed for me in this edition requires that, after the *Etymologies* and the *Differences of Things and Words*, I give a place to the Glossary, which deals with nearly the same subject and may be useful for understanding and explaining all writers, both sacred and profane. I shall append the observations of the most learned men, by which obscure passages may be clarified, corrupt ones corrected, and ancient material distinguished from more recent.

## CHAPTER LX  
### Allegories of the Old and New Testament—not to be attributed to some Isidore of Córdoba or another, but to our Isidore of Seville; editions; old manuscript copies

### 1

Braulio describes this book as follows: “One book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*, in which he shows what the persons mentioned signify mystically.”

These words were taken from the prologue of the work addressed to Orosius: “Certain very well-known names,” Isidore says, “are read in the Law and the Gospels, which are imaginatively concealed beneath allegory and require some interpretation,” and so forth.

Although these matters are sufficiently clear in themselves, the Pseudo-Dexter seized upon Orosius’s name as an opportunity for inventing a story and records the following under the year 423: “At this time Isidore the Younger, bishop of Córdoba, writes a book of Allegories to Paul Orosius of Tarragona.”

The architects of such fables distinguished two Isidores of Córdoba: one assigned to the year 384 and the other to the year 423, whom they consequently called the Younger. This might perhaps be entirely dismissed, unless Cave also had thought that the Allegories could plausibly be attributed to Isidore of Córdoba, because they were written to Orosius, his contemporary—*sýnchronos* (σύγχρονος). Cave adds that such allegorical commentaries are not listed among Isidore’s works either by Braulio or by Ildefonsus; Bivarius likewise presses this point in his commentary on Pseudo-Dexter.

### 2

As for Braulio, we have just seen how false this is. Concerning Ildefonsus, I do not wish, with Bayer, to suspect that the book *On Secrets*, which he mentions, is the same as the *Allegories*. Ildefonsus’s words fit much better the *Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments*, or *Questions on the Old Testament*. But certainly the silence of Ildefonsus, who passed over many other works of Isidore as well, ought to carry little weight against Braulio’s clear testimony.

Cave himself is not sufficiently consistent, since under the year 595 he names the *Allegories* among Isidore’s extant works. Nor do the other recent scholars—Oudin, Cellier, and Fabricius—doubt the matter.

Dupin perhaps understood this same work in volume V of the *Ecclesiastical Library* when he said that Isidore wrote a book of Allegories on the Octateuch; he ought instead to have said, “on both Testaments.” But, in my opinion, he confused the *Allegories* with the *Questions on the Old Testament*. The same thing happened to Labbe in his commentary on Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. For he first mentioned allegorical commentaries and then added:

“Allegories, and so forth, or a little compendium of Allegories on the Octateuch, drawn from Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, Fulgentius, Gregory, and others.”

These are plainly the authors whom Isidore names individually in the preface to the *Commentaries*. Labbe immediately adds: “See Sixtus of Siena, who in Book VIII of the *Holy Library* accuses Trithemius of wishing to enlarge the abundance of Isidore’s labors.”

Trithemius did indeed, as it seems, enlarge certain other works, but he was right to distinguish the Allegories from the *Commentaries on Genesis*, and so forth.

### 3

Among earlier authorities Bayer adduces Honorius of Autun, who states that Isidore of Seville expounded the entire Old Testament allegorically. Honorius means the *Mystical Expositions of the Sacraments*, which are allegorical commentaries, but a different work from the one we call the *Allegories*.

Bayer likewise cites Trithemius, who lists the *Allegories* among the works of Isidore of Seville, though under a different opening. In Trithemius I see the *Allegories* listed twice: first, *Interpretation of the Old and New Testament*, Book II, “To my lord and servant of God”—that is, what others have as “To the holy and most reverend brother.” Then, *Book I of Allegories*. For, as I noted in chapter 47, Trithemius sometimes describes the same work twice under different titles.

Pastrengus, whom I cited in the same chapter 47, includes among the other works of our Isidore a two-book work addressed “To Horosius, bishop, on the Meanings of the Old and New Testament.”

### 4

Sigebertus himself, who first preserved—or perhaps invented for himself—the memory of Isidore of Córdoba, whom he calls the Elder in order to distinguish him from Isidore of Seville, says that he published *Commentaries on the Four Books of Kings* addressed to the holy Orosius, a Spanish priest. Nevertheless, he assigns the *Allegories* to Isidore of Seville: “To Orosius, a book on the meanings of names.”

Cotelerius, volume I, page 738 of the Antwerp edition of 1698, brings from his manuscript codex, among the titles of this Isidorian book in the Apostolic Fathers, the following: *On the Meanings of the Old and New Testament*.

### 5

Bayer further proves that the Allegories belong to Isidore of Seville from the simplicity of their style, which is not inconsistent with his character and age, whereas it rejects the beginning of the fifth century, or the period of Isidore of Córdoba, no less than the book’s address: “To the holy and most reverend brother Orosius,” which, as he says, comes from a milder and more polished age than the fifth century and from the decrepit period of the Latin language.

Moreover, would a bishop of Córdoba have honored the priest Orosius with the designation “brother”? When Bayer noticed that Orosius’s name had caused so much confusion among learned men and could find no Orosius in Spain who was a contemporary of Isidore and a bishop, he conjectured that the name Orosius had entered the parchments in place of Theodosius. Theodosius was bishop of Arcavica and signed the Council of Toledo under Gundemar in seventh place in the year 610.

He could have made a more plausible conjecture concerning Orontius, metropolitan bishop of Mérida, whose name is already found in the Spanish councils from the year 638 and who, perhaps, already held that dignity while Isidore was alive. In a similar way he might have suspected Honorius, bishop of Córdoba, who signed in eighth place the Second Council of Seville, over which Isidore presided.

Indeed, in some manuscripts the *Allegories* are written as “Horosius,” which could have arisen from “Honorius.” Or, if this Honorius was called a bishop of Córdoba somewhere, someone may perhaps have seized upon that as a basis for thinking that Isidore of Córdoba was the author of the *Allegories*.

### 6

When Nicholas Antonius discusses Isidore of Córdoba in Book III, chapter 2, he conjectures that Isidore of Seville addressed the *Allegories* to that abbot Orosius who is mentioned in two letters of Gregory the Great: one to the monks of the island of Monte Cristo and the other to the defender Symmachus, Book I, letters 49 and 50.

Although Isidore calls Orosius “brother,” this ought not to be an obstacle, since Isidore may have written to Orosius before he became a bishop, or Orosius himself may at some point have been elevated to episcopal dignity.

The latter possibility should perhaps be preferred, since in the *Allegories* Isidore already makes use of the authority of Gregory the Great, something he could scarcely have done while he was not yet a bishop.

In the allegory of the servants in the New Testament, Cyprian Suarez (whom Nicholas Antonius says is Joannes Grialius, perhaps to indicate the edition), who added notes, makes the following observation:

“Others say of the first servant: ‘He signifies Saint Gregory,’ of whom he was especially a student; for Gregory treats the present allegory in this manner.”

### 7

We rejected in chapter 16 the opinion of Pellicer, expressed in his observations on the *Chronicle* which he thought belonged to Dulcidius of Salamanca, that Isidore, bishop of Setabis, near the end of the sixth century, was the author of the work *On the Meaning of Names*. Nor can that opinion rest on any foundation, whether this title appears to refer, as it seems, to the *Allegories* or to the Isidorian Glossary.

What, then, shall we say about Vatican Codex 287, in which Ambrose is said to be the author of the *Allegories*? After other works of Ambrose, the same book—Isidore’s *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* and *Allegories of the Old Testament*—is attributed to him. At the end of the work of the *Allegories* it is noted:

“Here ends the book of the blessed Ambrose, archbishop of Milan, on the Figures of the Old Testament.”

Clearly someone found these works among other works of Ambrose and, because the name was either absent or did not appear clearly enough, attributed them to Ambrose. Nor should the authority of that codex, written in the fifteenth century, carry any weight against so many other and earlier testimonies of codices and writers.

### 8

Isidore’s *Allegories* appear in the editions of all his works, and in the Royal Library of Madrid with the notes of Cyprian Suarez, which Grialius described in the preface discussed in chapter 36.

They had previously appeared at Hagenau together with other works of Isidore under this title:

“Two books of Blessed Isidore, bishop and most ancient theologian, *On the Birth, Passion, and Resurrection of the Lord, and on His Kingdom and Judgment*. The same author’s short treatise *On the Life and Death of Certain Saints of Both Testaments*. Also, certain *Allegories Excerpted from Both Testaments*, together with the *Book of Prefaces*—correct to *Proems*. All these works have been excerpted from two very ancient codices, and until now have been seen by absolutely no one. At Hagenau, by Johannes Secerius, in March of the year 1529.”

In the four *Allegories* a letter to Orosius, “brother,” and so forth, is placed at the beginning.

### 9

The manuscript copies I have observed are the following.

Vatican Codex 287, where the *Allegories of the Old Testament* are falsely attributed to Saint Ambrose; it is discussed in chapter 93.

Vatican Codex 629, discussed in chapter 94.

Regio-Vatican Codex 231, discussed in chapter 99, with this title:

“Book on the Interpretation of Certain Names of the Old and New Testament. Isidore to Orosius, lord and servant of God. Certain [names], and so forth.”

The compiler of the inventory, deceived, I think, by the authors of the pseudo-chronicles, wrote the title as follows: “Isidore of Córdoba, *On the Interpretation of Certain Names*, and so forth, to Orosius, priest of Tarragona.”

The *Allegories* without the author’s name occur in Regio-Vatican Codex 1823, discussed in chapter 101.

In Palatine Codex 277, discussed in chapter 102, the *Allegories* are preceded by this rubric:

“Isidore to the holy and most reverend brother Orosius.”

In Urbinate Codex 100, chapter 104, the same rubric appears, preceded by the title:

“Here begins Isidore’s book addressed to Orosius.”

In the same codex there is also a *Book of Soliloquies to Orosius the Father*, perhaps through a scribal error: the scribe took the name Orosius from the *Allegories* and, I think, substituted “father” for “priest.”

It should be noted that the oldest parchments read *reverentissimo fratri* (“most reverent brother”), not *reverendissimo* (“most reverend”); the latter word subsequently prevailed. In the manuscripts of the councils of Spain as well, this epithet is expressed in the same way, *reverentissimus*, as I observed in the oldest codices of the Vatican Library.

## CHAPTER LXI  
### The book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is asserted to be Isidore’s; editions and manuscript codices of this book; Isidore’s assertion of the preaching of James the Greater in Spain is confirmed; certain examples of the same work interpolated and abridged; whether the genuine book was corrupted by some interpolator

### 1

The agreement of ancient writers and manuscript copies of Isidore’s works concerning Isidore as the author of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is so constant that it is greatly surprising that certain more recent scholars should have thought of denying this, or even of calling it into question.

I pass over the astonishing hallucination of Vossius, who said that Callistus II, the Roman pontiff of the twelfth century, was the author of the book *On the Life and Death of the Saints*—that is, the work which is read among Isidore’s works—as Oudinus in volume II, page 1006, and Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca Media*, under “Callistus II,” have already noted.

Who would not be astonished at the confidence of Natalis Alexander, who in the first century of his *Ecclesiastical History*, dissertation 15, proposition 2, says that it was already established among learned men that the book *On the Life and Death of the Saints*, which circulates under the name of Saint Isidore, was not truly the genuine offspring of Saint Isidore?

I know that some learned men doubt whether this work is Isidore’s, and that some openly deny it to Isidore. But since others, neither less learned nor fewer in number, assert and vindicate the work as Isidore’s, by what right can Alexander defend his statement that this was already established among learned men? Someone could easily reply to him that it is now established among learned men—and that it was formerly always established among everyone—that Isidore was the author of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints*.

### 2

Baronius, Cennius, and all who oppose the arrival and preaching of Saint James in Spain assert or suspect, as Bayer observes, that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints* was fabricated, falsely attributed to Isidore, and corrupted and interpolated.

Mansi, however, in his notes on Alexander, counts Cennius among those who defend the Spanish preaching of Saint James, in *On the Antiquity of the Spanish Church*, volume I, dissertation 1, chapter 2.

Cennius wishes to defend the preaching of Saint James in Spain solely from tradition, although no mention of it appears in the monuments that preceded the discovery of the body. The judgment with which he did this is sufficiently shown by these two examples.

He denies that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is Isidore’s because it attributes a canonical epistle to the apostle James the Greater, “a thing,” he says, “which is found to have been done by no human being.” What could be more ignorant? Among those who have written in favor of James’s arrival in Spain, he could have found a catalogue of those who either explicitly attributed the canonical epistle to James the Greater or at least judged that attribution probable.

Furthermore, he asserts that nothing is advanced even if the hymn of the Mozarabic Breviary, in which the preaching of Saint James in Spain is affirmed, were attributed to Saint Ildefonsus, because Ildefonsus, he says, flourished long after the time of Isidore.

What could be more false or absurd? Ildefonsus was Isidore’s pupil and died in the year 667. The body of James was discovered in Galicia during the time of Alfonso the Chaste, who began to reign in the year 795. Cennius denies that any monument of James’s preaching existed before that time, and thinks that nothing is advanced even if the hymn in which the preaching is established is attributed to Ildefonsus.

Yet Cennius boasts that he writes not to please the Spaniards, as the Bollandists do, but in the interest of truth.

### 3

Constantine Cajetan, in his eulogy of Isidore, page 29, quotes Baronius’s words from the note on July 15 in the *Roman Martyrology* concerning this book:

“Whether it is Isidore’s is not improperly brought into question, since several falsehoods unworthy of Isidore are found joined together in it.”

But he immediately replies:

“Nevertheless, Baronius would not really have said this unless Isidore had taught James’s evangelical journey to the Spaniards, which Baronius himself denies.”

But Baronius must be understood differently. At one time he supported the preaching of Saint James in Spain, even though he denied that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* was the offspring of Saint Isidore.

Cajetan adds that he had proved through a particular investigation that highly trustworthy writers, including others before Isidore, had confirmed Saint James’s apostolate in Spain.

Mariana, in his treatise *On the Arrival of Saint James in Spain*, and Flórez, volume III of *Sacred Spain*, pages 106 and following, say that they do not know what Baronius calls the falsehoods unworthy of Isidore.

If anyone is troubled by the words concerning James the Greater, “He was buried in Marmarica,” the answer is easily given: a scribal error entered the text, as may be gathered from the old Toledan Breviary:

“And, as blessed Isidore says, he was buried in a marble chest.”

A manuscript lectionary of Alcalá agrees with this reading. Other ancient documents allude to the Compostellan tomb with expressions such as “an arched house,” “marble chests,” and “beneath marble arches.”

Perhaps, as someone conjectured in Mariana, the original reading was *marmoris arca* (“a chest of marble”), from which, through a slight alteration, *marmarica* arose.

Others, such as Gaspar Sanchez and Mauro Castella, have conjectured *Tamarica*, since the Tamarici are a people of Galicia; but this is less convincing.

My own conjecture would be that *Marmarica*, or some similar name—for proper names are everywhere found corrupted in manuscripts—was the name of the place where James was first buried, either within or near the city of Jerusalem.

### 4

Nevertheless, the accounts concerning Saint James’s tomb in *Sacred Spain*, volume XIX, page 38, should be compared, as they are related from the *Compostellan History* and other monuments.

Theodore and Athanasius, disciples of Saint James, ordered that they be buried on either side of the holy apostle’s tomb. In a certain codex of the *Compostellan History*, preserved in the Major College of Salamanca called the Archbishop’s College, there is at the beginning an image of a bishop beneath arches, looking at a certain large tomb covered in the middle, with two smaller ones on either side without covers.

In the *Compostellan History* itself, Saint James’s body is said to have been buried beneath marble arches. In many charters of the kings of Spain, reproduced in volume XIX of *Sacred Spain*, the place is variously designated: “beneath marble chests,” “into the place of the marble chests,” “we have the tomb in marble arches,” and “the base of the marble chest in Galicia.”

It may be questioned whether, from those three arches—or tombs—which I mentioned, the name was originally given as *Arcae marmoreae* (“marble chests”), or whether the designation of the place arose from the arches beneath which the tombs are situated, namely *Arcus marmorei* (“marble arches”), and was corruptly changed into *arcae marmoricae* (“marble chests”).

For the rest, amid such great variety of codices and readings, I shall select the reading found in Saint Isidore by the Casanatense Codex G. III, 1, a parchment folio manuscript from approximately the eleventh century:

“He was buried in an *arca mamorea*.”

This reading is confirmed by the conjecture of the most distinguished scholars and by the readings of the Toledan Breviary.

In the Casanatense manuscript, however, *archa* is written for *arca*, and the following variant readings have been noted in an old hand: “Acha marita,” or “in Achaia Marmorica.” From *Acha marita* someone might perhaps conjecture *acta maritima*.

### 5

In the interpolated *Chronicle of Isidore*, which Lucas of Tuy published in his compilation of chronicles, another reading is suggested:

“Peter and Paul were buried at Rome; Andrew at Patras, a city of Achaia; James the son of Zebedee in a marble fortress (*arce marmorica*), and carried into Galicia, the last province of Spain.”

But in the margin it is noted: “in the marble chest.” In my opinion, the author intended the sentence to read:

“James the son of Zebedee was carried in the marble chest into Galicia,” and so forth.

### 6

To review the authors who attribute the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints* to Isidore, we must begin with Braulio.

“One book,” Braulio says, “*On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, in which he briefly recorded their deeds, their rank as well, and their death and burial, in concise statements.”

You see that not only the title but also the subject of the work is clearly set out from Isidore’s own prologue:

“The origins, or deeds together with their genealogies, of certain holy Fathers and most noble men have been set down in this little book; their rank as well, and their death and burial, have been noted in concise statements.”

One would have to be blind not to see Isidore’s book, the one we now possess, expressed in Braulio’s description.

### 7

Ildefonsus begins his eulogy of Isidore with this book:

“He wrote works both outstanding and far from few—that is, the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*.”

Other writers on illustrious men adhere to him: Sigebertus of Gembloux, who had seen neither Braulio nor Ildefonsus, as Nicholas Antonius observes from a comparison of the three; Pastrengus and Trithemius, cited in chapter 47; and before them Notker Balbulus, who died at the beginning of the tenth century and lists among Isidore’s other works a book *On the Fathers of the Old and New Testament*.

### 8

Nicholas Antonius further adds Ferdinand Pérez de Guzmán—correct to Diego López de Almella—in the Spanish work *El Valerio de las Historias*, written under John II, king of Castile; John Eisengrein, Lippomanus, Surius, Philip of Bergamo, Possevinus, and Andrew Schottus, whom, he says, we call above all the defender of this writing, since he promised in his scholia on Photius’s *Bibliotheca*, codex 1, that he would publish a work on the writings of the holy Fathers that had been called into question and defended.

### 9

Among the older writers who acknowledged Isidore as the author of this book, Nicholas Antonius brings forward Bede, who flourished in the eighth century and died nearly one hundred years after Isidore’s death.

Shortly before his death, Bede wrote, as one of his disciples relates in his life, certain excerpts from the books of Bishop Isidore.

There still exists Bede the Venerable’s *Collections*, or *Excerpts*, gathered from the most approved opinions of the doctors of the Church, in volume III of his works. In this book many passages are reproduced in the same words from the work *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, especially the chapter on the division of the apostles. James is specifically said to have received Spain for announcing the Gospel.

These are certainly the excerpts from Isidore’s books that Bede’s disciple praises.

### 10

I do not wish to conceal that Natalis Alexander and several other critical scholars do not regard such collections as the genuine offspring of Bede, because they think them full of absurdities.

First, however, it should be observed that not everything that may seem absurd in our own age either really is absurd or ought to have seemed absurd to ancient writers, who generally received the narratives of others in good faith.

Who would dare deny that Saint Gregory the Great is the author of the *Dialogues* because they contain many things that most people now consider unworthy of belief? Some do dare, certainly, but they are refuted by such powerful arguments that they ought to be ashamed of their rashness.

Furthermore, the authors of collections are more deserving of excuse if they present some things that are somewhat absurd or less credible. Their purpose was not so much to distinguish truth from falsehood as to gather together the statements of others and submit them for judgment by others.

Moreover, the *Collections* circulated under Bede’s name are either entirely Bede’s, or the work of a contemporary author, or of someone not much later, since they are found transcribed in very ancient parchments.

### 11

Nicholas Antonius next cites the author of a sermon *On the Assumption of the Virgin Mary*, formerly attributed among other works to Saint Augustine but now rejected into the appendix of the Maurist edition, volume V, sermon 208.

Labbe, Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca Media*, and others believe this sermon to be the work of Fulbert of Chartres.

Mabillon, in the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints*, century III, part II, page 266, asserts that in a certain Cluniac codex the same sermon is attributed to Autbertus, or Ambrose Autpertus.

Fabricius, under “Ambrose Autpertus” in the *Bibliotheca Media*, distinguishes this Autpertus, or Autbertus, abbot of Saint Vincent at the sources of the Volturnus, who flourished in the eighth century, from Autpertus, abbot of Monte Cassino, who belonged to the ninth century. He says that some attribute to the latter a second sermon *On the Assumption of Mary*, found among the Augustinian sermons on the saints and in Combefis’s preaching library.

Vatican Codex 1269, from the eleventh or twelfth century, presents the sermon in question among other homilies for the octave of the Assumption, preceded by this rubric:

“Sermon of Ambrose Autpertus for the octave of Saint Mary.”

It begins:

“Beloved brothers, the very venerable day is here,” and so forth.

The rubric was written out in an old hand, but in such a way that something else appears to have been written there earlier.

### 12

In this manuscript sermon, which is certainly by an ancient author, we read as follows:

“But neither is any writer among the Latins found to have said anything openly about her death. For when Ambrose, of blessed memory, was treating that Gospel verse which Simeon spoke to the Lord’s mother—‘And your own soul a sword shall pierce’—he says: ‘Neither history nor the literal sense teaches that Mary ended her life by the sword.’

“Hence Isidore also says: ‘It is uncertain whether by this saying he meant the sword of the spirit or the sword of persecution.’”

Here you have Isidore’s statement in the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, chapter 67, concerning Mary, and nowhere else to be found in Isidore:

“Some assert that she departed this life through a cruel death, on the grounds that the righteous Simeon, embracing Christ in his arms, prophesied to His mother, saying: ‘And your own soul a sword shall pierce.’

“It is uncertain, however, whether he said this with reference to a material sword, or to the powerful word of God, sharper than every two-edged sword. Yet no historical account specifically teaches that Mary was killed by the stroke of a sword.”

13. Bayer, in his notes to the *Bibliotheca Hispanica*, who takes up the same case, cites several more recent writers who attribute the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* to Isidore: Gesner’s epitomator, Bellarmine, Johann Gerhard Vossius, Cave, Oudinus, Albert Fabricius, Cellier, and Placcius, who, in the *Theatrum Anonymorum et Pseudonymorum*, under “Isidore of Seville,” no. 1484, does not even dare to utter a word against Isidore as the author of this book. Among earlier authorities he cites the author of the *Life of St. Isidore* in the Bollandists, vol. I of April, and a certain Spanish bishop, Ascaric, in an as yet unpublished letter to Tuseredus.

He encountered this letter while examining the Escorial manuscript of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, designated D.III. and Plut. I, no. 3, written by the priest Dominicus in the Spanish era 1085, that is, in the year of Christ 1047, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of September, as is stated at the end. Its title, in poorly formed Latin, is: “Ascaric’s letter to Tuseredus, servant of God, concerning the very bodies of the holy sleepers who rose with Christ, etc.” There, after explaining the opinion of certain people who asserted that the bodies of the holy Fathers who had risen with Christ had “returned to their own tombs,” he adds that they bring forward, like dull-witted people, the decree of blessed Isidore—that is, concerning Adam and the three patriarchs—without understanding that he reports them as resting in their own sepulchres at Arbe; and that they are foolish and confused when they say that Isidore did not know whether those bodies had been raised at the Lord’s command, or that he had not seen them with his own eyes if they are in their tombs—or if they are not—but merely relates the ancient history of the patriarchs’ life or death from Genesis.

14. Although these words are obscure, they clearly indicate chapter 1 of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*: “Adam, however, was buried in the place of Arbe, which place received its name from a number, namely, four, for three patriarchs were buried there, and Adam was the fourth.” It is uncertain in what century this Ascaric lived. From the unfinished and harsh style of his Latin, which plainly inclines toward the Spanish vernacular, Bayer concludes that the author lived in the ninth century or at the beginning of the tenth. Certainly, in the eleventh century, when the manuscript was written—or earlier—it was established among the Spaniards, namely between Ascaric and those who disagreed with him, that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* was Isidore’s work.

15. My own conjecture, however, is that Ascaric, the author of the letter, was the bishop of Braga—namely, the man who in the eighth century asked Elipandus by letter whether Jesus Christ was the adopted Son of God or his natural Son, and who embraced Elipandus’s error.

Ascaric’s letter is written not in the proper Latin of educated men, but in the idiom then used among the common people; in this respect it is therefore very similar to Elipandus’s familiar letter to Felix of Urgel, which Flórez published in vol. V of *España Sagrada*, p. 577, and which Ducange cited, nos. 29 and 31 of the preface to his *Glossarium mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, as an example of the Latin vernacular. It begins: “Lord Felix, I report to you that, at the end of July, he received your letter, etc.”

Jonas of Orléans, in his work against Claudius of Turin, reports that Elipandus tried to infect Asturias and Galicia with his insane doctrine; Jonas himself had once seen some of his disciples among the Asturians. Thus Ascaric likewise explains to Tuseredus the controversy that had arisen some time earlier in the regions of Asturias. Flórez, in vol. XV of *España Sagrada*, p. 169, places Arcaric, Ascaric, or Ascarius, bishop of Braga, in the year 785; but he adds that Pagi, Fleury, Basnage, the author of the *Catalogue of the Bishops of Braga*, and others identify him as the bishop of Braga without adducing any reason.

16. In support of the same position, Nicholas Antonio cites all the editions of this work that acknowledge Isidore as its author, including one which he says was produced at Hagenau by Secerius, together with the books *On the Nativity of the Lord*, *Allegories*, and *Prologues*, in 1524. I think the year should be corrected to 1529; for I do not believe this to be a different edition from the one I described in the preceding chapter.

Fabricius mentions another, earlier edition, without place or year, in quarto, and also the Basel edition in the *Orthodoxographi* of 1569, in folio, part II, p. 1736. An edition of this same little book lies concealed in a work not sufficiently familiar in our regions, under the following title:

“Three books on the Life and Death of Moses, with observations by Gilbert Gaulmin of Moulins. Added are the excerpts of Pseudo-Dorotheus of Tyre and other ancient writers concerning the lives of the prophets, apostles, and the seventy disciples of Christ, in Greek and Latin. 2. The sayings of Ben Sira and other Eastern writers, previously published by Paul Fagius and Johannes Drusius. 3. The brief ecclesiastical *Menologion* of Nicephorus Callistus. With a preface by Johann Albert Fabricius. Hamburg, at the expense of Christian Liebezeit, 1714.”

In octavo. Thus, on p. 512 of this collection, there appears Isidore’s book under the title: “The blessed Isidore the Younger, archbishop of Seville, *On the Life and Death of the Saints Who Pleased God*.” The prologue is absent. The index for both Testaments occupies eighty-seven chapters.

Fabricius himself, who had prepared this edition, silently omitted it from his *Bibliotheca mediae aetatis*. It is similar to the Hagenau edition already mentioned, from 1529; but the Hagenau edition contains a preface and bears this title: “The book of blessed Isidore, bishop, on the life or death of the saints who pleased God.” In the preface, certain words are placed in the wrong order, as follows: “A preface concerning the origins of certain most noble and holy men … when they are read in brief discourse, who held precedence in the praises of Scripture.”

17. Nicholas Antonio next appeals to the old manuscript copies of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. These bear no other author’s name than Isidore’s, except when, by error, they assign it to Fathers older than Isidore, Jerome and Ambrose, as I shall explain later.

Among other works of Isidore, the oldest manuscripts in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris contain this book. In the sixteenth century, Jerome Zurita praised a manuscript more than five hundred years old in his *Annals*. In the same century, another parchment manuscript, two hundred and fifty years old, was in the library of Antonio Agustín; another was copied in the Imperial Library in 1475, as Peter Lambecius testifies.

The editor of the Hagenau edition had two other very ancient manuscripts before his eyes. Peter of Fuentidueña collated eight copies; he corrected this book for the royal Madrid edition, as Juan Grial relates in his preface. The same book is preserved with other manuscripts in the Ambrosian Library. Bayer notes that the Escorial Library contains two manuscripts of this work, though not especially ancient, and that the Royal Paris Library contains eight, as appears from its catalogue.

It should be observed that Bivarius, under the year 37 of the *Chronicle of Dexter*, asserts that Peter of Fuentidueña, or Fontidonius, collated eighteen ancient manuscripts. This is a printer’s error for eight manuscripts. The same Bivarius criticizes Grial and Loaisa, who, he says, also corrected the edition, because in the eulogy of Saint James the Greater they substituted *praedicavit* (“preached”) for *scripsit* (“wrote”). For his part, together with Juan de Salazar, in *On the Coming of Saint James* and elsewhere, he maintains that the canonical letter commonly attributed to Saint James the Less was written by Saint James the Greater, as the manuscript copies of Isidore prove.

18. Since Nicholas Antonio only briefly indicates Peter de Marca’s testimony concerning a certain very ancient manuscript, we should set it out more fully. In a letter to Henri Valois concerning the time when the Christian faith was first received in Gaul, Peter de Marca first transcribes Ussher’s words from chapter 2 of *On the Antiquities of the Churches of Britain*:

“Freculph’s account of Philip’s apostolate in Gaul, cited by William of Malmesbury, he copied word for word from Isidore’s book *On the Fathers of Both Testaments*, chapter 73. … The same Philip is also said to have preached Christ to the Gauls in the little book on the feasts of the apostles that is found in the manuscript Hieronymian Martyrology, from which Isidore transcribed almost everything into his book *On the Fathers of the New Testament*.”

The Parisian prelate adds:

“I thought I should append the testimony of a very ancient manuscript from the library of Saint-Germain in Paris, in which this treatise of Isidore, copied more than eight hundred years ago, is contained together with other books by the same author. … Nor should it be concealed that in the same manuscript one reads that Spain was given to the apostle James and that he preached the faith to the Spaniards. The authority of this ancient manuscript ought to remove from some minds the suspicion that the reading in earlier editions may perhaps have been corrupted by someone zealous for the Spanish side.”

Since such a manuscript was written in the eighth century or shortly afterward, all suspicion that the reading was corrupted in a later period ought certainly to disappear.

I should also note here that Saint Philip’s preaching in Gaul, which Saint Isidore likewise asserts, is not considered equally certain with Saint James’s preaching in Spain: first, because Isidore deserves greater credibility when speaking about domestic matters; and second, because, since Philip preached Christ in Galatia, and Galatia was also called Gaul, while the Galatians were called Gauls, as some observe, it can readily be understood either that “Gaul” entered manuscript copies in place of “Galatia,” or that Isidore and others who speak in a similar way should be interpreted as referring to Galatia.

19. Since Ussher, in the place cited, observes that the same things that are found in Isidore concerning the preaching of the apostles are also read in Julian of Toledo’s commentary on the prophet Nahum, we must carefully examine Julian’s authority here. After other material, chapter 81 of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* reports:

“For Peter received Rome, Andrew Achaia, James Spain, John Asia, Thomas India, Matthew Macedonia, Philip Gaul, Bartholomew Lycaonia, Simon Zelotes Egypt, Matthias Judaea, James the brother of the Lord Jerusalem, and Judas the brother of the Lord Mesopotamia. But no particular lot is assigned to Paul with the other apostles, because he is chosen as teacher and preacher among all nations.”

20. Now hear the words of Julian of Toledo in his commentary on the prophet Nahum, p. 309 of vol. II of the *Toledan Fathers*:

“These, then, were the feet of the Lord, who carried him throughout the whole world by preaching. For Peter carried him to Rome, Andrew to Achaia, John to Asia, Philip to Gaul, Bartholomew to Parthia, Simon to Egypt, James to Spain, Thomas to India, Matthew to Ethiopia, Judas Thaddaeus to Mesopotamia, and James son of Alphaeus kept him in Jerusalem.”

“Each spread Christ according to his allotted portion, without stain;

But through Paul he is scattered throughout the whole world.”

21. The difference between Isidore and Julian is that Julian omits Matthias; he assigns Ethiopia to Matthew and Parthia to Bartholomew, whereas Isidore assigns Macedonia to Matthew and Lycaonia to Bartholomew. Perhaps, however, since the manuscript from which Henry Canisius extracted this commentary of Julian was corrupted by errors, the difference should be attributed to the copyist.

22. Julian himself, in book II of *On the Proof of the Sixth Age against the Jews*, p. 118 of vol. II of the *Toledan Fathers*, although he does not enumerate all the apostles who proclaimed Christ throughout the various regions of the world—because this was then less necessary to his argument—nevertheless indicates this same distribution.

After recounting that Peter preached the faith without the Jews raising against him any difficulty concerning Daniel’s seventy weeks, he continues:

“By this same and a similar rule, James enlightened Jerusalem, Thomas India, Matthew Macedonia; and the whole remaining apostolic multitude preached and testified by similar teaching that Christ, the Son of God, had come into the world.”

23. There can be no doubt that in this book Julian had in mind the distribution of the apostles mentioned by Isidore in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. In this passage, indeed, Macedonia is assigned to Matthew, as in Isidore. But because the preaching of James the Greater and of the other apostles is omitted here, although it is expressly mentioned in the commentary on the prophet Nahum, those who reject the preaching of James the Greater in Spain—although they attribute the work *On the Proof of the Sixth Age* to Julian—nevertheless deny that Julian’s commentary on Nahum is genuine.

Fabricius says that Dupin, in attempting to deprive Julian of this commentary in vol. VI of the *Bibliothèque ecclésiastique*, p. 36, uses two arguments that are not wholly conclusive: the silence of Felix of Toledo and a difference, as it seems to him, in style and manner of composition.

The most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, who brought out an edition of the *Toledan Fathers* adorned no less by the brilliance of its scholarship than by the elegance of its typography, defends the work as Julian’s in the notice to the reader placed before the commentary and reduces the opposing arguments to nothing.

24. Natalis Alexander observes, by contrast, that although learned men had previously acknowledged Julian as the author of this commentary without any reason for doubt, he himself began to doubt for no other apparent reason than that the commentary asserts Saint James’s preaching in Spain.

Alexander examines three arguments. The first is that the work was published from a single manuscript, mutilated on every side and full of errors. This argument collapses of itself. For many works are attributed to an author from only one manuscript—and, if you wish, from one that is mutilated and corrupt.

The second is that it explains only four or five verses of the prophet Nahum. What is surprising in that, since the work is incomplete?

The third is that the Leonine verses indicate a more recent author than Julian:

“Each spread Christ according to his allotted portion;

Through Paul alone he is scattered throughout the whole world.”

The Bollandists, in their preliminary commentary on the *Life of Saint James*, vol. VI of July, part II, § 7, reply that the first verse contains no metrical number, and that the second is not Leonine, since its middle does not rhyme with its end; they say that the lines can only be called similarly ending, a phenomenon very common among ancient poets and sometimes occurring without any artistry at all.

I do not see, however, why the Bollandists say that the first line contains no metrical pattern, for it is a hexameter:

“Each spread Christ according to his allotted portion, without stain.”

Here the *e* in *sorte* is lengthened either by the rule of caesura, as Christian poets, especially those of the seventh century, commonly lengthened vowels, or because of the two consonants beginning the following word. There are also many examples of similarly ending verses, such as *sorde* and *orbe*, among poets older than Julian. If desired, compare my *Hispanic Hymnody*, in the preliminary dissertation, no. 215 and following.

In Eugenius of Toledo, Julian’s teacher, poem 1 of book I, the following two lines occur together:

“Neither shall I injure anyone by guilt, nor be injured by guilt,

So may I be able to wish well, that the power of wrongdoing may depart.”

Here the words *laedam*, *laedar*, *queam*, and *recedat* answer one another in sound.

Observe also that Natalis Alexander, when discussing Saint Julian of Toledo in the seventh century, asserts without any hesitation:

“He also wrote commentaries on the prophet Nahum, which, having been edited by Henry Canisius from a manuscript in the Bavarian Library, were transcribed into the patristic collections.”

Guilielmus Cuper, in his *Brief Defences of the Spanish Preaching of Saint James*, among the *Apologies for the Acts of the Saints*, p. 874 and following, no. 114, suspects that Saint Julian’s words should be read:

“Each spread Christ according to his allotted portion;

Without an allotted portion, however, through Paul he is scattered throughout the whole world.”

Perhaps two hexameters came from Julian’s pen even though he was not thinking of composing two hexameters; the same thing has happened to others more than once.

25. Mamachi, agreeing with Natalis Alexander, denies the preaching of Saint James in Spain in such a way that he simultaneously asserts that learned men deprive Julian of Toledo of the book of commentaries on Nahum. From the number of learned men he would presumably remove Miraeus, Fabricius, Labbe, Nicholas Antonio, Cardinal Aguirre, the Marquis of Mondéjar, the Bollandists, and countless others. Otherwise, why does he not rather say that learned men attribute the book on Nahum to Saint Julian?

Mamachi, together with Dupin, presses the silence of Felix in his eulogy of Julian. But since it is established that Felix did not mention the *Life of Saint Ildefonsus*, which Julian certainly wrote, and since there was a stronger reason for him to remain silent about an unfinished work, such as the commentary on Nahum, why should Mamachi place so much confidence in this negative argument?

Recently I myself found, in very ancient Vatican parchment manuscripts, a work of Saint Julian of Toledo omitted by Felix. I shall discuss it more fully in chapter 103, where I describe the Palatine manuscript 1746.

26. Cellier, together with the same Dupin, objects that the style and manner of composition are different. But on what basis do they infer this difference? And why, if such a difference exists, should it not be attributed to different ages of the same author, to different periods, or to a different purpose?

Fabricius observes that in this commentary the opening verses of the first chapter of the prophet Nahum are explained at greater length, with the freedom customary in those times of wandering through various senses. Why, then, could Julian not have followed the practice of his age in this commentary, even though in other works he wrote according to a particular method of his own?

27. Since Natalis Alexander admits that Saint James’s preaching in Spain is asserted by Freculph, Walafrid, Notker, Melellus, a monk of Tegernsee, Zacharias Chrysopolitanus, Otto of Freising, and others either of the same period or of the following one—because all these authors embraced without examination the opinion which, he says, became prevalent after the eighth century—we must see whether this reported distribution and preaching of the apostles is confirmed by other testimonies from before the ninth century, that is, before the beginning of which the body of Saint James was discovered in Galicia.

Mariana, in the work cited, *On the Coming of Saint James*, chapter 7, brings forward Venantius Fortunatus, a contemporary of Isidore, who testifies that James’s teaching was not confined within the borders of Judaea in a poem in praise of Saint James:

“The sound of the Lord’s worshipper goes forth throughout the whole world,

Nor is there any place where his lofty glory is absent.”

And, after much else:

“Here he teaches the Gentiles and rebukes the Jews,

Sowing faith throughout the world and making it fruitful for God.”

Mariana adds that he did not find these verses among Fortunatus’s poems, but that he had taken them from the third homily of Calixtus II in praise of Blessed James. The first couplet occurs in book I, poem 9, which concerns the basilica of Saint Vincent of Vernemetum, not praise of Blessed James. Yet in both Fortunatus and Calixtus it reads: “The sound has gone forth throughout the whole world.” Several other couplets were taken from Fortunatus’s poem 2 of book V, in praise of Martin of Dumio, to whom he writes. There is therefore little reason to trust this cento-like poem in praise of James.

28. It had long been established among learned men that Saint Beatus of Liébana, who vigorously refuted the Adoptionist heresy, had published a commentary on the Apocalypse. Flórez eventually committed it to print, observing that Beatus wrote on the Apocalypse in the year 784.

In the prologue to book II, p. 97, Beatus says:

“These, then, are the twelve disciples of Christ, preachers of the faith and teachers of the nations. Although they are all one, each of them nevertheless received his own allotted region in which to preach throughout the world: Peter, Rome; Andrew, Achaia; Thomas, India; James, Spain; John, Asia; Matthew, Macedonia; Philip, the Gauls; Bartholomew, Lycaonia; Simon Zelotes, Egypt; Matthias, Judaea; James the brother of the Lord, Jerusalem. But no particular lot is assigned to Paul with the other apostles, because he is chosen as teacher and preacher among all nations.”

The copyist omitted Judas Thaddaeus, whom Beatus, as he had said shortly before, reports as having been sent by ecclesiastical history to the city of Edessa, to King Abgar.

Beatus adds concerning the apostles: “This is the holy and chosen seed, the royal priesthood sown throughout the whole world.” From this it is understood that the apostles visited the provinces assigned to them.

Moreover, Beatus’s words are themselves Isidore’s words from chapter 82 of *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. In the prologue to book I, Beatus names Isidore among the others whose opinions he is about to set out.

29. That Saint James the Greater preached in Spain is demonstrably inferred by comparing the words of Jerome and those of his teacher Didymus of Alexandria. Jerome says in chapter 34 of Isaiah:

“The Spirit of the Lord gathered the apostles, gave them their lots, and distributed them, so that one might go to the Indians, another to the Spains, another to Illyricum, and another to Greece.”

Didymus speaks similarly about the distribution of the apostles in his books *On the Trinity*, finally published at Bologna in 1769 with notes by the distinguished scholar V. C. Mingarelli:

“Namely, by this arrangement: one of the apostles residing in India, another in Spain, and another distributed by him in a different region as far as the ends of the earth.”

Mingarelli demonstrates in a note that the preaching in Spain asserted by Didymus must be understood of James the Greater, not Paul or another apostle. He also cites the words of Bluman’s Martyrology, as transmitted by Florentinius, concerning James the Greater:

“This man is said to have preached in Spain and the western regions; he died by the sword under Herod; and he was buried in Marmarica of Achaia on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.”

This Martyrology was written in the year 772. Flórez, in vol. III of *España Sagrada*, p. 117, adds two other ancient Martyrologies supporting the same view, one from the eighth century and the other from the beginning of the ninth, specifically one written in the year 804.

I should also note that the verses of Walafrid cited by Natalis Alexander—

“First he converted the Spanish peoples by his teaching,

Turning barbarian hosts by divine words”—

are also found among poems published under the name of Alcuin, who flourished in the eighth century; they may therefore be older than Walafrid.

30. Finally, we must produce the hymn from the Mozarabic Breviary for 30 December, on which the feast of Saint James is celebrated in that office:

“Peter to Rome, and his brother to Achaia,

Thomas to India, Levi to Macedonia,

James to Jebus, and Zelotes to Egypt,

Bartholomew holding Lycaonia,

Matthias Pontus, and Philip the Gauls.

Then the great sons of thunder,

Shining after attaining the heights

Of both lives through the prayer of their illustrious mother:

John alone ruling Asia with his right hand,

And his brother possessing Spain.”

Natalis Alexander thought he had cut the knot by asserting that this Toledan Office had not been approved by the Roman Church. But that is not what we are asking. The question is whether, before the ninth century, the opinion of Saint James’s preaching in Spain had gained currency. If, therefore, it is clear that in the Isidorian office—which was celebrated throughout Spain in the seventh and eighth centuries—that preaching is openly asserted, we shall have obtained what we seek.

It is remarkable that Alexander immediately adds: “It is more probable to assert that Saint James never went to Spain, because the Roman Church denies it, than to assert that he went there, because the Spanish Church transmits the tradition.” When, I ask, did the Roman Church deny that Saint James went to Spain? In the Roman Breviary revised by order of Saint Pius V, James’s preaching in Spain is expressly affirmed. Under Clement VIII, according to the judgment of Baronius, this was replaced by the statement that it was the tradition of the churches of Spain. In 1625, after the matter had been fully discussed, the text now read was restored:

“After the ascension of Jesus Christ into heaven, he preached his divinity in Judaea and Samaria and brought many to the Christian faith. Soon afterward he went to Spain, where he converted some to the faith; from their number, seven were later ordained by blessed Peter as bishops and sent first to Spain.”

31. In the Quignon Breviary, whose history I explained in Appendix 2 to my *Hispanic Hymnody*, the matter was narrated as follows: “He is said to have visited Spain and converted only nine men there.” This was how the first edition of the Breviary, from 1535, read, though it was known to few.

When the revised Breviary was reprinted the following year—the form that many people used for several years in reciting the canonical hours—it was reformed as follows: “Isidore states that he visited Spain and preached the Gospel there.”

These same words occur in the old Breviaries of Sigüenza, Coria, Ciudad Rodrigo, and Palencia, which Mariana cites in chapter 8 of *On the Coming of the Apostle James into Spain*. The Breviary of Tuy expresses the same opinion in different words: “James also went to Spain to preach, as Isidore states.” That of Salamanca reads: “Isidore states that he visited Spain and preached the Gospel there.” The Breviary of the Order of Preachers reads: “He went to Spain and preached the Gospel there, as Isidore states.”

All these not only confirm James’s preaching in Spain, but also demonstrate that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is legitimately Isidore’s. Other Breviaries assert Saint James’s coming to Spain without mentioning Isidore, such as those of Pamplona, Zaragoza, Valencia, Badajoz, Burgos, Seville, Braga, Astorga, Segovia, Compostela, the Order of Saint James, and the two Breviaries of the Carmelite Order, one published at Venice in 1568 and the other in 1586.

32. The opinion concerning James’s preaching so occupied the minds of the ancients that it was even recorded on an old geographical map drawn approximately in the tenth century. In Royal-Vatican Codex 571, folio 71 verso, there is a geographical map on which the East is depicted in the upper part and the West in the lower; on the right side are the Altars of the Philaeni, and on the left Rome, Spain, and so forth.

In farther Spain, near the river Miño, this inscription appears: “Here James preached.” Likewise, near Mount Eryx: “Here Saint Andrew preached.” Elsewhere: “India, where Bartholomew preached.” Elsewhere again: “India, where Thomas preached.”

33. This common tradition perhaps receives even greater force from the fact that it was not accepted without examination. Despite opposition from some, whether through ignorance or envy, it ultimately prevailed everywhere; and in the very tenth century the authors of the contrary report were overcome by the words of our Isidore, although he was cited without his name being expressly given.

Caesarius, abbot, wrote a letter to Pope John. Flórez, who published it in vol. XIX of *España Sagrada*, understands this to mean John XII and dates the letter to approximately the year 962. Baluzius, who first published it in vol. VII of the *Miscellanea*, understands the pope to be John XIV, who began to reign in 984.

Caesarius had been consecrated archbishop of Tarragona by the bishop of Compostela and other archbishops. Since, however, some bishops of the province of Tarragona—especially those who obeyed the kings of the Franks—were unwilling to receive him, Caesarius wrote to the pope and, among other things, said:

“These men whose names have been written and mentioned above said that this apostolate, which is called Spain and the western regions, was not the apostolate of Saint James, because that apostle, having been killed here, came here in no way alive. And I gave them this answer, etc. O Lord, you should know that Peter received Rome, Andrew Achaia; James, who is interpreted as the son of Zebedee, the brother of John the apostle and evangelist, preached in Spain and the western regions; and John died after being struck down by the sword under Herod; and Philip preached in Galatia, etc. O holy Father, I say that he who contradicts this truth is a contradictor of the Lord and of the law.”

The provinces are assigned to the apostles by this author as they are by Isidore, except that he has Galatia for Gaul, as many read in Isidore; others also write Galatia in Isidore.

34. I could cite an earlier author, Eusebius of Caesarea, if the work read in Royal-Vatican Codex 2034, a manuscript of the fifteenth century, were genuinely his. The rubric on p. 90 reads:

“Here begins the Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea, companion of Pamphilus the martyr. Chapter one: On the first age. In the beginning of time, before any day, God the Father, in the Word and through his Word, made from nothing the matter of all things.”

It ends:

“Now, as it is said, the Council of Nicaea was held in the twentieth year of Constantine’s reign. Thus far Eusebius of Caesarea, companion of Pamphilus the martyr, brought his Chronicle. From this point Jerome arranged the history of his own time. During the same period, Helena, etc.”

In chapter 13 of this Chronicle I find the following:

“John rests at Ephesus. James the Greater, returning from Jerusalem to Spain, was beheaded. Thomas was pierced in greater India with a lance.”

35. In any case, this entire Chronicle is either wholly spurious or very heavily interpolated by some Gallic writer, as it seems. For many things are reported concerning the preaching of the faith in Gaul, and specifically concerning a church founded by Saint Savinian at Sens while Saint Peter was still alive; this church was called the Church of the Living Saint Peter.

Certain proofs of its forgery or interpolation are that Jerome is praised in chapters 15 and 16 and is called “Blessed,” and that near the end of chapter 16 one reads:

“That Constantine was baptized by blessed Sylvester is declared by the acts of that same pontiff.”

The continuation of Jerome suffers from the same defect. In red ink, the first hand wrote in its margin: “This does not appear to be Jerome’s style.” It ends:

“The Alans in the mountains of Spain, who are now called Vascoli [perhaps Vascones]. Thus far Jerome the priest arranged the history of his own time.”

36. We have said these few things about Saint James’s preaching in Spain as the occasion required. In his notes to Natalis Alexander’s history, Mansius compiled a catalogue of those who undertook to defend it.

He names Johann Albert Fabricius, who in chapter 16, § 2, of his *Salubrious Light of the Gospel* reviews the more recent defenders down to his own time; Father Guilielmus Cuper of the Society of Jesus in the *Acts of the Saints*, appendix to vol. VI of July; Father Godefridus Henschen in the dissertation attached to vol. I of April; Father Adrian Daude of the Society of Jesus in book I, § 3, of his *Universal History of the Roman Empire*, *Ecclesiastical History*, and in observation 5 on chapter 2 of book I; and Cajetan Cenius in vol. I, dissertation 1, chapter 2, of his *Antiquities of the Spanish Church*, together with other Spaniards listed in the *Acts of the Saints*, appendix to vol. VII of July.

Among more recent writers of the seventeenth century we must count Juan Dávila de Roa, whose manuscript treatise *On the Personal Preaching of the Apostle Saint James in Spain* is preserved in Codex 472 of the Royal-Vatican Library. Bayer attempted to assign it to the thirteenth century in his notes to the *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book VIII, no. 284.

There is another disputation, *On the Coming and Preaching of Saint James in Spain*, in the old Vatican Library, Codex 5540, paper manuscript in folio, by an unknown author. It begins: “We now undertake …”

37. To return to the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints*, on whose account the controversy over Saint James’s preaching in Spain arose: the Marquis of Mondéjar proves in many ways that it should be attributed to Isidore, in chapter 20 of *On the Preaching of Saint James*. He appeals to numerous manuscripts from Spain, Gaul, Germany, and Britain, as does Mariana in his treatise on the same subject; Flórez in vol. III of *España Sagrada*, p. 100 and following; and the distinguished continuator of *Hispania Sacra*, Risco, in vol. XXX, treatise 66, chapter 6, no. 12.

As Bayer observes, Benedict Clement of Arostegui fully exhausts the argument in his dissertation *On the Preaching of the Apostle James the Greater in Spain*, Naples, 1743, p. 10 and following. We may add a few pieces of evidence from old parchment manuscripts.

38. In the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*, no. 58, I described Vatican Codex 242, which contains Sedulius Scotus’s explanations of the four evangelists. Sedulius flourished in the ninth century. The manuscript, however, is marked by so many additions and corrections in the same original hand that one may rightly accept it as an autograph.

Sedulius first explains Jerome’s preface to the four evangelists, and concerning Matthew he says:

“Matthew, by surname Levi, is so called because he derives his origin from the lineage of the tribe of Levi. *MATHA* in the Hebrew language means ‘gift’; hence *Matthew* is interpreted as ‘gifted,’ because it was granted to him that he should be not only an apostle but also an evangelist. He also took his surname from his tribe, Levi. Chosen by Christ from the tax collectors, he first preached the Gospel in Judaea; afterward he preached in Macedonia. He rests here in the mountains of the Shepherds.”

Beside the words “He also, etc.,” the same hand added in large letters in the margin: “ISID.” These words were certainly drawn from chapter 75 of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, where some manuscripts read “in the mountains of the Parthians.”

Thus, concerning Mark and Luke also, Sedulius takes certain words from Isidore, although he does not cite him again by name. Concerning John the Evangelist, he takes a long account from chapter 72, from the words “He, in the sixty-seventh year” to the end of the chapter, including “at Ephesus, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.”

39. We have had in our hands several more manuscript copies that place Isidore’s name at the head of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. I pass over others in which an account of Saint John the Baptist is presented under Isidore’s name—specifically from chapter 72 of the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. I shall discuss these below, when I deal with the sermons, in chapter 72.

### 40.

In Vatican Codex 287, from the fifteenth century, there is a book *On the Origin, etc.*, mutilated at the end of its first part and lacking the second, wrongly attributed to St. Ambrose, as I shall explain in chapter 93. In Vatican Codex 629 the author’s name is absent, but other works of our Isidore immediately follow. See chapter 94. In the old Royal Vatican Codex 309 there is an abridgment of this book without the author’s name. See chapter 100. In Palatine Codex 216, discussed in chapter 102, there is chapter 72—or, in another reckoning, 73—on St. John the Baptist, but inserted into a certain homily, without the author’s name and with certain additions that I find in another book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, which I am preparing for publication. In the same place, Palatine Codex 277 contains, without Isidore’s name but after other works of Isidore—whose titles likewise lack the author’s name—the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, together with its prologue. The codex is extremely old. In Palatine Codex 1448, dating approximately from the tenth century, chapter 103 contains an abridgment of this same book without the author’s name, which I shall print after comparing it with other manuscript codices. I believe, however, that it was composed no later than the ninth century. In Urbinate 100, chapter 104, there is *Isidore, On the Death of the Fathers, etc.*, as in the printed editions. The same is found in Urbinate 382, at the same chapter 104: *Isidore, bishop of Seville, On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Fathers, etc.* A similar copy is found there in Urbinate 392. In Ottobonianus 1720 the same book occurs among other works of Isidore, but without the author’s name being explicitly given; see chapter 106. In Casanatensis Codex G. III, I, which I shall describe in chapter 107, the same book is attributed by the first hand to St. Jerome, and by the second hand to St. Isidore; certain other passages taken from the *Etymologies* follow it without any new mention of the author.

[Col. 0398A]

### 41.

From Zaccaria’s papers, in chapter 44, I listed the Veronese Codex, the Florentine Medicean Codex, another Florentine Codex of St. Mark, the Albanian Codex, and the Malatesta Codex; in all of these the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is attributed to Isidore. In chapter 46, from a catalogue of the library of the monastery of Pomposa compiled in the eleventh century, I indicated a book of St. Isidore *On the Life, Origin, and Death of the holy Fathers who are celebrated in the praises of Scripture*. It was also reported there that Leofric, or Leofrid, who lived in the eleventh century, gave the monastery of Exeter Isidore’s *Etymologies* and the *Passions of the Apostles*; Nic. Antonius confidently considers the latter work to be the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. In chapter 55, from Muratori, I described the Ambrosian Codex, written more than a thousand years ago, which listed among other works of Isidore a book *On the Lives of the Saints*. I believe this to have been this very book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*.

### 42.

Bandini, in volume IV of the *Codices Latini* among the manuscripts of Santa Croce, shelf 21, describes Codex 11, which contains Isidore’s three books of the *Sentences*, the book of the *First Things*—read *Prologues*—and also Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Life, or Death, of the saints who have gone before us in the Lord*, with prologue and table of contents, as in Grialius’s edition. The *Allegories* follow, as in the printed editions, together with an untitled book (*Synonyma*), which begins: “Recently a certain little document came into my hands.” It ends: “complete through practice what you have learned through exhortation,” at the penultimate chapter of the printed editions. There is no division into books. Other works, especially those of St. Augustine, are also found in this parchment codex, a large quarto from the thirteenth century, with rubricated titles and colored initials.

[Col. 0398C]

### 43.

The same Bandini, in the same place, shelf 22, describes Codex 12, a large quarto parchment manuscript from the thirteenth century, containing this same book together with other works of Isidore: namely, no. 6, *On the Nature of Things*, etc.; no. 12, *Isidore, bishop of Seville, On the Origin, Life, and Death of the holy Fathers*, etc. Appended is a notice concerning the twelve apostles who were sent throughout the whole world to preach. No. 13 is Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*. Two chapters are added: the first on Valerian, bishop of Calagurris; the second on Prudentius, which reads as follows:

> Prudentius of Calagurris, a distinguished versifier, published many works against heretics and pagans in various meters, and sang our doctrine with the greatest clarity.

The books of Gennadius, Isidore, and Ildefonsus *On Illustrious Men* follow.

[Col. 0398D]

The chapter on Prudentius strongly confirms the opinion of those who call him Prudentius of Calagurris, especially since a similar codex is preserved in the Vatican Library. Bayer, in a note to *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, book II, chapter 10, observes that this very material is found in the Emilian Codex of the councils, written in the tenth century, and in the Escorial manuscript called the Vigilian, also of that century—except that Jerome’s book ends with chapter 135, which concerns Sedulius, and chapter 136, which concerns Jerome himself. The words “Thus far Jerome” are added. “From this point onward, Gennadius, bishop of Massilia”; and after Valerian, who is the first entry, one reads: “II. Prudentius of Calagurris,” etc.

It is evident, however, that these codices have been interpolated, if only because Jerome could not have mentioned Sedulius, at least not in the eulogy commonly circulated under his name and actually belonging to Gennadius. Perhaps this is how it arose that the eulogy of Sedulius, written by Gennadius, is attributed by some to Jerome. I discussed this in the prolegomena to Sedulius, nos. 6 and 7. Nor should Gennadius be called bishop of Massilia, but a presbyter. I have discussed Prudentius’s birthplace at greater length in the *Prudentiana*.

### 44.

Flórez, in volume III of *Hispania sacra*, pp. 107 ff., observes that St. Jerome’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* was translated into Greek by Sophronius, Jerome’s contemporary, with many additions. Isidore adopted some of these in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, for example the statement that James the Greater preached to the twelve tribes of the Dispersion, and that Simon the Cananaean succeeded James the Lesser in the see of Jerusalem. The latter, however, is false, for Simeon succeeded him.

[Col. 0399B]

Thus Isidore, following an Eastern author on Eastern matters, fell into error. Flórez thinks that other material omitted by Isidore was added to Sophronius by the Greeks after Isidore’s time, such as the account of the eunuch of Candace and of Crescens found in Sophronius. Flórez calls him “the eunuch Candace”; this is an error—or a lapse of memory—shared by some others, instead of “the eunuch of Queen Candace.”

### 45.

I shall now briefly examine the opinion of Burriel, reported in a letter to Pedro de Castro in chapter 40. Burriel thought that, since he had found in Gothic Bibles written in Spain, as he believed, before the Moorish invasion, a historical eulogy before each prophet—the same eulogy that is found in St. Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*—these eulogies had been composed by Isidore so that they might be placed before the individual prophets in the Bibles. He holds the same opinion concerning the prologues. The prologues contained in those same Bibles were then joined together to form the book of *Prologues*, and the historical eulogies of the prophets, likewise joined together, formed the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. He adds that Book II—that is, the eulogies of the Mother of God and of the apostles—may perhaps have had a different author.

[Col. 0399C]

This opinion cannot be maintained, at least as far as the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is concerned. The reason concerning the prologues appears to be different, as I shall say in the following chapter. First, the ancient manuscript copies assign both books to Isidore, and many ancient writers fully adhere to this attribution, as we have seen. Secondly, it is more reasonable to believe that the eulogies of the prophets were taken from Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* and inserted into the Bibles than that the book itself was assembled from the combined eulogies of the prophets.

[Col. 0399D]

For the book *On the Origin and Death of the Holy Fathers*, even when the Fathers of the New Testament are excluded, consists of sixty-four chapters, beginning with Adam, Abel, and so forth, and extending to the Maccabees, whereas there are few sacred writers whose eulogy ought to have been placed at the beginning of their works.

### 46.
