Moreover, if we wish to imagine that Isidore first composed only the eulogies of the prophets and later turned his attention to compiling the book, there is no reason why we should say that he stopped with the eulogies of the Old Testament and did not proceed to praise the Fathers of the New Testament. The entire book, which embraces both Testaments, bears Isidore’s name; and its prologue mentions the praises of Scripture without distinguishing the Old Testament from the New.

[Col. 0400A]

Why would Isidore have omitted a historical eulogy of the writers of the New Testament if he had set out to praise the sacred writers? I pass over the fact that those Gothic Bibles of Toledo do not possess the antiquity that Burriel supposes, as I shall show in chapter 87. Burriel does indeed report that an ancient parchment codex is preserved in the royal convent of St. John of the Kings at Toledo, containing only the Lives of the Fathers of the Old Testament; but he notes that its table of contents also promises the Lives of the Fathers of the New Testament.

### 47.

Even if the table of contents did not promise those Lives, there would still be no basis for inferring that the Lives of the Fathers of the New Testament had not been written by Isidore. This often happens in similar works, as I shall also say concerning the prologues in the following chapter, no. 5: either because a codex is mutilated, or was copied from another mutilated one, or because some people occasionally extracted from an entire work only what seemed most useful to them.

[Col. 0400B]

There is also some reason why the portion dealing with the Fathers of the Old Testament might have been selected. A work recently appeared at Rome, published by Giunchi in four quarto volumes, and praised in the *Roman Ecclesiastical Journal* of 27 September 1794. It bears the following title:

> *On the Illustrious Men of the Old Testament and the Principal Analogies Which Their Persons, Words, Deeds, etc., Have with Jesus Christ and His Church. Essays by the Priest Bernardino Famiani.*

The Italian title is: *Degli uomini illustri dell’Antico Testamento, e delle principali analogie, che le lor persone, i lor detti, fatti, etc., hanno con Gesù Christo e colla sua Chiesa. Saggi del sacerdote Bernardino Famiani.*

There is also a work by George Cassander entitled *On Illustrious Men from Adam to the History of the Kings*, Cologne, 1551, octavo.

### 48.

Burriel praises another Gothic codex containing Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, substantially different from the printed editions.

[Col. 0400C]

I possess two copies that differ from the printed editions. One is the Veronese copy among Zaccaria’s papers, as I said in chapter 44; it is an abridgment of Isidore’s book. The other was copied from Royal-Vatican Codex 199, which I shall discuss in chapter 99. It is longer than the commonly circulated Isidorian book in many chapters, shorter in others, omits much, adds some new material, and lacks its beginning. I shall place both among the doubtful or spurious works.

The acephalous book begins:

> “Concerning holy Abraham, who was the first way of believing.”

This is taken from the first verse of Prudentius’s prologue to the *Psychomachia*:

> “The faithful old man, the first way of believing,  
> Abram, late father of the blessed seed.”

It ends with the eulogy of Stephen the protomartyr, which is entirely absent from the printed editions. There is no distinction between the first book, on the Old Testament, and the second, on the New. Fifty-five Fathers and saints from both Testaments are praised. Before the apostles there is a brief chapter, *On the Apostles in General*. After St. Matthias there is again another chapter on the apostles in general, their division, and their preaching.

### 49.

Another chapter follows, *On the Apostles Who Had Wives*. Here it should be noted that the author of the book—or at least of this chapter—claims to be contemporary with St. Clement, the disciple of the apostles. “Concerning the apostles,” he says, “who unquestionably had wives, I heard St. Clement say the following; he was their companion and their disciple, and was the third after Pope Peter in Rome.”

In both of these books *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, the preaching of James in Spain is announced just as it is in the printed editions.

[Col. 0401A]

In the first: “James, son of Zebedee, evangelizing in Spain”; in the other: “a preacher to Spain and the western regions.” In describing Palatine Codex 216 in chapter 102, I report a fragment of the Life of St. John the Evangelist taken from this fuller book, but without the author’s name.

### 50.

The genuine book of Isidore *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* should be considered to be the one already published and bearing Isidore’s name in the oldest copies. Some critics nevertheless still doubt whether it has been corrupted by an interpolator.

Papebrochius, in *Responsio ad exhibitum errorem*, part II, accusation 9, appears to follow Petavius. Petavius considers a similar book *On the Origin and Death of the Prophets*, falsely attributed to Epiphanius, unworthy of him, but declares that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints*, which bears Isidore’s name, is genuinely his work, contrary to Baronius. “Nevertheless,” Petavius adds, “I would believe it to have been corrupted by some interpolator.”

But no sane person will judge material confirmed by the common agreement of all copies, especially ancient ones written in different regions of the world, to be interpolated without some evident reason. Otherwise nothing in the works of ancient writers, however legitimate, will be safe or protected from the rashness and audacity of shameless critics.

A different judgment may be reached concerning material found in some codices but absent from others. An example is what Papebrochius reports in part I, accusation 14: he possesses a single manuscript from the library of the Dominican Fathers at Soest, in which the Life of St. Catherine had the following beginning:

> “The Conception and Life of Blessed Catherine is described by Blessed Isidore in his book *On the Origin and Death of the Just*.”

Papebrochius replies that the book *On the Origin and Death of the Saints*, published under Isidore’s name, contains only the Lives of the Fathers of the Old and New Testaments, and therefore adds that the material concerning St. Catherine belongs to a much later author. I myself have found no copy of Isidore’s book in which the Life of St. Catherine is contained, even as an addition.

## CHAPTER LXII  
### St. Isidore’s Prologues to the Books of the Old and New Testaments. Zaccaria’s Prologue to This Work

### 1.

I explained Burriel’s opinion concerning Isidore’s *Prologues* in the preceding chapter: namely, that they had been composed by Isidore to be placed before the individual books of the Bible and were later joined together into a single collection.

The title itself, *Prologues*, makes this opinion quite probable. Isidore himself may nevertheless have published these prologues assembled in a single volume so that others might more easily have before their eyes and in their hands the contents of all the books of sacred Scripture. From this volume, others may have placed the prologues before the individual biblical books in certain copies.

In the copy of the Gothic Bible preserved at Toledo, these prologues are inserted in their proper places, but not absolutely all of them, as Burriel himself indicates.

### 2.

Braulio and Ildefonsus certainly attest that Isidore compiled the book of *Prologues*. Braulio writes:

> “He distinguished, in a single book of Prologues, what each book of sacred Scripture contains by means of a brief description.”

Ildefonsus writes: “the book of *Prologues*.” These words were omitted at the beginning of the royal Madrid edition, where this chapter of Ildefonsus’s book on Isidore is transcribed. Misled by this omission, as I have already noted elsewhere, Nic. Antonius believed that nothing concerning the book of *Prologues* was found in Ildefonsus. In a similar way, Rodríguez de Castro, volume II of *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 296, erred when he placed the books of *Prologues* and *On Ecclesiastical Offices* among the works of Isidore omitted by Ildefonsus.

Sigebertus and others generally agree with Braulio and Ildefonsus. Nic. Antonius says that Isidore followed Jerome’s arrangement in the *Galeate Prologue*. But since Jerome published the *Galeate Prologue* in defense of his own translation, the purpose of Isidore’s book is better understood from Braulio’s words.

[Col. 0402B]

### 3.

In some copies the prologue of the book beginning “The Fullness of the Old and New Testament, etc.” is absent. In it all the books of sacred Scripture are briefly listed, so that each may subsequently be treated more distinctly.

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca media*, says that the Western Church’s view at that time concerning the canon of the sacred books can be well understood from this and other writings of Isidore, as Richard Simon observed in his criticism of Dupin’s *Bibliothèque ecclésiastique*, volume I, pp. 252 ff. Simon also notes, pp. 259 ff., that the Latin version of the biblical books does not always follow Jerome’s version, but sometimes another version, as in the Psalms, where it follows the Roman or Italian Psalter. I have discussed elsewhere the Latin version used by Isidore.

[Col. 0402C]

### 4.

According to Nic. Antonius, who observes this from Grialius’s preface, the work was corrected and prepared for publication through the comparison of seven codices by Juan Mariana, of the Society of Jesus, a singular ornament of Spain. It had previously appeared not only in the Bignaean edition but also in the Haguenau edition of 1529, together with certain other works of Isidore.

Rodríguez de Castro, volume II of *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 300, asserts that in Grialius’s edition the *Prologues* continue into Book I of *The Offices* under the same numbering of books and chapters, so that the *Prologues* and Book I of *The Offices* together consist of twenty-five chapters. This is entirely false. The *Prologues* are not divided into numbered chapters, and Book I of *The Offices* does follow the *Prologues*, but by itself contains forty-five chapters from beginning to end.

The aforementioned Nic. Antonius indicates a manuscript of the *Prologues* in the Ambrosian Library. Bayer adds two in the Escorial Library. In chapter 46, from an old catalogue of the monastery of St. Nazarius, a codex of the *Prologues* was indicated; two more were listed from the catalogue of the monastery of Bobbio. In chapter 61, one was listed from the Florentine library of Santa Croce, not to mention many others.

[Col. 0402D]

### 5.

The manuscript copies of the *Prologues* that I have seen and compared are the following. Vatican Codex 287 contains only the prologues to the Old Testament; I shall discuss it in chapter 93. Vatican Codex 641, which I shall discuss in chapter 94, presents the prologues to the Old and New Testaments under the title *Prefaces*, omitting the general preface but adding a chapter on Esther, which is absent from the printed editions.

Without Isidore’s name, the *Prefaces* of the books of the New Testament are found in Royal-Vatican Codex 231, which I shall discuss in chapter 99; they end shortly after the beginning. In Royal-Vatican Codex 310, which contains several works of Isidore, there are two books of *Prologues* with a prologue, but the author’s name is not expressly given. See chapter 100.

In Palatine Codex 277 the same *Prologues* occur, with Isidore’s name added by a later hand; see chapter 102. In Urbinate 100, chapter 104, there are the *Prologues* of both Testaments with a prologue. In Ottobonianus 278, chapter 105, there is an excerpt from the *Prologues* concerning St. Paul the Apostle.

## 6.

When the distinguished Zaccaria decided to begin an Isidorian edition with this work of *Prologues*, he had conceived his own prologue as follows:

> **The Prologues of St. Isidore, Bishop of Seville, to the Books of the Old and New Testaments. EDITOR’S PROLOGUE.**

[Col. 0403B]

We are about to publish the works that St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, composed concerning the volume of sacred writings, and we begin with his prologues to the books of both Instruments—the Old and the New. No one will deny that these were written by Isidore, since they are explicitly mentioned both by St. Braulio of Zaragoza in his preface to the works of the most holy bishop and by St. Ildefonsus in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9. Following them, Sigebertus, in chapter 55 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, says of Isidore:

> “He wrote a book of Prologues to the books of the Old and New Testament, which the Catholic Church receives into the canon.”

### 7.

They appeared in the Bignaean and Breulian editions of all Isidore’s works, and also in the Madrid edition, corrected against seven manuscript codices by Juan Mariana, a most learned member of our Society. He also illustrated them with brief but, as usual, highly learned annotations. In addition to these three editions, we used an equal number of manuscript books to review the text, and we have thought it worthwhile to make a few observations about them here.

### 8.

The first of these codices is preserved in Florence, in the famous library of the Franciscan Fathers whom we call Conventuals, at Santa Croce. It is designated Codex 233, shelf 29, and is placed in that part which faces the church itself.

The works copied in it are numerous and occur in the following order: Isidore’s *On the Supreme Good*; his book of *Prologues*; his *Origin and Life, or Death, of the Saints Who Departed in the Lord*; his *Allegories to Orosius*; his *Synonyms*; his book of *Differences*; the *Dialogue of St. Augustine, Bishop, to Orosius*, beginning “Although many highly learned men”; or St. Augustine’s book to Paul and Eutropius, bishops of Spain, concerning the questions of Caelestius on the perfection of righteousness; his book *To Virgins*, beginning “Since the changeable mind of mortals”; his book *On the Four Virtues of Charity*, beginning “The desire for charity”; his book *On the Ten Plagues*, beginning “It is not without cause, brothers”; his book *To Dulcitius on the Souls of the Dead*, beginning “Since we read”; his book *On the Consolation of the Dead*, beginning “It reminds us”; and finally his book *On the Entrance of Bishops*, beginning “He who does not enter through the door.”

### 9.

The second codex is preserved at Cesena, in the library of the Malatesta princes, also among the Franciscan Conventuals. It appears to have been written in the fifteenth century. It is designated 2, shelf 13, and is placed on the right-hand side as one enters the library.

This codex also contains many brief works, both by our Isidore and by others, in the following order:

1. St. Bonaventure’s *Inductions to the Understanding of Sacred Scripture*. At the end of the work it is called *An Introductory Treatise on the Understanding of Sacred Scripture and the Christian Faith*. The following is then added: “This book was published by the Reverend Father Brother Bonaventure of the Order of Friars Minor, cardinal of the Apostolic See, and is a compendium of theology and the Christian faith.”

2. A little book translated from Arabic into Latin by Brother Alfonso Bonihominis, a Spaniard, and dedicated to the Most Reverend Father in Christ, Brother V., Master of the Order of Preachers. It concerns the Messiah and is, as I find noted on the final page, a letter of Rabbi Samuel the Israelite (sic), a native of the city of the king of the Moroccans, sent to Rabbi Isaac, master of the synagogue at Sublimeta in the aforementioned kingdom.

3. Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, *Book of the New Testament*, which is a fragment excerpted from Book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

4. St. Isidore’s *Book of Prologues*.

5. His *On the Life and Death of the Holy Fathers*.

6. St. Isidore’s *Chronicle*.

7. His book of *Differences*.

8. His *Sermon against the Arians*.

9. His work *Against the Jews*.

### 10.

A third codex, much older than these, is the Veronese chapter’s parchment manuscript, as it is called, a large quarto, designated 54. The distinguished Marquis Maffei discusses it in the first part of his *Veronese Manuscript Library*, p. 88, in the following words:

> “In a book of the same format, likewise old, and written in a character that for the most part approaches typography, the following works are contained.
>
> “1. The book of *Prologues* begins with a dialogue of Jerome the presbyter. It does not mention *praemia*, nor is it a dialogue or a work of St. Jerome; it is rather Isidore’s work, concerning which Braulio says: ‘one book of Prologues.’
>
> “2. *The Life or Death of the Saints Who Went Before Us in the Lord.*
>
> “3. ‘The Little Works of St. Isidore Begin,’ as though the works preceding them belonged to someone else. There follows a book wrongly attributed to another Isidore by the spurious chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter: *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*. It appears to have received this title from Braulio.
>
> “4. ‘The Testimonies of Divine Scripture Begin.’ We published this collection of passages from this very codex in the second volume of our *Literary Excursions through Italy*.”

### 11.

These are the codices with which I compared the earlier editions of this Isidorian book. But I also unexpectedly obtained another resource from Rabanus Maurus, a most learned writer of the ninth century.

I had read in the Englishman Cave’s *Literary History*, p. 456 of the 1720 edition, that William of Malmesbury, in the preface which Peter Allix published from the Lambeth Library, reproached Rabanus with a charge of notable plagiarism—as though he had copied two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* word for word from Isidore, Augustine, and Gregory the Great’s *Pastoral Rule*, and had also compiled other brief works from the same Isidore and from Bede.

Perhaps I would have found more on this subject in the dissertation that John Francis Buddeus published in 1724, *On the Life and Teaching of Hrabanus Magnentius Maurus*; but I did not have access to it. Nevertheless, prompted by Malmesbury’s accusation, I turned to Rabanus’s twenty-two books *On the Universe*, or *Etymologies*. In the Codex of Charles de Montchal, archbishop of Toulouse, preserved in Labbe’s *New Library of Manuscript Books*, p. 176, they are carefully prefaced with material concerning the proper meanings of words and the mystical significance of things. I suspected that Rabanus had transferred much from Isidore’s *Etymologies* for his own purposes, and I found that this was indeed the case.

When I discovered that Book VI, chapter 3, entitled “A Brief Note Indicating What Is Contained in the Sacred Books,” was missing from Isidore’s corresponding sixth book of the *Etymologies*, it occurred to me that Rabanus had incorporated Isidore’s little book of *Prologues* in that chapter. I therefore compared the two, and observed that, as I had conjectured, one had been copied from the other.

For this reason I compared Isidore’s *Prologues* with that chapter of Rabanus, in order to present them as Rabanus had read them in the ninth century. For this purpose I used a very rare edition of Rabanus’s work, exceptionally elegant whether one considers its type or its paper, preserved in the library of our household college at Modena. It is a large folio edition prepared in the fifteenth century.

Orlandi mentions it in his book entitled *The Origin and Development of Printing*, p. 96, and correctly says that it appeared without any indication of year, place, or printer, although it was produced before the year 1500. Since he had not actually seen it, however, he knew neither what the work contained nor how splendidly it had been printed. The capital letters of the individual chapters are painted in blue or red, while the other larger letters, glowing red with cinnabar, greatly enhance its appearance.

To avoid having to name the codices or editions repeatedly in every place, we shall use the abbreviations given here, together with their meanings.

### 12.

The abbreviations that Zaccaria used were these:

- **B. E.** — Bignaean edition.
- **Br. E.** — Breulian edition.
- **M. E.** — Madrid (Grialian) edition.
- **F. C.** — Florentine Franciscan Codex.
- **C. C.** — Cesena Franciscan Codex.
- **V. C.** — Veronese Chapter Codex.
- **R.** — The final chapter of Book III of Rabanus.

As I noted earlier, the variant readings that he had planned to arrange and place beneath the text had indeed been begun, but they did not proceed beyond the title of this book. Nor do I find in his papers any discrepancy in the text from the one reported in that most ancient edition of Rabanus—or Rhabanus. Nevertheless, I do not consider this a great loss.

### 13.

Mucciolus, in volume I of his catalogue of the manuscript codices of the Malatesta Library, p. 57, shelf 13, Codex 2, discusses a codex containing St. Bonaventure’s introductory treatise on the understanding of sacred Scripture and Rabbi Samuel’s letter concerning the Messiah, translated by Alfonso Bonihominis, a Spaniard.

The following works succeed them:

> “A brief work of St. Isidore of Seville concerning the writers of the New and Old Testament. His letter to the presbyter Orosius. His brief chronicle concerning the Life, Origin, and Death of the Holy Fathers who are praised both in the Old and in the New Testament. His chronicle abbreviating the histories from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of the emperor Evadius—also called Heraclius—and the fourth year of the religious prince Sisebut, the year 5820. His book of *Differences*. St. Isidore’s sermons: one against the Arians and two against the Jews. A discourse concerning the substance of the soul, its power, and other matters pertaining to it.”

The codex is from the fourteenth century.

### 14.

I do not know whether the inscription was made by an ancient copyist or by the compiler of the catalogue: “On the Writers of the New and Old Testament.” This should be referred to the book of *Prologues*, not to the book *On Illustrious Men*.

Mucciolus observes that in the *Chronicle of Histories* the codex indicates the era of Sisebut’s reign; he adds that, as far as he knows, this is not so easily found in other codices. Yet nothing is more common in the codices and editions of the *Chronicle*. It notes the year 5820, which, according to the Roman Martyrology, corresponds to the year 614 and to the fifth year of the reign of Heraclius.

### 15.

Concerning the sermon against the Arians, which begins “Come, Lord,” and is attributed to St. Isidore, Mucciolus observes that in another extremely old Malatesta codex, the *Etymologies*, written in the seventh century—though I shall assign it to the ninth century—it is attributed to St. Augustine. On a label attached to the shelf, however, two sermons against the Jews are wrongly attributed to Isidore of Toledo.

From this I infer that those two sermons against the Jews are not different from the two books *Against the Jews*, or from fragments of them, since in other codices also these two books are attributed to Isidore of Toledo. I find my suspicion confirmed by the words that Mucciolus, p. 58 n., testifies were read after Isidore’s works:

> “Here end the chapters of Isidore against the Jews.”

As for the sermon against the Arians, I do not find it listed by Mucciolus when he describes the codex of the *Etymologies*, volume II, p. 144, where he lists other brief works attributed there to St. Augustine, although these are considered spurious. Among them is a brief work *On the Soul and Its Powers, etc.*, which may perhaps be identical with the *Discourse concerning the Substance of the Soul, Its Power, and Other Matters Pertaining to It* appended in this codex to other works of Isidore. But when Mucciolus compared this brief work, he discovered that it was Cassiodorus’s book *On the Soul*.

## CHAPTER LXIII  
### Isidore’s Book on Numbers, Now to Be Published for the First Time from the Royal Library of Turin. Other Writers on the Mystical Significance of Numbers. Another Unpublished Work on Numbers Preserved in the Vatican Library: Whether It May Be Attributed to Isidore

[Col. 0406B]

### 1.

Braulio clearly mentions the work *On Numbers*:

> “One book on Numbers, in which he touched in part upon the discipline of arithmetic because of the numbers inserted into ecclesiastical Scripture.”

Other ancient writers are silent about it, as are most more recent writers. Others, such as Cave and Ceillier, list the book *On Numbers* among Isidore’s lost works. Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca media*, thinks it is not different from certain chapters of Book III of the *Etymologies*, in which arithmetic and numbers are discussed.

But since Braulio, who arranged the *Etymologies* in order, declares that the book *On Numbers* was a work distinct from the others, Fabricius’s conjecture must be rejected entirely.

[Col. 0406C]

### 2.

A work is preserved in the Royal Library of the Academy of Turin, from which I have obtained a copy transcribed in Zaccaria’s papers. Bayer, as he reports in a note to Nic. Antonius, also made a copy in the year 1754. He says that the codex he saw was from the thirteenth century and entitled *On Numbers and on the Number Forty*. Perhaps this was the title recorded in the catalogue.

In Zaccaria’s copy I find only the following:

> “The Book of Numbers Begins. The Chapters Begin.”

After the table of chapters comes:

> “What Is a Number?”

Nothing else concerning this work could be found in Zaccaria’s papers. I described the codex in chapter 43, from the catalogue of the Royal Library of Turin.

### 3.

Some may ask whether this should be considered a genuine work of Isidore. I certainly think that it should. For if one considers its subject, it agrees completely with Braulio’s words: it deals with the mystical interpretation of the numbers inserted into ecclesiastical Scripture, preceded by a brief account of the discipline of arithmetic.

This book should not be referred to the work *On Computation*, which Trithemius lists among Isidore’s works, apparently alluding either to chapter 17 of Book VI of the *Etymologies*, on the Paschal cycle, or to some larger work on this subject, or to a work on speech by means of the fingers, attributed somewhere to Isidore, concerning which I have written elsewhere.

Nor should the book *On Numbers* be identified with a certain brief work or fragment marked in Ottobonianus 6 by the following rubric:

> “Likewise, on number, by Isidore: Cardinal numbers are, etc.”

There several kinds of numbers are listed, including cardinal and ordinal numbers. This fragment belongs rather to the *Etymologies*. I shall discuss that codex in chapter 105.

The numbers inserted into ecclesiastical Scripture, as Braulio calls them, can be none other than the numbers that occur in sacred writings, whose allegories and mysteries are explained in this book.

[Col. 0407A]

### 4.

The work’s style also bears the mark of Isidore’s character, as do its method of interpretation and its varied sacred and secular learning collected from many writers. Certain phrases are also characteristic, as when, in chapter 2, an infinitive is used without a verb governing it:

> “and to be the sole measure and cause of increase, and the condition of decrease,”

where something must plainly be supplied, or something similar. This occurs frequently in Isidore’s printed works and still more often in the manuscripts.

The prologue likewise recalls the Isidorian simplicity evident in other prologues of his:

> “It is not superfluous to attend to the causes of numbers in the holy Scriptures, for they contain a certain teaching of knowledge and very many mystical sacraments. Therefore, since you have wished it, I have decided briefly to set forth the principles of certain numbers.”

The same thought is found in Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4:

> “The meaning of number must not be disregarded, for in many passages of the holy Scriptures it is clear how great a mystery they contain. For it was not without reason that it was said in praise of God: ‘You have ordered all things by measure, number, and weight,’ etc.”

He gives examples from the numbers six and forty, which also appear in this work, together with certain other material concerning the doctrine of numbers taken from the same Book III of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0407C] 5. Epiphanius preceded Isidore in the mystical exposition of certain numbers in a brief work entitled *On the Mysteries of Numbers*; many, however, hold that it was written by another Epiphanius. For there were several Epiphaniuses, including bishops of Cyprus, besides the most celebrated author of the book *Against Heresies* and other works. Eucherius, bishop of Lyons, says the following about numbers in chapter 11 of his *Spiritual Formulas*:

> Let us also briefly arrange the numbers which the mystical logic of examples has made especially prominent among sacred subjects, from one to one thousand, omitting many.

Morhofius made the following observations on the mysteries and doctrine of numbers in *Polyhistor*, volume I, book I, chapter 12, no. 19:

> In the mathematical 519 sciences, what is there that is not divine? Here the doctrine of numbers first presents itself, and it rightly deserves to be called wholly divine. How great and how mysterious the powers of numbers are has not even to this day been sufficiently understood. Pythagoras, who knew this well, found no more suitable way to conceal the secrets of his philosophy while nevertheless disclosing everything to those capable of understanding, than to hide them in his numbers, which one might rightly call formal numbers. For when numbers are mentioned, what is meant is nothing other than the hidden proportions, progressions, operations, and revolutions defined by God himself. How, then, could it not be exceedingly difficult to sketch in them all the mysteries of divine and human wisdom? Let no one believe that it happens by chance that sounds are completed by seven and numbers by nine, and that from this they are brought back through the same ἀνακυκλώσεις [recurrences or cycles] into the hundreds and thousands. There the forms of hidden things lie concealed, and through these they are, as it were, prefigured. In these [Col. 0408A] things, as though in darkness, those authors grope who nevertheless see, as it were, through clouds—authors whose complete volumes on the mysteries of numbers are extant, and so forth.

6. In the same work, book II, chapter 7, no. 50, Morhofius observes, on the authority of Ghilinus in *Theatrum hominum litteratorum*, p. 219, that Theodotus Hosius wished to restore the Pythagorean doctrine of numbers in a book entitled *Rhythmic Meditations*, divided into two parts, one of which promises the theoretical and the other the practical branch of the science of knowing through numbers, or the restored doctrine of the Pythagoreans. Morhofius did not know whether this book had been published. Iamblichus of Chalcis was also versed in this Pythagorean doctrine of numbers; his works include *Introduction to Nicomachus’ Arithmetic* and *Theological Arithmetic*. Among more recent writers there were Peter Bongus, or Bungus, *On the Mysteries of Numbers*, and, more accurately, Meursius in *The Pythagorean Denarius*.

7. After Isidore, numbers—especially insofar as they concern ecclesiastical matters—were treated by Rabanus Maurus, whose works draw extensively on Isidore. On this subject, see Vatican Codex 939, to be discussed in chapter 95. The published work is found in Baluzius, *Miscellany*, book I, p. 1, under the title *Rabanus Maurus, Abbot of Fulda, Book on Computation*:

> To his beloved brother Macarius, the monk, Hrabanus, a sinner in Christ, sends greetings. We have read that it is written, etc. Since I have often heard you, venerable teacher, discussing numbers, etc.

Chapter 2 begins:

> Hence Isidore says: “The coin gave its name to the number,” etc.,

from book III, chapter 3, of the *Etymologies*. He also treats the significance of numbers by means of the fingers, time, the nineteen-year cycle, epacts, and so forth. Fabricius, in his *Bibliotheca medievalis*, also lists among the other works of Odo, abbot of Morimond in the twelfth century: *On the Meanings of Numbers*; *On the Figures of Numbers*; *On the Knowledges and Interpretations of Numbers*; *On the Meanings of Unity*; and *On the Analytics of the Ternary*.

8. Vatican Codex 919, a parchment manuscript in sixteens, p. 7, contains a fragment of an anonymous work on numbers:

> Likewise, numbers, etc.

Again, on p. 204, there are certain materials on numbers, followed by a treatment of ordinal numbers; and again, turning to the knowledge of numbers:

> A possesses the number five hundred in direct order.

John of Nijmegen transcribed these verses in book I, chapter 10, of *On Numbers*, though with some discrepancies from those found in the manuscript of Huguccio, as Ducange observed under the letter A. In [Col. 0408D] another Vatican Codex, no. 3101, written by Benedict the acolyte in the year 1077, there are works of Hermannus Contractus, including *Also, on the Number 22, Beautiful Things Worth Knowing: Now the First*, etc. Perhaps this is a book *On the Number 22*. Hermann had died shortly before, namely in 1054. The anonymous author of Melk says that he wrote *On the Principal Rules of Computation*; Trithemius attributes to him *On the Conflict of Rithmomachy*. The Vatican Ottobonian Codex 819 contains an Italian manuscript treatise on the mystical number seven:

> The septenary is, etc.,

by Raphael Aquilinus. The Ottobonian Codex 3140 likewise contains an anonymous Italian manuscript booklet, *On the Quaternary Number*.

9. For the use made by the Fathers of mystical interpretations of the numbers in sacred Scripture, one may consult Sirmondus in his note on Augustine’s sermon 19, volume I of Sirmondus’s edition of Augustine’s works, column 338. There he discusses the number of fish, 153, which the apostles caught in the Sea of Tiberias after Christ’s resurrection. One may also consult Cotelerius’s edition of the *Apostolic Fathers*, volume I, p. 29, in the note on the Epistle of Barnabas, where the number 318 of Abraham’s household servants is discussed. I treated this matter more fully in *Prudentiana*, chapter 20.

10. Although I believe the book *On Numbers* preserved in the royal library at Turin to be a genuine work of Isidore, I shall now examine another work concerning which there may be some question whether it is Isidore’s. It occurs in Codex Regio-Vaticanus 199, discussed in chapter 99, after Isidore’s three books of *Sentences* and his interpolated book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*. From this latter book I inferred a paraphrase of the Gelasian Decree on books to be received and not received, which I included in the appendices 521 to Sedulius’s edition.

A rubric has been added by some ignorant copyist: *Certain Matters Concerning Our Lord Jesus Christ*. The reason is that the prologue begins:

> With the help of our most high Lord and the granting of our most merciful Savior,

but the author immediately explains the subject of the book, continuing:

> I wish to write briefly, yet usefully, about number and its mystery.

The author intended—and perhaps succeeded—in extending the exposition to the number 24. But the work is mutilated, and shortly after the beginning of the mystical exposition of the number three it breaks off.

11. The author takes much from what Isidore briefly indicated in his book *On Numbers*; but since he generally wanders further in explaining the matters themselves, he sometimes turns to transcribing other works of Isidore. Thus, in the exposition of unity, when he discusses the soul, he writes:

> For although the soul is one thing, it possesses within itself many forms and adornments: while it breathes, it is spirit; while it perceives, it is sense; while it understands wisely, it is mind; while it understands, it is intellect; while it rightly distinguishes, it is reason, etc.

These words are taken from Isidore’s book *On the Differences of Things*, no. 29, *On the Difference between Mind and Soul*:

> Since the soul is one and the same: while it contemplates, it is spirit; while it perceives, it is sense; while it understands wisely, it is mind; while it understands, it is intellect; while it distinguishes, it is reason, etc.

This could provide some reason for doubting whether this book *On Numbers*, found without an author’s name in the Codex [Col. 0409D] containing other works of Isidore, is Isidorian. For it was Isidore’s practice to draw and repeat many passages from his other books throughout his works.

12. But there is a stronger reason for conjecturing that this work was attributed to Isidore somewhere. For when the number two is explained and two kinds of penitence are described, we read:

> Longinus opened the Savior’s side with a lance, and not only found forgiveness, but also deserved to have the honor of the episcopate, the glory of martyrdom, and a crown.

Salmeron, volume X, treatise 48, gives similar words:

> Longinus opened the Savior’s side, and, though deprived of sight in one eye, by the touch of Christ’s blood he was enlightened outwardly and inwardly by the light of faith and was baptized by the apostles; and after a long time in the desert he obtained the honor of the episcopate and the crown of martyrdom.

[Col. 0410A] In the margin he cites: “Isidore of Seville.” Collius likewise quotes the same words in his treatise *On the Blood of Christ*, book IV, chapter 1, from a recent, as he says, student of sacred Scripture who cites Isidore. But in chapter 3 he adds:

> Nor, so far as I know, can these words of St. Isidore readily be found.

Similarly, Barradas, treatise 4, book VII, chapter 22, after reporting the same words, concludes:

> This is what he says—Isidore—but I have not been able to find it.

13. This question was raised by the distinguished Francis Alexius Fiori, then of the Society of Jesus, who recently died piously at Bologna. In a letter sent from Mantua on 9 June 1758 to Zaccaria, who was planning to publish Isidore’s works, he asked in what place Isidore had uttered those words. I find no reply from Zaccaria. But when I found almost the same words in this manuscript work *On Numbers*, it occurred to me that Salmeron—or someone from whom Salmeron copied them—had come upon this work *On Numbers*, prefaced with Isidore’s name. For in his other works there is neither trace nor indication of them. The work *On Numbers* omits the statement that Longinus had been deprived of sight in one eye, etc., but expressly explains the honor of the episcopate and the crown of martyrdom. Perhaps Salmeron, or someone possibly earlier than him, appealed to Isidore for this opinion while asserting the remaining details from other sources.

14. Collius provides an excellent confirmation of this. In chapter 1 of book IV he cites Isidore twice: once, in connection with the blindness in one eye of the soldier who opened Christ’s side, using Salmeron’s words; and again in connection with the martyrdom of the same soldier. He says:

> There are also those who consider St. Isidore a patron of this opinion, introducing him as saying: “Longinus opened the Savior’s side with a lance, and not only found forgiveness, but earned the honor of the episcopate and the crown of martyrdom.”

These are the same words found in the unpublished book *On Numbers*, except that where the manuscript reads “and deserved to have the glory and crown of martyrdom,” Collius has “and earned the crown of martyrdom.” Collius adds:

> Yet such authors remain silent about the place where these things were recorded by Isidore—and perhaps not without reason, since until now I have nowhere encountered such agreement with Isidore in his writings.

15. The Bollandists discuss St. Longinus the martyr on 15 March, the man who pierced the Lord’s side with a lance. They observe that in the tragedy *Christ Suffering*, by Apollinaris of Laodicea—or, more probably, by some other fourth-century author rather than Gregory Nazianzen—there is an allusion to that metaphorical mode of expression by which it seems to have commonly circulated among Christians: when Christ’s side was opened, the eyes—namely, the eyes of the mind—of the man who had thrust the lance were also opened. The ignorance of the uneducated populace turned this into a reference to bodily eyes. Nor do they acknowledge the authority of Isidore, which some have cited for the blindness of one eye. They say nothing about the episcopate of Longinus, whether he was the soldier who struck the Lord’s side with a lance or the centurion who confessed the Lord. Nor does Collius, who in the cited passage discusses the controversy over Longinus’s blindness at length, name any other author besides Isidore in connection with his episcopate. Other serious authors, however, held the opinion that his eyes became dim or that he was blind in one eye, including St. Vincent Ferrer and Ludolph of Saxony, whom Collius cites. Collius concludes that this fiction arose from a misunderstanding of the words of John the Evangelist:

> And he who saw it has borne witness,

which John spoke about himself, but which some wrongly transferred to the soldier who pierced Christ’s side.

# CHAPTER LXIV  
## Questions on the Old and New Testament Not Yet Published

### What Is Isidore’s Work *On the Difference of the New and Old Testament*, or *On the Harmony of the New and Old Testament*, Cited in Collections of Canons?

1. I have not yet seen a more distinguished codex of Isidore’s works, or one that displays clearer evidence of antiquity, than Vatican-Palatinus no. 277. It is written in Roman majuscule letters of the kind in which some manuscripts of the eighth or ninth century are written; and there is certainly no reason why it could not be assigned to Isidore’s own century, namely the seventh. It contains Isidore’s prologues, the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*—though here without any title naming its author—*Allegories* with Isidore’s prologue to Orosius, and, besides certain other works to be examined in their proper places, on p. 29 the rubric:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begin the Questions of Saint Isidore, both on the New and on the Old Testament.

There are sixty-one questions, each followed by its answer. Question 1 is:

> Tell me, what is there between the New and the Old Testament?

The answer is:

> The Old is the sin of Adam, etc.

[Col. 0411C] 2. I therefore present these questions as a genuine work of St. Isidore, relying on the authority of so distinguished a codex and finding nothing that stands in the way, but much that draws me toward the same conclusion. Although some may perhaps think that Braulio and Ildefonsus did not mention this book, that will not disturb me, not only because Braulio and Ildefonsus openly state that they did not list all of Isidore’s works, but also because I seem to see a mention of this work in both authors.

Braulio says:

> The two books of QUESTIONS, whoever reads them will recognize in them a great store of the old interpreters.

Ildefonsus says:

> He also collected from various authors what he himself calls the expositions of the mysteries of the sacraments; when these were gathered together into one, the book was called QUESTIONS.

3. Until now, Braulio’s and Ildefonsus’s words seemed to signify nothing other than the *Exposition on Certain Books of the Old Testament* that is extant. But now that these questions on the Old and New Testament have been discovered, it will readily be possible to persuade anyone that they are included in the work which Isidore entitled *Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments*; others, perhaps because these questions preceded the commentaries, called the work—or the works—two books of *Questions*. The reason the questions preceded them was that most of them dealt with explaining some universal matter, or one pertaining to both Testaments.

Grialius says in the preface to the edition [Col. 0412A] that he found an exposition of the mysteries of the sacraments in a not very old codex of the monastery of Oliva, marked with the title *Questions*. In that codex, individual expositions have their own questions placed before them. But since he adds that the questions in this codex do not seem to him to be the same as those mentioned by Ildefonsus, he leaves us uncertain whether he is speaking of the commentaries themselves, which in that codex were arranged through questions and answers, or of various other questions such as ours. For this reason, when Nicholas Antonius speaks in book V, no. 139, of the *Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments* and of the book or books of *Questions*, he says, in connection with our subject:

> John Grialius seems to distinguish them, but, as we believe, without any adequate reason.

4. Someone might doubt whether questions of this kind were expounded by Isidore at Braulio’s request. For Braulio, in his letter to Isidore, the one that begins *So that it may be filled*, in which he asks that the *Etymologies* be sent to him, continues:

> When these things have been completed, I shall have questions concerning the sacred and divine pages, the exposition of which the light of your heart would disclose to me, if you would nevertheless command us too to shine—or perhaps, if it might help us—to unlock the obscurities of divine law. Nor, if I receive what I ask, will I remain silent about them; rather, you will open the way for the confidence necessary to undertake them.

Nevertheless, I think that the questions now extant are not those of which Braulio speaks. First, Isidore would not have failed to say that he was answering Braulio’s inquiry, prefacing the work with some brief prologue. Second, these questions, like the *Allegories*, the prologues, and the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, seem to have been fully written and explained [Col. 0412C] in order to open an easier path to continuous commentaries on sacred Scripture. Finally, Braulio wished to propose his questions after Isidore had completed the *Etymologies*, which appears to have been Isidore’s final work.

5. As in other books, so also in this one St. Isidore takes sentences and sometimes words from his other works. Thus, in question 2, on the number of books of the Old and New Testament:

> According to the seventy-two languages, seventy-two books are understood,

from book I of *The Offices*, chapter 11. Likewise, in question 9:

> Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside and not to benefit,

from book II *On the Offices*, chapter 5. And in question 37:

> There is one soul which, while it contemplates, is spirit; while it perceives, is sense, etc.,

from the book *On the Differences of Things*, no. 29, *On the Difference between Mind and Soul*. The sentence about the bishop also occurs in the *Dialogue of Questions* among the doubtful or spurious works of Augustine, as the final question. For one of the Fathers elegantly expressed the thought:

> Let him know that he is not a bishop who desires to preside and not to benefit.

It is taken from Augustine, book XIX of *The City of God*, chapter 19:

> Let him understand that he is not a bishop who has loved to preside and not to benefit.

6. Since this book of *Questions* begins, “Tell me, what is there between the New and the Old Testament?”, I began to suspect that it had somewhere been entitled *On the Difference of the New and Old Testament*. For Gratian, in distinction 34, chapter 5, prefaces the following words with Isidore’s name:

> Likewise Isidore, *On the Difference of the New and Old Testament*:

> A Christian, I do not say is permitted to have many women, but not even two at the same time, unless only one is a wife or a concubine in place of a wife.

Joseph Catalanus, I think, had this passage in view in his note on St. Jerome’s letter *On the Integrity of Clerics*:

> Observe that, according to the First Council of Toledo, canon 17, a concubine is called a wife who had not been admitted to the full right of marriage. Thus also Isidore, in the book *On the Difference of the New and Old Testament*.

Such words of Isidore are found neither in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 20, entitled *On the Difference of the Testaments*, nor in the book *On the Differences of Things*, no. 33, *Between the Law and the Gospel*, etc., nor in book II *Against the Jews*, or *On the Calling of the Gentiles*, where some matters concerning both Testaments are discussed. They are also absent from this book of *Questions*. Yet [Col. 0413B] this would certainly have been an appropriate place to establish a question concerning wives and concubines in the Old and New Testaments.

If Isidore did debate this matter, then, given the great freedom of copyists, it would not be surprising if some incompetent person omitted it because he did not understand that a Christian was permitted to have a concubine in place of a wife—that is, a true consort who had not been admitted to the full right of marriage. Such women were then permitted and were regarded as wives taken with less solemnity.

For my part, I would rather believe that Gratian cited these questions, originally entitled *On the Difference of the New and Old Testament*, from their very beginning, than that he was referring to some chapter of another work, each of which possesses its own title, as a work distinct from the rest. Berardus, cited above, discusses this title in chapter 32, no. 7.

7. It is clear from the letter of Burriel, transcribed in chapter 40, that he had borrowed from a friend a Gothic codex containing several works of Isidore and a certain acephalous book of brief questions on sacred Scripture in the form of questions and answers. Burriel himself doubted whether it should be assigned to Isidore. If he had indicated even one question, it would be possible to judge whether it agreed with ours.

In a Vatican Codex of the eighth or ninth century there is also a book of *Questions on Sacred Scripture*, mutilated at the beginning but different from ours. The first question encountered is:

> In how many ways did John understand that he must be baptized by Christ?

The last is:

> Why is Jesus called a child when infancy ends at seven years and boyhood closes at fourteen?

The answer is:

> This is certainly clear: Jesus came in order to minister and to hunger—[I would read “to serve”]—because the Son of Man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister, etc. For every minister, and every servant, is called a child, etc.

There are also other questions which, in the Gothic Regio-Vatican Codex 1823, among other works of Isidore, bear the title:

> On More Difficult Questions of the Old and New Testament. 527

The first question is:

> By what testimonies of Scripture is the Trinity confirmed?

The author’s name, in a different but sufficiently ancient hand, is given as Eucherius, bishop. In fact, these are the two books of Eucherius of Lyons, *Instructions for His Son Salonius*. After the first book, a more recent hand notes that the final seven lines are absent from the printed editions. In the manuscript, the questions end at the Epistle to the Colossians, [Col. 0414A] “Jewish Christians.” Immediately follows the rubric:

> Prologue on Hebrew Names: Since, dearest son, in the preceding book, etc.

At the bottom of the page an ancient hand, different from the first, has written:

> Here ends the book of Questions on the New and Old Testament. This is the first book of the *Instructions*; the second book is *On Hebrew Names*, with various terms, etc.,

as in the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of Lyons, volume VI, p. 853. There the first book, after the question on the Epistle to the Colossians, continues through the Apocalypse. The question on the Epistle to the Colossians is incomplete in the manuscript.

# CHAPTER LXV  
## *Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments*, or Questions or Commentaries on Certain Books of the Old Testament

### Whether Isidore Published Literal Commentaries on Sacred Scripture; Whether He Authored the Ordinary Glosses; Whether There Is Another Work, Not Yet Published; Other Commentaries; Interpretation of Job

[Col. 0414B]

1. After the works of Isidore that in some way pertain to the exposition of sacred Scripture in general, we now turn to the extant commentaries on individual books. Literal commentaries would certainly deserve priority if it were established that they were written by Isidore and still preserved somewhere. But since the only literal glosses known to me are certain ones that we can assign to Isidore only by conjecture, I shall first discuss his genuine allegorical commentaries and treat the others afterward.

2. In the preface to his Isidorian edition, Grialius discusses this work at length; it should be reread above, chapter 36. I shall add only that Latinius, *Bibliotheca selecta*, [Col. 0414C] p. 173, long ago observed that in Eucherius, printed at Rome in 1564, there are commentaries on Genesis and on the books of Kings in which several passages of St. Gregory the pope and words and deeds of Isidore are cited. He also adds that the work appears to have been written by a man in Britain. Nicholas Antonius confirms this with several passages that he cites.

The Bignaean edition gives the following title:

> Blessed Isidore the Younger, archbishop of Seville: commentaries on the Old Testament.

Breulius followed this title. Manuscript copies differ extraordinarily. Nicholas Antonius reports the title *On the Pentateuch* from a codex of the Medici library and from another belonging to St. Isidore of León. In another codex he observes that the material concerning the books of Kings exists separately. From the manuscript papers of Alfonso Chacón preserved at Rome in the monastery of St. Isidore of the Irish Friars, he produces the following inscription:

> Explanation of the History of the Divine Law.

From a manuscript codex of the Ambrosian Library at Milan:

> Commentaries of St. Isidore on the Pentateuch, Joshua, and Kings.

The inscription *Exposition*, or *Explanation of the History of the Divine Law*, also appears in some of our manuscripts, following an old custom borrowed from the Hebrews, according to which a title consisted of the opening words of the book. For the prologue of this commentary begins:

> The history of the sacred law.

3. Since Nicholas Antonius had named only Isidore’s expositions on the books of the Pentateuch, Joshua, Judges, Ruth, Kings, and Ezra, Bayerius added in a note:

> And also on the books of Maccabees, as in two Escorial Codices, from which Grialius printed some passages in volume II, p. 236.

There is indeed, not only in Grialius’s edition but also in the Bignaean edition and others, a short chapter on the martyrdom of the Maccabees. But since Bayerius says that Grialius cites some passages on the books of Maccabees from the two Escorial Codices he cites, he seems to imply that other material still lies hidden in those codices and has not yet been printed. Perhaps, however, he did not compare the manuscripts with the printed editions and therefore supposed that the manuscripts contained more than the printed texts, since, as I have said, the printed editions contain only a very brief chapter. In addition to those two Escorial Codices, Bayerius cites three other Escorial Codices of the same work of mystical expositions, but he does not transcribe a specific title from any of them.

[Col. 0415B] 4. Rodriguez, volume II of *Bibliotheca Hispana*, pp. 326 and following, lists several Escorial Codices containing an exposition of the books of the Old Testament. A parchment codex in quarto, II R. 14, appears to be from the thirteenth century. The following titles are written on its cover:

> “Isidore on the Pentateuch. Also, a treatise on the Lord’s Prayer. Also, Master Compostellanus, *On the Consolation of Reason*. Also, certain very useful theological questions. Also, a summary of Master Alanus on the art of preaching. Also, another treatise on the Lord’s Prayer.”

The work bears this inscription:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the Codex of Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville: an exposition of the five books of Moses and of the remaining books of the Old Testament, collected from various authors into one work and explained more fully. The history of the sacred law was carried out and written down not without some foreannouncement of future events, etc.”

5. In Codex II R. 9, a parchment manuscript of the fourteenth century, with clear, large lettering, there is the same exposition. The following note is on the cover:

> “This volume contains the following: the moral exposition of Blessed Isidore on the five books of Moses, namely Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Judges, and Kings. Also, at the end of the book, the *History of Dares Phrygius on the Destruction of Troy*.”

A Spanish note adds that the book belongs to the library of the Blessed Virgin of Guadalupe; it is signed “Belasco.” The title is:

> “In the name of the supreme God, amen; the sign of Christ. With the cooperation of the Holy Spirit, the preface of Isidore begins. The exposition of the Pentateuch is complete.”

6. Codex II, L. 8, a paper manuscript of the thirteenth century, bears this more recent title:

> “The exposition of St. Isidore on Genesis, and certain other works; and St. John Chrysostom, *On Contrition of Heart*.”

In this codex the exposition is likewise complete. In addition, there is a book of St. Isidore entitled *Collectum*, about which we shall say more in chapter 85.

7. Codex III, Q. 21, in quarto, a parchment manuscript apparently of the thirteenth century, with many ligatures, bears the following title:

> “The preface of Isidore, bishop, begins, in the book of Genesis.”

Rodriguez adds that this codex contains the exposition through the book of Jeremiah. Here I wish for a clearer explanation: does it also contain an exposition of Jeremiah, which is certainly absent from the printed editions, or at least some other material that has not yet been committed to print? The book [Col. 0416A] formerly belonged to the so-called Major College of Alcalá.

8. Codex III, P. 7, a parchment manuscript apparently of the fifteenth century, bears this more recent inscription:

> “Isidore on the Pentateuch and First Kings.”

The exposition of Genesis is mutilated. At the end there is the following subscription:

> “Peter of Castro, a noble boy, wrote this little book with his fingers. He wrote the book on very poor parchment: he wrote carefully, but not carefully enough.”

530 9. Codex III, P. 17, in octavo, a parchment manuscript apparently of the fifteenth century, with red titles and initials, bears on its first page the following inscription in a more recent hand:

> “Epitome of the Histories of the Old Testament by Isidore.”

Bayerius, who had once examined the codex, added:

> “Not an epitome, but Isidore’s complete work.”

The title of the codex reads:

> “Here begins the Eptameron of Blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville.”

The work begins:

> “The history of the sacred law was carried out and written down not without some foreannouncement of future events. Nor would such a manifold shadow of accomplished events pertain to the prefiguration of the mystery unless the Apostle, teaching, were to say: ‘The law has a figure of the good things to come, not the very image of the things themselves.’”

It ends:

> “the names of his two daughters: the name of the firstborn was Merob, and the name of the younger Michol. David, son of the Ephrathite.”

The codex formerly belonged to the library of the church of St. Antoninus at Palencia, as an old inscription records; it was removed from there in 1578.

10. Although Nicholas Antonius does not mention an exposition by Isidore on the books of Maccabees, he observed, on the authority of the Englishman Robert Cook and Vincentius Placcius, *On Pseudonymous Writers*, p. 209, that the prologue to the books of Maccabees, which is usually included among Jerome’s works, is Isidore’s. In Erasmus’s edition of Jerome’s works, at the beginning of volume I, it is noted among the doubtful works:

> “There are two prefaces to the books of Maccabees, with the same beginning: ‘The books of the Maccabees.’ They do not seem to me to be Jerome’s. The beginning of the Isidorian booklet is different.”

Cocus, however, in Placcius, does not speak under the heading “Jerome” of this booklet but of a fragment of Isidore’s *Prologues* included in the Bibles printed at Antwerp in 1570. Roffensis, Bunderus, and Alfonso de Castro cite it as Jerome’s prologue, while Erasmus, Scultingus, and others disagree.

11. Some have doubted whether the extant commentaries on the Old Testament, or at least on Genesis, are Isidore’s. Placcius, under the entry “Isidore” in *On Pseudonymous Writers*, reports the following from the *Mastrichtian Symbola*:

> “In the seventh century there was Isidore, bishop of Seville, an educated man, distinguished by many writings, who, in his commentary on Genesis—if indeed it is his and not that of Ildefonsus of Toledo, who nevertheless flourished in the same period—in chapter 7, etc.”

Samuel Andreae, in his disputation *On the Salvation of Adam*, thesis 28.

This author gives no reason why he would either deprive Isidore of such a commentary, contrary to the testimony of so many ancient writers, or assign it to Ildefonsus without any evidence.

531 12. There is a greater controversy concerning the commentary on the four books of Kings. Theophilus Raynaudus, *On Evil and Good Books*, part I, question 10, says:

> “Commentaries on the four books of Kings are commonly attributed to St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, but the true opinion is that they were written by that Isidore the Elder, also a bishop in Spain, whether of Córdoba or of Badajoz; nor are there lacking those who make him bishop of Zaragoza.”

But if Raynaudus is so uncertain about that older Isidore, why does he call it the “true opinion” that the commentaries were written not by our Isidore but by another, an Elder? And Isidore of Badajoz is certainly younger than our Isidore. Later writers invented the Isidore of Zaragoza; among the ancients, Sigebertus was the first to name the Isidore of Córdoba and to designate him as author of the commentary on the four books of Kings. I investigated the cause of this error when discussing the different Isidores in chapter 16.

13. In fact, the commentaries on the books of Kings are joined in manuscript codices to the other works that precede them, connected in a single continuous text and under the name of the same author, and adorned with sentences of St. Gregory the Great, so that it is in no way permissible to think of a different and earlier author. The beginning of the commentary on the First Book of Kings also suggests this connection in a certain way:

> “After the book of Judges comes Kings. And consider the sequence of times: first Judges, afterward Kings; just as there will first be judgment, afterward a kingdom.”

Labbeus, in his commentary on Bellarmine’s book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, is also in some way uncertain. First he asserts that Isidore the Elder of Córdoba dedicated his commentaries on the books of Kings to the historian Paulus Orosius around the year 412; then he merely notes that some prefer to assign the commentary on the four books of Kings to Isidore of Córdoba.

In only one codex, Vatican Codex 5002, discussed in chapter 97, do I find any doubt raised concerning the author of the commentary on the four books of Kings. After the exposition of the preceding books, this note is found:

> “Up to this point are excerpts of Isidore, bishop; what follows are excerpts by Bede the priest.”

But this single codex, against so many others, deserves no credence—especially since it names Bede as the author, although no one had thought, or now thinks, of him in this connection.

14. Nicholas Antonius rightly exposes the error of Ambrosius Morales, who thought that the work *Expositions of the Mysteries of the Sacraments* was identical with the work entitled *On the Highest Good*, or *Sentences*. Morales also reports that in the Spanish monastery of Espina, of the Cistercian 532 Order, there is a notable volume containing an exposition on the Pentateuch, or a catena drawn mostly from various unknown authors, among whom Isidore is frequently cited, presumably from these commentaries. He further understands Raymundus Martini, the Dominican writer of the thirteenth century, to allude to these commentaries. In part II of his *Dagger of Faith against the Jews*, chapter 3, section 12, Raymundus praises Isidore’s gloss on 2 Kings, chapter 2:

> “Go up, baldhead,” etc.

This belongs to the so-called patristic catenae on sacred Scripture, about which we shall say more below. For in such catenae the expositions of the Fathers are sometimes called glosses.

15. Besides the editions of Isidore’s *Expositions* included in collections of his other works, the following commentaries were published separately under this title:

> *The Most Learned and Very Brief Expositions on Genesis, etc., by St. Isidore, Bishop of Seville, a Most Ancient Theologian.*

Rouen, printed by Franciscus Vaultier, 1647, in octavo.

This edition contains only the expositions of the Old Testament that had already been published at that time. It appears, however, to have been reprinted from an older edition published at Cologne in 1530, in octavo, at the expense of Peter Quentel, with a similar title:

> *The Most Learned and Very Brief Expositions on Genesis by Isidore, Bishop of Seville, a Most Ancient Theologian,*
etc.

### 16

Since not only all the manuscripts but also all the printed editions agree in praising Isidore of Seville as the author of this work, what could Angelo Rocca have had in mind when, in the *Index of Theological and Scriptural Works*, vol. II, p. 110, omitting Isidore of Seville, he listed commentaries on both Testaments by Isidore the Younger of Córdoba? As I said, some attribute commentaries on the four Books of Kings to Isidore of Córdoba, whom they call the Elder [Col. 0418B]; but even this cannot be admitted against the testimony of so many manuscripts, even if one should wish to conclude from Sigebert that Isidore the Elder of Córdoba composed some other, different commentaries on the four Books of Kings.

### 17

I discussed the manuscript copies collated for the Zaccharian edition in chapter 43. I shall briefly indicate here what I have seen. In chapter 94 I shall catalogue Vatican Codex 626, in which these commentaries are called an *Exposition*, with certain additions that must be relegated to the Appendices. I have recently spoken of Vatican Codex 5002. In the Royal-Vatican Codex, of which I shall speak in chapter 100, the title is *Treatise on the Book of Genesis*; and at the beginning: “Preface of Bishop Isidore on the Book of Genesis. Isidore sends greetings to the reader.” In Palatine Codex 275, chapter 102, the commentary of Isidore is preceded by the following verse:

> Isidore, while dictating, openly adhered to Bresit [*Bereshit*];

and perhaps certain things in that Codex come from the literal commentaries, as I shall say at that point. In the same place: in Palatine Codex 276, *A little exposition of Saint Isidore on the Books of Kings*, with certain previously unpublished fragments inserted. In Ottobonian Codex 53, chapter 105, after the preface on the Old Testament there is the title *Exposition of the Book of Genesis*, etc., as commonly found in the printed editions.

### 18

What reason might I suppose for the fact that, although Isidore himself gave his commentaries a title, manuscript and printed books vary so greatly in the inscription of this work? From Ildefonsus we learn that Isidore called them *Expositions of the sacraments of secrets* [Col. 0418D]. Grialius wished to restore the original title and entitled it *Expositions of mystical sacraments*, because Isidore says in the prologue: “and they are full of mystical sacraments.” But Isidore could have called “mystical sacraments” in the prologue what he called “sacraments of secrets” in the heading. I shall therefore more readily retain *Expositions of the sacraments of secrets*.

John the Deacon, in the *Life of Saint Gregory*, book IV, chapter 77, used the name “exposition” when speaking of these commentaries:

> Isidore, bishop of the city of Seville, admired the harmony of Gregory’s eloquence in his *Exposition of Genesis*: “These things,” he says, “were taken from the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, [Col. 0419A] Augustine, Fulgentius, and, in our own times, the exceptionally eloquent Gregory.”

### 19

Grialius observes in a note that Isidore was indeed a devoted student of Fulgentius, but that he himself found no passage of Fulgentius in these *Expositions*; consequently he omitted the name of Fulgentius from the text, and it is likewise omitted in certain old copies. But since John the Deacon in the ninth century read the name of Fulgentius in Isidore’s prologue, and the ancient copies agree, it must certainly be retained: first, because it is difficult to assert that nothing of Fulgentius is found in these commentaries of Isidore; second, because other similar commentaries of Isidore seem to be missing; and finally, because Isidore may have excerpted something from other books of Fulgentius that have not survived to us.

[Col. 0419B] ### 20

The fact that Isidore occupies himself with extracting mystical and allegorical interpretations is not at all blameworthy, not only because he had already explained the literal sense, as I shall say shortly, but also because he followed very weighty guides and pursued this path for sound reasons. Petrus Lazeri discusses this subject at very great length and with great learning in the preface to Bruno of Segni’s commentary on the four Evangelists. He says:

> These same explanations are exceedingly frequent in the writings of the Fathers. If you wished to remove them from their writings, almost the whole of works of this kind would perish.

Besides Gregory, Bede, and Origen, he cites and praises Hilary, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine as Fathers most approved and highly esteemed by the judgment and acclaim of all. He then gives reasons why the Fathers were frequent in allegorical interpretations [Col. 0419C]—namely, so that they might season the harsher precepts of morality with a certain not ungenteel flavor, especially because, since they often had to address the people, they would have had sleepy hearers if they had not employed allegorical and mystical interpretations. Such interpretations could not fail to please educated and intelligent hearers as well.

### 21

Lazeri also explains the custom of the ancient Fathers, by which they freely took words from other, earlier writers, as though plucking flowers from different meadows, and often repeated in other works what they themselves had said elsewhere. Nor does this writer labor to bring forth novel interpretations or to coin new opinions; rather, he plucks, as it were, flowers from the ancient Fathers—namely, thoroughly approved explanations, instructions, teachings, and statements—so that he seems to have wished for nothing else than that whoever read his commentary should possess in it whatever useful and excellent things were found in all the others.

Braulio said this about Isidore:

> “The two books of Questions, in which whoever reads them recognizes a great store of the ancient interpreters.”

And Isidore says in his prologue:

> “Gathering together the opinions of the ancient ecclesiastical writers, we have brought them to hand like flowers gathered from different meadows.”

### 22

A little later Lazeri continues:

> “Nor will anyone find it difficult to believe that this was not first done by the author, nor that it is something new for those who addressed sermons to the people to borrow them from their other works, if they observe that in Augustine and other Fathers many passages of homilies consist of the same opinions, and even the same words, as those found in their other, more carefully wrought works. We should suppose that they did this either to spare themselves work that was not strictly necessary, or because they distrusted their ability to express those things more suitably than they had already done; or this resulted from the frequency of these homilies and sermons, which left no time for meditation and reflection.”

He observes that Bernardinus Ferrarius discussed this frequency of sermons at length in *On the Rite of Sacred Preaching*, chapter 18, and Bingham in volume VI of the *Origines Ecclesiasticae*, book XIV, chapters 4, 5, and 6. In the *Collection of Dissertations in the Italian Language*, begun through Zaccaria’s efforts and still continued after his death, volume XI, p. 126, there is a dissertation by Zaccaria entitled *Dissertation delivered at Lucca in the Academy of Ecclesiastical History on 26 March 1753, later revised and enlarged, on the ancient ecclesiastical sermons* [Col. 0420B], in which he praises several other writers on the same subject.

### 23

Isidore, moreover, willingly employs words not only in these commentaries but also in his other works—words that he had previously used himself no less than those found in the writings of other Fathers. In the commentaries, however, his principal aim was to gather together the various expositions of the Fathers into one work and present them to his readers. Perhaps he himself was the first consistently to follow this order and method of interpretation. After him many expounded the Sacred Scriptures in a similar way, whether or not they named the Fathers from whom they borrowed their words and interpretations. Their method was nearly that which Sixtus of Siena reports concerning Bede in book IV of the *Bibliotheca sancta* [Col. 0420C]:

> “In his Rhapsodies, or Stromata, or Collections, he gathered mystical rather than historical expositions from the most approved opinions and sayings of the doctors of the Church, collected here and there in interrupted and interpolated fashion, inserting some things of his own as well, in imitation of their meaning, wherever appropriate, so that the various discourses and periods of the Fathers might either cohere with one another more suitably or be made shorter and clearer.”

Ildefonsus, Isidore’s disciple, borrowed many things not only from his teacher but also from Augustine and Gregory, especially in the work entitled *Annotations on Knowledge of Baptism*, as the passages carefully indicated in the margins of the Madrid edition of the Toledan Fathers show. Nor did Ildefonsus himself conceal this; for in his prologue he says:

> “We do not propose novelties unknown to our predecessors, but either unlock the admonitions or insights of the ancients, or record them for memory.”

### 24

Among the *Opuscula of Certain Ancient Writers*, published at Bologna in 1755 with a review by the learned Trombellius, there are commentaries by Claudius of Turin on the Books of Kings. Claudius says in their prologue:

> “And because you often ask me for the resolution of many matters, especially in the Pentateuch and the Book of Kings . . . and in these matters I have satisfied your questions not from my own ingenuity but from the judgment of illustrious teachers, not from my own rashness but from the authority of others—not as much as I ought, but as much as I could,” etc.

Trombellius observes in a note that Claudius sometimes copies the *Expositions* of our Isidore, though occasionally with different wording and with the order somewhat altered. It is established that other authors of commentaries and homilies likewise benefited from this and other works of Isidore—namely Bede, the pseudonymous Eucherius of Lyon, author of the commentaries, Rabanus Maurus, Martin of León, and others [Col. 0421A].

### 25

From this method of interpretation, in which the expositions of the ancient Fathers were gathered here and there, arose the collections called *Catenae* on Sacred Scripture, which also appear in printed Bibles. The edition considered the best of this kind is the following:

> *The Holy Bible with the Ordinary Gloss, originally collected by Strabo of Fulda, but now enriched with new explanations of the Fathers, both Greek and Latin; with the passages for matters previously cited confusedly also indicated; and with the Postilla of Nicholas of Lyra, together with the additions of Paul of Burgundy and the replies of Matthias Thoringus, purged of countless errors and arranged in a more convenient order, by Fr. Francis Feuardent of the Order of Friars Minor, John Dadreus, and James de Cuilly, doctors of theology of Paris. Lyon, 1590, six folio volumes.*

Feuardent, in his dedicatory letter to Sixtus V, names Ambrose of Laon—whom others call Anselm—as the author of the ordinary and interlinear gloss after Strabo of Fulda. Following Jerome’s prologues are the introductory sections of the ordinary gloss on Genesis. After others, Isidore and Bede are cited under the mystical sense.

The beginnings of the human race, with which it began to enjoy the light itself, are suitably compared with the first day, on which God made light. And this age should be considered like the infancy of the entire age of the universe, etc. In chapter 1 of Genesis, at the words “And the Spirit of the Lord was borne over the waters,” Isidore is cited:

> “That is, the wavering hearts that had lost the tranquillity of the mind because the Spirit did not rest upon them,” etc.

In the same way, Isidore’s *Expositions* are inserted into the first books of Sacred Scripture, including the four Books of Kings. Isidore is also cited in connection with the Book of Job, but only certain words of his are brought forward, from the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*.

### 26

There are many handwritten codices in which such *Catenae* of the Fathers are preserved—namely, the Holy Bible, or certain parts of it, with scholia or glosses from the commentaries of the Fathers, specifically including Isidore’s. Blandinius, in volume I of the *Latin Codices of the Medicean Laurentian Library*, plut. 16, no. 38, describes a thirteenth-century codex of Deuteronomy with scholia whose authors are Rabanus . . . Isidore, etc. In the same place, plut. 17 [Col. 0421D], no. 14, there is a twelfth-century codex of Exodus with a commentary from the works of Rabanus . . . Isidore, etc.; and no. 17 contains Leviticus with commentaries by Hesychius . . . Isidore, etc. In volume IV, plut. 9, Codex 3 of Santa Croce, on parchment and from the fourteenth century, he likewise reports *Postillae of Various Holy Fathers on the Octateuch*, including those of Ambrose, Isidore, etc.

### 27

Genesis and Exodus with the glosses of the ancients—Jerome, Isidore, Strabo, etc.—are found in parchment Vatican-Palatine Codex 59, approximately from the fourteenth century. Isidore’s gloss begins:

> “The beginnings of the human race, with which it began to enjoy this light, are suitably compared with the first day, on which God made light,” etc.
