Parchment Vatican-Palatine Codex 60, from approximately the same period, presents Leviticus, Numbers [Col. 0422A], and Deuteronomy with the ordinary gloss, etc. Isidore begins:

> “Every variety of sacrifices prefigured the sacrifice of Christ,” etc.

These and other passages from Isidore’s commentaries, brought forward under his name in the *Catenae*, have been freely taken from them, not copied word for word. Isidore’s *Exposition of Leviticus* begins as follows:

> “The following book, Leviticus, explains the varieties of sacrifices, whose type bore the image of Christ’s Passion.”

### 28

The old Vatican Library offers us several codices of this kind. Codex 52 contains Genesis with expositions by the Fathers—Isidore, Jerome, Augustine, Bede, and Gregory—and with moral, interlinear, and other glosses. Codex 54 contains Genesis and Exodus with expositions by Isidore, etc., and Strabo, together with mystical, allegorical, and interlinear glosses. Codices [Col. 0422B] 55 and 56 contain the same, with Isidore’s expositions, etc. Codices 57 and 58 contain Exodus with Isidore’s expositions, etc. Likewise, Codices 59, 60 through 66, record Isidore’s expositions either on Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy, Joshua, Judges, or the Books of Kings.

### 29

Commentaries by Isidore survive on all these books of Sacred Scripture, from which scholia, glosses, or expositions were excerpted to form the *Catenae* of the Fathers. But Vatican Codex 107 contains the prophecies of Ezekiel with an exposition by Jerome, Gregory, Isidore, etc. Other codices likewise mention Isidore’s *Expositions* on other books of Sacred Scripture; but, as I shall explain more distinctly shortly, only certain words of Isidore are taken from various of his minor works [Col. 0422C] to explain one passage or another.

### 30

Here is the place to ask whether Isidore expounded all the books of the Old and New Testaments [538], and whether, besides those commentaries commonly preferred by the editions, others exist somewhere. From Braulio and Ildefonsus we can by no means demonstrate that Isidore composed continuous commentaries on the whole of Sacred Scripture.

Regarding the Old Testament, Bayerius produces two authorities: Sigebert of Gembloux and, before him—as he thinks—Honorius of Autun. He should have said that Sigebert was earlier than Honorius; for Sigebert is said to have died in 1113, whereas Honorius flourished around the year 1120. Sigebert says:

> “He runs through the whole Old Testament by explaining it simply.”

Honorius says:

> “He expounded the whole Old Testament in two ways, historically and allegorically.”

Trithemius, however, enumerates all the books of the Old and New Testaments individually and testifies that Isidore published commentaries on all of them, as you may reread above in chapter 47. Hence, it seems, Eisengreinius praised Isidore’s commentaries on the Gospels and the Pauline Epistles as highly learned [Col. 0422D].

### 31

Nicholas Antonius thinks that Trithemius’s words may refer to the book of *Prologues*, or *Expositions of the Mystical Sacraments*, and for this purpose he cites Ambrosius Morales, Bellarmine, and Padilla. But Trithemius most certainly distinguished the *Prologues* and the *Expositions* that survive from the *Expositions* on the other books of the Old and New Testaments. It is therefore more reasonable to believe that Trithemius asserted this partly [Col. 0423A] because he was influenced by the authority of Sigebert and Honorius, and partly because some trace of literal commentaries on the whole of Scripture appears in the prologue to the allegorical exposition of Genesis:

> “And because long ago the whole discourse was composed by us according to the letter, it is necessary that the allegorical sense follow upon the foundation of the history.”

Grialius complains in a note about the loss of this literal commentary, unless, he says, it is what is called the ordinary gloss.

### 32

Nicholas Antonius replies that the ordinary gloss is commonly attributed to Strabo of Fulda. He continues:

> “Perhaps we understand these words of Isidore not incorrectly in this way: that he had the Holy Bible written by his scribes—that is, the text of the sacred books—and at the end of each chapter or section he appended these mystical expositions of his own, like a gloss.”

By this, he seems to refer to the words at the beginning of chapter 1:

> “We read how the creature of heaven and earth was historically created from the beginning of the principle; but let us understand how it is received spiritually in the Church by the teachers.”

But apart from the fact that these very words of chapter 1 can quite suitably be referred also to the literal commentary [539], Isidore certainly asserts in the prologue that he had long ago composed the entire discourse according to the letter. Consequently, it can scarcely be understood that he appended his *Expositions* at the end of each chapter or section like a gloss, if the discourse already composed according to the letter was itself the text of the sacred Bibles written by Isidore’s scribes. Moreover, since an explanation of the literal sense must precede an explanation of the mystical sense, when Isidore says, “It is necessary that the allegorical sense follow upon the foundation of the history,” he clearly means that in the foundation of the history not only the letters of the text preceded but also the exposition of the literal sense.

### 33

Isidore often distinguishes and explains the different senses in which Sacred Scripture is to be understood. He states explicitly in book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 18:

> “The divine Law is to be understood in three ways: first, historically; second, tropologically; third, mystically. Historically, according to the letter; tropologically, according to moral knowledge; mystically, according to spiritual understanding. Therefore one must hold the faith historically in such a way that we must also interpret it morally and understand it spiritually.”

There can scarcely be any doubt, therefore, that before Isidore undertook to expound the other senses of Sacred Scripture, he explained the literal sense, and that he indicated this very thing when he said that the whole discourse had been composed by him according to the letter, after which the allegorical sense necessarily followed.

### 34

Grialius’s conjecture about the ordinary gloss could have some foundation in Sigebert’s words:

> “He runs through it by explaining it simply.”

But since there could have been—and in fact are—other glosses similar to the one called ordinary, we need not concern ourselves greatly with the ordinary gloss. It will be enough if Isidore ran through Sacred Scripture with a simple exposition of glosses.

Scholars are sufficiently agreed about the ordinary gloss that Walafrid Strabo was its author, or at least that he received it from the teaching of Rabanus Maurus. Editions of these works are presented in volume V of the *Literary History of France*, p. 62. Since Rabanus, Walafrid’s teacher, was a devoted student of Isidore and compiled his writings, we can readily understand that much in the ordinary gloss was drawn from Isidore’s storehouse. In favor of Rabanus as the author of the gloss is Notker Balbulus, chapter 4 of *On Illustrious Men*:

> “If you want little glosses on the whole of Divine Scripture, Rabanus, archbishop of Mainz, is sufficient.”

### 35

There are other glosses by Hugh of Saint-Cher; other marginal and interlinear glosses by Anselm of Laon; and another masterly gloss on the Psalms, or *major gloss*, by Peter Lombard. In the appendices to the commentaries of Menochius, glosses on the divine books by Robert of the Sorbonne have been published, in which we likewise find many excerpts from Isidore’s books.

Turneminius, who arranged for those glosses to be published, observes that Robert of the Sorbonne sometimes cites the texts of the Fathers differently from the way they are now read, and that he often found his reading both more probable and more convenient. Robert was a penitentiary or chaplain of Saint Louis, king of France, and laid the foundations of the Sorbonne College in the thirteenth century [Col. 0424B].

### 36

Ducange, in the preface to his *Glossary of Medieval and Later Latin*, no. 49, discusses various glosses—both unpublished and published—on the writings of both Testaments. Some, by uncertain authors, lie hidden in libraries; others name their authors. Among the latter, the glosses bearing this title in the codices of the monasteries of Corbie and Saint-Germain of Paris, and in the College of Navarre in Paris, are especially notable:

> “A little work on difficult biblical words by William Brito of the Order of Friars Minor, from the glosses of the saints.”

Brito died in 1356; perhaps the *Synonyma* published at Paris in 1508 are also his. Among the biblical glosses Ducange mentions the book entitled *Mammotrectus*. The author reveals the reason and etymology of this name in the prologue:

> “And because such a course resembles the practice of a teacher who directs the steps of little children, it can be called *Mammotrectus*.”

The author perhaps wrote, or intended to write, *Mammothreptus*, from the Greek μαμμόθρεπτος. This book is attributed to Marchesinus of the Order of Friars Minor, who lived around the year 1300 or, as others wish, around 1450. The work was printed at Mainz, at the very beginnings of printing, in 1470 by Peter Schöffer of Gernsheim.

### 37

If I say that Isidore opened the way for the production of biblical glosses of this kind [Col. 0424D], there will certainly be no shortage of plausible reasons by which to demonstrate it. Royal-Vatican Codex 310, from approximately the ninth century, gives the following title among other works of Isidore:

> “Here begin glosses composed from the New and Old Testament, or from the *Etymologies*, spiritually.”

Perhaps *specially* should be read instead of *spiritually*, since the two adverbs are usually written with the same abbreviation of letters, as Mariana observes in a note on chapter 3 of book I of Isidore’s *Against the Jews*.

There is a very extensive glossary, beginning:

> “Abavus, the father of one’s great-grandfather, that is, the grandfather of one’s grandfather. *Abba*, father. It is a Syriac word.”

It ends:

> “Zizania, darnel.”

Certain items occur that are found neither in Isidore’s *Etymologies* nor among biblical vocabulary, such as:

> “Abasu, *infima domus* (‘the lowest house’),”

instead of which other glossaries have:

> “Abaso, the lowest house.”

> “Abusitatus, less well equipped in knowledge.”  
> “Adverruncat, he makes very much true.”  
> “Altruncat, he turns away, alienates.”

### 38

Glosses arranged according to the books of Sacred Scripture, which I found after the *Etymologies* in old manuscript Codex 1 of the Vatican Archives, described in chapter 107, can much more probably be attributed to Isidore. The end of the *Etymologies* and the beginning of the glosses are missing, and therefore it cannot be discovered whether the glosses originally bore the author’s name.

But both the glosses and the etymologies were written in the same ancient hand. The glosses extend only as far as chapter 3 of the Second Book of Kings, either because the scribe neglected to copy the rest or because he encountered a mutilated exemplar. The title of a book listed in the twelfth-century catalogue of Göttweig, discussed in chapter 46, no. 8, could certainly be applied to these glosses—namely, *Isidore briefly on the whole library*, that is, on the whole of Sacred Scripture, as I then interpreted it.

I intend to place these glosses, although incomplete, among Isidore’s doubtful works. For, apart from the fact that many things in them are certainly Isidorian, several considerations suggest that they belong to Isidore’s literal exposition. Among these is the fact that many words are explained in them which will not easily be found in other Bibles, except in the Gothic Toledan Bibles with Isidore’s prologues—Bibles which Burrielius, in his letter to Don Pedro de Castro, thought had been arranged and organized by Isidore himself. The oldest edition of the Toledan Bibles does indeed derive from copies of Jerome’s version that Jerome himself sent to Spain [Col. 0425C], as I shall relate more fully in chapter 87.

### 39

I shall give some examples from the various readings of the same Toledan exemplar edited by Blanchinus in the *Vindications of the Latin Vulgate Edition*. In Genesis chapter 35, verse 5, our Vulgate reads:

> “They did not dare to pursue those who were departing.”

The Gothic Toledan exemplar reads:

> “Those who were yielding.”

The glossator has:

> “Obeying.”

Augustine, *Questions on Genesis*, question 112:

> “And they did not overtake the sons of Israel.”

In Genesis chapter 47, verse 11, our Vulgate reads:

> “In the best part of the land.”

The ancient version:

> “In the best land.”

The Toledan Bible:

> “In the best soil of the land.”

The glossator likewise reads: “in the best soil of the land.” But perhaps he distinguished the phrase as “in the best of the land, the soil of Ramesses”; for the ancient version reads, “in the best land, in the land of Ramessem.”

There are many variant readings of this kind that our glosses share with the Gothic Toledan Bibles [Col. 0425D]. You will search for them in vain either in Jerome’s Vulgate version as it is now circulated, or in the ancient version, or in the various versions that Peter Sabatier collected with the greatest care from the Holy Fathers. I shall note these distinctive readings individually in the notes to the glosses.

### 40

Similar biblical glosses are found in Royal-Vatican Codex 215, perhaps written in the time of Charlemagne, Carloman, and Louis. They are mentioned at the end of the continuation of Isidore’s Chronicle; concerning Charles it says:

> “The thirty-seventh year of whose reign is now being celebrated.”

The glosses on Genesis begin as follows:

> “Here begins the Book of Genesis.  
> In the beginning—in the order of created things.  
> Heaven and earth—unformed matter, from which heavenly and earthly things were formed.  
> Empty—useless.  
> The Spirit of God was borne over it—that is, Providence, in the manner in which he created all things.”

Glosses on Jerome’s prologue precede these, but they are written in fading letters and can scarcely be read. Although these glosses often agree with the glosses to be published from the Vatican Archives Codex, they nevertheless more frequently differ from them.

### 41

Codex 202 of the old Vatican Library, which I shall describe in chapter 93, contains sayings of the lord Isidore “on the Book of Genesis according to the letter.” As I shall explain then, these are not found in the allegorical commentary and therefore may perhaps be a fragment of the literal commentary.

In Palatine Codex 275, which I shall discuss in chapter 102, among various literal expositions by other authors on certain passages of Sacred Scripture, there are also several interpretations by Isidore [Col. 0426B]. These do not belong to the moral commentaries that we possess and, considering the nature of the matter, come closer to literal commentaries.

### 42

Since certain commentaries on some books of Sacred Scripture are indicated in catalogues of manuscript codices, or are even circulated in printed editions, which, although marked with Isidore’s name, are not his—or about which there may rightly be doubt whether they are his—something must now be said about each of them.

Those things that can be attributed to Isidore from the editions of the Bibles with the ordinary gloss—whether in the Book of Job, Ezekiel, the twelve minor prophets, the four Gospels, the Pauline Epistles, or the Acts of the Apostles—are not drawn from his particular commentaries on these books [543], but from opinions and expositions found in various works of his, or works attributed to him.

### 43

After the explanation of the divine law’s history—a title by which the *Expositions of the Sacraments of Secrets* are called in Vatican Codex 627, which I shall catalogue in chapter 94—there follows in the same Codex a work without title or author’s name, beginning:

> “Whoever speaks about God must necessarily take care,” etc.

In the inventory of the Vatican Library it is entitled *Isidore’s Interpretation of Job*. But in reality it is neither an interpretation of Job nor a commentary on Job, but certain *Sentences* and more extensive commentaries on several different passages of Sacred Scripture. Nor is there any indication or reason why this miscellaneous work should be attributed to Isidore. It also appears to have been written in a different script from Isidore’s preceding commentaries [Col. 0426D], although from approximately the same period, namely the twelfth century.

### 44

Since the words placed first are taken from the dedicatory letter of Gregory the Great to Saint Leander, to whom he dedicated his exposition of the Book of Job, perhaps someone derived from this the title *Interpretation of Job*. We may also suspect that this is the work mentioned in Braulio’s fuller, or interpolated, preliminary notice concerning Isidore’s books:

> “At the request of Pope Gregory the Blessed, he abridged the books of the *Moralia* in concise form.”

Taio, in chapter 22 of book II of the *Sentences*, entitled *On the Interpreters of Divine Scripture*, begins with the same words of Gregory:

> “Whoever speaks about God must necessarily take care to admire whatever instructs the morals of the hearers [Col. 0427A],” etc.

It therefore appears that the work in this Codex is a collection of *Sentences*, especially from the books of Saint Gregory; as I glance through the Codex, I recognize his words. At the beginning, as I said, there is no title, but as the work proceeds, on page 127, the title *Exposition* is added without anything further. It ends:

> “And so those who do not cease to weep over their sins, but again commit sins for which they must weep, are washed, yet are by no means clean.”

Some further similar material follows in a smaller script; the work nevertheless appears to be incomplete.

### 45

Grialius added to the other works of Isidore an *Exposition on the Song of Songs*, found by Cyprian Suarez in only one manuscript and attributed to Isidore on the basis of Braulio’s interpolated, or fuller, preliminary notice, although the authorship was not clear to him, as we saw in his preface.

But when he adds that the words of the fuller preliminary notice—“He elucidated the Song of Songs with a fluent exposition”—do not fit a very brief exposition, it should be observed that in Braulio’s fuller preliminary notice among the Bollandists, chapter 11 of the *Life of Saint Isidore*, the reading is *second exposition*, not *fluent exposition*. This may have been intended to distinguish it from another exposition on the Song of Songs, which is published among the works of Saint Gregory the Great, as I shall now say.

Fabricius, in the *Old Latin Library*, book III, chapter 16, no. 12, lists among the spurious works of Cassiodorus an *Exposition on the Song of Songs*, published at Freiburg in 1538 in folio together with Aponius’s *Commentary on the Song of Songs*, and in Garetius’s edition of Cassiodorus. He says:

> “A compendium of it occurs among the works of Isidore of Seville.”

That is, Breulius transferred it into his own edition from the royal Madrid edition. Garetius, in his preface to the works of Cassiodorus, praises that spurious exposition of Cassiodorus and correctly observes that the exposition attributed to Isidore is its abridgment.

This abridgment may be thought to have been made by some Spaniard, because the words “Voice of the Church, Voice of Christ” are inserted, as in the Gothic Toledan Bibles: “Voice of the Church, Voice of Christ.” Zaccaria had assigned the *Exposition on the Song of Songs* a place among the works spuriously attributed to Isidore.

### 46

A fuller *Exposition on the Song of Songs* exists among the works of Gregory the Great, which, as Fabricius testifies in the *Medieval Library*, is attributed to our Isidore in certain codices. Perhaps this is the reason that in the recent edition of Isidore’s works, volume II, among the appendices, p. 50, a certain epigram on the Song of Songs is attributed to Isidore:

> “This man sang it,” etc.

Yet, as is stated there, this epigram was excerpted from a tenth-century codex or one beginning the eleventh, after an exposition—so the codex says—of Blessed Bishop Isidore on the Song of Songs.

I do not know whether the brief exposition on the Song of Songs mentioned above is intended, or another, fuller one, which most people attribute to Saint Gregory the Great. Placcius, however, under “Gregory I, Roman pontiff,” states from Coco, p. 410, and Pamelius that Gregory’s commentary on the Song of Songs is attributed to Isidore in all manuscripts.

In old Vatican Codex 650, after this very commentary on the Song of Songs—which is now usually attributed to Gregory the Great and is said to be Isidore’s in some or many codices—the same epigram is found. We shall present it corrected from this Codex among Isidore’s other doubtful poems.

The commentary in our Vatican Codex bears no author’s name [Col. 0428A]; but the work of the most learned Maurists has already established that it should not be taken away from Gregory. All these expositions are distinct from the exposition of Justus of Urgell on the Song of Songs, which Isidore mentions in chapter 34 of *On Illustrious Men*. In that work too, as in the Gothic Bibles, the words “Voice of the Church, Voice of Christ” are repeated. On this, compare the *Acts of the Saints*, volume VI, p. 773.

### 47

Fabricius likewise reports in the place cited that an *Explanation of the Prophet Daniel*, and one on Susanna, are preserved under Isidore’s name in a manuscript in the Leiden library, according to the Catalogue, p. 329. We cannot judge whether it is the work of another author or some fragment from Isidore’s works.

### 48

Bandinius lists the *Postillae of Brother Landulph of Naples on the Gospels*, in which the authority of Isidore is cited along with that of other Fathers, in volume IV, plut. 36, Santa Croce Codex 5, on parchment and from the fourteenth century. He suspects the compiler to have been Landulph, or Landenulph, of the Order of Friars Minor, a student of Scotus and archbishop of Amalfi in 1330.

Isidore’s explanations could easily have been drawn from various of his works, in which Gospel words often occur and are explained. In Braulio’s interpolated preliminary notice we read:

> “He labored with no small diligence on an exposition of the books of Moses, the Psalter, and the four Gospels.”

In chapter 104 I shall describe Urbinate Codex 11, which contains a French version of a *Catena of the Fathers on the Gospels*, from Isidore and others. In the *Catalogue of the Manuscript Codices of the Sforza Library*, preserved in the Vatican Ottobonian Library under no. 2355, p. 3, there is listed an *Exposition on the Gospel of Luke from the Fathers, Isidore, etc.*, a sufficiently ancient parchment manuscript.

49. I also find in Bandini some mention of an Exposition of Isidore on Paul’s Epistle to Philemon. For in vol. IV, Plut. 34, Cod. 7 of S. Croce, a parchment manuscript of the thirteenth century, in large quarto, he says that there is a lectionary of saints. The Fathers from whom the readings were excerpted are named: Alcuin, etc.; Pope Damasus on John; and, in the *Catalogue of Pontifical Writers*, Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo . . . Isidore, in the *Sermons*, and on the Epistle to Philemon. *Against the Jews* . . . Peter Comestor, etc. In the index it is more clearly read: “on the Epistle to Philemon, and against the Jews.” In Isidore’s works [Col. 0428D], and in the index of passages of Sacred Scripture compiled by Breulius, I do not see the Epistle to Philemon cited even once.

50. It remains for me to speak about the Apocalypse, concerning which we can infer that Isidore published commentaries from the preface of Beatus 546 to his own commentaries on the Apocalypse, published at Madrid in 1770 by the work of Enrique Flórez. Beatus, who vigorously opposed the errors of Elipandus in the eighth century, says in the preface to his commentary on the Apocalypse that he gathered his material from Jerome, Augustine, Ambrose, Fulgentius, Gregory, Tichonius, Irenaeus, Victorinus, Apringius, and Isidore. This proves only that Beatus inserted into his commentary certain interpretations of Isidore taken from various works of his.

Some have falsely believed that this commentary is the very work which Isidore says was composed by Apringius in ch. 30 of *On Illustrious Men*. Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca manuscriptorum* [Col. 0429A], among the Codices Sangermanenses, names Cod. 255, “Isidore on the Pentateuch and Apocalypse.” What this may be, we cannot determine.

To understand how familiar Beatus was with Isidore’s works, one should note that he says he inserts the sayings of the Fathers, “so that,” he says, “our discourse might be strengthened by the opinions of the Fathers.” These words conclude Book II of Isidore’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in many manuscripts. Beatus adds that he dedicates the work to Etherius, “so that,” he says, “I may make him, as my companion in religion, a co-heir of my labor.” Thus Isidore writes in the dedicatory letter of his books *Against the Jews* to his sister Florentina: “So that I may make her, as my companion in blood, a co-heir of my labor.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. Isidore’s Two Books against the Jews, Addressed to His Sister Florentina, on the Catholic Faith from the Old and New Testaments. Editions, Manuscripts, and Translations.

[Col. 0429B]

1. These two books are given different titles by different authors. In the Bignaean edition the title is: “Of Blessed Isidore the Younger, archbishop of Seville, to his sister Florentina, on the birth of the Lord, his passion and resurrection, his kingdom and judgment.” For the second book, *On the Calling of the Nations*, Breulius followed Bignaeus, as he usually does.

Nicolaus Antonius reports an edition printed at Venice in 1483, in quarto, by Peter Loslein, with the title “Isidore against the Jews.” In it only the first of the two books is found, mutilated and differing in many respects. Some blasphemous Jewish tales about Christ and Mary, drawn from the books of the Talmud, are appended; there was no need at all to publish them.

Fabricius, however, states in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi* [Col. 0429C] that Book II, *On the Calling of the Nations*, together with the preceding book, *On the Birth of the Lord*, etc., constitutes the two books *Against the Jews* published at Venice in 1483, in quarto; or *Against the Wickedness of the Jews*, published at Hagenau in 1529, in quarto, by Johann Secerius; at Venice in 1584; and in the *Ocean of Law*, or *Treatise of Treatises*, vol. XIV, p. 23. In this collection the title is: “A Treatise of Isidore, bishop of Seville, against the Jews.”

I described the Hagenau edition in ch. 60, no. 8. The final chapter of Book I is entitled “Conclusion of the Work” in the table of chapters of that edition, but in the text it is “Epilogue of the Work.”

2. The Venetian edition of 1483 praised by Nicolaus Antonius and Fabricius may perhaps be the one preserved in the Alexandrian Library of Wisdom at Rome. It begins: “Isidore against the Jews. To the lady and beloved sister Florentia, Isidore” [Col. 0429D]. “Certain things which, in various ways,” etc.

This is the first book against the Jews. The chapters are not numbered. The last is: “That the Jews, blinded, ought to have denied Christ, and all that had been prophesied concerning Christ.” It ends: “We declare his kingdom and judgment.” In the Madrid edition: “We have declared.”

The edition continues: “See the blindness of the Jews contained in their Talmud.” It concludes: “Here ends the little book of the lord Isidore, bishop, on the Catholic Faith and the New and Old Testament, published against the impious Jews, who, led by sacrilegious blindness, wrote in their Talmud,” etc. Certain old-womanish Jewish tales are explained. Then follow the testimony of Josephus the Hebrew and Pilate’s letter about Christ. At the end are some excerpts from the readings for the office of blessed Isidore: “A wondrous thing: on a certain night of the Lord’s nativity,” etc.

[Col. 0430A]

3. In these readings it is related that, after Leovigild’s death, blessed Isidore, publicly reproving the heresy in question, yearned to attain the palm of martyrdom. Then, where Roderic of Cerrato says of St. Leander “I do not know, or it is unknown, by what omen he was anticipated,” here one reads: “It is unknown by what spirit he was led.” Compare ch. 14.

The edition is a small quarto, in a sufficiently elegant Roman type. The copy in the Alexandrian Library has its first page decorated with red and gold paintings. Neither the place nor the year of publication appears. In the catalogue, or inventory, of the Alexandrian Library it is assigned to the year 1483 and to the printer Peter Loslein; but, in my opinion, this is for no other reason than that four books *On Contempt of the World* are bound together in the same volume. In this edition they are attributed to Jean Gerson, chancellor of Paris, and were printed in a very different type at Venice in 1483 by Peter 548 Loslein of Langecen.

Jean-Baptiste Audiffredi, in his work *On Roman Editions of the Fifteenth Century*, p. 356, mentions this edition, which he says is preserved in the private library of our most holy lord Pius VI and in the Vallicelliana. But he says that it may not be Roman. Nicolaus Antonius, relying on the catalogue of the Alexandrian Library, named Peter Loslein as the printer and Venice as the place of publication.

4. In these two books Isidore refutes the Jews. Perhaps following his example, Julian of Toledo entitled his three books *The Sixth Age of Demonstration*, or *On Christ’s Coming against the Jews*. Likewise, among the ancients, Rabanus Maurus and Agobard, or Amulo of Lyon, wrote against the Jews; Fabricius should be consulted concerning them [Col. 0430C].

Among the works of certain ancient Fathers published by Stevartius at Ingolstadt in 1616, p. 399, the names of those who wrote against the Jews are listed, although our Isidore is omitted, even though he should have been listed first. Thomasinus reports that in the Venetian library of St. Antony there is preserved a very ancient Codex entitled “St. Isidore against the Jews.”

Others, however, give other titles. In ch. 46 this work was identified from the catalogue of the monastery of St. Nazarius at Laurissa as *On the Birth of the Lord*. Perhaps it is not different from the work called in the *Monasticum Anglicanum* “Isidore’s Book on the Miracles of Christ,” and in the *Chronicle of Fontenelle* “Isidore’s Book of Testimonies concerning Christ and the Church,” cited in ch. 46.

For the Zaccarian manuscripts, compare ch. 43. In them this same work is sometimes called *Against the Jews*, or *Against the Jews concerning Christ*; sometimes *The Catholic Faith*; sometimes *On the Lord’s Passion*; and sometimes *The Testimonies of the Prophets concerning Christ*.

5. Juan de Mariana, who appended brief but, as Nicolaus Antonius says, exceedingly learned notes to the Madrid edition of these two books, took the title from two Gothic manuscripts, which, as Mariana then stated, were known to have been copied six hundred years earlier, since the five other manuscripts he had obtained differed greatly. The title of the Gothic manuscripts is:

“On the Catholic Faith from the Old and New Testament against the Jews, addressed to his sister Florentina.”

In his notes Mariana names two manuscripts from Tarragona, a larger and a smaller one, on which he chiefly relied, and one from Seville [Col. 0431A]; he says nothing about the others he saw.

He makes no mention whatsoever of a certain addition appended at the end of Book II, after the words “in which he dwells forever,” in the Bignaean and Breulian editions. It concerns the *Forms of Spiritual Understanding*, about which I shall speak in ch. 86. Such an addition is also absent from our manuscripts.

Nicolaus Antonius states that the title of the work agrees with that of the Gothic manuscripts and with the oldest manuscript copy in the Barberini Library. Compare the excerpts from the Zaccarian papers in ch. 43. For I think it is the same Codex said to belong to the eighth century; but the title of the Codex differs from the one Mariana gives. Perhaps Nicolaus Antonius is referring to a later title, for shortly afterward he says that the title of Barberini Codex no. 230 had been worn away by age [Col. 0431B].

Bayerius, in his notes to the *Bibliotheca* of Nicolaus Antonius, testifies that one manuscript of this work is preserved in the Escorial Library, but gives no information about its title.

6. Perhaps this is the Codex which Rodriguez describes in vol. II of his *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 324, among the other manuscripts of the Escorial Library. It is a parchment octavo manuscript of the fourteenth century. Among other works by different authors it contains Book I *Against the Jews*, very different from the printed text, as Rodriguez infers from the title of the work and of its chapters.

The title of the work is:

“Here begins Isidore’s book against pagans, heretics, and Jews. To the lord and beloved sister Florencia.”

The prologue begins in a corrupt form:

“Certain things which God pronounced in the books of the Old Testament concerning the birth of the Lord and our Savior according to his divinity, or concerning his incarnation, etc., I shall make a co-heir of my labor. Let us therefore begin with his birth, by which he was begotten by the Father before the ages. That Christ is the Son of God, begotten by God the Father.”

The other chapters proceed in the same way, but are divided differently from the arrangement found in Grialius.

7. There are also, among the chapters themselves, several titles expressing a new subject. Thus, after the first six chapters:

“Let us begin to speak about his name.”

After another chapter:

“On Christ’s lineage according to the flesh, because he derived his origin from the seed of Abraham.”

After three more:

“On the place where he was to be born, in Bethlehem, according to the prophecies.”

After another four:

“On Christ’s virtues and miracles according to the prophets,” etc.

This title perhaps gave occasion to those who praised Isidore’s work *On the Miracles of Christ*. Although Rodriguez considers this manuscript’s book very different from the printed version, I believe that the difference lies only in the division of the books and in certain variant readings, which are common in all manuscript Codices, even the best ones.

8. Most manuscripts and printed editions 550 agree on the name of Isidore’s sister as Florentina. In some manuscript martyrologies she is called Florentiana. Marinus the Sicilian incorrectly called her Flora; the first edition of 1483 likewise incorrectly called her Florentia, as Nicolaus Antonius says.

It must nevertheless be admitted that the name Florentia also appears in many manuscripts, and is likewise found in many martyrologies, as well as in the Breviary and even in the Mozarabic Missal among the more recent offices. Nor is it perhaps unreasonable that Florentia was accustomed to be called by either name—Florentia or Florentina—or by both together, Florentia Florentina, just as Claudius Claudianus and similar names existed among the Romans [Col. 0432A].

Concerning this most holy sister of Isidore, one may consult chs. 2, 17, and 18.

9. We know that what happened with certain other works of Isidore also happened with these two books *Against the Jews*: they were translated into vernacular languages.

Fabricius reports in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi* that Johann Philipp Palthenius of Greifswald published, together with Tatian’s *Harmony*, a notable fragment of an ancient Theodisc translation of this work, from a Colbertine Codex which Baluzius had supplied, and enlarged and illustrated it with a substantial glossary. The work was published in quarto in 1706 and reprinted in vol. I of Schilter’s *Thesaurus of Teutonic Antiquities*, Ulm, 1727, in folio.

In Palthenius’s edition Isidore’s fragment appears on p. 239 and begins: “And the cardinal points of the earth,” etc. [Col. 0432B] The title of the following chapter is: “That Christ is God and Lord: After the mystery of Christ’s divine birth had been declared,” etc.

The final chapter is: “That Christ was born from David’s stock: Behold from which tribe.” It ends:

“This passage reads thus in Hebrew: ‘And his resting-place shall be glorious.’ Certainly, because when he died his flesh did not see corruption, according to the saying of the Psalm: ‘Nor will you allow your Holy One to see corruption.’”

Palthenius says in his preface that the script of the Theodisc fragment of Isidore is Merovingian, from the seventh century. Mabillon, in *De re diplomatica*, p. 49, says that such a fragment could be presented as the oldest monument of Teutonic antiquity of this kind.

It should be noted that in the Casanatense Index this Theodisc translation is described less accurately as having been made from Isidore’s “Sermon on the Birth, Passion, etc.” It belongs, in fact, to Book I *Against the Jews*, chs. 2, 3, etc.

10. Another translation of Isidore’s books *Against the Jews* into Italian is indicated in Vatican Codex 5420, a parchment manuscript which formerly belonged to the books of Francesco Peña of Spain, the celebrated dean of the Sacred Rota. See ch. 98, where I shall point out that it is not a translation of the two books, but only of the first, and that it has been abridged.

Its title is:

“Saint Isidore, teacher and bishop, confounds the Jews. To his sister, etc.”

11. The manuscript copies of the work *On the Catholic Faith against the Jews* that have come into our hands are the following.

Vatican Codex 939, to be described in ch. 95, contains only excerpts from this work. Vatican Codex 1268, also to be described in ch. 95, similarly contains certain testimonies extracted from Book I *On the Passion of Christ* [Col. 0432D].

In Vatican Codex 4327 these two books on Christ against the Jews are attributed to Isidore the Younger. See ch. 97. The same is true in Vatican Codex 4918, in the same chapter.

In Royal-Vatican Codex 421, to be discussed in ch. 100, there is a fragment of these books.

In Palatine Codex 278, to be discussed in ch. 102, these two books are preceded by the note:

“In this volume are contained the rejections of the Jews and the calling of the nations.”

The final chapter of Book I is called “Conclusion of the Work: Summary.” In Palatine Codex 279, in the same place, we read: “The book of holy and most blessed Isidore to Florentina,” etc. The final chapter of Book I is “Summary.” Book II is mutilated.

In Urbinate Codex 100, ch. 104, there is a “Preface, or Recapitulation, of the Catholic Faith, or Conclusion of the Work of Isidore, bishop of Seville” [Col. 0433A], followed by:

“To his holy sister Florentina, Isidore, bishop of Toledo,” etc.

I have already noted the error by which Isidore is falsely called bishop of Toledo; the same error occurs in other Codices in which the books *Against the Jews* are recorded.

In this Codex Book I is called *Against the Jews*, and Book II *On the Calling of the Nations*. In Ottobonian Codex 945, ch. 106, the books *Against the Jews* appear as in Vatican Codex 4918.

## CHAPTER LXVII. The Three Books of St. Isidore’s *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*. Editions and Manuscript Codices of This Work; the Spanish Translation. Julian of Toledo, Taio, Peter Lombard, and Other Writers of *Sentences* after Isidore. Whether a Fourth Book of *Sentences* Has Been Falsely Attributed to Isidore. Bayerius’s Learned Observations on This Fourth Book.

[Col. 0433B]

1. Braulio clearly identified these books: “The three books of *Sentences*, which he adorned with flowers from the moral works of Pope Gregory.”

Ildefonsus understood nothing else when he wrote of “the book of the *Sentences*,” that is, the work, Codex, or volume of the *Sentences*. For works commonly divided into several books were designated by the singular term “book.” In referring to this very work, Balbulus and others likewise called it the book of the *Sentences* together with Ildefonsus.

Nor should the learned Scipio Maffei have sought in Ildefonsus’s words a work different from the three books of the *Sentences*. He says in the *Bibliotheca of Verona Manuscripts*, p. 89, after the *History of Grace*, where he describes a Codex containing testimonies of Sacred Scripture distinct from the *Sentences*:

“This thought also occurred to me: that this work of Testimonies is being indicated when the *Sentences* of Isidore are praised by ancient writers. For this designation fits it much better than it does the books *On the Supreme Good*, which are also three, whereas Ildefonsus counts one book of *Sentences*.”

In the same way Ildefonsus calls the book *On the Kinds of Offices* a book, just as he calls the book of *Sentences*, although the former consists of two books; for he did not say that the *Sentences* consisted of one book.

2. The Eighth Council of Toledo explicitly cites, with great praise of Isidore, the second book of the *Sentences*, as Loaisa also observes in his note to the title of the book. Samson, abbot of Córdoba, in the ninth century, Book II, ch. 1 of his *Apologetic*, reports:

“For the eminent teacher Isidore, illustrious in merits and eloquence, says in the books of the *Sentences*: ‘God does not fill heaven and earth for that reason,’ etc.”

As for Loaisa’s statement that all manuscript Codices agree in the title *Sentences*: if he means all the oldest ones, I have likewise observed this in those I have seen. Yet I have encountered many that are not so ancient, which bear the title *On the Supreme Good*, as you may also observe in those I listed from the Zaccarian papers in ch. 43.

Nicolaus Antonius reports two examples bearing this same title: one formerly in the Paduan library of the Lateran Canons, and the other in the monastery of St. Francis in the Pincian district of Rome, which Morales mentions in his already published book *The Holy Journey*.

Bayerius identifies at least eight Codices of Isidore’s *Sentences* in the Escorial Library, three of them older than the year 1000; but he does not give their individual titles.

Ulricus Engelbertus of Strasbourg, a distinguished thirteenth-century theologian of the Order of Preachers, perhaps assigned the title *On the Supreme Good* to one of his major works from its subject matter. This manuscript is preserved in the Corsendonc Library, according to Valerius Andreas, *Bibliotheca Belgica Manuscripta*, II, p. 70.

In the inventory of the Vatican Library, Codex 131 bears the title:

“Six books of Ulric of Argentina, of the Order of St. Augustine, *On the Supreme Good* 553. 1. On the praise of the Scriptures,” etc.

I would believe this to be the same work that Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, attributes to Ulric of Argentina on the authority of Valerius Andreas, and records under the entry for Ulric Engelbertus of the Order of Preachers.

3. In the Zaccarian papers I find the beginning of a certain Italian version of Isidore’s *Sentences* described as follows:

“Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*. Ch. 1. The supreme good is God himself, because he is unchangeable and cannot in any way be corrupted,” etc.

It is not stated where this translation is preserved.

Fabricius believes that Sigebert calls the books of the *Sentences* the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. For the work attributed to Isidore under this title in the Bignaean edition, he says, has Gennadius of Marseille as its author.

Bayerius adds that Placcius, on the authority of Robertus Coco, p. 131, asserts that the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is wrongly attributed to blessed Isidore. Whether, he says, Placcius referred this to Isidore’s work of the *Sentences* is uncertain.

Indeed, I am certain that he is speaking of the *Book of Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which some attribute to Augustine, most to Gennadius of Marseille, some to Isidore, and—more correctly, as I shall say in its proper place—to Bracarius, bishop of Seville.

Elipandus, in his letter to the heretic Migetius, which Flórez first published in vol. V of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 543, praises these books as follows:

“Concerning these matters blessed Isidore, that eminent teacher, also speaks in his dogmas, saying: ‘The Scriptures of the heretics,’ etc.”

But Elipandus commonly calls various other works of Isidore, Ambrose, and others by the name “dogmas.”

4. Several councils mentioned in ch. 31, the collectors of canons, and other ancient ecclesiastical writers give the title *Sentences*, including Ratramnus, *On Predestination*, Book II; Jonas of Orléans, *On the Instruction of the Laity*, Book I, ch. 10; and the ancient catalogues of libraries in ch. 46, besides the writers *On Illustrious Men* whom I cited in ch. 47.

Some more recent writers, however, give both titles. Pastrengus, moreover, seems to mention two distinct works. Their oldest witness, Balbulus, a tenth-century writer, declares Isidore’s book of the *Sentences* to be exceedingly useful [Col. 0434D].

Two manuscript Codices appear to agree in the same title *Sentences*: Nicolaus Antonius reports, on the authority of Ambrosius Morales, that they are preserved in the monasteries of St. Facundus and of St. Isidore at León, together with others in the Ambrosian Library.

5. The older editions, however, title these three books *On the Supreme Good*. I discussed an old Italian edition, around the year 1470, of the work *On the Supreme Good* together with the *Etymologies* in ch. 54. There I also mentioned another similar Venetian edition of 1483 and another Venetian edition of 1493.

Fabricius praises an old duodecimo edition without place or year and cites Theophilus Sincerus’s *News concerning Old and Rare Books*.

[Col. 0435A]

6. Maittaire reports editions of the three books *On the Supreme Good* at Louvain, in quarto, by Johann of Westphalia, 1486, and at Paris, in octavo, by Pigouchet, 1491.

Thus, in vol. I, p. 475:

“Three books of Isidore of Seville *On the Supreme Good*, printed by me, Johann of Westphalia, in quarto, at the University of Louvain, 1486.”

And again, p. 536:

“Isidore *On the Supreme Good*, printed by Philippe Pigouchet.”

“P. Philippe Pigouchet with the emblem of the Pelican; E. G., that is, Enguilbert George, of Marnef,” etc.

7. Maittaire says that in 1493 an edition of the three books *On the Supreme Good* was produced at Paris in octavo and at Leipzig in quarto by Arnold of Cologne.

Orlandus reports it as follows: *On the Supreme Good*, Venice, 1494, by Bonetus Locatellus; and by the same printer in 1493, quarto; Leipzig, 1493.

8. The same work was published at Paris in 1495, in octavo, by Étienne Jehannot, in the Rue Saint-Jacques, on 27 August, [Col. 0435B] under the title “Isidore *On the Supreme Good*,” according to Maittaire.

9. The three books *On the Supreme Good* were also published at Paris by Jean Petit in 1519, in duodecimo, according to Nicolaus Antonius and Fabricius; and at Venice in 1533, according to Nicolaus Antonius and Gesner’s epitome.

10. Another Parisian edition was published by Jean Roigny in the Rue Saint-Jacques, under the Basilisk and the Four Elements, in 1538, with the title *On the Supreme Good*. It will be described more fully in the following chapter when its preface is presented.

11. Margarinus de la Bigne gave it the title *Sentences on the Supreme Good*, and in the index of works, *Sentences, or On the Supreme Good*. He says that he published the work after the revision of Jean Aleaume, doctor of the Sorbonne, adding a preface, namely the letter to Massona, which is found on the verso of p. 60 in vol. II.

This letter commonly precedes the books of the *Sentences* in many manuscripts, but improperly, as I shall explain in ch. 73 when I discuss the letter; Gratian too cited it as the preface to the books of the *Sentences*.

12. An edition of the same work followed, prepared and revised by Loaisa:

“Three books of the *Sentences* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, corrected and illustrated with notes by García Loaisa. Turin, at the press of John Baptist Bilaq, 1593, in quarto. Addressed to Philip, prince of Spain; 450 pages.”

In the same place and year:

“Chronicle of Don Isidore, archbishop of Seville, corrected and illustrated with notes by García de Loaisa, archdeacon of Guadalajara; in quarto, 96 pages, addressed to Philip II.”

This is Fabricius’s judgment concerning Loaisa’s notes in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*:

“They contain much learning; but it was wholly lacking in critical judgment when, on p. 483, Loaisa wrote: ‘In our own most ulcerated times, Oecolampadius’s volume against the sacrament of the Eucharist is attributed to Bertramus the priest, addressed to Charlemagne; Carolostadius’s work against images to Charlemagne himself; and a certain book of Calvin’s to Alcuin, Charlemagne’s teacher.’”

These words occur in the notes to Book III of the *Sentences*, ch. 12, p. 83, of the royal Madrid edition. Fabricius omitted what Loaisa immediately added in support of his statement: “As Sixtus learnedly noted in his *Bibliotheca*.”

Read again what I said about Ratramnus’s, or Bertram’s, work in ch. 30, no. 18. Nevertheless, I neither defend Sixtus on this account nor wish wholly to excuse Loaisa.

13. Since the books of the *Sentences* had not been properly printed at Turin, Loaisa undertook a second revision so that they might appear more accurately in the royal Madrid edition. Breulius too, at the end of his edition, inserted Loaisa’s notes together with others taken from the royal Madrid edition.

The Turin edition contains certain features absent from the Grialian and Breulian editions. In addition to the variant readings more frequently explained in the margin and notes, Loaisa distinguished the *Sentences* by numbered order and indicated in the margin the passages of the Fathers from which they were taken.

These marginal notes were likewise reproduced and added in the Breulian edition published at Cologne.

14. Isidore’s *Sentences* are not slightly commended by the fact that the Venerable Thomasius had decided to print the three books, together with other works, in his system of theological instruction, which he had planned from selected works of the ancient Fathers.

His *Catalogue of the Ancient Fathers’ Theological Institutions, which Clearly and Briefly Explain Theology, Whether Theoretical, Commonly Called Speculative, or Practical* was published. Among the other works were “the three books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*, of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, who died in 636.”

They belong to both branches of theology, especially practical theology, and are largely excerpted from the moral works of St. Gregory the Pope. They appear among the works of St. Isidore and were separately published by Gaspar—correct this to García—Loaisa.

Vezzosius, who carried out the plan of the Venerable Thomasius, observes this in his notes to the *Catalogue*:

“In the first edition of the *Catalogue*, through a scribal error, it was read that this holy bishop had four books of *Sentences*, although there are only three” [Col. 0436C].

All the other editions of the *Catalogue* preceding ours followed that error.

15. Vezzosius published four volumes of theological institutions under the following title:

“Institutions of Theology of the Ancient Fathers by the Venerable Joseph Maria Cardinal Thomasius, which plainly and briefly set forth theology, whether theoretical or practical. Revised and enlarged with notes by Antonius Franciscus Vezzosius, C.R. Rome, 1769. From the press of Marco Palearini; large quarto.”

Vezzosius prefaces the Isidorian work in vol. I, preface, no. 13:

“There are three writings of the most holy Fathers which constitute the fourth part of our work. The last of these is the three books of the *Sentences* of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, or, as others have written, Isidore the Younger, to distinguish him from another Isidore [Col. 0436D] who preceded him by one hundred years in age and held the bishopric of Córdoba.

“Those books, composed for the most part from the *Moralia* of Gregory the Great, after touching upon theoretical theology at the beginning, turn to that which directs conduct. We now give them reprinted according to the Paris edition of 1601, prepared by Jacques du Breul, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. We compared them, recording the variants in the margin of the page, with two other copies: one published by Margarin de la Bigne, a Parisian theologian, in 1580, and another at Turin in 1593 by García Loaisa, who adorned the same books with learned observations.”

16. Vezzosius appears to have erred in saying that Isidore of Córdoba lived one hundred years before Isidore of Seville, rather than two hundred. For, as he himself observes in his note to the title of Book I of the *Sentences*, it is established that Isidore of Córdoba flourished not long after the beginning of the fifth century after Christ.

But in truth it is not even sufficiently established that this Isidore of Córdoba ever existed.

As for what he says in these notes—that the Parisian editions, the Bignaean and Breulian, are considered more trustworthy by the consensus of learned men—this shows that he neither collated the royal Madrid edition nor knew what learned men thought of these three Isidorian editions.

Vezzosius further asserts that the editions of Margarinus and Loaisa are as alike as an egg is to an egg. This too is false [Col. 0437B]. Although Loaisa generally retains the Bignaean reading in the text, he frequently gives another reading in the margin and notes. He also adds in the margin the passages of the Fathers from which the *Sentences* were taken; this is found neither in the Bignaean edition nor in the first Breulian edition.

Vezzosius nevertheless printed the Breulian text, adding at the foot of the page variant readings from the Parisian Bignaean and Turin Loaisan editions, together with brief notes, which we too shall reprint.

17. These editions make sufficiently clear the esteem in which the books of the *Sentences* were always held [Col. 0437C]. The same is no less evident from manuscript copies, which frequently occur in libraries, and from other ancient monuments.

Claudius Castellanus reports in his notice to vol. I of his *Martyrology* that the custom became established in many churches of reading the works and *Sentences* of St. Isidore after the Martyrology.

Several manuscript copies have already been indicated in this chapter; others will now be briefly mentioned.

In ch. 61 a Florentine Codex of St. Croce containing the *Sentences* was described. Bandini, in vol. IV of the *Latin Codices of St. Croce*, Plut. 21, reports another Codex, no. 8: “Three books of the *Sentences*, preceded by a table of chapters. Then the *Dialogues* of St. Gregory the Great.”

The Codex is a square-format parchment manuscript of the eleventh century, with rubricated titles and initials, some of them decorated, as Bandini says.

In the same place, Codex 9: “Three books of the *Sentences*, as in the preceding Codex. Then the *Book of Exhortations* of St. Augustine.”

The Codex is a parchment folio manuscript of the eleventh century, written with the greatest care in a rounded and clear script, with rubricated titles and initials, some of them colored.

18. In Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. I, at the end of the first part, after the treatise *On the Grace and Virtue of the Mother of God* by Engelbertus, who died in 1331, the scribe’s subscription reads:

“Here ends Engelbertus, etc., written by the hand of the monk of the Throne of the Blessed Virgin and a priest of the Carthusian Order.”

In the margin: “Don Peter, later prior.”

It is added that he served as prior from the year 1395, wrote several works in elegant script on parchment, including Isidore *On the Supreme Good* in 1380, the *Collations of the Fathers*, and Conradus *On the Five Alleluias* [Col. 0438A].

It would be necessary to explain what “monk of the Throne of the Blessed Virgin” means. But in Ducange, even with the supplement, I find nothing suitable. Under the word *thronarius*, Ducange says that the term is suspect, and that perhaps it should be restored as *Centenariis* or *Officialibus*. But perhaps *thronus* and *thronarius* mean one who attends or serves at a throne; or *Thronus* may be the name of a monastery.

558 19. Rodriguez de Castro, vol. II of his *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 321, describes an Escorial Codex in II, c. 19, a folio manuscript of the fifteenth century, with chapter titles in red and initials either red or purple, containing the books of the *Sentences* in Spanish.

On the first folio is this note:

“This book was made by Saint Isidore, who was archbishop of Seville and a doctor.”

There follows a table of chapters: “First chapter, on the Supreme Good,” etc. All 140 chapters of the three books are indicated, without any division into books and under one continuous numerical order [Col. 0438B].

The work begins:

“God is the Supreme Good, for he is without change and without any corruption.”

It ends on fol. 109:

“But those we ought not to mourn, for paradise receives them into itself with great joy.”

“Here ends Isidore *On the Supreme Good*. Thanks be to God.”

20. Rodriguez says that the author of this translation was Alfonso Martínez de Talavera. Nicolaus Antonius, Book X, no. 324, mentions Alfonso Martínez of Toledo, who served in the chapel of King John II and is better known by the dignity of archpriest of Talavera than by his own name and that of his family.

But neither he nor Bayerius, in his notes, lists the Spanish translation of Isidore’s *Sentences* among Alfonso’s works.

21. There is another Escorial Codex in IV, f. 8, a parchment octavo manuscript, elegantly written by Diego de Astigia [Col. 0438C] in 1467. It contains:

“The *Treatise of Synonyms* of the most blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville.

“The *Treatise of the Sentences*, or *The Supreme Good*, of the same most blessed Isidore.

“The *Book on Conscience* of blessed Bernard, abbot.

“A sermon of the most blessed Augustine *On the Modesty of Women*.

“Another sermon of the same most blessed Augustine *On the Fire of Purgatory*.”

At the end is the following subscription:

“I, Diego de Astigia of the diocese of Seville, wrote this book. I completed and corrected it to the honor and glory of the most holy Trinity and of the most blessed Virgin Mary, and to the praise and memory of the most blessed Isidore, archbishop, at the command of my lord Juan Alfonso de Logroño, canon of the same church.

“On Thursday, the feast of Saint Fulgentius, the aforesaid Isidore’s brother, on the fifth day of January, in the year from the birth of the Lord 1467 [Col. 0438D].

“May Christ, the righteous one born of the Virgin, pardon me, and may the everlasting honor of him who is three and one be praised. Amen.”

22. Another Escurial Codex, in folio, apparently from the fourteenth century, on parchment, written in a large and elegant script, shelfmark III, R. 21, is incomplete. Its 559 titles are red, and its initials are in various colors. Another, likewise in folio, on paper, from the thirteenth century, with rubricated titles and initials ornamented in different colors, bears this inscription: “Saint Isidore of Spain, on Astronomy, or on the Nature of Things. Also, the Book of Sentences.” [Col. 0439A] Rodriguez likewise praises an Escurial Codex containing Isidore’s exposition of the Pentateuch and the work of the Sentences consisting of four books—that is, with a fourth book added to Isidore’s three genuine books, concerning which there will be discussion below.

23. Passing over the other manuscript Codices of the Sentences, mentioned in chapter 46 and elsewhere, I shall draw up a list of those which I myself saw in the Vatican Library or in other libraries of Rome. Vatican Codex 632, which I shall discuss in chapter 94, presents these three books under the title of the Sentences, preceded by a letter to Massona. Vatican Codex 633, which will likewise be examined there, retains from an old hand the inscription “of the Sentences,” and from a more recent hand “of the Supreme Good.” Vatican Codex 657 likewise bears the title “of the Supreme Good,” but was not written before the fifteenth century. Vatican Codex 5992 was written at the same period; I shall discuss it in chapter 98. It contains Book I of the Sentences and the beginning of Book II, under the first title “A Certain Theology,” and under a later one [Col. 0439B] “of the Supreme Good.”

In Regio-Vatican Codex 199, which I shall discuss in chapter 99, there is only the recent inscription: “Book of the Sentences of the Divine Isidore of Seville.” There, too, the old Regio-Vatican Codex 255 displays a peculiar title: “Here begins the Book of Spermologon of Isidore,” perhaps because the spermologus is a bird that gathers seeds, just as Isidore gathered the sentences of the Fathers. In Regio-Vatican Codex 1823 there are three books of the Sentences, mutilated at the beginning, as I shall say in chapter 101. In the same place, Regio-Vatican Codex 2093 contains three books of the Sentences under this title: “Chapters from the Book of the Sentences of the Lord Isidore.” The third book is incomplete.

In Palatine paper Codex 267, chapter 102, the work is entitled “On Ecclesiastical Instruction,” “On the Supreme Good,” and “Sentences,” and is divided into four books. In Pal. 280, on paper from the fifteenth century, chapter 102, the title is “Isidore on the Supreme Good.” The title of this book is “Isidore [Col. 0439C] the Spaniard in the Sentences.” In Pal. 602, chapter 103, the title is: “Three Books of the Sentences of Isidore, which, if examined attentively, are like general canons.” In Urbinate 106, which I shall discuss in chapter 104, perhaps from the fifteenth century, the work is entitled “On the Supreme Good,” with a preceding letter to Massona in place of a preface. At the end of Books II and III the title “of the Sentences” appears. In Urbinate 1504, on paper, chapter 104, the title is: “Isidore’s Book on the Supreme Good: these are three books of the Sentences.”

560 Excerpts from the Sentences occur in Ottobonian Codex 6, chapter 105. Others occur in Ottobonian 122, in the same place. In Ottobonian 128, approximately from the fourteenth century, the title is “Ysidorus on the Supreme Good,” without any division of the books by the first hand, and with a continuous numerical sequence of chapters. In Ottobonian 139, in the same place, there are fragments from these books. In Ottobonian 159, approximately from the fourteenth century, there are three books “on the [Col. 0439D] Supreme Good.” In Ottobonian 336, from the same period, chapter 105, there are “three books of the Sentences of Saint Isidore, Doctor of the Church.” In Ottobonian 508, chapter 106, approximately from the fourteenth century, there are “sentences excerpted from Isidore in the book on the Supreme Good.” In Ottobonian 1737, chapter 106, the recent title is “Isidore’s Books on God.” In chapter 107 I shall catalogue two Codices of the Sentences in the Angelica Library, another in the library of the Roman College, and another collated by me.

24. [Col. 0440A] Isidore appears to have been the first to propose, in these three books of the Sentences, a certain system of theological questions arranged in distinct classes. Peter Lombard imitated its title and purpose, thereby opening a clearer path for scholastic theology and acquiring the name “Master of the Sentences.” Perhaps Isidore himself would have preempted that name, had he not already become accustomed to being called by the more distinguished title derived from his work the Etymologies.

There had indeed existed before Isidore—leaving aside the books of Sentences among jurists—the Sentences of the Egyptian Fathers, by an unknown Greek author, translated by Martin, abbot of Dumium and bishop of Braga. Rosweyd published them in the appendices to the Lives of the Fathers, having received them from the Toledan library through Christopher de Castro, a theologian of the Society of Jesus and professor of sacred letters at Salamanca. These Sentences, however, present only certain spiritual sayings of monks, connected with one another by no arrangement. Nor is the collection of Sentences excerpted from [Col. 0440B] the works of Saint Augustine by Saint Prosper very different; I shall discuss it in chapter 83, no. 7.

If Isidore perhaps took the title for his own work from that source, he advanced the undertaking much further by arranging the topics in some order and assigning to their respective sections the statements of sacred Scripture and of the Fathers. What many say—that Isidore’s work consists for the most part of Gregory’s sentences—must be understood to mean that Isidore principally follows Gregory, although he also frequently cites the words of sacred Scripture and adheres to the opinions of several Fathers, including Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Eucherius, Cyprian, and others, as can be seen in Loaysa’s notes.

561 25. Since Isidore plainly provides the model which the Master of the Sentences certainly had before his eyes—for he praises Isidore’s books of the Sentences [Col. 0440C] and derives much from them—I do not know why Mabillon, followed also by some other Spaniards, asserted on page 317 of volume I of the Analecta that it seemed to him that Taio of Zaragoza was the first, after whose example others, together with Peter Lombard, composed collections of theological sentences of this kind. Schoettgenius confidently says in volume VI of Fabricius’s Bibliotheca medii aevi: “Thus Taio was the first to collect sentences, and in this very labor of composition he preceded Peter Lombard.”

Mabillon published in the volume of the Analecta just mentioned Taio’s preface to Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, concerning the five books of Sentences which Taio had collected from the works of Saint Gregory the Pope, together with the beginning of the work. He could therefore easily have recognized both that Taio himself composed his books of Sentences by following and imitating Isidore’s example, and that [Col. 0440D] Peter Lombard could have benefited far more from Isidore than from Taio.

In his preface to Quiricus, Taio says that he gathered and extracted from the sacred volumes—namely, from the books of the Sentences of the holy Pope Gregory of Rome—chapters divided into five little books, or rather enclosed within the text of the Codex. A little later he adds: “But because we were wholly unable to find in the little works of that same holy pope the chapters of certain titles needed to complete the subject, we took care to gather a few passages from the books of Saint Augustine, bishop.” But the Sentences of Isidore are much [Col. 0441A] more extensive and are confirmed by the testimony of a greater number of Fathers.

26. Taio’s five books of Sentences were published a few years ago at Madrid by Father Manuel Risco, the most learned continuator of the España Sagrada, in volume XXXI, beginning on page 171. They were taken from an old Gothic Codex of Saint Emilianus, and were preceded by Taio’s letter to Eugenius of Toledo, from Baluze, in which he speaks of another collection made by him from passages of Saint Gregory illuminating the Old and New Testaments, as well as by the preface to Quiricus and Quiricus’s reply.

The end of chapter 33 and the whole of chapter 34 of Book V are nevertheless missing, as Risco observes; indeed, chapter 35 is also absent, as is clear from a parchment copy of the same work from the fifteenth century, preserved in the Medicean Laurentian Library, Plut. 21, Codex 18, listed above in chapter 43. From it I have [Col. 0441B] had transcribed in my papers Taio’s preface to Quiricus, Quiricus’s letter to Taio, which is appended to the entire work, the table of chapters of the five books, and several chapters as specimens.

The titles of the chapters 562 differ somewhat from those in the printed edition. In Book III the manuscript index gives fifty-five chapters, whereas the edition contains only fifty-four; namely, the edition lacks the chapter on Widows, which is indicated in this manuscript after chapter 7, “On Married Persons.”

27. But when I had friends carefully inspect the manuscript Codex itself, I was informed that although the index does indeed record chapter 7, “On Married Persons,” it is entirely absent from the body of the work, and that only [Col. 0441C] fifty-four chapters are found, as in the edition.

The inscription of Taio’s letter is as follows:

“To the venerable and most holy lord Quiricus, bishop, Gaius, the unworthy bishop of the city of Zaragoza, surnamed Saorohel.”

The copyist’s error, “Querico” for “Quirico” and “Gaius” for “Taius,” can easily be excused. But what is this that Taio is said to have as a surname, “Saorohel”? At the end of the work, however, a new name appears: “Here ends the Book of the Sentences of Bishop Samuel. Praise be to God.” Unless perhaps here too “Saorohelis” should be read, or “Samuel” should be restored at the beginning in place of “Saorohel.”

Neither Nicolás Antonio nor Bayerius, in the Bibliotheca Hispana, mentions either surname. By the continuator of Fabricius’s Bibliotheca medii aevi he is called “Taio, or Taius, surnamed Samuhel.”

I shall state what I think. Somewhere there existed a Codex of Taio, whose owner was a certain Samuel; hence the book was called Samuel’s. When, therefore, a copyist saw that the work was called both Taio’s and Samuel’s, he believed that Taio and Samuel were one and the same author.

I confirm [Col. 0441D] this conjecture with a particular observation. In the very old catalogue entitled Breviarium librorum S. Nazarii—that is, in Laurissa, Vatican-Palatine Codex 1877—the former owners of certain books are named. Among them are these: “Also the Missals which belonged to Samuel, Babo, and Randulf. Samuel’s collections from the little works of Saint Gregory.” I believe this to be Taio’s book, which once belonged to Samuel. After many other entries, the same catalogue lists “the Book of Tagio [Taio], assembled from the little works of Saint Gregory.”

28. [Col. 0442A] Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that this surname Samuel, attached to Taio, is extremely ancient. For in the Thuanaean Codex, which Mabillon thought had been written eight hundred years earlier, the inscription of the letter is:

“To the venerable and most holy lord Quiricus, Taio, the unworthy bishop of the city of Zaragoza, surnamed Samuel.”

But in the Gothic Codex of Saint Emilianus of La Cogolla, from which Risco published the five books of Sentences, the only title was this: “Here begins the Book of the Sentences of the Lord Gregory, Pope of Rome, extracted from the books of the Moralia.” Nor is the surname Samuel added in Taio’s letter to Eugenius.

Indeed, even if Taio truly had borne the surname Samuel, I would still hardly believe that he wrote: “Quiricus, Taio, the unworthy bishop of the city of Zaragoza, surnamed Samuel,” when, according to customary usage, he could have said more simply: “Taio Samuel.”

[Col. 0442B] 29. From comparing Taio’s books with Isidore’s work, it is possible to infer that Taio not only had Isidore’s Sentences before him, but also formed most of his titles from them. He nevertheless took care not to introduce sentences or words of Gregory which Isidore had already collected.

I present the titles of the first three chapters of Book I.

**Taio.** Chapter 1: “That God exists immutable, supreme, and eternal.”  
2. “On the immensity, or omnipotence, of God.”  
3. “That God is invisible or incomprehensible” [the text has *de id*, for *de eo*, “that he”].

**Isidore.** Chapter 1: “That God is supreme and immutable.”  
Chapter 2: “That God is immense and omnipotent.”  
Chapter 3: “That God is invisible.”

Taio often places the chapters in a different order. [Col. 0442C] Thus, in Isidore, chapter 4 follows: “That the Creator is recognized from the beauty of creation.” In Taio this is chapter 9, in these words: “That from the beauty of creation invisible eternity is recognized.”

Isidore’s chapter 5, “That certain forms from our customary usage are referred to God,” is Taio’s chapter 10: “That from human affections certain forms are referred to God,” as it stands in my papers; but it would be preferable to read *referantur* with Isidore. For that Isidore himself supplied the titles to this work is sufficiently shown by the fact that Taio, who succeeded Braulio, already read them in this form, as the comparison makes clear.

30. Someone may perhaps argue that Taio arranged his system of theological sentences in a better order. [Col. 0442D] For in his preface to Quiricus he himself explains the method of the entire work, which he also expressed in these verses, according to Mabillon:

> Whoever, reader, loves to learn the sacred law,  
> Read through this book of our study.  
> You will easily find whatever you may wish to know;  
> It bears all things in flower and carries verdant meadows.  
> It feeds the sheep of the Lover, Christ’s innocent creatures;  
> It shows the lofty homeland and the mighty kingdom,  
> The Tartarean fires and sorrows without end.  
> Behold, Christ is present to bestow the kingdom upon the blessed;  
> 645 But upon the impious, by contrast, he bestows dreadful punishments.  
> Sublime soul, climb toward the royal halls of heaven.  
> Hasten eagerly, lest you lack such great rewards,  
> And look down upon the dreadful flames of the pitch-black spring.

These verses are not altogether bad for the literary capacity of their age, but, as it seems, they have been corrupted in certain places through the carelessness of copyists. For example, perhaps the author wrote *regemque potentem*, “the mighty king,” rather than *regnumque potentem*, “the mighty kingdom.” [Col. 0443A] Nicolás Antonio wished to infer from this epigram that Taio was a competent poet.

31. As for the method of the Sentences, Isidore followed in his first book the very method which Taio proposed for himself. For Taio says in his preface to Quiricus:

“Beginning with the Trinity of the immutable essence of the almighty Lord, and with the origin of the world and the formation of mankind, continuing up to the consummation of this age.”

Isidore’s Book I treats of God and his attributes, the origin of the world and the formation of mankind, Christ, the Holy Spirit, the Church, both Testaments, the resurrection, Gehenna, and the glory of the saints; the last of these is chapter 30 of Book I.

In the remaining two books he explained the theological and other virtues, [Col. 0443B] discussed sins and vices, and described the duties of bishops, rulers, and others.

32. Just as Taio imitated Isidore by extracting chiefly from Gregory’s sentences, so at the same time Julian of Toledo followed the same method of excerpting from Augustine’s books. To this belong what Felix, the author of Julian’s Life, reports: “Excerpts collected from the books of Saint Augustine against Julian the heretic.”

These are those highly elaborated six books of Augustine—or, in Augustine’s own judgment, *Retractationes* II, chapter 62—against Julian, bishop of Eclanum. Nicolás Antonio discusses them in the *Bibliotheca vetus*, followed by our Augustinian, Henry de Noris, in Book I of his *History of Pelagianism*.

[Col. 0443C] I confess that I hesitated somewhat over these words. Why, indeed, does Nicolás Antonio call Noris “our Augustinian”? Was Noris perhaps a friend of Nicolás Antonio, and did Nicolás Antonio intend to signify this? Or can this confirm the suspicion of some that certain spurious works have slipped into Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca vetus*?

Among Julian’s other works, the same Felix lists a Book of Sentences briefly and summarily collected from the decade of the psalms of Blessed Augustine. 565 “The statement is obscure,” says Nicolás Antonio, “unless he intended to indicate only the first decade of the psalms.” Perhaps it would be better to read “from the decades,” for Augustine divided his interpretation of the psalms into several decades.

[Col. 0443D] Bayer’s conjecture concerning a special Psalter of Augustine, placed among the spurious or doubtful works of the holy Doctor and intended for the use of his mother Monica, is less convincing. The discussion of Augustine’s decades of the psalms will recur in the notes to Isidore’s letter to Braulio.

33. But no judgment can be passed concerning what Julian’s Sentences were like, since they no longer exist. It is enough to observe that Peter Lombard could have benefited greatly from this work of Julian, had it been available to him, since he composed his own Sentences chiefly from Augustine.

As for the other Sentences of Isidore and Taio, especially Isidore’s, the question still remains whether Peter Lombard benefited from them to such an extent that he can be charged with plagiarism.

This is not the place to discuss the six books of the Sentences of Saint Bruno of Asti, once attributed to Saint Bruno, founder of the Carthusians. [Col. 0444A] They are concerned only with explaining the figures of the Church from the testimonies of sacred Scripture.

Since Peter Lombard proposed to gather theological sentences from various books of the Fathers into a single body, it should not seem surprising if he reproduced certain features on Isidore’s model. Some likewise argue that he took much from the books of John of Damascus on the Orthodox Faith, and from the writings of his teacher Peter Abelard, especially from the five books of *Christian Theology* and from the Book of Sentences *Sic et Non*, or *Introduction to Theology*.

Nor should Hugh of Saint Victor be passed over. He died in the year 1140 or 1142, and in the third volume of his works there is a *Summa of the Sentences*, or of theological learning, arranged in seven treatises in a sufficiently suitable order.

[Col. 0444B] Some add that Master Bandinus preceded Peter Lombard in his *Summa theologica*, or in his four books of theological Sentences, later published at Vienna in 1519. Others, on the contrary, maintain that Bandinus’s work appears to be an epitome of Peter Lombard’s Sentences.

Hugh Mathoud of the Congregation of Saint Maur, who in 1651 committed to print the eight books of the Sentences of Cardinal Robert Pulleyn and the five books of the Sentences of Peter of Poitiers, argues that this Robert Pulleyn, who died around 1150, was the first scholastic theologian.

566 34. [Col. 0444C] I consider it certain that Peter Lombard’s scholastic method was his own: in Book I of the Sentences he encompassed the doctrine of the one and triune God in forty-eight distinctions; in Book II, creation, the angels, fallen humanity, and the grace of God in forty-four distinctions; in Book III, the incarnation of the Word, love of God and neighbor, and virtues and vices in forty distinctions; and in Book IV, the sacraments and the four last things in fifty distinctions.
