It will surely be extremely difficult, within this method of scholastic theology, which was once especially pleasing to theologians, to convict the Master of the Sentences of plagiarism, particularly since he introduces his work as follows:

“Containing in a brief volume the sentences of the Fathers, with their testimonies added, so that one who is searching need not unfold the multitude of books; the brevity offers without labor what is sought.”

[Col. 0444D] Among the Fathers he often expressly cites Isidore, including from his books of the Sentences.

35. Perhaps, however, because Peter Lombard’s Sentences consist of four books, someone was led to attribute a fourth book of Sentences to Isidore as well, although the Codices from which this fourth book was copied appear to be older than Peter Lombard.

The fourth book of the Sentences appeared among the appendices to the recent Madrid edition, taken from certain Codices in which it bears Isidore’s name, as the editor states in the preface to volume I. Bayer also indicates in a note to the *Bibliotheca Hispana* an Escurial Codex from the twelfth or thirteenth century in which it occurs.

[Col. 0445A] There are sixty-five chapters. After their table, this note is added from some manuscript, as I suppose:

“Here end the four books of the Sentences of the Lord Isidore. The title is: ‘Here begins the fourth book, on rulers and how they ought to conduct their way of life.’”

The compiler excerpted his Sentences solely from the books of Saint Gregory. In a note to the title the editor explicitly says: “This book is excerpted word for word from the books of Taio’s Sentences.” He then indicates the chapters in their respective places which correspond to the chapters of Taio’s books; for the excerpts were not made in any definite order, and some sentences also appear to have been transposed.

I therefore cannot agree with Bayer, who asserts that this fourth book of the Sentences was added in the latest Madrid edition as though it were Isidore’s. This had to be said again because he twice brings the same charge against the Madrid editor, whom he says was miserably deceived and later openly acknowledged his error.

And indeed, 567 he adds, in the Escurial Codex [Col. 0445B] from the twelfth or the beginning of the thirteenth century, shelfmark t, Plut. 2, no. 7, from which the book was taken, the fourth book of the Sentences follows the three books of Isidore on the same subject in a continuous line of writing, so that anyone could easily stumble over the same obstacle. It will be much easier to do so if, at the end, as I said earlier, it is noted that Isidore’s four books of the Sentences are complete.

In reality, however, this book was placed in the latest Madrid edition among Isidore’s spurious works, not among the genuine or doubtful ones.

36. Other chapters of the Sentences seem to have been drawn from the same manuscript Codices and appended in the recent Madrid edition to the fourth book of the Sentences, under this inscription:

“Here end the four books of the Sentences of Saint Isidore. Here begin other chapters of the Sentences of the same author.”

There are only two chapters. The first has no title and deals chiefly with abstinence; it is taken from Saint Gregory the Great, as the editor observes in his notes. The second concerns Pride, Desire, Envy, and Boasting. In the preface to volume I the editor notes that it was taken from chapters 3, 4, 9, and 10 of Book III of Julian Pomerius’s *On the Contemplative Life*, a work incorrectly attributed to Saint Prosper in many editions. [Col. 0445C]

37. If someone nevertheless maintains that this collection, the fourth book and the other chapters of the Sentences, can also be attributed to Isidore, he will not easily be refuted.

The learned author of the preface presented in chapter 38, nos. 56 and following, certainly believed that the fourth book of the Sentences agreed especially well with Isidore, before Taio’s books of Sentences had appeared.

But even after the publication of Taio’s books, there remains room for inquiry. Since the sources from which the sentences were drawn were equally available to Isidore and Taio, it is not at all unreasonable that Isidore either prepared this collection separately for his own use or wished to add a fourth book after publishing the three books of Sentences—although this fourth book was not preserved in all copies.

[Col. 0445D] If that is so, Taio benefited from this fourth book as well, just as I am certain that he benefited from the first three. This is so not merely because many things occur in Taio which are found in Isidore’s books but not in the works of others—for that may perhaps result from the loss of the works of those others—but chiefly because Taio often took the very titles of the chapters from Isidore, as I have already noted.

[Col. 0446A] Furthermore, he joins certain passages from the ancient Fathers under the same titles and in the same order as Isidore, and proceeds in precisely the same style.

38. Rodriguez de Castro, in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, page 332, does not appear entirely to agree with the opinion proposed in the latest Madrid edition, namely, that the fourth book of the Sentences was excerpted from Taio’s books. For the purpose of forming a judgment on this matter, he thinks Bayer’s observations should be kept before us when reviewing this Codex. He quotes them from Bayer’s *Adversaria*, and we reproduce them here.

**Bayer’s observations on the fourth book of Isidore’s Sentences found in an old Escurial Codex**

39. [Col. 0446B] “The four books of the Sentences of Saint Isidore of Seville, otherwise known as *On the Supreme Good*. Anyone who has read in Grial, Nicolás Antonio, Gesner, and others that only three books on this subject, and under this title, were written by the holy Doctor will surely be surprised. The same thing happened to us when we first encountered our Codex.

But a Codex written in the thirteenth century, and apparently copied from another, much older one, testifies otherwise. After those three books of the Sentences, which all bibliographers attribute to Saint Isidore, have been recorded in precisely the same order of titles as in Grial’s printed edition—with only a few, and very minor, exceptions—the fourth book is appended by the very same hand as the preceding book and without interruption in the thread of the exposition.

It appears under a major rubric very similar to those which the scribe assigned after the completion of Books I and II, namely: ‘The third book is complete. Here begin the chapters of the fourth book.’ Without leaving any blank space, the rubrics of that book are appended in this order: ‘On rulers,’ and so forth, as in the printed edition.”

40. The numbering of the rubrics proceeds to number sixty-five. But they appear to contain an error, since rubric 51, “On the Concord of Good Things,” which occurs in the body of the work, was omitted.

[Col. 0446C] Immediately afterward, the following major rubric occurs in the Codex: “Here begins the fourth book, on rulers and how they ought to conduct their way of life.” This follows the sixty-four minor rubrics that precede it, each assigned its own chapter.

The entire book consists of thirty-three and a half quarto leaves. I shall return to it shortly. For now, let us present the remaining contents of the Codex, and so forth.

Now let us return to the fourth book of Isidore’s Sentences, as we promised above.

41. [Col. 0446D] After those illustrious ten men who, by order of Philip II, king of Spain, labored to investigate and correct the works of this holy Doctor—namely Álvaro Gomes, Pedro Pantino, Roland Wicelius, García de Loaysa, who devoted himself to correcting the very books of the Sentences under discussion and for that purpose examined thirteen entire Codices, including two Lombardic ones; J. B. Pérez, our countryman in more than one respect; Pedro Fontidonio; Cyprian Suárez; Juan de Mariana, both of the Society of Jesus; and Pedro Chacón, whose labors John Grial collected and recast—after so many distinguished men who cultivated and adorned this field, the profound silence concerning a fourth book of Isidore’s Sentences makes it seem entirely unsafe, and full of confidence and rashness, to attribute it to the holy Doctor.

It is scarcely possible that, among such a large number of Codices of Isidore, not one of those men should have encountered a Codex like ours in which this book had been written, whether by an ancient or a recent hand.

Nevertheless, I considered it wrong to leave entirely unmentioned the arguments which seem to support attributing this book to Isidore, or at least to raise a doubt. I shall therefore bring them forward for judgment by the learned. First, that this book is not Gregory the Great’s—which I had long suspected, when I observed that its first chapter, “On Rulers,” was largely copied verbatim from Gregory’s *Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 2 (Father Joseph of Segovia’s note written in the margin of the Codex at that place drew my attention to this)—is plainly indicated by the fact that in chapter 40, “On the Eight Principal Vices,” Gregory himself is cited with praise.

[Col. 0447A] There we read: “The eminent Doctor Gregory, while explaining that saying spoken by the Lord to blessed Job, indicates…”

42. Second, there is the order of the writing and books in our Codex. It too is not especially recent—for it seems to have been written in the thirteenth century—and it was copied from another, older Codex, either Gothic or altogether of Gothic character. Anyone who observes the frequent Gothicisms scattered throughout our Codex will certainly agree with me on this.

For in it we find *domnus Isidorus*, “Lord Isidore,” [Col. 0447B] and *domnus Nicolaus*, “Lord Nicholas,” in place of *dominus*, according to the usage of that period, as we have noted elsewhere. Likewise *adolari* and *adolantes* for *adulari* and *adulantes*; *jubilum* for *jubilus*; *conlabsus* for *collapsus*; *palfebre* for *palpebre*; *strionis* for *histrionis*; *abtius* for *aptius*; *temeritudinem* for *temeritatem*; *Incipit dicta* for *Incipiunt dicta*; *dignitate precelles hac fide* for *praecellis ac fide*—along with many other forms which we have noticed in passing.

43. The history of the translation of the body of Saint Isidore, in which we first said that the year of Christ 1071 was mentioned, was taken from elsewhere and attached out of order to our already completed Codex together with the Martyrologies, or readings, which we reported above.

44. Third, our Codex seems to have been written in some old monastery of our Spain, perhaps at Oña, or the monastery of Ona, as will shortly be said, for the instruction of novices in piety. Consequently, in the library of that place, while older Codices were preserved among the monks in their monasteries, the complete work of Blessed Isidore’s Sentences, divided in this manner into four books in our Codex, could have been kept.

45. [Col. 0447C] That it was once intended for monastic use is clear from the fact that in the inventory of books which we mentioned earlier we read: “The Psalter of the Parisian Cantor”—namely, Peter Lombard, the scholastic cantor and bishop, concerning whom see Gesner under “Peter the Cantor”—“which the lord abbot ordered to be made.”

There is also the note written near the end of the Codex, namely:

“On 27 March, in the year from the birth of the Lord 1387, Peter Fernández de Crañon, bachelor in canon law, in that year in which he received the monastic habit, completed reading this book.”

This monastery appears to have been Oña because twice, on the last folio of the same book, which had previously been left blank, the following is written:

“Clement, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Oña in the church of Saint Saviour, etc.”

Certainly it once belonged to the regions of Old Castile, Asturias, or Galicia, as the vernacular dialect of those regions preserved in the inventory indicates. There we read:

“Two *domingales* (Sunday books), one new and the other old; two *colectarios* (collectaries), one new and the other old.”

46. [Col. 0447D] Finally, and in my view much more powerfully and immediately relevant than the preceding arguments, this fourth book under discussion does not appear to be a new work proceeding from Isidore himself or from any other author, but rather a completion of the three preceding books on the same subject.

Its subject matter and rubrics fit and attach themselves most suitably to the rubrics and subject matter of the earlier books, so as to form with them one complete body—a circumstance that very rarely occurs in works by different authors. Nor is there any overlap or confusion between the rubrics of the earlier books and those of the fourth book.

47. Although the following rubrics may appear not very different from one another, namely:

[Col. 0448A] **The three books of Isidore’s Sentences published by Grial**

1. Book II, chapter 33: “That vices arise from vices, and virtues from virtues.”  
2. Book III, chapter 35: “On Simulated Virtues.”  
3. Book III, chapter 5: “On the Temptations of the Devil.” Book III, chapter 6: “On the Temptations of Dreams.”  
4. Book III, chapter 20: “On the Tepidity of Monks.”

48. **The fourth book of the Sentences in our Codex**

1. Chapter 18: “That virtues arise from virtues, and vices from vices.”  
2. Chapter 17: “On Certain Vices That Pretend to Be Virtues.”  
3. Chapter 13: “How Many Kinds of Dreams There Are.” Chapter 14: “On Nocturnal Illusions.” Chapter 15: “On Satan’s Various Arguments.”  
4. Chapter 5: “On the Tepidity or Idleness of Monks.”

49. Although, I say, there is in these and perhaps other passages a very great similarity between the rubrics of the printed edition and those of our Codex, the treatment in the two places is nevertheless far different, as I learned by testing the matter.

Moreover, when we read our book cursorily and in excerpts, nothing occurred to us that seemed unworthy of so great a Doctor, more recent than his age, or otherwise such as to cause us serious doubt.

50. On the contrary, its style, if not identical, is certainly by no means foreign to Isidore’s style: it is full-bodied and smooth, and extremely rich in sentences and passages of Scripture. [Col. 0448B] It is also borrowed from the *Moralia*—this is the second indication—and from other works of Gregory the Great. [Col. 0448B] The entire chapter 13, “On the Kinds of Dreams,” is transcribed in almost exactly the same words and in its entirety from Book IV, chapter 48, of Gregory’s *Dialogues*, as will be clear to anyone who compares them.

This supports attributing the book under discussion to Isidore. For, as Braulio says in his Life of him: “He wrote three books of Sentences, which he adorned with flowers from the books of Pope Gregory’s *Moralia*.”

But, he says, three and no more. I admit it. Yet Braulio did not encompass all Isidore’s writings, as he himself acknowledges; he mentioned only those that came to his memory.

51. The same Braulio, writing about the work of the Etymologies, says that it was divided by Isidore into chapters, not books; and that, because Isidore had undertaken it at Braulio’s request but left it incomplete, Braulio divided it into fifteen books, although twenty are counted in all. No one therefore excludes the last five books from Isidore.

Something similar could certainly have happened with the books of the Sentences.

52. [Col. 0448C] In the eulogy of Braulio which Grial prefixed to Isidore’s works, however, he substituted “I divided it into twenty books” for “fifteen.” I do not know where he obtained this reading, since the old manuscript Codices invariably read “fifteen.”

At least, I have so far encountered none that does not have this reading, except one Ovetan Codex copied by Moralius, in this royal library, shelfmark b, III, no. 14. In its text “five” is written, but this is an error for “fifteen,” which word is supplied in the margin.

53. Furthermore, another Codex of the same library, shelfmark et IV, no. 23, copied from a very ancient one, has “fifteen.” Especially noteworthy is Codex Q, Plut. 2, no. 21, written in the year of Christ 743, or Era 781, which likewise has “fifteen.”

Nor do I fear that the Toledan Codices, which I shall consult on another occasion, will disagree with this reading, if God grants his approval.

54. And this is what concerns the reasons for doubting whether our fourth book of the *Sentences* should be attributed to the holy Doctor Isidore. But whether the three larger rubrics that follow this fourth book—namely, 1. “Also, the chapters of various sentences”; 2. “On pride, desire, envy, and boastfulness”; 3. “Here begins an exhortation to humility”—whose author is not identified in our Codex, ought to be attributed to Isidore or to someone else, whoever may ultimately have written the fourth book of the *Sentences*, is not for us to determine, nor do we have time to judge the matter, especially since we have already lingered more than enough over the description of this Codex.

55. This was Bayer’s position. Rodriguez had placed certain words in the wrong location, namely, from “and borrowed from other works of Gregory the Great” up to “it will become clear after the words ‘it will be necessary to consult them, if God grants it.’” I restored the passage conjecturally. Bayer held this view before Taio’s books of the *Sentences* came to public notice; afterward he entirely abandoned it. Yet it must be admitted that some reason for doubt still remains.

What he argues in chapter 48 concerning fifteen books of the *Etymologies* instead of twenty has been rejected by us. Braulio says that the work of the *Etymologies* was distinguished by Isidore with titles; Bayer reports “chapters” instead of “titles.” The little work entitled *Exhortation to Humility* is usually attributed to Saint Martin of Dumio, as I shall say in chapter 84.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. Prefaces to the Books of the *Sentences* in the Paris edition of 1538 and in García de Loaysa’s edition. Excerpts from the Books of the *Sentences*. Prefaces to the Excerpts from the *Sentences*, namely, to the book entitled *On Converts* and to another entitled *On Prelates*

1. The title of the Paris edition of 1538, joined with a substantial encomium of Isidore, runs as follows:

> “The three books of the blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the Highest Good, most useful to every class of humanity. In these books that divine man has briefly gathered together, under certain commonplaces, all matters both human and divine that many philosophers and theologians have sought out and handed down in numerous volumes for the attainment of that highest end. Now for the first time most faithfully purged of the foulest and most dreadful errors through the study and labor of the most learned Joannes Aleaume, Parisian doctor of theology. Paris, at the house of Joannes Roigny, on the road to Saint James, under the Basilisk and the Four Elements, 1538.”

At the end:

> “Paris: printed by Joannes Lodoicus Tiletanus at the expense of the most honorable bookseller Joannes Roigny, 1538.”

The edition is in octavo, and the following prologue is prefixed to it.

### Greetings to the candid reader

2. What kind of man Isidore was, and how great—once bishop of Seville, renowned for the highest integrity—and how extensive was his knowledge and learning in treating divine and human matters, are most clearly shown not only by his many other works but especially by these three books on the Highest Good. For nothing, it seems to me, has been omitted by him that could contribute to knowledge of important subjects.

Beginning with God, that supreme Craftsman, he ranges through everything else in such a way that he seems to have omitted nothing that could be either useful to know concerning any matter or worthy of remembrance. For, as he reviews all the orders of humanity, he prescribes to each of them something like a definite duty.

I pass over the incredible variety of all things, whose observation must affect every mind with an extraordinary pleasure. For whether you desire instruction in life and morals or a marvelous gathering of divine and human matters, these books will supply everything in the fullest abundance. Indeed, if you devote yourself diligently to them, you will be able to discuss any subject proposed at length and sometimes even with admiration.

Yet these very books, so miserably disfigured and by now abandoned by nearly everyone because of the countless errors, Joannes Aleaume, a most learned doctor of theology, brings back to the light and presents anew. With the same diligence with which he recently restored Peter Lombard’s work of the *Sentences*, he has restored them for the benefit of all to their former integrity and clarity. Since he has always shown such exceptional willingness to assist cultivated and studious men, I judge that greater and more refined works may be expected from him. Farewell.

3. From this edition and from Joannes Aleaume’s emendation, Margarinus de la Bigne reprinted the books of the *Sentences*. Thus, in both editions, the following are the concluding words of the third book, which are absent from most copies:

> “For this is the disposition of Christian compassion: that a sacrifice be offered to God for each dead person. Hence it is written: ‘And when a person is dead, do not withhold mercy from him.’”

Several editions of Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, revised through the same Joannes Aleaume’s efforts, are listed in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*. Yet they all postdate 1538, although the preface reproduced above implies that Peter Lombard’s *Sentences*, corrected by Joannes Aleaume, had appeared shortly beforehand.

4. The dedicatory letter of García de Loaysa to Prince Philip, later Philip III, king of Spain, prefixed to the edition of Isidore’s *Sentences*, must not be omitted by us, since it was repeated in the Madrid editions.

### García de Loaysa sends greetings to Philip, prince of the Spains

5. The wise natural philosophers teach that moral knowledge, which the Greeks call *ἠθικήν* (*ethikēn*, “ethics”), is alien to youth because of the ardor and instability of that age. But the condition of princes is different. Virtue comes to them before its time, especially when they have been imbued with Christian faith and religion, by which rebellious impulses are softened in the flower of adolescence and human conduct is kept within its duty by divine institutions.

He who wrote to a young man knew this most aptly:

> “Flee youthful desires; pursue instead justice, faith, charity, and peace with those who call upon the Lord from a pure heart.”

Therefore, most gracious prince, I judged that these books of the *Sentences*, written by the blessed Isidore—born of Gothic royal blood and bishop of Seville—should be dedicated to you at this stage of your life. Using manuscript Codices, I corrected them, giving some light to obscure passages by notes and lending antiquity to new errors.

In these books you will read the entire Christian duty, by which you will shape your mind toward every kind of virtue, so that you may pass your youth honorably and splendidly, restrain yourself from lusts, and diligently exercise yourself in labor, in endurance of mind, and in the study of letters. Thus, in prudent old age, you may rest in the love of divine things with the highest authority and esteem.

Since there are two roads by which we advance toward the royal palace of wisdom—speech and reading—I wish you to labor in both. Since you have been called to the summit of human government, once you have obtained the principate you must direct the world subject to you, through the difficult discipline of governing, toward a tranquil way of life, as toward the safest harbor.

You will achieve this, relying on divine protection, if you add practical experience to the voice of your teacher and, above all, to the reading of books. You will learn this from your most wise and powerful father, as from an exceedingly skilled master of government. To him the noble exclamation of Marcus Cicero applies better than to anyone:

> “O fortunate man, from whom no one dares ask an improper thing!”

At the same time, you will learn that the greatness of fortune changes the mind in this one respect: you can benefit your peoples only as much as you desire to do so through the best government. Farewell.

6. Many excerpts, as they are called, occur from these books of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences*, not only in manuscripts but also in printed works. I shall not now discuss certain sermons excerpted from these books, such as the sermon *On Temptations* and the sermon *On Angels*, since there will be a proper place for discussing the sermons.

Concerning other excerpts inserted into several councils, see chapter 31. Hugo Menardus, in the prolegomena to his *Concord of Rules*, reports that in the Floriacensian Codex, from which he extracted the *Concord*, there are certain sentences on virtues and vices, chiefly concerning monks, drawn from many Fathers and specifically from Saint Isidore in the *Sentences*.

Menardus thought this to be Benedict of Aniane’s book, collected from the homilies of the holy Fathers and mentioned by Ardo Smaragdus. Holstenius, however, disagrees, believing that the *Appendix* and *Codex of Rules* published by him are the work mentioned by Smaragdus.

In Vatican Palatine Codex 216 there is an *Excerpt*, or, as it is called there, an *Excarpsum*, from Saint Isidore’s book *On the Scourges of God*, namely from book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 1. In the same Codex there is another excerpt of Isidore, without its location being indicated. It begins:

> “Most beloved, keep death before your eyes at every hour,” etc.

The opening words are from book I of the *Synonyms*, after the middle, through “sins are wiped away through repentance.” In the manuscript the reading is: “Through repentance all sins are extinguished.”

The manuscript continues:

> “He practices repentance worthily,” etc.,

as far as the end of book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 13.

7. Canisius published certain chapters of book II of the *Sentences* in volume V of his *Antiquae Lectiones*, believing that he was bringing to light for the first time a book of Isidore’s not previously published, entitled *On Converts to Monks*.

Regarding this title, Barthius writes in *Adversaria*, book XVIII, chapter 1:

> “Furthermore, from these and similar expressions, in the Latin Church those who, having laid aside concern for earthly affairs, pursue true blessedness alone are specifically called converts. And there exists a distinct little book of Isidore’s on converts, which must be understood under that title.”

To this also belongs Blessed Paulinus’s letter to Victricius, bishop of the Morini. Add the words at the end of Cassiodorus’s preface to the *Tripartite History*:

> “Here ends the preface of Cassiodorus the Senator, now converted, by the Lord’s favor.”

As Fabricius correctly explains this under the entry “Cassiodorus” in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, these words do not establish that Cassiodorus, formerly a pagan, then became a Christian. Rather, they can and should be understood of the monastic life, which, weary of courtly affairs, he preferred to secular life in the last years of his life.

Properly speaking, however, converts were those who renounced the world and approached a monastery, even though they had not yet been admitted into the company of monks, as can be gathered from chapter 4 of Isidore’s *Rule of Monks*.

Basnage himself did not approve the suspicion that the wording of a certain epitaph of Isidore might indicate a work entitled *The Form of Repentance*, *On Converts*, as appears from his words, which I shall report in chapter 71.

In Canisius the title and preface are as follows:

> “Saint Isidore on Converts, or to Monks, now published for the first time from manuscript parchments of the celebrated monastery of Saint Gall.”

### To the reader

8. We found this little work in the manuscript parchments of the monastery of Saint Gall, preceded by the following title:

> “Saint Isidore on Converts.”

At the end of the final page:

> “Isidore to the monks.”

It does not appear in the recent edition of Isidore by Jacobus du Breul, which he prepared carefully and in which he included many works that had not previously seen the light.

For my part, I am glad to have found this manuscript Codex, however much it is written not only in a fleeing hand but in one scarcely legible and extremely corrupt. Nevertheless, I regard as a true treasure anything that can be recovered from the remains of the works of Saint Isidore of Seville.

Here I am thinking only of the Younger Isidore. I neither wish nor dare to attribute it to Isidore the Elder, likewise of Seville, or to Isidore of Córdoba. The work itself testifies that it belongs to Isidore in chapter 10, in these words:

> “Woe to me, wretched Isidore, who both neglect to repent of past deeds and continue to commit deeds requiring repentance.”

9. I do not sufficiently understand which “Elder Isidore of Seville,” distinguished by Canisius from “Isidore the Younger of Seville,” he means. Compare chapter 16, *On the Various Isidores*.

Constantinus Cajetanus, who published this among other little works of Isidore, recognized that it had been taken from the books of the *Sentences*, as can be seen in the following notice of his concerning the notes and variant readings.

10. Henry Canisius, that most diligent investigator of ancient monuments, made this book of Saint Isidore, *On Converts to Monks*, public after all the editions of Isidore’s works, from a manuscript Codex of the monastery of Saint Gall in Switzerland. He testified that the Codex was preceded by the title:

> “Of Saint Isidore on Converts,”

and that at the end of the final page it read:

> “Isidore (*On Converts*) to the monks.”

Indeed, in chapter 10 of the same book, Isidore proves himself to be the author when he says:

> “Woe to me, wretched Isidore, who both neglect to repent of past deeds and continue to commit deeds requiring repentance.”

These are also Canisius’s arguments by which he attempts to establish that this book was written by none other than Isidore of Seville.

But in truth I cannot help wondering at Canisius, otherwise a man of perceptive intellect—and likewise at Antonio Possevino, who praises him for publishing this book—for failing to notice the one point that completely proves the book to be by none other than Isidore of Seville. For it is so certain that this very book was excerpted from Isidore’s second book of the *Sentences* that, from chapter 8 through chapter 17, with chapters 38 and 39 added, the portion of Isidore’s *Sentences* in which the entire subject of converts is discussed and completed contains nothing other than thirteen chapters of the same book *On Converts to Monks*.

Moreover, the titles of the chapters in both books are identical, and, apart from a few alterations, the sequence of words is the same throughout.

Isidore also treated this very doctrine of converts in its entirety in chapter 4 of his *Rule of Monks*. Nor was this practice unfamiliar to our Isidore, as his other books clearly demonstrate. In the work *On Contempt of the World*, many things are repeated that he also wrote in the books of the *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*. The same judgment may be made concerning the other work *On the Rule of Living*.

We should not, however, on this account lay the blame upon Isidore. He was born for the benefit of the Christian commonwealth and had resolved, according to the opportunity afforded by time and place, to be of assistance both to the wise and to the foolish.

11. Collections of passages from Isidore’s books *On the Highest Good* are found in Vatican Codex 4414, page 135, on parchment. It begins: “The divine immensity,” etc. I have listed similar Codices containing excerpts from the books of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences* in chapter 67, section 23.

12. Nicolás Antonio mentions Isidore’s book *On Prelates*, published together with Valerian of Cimelium’s sermon *On the Good of Discipline* by Goldastus at Geneva in 1602, in octavo; yet he admits that he had not seen the book himself.

This too is an excerpt, or fragment, of book III of the *Sentences*. I eventually obtained the book, which is not particularly easy to find in Rome. Here is the title:

> “The Sermon of Saint Valerian on the Good of Discipline. A fragment of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, on Prelates. Melchior Hamenveltius Goldastus published it together with his collections, in which many passages of numerous authors, especially of the Fathers, are either explained, corrected, or newly published. Printed by Petrus de la Roviere, 1601, in octavo.”

Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Valerian of Cemelium” (Goldastus writes “Cimelensis”), notes that the book is in octavo, not in duodecimo, as the authors of the *Literary History of France*, volume II, page 331, state. Nicolás Antonio gives the year 1602, through an error, I think.

He also mentions a certain book of Dositheus the Master, published at the same time. In my copy it is bound together with this work, but with a different pagination and a new title:

> “Book III of Dositheus the Master, containing the sayings and letters of the divine Emperor Hadrian. Melchior Hamenveltius Goldastus enlarged, corrected, and illustrated it for the most part. Printed by Petrus de la Roviere, 1601.”

The place of publication is not stated here, but I readily agree that it was Geneva.

After Saint Valerian’s sermon and Saint Isidore’s fragment *On Prelates*, Goldastus added *Collections*, or notes, on Saint Valerian, and then notes on Saint Isidore, prefaced by the following notice.

13. ### Collections on Saint Isidore’s *On Prelates*

In the manuscript Codex there is a continuous sequence and uninterrupted series of these treatises, so that, as they are joined together here from it, the two may seem properly connected and mutually fitted together.

We shall readily demonstrate that this was done from very bad exemplars and through a most perverse kind of error.

First of all, Valerian himself clearly advances this opinion, writing explicitly at the end of his sermon:

> “There were indeed still many things, beloved, which the consideration of discipline urged us to disclose. For the time being, however, we thought these should be postponed, lest a lengthy account become wearisome to idle ears. Certainly, lest we seem to have omitted anything from this work, we shall strive to discuss at a later time those matters that pertain to religious practices.”

If he fulfilled this promise, and if he wrote anything beyond it, no one has informed me, nor made me certain of what was uncertain—not even those who prepared the editions of Augustine, whom it would have especially suited to do so. Indeed, anyone who carefully examines the preceding material and wishes to reflect upon it diligently, unless he harbors an insincere state of mind, will never deny that these passages are not by the same author:

> “For they are not so dissimilar in subject, but nevertheless—”

> “They are made in a different manner of expression and style.”

For they are interrupted throughout; they are not continuous, do not cohere with one another, but resemble a kind of cento, stuffed or stitched together from many and diverse sentences.

I think this is what happened. A pious monk, wishing to produce something for the public good, saw that the matters to which Valerian had pledged and bound himself were being sought in vain. He therefore took from Isidore what he thought should be added concerning religious practices, using it to supply the omission, and at the same time instructed the princes in discipline, as he judged Valerian would have done.

Unless someone should rather hold that Isidore himself copied these things—something that was customary and habitual for him in that large work—from the longer volume of the bishop of Cimelium and then included them as his own in the books of the *Sentences*. Or perhaps a monk, or someone else who had read Isidore’s writings, later existed who preferred his epitome to the complete author, either to serve the convenience of others through misplaced diligence or to evade the labor of writing through sluggish negligence.

Whatever the truth may be, as far as could be seen from ancient sources, they attribute this material to Isidore: the authors of the Council of Paris, of the Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious, of the Synod of Mainz under the emperor Arnulf, Rabanus Maurus, Gratian, and others, whom I shall mention in their proper places.

This fact can abundantly establish that the work always has been, and still is, of an authority not to be despised, and that it is fully worthy of the small amount of time I shall devote to elucidating it.

It certainly contains notable and brilliant testimonies not only against the monstrous madness of the Anabaptists, the Müntzerites, and people of that kind, but also against those who, in defending divine worship and protecting the public and holy peace of the Catholic Church, deny that Christian magistrates have any role with respect to heretical and disorderly people.

The edicts of many excellent kings and emperors, established and sanctioned by the holiest examples, and the eternal divine laws themselves, oppose them sufficiently and more than sufficiently.

Nor can the mad interpretations of the mad Origen on the thirteenth chapter of Romans provide anyone with protection or defense. For Blessed Jerome caused his perverse errors and delirious dreams, inspired by the Anabaptist spirit, to be utterly overthrown.

There is also an exceedingly elegant and learned book *On the One Religion*, written by the distinguished Justus Lipsius, from which many very weighty and well-proven arguments on this subject may be drawn.

14. Goldastus’s *Collections* seemed to me not unworthy of having their place in an edition of Isidore, provided that suitable notes were added. Through these notes, certain opinions of the heterodox author that depart from the true Catholic religion may be refuted so clearly that they can do our readers no harm.

## CHAPTER LXIX. Two Books on Ecclesiastical Offices Attributed to Isidore. Editions. The Preface of Joannes Cochleus. Excerpts. Little Works on Various Kinds of Monastic Life and on Receiving the Sacred Eucharist: Preface to These Fragments. Manuscript Codices

1. Braulio described Isidore’s outstanding work *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in his *Preface* in these words:

> “To his own brother Fulgentius, bishop of Astigi, two books on the Offices, in which he drew out, in his own style and not without the authority of his predecessors, the origin of the offices and the reason why each one is performed in the Church of God.”

Braulio is repeating what he had read in Isidore’s letter to Fulgentius:

> “You ask me about the origin of the offices, etc. … I have sent you a little book on the origin of the offices, arranged from the oldest writings of authors and commented upon as the subject required, in which I have drawn out many things in my own style, etc.”

Ildefonsus briefly indicated this work, calling it a book *On the Kind of Offices*. These words were omitted by Grialius at the beginning of his edition, where he transcribed this chapter 9 of Ildefonsus, and they led Nicolás Antonio and Rodríguez de Castro into the error of believing that Ildefonsus had not remembered this work of Isidore. Bayer was greatly surprised by this, as I noted long ago.

2. Since innumerable manuscripts, including very ancient ones, and all printed editions consistently attribute to Isidore the work that Braulio and Ildefonsus so plainly ascribe to him, what reason could Baronio have had for opposing them so strongly as to consider it spurious? Cave, who makes this claim, does not identify Baronio’s passage.

Bayer cites Baronio’s work, unknown to me, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, under the year 630, page 239—or 259, since the second numeral cannot be clearly distinguished in my copy. I thought that “Baronio” had entered in place of “Bellarmino,” but I do not find this claim even in Bellarmino.

Nicolás Antonio observes that Sigebert and Jonas of Orléans, book II of *On Lay Formation*, chapter 1, in volume I of Dacher’s *Spicilegium*, page 64, mention this work of Isidore. He further reports from Possevino’s *Apparatus sacer* that Alcuin transcribed the whole of chapter 29 in his work *On Divine Offices*.

Pezius, in the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, section 13, reports that in the library of the Benedictine abbey of Saint Peter at Salzburg there is a thirteenth-century Codex of Master Praepositinus, *On the Divine Office and the Daily Office*. On its first page are recorded the names of those who wrote books on the divine offices—Isidore, Rabanus, and others.

This same Rabanus transcribed several passages from Isidore’s books *On Offices* into his *Instruction of the Clergy*. Cave, in opposition to Baronio, also adduces the testimonies of Bede, Fulbert of Chartres, and Freculf of Lisieux.

Balbulus speaks excellently of Isidore’s books *On Offices* in chapter 47, already cited. Among other works of Isidore addressed to Solomon, later bishop of Constance, he reports as follows:

> “Also another work on ecclesiastical offices and orders, which will be especially necessary for you, a future priest by the grace of God. In it you will find the entire rationale and the names of the individual feasts and fasts, so that you may announce to the people of God beforehand the stations that are to come,” etc.

The anonymous author of a monastic rule, whom I shall discuss in chapter 71 and whom Martène believes to have lived not long after Saint Isidore, reports in chapter 5:

> “Concerning these days Saint Isidore says in his book *On Offices*: ‘After Easter until Pentecost,’ etc.”

He takes other material from the same books in the same place.

Saint Ildefonsus himself, in his work *On Knowledge of Baptism*, repeatedly produces several chapters from Isidore’s books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. He does not mention Isidore’s name, contenting himself with saying in the prologue, as he does of the other Fathers from whom he learned, that he was presenting not his own novelties but the teachings of the ancients. Ildefonsus, as is well known, was Isidore’s disciple.

The Anonymous of Melk, Pastrengus, and others cited in the same chapter 47 also mention these books *On Offices*.

3. Catalogues of ancient libraries, mentioned in chapter 46, frequently list Isidore’s books *On Offices*. In the very ancient library of the monastery of Bobbio, five books of Isidore *On Offices*—that is, five copies—are said to have existed.

Four manuscript Codices, whose collations I possess in the Zaccarian papers, were described in chapter 44. Joannes Grialius corrected two manuscript copies of the same books, as he himself relates in the preface; Breulius worked from one manuscript Codex of Saint-Germain-des-Prés.

Bayer says that another copy exists in the Escorial library, bearing the title:

> “Two books to Fulgentius on the Nature and Origin of Ecclesiastical Offices.”

I shall soon indicate the Vatican Codices.

4. The oldest edition of this work, which Nicolás Antonio believed belonged to the year 1510, was in fact completed only in 1534. Here is the title:

> “The two books of the blessed Isidore, formerly archbishop of Seville, on Ecclesiastical Offices, published by him 900 years ago and now restored to the light from an ancient Codex. Leipzig, 1534, under the illustrious and orthodox prince Lord George, duke of Saxony, etc. In quarto.”

At the end:

> “Printed at Leipzig by Michael Bloum in the year of the Lord 1534.”

Book II ends:

> “who would give the Holy Spirit to those already baptized,”

as that chapter ends in the Bignaean edition. Two chapters are omitted which are added in the Bignaean and Breulian editions, concerning suffrages.

Bignaeus at the beginning of his edition, and Breulius at the beginning of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, transcribed part of Cochleus’s dedicatory letter. It seemed appropriate to us to reproduce it here in full.

### Joannes Cochleus sends greetings to the distinguished man of exceptional piety and learning, Lord Robert Ridley, Englishman, eminent doctor of arts and sacred theology, and secretary to the most reverend Lord Cuthbert, bishop of Durham, etc.

5. If distance of place, the adversity of the times, and human malice so stubbornly stand in my way, my dearest Ridley, that my heart and my gratitude toward you, a pious, learned, and deserving friend, cannot be made known to you through private letters, then I must finally try another path—perhaps through public booklets I may be able to prevent myself from appearing perpetually silent, forgetful, and ungrateful toward all your pious efforts and benevolent services on my behalf.

Certainly I might rightly seem so to you when my letters reach you so rarely. I have often written to you from this city; I wrote from Augsburg three years ago, when our unconquered emperor Charles V had gathered there the princes and nobles of the entire Holy Roman Empire for the sake of public welfare and peace.

I also wrote from the imperial diet at Regensburg through the royal ambassador, Lord Thomas Cranmer, a learned man and distinguished theologian. His conversations were all the more pleasant to me because he gave no slight testimony to your piety and learning, affirming that you had once been an outstanding teacher of philosophy to him.

Finally, I wrote from Mainz, trusting to the vessels of the Rhine that travel from there all the way to the British Ocean.

If the malignity of the times amid the new German sects does not hesitate to frustrate my wishes in so many ways, I hope that, in keeping with your great humanity, you will forgive me while I seek another route by which my spirit may become known to the sweetest of my friends, than whom I have never had a more candid one.

For with singular kindness and, as I think, an entirely divine providence, you first made yourself known to my smallness through letters. You freely offered me your friendship and immediately adorned it with so many efforts to do me good and with carefully sought opportunities to earn my gratitude; you have confirmed it more and more each day.

I could rightly seem made of iron, even harder than steel, and more stupid and senseless than any stone, if the many services of so pious and sincere a friend did not stir me to mutual love and the gratitude of heart that ought to be expressed and displayed by every possible sign.

Yet to return worthy thanks to you and repay the proper obligations is beyond my power, my sweetest and most learned Ridley. For you have doubtless understood from some of my little books, published long ago, how scanty is the household store of my learning and how slight my ability.

Since the letters I usually write to you privately are stealthily intercepted by malicious people, and since my little books, which the incessant malice of the new sects extorts from me, are not worthy of reading, I have resolved to seek other messengers for you—messengers whom the wicked will fear more than private letters and whom your learning will more readily admit into conversation.

From that venerable company and order now comes holy and learned Bishop Isidore. Among the Spaniards, on account of the exceptional holiness of his life and the piety, uprightness, and abundance of his learning, he was not only dear and admirable to kings and peoples; he also stood out with distinction in the public councils of the Fathers and surpassed all in authority.

Thus, in the Eighth Council of Toledo, the Fathers deigned to exalt him with public praises in these words:

> “Isidore, the distinguished teacher of our age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him, but not least in comparison of learning—and, what is greater, the most learned man of the closing centuries, to be named with reverence,” etc.

I therefore publish two little books by this man, so long ago proven and authoritative, as messengers and witnesses of my gratitude and goodwill toward you. I had not previously seen them in print.

I found them in an ancient Codex at Mainz, joined to the ancient books of Amalarius of Trier, once archbishop under Charlemagne, which he composed on the divine offices.

May God grant that, according to my wish and intention, they may appear in such a form that they will please you, effectively admonish our bishops and priests of their duty with beneficial effect, and recall the leaders and defenders of the new sects from their impious undertakings. May they also salutarily deter and turn them away from their barbarous war of giants against the ancient sacred rites and ceremonies of the Church.

May he grant this who is the source of every good gift and every perfect gift. Farewell.

From Dresden in Meissen, on the Elbe, on the third day before the Kalends of January, in the year of the Lord 1534.

6. Many afterward arranged for Cochleus’s edition to be reprinted as newly corrected and revised against manuscript copies. Yet it may be questioned whether this was added through the booksellers’ fraud.

Prateolus Marcossius seems to have had some role in arranging this edition. I give its title:

> “A dialogue on the examination of those who are initiated into sacred orders, useful and necessary not only for priests but also for all Christians, by Friar Francisco Ponissono. Appended to it are those truly golden books of blessed Isidore the Spaniard, formerly archbishop, on the Origin of Ecclesiastical Offices, published by him nine hundred years ago and now restored to the light from an ancient Codex and purged of errors to the last detail by Gabriel Prateolus Marcossius. Paris, at the house of Guillaume Cavellat, 1561.”

It is in the smaller format. In a dedicatory letter dated at Paris from the Becodian college on 6 December 1560, Prateolus Marcossius praises Francisco Ponissono’s first little work.

7. He then adds the following concerning our Isidore:

> “For his sake also, and for the benefit of you and all the pious, we have arranged to append, after first purging them of countless errors, those truly golden little books of blessed Isidore the Spaniard, formerly archbishop, on the Origin of Offices—namely, books that we judge to be no less necessary for our own age than for the former age in learning ecclesiastical doctrine.

> “Since I understood that they were sufficiently commended partly by their own dignity and excellence, and partly by the epistolary addition of Joannes Cochleus, a man both exceptionally upright and learned, placed at the threshold of the work, we did not wish to pass any other judgment upon them. We have therefore purged all these little books to the last detail and restored them to their original integrity, etc.”

8. But if we wish to draw an argument from the title of the work, we shall judge Cochleus’s edition to be corrupt, not corrected. For the title on page 56 is transcribed from Cochleus as follows:

> “The two books of the blessed Isidore, formerly archbishop of Seville, on the Origin of Ecclesiastical Offices, published by him four hundred years before the years of the Lord, and now restored to the light from an ancient Codex.”

On the title page of Cochleus’s edition one reads *ante annos D. CCCC*, that is, “nine hundred years ago,” not “four hundred years of the Lord ago.”

In Prateolus’s edition, after the final words of Cochleus’s edition, “who would give the Holy Spirit,” two chapters are added: “On the Suffrages of the Church” and “Whose Suffrages Are Beneficial.” These are not indicated in the table of chapters and may perhaps have been taken from another Paris edition of 1539, which I shall discuss shortly.

9. Fabricius lists other editions of the books *On Offices*, namely one from Cochleus, Paris, apud Vivantium Gautherot, 1542, in a smaller format; another from 1564, in octavo; and one in the *Orthodoxographi*, Basel, 1569, folio. He also lists one in Melchior Hittorp’s collection of writings on the Catholic offices of the Church, Cologne, 1568, folio, where the two final chapters of the second book—“On the Suffrages of the Church” and “Which Suffrages Are Beneficial”—are lacking. In their place one reads the conclusion: “These are a few things from many,” etc., as in Grialius’s edition. I have already noted that those two chapters are also absent from Cochleus’s edition.

These two books *On Offices* also appear in the Roman Collection of Writers on Ecclesiastical Offices, 1591, folio; Paris, 1610, folio; in the *Library of the Fathers*, Paris, 1644, vol. X; and in the *Auctarium*, 1624. Fabricius adds: “It also appears in the *Acta Sanctorum*, vol. I, April, p. 345.” In my opinion, however, this has been inserted here contrary to the author’s intention; Rodriguez carelessly copied the error in vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 335. The two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* are neither in the *Acta Sanctorum*, nor can any reason be devised why they should be there.

A little earlier, no. 7, Fabricius had remarked concerning the *Lament of Repentance* that Lucas of Tuy should be consulted in Isidore’s *Life*, ch. 6, vol. I of the *Acta Sanctorum*, April 3, pp. 340ff. The *Lament of Repentance* does indeed occur in the *Acta Sanctorum*; and perhaps the note concerning this little work was transferred prematurely to the books *On Offices*.

10. Fabricius omitted the edition of 1561, which I described, as well as another preserved in the Alexandrian Library at Rome. The latter reproduces Cochleus’s edition in twenty-fourmo: Paris, 1539, apud Joan. Foucher, “under the Florentine shield, on the road to Saint James.” After the words “they would yield up the Holy Spirit”—the final words in Cochleus’s edition—this edition adds the two chapters “On the Suffrages of the Church” and “Which Suffrages Are Beneficial.” These chapters are absent from some copies and are not even indicated in this edition’s table of contents. I recently compared this edition.

Its title is the same as that of Cochleus’s edition, and it has the same preface. It does not indicate from where those two final chapters mentioned above were taken.

11. Fabricius suggests that the *Exegesis on the Canon of the Mass*, published in Paris in 1548, in octavo, was drawn from this work of Isidore. Zaccaria states this explicitly in the *Bibliotheca Ritualis*, vol. II, under the year 595:

> “From this work of Isidore—specifically, from book I, chapter 36—the passage on the institution of the Lenten fast was extracted, which Boxhorn promised in his notes on Claudius Albinus Spartianus to publish, as well as the *Exegesis on the Canon of the Mass*, Paris, 1548, in octavo.”

Fabricius did not assert that the fragment on the institution of the Lenten fast was taken from this work of Isidore; he merely conjectured it. It may instead be Saint Isidore’s sermon on fasting, which is recited in the Mozarabic Breviary, as I shall explain more fully in chapter 72. The *Exegesis*, or exposition, of the Mass, however, is certainly altogether different from these books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; it will be discussed separately in chapter 84.

12. Boetius Epo printed certain fragments of Saint Isidore, which he himself believed had not yet been published. In fact, however, they already existed in Isidore’s work *On the Divine Offices*, which had by then been circulated in print. Epo appended these fragments to a work of Saint Julian entitled:

> “The three books of the *Prognostica*—that is, *On the Future Age*—of the ancient ecclesiastical writer Julian, once archbishop of Toledo, brought to light from very ancient manuscripts discovered in the Marchiennes Library by Boetius Epo Rordahusanus, a Frisian, professor of both laws and royal ordinary professor at the Academy of Douai. With a preface by the same Boetius Epo addressed to Our Lord Philip, Catholic King. Douai, printed by Louis de Winde, 1564. In octavo.”

After book III come “some very elegant fragments of Saint Isidore of Seville, a most holy man, concerning the various kinds and institutions of the monastic life; also concerning the reception of the Eucharist.”

The first fragment is the whole of chapter 16 of book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. The second is part of chapter 18 of book I:

> “Some say that, unless some intervening sin prevents it, the Eucharist ought to be received daily,” etc., continuing to “may approach more worthily”—or, as in Grialius’s edition, “may more worthily approach.” The passage establishes for whom daily or frequent reception of the Eucharist may be beneficial.

13. The first fragment, concerning the six kinds of monks, seems long ago to have existed separately from the rest of the work in other codices. It still exists in Codex Casanatensis D. IV, 23, which I shall describe in chapter 107.

I also refer here to the fact that among the works published under the name of Saint Valerius the Abbot, who flourished in the seventh century, in vol. XVI of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 387, there is a work entitled *Sayings of Saint Valerius on the Kinds of Monks*:

> “Here there arises a seventh kind of monks, recently added and worse than the earlier ones,” etc.

Flórez adds this note:

> “From the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 3, § 7. Since, according to Menardus, only an incomplete chapter on the kinds of monks is cited, we may hope that Saint Valerius’s fuller codices will be discovered.”

But anyone who reads Isidore’s six kinds of monks will easily understand that Valerius added a seventh kind, since Valerius’s own words show that he had worked through the books *On Offices*. He says:

> “As it is written: possessing the sign of religion but not the merit of religion, like hippocentaurs, with neither horse nor human characteristics distinguished, as was said above.”

That is, in the same book II, chapter 3:

> “Possessing the sign of religion but not the office of religion, like hippocentaurs, neither horses nor human beings,” etc.

In the *Concordia Regularum*, Saint Valerius’s *Sayings* are preceded by chapter 16 of book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, with Menardus’s notes, which I shall present in their proper place.

Epo prefixed to these fragments a dedicatory letter, which reads as follows.

**To the prudent, learned, and pious man, Lord Arnold Gantois, bishop of Marchiennes, Boetius Epo sends greetings.**

14. Among those exceedingly ancient books, Arnold Gantois, most distinguished prelate, which James the Great, your predecessor, a learned and cultivated man, had allowed me to take from your library, and which you yourself sent to me, were these fragments of Isidore, bishop of Seville. As far as I know, they had never before been printed. Isidore was renowned both for the multitude of his writings and for the integrity of his life. Abbot Trithemius noted that he flourished in the year 630 of Christ the Redeemer, during the reign of Sisebut, king of the Goths in Spain, and that on account of his most holy life he was included in the catalogue of the saints. These fragments are surely most worthy of being continually in the hands of all people, but especially of members of your order.

Several of the ancients wrote about monastic institutions, most extensively John Damascene and John Climacus, both Greeks, and most recently our friend Matthew Galenus Vestcappellius, a most diligent observer of theological antiquity. Yet no one has treated this subject more briefly in words, more clearly in substance, or more conveniently in method than Isidore. I thought it my duty to present this little gift especially to you: first, so that I might honestly report to you the source from which I had received it; and second, so that through this Isidore some assistance might be provided for you as you compete in glory with the most praiseworthy and holy archimandrites of these regions, who are earnestly striving to administer their monasteries properly and laudably according to the example and imitation of the ancient monks. Among the foremost in this praise has distinguished himself the excellent John Lentallerus, prelate of Anchin, your neighbor and friend.

For either I am greatly mistaken, or, if those three best kinds of monks which Isidore describes should arise and return, as it were, by a restoration of civil rights, the monastic life will receive the highest praise and will very easily vindicate itself from the contempt and disdain into which—because of the luxury, arrogance, and ignorance of many monks of the preceding age, or, as we commonly say, of religious persons, no less than of secular people—it had for a time almost fallen and in part still lies.

15. You will therefore receive this service of mine toward you with a humane and kindly spirit, and you may expect greater things from me on another occasion. For I possess two copies of Peter of Riga, an ancient Christian poet and, as it appears, a very great theologian. He rendered in elegiac verse the historical books of the entire Old and New Testaments, as well as the Pentateuch of Moses, except for the prophet Job, the Song of Songs, and the Acts of the Apostles, which he completed in heroic verse. He also expressed all the allegories with great skill and, where there was no place for allegory, applied the history to morals. In this manner of interpretation he followed Origen especially and Jerome.

The work is immense and has never yet been printed; it has lain hidden in darkness. If my resources permit, I shall carefully collate the material first from the various copies, insofar as my profession of law allows during certain spare hours, and, God willing, I shall see that it is restored to the light.

I also possess a little work by Matthew of Vendôme, likewise a Christian poet, who treated only Tobit in elegiac verse. Both works are entirely worthy of being brought to light; it is regrettable that treasures of this kind have remained concealed for so long.

Farewell, 1564.

16. Stevartius published a collection of certain ancient ecclesiastical authors under the following title:

> “A single volume of distinguished authors, both Greek and Latin, gathered from various libraries and now ordered by Petrus Stevartius of Liège to come forth into the light for the first time and to benefit the public. Ingolstadt, from the Ederian press, 1616, in quarto.”

On page 797 of this volume there appears *The Blessing of God*, that is, a short commentary on how God should especially be blessed and praised through the psalms. It was composed for the most part from Cassiodorus and Isidore by an anonymous writer, apparently a monk of Regensburg, for Bathuricus, bishop of Regensburg, etc. This author flourished in the year 814 and thereafter.

He offers the bishop these little flowers:

> “which,” he says, “our holy Fathers and teachers of the Church have expounded—namely Jerome, Augustine, Cassiodorus, that great and eloquent man. I have also incorporated Isidore’s instructions concerning antiphons, responsories, and other matters, as well as those of Bede, that outstanding teacher.”

Much material from Isidore’s *On Offices* has been inserted here. Similar material was reproduced in the same way in the Basnagian edition of Canisius’s *Lectures*, vol. II, p. 38.

17. It remains for us to list the manuscript copies which we have collated or examined. In Vatican Codex 641, which I shall describe in chapter 94, are the two books *On Offices*, together with the prologues to the Old and New Testaments, said to be by Isidore the Elder. Vatican Codex 1146, discussed in chapter 95, contains only certain fragments of this work. In the very ancient Vatican manuscript 5765 is book II, mutilated at the end; see chapter 98. In the very ancient Regio-Vatican manuscript 191, discussed in chapter 99, the two books *On Offices* occur much as in the Royal Madrid edition. In Regio-Vatican Codex 256, discussed in chapter 99, is the heading: “Isidore, *On Clerics*: All [clerics],” etc.—that is, from book II, chapter 1, *On Offices*. Other fragments concerning clerics occur in Regio-Vatican manuscript 982, chapter 101. There is a fragment from book II *On Offices* in Ottobonian Codex 6, chapter 105. In Ottobonian 122, at the same place, are “Two books *On Offices* of Lord Isidore”; they end as in Grialius.

## CHAPTER LXX. Isidore’s *Synonyma*, or *Soliloquies*. Editions. Preface to the edition of 1532. Italian translation of the *Synonyma*. Breul’s notice. A heretical corrupter of the *Synonyma* punished by divine judgment. Manuscripts. Several works derived from the *Synonyma*.

1. Braulio, Ildefonsus, and Isidore himself mention the *Synonyma*. Braulio says: “He composed two books of *Synonyma*, by which, through the intervening exhortation of reason, he raised [the soul] to consolation and to the hope of obtaining pardon.” Ildefonsus says: “The Book of Lamentation, which he himself called *Synonymorum*”; where some read *Synonyma*, others corruptly *Synonymam*, just as some manuscripts have *Synonymam* for *Synonyma* in Saint Isidore’s own prologue. *Synonymiam* would not be a bad reading, from Isidore himself, whose definition of *synonymia* I shall shortly give.

Braulio had asked Isidore to send him the *Synonyma*; accordingly Isidore sent them, as is clear from his letter to Braulio while the latter was still archdeacon: “We have sent you the little book of *Synonyma*, not because it is of any usefulness, but because you wanted it.” Some take this letter, which also speaks of other matters, as the preface or dedicatory letter to the *Synonyma*. In fact, however, the *Synonyma* had already been written when this letter was sent to Braulio, as is clear even from the quoted words of the letter. Saint Julian of Toledo also mentions the *Synonyma* in his unpublished work *On Grammar*, no. 346: “For example, if you say to me, ‘Who wrote the *Etymology* [perhaps *Etymologies*]?’ I say, ‘Isidore.’ See: by uttering the name Isidore, I indicate both the things that were done and who did them. Likewise, you ask me, ‘Who [wrote] the *Synonyma*?’ I say, ‘He himself.’”

2. There appears to be no reason to doubt the title which the author himself supplied to the work. Nevertheless Mariana added *On the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul*, because he found those words in the Guadalupe and Seville manuscripts, and because, as he says, by common usage the name *Lamentation* seems to have been employed from Ildefonsus’s own time, since he calls it the *Book of Lamentation*, etc. Certainly Isidore says in the prologue to the reader: “There recently came into my hands a certain little sheet, which they call *Synonyma*; its form persuaded my mind to compose a certain lament for myself and for the wretched”—that is, for himself and for sinners; for this is what the words *mihi vel miseris* signify. Thus there is no incongruity in adding *On the Lamentation of the Sinful Soul* to the title *Synonyma*.

Moreover, four manuscripts used by Mariana, who corrected this work from ten manuscript copies, give the more common title, *Synonyma*. On this subject Mariana says more in his note on the title of the work; he again discusses his manuscripts in notes on book I, chapters 1, 4, 7, and 18, and book II, chapters 2, 3, and 7. One of these manuscripts has the title “Dialogue between Reason and Desire”; three have *Soliloquies*. This variation may be observed in chapter 46, where Isidore’s works are listed from ancient catalogues and the *Synonyma* are recorded among the oldest books of Queen Gisela; also in chapter 47, in the testimonies of writers *On Illustrious Men*, and in chapter 43, where the manuscripts whose collations survive in Zaccaria’s papers are discussed—not to mention the Vatican manuscripts to be reported later. Labbe, in the *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, p. 277, reports that the two books of *Synonyma* by Isidore the Younger occur in the library of the Most Christian King, Codex 513. Rodriguez, vol. II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, pp. 323 ff., records two Escorial manuscripts of the *Synonyma*: one, already described, also containing the books *Sentences*; the other, a quarto paper manuscript of the eleventh century, or, as he says, the beginning of the twelfth—perhaps meaning cotton paper.

3. Since Isidore says in the prologue that he was moved to compose this work by a certain little sheet which had come into his hands and which “they call *Synonyma*,” the question arises whether this is to be understood of Cicero’s *Synonyma*. For many manuscripts read “a certain little sheet of Cicero.” Mariana thought that the word *Ciceronis* should be deleted, because it is absent from most manuscripts and because the inscription of Cicero’s little book of *Synonyma* to Lucius Vetturius was falsely attached to it. I collected much concerning such *Synonyma* of Cicero in chapter 56. For my part, it seems difficult to believe either that in Isidore’s time that little work already bore Cicero’s name, or that Isidore had regard to that book, even if it then existed, whether marked with Cicero’s name or another.

4. For Isidore composed a lament for himself, imitating, he says, assuredly not the eloquence of that work, but his own purpose. Yet what eloquence or rhetorical merit can be imagined in a work containing only certain synonymous nouns, piled together without order, from which no sense arises? Moreover, Isidore affirms that the form of that little sheet persuaded his mind to compose a lament for himself and the wretched, or sinners. What distinctive feature does the form of the circulating *Synonyma* of Cicero possess that could incite anyone to compose a lament?

Nicolaus Antonius conjectures that Isidore imitated Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, while at the same time serving piety and eloquence in so salutary a matter. This perhaps bears on Braulio’s statement that these books were composed for the consolation of the soul, and on the fact that some entitle the same work *On Spiritual Consolation*. Nor, I think, did the author of the Spanish work entitled *Valerius of Histories* intend to indicate another work of Isidore when he praised, among other writings of his, one *On the Consolation of Souls*—although Nicolaus Antonius seems to refer this to another little work of Isidore, published by Breul, *Exhortation to Repentance with Consolation*, discussed below. Others think that the book indicated by Isidore is Cicero’s *Consolation*, or little work *On Mitigating Grief*, written upon the death of his daughter Tulliola. If so, “a little sheet of Cicero” could be retained in Isidore’s prologue.

5. But since Isidore says that the little sheet he mentions is called *Synonyma*, that designation cannot possibly be understood of Boethius’s *Consolation of Philosophy*, or of Cicero’s other *Consolation* upon Tulliola’s death. It would be otherwise if this preface were placed before the little book *On Contempt of the World*, in the manner in which Breul publishes it: “There came into my hands a certain book of Cicero, whose form persuaded my mind,” etc. Breul notes: “He means Cicero’s *Consolation*, by which he consoled himself, grieving at his daughter’s death. You have it at the end of the fourth volume of his works.” Indeed, Cicero’s *Consolation* has perished; the extant work is spurious and, it is believed, fabricated by Carlo Sigonio.

As for Isidore, the old copies of the *Synonyma* give the prologue as we report it: “a certain little sheet, which they call *Synonyma*,” or “a certain little sheet of Cicero, which they call *Synonyma*.” The little book *On Contempt of the World* proceeds in the manner of the *Synonyma* and consists for the most part of Isidore’s *Synonyma*, as Breul also noted; for that reason he doubts whether it was compiled by another.

6. Therefore I would more readily believe that Isidore is speaking of some work, though unknown to us, which, composed under the title and in the manner of *Synonyma*, may have served as a model for Isidore’s composition. In this fashion, indeed, Ildefonsus later imitated Isidore’s *Synonyma*. Cixila, author of Ildefonsus’s *Life*, says: “And he elegantly composed his little book *On Virginity*, in the manner of *synonymia*, filled with testimonies from the Old and New Testaments,” etc. Perhaps one should read *more synonymorum*, “in the manner of the *Synonyma*.” But it is preferable to retain *synonymiae*, for Isidore says, book II of the *Etymologies*, chapter 21: “*Synonymia* occurs whenever, in connected speech, we signify one thing by several words, as Cicero says: ‘You do nothing, undertake nothing, think nothing.’ Likewise: ‘I shall not endure it, I shall not suffer it, I shall not permit it.’”

I possess a rather uncommon edition in which the *Life of Ildefonsus* is attributed to Saint Eladius, bishop of Toledo, and where one reads *more synonymo*, “in a synonymous manner.” Its title is: “The book of the divine Ildefonsus, bishop of the Church of Toledo, a man most learned in sacred literature, *On the Praises of the Virgin Mary and on Her Virginity against the Hebrews*, now first brought to light. His *Life* is appended, together with the preface in which his exceedingly pious confession is expressed. Basel, 1557, octavo.” Basil Millanius of Cassino had the work published from a manuscript copied in the tenth century by Gomesanus, monk of Albelda, for Bishop Gothiscalc, or Gothescalc. I call Gomesanus a monk of Albelda because, although the cited edition reads “abbot of Ildensis,” Nicolaus Antonius frequently calls him abbot of Ildensis, and Risco likewise, vol. XXXIII of *Hispania Sacra*, treatise 69, chapter 12, calls him abbot of Hildensis, Andreas Marcus Burriel was nevertheless the first in his manuscript notes to restore the passage and demonstrate that *Albaildensis*, or *Albeldensis*, should be read in place of *abbas Ildensis*, as Bayer observed, book V, chapter 6, nos. 285 and 289, and again among writers of uncertain date, p. 367. As for Eladius, or Helladius, named as author of Saint Ildefonsus’s *Life*, although another Toledo manuscript of the twelfth century agrees, it nevertheless appears certain that the name of Helladius intruded in place of Cixila’s. Nicolaus Antonius and Bayer’s notes may be consulted on this matter.

7. But must we also contend to attribute this work to Isidore? I see that Berard, whose words I copied in chapter 32, no. 37, calls it into doubt. But on what flimsy grounds! Isidore, he says, calls Braulio, in the prefixed letter, “archdeacon” and “brother,” though elsewhere he calls him bishop. What is this against the *Synonyma*? The letter may be charged with falsity without overthrowing the authority of the *Synonyma*. But then what does the other point prove against the letter? Berard adds: “In that letter Isidore is represented as awaiting the decade of Saint Augustine, adding, ‘I ask that you somehow make me known to it’; these words cannot suitably refer to Augustine, long since dead.” But Berard did not understand Isidore’s expression. Isidore says, *cognitum me ei facias*—that is, “make it known to me.” For that was how people then spoke, as I shall show elsewhere.

8. The *Synonyma* were often printed separately; Fabricius lists them among the other works of Isidore. In the Baluzian library catalogue, p. 16, occurs “The *Soliloquies* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Palatine, from an old edition, without place or year, folio”; this he recognized as identical with our Isidore’s *Synonyma*, or *Soliloquies*. In the catalogue of the Duke de la Vallière’s books, no. 787, this same edition seems to be listed as follows: “The Book of the *Soliloquies* of Isidore, bishop of the city of Palatine, printed about 1472, folio, without indication of place or printer.” It is established that *Palatinensis* was written for *Hispalensis*. Montfaucon likewise mentions, under the same erroneous title, the *Soliloquies* of Isidore, bishop of Palatine, among the manuscripts of the library of Saint-Victor in Paris.

9. The same catalogue, no. 4405, establishes that Isidore’s work *On Spiritual Consolation*, or *Synonyma*, appeared in 1473 from the press of Johannes Veldener, with no place designated. Maittaire’s alphabetical appendix lists Isidore’s *Soliloquies*, quarto, Marsipoli, 1479. Orlandi records Isidore’s *Synonyma on Man and Reason*, Antwerp, 1488, quarto. Fabricius likewise records the Antwerp edition of Isidore’s *Synonyma* of 1488, quarto. Rodriguez de Castro records a Deventer edition of 1491, quarto, printed by Richard Paffroed. Maittaire, vol. I, p. 538, gives the title: “The *Synonyma* of Isidore on man and reason, with the dialogue of the sinner and the Crucified, by Richard Paffroed in Bishop’s Street, 18 November 1491, quarto. Deventer.”

10. I saw another edition in the Angelica Library in Rome, octavo, Venice, printed by Simon of Luere, 1512; it was reprinted there in 1516. This second edition survives in the same Angelica Library and in the Roman library of the Discalced Trinitarian Fathers of Saint Charles at the Four Fountains. *Isidore on Man and Reason Consoling through Synonyms.* At the end: “Here end the *Synonyma* of Saint Isidore of Seville, printed at Venice by Simon of Luere, 10 March 1512.” The other edition was printed in the same manner at Venice by Giorgio de Rusconi on 23 June 1516, duodecimo.

This edition has Isidore’s prologue beginning, “In this following book,” etc., and another: “There recently came into my hands a certain little sheet of Cicero, which they call *Synonymam*,” where the more correct books read, “a certain little sheet, which they call *Synonyma*.” This edition also contains a note appended at the end, commonly lacking in other manuscript and printed copies:

> “Into whosoever’s hands this little book may come, I ask and with great humility beseech that he himself read it more frequently, and that he not merely permit but urge others to write and copy it, so that from his own and others’ progress he may receive a double reward from the Lord. I address a human being, because there are many, perhaps even some religious persons, who wish to possess many books, sufficiently neatly and beautifully bound, and keep them shut up in bookcases, so that neither do they themselves read them nor grant them to others to read. They do not know that it avails nothing to have books and not read them because of worldly hindrances. A well-covered and elegant book, if it is not read, does not make the soul clean. But the book that is constantly read, and cannot be beautiful outwardly because it is often handled, makes the soul beautiful within. For the regard of the Father of mercy, and from the solicitude of a pastor, however unworthy, we have written in this book simple admonitions necessary for parishes, which [perhaps *quam*, ‘which’] holy priests or deacons ought to recite to the peoples committed to them on the greater feast days. In kindly spirit I have undertaken to fulfil this task, and before God I have discharged my conscience. But if any priests or deacons have so bound themselves, indeed, with earthly impediments that they cannot recount those sermons to the people more frequently, let them see how they can render account before Christ’s tribunal for the Lord’s flock entrusted to them.
