Yet we believe in God’s mercy, that he will deign to inspire all clerics, and especially priests and deacons, so that they may not incur guilt through negligence but rather merit eternal reward through constant preaching. And therefore I have written a letter to your Excellency, which attests that in pious affection you are solicitous for priestly honour and reverence. For in this you all show yourselves faithful guardians of God, when you love his priests with due favour and veneration. Here end the *Synonyma* of Saint Isidore of Seville,” etc.

11. I saw another edition of the *Synonyma* in the Vatican Library, no. 1487, with this title: “Dialogue of Isidore, bishop of Seville, *anthrōpou kai logou*—that is, of man and reason. The same author’s *Soliloquies*: a little work, by Hercules, comprising in a concise and convenient brevity the pattern of Christian piety and life; small indeed in size, but greatly to be valued for its holy instructions. Never before printed. Cologne: Johannes Prael, 1522.” Octavo. The editor thought that the *Synonyma* had not yet been printed, though so many editions as I have listed, and perhaps more, had already preceded it. The editor calls the first book of the *Synonyma* a *Dialogue*, the second *Soliloquies*. After the dedicatory letter, soon to be described, follows an elegiac poem in praise of Rutger Sueder, canon of the Church of Our Lady at the Steps in Loon and rector of the monastery of Saint Maximin at Cologne, in whose library this book of Isidore is said to have been found. Then follows: “Preface of Isidore, bishop of Seville, to his dialogue and *Soliloquies*,” beginning: “There recently came into my hands a certain little sheet, which they call *Synonymam*,” etc. This should be corrected to *Synonyma*. The second book is entitled “Second Dialogue, or *Soliloquies*.” It ends nearly as do the common editions: “You please me beyond my life, unto ages of ages. Amen.” There is added from Trithemius: “This Isidore flourished under Heraclon,” etc. The dedicatory letter of Johannes Volscius follows.

> **Johannes Volscius of Loon, their humble rector, wishes Christian piety to the religious and pious Catherine Herrel, lady and mistress in Christ; to the venerable Elisabeth Berstoltz, prioress; and to all the virgins, distinguished by purity of chastity, of the monastery of Saint Maximin in Cologne, his dearest daughters in Christ.**

12. As I was turning over and arranging, religious lady in Christ, venerable prioress, and dearest virgins all, the various books successively left to your monastery by your rectors, my predecessors and yours, there happened to fall into my hands, enclosed in a certain lectern, a little parchment book written in very ancient characters. Its title was: “The Book of Saint Isidore, Bishop, in which Man and Reason speak.” Although at first sight this little book appeared most humble, on closer inspection it seemed to me most devout and at the same time most elegant; for in it, as in a dialogue, two persons—Man lamenting and Reason admonishing—enjoy a salutary conversation.

13. In addition to the candid confession of a man recognizing and bewailing himself, and to the very lucid, elegant, and abundant pious and Christian admonition of Reason, urging him toward the best things, you will find in it a wealth of things and words.

14. For this reason alone I judged it most unfair that this little book of Saint Isidore the bishop, divided into two little works, should any longer be withheld from the sight and reading of your charities and of other pious and learned people. Moreover, because of the wonderful fruit of Christian religion and piety with which it abounds, even if it possessed no charm of words or beauty of style, it nevertheless seemed worthy to be issued in the form of a handbook, because of the pious exhortations contained in it to the pursuit of virtue.

15. This Isidore, surnamed the Younger, bishop of Seville after Leander, disciple of Blessed Pope Gregory, a man most learned in the divine Scriptures and second to none of his age in secular letters, shone forth, subtle in intellect, clear in understanding, measured in expression, distinguished no less by holiness and the variety of his miracles than by learning. But, dearest lady and virgins in Christ, no one offered himself to me before your charities as a person to whom I could more fittingly and conveniently dedicate these little books found in your house; for you are not only most diligently occupied in observing the rule of Saint Aurelius Augustine, your bishop, and your constitutions, but also most attentive in reading sacred—and therefore pious—books.

16. Receive, then, with placid and kindly countenance these two books of Saint Isidore the bishop, brought forth from darkness into light chiefly under your auspices, and printed in a thousand copies in bronze type by your neighbour, the printer Johannes Prael of Suerten, at my urging and through my effort. By their constant and attentive reading you will doubtless become better. May he who is the best and greatest of all deign to grant this to your charities. Farewell. From your house of Saint Maximin at Cologne, in the year from Christ’s birth 1531, on the Ides of December.

17. Nicolaus Antonius testifies that the *Synonyma* were translated into Italian by Giuseppe Alchaino and published at Venice in 1570. This version occurs in the Angelica Library in Rome under the title: “The *Soliloquies* of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Hispoli [sic], in which Man and Reason are introduced, who bewail human miseries and treat of the true rule of good living. To these have been added two most useful works: namely, the moral *Sentences* of Blessed Abbot Nilus, and Rabanus’s book *On Virtues and Vices*. Newly translated by the Reverend Father Fra Iseppo Alchaino of the Order of Preachers. Venice: heirs of Marchiò Sessa, 1530.” Sextodecimo.

Alchaino dedicated his translation to Father Camillo Spera, elected vicar of the province of Saint Dominic, on 16 April 1570, in the Venetian convent of Saints John and Paul. First comes the prologue, called by Alchaino the work of an uncertain author, “in this book”—that is, “In this following book,” etc. Then comes the *Life of Isidore* written by Braulio, which Alchaino says he believes had not previously been printed. The author’s prologue precedes the work: “A short while ago there came into my hands a little book of Cicero, called the *Synonyms*.” The prologue ends: “And Archbishop Isidore of Spain represents the person who weeps.”

In the second book, after the words “I say that you are dearer to me than life itself,” which are the end of the work, Reason continues: “O grieving soul, why do you toss, struck by storms?” etc. The margin notes that this is not found in the Venetian Latin copy. It ends: “to make adverse things prosperous, he who lives and reigns,” etc. This is the little work published by Breul under the title *Exhortation to Repentance with Consolation and the Mercy of God*. Alchaino adds an epilogue to the book and the author’s exhortation to the reader: “Humbly, and with all my heart, I pray,” etc., which I transcribed above from the Venetian Latin edition of 1512. Alchaino falsely attributes this exhortation to Isidore, and carries it only as far as the words “if in this they have not been negligent. And so be it. The end.” After the words “makes the soul beautiful,” he omits “For the regard of the Father of mercy, and [the solicitude] of a pastor, however unworthy.” He reads *parochis* (“for parish priests”) for *parochianis* (“for parishioners”), and shortly afterwards *quam*, as I conjectured, for *quas*. In Braulio’s prefatory notice, it should be noted that Alchaino already read “bishop of Astigi . . . in twenty books.” See chapter 3, no. 21, and chapter 48, no. 12.

596

### 18.

In the editions of all Isidore’s works, the *Synonyma* have been arranged in various ways. Bignaeus presents the entire work as one continuous text, without any division into books. He omits Isidore’s prologue, *Venit ad manus meas*, which he prefixed—with some differences—to the work *De contemptu mundi*, placed by others among Isidore’s doubtful writings. In place of this prologue there is another preface [Col. 0468A], not by the author but by someone else, which is also found in the oldest manuscripts: “In the following book,” etc. The words “Isidore, archbishop from Spain” show that the author of the preface was not a Spaniard. Bignaeus, however, gave the work simply the title: *The Synonyma of Isidore of Seville, Bishop*.

### 19.

Breulius’s edition proceeds as follows: *The Synonyma, or Soliloquies, of Isidore, Bishop of Seville*. Argument. “In the following book, which is called the *Synonyma*,” etc. It is followed by: “In the name of the Lord, to Braulio, most beloved and dearest brother in Christ, archdeacon, Isidore. Since I am unable to enjoy your company,” etc. Breulius thought that this letter had never previously been published; but it had already been included in the Madrid edition among Isidore’s other letters, where it more properly belongs. After the letter [Col. 0468B], Breulius added this notice:

### 20.

> “This letter, never before printed, was supplied to us by the manuscript Codex V of the Most Illustrious Paulus Petavius, counsellor in the royal senate of Paris. It was followed by another letter from the same Isidore to the reader. Since below it serves as the preface to the book *De contemptu mundi*, and since it is reported more faithfully there—the word *schedula* having been changed into *librum*, although *schedula* is wholly inappropriate to this passage—we have judged that it should be omitted here. The work which Isidore called the *SYNONYMA* is called *SOLILOQUIA* in this manuscript, and is divided into two books. John Trithemius also has this division in his work *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and we retain it; nevertheless, we consider that *Soliloquia* applies more particularly to the second book, in which the human being alone speaks. That book [Col. 0468C] is also divided into chapters or commonplaces, whereas the first flows as one continuous text.”

### 21.

Breulius admits that the Petavian Codex agrees with most others in Isidore’s prologue: “A certain little sheet recently came into my hands,” etc. There was therefore no adequate reason for omitting it here. Nor do I approve his statement that in the second book only the human being speaks; for the second book is likewise a dialogue between the human being and Reason, and in it Reason speaks much more than the human being.

### 22.

In the Madrid edition the title of the work is: *Book I of the Synonyma concerning the lamentation of the sinful soul*. The earlier prologue is: “In the following book, which is now called the *Synonyma*,” etc. The second prologue is: “Isidore sends greetings to the reader. A certain little sheet recently came into my hands [Col. 0468D], which they call the *Synonyma*,” etc. It is then followed by Book II of the *Synonyma*, in which, as in the first book, a dialogue is established between the human being and Reason, with these words explicitly marking the speakers: “Human Being,” “Reason.”

### 23.

While we are discussing Isidore’s *Synonyma*, the miracle of the divinely inflicted punishment suffered by a certain Albigensian heretic, who attempted to corrupt that work, must not be passed over in silence. I have said something about heretics who corrupted ancient manuscripts in chapter 7 of the *Prolegomena* to Sedulius. That such frauds by heretics are ancient is evident from Book I, chapter 3, of Sulpicius Severus’s *Dialogues on the Miracles of Saint Martin*:

> “The bishops recalled certain passages written too rashly in Origen’s books. His defenders, not daring to uphold them, said that they had instead been fraudulently inserted by heretics [Col. 0469A]. … Nor is it surprising if heretical fraud had operated in books that were unorthodox and recently written, since in some places it had not feared to cut into the evangelical truth.”

### 24.

John Baptist Gener had prefixed to Part III of his *Theology*, Treatise 2, Book III, on the moral virtues, a polemical preliminary discourse, *On Errors against the Truth, or On the Frauds of Heretics*. The volume had begun to be printed but remained incomplete, and what had already been set in type was not widely circulated. Nevertheless, I saw a copy of this unfinished volume. In that preliminary discourse the sixth fraud of the heretics is stated as follows:

> “At times, with incredible impudence, they corrupt and falsify the sacred books.”

Gener proves this by citing testimonies from Rufinus, Book I of the *Invectives* [Col. 0469B], in Jerome, volume IV of the new edition, p. 366, and volume V, p. 250; from Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 12, where Loaisa’s notes should be consulted; from Lucas of Tuy, Book II, chapter 8, and Book III, chapter 1, in volume XXV of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, pp. 221 and 240; from Irenaeus, Book I, near the beginning; from Tertullian, *On the Prescription against Heretics*, chapter 17; and from Dionysius, bishop of Corinth, apud Eusebius, Book IV of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 23.

### 25.

The tenth fraud of the heretics is this: they have been discovered mutilating and corrupting the writings of the holy Fathers and other ecclesiastical books. The evidence comes from Jerome, *Apology against Rufinus*, Books I and II; Isidore, Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 12; and Lucas of Tuy, *Against the Albigensians*, Book III, chapter 13, who writes:

> “It has been stated above that heretics pervert the divine Scriptures, either by cutting out what is true [Col. 0469C] or by inserting what is false. I now think it should be explained how, through certain alterations of titles, they introduce ambiguity into the Church of God, so that they may more easily be given the opportunity to deceive. For in the books of the holy Fathers they place foreign titles, so that a sermon published by Augustine is given the name of Ambrose, while one published by Ambrose bears the title of Augustine, Jerome, Gregory, or Isidore. A work published by Isidore is made to contain the name of Maximus or Fulgentius, and so with the others, so that the authorities of the holy Fathers may be regarded by us as uncertain. The enemies of God do this especially in parish churches, etc.”

Nor should this seem surprising, since many forgers of profane writers also existed among the ancients, as the most learned [Col. 0469D] Blasius Nasarre observes in his preface to Christopher Rodríguez’s *Hispanic Polygraphy*, citing Pliny, Book X, Letter 71, and Galen, *On the Nature of Man*, Book II, volume V, and in his commentary, Book V, p. 16.

### 26.

Certainly Lucas of Tuy is a reliable witness to what happened in the city of León in his own time. Thus he reports in Book III, chapter 17:

> “A certain heretic named Arnaldus came into Spain from the borders of Gaul, sowing the tares of heretical error. Among his other wicked activities was his practice of corrupting the minor works of the holy Fathers Augustine, Jerome, Isidore, and Bernard, removing what was true and adding what was false. He was a very rapid scribe, and he sold or gave the corrupted works of the saints [Col. 0470A] to Catholics, so that by such deception he might mislead and entangle the minds of unwary readers. It happened one day, when the feast of the translation of the most blessed confessor Isidore was being celebrated, that he was writing and corrupting the *SYNONYMA* of that confessor. It seemed to him that hot water was flowing from the roof of the house down upon his head. When he raised his right hand to wipe his head, his arm was broken as though it had been struck by a powerful blow, and he lost the sight of his eyes. … He began to blaspheme Christ’s confessor Isidore and to reveal the sect of his unbelief in abominable words. But, suddenly seized by the devil, he was cruelly tormented until he finally breathed out his spirit, etc.”

This heretic Arnaldus seems to have been buried in the city of León; for in chapter 9 of the same Book III [Col. 0470B] Lucas mentions “Arnaldus the heretic, buried in that city,” at whose intercession, as the heretics falsely claimed, miracles were performed.

### 27.

I have seen several manuscript copies of the *Synonyma*. The two books of the *Soliloquia*, with Isidore’s prologue, are found in Vatican Codex 473, which I shall discuss in chapter 93. The same books, under the title *Synonyma*, with Isidore’s prologue and a second prologue called the argument, are in Vatican Codex 628, discussed in chapter 94. The same place records Vatican Codex 650, in which the *Synonyma* are indicated at the beginning but are no longer extant. Vatican Codex 1290 contains an excerpt from Isidore’s *Soliloquia*, which I shall discuss in chapter 96. The very old Vatican Codex 4948, discussed in chapter 97, contains the *Synonyma* with only the prologue beginning *In subsequenti*, etc. In Vatican Codex 5077, in the same place, there are two books of the *Soliloquia* without any prologue. Royal-Vatican Codex 254, discussed in chapter 99 [Col. 0470C], presents Isidore’s Book of the *Soliloquia*, which in the printed editions is Book II. In Royal-Vatican Codex 310, discussed in chapter 100, there are two books of the *Soliloquia* of Isidore the Younger, with Isidore’s letter to Braulio, in which he speaks of this work on the *Synonyma*, and with Isidore’s prologue, *Venit nuper*, etc. In Urbinate Codex 100, chapter 104, there is a *Book of the Soliloquia of Blessed Isidore*, which begins “To Orosius the Father.” I believe this to be a scribal error, as I shall explain there. There are two books of the *Synonyma* with the prologue *Venit nuper*; but the work is interpolated, with many additions and many omissions. In Ottobonian Codex 958, chapter 106, there are the *Synonyma* as in Vatican Codex 4948. In Ottobonian Codex 869 there is a *Book of the Synonyma* with two prologues. The two printed books are present, but are not distinguished from one another. Casanatensian Codex G. VI, 7, discussed in chapter 107, contains an excerpt from Isidore’s book called [Col. 0470D] *Symonia*—a corruption of *Synonyma* or *Synonymia*.

### 28.

Several shorter works have been excerpted from the *Synonyma*. Bandini, in volume IV of his *Manuscript Codices*, Pluteus 19 of the library of Santa Croce, describes Codex 3, a twelfth-century parchment manuscript in large folio, most elegantly written, with painted initials and rubricated titles. Among other contents, on p. 134 it has a sermon “from the *Synonyma* of Saint Isidore”; another hand adds: “taken from his *Synonyma*.” It begins: “For reading teaches you what to avoid.” It ends: “Embrace everyone in gentleness and charity.” It is evidently taken from Book II of the *Synonyma*, the chapter on the eyes and leisure, near the end: “Reading teaches you what to avoid,” etc., through the beginning of the chapter on peace: “Love peace, cherish peace, maintain peace with everyone; embrace everyone in gentleness and charity.”

[Col. 0471A]

### 29.

The little book *On Contempt of the World* was also taken from the *Synonyma*, as was another entitled *A Rule of Living*. To the same category belongs the short work that we are to publish, *On the Formation of a Good Life*, or *Isidore’s Collection Concerning Tears*, as well as another entitled *Notable Sayings of Saint Isidore*, or *A Rule of Living*, which is to be transcribed from the Codex of the Borgian Library in chapter 107, no. 31. Although Breulius, in his preface to *A Rule of Living*, declares that he will never believe that so great a man ever intended to serve us “cabbage twice cooked,” I, on the contrary, believe that this was characteristic of Isidore and of the other Fathers: as circumstances required, they frequently transferred much material from earlier books into others. They did not seek to appear endowed with fertile originality, but to be as useful as possible to the people. It is certain that Isidore’s genuine [Col. 0471B] works contain much material repeated in exactly the same words. These and other similar little books will be considered individually when we examine Isidore’s doubtful works, namely in chapters 81 and 82.

## CHAPTER LXXI

### The Rule of Monks

The arguments of the Most Illustrious Petrus Emmanuel Hernandez, who considers that it should be denied to Isidore, are examined. The commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict that Constantine Cajetan attributes to Isidore are spurious. The Isidorian rule of Canons. Editions of the *Rule of Monks*. What is the final chapter concerning the rule of the Devout, derived from Martène?

### 1.

The testimony of Braulio concerning the rule of monks composed by Isidore is clear: “One book of a monastic rule, which he most suitably adapted for the use of his country and for the minds of the weak.” It may be questioned [Col. 0471C] whether Isidore had the same work in mind in his letter to Braulio, while the latter was still an archdeacon, beginning *Dum amici litteras*, where he says: “We have sent a gathering of rules through Maurentius, the chief clerk.” In the manuscript Codex of El Escorial, shelfmark B, Pluteus 1, no. 12, as Bayerius has noted, there is a *Rule of Monks* with this heading by Isidore: “We have sent a gathering of rules through Maurentius, the chief clerk.” This belief, then, that Isidore sent his rule at that time is an old one. Nor, in truth, is there anything that can weaken or undermine it. For *quaternio* referred to sheets fastened together; on this Ducange explains Alcuin’s verses, poem VII:

> “Many wondrous signs this bishop performed,
>
> Which are now properly written on squared sheets.” [Col. 0471D]

He also cites the authority of Eckehard the Younger, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*, chapter 16: “He sent … a gathering containing the whole account of Sandrat.” That some of Isidore’s works were written in gatherings is also established by the oldest catalogue of the library of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch, from which, besides other material, I previously cited in chapter 46: “Isidore’s work *On the Origin*—it seems it should be corrected to *On the Order*—of Creatures, in a gathering. The *Sentences* and the *Chronicle* in gatherings.”

### 2.

That the rule now extant is precisely the one Isidore wrote is forcefully argued by Nicolás Antonio:

> “There are many indications from which we know that this rule was written by Isidore. Not only the subject matter but also the wording agrees with his other books, as we are reminded in very brief notes.”

Smaragdus also praises this rule as Isidore’s in his *Diadem of Monks*, or exposition of Saint Benedict’s rule; he was a writer of the tenth century. So too does Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino in a work on the same subject. Gratian likewise uses its words in chapter *Cum excommunicato*, distinction 18, question 11, and before them Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot, in his *Concordia of Rules*, published by Hugh Menard, an author of the ninth century. Thus far Nicolás Antonio learnedly.

Martène believes that an author of a certain monastic rule lived not long after Isidore and Fructuosus. He published it in volume IX of his *Veterum Scriptorum Collectio*, column 161, from a Colbert manuscript written more than seven hundred years earlier. It begins: “The Lord’s Day, as Isidore says, the apostles therefore,” etc., from chapter 24 of Book I of the *Offices*. The anonymous author, besides other Fathers, cites Saint Benedict, Saint Caesarius, Saint Fructuosus, and Isidore [Col. 0472B] from the *Rule of Monks*. Thus in chapter 6, concerning Saint Fructuosus: “To live on vegetables alone,” etc.; and concerning Bishop Isidore: “Throughout the whole week let them use poor vegetable foods and pale legumes,” which is taken from chapter 9 of the *Rule of Monks*.

### 3.

That Peter of Monte Cassino, from whose manuscript commentary on Saint Benedict’s rule Constantine Cajetan published Isidorian fragments, was a monk and librarian of Monte Cassino and a deacon of Ostia around the year 1137, is stated by John Baptist Marus in chapter 47 of his *On Illustrious Men of Monte Cassino*. Vatican Codex 5718 contains Peter the Deacon’s exposition of Saint Benedict’s rule, on parchment in large folio, whose prologue calls Peter “a sinner.” Vatican Codex 5719, a parchment manuscript in folio, presents another exposition [Col. 0472C] of the same rule by an uncertain author. It begins: “And when he had gathered the crowds.”

Fabricius, in his *Bibliotheca media*, under the entry “Saint Benedict of Nursia,” compiled a list of the writers from whom Benedict of Aniane’s *Concordia* was composed, adding it to the pages of Menard’s edition, and indicated more than fifty passages in which Isidore’s rule is cited.

### 4.

Ancient manuscript copies that attribute the *Rule of Monks* to Isidore support the same conclusion. The Roman Correctors, when correcting Gratian’s *Decree*, had before them a copy of the *Rule of Monks of Saint Isidore*, brought from Spain. For the preparation of the royal Madrid edition, Petrus Ciaconius used one manuscript, and Grialius another, from Oviedo, written in Gothic—or Lombardic—script [Col. 0472D]. Another exists among the rules of the Fathers, written in Gothic characters, at the monastery of Saint Peter of Cardeña; another at the monastery of Saint Peter of Arlanza, as the Benedictine Fathers, witnesses from within those communities, affirm in Bivarius, p. 85, concerning Maximus and Nicolás Antonio.

From a copy of the Cologne Codex of the Regular Canons, which had itself been copied from another very ancient manuscript of Saint Maximinus near Trier, Holstenius published the same Rule of Isidore in Part II of his *Codex of Rules*, p. 196. I recently mentioned one manuscript at El Escorial. Bayerius also lists another Gothic Escorial manuscript, from the ninth or early tenth century, shelfmark A, Pluteus 1, no. 13, with the title: “An ancient collection of monastic rules and of holy virgins consecrated to God.” In it Isidore’s rule bears this heading [Col. 0473A]: “Here begins the rule of Saint Father Isidore the abbot.” It is sufficiently clear that the title “abbot” was attached to our Isidore of Seville by someone who already believed him to have been a monk and therefore to have presided over monks.

### 5.

Mabillon discusses Isidore’s rule in volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, pp. 73, 361, and 397. From Yepes, year 646, chapter 3, he reports that at the monastery of Saint Peter at Arlanza there was preserved a codex entitled *Rules of the Fathers*, containing the rules of Macarius, Pachomius, Basil, Benedict, Fructuosus, and Cassian; and another likewise at Saint Peter’s in Cardeña, containing the rules of Posthumus, Macarius, Pachomius, Basil, Cassian, and Benedict. Mabillon therefore thinks that at that time several rules were customarily read together in Spanish monasteries, at least as spiritual books.

He also concludes that Isidore [Col. 0473B] and Fructuosus adapted the Benedictine rule to local usage, on the basis of those two codices in which, he says, the rule of Saint Benedict is combined with the rules of Isidore, Hildefonsus—this should apparently be corrected to Fructuosus—and others.

### 6.

Mabillon, however, should have demonstrated that those codices were not later than Isidore’s time. He does indeed compare certain canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided, with several passages of Isidore’s rule, which he maintains were taken from the Benedictine rule. But why should we not say that both Benedict and Isidore watered their little gardens from some common and more ancient source? Indeed, since it was Isidore’s practice to copy many words continuously from the Fathers whom he had read, and since in the case of the Benedictine rule there is no evidence that he did this by collation [Col. 0473C], we shall more correctly conclude that he had not read it through.

Mabillon produces from a very ancient Codex of Lérins a pact that the monks made with the abbot of the monastery of Honoriacum, prefixed to Isidore’s rule. He also observes that a similar pact is found at the end of Saint Fructuosus’s common rule. Mabillon says that he is uncertain which monastery Honoriacum was; yet on p. 398 he suggests that Isidore himself was the author of the pact, or profession, as we call it, of the monks of Honoriacum. I am not convinced that this can be inferred from that single Codex of Lérins. I therefore believe that the pact of the monastery of Honoriacum should be relegated to Isidore’s doubtful works.

### 7.

Basnagius, in an observation on Halitgarius’s *Penitential* [Col. 0473D] in the *Thesaurus of Monuments*, Part II, volume II, p. 86, applied certain verses from Isidore’s epitaph to the rule of monks, but not very suitably:

> “As he sincerely believed, so sincerely he published
>
> the form of repentance.”

“This form of repentance,” Basnagius says, “which Isidore published, could indicate the treatise *On Converts*.” Since, however, none of the ancients mentions this little work, I would rather interpret the epitaph as referring to the rule of monks that the bishop of Seville had composed and that occupies a place among the rules published by Holstenius at Paris.

The author of that epitaph, who lived many centuries after Isidore, as is clear from chapters 7 and 13, seems to have understood [Col. 0474A] either the *Exhortation to Repentance*, published by Breulius, or the *Lament of Repentance*, which was inserted by the Canon of León into the *Life of Saint Isidore*, where the epitaph first appeared. It was published by Breulius and subsequently also by the Bollandists under April 4.

### 8.

Once Basnagius’s opinion has therefore been rejected, so many ancient monuments from other sources support recognizing the rule of monks as Isidorian that no one has yet attempted to oppose it. Natalis Alexander, in the sixth century, chapter 6, article 5, after stating that the monk Donatus—who was a contemporary of Gregory of Tours—first brought to Spain monastic discipline regulated by definite laws and institutions, added:

> “Saint Isidore of Seville handed down to the monasteries of Spain [Col. 0474B] a rule extracted from the rules of the earlier Fathers.”

That is certainly how matters stood. As I noted in chapter 19, canon 1 of the Council of Huesca, in the year 598, prescribed that bishops should assemble the abbots of the monasteries annually and demonstrate the rule by which life was to be conducted. Since the monks, from whose hands we have received nearly all of Isidore’s other works, should have taken greater care in copying this rule, who could doubt that it was preserved in those most ancient manuscripts which bear Isidore’s name as author?

Braulio also, when he says that Isidore “adapted the rule for the use of his country and for the minds of the weak,” points to the prologue we possess:

> “Moreover, whoever among you strives to pursue the whole discipline of the ancients, let him proceed as far as he wishes and move with an easy course along that lofty and narrow [Col. 0474C] boundary. But whoever is unable to fulfill such great commands of those who came before should set his steps upon the boundary of this discipline and resolve not to turn aside beyond it, lest, while seeking a deviation toward lower things, he lose both the life and the name of a monk.”

### 9.

Nevertheless, the arguments that the Most Illustrious Hernandez set out in his notes to Zaccaria’s *Conspectus of the Edition*, chapter 42, no. 31, are such that they should not be passed over without careful examination. He denies that the rule circulated under Isidore’s name belongs to Isidore, and considers it the product of some unknown monk—not even a Spanish one—who lived after Isidore. For the author of the rule, in chapter 5 of Holstenius’s edition, cites Isidore’s words from Book III, chapter 21, of the *Sentences* under the name of “a certain Father.”

To begin with this first argument, I wish that this most learned [Col. 0474D] man had noticed that the rule could be Isidore’s even if it had been interpolated in some passage or in some manuscript. From the careful comparison of countless manuscript codices that I examined for Isidore’s edition, I reached the conclusion that scarcely any work of Isidore has not been interpolated in many copies since the ninth and tenth centuries. For around that time this practice—or rather corruption—had become widespread, especially in the Frankish empire: the works of the ancient Fathers were copied with many additions inserted from elsewhere that seemed relevant to the same subject.

### 10.

There was a particular reason for this to happen in the rule of monks: either because different customs prevailed in certain [Col. 0475A] matters in the various monasteries for whose use the rule was intended, or because a fuller explanation of the same point sometimes seemed necessary or useful. Once this is granted, Hernandez’s arguments will easily be weakened.

First, we must ask whether what is not believed to be Isidore’s is found in every copy. If it is not, the interpolation is obvious in itself. Then, if something appears that could in no way have Isidore as its author, yet is present in all manuscript codices, the interpolation must be inferred from conjectures.

The words attributed to a certain Father in chapter 5 of Holstenius’s edition, which are Isidore’s in Book III, chapter 21, of the *Sentences*, are these:

> “For many of the monks, according to the judgment of a certain Father, entangled in secular activities and public business [Col. 0475B] through love of their relatives, while wishing to benefit their kin, have lost their own souls,” etc.

In the Madrid edition, chapter 19 corresponds to chapter 5 of Holstenius’s edition. After the words “are instructed by observing,” the entire passage that Holstenius inserts is omitted: “No monk,” etc., through “It must not be presumed”; and consequently the sentence “For many of the monks,” etc., is omitted. It is inserted in Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 21, though not in the same words.

The first answer, then, may be that Holstenius’s edition is interpolated at this point and does not reproduce Isidore’s words. Furthermore, Isidore presented the aforesaid sentence in Book III, chapter 21, from Gregory, Book VII of the *Morals*, chapter 30. The words “according to the judgment of a certain Father” therefore indicate Gregory, not Isidore. The sentence in the *Rule* [Col. 0475C] does indeed seem to be expressed more closely from Isidore’s *Sentences*, Book III, than from Gregory at the cited passage; but the substance is the same in both, and therefore Gregory is the original author.

Breulius cites chapter 18; Grialius, chapter 17; in the Maurist edition it is chapter 30. It is also characteristic of Isidore to cite a certain Father without naming him, as in Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 48:

> “For, as a certain Father says, everything that rises above others is afflicted more by sorrows than it rejoices in honors.”

This saying is Gregory’s, Book XXXIII of the *Morals*, chapter 19.

### 11.

Hernandez says that the author of the rule was a monk because, addressing monks in the passage cited, he says: “Therefore we too must be free from the activities of the world,” etc. He absolutely denies that Isidore was ever a monk. I, on the contrary, would find it easier to count [Col. 0475D] Isidore among the monks—of the kind who lived in Spain in that century, such as Leander, Isidore’s brother, Ildefonsus, his disciple, and other men of the highest standing—than to deny the rule of monks to him.

But, leaving aside the fact that these very words, “Therefore we too must be free,” etc., are absent from the royal Madrid edition, which should be preferred to Holstenius’s, I do not think it follows from the words quoted that the author of the rule was a monk. A bishop addressing monks could say what is common to all ecclesiastics: all ecclesiastics ought to be free from the activities of the world.

This is also supported by the fact that Isidore frequently transfers the sayings and words of other Fathers into his own works. That he followed this practice in the rule of monks is sufficiently clear from the preface itself. From [Col. 0476A] the same preface and from the epilogue it may be gathered that the author of the rule was not a monk, for he addresses monks as someone separated from their state. Thus in the preface:

> “Following the example of those Fathers, we have dared to select these few things for you. … Moreover, whoever among you strives to pursue the whole discipline of the ancients,” etc.

### 12.

In the epilogue:

> “Therefore, O servants of God and soldiers of Christ, despisers of the world, we wish you to observe these things in such a way that you may keep the greater commandments. Receive, then, among those commandments this admonition of ours also, guarding with humble heart what we say and willingly accepting what we administer, so that glory from the fruit of the work may come to you, and forgiveness may be granted to us in answer to the prayer we offer for this admonition. May almighty God guard [Col. 0476B] you in all good things, and, as he began, so may he also strengthen his grace in you.”

If, then, the words objected by Hernandez proved that the author was a monk, they should rather be considered spurious, since they contradict the preface and the epilogue, than should the whole work be denied to Isidore. But, as I have said, those words could appropriately have been spoken by a bishop who was not a monk, just as Isidore says similar things in Book III of the *Sentences*, chapter 21, where he discusses monks occupied with worldly cares:

> “Just as we must not hate our soul, but must hate its carnal affections, so neither must our parents be hated by us,” etc.

### 13.

Hernandez believes that the author of the rule was not Spanish because the monastery of Honoriacum, or Honorianum, as it is read in Holstenius’s [Col. 0476C] edition, for which the rule appears to have been written in that edition, is entirely unknown among the Spaniards.

This conjecture could establish only that the title concerning the monastery of Honorianum, which was printed by Holstenius, had been added, especially since it is omitted in the editions of Grialius and Breulius. But even this is not established, for no mention of a monastery of Honorianum or Honoriacum appears outside Spain either.

Since other peoples have investigated their ecclesiastical and monastic antiquities no less diligently than the Spaniards, and since it is easier for the memory of Spanish monasteries to have perished through the invasion of the Moors than that of monasteries in other nations, fairness in judgment requires us to conclude from the rule itself that a monastery [Col. 0476D] called Honoriacum existed in Spain, or perhaps in those parts of Gaul that were subject to the Gothic kings.

Cellier says that it was situated in Baetica; I think he does so because this is more consistent with reason: namely, that Isidore wrote the rule for the monks of his own province rather than for those of another. It is not absurd, however, that he should have sent a rule composed for the monks of Baetica to others who requested it, just as we have said he sent it to Braulio.

### 14.

Braulio’s words “for the use of his country” indicate more strongly that the rule was arranged by Isidore for Baetica than for any other province of Spain. For it is clear from the Second Council of Seville, over which Isidore presided, that Baetica contained many monasteries, both ancient and recently founded:

> “At the tenth session, at the request of the Fathers of the monasteries [Col. 0477A], we unanimously decreed that the monasteries recently founded in the province of Baetica, as well as those that are ancient, should remain firmly established with an immovable and unshaken stability.”

It is therefore a plausible conjecture that Isidore prescribed the rule for one of the newly founded monasteries, which bore the name Honoriacum or some similar name. Since proper names are found corrupted in most manuscript codices, and since the monastery itself is called Honorianum in Holstenius’s edition but Honoriacum by Mabillon and others, one need not strongly resist someone who wishes to substitute for *Honoriacum* a somewhat similar name of a Baetican monastery whose memory still survives.

But although, as I have said, there were many monasteries in Baetica and in Spain in Isidore’s century, there are certainly not [Col. 0477B] many whose distinct names have come down to us. Information about some of them is found in only one or another ancient monument, as with the monastery of Honoriacum in Saint Isidore’s *Rule* and in the pact that the monks of the monastery of Honoriacum made with their abbot, published by Mabillon in volume IV of the *Benedictine Annals*, p. 397.

Paul the Deacon of Mérida reports the following about Masona in chapter 9 of the *Life of the Fathers of Mérida*:

> “At the very beginning of his episcopate he founded many monasteries and enriched them with extensive estates.”

Who, I ask, ever set down all the names of those monasteries?

### 15.

Hernandez derives another argument from the fasts prescribed in chapters 11 and 12 of Holstenius’s edition of the *Rule of Monks*. These, he says, differ utterly [Col. 0477C] from those that Isidore describes in chapter 38 and following of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

It must nevertheless be observed that the fasts are prescribed in the rule for monks, whereas in the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* they are prescribed for all Christians.

Regarding the first fast, therefore, which is the Lenten fast, Isidore treats it in chapter 37 of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. In the *Rule*, chapter 11, he says:

> “The first fast is the daily fast of Lent, during which a stricter observance of abstinence will be maintained by the monks,” etc.

Isidore explains the second fast in the cited chapter 33 of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “According to the canons,” he says, “it begins on the day after Pentecost.” In the *Rule*, however, in the cited chapter 11, he explains the same fast more distinctly:

> “The second fast, which is observed on alternate days, begins on the day after Pentecost and extends to the autumnal equinox, namely, for three days in each week.” [Col. 0477D]

Here you see that the opening words appear to have been taken from the book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

Isidore establishes the third fast in chapter 39 of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices* on the eighth day before the Kalends of October; it is called the fast of the seventh month. He then places the fourth fast on the Kalends of November.

In the *Rule* these two fasts are joined and continued. Thus, in the cited chapter 11:

> “The third follows: a daily fast from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the Lord’s Nativity; during it the daily fasts are in no way relaxed.”

This applies, of course, to the monks whom Isidore was instructing.

### 16.

A greater difficulty remains concerning the fourth fast prescribed in chapter 11 of the *Rule*:

> “The fourth daily fast likewise begins after the day of the Circumcision and continues until the solemnities of Easter.”

This fourth monastic fast was joined [Col. 0478A] to the first, the Lenten fast; during Lent they abstained not only from meals but also from wine and oil.

What does not accord with Isidore’s teaching is that this fourth fast should begin after the day of the Circumcision. For in chapter 41 of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices* he himself states that the Church instituted the fast of the Kalends of January because of the error of paganism. The same is prescribed by canon 10 of the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided in the year 633. The beginning of the fourth fast, therefore, should have been placed on the Kalends of January.

What is more, as Hernandez observes, Isidore never mentions the feast of the Circumcision, although the church of Spain did not begin to celebrate such a feast until after his death. Nor is there any monument [Col. 0478B] older than law 11, title 1, Book II, of the Visigothic laws, dating from about the year 650, under King Recceswinth.

17. I admit that some interpolation seems necessary at this point, but one that may in some way have proceeded from the author’s intention. For Isidore took the beginning of the fourth monastic fast to be the Kalends of January, because on that day a solemn fast had been instituted for everyone. But as soon as the feast of the Circumcision began to be celebrated in Spain, the contrary consideration persuaded people to begin the fourth fast after the feast of the Circumcision, rather than on the day itself. Since, therefore, the rule was in the monks’ hands for exact observance, or even had to be read aloud publicly, so that the explicit beginning of the fast on the Kalends of January might not cause confusion [Col. 0478C], the words “after the day of the Circumcision” were substituted. If anyone nevertheless wishes to proceed with the utmost strictness, he may also maintain that these very words are Isidore’s, following the authority of the eminent Lesleus in his note to the Mozarabic Missal, p. 492. From Isidore’s rule he infers that the solemnity of the Circumcision began to be celebrated before Isidore’s death; by the middle of the seventh century it was listed among the principal festivals in the laws of the Visigoths, on which even the courts were closed. He denies that before this period any certain testimony to this festival can easily be found; from Spain it soon spread to Gaul and thence to Germany.

18. Thus far I have compared the fasts established in the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* with the fasts of the rule of the monks in the royal Madrid edition. In Holstenius’s edition, chapter [Col. 0478D] 11 concerns the Feriae, and chapter 12 the Fasts. Omitting other variations, which are irrelevant to the matter and are attributable to copyists, after the words “the fasts are interrupted” Holstenius inserts the following, omitted in the Madrid edition: “provided, however, that they have not been general.” The chapter on Fasts agrees in both editions, and does not differ in any statement. Since, therefore, the rule concerning fasts as set out in the Madrid edition may have Isidore as its author, the same must be said of this part of the rule in Holstenius’s edition, since the few added words, “provided, however, that they have not been general,” present no difficulty. Perhaps they were added at a later time, for purposes of explanation, in some monastery where the rule was in force, by some private monk [Col. 0479A], so that it might be understood that the permission granted by the rule to interrupt the fasts while one of the brothers was being converted, or while brothers from other monasteries gathered for a visit, could not be extended to fasts which the Church prescribed for everyone to observe.

19. The objections which Hernandezius raises at the end are less significant—namely, that the order of the chapters of the rule is very different in Holstenius, Grialius, and Breulius, and that Holstenius has two chapters consisting of certain additions, which are absent from the other two. From the recension of manuscript copies in the Vatican Library, which I shall undertake later, it will plainly appear that scarcely any work of Isidore exists that is not exposed to this kind of difficulty. This is already sufficiently clear from the comparison presented above of the codices of Zaccaria’s edition and others, and indeed from the notes of Grialius’s edition [Col. 0479B]. Isidore’s works were in almost everyone’s hands. What wonder, then, if his works were subjected to transpositions of chapters, additions, alterations, interpolations by unskilled copyists—or, what is worse, by shallow and audacious men?

Vives says excellently in book I of *On the Corruption of Learning*:

“But indeed, in copying, the greatest blame has always rested on them: copyists were almost invariably rather unskilled men, who supported their modest means by transcribing books; not rarely they were also women and consecrated virgins . . . Sometimes those who wrote did not know how to read and confused everything . . . In the case of other authors, not only did half-learned men pursue the copyists’ errors, but they also attacked passages that had been correctly written yet were beyond their own understanding. Thus they corrupted sound meanings, and for one error which they tried to erase, they sprinkled four [Col. 0479C] more. We see that, as each of the ancient writers has been in the hands of scholars during these five hundred years, so he has come down to us more corrupt.”

20. In reviewing Isidore’s works, especially those concerned with shaping human conduct, one consideration must repeatedly be kept in mind: the author himself appears to have circulated the same little works several times, with additions and minor alterations according to circumstances. Thus, when he was obliged to hand down rules of life to monks based on the prescriptions of the canons, he may have altered or expanded certain matters for different monasteries, places, and times. Later, when copyists collected these materials into a single body, some manuscripts came to display a certain disorder of subjects and chapters.

[Col. 0479D] 611

21. Zaccaria found no manuscript copy with which he could compare Isidore’s rule. Holstenius, although he subjected some of the rules of the ancient Fathers to comparison with manuscript copies, added no variant readings to Isidore’s rule. This indicates that he found no manuscript of that rule with which he could compare his own exemplar. Nor was I able, among so many Vatican manuscripts, to find one containing Isidore’s *Rule*.

22. The more extensive commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, which Constantine Cajetan attributes to Isidore, should not be separated from the *Rule of the Monks* if they were genuine, and not rather spurious; something has already been said about them in chapter 19, when the claim that Saint Isidore was a Benedictine monk was rejected [Col. 0480A]. Cajetan published fragments of such commentaries from Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino. Yet, whatever Cajetan boasts in his introductory note to the annotations, almost all of them are drawn from the *Rule of the Monks*: some from other extant works of Isidore, and perhaps a few from works that have perished. Nor is everything that Cajetan reports from Peter of Monte Cassino as though it were Isidore’s actually Isidore’s; some passages belong to Peter himself, who expands Isidore’s thought, as will be clear to anyone who compares them. We shall relegate these fragments to the appendices, with Cajetan’s notes attached. His prefatory notice runs as follows:

*Notes and variant readings of Constantine Abbot Cajetan on Isidore’s fragments concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict.*

23. What we have reported thus far consists of certain fragments surviving from Isidore’s commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, lost through the ravages of time. We have extracted them not only from Peter the Deacon of Monte Cassino, who wrote approximately five hundred years ago, but also from Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in Lorraine, who lived eight hundred years ago. For, among others who explained Saint Benedict’s Rule, these men bring forward as evidence the statements of Isidore of Seville concerning that same rule.

Accordingly, we collected both the rule itself and Isidore’s fragments from the commentaries of Peter the Deacon, preserved in manuscript form in the library of Monte Cassino. From Smaragdus, whose exposition has already been published and is in circulation, we noted only variant readings, to be recorded somewhat farther below. Moreover, anyone who compares these fragments with Isidore’s *Rule of the Monks* will recognize with certainty that their author was this Isidore of ours; indeed, that this very *Rule* is nothing other than a kind of abridgment of the commentaries on Saint Benedict’s Rule. They are so similar to one another in both style and subject matter—or, more truly, they are so identical [Col. 0480C]—that this is unmistakable.

Finally, since some writings by Isidore of Seville on the Rule of Saint Benedict survive which are found neither in his own *Rule of the Monks* nor in his other books, it must undoubtedly be admitted that Isidore composed more extensive commentaries on it. But more on this elsewhere.

24. Some also report that Isidore composed a *Rule for Canons*, and they are not entirely mistaken. But this rule, as I explained in chapters 19 and 31, is the *Rule for Canons* proposed at the Council of Aachen, which was composed from the sentences of the holy Fathers, especially those of Isidore.

25. Isidore’s *Rule of the Monks* first appeared in the royal Madrid edition; it was subsequently reprinted in Breulius’s edition and in the second, recent Madrid edition [Col. 0480D]. Lucas Holstenius prepared his collection of rules under this title:

“*A Codex of Rules which the Holy Fathers once prescribed for monks and holy virgins to observe, collected long ago by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane. Lucas Holstenius, Canon of the Vatican Basilica and prefect of the library, edited it, arranged in three parts and enlarged. Rome: printed by Vitalis Mascardus, 1651, quarto.*”

In that old *Codex of Rules*, a preface precedes Isidore’s rule:

“*Here begins the preface of Isidore, bishop of Seville, to the Rule of the Monks. Isidore to the holy brothers established in the monastery of Honorianus. There are many things, etc.*”

The title of the preface is lacking in the editions of Isidore’s works. As I noted above, Mabillon calls the monastery Honoriacense. The chapters of Saint Isidore’s rule in the Codex of Saint Benedict of Aniane [Col. 0481A] number twenty-three; in the editions of Isidore’s works they number twenty-four. Nor is the order of the chapters the same, but in the actual contents there is little difference.

Holstenius, who died shortly before the *Codex of Rules* appeared, had stated in his preface that this codex was the very one about which Hugh Menard says in his note to the *Acts of Saint Benedict of Aniane*:

“In the testament of Saint Gennarius, bishop of Asturia, among the books which he gave to the monastery of Saint Peter of the Mountains, there is listed a *Book of Rules of Illustrious Men*. Whether it is the same as the book collected by our Benedict is not entirely certain.”

26. Holstenius’s *Codex of Rules* was printed again at Paris in 1663, quarto, and in a new collection of rules under this title:

“*Lucas Holstenius’s Codex of Monastic and Canonical Rules, once collected by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, now enlarged, expanded, and divided into six volumes; illustrated with critical-historical observations by Father Mariano Brockie, prior of the monastery of Saint James of the Scots at Regensburg. Augsburg, 1759, folio. There, volume I, pp. 187 ff.: Rule of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, for Monks.*”

*Critical observation of Father Mariano Brockie on the Rule of Saint Isidore.*

27. The author of this rule is Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, successor of Saint Leander in the episcopate and his uterine brother, who died in 636 and was entered in the calendars of the saints. For this most holy bishop seems to have written the rule before attaining the episcopate, since he had followed the monastic life from his earliest years. Yet whether he began his novitiate in this monastery of Honoriacum [perhaps *Honoriacense*] is rightly doubted, since he composed the present rule, comprising twenty-three chapters, to instruct its monks and strongly commended to his monks other rules of monastic life written by the holy Fathers.

Although we are now unaware of the location of this monastery, we may nevertheless easily suppose that it had been imbued with Benedictine institutions, since the Rule of Saint Benedict had long before been promulgated among the Spaniards through Saint Aemilianus and Saint Leander had embraced it. Finally, if we examine this Rule of Saint Isidore carefully, we must recognize that it too was drawn from Benedictine discipline. For it prescribes manual labor, fasts, readings, the divine office, and other monastic duties in the same manner; it also requires the monks to sleep in the same dormitory and eat at the same table, and orders a dean to supervise every group of ten. All these things appear to have been taken from the Rule of Saint Benedict, which he therefore proposed for observance by his monks, with a few additions better suited to the place and region [Col. 0481D]. Hence there are authors who assert that both rules were observed simultaneously in the same monastery.

28. In this edition the preface is entitled: “To the holy brothers established in the monastery of Honoriacum, Isidore.” It is preceded by chapter 24 from Martène, or the *Sentence concerning the Rule of the Devout*. Again, on p. 404, the editor produces the same *Sentence concerning the Rule of the Devout* for variant readings according to Holstenius:

“In the old codex,” he says, “which contains the monastic ordinances of the holy Fathers, the following two constitutions were also read after Saint Isidore’s Rule: one belonging, I do not know to whose rule of the Devout; the other belonging to the Second Council of Seville.”

The constitution of the Second Council of Seville is chapter 11: “In the eleventh session,” etc. Perhaps this is how it is found in the Paris edition of Holstenius’s *Rules*. In the Roman edition, at least, I find nothing of the kind.

614

29. Martène, volume IX of the *Veterum Scriptorum Collectio*, column 160, added, from an Elno manuscript written, as he himself then said, eight hundred years earlier, the final chapter—or chapter 24 or 25—of Isidore’s *Rule*, under this title: *Sentence concerning the Rule of the Devout*: “Let no one go to visit them,” etc. Rodriguez took the opportunity for his error from this, asserting in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, p. 336, that Isidore’s *Rule of the Monks* had been published in volume IX of Martène’s collection, although only the final chapter just mentioned was printed there.

30. Hugh Menard formerly published a *Concordance of Rules* with this title:

“*Concordance of Rules, by Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, now published for the first time from the library of the monastery of Fleury, and illustrated with notes and observations, by Father Hugh Menard, a Benedictine monk of the Congregation of Saint Benedict, otherwise called Cluniac, and of Saint-Maur at Paris; from the press of Jérôme Drovat, 1638.*”

There are two quarto volumes, but the numbering of the chapters and pages continues in the same sequence. In the preface, concerning the rules of this concordance and their authors, Menard says briefly of Isidore on p. 62:

“The Rule of Saint Isidore, bishop, is that of the great Isidore, bishop of Seville, which appears among his works published at Cologne in 1617. Saint Braulio lists it among Saint Isidore’s writings, etc. It does not differ greatly from Saint Benedict’s rule. Some material, however, is drawn from other works of Isidore, as in chapter 3, ‘The Statements of Saint Isidore concerning the Kinds of Monks,’ from book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15, or 16.”

We shall not omit Menard’s learned notes. This *Concordance of Rules* proceeds in a different order from the *Codex of Rules* collected by the same Saint Benedict of Aniane and edited by Holstenius. In the *Codex*, the rules of various authors are woven together in a continuous flow of discourse; in the *Concordance*, the text of Saint Benedict’s Rule is first set out under various titles, and excerpts from the rules of other authors are compared with it here and there.

Benedict of Aniane introduces the work in prose and verse. From the verse come these lines:

“Benedict and Isidore, Basil also, stand forth,

Illustrious men, whose sayings resound throughout the world.”

615

## CHAPTER LXXII. Sermons Ascribed to Saint Isidore. Whether Any Are Genuine, and Which Ones. Saint Isidore’s Sermon in the Mozarabic Breviary for the Removal of Flesh. Several Sermons of Isidore Excerpted from His Works in Homiliaries.

[Col. 0482D]

1. I have no doubt that Isidore, in the course of his episcopal office, often delivered sacred addresses to the people, and that many homilies of this kind were committed to writing and handed down to posterity. Whether a collection of Isidore’s sermons ever existed in a particular volume, however, does not appear equally certain. The anonymous twelfth-century writer of Melk, cited above in chapter 47, suggests this:

“Moreover, he transmitted to posterity many sermons, delivered at different times and written in an excellent style.”

Sigebert, more clearly, in the same century, and much later Trithemius, say that Isidore wrote a *Book of Sermons*. I do not know whether what Montfaucon mentions in the *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, among the codices of the Ambrosian Library at Milan, belongs here: “homilies of Isidore and certain other works.” The more ancient authors are silent. Perhaps a large part of Isidore’s sermons had been inserted by Isidore himself into his other commentaries, as was the custom of other Fathers. As a result, a collection of his sermons may have been neglected by copyists of books as less necessary.

Nevertheless, one must hold that a given sermon is Isidore’s if this is established by ancient records, or if in old copies a sermon is attributed to him whose style is not unworthy of him.

2. As I explained in chapter 44, I possess among Zaccaria’s papers three sermons attributed to Saint Isidore, all of which Zaccaria considered spurious in his published *Survey of Isidore’s Edition*. The first of these is a sermon against the Arians. It exists not only in the Codex Caesenas Malatestianus, inscribed with Isidore’s name among his other works, but is also assigned to Isidore in an eleventh-century catalogue of the monastery of Pomposa, with the same opening indicated above, as I observed in chapters 44 and 46.

From the Canon of León, the author of Saint Isidore’s life, and from the Spanish breviaries, I reported in chapter 18 that Isidore, while still a young man, had vigorously attacked the Arian heresy. Certainly I find nothing in this sermon that could not have proceeded from Isidore; nor would anyone perhaps be mistaken who believed that it was composed by him in his youth.

3. The second sermon is in praise of Saint Aemilianus, transcribed from a very ancient manuscript of the archive of Vercelli, under this title: “Sermon of Blessed Isidore on the feast of Saint Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli” [Col. 0483C]. Formerly, as I suppose, this sermon was recited in the church of Vercelli on the day when Saint Aemilianus’s feast was celebrated, perhaps before that church abandoned its own particular rite, called Eusebian after Saint Eusebius, and adopted the Roman rite. John Andrew Iricus clearly attests to this in book I of his *History of Trident*, p. 11.

John Stephen Ferrerius, bishop of Vercelli, in his work *On the Life and Deeds of Saint Eusebius of Vercelli and of His Successors in that Episcopate*, Rome, 1602, quarto, printed by Aloysius Zannettus, mentions that the same sermon exists in the most ancient archive of the church of Vercelli, identifying it by its opening words: “The ecclesiastical man, crucified to the world through the mortification of his own flesh, ought also, according to his stewardship, etc.”

He relates that Saint Aemilianus [Col. 0483D], whose feast day is celebrated in the church of Vercelli on the third day before the Ides of September, originated in the town of Libyus in Aragon; that, already bishop of Vercelli, he attended the third, fourth, and sixth Roman councils under Pope Symmachus, in the years 501, 502, and 504; and that his body was discovered and transferred to the principal church of Vercelli in 1181, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June. Niccolò Antonio wished this to be recorded so that the citizens of Aragon, and especially of the town of Libyus, would not remain unaware of it.

4. This, then, may have been the reason why Isidore celebrated Saint Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli. Yet I have an objection. Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, committed to writing the life of Saint Aemilianus the priest, who is said to have died in 564. It was published in Bivarius’s commentary on Maximus, in Tamayo’s *Martyrology* on 12 November, and in volume I of the *Acts of the Benedictine Saints* [Col. 0484A].

There is much controversy over which Aemilianus Braulio praised. Most Spaniards believe that he was Saint Aemilianus the Hooded, commonly called “of La Cogolla.” The Aragonese contend that he was Aemilianus, the hermit of the kingdom of Aragon, whose sacred remains are preserved in the town of Torre la Paja. Authors who fabricated spurious chronicles add several other details. “I likewise regard Helecan as a fabrication,” says Niccolò Antonio, book V, no. 237, “who, intent on resolving this question as well, chatters that he was the bishop of Vercelli who is venerated among the Aragonese—or else he was misunderstood by Bivarius himself.”

5. In the Mozarabic Office, the feast of Saint Aemilianus, abbot and confessor [Col. 0484B], is celebrated on 12 November. Everything is common, except for an iambic senarius hymn, believed to have been written by Braulio. For Braulio himself testifies at the end of the dedicatory letter to the *Life of Saint Aemilianus* that he composed a hymn in praise of this holy confessor. Certainly the hymn is elegant, and may appear above the capacity of the seventh century. It begins:

“O great Christ, illustrious ruler of all things,

to whom the stars of heaven are perpetually obedient,

grant us chaste and sober prayers, favorable at the annual feasts,

which may appease your clemency.”

It proceeds without metrical fault, except in certain places where a scribal error is easily detected, especially since similar mistakes of writing are frequently observed even in the hymns of Prudentius that occur in the Mozarabic Breviary. In the third verse the author perhaps wrote “These vows,” and in the fifth, “Which may appease your clemency.”

6. Since, therefore, the memory of this Aemilianus was famous among the Spaniards—and he is certainly very different from Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli—someone might suspect that Saint Isidore’s sermon was written in praise of Saint Aemilianus the Hooded, and that the people of Vercelli later applied it to their bishop Aemilianus.

I am nevertheless certain that someone composed a sermon in praise of Saint Aemilianus, bishop of Vercelli, from book III of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences*, and prefixed Saint Isidore’s name to it for this reason: apart from a few words by which the subject of the sermon is adapted to Aemilianus, the entire sermon is composed from chapters 33, 36, 42, and 43 of book III of the *Sentences*, reproduced in full [Col. 0484D]. This sermon must therefore be relegated to the appendices, among other works pieced together from Isidore’s books.

7. The third is a sermon ascribed to Isidore in a thirteenth-century codex, against gluttony, pride, and greed. This homily is devout and effective against the vices, but I cannot bring myself to believe that it is Saint Isidore’s. It bears the scent of later centuries in its more distinctly elaborated teaching about two angels: one a good guardian at the right hand of each individual, the other an evil tempter at the left. The scholastics indeed hold this by common agreement and generally confirm it with certain testimonies of the ancient Fathers. But it is presented in this homily more distinctly and explicitly, as I have said, than seems compatible with the age of Isidore [Col. 0485A].

I would say the same about the punishments of hell, which seem to be described in the style of more recent times. Saint Augustine is praised in this homily as though he had asserted that, on the day of the Lord’s resurrection, the souls of the righteous visit the tombs of their bodies and say, “Farewell, good companion,” and so that the souls of the damned reproach their own bodies: “Alas, alas, wretched body,” etc. Yet I believe you will find nothing of the kind in Augustine, nor in any reputable ancient author.

8. Although many have carefully reviewed Isidore’s books and little works, no one has identified the homily that is recited under his name in the Mozarabic Breviary. It appears on Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, p. 135 of the new Madrid edition, with this inscription: “Sermon of our most blessed Father Isidore, bishop, for the removal of flesh” [Col. 0485B]. It begins: “Dearest brothers, I beg and exhort you, on this lawful and most sacred day, etc.”

Eugene Robles mentions this homily in his description of the Mozarabic Office, inserted in the book *On the Life and Deeds of Cardinal Ximenes*, chapter 26:

“Appropriately, Saint Isidore’s sermon is inserted in the breviary. He enlarged this office for the day of the revelries, or Mardi Gras, which is immediately followed by Ash Wednesday.”

This is rendered into Latin from Robles’s Spanish book in Blanchini’s prolegomena to the *Gothic-Hispanic Orational*, p. 120. In his Spanish work, which I possess, Robles calls it a solemn sermon and calls the day on which it is recited *martes de Carnestolendas*; this is how the Spaniards speak, whereas others call it *Carnisprivium*. Although Robles was a priest attached to the chapel of Toledo, where the Mozarabic Office is celebrated, he nevertheless designated the day on which Saint Isidore’s sermon is recited with insufficient accuracy.

9. For Isidore’s sermon was not appointed for the office of Tuesday, or the third feria, for the removal of flesh—there is no proper office for that day in the Mozarabic Breviary—but for the office of Wednesday, or the fourth feria of the Ashes, which is inscribed “at the beginning of the fast.” It was placed at the end of that office. Robles may have been misled by the title of the homily, “for the removal of flesh.”

In former times, however, not only were the days immediately preceding the Lenten fast called by this name, but the beginning of the Lenten fast itself was also so called. Ducange defines *Carnisprivium* as “the time when the faithful begin to be deprived of meat and to abstain from it before the Lenten fast.” The Maurists add: “Sometimes it is used for the first days of the fast.”

10. Otherwise, as I believe, Isidore’s sermon was not composed for Ash Wednesday but for the First Sunday of Lent. In the ancient Gothic Office, this Sunday was called “for the removal of flesh,” because the Lenten fast began on the Monday after the Sunday that we call Quadragesima, as can be seen in Blanchini’s *Gothic-Hispanic Orational*, p. 63.

Thus the Gothic Spaniards held no office on the Wednesday at the beginning of the fast, or on Ash Wednesday. The Mozarabes later took the office of blessing ashes and placing them on the heads of the faithful, which is not older in the Church than the eleventh century, largely from the Roman Toledo Missal, with certain elements taken from elsewhere. Compare Lesleus’s notes to the Mozarabic Missal, p. 503.

11. In the Toledo Missal, after the ashes had been imposed, the following was prescribed:

“After this, they all proceeded to the procession; when the procession was finished, let a sermon be given; when it is finished, let them begin the Mass.”

The Mozarabes transferred the same rubric into their missal. In place of this sermon, Saint Isidore’s sermon “for the removal of flesh” was inserted in the Breviary. It seems, in fact, originally to have been adapted to the First Sunday of Lent, as can be inferred from the Gothic office of that day itself.

The sermon concerns fasting and almsgiving, especially the almsgiving to be practiced by those who cannot fast. This twofold subject is indicated in the Mozarabic Breviary for the First Sunday of Lent, p. 139:

“Behold, the days of the great Lord of almsgiving and fasting will come; be ready to do good to the oppressed, widows, and orphans, etc.”

There follows a prayer found in the *Gothic-Hispanic Orational* under the title “For the removal of flesh, after Matins,” p. 64. It begins: “God, who command us to give alms, etc.”

12. Among Isidore’s works, Niccolò Antonio listed a book *On the Institution of the Lenten Fast*, which, as he says, still lies hidden. He quoted the words of Marcus Zuerius Boxhornius in his note to the *Historians of Augustan History*, in Spartianus’s *Life of Clodius Albinus*:

“I cannot conceal from the learned reader and student of ecclesiastical antiquity the joy I feel at this point: namely, that in recent days I have discovered an illustrious and quite substantial fragment of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the institution of the Lenten fast [Col. 0486C], which elsewhere and in a more suitable place, if God grants me life, I shall make public.”

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca Media*, no. 21, suspects that this fragment is the same as chapter 36, or 37, of book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Perhaps so. But since Boxhornius calls it a “quite substantial fragment,” it corresponds more closely to our sermon, which is two-thirds longer than the cited chapter 37.

Whether, then, this homily exists in some other manuscript or not, since the Mozarabes adopted it as a genuine work of Isidore, and since there is no reason to lead us in the opposite direction—indeed, since it is especially worthy of so great a teacher—we have judged that it should be placed among Isidore’s authentic works.

[Col. 0486D]

13. I readily believe that Boxhornius was speaking of chapter 37 of book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, since in other manuscript codices as well Isidore’s teaching on fasting is found drawn from book I of the *Offices*. Boxhornius could have spared us this investigation if he had indicated some words from his fragment.

Bandini describes Codex 1 in volume I, *Catalogue of the Latin Codices of the Medicean Library*, pluteus 14, as follows:

“Homilies of Saint Ambrose—or rather homilies and sermons that were read in the church from the Advent of the Lord until Holy Saturday, selected from the works of Saints Ambrose . . . Isidore, bishop, etc.”

There, on p. 136, is “a sermon of Saint Isidore, bishop.” It begins:

“The times of fasting according to the Holy Scriptures are four, during which, through abstinence and the lamentation of repentance, supplication must be made to the Lord.”

This is the beginning of chapter 37 of book I of the *Offices*. The sermon ends:

“And it celebrates the universal fast by this observance.”

This is the conclusion of chapter 40 of the same book. But in the royal Madrid edition it reads:

“And it celebrates the universal fast by observance.”

This sermon encompasses not only the institution of the Lenten fast but also that of the other fasts. Bandini also records the same sermon under Isidore’s name in volume IV, pluteus 36, codex 4 of the library of Santa Croce, a parchment manuscript of the twelfth century, although here Bandini calls it a sermon on Lent.

14. The Vatican Library contains other codices in which Isidore’s exposition of fasting is set out. In the large-format parchment Vatican Codex, p. 76, there is “Isidore’s sermon on the Lenten fast,” beginning: “During the time of fasting.” The same sermon, with the same beginning, appears in the Vatican paper manuscript 6454, p. 205.

15. After other excerpts from Isidore’s *Sentences* and *Synonyms*, the Palatine Vatican Codex 216, dating approximately from the eleventh century, presents a short work under the title of a book, though it should rather be classified among homilies, namely, on folio 90 verso:

“Here begins the book of Saint Isidore on the day of judgment and the despair of sinners: ‘I beg you, dearest brothers, etc.’”

The inscription should rather have been: “Here begins a sermon on the day of judgment,” since an excerpt from Isidore on the despair of sinners, taken from the books of the *Sentences*, preceded it.

Whether the *Sermon on the Day of Judgment* is genuinely Isidore’s, I would not dare to determine. Certainly it does not appear to be excerpted from his extant works. Nor is it unworthy of being read among the appendices, although it has already been published among the sermons of Saint Augustine [Col. 0487C]. The Louvain scholars considered it doubtful; the Maurists considered it spurious and a genuine work of Caesarius. In the Palatine Codex, some passages are omitted and others are presented in a confused and disordered sequence.

16. I transcribed two sermons from the very ancient Vatican Palatine Codex 67, which I shall discuss more fully in chapter 102: one expressly ascribed to Isidore, and another that immediately follows and also appears to be ascribed to the same Isidore. The codex is assigned to the eleventh century and is listed by Blanchini in volume II of the *Fourfold Evangelistary*, p. 604; a specimen of its script is also provided there after p. 60.

Blanchini says that the codex contains the following:

“Homily of Saint Isidore, which begins: ‘Brief is the happiness of this world, etc.’ Also, a sermon on the false friend: ‘Protector and nourisher, etc.’”

Blanchini does not explain whether this sermon too is Isidore’s. In fact, after that brief homily, which occupies only a few lines, the title appears: “Here begins a sermon on the false friend,” without the name of the same or another author being added.

The script of these two sermons is the same, though different from the script of the psalms that follow and of the commentary on the psalms. Neither their style, subject matter, nor statements contain anything that is not thoroughly appropriate to our Isidore. Thus not only the homily under the title “Here begins the homily of Saint Isidore,” but also the sermon that follows the very brief homily, entitled “Here begins a sermon on the false friend,” may rightly be placed among the doubtful sermons.

17. Among the seven little works which Constantine Cajetan proposed to append, after reviewing and annotating them, to a new edition of Isidore’s works, there are two sermons: one for the day of the Lord’s Nativity, the other on the holy angels. To the sermon on the Nativity of the Lord he added the following notice:

“First, concerning Isidore’s name, I found it written in different ways, not only in copies but also in printed books: some wrote it *Hisidorus*, *Hisydorus*, or *Hysidorus*; others *Ysidorus* or *Isidorus*. Of all these readings, however, the one by which he is written *Isidorus* pleased us most.

“That Isidore wrote a *Book of Sermons* is testified not only by Trithemius and Sigebert of Gembloux, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, but also by Braulio, when he says: ‘There are also many other little works of this man, inscribed in the Church of God with great adornment.’ Yet we especially lament that the wretched condition of those times consumed very many of his sermons, as well as many writings of various kinds [Col. 0488B].
