“That this sermon on the Nativity of the Lord was composed by Isidore of Seville is indicated, besides its phrasing, certainly familiar to Isidore, by Conrad Gesner—an author of condemned memory though he was—who noticed it in his *Bibliotheca* from Alcuin’s *Homiliary*. It is also certain that Alcuin himself collected that work from the holy Fathers at the command of Charlemagne; we have read it in manuscript at Monte Cassino, while at Basel it was printed in the year of the Lord 1498.”

### 18

Cajetanus applies Braulio’s words, “many little works, and inscribed in the Church of God with great distinction,” to the Book of Sermons; yet they indicate any number of other books. In Alcuin’s *Homiliary*, Venice 1551, fol. 25, and Cologne 1569, p. 67, one reads a sermon of St. Isidore for the day of the Lord’s Nativity: “The day of the Lord’s birth,” etc. It ends: “because Christ was born, who lives,” etc. *Homilies and Meditations for the Feast of the Nativity of Jesus*, collected by Christian Daumius, appeared at Zwickau in 1670, in octavo; there, no. 12 contains Isidore’s sermon on the Nativity, taken from the *Homiliary of the Doctors*. It is the same sermon and the same *Homiliary* published under Alcuin’s name. That this work is wrongly attributed to Alcuin is also observed, apart from the point, in the Spanish version printed at Valencia in 1552, fol., entitled *Homiliario recopilado por Alcuino*, in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, where it is attributed to Paul the Deacon [Paulus Winfridus], and several editions produced from the year 1482 onward are listed, though the two editions I mentioned are omitted. In the year just past, 1795, the *Homiliary of Alcuin* began to be reprinted at Madrid from the version of the bachelor Juan de Molina, which is itself the old version, in three quarto volumes.

### 19

As for the author of the sermon on the Lord’s Nativity, others have already observed that it is truly by St. Isidore, since the entire sermon differs in no respect from chapter 26 of Book I of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, except for certain variant readings that easily enter manuscript copies—for example, at the end, “that Christ was born” instead of “the day on which Christ was born.” I found the same sermon in ancient Vatican parchment manuscripts, for example in Codex Regio-Vaticanus 125, concerning which I shall speak in chapter 99.

### 20

The sermon on the angels is longer; Constantinus Cajetanus published it as though it had not previously been edited. He also added notes and variant readings, prefacing them with the following notice:

In one or two of the older manuscript Lectionaries of the Casinensis Library, shelfmarks 75 and 236, and in two Codices of the Vatican Library, shelfmarks 1296—corrected to 1269—and 3836, there is this sermon of Isidore on the holy angels. In them, however, it is inscribed only to St. Michael the Archangel.

I truly consider whatever can be recovered from the remnants of the works of Isidore of Seville a treasure. He alone is my concern here; I do not even wish to entertain the suspicion that the sermon should be attributed to Isidore of Córdoba or Isidore of Beja. For it is certain that three men in Spain, all distinguished for their reputation for learning and integrity, bore the name Isidore, though they did not live at the same time: Isidore of Córdoba, the bishop who, because of his antiquity, received the surname “the Elder” and lived in the time of the emperor Honorius; Isidore of Seville, whose activities we have already explained; and finally Isidore of Beja, who, being two generations later—for he lived long after Isidore of Seville—was called “the Younger,” although Isidore of Seville was sometimes distinguished from the Cordoban by that same designation. Beware, reader, lest the identical surname lead you into error.

### 21

Cajetanus identifies the first Vatican Codex by the number 1296, but it must be read as 1269, as he himself indicates in his notes. That Codex is certainly now catalogued in the Vatican Library under the number 1269; I shall describe it in chapter 95.

It is worth noting, however, that Cajetanus attributes three readings concerning the angels to Isidore alone, although this is not clear from the Vatican manuscripts. Indeed, in Codex 1296, only the reading beginning “The name of angels,” and continuing through “restored to the angels,” is attributed to Isidore; the other two are attributed to St. Gregory the Great. For once the reading “The name of angels” has ended, the rubric immediately follows: “Of St. Gregory, pope, as above: Sometimes,” etc. Again: “Likewise, of the same, as above: Sometimes through angels.” Codex 3836, an older manuscript which I shall discuss in chapter 97, lends Cajetanus somewhat more support. There, after the reading attributed to Isidore—“The name of angels,” etc.—a rubric is added without an author’s name: “Likewise, as above: But sometimes,” etc.; and again, after this reading, the rubric appears: “Likewise, of the one mentioned above: Sometimes through angels,” etc. Yet it seems certain that the copyist omitted the author’s name when he wrote the rubric for the reading beginning “But sometimes.” For other Codices that transmit St. Isidore’s sermon on the angels likewise assign only the reading “The name of angels,” etc., to Isidore.

### 22

A twelfth-century *Homiliary* is described by Bandini in volume IV of the *Codices Latini*, shelfmark Plut. 33, Codex 4 of Santa Croce. On page 193 one reads: “A sermon of St. Isidore, bishop, on St. Michael the Archangel. ‘The name of angels,’” etc., through “restored to the angels.”

In Vatican Codex 1271, which contains an ancient Lectionary, the same sermon is listed in the inventory without an author’s name: “For the celebration and victory of St. Michael the Archangel. ‘The name of angels,’” etc.

### 23

The sermon on the angels attributed to Isidore in the manuscripts is the entirety of chapter 10 of Book I of the *Sentences*. The passages added by Cajetanus under the same title, but attributed in the manuscripts to Pope Gregory, are taken from Gregory the Great, Book XXVIII of the *Moralia*, chapter 1, no. 3, except for the passage concerning Daniel. Specifically, Gregory’s words are “But sometimes,” etc., through “he perceived what was to come.” What follows—“As in the case of Daniel,” etc., through “to the end of days”—is absent from Gregory’s works.

The remaining passage beginning “Sometimes through angels,” through “may see what is to come below,” is taken from the cited work of Gregory, nos. 6 and following. Whether Isidore incorporated the discussion of angels treated by St. Gregory into a sermon, inserting the words concerning Daniel, or whether someone else did so, cannot easily be determined. For, as I have often stated, I do not consider it unworthy of Isidore to have gathered the opinions and fragments of ancient Fathers into a single body. This was his practice, and it was also the practice of the other Fathers.

### 24

In the *Homiliary* of the Library of Santa Croce, which I mentioned shortly before, page 34 lists a sermon of St. Isidore, bishop, on the Life of St. John the Baptist. Bandini observes that in another Codex it is without a title. In my opinion, this sermon contains nothing different from chapter 72, or 73 in some copies, of Isidore’s *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*. Other Codices of ours bear a corresponding title, such as Regio-Vaticanus 125, which I shall discuss in chapter 99.

### 25

A sermon on the Trinity, beginning “Also in many ways,” is attributed to Isidore in Vatican Codex 6451, page 248. It is taken from the *Etymologies*, Book VII, chapter 2.

Among the homilies of the Veronese Codex, which I discussed in chapter 44, no. 50, there are sermons from St. Isidore’s book *On the Passion of the Lord*: “They were gathered together,” etc., namely from Book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 19, and so forth.

From chapter 43 of Zaccaria’s *Adversaria*, a Codex of Isidore’s *Sentences* in the Florentine Library of San Marco was catalogued; it was said to contain “a sermon of St. Isidore on penance.” But since its beginning is attributed as follows—“From the moment when each person begins to be righteous, from the moment when he becomes his own accuser”—I readily understand that it is chapter 13 of Book II of the *Sentences*, whose title is “On the Confession of Sins and Penance,” and whose beginning is the same: “From the moment when each person,” etc.

### 26

In Regio-Vatican Codex 261, which I shall describe in chapter 100 after several other works and certain sermons of St. John Chrysostom—the “Golden-Mouthed”—there is, on page 175, a sermon of St. Isidore on the temptations of the devil. It begins: “The mind of the righteous person is assaulted in this life by many temptations of calamities.” It ends: “without doubt he avoids the crime committed.” It is the complete fifth chapter of Book III of the *Sentences*, bearing the same title, “On the Temptations of the Devil,” with certain variant readings of little importance.

### 27

What sort of sermon of St. Isidore, from the *Synonyms*, is listed in a certain Florentine Codex, I explained in chapter 70.

The catalogue of the royal library of Paris lists several sermons of Isidore. Most have the same titles as sermons already mentioned. Others, although bearing different titles, do not seem to differ from those already discussed; or at least it may be inferred that they have been excerpted from Isidore’s works. The following are the principal items to be noted in that catalogue:

- Codex 6623, parchment, twelfth century: two homilies of St. Isidore, bishop, the first on the three causes of sins, the second on the life of this world.
- Codex 5302, twelfth century, no. 79: a sermon of St. Isidore on Septuagesima.
- Codex 3806, parchment, fourteenth century: a sermon for Pentecost, excerpted from a book of St. Isidore.
- Codices 1713, eleventh century, and 1714, twelfth century: a sermon of St. Isidore on wickedness.

Jac. Philippus Tomasinus, in the *Bibliotheca Patavina Manuscripta*, page 30, lists a sermon of Isidore on evil days.

### 28

Among the appendices to the new Madrid edition, page 45, there was placed, from a certain manuscript Codex, a sermon of Isidore, bishop, on the Body and Blood of the Lord at Easter: “The greatness of heavenly things,” etc.

The editor warned in his prologue that this sermon must be rejected as the work of St. Isidore. It is Homily 7 of St. Caesarius of Arles on Easter, in volume II of the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1624.

Bayer, in his notes to *Bibliotheca vetus*, Book IV, no. 179, testifies that this sermon exists in a thirteenth-century Codex at El Escorial, with the heading: “A sermon of Isidore, bishop, on the Body and Blood of Christ at Easter.”

I believe this is the sermon mentioned by Pastrengo, who included in his catalogue of Isidore’s works one treatise “On the Body and Blood of the Lord,” which agrees with Trithemius: “One book on the Body and Blood of the Lord.” Zaccaria observed in his *Conspectus* that a sermon “On the Body and Blood of the Lord,” published under the name of Eusebius of Emesa, is attributed to Isidore by Martène on the authority of two ancient Codices.

# CHAPTER LXXIII  
## Which letters of Isidore are genuine, and which spurious or doubtful? Genuine letters include not only those to Braulio, but also those to Leudefredus and Massona

### 1

In his catalogue of Isidore’s works, Trithemius placed last a Book of Letters to Various Persons. Since he did not give its beginning, I include it among those books that Trithemius did not see. I mentioned in chapter 46 that Isidore’s letters were burned with other books at the Canons’ house of St. Nicholas in Padua in the year 1395.

Since several letters of Isidore to Braulio are usually prefixed to the *Etymologies* in manuscripts, it would not be surprising if someone had inscribed an entire Codex with the title “Letters of Isidore.” In Maittaire’s alphabetical appendix are listed “Letters of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza,” folio, Venice 1483; this must be understood as referring to the letters prefixed to the work itself, the *Etymologies*.

Neither Braulio, nor Ildefonsus, nor Sigebert mentions Isidore’s letters, since, as Nic. Antonius says, they scarcely deserve to be counted among his works.

### 2

Certain letters of Isidore were prefixed to the works themselves in the place of dedications. These are: the short letter to Braulio in which he sends the *Etymologies*, beginning “Here you have”; the preface to the *Allegories* addressed to Orosius; the two prologues to Books I and II *Against the Jews*, addressed to his sister Florentina; the dedication of *Ecclesiastical Offices* to his brother Fulgentius, bishop of Écija; the preface to the *Rule* addressed to the monks of Honoriacum; and the dedicatory letter of the book *On the Nature of Things* to King Sisebut.

Such dedicatory letters should not be removed from their proper places. Those who place several other alternating letters of Isidore and Braulio before the *Etymologies* act less correctly merely because they found them arranged there in many ancient manuscript Codices. The same is true of those who present Isidore’s letter to Massona as the preface to the Books of the *Sentences*, or who place Isidore’s letter to Braulio, “Because I am unable,” before the *Synonyms* as a dedication.

Although in certain ancient parchments copyists joined these letters to the celebrated works of Isidore, it is nevertheless more appropriate to assemble in one body all the letters that are not prefaces to other works.

Benedict XIV discusses two letters of Isidore to Braulio, who was serving as archdeacon, in a letter to the archbishop of Zaragoza, by which he sent new readings and a collection for the office of St. Braulio, revised and approved by himself. In the first letter he observes that the heading reads “My dearest son,” while at the end it says “My most beloved lord,” a form of deference that he thinks a bishop ought not to display toward a subordinate archdeacon. The second letter is addressed “To the beloved brother Braulio.” The supreme pontiff concludes that Braulio had been archdeacon in the Church of Seville, contrary to the view held by the archbishop of Zaragoza. He believes that Braulio had once been Isidore’s disciple.

### 3

For the royal Madrid edition, Juan Bautista Pérez collected Isidore’s letters and provided them with notes. In note d to the first letter, he names one Complutensian Codex and refers generally to others; in the note to the twelfth letter, “It is usually completed,” etc., he mentions the Gothic Codex of Oviedo and a Roman Codex, as well as other manuscripts in general.

He published thirteen letters:

1. To Leudefredus.
2. To Braulio the archdeacon: “While friends.”
3. To Braulio the archdeacon: “Because I am unable.”
4. To Massona.
5. To Helladius.
6. To Claudius the duke.
7. To Redemptus the archdeacon.
8. To Eugenius.
9. Isidore to Braulio: “With every desire.”
10. Braulio to Isidore: “O pious lord.”
11. Isidore to Braulio: “Because I have learned that you are safe.”
12. Braulio to Isidore: “It is usually completed.”
13. Isidore to Braulio: “Your Holiness’s letters.”

### 4

As I have said, the five alternating letters of Isidore and Braulio prefixed to the *Etymologies* are found not only in most editions but also in many extremely ancient manuscript copies.

The Leonese Canon inserted two of these letters of Isidore to Braulio into the *Life of St. Isidore* in the *Acta Sanctorum*, April 1, chapter 7, page 344 and following, namely:

“Addressed to Braulio, his disciple. To Braulio, most beloved in the Lord Christ, archdeacon, Isidore: ‘While friends write,’ etc.”

“Addressed to the holy Braulio. To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, Isidore: ‘Your Holiness’s letters.’”

One letter of Braulio to Isidore is also inserted:

“Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, to Isidore: To my lord, truly the lord and chosen one of Christ, Isidore, foremost of bishops, Braulio, the worst of sinners and an unworthy servant of God’s saints: ‘It is usually completed,’ etc.”

No notes are appended to these three letters or to the letter to Eugenius; but notes are appended to the letter to Massona and to the other letter to Leudefredus, especially from Nic. Antonius.

Again, in chapter 8, perhaps outside its proper place, other letters are interspersed without their own headings and with brief Bollandist notes, namely:

“Letter of St. Isidore to Braulio: ‘Because I am unable.’”

“Letter of Braulio to St. Isidore: ‘O pious lord.’”

“Reply of St. Isidore: ‘Because I have learned that you are safe.’”

Risco, in volume XXX of *Hispania sacra*, published Isidore’s letters to Braulio and Braulio’s to Isidore, adding several annotations of his own.

### 5

Almost no one disputes the alternating letters of Isidore and Braulio. Nor do I see that most critical scholars doubt the letter to Leudefredus. Gratian attributes it to Isidore in chapter 1 of Distinction 25; Ivo of Chartres does so in Part VI of the *Decretum*, chapter 20, and in letter 73 of the Paris edition of 1585.

If, however, we examine the letter of Isidore addressed to Leufredus, bishop of Córdoba, it can plainly be understood that it does not concern an archdeacon, and so forth.

In Regio-Vatican Codex 1026, which contains a collection of canons entitled *Polycarpus*, there is a letter of Isidore, bishop of Seville, addressed to Ludefredus, bishop of Córdoba, but it is mutilated at the end, as it is in Gratian.

Cellier calls this letter an epitome of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, insofar as it concerns ministers serving at the altar. For this reason Breulius appended the portion of the letter that he had found to the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Then, on page 693, he added the missing fragment among the letters, prefacing it with this brief notice:

“To the books of St. Isidore *On Ecclesiastical Offices* we have appended his letter on the same subject, which he wrote to Ludifredus, otherwise Leudefredus, bishop of Córdoba—not, however, in its entirety, but as we read it in Gratian’s *Decree*, Distinction 25, ‘Having read,’ and in Ivo of Chartres, Part 6 of his *Decree*, chapter 20, and also in manuscript Codices. Most recently, however, having obtained the final part that was missing, we now present it to the reader without repeating the earlier portions, which may be found above, on page 615.”

The Roman Correctors had already noted in their edition of Gratian’s *Decree* that the complete letter existed in a Codex of the Dominican monastery, namely in the Codex of the Dominican Library above the Minerva.

### 6

The Council of León, held in 1091, decreed—as Lucas of Tuy reports in his *Chronicle*—that ecclesiastical offices in Spain should be regulated according to the Rule of blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville.

Rodrigo of Toledo says briefly in Book VI, chapter 30: “They established many things concerning the offices of the Church.”

Many, following Aguirre in his notes to the *Councils of Spain*, interpret these words as referring to Isidore’s letter to Leudefredus, since the Gothic rite had already been abolished in Spain at that time.

They could, however, be understood as referring to Isidore’s two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. In them, along with other matters, both the contents of the letter to Leudefredus and those things that can be adapted to the Roman ecclesiastical rite are explained.

### 7

Loaisa published this letter to Leudefredus in his notes to the Eighth Council of Toledo, from a very ancient Escorial Codex called the *Vigilano* after its copyist Vigila, and the *Albeldense* after the monastery in which it was written. Risco discusses it in volume XXXIII of *Hispania sacra*, treatise 69, chapter 12.

The Codex was written by the monks Vigila, García, a disciple of Vigila, and Sarracino. At the end of the volume are ametrical acrostic verses whose first and final syllables yield the following sentence:

“Vigila and Sarracino produced this in Era 1014.”

Other acrostic verses follow, the first of which is: “O Word of God, brought forth from the Father’s mouth.”

The year 1014 corresponds to A.D. 976.

Labbe took the letter from Loaisa and printed it in volume VI of the *Councils*, column 420. Its title is:

“Letter of blessed Isidore the Younger, bishop of the Church of Seville, addressed to Leudefredus, bishop of the Church of Córdoba.”

A portion of this letter to Leudefredus, under Isidore’s name, is included in a work containing various ancient materials edited by Stevartius and entitled *Canons on the Office of Priests*, by an uncertain compiler, page 675:

“Examples of Isidore to Bishop Lamfidus [sic]: ‘To the psalmist: let him sing the responsory on Sundays or on other festivals,’” and the rest.

“Thus far Isidore on ecclesiastical orders.”

This material is indicated as having been taken from Burchard.

The catalogue of manuscripts in the royal library of Paris lists two Codices of the letter to Lanfredus, or Ludifredus.

### 8

Nic. Antonius believes that Leudefredus may be the same person who is called Leudeficus, bishop of Córdoba, in the subscriptions to the Fourth Council of Toledo.

There is no remaining reason for doubt, since in the edition of the Councils of Spain by Loaisa and Aguirre, beside *Leudeficus* the variant *Leofredus* is noted in the margin. The same Cordoban bishop subscribes to the Sixth Council of Toledo as *Laufredus*, and at the Seventh Council of Toledo Valentinianus, archpriest, subscribed while acting in place of Leudefredus, bishop of Córdoba.

In the Vatican manuscript Codices in which I found Isidore’s letter to Leudefredus, there is similar variation in the transcription of the name.

Flórez says that he does not know where Loaisa obtained the name *Leudeficus*, since it is not read that way in the older editions or in the Escorial and Toledo manuscripts; see volume X, page 235.

### 9

In the Escorial Codex that I described from Rodríguez, chapter 55, there is a Spanish version of several of Isidore’s letters, including the letters to Massona, to Eugenius of Toledo, and to Leudefredus, who is called *Leofredo* in Spanish.

In ancient manuscripts the letter to Leudefredus is usually joined to the letter to Massona, as in Vatican Codex 1344.

### 10

The exceptionally learned Hernando supposes that the letter to Leudefredus is the product of some patchwork compiler, cobbled together from Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, because it is found in certain Codices containing an impure collection attributed to Isidore the Merchant, as the Ballerini report in volume III of the works of St. Leo, page CCXXXV.

This, however, presents no obstacle, since the letter exists in other copies entirely free from such falsifications, as in the *Vigilano*.

He adds that certain words in the text of Breulius’s edition and in Pérez’s notes concerning the office of the archpriest are foreign to the discipline of those times. But this proves not that the letter is false, but that it is found interpolated in some copies, as is the case with many other works of Isidore.

Thus, in Vatican Codex 3788, page 11, under the rubric “From the sayings of Blessed Isidore to Landefredus [sic], bishop,” certain statements concerning priests are presented that are spurious and absent from other manuscripts. I shall describe the Codex in chapter 97. I shall relegate the passages concerning priests to the appendices.

Berardus, whose words appear in chapter 32, no. 14, also inclines toward the view that this letter is apocryphal.

### 11

Isidore’s letter to Massona occurs extremely frequently in ancient sources. A fragment of it is found in Hatligarius’s collection of canons and in chapter 1 of the *Penitential* of Rabanus Maurus, edited by Antonius Augustinus. It is also found in Rabanus’s letter to Heribald, bishop of Auxerre, published by Peter Stevartius and later printed by Étienne Baluze after Regino’s work *On Ecclesiastical Disciplines*.

Algerus used it in the preface to Book I of *On Mercy and Justice* in Mabillon’s *Analecta*; so did Burchard, Book XIX, chapter 73; Ivo, Book III, title XI, chapter 17, of his *Decrees*; and Gratian, chapter “Lord,” 28 of Distinction 50, and chapter “This very thing,” 33 of Question 2. The annotators add the author of *Polycarpus*, Book IV, title 39; Anselm, Book VIII, chapter 37; and again Ivo, Part 8, chapter 398, and Part 15, chapter 91.

Nic. Antonius observes that Gratian’s heading “This very thing” contains something more, since it reads:

“Concerning these matters Isidore writes thus to Massona, bishop, in the preface to the book *On the Highest Good*.”

Nic. Antonius continues that it is not yet clear which books Isidore called the *Books of the Sentences*, or *On the Highest Good*. Nevertheless, this letter contains nothing resembling a preface.

### 12

That is indeed the case. The letter to Massona has neither the appearance of a preface nor that of a dedicatory letter, and it has no connection whatsoever with the Books of the *Sentences*.

Flórez, in volume XIII of *Hispania sacra*, first edition, page 205, against Moreno de Vargas—who had inferred from Gratian’s chapter “This very thing” that the Books of the *Sentences* were dedicated by Isidore to Massona—observes that in the Paris edition of Gratian of 1552 the words “in the preface to the book *On the Highest Good*” are absent. He maintains that the words quoted by Gratian are in no way part of the Books of the *Sentences*.

Nevertheless, in the corrected Roman edition of the *Decree*, Gratian speaks with the authority of ancient manuscript Codices. In two parchment copies of the Books of the *Sentences* in the Angelica Library at Rome, the letter to Massona takes the place of the prologue.

One of them, in small quarto, bears this rubric:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the book of St. Isidore, bishop. The prologue begins. To the holy and meritorious brother Massona, bishop, Isidore, bishop. When your religious servant Nicetius came to us,” etc.

It is not complete but ends:

“To attain according to the former ranks.”

Immediately follows the rubric:

“The chapters of Book I begin.”

The other Codex, in small folio, is marked with a similar rubric:

“The first Book of the *Sentences* of Lord Isidore, bishop, begins: his letter to Massona, bishop. To the holy and blessed brother Massona, bishop, Isidore. When your religious son Nicentius came to us,” etc.

It ends:

“Either the older or the weightier authority stands.”

This is the end of the letter. Other copies have “is” or “exists” for “stands,” and some add: “Given on the day,” etc.

I described two Codices in chapter 43, nos. 27 and 30, one Lucan and the other Florentine, from San Marco; in both, this same letter is prefixed to the Books of the *Sentences* in place of a prologue. A third Codex of this kind, from Pistoia, is added there at no. 31.

Two similar Vatican Codices are among those listed in chapter 67, no. 23. Bignaeus likewise added the letter to Massona to the Books of the *Sentences* as a preface, from the Library of Saint Victor, as I explained in chapter 35.

### 13

The name Massona is written in various ways in the manuscripts. In the Third Council of Toledo, held in 589, and in another Council of Toledo, held in 597, over which he presided, he is called *Massona*. In some copies, however, the form is *Mausana*, in others *Mausona*, and in others *Masona*.

On this name, see Antonius Augustinus’s notes to Rabanus’s *Penitential* and Tamayus de Vargas’s notes to chapter 9 of Paul of Mérida’s *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*. In some places he is incorrectly called *Mesanus*, *Massanus*, or *Massenus*. *Masson* or *Mason* perhaps deviates less from the original; for Masson could have been called either *Masson* or *Massona*.

*Mansonem* or *Mastonem* is corrupt for *Massonem*, as it is read in the catalogue of old Pomposa from the eleventh century, as I indicated in chapter 46.

Massona was metropolitan bishop of Mérida from before the year 573 until 606. He was distinguished for learning and holiness of life and was, as Nic. Antonius calls him, the most eminent man of his age.

To these words Bayer adds that in an ancient Breviary of the Escorial Library, dating from the twelfth century or the beginning of the thirteenth and perhaps once belonging to the Church of Mérida, after the feasts of Saints Laurence, Nunilo and Alodia, Servandus and Germanus, Acisclus and Victoria, and Eulalia of Mérida, the following prayer occurs:

“Mercifully grant us, we ask, O Lord, your mercy, through the intercession of your holy confessors and bishops Damasus and Massona, and be propitious to us sinners through their assistance.”

Bayer thinks that the commemoration of Damasus in this Breviary lends some support to his Lusitanian origins. I would have this understood, however, as referring to ancient Lusitania, whose capital was Mérida in Extremadura, now situated outside New Lusitania, or Portugal.

### 14

There is controversy among critical scholars as to whether Isidore’s letter to Massona is genuine. Morinus, Cellier, Dupin, Aguirre, and others cited by Placcius, no. 1484, consider it falsely attributed to Isidore.

Bayer indicates the relevant passages individually in his notes to Nic. Antonius, and Hernando, on the basis of Espen and others, concludes in his notes to the *Prospectus* of Zaccaria’s edition that the letter is doubtful, although the Bollandists and Flórez reach the opposite conclusion.

See also the preface of the distinguished scholar transcribed in chapter 38, no. 37.

The older scholars recognized it as legitimate without subjecting it to examination. Flórez, in volume XIII of *Hispania sacra*, page 204, briefly defends the letter against Cellier on the grounds that it bears the stamp of Isidore’s style and contains nothing contrary to Isidore’s doctrine.

Oudin and Natalis Alexander join those who consider the letter spurious. Their arguments amount to this: the doctrine of the letter is contrary to Isidore in Book II of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 5, and in the letter to Helladius.

Dupin, in volume V of the *Bibliothèque ecclésiastique*, suspects that it was fabricated by the person who forged the famous collection of canons and decretals under the name of Isidore the Merchant. Those who wish to appear devoted to the stricter ancient discipline generally hold approximately this view. Berardus, cited in chapter 32, no. 40, agrees with them.

### 15

For my part, if I see correctly, the letter to Massona is not only thoroughly worthy of Isidore when considered in itself, but also presents nothing contrary either to the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* or to the letter to Helladius.

I pass over the fact that this letter to Helladius itself appears spurious to others, perhaps for still weightier reasons. Certainly the letter to Massona should not be rejected because it contradicts the letter to Helladius, nor the latter because it opposes the former.

There is no disagreement between these letters, as I have said, unless the letter to Massona is said to disagree and conflict with itself.

From the letter to Helladius and from the cited passage *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, it is argued only that after a carnal lapse the dignity of the former rank is in no way to be restored.

The words of the letter to Helladius are:

“We ask that, once this same fallen man has been presented to your holy assembly and his confession has been acknowledged by you, he be deposed from the rank of priesthood by synodal judgment. … For he must know that he has lost the name and office of priest who has lost the merit of holiness. Therefore, by the decree of your judgment, let him continually lament the crimes he has committed through his lifelong penance; let him mourn the dignity of the priesthood, which he lost through evil living,” etc.

The passages in which Isidore discusses the holiness of the priest in the cited place, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, are less forceful:

“That a person who, after baptism, has been seized by some mortal sin is not to be promoted to the priesthood, the law itself bears witness. … But why should I say more? If one who has already been placed in the episcopate or presbyterate commits some mortal sin, he is withdrawn from office, how much more must one found to be a sinner before ordination not be ordained? … For one who accuses another of sins must himself be free from sin.”

### 16

Isidore asserts all these things—and perhaps in even stronger words—in the letter to Massona, but in such a way as to reconcile them with canon 19 of the Council of Ancyra, which prescribes that after a carnal lapse the rank of honor is to be restored after penance.

“But,” he says, “from what your venerable fraternity subsequently made known in your letters, no diversity of decrees is to be understood in such judgments: in one place it is read that after a carnal lapse a person’s rank is to be restored following penance, while elsewhere it is read that after such a crime the merit of the former rank is in no way to be restored.”

Do you see that Isidore even in this letter maintains that after a carnal lapse the merit of the former rank is in no way to be restored?

Now hear Isidore himself reconciling apparently different canons:

“For the canon commands those to return to their former offices whose satisfaction in penance or worthy confession of sins has preceded them. But, on the other hand, those who are not corrected from the vice of corruption, and who, after committing that very carnal offense, attempt with a kind of superstitious rashness to justify it, receive neither their rank of honor nor the grace of communion. … These deservedly incur the condition of dignity taken away, who are known to have received the remedy of life through the amendment of penance.”

And after several further points:

“Behold, insofar as I have been able, I have clearly explained through sacred testimonies the ancient and fully authoritative judgment of the Council of Ancyra. I have shown that the person who has learned to bewail his sins through the satisfaction of penance can be restored to his proper honor; but the person who does not mourn what he has done, and instead commits the things that ought to be mourned without any religious shame or fear of divine judgment, can in no way be restored to his former rank.”

### 17

Isidore’s doctrine, therefore, consistent with itself in every respect, is this: whoever has lost the rank of his dignity through a carnal lapse or any other grave offense can never recover it unless he produces worthy fruits of penance, so that he may be known to have received the remedy of life through amendment.

For this reason, in the cited passage *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, he concludes:

“Let him who neglects to do what is right cease to teach what is right. For the person who strives to admonish others to live well must first correct himself.”

If the letter to Helladius indicates that perpetual penance is to be imposed on the bishop of Córdoba, perhaps certain more serious crimes demanded this. For it says that he had been plunged from the height of honor into the deep ruin of crimes and must mourn:

“Let him mourn the condition of his soul, which he has polluted with such a great mire of corruption.”

Nevertheless, the possibility of restoration seems to be suggested when it adds:

“Perhaps the Holy Spirit will at some time extend a hand to him, so that through worthy satisfaction he may deserve the remission of sins.”

Moreover, one thing is that the penance imposed should be perpetual from the penitent’s side, so to speak, because he himself could not lawfully demand restoration; another is that it should lie within the power of a bishop or council, out of indulgence, to admit to his former rank a fallen priest or bishop who had shown particular signs of penance and contrition.

### 18

That the doctrine concerning the restoration of a fallen priest taught by Isidore in the letter to Massona was not contrary to the discipline of the Spanish Church can be inferred from the letter of Innocent I to the Fathers of the Council of Toledo, from canon 10 of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo, held in 683, and finally, more clearly, from canon 5 of the Council of Lérida, held in 564—elsewhere dated 524—where the following is decreed:

“Those who serve at God’s altar, if they suddenly fall through the lamentable weakness of the flesh and, with the Lord looking favorably upon them, should duly perform penance, so that, with the body mortified, they offer God the sacrifice of a contrite heart, shall remain under the power of the bishop: he may either not suspend those who are truly afflicted for long, or separate the negligent from the body of the Church for a longer period. This condition is to be maintained, however: they may recover their places in their offices, but they may not thereafter be promoted to higher offices,” etc.

Add also the letter of Bachiarius, a Spanish writer of approximately the year 400, to Januarius, *On the Restoration of the Fallen*, or *On Receiving Back the Fallen*.

19. Isidore’s letter to Massona was published in the *Acta Sanctorum* [Col. 0499A] under 4 April, together with others that an anonymous Canon of León inserted into the *Life of St. Isidore*. Constantine Cajetan mentions other editions; he printed this same letter, furnished with his notes, among seven other works of Isidore. He prefaces his notes and variant readings as follows:

Before this complete letter of Isidore was widely read, a fragment of it could be found in the *Book of Penitents* of Rabanus Maurus, chapter 1, which Antonius Augustinus, archbishop of Tarragona and a most learned student of antiquity, published and annotated together with other ancient penitentials. It is also found in Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 50, chapter 28, “To the holy Lord”; in Burchard, book XIX, chapter 73; in Ivo, book III, title 11, chapter 17; and elsewhere. But Joannes Grialius and Jacobus Breulius, who prepared a recent edition of Isidore’s works, gave this letter in full, whereas previously it had survived in mutilated form. So too did Henricus [Col. 0499B] Casinius, from manuscript parchment codices of the monasteries of St. Gall among the Swiss, and of Weingarten in Germany. Therefore, from all these cited codices, we have thought it worthwhile to record the variant readings.

636 20. Different writers assign different dates to the letter. Grialius gives the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of Witeric. Niccolò Antonio reports the eleventh day before the Kalends of March. Others give the second day before the Kalends of March. Canisius assigns the fourth year of King Witeric. Most give the third year, which corresponds to the year 606, since Witeric began to reign in 603. Breulius is far from the truth: having published the letter from the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés and indicated Witeric’s third year, he added this note in the margin: “It was the year of Christ 609.” For this Wicteric began to reign in the era 645, that is, in the year 607. He cites as authorities Roderic of Toledo [Col. 0499C], book II *On the Affairs of Spain*, chapter 16; Roderic Sánchez, part II, chapter 12; and Vasaeus in his *Chronicle* under that same year. Yet Breulius himself, in Isidore’s *History of the Goths*, placed the beginning of Witteric’s reign in the era 642, that is, in the year 604. Corrected editions, however, give era 641, or the year 603. More recent historians are themselves mistaken, or the copyists corrupted the era-numbers. Cajetan adopts Breulius’s opinion in his notes, but without being led to it by any new argument. In many manuscript copies the words specifying the exact day and year on which the letter was issued are entirely absent.

21. We found a copy of the letter to Massona in Vatican Codex 632, before the books of the *Sentences*, concerning which see chapter 94; there it is dated the day before the Kalends of March. In Vatican Codex 1344 it is dated the second day before the Kalends of March [Col. 0499D], addressed to Massona, and preceded by the letter to Leudefredus, concerning which see chapter 96. It is also found in the very ancient Vatican Codex 5751, concerning which see chapter 98; in a Palatine manuscript of approximately the tenth century, chapter 103, dated the day before the Kalends of March, in the fourth year of the reign of our lord King Witeric; and in Urbinate 106, chapter 104, dated in the third year. The same is true of Ottobonianus 14, chapter 105, and Ottobonianus 312 at the same place. This same letter to Massona is indicated in many library catalogues; and the Royal Library of Paris is said to possess six codices in which it appears, as the catalogue makes clear.

22. Since the letter to Massona is unanimously ascribed to Isidore by ancient documents and the earliest writers, it ought in no way to be discredited by its occurrence among the letters of St. Boniface, martyr and bishop of Mainz [Col. 0500A]—letter 72 in the Mainz edition prepared by Nicholas Serarius in 1605. Indeed, it is rather helpful that it is also attributed to Isidore in that collection of letters: “To the holy Lord, etc. Isidore, bishop, to Massona, bishop.” At the beginning, *Nicitio* is written for *Nicetio*. 637 It ends: “whose authority, whether more ancient or stronger, remains; amen.” There follows a fragment which Serarius thought belonged either to that same letter 72 or to another whose beginning was missing: “Sometimes also, according to the merit of the peoples, etc.” In reality, however, it is a fragment from book II, chapter 5, of Isidore’s *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, extending to the words “must be free from sin”; it deals with the same subject. Such confusion and mingling of ancient works is frequent in manuscripts. As for the letters of Boniface themselves, and the dates at which they were written, since the printed editions contain erroneous [Col. 0500B] chronological notices, there is a dissertation by Mansi in volume I of the *Supplement to the Councils*, column 551, where he discusses the exchanged letters of Pope Zachary and St. Boniface. Serarius added some brief notes to the letter to Massona, as he did also to the Isidorian fragment *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, which he designated as letter 73.

## CHAPTER LXXIV  
### Are the Letters Inscribed in Isidore’s Name to Helladius, to Claudius the Duke, to Redemptus the Archdeacon, and to Eugenius Genuine?

1. In the prospectus of the Isidorian edition, Zaccaria promised that he would discuss at length Isidore’s letters to Massona, Helladius, Claudius, and Eugenius, against certain hypercritical scholars; by this he implied that he regarded them all as genuine. Yet I find nothing written or noted [Col. 0500C] concerning the letters in his papers. Regarding the letters to Helladius, Redemptus, Claudius, and Eugenius, the preface of that most learned man reproduced in chapter 38, numbers 36, 37, and 38, deserves to be read again. First, in the case of the letter to Helladius, Hernandez’s arguments in the notes to Zaccaria’s prospectus of Isidore’s works deserve particular consideration. Cellier, Fabricius, and Oudinus seem to acknowledge the letter; Dupin considers the letter to Massona spurious because he regards it as contrary to this other letter, while he declares the letter to Helladius consistent with Isidore’s doctrine in the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Bellarmine and Cave do not mention it, and neither Perez nor Grialius indicated where this and the following three letters were taken from, as Bayer observes.

[Col. 0500D] 638 2. Mabillon, in volume I of the *Benedictine Annals*, asserts that Isidore’s letter to Helladius is authentic; from it, he continues, the other letter fabricated in Isidore’s name to Massona, which approves the restoration of fallen priests, is shown to be false. But why should the letter to Helladius not rather be rejected than the other letter to Massona, which is supported by so many ancient testimonies? Indeed, Mabillon himself, in volume II of the *Benedictine Annals*, page 138, seems to accept both letters as true and genuine. It must therefore be investigated on what authorities or manuscript copies the authenticity of the letter to Helladius rests. Perez cites no manuscript in his notes. Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 20 of his *Chronicle*, appeals to an ancient Complutensian codex. Yet in that codex [Col. 0501A] the letter is said to have been written by Isidore to Helladius and to the Third Council of Toledo—a glaring error. For at the time when the Third Council of Toledo was held, the see of Toledo was occupied not by Helladius but by Euphemius, and that of Seville by Leander, not Isidore. Moved by this consideration, Padilla, century VII, chapter 33, began to doubt the letter, against Pedro de Alcocer, who sought to infer from it the primacy of the see of Toledo, although Padilla argues that even if the letter be admitted, the primacy of Toledo cannot properly be established from it. Padilla calls the codex cited by Morales, book XII, chapter 21, Ovetensian; Hernandez calls it Complutensian; but it is one and the same codex.

3. Nicholas Antonio inferred that the apostolic delegation entrusted to Isidore is indicated in some fashion in this letter. “This is,” he says, “Helladius, bishop of Toledo, [Col. 0501B] who lived at the same time as our Isidore, during the reigns of Sisebut, Suinthila, and Sisenand, and whose principal concern was to convene a council to settle the case of a suffragan bishop. That Isidore considered the matter not unrelated to himself may perhaps be explained by supposing that he intended in some way to indicate that an apostolic delegation, or the rights of a primate, had been entrusted to him.” I do not, however, see at all why the bishop of Córdoba should be called a suffragan of Toledo, since the bishop of Córdoba was a suffragan of the metropolitan of Seville. This bears on the statement in the letter that the person who was to be judged was the Sevillian priest of the church of Córdoba, as Flórez believes in volume V, page 540, although Juan Bautista Pérez suspects that the word *Hispalensis* is superfluous. Flórez, as I said in chapter 22, [Col. 0501C] considers the letter to Helladius highly consistent with the ecclesiastical discipline that prevailed in Spain at that time, without in any way establishing from it the primacy either of the see of Toledo or of Seville.

4. But this is the principal point that Hernandez presses against the letter. Even if, he says, the inscription or address to the Third Council of Toledo is attributed to the negligence of some copyist, the doctrine of the letter is contrary to canon 6 of the Second Synod of Seville, canon 28 of the Fourth Synod of Toledo, and title 13 of the collection of Martin of Braga. Let us therefore compare the letter to Helladius with these canons. First, the letter is addressed not only to Helladius but also to some council then assembled at Toledo. Its title reads: “To my lords and servants of God, Helladius [Col. 0501D] and the other bishops assembled with him: Isidore.” Isidore asks that the bishop of Córdoba, having fallen through carnal sin and having been presented to your holy assembly, be removed from the priestly rank by synodal judgment once you have recognized the declaration of his confession.

5. Now title 13 of Martin of Braga’s collection asserts that a bishop is to be judged by the bishops who are in his province; and if the bishops disagree among themselves in judgment, another metropolitan from a neighboring province is to be summoned, so that through him what accords with right may be confirmed. Canon 6 of the Second Council of Seville, however, decrees that priests or deacons cannot be deposed by one bishop, but only by synodal judgment. At the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 28, it was defined that if a bishop, priest, or deacon unjustly expelled from his rank is found [Col. 0502A] innocent in a second synod, he cannot remain what he had been unless he receives back his lost rank before the altar, and so forth.

6. Of these provisions, title 13 of St. Martin of Braga’s collection comes closest to the matter. It does not so much prescribe as indicate what was apparently the established practice: that a bishop should be judged by the bishops of his province. Why, then, was the bishop of Córdoba not judged in the Synod of Seville? Or, if he was judged, why was he not deposed? Why does Isidore ask that he be deposed in the Council of Toledo? Nor can one answer that he had appealed, since Isidore speaks of deposition to be carried out in the Council of Toledo, not of a sentence to be confirmed; and there was no reason for the bishop of Córdoba, who confessed the crime, to appeal. This is certainly no slight difficulty, [Col. 0502B] but it is not so great as to prove the letter to Helladius spurious. I have no doubt that the discipline of the Spanish Church was that the cause for a bishop’s deposition should be examined in the council of the province to which he belonged. But why could that discipline not be set aside, for just reasons, in a particular case? How often do circumstances arise in a matter that necessarily prevent it from proceeding along the ordinary and familiar path? This is why we are sometimes deceived in judging ancient events. We are surprised by certain facts and often do not believe them because, separated from their circumstances and presented to us in isolation, they create a difficulty that we cannot explain because we do not know the causes.

7. In the present case, however, a plausible explanation [Col. 0502C] immediately presents itself for why the bishop of Córdoba ought to have been judged in the Council of Toledo rather than elsewhere. If the crime of the bishop of Córdoba, as appears likely, was not only manifest but also extremely serious and required immediate punishment, while the Council of Seville could not be convened at once, whereas the Council of Toledo had already been summoned at that very time for other reasons, why could the case not be settled in the Council of Toledo, especially with the consent of Isidore, the metropolitan? For Isidore’s words, “once you have recognized the declaration of his confession,” do not indicate that the case had already been examined in some Council of Seville. They indicate only that Isidore, as metropolitan, already knew either that the bishop of Córdoba confessed the crime or that he had been caught in so obvious a crime that he seemed unlikely to deny it. Other similar explanations can be imagined [Col. 0502D]—for example, if the king had wished a very serious case to be heard in the royal city, or if the bishop of Córdoba had committed the crime in that same royal city.

8. What Hernandez argues carries less weight: that the author of the letter does not appear to be a bishop because he uses the words, “Pastoral concern rests upon you,” and so forth. Isidore is not addressing Helladius alone, but the entire council, whose judgment he says such more serious cases involving priests belong to. It is not easy to determine in what year this Council of Toledo was held. Helladius died at the beginning of 633, after eight years in the episcopate. The case of the bishop of Córdoba [Col. 0503A] was therefore examined between the Second Council of Seville, in 619, and the Third Council of Toledo, in 633. Honorius, bishop of Córdoba, signed the acts of the Second Council of Seville; Leudefredus, likewise bishop of Córdoba, signed those of the Third Council of Toledo—namely, the man to whom, as we have said, another letter of Isidore survives. 641 The identity of the deposed bishop is unknown. In the fictitious chronicle of Julian Pérez he is called Heleca, the successor of Honorius; but Flórez shows in volume X, page 233, that this is stated without any foundation, and there again confirms that Isidore’s letter to Helladius appears genuine to him. Ildefonsus composed a eulogy of Helladius in his book *On Illustrious Men*. A funerary poem for the same Helladius is also attributed to him; some consider it spurious, others genuine but somewhat interpolated. See volume I of the *Toletan Fathers*, page 444, together with the notes. Mabillon, in volume I of the *Benedictine Annals* and in the second Benedictine century [Col. 0503B], page 139, accepts part of the same epitaph as genuine and calls part of it plausible.

9. Whether the letter to Claudius the duke is a genuine work of Isidore is a more sharply disputed question among learned men. Bayer asserts that nearly all bibliographers consider it spurious. Nicholas Antonio, however, should not be counted among them, although some might infer this from Hernandez’s words. For when Nicholas Antonio lists this letter among Isidore’s others, he gives no reason for doubting it and cites no dissenting authorities. Nor do the other bibliographers reject it so universally as Bayer claims. Indeed, after censuring the letters to Massona and Redemptus as fabricated, Natalis Alexander proceeds to assert admirably, in the letter to Claudius the duke, chapter 1, that the primacy of the Roman pontiff is by divine right [Col. 0503C]: “Thus we know,” and so forth. And in the letter to Eugenius, bishop of Toledo, he says: “As for what is said concerning the equality of the apostles,” and so forth.

10. Here is the principal reason that moves heterodox writers to reject both these letters. Oudinus further says that the letter to Claudius was fabricated after the controversies over the procession of the Holy Spirit that arose in the time of Photius; that it reeks of the scholastic loquacity of the twelfth or thirteenth century; that the word *prelate*, used for bishop, belongs to a later age; that obedience to the Roman pontiff is being deliberately emphasized—concerning which, he says, the ancient Church maintained the deepest silence—and that the Athanasian Creed is mentioned. None of these arguments prevents me from attributing the letter to Isidore [Col. 0503D], whom I otherwise consider worthy of it and whose style, I think, would not easily have been imitated by authors of the twelfth or thirteenth century. Lucas of Tuy, book II *Against the Errors of the Albigensians*, chapter 9, quotes words from this letter to Claudius the duke against the heretics: “What you have reported, that you have heretics,” and so forth. Another reading has: “What you have stated.” Nor does Mariana, in his marginal note, doubt that the letter is genuine.

11. First, it ought not to seem strange if, in Isidore’s time, some question concerning the procession of the Holy Spirit from the Father and the Son was raised in Spain. It is well known that, from the First Council of Toledo onward, the symbol and profession of faith were customarily expounded in the councils of Spain in such a way that the Holy Spirit was explicitly said to proceed from the Father and the Son. At the Third Council of Toledo, [Col. 0504A] in which the Goths were converted to the faith under the leadership of Leander, the Constantinopolitan Creed is found with this addition: “And we believe in the Holy Spirit, the Lord and giver of life, proceeding from the Father and the Son.” The same Third Synod of Toledo, chapter 2, decreed that throughout all the churches of Spain and Gaul, according to the form of the Eastern Churches’ Council of Constantinople—that is, of the one hundred and fifty bishops—the creed of faith should be recited, so that before the Lord’s Prayer was said it might be sung aloud by the people, and so forth. The Constantinopolitan Creed with the addition “and the Son” is intended. It had been introduced under this title: “The holy faith expounded by the 150 Fathers of the Council of Constantinople, in agreement with the great Synod of Nicaea.” Indeed, the same words, “proceeding from the Father [Col. 0504B] and the Son,” are found in the creed recited in the Mass of the Gothic rite. Since this is so clear, I do not know why the most learned theologian Petavius, *On the Trinity*, book VII, chapter 2, number 2, should not only say that it is unknown when this addition to the creed was instituted, but also expressly deny that the Spanish councils—and specifically the Third Council of Toledo—added anything to the creed itself, although he admits that they placed in the profession of faith the statement that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son.

12. At the time when this custom was becoming widespread in Spain, many Greeks were living there, either mixed among the Roman soldiers or residing in cities subject to the emperor of Constantinople. We may reasonably believe that some of them were infected with heresy, without for the moment mentioning the other Arians who remained in Spain even after the public conversion of the Gothic people, as is clear from our histories. This, then, may be connected with what the author of the letter to Claudius says: “But you have stated that you have heretics [Col. 0504C] with whom you dispute continually and whom you strive to recall to the Catholic faith,” and so forth. This Claudius was evidently a duke under King Reccared, whose virtues St. Gregory praises most highly in book VII, letter 125, elsewhere numbered 124; he is also praised in Isidore’s *History of the Goths*, in the *Chronicle* of John of Biclaro, and in the *Lives of the Fathers of Mérida*.

13. The addition “and the Son,” established with such solemnity at the Third Synod of Toledo, was therefore especially offensive to the Greeks, as well as to other heretics. Isidore did not omit it in his *History of the Goths*, under era 624, where he says of Reccared: “That most religious prince [Col. 0504D] himself attended the council and confirmed its proceedings by his presence and signature, renouncing with all his people the perfidy that the Gothic nation had learned up to that time under the teaching of Arius, and proclaiming the unity of the three persons in God: that the Son was consubstantially begotten from the Father; that the Holy Spirit proceeded inseparably from the Father and the Son; and that he was the one Spirit of both, whence they are also one.” Perhaps the heretics, concealing the more evident part of their error, thought that they could act more safely against the addition “from the Son.” For although many of the ancient Greek Fathers also rightly held that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son, some nevertheless did not speak so clearly, and many even argued that the phrase should be added to the creed.

[Col. 0505A] 14. Natalis Alexander, dissertation 18 on the ninth and tenth centuries, denies that Theodoret should be heard in the controversy over the procession of the Holy Spirit. He was carried away by excessive ardor in his dispute against St. Cyril and was the first to propagate the error that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father alone, in his refutation of Cyril’s twelve anathemas. Theodoret’s words are:

“But if he argues that the Spirit is properly the Spirit of the Son, inasmuch as he said that it is of the same nature as the Son and proceeds from the Father, we shall agree and accept that expression as pious. But if he asserts that the Spirit exists from the Son and through the Son, we shall reject this as blasphemous and impious. For we believe the Lord who says, ‘The Spirit who proceeds from the Father’; and likewise the most divine Paul, who says, ‘We have not received the spirit of the world, but the Spirit who is from God the Father.’”

15. Why, then, could some people in Spain not have raised this question in similar words and pressed the Catholics when they noticed that the word “and the Son” had been added to the creed? The reason why the Spaniards added that word may be sought in Ratramnus, book II *Against the Greeks*, who was writing around the year 868:

“Then, when the Arian madness sprang up again and sought to establish that it was not orthodox to say that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father—for this seemed blasphemous because it appeared to profess that the Father was the Father of two, namely the Son and the Holy Spirit—the teachers of the Church, determining that this blasphemy too must be driven away, added to the creed that the Holy Spirit proceeds also from the Son, lest, if he were said to proceed from the Father alone, he should be thought to be the Son and should not be called the Spirit of the Son.”

16. The Arians, or other Greeks living in Spain, seem to have been silenced by Isidore’s authority and that of the Councils of Toledo, and they did not pursue the controversy over the procession of the Holy Spirit or the addition “and the Son.” The practice of reading or singing the Constantinopolitan Creed with the addition “and the Son,” common to the Gothic Churches of Spain and Gaul, subsequently spread to other parts of Gaul and of the Gallo-German Empire, especially under the rule of Charlemagne, whose dominion included part of Spain as well. In the year 809, therefore, a certain John, a monk of Jerusalem, revived the same question. A council was convened at Aachen against him, and an embassy was also sent [Col. 0505D] to Pope Leo III. Although the doctrine of the Holy Spirit’s procession was established, the pope refused to approve the practice of singing the creed during the solemn celebration of Mass, and even less with the addition “and the Son.” He advised that, if possible, the practice should gradually be abolished, as is clear from the acts of the embassy preserved by Labbe in his collection of councils. Yet in the same century, either under Nicholas I or around his time, the Roman Church also adopted it, as may be inferred from Photius’s encyclical letter against Nicholas.

17. It is clear from these facts that the letter to Claudius should not be judged spurious because it discusses procession from the Father and the Son and the addition “and the Son.” I would nevertheless readily believe that some words were interpolated on the occasion of the controversy between the Greeks and Latins. The letter reads:

“Therefore certain Greeks [Col. 0506A] insolently strive to reproach the Latins because, in the profession of the holy faith, they sing with heart and mouth to God: ‘Who proceeds from the Father and the Son’; whereas in the councils mentioned above it was written, ‘He proceeds from the Father,’ and the holy Roman Church approves and believes that the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father and the Son. This prohibition mentioned above,” and so forth.

The words “and the holy Roman Church … believes” seem superfluous and out of place, especially since the letter first defends the addition and then confirms the doctrine. These words, therefore, may perhaps have been added to the genuine letter.

18. Nor are the other objections raised by Oudinus any more serious. If he detects in the letter to Claudius some kind of scholastic loquacity [Col. 0506B], another person could easily reply that the letter breathes Isidorian gravity. He denies that the word *prelate*, used for a bishop, belongs to Isidore’s age. But just as Isidore frequently calls bishops and other priests *superiors*, *prelates*, *rulers*, and other such names in book III of the *Sentences*, and devotes an entire chapter of book II of the *Synonyms* to prelates and subjects, where he discusses superiors and subjects of every kind, so in this letter he says, “the other prelates of the Church,” and so forth. By this word Isidore ordinarily understands those who possess authority to command. There is also a book attributed to Cyprian entitled *On the Simplicity of Prelates*; but its ancient and genuine title is *On the Unity of the Church*.

19. Oudinus claims [Col. 0506C] that among the ancients there was the deepest silence concerning obedience to the Roman pontiff. Catholic theologians have sufficiently and more than sufficiently refuted this claim. Clear evidence exists of the ancient Spanish Church’s observance toward the Roman see. One may consult the *Collection of the Spanish Councils*, arranged by Pueyo in the form of canon law. Its title I concerns the Roman pontiff and is divided into six chapters [Col. 0506D]; title II concerns the vicars and legates of the apostolic see and consists of four chapters. In the preface to the genuine collection of the canons of the Gothic Church—older even than Isidore, unless one wishes to make him its author—we read the following in Marca, *On the Ancient Collection of Canons*, Ballerini, and others:

“They also submit the decrees of the Roman prelates, in which, because of the eminence of the apostolic see, there exists an authority equal to that of councils.”

The Second Council of Seville, which Isidore presided over, agrees with this in chapter 2:

“That thirty-year objection imposes silence; for this is commanded both by the edicts of secular rulers and by the authority of the decrees of the Roman prelates.”

In chapter 40 I gave a Latin translation of Burriel’s letter, in which he asserts that the perpetual observance and obedience of the Spaniards toward the Roman pontiffs is most clearly demonstrated by our ancient collection of canons. I shall not omit the testimony of the most religious King Sisebut, who died before Isidore, from his letter to Adualvald, king of the Lombards, in Flórez, volume VII of *Sacred Spain*, pages 321 and following:

“‘The teacher of the nations, following in the footsteps of his master, declares [Col. 0507A] in these words: One God, one faith, one baptism.’ He clearly and plainly taught that there is one confession of believers for the worship and veneration of God, which the following Roman Church received as handed down by the apostles and, when rightly asked, after uprooting the crops of the heretics, handed on with maternal affection.”

St. Braulio, Isidore’s friend and, as many believe, his disciple, also addresses Honorius I in this manner in the letter in which he defends the deeds of the Spanish Fathers in the name of the Sixth Council of Toledo, volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, letter 21:

“You fulfill very well and most suitably the duty of your chair, bestowed upon you by God, when, with holy concern for all the churches, with the light of doctrine shining before you, and stationed as a watchman, you provide worthy defenses for the Church of Christ; when you pierce with the divine sword of the word and the heavenly weapon of zeal those who mock [perhaps: divide] the Lord’s tunic; and when, in the likeness of Nehemiah, by your zeal and vigilance you cleanse the holy house of God, our mother, of wicked transgressors [Col. 0507B] and abominable deserters.”

20. Oudinus objects to the mention of the Athanasian Creed in the letter to Claudius. What follows from that? Learned men agree—even those who deny that the creed was composed by Athanasius—that it is nevertheless extremely ancient, since it was found in an old codex written in the time of Gregory the Great. Whether, then, Vigilius of Tapsus published the creed under Athanasius’s name at the end of the fifth century, as many hold, or whether, as others prefer, Vincent of Lérins did so at the beginning of that century, it is certain that Isidore could have cited it under Athanasius’s name. See Natalis Alexander, century IV, chapter 6, article 8. He observes that at the Synod of Autun in the year 670 the clergy were ordered to recite the Creed of St. Athanasius, and that as early as the year 633 some passages from this creed appear to have been transcribed [Col. 0507C] in the profession of faith issued by the celebrated Fourth Council of Toledo, presided over by our Isidore.

21. Oudinus confidently declares that the letter to Redemptus was fabricated by the same author and adds: “All learned men hold this opinion.” Labbe, in his commentary on Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, indeed considers the letter false and thinks it was written after the controversy over unleavened bread. So do Cave, Cellier, Dupin, the authors of the supplement to the *Acta Eruditorum*, volume II, section 9, page 475, and others cited by Placcius, number 1484. Fabricius, number 23, merely says that it is considered suspect by highly learned men. It also appeared suspect to Flórez, volume XIII of *Sacred Spain*, page 319. Natalis [Col. 0507D] Alexander, who accepts the letter to Claudius, asserts that this one was fabricated after the controversy over unleavened bread arose between the Greeks and Latins, and thus after the Photian schism. Nicholas Antonio, after observing that Cardinal Bona, book I of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 23, also brands the letter as spurious, and that Mabillon, who argued against Cardinal Bona on the matter of unleavened bread, placed among the doubtful works an argument drawn from this letter that otherwise appeared extremely strong, in his dissertation *On Unleavened and Leavened Eucharistic Bread*, chapter 6, remains himself somewhat uncertain. He asks how Isidore could have written to his archdeacon Redemptus. “Perhaps,” he says, “Isidore was at that very time engaged at the royal court, as may be inferred from the tenth letter among Isidore’s letters to Braulio.” Flórez, as I showed in chapter 6, [Col. 0508A] doubts whether Redemptus the cleric of the church of Seville, the author of the account of Isidore’s death, was the same as Redemptus the archdeacon to whom the letter is addressed. He rather believes that the latter was Redemptus, archdeacon of Mérida, who flourished at the same time. This may be suggested, as Flórez likewise confirms in volume XIII of *Sacred Spain*, by the fact that the author of the account of St. Isidore’s death is called a cleric, whereas the other is called an archdeacon. Although the designation “cleric” is in a sense a general one, there was nevertheless already some distinction between the terms *cleric* and *deacon*, as appears in the case brought between the bishops Martianus and Habentius at the Sixth Council of Toledo, in Pueyo, page 690: “Through Timothy, then a cleric but now a deacon.”

[Col. 0508B] 22. Bayer sets out arguments that may make the letter to Redemptus seem suspect: its style appears to reflect the modern manner of disputing in the schools; the words “but the linen cloths, which we call corporals” seem to breathe an age later than that of Isidore; and it discusses unleavened and leavened bread long before the dispute over this matter arose between the Latins and Greeks. He observes that Mabillon and Cardinal Bona seem to have read only one of the three letters of Leo Acridens, archbishop of Bulgaria, to Leo IX on this subject, published in Latin by Baronius under the year 1053, whereas he himself once transcribed all three from a Greek codex of Antonius Augustinus. In them, however, he found nothing that could have given Isidore an occasion to write to Redemptus. Nevertheless, [Col. 0508C] Bayer offers several further arguments in defense of the letter against the charge of forgery. 648

“Why could Isidore not have written this letter before the dispute between the two Churches over unleavened and leavened bread, on the occasion of the scruple that, as the letter itself says, had arisen in Redemptus concerning this and other matters of ecclesiastical discipline? It contains no mention of a controversy between the two Churches, as Mabillon was convinced, not even the slightest trace or indication of one.”

He adds that the letter contains nothing absurd or unworthy of Isidore, that its doctrine agrees admirably with Catholic dogma, and that its style is not wholly unlike Isidore’s. “Let those judge these matters,” he concludes, “whose minds are attached to the study of the discipline of the ancient Church.”

23. To begin with the word *corporals*, the phrase “which we call corporals” may perhaps be a gloss [Col. 0508D] that entered the text from the margin. Yet it is not easy to accept that this meaning of the word was not in use in Isidore’s age, since the word is employed in this way in Gregory the Great’s *Book of Sacraments*, in the Roman Order, in the old Frankish Missal, page 400, in the *Capitularies of Charlemagne*, chapter 234, book VII, and by Alcuin, Amalarius, and other ancient writers cited by Ducange. In the Gothic-Hispanic Missal, page 219, in the preparation for Mass, we find this prayer:

“For spreading out the corporals, the priest says: ‘In your sight, Lord, we ask that these our gifts may be pleasing to you, so that we may be able to please you. Lift up your gates, princes, and be lifted up, eternal gates, and the King of glory shall enter,’ and so forth.”

But it must be observed [Col. 0509A] that among the Gothic-Hispanic peoples *corporals* did not mean the cloths on which the body of the Lord is placed according to the Roman rite. They meant the cloths with which the sacred gifts and the altar itself were covered by the deacon. Perhaps, therefore, in the rubric of the Gothic-Hispanic Missal one should read “for lifting up the corporals,” unless the covering was lifted in such a way that it was immediately spread over the altar. For in the Mass of the first Sunday of Advent, page 2, there is another rubric: “Leaving the paten upon the corporals.” Or—and this seems more likely to me—the chalice and paten were placed upon the corporals, and some folded outer portion of the corporals was spread over them, as may be inferred from what Cardinal Bona discusses in *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 25, number 11. The Council of Coyac, held in the diocese of Oviedo in the year 1050, agrees with this: “Under the chalice, and above it, a clean and undamaged linen corporal.” [Col. 0509B] The Gothic-Hispanic peoples and the Mozarabs always kept the bread and the Lord’s body on the paten.

Source preparation: Supplied textual variants, foreign-language text, and column transitions retained.

649

### 24.

The controversy in the letter to Redemptus, then, seems not to concern the cloths that we call *corporalia*, but the veil, or cloths, with which among the Goths the deacon covered the sacred gifts. This veil, or *pallium*, is now usually made of silk and interwoven with gold; but, as can be inferred from the letter, formerly—at least in many Western churches—it was linen. Gregory of Tours, book VII, chapter 2, calls it a covering with which the Lord’s altar is covered together with the offerings: “which is placed over the altar’s gifts.” Nor do the words of the letter differ from this: “They provide silk cloths, but we linen cloths, which we call *corporalia*, for the adornment of so great a sacrifice.”

Many centuries later, in Spain, this same *pallium* with which the chalice is covered still retained the name *corporale*, as is clear from the law of Alfonso IX, part I, title 4, law 57:

> Corporales son dichos aquellos pannos blancos, que ponen sobre el caliz, con que lo cubren, quando face el clerigo el sacramento del Corpus Domini, e estos no deven ser de sirgo, nin de panno tinto, mas de panno de lino puro e blanco.

“Those white cloths are called *corporales* which they place over the chalice and with which they cover it when the cleric performs the sacrament of the Lord’s Body. These ought not to be made of silk or dyed cloth, but of pure and white linen.”

Yet, according to different periods and regions, the name *corporale* is found applied to different cloths serving the altar, as may be seen in Ducange under the entries *Corporale*, *Palla*, and *Substratorium*.

[Col. 0509C]

### 25.

Someone might perhaps identify another indication of a more recent style in the words of the letter to Redemptus: “Since they are not of the essence, or substance, of the sacrament.” But certain expressions now common among theologians have a foundation in the ancient Fathers. [Col. 0509D] The use of the preposition *de* is so varied and remarkable even among the best authors of Latin that it would be difficult to recognize any novelty in the phrase under discussion.

As to whether, before the controversy over unleavened bread arose between the Latins and Greeks, some scruple concerning this distinction could have arisen in Redemptus—or indeed whether, even in Isidore’s time, certain Easterners may have attempted to criticize the practice of the Latins—there is certainly no reason for us to deny it. For if the causes of the disagreement were the same, why could there not also have been beginnings which nevertheless did not erupt into open conflict and schism until many centuries later, after other controversies had arisen?

[Col. 0510A]

Thus the Greeks reproached the Armenians, who, falling into the Eutychian heresy, had begun to use unleavened bread. An old formula of the Armenians returning to the Catholic faith and to concord with the Greek Church, transcribed by Cotelerius in his notes on book V of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, expressed this anathema:

> If anyone does not put leaven and salt into the bread of the offering, nor water together with the wine into the holy chalice, let him be anathema.

Certain words of Gregory the Great are also cited by the patriarch of Constantinople, Gennadius, on behalf of the Council of Florence, and by Saint Thomas, part III, question 74, article 4, as well as in the *Catena* on Matthew, as though taken from Gregory’s register. But, as learned men have already observed, they are found in none of Saint Gregory’s works. They read as follows:

[Col. 0510B]

> It is customary to trouble many people why, in the Church, some offer unleavened breads and others offer leavened ones. The Roman Church offers unleavened breads, etc.; but whether it is celebrated with unleavened or with leavened bread, we receive the body of the Lord and of our Savior.

### 26.

The greatest difficulty in this matter, however, lies in the question whether, in Isidore’s time, the use of unleavened bread existed in the Latin Church, and especially in the Gothic-Hispanic Church. For the most learned men disagree among themselves.

Mabillon, in the preface to the third century of the Benedictine order and in his separate dissertation on unleavened and leavened Eucharistic bread, and Christian Lupus, volume III of the *Scholia on the Decrees and Canons of the Councils*, in his dissertation on the acts of Saint Leo IX, chapters 7 and following, maintain that from the very beginning of the faith’s reception the Latin Church had perpetually used unleavened Eucharistic bread.

[Col. 0510C]

Against them, Sirmond, in his dissertation on unleavened bread, argues that the solemn use of leavened bread in the Latin Church lasted for eight hundred years and more, and that unleavened bread was not adopted until after the schism of Photius. Cardinal Bona, book I of the *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 2, followed this opinion, except that he does not exclude unleavened bread from the Latin Church in those earliest centuries altogether, as Sirmond does.

Natalis Alexander sets out the arguments for both sides with the greatest care in dissertation 11 on the eleventh and twelfth centuries, article 3, but does not dare to decide in favor of either position. He is somewhat inconsistent with himself, however, since in century VII, chapter 3, article 22, he says that it is established from canon 6 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo that the Spanish Church used leavened bread at that time, while in chapter 4, article 4, he denies that the letter to Redemptus is Isidore’s, because in that period the Spanish Church consecrated leavened bread.

[Col. 0510D]
