In the present dissertation he observes that both parties cite canon 6 of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo in support of their own position, and concludes: “Let the reader judge which opinion he should favor.” I believe that the words of the Council of Toledo can be reconciled with both positions, and therefore favor neither.

650

### 27.

The council, in chapter 6, reproves those who

> do not offer upon the Lord’s table, for the sacrifice, clean breads carefully prepared, but indiscriminately, in whatever way necessity impelled or inclination compelled each person, remove from the breads prepared for their own use a small cake, shaping it into a round form, and offer it upon the altar with wine and water as a sacred libation. No such action, however, is found to have been performed anywhere in the history of sacred authority.

It then proves [Col. 0511A] that Christ took a whole loaf, blessed it, and broke it, and continues:

> What else did he institute for us except that, taking a whole loaf, we should place it upon his altar table to be blessed, not a piece of bread, which we clearly see that our Head did not do? For if a person takes particular care of the necessities of his own life, how much more ought he to display the proper cleanliness in the worship of God? Therefore, wishing to put an end to this rashness or ignorance, our assembly has unanimously decreed that bread to be sanctified upon the Lord’s altar by priestly blessing shall not be presented in any other form than whole, clean, and carefully prepared, and not something large, but only a modest offering, according to what ecclesiastical custom retains. Its remnants [Col. 0511B] may either be more easily preserved for safekeeping in a small container without any damage, or, if it is necessary to consume them, they should not weigh down the stomach of the person who has taken them with the burden of a heavy stuffing.

### 28.

Something is perhaps missing between the words “which we clearly see that he did” and “For if a person.” The council’s meaning is certainly that the bread to be sanctified ought to be placed upon the altar whole, clean, carefully prepared, and of modest size.

It appears that by that time there had already arisen in Spain some beginning of the little pieces that are now distributed to communicants after consecration. The council condemns this because it was contrary to ancient custom: Christ took a whole loaf, blessed it, broke it, and gave it to his disciples. Unless I am greatly mistaken, the text should read: “they remove *crustula* into a round shape, and offer them,” etc.

[Col. 0511C]

For although *crustula* can be feminine, derived from *crusta*, here it seems better to understand it as neuter plural, derived from *crustum*. As Servius observes in his note on book VII of the *Aeneid*, verse 114:

> We use *crustum* and *crusta* in the neuter for things that can be eaten, but in the feminine for things that we cannot eat.

Nor can the council’s meaning be otherwise. It is speaking of bread that was to be taken whole and broken into pieces for distribution; its remnants were either to be preserved in a small container or consumed. The example of Christ is repeated: he took a whole loaf—not a morsel—and, after blessing it, broke it and gave it piece by piece to his disciples.

652

Therefore, those who offered a single round piece of bread, that is, one morsel, upon the altar—namely, for the priest who alone was offering—are not being reproved. Rather, the council reproves those who brought several round pieces to the altar and afterward, once they had been sanctified, gave them to the communicants without breaking them.

[Col. 0511D]

### 29.

What form or shape the bread to be consecrated once had, and how it came to the form of the hosts and pieces that we now use, is investigated with the greatest care by Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 23. But he traces the origin of hosts and pieces to later centuries. This is true if the subject is the common practice received in the churches. Otherwise, its beginning must be traced to the custom censured at the Council of Toledo, which afterward prevailed in an improved form, purged of the fault that the Council of Toledo likewise condemned: namely, that these round pieces were made from bread used for ordinary purposes.

In this respect, where the council wishes the bread to be sanctified to be clean and carefully prepared, Mabillon argues that unleavened bread is prescribed. Sirmond, Cardinal Bona, and others infer that leavened bread is not excluded, since no express mention of it is made, as would have been necessary. Christian Lupus also agrees with them, although from this he argues that the use of leavened bread was proper to the Spanish Church and not common to the Latin Church.

[Col. 0512A]

I again affirm that the chapter of the Sixteenth Council of Toledo can be consistent with both opinions. The words “clean and carefully prepared” sufficiently suggest unleavened bread, if its use was otherwise in force at that time; but they may also signify the special care and diligence—or, more precisely, the careful preparation—required to make even leavened bread from the finest flour. The dispute must therefore be settled from other evidence, and it is not ours to resolve it.

I nevertheless believe that the Council of Coyaca, held in the year 1050, favors the opinion of Sirmond and Cardinal Bona:

> Let the host be of wheat, sound and whole; or, according to another reading, of selected wheat.

Here there is no mention of unleavened bread, as would have seemed necessary if that had been the common practice.

653

Joan Gotter’s *History of the Controversies concerning Unleavened Bread*, etc., was published at Leipzig in 1737. Meanwhile, the letter to Redemptus must at least be regarded as doubtful on this point.

[Col. 0512B]

### 30.

[Col. 0512C]

As for the statement in the same letter that the vessels used for the offering of the sacrifice ought preferably to be made of metal rather than wood or earthenware, this seems to have been said on the basis of ancient custom. The recently cited Council of Coyaca says:

> So that they may not sacrifice with a wooden or earthen chalice.

If you have the opportunity, read Cardinal Bona, *Liturgical Matters*, book I, chapter 25. In paragraph 2 he concludes that the orthodox Church has always and everywhere agreed that priests should use golden or silver chalices.

The same most learned cardinal also reports much concerning the linen cloth called the *corporale* in the same work, paragraph 11; this is consistent with the letter to Redemptus.

The ancient Fathers likewise held that the words of the heavenly oracle were not subject, as the author of the letter to Redemptus says, to the rules of Priscian or Donatus. Gregory the Great, in his letter to Leander prefixed to the *Exposition on Job*, says:

[Col. 0512D]

> I consider it entirely unworthy that I should restrict the words of the heavenly oracle under the rules of Donatus.

For these rules have not been preserved by any interpreters in the authority of Sacred Scripture.

### 31.

Something remains to be said about the letter to Eugenius. Perez, in his notes, asserts that this Eugenius was Eugenius II, bishop of Toledo and successor of Justus. For this reason some have thought that the inscription was false, because they believed that Justus died after Isidore; Oudinus refutes this, although he says that the letter belongs to the same forgery and author as the preceding letters.

Florez, volume V of *Sacred Spain*, page 267, regards the letter as genuine, but does not think it was written to Eugenius of Toledo. Since Justus, his predecessor, died in the year 636 around the middle of March, [Col. 0513A] Eugenius’ consecration must be placed near the end of that same month, and not earlier; Isidore, however, died at the beginning of the following month, April. It therefore does not seem that enough time elapsed for Isidore to have been able to send a letter to Eugenius once he had become bishop.

Moreover, the letter seems rather to have been addressed to a bishop long established in office:

> Receiving through the messenger Verecundus the letter of your holiness, we give thanks to the Creator of all things, who deigns to preserve for His holy Church the health of your mind and body.

Florez therefore thinks that the letter was addressed to Eugenius of Egara, who signed the Fourth Council of Toledo together with Isidore. The inscription certainly does not identify the bishop’s see, and the chronological argument explained by Florez weighs against Eugenius of Toledo. [Col. 0513B]

654

### 32.

Lucas of Tuy inserted part of this letter to Eugenius into his work on the Albigensian heresy. Mariana too, in book VI, chapter 6, of his *History of Spain*, infers from it the friendship that existed between Isidore and Eugenius II of Toledo. In his notes on Lucas of Tuy, book II, chapter 1, Mariana asserts that the letter exists in an ancient codex of the church of Toledo.

Lucas praises Isidore as its author, but does not name the work or passage from which he took the words. Natalis Alexander asserts that Isidore, in this letter as in the other addressed to Claudius, admirably confirms the divine right of the Roman pontiff’s primacy.

Oudinus, as I have said, together with Dupin, Dallaeus, Tentzel, and others—especially those outside the orthodox confession—openly call the letter fictitious, both because of its professed obedience toward the Roman pontiff and because it introduces a reference to the Athanasian Creed. I already refuted these two objections when discussing the letter to Claudius.

There is therefore less reason to doubt that this letter is Isidore’s than there is to doubt the preceding letter to Redemptus. There may even be greater reason to assert that Isidore wrote it, since Lucas of Tuy is already found citing it. Yet, because Tuy’s authority is not sufficiently firm or ancient, and because more reliable examples from an earlier age have not been produced, I shall pronounce these four letters at least doubtful.

[Col. 0513C]

# CHAPTER LXXV

## On Other Letters Attributed or Falsely Ascribed to Isidore. The Spurious Medical Letter of Isidore. Whether Isidore Wrote Any Work on Medicine

[Col. 0513D]

### 1.

The canon of León, author of the *Life of Saint Isidore* among the Bollandists, reports that while still a young man Isidore wrote a letter to Gregory the Great on blessedness. No mention of it is found among earlier authors, as I observed in chapter 18, number 9; nor do I think that a copy of it can be found anywhere.

### 2.

In Vatican Codex 3791, after Isidore’s letters to Leudefredus and Massona, there is the following inscription:

> Here begins Isidore’s letter on the names of the heretics who disturbed the unity of the Church.

But this has been extracted from book VIII, chapter 5, of the *Etymologies*: “There are also certain heretics,” etc. Additional material is taken from chapter 6 under the title “Some Matters Concerning the Philosophers of the Nations.” This letter will be discussed again in chapter 86.

655

[Col. 0514A]

### 3.

Another letter under Isidore’s name occurs in a fairly ancient Vatican Codex, 4418, described in chapter 97. Among other medical works, it is thus inscribed on page 167 verso:

> Here begins the letter of Isidore the Spaniard.

Again, on page 108, in a more recent hand:

> Letter of Isidore: There are four winds and four corners of the sky, etc.

The letter appears to have been composed by a Christian who took certain material from Isidore, namely from book IV of the *Etymologies*, which concerns medicine, and from other places.

Fabricius, volume XIII of the *Greek Library*, page 746, lists among ancient physicians Isidore of Antioch, cited by Galen, and Isidore of Memphis, cited by Aëtius. He adds that Isidore of Seville is counted among physicians by Tiraquellus because of what he wrote on the properties of things, as well as because of much other material relevant to medicine, especially in books XI, XII, XVI, and XVII of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0514B]

I do not know whether, when he speaks of “the properties of things,” he means the work mentioned by Sigebert:

> He also wrote two books on the Differences of Words, or on the Properties of Things,

or whether he merely means that Isidore wrote extensively about the properties of things in the books of the *Etymologies*.

### 4.

In the Roman Angelica Library there is a parchment codex in quarto, dating approximately from the fourteenth century, entitled *Isidore and Others on Medicine*. It begins:

> Meanwhile, I advise you, physician, just as I was advised by our teachers, etc.

It ends:

> is known to be possible. Here ends Isidore.

The work addresses a certain nephew of its author. It does not say that the author is Isidore of Seville. There follow several anonymous works:

> Medicine is that which either protects or restores the body, etc.

This is the imperfect fourth book of Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Then begins the *Golden Book*:

> If there is pain in the head, etc.

Here ends the *Golden Book*. Next begin the treatments of Master Bartholomew:

> Hydrophobia is an illness, etc.

The codex appears to be mutilated at the end.

[Col. 0514C]

### 5.

I suspect that during the Middle Ages there was some Isidore who attempted, to the best of his ability, to shed light on medicine through Latin literature. For in Vatican Codex 2439, also on parchment and in folio, after Averroes’ commentary on Avicenna’s *Cantica*, translated from Arabic by Master Armengandus Blaxius of Montpellier, there are, on page 45, the aphorisms of John of Damascus with a commentary attached.

The aphorisms begin:

> May God deliver you, dearest son, from the wandering error.

The commentary begins:

> John of Damascus, when transmitting certain medical rules, prefixed a preface to his work.

At the end there is this rubric:

> Here end the aphorisms of John of Damascus, son of Serapion, with the commentary of blessed Isidore.

[Col. 0514D]

The codex dates approximately from the fourteenth century. Neither Armengandus Blaxius nor any medical Isidore is mentioned by Fabricius in his *Library of the Middle Ages*.

John of Damascus, the physician, is the very man whom Fabricius, in volume XIII of the *Greek Library*, says wrote a book of 160 aphorisms to his son and assigns to approximately the end of the eighth century. Although he promised to discuss John of Damascus, son of Serapion, in his treatment of Serapion, he produced only the following:

> John Serapio, or, as others call him, the son of Serapion, an Arab physician around the year of Christ 1070, lived many centuries after Serapion the Alexandrian physician, etc.

[Col. 0515A]

He adds:

> We have several writings of that Arab, whom some incorrectly assign to the eighth century, translated into Latin, etc.

Yet Fabricius himself assigns the author of the aphorisms to the eighth century. Whatever the truth may be, our Isidore certainly could not have published a commentary on the aphorisms of a writer who lived so much later.

656

### 6.

If, as I believe, there was some Isidore who, during the Middle Ages, professed his name among medical writers, it was easy for foolish scribes to believe that the author was Isidore of Seville, whose fame had spread everywhere.

Perhaps the author of the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle*, attributed to Ildefonsus and either entirely fabricated or extensively interpolated, took the opportunity from this to disseminate certain claims about Isidore’s medical books, allegedly falsified by the likewise fictitious Theodiscus, Isidore’s successor:

[Col. 0515B]

> The most blessed Isidore was succeeded by Theodiscus, a Greek by nationality, etc. He corrupted certain books on the Nature of Things and the Art of Medicine, as well as on the Notarial Art, which Father Isidore had composed in eloquent style and which had not yet been made public, out of hatred for the faith, cutting out what was true and inserting what was false; and through a certain Arab named Avicenna he translated them from Latin into Arabic.

### 7.

Nicolaus Antonius rightly rejects this entire fable. He thinks that the error arose from such an interpolated chronicle among those who believed Avicenna to have been a Spaniard. Yet Avicenna, the chief of the Arab physicians, appears to have been neither born in Spain nor ever to have gone there, and he lived only in the eleventh century, [Col. 0515C] as is shown in book VII, chapter 2, where Antonius observes that others distinguish two Avicennas without any foundation.

Moreover, it seems ridiculous to say that Theodiscus, out of hatred for the faith, cut out true material and inserted false material in books on medicine and natural things, when this ought rather to have been referred to books written on sacred matters.

It is uncertain whether the pseudo-Ildefonsus, by “the notarial art,” meant that superstitious art which Cornelius Agrippa explained in an entire book under the title *The Key of Solomon*, and which Delrio, Torreblanca, Alberghinus, and others discuss—an art that certainly cannot be attributed to the most holy Isidore without the greatest injustice—or whether he meant the notarial art that teaches writing by signs, which even the Jews of a later age knew. On this subject, see Muller, *Miscellanies*, book II, chapter 13.

[Col. 0515D]

This latter notarial art is even less suitable for being corrupted out of hatred for the faith. Pinius, in his treatise on the Hispanic Liturgy, chapter 4, conjectures that the corruption of certain copies of the Mozarabic liturgy may be attributed to the same fictitious Theodiscus. He says this because he trusted Baronius, who, under the year 794, reports that Theodiscus was the first in Spain to assert that Christ the Son of God was adoptive. Thus errors easily spread.

### 8.

Berardus, who published the genuine canons of Gratian, repeats the same old story in part III, page 481, and concludes as follows:

> From this everyone can infer how much care is required in studying the books attributed to Isidore. If anything in them can cause offense, it must certainly be attributed not to Isidore but either to Theodiscus or to Avicenna.

Rodriguez, volume II of the *Spanish Library*, page 344, misrepresents Nicolaus Antonius’ position. He says that Antonius composed an apology for Theodiscus, to whom some had attributed the error of the Adoptionists, whereas Nicolaus Antonius maintains that no bishop Theodiscus of Seville ever existed at all.

[Col. 0516A]

### 9.

It has already been demonstrated in chapter 12 that there was no Theodiscus who held the see of Seville after Isidore. Nevertheless, I would not for that reason consider Lucas of Tuy the author of the continuation of the chronicle attributed to Ildefonsus, or its interpolator, as many believe.

For Rodrigo of Toledo, who was Lucas’ contemporary or perhaps even earlier, also seems to have read the same continuation, as appears from book II of *On the Affairs of Spain*, chapter 21, where he says of Chindaswinth:

> He diligently ordered the books of the holy Fathers to be sought out and the institutions of blessed Isidore to be firmly observed. By synodal judgment he sent the treacherous Theodistus, bishop of Seville, into exile and, with the approval of the entire council, confirmed for the Church of Toledo the dignity of the primacy which it had possessed from ancient times.

Rodrigo says nothing explicitly about the corrupted books of Isidore, either because it was sufficient for his purpose to call Theodiscus or Theodistus treacherous, or because he perhaps obtained a less corrupt copy of the continuation of Isidore’s *Chronicle*, as I have already noted in the cited passage.

658

[Col. 0516B]

### 10.

Someone might include among Isidore’s letters the little work *On the Institution of a Good Life*, discussed in chapter 82, since it bears the title of a letter in Vatican-Palatine Codex 832. [Col. 0516C] Yet there it is wrongly attributed not to Isidore but to Ambrose, on page 80 verso:

> Here begins the letter of blessed Ambrose, archbishop, on Morals and an Honorable Life: Dear son, love tears, etc.

# CHAPTER LXXVI

## On Isidore’s Book *On the Nature of Things*, Addressed to King Sisebut. Editions, Manuscript Codices, and Excerpts. A Chapter of This Book Not Yet Published. An Astrological Poem Added to This Book, Perhaps by Isidore; a Metrical Epitome of the Same Book, Not Yet Published, Perhaps by Saint Eugenius of Toledo

[Col. 0516D]

### 1.

“I have not yet seen anyone,” says Bayer, “who brings a case against Isidore concerning this work.” This is certainly worth noting amid such freedom and variety in judging Isidore’s genuine works.

Florez published the letters, some brief verses, and the *Acts of the Martyrdom of Saint Desiderius* of King Sisebut, whose learning and eloquence Isidore celebrates not only in the dedicatory letter but also in his *History of the Goths*. These works sufficiently confirm Isidore’s judgment of the king’s education, although Sisebut wrote in a language that was only slightly Latin and inclined toward the vernacular.

The work is clearly described by Braulio:

> One book on the Nature of Things, addressed to King Sisebut, in which he resolves certain obscure questions about the elements, both through the investigation of ecclesiastical teachers and through that of the philosophers.

Ildefonsus gives a shorter description:

> A book on the Nature of Things, addressed to Prince Sisebut.

Sigebert and others likewise retained the title *On the Nature of Things*. Nicolaus Antonius thinks that this is the work which Trithemius cites under the name *Cosmography*. Scriverius observed that this title appears in the Pithoean Codex, in his annotations on Vegetius’ 1670 edition, volume II, after Stewechius’ commentary, page 54.

But since Trithemius sometimes represents certain works under different titles, I believe that the work is not different from what he elsewhere calls *On Computation and the Nature of Things* and elsewhere *On Astronomy*.

659

[Col. 0517A]

### 2.

There seems to be no doubt that the book on Astronomy recorded by Trithemius is the very work *On the Nature of Things*. For the beginning given by Trithemius—“To the most dear lord and son”—corresponds to Isidore’s dedicatory letter to Sisebut.

Nicolaus Antonius lists among the works mentioned by Trithemius but unknown to others a book on Astronomy, which he himself also suspects to be the book *On the Nature of Things*. [Col. 0517B] Nevertheless, he adds that in the Medicean Library there is an Isidore *On the Stars*.

This codex still exists, entitled *Isidore’s Book on the Stars of the Sky*. Yet it is plainly the same as the book *On the Nature of Things*, as is evident from the comparison with the Zaccarian collations mentioned in chapter 44.

Nor are similar titles lacking in other manuscript copies of the book *On the Nature of Things*, as in Royal-Vatican Codex 1573. Bayer also describes a Toledo Codex entitled *On the Stars of the Sky*, addressed to Sisebut. Others call it an astronomical book; and in the Augsburg edition of 1472, cited by Fabricius, it is entitled *On the Response of the World and the Ordering of the Stars*.

In the Escorial Codex described by Rodriguez, volume II of the *Spanish Library*, page 327, dating from the eleventh century, the title is *Saint Isidore of Seville on Astronomy or the Nature of Things*. In the same codex there follows *The Book of Sentences*, namely Isidore’s.

[Col. 0517C]

### 3.

Nicolaus Antonius also wonders that the work *On the Nature of Things* is called the *Book of the Wheels* in the manuscript codex of Paul Petau, cited by Scriverius.

Nor does he agree with Scriverius, who wished to change *Rotarum* into *Notarum*. Instead, he considers more plausible the conjecture that *Rotarum* arose from *De Natura rerum* when the title was written in abbreviated form.

He nevertheless judges it more likely that the title *Book of the Wheels* was fabricated by some exceedingly incompetent copyist from the wheels, or circular figures, which Isidore uses frequently in this book—especially since he found the same title in the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*. On this, compare the above, chapter 46, where the same title *Book of the Wheels* is placed above the true title in another codex of the monastery of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch.

Our Royal-Vatican Codex 310 likewise bears this inscription. The Milanese Codex is entitled *Liber Rotar.*, which Muratori did not understand when he described the codex, as I said in chapter 55. Perhaps the final letters of *Rotarum* had been worn away by age.

[Col. 0517D]

### 4.

Grial, who undertook to correct this book for the Madrid edition, says that the title *On the Nature of Things* is preferable, since Bede too, following Isidore’s example, entitled his book *On the Nature of Things*, although Isidore’s book is elsewhere entitled *On Astronomy*, *On the World*, or *On the Natures of Things*.

Mansi, in his description of the Lucchese Codex mentioned above in chapter 44, records a work by a certain James under the following title:

> Here begins *On the Nature of Things*.

It deals with the earth, the world, the elements, the stars, meteors, and so forth. Its preface is in verse:

> He has briefly surveyed in swift headings the diverse natures of things and the broad periods of passing time.

Mansi was planning to publish this little work. He believed the author to be James the deacon, whose synopsis of Alcuin’s letter follows. I think it is Bede’s already published work.

In the ninth century, Alvarus of Córdoba called Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things* in his *Bright Index*, number 15:

> But blessed Isidore, “our light” [Latin *lumen noster*; conjectured *nostrum*, likewise “our light”], proclaims in his book *On the Nature of Things*, in clear discourse and by the apt figure of a certain star, *Horione* [corrected *Orionis*, “Orion”], that at the time of martyrdom scandal arises for the carnal-minded and the less learned.

[Col. 0518A]

### 5.

As I said from Fabricius, this book was published in 1472. [Col. 0518B] Bandini agrees in volume IV of the *Latin Codices of the Laurentian Medicean Library*, shelf 27, codex 9 of the Library of Santa Croce. The edition was unknown to Margarino de la Bigne, who believed that he was the first to publish the work in 1580.

The same book was subsequently reprinted in the royal Madrid edition of Isidore’s works, in the Breulian editions, and in the recent Madrid edition. In the royal edition, however, the final chapter, *On the Parts of the Earth*, was omitted.

In the recent Madrid edition, this chapter was added among the appendices, page 51, from an Oviedo Codex written in the seventh century and from another Oxford codex, written in the twelfth century or around the beginning of the thirteenth. The editor, who adds some variant readings from the Oviedo Codex, observes that in the center of the figure in chapter 11, marked in red letters, one reads:

> Remember Eulogius the sinner.

This Eulogius, he adds, appears to have been the scribe or possessor of the book. In an appended note, it is questioned whether he was Saint Eulogius, the martyr of Córdoba. Saint Eulogius suffered martyrdom in the year 859; therefore, if the book belongs to the seventh century or, as others think, the eighth, this holy martyr could only have been its possessor.

[Col. 0518C]

### 6.

The same editor observes that, after the chapter which is now the last, *On the Parts of the Earth*, another passage is added in the same Oviedo Codex concerning Asia and its parts. These are chapters 3, 4, and 5 of book XIV of the *Etymologies*. He makes the not implausible conjecture that they once genuinely belonged to the book *On the Nature of Things*, which preceded the *Etymologies*, but were later inserted by Isidore into the *Etymologies* and omitted from most copies of the book *On the Nature of Things*.

Bayer, in his notes on the *Ancient Spanish Library*, observes that the very ancient codex once belonging to the Church of Oviedo, [Col. 0518D] which Grial calls Lombardic, now exists in the royal Escorial Library. It consists partly of Lombard cursive writing, which we call the Ataulphic script, and partly of square, or ordinary Roman, writing. It appears to have been written in the eighth century, and not very late in that century. From this codex, he continues, Isidore’s previously unpublished chapter 47, *On the Parts of the Earth*, passed into the latest Madrid edition of 1778.

He is mistaken in thinking that this chapter had not been published earlier, since it appears both in the Bignan edition and in the two Breulian editions. Since it is found not only in the printed editions and in most of our manuscript codices but also in that very Lombardic codex which Grial used above all, it may be inferred that its omission from Grial’s Madrid edition resulted from someone’s carelessness.

[Col. 0519A]

If it was deliberately omitted because it is absent from some manuscripts, the editor ought to have explained why he excluded a chapter already found in the Bignan edition, present in many very ancient parchment manuscripts, and containing nothing unworthy of Isidore.

### 7.

Some excerpts from the book *On the Nature of Things* occur in manuscript copies. Thus, in Royal-Vatican Codex 571, among other excerpts drawn from the Fathers, there is a passage on the signs of stormy or clear weather on page 13. This is the complete chapter 38 of Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*. There is another excerpt in Casanatense Codex D. IV, 23, discussed in chapter 107.

### 8.

Nicolaus Antonius mentions one manuscript codex of the book *On the Nature of Things* from the Milanese Library. Bayer mentions three Escorial codices and one from Toledo, which Burriel also recalls in his letter.

At the end of chapter 44 I listed four codices—one Lucchese and three Florentine—whose variant readings Zaccaria had prepared for himself. Among the Albornozian codices of the *Exposition on Genesis*, etc., a book of Isidore *On the Nature of Things* is indicated at the beginning.

Among the codices of the *Etymologies*, as I have already observed, the book *On the Nature of Things* is found in some places as a part, or final book, of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0519B]

### 9.

Bandini, volume IV of the *Latin Codices of the Medicean Library*, shelf 27, of the Library of Santa Croce, describes Codex 9, which contains the work *Etymologies*, as I said elsewhere.

On page 175, number 3, there is:

> The illustrious little book of Isidore the Younger, on Astronomy or the Nature of Things.

Its prologue begins:

> To the lord and son Sisebut, etc.

There is a table of forty-five chapters. [Col. 0519C] The last concerns Mount Etna and ends:

> to punish sinners, who will be tormented forever and ever.

The Madrid edition adds some other material, and the Bignan and Breulian editions add another complete chapter.

In the same codex four chapters follow. The first is:

> On the names of the stars and the reasons why they received their names.

The second:

> On the precedence and antegradation of the stars.

The third:

> On the precedence and antegradation—read *retrogradation*—of the stars.

The fourth:

> On the state of the stars.

These are the four final chapters of book III of the *Etymologies*. Other chapters on the world follow, namely the first ten chapters of book XIII of the *Etymologies*.

On page 188 the entire tenth book of the *Etymologies* occurs. In this codex it is somewhat longer than in the printed editions, since it contains certain additions at the end, as Bandini observes.

[Col. 0519D]

Another Codex *On the Nature of Things* is listed by Bandini under shelf 22 of the Library of Santa Croce, number 12. It is a parchment codex of the thirteenth century, entitled *On the Stars of the Sky*, similar to Codex 39, shelf 29, which I discussed in chapter 44.

10. I have examined quite a few manuscript copies of the book *On the Nature of Things*, none of them negligible. The Codex Regio-Vaticanus 255, to be described in chapter 99, presents the work *On the Nature of Things* under this later title: “Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*.” The codex is old, perhaps from the ninth century. Not much later is the Codex Regio-Vaticanus 310, discussed in chapter 100, in which the book *On the Nature of Things* is entitled “Isidore’s Book of Wheels.” In the Codex Regio-Vaticanus 571, also discussed in chapter 100, there is a fragment of this book. In the Regio-Vatican Codex 1260, chapter 101, the complete work appears without a title; it begins: “To Sisebutus, lord and son, Isidore.” The final [Col. 0520A] chapter concerns Mount Etna; there are verses on the winds and the poem beginning “You perhaps, in the grove,” etc. In the Regio-Vatican Codex 1573, chapter 101, the title is “Book of the Stars of Heaven, published by Isidore.” It contains chapter 47, “On the Parts of the Earth.” In the Palatine Codex 834, discussed in chapter 103, it begins: “Here begins the book *On the Stars of Heaven* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.” In the Palatine Codex 1448, approximately of the eleventh century, there is “The Book of Wheels of Saint Isidore, bishop”; it contains chapter 46, “On the Names of the Sea and Rivers,” not yet published. This is chapter 48 in the Palatine Codex 834. The same chapter exists in the Urbinate Codex 100, discussed in chapter 104, where this book is entitled *On Astronomy* and is appended to the *Etymologies* as book 23 and the final book; at the end it is enlarged by a short work *On the Sky*, which is likewise attributed to Isidore. It is also found in the Albanian Codex, which I shall discuss at greater length in chapter 107.

[Col. 0520B] 663

11. A new chapter, “On the Names of the Sea and Rivers,” is to be brought forward by us from manuscript codices, namely, after chapter 22, on the Nile. Although it is lacking in the printed editions and is also absent from many handwritten copies, I am certain that it is by Isidore’s hand. For who else after Isidore’s time would have known how to insert passages from ancient authors so skillfully, as is evident in this chapter? This chapter corresponds to the remainder of the work, concerning which the words of Scriverius on Vegetius, reported by Niccolò Antonio and quoted by Fabricius, should be noted:

> Certainly, a work not unworthy of consideration, and deserving the judgment of a learned man. Many fragments of Nigidius, Varro, Suetonius Tranquillus, and others are to be drawn from it.

In this chapter Isidore adduces words of Tranquillus in the *Prata*, of Virgil, of Naevius in the *Punic War*, of Atta in the *Togatae*, [Col. 0520C] of Pacuvius, and of Augustus, from whom he quotes: “We came to Naples, though on a blind wave.” This fragment may be added to the other passages of Augustus collected by Rutgersius, no less than the words of Tranquillus, Naevius, Pacuvius, and Atta quoted in this chapter may be placed among the fragments of ancient poets, which many have already published. The aforementioned chapter exists in the Albanian Codex, in the Lucchese Codex, and in many Vatican codices, as may be observed in the catalogue recently set out for them.

12. In some manuscripts, a certain astronomical poem in hexameter verse is appended to the book *On the Nature of Things*, beginning “You perhaps, in the grove,” etc. In the recent Madrid edition this poem was transcribed, where it is called a most elegant eclogue. It was taken from a very old Oviedo Codex, in which it was placed between chapters 46 and 47, and from another fourteenth-century codex, namely the Escorial one, as I infer from Bayer’s note to the *Bibliotheca Hispana*. Bayer calls it a little poem *On the Sun*, though it is elliptical and miserably mutilated. Its beginning among the appendices of the new Madrid edition is: “You perhaps, in the groves.” It ends: “Light, and assailing his brother with straight rays.” The poem is corrupted by many errors in that edition. I shall publish it corrected not only from the Regio-Vatican manuscript 255, in which it is found after the book *On the Nature of Things*, but also from the early editions.

13. Both the Madrid editor and Bayer seem to have been unaware that this kind of astronomical poem had been published in print long before, and more than once. It appears in the *Anthologia Latina*, p. 494 of volume IV of the Pisan edition of the *Poetae Latini*, where at the end it is indicated that something is missing after the verse “The moon moves,” etc.; for this is how it must be read, [Col. 0521A] 664 not as in the Madrid edition, “Let the light go.” In the Regio-Vatican manuscript 255, no sign indicates that the poem is incomplete; its final verse, however, reads:

> The moon moves, assailing her brother with straight rays.

The Madrid edition has *argens*, the Pisan edition *arcens*, in place of *urgens*.

The poem first appeared among the ancient poems of P. Pithou. Fabricius discusses that edition in book IV, chapter 1, of his *Bibliotheca Latina*. He calls it a fragment by an uncertain author, *On the Decline of the Moon*, or *On Astronomy*, beginning: “You perhaps, joyful in the place.” But it should read: “You perhaps, slow in the grove.” He observes that the attribution to Fulgentius was indicated in the title on the basis of an insufficient conjecture; that it is appended in manuscripts to Isidore’s book *On Astronomy*; and that Pithou and Petrus Daniel, in Turnebus, *Adversaria* XIX.3, conjectured that it was by Varro Atacinus. Salmasius argues against them on p. 1131 of his Paris edition of Solinus.

14. Gerardus Johannes Vossius, in chapter 5 of *On Latin Poets*, believes that this is a fragment of an astronomical poem and that Isidore may be its author, since it is often appended to his works without the author’s name being given. He reports that a very learned man conjectured it to be by Varro Atacinus. Since the name of Fulgentius was prefixed solely on the basis of conjecture, as Pithou agrees in his notes, and since the ancient copies of Isidore’s *Astrology*, to which it is generally appended, bear no title naming an author, it seems to follow that the poem is either by Isidore or by one of the earlier writers whom Isidore willingly used. In the very old Oviedo Codex, moreover, these verses are inserted into the text itself before the final chapter [Col. 0521C], which suggests that this was done by the author of the book. The poem’s proper place, however, would be after chapter 21, on the eclipse of the moon. The author’s purpose there is to explain the moon’s eclipse, adding a few remarks about the sun’s eclipse. Nor do I see why most people call the poem incomplete: the poet fully carries out what he proposes at the beginning, namely to speak about the moon’s eclipse.

15. The authority of the Florentine Codex of San Marco 604, approximately of the ninth century, supports the conjecture with greater confidence that this little poem is by Isidore. In it certain fragments of the *Etymologies*, though interpolated, are presented, namely the section on the inventors of letters. Among its peculiar readings are the following:

> The philosopher and cosmographer Aethicus distinguished the characters of letters that he invented in the manner noted below; and blessed Jerome, the presbyter of good memory, took care to transmit them in Latin together with his book, the *Cosmographia*, etc.

The characters of the letters follow, and then this rubric:

> Here begins, in the more polished style of Isidore the presbyter: “You perhaps, slow in the grove,” etc.

[Col. 0521D] 665

These verses appear contaminated by many errors, as I gather from the specimen that my friend Rochus Menciaca sent me. Other Isidorian fragments follow, concerning the day, the week, the month, the year, etc. I do not understand why Isidore is called “the presbyter,” unless we are to say that he composed this astronomical poem while still young and a presbyter.

16. I find a fragment of this little poem under the name of Sisebutus among Muratorius’s *Anecdota*, volume III, p. 160, [Col. 0522A] inserted into an anonymous work *On Computation* from a very ancient codex of the Ambrosian Library. The book is compiled from many short works on computation, the calculation of Easter, the cycle, etc.; it was assembled in the year 810 or, at most, a few years later, as can be inferred from chapter 153 and other passages. Some material was taken from Isidore. The title of chapter 106 is: “Likewise, Sisebutus speaks about eclipses of the sun and moon”:

> Why, when weary, does the moon grow dim in its circular sphere, etc.?

The verses proceed, corrupted by many errors, to the final verse:

> The moon was [or: “The moon had been”] accusing her brother with straight rays,

which should be corrected to:

> The moon moves, assailing her brother with straight rays.

17. The reason why these verses are attributed to Sisebutus may be sought in Isidore’s own book *On the Nature of Things*, [Col. 0522B] dedicated to Sisebutus, to which they are commonly appended or in which they are inserted. In fact, toward the end of this book on computation, or collection, there is Isidore’s work *On the Nature of Things*, which Muratorius indicates on p. 208 as follows:

> “To Sisebutus, lord and son, Isidore: Although you surpass others in talent and eloquence,” etc.

Muratorius omits the work, but adds from the codex several verses:

> The year of the sun is contained  
> In four seasons. They end:  
> A three-year period, a two-year period,  
> And twice three, having been passed over.  
> The rest is lacking.

18. Nevertheless, it would not be unreasonable to believe that Sisebutus, distinguished in talent and learning, as Isidore says and others confirm, was the author of the poem. From his letter to Theudila, written when he had exchanged secular dress for the monastery, we gather that Sisebutus was also a friend of the Muses. For he concludes the letter with three couplets addressed to Theudila, preceded by a verse from book I of Dracontius’s *On God*, verse 128:

> Great everywhere is God, the never-changing creator.

In the editions of Dracontius it had been read:

> Bright everywhere is God, the never-changing creator.

I published Dracontius’s poem, contained in three books, from a Vatican manuscript in Rome in 1791. In that manuscript the reading was:

> Bright everywhere is God, the creator who can never be stained.

This reading is confirmed by two other Vatican codices, 3853 and 5884, which I saw later; in them Dracontius’s poem likewise appears under the name of Aurelius Augustine. Sisebutus’s second couplet reads:

> He who granted you the divine vow,  
> May that same one grant you, Sandrimer, a living soul.

It seems that this should be corrected to:

> May that same one grant you, Sandrimer, blessed one, the way.

The final verse is:

> May Christ, everywhere gracious, be for you the light of life.

In a Toledo manuscript it reads:

> May life be your light.

It may be restored as:

> May life and light be yours.

19. I found another poem, in some measure related to the same book *On the Nature of Things*, appended to that book in the Albanian Codex. It is, as it were, a metrical compendium of several chapters of the same work. [Col. 0523A] Some prose precedes it:

> At the very beginning, etc.,

concerning the first seven days of creation. Then comes the rubric:

> Likewise, verses on the same subject:

> The first day in the world took up the beginnings of light.

These are the seven verses of Saint Eugenius of Toledo, which are found among his poems and have also been printed in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, p. 17. The following rubric appears:

> Likewise, verses on the sun:

> The rising sun strips away the entire face of the stars, etc.

These verses belong to chapter 27. There follow verses on Arcturus, Boötes, the Pleiades, Orion, Lucifer, evening, the comet, Sirius, the twelve signs, thunder, lightning, the rainbow in the sky, clouds, rains, snow, ice, and winds.”

20. The final verses, namely those on the winds, are the very ones appended in the Bignaean and Breulian editions to the text of chapter 37 under the title: “Little verses on the winds named above.” Breulius notes in the margin that these verses are not found in the manuscript codex. Grialius observed that they are absent from other manuscripts but exist, separated from Isidore’s work, in the Gothic Oviedo Codex, and are more correctly written there than in the printed editions; since they did not seem altogether inelegant and appeared to him older than Isidore, he proposed them in a note. But since these little verses on the winds seem to have come from the same author as the others, being written in the same context in the Albanian Codex, they should not be considered older than Isidore. For the others follow Isidore’s words so closely and clearly that they do not even omit his mystical allegories. In the Ottobonian Codex 6, discussed in chapter 105, the same verses on the winds are presented without the author’s name, and likewise in the Gothic-Hispanic Orational of the Veronese Codex, as Maffei indicates in his description of that codex, chapter 88, number 93.

21. Whom, then, shall we regard as their author? I see no reason to deny Eugenius of Toledo the authorship of verses of this kind; indeed, there is substantial reason to attribute them to him. Since all the verses flow together in the same context, the same person should be regarded as their author. I have already stated that Eugenius was the author of the first seven little verses. Eugenius evidently took pleasure in explaining natural phenomena in brief poems, as is sufficiently clear from his books of poetry. Perhaps the rubric that once preceded the whole poem, now so worn away by age that it can no longer be read, indicated the poet’s name—Eugenius, as I believe. But whoever the author of this poem may finally prove to be, since it has not yet seen the light of publication and belongs either to the explanation or to the commendation of Isidore’s book, it will rightly and deservedly be included by us among the Appendices.

# CHAPTER LXXVII

**Our Isidore of Seville is the true author of the Chronicle, which is different from the Chronicle of Isidore of Pacensis. The abridgment of the Chronicle inserted by Isidore himself into the *Etymologies*.**

1. Since certain people, especially from the ninth century onward and at various times thereafter, exercised great license in interpolating, enlarging, and mutilating the works of ancient writers, this extreme recklessness was particularly active in corrupting books of certain kinds: collections of canons, calendars, chronicles, and histories. I am not one who immediately judges that all corrupters of works of this kind acted with deliberate fraud. Some, as it seems to me, copied books for themselves, or had them copied, in such a way that they inserted various additional materials—whether from the glosses and additions of others or from their own resources—on the same subject, so that these might sometimes prove useful. Yet they did this on the worst possible model, since they allowed others easily to be deceived: those others honestly attributed everything written in a book to the author whose name appeared at its head. They could have prevented this evil with a few words, if they had indicated that the work was a compilation or had been assembled from various sources. But there were also men who made money from copying books and therefore promised themselves a higher price from the name of some great author displayed on the title page.

2. This corruption of codices and confusion of mixed materials is found in many copies of Isidore’s works, and especially in copies of the Chronicle, [Col. 0524B] 668 all the more because Isidore’s name was famous everywhere and his writings were very widely disseminated. In particular, when I speak of the Chronicle, this is why it has happened that Isidore has been denied part of his own genuine Chronicle, while other works, either not his or interpolated, have been attributed to him. Ildefonsus does not mention the Chronicle, since he did not undertake to review Isidore’s historical books. Braulio, however, does so, and describes the work clearly: “One book of chronicles from the beginning of the world to his own time, collected with excessive brevity.”

3. I would not interpret Braulio’s words as though he disapproved of Isidore’s brevity. Rather, he praises the fact that Isidore skillfully included a history of events and times from the creation of the world in a brief chronicle, much as Isidore himself, in chapter 38 of *On Illustrious Men*, describes with praise and commendation a brief history by Victor of Tunnuna as outstanding and worthy of remembrance. This must nevertheless be understood in such a way that Braulio is referring not only to the abridged Chronicle found in the *Etymologies*, but also to another, more extensive work published separately. For even this work, considering the abundance and magnitude of the matters it explains, may be called excessively brief—that is, very brief.

4. The oldest writers praise Isidore’s Chronicle. I discussed the words of Fredegarius Scholasticus, who flourished in the same seventh century as Isidore, in chapter 33, against Niccolò Antonio, who believed that Fredegarius had scarcely shown himself certain that Isidore was the author of the Chronicle. In the eighth century Elipandus invoked the authority of blessed Isidore from this Chronicle in his letters to Charlemagne and Alcuin, as I said in the same chapter 33. In that same eighth century, even before Elipandus, Isidore of Pacensis, who continued Isidore’s Chronicle, refers to Isidore’s Chronicle near the end of his own in these words:

> According to the ecclesiastical history of the lord Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, in book I, in the sixth age; or now, according to the chronicle of the lord Isidore.

After the Chronicle of John of Biclaro, Florez, in volume VI, appendix 9, added from the Complutensian Codex an epilogue composed in the year 742, whose author says:

> Up to the year 654, in which blessed Isidore composed his chronicle, in the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius and the fourth year of Sisebutus, king of the Goths, etc.

Likewise, at the beginning of the twelfth century, the author of the Silos Chronicle says in section 2:

> This is clearly explained in the Chronicle, which Isidore, servant of Christ and bishop of the church of Seville, wrote in concise form from the beginning of the world up to the time of Heraclius, Roman emperor, and Sisebutus, the most religious ruler of the Spaniards.

[Col. 0525A] 669

I pass over the ancient Spanish writers who quoted words from Isidore’s Chronicle without praising its author: Beatus, in the eighth century, in his *Commentary on the Apocalypse*, and Dulcidius, or another author of the ninth-century Chronicle of Albelda.

5. So many testimonies of the ancients, to say nothing now of ancient manuscript copies, clearly show that our Isidore was the author of the Chronicle circulated under his name, as the very old catalogues and most bibliographers cited in chapters 46 and 47 also agree. Particularly explicit is the testimony of the eleventh-century catalogue of the monastery of Pomposa:

> Chronicles of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, describing a brief history from the beginning of the world to the time of Heraclius.

The anonymous writer of Melk also understands the Chronicle to be meant when, among Isidore’s works, he praises an abridgment of the ages. Nevertheless, some more recent writers, especially after the fabrication of the famous chronicles, disagree. Theophilus Raynaudus, Johannes Harduinus, and others seem to agree with them in Vincentius Placentius’s *Theatre of Anonymous and Pseudonymous Authors*, no. 1484.

First, Bivarius attempted to explain the matter in this way in his *Pseudo-Dexter*, under the year 384, no. 8:

> Isidore the Elder of Córdoba continues the Chronicle from the first consulship of Theodosius.

Niccolò Antonio observed that these words do not appear in the fragment of the Estepa Codex; consequently, they were added later by someone who, less cautiously, invented the elder Isidore of Córdoba named by Dexter, in comparison, of course, with Isidore of Seville, who flourished long after Dexter’s time. To excuse the imprudence of Pseudo-Dexter, Bivarius invented two Isidores of Córdoba: one, the Elder, author of the Chronicle; the other, the Younger, author of the *Allegories on Orosius* and of commentaries on the books of Kings and on the Gospel of Luke. He therefore believes that the Chronicle written by Isidore of Seville was taken for the most part from the Chronicle of that elder Isidore of Córdoba, and that Lucas of Tuy inserted Isidore of Córdoba’s Chronicle into other chronicles, thinking it to be the work of Isidore of Seville.

6. These arguments are foolish. The claim that Isidore of Córdoba wrote a Chronicle is reported only among the fabrications of Pseudo-Dexter. Although Lucas of Tuy produces under Isidore’s name many things that do not occur in Isidore’s Chronicle, this does not show that he found them in some earlier Chronicle of Isidore of Córdoba; for he likewise reports many things concerning a period that could not have been explained by Isidore of Córdoba. It shows only that Lucas of Tuy used a Chronicle of Isidore interpolated in every part, as I shall soon explain.

[Col. 0526A] 670

7. Joseph Pellizerius took the opposite course. He maintained that the Chronicle commonly attributed by everyone to Isidore of Seville was written by Isidore of Pacensis. Bandinius, in volume I of the *Codices Latini of the Laurentian Medicean Library*, plut. 20, describes Codex 54, of the eleventh century, written with exceptional elegance. It contains “the chronography of Isidore the Younger,” with a prologue beginning “Julius Africanus,” etc.; these words occur in the prologue of Isidore’s Chronicle shortly after the beginning. The book begins: “When Adam was,” etc. It ends: “The consummation of the age is.” In the catalogue index it is announced as follows:

> The chronography, with prologue, of Isidore the Younger, likewise bishop of Zaragoza, invented by Joseph Pellizerius.

This should not be understood as though Pellizerius invented the *Chronography* itself, but rather that he invented for himself the author of that Chronicle: in reality it was written by Isidore, bishop of Seville, but Pellizerius made him another Isidore, a native of Seville and bishop of Zaragoza. At one time, namely in his *Observations on Dulcidius*, fol. 16, he held this view. But in his book *On Maximus of Zaragoza*, fol. 29, he attempts to prove at length that Isidore of Pacensis was the author of the Chronicle published under the name of Isidore, bishop of Seville.

Bandinius transcribed Fabricius’s words in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, perhaps without grasping his meaning. Fabricius says:

> Isidore the Younger of Seville, likewise bishop of Zaragoza, invented by Joseph Pellizerius, as I believe I mentioned on p. 123.

He had prefaced this with:

> The fictitious Isidore of Zaragoza, whom Joseph Pellizerius makes the author of the double Chronicle, should more properly be included among the writings of Isidore of Seville.

I omit the arguments that Pellizerius derives from Ildefonsus’s silence, as well as from the suspicion he raises against Braulio’s heading concerning Isidore’s books, as though that heading were not genuine; for we have already discussed that controversy in chapter 3.

Pellizerius’s principal argument is therefore drawn from the preface to the chronicles of Pelagius of Oviedo, who in the twelfth century collected several chronicles into a single body. They are still preserved in an Oviedo Codex, written partly by Pelagius’s own hand and partly at his command. The title of the codex is:

> Book of Chronicles from the Beginning of the World.

Niccolò Antonio adds “up to the year 1170,” but Florez says that these words are absent from the manuscript, in volume IV of *Hispania Sacra*, pp. 200 ff., where he accurately transcribes the entire prologue of the book. Pelagius, the compiler of the chronicles, or of the “patchwork History,” introduces it as follows:

> Dearest brothers, if you read this Chronicle that you see here with a good disposition, you will find how Isidore the Younger, bishop of the Church of Pacensis, wrote fully, just as he read in the Old and New Testaments and understood through the Holy Spirit, from Adam to Noah, and to Abraham, Moses, and David, and up to the coming of the Redeemer; and concerning the judges and kings in Israel, and the Roman kings or emperors, and concerning the Vandals and Alans, as well as the Suevian kings of Spain, just as he investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors. And blessed Isidore, in whom the Church of León now rejoices, wrote as fully as he could concerning the kings of the Goths, from the first Athanaric up to Wamba, the Catholic king of the Goths.

8. From this Pellizerius concludes that Pelagius of Oviedo attributes to Isidore of Pacensis the Chronicle from the beginning of the world and the History of the Vandals and Suevi, while attributing to Isidore of Seville only the History of the Goths. There can be no doubt that this was Pelagius’s intention, if the preface truly belongs to him. Niccolò Antonio, however, in book V of the *Bibliotheca*, no. 121, questions whether the prologue, teeming with the most shameful errors, is the offspring of Pelagius of Oviedo. Again, in book VII, no. 49, when discussing Pelagius, he says:

> I am easily persuaded, unless those handling the book establish from elsewhere that the opposite is true, that this preface is not by Pelagius but by another, later person who wished to compile a summary of the matters contained in the book.

Bayerius adds this note:

> Our author seems to have struck the matter exactly: although there are so many additions in the previously praised Complutensian Codex, as we have seen, the preface that caused him such great confusion is absent from it.

9. To compare these copies of the chronicles with one another, the codices themselves must be described. The Complutensian Codex, now the Royal Madrid Codex, contains, without a general title for the chronicles and without the preface:

1. The cities ruled by the Gothic kings and their bishops.
2. Brief annals by years, from the year 38, in which Christ was born, to the year 1073.
3. Under a larger rubric: “Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, says: On the Origins of the More Famous Cities of Spain.”
4. A book of chronicles, or a register, from Adam to the Flood, and four sequences of kings: Roman, Gothic, Asturian, and Saracen. Here I understand the Chronicle of Isidore and the Histories of the Goths, Vandals, and [Col. 0527C] Suevi to be inserted.
5. A chronological order of the ages of the world by blessed Julianus Pomerius, archbishop of Toledo. The work is falsely attributed to Julianus, who never bore the surname Pomerius.
6. An excerpt from the Chronicle of Sebastian of Salamanca.
7. The Chronicle of Sampirus of Astorga.
8. The Chronicle of Pelagius of Oviedo.
9. [Col. 0527C] 672 *On the Repentance of Solomon*.
10. The decrees of King Alfonso and Queen Geloira, and various minor pieces.

10. Morales, Sandoval, and Pellizerius, as reported by Niccolò Antonio, mention the Oviedo Codex of Pelagius, written partly by Pelagius’s hand and partly at his command, as I have said. While Niccolò Antonio was writing, the codex was in the Reynosian Library, that is, in the library of Don Diego de Arce Reynoso. Pellizerius testifies that he had seen it there at some point, unless perhaps Pellizerius possessed another, different copy. For Morales too had found two similar codices of Pelagius’s chronicles in the church of Oviedo, and he seems also to have had several copies at hand containing the same chronicles, though with a different appearance and title from those under which they were published. Niccolò Antonio observes this and confirms it by comparing the testimonies. In book X, no. 245, he asserts that the codex of the church of Oviedo seen by Sandoval is the very one that had belonged first to García de Loaysa and then to Don Diego de Arce Reynoso, bishop of Plasencia, and therefore to the Reynosian Library.

Primary attention must therefore be given to the autograph Oviedo Codex, whose title, according to Pellizerius, is:

> Book of Chronicles from the Beginning of the World up to the Year 1170.

Niccolò Antonio rightly observes that this title is doubtful. For how could Pelagius, who had already died in or before the year 1168, have carried the chronicles as far as the year 1170? Bayerius replies in a note that this title is absent from the Complutensian Codex, but that Pelagius truly did compile his patchwork history up to the year 1170.

11. Bayerius saw little of the matter here, because he paid no attention to the year in which Pelagius died. If the Complutensian Codex extends to the year 1170, he should have concluded that the Chronicle had been enlarged by some continuator, and not carried that far by Pelagius—or, alternatively, that Pelagius had lived until the year 1170. Florez had already provided guidance on this very point in volume IV of *Hispania Sacra*, pp. 200 ff. As I have mentioned, he shows that the words “up to the year 1170” are absent from the Oviedo Codex. He nevertheless reports that Pelagius exchanged this life for death around the year 1143, or the year 1181 in the Spanish era, and that the codex contains nothing accomplished after that time. He adds that the genealogies of the Gothic kings were written by Pelagius’s own hand, while the rest, including the disputed preface, was written by another hand, but in such a way that it is easily understood that everything was committed to writing at Pelagius’s direction.

I shall remark in passing that the genealogies written by Pelagius’s hand may be a work older than Pelagius, mentioned in the ninth-century Chronicle of Albelda, in volume XIII of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 462:

> The Book of Genealogies likewise asserts that the Goths came from Magog, the son of Japheth, and that Gothia and Scia were named from Magog.

We may suspect that this old work of the Genealogies, like other works, was interpolated by Pelagius. Florez, along with Morales, maintains that Pelagius himself was the author of the prologue. He believes that this is not prevented by Niccolò Antonio’s conjecture that the prologue speaks of Pelagius as a person distinct from the one speaking:

> And from Veremundus the Gouty up to King Alfonso, son of Count Raymond and Queen Urraca, Pelagius, bishop of the church of Oviedo, just as he investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors, wrote as fully as he could concerning the Gothic and Aragonese kings.

12. Pelagius could have spoken of himself in this way, either to preserve the order he had followed in mentioning the other writers or because he perhaps would not have minded if someone else were believed to be the author of the prologue. But whether Pelagius himself was the author of the prologue or another contemporary was, it is entirely foolish to attribute the Isidorian Chronicle, extending from the beginning of the world, to Isidore of Pacensis, against so many earlier writers who support Isidore of Seville—not even excluding Isidore of Pacensis himself, who, as I have said, praises “the Chronicle of the Lord Isidore” when discussing the year in which Christ was born.

The style of our Chronicle also differs much more from the barbarous and unpolished language of Isidore of Pacensis than the periods of the two Isidores differ from one another. In Isidore of Seville one sees a man retaining clear traces of pure Latin expression; in Isidore of Pacensis, by contrast, one sees a writer miserably disfigured by the barbarous Moorish mixture.

Pelagius of Oviedo himself certainly deserves no credibility, especially in matters of antiquity. As Mariana observes in the manuscript prologue to Pelagius’s Chronicle, cited by Florez, he was commonly called “the fabulous.” The same Florez reports that in the Batres copy of Pelagius’s chronicles, which belonged to Fernando Pérez de Guzmán, grandfather of García Lasso de la Vega, the following order was found. After the prologue came the chronicles of the Vandals and Suevi and the History of the Goths. These are the very works of Isidore of Seville, but interpolated. Next came the *Supplement of Don Ildefonsus*, which is either a continuation wholly attributed to Ildefonsus or a work corrupted by fables by someone else. Then came the *Number of the Sees of Spain*, a fictitious division of the bishoprics said to have been made by Wamba but, as many now agree, entirely fabricated by Pelagius of Oviedo himself and circulated under the name of Idacius, or Itacius—perhaps because Pelagius had read that a certain Idacius had been an author of a Chronicle. That Idacius, however, flourished long before Wamba’s time.

13. These materials appear in a different order in the autograph Oviedo Codex. There, after this fictitious Itacius and the History of Sampirus, comes the *Corographia of Isidore the Younger*, which is the Chronicle of our Isidore. He may have been thought to be Isidore of Pacensis because it was found in some codex under the title “the Younger,” as can be seen in the Florentine Codex reviewed above, where the title is more correctly given as “The Chronography of Isidore the Younger.” For the Spaniards commonly called Isidore of Seville “the Elder” and Isidore of Pacensis “the Younger”; outsiders, however, often also called Isidore of Seville “the Younger.”

The same Oviedo Codex continues:

> Here begins the written chronicle of the Gothic kings up to Wamba, the Catholic king.

This is the History of the Goths by our Isidore, but, in my view, with the continuation called in the Batres Codex the *Supplement of Don Ildefonsus*. Next comes the *History of Paul’s Rebellion against Wamba*, by Julianus, incorrectly surnamed Pomerius there. Various letters, the chronicles of Sebastian, Pelagius, and others are appended. Interpolations by Pelagius clearly appear in this Oviedo Codex, sometimes even with the words “Addition of Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo” inserted.

14. If we examine the very prologue of the Oviedo Codex, it will be clear from that alone that no credence should be given to a document filled with the most evident historical errors and anachronisms. Isidore of Seville is said to have written the History of the Goths in full up to King Wamba, although Isidore flew to heaven in the year 636, whereas Wamba did not begin to reign before the year 672.

The prologue continues:

> And from the aforesaid King Wamba up to Pelagius, the Catholic king of the Goths, blessed Julianus, archbishop of the see of Toledo, who repeatedly transferred to Asturias with King Pelagius the chest containing the relics of the saints, with which the church of Oviedo now glories, and who, just as he investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors, wrote as fully as he could.

Yet Saint Julianus had already died by the year 690. How, then, could he, after the invasion of the Moors, which occurred in the eighth century, either have continued the History of the Goths or have carried the sacred relics to the Asturians?

Hear the remainder:

> And from King Pelagius up to Alfonso the Chaste and Catholic king of the Goths, Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, just as he investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors, wrote as fully as he could.

Here Pellizerius himself admits that the author of the prologue is mistaken. For the continuation of the history from Pelagius to Alfonso the Chaste was not written by Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, but by Alfonso III, who sent it to Sebastian. Nevertheless, the question remains unresolved. Some, with Mariana, suspect that the Chronicle was composed by Sebastian but published under the king’s name. The letter prefixed to the Chronicle in Alfonso’s name, however, is meaningless and appears mutilated; nor can it be adequately inferred from it who the author of the Chronicle was.

15. The prologue continues:

> And from Alfonso the Chaste up to King Veremundus the Gouty, Sampirus, bishop of the church of Astorga, just as he investigated and heard from his elders and predecessors, wrote as fully as he could concerning the Gothic kings.

These statements about Sampirus, who came closest in time to Pelagius, are more consistent with the truth, although the writers differ even here. Morales attributes to this Sampirus the account of the chest of relics transferred to Asturias, while Sandoval published it under the name of Sebastian of Salamanca.

### 16

Whatever the case may be, one ought by no means to place confidence in the author of the prologue to Pelagius’s system of chronicles, who was so disgracefully mistaken in ancient matters when he ascribes the Chronicle of Isidore of Seville to Isidore of Beja—whether he was deceived, as I have said, because he found it inscribed with the name of Isidore the Younger, or because he saw a copy of the Chronicle brought by Isidore of Seville down to the time of Sisebut and continued by Isidore of Beja, to whom he ultimately attributed the whole work. When John Vasaeus encountered a similar confusion in manuscript copies of the chronicles, he fell into serious difficulty, from which, nevertheless, he extricated himself not unsuccessfully in Book I of his *Annals*, chapter 4:

> “Isidore, bishop of Beja, also wrote a Chronicle of Spain; but if that is the Chronicle which I have seen marked with his title, I should call it a portent rather than a chronicle, so monstrously did he write, and in Gothic rather than Latin. Certainly I had to sweat over it as though over some new and unheard-of language before I could understand it.”

Thus far Vasaeus accurately depicts the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja in its true colors. Resende, in Book IV of his *Antiquities of Lusitania*, and Mariana in his prologue to the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja agree concerning its harsh and uncultivated style. [Col. 0530C–D]

### 17

Vasaeus continues:

> “I also found another Chronicle, under the title of Isidore the Younger, 676 as though it were his [that is, Isidore of Beja’s], extending from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of Suinthila, king of the Goths, which was the year of our Lord 626. But I am firmly persuaded that this Chronicle belongs to Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, not to Isidore of Beja, especially since Saint Isidore himself also testifies in his *Etymologies* that he brought his Chronicle down to that same year . . . Nor does the designation ‘the Younger’ stand in the way, since it suits Isidore of Seville, not this Isidore of Beja. Saint Isidore is called ‘the Younger’ because of Isidore of Córdoba, and so forth . . . I have examined these matters at greater length because of the conflicting opinions, and have stated my own view; I shall readily yield if anyone brings forward more certain evidence.”

As we have seen, Vasaeus is correct: no doubt on this matter now remains. Although he says that Isidore’s Chronicle was brought down to the fifth year of Suinthila, he nevertheless means the commonly published Chronicle of Saint Isidore, which ends in the fifth year of Sisebut. The manuscripts differ: either, as Loaisa conjectures in his notes, someone transferred into the fuller Chronicle a conclusion from the abridgment incorporated in the *Etymologies* and extended to the fifth—or, in some copies, the seventh—year of Suinthila; or, as I rather believe, Isidore himself, having first published the Chronicle down to the fourth year of Sisebut, continued it in a particular copy with the subsequent years. From this arose the variation in the conclusion found in manuscript copies. Some say that Isidore produced a second edition of the Chronicle; but this is unnecessary, since Isidore could have added a continuation to his copy without issuing a new edition. [Col. 0530D–0531B]

### 18

Vasaeus, in the passage cited above, also mentions another Chronicle attributed to our Isidore:

> “I certainly saw in the same manuscript another Chronicle inscribed with the name of Isidore, bishop of Seville; but since it ends in the last year of Trasamund, king of the Vandals in Africa, I believe it to belong rather to another author, and to that African author, than to Saint Isidore of Seville—especially since it deals more with the kings of the Vandals in Africa than with the Goths in Spain.”

Since this Chronicle has not come into our hands, we cannot pass judgment upon it; but Vasaeus’s arguments by themselves sufficiently establish that it is not Isidore’s. It would not, however, be useless to publish it if by that means the history of the Goths in Spain and of the Vandals in Africa could in some way be illuminated. But who will indicate where it now exists—if indeed it still exists, and has not perished, like many other manuscripts, through irreparable loss? [Col. 0531B–C]

### 19

To return to the genuine Chronicle of Isidore of Beja: it was first printed by Sandoval at Pamplona in 1615 under the following title: *Isidore, bishop of Beja: Epitome of the Emperors and of the Arabs, together with a Chronicle of Spain, from the Gothic Codex of Alcalá and the Codex of Osma*. Mariana reports in his prologue that the name of the author is absent from the Codex of Osma.

It was printed again at Madrid in 1729, corrected by M. Fr. Francisco Berganza from two copies: one copied by Juan Bautista Pérez from an old Codex of Osma, the other from the Gothic Codex of Alcalá, by order of Ambrosio de Morales. Finally, Flórez published it in volume VIII of *Sacred Spain*, revised against the first two editions, a membranaceous manuscript Codex of Alcalá, though not Gothic, Mariana’s manuscript, whose prologue he transcribes, and several readings observed by the prelate de Marca.

The heading is:

> “Here begins an epitome of the emperors, or the annals of the Arabs, and a chronography of Spain, collected in one volume.”

At the beginning the Chronicle gives the Spanish Era 649 and the year of the world 5837, in which Heraclius died. The Era given at the outset therefore designates not the year in which the emperors began to reign, but the year in which they died. Isidore of Beja accordingly carries the history from the beginning of Heraclius, in whose fifth year the Chronicle of Saint Isidore ends, down to the year 754; consequently, it is not the Chronicle of Hydatius, as some have claimed, but that of Isidore of Seville that he continued. [Col. 0531C–0532A]

The Chronicle of Isidore of Beja itself appears to have been continued by someone else. Ambrosio de Morales reports that he saw a Chronicle of Isidore of Beja extending beyond the nine-hundredth year of salvation, from which Mariana questioned the period in which Isidore of Beja lived. But, as Flórez observes, Ambrosio de Morales was often mistaken in describing such chronicles and distinguishing their authors; and continuations added by later hands frequently occur in manuscript copies.

Du Pin, in the preface to volume IV of the *Ecclesiastical Library*, casually stated that he did not use the authority of the Chronicle of Isidore of Beja because it was not an unquestionable document. But, I think, he intended to name Pseudo-Dexter, or some other fabrication of the seventeenth century, not our Isidore of Beja. [Col. 0532A–B]

### 20

I have indicated more than once that an abridgment of the Isidorian Chronicle was included by Isidore himself in the *Etymologies*. When Isidore undertook to compose his encyclopedic work entitled the *Etymologies*, he reduced to a shorter form much of what he had published in his other works and inserted it into the *Etymologies*. Thus, in Book V, after various discussions of years, ages, and related matters, he entitled chapter 37 *On the Division of Times*. This chapter is an epitome of the somewhat extended Chronicle; for it ends: “Heraclius is now in the seventeenth year of his reign,” and so forth, whereas the Chronicle itself reaches only the fifth year of Heraclius. Other manuscripts of the Chronicle in the *Etymologies* designate the tenth year of Heraclius, while others give different years.

This much, however, is certain: after the longer Chronicle had ended in the fourth year of Sisebut and the fifth year of Heraclius, Isidore reduced the same subject to an abridgment in his etymological work, which was his last. Bellarmine paid no attention to this chronology when he supposed that the Chronicle published under Isidore’s name had been taken from the *Etymologies*. Labbe rejected this view all the more because the separate Chronicle is much fuller than the Chronicle in the *Etymologies*. Nor is it unusual for the same writer, when circumstances require it, to contract his labors from wider bounds into a kind of narrower circle. [Col. 0532B–C]

### 21

I have no doubt that Isidore himself abridged his Chronicle in the *Etymologies*. Why, then, should we attribute to Braulio, as Oudinus conjectures with Labbe, an interpolation of the Chronicle in Isidore’s *Etymologies*? What will remain secure in the *Etymologies* if we declare Braulio to be the author of this or another chapter for no other reason than that Braulio divided the work into books distinguished only by their titles?

The case is different with a certain note added to the Chronicle in the *Etymologies* in the Breulian edition, where Suinthila is mentioned and certain statements are repeated from the prologue to the fuller Chronicle. Vossius, in Book II, chapter 25, of his *History of Latin Literature*, more plausibly believes that this note was added not by Isidore but by someone else, since the words are absent from his old, excellent-quality manuscripts. They are also absent from most of our manuscripts, and Grial omitted them correctly.

Nevertheless, Grial—as did the ancient copies—notes the seventeenth or eighteenth year, certainly a year later than the fifth year of Heraclius. This appears unquestionably to come from Isidore’s own hand. For when he composed the epitome of the Chronicle after the fifth year of Heraclius, he ought to have stated the year then current, not the fifth year of Heraclius, in which the fuller Chronicle had ended. [Col. 0532C–0533A]

### 22

Examples of the shorter Chronicle exist in manuscript copies, even separately from the rest of the body of the *Etymologies*. By this Chronicle I mean the two very ancient manuscripts described by Joseph Blanchinus in his *Catalogue of Golden, Silver, and Purple Manuscripts Collected from Various Authors*, volume II of the *Fourfold Gospel Book*, page 593. 679

The first Codex contains the sacred Latin Bible which Theodulf, later bishop of Orléans, had arranged to have copied around the year 790; Sirmond discusses it in volume II of his works, page 1046. It is a membranaceous in-folio Codex:

> “Certain verses of Theodulf, as Sirmond says, were written in golden letters on the front of the book.
