Other verses, copied in silver letters, were placed before the short Chronicle of Isidore—which is attached to the Bible before the New Testament—and before Eucherius’s little work on the interpretation of Hebrew names, and the work on Greek names with a key, which some have regarded as belonging to Melito, bishop of Sardis.”

Blanchinus adds that the verses were written in golden letters on purple parchment, while Isidore’s Chronicle and Eucherius’s little work were written in silver. This remarkable monument was preserved in the Mommian library, or that of the lord de Mosmes. [Col. 0533A–B]

### 23

A similar Codex, perhaps copied from the preceding one, existed in the church of Our Lady of Le Puy, donated by Theodulf himself. It contained the Latin Bible with the chronography of Saint Isidore, a book on Hebrew names, another on the exposition of various things, and a treatise on God, his attributes, and various moral matters, together with Theodulf’s verses, which were also read in the preceding volume. [Col. 0533B–C]

### 24

The shorter Chronicle inserted in the *Etymologies* frequently occurs in manuscript copies of the *Etymologies*, with the tenth year of Erwig and the Era then current recorded at the end. This was done by Ildefonsus or another contemporary in his copy of the *Etymologies*, and the addition subsequently remained in other copies.

For this custom prevailed, among the Spaniards as among other peoples, that learned writers continued to copy chronicles, or at least appended the year then current. In an old Medicean manuscript there are certain genealogical tables from Adam to the Incarnation of Jesus Christ, perhaps taken from Isidore. A certainly Spanish scribe appended the following note:

> “From the Incarnation, however, of our Lord Jesus Christ to the present first year of the glorious Wamba, and so forth. From the beginning of the world to the coming of the Lord: 5,195 years.”

I suspect that this was added by the scribe rather than by the original author of the genealogies. [Col. 0533C–D]

### 25

In Vatican Codex 1869, discussed in chapter 96, the Chronicle in the *Etymologies* is entitled *On the Description or Division of Times*. It precedes the history of Freculphus. I shall discuss other similar copies in the following chapter, when I review the Vatican Codices of the Isidorian Chronicle. [Col. 0533D–0534A]

## CHAPTER LXXVIII

### The Interpolated Chronicle of Isidore, which Lucas of Tuy included among his own Chronicles

The Chronicle of Melito, identical with the Isidorian Chronicle but differently interpolated, and more often mutilated and abridged. Editions of the Isidorian Chronicle; Loaisa’s prologue; a published Italian translation; another Spanish manuscript translation; manuscript copies of the same Chronicle.

### 1

Lucas of Tuy composed a certain system of chronicles in four books. The first book contains an expanded version of the commonly published Chronicle of Isidore. The second contains Isidore’s Histories of the Vandals, Suevi, and Goths. The third contains a continuation of Isidore’s chronicles attributed to Ildefonsus, together with other material. Part of the third book and the whole of the fourth are the work of Lucas himself of Tuy.

Since the Chronicle which Lucas of Tuy published under the name of Saint Isidore, doctor of the Spains, contains several things absent from the commonly published Isidorian Chronicle, two questions may first be asked: whether the fuller or the shorter Chronicle is the true and genuine product of Isidore; and, if we say that the fuller Chronicle has been interpolated, as seems certain, whether Lucas of Tuy was the author of the interpolation.

The first question presents no difficulty. Since copies of the shorter Chronicle far older than Lucas of Tuy, who flourished in the thirteenth century, exist, it must be concluded without hesitation that the additions visible in manuscripts of later centuries do not come from Isidore’s hand—especially since, as I have often observed, people of a later age exercised such license in expanding and interpolating chronicles. [Col. 0534A–B]

### 2

“Then,” someone may object, “did Lucas of Tuy pass off as Isidorian material what he himself had drawn from his own storehouse and inserted into the Isidorian Chronicle?”

Lucas does bear some reproach in this respect, from which I attempted to clear him in chapter 13. As for the Isidorian Chronicle, Nicolás Antonio, who otherwise is not especially favorable to Lucas, gives the following judgment:

> “To those who ask whether this expansion belongs to Tuy or to someone else, I shall freely say that what is inserted by him into the Isidorian Chronicle does not seem to me to come from Tuy’s pen, but from an author of a more Latin and polished age. Yet since nearly everything Isidorian exists in this, so to speak, interpolated Chronicle, it seems more consistent with the truth that the genuine Chronicle of Isidore of Seville is the one in everyone’s hands, while the work of another, later author was reduced to the form which Tuy believed in its entirety to be the work of Isidore’s hand. This is more plausible than the view of one who, following Bivarius, might suppose that Isidore of Córdoba left in writing the Chronicle used by Tuy, and that this Chronicle, stripped or excerpted by Isidore of Seville, is the Chronicle bearing his name.” [Col. 0534B–D]

### 3

Above, I refuted Bivarius’s exceedingly slight conjecture that Isidore of Córdoba was the author of a certain Chronicle. I willingly approve Nicolás Antonio’s judgment, by which he absolves Lucas from the charge of interpolation. Certainly, I believe that Lucas encountered Isidore’s Chronicle already expanded, and I have shown in chapter 13 that he should not readily be branded an inventor of fables.

A papyrus Codex of the old Vatican Library, no. 7004, contains the Chronicle of Lucas of Tuy, beginning “The blessedness of power,” and so forth, together with a letter from Francisco Peña, a man deeply devoted to antiquities, to Cardinal Baronius concerning the author of the same history, and a Spanish letter from Alfonso Spinosa and García de Salazar concerning that history.

I believe this is the Codex of which Baronius writes under the year 636, no. 9:

> “This is Tuy’s work, which Francisco Pegna, my most devoted friend, a Roman Rota auditor, allowed us to copy from the original.”

There Baronius attributes to Tuy the material which Tuy presents from Ildefonsus’s supplement to the Isidorian Chronicle.

Rodríguez, in volume II of the *Spanish Library*, page 327, lists an Escorial Codex of the sixteenth century, or perhaps later, with the following title:

> “Genealogies from the New and Old Testament. The History or Chronicle of Saint Isidore, with a prologue by Lucas of Tuy. Continuation by Saint Ildefonsus. Continuation by an unknown author, perhaps Lucas of Tuy. The lies of Archbishop Turpin concerning Charlemagne. From Isidore: on the entry of the Vandals, Goths, and Huns.”

At the beginning it is noted that the Codex was copied from a very ancient book of the church of Oviedo, written in Gothic letters. At the end is added:

> “These things have been transcribed from an ancient handwritten Codex preserved by Brother Michael of Medina, of the Franciscan order. The remainder, down to García, son of King Adefonsus, is missing.”

The final work of the Codex is evidently incomplete: it is an excerpt from Isidore on the entry of the Vandals and so forth. Its beginning is:

> “Here begins the order of the times in which the Suevi, Vandals, Alans, and Goths entered Spain, published by Lord Isidore, archbishop, and briefly collected in the Era 444.”

There is an error in these Era numbers. [Col. 0534D–0535C]

### 4

Pagius and others introduced a certain Melito the Spaniard, a contemporary of Isidore of Seville and author of a certain Chronicle. Bayerius, however, makes no mention of him in his notes to the *Ancient Spanish Library*, perhaps because he did not recall what Flórez had set down in writing in volume VI of *Sacred Spain* concerning this Melito and his Chronicle.

Under the years 567 and 614, no. 41, Pagius identifies from the Colbert Library a work by the Spanish writer Melito with the title *A Brief Exposition of Times*. Montfaucon agrees in volume II of the *Library of Manuscripts*, page 924, under the title *Melito’s Exposition of Times*.

Since this Chronicle of Melito extends to the fourth year of King Sisebut and stops there, it appears certain that its author was Spanish. Under the year 614, no. 41, Pagius quotes the final words of Melito’s Chronicle and supposes that Isidore took from Melito those very words concerning Heraclius and Sisebut, while adding fifteen further years in Book V of the *Etymologies*.

In a note, Mansi observes that the words recovered from the Colbert manuscript and attributed by Pagius to a certain Melito also occur in a manuscript Codex of the Isidorian Chronicle at Lucca, from the ninth century or perhaps even the eighth. After noting the error in the numbers, he concludes:

> “The same account may readily have been given by Melito. From the fragment preserved by Pagius, it is clear that Isidore copied Melito, on the basis of what we have quoted from our Codex. Thus Melito too may perhaps have written this, and it entered the Colbert Codex differently only through the carelessness of a copyist.”

### 5

Since the question is whether Isidore copied Melito or, conversely, Melito copied Isidore, Mansi did not express his position very clearly. But, as I understand it, against Pagius he maintains that it was not Melito who copied Isidore, but Isidore who copied Melito. That is why he calls his own Lucca Codex a Codex of the Isidorian Chronicle.

The matter must be explained more precisely. Pagius argues that Melito wrote his Chronicle in the fourth year of Sisebut, since he immediately adds that the times following were known to God, whereas Isidore, as I was just saying, extended his Chronicle in the *Etymologies* by another fifteen years. Here Pagius seems to have been unaware of the Isidorian Chronicle commonly circulated, which is distinct from the abridgment inserted into the *Etymologies*.

Yet as early as the year 567, no. 4, he had compared Melito’s Chronicle with the Chronicle of Isidore published by Schelstratius. I shall quote his words:

> “Thus Melito, word for word, who states that he completed his work in the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius and the fourth of Sisebut—that is, in the year of Christ 614 or the following year. That he was a Spaniard is shown by the mention of King Sisebut in so short a Chronicle. We therefore possess a contemporary author who writes nothing that he did not receive from earlier authors. The Codex was written approximately eight hundred years ago. Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, likewise has the same material, as a contemporary author, in his short Chronicle, recently published by Schelstratius from the Urbino-Vatican Library.” [Col. 0535D–0536C]

### 6

Who would not be astonished at this in so acute a man, and one so experienced in comparing chronicles? He asserts that Isidore took certain material from Melito, not that Melito took it from Isidore, because Isidore extended the Chronicle in the *Etymologies* by another fifteen years. Yet he had seen the Chronicle of Isidore printed by Schelstratius, which ends in the same fourth year of Sisebut and in the same words as Melito’s Chronicle; and this Schelstratius repeatedly compares with the fuller Isidorian Chronicle found among Isidore’s works, which likewise ends in the fourth year of Sisebut.

Who could persuade himself that two writers composed a Chronicle in the same fourth year of King Sisebut, using the same statements and words? For the Chronicle which Pagius attributes to Melito and the Chronicle preserved in the Urbino-Vatican Library under the name of Isidore differ in no other way than two copies of the same work, distinguished by several variations in wording and perhaps by a brief interpolation.

Nor does the Isidorian Chronicle, differing from the published version and closely resembling the Chronicle called Melito’s, exist only in Urbino-Vatican Codex 609, now 392, which Schelstratius consulted. It also exists in Codex 606 of the same Urbino-Vatican Library, now 382. There, after other works of Isidore, on page 186, is the rubric:

> “Here begins the book of the Chronicles of Isidore, bishop of Seville, from the beginning of the world to the reign of Heraclius Augustus and the principate of King Sisebut. Preface.”

The same title occurs in the other Codex, 609, otherwise numbered 392. Everything in the two copies agrees so closely that one appears to have been copied from the other, or both to have derived from one and the same source.

Schelstratius gives the title as follows:

> “The Chronicle of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, from Gaius Caesar to the emperor Heraclius and the principate of King Sisebut, from manuscript Codex 609 of the Urbino-Vatican Library, 684 very different from the published version. Here begins the sixth age of the world, and so forth.”

In the margin it is noted that the Chronicle was compared with another Vatican manuscript and with the printed editions. [Col. 0536C–0537A]

### 7

What, then, are we to think about Melito? Saint Mellitus, the first bishop of London, certainly flourished in Isidore’s time and died in 624. Yet there is no reason for us to suppose that he was the author of our Chronicle. If someone should conjecture that the Colbert Codex was copied from a Codex once owned by some Melito, and that the name of Melito spread from this circumstance, he would perhaps say nothing absurd.

Long ago Flórez suspected that the name belonged to the copyist of the Isidorian Chronicle. He also observed that, in the copy he had arranged to have made from the Colbert Codex, the work bore the following title:

> “Here begins a brief exposition of times,”

without the addition “of Melito.”

Since Flórez not only advanced this suspicion but also questioned whether the scribe who reduced the Isidorian Chronicle to an abridgment was Spanish, why did he title appendix 11 *On the Chronicle of Melito, a Spanish Writer, Not Yet Published, and on the Chronicle of Isidore*?

The true title of the work would be:

> “The Chronicle of Isidore abridged by someone outside Spain and interpolated in certain places, attributed somewhere to Melito.”

To support the possibility that Melito was the author of the Chronicle, Flórez points out that it sometimes adds:

> “Thus far Jerome; thus far Prosper.”

He immediately resolves the argument, however, by replying that some scribe may have abridged Isidore’s Chronicle for his own use, and that a curious man may have added those words.

It seems more plausible that the person who reduced the Chronicle to an abridgment added those words along with certain others. Learned men sometimes copied books for themselves, and scribes themselves were often only superficially learned. This is sufficient to explain how the copyist and epitomator of the Isidorian Chronicle could have noted:

> “Thus far Jerome; thus far Prosper.”

I have found the same note in several copies, including Vatican Codex Palatine 239. It is also known that additions of this sort sometimes entered the text from marginal notes added by the author or by others. [Col. 0537A–D]

### 8

Finally, since Flórez remained uncertain about the author of the Chronicle attributed to Melito, he published the Isidorian Chronicle under the following title:

> “The Chronicle of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville (and Mellitus).”

Thus he printed in a different type the material omitted from Melito’s Codex, and in the notes he supplied what had been added to Isidore’s Chronicle in that same Codex, while also recording several variations in wording. For the present, it will be enough for us to note generally that much is omitted from the Melito Codex and little is added; we shall present these matters in their proper places.

That such a copy of Melito is in reality an abridgment, and not conversely a fuller Chronicle expanded and interpolated from the Isidorian one, is manifest in many places. Near the end, Isidore wrote:

> “Thereafter Heraclius is in the fifth year of his reign. At its beginning the Slavs took Greece from the Romans, and the Persians took Scythia and Egypt, together with very many provinces. In Spain also Sisebut, king of the Goths, captured certain cities belonging to the Roman army.”

The epitomator Melito—or whoever he was—contracted or rather mixed and confused these statements as follows:

> “Thereafter Heraclius is in the fifth year of his reign. Sisebut, the most glorious prince of the Goths, subdued for himself by war very many provinces in Spain, cities of the Roman army.”

As you can see, he improperly transferred “very many provinces” from its original place to another.

Whether Melito was the epitomator of the Chronicle, merely the owner of the Codex, or whether the word “Melito” was accidentally added to the Codex by someone, cannot easily be determined. But I would contend, with every confidence, that the person who abridged and interpolated Isidore’s Chronicle in this manner was not Spanish.

First, as Flórez has already observed, when Isidore says near the end:

> “Thus, from the beginning of the world to the present Era 554, there are…”

the abridger, had he been Spanish, would not have altered this to:

> “Thus, from the beginning of the world to the present year of Heraclius, there are…”

Second, a Spaniard would certainly not have omitted certain distinctive glories of Spain reported in the Isidorian Chronicle, such as the entry under the year of the world 5773:

> “At that time Martin, bishop of Braga, was renowned throughout Galicia for his wisdom and his teaching of the Catholic faith.”

And under the year 5801:

> “At this time Leander, bishop in Spain, became renowned for the conversion of the Gothic people through his teaching of the faith and of the sciences.” [Col. 0537D–0538C]

### 9

Although we find an interpolated Isidorian Chronicle in the Codex of Pelagius of Oviedo from the twelfth century and among the chronicles of Lucas of Tuy from the thirteenth century, and although we admit that this interpolation was probably made in Spain, it is certain from other evidence that traces of an interpolated Isidorian Chronicle outside Spain are older. This is clear from the Melito Codex 686 and from other manuscript copies, which I shall review shortly, in which the same Chronicle is found interpolated and continued in Gaul or Germany.

Indeed, during the eighth, ninth, and tenth centuries, when such ancient monuments began to be interpolated, it will be difficult to find even the slightest trace of this fraud in Spain. The Spaniards, partly oppressed under the yoke of the Moors and partly constantly waging war against the Moors, had no leisure to fabricate new documents or to enlarge and alter old ones. [Col. 0538C–D]

### 10

Nor is this contradicted by the apparent fact that Julian of Toledo had read an abridged Isidorian Chronicle like that of Melito, since on one occasion, in the abridgment of the Chronicle which he presented in Book III of *On the Demonstration of the Sixth Age*, he gives similar wording.

First, even if the Chronicle had been reduced to an abridgment outside Spain, it could nevertheless have come into Julian’s hands. Second, since Julian abridges most things, he could easily on occasion have abridged them in the same way, as is clear from the example presented in the note to Julian.

Isidore wrote:

> “In the second year after the Flood, Shem, when he was one hundred years old, begot Arphaxad.”

In the Melito copy:

> “In the second year after the Flood, Shem begot Arphaxad.”

Julian likewise published the shorter form. Even if he had not seen Melito’s copy, since he omits similar material elsewhere, he could, as I have said, have omitted the words “when he was one hundred years old.” These words are also omitted in the Chronicle of Isidore inserted into the *Etymologies*, where we read:

> “In the second year after the Flood, Shem begot Arphaxad.”

There is no doubt that Julian had read the *Etymologies*. [Col. 0538D–0539A]

### 11

Let us now review the editions of the Isidorian Chronicle.

In the Vatican Library, no. 2863, there is a little work of Isidore—written “Isiodore” in the manuscript—on times. It begins:

> “A brief account of times through the generations…”

It is full of errors, as is evident from the beginning. The prologue ends:

> “So that the times past may be known.”

In many places it has been abridged. The Chronicle ends:

> “Heraclius is now in the fifth year of his reign. Sisebut, king of the Goths, converted the Jews to the faith of Christ and certain cities of the army in battle [supply: ‘subjugated’]. Thus, from the beginning of the world to the Era ‘delivi’ [sic; for DCLIV, 654], that is, the fifth year of the emperor Heraclius, there are 5,816 years. The remainder of the age…”

In corrected editions the number is 5,814.

In the Vatican Library this abbreviated work is bound together with another Chronicle excerpted from Jerome, Eusebius, and others, and published at Rome in the house of the nobleman Giovanni Filippo de Lignamine in 1474. The type and paper do not appear to differ. [Col. 0539A–B]

### 12

Giovanni Battista Audiffredi, a man distinguished in every field of study and pre-eminent in knowledge of early editions, describes this edition on page 385 of his work *On Roman Editions of the Fifteenth Century*. He says that it is preserved in the library of His Holiness Pope Pius VI and by the abbot de Rossi, whose many early editions passed into the Corsinian Library.

He says that it is a small quarto, in large Roman type, by Giovanni Filippo de Lignamine, and conjectures that it belongs to the year 1473. He adds that another small quarto edition is preserved in the Casanatense Library, in the Gothic type of Stefano Planck, or Plaunck. The place of publication is not specified. Some have incorrectly thought that it was an octavo. The Chronicle ends in the fifth year of Heraclius; its title is *A Little Work on Times*. [Col. 0539B–C]

### 13

Nicolás Antonio, citing Labbe in the *Library of Manuscripts*, reports that Isidore’s Chronicle was published under the title *On Times* in 1474; this may perhaps be the first Roman edition. Fabricius lists an edition from 1477 under the same title. Maittaire mentions none of these editions in his *Annals of Printing*.

In the following century, in 1577, it was published in octavo under the title *Chronology*, by Thomas Guarinus, together with the *Chronology* of Gerard Mercator and that of Matthaeus Beroaldus, at Basel. [Col. 0539C–D]

### 14

García, or Garsias Loaisa, labored admirably to produce a corrected edition of the Chronicle. His edition, illustrated with his notes, appeared not at Madrid, as Nicolás Antonio says, but at Turin. The title is:

> *The Chronicle of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, corrected and illustrated with scholia by García de Loaisa, archdeacon of Guadalajara, and so forth. At Turin, by Giovanni Battista Bilaquam, 1593, in quarto.*

It appeared in the same year and place as the *Book of Sentences*, as I have already noted.

Loaisa’s dedicatory letter is as follows:

> To the Most Powerful and Catholic Philip II, king of the Spains, García de Loaisa sends greetings.

### 15

To present an exact and accurate account of a long period of time is a laborious undertaking, filled with great difficulties. The events and definite occurrences of the past are first entrusted to the shifting and unstable memory of human beings, rather than consecrated through writing and books to the eternity of time. The annals themselves are exposed to countless injuries inflicted by mortals: first, to the disturbances and passions of writers, since each person seeks to make the glory of his own people and homeland immortal by commemorating their splendid achievements; then, to the upheavals of states and the invasions of provinces, which destroy everything by fire, sword, revolt, and the violence of the populace. Finally, although memory of past events strives to preserve the uncorrupted truth of time, through the remoteness of time itself it grows old and antiquated, and as the course of the years slips toward destruction, it too collapses into ruin.

Yet although this is so, among the qualities that make a man learned, accomplished, and complete in almost every respect, one is especially important: amid the uncertainty and obscurity of events, to investigate diligently the truth, certain and clear, and to trace the unusual and hidden paths of history. For nothing is more excellent—whether for increasing wisdom, confirming prudence, governing the reins of empire piously and moderately, understanding the character of the commonwealth and restraining the movements of the people, or suppressing the designs of domestic enemies—than to possess a known and thoroughly examined understanding of the public memory of past events, the accidents and outcomes of history, and the experience of all ages and peoples. All these things are embraced within the single compass of chronology.

Receive, therefore, Most Powerful Philip, a Chronicle published by Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, the light and crown of the royal Gothic nation. In you religion, devotion to the Christian name and worship, singular clemency, and a certain admirable and wholly divine wisdom in governing—strengthened, as though by experience, through the longest practice in affairs—shine forth.

At Your Majesty’s command I undertook to correct this Chronicle and illustrate it with notes, so that it might return to you, from whom it originated, as to an immense ocean of all virtue and justice. It may not be adorned as it ought to have been, but it has been worked over with as much diligence as I could bring to it.

It is especially pleasant and dear to me, and always before the eyes of my mind, to comply earnestly with Your Catholic Majesty and to serve you with a humble spirit; to dedicate your royal and august name, insofar as I can, to immortality; and continually to offer prayers for you to Christ the eternal King, that amid the cares and anxieties of so many kingdoms you may remain unharmed, steadfast, and safe.

Farewell. [Col. 0540A–C]

16. I said Taurini, not Madrid, as Nic. Antonius reports, no. 110, that the Chronicle of Isidore, illustrated with Loaisa’s scholia, was published—unless perhaps the Turin edition was preceded by another from Madrid. For the explicit words of Nic. Antonius offer some reason for doubt: “Garsias Loaisa published it anew at Madrid, more richly furnished with his notes, together with the books of the Sentences, of which we shall speak presently, when he was still tutor in letters to Philip III, while his illustrious father was living, and had not yet been inducted into the see of Toledo, which he later obtained.” But since, when he was about to speak of the books of the Sentences, he directs the reader elsewhere and at that place mentions only the Turin edition, one must altogether believe that the name “Madrid” slipped in for “Turin” when the edition of the Chronicle was being mentioned. I am more surprised that in the new Spanish Library, enlarged even by a second revision and recently published at Madrid, when Loaisa’s eulogy is composed, no mention is made by Nic. Antonius of the edition of the books of the Sentences or of the Isidorian Chronicle prepared by Loaisa, nor of the labor which Loaisa, together with others, contributed to completing the royal Madrid edition of the Works of St. Isidore. [Col. 0540D–0541A]

17. In the Parisian Bignaean edition of the Works of St. Isidore the Chronicle was omitted, although it had long since been published. Breulius did publish it, but in the catalogue of books an asterisk is placed beside it, indicating that the work was then appearing for the first time—not for any other reason than that it had been omitted by Bignaeus. At the same time, the following title is given: “Chronicle from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of Suinthila” (correct: the fourth of Sisebutus), “king of the Goths, emended by Garsias Loaisa and illustrated with scholia.” Breulius omitted Loaisa’s dedicatory letter to Philip II and prefixed in its place the words of Vaseus on Isidore’s Chronicle cited above, chapter 77, nos. 16 and 17, and reproduced by us. [Col. 0541A–B]

18. Audiffredus describes an old Italian version of Isidorian’s Chronicle in his Catalogue of Italian Editions of the Fifteenth Century, p. 212:

> “Here begins the Chronicle of Saint Isidore the Younger, with some additions taken from the text and histories of the Bible, and from the book of Paulus Orosius, and from the passions of the saints. At the end: ‘The Chronicle of Saint Isidore the Younger was completed in Cividale del Friuli, in the year of Our Lord Jesus Christ 1480, on 24 November. May our Lord God always be praised.’”

This edition exists in the Casanatense Library, in Gothic type, small quarto. Nic. Antonius possessed a copy of this edition; he says that it is octavo, and observes that the translator interpolated much into Isidore’s text and continued the work down to the death of the emperor Frederick II, and the year 1250. But I would rather believe that the Italian translator happened upon an old copy already so enlarged and continued, of the kind of which I have found many. A Latin chronicle of this sort exists in the Escorial Library, written in the fourteenth century. There the first work is “The Chronicle of Nichobaldus”; next comes “The Chronicle of Saint Isidore the Younger, with certain additions extracted from the text and histories of the Bible, and from the book of Paulus Orosius and the passions of the saints,” containing within itself the six ages of the world, namely, from the beginning of the world, when God in the beginning created heaven and earth and the first man Adam, down to the present day, which is in the year 690 of the Lord from the incarnation, 1335, in the time of Pope Benedict XII, who resides …” Other material appears to be missing. For thus Rodriguez describes the codex in volume II of the Spanish Library, p. 328. [Col. 0541B–D]

19. Audiffredus, in the same place, p. 402, records another edition of the Italian version of Isidorian’s Chronicle, rare, in Roman type and small quarto, preserved in the Corsiniana Library:

> “It reports (I read: “Referisce”) and relates the present work, the Chronicle of Saint Isidore the Younger, with certain additions taken from the text and histories of the Bible, and from the book of Paulus Orosius and the passions of the saints. At the end: ‘The Chronicle of Saint Isidore the Younger ends, corrected and revised by Baptista Alexander Iaconellus of Rieti, printed at L’Aquila by Master Adam of Rothweil, a German, in the year of Our Lord 1482, on 5 October. Praise to God, amen.’” [Col. 0541D–0542A]

20. Rodriguez, volume II of the Spanish Library, p. 328, indicates from an eleventh-century Escorial codex a Spanish version of Isidorian’s Chronicle, but as it appears in the collection of Pelagius of Oviedo. Its heading is:

> “General history collected from various authors, namely from Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville; Julianus Pomerius, archbishop of Toledo; Saint Piro, or Samphiro, or Zafiro—for different historians call him by these names—bishop of Astorga; and Pelayo, bishop of Oviedo.”

21. Manuscript copies of Isidorian’s Chronicle are encountered everywhere in libraries. Fabricius reports that in the Vossian manuscript of the Leiden Library it is entitled “Chronicle of the Six Ages of the World,” while on the pages themselves it bears the title “Image of the World.” Labbeus and Oudinus mention a codex of the Jesuit College of Clermont, written in the seventh century. Oudinus adds the Corbie Codex, later belonging to Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris, of the seventh or at least the eighth century. Bayerius asserts that at least three copies, and ones of no ordinary antiquity, are preserved in a single Escorial library. In the library of the University of Siena there is a Chronicle of St. Isidore with a supplement down to the year 1316, a parchment quarto codex of the fourteenth century. At the end one reads: “The end of this work, written by the hand of my lord Christoforus of Acquapendente.” Antonius Ponzius, volume XI of the Spanish Journey, p. 220, says that in the monastery library of León there is a chronicle of St. Isidore continued down to King Alfonso VI. From the Zaccarian notebooks, chapter 44, I have described the Lucca, Pistoia, Florentine San Marco, Cesena Malatesta, Albanian, and Modena codices. [Col. 0542A–C]

22. The following are manuscript copies of Isidorian’s Chronicle that I myself have seen. Vatican Codex 629, to be described in chapter 94. Vatican Codex 1348, concerning which see chapter 96; there the Chronicle is interpolated and is attributed rather to the work of Augustine and Jerome than to Isidore. Vatican Codex 1974, in the same chapter 96. Regio-Vatican Codex 215, chapter 99, in which it is entitled “The Book of the Chronicles of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis.” In Regio-Vatican Codex 1852, chapter 101, the Chronicle, whose author is said to be Isidore of Hispalis, is continued by a certain Peter. In the same place, in Regio-Vatican Codex 2034, “A Brief Chronicle of Isidore,” with a note added concerning the tenth year of King Receswinth. In Palatine Codex 239, approximately of the tenth century, concerning which see chapter 102, “The Book of the Chronicles of Saint Isidore the Younger,” apparently interpolated in Gaul. In Urbinate 100, chapter 104, “The Book of the Chronicles of Saint Isidore, bishop of Hispalis,” etc.; the Chronicle is interpolated and continued outside Spain. In Urbinate 382, chapter 104, “The Book of the Chronicles of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis,” etc., interpolated in Gaul. A similar copy exists in Urbinate 392, in the same place. Also in Urbinate 585, in the same place: “A Brief Chronicle of the Etymologies,” with certain passages inserted, apparently by some Cassinese monk. In Ottobonian Codex 1720, a somewhat interpolated Chronicle, concerning which see chapter 106. In Ottobonian Codex 1758, in the same place, an interpolated and continued Chronicle. In the library of the Roman College there is a manuscript chronography—or, as it is incorrectly written, “conography”—of Isidore the Younger, as I shall say in chapter 107. [Col. 0542C–0543A]

# CHAPTER LXXIX

The History of the Kings of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi defended as Isidore’s against Pellizerius. Manuscript codices differing from one another; editions likewise different. The Chronicle of the Visigoths called Wulsa’s: is it St. Isidore’s? Notice concerning this Chronicle from the edition of the Toledan Fathers. An interpolated copy of the History among the chronicles of the Tudense. Another mutilated copy, apparently dating from Isidore’s time, and the reason for this. Isidore’s words concerning St. Hermenegild, explained as referring to his war against his father. The remarkable silence of Isidore and other Fathers of the Gothic Church concerning the glorious martyrdom of St. Hermenegild. The compliance of the bishops of the Gothic Church in certain difficult actions of the kings.

1. Placcius, in the *Theatrum Anonymorum et Pseudonymorum*, does not bring a suit against the History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi. Pellizerius, however, had brought one, using the same arguments by which he attempts to deprive Isidore of the Chronicle, as I said in chapter 77. As far as the History of the Goths is concerned, it is established from the very prologue to the chronicles of Pelagius of Oviedo—which Pellizerius otherwise cites in support of his position—that it is the work of Isidore of Hispalis:

> “And blessed Isidore, concerning whom the church of León now rejoices, wrote as fully as he could concerning the kings of the Goths, from the first Athanaric down to Wamba, the Catholic king and king of the Goths.”

The author of the prologue is indeed mistaken in attributing to Isidore the continuation of Isidore’s History down to Wamba. Alfonso III, King the Great, falls into a similar error in the letter with which he sends his Chronicle to Sebastian—or whoever else its author may be:

> “And because Isidore, bishop of the see of Hispalis, has fully taught the chronicles of the Goths down to the time of the glorious King Wamba, we shall briefly indicate to you certain matters from that time, just as we have heard them from our ancestors and predecessors and have learned them to be true.”

The word *cognovimus* should be read, rather than *cognobimus*. This letter was published by Joseph Pellizerius himself at the beginning of the Chronicle of Dulcidius of Salamanca. [Col. 0543B–C]

2. Works enlarged by appendices from other authors are sometimes attributed in manuscript codices only to the original author, and sometimes only to the continuator. Hence there is frequent opportunity for error in identifying authors. In this very book before us, the monk who wrote the Chronicle called Exiliensis falls into the same error. In the eleventh century he attributes to Isidore the History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi in such a way that he also assigns to Isidore the account of Paul’s rebellion against Wamba, which was composed by Julianus of Toledo long after Isidore:

> “They are written,” he says, “in the book of Blessed Isidore, who, among fourteen other works edited by him, carefully composed an account of the deeds of the Vandals, Suevi, and Goths.”

But since not only King Alfonso the Great and the author of the Exilian Chronicle, but also the author of the prologue to the chronicles of Pelagius of Oviedo attribute the History of the Goths to Isidore, Pellizerius is scarcely consistent with himself when, thinking that the author of the prologue is mistaken on this point, he seizes upon his testimony in order to deprive Isidore not only of the Chronicle but also of the History of the Vandals and Suevi, because the prologue says that Isidore of Pacensis wrote from Adam onward, and concerning the kings of the Vandals, Alans, and Suevi in Spain. By these words he perhaps understands the extant History of the Vandals and Suevi by Isidore; but when King Alfonso asserts that the History of the Goths belongs to Isidore, he seems also to understand the History of the Vandals and Suevi. These histories are so interconnected that some people formerly called all three by the single name “History of the Goths.” Lucius Marinus and Eisengreinius, however, were mistaken in reporting that Isidore wrote a History of the Lombards. [Col. 0543C–0544A]

3. Pellizerius suspects that the History of the Goths inscribed with Isidore’s name is the work which Isidore himself praises in the final chapter of *On Illustrious Men*, in the entry on Maximus of Zaragoza:

> “He also wrote, in a brief style, a little history of what was done in Spain during the times of the Goths, in historical and composed language.”

By this opinion he attempted to expel from its proper place another pseudo-chronicle of Maximus fabricated in the seventeenth century. But the falsity of the fictitious Chronicle of Maximus is sufficiently evident in itself, and the History of the Goths agrees so well with Isidore that it cannot be attributed to Maximus. Maximus ceased to live not long after the year 610. The History of the Goths, however, proceeds in the same style down to the time of Suinthila, or the year 621. [Col. 0544A–B]

4. Add the words of Braulio, whose authority has already been defended elsewhere against Pellizerius:

> “One book on the origin of the Goths and the kingdom of the Suevi, and also a history of the Vandals.”

Nic. Antonius compares with this the words of the author of the History, from the preface addressed to King Sisenand, published in the chronicles of Lucas of Tuy:

> “Since you have requested that you be informed concerning the origin of the Goths of Spain” (he says that this should be read together in that form), “of the Suevi, Vandals, and Alans, and how they ruled Spain, etc.”

If these words truly belonged to the first author of the History of the Goths, they would agree exceedingly well with Braulio. But since they were taken from the system of the chronicles of Lucas of Tuy, in which many things have been interpolated, no strong argument arises from them—except that the Tudense believed Isidore to be the author of the History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi. Braulio’s opinion, however, needs no confirmation. Thus Gerhardus Joannes Vossius, in *On Latin History*, book I, part II, chapter 25, writes concerning Isidore:

> “He also composed a history of the origin of the Goths, the kingdom of the Suevi, and the Vandals; Braulio mentions this work, etc.”

And concerning the year of Isidore’s death:

> “And the previously mentioned Braulio, whose testimony above all others deserves credence.”

Nor is the silence of Ildefonsus an obstacle, although he passed over in silence other works of Isidore, especially his historical works. [Col. 0544B–D]

5. In a letter to Peter of Compostela, dated 1199, Innocent III recognized as genuine the testimony he had produced from Isidore’s History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi in support of the rights of his see:

> “Isidore, however, in his chronicles, under the title ‘Concerning the Suevi,’ testifies that Remismundus crossed over to Lusitania, etc.”

Thus in the History of the Suevi, under era 502:

> “Remismundus, etc., from there crosses over into Lusitania.”

It should be noted that the title “History of the Goths” includes the chronicles of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi, divided into separate titles. The History of the Goths occupies the principal portion; what is added concerning the Vandals seems rather to be an appendix. Trithemius, however, speaks of Isidore’s “History, or Chronicle, book III.” And perhaps the reason that the catalogues of the ancients do not frequently make explicit mention of Isidore’s History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi is that many understood all these histories under the name “chronicles,” although some professed that they were omitting those works of Isidore that belong to secular literature.

In the edition of Isidorian’s History of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi prepared by Lindenbrog, these words of Leo of Monte Cassino, book III of the *Cassinese Chronicle*, chapter 62, concerning Isidore’s History, are explained as follows:

> “Desiderius ordered the following codices to be transcribed: … the History of the Lombards, Goths, and Vandals; the History of Bishop Jordanes concerning the Romans and Goths.”

The author of the ninth-century Chronicle of Albelda also simply calls Isidore’s History “the Chronicle of the Goths,” in volume XIII of *Sacred Spain*, no. 84, p. 462:

> “And because the nation of the Goths came from Magog, the Chronicle of the Goths affirms that the Goths are a most ancient nation,” etc.

This is the beginning of Isidorian’s History. [Col. 0544D–0545B]

6. Neither the distinguished Zaccaria nor I have been able to see any manuscript copies of the History of the Goths, except that in Vatican-Palatine Codex 927, p. 122 verso, I found a fragment of the History of the Goths, without the name of Isidore as author. Its title is: “On the First Arrival of the Goths in Italy and the Capture of Rome.” Under the year 437 of the era, the fourth year of the reign of Honorius and Arcadius. Grotius incorrectly has “the year 437 of the era” in a different form. This fragment ends at the year 448 of the era. “He is murdered amid domestic intrigues.” It agrees with the editions of Grotius and Labbeus in those passages which, after the earlier material had been deleted, the Lombard hand had attributed to the ancient Clermont copy. A few other, less important differences occur, such as the year 447 at the end:

- “He died in Italy.”
- Grotius: “He died Italy.”
- Labbeus: “They died in Italy.”
- The royal Madrid edition: “He died in Italy.”

In Ottobonian Codex 1758, concerning which I shall speak in chapter 106, there is a genealogy of the kings of Spain, with much material drawn from Isidore’s History of the Goths and Vandals. [Col. 0545B–C]

7. It is not known which manuscripts John Baptist Perez used in correcting this History for the royal edition. He presented it fuller and much more accurately corrected than it had previously appeared. Fabricius was deceived when, in the *Bibliotheca media*, he states that the Chronicle, or History of the Goths, was published at Turin with the scholia of Garcia de Loaisa in quarto. Loaisa, however, published at Turin in that year the Chronicle from the Creation of the World, not the History of the Goths, illustrated with his scholia.

The History of the Goths first appeared, so far as I know, in Paris together with the twelve books of Visigothic laws, at the shop of Sebastianus Nivellius in 1579, in folio, from the library of Petrus Pithoeus. It was then reprinted in the Bignaean edition of Isidore’s Works in 1580. Bonaventura Vulcanius, at Leiden, appended the same Isidorian History of the Goths with his notes after Jordanes, beginning at p. 203. This edition was completed in octavo in 1597, with the addition of a brief Chronicle of the Visigoths, which some attribute to Bishop Wulsa. [Col. 0545C–0546A]

8. Lindenbrog’s edition is similar, under the following title:

> “Three ancient writers of the histories of various nations: Jordanes the bishop, on the succession of kingdoms and times; his History of the Origin of the Goths; Isidore of Hispalis, on the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi; his Chronicle of the Kings of the Visigoths; Paul, son of Warnefrid, the deacon, on the deeds of the Lombards, six books. Fridericus Lindenbrog revised and illustrated them with observations. Hamburg, at the shop of Michael Heringius, 1611, quarto.”

Florezius was unable to obtain this edition, although he wished to compare it with the Aguirrian edition of the Chronicle called Wulsa’s. The “Chronicle of the Kings of the Visigoths,” which Vulcanius and Lindenbrog append, presents only the years during which the kings reigned, preceded by a brief preface and the following heading:

> “Chronicle of the Kings of the Visigoths. In the year 400 of the era, Athanaric becomes the first king among the Goths,” etc.

This is the very Chronicle that is falsely inscribed with Wulsa’s name and attributed by some to Julianus of Toledo. Vulcanius and Lindenbrog, apparently on the basis of manuscript codices, attribute this brief Chronicle to Isidore. Nor does any contrary consideration appear, if we understand that Isidore carried the Chronicle down to King Sisenand and that Julianus—or someone else—continued it from there to Ervig. For in Ervig the Chronicle ends in Lindenbrog’s edition.

Fabricius noted in the *Bibliotheca media* that this Chronicle was missing from the editions of Isidore’s Works; we shall therefore assign it a place among the appendices in our edition. John Baptist Perez gives the following judgment concerning it in his prologue to the corrected Councils of Spain, in Aguirre, volume I of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 13:

> “We have taken the later kings from the very brief but golden chronicle of Bishop Wulsa, which exists in a certain book of the royal library and in other ancient copies. We have no reason to doubt its reliability in writing, since the times recorded by it agree so exactly with the councils, and since it defines the months and days of the later kings in such minute detail that it scarcely seems to have been written after the destruction of Spain.” [Col. 0546A–C]

9. This same Chronicle was published in the appendix to volume II of the Works of St. Julianus of Toledo, in the *Toledan Fathers*, p. 385, and was continued even to Witiza, at which time Julianus had already ceased to live. The Chronicle does indeed appear to have been continued by several persons; this is also sufficiently probable for another reason. For if, for example, Ildefonsus received the Chronicle of the Visigoths composed down to Sisenand, he himself could have added the kings who succeeded thereafter; Julianus could have added others after Ildefonsus, and someone else could have added others after Julianus. As I have said, it is my intention to relegate this most useful little work to the appendices, prefacing it meanwhile with the notice of the learned editor of the Toledan Fathers cited above. [Col. 0546C–D]

10. We conclude this very brief appendix with the few works falsely attributed to St. Julianus: namely, the Chronicle of the Kings of the Visigoths, frequently called Wulsa’s; then two poems and four epitaphs. Do you ask who attributed these to Julianus? The man who, under the forged names of Julianus and Liutprand, fabricated those widely circulated chronicles, distinguished by so many fables.

As for the Chronicle of the Visigoths, although it is truly a golden work—as the highly learned John Baptist Perez called it in the prefatory letter to volume I of Cardinal Aguirre’s collection of the Councils—and although Spain’s sacred and secular chronology has been illuminated by its light to an extraordinary degree, nevertheless there is no sufficiently solid argument by which it can be attributed to St. Julianus. The whole work, as it now exists, extending down to the reign of Witiza, cannot belong to Julianus. Nor, even if it is said that its final chapters were written by some continuator of the earlier Chronicle—which, when we consider the individual passages and observe the differences between one section and another in the designation of years and days, is virtually evident and established—can Julianus be called the author of the earlier part of the Chronicle.

For if we can arrive at anything by conjecture from certain older codices in which the present Chronicle extends only to the beginning of Ervig’s reign, as is evident from the Aguirrian and Vulcanian editions in the notes to Jordanes’ History of the Visigoths, it follows rather that its author was someone other than our Julianus. Julianus died under Egica and would hardly have passed over in silence both the death of Ervig and Egica’s accession to the throne.

Moreover, if one adds that the aforementioned Chronicle is not mentioned at all by Felix in his eulogy of Julianus—although he carefully recorded the history of King Wamba—it must be concluded that this work was rashly attributed to St. Julianus.

If you ask for its true author, we are entirely ignorant. As for the fact that it is called Wulsa’s and commonly attributed to a writer of that name, whom some have even called a Spanish bishop, it is, in our judgment, a foul error arising from the fact that some scribe carelessly copied “Wulse-Gothorum” for “Wise-Gothorum,” which is what appears in ancient copies; from there the mistake spread to others. Certainly the name Wulsa is nowhere found among the writers of that period, much less among the bishops of Spain.

On this subject P. Florez should be consulted, volume II of *Sacred Spain*. We reproduced the present Chronicle from his edition, likewise adding in the margin many variants from the codex of John Baptist Perez that he had omitted, from the manuscript we have often mentioned. [Col. 0546D–0547C]

11. I find another epitome of the History of the Kings of the Goths in Regio-Vatican Codex 667, formerly 1009, written, as I think, by some foreigner from our chronicles, from the beginning of the Gothic kingdom down to the invasion of the Saracens. It precedes the History of Wamba edited by St. Julianus of Toledo and bears the title “Chronology and Succession of the Gothic Kings.”

The codex is more recent, but was copied from another, older one, written in the year 1127 by Petrus Willelmus Armarius, concerning whom I shall speak more fully in chapter 100. I believe that the Chronicle was first composed in the ninth century. Since I do not yet know it to have been printed, and since it may be useful for illustrating Isidorian’s Chronicle or History of the Goths, it may appropriately be placed among the appendices, especially since it everywhere breathes antiquity. [Col. 0547C–D]

12. Breulius published an imperfect History of the Goths without the Chronicle of the Visigoths, from an edition that I believe was the Bignaean edition of Isidore’s Works. His negligence is not slight, since he had before him the royal Madrid edition, in which that History had appeared fuller and more accurately corrected, before he completed his own edition, and since he appended much from the same royal edition at the end of his own.

In the same mutilated form the History of the Goths appeared among Goldast’s *Writers on Suevic Affairs*, Frankfurt 1605 and Ulm 1722. But why should it be surprising that Goldast, Lindenbrog, Baronius, Pagius, and other foreigners were unaware of the Madrid edition of the History of the Goths, when Cardinal Aguirre, in volume II of the *Councils of Spain*, p. 183, likewise published the same History not in its entirety—not from the royal edition, nor from the second edition of Grotius, nor from the third edition of Labbeus—but mutilated, as it appeared in the earliest editions and as it was printed in volume III of Andrea Schott’s *Illustrated Spain*, p. 847?

Florezius rightly wonders at the same thing in Aguirre’s book *On the Illustrious Men of Isidore*, and anyone will wonder who has otherwise perceived the learning of that most learned cardinal. Fabricius, however, is not to be heeded in the *Bibliotheca media*, where he asserts that the History of the Goths appeared in Aguirre’s *Councils of Spain* much fuller and more corrected than in Vulcanius, Lindenbrog, and the other first editions—perhaps because he thought that Aguirre had used more accurate editions.

Aguirre’s title, volume II, p. 183, is:

> “History or Chronicle of the Goths, Vandals, Suevi, and Visigoths, by St. Isidore, archbishop of Hispalis.”

And on p. 189:

> “Chronicle of the Kings of the Visigoths, partly from Isidore, partly from Wulsa.”

He briefly introduces it as follows:

> “The chronology of the councils and of the other ancient monuments of Spain that are published in this work can scarcely become known unless a historical index of its kings is placed before one’s eyes, with the proper epoch assigned to each. This is supplied by St. Isidore of Hispalis in his brief History, from the era of Caesar 214—that is, the year of Christ 176—to the era 666, that is, the year of Christ 628, when Sisebutus, king of Spain, had already died, while Isidore was still alive. For the Goths and the other kings included in this little book did not invade Spain in the era 214, nor even much later, but only at the beginning of the fifth century, around the era 449, or the year of Christ 411, in the first year of Theodosius the Younger, when the Bracaran Council is said to have been celebrated under Pancratianus, which we have presented under that year. The Chronicle of Idatius corresponds to this method of reckoning. See the shorter chronology of the same Gothic kings, published at the beginning of volume I, p. 15 onward, from the same Isidore and Bishop Wulsa, which begins with Athanaric.” [Col. 0547D–0548C]

13. Therefore the editions of Isidorian’s History that must be preferred above all others are the royal Madrid edition, the second edition of Grotius, the third of Labbeus, and the fourth of Florezius. In volume VI of *Sacred Spain*, he published that History after comparing the three preceding editions with one another, adding the variants of the readings and illustrating it with certain of his own notes and others by the ancient Perez. [Col. 0548C–D]

Hugo Grotius arranged his collection of Gothic affairs during his lifetime; after his death it was published under the following title:

> “The History of the Goths, Vandals, and Lombards, partly translated and partly arranged by Hugo Grotius. Prefixed are his Prolegomena, in which the order and chronology of the Gothic kings are given together with their eulogies. Appended are appellative names and Gothic, Vandalic, and Lombard words with explanations. Amsterdam, at the shop of Louis Elzevir, 1655.”

The editor says in the prologue that he obtained the Isidore whom Grotius could not possess from the library of Isaac Vossius. The Vossian copy had been transcribed from the Clermont Codex, concerning which more shortly.

The title on p. 705 of the collection is:

> “The Chronicle of Blessed Isidore, archbishop of Hispalis, of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi in Spain, now appearing at last, enlarged by more than half, from the library of Isaac Vossius.”

Grotius had prefaced his Prolegomena on p. 63 with these words:

> “Besides brief accounts of Ostrogothic and Vandal affairs, Isidore brings the deeds of the Visigoths down to his own times, having collected what elsewhere we should seek with no little labor in scattered form.” [Col. 0548D–0549A]

14. After Hugo Grotius’s collection of Gothic affairs had been printed, a new bibliography of manuscript books appeared in Paris in 1657, in folio, through the work and care of Philippus Labbeus, S.J. In volume I of this excellent work, p. 61, there appears the following:

> “The Histories of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi by St. Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, much fuller and more accurate than those hitherto published. From the manuscript codex of the Jesuit College of Clermont in Paris, in which there are also, by an uncertain author, accounts of the deeds of Constantine the Great; uncertain chronicles concerning the affairs of the emperors Zeno and Anastasius, as well as of King Theoderic; likewise from other chronicles concerning the affairs of the emperor Justinian, and thereafter down to Charles Martel, etc.”

It begins:

> “On the Praise of Spain by St. Isidore: ‘Of all lands,’ etc.”

In the catalogue of what is contained in the first volume, section 1, no. 3, Labbeus prefixes the following:

> “The Histories of the Kings of the Goths, Vandals, and Suevi by St. Isidore, bishop of Hispalis in Baetica, much fuller and more accurate than those hitherto published, from the excellent parchment codex of the Jesuit College of Clermont in Paris, etc.”

The Dutch printers, who recently—while this volume of ours, begun three years earlier, was still under the press—published those three histories together with Hugo Grotius’s collection of Gothic affairs, ought to have observed that they used no manuscript codex from a Dutch library, but rather a copy of the Reverend Father Jacobus Sirmond, S.J., *τοῦ μακαρίτου* (“the blessed/deceased one”), who had transcribed it from this very codex. [Col. 0549A–C]

15. The Dutch editor and Labbeus prefixed to the History of the Goths from the Clermont manuscript a eulogy of Spain that had not previously been published:

> “Of all lands, etc.”

This was reprinted by Florezius and, in the second edition of *Sacred Spain*, collated with and corrected against the manuscript copy of the León Codex. The León Codex does not appear to have contained the History of the Goths, since Florezius records from that codex variants in the eulogy, not in the History.

In the Clermont Codex this praise is prefixed as a kind of preface to the History of the Goths. Nic. Antonius calls it a preface eminently worthy of being read, and it is indeed so composed that it appears to have been prepared by Isidore for this purpose. There is no reason to deny that it belongs to Isidore. [Col. 0549C–D]

16. Another, much fuller copy of the History of the Goths is found among the chronicles of Lucas of Tuy, volume IV of *Illustrated Spain*. Fabricius asserts that a more complete Chronicle of the Goths was published together with the codex—or the twelve books of Visigothic laws—from the library of Petrus Pithoeus, and in volume III of *Illustrated Spain*, rather than in book II of the Chronicle of Lucas of Tuy, volume IV of the same *Illustrated Spain*. This is not sufficiently clear. For in Lucas the Chronicle is even fuller than the Chronicle of the Clermont Codex, whereas the Pithoean Chronicle is very incomplete and mutilated in many places. Perhaps Fabricius intended to suggest that the Chronicle in the Tudense is less authentic.

In book II of his chronicles, the Tudense prefixes his own prologue:

> “It is fitting for men, etc.”

There he says:

> “Now we turn our hand to the deeds of the Gothic kings, presenting in the second book of the work the Chronicle of Isidore, teacher of the Spains. For earlier we had presented the Chronicle from the creation of the world.”

This is followed by the Prologue of Blessed Isidore:

> “To Sisenand, lord and most beloved son, king of the Goths, Isidore: Since you have requested information concerning the origin of the Goths, etc.”

Then:

> “Two years before the invasion of the Roman city, in the era 443, when it was stirred up, etc.”

The History of the Suevi follows:

> “In the era 446, the Suevi, under their prince Hermeric, entered Spain together with the Alans and Vandals, etc.”

The History of the Suevi ends. Then comes the History of the Goths:

> “The most ancient origin of the Goths, etc.”

This is the capitulation in Labbeus’s edition. The Tudense distinguishes the material in such a way that he calls the general Chronicle from the creation of the world the first book of Isidore’s Chronicles, and the chronicles of the Vandals, Suevi, and Goths the second book of Isidore’s Chronicles. [Col. 0549D–0550B]

17. Copies of the History of the Goths can therefore be reduced to three classes. The first is the mutilated and incomplete History, such as was published from the Pithoean Library; the second is the fuller and more accurate History in the royal Madrid edition and subsequently from the Clermont Codex; the third is the History interpolated by a later hand, as found in Lucas of Tuy.

The first edition, mutilated, begins:

> “It is certain that the kingdom of the Goths is the most ancient.”

The second, fuller and genuine, begins:

> “It is certain that the nation of the Goths is the most ancient.”

The third, interpolated, begins:

> “The most ancient origin of the Goths is from Magog.”

The first edition, incomplete, ends in the era 656, at the death of Sisebutus. The second, fuller, adds the eulogy of Suinthila and his son Riccimirus, down to the fifth year of Suinthila, era 661. It is followed by:

> “Likewise, a recapitulation by the same Isidore in praise of the Goths.”

The third, interpolated edition takes its beginning from this eulogy of the Goths and also contains the praises of Suinthila, but makes no mention of Riccimirus.

As for what Nic. Antonius indicates—that, with the exception of Labbeus, others are completely silent concerning Riccimirus, chosen by Suinthila as his partner in the kingdom—that is certainly not so. The words concerning Riccimirus had already been published in the royal Madrid edition, to say nothing of Grotius’s edition, which derives its origin from the Clermont Codex. [Col. 0550B–D]

18. In the first, mutilated edition, the Vandalic History begins:

> “The Vandals with the Alans and Suevi.”

It ends:

> “And seven months.”

In the second, more correct edition:

> “Era 449, two years before the invasion.”

In Labbeus:

> “Era 404.”

And in the copy in the library of the Roman College, a note in the margin of the manuscript says:

> “I think 444 should be read.”

It ends:

> “Down to the death of Gilimer.”

In the interpolated edition the beginning is:

> “Two years before the invasion of the Roman city, in the era 444, when it had been stirred up.”

A prologue, or dedicatory letter to Sisenand, precedes it; this is absent from the genuine copies. Some things are omitted, others added. [Col. 0550D–0551A]

### 19

Nicolaus Antonius says that the *History of the Suebi* is everywhere the same. Yet here too some difference is observed. The first, less complete edition begins: “The Suebi, under their king Hermeric, entered Spain together with the Alans and Vandals,” etc. It ends: “he remained for one hundred and twenty-six years.” The second, more accurately corrected edition reads: “In the year 447 of the Spanish era, the Suebi, under their prince Hermeric, together with the Alans,” etc. It ends: “which is said to have lasted 177 years.” The interpolated edition [Col. 0551B] begins: “In the year 446 of the Spanish era, the Suebi,” etc., as in Labbe’s edition; its ending is also the same. Perhaps the variation of wording observed in this *History of the Suebi* comes from the hands of copyists, not from the deliberate work of any interpolator. For the three different editions agree sufficiently with one another in this respect.

### 20

Leaving aside what some later writer inserted into or omitted from Isidore in the *History of the Goths* adopted by Lucas of Tuy, it is especially worthy of consideration that a difference is observed between the abridged and fuller editions in their particular narration of Gothic history. This difference seems ancient to me, and to belong to the Isidorian age, perhaps even to Isidore’s own hand.

The fuller edition contains Suinthila’s eulogy in an extended passage:

> “In the year 659 of the Spanish era, in the tenth year of the reign of Heraclius, the most glorious Suinthila, by divine favor, assumed the scepters of the kingdom. Having obtained the office of duke under King Sisebut, he subdued the Roman camps and defeated the Ruccones. But after he had ascended the summit of royal power, he took by battle the remaining cities which the Roman hand held in Spain, and, with wondrous good fortune, carried away a glory of triumph greater than that of the other kings. He was the first to possess the monarchy of the whole of Spain within the strait of the Ocean—a distinction granted to none of the rulers before him. By that battle he increased, etc.”

After many outstanding exploits, it continues:

> “Besides these praises of military glory, there were in him many virtues of royal majesty: faith, prudence, diligence, careful judgment, vigorous concern in governing the kingdom, exceptional generosity and liberality toward all, and a mercy toward the needy and destitute that was sufficiently prompt; so that he deserved to be called not only the ruler of peoples but also the father of the poor.”

### 21

Isidore then pursues the praises of Riccimir, or Racimir, who had been taken into partnership in the kingdom by his father, and concludes the *History of the Goths* in the fifth year of Suinthila’s reign, whom he calls “the most glorious prince.”

Perezius appended this brief note: “This was written while Suinthila was alive.” Yet Suinthila was condemned at the Fourth Council of Toledo, at which Isidore subscribed. Here is the reason why I think that the *History of the Goths*, although certainly written by Isidore, originally extended only to the fifth year of Suinthila; afterward, however, either by Isidore himself or by another contemporary who wished to please King Sisenand, his successor, certain copies were mutilated at the end, from which the first, less complete edition was produced.

Concerning Sisebut, who preceded Suinthila, Isidore had written while Suinthila was alive:

> “Some say that this man was killed by a disease peculiar to him, others by drinking an excessive quantity of medicine; he left behind his son Recaredo, who, after his father’s death, departed when death intervened after only a few days of rule.”

Thus the Claromontanus Codex. In place of *abiit* it has *habetur*. I would prefer *obiit*.

After Suinthila had later been condemned, the *History of the Goths* ended as follows, with these words somewhat altered and partly omitted:

> “Some say that this man was killed by illness, others by POISON. These are the years of the Gothic kings, from the beginning of King Athanaric up to this Sisebut: 251 years, 665 of the Spanish era. The Gothic Chronicle ends.”

The introduction of the suspicion of poisoning—of which no mention had been made while Suinthila was alive—shows that the *History of the Goths* was deliberately truncated after Suinthila’s condemnation. Perhaps some persons from Sisenand’s faction charged Suinthila with having killed Sisebut by poison.

The royal Madrid edition, derived, as I think, from Lucas of Tuy, combined the three reported causes of Sisebut’s death:

> “Some say that he was killed by a disease peculiar to him, others by an excessive draught of medicine, others by poison.”

### 22

It certainly seemed most appropriate that so many exceptional praises bestowed by Isidore upon Suinthila should, as far as possible, be erased from the *History of the Goths* after Suinthila had been condemned by the solemn national decree of the Fourth Council of Toledo.

The fathers of that council, convened by Sisenand, established as their final chapter “concerning admonishing the people not to offend against the prince, concerning the election of princes, and concerning the violation of the faith promised to princes, so that anyone who offends in this matter is to be regarded as excommunicated and anathematized; and concerning the execration of Suinthila, his wife, and his offspring; likewise of his brother Geilanus and their possessions. This, therefore, is the execration of Suinthila.

“Concerning Suinthila, who, fearing his own crimes, deprived himself of the kingdom and stripped himself of the insignia of power, we have decreed, with the consent of the nation, that neither he nor his wife, because of the evils they committed, nor their sons shall ever be joined to our fellowship, nor shall we ever promote them to the honors from which they were removed on account of their iniquity. And just as they are regarded as strangers to the height of royal power, so also let them remain strangers to the possession of the property which they acquired from the resources of the wretched [Al., *auxerant*; perhaps *auxerunt*], except for whatever our most pious prince may have granted them out of mercy. The same applies to Geilanus, the brother of the aforementioned Suinthila both by blood and by crime, etc.”

### 23

It is indeed difficult to reconcile Suinthila’s many crimes with the eulogy composed for him by Isidore. Some say that he was initially an excellent prince but afterward fell into vices and crimes. Yet when, in the year 626, Isidore praised him as endowed with such conspicuous virtues that he deserved to be called the father of the poor, is it credible that by the year 631, when he was deprived of the kingdom by Sisenand, he had fallen into such great wickedness that he could even be accused of having acquired his possessions from the resources of the wretched?

What then? Shall we believe that Isidore lied? Certainly not. One course therefore remains: to say that the virtues which Isidore praised in Suinthila in 626 really did appear in him, while his vices were meanwhile concealed; later they may have broken out more openly and perhaps been exaggerated by Sisenand’s friends, so that his crimes might be condemned more forcefully in the council.

Although the council’s decree says that Suinthila, fearing his own crimes, deprived himself of the kingdom and stripped himself of the insignia of power, it is nevertheless sufficiently clear in itself that Suinthila did this because he was compelled by Sisenand’s faction. This is confirmed by Isidore of Pacensis, who wrote more freely in the following eighth century, after the Moorish invasion. Of Suinthila he says:

> “He deservedly assumed the scepters of government in the Gothic kingdom.”

Of Sisenand, however:

> “Having seized the Gothic kingdom through tyranny, he was established on the royal throne for five years.”

These statements were taken from the older continuator of the *Chronicle of Biclarensis*, first published by Florez in volume VI of *Hispania sacra*, who was writing around the year 720.

### 24

But the most holy bishops who governed the Gothic Church possessed such prudence and economy that, insofar as it lay within their power, they strengthened the people’s obedience and submission toward their rulers and removed every occasion for revolt.

Thus Isidore, while Suinthila held the kingdom, commended his virtues as best he could. The same Isidore and the other fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo favored Sisenand, whose rule had already been secured, and praised his piety and religion, because he remained concerned not only with human affairs but also with divine matters; because, prostrate on the ground before the priests of God, he asked with tears and groans that the Lord be entreated on his behalf.

This same prudent policy opens the way to explaining a considerable difficulty which has long troubled the most learned men concerning this Gothic history of Isidore.

### 25

That difficulty was raised in chapter 36 of Grialius’s preface. Isidore says of Leovigild, under the year 606:

> “Then he overcame his son Hermenegild, who was tyrannizing against his authority.”

Grialius replies that no one ought to be offended by the unusual expression “tyrannizing,” nor should the *History of the Goths* on account of that expression be denied to Isidore, since Roderic of Toledo used the same wording in the same context.

Nicolaus Antonius, on the other hand, observes that Roderic could have taken such words from this *History of the Goths* without regarding it as Isidorian. He therefore defends Isidore on the basis of the customary sense of the word among both Greeks and Latins, who used the names “king” and “tyrant” interchangeably. Plato and Aristotle used “tyrant” for a just ruler. Among the Latins, so did Virgil, Horace, Avienus, and others, as is evident even from ordinary lexicons.

For Isidore’s case, however, Nicolaus Antonius adds that he has John of Biclaro, who spoke in the same way of Hermenegild in the third year of the emperor Tiberius:

> “His son Hermenegild, assuming tyranny through the faction of Queen Goswintha, shut himself up in the city of Hispalis after fomenting a rebellion.”

### 26

These words of John of Biclaro, which Nicolaus Antonius cites in his own defense, rather tell against him. For, while he wishes to prove that Hermenegild was called a tyrant by Isidore in the sense of a just ruler, he produces words in which Hermenegild’s tyranny is joined with rebellion. He himself recognized this:

> “Perhaps,” he says, “Biclarensis disapproved of the prince’s action, since he was then flourishing in Spain, although he had been harshly treated by the heretical king Leovigild.”

### 27

I therefore ask: when Isidore asserted that Hermenegild had tyrannized against his father’s authority, did he disapprove of the prince’s action?

I add that the word “tyrant” was at times taken in a favorable sense, but as time went on it was always, or almost always, taken in an unfavorable one. My authority is our Isidore himself, in book I, chapter 31, and book IX, chapter 3 of the *Etymologies*.

Although neither Isidore nor Biclarensis understood Hermenegild’s tyranny as cruel and barbarous rule, they could understand it as power seized contrary to right and justice. This is suggested in Isidore by the added words “against his authority.” For Isidore seems to imply that Hermenegild tyrannized against his father’s authority because he invaded his father’s power without any right.

Isidore regularly uses the word “tyranny” in this sense in the same *History*, as in the year 639 concerning Liuva:

> “Witericus, having seized tyranny, deprived him, while innocent, of the kingdom in the first flower of his youth.”

Moreover, in the *History of the Suebi*, does Isidore not call Hermenegild a rebel? Near the end, concerning Miro, king of the Suebi, he writes:

> “Then he went to Hispalis to assist Leovigild, king of the Goths, in attacking his REBELLIOUS SON.”

### 28

Joseph Perezius, in his most learned ecclesiastical dissertations published at Salamanca in 1668—of which favorable mention was made in the *Journal of the Learned* at Parma in 1690, p. 81—dealt with the words relevant to this question on p. 272:

> “But this surpasses all wonder: that the same Biclarensis, hostile to Leovigild the Arian and exiled by him, should write this concerning the holy martyr: ‘King Leovigild gathers an army to attack his tyrant son.’ Yet far more wondrous is Isidore, the brother of Leander, whom he regarded as a parent, who favored the Catholic party of Hermenegild and did not silently tolerate Leovigild’s crimes, and whom our historians report to have been related by blood to the martyr-prince—this Isidore, I say, seems almost incredibly to have committed these words to writing concerning Hermenegild: ‘He overcame his son Hermenegild, who, after being besieged, was tyrannizing against his authority.’ And although, concerning the miracles that occurred during his passion, Gregory the Great is an abundant witness, both writers maintain a profound silence . . . Yet despite the fact that they bristle with so many difficulties, all learned men accept them and do not bring either the *Chronicle of Biclarensis* or that of Isidore under suspicion of forgery [νοθείας].”

The Aguirrian collection of the councils of Spain had not yet been made public.

### 29

To extricate himself from these difficulties, Cardinal Aguirre argues, in volume II of *Concilia Hispaniae*, p. 422, that the *Chronicle of Biclarensis* was corrupted by some Arian in all the passages where Hermenegild’s tyranny and rebellion are asserted, since it makes no mention of his martyrdom.

But the learned cardinal labors in vain. Since all manuscript copies agree, and since many other clearer testimonies against the Arians in the chronicles of Biclarensis and Isidore remain untouched, he will not easily find supporters for his opinion.

Gregory of Tours, whom the most eminent Aguirre cites in his support, was also writing outside Spain at the same time and spoke of Hermenegild in a similar way, in book VI of the *History of the Franks*, no. 43:

> “The wretched man did not know that divine judgment was impending upon him, since he was contemplating such things against his father, however heretical he might be.”

Certainly no sane person will claim that these words were inserted in Gaul into the manuscripts of Gregory of Tours by some Arian heretic.

### 30

For this argument to be explained more clearly, several questions must be distinguished:

1. Whether Hermenegild acted unjustly when he undertook war against his father.
2. Whether, at least, the case was doubtful, so that some judged Hermenegild’s cause just and others judged it unjust.
3. Whether, even if Hermenegild clearly undertook an unjust war against his father, he nevertheless died a true martyr.
4. Whether, before the Moorish invasion of Spain, our writers mentioned the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild, or rather what the cause was of such silence concerning that martyrdom.

We cannot readily determine the first question, since we are unable to examine all the circumstances on which the justice of the war depends.

Florez, volume VI, p. 377, declares that Hermenegild initiated an unjust war against his father, and that certain cities adhered to Hermenegild for no other reason than that his father was a heretic.

From the *Chronicle of Biclarensis* under the year 579 it is clear that King Leovigild gave his son Hermenegild the daughter of Sisbert, king of the Franks—Ingund—in marriage, and granted him part of the province to govern.
