Once Hermenegild had been established as king, who can deny that some just cause might have arisen for him to defend the rights of his kingdom against his father?

### 31

Concerning the cause of the war, Biclarensis adds only this:

> “Therefore, while Leovigild was ruling in peaceful tranquility, the security of his opponents was disturbed by domestic strife [Al., ‘by domestic security’]. For in that same year his son Hermenegild, assuming tyranny through the faction of Queen Goswintha, shut himself up in the city of Hispalis after fomenting a rebellion, and induced other cities and fortresses to rebel with him against his father.”

He calls it “domestic strife” because the origin of the disagreement seems to have arisen from a quarrel between Ingund, the wife of Hermenegild, and Goswintha, the wife of Leovigild.

Florez contends that one should read “through the faction of Queen Ingund,” since Ingund is believed to have moved Hermenegild to wage war against his father. This is sufficiently probable. But since Ingund was Catholic, Goswintha Arian, and Florez himself agrees that Goswintha gave occasion for the quarrel—indeed, since Goswintha was, as Gregory of Tours says in book V, chapter 39, the chief cause of this crime, that is, of the persecution raised by Leovigild against the Catholics—whether one reads “through the faction of Ingund” or “through that of Goswintha,” there remains room to ask whether Leovigild, first moved by Goswintha, or Hermenegild, moved by Ingund, gave the cause for the war, and to which side justice favored.

For what if Leovigild, knowing that Hermenegild had converted to the Catholic faith, was the first to begin harassing his kingdom? Nor is this difficult to believe, since, as Isidore writes in the *Chronicle*, Leovigild, “filled with the fury of Arian perfidy,” began a persecution against the Catholics, banished many bishops into exile, took away the revenues and privileges of the churches, and also drove many by threats into the Arian plague, etc.

Would he have tolerated calmly the Catholic religion flourishing in Hermenegild’s kingdom, especially under Leander’s influence, and Catholics whom he had harassed taking refuge there?

Now hear Gregory the Great, who, after recounting Hermenegild’s conversion in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31, continues:

> “His Arian father, in order that he might return to the same heresy, attempted both to persuade him by rewards and to terrify him with threats.”

These circumstances seem to have given rise to the war. Saint Gregory immediately adds:

> “And when he answered with the greatest constancy that he could never abandon the true faith which he had once recognized, his angry father deprived him of the kingdom, etc.”

Gregory of Tours speaks more plainly of Hermenegild in book VI, chapter 39:

> “Moved by her preaching, he was converted to the Catholic faith; and when he was being confirmed, he was called John. When Leovigild heard this, he began TO SEEK PRETEXTS by which he might destroy him. But Hermenegild, understanding this, joined himself to the emperor’s party, etc.”

### 32

But Biclarensis and Isidore condemn Hermenegild’s action and represent it as a rebellion. This belongs to the second question.

For, as it seems to me, Hermenegild’s cause at that time was doubtful: some, as often happens, believed the reasons for the war adequate, while others considered them worthless.

I certainly think that Leander, a most holy and learned man, did not disapprove of Hermenegild’s war. As I showed in chapter 18, Leander was sent by Hermenegild to Constantinople to obtain assistance from the emperor against Leovigild. This is suggested by Gregory the Great’s words:

> “The embassy of the king of the Visigoths, entrusted to you on matters concerning the faith, had brought you there.”

After Hermenegild had been defeated and Recaredo was already reigning, at the time when Biclarensis was writing, either Leovigild’s reasons against Hermenegild had become clearer, or they had somehow acquired greater force from the outcome itself. Nor was it appropriate for those who perhaps still remained supporters of Hermenegild to be incited to new disturbances by reviving their former arguments in his favor.

### 33

The third point that I said must be investigated is absolutely certain: Hermenegild died a true martyr, even if we are willing to grant that he had begun an unjust war against his father.

It is irrelevant that Gregory of Tours, writing outside Spain and perhaps not knowing the whole course of events, called the wretched Hermenegild “wretched.” Concerning this passage of Gregory of Tours, Baronius writes under the year 584, no. 4:

> “But how prudent he was in this, let him judge for himself, since he calls Hermenegild WRETCHED, etc.”

As though the Lord had not warned him that devotion to God must be placed before father, mother, and everything else.

But we must consider above all the cause of the death inflicted, which Gregory of Tours seems not to have known. In my opinion, he constructed his account from the report of Oppila, the envoy sent by Leovigild to Chilperic. For Leovigild feared that Childebert might raise an army to avenge the wrong done to his sister, as Gregory relates in book VI, chapter 4, where he recounts the conversation he had with Oppila concerning religion.

Hermenegild was ordered by his father to be killed because he refused to renounce the Catholic religion, as the exceptionally reliable witness Gregory the Great fully narrates in book III of the *Dialogues*, chapter 31. He celebrates Hermenegild’s glorious martyrdom with the highest praise.

The ancient martyrologies of Usuard, Ado, Wandalbert, and Fulda agree. The same martyrdom of Hermenegild is proclaimed in many ancient chronicles.

It is also useful to observe that Gregory the Great’s *Dialogues*, which contain the history of Saint Hermenegild’s martyrdom, were not unknown to our Gothic fathers. For Ildefonsus praises them in chapter 1 of *On Illustrious Men* as follows:

> “He preferred to call this work the *Book of Dialogues*: in these books the diligent reader can easily recognize how many divine mysteries lie hidden and what wondrous lessons they contain concerning love of the heavenly homeland.”

Paul the Deacon of Mérida also wrote *On the Life and Miracles of the Fathers of Mérida*, so that, as he says in his preface, no one might doubt what “Gregory, the most holy and outstanding prophet, bishop of the city of Rome, inflamed by the spirit of the Paraclete’s gifts, set forth in the books of the *Dialogues* in a truthful style.”

But here again a greater reason for wonder arises. Paul not only had before his eyes Gregory the Great’s account of Saint Hermenegild’s martyrdom, but also copied certain words from Gregory’s narrative, while deliberately omitting any mention of Hermenegild.

Hear Gregory:

> “After his death, King Recaredo, FOLLOWING NOT HIS PERFIDIOUS FATHER BUT HIS MARTYR BROTHER, converted from the depravity of the Arian heresy and brought the whole nation of the Visigoths to the true faith, so that . . ., etc.”

Now consider Paul’s words in chapter 16:

> “After his most cruel death, the venerable prince Recaredo, his son, FOLLOWING NOT HIS PERFIDIOUS FATHER BUT CHRIST THE LORD, converted from the depravity of the Arian heresy and brought the entire nation of the Visigoths to the true faith through wondrous preaching.”

You see how Paul, in order not to name Hermenegild a martyr, even lost the elegance contained in Gregory’s words. For “following not his perfidious father but his martyr brother” is much more elegant than “following not his perfidious father but Christ, he converted from the depravity of the Arian heresy,” etc.

Paul was writing in Isidore’s time and, I think, passed over Hermenegild’s martyrdom in silence for the same reasons.

### 34

What, then, was the reason that the ancient Spanish writers left us scarcely any testimony concerning the martyrdom of so glorious a man? This is the fourth question.

For it is beyond dispute that scarcely any mention of his martyrdom is found among our ancient fathers or writers. Biclarensis, concerning Hermenegild’s death, says only under the year 585:

> “Hermenegild is killed by Sisbert in the city of Tarragona.”

And immediately, under the year 587:

> “Sisbert, the slayer of Hermenegild, is destroyed by a most shameful death.”

Biclarensis may perhaps have wished to win favor with Recaredo, who was then reigning and who might have been displeased to hear that his brother Hermenegild had suffered martyrdom by his father’s unjust command.

Gregory of Tours, who otherwise called Hermenegild wretched, relates that Leovigild had sworn that Hermenegild would not be humiliated; nevertheless, after Hermenegild had thrown himself at his father’s feet, he ordered his son to be sent into exile dressed in vile clothing, and afterward also delivered him to death.

What of Isidore, who remained entirely silent about Hermenegild’s death while writing in the time of Sisebut or Suinthila? Grialius and others suspect that something is missing from Isidore in which Hermenegild’s martyrdom was asserted.

There are indeed two Isidorian chronicles in the Urbino-Vatican Library, no. 382, formerly 606, and no. 392, formerly 609, in which the matter is expressed as follows:

> “The Goths, divided into two factions on account of Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild, are devastated by mutual slaughter, and he himself is crowned with martyrdom.”

But since these chronicles are interpolated in many places, including outside Spain, and since the ancient copies of the genuine Isidorian *Chronicle* lack these final words, we cannot cite Isidore in favor of Hermenegild’s martyrdom, nor even suspect that the *Chronicle* is mutilated in this passage. For who would have wished to delete those words from the most ancient copies, and for what reason?

### 35

Nicolaus Antonius takes another path:

> “Whatever may be said about this omission, whatever the author of the history may have been, provided that he was a Catholic, he deserves to be challenged. The work is nevertheless so brief that he appears to have wished to touch only upon the chief matters relating to the deeds of the kings. Yet the matter itself seemed to demand that, once Hermenegild had been mentioned in the *Chronicle*—or certainly in the *History of the Goths*, where other minor details are narrated at greater length—at least two words should have been added concerning his martyrdom. The example of Paul of Mérida, discussed in no. 33, also suggests that Isidore deliberately omitted mention of the death of Saint Hermenegild.”

### 36

The difficulty is increased by the fact that most other writers of the Gothic Church did not mention the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild, nor was an office performed for him by the Goths, or by the Mozarabic peoples who succeeded them, in their liturgies.

Perhaps no other Gothic father can be cited in favor of Saint Hermenegild’s martyrdom except the one whose work Florez first published only a few years ago in volume XVI of *Hispania sacra*: Saint Valerius the abbot. Having celebrated bands of martyrs in his treatise *On the Vanity of Secular Wisdom*, section 8, and more than a century having already passed since Hermenegild’s death, he says incidentally:

> “From the royal height we recall Caesar Crispus by name, Hermenegild, king of the Goths, Aucuia, king of the barbarians, Hippolytus the duke, Georgius the count, and a queen named Alexandria.”

The names Aucuia and Alexandria are perhaps corrupt. Crispus certainly should not be counted among the martyrs.

Yet Gregory the Great, relying on the testimony of Spaniards, gives an extensive account of Hermenegild’s martyrdom. He begins his narrative thus:

> “As we have recently learned from the report of many who come from the regions of Spain, King Hermenegild, etc.”

Some distinguish the words as: “we have learned; recently, King Hermenegild,” which I said in chapter 18 seemed less satisfactory.

The same holy doctor also provides testimony concerning the honor shown to Hermenegild by the Spaniards:

> “And so it came about that his body, as that of a martyr, ought rightly to have been venerated by all the faithful.”

There must therefore have been some political reason, originating in the time of Recaredo himself, why the Spaniards of that age were unwilling to commit Hermenegild’s martyrdom to writing.

I attribute this cause not so much to Recaredo’s wish to protect the memory of his father Leovigild, or to his attempt to extinguish the faction of the Spaniards who had supported Hermenegild, as to the fact that, while Hermenegild’s son was still alive, Childebert and Guntram, kings of the Franks, were plotting new measures against Spain, intending also to avenge the injuries which they believed had been inflicted upon Childebert’s sister Ingund and Hermenegild’s wife.

### 37

Paul the Deacon, in book III, no. 21 of *On the Deeds of the Lombards*, speaks to our point as follows:

> “Meanwhile, King Childebert of the Franks, waging war against the Spaniards, defeated them in battle. The cause of this conflict was as follows: King Childebert had given his sister Ingund in marriage to Hermenegild, son of King Leovigild. Through the preaching of Leander, bishop of Hispalis, and the exhortations of his wife, Hermenegild had been converted from the Arian heresy, from which his father suffered, to the Catholic faith. His impious father killed him by striking him with an axe on the very holy day of Easter. After the funeral of her husband and martyr, Ingund fled from Spain and, while attempting to return to Gaul, fell into the hands of soldiers stationed on the frontier against the Spaniards and Goths. She was captured with her young son and taken to Sicily, where she ended her days; but her son was sent to the emperor Maurice at Constantinople.”

Paul does not explain in what year the war occurred in which the Goths were defeated by Childebert, nor is this Frankish victory confirmed by the testimony of other historians. For after Hermenegild’s martyrdom Childebert took up arms against the Goths twice and was twice defeated with great slaughter of his forces—first in 585, then in 589, as Pagius calculates.

### 38

Gregory of Tours, speaking in book VIII, chapter 28, of the events in the tenth year of King Childebert—that is, the year of Christ 585—writes:

> “Ingund, abandoned by her husband while he was with the emperor’s army, died and was buried in Africa while she was being escorted to that prince with her young son. Leovigild, however, delivered his son Hermenegild, whom the aforementioned woman had borne, to death. Moved by these events, King Guntram sent an army into Spain, etc.”

This war, while Leovigild was still alive, was conducted by Recaredo, who, as Biclarensis records, returned victorious to his father and his homeland.

Then, in the year 587, as Gregory of Tours narrates in book IX, chapter 16, Recaredo, already a Catholic, sent envoys to Childebert and Guntram to establish peace and friendship. Childebert received them kindly, but Guntram replied:

> “What faith can they promise me, or how ought I to trust those who delivered my niece Ingund into captivity, through whose treachery both her husband was killed and she herself died in exile? I therefore do not accept Recaredo’s embassy until God orders me to avenge myself upon these enemies.”

The war of 588 followed. In it Claudius, duke of Lusitania, completely destroyed the Frankish army, as Biclarensis, Gregory of Tours, Isidore, and others unanimously relate.

### 39

While matters were therefore in this condition, it is not surprising that the Spanish writers were not very favorable to Hermenegild’s cause, especially since his son Athanagild was still living at Constantinople.

How long he lived is uncertain. But letters from Queen Brunichild and King Childebert of the Franks addressed to him as king and grandson are extant in volume I of Chesne’s *Historical Writers of the Franks*, p. 867, and in the appendix to the Maurist edition of the works of Saint Gregory of Tours.

I see that the most eminent Aguirre, in volume II of *Concilia Hispaniae*, p. 407, refers to a manuscript dissertation by Don Juan Lucas Cortes, in which Cortes demonstrated from ancient monuments that, through Athanagild, the son of Saint Hermenegild, the kings of Spain descended after several intervening generations.

Once this political reason for remaining silent about Hermenegild’s martyrdom had taken hold in the minds of the Spaniards, it was easier for the silence to continue thereafter, until, when the glorious martyr’s cult had been widely celebrated in foreign martyrologies and histories and Spain’s circumstances had likewise changed, public veneration was rendered to him in Spain.

### 40

These facts sufficiently prove the deference which I mentioned that the ancient bishops of Spain showed toward kings, often concealing many things lest offense or disturbance arise.

There are many other matters I could add, but since this discourse has become longer than I expected, I shall mention only one which also concerns Isidore’s history of the Goths.

At the end of the *Chronicle*, concerning Sisebut, he says:

> “He converted the Jews subject to his kingdom to the faith of Christ.”

Sisebut was evidently still alive at that time, and therefore Isidore prudently refrained from disapproving of his action.

But in the *History of the Goths*, after Sisebut’s death, he openly expressed his own judgment:

> “At the beginning of his reign, when he moved the Jews toward the Christian faith, he certainly possessed zeal, but not according to knowledge; for by force of power he compelled those whom he ought to have invited by the reason of faith.”

The other bishops held the same opinion, although no one is known to have opposed Sisebut’s law. For in the council convened at Toledo in the year 633, chapter 57, they ordered that thereafter no one should be compelled to believe [perhaps: “that force should be brought to bear on no one to believe”] . . . “as happened in the time of the most religious prince Sisebut,” etc.

### 41

There is a particular observation by Thomassinus, in volume III, book I, chapter 40, no. 14 of *On the Old and New Discipline of the Church*:

> “Nor is it contrary to truth that exceptionally holy men could sometimes turn aside for a time from the straight path and from the exact observance of canonical rules, whether through thoughtlessness, whether swept along by the force of custom, or whether, through some bond of charity of which I know not what kind, they adapted themselves to the will of the prince, from which they afterward hoped that richer fruits would return to the dignity and welfare of the Church.”

But this is more certain: many circumstances of such matters generally remain hidden, and if they were revealed, little labor would be needed in composing the defense of the most holy fathers of antiquity.

## CHAPTER LXXX

### Isidore’s Book *On Illustrious Men*: Editions of This Book and Manuscript Copies; Zaccaria’s Preface; Hardouin’s Ravings against Most Writings of Antiquity Criticized

### 1

Braulio’s preliminary notice concerning Isidore’s books is usually appended to Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*. That this was done in accordance with Braulio’s intention is clear, for he says:

> “One book, *On Illustrious Men*, to which we have appended these materials.”

Ildefonsus did not mention the book *On Illustrious Men* in his eulogy of Isidore, as Oudinus and Cellier observe. But they should have added that there was a sufficient reason for Ildefonsus’s silence: in his preface to the supplement, or continuation, of that same book, he clearly referred to it:

> “Next, the most prudent man, Isidore, bishop of the see of Hispalis, following the same course, added to the record whatever excellent men he found; for he departed without having investigated everything.”

And at the end of the preface:

> “Indeed, the blessed Gregory of holy memory had been recorded by Isidore; but because he did not say as much about Gregory’s works as we ourselves have discovered, we have removed his brief notice and recorded in fuller style whatever we know about him.”

Most other writers, cited in chapters 46 and 47, likewise attribute this same book to Isidore.

Sigebert of Gembloux, however, who also wrote a book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* and reviewed Isidore’s works, did not mention Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*. Nor does he seem to have read it, as Suffridus Petri observes in his dedicatory epistle and in his note on chapter 98 of Gennadius. Consequently, many persons are mentioned in both the works of Isidore and those of Sigebert.

Oudinus and Cellier excuse Sigebert’s and Ildefonsus’s silence on the ground that they did not mention Isidore’s historical works.

## 2.

There are, nevertheless, thus far three published copies: the first, shorter, comprising thirty-three chapters; the second, fuller, extending to forty-six chapters; and the third, consisting of those first thirty-three chapters with thirteen others appended as by an uncertain author, although in the fuller copy they are ascribed to Isidore. I would suppose that some error lies in another catalogue of Isidore, cited by Bayer in his note on Book V, no. 216 of the *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*, as follows:

> In the Cotton Library, in the manuscript *Julius*, letter F, no. 7, page 14, there is a *Catalogue of Illustrious Men, or Ecclesiastical Writers, from the Passion of Christ to the fourteenth year of Theodosius*, from Isidore of Seville. The book *On Illustrious Men*, comprising thirty-three chapters, the first of which is on Hosius, appeared in the earliest editions, such as Bignaeus’s and others. Grialius published the fuller book, consisting of forty-six chapters, with Isidore’s brief preface, illustrated by the notes of Joan Baptista Pérez, which Labbe calls “most learned” in his dissertation *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

But Labbe, along with many others, is mistaken in thinking that the notes of the Royal Madrid edition were composed by Loaisa. Whatever the truth may be concerning the assertion made by some that Loaisa joined his efforts with Grialius so that the corrected Royal edition might be published, this book was reprinted by Breulius. He first published the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers* as he found it in Bignaeus’s edition; then, having obtained the Madrid edition before completing his own, he took from it the expanded book *On Illustrious Men*, though in reverse order. For he placed first Ildefonsus’s book on the same subject, although he later recognized that it ought to have been placed afterward.

## 3.

Loaisa included in his *Collection of the Councils of Spain* the thirty-three chapters of Bignaeus’s edition and, after Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*, added thirteen further chapters, beginning with Pope Xystus and so forth, which he published without assigning them to any certain author. Others followed Loaisa’s example; and, astonishingly, Aguirrius himself did so in his *Collection of the Councils of Spain*, although he appears to have been entirely unaware of the Royal Madrid edition of Isidore’s works. For in the book of St. Ildefonsus he omitted the first chapter, which concerns St. Gregory the Great and is present in the Madrid edition, because he did not find it in Loaisa’s edition.

The Madrid edition is certainly to be preferred, as Zaccaria also acknowledged in the preface soon to be presented, although he himself wished to retain the order of Fabricius’s 716 edition because he had undertaken to have Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library* printed again.

## 4.

Florez published the same book of Isidore in Volume V of the *Hispania sacra*, revised with some notes of his own and following the standard of the Madrid edition. The most learned editor of the works of the Toledan Fathers also followed that edition in Volume I; in Volume II he illustrated it with learned observations on the *Life of St. Ildefonsus*, written by St. Julian, and on the *Life of St. Julian*, composed by Felix, bishop of Toledo. These two lives had appeared in the Madrid edition after Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*.

We cannot depart from this edition. There are indeed several codices in which the book begins with Hosius, such as the Codex Emilianensis mentioned by Bayer, written in the year 994, where, on folio 346, it reads: “Thus far Gennadius. From this point Isidore of Seville begins. 1. Hosius of Córdoba.” But besides the codices praised by Zaccaria, there are others that present the complete work in the form reviewed by Pérez, as will presently become clear.

Two codices also described by Bandini in chapter 44—the one Medicean, the other Florentine of Santa Croce—begin with Xystus, although Bandini adds that in the Medicean Codex, which he says resembles the Florentine Codex of Santa Croce, there are only thirty-eight chapters, arranged in a different order as well. Indeed, the final chapter is identified as being on Severus, whereas in the printed editions and most other manuscripts the book ends with Maximus of Zaragoza.

Although Nicholas Antonius was at times uncertain concerning the author of the thirteen chapters that Loaisa published separately, he nevertheless declared in Book V, no. 112, that it was fair to acknowledge Isidore as their author. Nor does anything oppose this judgment, expressed when he is discussing Isidore, merely because he later appears to doubt the matter. Since the *Old Library* is a posthumous work, and since what appears later in arrangement may often have been written earlier in time, we must hold that he first doubted the matter and committed that doubt to writing; then he abandoned his doubt, though—prevented by death—he did not erase what had already been written, as it were, in the wrong places, and left the work unfinished.

## 5.

I have seen the following handwritten codices:

- Vaticanus 1974, in which there is a *Life of Orosius*, attributed by some to Isidore in the book *On Illustrious Men*, but falsely, as I shall say in chapter 96. We shall relegate that *Life* to the appendices.
- Vaticanus 4827, chapter 97, containing Ildefonsus’s continuation of Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*.
- Regio-Vaticanus 119, Codex 717, discussed in chapter 99, in which only chapter 27—elsewhere chapter 14—on St. Fulgentius is found.
- Regio-Vaticanus 349, discussed in chapter 100, which contains the book *On Illustrious Men*, beginning with Xystus and adding Isidore’s eulogy by Braulio.
- Another Regio-Vaticanus, 551, in the same collection, begins with Hosius, as in Bignaeus’s edition.
- Urbinas 60, discussed in chapter 104, contains only the chapter on St. John Chrysostom.
- Urbinas 382, chapter 104, contains the book *On Illustrious Men* with Braulio’s preliminary notice and Ildefonsus’s continuation, in approximately the order found in Grialius.
- Ottobonianus 302, chapter 105, contains the chapter on the life of St. Julian of Toledo.
- Ottobonianus 849, chapter 106, contains the book *On Illustrious Men* in thirty-three chapters, with Braulio’s preliminary notice, beginning with Hosius.
- Ottobonianus 1720, chapter 106, has no title or preface: “On Pope Xystus,” and so forth, followed by Braulio’s preliminary notice on St. Isidore and St. Ildefonsus’s book *On Illustrious Men*.

## 6.

Zaccaria had prepared an edition of this book together with others on the same subject before he conceived the plan of printing all Isidore’s works. I possess his notes, collected from various authors, which I shall use in their proper place, and the preface that I append.

### Isidore’s Addition to the Books of St. Jerome and Gennadius on Ecclesiastical Writers Begins

### Preface to This New Edition

## 7.

I have preserved the title and order of Fabricius’s edition so that this edition might not depart too far from it. There were, however, reasons urging that both should be changed.

As for the title, since Braulio—that most ancient writer on Isidorian matters—expressly teaches that this book was entitled *On Illustrious Men*, it is surprising that Loaisa, Miraeus, Aguirrius, and others, passing over that title, coined this other one: *Addition to the Books of St. Jerome and Gennadius on Ecclesiastical Writers*.

## 8.

I shall speak of the order after reviewing the editions of this little book. These may be divided, as it were, into two classes.

The book was printed together with the other works of the Holy Doctor: in Paris in 1580, under the care of Margarino de la Bigne; in Madrid in 1599, with the notes of Joan Baptista Pérez, then a canon of Toledo and afterward bishop of Segorbe; and again in Paris in 1601, through the work of Jacobus du Breul.

In addition, when Suffridus Petri of the Carthusians [delete “of the Carthusians”] undertook to bring together in one volume those who had composed catalogues of ecclesiastical writers, he also published Isidore’s book at Cologne in 1580. 718 Garcia Loaisa likewise inserted it in his Madrid edition of the *Councils of Spain* in 1593.

To these was added the Frankfurt edition of Andreas Schottus, a most learned member of our Society, who had this very little book printed again in the *Hispania illustrata*, explained with his own notes. In 1629 Miraeus enlarged his *Ecclesiastical Library*, published at Antwerp, with the same book. Cardinal Aguirrius also—Volume III of the *Councils of Spain*, pages 71 and following—published this little work corrected and illustrated, with his own observations written in the margins and Schottus’s notes relegated to the end.

I pass over the Fabricius edition now before us.

## 9.

That Madrid edition, based on seven manuscripts, but especially on the copy from Font-Saint in the diocese of Coria, consists of forty-six chapters and begins with Xystus, bishop of the city of Rome.

Of the first fourteen chapters, if the fifth, on Hosius, is excepted, the other editions either omit the remainder entirely or append them as an appendix by an uncertain author to Isidore’s and Ildefonsus’s little books, beginning the Isidorian commentary with Hosius.

I for my part believe that these chapters genuinely belong to Isidore, together with the brief preface that will be found below. For there is nothing in these chapters [I supply *exstat*, “is found”] that is unworthy of Isidore.

Vossius says of Isidore (*On Latin History*, Book II, chapter 25):

> He also composed a little work on forty-six illustrious men, which exists in manuscript at Cambridge in the library of St. Benedict’s College, and at Oxford in Merton College.

These words indicate not merely any sort of work, but precisely that work divided into forty-six chapters which we possess in the Madrid edition. Thus the authority of two English codices reinforces that of the Spanish codex.

The brief preface that Miraeus objects to presents no difficulty if, with the most learned Pérez, it is referred to the books of Jerome and Gennadius. The order therefore ought to be changed, and the Madrid edition ought to be reproduced in full.

## 10.

Although I have not, as was proper, rejected either the title or the order of Fabricius’s edition, I have nevertheless collated much material so that this little book might appear in our edition as complete as possible.

I compared Fabricius’s edition with those of Madrid and Aguirrius and extracted the various readings from both. I also added the notes of Miraeus and Fabricius to my own, and did not omit the observations of Pérez, Schottus, and Aguirrius.

In this I followed the example of those who publish ancient authors with the notes of the Variorum. For I do not approve of Fabricius’s method, which I nevertheless retained for Jerome and Gennadius: sparing the printer and expense, and accommodating the haste of one who was publishing these various commentaries separately. Instead, I assigned each to its proper place, adding only the author’s name when presenting the observations of others, so that they might easily be distinguished from my own.

But I now turn to the book itself.

## 11.

From this preface it is clear that Zaccaria had planned to reprint Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library*. Although he mentions the printer’s haste, the undertaking was not brought to completion.

Among the papers of Zaccaria, now deceased, I saw a large bundle of sheets 719 intended for the edition I have mentioned, together with Fabricius’s *Ecclesiastical Library* itself.

What he says about the title is correct. Isidore followed Jerome and Gennadius; but Jerome’s own book is called by many *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, a title not alien to Jerome’s intention. For in Letter 89 to Augustine he asserts that the title of his book is called *On Authors* by many unskilled correctors, although it ought to be called *On Illustrious Men*, or more properly *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Isidore appears to have chosen the earlier title, *On Illustrious Men*, as may be inferred from Braulio.

Since I have brought forward both of Zaccaria’s prefaces, prepared by him for the publication of Isidore’s works, why should I either suppress his other labors in silence or claim for myself whatever glory might arise from them?

I hear that some people, although they have not yet seen what I am about to commit to print, commonly boast that I do not even mention Zaccaria. In this they are greatly mistaken for many reasons.

For if I consistently restore to each person what belongs to him, as may be seen on nearly every page, even when the matter concerns writings not generally known, why would I begrudge Zaccaria his praise?

Moreover, my own works, whatever their quality, differ so greatly from Zaccaria’s that even if I understand that glory would flow back to me from them were I their author, I still could not freely acknowledge them as my own unless I denied that the things I actually produce by my own efforts were mine.

If there are nevertheless some who possess too little judgment to distinguish different styles, they may, if they wish, see in the Zaccarian papers preserved by me—and readily shown to anyone—what Zaccaria actually accomplished.

For the signs of a work begun, followed after a few lines by its abandonment, are so evident that this may serve as a remarkable example of Zaccaria’s customary manner of writing. We are now less surprised that, although Zaccaria had long promised to reprint the history of the Council of Trent by Cardinal Pallavicino, greatly enlarged with notes and confirmed by documents, and although he had finally begun publishing it at Faenza, he nevertheless left it so incomplete that after his death the editor had to seek some learned man who would sprinkle the later volumes with a few slight notes, so that the edition might somehow be completed.

Indeed, Zaccaria, a man as learned as he was, who had a thorough knowledge of the innermost recesses and sources of scholarship, followed this practice in publishing many works, especially in illustrating the books of other authors: he arranged the writings and simultaneously sent them to the press, guided by much the same principle that Joachim Fortius himself followed and prescribed for others in chapter 24 of *On the Method of Study*:

> Tell the printers to prepare themselves: tell them that you wish to give them a book to print, even if you have not prepared a single page. Then you can easily conceive the whole appearance of the volume in your mind; next, lightly describe its individual parts in the manner of the plot of a comedy; finally, you will be able to complete each day as much as will be sufficient for them.

When you have begun something in this way, you must finish it, whether you wish to or not.

## 12.

In the prospectus of the Isidorian edition, Zaccaria promised that, using Dupin’s arguments, he would defend Isidore’s authorship of the book *On Illustrious Men* against Hardouin’s opinion.

Since no mention of this matter appears in the preface, nor of the other codices whose collation he had prepared for reviewing this book, it is evident that he had thought of publishing this book of Isidore’s long before, as I recently said, he conceived the plan of preparing an edition of all the works.

The arguments of Dupin that he hints at concern the authority of Braulio and Ildefonsus, which I have presented, and the testimony of Honorius of Autun. Dupin adds that he does not cite the words of Isidore of Badajoz because his *Chronicle* is not an undoubted document.

But neither Isidore of Badajoz mentioned Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, nor is his *Chronicle* of doubtful reliability—unless perhaps in the judgment of some foreigner ignorant of Spanish affairs, who thought that the *Chronicle* of Isidore of Badajoz should be placed among the chronicles fabricated in the seventeenth century by Pseudo-Dexter and others.

Against Hardouin’s opinion, Dupin insists that the style of this book resembles that of Isidore’s other works and that everything narrated in it agrees remarkably with truth and chronology.

## 13.

What Hardouin’s arguments were is not clear. Dupin merely reports that the author of the *Defense of the Letter of St. John Chrysostom to Caesarius* attributed this opinion to Hardouin: that Isidore’s book, like many others, had been fabricated in Gaul in more recent times. The author of that *Defense* promised that he would at some point present proofs of this claim.

If Dupin had fully understood Hardouin’s system, I think he would not have taken much trouble to refute it, especially by bringing forward the testimonies of Braulio, Ildefonsus, and Honorius of Autun, which Hardouin placed in the same period as Isidore’s book.

For Hardouin’s paradoxes—or rather his learned deliriums—were directed toward the claim that only in the fourteenth century all the ancient books now in our hands, except the Latin Bibles and a few others selected at his pleasure, had been fabricated by some society of atheists.

Hardouin sang a palinode, if indeed a man already, as I believe, deprived of reason could seriously conceive or retract so absurd a system.

We should not linger over its destruction. It is enough to point to the observations of the Fathers of Trivulzio in their *Ephemerides* for 1761, article 169, Volume II, October; and to the dissertation of Monsieur Maleville, Volume II of his work *On Natural and Revealed Religion*, translated from French into Italian and published at Rome in 1792, Volume I of the *Collection of Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*, by the distinguished Francis Anthony Zaccaria.

Just as Hardouin doubted Isidore’s book, so in this very year, 1796, Marcellinus Molkenbuhr of the Order of Friars Minor, in critical dissertation 18, chapter 4, has attempted to prove that St. Jerome’s catalogue *On Illustrious Men*, which Gennadius and Isidore followed, is spurious.

Although Molkenbuhr possesses much learning and great acumen, his arguments in this and similar controversies that he raises lead plainly to skepticism.

## 14.

Someone might doubt whether the expanded book of Isidore *On Illustrious Men* exists anywhere beyond the commonly published version.

For in the *Proper Offices of the Saints of Spain*, on 9 August, the lessons for the second nocturn of the holy martyrs Justus and Pastor are recited from the book of St. Isidore and the book of St. Ildefonsus *On Illustrious Men*, as the preceding rubric states; yet in the published book of Isidore no mention of those martyrs occurs.

But, as I think, the rubric has been attached incorrectly. Its basis may nevertheless have been that the hymns recited in the Isidorian office in praise of these martyrs are attributed by some to St. Isidore, as I shall say in the next chapter; or rather, that in Ildefonsus’s book, which is usually joined to Isidore’s book, chapter 2 praises Asturius of Toledo, who, as the passage relates, discovered the bodies of the holy martyrs after being warned by divine revelation.

For a similar reason I believe Notker was mistaken. Having seen Gennadius and Ildefonsus, bishop of Toledo, *On Illustrious Men* in one volume, he twice called Gennadius a bishop of Toledo in his own book *On Illustrious Men*, namely in chapters 7 and 11, 722 whom he declares to have treated this subject after St. Jerome, without mentioning Isidore and Ildefonsus—the latter of whom he ought to have called simply “the bishop of Toledo.”

Likewise, when Petrus Crinitus says in Book V of *On Latin Poets*, chapter 90, that Isidore testifies that Prudentius was trained in Latin letters with great diligence and equal zeal, he perhaps intended to name Gennadius, not Isidore.

I spoke shortly before of the *Life of Orosius* attributed to Isidore, when I listed the manuscript codices.

# Notice

Since Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* is, in the system I have decided to follow, the last among his genuine and certain works, and since this first volume has already reached its proper extent, what remains to be said about doubtful or spurious works must necessarily be reserved for the second volume.

In that volume, besides discussions of many other writings of lesser importance, I shall treat more fully the antiquity and translation of the Gothic Bibles, the Gothic liturgy, the genuine Spanish collection of sacred canons and the other, spurious, Pseudo-Isidorian collection, as well as the Code of Visigothic Laws.

In all these matters most people believe that Isidore played a major part, and it will be worthwhile to investigate what his role actually was.

Nor would I wish to omit from my Isidorian studies a diligent and accurate review of more than one hundred and seventy codices in the Vatican Library, in addition to those of the other libraries of the City that contain Isidore’s works.

This, apart from the fact that it may provide some benefit to literary history, in a certain sense redounds to Isidore’s glory and contributes greatly to the elucidation of his writings.

# ISIDORIANA

## To His Most Eminent and Most Reverend Highness, the Lord Don Francisco Antonio de Lorenzana y Buitrón, Priest-Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, Archbishop of Toledo, Primate of Spain and Grand Inquisitor, Grand Chancellor of Castile, Councillor of State to the King, Decorated with the Grand Cross of the Illustrious Royal Spanish Order of Charles III, etc.

### Faustinus Arevalus

When, at the beginning of this very year, I sent you, Most Eminent Prince, the first volume of the Isidorian edition, inscribed and dedicated to you, I thought that this was sufficient for you to understand that the remaining volumes, which would follow, should likewise be sent to you by the same route, even without a new letter.

For how could I have foreseen that in this very year you would come to Rome on a most honorable embassy entrusted to you by Charles IV, the Catholic and most pious King, to the Most Holy Lord Our Pope Pius VI, and that I would be permitted to approach your most eagerly desired presence, enjoy your most gracious conversation, and place this second volume in your most sacred hands as a kind of gift of welcome?

Now, amid the joyful acclamations of the Roman people and of every order, by which all proclaim you with one voice—your reputation, though sufficiently great in itself, being nevertheless praised as far greater—nothing remained for me by which I might congratulate you except to hasten the work undertaken under your authority, and owed to you in every respect, and to continue, insofar as I could, to place the works and teaching of Isidore, the Doctor of Spain, in a favorable light.

It has happened most conveniently, and I greatly rejoice at it, that, in accordance with the plan and purpose of the entire work proposed to me, many matters occur especially in this volume that belong to you by a particular right and that, as I both augur and hope, will not be displeasing to you.

For I must treat the Gothic Bibles, which are reverently preserved in the holy Church of Toledo; the Isidorian Office, or ancient Toledan Office; and the ancient laws of Spain, which are known to have been enacted chiefly at Toledo.

The Fourth Council of Toledo also must be illustrated by a new recension. It was the most celebrated of all the councils held in Spain, Isidore presided over it, and, in the opinion of the most learned men, he arranged its canons.

Why should I mention those matters that concern your most noble homeland, that ancient royal city, León? In that city your family, from the remotest antiquity, through an unbroken succession, by reliable monuments and memorial records, has preserved, defended, and advanced the splendor and dignity of the highest nobility with ancient fidelity and ancestral self-restraint.

For, besides the life of Isidore written by a certain canon of León, there is readily available the translation—celebrated long ago—of the body of our most blessed Doctor from Seville to the city of León, together with the extraordinary enlargement of his posthumous glory through innumerable miracles wrought by Almighty God at the tomb where his sacred remains rested, day and night, beneath the most august Eucharistic sacrament, exposed to perpetual veneration.

For the rest—and I shall close the letter with the words of Braulio to Isidore himself, for I find none more suitable either to my prayers or to your merit—I earnestly beseech the piety of the Most High Creator that, for the integrity of your faith and the stability of His Church, He may preserve the crown of your blessedness for a long time.

# ISIDORIANA, OR PROLEGOMENA TO THE EDITION OF THE WORKS OF ST. ISIDORE OF SEVILLE

## Part Three: On the Doubtful Works of St. Isidore and on Other Works Attributed to Him

### Chapter 81

Verses in the Library of St. Isidore. Other Poems Attributed to Isidore. The Hymns of St. Agatha and of the Holy Martyrs Justus and Pastor. An Exhortation to Repentance: *The Lament of Repentance*. Several Alphabets Attributed to Isidore. A Prayer for the Amendment of Life, and Another Against the Devil’s Snares, Appended to *The Lament of Repentance*. What the *Confession of St. Isidore*, Published by Constantine Cajetanus, Is. Other Prayers of St. Isidore from Alcuin.

## 1.

In the first volume, when the discussion turned to the certain works of St. Isidore, it often seemed appropriate, as occasion arose, to discuss other works that were not equally certain.

Now our entire discussion is directed toward examining those works that either are not certainly Isidore’s or may appear to have been falsely attributed to him.

Joannes Tamayus de Salazar was the first to publish, in his *Spanish Martyrology* under 4 April, the poems of the library of St. Isidore from manuscripts. Nicholas Antonius said that, in response to his generosity, one might sing Virgil’s line:

> I fear the Greeks, even when they bring gifts.

For the manuscripts of Tamayus are not what they wish to appear. It commonly happens that a liar is not trusted at all, even when he occasionally reports the truth.

Later Muratorius, unaware that they had already been published, issued the same poems among his *Anecdotes*, Volume II, under this title:

> 2. Very ancient verses that were once read in the library of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville.

Fabricius took them from Muratorius and reprinted them at the end of Volume V of his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

Although I had read in Muratorius that the verses had been taken from a very ancient codex, nevertheless in the *Prolegomena to Prudentius*, page 207, I had expressed some doubt as to whether the codex really was very ancient.

## 2.

Afterward, having obtained other arguments by which I came to believe that the verses were genuinely very ancient, I hinted at this in the *Prolegomena to Juvencus and Sedulius*, and now I openly affirm that no doubt can remain that verses of this kind have a very ancient author and, as we may believe, Isidore himself, although this is not entirely clear.

The same verses were published by Florez in Volume IX of the *Hispania sacra*, collated with Muratorius’s edition and with a manuscript of the Royal Library of Madrid.

Among the appendices to the recent edition of St. Isidore’s works, they were printed twice from the same Royal Library codex: first on page 47, with various readings, as well as the errors of the codex and several divergences from Tamayus’s edition; and again on page 67, as they had been edited by Florez, with Florez’s Spanish notes appended, which were then poorly translated into Latin at the end.

The inscription in the Royal Library codex is:

> Here begins the title of the library edited by Lord Isidore.

Florez notes that Muratorius allows these verses to be attributed to Isidore, whereas the title of the manuscript codex clearly establishes this.

## 3.

As for the antiquity of these verses, of which I was speaking, no one should doubt it, since, besides the codices of the Milanese and Madrid libraries, I have found them in other very ancient manuscripts as well.

Whether Isidore is the author is not equally certain.

Without naming the author, Julian of Toledo quotes one of these verses in his as-yet-unpublished work *On the Art of Grammar*, no. 355:

> I, once the truest teacher of Origen;

although in some printed editions it is incorrectly read:

> I, therefore, Origen, once the truest teacher.

Notker Balbulus excerpted another without naming its author in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 5:

> As it has been said before us: If Augustine is present, he alone is sufficient for you.

In Codex 421 of the Library of the Queen of Sweden, page 31, this inscription is expressly given:

> Eulogies of certain Fathers, by an uncertain author.

They are eulogies of Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, from the verses of Isidore’s library.

## 4.

This would not be particularly troubling unless there were also other codices in which an author other than Isidore was indicated.

Parchment Codex 3 of Queen Christina’s Library, 571, page 6 verso, presents the eulogy of St. Augustine under this title:

> Jerome’s verses to blessed Augustine: “He lies,” etc.

Immediately afterward it gives the eulogy of St. Jerome, as though composed by Augustine:

> Augustine to Jerome: “Bethlehem celebrates you,” etc.

It will be difficult to persuade learned men of this. These verses appear to have been written in a later age of Latin, and among the authors praised are several later than Augustine and Jerome, such as Sedulius, Gregory the Great, and Leander.

A more serious difficulty may be created by Codex 1 of the Vatican Archives, dating from approximately the tenth century. It contains Isidore’s *Etymologies*, and after Isidore’s dedicatory letter to Braulio—“Behold, as I promised you,” etc.—the following appears:

> Here begins Isidore’s book of the *Etymologies*. Prologue. There are here many sacred things, etc.

These are the first six verses, as in Muratorius.

The eulogies of the Fathers follow in this order: Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, John Chrysostom, Cyprian, Prudentius, Avitus, Juvencus, Sedulius, Eusebius, Orosius, and Gregory.

Then, in place of Leander’s title, Isidore is presented, together with the distich:

> You are not considered inferior to the ancient teachers,  
> Isidore, bishop. Your words teach this.

## 5.

There may be some controversy as to whether verses of this kind were written in the codices themselves or attached to statues or images of the authors, which were customarily placed above the shelves containing their works. Claudius Clemens discusses this practice at greater length in his work *On the Arrangement of a Museum or Library*, Book I, section 8 of chapter 3.

The following may be referred to this practice. Under the title “Cosmas, Damian, Hippocrates, Galen,” instead of a distich, it says:

> Those famous masters of medicine whom the world celebrates,  
> This present image marks as painted men.

But in my opinion this distich refers rather to an image of the authors that was customarily attached to the beginning of codices, as I shall demonstrate with many examples in chapter 105, nos. 32 and following.

Rusticus, in his letter to Eucherius of Lyon, published by Sirmond in Volume I of Sidonius’s works, speaks of a certain library in which, among images of various orators and poets adorned with epigrams, some verses of Virgil had been placed:

> Virgil the poet, etc.

Our Isidore traces the origin of placing images of authors in libraries to Pollio in Book V, chapter 5 of the *Etymologies*.

Some people inscribed verses on the bookcases themselves, as may be inferred from carmen 3 of Ennodius of Ticinum, concerning the epigrams made for the bookcases of Lord Faustus:

> You fashioned harmonious poems for diverse books;  
> Let the writing gladly receive what it has bestowed.

Perhaps another poem of the same Ennodius, no. 123, refers to this, under the title:

> In the chamber, above the codices placed in order.

After Isidore’s eulogy this title is added:

> To all readers of this codex:  
> Here is contained the broadest sequence of laws.

That is, the eulogy of Theodosius, Paulus, and Gaius, with the names omitted that appear as the title in the printed editions.

From this it may be inferred that verses of this sort were attached either by Isidore or by another author to the Code of Laws. I would believe the same of the other verses, which I suspect were affixed to the books of the authors praised, collected by Braulio or someone else from them into a kind of unified corpus, and marked with the title “Library of Isidore.”

Perhaps these were the codices that Isidore sent to Braulio together with the work of the *Etymologies*. Isidore says of them in his letter beginning “Your Holiness,” etc.:

> I sent the codex of the *Etymologies* on the journey together with other codices.

If this is so, it is sufficiently plausible that Isidore composed these poems in praise of the authors, and that Braulio added Isidore’s eulogy. Another person, thinking that all the verses were Isidore’s, may have substituted “the poet Leander,” together with Leander’s title, for “Bishop Isidore.”

It could also have happened that Isidore praised Leander in that distich and that someone else transformed the same eulogy into one of Isidore.

## 6.

For the present, this much is certain: in the very ancient Milanese codex it is asserted that these verses were once read in Isidore’s library; in another Madrid codex, that the title of the library was edited by Isidore; and I say nothing of Tamayus’s manuscript copy.

Moreover, Codex Regio-Vaticanus 215, dating from approximately the ninth century, quotes on page 125, among other verses used to confirm rules of prosody, the following verse from Isidore, as it expressly states:

> Our library too proclaims you through your books,

which appears in the eulogy of Jerome.

The Vatican-Palatine Codex 276 is also very ancient. On page 39 verso, after Isidore’s exposition of the books of Kings and Maccabees, it has this inscription:

> These are the verses of Isidore Palanensis [read: Isidore of Seville], bishop.

The title of the library is:

> There are here many sacred things, etc.

## 7.

But will it stand in the way of these arguments that these first six verses are found attributed somewhere to St. Damasus? Not at all.

They do not bear the style of Damasus, who never in his own verses made the *a* of the singular ablative of the first declension short, as poets of later periods commonly did. Isidore, however, has, in verse 4:

> You see meadows full of thorns and an abundance of flowers.

Beware, therefore, of Eugenius de Levis, who, in his *Anecdotes* published at Turin, not knowing that the first six verses of Isidore’s library—“There are here many sacred things,” etc.—had already been published, issued them under the name of Damasus on pages 17 and following. He believed them to be very similar in style to Damasus’s other poems and found them attributed to Damasus in a parchment codex of the Novalician Library, dating, as he says, perhaps from the ninth or tenth century, which contained the Epistles of St. Paul with St. Jerome’s prefaces.

The same Levisius falsely attributes two other poems to Damasus, although they agree neither with Damasus’s style nor with his period.

## 8.

Since in the Palatine-Vatican Codex I mentioned the inscription “Title of the Library” is prefixed as something particular to these six verses, while in the Novalician codex just mentioned the poem is said to concern the Epistles of the holy apostle Paul, someone may reasonably doubt whether the name “library” ought to be understood as referring to the sacred Scriptures, a meaning very common in ancient times, including in Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 5.

The two final verses most clearly suggest this interpretation:

> Here the venerable volumes of the Law shine forth in pairs,
Here the new and the old are joined together. Muratorius, Fabricius, Florezius, and others printed *gemmae* instead of *geminae*. In manuscripts, indeed, *m* is often confused with *in*; but the sense clearly requires *geminae*, as it is read without any uncertainty in our manuscripts of the Vatican Archives and the Vatican-Palatine Library, to which is added the Novalichian Codex cited by Levisius.

**9.** It was also the custom of the ancients to place similar verses before or after Bibles. In the second part of the poems of St. Eugenius of Toledo, poem 59, the title is: “Verses in the Library.”

> The books which the rule of faith commends us to know,  
> our present library contains.

> It bears the five venerable volumes of the Law.

And thus he continues concerning the books of the New and Old Testament; as you see, in the words “the venerable volumes of the Law” he reproduced Isidore. Alvarus of Córdoba imitates Isidore even more clearly. His poem appears in volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 281, under the title “Verses of Alvarus in the Library of Leovigild”:

> Here are many sacred things, and truly clear in doctrine;

and in verse 3:

> Here the new and the old alike are clearly adorned.

By that ninth century the practice had begun to gain strength of using the nominative in place of the ablative, as *vetera* in verse 6 for *veteribus*. This was commonly observed by Alvarus and his contemporaries. Florezius therefore ought not to have troubled himself over the words of Abbot Speraindeus addressed to Alvarus. He printed them as follows:

> I shall produce the testimonies of the Holy Scriptures, and, together with the sayings of the learned, I shall connect what I shall write in reply.

He added the note: “Read: *cum doctorum dictis atque vero*.” Rather, the connected wording should be retained: *cum doctorum dicta ut quivero, connectam*—that is, “I shall connect, as I shall be able, the sayings of the learned.” Thus, in the reply to the second part of Alvarus’s question:

> For while I derive this question from the persons of the sayings of Scripture, etc.

**10.** In Alvarus’s verses Florezius conjectures that one should read: *Septuaginta duos mittens sub vagina biblos*; the manuscript has *sub vargina*. I would prefer *sub margine*.

In the same volume XI of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 525, there are “Verses of Cyprian, archpriest of Córdoba, at the request of Zoilus, his son, placed at the end of the library which he had written for Saturninus, archdeacon.” Zoilus, a transcriber of Bibles, speaks as follows:

> I, grateful Zoilus, strive to repay to you the vows of praise,  
> to Christ the Redeemer, etc.

The first verse will stand properly if the word *Zoilus* is removed, since it may have entered from the inscription, or else if the word *gratus* is removed.

In these verses the Bible is called simply “a case” (*theca*), without any additional qualification. In other verses by the same Cyprian, however, which precede them on p. 522 and were written at the request of Adulfus for another copy of the Bibles, it is called “a case of books” (*librorum theca*).

You may read certain other poems of this kind in Blanchinus, volume II of the *Evangelarium Quadruplex*, p. 593 and following, where *bibliotheca* occurs with the same number of syllables as in Isidore:

> Blessed King, may the library please you, Charles,  
> which contains two Testaments to be read again.

**11.** Nevertheless, it cannot be said that all those first six verses were attached as a title to Isidore’s library and intended to refer to the sacred books, since it is asserted that many sacred things and many worldly things are there, and that there are roses as well as thorns. I therefore think that the final couplet,

> Here the twin books shine, etc.,

was composed for some codex of the Old and New Testament. The two preceding verses were intended either for a library—that is, a place where books are stored—or perhaps for some codex containing a mixture of sacred and profane materials, specifically poems; for verse 2 reads:

> If any of these poems please you, take it and read it;

although this verse is missing from the Codex of the Vatican Archives.

The Madrid Codex of the Royal Library also differs from the others in its first title. It applies the first title, “of the library,” to those verses which in the other codices are understood to concern the volume of the Laws; then it adds: “Another title: Here are many sacred things, etc.” In doing so, it omits the last two verses, which concern the New and Old Testament:

> Here the twin books shine, etc.

That the very ancient opinion was that the verses in question had been composed by Isidore himself to be attached to his library—that is, to his book cupboard—is demonstrated by the oldest catalogue of the Library of Lorsch, which I reviewed in chapter 46. There, among Isidore’s works, is listed:

> A summary of the same author on the books of sacred history, and the verses which he himself composed and wrote on his book cupboards.

**12.** In the new Madrid edition of the works of St. Isidore, p. 50 of the Appendix, eight hexameter verses are added which, it is said, were found in Codex 4, 6, 17 of the Library—presumably the Royal Library—after Blessed Isidore’s exposition of the *Song of Songs*:

> Solomon sang this, etc.

I too saw these same verses in Vatican Codex 650, concerning which see chapter 94, after the exposition of the *Song of Songs* commonly attributed to Gregory the Great; and in another Casanatensian codex, G. III, 1, concerning which see chapter 107, before Bruno of Asti’s exposition of the *Song of Songs*. On the basis of these witnesses I shall present a more accurate text.

For the present it is enough to point out that immediately after the first verse comes:

> He who holds the excellent things, etc.,

with no intervening blank space for another verse, as the Madrid edition indicates. The sense proceeds correctly even if no additional verse is supplied. Compare what I said about these verses in chapter 65, where I discussed the exposition of the *Song of Songs*.

**13.** There are other poems circulated under Isidore’s name. Montfaucon, in the *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, praises Codex 1512 of the Colbertine Library of the Royal Library of Paris, containing poems by Sedulius, Isidore the Younger, and Eugenius of Toledo. This, I think, is the codex identified in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris as 1093, partly of the ninth, partly of the tenth, and partly of the fourteenth century. Besides Sedulius and Dracontius, it contains several poems of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville.

Tamayo de Salazar, in the *Hispanic Martyrology* under 20 March, attributes to Isidore the epitaph of St. Martin of Dumio, born in Pannonia, etc., which Sirmond published after the poems of Eugenius of Toledo, p. 58, and appears to assign to Martin himself. Indeed, Martin speaks of himself:

> And following you, my patron, your servant Martin, bearing  
> the same name, though not the same merit, here rest in Christ’s peace.

Isidore would certainly not have said this of the most holy man Martin.

Bayer, in his notes on *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*, book V, 8, no. 181, observes that in an Escorial Codex of the beginning of the eleventh century, entitled *Forum judicum*, or the Laws of the Visigoths, there follows book three a short poem on the degrees of kinship under the heading:

> Verses of the lord Isidore on affinity, or the degrees of human relationships.

It begins:

> Behold those born hanging from the tree of law.

These verses, I think, present Isidore’s teaching concerning blood relatives and relations by marriage in book IX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 6 and following, and resemble other verses which I shall produce from Codices of the Palatine Library, nos. 282 and 283. I believe, however, that someone other than Isidore was their author.

**14.** Fabricius, together with the Bollandists under 5 February, p. 596, attributes to Isidore two hymns in honor of St. Agatha. One begins:

> Be present, most faithful people,

and the other:

> The illustrious feast appears, gleaming.

These two hymns do indeed occur in the so-called Isidorian Breviary, but that is no reason to say that they were composed by Isidore unless this is established from another source, since many other hymns by other authors are found in the same Mozarabic Breviary.

For this reason I said in chapter 3, no. 6, that Constantine Cajetanus had rashly attributed to St. Isidore the hymn *Urbis Romuleae*, for the feast day of the Seven Apostles.

And to state plainly what I think: these two hymns of St. Agatha are neither Isidore’s nor of his period. Hernandez, in his notes on the prospectus of Zaccaria’s edition, declares that they should be removed from Isidore’s works.

Both are merely rhythmic; the second entirely rejects the laws of meter. Although some verses of the first are metrical—for it is easy to produce an iambic dimeter even without deliberate effort—and although some others might perhaps be improved by correction, the author does not seem to have taken care over meter.

What is more decisive is that the first hymn mentions, as I believe, the rule of the Muslims, in stanza 12:

> You who once rescued your fellow citizens  
> from a great fire,  
> now restore us to freedom,  
> when the worst yoke has been removed.

What is this “worst yoke”? Perhaps those who maintain that the proper offices did not enter the Mozarabic Breviary and Missal after the destruction of the Gothic kingdom will answer that the hymn refers to the Gothic rule, before the Goths converted to the Catholic faith.

But apart from the fact that “the worst yoke” suggests the tyranny of the Muslims more naturally, it is difficult to believe that at the time before the conversion of the Goths such barbarous hymns were composed, when some measure of good Latin still remained in Spain. I have other reasons for thinking that the proper Gothic offices received some additions during the period of the Mozarabic rite, which I shall explain in a more suitable place.

The feast of St. Agatha is indicated in Francesco de Pisa’s Gothic-Hispanic Calendar, but it is omitted from the Gothic Orational of Verona.

**15.** Older and more elegant than the hymns of St. Agatha is the hymn for the feast of the martyrs Saints Justus and Pastor, on 6 August:

> O eternal Word of God, uttered from the Father’s mouth,  
> you who apply an instrument to the weakness of infants, etc.

Whether one considers its Latin or its metrical rules, this hymn may be assigned to the Isidorian age or to a somewhat earlier period.

Blanchinus, in his notes on the Gothic Orational, together with Tamayo in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, attributes this hymn to Asturius, bishop of Toledo and the first bishop of Complutum, to whom the bodies of the holy martyrs had been divinely revealed. Florezius considers this sufficiently plausible, volume VII of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 177.

In the proper Hispanic offices, nine stanzas of the same hymn are recited at Vespers, beginning with the third stanza:

> Behold Justus, behold Pastor, both joined by blood,

preceded by the rubric:

> Hymn of Blessed Isidore.

This does not happen in the other cases, even when the hymns have been taken from the Isidorian, or Mozarabic, Breviary.

I also said in the preceding chapter that the lessons for these same martyrs, extracted for the second nocturn, are said to come from Isidore’s book and from Ildefonsus’s *On Illustrious Men*. I certainly do not place great authority in rubrics of this kind; but neither do I see any reason to attribute the hymn to anyone rather than Isidore. As I said, it seems to me to bear the character of Isidore’s age.

The first verse,

> O eternal Word of God, uttered from the Father’s mouth,

is also the beginning of a hymn in praise of the apostle St. James, which is found in the Isidorian Breviary. I have revised several verses of the hymn of Saints Justus and Pastor according to the requirements of chant and meter in the *Hispanic Hymnody*.

**16.** I have discussed sufficiently, in proportion to the importance of the matter, in chapter 76 what sort of astrological poem it is that begins:

> You perhaps in the grove, etc.,

and whether it is Isidore’s. In the same place I spoke of a metrical abridgment of the book *On the Nature of Things*, which I would prefer to attribute to St. Eugenius of Toledo.

Certainly, the verses of the first poem concerning the seven days belong to Eugenius, as is clear from his works and from several Vatican manuscripts. In Palatine Codex 930, however, the title has been erased.

This codex contains several as yet unpublished letters of illustrious men. Although a more recent rubric states that few of them are good and most are useless, they would nevertheless not be printed without benefit. I shall therefore, I think, please some readers if I describe the codex with somewhat greater care.

It is a parchment quarto, written in a small script of approximately the tenth century, mutilated at the beginning. The letters are from princes, bishops, abbots, and others. Verses are interspersed, some of which seem to belong to the authors of the letters, as in the first:

> For the sake of him whom we all believe to be supreme,  
> give me what I have asked, that you may hold the joys of heaven.

On the verso of p. 4, Abbot Humbert writes to the empress C. On p. 5 is a letter of Bobbo, archbishop of Worms, as can be gathered from other letters. On p. 9, verses of Juvencus are quoted without the author’s name:

> … But he  
> in whose hands the farmer’s spade is held,

Juvencus says in book 1, verse 378:

> And in whose hands the farmer’s spade is held.

**17.** On pp. 14 and following come abusive letters to Charles and Charles’s letters to Dietheric, etc. The subject is Lothair, whom Charles succeeded.

On p. 20 certain enigmatic verses are inserted. With an explanation supplied later, they teach how the sound of bells can be made clearer. The discussion concerns five bells of Cologne, for which a specific measure of the clapper is prescribed.

On p. 41 there is a letter from the clergy of Worms and Mainz to the emperor H., that is, Louis, as pious as he is wise, against Frederick of Utrecht.

On p. 47 are verses of Eugenius of Toledo on the plagues of Egypt, without the author’s name:

> The first plague of Egypt, etc.,

book I of the poems, no. 20.

On the verso of p. 48 is the heading:

> Here begin the sayings of philosophers on speaking against complainers about all things.

I shall cite certain words of Cicero which do not occur to me in his works.

Cicero’s definition:

> There are no more hidden plots than those which lie concealed under the appearance of duty, under some name of relationship. For you can easily avoid an adversary who is openly hostile by taking precautions; and the Trojan horse deceived precisely because it falsely assumed the form of Minerva. The common enemy of all is he who is the enemy of his own people.

At the end are the verses I have already mentioned, by Eugenius of Toledo, on the seven days. In verse 2 one reads *splendifluus*, and in verse 6 *reptans hominesque sagaces*; the remainder agrees with the published text.

**18.** If we wish to assign a place among the appendices to certain poems found in ancient codices of Isidore, a short poem may perhaps not seem unworthy of inclusion. It precedes the books of the *Etymologies* in the most ancient Royal-Vatican Codex 1953, of the eighth or ninth century, after Isidore’s letters to Braulio and Braulio’s letters to Isidore.

These are verses in praise of the Mother of God, and they might appear to be an invocation for the completion of the work, unless the fact that they are written in a different, although ancient, script presents some slight obstacle.

I would rather attribute such verses to Ildefonsus than to Isidore, for Ildefonsus’s devotion to the Blessed Virgin is famous, and Julian of Toledo reports in his Life that the fourth book of Ildefonsus’s works was composed in a mixture of verse and prose.

This copy of the *Etymologies* appears to have been collated with another in which Ildefonsus added something at the end of book V after a brief chronicle. For in an ancient script, though not by the first hand, one reads:

> All time is reckoned from the beginning of the world up to the present tenth year of the glorious Recceswinth, which is era DCLXVI, years V DCCCLVII.

The remainder of the sixth age is known to God alone.

At this time Ildefonsus presided over the see of Toledo. Just as he expanded Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men* and brought it down to his own time, so he is also said to have continued the *History of the Gothic Kings*.

**19.** In the observations of the distinguished Hernandez on the prospectus of the edition outlined by Zaccaria, which I presented in chapter 42, it is noted that the *Exhortation to Repentance*, included by Breulius among Isidore’s works, is almost entirely metrical.

The learned man is right to observe this, provided that we do not understand “meter” in its proper sense, but in a broader sense—that is, as political verses, in which prosody is not observed. For in that *Exhortation*, which until now has been published in the manner of prose, there is no properly metrical verse, that is, none composed with the correct quantities of syllables.

Verses in which the law of meter is disregarded are called rhythmic—not in the ordinary sense in which *rhythm* means the concord of sounds, but insofar as rhythm denotes numerical pattern. For what is observed is the number of syllables, not their quantity. The Greeks also call such verses “political.”

The verses of the *Exhortation to Repentance* preserve the number of syllables proper to hexameter verses and resemble those used by Commodianus in his *Instructions*, which begin:

> Our preface points out the way to the wanderer,  
> and a good prospect when the end of the age shall come.

In the same way the *Exhortation to Repentance* should be divided:

> Why do you waver, soul, shaken by storms of sorrow?  
> How long will you be troubled by manifold thought?  
> Confused mind, wearied by tedium, taking the byways of the journey.

And so the work should be copied throughout—not, as Breulius published it, as continuous text in the manner of prose.

**20.** From a manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Maur Fossatensis, formerly a regular house, Nic. Faber had this little work transcribed; Breulius then received and published it. It was omitted from the recent Madrid edition of the works of St. Isidore, as were several other works added by Breulius to the Madrid royal edition.

Breulius’s title is:

> Exhortation to Repentance by St. Isidore, archbishop, with consolation and the mercy of God, addressed to a soul fearing the future judgments.

Nic. Antonius suspects a corruption beginning with *misericordia* (“mercy”).

I do not know whether another manuscript copy exists, or whether it differs from the one which Conrad Gesner affirmed in his time to be preserved in the Zurich Library in his *Bibliotheca*. For that Zurich Codex also contained the three or four little works which Breulius published together.

I find no one before Hernandez who questioned whether this work and the three others which Breulius appended—namely, the *Lament of Repentance*, the *Prayer for the Correction of Life*, and the *Prayer against the Snares of the Devil*—were genuine productions of Isidore.

Oudin says that there is nothing in them by which they should be removed from Isidore. Cellier asserts that none of these four little works contains anything unworthy of Isidore.

Nic. Antonius says of the *Exhortation to Repentance*:

> It is not contrary to the style, purpose, or practice of our most pious writer.

As for what he adds—that the vernacular author of the book entitled *Valerio de las historias* remembered, among other works of Isidore, book VI *On the Consolation of Souls*—I do not refer this to the *Exhortation to Repentance*, but to the *Synonyms*.

**21.** Theophilus Spizelius assigned this work and the next two a place, from Breulius’s edition, in his systematic collection of works entitled *Selected Monuments and Documents of the Ancient Learned Men and Ecclesiastical Writers Concerning True and Sincere Conversion to God*, Augsburg, 1685.

He first placed the *Exhortation to Repentance*, or prayer, beginning:

> God of all wonders, etc.,

then added the *Alphabet of the Penitent*, and finally the *Exhortation*, which he calls the second, to repentance, with consolation, addressed to a soul fearing the future judgments. Breulius places this last work first.

Spizelius’s preface to these three works of Isidore is as follows.

**22.** Having shown in the tenth section of our *Institution* that, after devoting very great effort to profane studies, he became a most distinguished convert to sacred *metanoia* and, turned from vain to sound studies, held forth as it were a torch to learned persons sincerely repenting, we shall now present that same Isidore, especially conspicuous for his eminent and illustrious proclamation of repentance; and shall learn with what fervor of piety he exhorted mortals wandering from the path of Christian virtue to the practice of repentance by his own example, and stirred them to amend their most corrupt life and morals.

One point deserves particular attention: when Isidore of Seville was near death, following the example of the doctor of Hippo, he summoned that ancient companion of his, repentance, so that he might die, as it were, in her hand and bosom. We shall cite as witness the cleric Redemptus, who thought it necessary to record the death of blessed Isidore and to commemorate his final deeds and words:

> Stretching out, etc.

Compare Constantine Cajetanus’s trilogy of holy bishops, etc.

**23.** I would not wish to approve what Spizelius calls Isidore’s “vain studies,” unless by this he means profane studies, from which, nevertheless, no small benefit flows into the sacred disciplines.

In the *Exhortation to Repentance*, Hernandez considers the mention of Cyprian the magician, later a priest and martyr, foreign to Isidore, since none of Spain’s sanctorals mention him.

The words of the *Exhortation* are:

> And thus Surius, Cyprian, from magician a priest and martyr.

Hernandez suspects that one should read:

> And thus the Syrian Cyprian,

and, as to why the author should be thought to have written *Surius* or *Syrus*, he refers the reader to the Bollandists under 26 September.
