There, in no. 75 and following, the Bollandists show that St. Cyprian, who had previously been a magician, was not from the Syrian city of Antioch, but from another city of the same name, perhaps Antioch, the metropolis of Pisidia.

Certainly the rhythm would not hold if *Surius* were read; *Syrus* could stand. But I think one should read:

> And thus Cyprian, from magician a priest and martyr,

with the name *Surius* rejected to the margin, where this note now appears:

> Concerning him, volume V of *The Saints*, 26 September,

without the name of the author who discusses Cyprian in that volume.

Breulius therefore wrote in the margin: “Surius, concerning him, volume V of *The Saints*, 26 September.” Through the compositor’s carelessness, the name *Surius* entered the text from the marginal note.

Everything fits remarkably well. Under 26 September, Surius, in volume V of *The Lives of the Approved Saints*, presents from Metaphrastes the Life and Martyrdom of Saints Cyprian and Justina. There he remarks that Metaphrastes appears to have fallen into error in saying that this Cyprian was bishop of Carthage.

**24.** There is no reason to regard as unworthy of Isidore the mention of Cyprian, first a magician and afterward a bishop and martyr. Why could Isidore not have believed what the very learned men Gregory of Nazianzus and Prudentius—whom Isidore is known to have read—openly affirmed, and what Metaphrastes and others later transmitted?

I have said more on this subject in my commentary on hymn 13 of the *Peristephanon*. I do not now have time to repeat why, in this question, one should believe the most authoritative writers, who assert that Cyprian practiced magic before his conversion, rather than later authors, however critical, who employ a negative argument.

**25.** From the manuscript codex of the library of Saint-Maur Fossatensis, Breulius also published the *Lament of Repentance*, arranged according to two alphabets, except that three letters—A, B, and N—are extended over a greater number of verses, in which the speaker pleads for the forgiveness of sins.

Nic. Antonius calls the work metrical; I would prefer “rhythmic,” in keeping with the practice of the age, which observed sound alone and not the strict laws of prosody. The verses retain the number of syllables proper to trochaic meter, while disregarding quantity.

> Hear, O Christ, the sad and bitter song,  
> which the stricken and contrite spirit modulates.  
> See the streams of tears, and listen to the groans.

This is the first stanza, and the remaining stanzas proceed in the same manner, numbering 110.

**26.** This same poem, but mutilated and containing only sixty-two stanzas, appears in the Life of Isidore by a certain Canon of León, commonly thought to be Luke of Tuy, published by the Bollandists.

The author of the Life introduces it as follows. Nic. Antonius, who sent the Bollandists a copy of this Life, reports the passage in the library:

> After he had published the alphabet of the uneducated, the verbal alphabet, the alphabet of theological distinctions, and the alphabet of books, he wrote an alphabet of prayer, bringing the work to an end with a prayer; he wrote an alphabet lamenting the future errors of the Gothic people and their downfall, in which he daily sang psalms to the Lord. We have thought it appropriate to record this in the present work. Here begins the alphabet of prayer for repelling the assaults of the adversary and obtaining the grace of God, published by Isidore of Seville, archbishop of the Church, of holy memory.

From this title the preceding words may perhaps be emended to read: “bringing the work to an end with a prayer, he wrote an alphabet of prayer”; or, as the Bollandists punctuate it: “bringing the work to an end with prayer, he wrote an alphabet of prayer.”

Ambrosius Morales, book XII, chapter 21, testifies that he read this poem in a manuscript book of the College of Complutum. Bayer asserts that it is found in two copies in the Escorial Library.

Nic. Antonius is surprised that such an alphabet is missing from the Madrid royal edition. It is even more surprising that it is missing from the recent Madrid edition.

The editor says in his prologue that it was not included in his edition because he was informed only belatedly that it existed in the *Acta Sanctorum*. But what shall I say of the negligence by which he neither read Nic. Antonius himself nor kept before his eyes Breulius’s edition, which is by no means rare?

**27.** Hernandez raises no objection to the *Alphabet of Repentance*. Nevertheless, together with the *Exhortation to Repentance* and the two prayers that follow, he rejects it as apocryphal.

There is, however, a special reason for attributing this alphabet to Isidore. It is known to exist in many manuscripts; the author of the Life attributes it to him; and long before Sigebertus listed among Isidore’s other works:

> The Lament of the Penitent, arranged alphabetically, with a prayer added.

From this, I think, Trithemius designated it:

> The Lament of the Penitent, book I.

The author of St. Isidore’s Life asserts that in this alphabet of prayer Isidore lamented the future errors and downfall of the Gothic people. Perhaps he had in mind these words:

> You have made the hand of the plague weigh more heavily upon me,  
> crushing my flesh with the punishment of dreadful scourges,  
> with slaughter, iron, filth, pestilence, and the prison of darkness.

But prayers of this kind, whether composed in verse or prose for the use of penitents, generally included both all the sins human beings are accustomed to commit and the punishments God is accustomed to inflict, so that they might be recited indiscriminately by everyone. There is no need, therefore, to resort to a prophecy concerning the destruction of the Gothic people.

The author is certainly ancient, learned, and pious; nor do I see why we should depart from Isidore. In the final stanza the author himself called the poem an alphabet:

> Now, keeping watch, I shall sing the glory as I finish the Alphabet.

**28.** As for the other alphabets mentioned by the author of the Life, we have been unable to discover anything about them from other sources.

Nic. Antonius, in the *Bibliotheca vetus*, first calls one of them the “Alphabet of the uneducated.” But since the work was posthumous, it may perhaps have happened that his words were not properly understood by the editor.

For the Bollandists, from the copy Nic. Antonius sent them, report the wording as follows:

> After he had published the *Alphabetum Papiae judicum* [“Alphabet of the judges of Papia”; reading uncertain], the verbal alphabet, etc.,

and add in a note:

> Perhaps *Patriae*?

Nicolaus Antonius notes that this error cannot be corrected, since no one remembers any such alphabet.

Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca media*, conjectures that one should read:

> The Alphabet of patronymics.

Since the author of the Life joins these alphabets together, he seems to imply that all were similarly composed in verse or rhythm.

Otherwise, we might suspect that under these titles are concealed lists of words arranged alphabetically: the names contained in book X of the *Etymologies*, the book of the *Differentiae*, in which distinctions between words are explained in alphabetical order, or some glossary long famous under Isidore’s name.

Book X of the *Etymologies* may indeed also have circulated separately. I judge the same concerning certain other books or titles: the *Etymologies* was largely formed from them, whether they had been reduced to an abridgment or left entirely unchanged.

A work with the title *Alphabet* and no author appears in parchment octavo Codex 164 of the Royal-Vatican Library:

> Alphabet of narratives useful for rightly shaping one’s life.

Pezius, in the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, no. 12, lists from the Melk Library an *Alphabetary of Divine Love* by Nicholas Kempli of Strasbourg, a Carthusian.

**29.** The prayer which Breulius published from the aforementioned manuscript must not be separated from the *Alphabet of the Penitent*. It bears the following title:

> Here begins the prayer of St. Isidore, archbishop, for the correction of life, to lament sins continually.

Sigebertus joined it to the *Lament of the Penitent*:

> The Lament of the Penitent, arranged alphabetically, with a prayer added.

Indeed, the author himself says at the beginning:

> Therefore, rising up and addressing you with cries of lamentation, knocking at the hearing of your mercy with manifold prayer, through the alphabet which I prefixed, moistening each of its letters with a stream of tears.

Perhaps one should read *rigavi*, “I moistened,” instead of *rigans*, “moistening.”

Hernandez offers two arguments for refusing to attribute this prayer to Isidore. First, the author uses the common Latin version of Holy Scripture, which, he says, was not used in the seventh century either by the holy Fathers or by the Spanish interpreters. Second, the statements made in the prayer concerning repentance and satisfaction are taken from book VI, final chapter, of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, and from book II, chapter 13, of the *Sentences*.

**30.** As regards the Latin version of the Bible, it is by no means surprising if Isidore sometimes cites the words of Holy Scripture differently from the way they are read in the Gothic Bibles. Since he was especially versed in the writings of other Fathers, and for the most part spoke in the words of others rather than his own, it follows that passages of Holy Scripture cited by him ought not always to be referred to the version found in the Gothic Bibles. The learned Mariana precisely touched the point in his notes on book I *Against the Jews*, chapter 2:

> This Psalter of Isidore, used by the Mozarabs, we shall hereafter call Hispanic, in comparison with the Roman and Gallican Psalters. Throughout this work Isidore adduces testimonies from all these Psalters, as was more convenient or as memory more readily suggested. He also uses indiscriminately, in the other books of Holy Scripture, Jerome’s version and the old Vulgate Latin edition; for both circulated in his age, as Gregory teaches at the beginning of the *Morals*, and Isidore himself indicates in book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4 … Often also, as he did in this place, he weaves together a single testimony from various translations.

**31.** Weak, then, is the argument drawn from the words of Holy Scripture cited in the *Prayer* to prove that it is not Isidore’s. Yet I do not understand why Hernandez denies that the Vulgate version of the Bible was in use among Spaniards in the seventh century. For what other version do the Gothic Bibles present—except for the Psalter, which agrees with the Psalter of the Basilica of St. Peter—than the very version of St. Jerome recognized in our Vulgate? There are indeed some discrepancies between the Gothic Bibles and the Vulgate version as we now have it; but this difference must be attributed to the diversity of manuscripts, or even to the fact that Isidore, as some think, revised the version found in the Gothic Bibles—though I consider this less certain. But the Gothic Bibles must be discussed more fully elsewhere.

For the present I merely observe that the *Prayer for the Correction of Life* contains some passages of Holy Scripture taken from the Gothic Bibles, as, from Jeremiah, chapter II, verse 23: *cursor levis explicans vias tuas*, “a swift runner tracing out your ways.” Thus read both the *Prayer* and the Gothic Bibles; the Vulgate has: *vias suas*, “her ways.” Nor does Sabatier produce from the old Italic version or from the Fathers the reading found in the Gothic Bibles and the *Prayer*. I have no doubt that many more such instances will occur to anyone who compares the *Prayer* with the Gothic Bibles themselves, which are kept at Toledo. For the *Prayer* contains many things that plainly differ from the reading of our Vulgate.

**32.** Nor should it matter much that certain things in the *Prayer* may seem drawn from the books of the *Etymologies* and the *Sentences* (for this was Hernandez’s second argument). For I have often already observed, and shall not tire of observing more often, that Isidore’s manner of writing was to compile from his own writings no less than from those of others whatever was suitable to the matter. It is certain that most other Fathers did this as well, especially those of the later age; and unless we assume this in Isidore, we could easily call almost all his works into question.

**33.** Breulius appended the *Prayer of Saint Isidore against the Snares of the Devil*, which is brief and was composed either for the *Alphabet of the Penitent* itself, or for another of those lost alphabets, or perhaps for the *Exhortation to Repentance*, which, as we have seen, likewise consists of rhythmic or political verses. Hernandez advances nothing particular against this prayer, but insists that it is by the same uncertain author as the prayer for the correction of life.

He more rightly declares that the prayer published by Constantine Cajetanus differs in no way from the final chapter or section of book I of the *Synonyms*. Cajetanus entitled it:

> Prayer, or confession, of Blessed Isidore, bishop and doctor.

He added this note:

> Apart from the fact that we remember having copied this prayer, composed by St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, from a very ancient manuscript codex in the library of our monastery at Subiaco, we have nothing else concerning it worthy of observation.

But since Cajetanus reproaches Canisius and Possevinus for failing to notice that the book *On Converts* is contained in Isidore’s books of the *Sentences*, he has no excuse for failing to discover this, his own *Prayer*, in the books of the *Synonyms*. It was later published by Tamayo de Salazar in the *Hispanic Martyrology* under 4 April; and Bandini notes it from the Florentine library of San Marco, volume IV of the Latin codices, pluteus 19, parchment Codex 10 in octavo, of the thirteenth century, formerly for the use of Brother Antonio Bindi of the Order of Minors. It contains certain works of Gregory the Great and others, and on p. 361 the prayer of Blessed Isidore, beginning *Succurre mihi* (“Come to my aid”) and ending *Trinitas sancta*, etc., as in Cajetanus.

34. Alcuin transcribed certain prayers of Isidore, of which others make no mention, in the work entitled *Offices for the Weekdays*, or *Psalms arranged according to the individual days of the week, which are sung in church, together with prayers, hymns, confessions, and litanies*. On Thursday there is Isidore’s Prayer for All Christians: “O Lord God, graciously hear,” etc. On Saturday: “Prayer of Saint Isidore: Blessed are those servants whom, when the Lord comes, he will find watching. Blessed is the vigil,” etc. After the litanies, among other prayers, there is “Prayer of Saint Isidore: You, Lord, true teacher, giver, advocate, and judge,” etc. Also one of the same author: “With what weeping shall I begin to weep for my evils? With what tears shall I mourn my crimes?” etc. [Col. 0588D] Immediately afterward: “Prayer of Saint Isidore: Help me, my God, before death comes,” etc.

These two prayers are excerpted from the books of the *Synonyms*, but they do not contain exactly the same wording; and perhaps Isidore himself included them in the ecclesiastical Offices. Otherwise, Alcuin also presents prayers collected by him from other works of the Fathers; and in this way he could likewise have composed prayers from Isidore, even though he had not seen the ecclesiastical books of Spain. The prayer “Help me, my God, before death comes,” taken from Book I of the *Synonyms* toward its end, is shorter in Alcuin than in Constantine Cajetan, who published it under the title “Prayer, or Confession, of blessed Isidore,” as I have just said.

## CHAPTER LXXXII. Certain works published under Isidore’s name, whose authorship is disputed

Some composed from Isidore’s *Synonyms*. The books *On the Rule of Life* and *On Contempt of the World*. *A Collection on Tears*, or a little work *On the Formation of the Good Life*. *The Mirror of Humanity*, or *The Method of Living Properly*.

[Col. 0589A]

1. Since many works have also been attributed to other Fathers—through the negligence of copyists, the perversity of men, the pious zeal of certain writers who wished to remain concealed, or finally by chance—although they are not truly theirs, it should be no surprise if several little works were also circulated under the name of Isidore, whose fame had spread widely during the Middle Ages. Among these may be placed certain excerpts, or little works pieced together from Isidore’s books, [Col. 0589B] although, as I have often suggested, I do not regard it as at all foreign to Isidore’s genius and practice that he himself might have arranged his writings in different ways according to circumstances and reworked them under different titles. The matter of the *Synonyms* was discussed in chapter 70: many small streams flowed from that source.

2. Margarinus de la Bigne published a little work *On the Rule of Life* from a manuscript in the library of Saint-Victor outside the walls of Paris. In my copy of Bigne’s edition, a manuscript note states that this book *On the Rule of Life* appears to be the latter part, or second book, of the work of the *Synonyms*. Yet although the *Synonyms* are not divided into two books in Bigne’s edition, that edition nevertheless contains under one title the two books that others distinguish: [Col. 0589C] and *The Rule of Life* is excerpted from the work of the *Synonyms* itself, though it is not arranged in such a way that it can be regarded as a separate book of that work. Bigne thought he was publishing this little work for the first time; but it had appeared long before.

3. In the Vatican volume of printed books, shelfmark 6963, quarto, several little works are bound together, apparently printed at approximately the same time. The first is Francesco Matarazzi of Perugia’s little work *On Composing Hexameter and Pentameter Verses*: Venice, 1468. Next comes Jacobus Publicius’s *On the Art of Oratory*. Also included is *The Art of Memory*, with illustrations. This is followed by *The Transmission of Morals*, containing the following graceful lines:

> Whoever wishes to be charming in morals and in life,  
> Let him attentively observe and gladly read the present things.

[Col. 0589D] A German interpretation follows. This opening, unless I am mistaken, having been appended somewhere to a leonine poem attributed to Facetus, furnished the occasion for inventing a poet called Facetus, because some people call the poem itself *Facetus*, from the last word of the first line.

Next follows a little treatise of Isidore’s *Synonyms*, *On the Governance of the Present Life*, not so pleasant as it is useful. Chapter 1: *On the Rule of Life*. “Act, my son, as is fitting,” etc. It ends: “lest you despise the good that you have received.” There are sixteen chapters, just as in Bigne’s edition; but here they are divided differently and the titles are absent. Chapter 11 in the old edition concerns instruction.

This old edition has the same type and similar paper as the other works that follow in the same volume, [Col. 0590A] namely, a *History of a Certain Spirit Conjured by the Prior of the Friars Preachers*—in the year 1423, in the city of Allecti—and Lucius Florus, said to have been printed at the end by Conrad Gallicus in the town of Leipzig in 1487.

Bound in the same volume is a curious *Letter on the Misery of Curates*, or parish priests. It begins: “It has always followed,” etc., “dearest John,” etc. The devils who commonly torment parish priests are listed: “The first devil of them all is the very patron,” etc. “The third devil is your cook, your mistress,” etc., “who, unless she were despised by everyone as a prostitute, would in no way have been made the steward of your household,” etc.

4. Breulius took the little work *On the Rule of Life* from Bigne’s edition, prefacing it with this brief notice:

“Isidore, *On the Rule of Life*. This rule of life [Col. 0590B] is excerpted here and there, for the most part, from Isidore’s *Synonyms* and from the book *On Contempt of the World*. It has as its author rather some compiler than Isidore. For it is not credible that so great a man ever intended to set before us twice-cooked cabbage.” Perhaps *apponere* (“to set before”) should be read in place of *opponere*. But, as I said, this argument is not as effective as some may think.

Although it is true that *The Rule of Life* is excerpted from the *Synonyms*, as Cellier, Bellarmine, Dupin, Cave, Placcius, and others agree, it can nevertheless still be questioned whether it was excerpted by Isidore himself. Bayerius testifies that it exists in the Escorial Library, shelf M, pluteus 3, no. 3. Nevertheless, it was omitted from both editions printed at Madrid. I shall publish a different copy from the Borgian Manuscript, of which I shall speak in chapter 107, no. 31.

5. Several little works bearing the same or a similar title are attributed to other authors. Vatican-Palatine Manuscript 327 contains Saint Bernard’s *Formula of an Honest Life*: “You ask me, brother.” In the same manuscript there is another anonymous work: “Your affection”; this occurs again in Palatine Manuscript 399.

Palatine Manuscript 386 contains Saint Augustine’s short treatise *On the Honesty of Religious Life*: “You ask me, brother.” In Royal-Vatican Manuscript 444 there is Saint Bernard’s *Formula for Living Honestly*: “If anyone.” In Vatican Ottobonian Manuscript 56 there is a sermon of Saint Bernard, *On Morals and the Honesty of Life*: “You have asked me.”

The Chisian Manuscript of Isidore’s *Sentences* also contains Bernard’s *Formula of an Honest Life*; but it is noted that the author is Bernard Silvester, who likewise wrote the letter *On the Proper Administration of Domestic Affairs* among the works of Saint Bernard. Bernard surnamed Silvester is the same as Bernard of Chartres, a twelfth-century writer. Fabricius attributes to him a letter to Raymond of Castro Ambrosius *On the More Useful Management of Domestic Affairs*, but not the *Formula of an Honest Life*. Some also give this title to an excerpt from Saint Jerome’s letter to Nepotian.

6. There is another *Formula of an Honest Life*, attributed to Seneca in Vatican Manuscript 993 and likewise in another Vatican manuscript, 1783. But in fact it belongs to Saint Martin of Dumio, or Braga, to whom it is attributed in Vatican Parchment Manuscript 634: *One Book of Martin, Bishop, on the Four Cardinal Virtues*, entitled *The Formula of an Honest Life*, [Col. 0591A] and on their excesses, that is, their vices. Its prologue is addressed to King Miro: “To the most glorious,” etc. “I am not unaware,” etc.

Vatican Paper Manuscript 5370 and Ottobonian Manuscript 1354 agree with it; these too contain the prologue to King Miro. It was published after others by Florez in volume XV of *Sacred Spain*. A similar title is *On the Formation of the Good Life*, or, as others have it, *of the New Life*, which is attributed to another work excerpted from Isidorian writings, as I shall say shortly.

7. Saint Isidore’s golden little book *On Contempt of the World* also appeared in Bigne’s edition, with Hubert Schutteput, canon of Louvain, identified in the catalogue of the works as its editor. Breulius admitted the work into his edition, prefacing it with this notice:

“In this little book many things are repeated which had earlier been stated in almost the same words in the books of the *Synonyms*, or *Soliloquies*; some of these, as time permits, we shall note. Finally, it has the same interlocutors, a human being and Reason, so that I wonder whether it was not compiled by someone else.”

Its preface begins: “A certain book of Cicero came into my hands, whose form,” etc. With some changes in wording, this is read before the *Synonyms* in the Madrid edition, as I said in chapter 70, where I also discussed Breulius’s opinion: he thinks that Cicero’s *Consolation* is indicated. This little book *On Contempt of the World* was omitted from both Madrid editions.

8. I saw a Venetian edition of this little book together with other works:

1. John Gerson, chancellor of Paris and a most celebrated doctor, *On the Imitation of Christ* and *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, Venice, 1555, sextodecimo. Most others attribute this work to Thomas à Kempis.

2. A little book by Saint Leo the pope, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*: “The apostolic voice cries out,” etc. Some also attribute this to our Isidore, as I shall say in chapter 84.

3. Saint Isidore’s golden little book *On Contempt of the World*: “A certain book came into my hands, whose form,” etc. The reference to Cicero is absent. It ends, as in Breulius: “retain the holy gift you have received.”

Another work follows, *On Contempt of the World*, or *On the Misery of the Human Condition*, whose author is Pope Innocent III. Fabricius praises another Venetian edition of the Isidorian little book, from 1523, octavo, in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*. He follows Breulius’s view concerning the *Consolation of Cicero* indicated in the prologue.

9. Nicholas Antonio considers the Isidorian work *On Contempt of the World* to be the same as the *Synonyms*, though somewhat altered, as is generally the case with whatever has come down to us from antiquity. But it is rather a summary, or excerpt, from the *Synonyms*, arranged so that new sentences are sometimes inserted, while at other times the same words of the *Synonyms* are repeated at length.

10. The title *On Contempt of the World* is also old in other works [23] and has been used by many. In chapter 41 of *On Illustrious Men*, Isidore reports that his brother Leander wrote one little book to his sister Florentina *On the Formation of Virgins and Contempt of the World*.

Vatican Manuscript 3499 contains a work of Eucherius, bishop of Lyon, *On Contempt of the World and Secular Philosophy*, addressed to his kinsman Valerian: “It is rightly alleged,” etc. In another Vatican manuscript, 4257, there is Bernard’s *On Contempt of the World*: “The world,” etc. Another Vatican manuscript, 1699, records a fragment of Seneca *On Contempt of the World*: “Although your lap,” etc., which perhaps belongs to Martin of Dumio’s *Formula of an Honest Life*.

Palatine Manuscript 193 presents a sermon of Saint Augustine *On Contempt of the World*: “Hear, brothers,” etc. There is another sermon *On Contempt of the World*, without an author’s name, in Royal-Vatican Manuscript 261: “See carefully how you walk,” etc. The spurious book of Augustine *On Contempt of the World*, volume IX of the Louvain edition, is the cited sermon, “Hear, brothers,” etc., which was included among the appendices to volume VI of the Maurist edition. Barthius, in *Adversaria* book LV, chapter 5, quotes certain words from a book entitled *On Contempt of the World* under the name of Roger.

11. Poems bearing this title also exist. [Col. 0592B] Ottobonian Manuscript 3325 contains a poem *On Contempt of the World*: “It is useful,” etc., by Brother Bernard of the Order of Friars Minor.

The manuscript is a paper codex of the fifteenth century. It also contains, under Ovid’s name, a poem *On the Mirror of Medicine*: “Nothing for you”; a comedy of Plautus, or the book of *Birria*—perhaps *Byrrhia*, which is the name of a slave in Terence’s *Andria*—*Greek Studies*, and Aesopic fables in verse: “That it may help and be useful,” etc. I noted in the *Urbinate* Manuscript 352 that these too exist, in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 70, where I observed that Labbe had intended to publish these fables, which he thought had not yet been printed. But they had appeared much earlier, and Fabricius lists several editions of many of them in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, book II, chapter 3, no. 1, in the notes. He observes that the author is called Accius by some, Salo by others, Romulus or Romalius by others, and Bernard by others. [Col. 0592C]

12. Bernard of the Order of Friars Minor, the author of the poem *On Contempt of the World*, is different from Bernard of Morlaix—or Morlac, or Morlav—of Cluny, who around the year 1130 wrote three books *On Contempt of the World* in dactylic leonine verse, repeatedly reprinted. Vatican Manuscripts 5158 and 5161 contain a poem entitled *Contempt of the World*: “Our little page to you,” etc., without an author’s name.

[24] 13. The authors who, in the famous controversy over the author of the book *On Contempt of the World* and *On the Imitation of Christ*, wrote either in favor of Thomas à Kempis, or of John Gersen the Benedictine, or of John Gerson, or of others, are carefully catalogued by Fabricius in *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under the entry “Kempis, Thomas.”

Palatine Paper Manuscript 414 is entitled: “Thomas à Kempis, *On the Imitation of Christ and Contempt of the World’s Vanities*.” In Palatine Manuscript 719: “An anonymous work, *On the Imitation of Christ and Contempt of All the Vanities of the World*: ‘Whoever follows me,’” an unfinished work at the end.

Ottobonian Manuscript 530 contains *Excerpts from John Gerson and Others for Private Use*: “Whoever follows me,” etc., which is the beginning of the same little book. This manuscript too is on paper.

In another Ottobonian manuscript, of a more recent period, no. 3155, there is an anonymous *Conjecture concerning the Books on the Imitation of Christ and Their Authors*. In another Ottobonian manuscript, likewise, no. 3164, there is Constantine Cajetan’s *Apology for John Gersen, Abbot of Vercelli, against Rosweyd*: I do not know whether it differs somewhat from the published version.

In Papebrochius’s *Chronological-Historical Endeavor toward a Series of the Roman Pontiffs*, dissertation 45 asks whether Peter of Corbaria may be believed to have had a share in the books *On the Imitation of Christ*, disputed between John Gersen and Thomas à Kempis.

14. Zaccaria placed the little book *On Contempt of the World*, circulated under Isidore’s name, among his genuine works, although he rejected as spurious the little works *On the Rule of Life* and *On the Formation of the Good Life*, which likewise derive from the *Synonyms*.

From a fifteenth-century Veronese manuscript, which I described in chapter 43, no. 35, he had decided to print the little book *On the Formation of the Good Life*, which he thought had not yet been published. But Tamayo de Salazar had already made most of it public in *Spanish Martyrology*, on February 25, p. 252. He entitled it *A Collection on Tears, or on the Formation of the New Life*.

He considers it a fragment of a letter, falsely attributed to Saint Isidore of Seville. “In my manuscript,” he says, “where this letter is written in Gothic letters, the following title is found: *Treatise of Saint Isidore of Seville on the Formation of the New Life*. In the margin, in the same letters, is this note: ‘Others attribute this letter to Saint Valerius, abbot of Bergidum, and assert that it was written to the presbyter Justus; this is more likely.’”

It ends: “and, when you have fulfilled the words of the law, you will attain eternal life.” He omits other material added in our manuscripts, as well as certain passages from the preceding material, and differs somewhat in many places. William Cave followed Tamayo’s opinion, which assigns the *Formation of the New Life* to Saint Valerius, in the year 680.

15. In the manuscript codices containing other works of Valerius of Bergidum—or, as Tamayo writes, of Virgitum—Florez, who published them in volume XVI of *Sacred Spain*, did not find the letter *On the Formation of the New Life* attributed by Tamayo to Valerius, and considers it inconsistent with Valerius’s style. Certainly, since the little work is excerpted from Isidore’s *Synonyms*, it can be attributed to Valerius only as an excerptor or compiler.

Bayerius is uncertain on this matter in his notes to the *Bibliotheca vetus*. In his note to book V, no. 216, he first says that Isidore’s *Collection on Tears* is found in two Escorial manuscripts, apparently different from the other little works on related subjects. It begins: “Beloved son, love tears; do not delay them.” It ends: “See, whoever you are who read these things, lest you despise in living what you consider while reading.”

He adds that this same work, with the same beginning and ending and under the title *Collection of Saint Isidore*, exists in the library of the monastery of Alcobaça, as appears from the catalogue published at Lisbon in 1775; Tamayo attributes it to Saint Valerius.

Again, in the same note, he adds that some attribute to Isidore the letter, or treatise, *On the Formation of the New Life*, which is rather thought to belong to Saint Valerius of Montanus, or Bergidum. He returns to the same subject in his note to book V, no. 370, where he observes that the *Formation of the New Life* in Tamayo and the *Collection on Tears* have the same beginning, but that the works may perhaps be different, although they derive from the same source. Finally, from a comparison of the two he concludes that the *Collection on Tears*, found in two Escorial manuscripts, is much fuller and at least twice as extensive as the treatise *On the Formation of the New Life* published by Tamayo.

[Col. 0594A] 16. The situation is as follows: whether the little work is entitled *A Collection on Tears*, or *On the Formation of the New Life*, or, as in the Veronese Manuscript, *of the Good Life*, or in some other way, as I shall soon say concerning the Vatican manuscripts, it is the same excerpt from the books of the *Synonyms*, partly also from the books *On the Rule of Life* and *On Contempt of the World*.

It is called *A Collection on Tears* from its opening, where tears are mentioned: “Beloved son, love tears.” This opening is taken from the chapter *On Always Mourn­ing Sins*, or, in other editions, *On Humility*. Another title is *On the Formation of the Good Life*, in the same way that a similar little work is entitled *On the Rule of Life*.

In chapter 44, no. 29, I described the Florentine Codex of Saint Mark, *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*. It contains a letter of blessed Ambrose, bishop, to one of his disciples, *On Morals and the Honesty of Life*, with the same beginning: “Beloved son, love tears.” I do not doubt that this is identical with our little work *On the Formation of the Good Life*. For elsewhere too I found some book of Isidore’s attributed in manuscripts to Ambrose.

In Vatican-Palatine Manuscript 832, under the title of a letter *On Morals and an Honest Life*, this little book *On the Formation of the Good Life*, somewhat abridged, is attributed to blessed Archbishop Ambrose, with the same beginning: “Beloved son, love tears,” etc. It ends: “See, whoever you are who read this”—perhaps “these things”—“lest you despise in living what you consider while reading.”

Vatican Manuscript 351, a parchment manuscript dating approximately from the fourteenth century, p. 217, presents this little book without a title: “Beloved son, love tears,” etc. It ends: “For love proceeds from reverence.” In the catalogue of works, written in the same hand or from the same period, this title appears: *The Synonyms of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville*.

A more appropriate title appears in Vatican-Palatine Manuscript 327, a paper manuscript about which I shall speak in chapter 103, p. 148: “Here begin the flowers of blessed Isidore: ‘Beloved son, love tears; do not delay them,’” etc. It ends: “is either justified or condemned. Here end certain excerpts, or flowers, of blessed Isidore.”

17. This is why, although the beginning of the little work is the same everywhere, its ending is different in almost all copies: when an excerpt is being transcribed, one person easily selects more and another fewer passages. Since the beginning is the same in all copies, it is reasonable to suspect that this work is ancient, perhaps dating from Isidore’s time, and that it acquired the variations observed in the manuscript codices through the hands of copyists.

The words that Bayerius quotes from the Escorial manuscripts as the final words of the *Collection on Tears* occur almost identically near the end of *The Rule of Life*. In the Veronese copy there are some passages that seem to have been taken from chapters 2 and 17 of Book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. But since these passages are themselves common to the *Synonyms*, perhaps the excerptor had only these before his eyes.

There is another little work likewise taken from the *Synonyms*, bearing the title *Sermon*, which I discussed in chapter 70.

18. *The Mirror of Humanity*, also excerpted from the books of the *Synonyms*, was published in the fifteenth century, as I infer from the style of its very old type. The copy that had belonged to the distinguished gentleman Don Pedro Manuel Hernández was sent to me by my eminent patron, Cardinal Lorenzana.

I believe that the little work was published without an author’s name; certainly the author’s name does not appear in this copy, nor does any date or place of publication. Its first words are:

“*The Mirror of Humanity.* Here two persons are introduced: the grieving human being and Reason offering admonition” (I correct *rationem* to *rationis*). “The human being: My soul, you are in distress,” etc. It should read, “My soul, you are not in distress”; other errors are similarly inserted throughout.

It ends: “Now you know what it is to live rightly; henceforth see that you do not despise in living what you have heard through admonition: let it be so, let it be so. Amen. Here ends *The Mirror of Humanity*, or *The Method of Living Properly*.”

The final words are corrupt. Nevertheless, the books *On Contempt of the World* and *On the Rule of Living Properly* end in almost the same way. A work with nearly the same title, formerly especially famous, is Rodrigo Sánchez de Arévalo’s *Mirror of Human Life*.

## CHAPTER LXXXIII. Other works published under Isidore’s name, doubtful or spurious

Testimonies of Sacred Scripture. *The Book on the Order of Creatures*. Dacher’s preface. *The Book of the Catholic Faith*. *The Profession of Faith*. *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. Vezzosi’s preface to this book. Pedro Manuel Hernández’s observations on Brachario, bishop of Seville, as the author of this same book.

1. The very ancient Veronese Manuscript, which I described in Maffei’s words in chapter 44, after the *Proems*, the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, and Isidore’s *Allegories*, presents *Divine Testimonies of Sacred Scripture*. Maffei considered this to be a collection by Isidore and intended to publish it.

Perhaps this work is indicated in the twelfth-century catalogue of Göttweig, of which I spoke in chapter 46, no. 8, under the explicit title: *The Sentences of Isidore from Both Testaments*. Although that collection of sentences contains not only testimonies of Sacred Scripture but also, after these, as it were in a second part, testimonies of certain Fathers, after Maffei’s death Zaccaria had included *Divine Testimonies of Sacred Scripture* among the other works of Isidore that he intended to publish, as I said in chapter 41. Yet he passed it over in silence in the published *Prospectus* of the Isidorian edition, because he had already made it public in his *Literary Journey through Italy*, p. 189, denying that it was a genuine work of Isidore. He prefixed a notice, which I reproduce here.

[28] 2. It was customary among the ancient Fathers to collect testimonies from Scripture and from the Fathers in order to establish some point, without adding any explanation or argument drawn from them. Most celebrated in this respect are Cyprian’s three books of *Testimonies against the Jews*. To these was recently added Saint Cyprian’s *Exhortation on Penance*, published in 1751 by the distinguished Father John Chrysostom Trombellius (*Anecdota Published by the Canons Regular of Saint Saviour*, volume II, part I, pp. 1 ff.).

The work commonly attributed to Prosper, *On the Promises and Predictions of God*, was written in approximately the same form. Leo the Great too, after the Ephesian Robber Council, sent to the East certain testimonies of the Fathers that he had collected against the Eutychian heresy. Vossius published them in Greek in his edition of Saint Gregory Thaumaturgus. Later, in a much fuller form and with the order altered, Leo wrote them to Emperor Leo and appended them to his letter, number 165 in the Ballerini edition and number 138 in the Cacciari edition.

What of Pelagius himself? As we learn from Saint Jerome in the first book *Against the Pelagians*, chapter 9, when writing books of *Testimonies* he acknowledged himself to be an imitator, indeed a fulfiller, of the work that blessed Cyprian the martyr wrote to Quirinus.

3. The author of the *Testimonies* followed these examples. Through the gift of the Veronese Manuscript, I am the first to bring him out of darkness. The distinguished Maffei describes this manuscript as follows in *The Veronese Library of Manuscripts*, part I, p. 88:

“In a book of the same format, likewise mixed and ancient, with a type that for the most part approaches the typographical, the following are contained:

1. The book begins with the *Book of Rewards*, a dialogue of Jerome the presbyter. It neither mentions rewards nor is a dialogue, and it is not a work of Jerome, but Isidore’s work of which Braulio speaks as one book of the *Proems*.

2. The life or death of the saints who have gone before us in the Lord.

3. ‘Here begin the little works of Saint Isidore,’ as though what precedes belonged to someone else. A book follows that the spurious chronicle of Pseudo-Dexter incorrectly attributes to a second Isidore: *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels*. It appears to have received this title from Braulio. William Cave lists it among the lost works, and even suspects that it never existed, since he doubts whether it is the same as the *Book of the Proems*; [Col. 0596B] yet it has been published more than once under the title *Allegories*.

4. ‘Here begin the Divine Testimonies of Sacred Scripture.’ It is a collection of sentences, first from the Old and New Covenants, then from the *Book of Conferences* and from Evagrius’s *Sentences to the Brothers*, unquestionably Evagrius Ponticus. Material is also excerpted from the books of Ambrose and Prosper, and testimonies are brought from the book of Saint Martin—not Martin, bishop of Tours, but the father of monks. I understand this to mean Martin of Braga, who founded several monasteries in Galicia and translated the sayings of the Egyptian Fathers from Greek.

“This is evidence that the manuscript was brought from Spain, or at least copied from a Spanish manuscript; for Martin of Braga would not be called ‘father of monks’ in any other province. Finally, this collection breaks off together with half of the book. Since I have examined several other collections of this kind, I consider it unpublished. Several things seem to suggest that it proceeded from Saint Isidore, although this has hitherto not been known.

“For the manuscript contains only Isidore’s writings; [Col. 0596C] the title prefixed to the preceding little book, ‘The Little Works of Saint Isidore,’ suggests that not merely one little work of his is to follow; the compiler excerpted chiefly from a fellow Spaniard; and finally, the work reflects Isidore’s character extremely well. Sixtus of Siena aptly says that Isidore had an insatiable desire to read, collect, and combine the sayings and sentences, or rhapsodies, of the ancient Fathers.

“The book of Isidore’s *Catholic Faith* is called by the same name as this collection in the chronicle of Fontenelle, according to D’Achery (*Spicilegium*, volume III, p. 241), namely, *Testimonies concerning Christ and the Church*. It would indeed be surprising if Isidore had contributed nothing here from Gregory the Great and Augustine; but the book is mutilated, as I have said, and the compilation is broken off.

“It also occurred to me that this work may be the one indicated when ancient writers praise Isidore’s *Sentences*. The designation fits it much better than the books *On the Supreme Good*, which are also three in number, whereas Ildefonsus counts one book of *Sentences*. Moreover, moral subjects are prefixed to the chapters, except the first, which concerns the one God and the distinction of the Persons.

“In support of this subject, the following verses from John’s Epistle are adduced: ‘For there are three who bear witness on earth, the Spirit, the water, and the Blood; and the three are one in Christ Jesus; and there are three who bear witness in heaven, the Father, the Word, and the Spirit, and the three are one.’”

4. Thus far Maffei. I readily agree with so learned a man that the *Books of Testimonies* presented here are the work of a Spaniard; but I shall never be persuaded that they are by Isidore of Seville.

Against Ildefonsus, who attributes one book of *Sentences* to Isidore, we set Braulio of Zaragoza, who expressly reports that three books of *Sentences*, sprinkled with the flowers of Saint Gregory the Great, proceeded from Saint Isidore. These are the books that are also headed *On the Supreme Good*.

Indeed, it would be absurd to attribute these *Testimonies* to Isidore while taking away from him, against the evidence of all manuscript codices, the books *On the Supreme Good*. But if we suppose that by the name “one book of Sentences” Ildefonsus meant not the books *On the Supreme Good* but these *Testimonies*, some critic, observing that Ildefonsus made no mention of the books *On the Supreme Good*, will readily press his silence in order to deny those books to Isidore.

For who would believe that Ildefonsus passed over in silence books that are both highly learned and particularly useful for confirming the Church’s doctrine, while not remaining silent about a little book of *Testimonies*, merely moral in subject and haphazardly scraped together from here and there?

Nor is the version of Scripture the same in Isidore as in this author of ours; rather, the two differ greatly from each other. As for Maffei’s statement that these testimonies are found in a codex containing nothing but Isidorian works, that has no force in the present matter. Those who have examined manuscript codices know that neither the titles of books nor the order in which they were written can be trusted sufficiently.

Let us examine this very manuscript. The first two little works seem to have been wholly rejected as Isidore’s by the person who copied the codex. The first was certainly rejected as a book of the *Proems*, since it is attributed to Saint Jerome; the second less openly, but, as far as we can infer, no less clearly, since immediately after that little work appears the title: “Here begins the *Little Works of Isidore*.”

Who, then, was the author of the little work? He was a Spaniard, I say again; perhaps even somewhat earlier than Isidore. For although the book is mutilated, we can easily suspect that the person who collected the testimonies of Martin of Braga shortly after the testimonies of Scripture would have placed Isidore’s sentences before the sayings of all the others, since Isidore’s name had always enjoyed such great renown among the Spaniards.

5. Whatever the truth concerning the author, no one will deny that this is a most useful little work. From it much may be extracted that will assist in comparing the Hieronymian version of Scripture with the others; and it supplies a new Spanish witness in favor of the Johannine testimony concerning the most holy Trinity.

It may also perhaps be useful to compare the passages of the Fathers quoted here with the published examples, but I had no opportunity to do so.

6. Concerning the method of publication, note the following. No division of the books appears in the manuscript. Yet since, except for one passage from Deuteronomy—and that passage is miserably corrupt—which was copied in the manuscript after the sentences of Cassian, the sayings of the Fathers follow the testimonies of Scripture in continuous order, and since the beginning of the work is headed “Here begin the Divine Testimonies of Sacred Scripture,” it occurred to me to divide the entire work into two little books, one presenting the testimonies of Scripture and the other the collected testimonies of the Fathers.

It was therefore necessary, in imitation of the title under which I said the book is inscribed in the manuscript, to devise another title with which to head the second little book.

In all other respects I took care to reproduce the manuscript itself scrupulously, preserving not only its old spelling but almost all its actual errors. It might perhaps have been useful to readers for me to add to each sentence the places where it occurs in Scripture or among the Fathers; but I had no leisure for that. At the beginning, however, I have supplied the references that I found written in the manuscript itself. This is enough on the matter.

7. Zaccaria was moved to deny that this little work is Isidore’s for one reason only: the version of Scripture is not the same in Isidore as in the author of the *Testimonies*, but the two differ greatly from each other.

Yet this is difficult to accept, especially since Zaccaria admits that the work is by a Spaniard, perhaps even somewhat earlier than Isidore; and since, for another reason, Isidore generally took the words of Scripture from the form in which he found them set out in the Fathers whom he transcribed. [Col. 0598A]

Maffei’s opinion, therefore, that the work proceeded from Isidore is not unreasonable. It could have happened that, after the three books of *Sentences* collected chiefly from Gregory and Augustine, Isidore arranged this new collection from Sacred Scripture and from his reading of other Fathers. That would provide a suitable reason why he contributed nothing here from Gregory and Augustine, which seemed strange to Maffei—even if the book were not otherwise mutilated and the compilation were not broken off.

One may ask which book of *Sentences* is meant when the final sentences are said to have been excerpted from it. I have no doubt that it is Prosper’s book, which Prosper collected from the works of Augustine and which was also published separately at Helmstedt by John a Fuchte in 1613, octavo.

Among all Prosper’s works, volume I, p. 316, of the Venetian edition of 1744, its title is: *One Book of Sentences Gathered from the Works of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Hippo*. Each chapter consists of a single sentence, with no orderly connection among them. Isidore’s labor was therefore much more useful: in his three books of *Sentences* he established a kind of theological system from Gregory, Augustine, and other Fathers, as was said above in chapter 67.

8. The book *On the Order of Creatures* appears to be attributable to Isidore, as I established with many arguments in chapter 23. There I also noted that I would publish it with variant readings collected with the greatest care by the distinguished Thomas Dendrade from a Florentine manuscript.

For now I shall add only what D’Achery prefaced concerning this work in his prologue to volume I.

9. The third place is occupied by the book of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the Order of Creatures, which he published at the request of Braulio, bishop of the city of Zaragoza. Although the cataloguers of ecclesiastical writers, both ancient and modern, have not mentioned it, its style and spirit seemed to me so plainly Isidorean that I thought no one could call its genuine authorship into question.

[Note: In this year, 1665, I found this book cited by Aeneas, bishop of Paris, in his treatise *Against the Greeks*, but under another title, namely: “Isidore on the Catholic Faith.”]

We publish a manuscript copied not long after the author’s time, obtained from our noble monastery of Saint-Remi at Reims. Isidore is too celebrated—an exemplary model of holiness and of every kind of learning—to require being sketched by the rough lines of my pen. Isidore Pacensis in his *Chronicle*, that same Braulio in his *Preface to the Books of St. Isidore*, Ildefonsus of Toledo, and Sigebert in his *On Ecclesiastical Writers* long ago celebrated him with many encomiums. He flourished in the time of Heraclius.

Yet the words attached to the title must by no means be passed over in silence: “To Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome.” To clarify them I added: “That is, of Zaragoza.” I confess that I was perplexed, since nowhere have I been able to observe that Zaragoza was ever called Rome by ecclesiastical writers—unless one should say that, just as Constantinople was called Rome, though for a different reason, the Spaniards formerly desired their principal city, a Roman colony, to be called Rome by a kind of imperial prerogative. I do not, however, wish to indulge conjecture on this matter; leaving the decision to sharper minds, I proceed to other subjects.

10. The book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, attributed to many others, was first—and uniquely—published among Isidore’s works by Margarin de la Bigne, from the library of the distinguished Peter Daniel of Orléans. He entitled it: “The little book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the doctrine and faith of ecclesiastical dogmas.” Breulius not only excluded such a work from Isidore’s writings, but also appended the following notice concerning it after his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*:

> “In the works of St. Isidore printed at Paris in the year of Christ 1580, there followed a little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which we removed intact after finding it among the works of the divine Augustine. Although it belongs neither to Augustine nor to Isidore, but to Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseilles who was not sufficiently Catholic, it is cited under his name by many writers: for example, by St. Thomas in *Quodlibet* 12, article 10; by the Master of the Sentences, book II, distinction 8; and by Walafrid Strabo in book 20 of *On Ecclesiastical Matters*. For this reason the Louvain scholars rejected this little book into the appendix to volume III of the divine Augustine, together with an antidote.”

11. Among the works which Trithemius assigns to Isidore, but which are unknown to others, Nicholas Antonius lists one book of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. From Placcius he observes that it was customarily attributed, besides Isidore, to Augustine, Alcuin, Fulgentius, and Pope Gregory. But apart from the fact that de la Bigne published a book under Isidore’s name from Peter Daniel’s manuscript, Trithemius seems to assign this work to Isidore on the authority of Sigebert. For Sigebert, among Isidore’s other books, mentions a book of *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

Although Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, suspects that Sigebert was referring to the three books of the *Sentences*—which Sigebert certainly does not mention under any other title—Trithemius understood a different work and, as it appears, that very work which is attributed to many others. I already noted in chapter 67 that Bayer had no sufficient reason to doubt whether Robert Cocus, who says that a book *On the Dogmas of the Church* was wrongly attributed to Isidore, was referring this to the books of the *Sentences*. For there can be no doubt that Cocus understood the book commonly called *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* by that name.

12. I do not know whether the following entry in the old catalogue of the Fulda library, dating approximately from the tenth century (Cod. Palat. 1877), should be referred to this book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: “A statement of faith by St. Jerome, and the creed composed by Theodore, archbishop of Britain, and the creed of the Twelve Apostles, and a treatise of someone on the same creed; a STATEMENT OF THE FAITH OF ST. ISIDORE; and a letter of Pope Damasus to Paulinus of Antioch.”

Perhaps “The Faith of St. Isidore” refers to a certain profession of faith which is inserted among the *Etymologies* in Codex 2 of the Vatican archives, discussed in chapter 107, as something belonging to them; it will therefore have a place among the appendices.

13. As for the fact that Aeneas of Paris cites Isidore *On the Catholic Faith* against the Greeks, Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, no. 12, explains this as referring to the two books *Against the Jews*, which are also entitled *On the Catholic Faith*.

Certain sentences from the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* are found in Isidore’s book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 24, whether Isidore took them from an older book or, rather, another later author took them from Isidore. For it is not as certain as many think that the work belongs to Gennadius. Since ancient manuscripts and ancient writers differ so greatly concerning the author of this little book, I would not dare to assign it to Isidore on the basis of the single manuscript cited by de la Bigne and the doubtful testimony of Sigebert—or even the clearer testimony of Trithemius.

In the inventory and catalogue of the Vatican-Urbino library, Codex 1504, page 62, a book of Isidore *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is listed: “Divine, etc.” But that paper manuscript contains only Isidore’s three books of the *Sentences* and his book *On the Differences of Things*. On page 62 there is a table of chapters and the beginning of the third book of the *Sentences*, which begins: “Divine wisdom, etc.”

14. In the old Vatican Library, Codex 458, a small parchment folio, among other works of Augustine, folio 113 records: “The same author, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*”; and it is again attributed to Augustine in Codex 466. But in the margin of the inventory there is this note: “In this little book there are also lacking the passages printed after chapters 21 and 24; and it is by Gennadius of Marseilles.”

Nevertheless, it is attributed to Augustine in Vatican Codices 473 and 514, and likewise in Vatican Codex 4982, under this title: “A little book against all heresies, on the Catholic faith: We believe in one [God], etc.” I shall describe Codex 473 in chapter 93.

The Ottobonian Codex 459 likewise records: “Definitions of Aurelius Augustine on Ecclesiastical Dogmas: We believe one [God], etc. A Catholic refutation by the same author of certain chapters: Since Christian [faith], etc.” It is a parchment folio.

Another Ottobonian manuscript, 612, parchment folio, has: “Augustine’s statement of the true faith: We believe, etc.” The Palatine Codex 191, on paper, has: “Augustine’s definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas: We believe one [God], etc.” Another Palatine manuscript, parchment no. 213, agrees with it.

But the Regio-Vatican Codex 83, on paper, is described in the inventory as follows: “The book of St. Augustine—or rather of Gennadius of Marseilles—on Ecclesiastical Dogmas.”

15. The Vatican Codex 655, parchment folio, expressly attributes it to Gennadius, page 170: “Gennadius, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: We believe in one God.” The following note is added in the inventory: “It truly belongs to Gennadius; it is also found in Alcuin.”

The same inscription is produced under the name of the Council of Nicaea in Vatican Codex 4152: “Definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas: We believe in one God, etc.” In a Regio-Vatican manuscript, parchment octavo, without the author’s name, it appears as: “Definition of Ecclesiastical Dogmas,” consisting of nine chapters and mutilated at the end.

Vatican Codex 1348, parchment of the eleventh century or later, contains a particular collection of canons. At its beginning is a treatise *On the Faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity*: “We believe there is one God.” It is a work compiled from the beginning of the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* and from other authors. It ends: “and to join the account together.”

16. These details are drawn from the Vatican manuscripts. Above, in chapter 43, I said that this little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* exists in an old Barberini manuscript of the eighth century or later, inscribed under Augustine’s name. In contrast, in chapter 44 I noted that it is attributed to Gennadius in an ancient Lucchese manuscript described by Mansi. That manuscript, however, differs greatly from the printed editions, as Mansi testifies, having brought forward several variant readings.

Mansi also mentions the same Lucchese manuscript in the supplement to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Gennadius.” He says that the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is represented there under this title: “Here begins [the book] on the Ecclesiastical Dogmas of the see’s bishop of Massilia.” The name of Gennadius is omitted here, perhaps through a typographical error.

Mansi suspects that one should read “of the ecclesiastical see,” but it would be better to construe the title as: “On the Ecclesiastical Dogmas of Gennadius, bishop of the see of Massilia.” An error of this kind, by which Gennadius was called bishop of Marseilles, has entered the works of many ancient writers.

Although the common opinion of modern scholars is that Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseilles, was the author of the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, the ancients differed greatly among themselves on this matter.

17. For, apart from the diversity of the manuscripts, Fabricius, in the *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, says that Abbo the abbot, John Scotus, and Rabanus stood for Augustine; that Peter Abelard and Gratian sometimes cited this book under Augustine’s name and sometimes under Gennadius’s; that the name of St. Faustus, bishop of Marseilles, was prefixed to the same little book in one manuscript; and that Ratramnus called the author Gennadius, bishop of Constantinople.

He lists many more witnesses for Gennadius of Marseilles, namely Pope Adrian I, Alcuin, Florus, the church of Lyon in its work against Gottschalk, Walafrid Strabo, Algerus, Peter Lombard, Thomas Aquinas, and Trithemius.

In the synodical letter of the Council of Frankfurt, held in 794, the same work seems to be assigned to Augustine in Labbe, volume VII of the Councils, column 1039. For after certain words of St. Ambrose, Augustine is cited:

> “Likewise, St. Augustine, in the book *Enchiridion*, etc. Likewise, in the *Exposition of the Catholic Faith*: ‘Therefore, not two Christs, nor two Sons, but one Son, God and man; for this reason we call him Only-begotten, remaining in two substances, just as the truth of his nature has conferred upon him.’”

These are the words of chapter 2 of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

Placcius, under “Aurel. Augustinus,” says that this book was wrongly attributed to Fulgentius, Gregory, and Tertullian. He says that Elmenhorst proved, in his notes on Tertullian, that it belongs to Gennadius, but that certain chapters were taken from the letters of Celestine and from the Councils, since they are absent from the manuscript in which the work is attributed to Gennadius.

Bernard Vinding, an Augustinian from Spain, in his *Corrected Augustinian Critic*, page 58, observes that chapter 53, on daily communion, is contrary to Augustine’s judgment.

18. Amid this variety of opinions, the most learned Hernandezius, in his observations on Zaccaria’s *Conspectus*, chapter 42, took a path different from all the others. He judges that the author of the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* was Bracharius, the fourth bishop of Seville after Isidore; on this subject he promises to publish a short dissertation.

Meanwhile, while rereading *España sagrada*, I encountered the following concerning Bracharius in volume IX, pages 24 and following. Bracarius, or Bracharius, distinct from Bachiarius, whose works were published by Muratori, Florio, and finally Flórez in volume XV of *España sagrada*, is listed fourth in the Emilian catalogue of the bishops of Seville, which I presented in chapter 24, after Isidore.

Flórez concludes that this Bracharius published some work from the second letter of John of Seville to Alvarus of Córdoba, which is the sixth among Alvarus’s published letters in volume XI of *España sagrada*. John of Seville says:

> “But among the things which Bishop Bracharius says in his dogmas must be recognized throughout his whole church, he established, among other things, the following: that human souls do not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once, etc.”

That this Bracharius was the same writer as Bracharius, bishop of Seville, is further proved by the fact that when John of Seville mentions him again, our author says:

> “Jerome says that the fifth opinion is more probable, and OUR BRACHARIUS also affirmed it.”

Alvarus of Córdoba, writing to John of Seville, expresses nearly the same meaning when he says, on page 114:

> “Hear your Isidore saying…”

and on page 140:

> “For your distinguished—indeed, our common—Isidore says in his *Differences* concerning blessed Fulgentius of Ruspe, etc.”

For Isidore was regarded as the common teacher of Spain.

19. What Bracharius had written was not clear to Flórez. But it is certain that John of Seville was alluding to the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*—not because the work seems to bear the title *Dogmas*, for by this common word the ancients understood any dogmatic books, but because Bracharius’s words reproduce the whole of chapter 14 of the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

Where John of Seville reads *nec in semel*, Flórez corrects it to *nec simul*; this is also how it is read in the edition of the theological *Institutions* by Father Thomasius. But the genuine reading is *nec insimul*, as is also indicated in de la Bigne’s edition, where the form is *in simul*. In manuscripts *e* often occurs for *i*, as in *insemel* for *insimul*. Nor is this adverb unknown among ancient authors of otherwise sound Latin.

A similar expression occurs in Alvarus, page 137, from St. Jerome: “Nor were they created *in semel*”—I read *insimul*—“in the beginning.”

It is therefore established by the authority of John of Seville, who flourished in the ninth century, that Bracharius, who appears to have held the see of Seville in the seventh century after the year 660, composed a work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* in order to instruct his church.

20. It is certainly difficult to find any other testimony so effective in favor of Gennadius, Augustine, or anyone else. Perhaps the title “of Seville,” incorrectly written in some manuscript, furnished the occasion for suspecting that the work belonged to Augustine; and someone may have changed *Hispalensis* into *Hipponensis*. Conversely, in the inventory of the Vatican Library, Palatine Codex 286, Augustine is called “of Seville”:

> “Here begin the homilies of the blessed Augustine, bishop of Seville, on the first canonical letter of the blessed apostle John, concerning charity, in the name of the Lord, amen. Preface: Behold now your holiness, etc. Homily: What was from the beginning, etc. Who is there who handles with his hands, etc.”

I discussed the great confusion surrounding the word *Hispalensis* in manuscript codices in chapter 24.

The same name “of Seville” may also have caused the work to be attributed in some places to Isidore rather than to Bracharius, a bishop unknown to most people. I do not, however, wish to conceal a certain difficulty that has arisen in my mind against believing Bracharius to be the author: while in Spain we find only one John of Seville who mentioned the work and attributed it to Bracharius, outside Spain this same work was being handled by many people even in the eighth century and was commonly inscribed under the names of others.

What, then, if John of Seville, finding Bracharius’s little book among some papers, believed Bracharius to be the author because he knew of no other? But judgment must be suspended until the dissertation of Hernandezius, which I mentioned, is published.

21. Since so eminent a man believed that the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* could be included among the Isidorian appendices, I decided to reprint it—not from de la Bigne’s edition, but from another edition prepared by Vezzosi in volume III of Father Thomasius’s *Theological Institutions*, with some notes and variant readings. He prefaces the work as follows:

22. Thomasius attributes the present work to Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, who is known to have flourished at the end of the fifth century, in the catalogue of his *Theological Institutions*, using words that seem to indicate that he had no doubt that it should be assigned to him.

The reasons others might have for doubting this are revealed in the *Admonition* which the most illustrious Maurist editors of St. Augustine’s works prefixed to it on page 75 of the appendix to volume VIII of the Paris edition of 1688. For the ancient manuscripts disagree among themselves when identifying its author: some attribute it to Augustine of Hippo, others to Bishop Paternus, others to Alcuin, and others to Gennadius.

In the same catalogue Thomasius praises the Maurist edition, but he seems to have preferred to it the edition found in volume II of the Antwerp edition of St. Augustine’s works of 1577, which also appears in volume I of the *Opuscula* of the same St. Augustine published at Venice in 1547. He does so because, as Thomasius himself says, several chapters had necessarily been added. Perhaps for this reason the Maurists, moved by that consideration, preferred their own copy to the other.

We ought not to hesitate to follow Thomasius. For the present we offer the Antwerp text, though collated and compared with the Maurist edition; since the latter’s variants are indicated in the notes, it seems to us equivalent to giving both versions.

23. In certain places Vezzosius explains in his notes the Catholic sense in which some propositions of this little book must be understood. Natalis Alexander, in dissertation 4, toward the end of the fifth century, denies that any trace of Semi-Pelagian error is present in this work, although he acknowledges Gennadius as its author.

24. “I answer secondly,” he says, “and, as it seems to me, more probably, that this book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* was published by Gennadius after he had recovered from the Semi-Pelagian heresy. For he sent a book on his faith to Gelasius, the Roman pontiff, as he himself asserts; and it is likely that this was the book he entitled *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*.

“Would he, however, have sent to Gelasius a book that reeked of Semi-Pelagian errors, when he knew that Gelasius had branded the books of Faustus and Cassian with the mark of censure because they had attributed the beginning of salvation to human powers? Therefore it cannot be inferred from this book of Gennadius what the opinion of the Semi-Pelagians was, since in it he is by no means a Semi-Pelagian.”

25. I had gathered these observations concerning the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* and its author when the dissertation I had mentioned, by the distinguished Peter Emmanuel Hernandezius, was sent to me from Spain. I decided to translate it from Spanish into Latin and insert it here.

## Observations by Peter Emmanuel Hernandezius on the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*

26. Since I have devoted some study and labor to arranging these observations, I shall consider this work worthwhile if I finally achieve what I set out to do: namely, to establish that the book entitled *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, wrongly attributed by some to Augustine and, with greater probability, by others to Gennadius of Marseilles, is the genuine work of a certain Spanish bishop who lived at the end of the seventh century.

First, however, I shall explain how I came upon this idea.

27. While reading volume XI of *España sagrada*, I encountered, among the letters of Alvarus of Córdoba, the sixth letter, sent by John of Seville to Alvarus, and noticed these words:

> “But among the things which Bishop Bracharius says in his dogmas must be recognized throughout his whole church, he established, among other things, the following: that human souls do not exist from the beginning among the other intellectual natures, nor were they created all at once [perhaps: ‘together’], as Origen imagines; nor are they sown together with bodies through sexual intercourse, as the Luciferians, Cyril, and many presumptuous Latins affirm, as though this followed from the course of nature. Rather, we say that only the body is generated through marital union; but by God’s judgment it is coagulated in the womb and fixed [perhaps: ‘fashioned’] and formed; and once the body has been formed, the soul is created and infused, so that a human being composed of soul and body may live in the womb and emerge alive from the womb, complete in human substance… Jerome says that the opinion is more probable, and our Bracharius also affirmed it.”

28. As I was reading this, it occurred to me that only a few days earlier I had read the same sentence—“that human souls do not exist from the beginning, etc.”—in volume I of the edition of St. Martin of León published at Segovia in 1782, where it was attributed to St. Augustine.

When I reread the passage and observed that the sentence was taken from chapter 14 of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, as stated in the marginal note on page 577, I attributed it, as a gift of divine providence, to the discovery by this route of the true author of that celebrated book.

At that time I therefore thought that I had established the matter clearly and that the author of such a work should immediately be announced as Bracharius, the bishop.

29. But when I turned my attention to weighing the arguments by which the same work is attributed to Gennadius, I found that this opinion was sufficiently probable. Its arguments must be overturned before our judgment—or rather the judgment of John of Seville, a writer of the ninth century—can be established.

I therefore pass over the opinion of those who think that the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is a work of St. Augustine. Among them are the aforementioned St. Martin of León, who flourished in the twelfth century, and the Master of the Sentences in some insufficiently corrected editions, and perhaps other more recent writers.

I shall say nothing about Gratian, who assigns the same book to Paterius, nor about Trithemius and others who attribute it to Alcuin. For my sole purpose is to refute the arguments of those who have identified the little book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* under the name of Gennadius of Marseilles.

30. It will nevertheless be useful first to know who these writers were, especially the earlier ones, since those who wrote in more recent times, from the twelfth century onward, drew this opinion from them.

The foremost is Pope Adrian I, who, in chapter 59 of his letter to Charlemagne, sent in the year 787, reports as follows:

> “In the sacred councils mentioned above, these testimonies of my most holy predecessors, the pontiffs, were presented: namely, that of St. Gennadius, bishop of Marseilles, concerning how the bodies or relics of the saints should be venerated. Chapter 40: ‘The bodies of the saints, and especially the relics of the blessed, must be honored with the utmost sincerity as the members of Christ; and the basilicas called by their name must be approached with the deepest affection and most faithful devotion, as places dedicated to divine worship. If anyone opposes this judgment, let him not be considered a Christian, but an Eunomian.’”

31. Neither the Louvain theologians nor the Maurist editors of St. Augustine’s works used this testimony of Adrian, which is the strongest of all, in support of Gennadius.

Adrian’s authority can be weakened only by saying that, among the other historical errors contained in these few words, one must count the attribution of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* to Gennadius. If these words did not belong to a Roman pontiff, Baronius would have openly rejected Adrian’s calling Gennadius a saint. For although Gennadius cleared himself before St. Gelasius of the stain of Pelagianism, many still consider him unpurged of the taint of Semi-Pelagianism.

32. Baronius’s judgment of Gennadius, under the year 490, no. 45, is as follows:

> “As for Gennadius’s doctrine, anyone who carefully reads his writings will understand that, while at times opposing Pelagius, he favored Pelagian errors. You will see that he must be cast into that class of Pelagians who, inwardly favoring Pelagian errors, appeared outwardly to oppose Pelagius.”

In the preceding number he had quoted Gennadius’s own words:

> “I, Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles, sent a work on my faith”—by which he was clearing himself of that error—“to the blessed Gelasius, bishop of the city of Rome.”

33. Norisius says the following concerning Gennadius’s Semi-Pelagianism in book II of his *History of Pelagianism*, chapter 16:

> “From the Semi-Pelagians’ praise of him and Prosper’s rebuke, no one can justly deny that he [Gennadius] was a Semi-Pelagian.”

If Norisius later frees Gennadius from this error, he does not do so without qualification, but only as far as concerns the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*, which he believed to be Gennadius’s.

34. Whatever the truth may be—even if Gennadius died in the Catholic faith, as the cited author of the *Annals* believes—it can never be maintained that he was a saint.

This is Adrian’s first error in a purely historical matter: he casually called Gennadius a saint. A second similar error follows, namely that he called Gennadius bishop of Marseilles. That is entirely false, since it is plainly established that he was only a presbyter, as Pagius states in his notes on Baronius, under the same year, no. 21: “Gennadius’s episcopate is wholly fictitious… for he was only a presbyter of Marseilles.”

35. The Louvain theologians and the Maurist editors of St. Augustine’s works defend this very point against Platina. The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume I, column 636 of the Paris edition of 1731, and others do likewise. They reject Sigebert of Gembloux for calling Gennadius a bishop. Baronius also fell into this error, influenced by the authority of Pope Adrian.

The blessed Notker Balbulus, who around the year 890 wrote his *Notice of Illustrious Men Who Intentionally Explained the Sacred Scriptures*, etc. (volume I of Pez’s *Anecdota*, page 1; Fabricius, volume V of the *Bibliotheca medii et infimae Latinitatis*, pages 143 and 308 of the Padua edition of 1754; *Gallia Christiana*, volume V, columns 900 and following, in the cited edition), is even more mistaken: he calls Gennadius, once and again, bishop of Toledo—unless this error belongs not to Notker but to those who published his work.

36. Since Adrian stumbled twice in a single line, it may reasonably be asserted that he was deceived in naming the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* by some testimony resembling that which led him to make those first two assertions.

37. It would be easy to maintain that the other advocates of the same opinion copied it from Adrian—who certainly preceded them—and that all were led astray by his authority. But I have chosen to defend my opinion by another route.

Once Pope Adrian’s testimony is rejected for the reasons explained, the testimony of John of Seville in favor of Bracharius is older than all the others.
