Walafrid Strabo, who lived in Germany at the same time that John of Seville lived in Spain, praises Gennadius as the author of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* in chapter 20 of his work *On the Origins and Developments of Ecclesiastical Affairs*. But it must be observed that Strabo’s testimony is later than that of John of Seville.

38. Strabo’s work was written only after the year 840, as Cellier demonstrates in his *General History of Sacred and Ecclesiastical Authors*, volume XVIII, page 673:

> “What he [Walafrid] says about the death of Louis the Pious proves that he composed this treatise [*On the Origins*, etc.] only after the year 840.”

But Gomez Bravo dates the exchange of letters between Alvarus of Córdoba and John of Seville to the years 820–830 (*Catalogue of the Bishops of Córdoba*, book II, chapter 2, page 115 of the latest edition), and Flórez does not disagree (*España sagrada*, volume XI, treatise 34, chapter 2, no. 43, page 37).

39. Thus at least ten years of greater antiquity stand on the side of the Spaniard, who knew nothing of the Germans’ opinion on this matter. The Germans, perhaps influenced solely by Adrian’s authority, assigned the book in question to Gennadius, presbyter of Marseilles.

In Spain, by contrast, there must have been more substantial testimony for the book to be attributed to Bracharius; for it is not to be believed that John invented this attribution.

Bracharius held the episcopate from 656 to 681. For in December 656 Fugitivus was still bishop of Seville, while in January 681 Julian, or whatever other bishop it may have been, was already governing the see of Seville and took part in the twelfth Council of Toledo (*España sagrada*, volume IX, treatise 29, chapter 6, nos. 19–34; and volume VI, treatise 6, chapter 14, no. 1, etc.; and the dissertation *On the Primacy*, section VI). Bracharius lived between these two bishops (*España sagrada*, volume IX, same place, no. 22, etc.).

40. John, a writer at the beginning of the ninth century, lived one hundred years later, or slightly more. For around the year 820, as we explained earlier, Alvarus addressed John as follows in letter 5, no. 2:

> “Believe me, brother—indeed, father in age.”

For John of Seville to have been called the father of Alvarus of Córdoba in that year, it is necessary to place John’s birth around the year 750, since Alvarus was born toward the end of the eighth century or at the beginning of the ninth.

John therefore assigned the work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* to Bracharius on the basis of some substantial foundation. He did so all the more because he was writing to Alvarus, a man of noble birth and exceptional learning, and there is no evidence that Alvarus rejected John’s opinion. Indeed, no later letter from one to the other survives after John’s letter in which Bracharius is mentioned.

Otherwise Alvarus seems to have been ignorant of the work’s true author; for in no. 7 of letter 5 he assigns the same work to Jerome, unless I am mistaken, although I rather think that passage is confused.

41. Having weighed the foundations of John’s and Walafrid’s assertions, I judge that John’s opinion should be preferred. Since it remained hidden until Father Flórez brought it to light, it is not surprising that no one adopted it.

It is nevertheless surprising that when Flórez first presented it in volume IX, treatise 29, chapter 6, page 220, he did not notice what work was being discussed. After publishing the fragment of the letter beginning “But among the things which Bracharius…,” he added on page 223:

> “It is unknown to us whether that work—the work of Bracharius mentioned by John of Seville—still exists; but the fragment quoted may serve to identify its author, if the work should appear.”

42. Thus, according to Flórez’s judgment, Bracharius is the author of whatever work contains the fragment. But, as we have seen, this is not as evident as he himself thought.

His arguments do make it clear that Bracharius was bishop of Seville. It may therefore be counted to the credit of the Church of Seville that, as we certainly believe, it produced a work celebrated everywhere from the span of ten centuries down to our own age. For in Germany, Italy, and Gaul it was already being read with approval near the end of the eighth century.

43. In the ninth century Florus the presbyter—or someone else writing under the name of the Church of Lyon—declared that a work of this kind had been tainted by Pelagian error while writing against the errors of John the Irishman.

In volume IV, part II, column 253 of the Paris edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum* of 1624, and volume XV, page 611 of the Lyon edition of 1677, there is a book written under the name of the Church of Lyon against John Erigena around the year 850. Florus is believed to be its author. In chapter 2 it contains the following:

> “But the claim that a human being cannot reach God without the exertion of his own labor is not Catholic but Pelagian. A definition of this kind is found in a little book entitled *Ecclesiastical Dogmas*. But entirely—as … and several other passages in the same little book, it is a Pelagian error.”

44. The Louvain theologians who corrected the edition of St. Augustine’s works held the same opinion. Among them was Henry Cuyckius, who corrected volume III. In the appendix, page 380 of the Antwerp edition, with the approval of the other theologians of that academy, he marked the book *On Dogmas* with this judgment:

> “This book is not by a Catholic writer, but by Gennadius, a presbyter of Marseilles in Gaul… belonging to the party of the Gauls, against which the Second Council of Orange was convened. Just as he frequently contains serious errors in his catalogue of illustrious men, so also in these *Ecclesiastical Dogmas* he contains certain things against which the reader must be on guard… Nowhere in this book does he mention original sin or the baptism of infants for the remission of sins. Although he names many heretics, he nowhere mentions Pelagius or the Catholic dogma issued against him. Instead, he carefully insists that souls are not transmitted by descent, because he knew that Pelagius based his own doctrine on that point.”

The Maurists transcribed this judgment in their edition and did not dissent from it.

45. But the learned Cardinal Norisius, considering these opinions in the place cited, so beautifully defends the work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* that nothing could surpass it:

> “I do not approve the judgments of these men. First of all, it is by no means Pelagian to say that labor is necessary for a human being to obtain salvation, if the labor proceeds not from the powers of nature alone but from the power of preceding grace… This is the doctrine handed down by the Council of Orange after canon 25… Nor can what he said—‘It is within our power to assent to saving inspiration’—be called Semi-Pelagian. For even when we choose the good, the will is prepared by the Lord. Hence St. Augustine says: ‘When the will is prepared for some but not for others by the Lord, one must discern what comes from his mercy and what from his judgment.’ Gennadius wholly adheres to this judgment.

“For in chapter 56, in a few words, he attributes the beginning and completion of salvation to the power of divine grace… When he discusses an evil work, he assigns it to the choice of free will alone; but when he discusses a good and holy work, he no longer sets before us choice alone, but God assisting and preparing the will so that it may choose the good.”

46. I had warned that Norisius’s defense pertained rather to vindicating the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* than Gennadius himself; and, as I think, this has now been confirmed. For it must be observed that all the passages brought forward are excerpted from that book. The defense concludes with these words of Vossius:

> We hope that those who know that he displays toward the monuments of antiquity the candor of mind which he wishes posterity to bring to the assessment of his labors will not disapprove this judgment of ours. …

Thus the work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* is free from every error, and its author, namely Bracharius, is likewise free from error, as our opinion maintains. Gennadius too, although he did not write it, may, so far as we are concerned, be considered free from error, as Baronius judged.

47. You have the weight of all the arguments by which this book ought to be restored to our Bracharius. The learned men to whose judgment I entrust them will judge how probable they are. But certainly, I think, they will not deny that they are at least as probable as those advanced for Gennadius of Massilia.

48. I have passed over in silence the opinion of Ratramnus, monk of Corbie, who, in chapter 5 of his book *Against the Objections of the Greeks*, assigned the work *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas* to Gennadius, patriarch of Constantinople, who died in the year 471. For I see no one who followed that opinion except the latest editor of Acherius’s *Spicilegium*, who, in volume I of the Paris folio edition of 1723, noted at the bottom of the page:

> Those who published this book of Gennadius, since they knew no writer of that name except the presbyter of Massilia, assigned to him another man’s offspring. Ratramnus refuted their ignorance in this passage, in the manner cited.

But since Ratramnus expressed this opinion around the year 867, the two earlier opinions that we have discussed are certainly prior to it. Nor do we know of others who, having read Ratramnus’s work, subscribed to his opinion; nor does its editor confirm it by any new argument.

49. Finally, it is worth observing that three writers of the same century—John of Seville, Walafrid, and Ratramnus—one in Spain, another in Germany, and the third in Gaul, gave such divergent judgments concerning the author of the same book, which all of them handled.

50. Having now completed these observations of mine, I have encountered two further matters to be noted concerning the same book in volume III of the works of St. Leo, edited by the Ballerini priests of Verona and published at Venice in 1757; yet neither contributes to discovering its true author. Those learned men mention, on page CLXXXIX and following, a ninth-century codex in which the work is attributed to St. Augustine. On page CCLXI they mention another codex, apparently of the eighth century, in which the person who abridged the work—or perhaps the scribe who excerpted certain passages—gave it this title: *From a letter of Pope Felix to the bishops of Sicily*. We readily follow the editors’ judgment, which is as follows:

> Perhaps the abbreviator prefixed Pope Felix’s name to it—that is, to the book *On Dogmas*—because he found this little work in some collection after Felix’s letter to the Sicilian bishops.

## CHAPTER LXXXIV

### The *Exegesis*, or *Exposition of the Mass*: Is It Isidore’s?

The work *On the Canon of the Mystical Offering* appears to be later than Isidore. Numerous and varied copies of the *Exposition of the Mass*. *Exhortation to Humility* by St. Martin of Dumio attributed to Isidore in some sources. *The Conflict of Vices and Virtues* attributed to many authors. Metrical abridgment of this work. French translation.

1. In the new Madrid edition of the works of St. Isidore, among the appendices on page 54, an *Exposition of the Mass* was published with this rather inelegant note:

> It seems contradictory to say that this exposition is by St. Isidore, because this liturgy was not in use in his time.

The margin indicates that the *Exposition* was taken from a ninth-century codex. It begins: “The Lord be with you: He greets the people,” etc. It ends: “and let all respond: Thanks be to God.” This little work had already appeared, as may be gathered from Nicolás Antonio:

> We saw an *Exegesis of the canon of the Mass*, published at Paris by Charles Guillard in 1548, in octavo, in the library of the Roman Sapienza.

The old catalogue of the Sapienza does indeed list this book; but it is now missing, whether stolen or placed out of order on some other shelf. Bayerius states in a note that the *Exegesis* was first published separately at Paris in the year 1648; but, as I think, there is a numerical error: 1648 should read 1548, the year given by Nicolás Antonio. I observed in chapter 69, section 11, that Fabricius and Zaccaria, who think that the Paris edition of the *Exegesis of the Mass* was excerpted from Isidore’s books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, have not looked carefully enough.

2. Bayerius gathers several arguments in defense of attributing the *Exegesis* to Isidore, against the editor’s note that he has quoted. That note, he says, is “much more Latin,” though not for that reason more truthful; it also appears in the preface to the same edition. He testifies that two codices of this *Exegesis* exist in the Escurial library. One was written in the year 954, as is stated in a contemporary hand in the same manuscript, under this heading: *Exposition of the Mass*, with no author indicated; it was from this copy that the work was reprinted in the new Madrid edition. The other is apparently from the late or closing years of the thirteenth century and bears Isidore’s name explicitly.

He therefore thinks, not without reason, that the work was attributed to Isidore by Trithemius, Eisengrein, Gesner, Fabricius, and others, especially since its doctrine and style are not inconsistent with Isidorian works. It is therefore surprising that it does not appear in Grialius’s Madrid edition.

3. Apparently distinct from the two codices cited by Bayerius is Escurial Codex IV, folio 9, described by Rodríguez de Castro in volume II of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, page 324, in octavo. It is a membranous manuscript of the tenth or early eleventh century, written in obscure characters, with many abbreviations and red titles and initials. It once belonged to the principal church of Seville and was at one time in the possession of Father Mariana, who returned it in 1583.

The title on the cover is: *Treatise on the Mass of Blessed Isidore. His book of Differentiae. Also his book of Prologues.* On the first folio:

> Here begins the *Treatise on the Mass*, published from beginning to end by the most blessed Isidore.

Rodríguez asserts that this treatise is altogether the same as the work *On the Canon of the Mystical Offering*, which, at the end of Hittorp’s collection *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, published at Rome in 1591, was conjecturally attributed to Hugh of St. Victor. If the codex is as old as Rodríguez indicates, Hugh cannot be the author of the work *On the Canon of the Mystical Offering*. I would judge that a book of this sort belongs to a later period and that, on the basis of its age, it could indeed be attributed to Hugh.

It explains the Roman canon of the Mass, but in a manner different from the *Exegesis of the Mass* published in the new Madrid edition, though there it was presented as Isidore’s, contrary, as I have said, to Bayerius.

[Col. 0609D] 4. Bayerius responds to the recent editor’s contrary argument as follows. Besides other liturgies of uncertain authority that circulate, Gelasius I composed the prefaces of the Sacramentary in the fifth century; then, in the sixth century, Gregory the Great reformed the Gelasian book. This rite continued in Spain until its downfall; afterward it was somewhat altered in the period of the Mozarabs, and in the eleventh century was restored by the authority of St. Gregory VII. It prevailed continually in Spain and still prevails there. This will become clear to anyone who compares the present order of the Mass with this *Exegesis* and with the example of the Gregorian Sacramentary published by Muratori in volume II of the *Roman Liturgy*, from a Vatican codex more than nine hundred years old.

Bayerius also possessed an old, five-hundred-year-old codex containing a Greek translation of the Gregorian liturgy, proceeding in the same order as our *Exegesis*. The Latin version is preserved in the Laurentian Medicean Library, volume II of the catalogue, shelf 29, no. 39, column 57, described under the title: *On the Order of the Mass and the Exposition of Its Words*. Bayerius adds that not only the use of the liturgy but also that of the Roman psalter continued in Spain in the time of the Goths. Finally, he concludes that Isidore could have written an exposition of the Roman liturgy for private use or for the use of others, even if that liturgy had not been received or customary in Spain during Isidore’s lifetime.

5. By these arguments Bayerius endeavors to vindicate the *Exegesis of the Mass* for Isidore. But in the part where he argues that the order of the Mass, which now prevails almost everywhere in the Latin Churches according to the Roman rite, also prevailed in Spain in Isidore’s time, his effort is entirely futile. The Gothic liturgy must be sought not in the Roman Missal but in the Mozarabic Missal, which still exists.

No one will deny that there is a great difference between the Mozarabic and Roman Mass, at least with respect to certain distinctive rites and prayers. Isidore himself, in his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, explains point by point not the parts of the Mass that is now Roman, but those of the Gothic Mass, now called Mozarabic. Nor did the Mozarabs depart from or alter the Gothic rite. Rather, after they had devoutly retained it, St. Gregory VII finally succeeded in having the Roman rite substituted for the Gothic, or Mozarabic, rite in the churches of Spain, with a few exceptions.

On this point Flórez differs greatly from Bayerius. In volume III of *Hispania Sacra*, pages 212 and following, he attempts to prove that the Spaniards had always preserved the order of the Mass originally received from the Roman pontiffs; that it later appeared different from the Roman order because the pontiffs themselves had introduced certain changes at Rome for legitimate reasons; and that Galicia, in the sixth century and until the year 633, when the Fourth Council of Toledo prescribed the same rite for all the churches of Spain, had a Roman Mass different from the ancient Spanish, or Gothic, Mass.

Yet although, at the very beginning of the Church, the same general manner of celebrating the Eucharist may have been observed at Rome and in Spain—which I believe to be true—little by little the supreme pontiffs at Rome and the Fathers of the Gothic Church in Spain separately added certain prayers and formulas of supplication. From this arose that great difference.

[Col. 0610D] 6. If, however, the Roman order of the Mass remained in use in Galicia, and perhaps in some other parts of Spain, until the year 633, as Flórez maintains, Bayerius’s other argument will appear more probable: namely, that Isidore could have written an exposition of the Roman Mass for private use or for the use of others, since it could have been useful to many Spaniards.

Here is the place to ask whether, in Isidore’s time, the Roman canon of the Mass was as it is represented in the *Exegesis*. Muratori’s codex, which Bayerius cites, is not far removed from that period. I too have encountered many ancient codices in which the Roman canon of the Mass that now exists is found, with only a few words altered.

The Vatican Ottobonian Codex 576 contains an old monastic missal on parchment, in quarto, written in Lombard script, or, as it is called, Beneventan, with musical notation older than that of Petrus Aretinus. It begins: “To you I have lifted up my soul, O God,” etc.; “Stir up your power, we beseech you, O Lord,” etc. Then follows the Second Sunday of Advent, etc., almost as in our Missals. There are Masses of St. Nicholas, St. Ambrose, St. Sylvester, and, after Epiphany, of St. Maurus the abbot, etc.

7. In Lent there are offices for weekdays and Sundays. On Holy Saturday there are several rites concerning the blessing of oil, salt, etc., and the following distinctive directions concerning baptism by triple immersion:

> “And thus, taking him from his hands, let him baptize him under a triple immersion, saying: ‘And I baptize you in the name of the Father’: let him immerse him once. ‘And of the Son’: let him immerse him again. ‘And of the Holy Spirit’: let him immerse him a third time in the form of a cross—first with the infant’s head turned toward the east and his feet toward the west; second toward the south; and third toward the north. When the infant has risen from the sacred font, let him make a cross of chrism on his crown with his thumb, saying the prayer,” etc.

Afterward comes the explanation of the Lord’s Prayer, customarily given by a priest: “Our Father, who are in heaven: This is the voice of freedom,” etc. Then follows an exposition of the Creed; the preparation of the litanies for the Mass, etc. The canon of the Mass follows: “Therefore, most merciful Father,” etc., as in modern Missals. There occur the words, “together with your servant, our pope N., and our abbot N.” There is also the *Memento*, as they call it, for the dead.

In the prayer “Deliver us,” etc., certain saints are added: “Mary, Mother of God, and blessed Michael the archangel, and your holy apostles Peter and Paul, Andrew, and your blessed confessors Martin, Gregory, Benedict, Maurus, and blessed Scholastica with all the saints,” etc. After the feasts of the saints comes the Order of Betrothal, with rubric, blessing of the ring, Mass, etc. There are also the Common of Apostles, Martyrs, and so forth. Several leaves are missing at the end. The codex perhaps belongs to the tenth century.

8. The canon of the Mass also occurs in the Royal-Vatican Codex 191, approximately of the tenth century, after Isidore’s books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* and certain other works. “It is truly worthy and just,” etc., continues to “Holy, holy, holy.” “Therefore, most merciful Father,” etc. “Our pope N., and all,” etc.

After the name of Damian, the following is noted in the margin as something to be inserted:

> “and those whose solemn triumph is celebrated today in the presence of your glory.”

Afterward: “He gave [it] twice to his disciples,” not “he did not give.” Then: “And therefore, remembering, we, your servants, O Lord,” etc., “may be filled with grace through Christ our Lord.” “To us also, sinners.”

The *Memento* for the dead is absent. It is likewise omitted in our *Exegesis*, which agrees very closely with the canon of the Mass in this codex.

9. The Vatican Codex 1146 is also extremely ancient, and in it the canon of the Mass is found almost as it is now recited. There we read:

> “Together with your servant, our pope N., etc.; Cosmas and Damian”—if it is the feast of the saints, this should be said, and also while celebrating the birthday of that blessed one or of those blessed ones—“Remember also, O Lord, those who have gone before us with the sign of faith and sleep in the sleep of peace.” Then they are recited, and after they have been recited, he says: “To them,” etc.

At the end the rubric reads:

> “This came from the monastery of Dionysius. The Exposition of the Mass begins. First in order,” etc.

I understand this to mean the Parisian monastery of St. Dionysius. I shall describe this codex in chapter 95. In examining other manuscript codices, several further examples of this kind will occur.

10. It is therefore established from ancient manuscript copies that the canon of the Mass now in use is extremely old, with only a few words perhaps added or altered according to the diversity of churches. Accordingly, on this point the person who contended that the *Exegesis* was Isidore’s work would not easily be refuted.

Nevertheless, the matter seems to me very doubtful. Nor do I think that in Isidore’s time, especially in Spain, the Roman pontiff was called “the Apostolic” as a title of distinction, as he is called in the *Exegesis* at the words:

> “Remember, O Lord, your male and female servants, and all who stand around.”

For the author continues:

> “The priest had previously prayed for the Apostolic and for his own bishop.”

11. I found this same exposition of the Mass in Vatican manuscript codices, but without the author’s name. In Vatican Codex 1146, a parchment folio manuscript, after several other anonymous expositions of the Mass, there is, on page 20, an *Exposition of the Mass*:

> “The Lord be with you. The priest greets the people and prays that the Lord may be with him.”

It ends:

> “let it be announced by the minister, and let all respond, ‘Thanks be to God, amen.’”

A recent note at the beginning states:

> “These excerpts appear to have been taken from Alcuin or from another author.”

The codex is approximately of the tenth century and contains much material concerning ecclesiastical rites; it will be described in its proper place.

I found the same exposition of the Mass in Vatican Palatine Codex 485, from approximately the same period. On the reverse of page 16 there is another exposition. First comes the prayer “Almighty God, have mercy,” etc.; then:

> “First in the order of the Mass, the antiphon for the entrance is sung,” etc.

On the reverse of page 18, after the prayer of the secret, the priest says:

> “The Lord be with you.”

The priest prays while greeting the people for the clergy and the congregation, etc. It ends on the reverse of page 27: “He commended the apostles.” Immediately there is a rubric:

> “Likewise begins another exposition of the Mass: ‘The Lord be with you’; the priest greets,” etc.

It ends: “and let all respond, amen. The exposition is finished. Again begins an exposition concerning the competent.”

The exposition beginning “The Lord be with you; the priest greets,” etc., is the one attributed to Isidore in some sources.

[Col. 0612D] 12. I find Isidore’s name in an approximately tenth-century work inscribed in the Ottobonian Codex *On the Order of the Mass*. But this is different from the *Exegesis of the Mass*, as is clear from the rubric itself:

> “On the order of the Mass, or on the prayers contained in it, in chapter 15 of Isidore’s book *On Offices*, namely book I: ‘The order of the Mass, however,’ etc., ‘the world completes.’”

What follows is:

> “Celestine, a Campanian by nationality and the forty-fifth pontiff at Rome, established that the antiphon—that is, the entrance—and David’s psalm should be sung before the sacrifice. Previously this was not done; only Paul’s Epistle and the holy Gospel were read.”

Other matters of this kind are then added. Isidore is cited again, and the measures prescribed by Roman pontiffs at various times are inserted, such as:

> “Damasus, the thirty-ninth pontiff in this order, a Spaniard by nationality, established that psalms should be sung day and night throughout all the churches. He ordered this for priests, bishops, or monasteries.”

13. There are many other examples of an *Exposition of the Mass* distinct from the *Exegesis* attributed to Isidore: some published, others unpublished; some with the author’s name, others without it.

In Vatican Codices 1143 and 1146 there is an anonymous exposition of the Mass beginning “First,” etc. In another Vatican codex, 1121, there is Albert the Great’s exposition of the canon of the Mass, from his book *On the Office of the Mass*: “In the natural body,” etc. In Vatican Codex 4862 there is Albert the Great’s *Exposition of the Mass*: “Behold, I shall explain.” In Vatican Codex 4074 there is Innocent’s *Exposition of the Mass and the Canon*: “Note the reasons why,” etc. In Vatican Codex 4578, a parchment folio manuscript, there is Remigius of Auxerre’s *Exposition of the Mass*: “The Celebration of the Mass.” In Vatican Codex 4396 there is an *Exposition of the Offering of the Mass*: “Therefore, most merciful Father.” In Vatican Codex 7150 there is an *Exposition of the Roman Mass*: “Whenever, against,” etc.

14. Royal-Vatican Library Codex 214, a parchment manuscript in quarto, contains Florus the Master’s exposition of the canon of the Mass: “In the mystery,” etc. Codex 435 contains an exposition of the Mass by an ancient writer: “First,” etc. Codex 446 contains an exposition of the Roman Mass: “Whenever,” etc., which is mutilated at the end. Codex 524 contains an exposition of the canon of the Mass under the name of Peter Damian: “The day before he suffered.” Codex 612, a parchment manuscript in octavo, contains an exposition of the Mass: “The male,” etc.

15. The exposition of the Mass by Brother Bernard of Parentinis, of the Order of Preachers—“Because,” etc.—is preserved in Vatican Palatine Codex 345. Henry of Hesse’s *Exposition of the Mass* is in another Vatican Palatine Codex, 717.

Another anonymous *Exposition of the Mass* is in Palatine Codex 1578, approximately of the tenth century. It begins:

> “The celebration of the Mass is conducted in commemoration of Christ’s Passion,” etc.

It ends:

> “as animals and beasts.”

The exposition of the Mass and of the Creed ends with these words. It appears to be the exposition of the Mass already described from the Florentine Codex of St. Mark in chapter 44, where I said that Isidore is cited.

16. Codex 6 of the Vatican Ottobonian Library, approximately of the tenth century and in octavo, contains several miscellaneous works. On page 9 it records:

> “Here begins the order according to which a bishop or priest ought to prepare himself for the divine offices. First, the psalm ‘How lovely,’ etc. A prayer for the state of the Church and for all the living, to whom we are indebted: ‘Receive, Holy Trinity, this offering for our emperor N. and his venerable offspring,’ etc., ‘and for the salvation of our congregation,’ etc.”

A prayer for the dead is also inserted. On the reverse of page 11 follows:

> “In the name of Christ begins the Exposition of the Mass: ‘The Mass, as blessed Isidore says, is so called from sending forth.’”

It is a brief exposition of the Roman Mass, mutilated at the end.

In another Ottobonian codex, 257, there is Paschasius Radbertus’s work *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, with a metrical prologue: “To approach the sacred things of the King,” etc. There is also what appears to be his *Exposition of the Mass*: “The Mass, as blessed Isidore says,” etc. In Ottobonian Codex 567 there is an *Exposition of the Mass*: “The Apostle says.” In another Ottobonian codex, 943, there is an *Exposition of the Mass* published in the monastery of St. Dionysius: “First in order.”

17. John Cochlaeus published at Mainz in 1559 a *Mirror of Devotion Concerning the Mass*, containing an exposition of the Mass from the Eystätt and Meissen manuscripts, reprinted by Hittorp from another manuscript. It begins:

> “The Mass is celebrated for many reasons,”

and is perhaps by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, among whose works there is an *Exposition of the Mass* beginning:

> “It must be avoided by priests,” etc.,

followed shortly by:

> “The Mass is celebrated for many reasons,” etc.

Thereafter appeared the *Mirror of the Mass from Certain Most Ancient and Very Old Fathers of the Catholic Church*, first laboriously compiled by John Cochlaeus and now revised, enlarged, and enriched by Brother Nicholas Aurificus of Siena, a Carmelite, Venice, at the press of Francesco Ziletti, 1572, in octavo.

The works included are Amalarius’s *On the Office of the Mass*; Walafrid’s *On Ecclesiastical Matters*; an *Exposition of the Mass* from two venerably ancient manuscripts, Meissen and Eystätt, beginning “The Mass is celebrated for many reasons,” etc.; Peter Damian’s book entitled “The Lord be with you”; Honorius of Autun’s *Gemma animae*; the *Micrologus*; Peter, abbot of Cluny’s *Nucleus Concerning the Sacrifice of the Mass*; Berno’s little book *On Certain Matters Relating to the Mass*; Hildebert’s verses *On the Mystery of the Mass*; the *Order of the Mass* by John Burchard; and Nicholas Aurificus’s little work *On the Antiquity, Truth, and Ceremonies of the Mass*.

In Dacherius’s *Spicilegium*, volume I, item 6, there is a letter of Isaac, bishop of Langres, on the canon of the Mass: “Behold what for a long time,” etc. Odo, bishop of Cambrai’s *Exposition of the Canon of the Mass* appeared at Venice in 1569, in a smaller format. It begins: “Therefore, most merciful Father,” etc.; “For it is worthy and just,” etc. John Burchard of Strasbourg’s *Order of the Mass* in Italian—*L’ordine della messa*—was published at Venice in 1566.

18. Since so many and such varied expositions of the Mass have appeared, and since Isidore’s doctrine was distinguished both in *Ecclesiastical Offices* and in explaining the liturgy, it is not surprising that an anonymous exposition was attributed to him somewhere, although it may not be his.

Bandini, in volume II of the *Codices Latini of the Medicean Library of Florence*, shelf 29, describes Codex 39, a parchment manuscript in quarto from the thirteenth century. He says that it contains works of St. Isidore and others, and under no. 9 records:

> “An anonymous work on the order of the Mass and the exposition of its words. It begins: ‘The Mass—blessed Peter …’ It ends: ‘produces the effect.’”

Under no. 22 he also records:

> “A concise exposition of the canon of the Mass. It begins: ‘The Lord be with you: the priest greets.’ It ends: ‘he is ordered to go home by the priest, with the Lord’s help,’ etc.”

Its beginning is the same as that of the *Exegesis* circulated under Isidore’s name; but the final words do not agree. Nor does the Florentine codex, apparently, attribute this second exposition to Isidore in any way.

19. Among the appendices of the new Madrid edition, on page 42, an *Exhortation to Humility* was published from a manuscript codex that bore Isidore’s name. It begins:

> “Whoever, by the nod of God,” etc.

But the editor observes that this *Exhortation* is by St. Martin of Braga, as is clear from volume XV of *Hispania Sacra*. Flórez had indeed published, among other works, St. Martin’s *Exhortation to Humility*, comparing two manuscript codices, one from Toledo and the other from the Madrid royal library, as well as Tamayo’s edition.

The little work, collated by me with Flórez’s edition and with the new Madrid edition of St. Isidore’s works, will appear much more accurately, namely among the doubtful or falsely attributed works of Isidore.

20. Cyprian Suárez emended the little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues* for the Madrid royal edition and inferred from manuscript codices, style, and the testimony of Sigebert that it was Isidore’s work.

John Grialius rather believed it to be a work of John Chrysostom *On the Struggle of Virtues and Vices*, which Isidore himself mentions in the book *On Illustrious Men*, but which was enlarged and interpolated at a later time and expounded in more than one way according to the differing ingenuity of interpreters.

After Nicolás Antonio had reported contradictory opinions on the matter, including those of Mabillon, who asserts that the author was Ambrose Autpertus, abbot of St. Vincent at Volturno in Benevento, and of Constantine Cajetan, who considers the author to have been some Benedictine of Milan, he declared that the discussion ought to be expanded.

[Col. 0615B] Bayerius notes that among modern writers only Cave attributes this little work to Isidore, on the basis of Sigebert and other evidence, as he himself says. He adds that Dupin, Placcius, Cellier, Oudin, and Fabricius attribute it to Ambrose Autpertus; Bellarmine lists it among works attributed to Isidore; and the work is not found in the Escurial library.

Labbe, too, on the basis of Sigebert and manuscript codices, attributes this work to Isidore; he observes in it a reference to the Rule of St. Benedict. Although Ildefonsus and Braulio do not mention the little book, he wisely observes that Braulio warned that Isidore had other works besides those he had listed. Constantine Cajetan composed a lengthy discussion of this little book on page 29, which it is worthwhile to reproduce here.

21. Finally, we have excluded from the catalogue of Isidore’s writings that book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which is attributed to various authors. For it is found among the works of Leo the Great printed at Paris in the year of our Lord 1511 and at Venice in 1553, but not in the newer editions. It also appears in volume IX of St. Augustine.

The theologians of Louvain rightly judged that it belonged to neither author, chiefly because of a certain narrative inserted into it about a monk tormented by a demon, and because of an epilogue mentioning St. Benedict, who was much later than these doctors.

In the works of St. Ambrose printed at Rome in the year of Christ 1585, this book is addressed to Simplicianus; but it was relegated to the latter part of volume V, together with other books whose authority—or perhaps authorship—is uncertain, and it was shortened by the removal of that narrative and its epilogue.

Arnold Wion (*Lignum Vitae*, book V, chapter 12, emblem 6) judged that the same book should be attributed to Gregory the Great. For he writes:

> “He is said also to have written one book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which is found under his name in the manuscript collection of our St. Benedict of Mantua. It is cited by many in support of this holy man, such as John Bertels, abbot of Luxembourg, in the eighth dialogue on the Rule of our holy father Benedict, and others. Finally, the style itself indicates that it belongs to no one other than St. Gregory.”

John Grialius, however, argues for St. Isidore in the preface to Isidore’s works on these grounds:

> “The little work was believed by an excellent man to be Isidore’s—just as he himself left it written—because of the codices bearing his name, its style, which perhaps does not differ greatly from the *Synonyma*, and Sigebert’s testimony. We, however, so as not to conceal anything, believe that this was the work which in Isidore’s own time circulated under the name of John Chrysostom. For this is what Isidore says of Chrysostom in his book *On Illustrious Men*: ‘There is also found, addressed to a certain most noble matron named Gregoria, an outstanding work of his, *On the Conduct of Life and the Formation of Character*, or *On the Struggle of Virtues and Vices*.’ Therefore, we shall attribute such numerous variations in the writings to the interpreters rather than to the copyists.”

22. For our part, we have wished, in some fashion, to restore these various and mutually conflicting opinions of writers to the radiance of a single truth. First, however, let me say, with the indulgence of Grialius and Wion, that the book under discussion is no more the work of Ambrose, Augustine, or Leo than it is that of Gregory or Isidore.

The argument drawn from its style is entirely invalid and wholly empty, since its style resembles not only the books of Isidore’s *Synonyma*, as Grialius maintained, but also, as Wion wished, the writings of Gregory. This is especially so because reasoning drawn from a writer’s diction or style—which is apt to vary with the changing force of meanings according to the subject or the time—is generally considered highly prone to error.

The second argument is drawn from the titles of manuscript codices. If this argument truly had force, one and the same book ought not to be assigned to more than one author whenever it is found inscribed with the names of different doctors in different handwritten volumes. Accordingly, it may be said without injustice that Sigebert, otherwise a most learned man, was deceived, since he wrote in Germany more than five hundred years after Isidore’s time.

Furthermore, Grialius himself does not appear consistent in his opinion. For he had first attributed this little work *On Virtues and Vices* to Isidore, but later asserted that it was the same work as that which Chrysostom wrote *On the Conduct of Life and the Formation of Character*. In order to maintain this position, he entirely denies the existence of the epilogue that is attached to the aforementioned book *On Virtues and Vices*.

But since these two little works differ from one another as widely as heaven from earth, there is no reason for Grialius to blame interpreters for this matter—and without charge or evidence at that. Nor is there any reason for Breulius to call the appended letter the epilogue of the same book, since that concluding section, being genuinely part of the book itself, is far removed from the purpose of a letter.

And because we can gather stronger arguments for the truth from the epilogue of the book itself, we thought it worthwhile for that reason to reproduce it here, taking it from very ancient copies. It runs as follows.

23.

> “But you, man of God, attend carefully to what I say, and believe me as I relate something even more astonishing. I recently learned what I am about to say from someone’s report.
>
> “A certain religious man, who lived in monastic dress, was in our own time assailed by an unheard-of temptation from the ancient enemy, to such an extent that the same malignant spirit repeatedly befouled fragments of his clothing, even while they remained outside him, with an unclean filth. It was so horrible, foul, and harmful that the portion of the garments which it had touched was thereafter fit for no use, although it had been washed.
>
> “When I was asked why almighty God had given such power over him to the crafty serpent, I replied that it was in order to display outwardly the uncleanness of his heart. For it would never have acted upon his outward clothing unless it had wholly corrupted the inner man, either by unbelief and blasphemy or, at least, by empty and vain glory. For the corruption within the heart flows outward through the clothing.
>
> “Although I did not see him myself, since I was far away, I nevertheless foresaw, as I think, that these things were truly in him. And if it is not so, is the event nevertheless thought to have happened without cause? It also happened so that the foulness might preserve purity of heart in him, lest the cunning enemy stain it with the blemish of vainglory, just as Paul (2 Corinthians 12), lest he become proud because of the greatness of his revelations, received a thorn in the flesh.
>
> “Let whichever of these explanations be the case—or, even if none of them is, will the final point that I am about to make nevertheless not be true? It is altogether true, it is true, what I say: that this external filth is not harmful to the soul if the soul itself strives to preserve inward purity of heart.”

24. [Note: [Col. 0615] It may easily be conjectured that this book was addressed to some monk.] “Meanwhile, as you yourself have taken care to indicate, I hear that certain people among you say that no one can be perfected in the land of his birth, taking as proof the Lord’s saying: ‘No prophet is acceptable in his own country’ (Luke 4). They must first be refuted by the reasoning of truth, and only then must it be shown how the statement is to be understood. Let those who say these things listen patiently, because, by failing to consider prudently the meaning of Holy Scripture, they despise nearly all the saints. For if the matter is as they assert, then all those converted from among the Romans who live among the Romans, all those from among the Greeks who live among the Greeks, all those from among the Italians who live among the Italians, all those from among the Gauls who live among the Gauls, all those from among the Iberians who live among the Iberians, all those from among the Germans who live among the Germans, all those from Aquitaine who live among the Aquitanians, all those from Britain who live among the Britons, and all those from the English who live among the English and lead religious lives will be imperfect.

“Behold, Paul and Antony, from among the Thebans, were perfected among the Thebans; behold, Hilarion, from among the Palestinians, was perfected among the Palestinians; behold, Macarius, from among the Egyptians, was perfected among the Egyptians; behold, the city of Oxyrhynchus was wholly perfected from among its own citizens. Behold—so that we may come to our neighbors—Protasius and Gervasius, remaining in this very city of Milan, in their own house [Note: [Col. 0617D] The author shows that he is writing this book at Milan.], and practicing the monastic life for ten years, were so perfected that they became martyrs. Or will our province alone perhaps be excepted from this rule, so that it has monks not from its own people but only from foreigners?

“It is therefore more important to strive to live wherever one may be according to the rule of the perfect, and not to turn aside from the path of perfection through the allurements of parents, relatives, or in-laws. Thus, certainly, according to the Savior’s saying (Luke 14), he will be able to renounce father, mother, brothers, sisters, wives, children, houses, fields, and everything that he possesses. I say this not to deny the highest praise to those who pass from kingdom to kingdom and from public life to the desert, but to show that even those who flee their homeland more through their affections than through their footsteps are happy and perfect.

“I therefore ask those who deny that this can happen among you to consider with vigilant care why the Lord did not say: ‘No prophet is perfected in his own country.’ But what else is to be understood there except that he said ‘acceptable,’ by no means ‘received’? And he wished this to be understood both of the ancient prophets and of himself, who among the unbelieving Jews were not accepted but rather despised, as Stephen said to them: ‘Which of the prophets did your fathers not persecute, those who foretold the coming of the Just One, of whom you have now been murderers and betrayers?’ (Acts 7).

“Who does not see how great the recklessness and presumption would be for anyone to assume for himself the name of prophet? Therefore rebuke such people with charitable affection, and always strive to live according to the Rule of the Fathers, especially that of the holy confessor Benedict. Do not depart from it, nor add anything to it, nor take anything away. For it contains everything sufficient, and nowhere is it deficient. May its words and commands lead its followers to the palaces of heaven.”

[Col. 0617D] 25. Behold, dearest brother, amid my other occupations I dictated and wrote this discourse for you during the nighttime hours, though with unpolished elegance. Since I realized that it exceeded the form of a letter, I preferred to call it a little book—*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*—in which, if you find anything conducive to edification, you ought to have it read and pass it on to others.

26. The foregoing material, which we have now related, is found not only in all the printed copies issued under the name of Augustine or Leo, but also in other very ancient manuscripts, such as those of the libraries of Monte Cassino and Saint Benedict at Mantua. Moreover, anyone who investigates the matter carefully may see that this Epilogue has a necessary connection with the book itself. Therefore, the copies printed under the name of Isidore must be judged altogether mutilated.

First, because the book’s conclusion is so cold that the reader’s mind remains suspended by the wording and seems to expect something more in it. For it reads as follows: “But you, man of God, attend with vigilant care to what I say, with the help of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.” Such an imperfect ending to a peroration would be wholly unworthy of Isidore—something I certainly do not believe—if it were in his book.

Second, because its final sentence, which elsewhere is abbreviated, must be connected with the sentence found in our copies if it is to be complete. For the example of a certain monk narrated there is merely an account of the illusions of the evil spirits directed against us, whose deceitful temptations had already been described immediately before the beginning of this same Epilogue.

Third, because the work itself is recognized as having been written by a monk—indeed, I will say a Benedictine—to a man of the same profession. This is especially clear from chapters 11, 12, and 13, which deal with vigils, psalmody, manual labor, stability of place, and similar exercises familiar to a Benedictine monk. But the purpose for which these matters are treated is indicated in chapter 15, where it says: “If, therefore, the pursuit of desire is so dangerous for secular men, how much more dangerous is it for those who, by habit and way of life, have already ceased to be secular, who have devoted everything they live to the Lord?”

Since all these matters possess an excellent—indeed, almost necessary—connection with the subjects discussed at the end of our copies, the account of their Epilogue must be judged wholly genuine, not patched together or fabricated.

Finally, this should be considered more than sufficient evidence in the same Epilogue: its author confesses that he composed the entire book. For he says:

“Behold, dearest brother, amid my other occupations I dictated and wrote this discourse for you during the nighttime hours, though with unpolished elegance. Since I realized that it exceeded the form of a letter, I preferred to call it a little book—*On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*.”

Therefore Joannes Grialius certainly asserted without justification: “As for the Epilogue, there is no need for us to labor over it, for it is evidently by another author. Nor ought the theologians of Louvain to have formed a conjecture about the author from the addition.” But let the defenders of Grialius tell me this: when he asserts that, in editing or correcting Isidore’s writings, the ancient manuscripts were of great use both to him and to other learned men—manuscripts written by the hands of Goths, Lombards, or Romans—why, when he comes to this book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, does he merely assert: “Nor could it be established how many ancient manuscripts he had obtained”? Nevertheless, I leave the matter to prudent men to judge.

27. Since the integrity of this book has therefore been established by the strongest arguments, neither Isidore nor Gregory should now be regarded as its author. For although the Benedictine monastic profession asserted of the book’s author suits them, other contents of the same book openly contradict that attribution.

When the objection is raised there, “No prophet is acceptable in his own country,” the response immediately continues: “For if the matter is as they assert, then all those converted from among the Romans who live among the Romans, all those from among the Greeks who live among the Greeks, all those from among the Italians who live among the Italians, all those from among the Gauls who live among the Gauls, and all those from among the Iberians who live among the Iberians and lead religious lives will be imperfect.” After only a few intervening words it adds: “Behold, so that we may come to our neighbors, Protasius and Gervasius, remaining in this very city of Milan, in their own house, and practicing the monastic life for ten years, were so perfected that they became martyrs. Or will our province alone perhaps be excepted from this rule, so that it has monks not from its own people but only from foreigners?”

The compiler of this book was therefore an Italian Benedictine. Although he omitted his own name out of humility, he by no means wished to conceal a doctrine profitable to the salvation of souls.

28. I saw a Venetian edition of this same little work, dated 1555, placed after the book *On the Imitation of Christ*, falsely entitled as by Jean Gerson, chancellor of Paris. It is followed by the little book of Pope Leo, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*: “The apostolic voice cries out,” and so forth. It closes with an Epilogue in which the city of Milan and Saint Benedict are mentioned. This Epilogue is absent from certain manuscript codices and from the editions of Saint Ambrose, Saint Isidore, and the Erasmian edition of Saint Augustine.

Vincent of Beauvais, *Historical Mirror*, book 22, chapter 27, places the little commentary on the *Song of Songs* and the book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* among the works of Gregory the Great; nevertheless, he adds that most people attribute it to Augustine. Bandini, volume 1 of the *Latin Catalogue of the Medici Library*, pluteus 19, drawing from Codex 29, written partly in the fourteenth and partly in the fifteenth century, gives under number 45 Augustine’s book *On the Conflict of Vices and the Machinery of Virtues*. It begins: “The apostolic voice cries out throughout the world,” and so forth. It ends: “and may you emerge victorious with Christ’s favor.” Other copies of this little book have a different ending. Instead of *machina virtutum*, perhaps *machia* should be read, that is, “the battle of virtues.”

29. The Maurist editors of the works of Saint Augustine place the work *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* among the spurious works, together with the Epilogue containing the words “in this very city of Milan,” and they interpret this as Benevento, where Ambrose Autpert was writing, being near Milan in comparison with the city of Oxyrhynchus, which had previously been mentioned.

They say that the work is cited under Augustine’s name by Gratian, 2.9.22, chapter “Nor by artifice”; that the manuscripts they themselves saw attribute it either to Ambrose, Leo, or Augustine; but that the words of chapter 16, “If, therefore, for secular men,” and of chapter 18, “If a prelate,” reveal the style of a monk. They also say that the work bears an affinity to Ambrose Autpert’s commentary on the Apocalypse.

The Maurist editors of the works of Saint Ambrose likewise cite a codex of the abbey of Saint Ebrulf that presents the same work under the name of Ambrose Autpert.

30. That Ambrose Autpert, or Autbert, wrote the book *On the Battle of Virtues and Vices* is established by the anonymous author of *Illustrious Men of Melk*, chapter 51: “Ambrose, also called Autpert, of the monastery of Agaunum, and so forth, also wrote, in the manner of Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, which is interpreted as ‘the battle of the soul,’ a book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*, which he also sent to Lantfrid, abbot and priest established in Bavaria.”

Pezius, in the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume 1, preface, page 41, number 65, says that in the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg there exists a codex eight hundred years old, *A Little Book on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, sent to Lantfred, priest and abbot established in Bavaria.

This is certainly the work indicated by the anonymous author of Melk. But since the beginning of the little book is not supplied, and since the anonymous author of Melk says that Autpert wrote it in the manner of Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, one might doubt whether Autpert’s work is in verse and therefore different from the work whose author we are now seeking.

The author of the chronicle of the monastery of Saint Vincent at the Vulturnus, in Duchesne’s *Writers of Gallic Affairs*, in the *Acts of the Saints of the Order of Saint Benedict*, third century, part 2, page 263, and in Mabillon’s notes to the *Life of Saint Ambrose Autpert*, attributes the book *On the Conflict of Vices* to this same Ambrose Autpert, abbot of Saint Vincent. Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals*, volume 2, page 237, under the year 776, discusses Ambrose Autpert, or Autbert, abbot of Saint Vincent at the Vulturnus and author of the commentary on the Apocalypse; but he says nothing about the book *On the Conflict*.

31. Fabricius, in his *Bibliotheca media*, distinguishes two Autberts: one, abbot of Saint Vincent at the sources of the Vulturnus, also called Ambrose, who died in 778; the other, abbot of Monte Cassino from 834 to 837, concerning whom Peter the Deacon writes in chapter 13, and John Baptist Marus in his notes.

He says that the older Autpert was the author of the commentary on the Apocalypse, as is sufficiently established elsewhere. He says that the other Autpert, the abbot of Monte Cassino, should be credited with various other works, including the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, frequently printed among the works of Saint Ambrose and Augustine; yet this work is not mentioned by Peter the Deacon or John Baptist Marus.

Most people believe that the same man—Ambrose Autpert, abbot of Saint Vincent at the Vulturnus—was the author both of the commentary on the Apocalypse and of the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*. They also infer from the name Ambrose that the name of Saint Ambrose of Milan came to be prefixed to the work in certain manuscripts. They consider the style of this little work and of the commentaries on the Apocalypse to be similar, as I have said.

The subscription in the two works is indeed similar. In both, the author speaks in his own person and states the title of the book. Blanchinus transcribed the subscription of the commentary on the Apocalypse from what appears to be an autograph Codex Regio-Vaticanus, in volume 2 of the *Fourfold Gospel*, page 603, having provided a specimen of its script after page 600. It begins: “In the name of the Holy Trinity, the exposition of the priest Autpert in the second part of the exposition of the Apocalypse.”

At the end of the book, in uncial letters: “Ambrose, also called Autpert, born in the province of Gaul, and so forth, composed and completed this work, which, because of the ease of understanding it, I called *The Mirror of the Little Ones*.”

But if Blanchinus says that the codex appears to be an autograph, why does he declare in his specimen of the script, plate 5, number 3, that the codex is from the tenth century? For Autpert, the author of the commentary on the Apocalypse, flourished in the seventh century, as is clear from the inscription itself.

32. The codices of the Vatican Library that contain the book *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices* disagree among themselves in identifying its author.

The name of Augustine appears in Vatican Codices 464, 468, and 4578; in Palatine Vatican Codices 208 and 314; in Vatican Urbinas 84; and in Vatican Ottobonianus 612.

They attribute it to Saint Ambrose in Vatican Codex 284 and Palatine Codex 171.

They attribute it to Blessed Pope Leo in Vatican Codex 5077, which will be described in chapter 97, and in Chisianus Codex, discussed in chapter 43, number 37, copied from Cardinal Bona, who adds: “The true author is believed to be Saint Isidore of Seville.”

In Vatican Codex 4314, parchment, quarto, it is listed as follows: “Of Ambrose Autpert, bishop, *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues: The apostolic voice cries out*, and so forth,” where the word “bishop” appears to have entered by mistake.

In Regio-Vatican Codex 17, parchment, quarto: “An anonymous little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues: The apostolic voice cries out*.”

Other books of the same subject and title exist in the Vatican Library, but they are different from the work under discussion.

In Vatican Codex 504 there is a *Dialogue on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues between Peter and Theodore*, without the author’s name: “It now seems necessary,” and so forth.

In Palatine Codex 1729, *The Anonymous Ethomachia*, that is, “the battle of moral virtues and vices”: “King Saul sent,” and so forth.

In Vatican parchment Codex 4347, a *Treatise on the Conflict of Vices and Virtues and on their Armed Engagement*, divided into chapters: “King Saul sent.”

This work is attributed to Saint Augustine in Palatine Codex 119: “Blessed Augustine’s *On Vices and Virtues*: King Saul sent,” and so forth.

33. The manuscript note of Lucas Holstenius in the *Inventory of the Old Vatican Library* concerning Codices 281 and 464 must not be passed over. He observes that the little book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which is found not only among the works of Saint Ambrose and Augustine but also among the works of Saint Gregory, is truly the work of the monk Evagrius, who entitled it *Antirrheticus* and had it translated into Latin by Gennadius, as Gennadius testifies in his *Catalogue of Writers*.

The same conclusion is suggested by the fact that in the *Inventory of the Palatine Vatican Library*, Codex 973, immediately after the entry for Isidore’s letter to Massona, the following is noted: “The anonymous contradiction, or conflict of chastity and impurity: ‘It is no great thing,’ and so forth.” It appears to be a fragment from the *Antirrhetica* of Evagrius.

It is certainly a fragment of the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, near the end, under the title “A Certain Doctor’s Opinion.” Impurity says: “It is no great crime,” and so forth. It ends: “the hidden things of human beings according to the Gospel.”

Gennadius’ words about Evagrius are these: “Besides the *Lives of the Fathers*, he wrote many things necessary for monks, among which are the following. Against the suggestions of the eight principal vices, which he either first noticed or learned among the first, he composed eight books from testimonies of Holy Scripture. Although I found this work in Greek in the same simplicity, I translated it into Latin when ordered to do so.”

From this Holstenius could have recognized that the work of Evagrius praised by Gennadius, divided into eight books and composed against the suggestions of the eight principal vices, differs greatly from the little book beginning “The apostolic voice cries out,” which consists of only one book and enumerates twenty-four or even more vices, setting corresponding virtues against them.

Evagrius’ work *On the Eight Vices* was published in quarto by Emeric Bigot, after the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom* written by Palladius.

34. If the Epilogue of the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, in which Milan and Saint Benedict are explicitly mentioned, was not added by another author, as Constantine Cajetanus maintains, it immediately becomes clear why neither Evagrius, nor Augustine, nor Saint Ambrose, nor Saint Leo, nor Saint John Chrysostom should be regarded as its author.

I also believe that neither Gregory the Great nor Isidore, and indeed not even Ambrose Autpert, abbot of Saint Vincent at the Vulturnus, composed the work’s Epilogue.

Regarding the others, the matter is clear. Regarding Ambrose Autpert, it is not obscure to me, although the Maurists adopt the contrary view. For I do not think that the words “in this very city of Milan,” and again, “Or will our province alone perhaps be excepted from this rule, so that it has monks not from its own people but only from foreigners?” suit Ambrose Autpert.

For in the subscription to his commentary on the Apocalypse he says that he was born in the province of Gaul, and he mentions the province in which he lived as follows: “of Arochis, duke of the same province in which I dwell.”

The author of the Epilogue therefore appears to have been some Benedictine, not a Milanese but someone residing at Milan, who perhaps prepared an old book with a new Epilogue for the instruction of others and addressed it to one of his own countrymen.

It may also be conjectured that the reading should be *in propria ac Mediolanensi*—“in his own and Milanese [city]”—or that *hac* should be deleted altogether.

[Col. 0622B] 35. Once the Epilogue has been separated from the rest of the body of the little book, it will still remain uncertain to whom among the ancient Fathers named the work ought to be attributed.

Nor can the opinion of Constantine Cajetanus cause any difficulty, since he maintains that the book is incomplete without the Epilogue, namely: “But you, man of God, attend with vigilant care to what I say, with the help of him who lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.” He says that this ending to the peroration would be wholly unworthy of Isidore.

Thus the book’s conclusion appears in Grialius. But it is immediately understood that the words “with the help of him,” and so forth, were added by scribes, since manuscripts commonly display these or similar words at the end of almost every other work.

The ending was therefore not inept: “But you, man of God, attend with vigilant care to what I say.” The meaning is understood as “what I have said”; and the same sense is also gathered when the Epilogue is added: “Attend to what I say, and believe me as I tell of matters even more astonishing.”

But the conclusion will be more suitable if the words of Vatican Codex 5077 are retained. There, on page 65, the rubric reads: “Here begins the little book of Blessed Pope Leo *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*: ‘The apostolic voice,’ and so forth.”

At the end: “Attend to what I say, and resist manfully the snares of so deceitful an enemy. Here ends the book of Blessed Pope Leo *On the Conflict of Virtues and Vices*.”

Some titles differ in wording from those of Grialius; for example, the manuscript has “Simulation suggests,” whereas the printed edition has “Hypocrisy says.” Certain chapters are also omitted. We may therefore suspect that the work, whether by Leo, Isidore, or some other ancient Father, was expanded and interpolated by a monk—not an unusual practice at that time—not only by the addition of the Epilogue but also by the addition of certain chapters. From this, the differing opinions about the author may have arisen.

Natalis Alexander, in the fifth century, chapter 4, article 8, points to certain passages from chapters 14, 16, 18, and 22 that have the flavor of a professor of monastic life and appear to have been borrowed from the rules of Saint Benedict. Yet, as I have said, these may have come from the hand of an interpolator.

62 36. The reason for placing this little work among Isidore’s other doubtful writings is supplied not only by the judgment of Cyprian Suarez, Grialius, and Cave, but also by that of Breulius and Cardinal Bona.

As I indicated, this very learned cardinal said that the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, attributed to Saint Augustine in the Chisian Codex, appears to be the work of Saint Isidore, among whose works it is found.

In his preface, Breulius presents certain material also described by Cajetanus, but in such a way that what Breulius calls a letter Cajetanus calls a narrative. The following, therefore, is Breulius’ preface.

37. We read that this book has been attributed to various authors. For it appears among the works of Saint Leo the Pope printed in Paris in the year of the Lord 1511, though not in the newer editions. It is also found in the ninth volume of Saint Augustine.

The theologians of Louvain correctly judged that it belonged to neither author, chiefly because a certain letter about a monk harassed by a demon had been attached to it, and because the Epilogue mentions Saint Benedict, who was much later than those doctors.

In the works of Saint Ambrose printed at Rome in the year of Christ 1585, this book is addressed to Simplicianus. But it was relegated to the latter part of the fifth volume, together with other books whose authors are not certainly known, and indeed without the aforementioned letter and Epilogue.

Following the excellent testimony of Sigebert of Gembloux, however, we believe that it is the work of Saint Isidore, because its style and manner of dialogue agree with the *Synonyma*, and because, as even the Spaniards report, many manuscript codices bear his name.

Accordingly, the editors did not hesitate to place this book among his works printed at Madrid in the year of the Lord 1599.

38. Poems on the *Conflict of Vices and Virtues* were also composed. To pass over Prudentius’ *Psychomachia*, Trithemius, in chapter 947 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, reports that Henry of Northeim, who was alive in 1494, wrote in verse and prose a *Dimetromachia* on the conflict of virtues and vices: “You, my laurel-bearing …,” and so forth.

39. Wipo, or Wippo the priest, chaplain of Conrad II and Emperor Henry III, wrote in the eleventh century, partly in rhythm and partly in leonine verse, certain proverbs for Henry, son of the Emperor Conrad. Their beginning is: “Here begins a composition containing one hundred proverbs.”

After many proverbs there follows a *Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, or compendium of the book under discussion, beginning as follows:

“Pride says: In all riches no one will be equal to you.

“Humility: You are a rotten worm; why, mortal man, are you proud?”

These verses were published in Martène’s *Ample Collection*, volume 9, page 1095, and later in Fabricius’ *Bibliotheca media*, at the end of volume 1.

Fabricius, however, reads *In cunctis operibus* (“In all works”), but meter and sense demand *opibus* (“riches”). *Humilis* (“humble”) was also printed instead of *Humilitas* (“Humility”), although in what follows the names of the vices and virtues are always expressed.

We shall present this little poem, as an epitome of the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, among the appendices.

[Col. 0623D] 40. I saw a French version of the little book *On the Conflict* in the Casanatense Library, in duodecimo, bearing the following title: *The Combat of Christians, translated from the Latin of Saint Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, together with the Life of the same Saint*. Paris, at the shop of Lambert Roulland, 1676.

It is preceded by a French preface on the conflict of Christians against demons. Then follows the book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*, which two doctors of the Sorbonne, the censors of the translation, call “the most excellent work of the eloquent Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, distinguished among the doctors and defenders of the Church for his intellectual gifts.”

There follow certain letters of Isidore of Pelusium, or, as he is called here, “of Damietta.” Then comes the *Life of Saint Isidore of Seville*, followed by a Spanish note:

“The life of this holy doctor, collected from what Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, Usuard, and other authors wrote about him, and from the ancient breviaries of Spain, in the following manner.”

Many things are related from monuments of a later age, or even collected from spurious chronicles, which we have already refuted: that Isidore had three sisters, Theodosia, Florentina, and Justina. Yet it is later suggested that Florentina and Justina were one and the same woman, who was called by both names.

41. The author of the *Life* reports, from a certain Spanish historian, that the boy Isidore was gifted in intellect but suffered from a defect of memory. He adds that the Arians sought to kill the young Isidore; that Isidore became a monk; that he was raised from the monastery to the episcopate; and that the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo entrusted Isidore with composing books on ecclesiastical offices, so that the same order might be preserved among the Spaniards in the divine offices.

Perhaps he meant liturgical books. For Isidore had composed two books on ecclesiastical offices long before the Fourth Council of Toledo and had dedicated them to his brother Fulgentius.

But how absurd is the claim of the same author of the *Life* that he attributes to the Fourth Council of Toledo—which Isidore presided over—a magnificent eulogy in which the Eighth Council of Toledo celebrated the praises of Isidore, who had long since departed this life: “The outstanding teacher of our age,” and so forth!

42. The French version begins: “It would be in vain,” and so forth. After the prologue: “Pride, that passion,” and so forth.

Chapter 25 is the final chapter, on heavenly and earthly love. It ends: “Despise perishable things and love heavenly things,” which are Augustine’s words and do not ordinarily appear in the editions of the Latin little book.

The work’s conclusion is appended, beginning as follows: “Although we have omitted many things that we could have placed here,” and so forth. From this it is sufficiently clear that the version is free and interspersed with certain extraneous material.

# CHAPTER LXXXV

Several little works falsely attributed to Isidore in manuscript codices: some excerpted from his works, some doubtful, some composed in imitation of him, and some certainly by other authors. The book *On the Twelve Abuses*. *On Genealogies*. *On the Church*. *On the Active and Contemplative Life*. *On the State of Perfection*. *On a Certain Filentulus Who Distributed His Property to the Poor*.

1. In chapter 23 I stated that a book *On the Order of Creatures* is attributed to Isidore in a twelfth-century codex of the Gaddiana Library, volume 3 of the *Latin Catalogue of the Medici Library* at Florence, pluteus 89, codex 31.

In the same codex, after other material, number 10, page 114, there are *Sayings of Saint Isidore on the Twelve Abuses*: “The first degree of abuse is a wise man,” and so forth. It ends: “may begin in the future.”

Bandini observes that this work exists in the appendices to volume 6 of the Maurist edition of the works of Saint Augustine, in the appendices to the works of Saint Cyprian edited by Baluze in 1727, and in the Oxford edition near the end.

In Palatine Codex 309 it is listed under Augustine’s name as *The Book on the Twelve Abuses of the World*. In another Palatine codex it is listed under Saint Cyprian’s name as *On the Twelve Abuses of the World*.

The index of the Lorsch Library, dating approximately from the tenth century and preserved in Palatine Codex 1877, as well as another index of the Fulda Library in the same codex and from nearly the same period, attributes to Augustine one book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World*.

In Regio-Vatican Codex 261 there is a work on the same subject by Hugh of Folieto, canon and prior of Saint Lawrence in Gaul during the time of Saint Gregory VII: *On the Cloister of the Soul, on the Twelve Abuses of the World, and on the Material Cloister of the Soul*. It was published among the works of Hugh of Saint Victor, although it is in fact by Hugh of Folieto, or Fulleio, concerning whom Labbe, Fabricius, and others write.

Hugh, however, deals only with the twelve abuses of the cloister: the negligent prelate, the disobedient disciple, and so forth, in imitation of the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World*.

65 2. Learned men agree that the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World* belongs neither to Cyprian nor to Augustine.

In the Oxford edition of Cyprian’s works, after the works of Bernard, abbot of Bonneval, page 46, the little work is reprinted under the following title: *A Treatise on the Twelve Abuses of the World, Wrongly Attributed to Cyprian and Augustine*, with certain variant readings appended, especially those collected through the care of Pamelius.

Pamelius suspects that the author was Ebrard or John Climacus. Goldastus, in his notes to the book or fragment of Saint Isidore *On Prelates*, supports Ebrard and criticizes Pamelius, as though Pamelius had not read the *Steps* of John Climacus, to whom he failed to give sufficient consideration in assigning the work to another author.

Goldastus does not say which Ebrard he himself means, since many Ebrards or Eberhards flourished at different times. Fabricius, under the entry “Eberhard of Béthune” in his *Bibliotheca media*, reports Goldastus’ opinion. But this Eberhard lived in the twelfth century, whereas the work *On the Twelve Abuses of the World* was already attributed to Cyprian by Jonah of Orléans in the ninth century, in his book *On the Instruction of the King*, chapter 3; Gratian, Ivo, and others followed him.

3. Natalis Alexander, in the third century, chapter 4, article 4, denies, on the judgment of all learned men, that this is a genuine product of Cyprian, proving it, he says, by the immense difference in style and by its citation of Holy Scripture according to Saint Jerome’s version.

Again, in the fifth century, chapter 4, article 8, he says that the book *On the Twelve Degrees of Abuses* belongs neither to Saint Augustine nor to Saint Cyprian. He adds that the final two degrees coincide, since the same thing is meant by “a people without discipline” and “a people without law.”

Since this little book belongs neither to Saint Augustine nor to Saint Cyprian, and since no argument is shown for attributing it to some Ebrard, is there any plausible reason why we should assign it to Isidore on the basis of the Gaddian Codex? I see nothing that would oppose such an attribution.

For Natalis Alexander’s view—that the final two degrees are not correctly distinguished—does not sufficiently persuade me. First, there is a difference between *plebs* and *populus*, because, as Isidore says in *On Differences of Words*, number 445: “The plebs differs from the people in this respect: the people is the general body of citizens together with the elders, whereas the plebs is the humble and rejected part.” Again, at number 472: “The people is the whole body together with the senate and Roman citizens, whereas the plebs is the inferior multitude.”

4. The abuse is likewise different when the plebs is said to be without discipline and the people without law. For discipline, as the author of the book explains, is “the orderly correction of morals and the observance of the preceding rules of the ancestors.”

By “a people without law,” however, the same author understands one who, while despising God’s words and the commands of the laws, falls into the same snare of perdition by various paths of error—that is, one who abandons God’s law and embraces the paths of error.

Thus the book *On the Twelve Abuses of the World* will not improperly occupy a place among Isidore’s other doubtful works, especially because in certain ancient copies the titles of those twelve abuses are listed after Isidore’s genuine works, as in the Lucchese and Pistoian codices, about which I spoke in volume 1, page 363, chapter 43, number 48.

5. Bayer reports in his notes to the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, book 5, number 216, that in the Escorial Library, letter *f*, pluteus IV, number 9, immediately after Isidore’s book *On Differences*, one reads:

“His book called *Genealogical*, or *On Surnames*. It begins: ‘There are two Adams: one the first-formed man, the other the son of Barda. There are two Enoses: one from Cain, the other from Seth. There are two Cainan[s]: one from Ham, the other from Seth,’ and so forth,” and continues as far as Marys, of whom it says there were ten.

Flórez, volume 11 of *Sacred Spain*, pages 47 and following, describes an ancient Cordoban codex containing several works of Paul Alvarus of Córdoba and certain others that he denies to Alvarus. Among them is a little book *On Genealogies*, with the same subject but a somewhat different beginning:

“There are two Adams: one is the first-formed man, the other is the second Adam, Christ.”

6. The Continuator of *Hispania sacra*, the distinguished Emmanuel Risco, vol. XXXIV, p. 165, reports that the Benedictine Fathers Rodriguez and Ibarreta discovered in the archive of the church of León a Gothic Bible, at the end of which is written:

> In the name of Christ this book was completed under the protection of Saint Mary and Saint Martin, in the monastery called Alb[...]. Recorded on the eighth day before the Kalends [...], in the 958th year of the era, happily, during the sixth year of the reign of our glorious king Ordoño.

After the Gospels there is a short treatise:

> It begins: “On Genealogies: There are two Adams, etc.”

Immediately afterward:

> “John the deacon wrote it.”
