In this tenth-century codex the anonymous *Book of Genealogies* is not attributed to anyone; for John the deacon, who appended his name, was not the author but the copyist of the book and, as I think, the very man who wrote the Regio-Vatican Codex 1823, discussed in chapter 101, no. 21.

Certainly he does not seem to be distinguishable from John who copied Saint Ildefonsus’s book *On the Virginity of the Mother of God*. At its end, as Bayer reports in his notes to book V of the *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*, no. 289, we read:

> In the name of Jesus Christ, this Codex was completed by John, an unworthy notary, in the year 992 of the era [A.D. 954], on the eighth day before the Ides of March, while King Ordoño reigned in León and Count Fernando Gundisalviz in Castile. Thanks be to God.

John was also called a deacon who, in the tenth century, copied the celebrated Hispalense Codex of the councils, discussed in chapter 108, no. 8.

Different from these is the John the deacon concerning whom Blasius Nasarre writes in his preface to Christopher Rodriguez’s *Polygraphia Hispanica*, p. 21. He reports that in the church of Saint Andrew at Madrid there is preserved a *Life of Saint Isidore the Farmer*, written by John the deacon and believed to be an autograph. Saint Isidore the Farmer died in the year 1130.

7. A certain short work on the Church, written in the form of a dialogue and bearing Isidore’s name, was supplied to me by the very ancient Vatican Palatine Codex 485, fol. 44 verso, under this title: *Isidore on the Church*.

It begins:

> Question: In what language is the Church, etc.?

It ends:

> “has the name.” The end.

Another title follows:

> Likewise, *On the Ministry of the Church*: “Although one may place the Church,” etc.

This seems to be part of the same short work, and perhaps the word “Likewise” indicates that Isidore too was its author. I would believe, however, that Isidore is not so much the author as another writer who drew upon Isidore’s extant books, and perhaps upon others that have not come down to us—especially in the first part, which contains the dialogue.

8. The three books *On the Contemplative Life*, which critical scholars have long attributed to Julianus Pomerius together with Saint Isidore in the *Book of Illustrious Men*, also bear the name of Saint Prosper in very ancient parchment manuscripts—for example, in the Regio-Vatican Codex of approximately the ninth century, no. 281, which I shall discuss in chapter 100.

In the same Codex these three books are preceded by a short work bearing the title:

> Here begin the *Sentences on the Differences between the Active and Contemplative Life of Blessed Isidore*: “There are two lives, through which all the elect,” etc.

Much in this short work comes from Isidore’s *Book on the Differences of Things*, but much else has been taken from elsewhere; nor is all of it unworthy of being counted among Isidore’s doubtful works, especially since I believe that this little book has not yet been published.

Taio of Zaragoza, in his books of *Sentences*, collected chiefly from Gregory the Great, entitled chapter 21 of book III *On the Active and Contemplative Life*. There too are several passages that occur likewise in our short work.

9. We should also publish another short work which, I believe, has not yet been printed. Bandini describes it in vol. I of the *Codices Latini bibliothecae Florentinae Mediceae*, pluteus 19, codex 29, as follows:

> “No. 47. A certain treatise of Saint Isidore, in which is briefly comprised everything pertaining to the state of perfection of any faithful person. It begins: ‘A monk, and every disciple of our Lord Jesus Christ, ought above all to possess a poor life without personal property.’ It ends: ‘with whom we should strive to live, by the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ,’ etc.”

The Codex is partly of the fourteenth and partly of the fifteenth century, and is written on paper.

My friend Rochus Menchaca, while examining the Florentine manuscripts for other studies that he has long been preparing, transcribed this short work for me with great courtesy and diligence, although it was written in an extremely difficult hand. Many sentences in it appear to have been excerpted from Isidore’s *Synonyms* and other books, and perhaps stitched together by some monk.

10. Bayer reports from Montfaucon that among other works of Isidore there is said to be, in a certain Medicean Codex, a work *On a Certain Filentulus*, who distributed all his property to the poor but nevertheless did not cease from fornication until his death. He adds that it appears in the most recent edition of the catalogue, vol. II, pluteus 29, codex 39.

But Bandini describes the Codex at the place cited in such a way that we can in no manner infer that the story of Filentulus is a work of Isidore. The Codex is a thirteenth-century parchment manuscript in quarto and contains works of Isidore and others. Its first item is *Saint Isidore on the Stars*, that is, *On the Nature of Things*. Items 2, 3, 4, and 5 are anonymous works. Items 6 and 7 are not explicitly called anonymous, but neither is an author’s name added, and in fact they are anonymous.

The same is true of item 8, which bears no author’s name:

> *On a Certain Filentulus, who Distributed All His Property to the Poor but Nevertheless Did Not Cease from Fornication until His Death.*

It begins:

> “In the days of the most holy Archbishop Arcadius there was a certain Filentulus at Constantia, who was said to be of the family of Olympius.”

It ends:

> “without which—bodily purity—no one shall see God.”

This same work on Filentulus is listed in the catalogue, col. 488, among the writings of anonymous authors. There is no reason to regard as Isidore’s offspring, even a doubtful one, a work that is attributed to him in no way either by the Codex or by the compiler of the catalogue, and whose beginning openly indicates another author.

## 69. CHAPTER LXXXVI. Other Books Attributed or Falsely Attributed to Isidore

*The Image of the World. On Harmony and Celestial Music. On Astronomy. On Heaven. A Little Work on Feet. The Second Orthography. Isidore’s Brief Work. The Itinerary Published under the Name of Antoninus. The Book on the Nature of Birds. Formulas of Spiritual Understanding. On the Seven Degrees of Kinship. Several Works of Isidore under the Same Title; Several Titles of the Same Work. Fragments of Works Adorned with Distinct Titles. Whether Isidore’s Book on Heresies Has Been Lost. Certain Works Falsely Attributed to Isidore. The Book on Adverse Fortune. The Catalogue of the Abbots of Monte Cassino.*

1. Honorius of Autun is certainly the author of the work entitled *The Image of the World*, concerning the arrangement of the earth, which has often been printed and treats of the globe of the entire world, the differences of times, and the succession of things.

Nevertheless, Zaccaria had promised in the first *Prospectus of the Isidorian Edition* that he would include this work among Isidore’s spurious writings, because it was found under Isidore’s name in a certain Codex and differed considerably from the printed version. He entirely abandoned this plan, as may be gathered from his second *Prospectus*; nor do I find in his papers any trace of an *Image of the World* to be published from the manuscript Codex of Father Gabriel Laget, as he had previously promised.

In the *Supplement to the Ecclesiastical History* of Natalis Alexander, published at Venice in 1777, the same Zaccaria listed Honorius of Autun, without mentioning the *Image of the World*. Of another work of his he says:

> “The *Gem of the Soul* is more extensive in certain manuscript Codices than in the printed copies.”

Vatican Codex 4088, which I shall discuss in chapter 97, attributes to Isidore a work *On the Form of the World*, or *On the Map of the World*, which is called *The Image of the World* in the margin and appears to differ little or not at all from Honorius of Autun’s *Image of the World*.

Tomasinus, in the *Catalogue of Manuscripts of Padua*, p. 73, records a Codex entitled *Isidore on the Image of the World*. Vatican Codex 6013, parchment, octavo, contains Honorius of Autun’s work *On the Image of the World*: “The world, therefore, is called ...,” which is its beginning after the prologue. Likewise, the Vatican Ottobonian Codex 1245, parchment, folio, contains the work of Honorius of Autun, *The Image of the World*: “Sevenfold,” etc.

2. *The Image of the World* can have no place among Isidore’s works unless perhaps by that name one understands Isidore’s *Chronicle* itself. For it is so called in a certain Vossian manuscript Codex, as I said near the end of chapter 78.

One may conjecture that this was the reason why someone attached Honorius of Autun’s *Image of the World* to Isidore—or perhaps because it is well established that Honorius took much from Isidore. He may also have taken from Isidore a fragment on celestial music, inscribed somewhere under Isidore’s name, which I shall discuss in the following section, and inserted it into the *Image of the World*.

The same title, *Image of the World*, has also been attached to other chronicles. Vatican Codex 5732 contains Peter of Ailly’s *Image of the World*: “In the first place,” etc. It was printed in folio, without place or year, together with other short works of his, including the *Epilogue of the Map of the World*, *On the Correction of the Calendar*, etc.

In Latin Turin Codex 589, of the fourteenth century, there is the *Second Part of the Chronicle of the Book of the Image of the World*, compiled by Brother James of Aqui, of the Order of Friars Preachers, etc. On this author, see Mansi in the *Supplement to Fabricius’s Bibliotheca media*, and Muratori, vol. III of the *Antiquities of the Middle Ages*, col. 917.

With the same title but on a different subject is the *Image of the World* composed by John, the beloved disciple of Christ, as seen in the theater of Lucerne. It was published, I believe, around the year 1650.

3. In a collection of various works on music, preserved in the Regio-Vatican Codex 1315, parchment, folio, which I shall discuss in chapter 101, after other sentences of Isidore on music and on metrical feet taken from the *Etymologies*, p. 86 verso contains the rubric:

> Here begins Isidore’s treatise on harmony and celestial music and on the seven consonances of the planets: “The moon is the first of the planets,” etc.

It ends:

> “We pass beyond the fire through the spheres of the planets; now we enter heavenly things. Here end Isidore’s sentences on music.”

The final words imply that this is a fragment of a longer work, and in fact it is found inserted into Honorius of Autun’s *Image of the World*. In many passages it quite plainly expresses Isidore’s teaching from the *Etymologies* and *On the Nature of Things*. But there are many other matters in it that one would search for in vain among his extant works.

Therefore, the short work attributed to Isidore in this Codex, together with other genuine works, and not unworthy of his intellect, will at least rightly be counted by us among his doubtful works.

4. This same short work is entitled *Isidore’s Treatise on Astronomy* in Vatican Codex 6878, which I shall discuss in chapter 98. This confirms my suspicion that Honorius may have inserted into his *Image of the World* a short work that Isidore had published separately from his other works.

Others assign this title, *On Astronomy*, to the book *On the Nature of Things*, as I shall shortly explain.

5. Different from this is the work *On Heaven*, found in Urbinate Codex 100, which I shall discuss in chapter 104, after the book *On the Nature of Things*; or, if one prefers, it may be called an addition to that book.

After the final chapter of the book there is the rubric *On Heaven*:

> “It is asked whether there is one heaven,” etc.

It ends:

> “the entire capacity of human understanding. The book of Isidore on astronomy and heaven ends happily.”

Perhaps it is an Isidorian work; certainly it will occupy its place among the doubtful works.

6. I am likewise uncertain about a short work prefixed to the beginning of the Regio-Vatican Codex 112, which I shall discuss in chapter 99. The Codex was written in the year 1012, as is clear from the subscription, and the work bears this title:

> “Isidore.”

The rubric follows:

> “Here begin the little discoveries concerning feet that are necessary for us. There are twenty-eight feet.”

It begins in black lettering:

> “The composition of feet is,” etc.

It ends:

> “are contained in equal-sounding words.”

Isidore’s *Etymologies* follow in the same beautiful Codex.

Isidore does discuss feet in book I, chapter 17 of the *Etymologies*, but this work differs from that chapter in many respects. It appears to have been excerpted from some more extensive work; for its first words are:

> “The composition of feet, of which we have already made some mention.”

Yet we should not entirely deny that it is Isidore’s work. The antiquity of the Codex suggests this, as does the fact that we know several books, or titles, of the *Etymologies* to have been published separately before they were gathered into one body and sent to Braulio.

Perhaps these and similar short works bearing Isidore’s name consist of the first disseminated titles or fragments of the *Etymologies*, which Isidore later modified somewhat or arranged in another order.

7. I offer the same judgment concerning Isidore’s *Second Orthography*. In the Albanian Codex of the *Etymologies*, a fairly ancient manuscript, after the middle of chapter 34 of book I, in the same hand in which the books of the *Etymologies* were written—or perhaps in an older hand—there is inserted a fragment under this rubric:

> “On the Indiction: ‘The indiction is so called,’ etc.”

It ends:

> “the city of Rome was being made illustrious.”

This is taken for the most part from *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 6, where Isidore is also cited, and may be referred to book VI, chapter 15 of the *Etymologies*, where the doctrine of the era is explained.

After the fragment on the indiction, in the same hand, there follows the rubric:

> “Here begins the second orthography: ‘Ara is written with a alone,’ etc.”

It ends:

> “Zebulun, Zotichus, Zeno, and the rest.”

Chapter 34 of book I of the *Etymologies* then continues. Since Isidore’s orthography has already preceded it in chapter 27, this seems to be called “second” as another orthography of the same Isidore.

8. Petrus Pithoeus, book II, chapter 1 of the *Adversaria*, lists a certain book of Isidore as follows:

> “A Notice of the Roman Empire, as well as Isidore’s *Brief Work*, makes four provinces of Lyon.”

I do not find this in Isidore—neither in book XIV, chapter 4 of the *Etymologies*, where he discusses Europe, nor in book XV, chapter 1, where he discusses cities, nor anywhere else. No title *Brief Work* appears among Isidore’s works.

Fabricius, in the index of his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, under the heading “Author of the Itinerary that travels under the name of Antoninus,” discusses at length this *Itinerary*, which cannot belong to the emperor Antoninus, since it mentions the names of cities that arose only after all the emperors named Antoninus had died. On this matter, see the *Trevoltine Memoirs* of 1711, p. 1258.

Fabricius observes that in some Codices, such as that of Thomas Gale, the author is called Antonius; while in others certain materials are read under the name of Bede, Marianus Scotus, or Saint Isidore, according to Goldast’s notes on Eginhard’s *Life of Charlemagne*, p. 215.

He adds, citing Nicolas Bergier in a letter to Camden among the *Camdeniana*, p. 368, that Hieronymus Surita introduced many errors into this *Itinerary* under the guise of corrections.

This, however, is contradicted by the testimony of Gerardus Johannes Vossius, chapter 70, § 24, *On the Mathematical Sciences*, who considers Surita’s commentary on the *Itinerary of Antoninus* exceptionally learned. Still, since Surita’s commentary is a posthumous work, it is not surprising that some blemishes may have crept into it.

9. Why the book *On the Nature of Birds*, or *On Certain Animals*, which appears to be attributed to Isidore in the Florentine Codex of Santa Croce, pluteus 27, no. 9, should be rejected as Isidore’s, I explained in chapter 55, where I reviewed the Codices of the *Etymologies*.

In that Codex, immediately after the catalogue of Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*, there is listed *A Certain Treatise on the Nature of Birds*. Then, on p. 69, there is an untitled book *On Certain Animals*, which the compiler of the catalogue suspects to be Isidore’s.

It is the very work that is earlier called *On the Nature of Birds*, and it begins:

> “In Psalm 101 David says: ‘I have become like a night raven,’ etc.”

The final chapter is on the pelican.

10. There exists the published work of Eucherius of Lyon, *Formulas of Spiritual Understanding*. I see that some have wished to attribute either this very book or another with the same title to our Isidore.

For in the readings of the Florentine *Office of the Proper Hispanic Rite* for March 14, we read:

> “Nor was the esteem that Saint Isidore deservedly held for her holiness and learning any less great. For, recognizing it most fully from his own education and first instruction, and wishing to repay some fruit for what he had received from her, he dedicated two books to her: one on the birth, passion, and resurrection of the Lord, his kingdom and judgment, which he testifies that he composed at Florentina’s request; the other on the calling of the nations. He also promises that he will send her the *Formulas of Spiritual Understanding*, by which she might be instructed in all divine Scripture.”

11. Perhaps someone inferred this from what is added in the Bignean and Breulian editions, in the epilogue to book II *Against the Jews*:

> “You say that the formulas of spiritual understanding should be composed and sent to you; out of my fatherly concern for you, I judged that they should be prepared and sent, so that, once she had received them, she might readily apply herself to understanding the sense of all divine Scripture.”

But these words and what follows are absent from the royal Madrid edition, nor have we found them in manuscript copies.

Even the meaning of this addition is not sufficiently clear. First, the *Formulas* are requested in Florentina’s name; then it is implied that Isidore, out of his concern as a father, considered sending the formulas even without being asked.

If one wished somehow to conclude that Isidore sent Florentina the *Formulas of Spiritual Understanding*, this could still be understood either of the *Allegories of Both Testaments* or of allegorical commentaries, part of which we possess.

12. A short work, or fragment, *On the Seven Degrees of Kinship*, is inscribed with Isidore’s name in Ottobonian Codex 1968, which I shall discuss in chapter 106. It is an exposition of Isidorian teaching and should be placed among the appendices.

13. Considerable ambiguity often arises in distinguishing Isidore’s works because some are customarily called by different titles.

The book *On the Nature of Things* is called in certain manuscripts the *Book of Wheels*. The work *On Differences*, or *On the Property of Language*, is sometimes called *Carnal and Spiritual Differences*.

The two books *Against the Jews*, as noted in chapter 66, are sometimes called *Testimonies concerning Christ*, and sometimes *On the Catholic Faith*. Perhaps the same work is entitled *On the Miracles of Christ* in the English Monastic Catalogue, *On the Mysteries of the Savior* in Sigebert, and *Mysteries of Sacred Scripture* in Trithemius—unless one prefers to understand this last title as referring to the *Allegories of the Old and New Testaments*.

14. Certainly the work *On the Names of the Laws*, which the Spanish author of Valerius’s *Histories* attributes to Isidore, belongs among the allegories. It begins:

> “Certain very well-known names of the law are read,” etc.

Braulio himself likewise entitled a work *Allegories*.

When Fabricius lists writings missing from Isidore’s editions, he thinks that the book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels* and the book *On the Mysteries of the Savior* are concealed in the *Prologues*, the *Allegorical Commentaries*, and the *Allegories*. But, as I said, the book *On the Names of the Law and the Gospels* unquestionably belongs to the *Allegories*.

15. The book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, mentioned by Trithemius and Pastrengo, does not appear to differ from the sermon *On the Body of the Lord*, which I discussed in chapter 72.

Trithemius’s book *On Cosmography* is the same as the book *On the Nature of Things*, although Trithemius mentions the same book under two other titles: *On Astronomy*, and *To the Lord and His Most Dear Son*, which is the beginning of Isidore’s letter to Sisebutus, and *On Computation and the Nature of Things*.

I do not think that the book *On Computation* attributed to Isidore is a work on computation, or on speaking by means of finger gestures, of the kind written by Bede, Rabanus, and others—as Fabricius discusses at length in book IV, chapter 6, no. 12 and following, of his *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*. Isidore treated that subject briefly in book I, chapter 26 of the *Etymologies*.

16. In Urbinate Codex 290, chapter 104, there is a fragment of book III, chapter 4 of the *Etymologies*, under the title:

> “Isidore in Praise of Computation.”

According to Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca media*, William of Ramesey, who died in 1180, wrote on Bede’s *On Times* and on Isidore’s *On Computation*. I understand this as referring to some fragment, either genuine or inserted into the *Etymologies*.

In the Florentine Codex of Santa Croce, which I discussed in chapter 55, the book *On the Nature of Things* is clearly entitled *On Computation and the World*.

In Vatican Codex 623, however, which I shall describe in chapter 93, a work *On Computation by the Fingers*, etc., is inserted among the *Etymologies*.

The book *On the Office of the Mass*, listed by Trithemius among Isidore’s works, may perhaps be the same as the *Exegesis of the Mass*, which I placed among the doubtful works in chapter 84.

17. The book *On the Property of Things*, which is cited by Sigebert and subsequently by Trithemius, does not appear to differ from the *Book of Differences of Things*, or even from the book *On the Nature of Things*.

In Montfaucon’s *Catalogue of Manuscripts* there is listed *Isidore on Various Short Works of the Fathers*, which is a commentary on Genesis, etc.

18. Other works of Isidore are cited here and there that appear to differ from the printed works, but they are nothing other than certain fragments of works marked with distinct titles.

I said in chapter 31, no. 2, that Isidore’s *Book on the Moral Conduct of Clerics* is not distinct from book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

For the work *On the Difference or Harmony of the New and Old Testaments*, see chapter 32, no. 7, and chapter 64.

Trithemius lists a book of Isidore *On the Trinity*. In Vatican Codex 4250, dating approximately from the twelfth century and discussed in chapter 97, there is a work that the catalogue describes as *Collected from Isidore’s Books on the Trinity*. It consists only of certain excerpts from book VII, chapter 4 of the *Etymologies*, with Isidore’s name added in the margin.

It begins:

> “The Trinity is the unity of three; it is called Trinity because the whole is made one from certain three things,” etc.

There follows:

> “The most blessed Jerome, a most learned man, skilled in many languages,” etc.

This is taken from book VII, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*. Yet these passages have not been copied word for word from Isidore; some have been abridged, while certain other material has been intermingled.

19. In Vatican Codex 2902, which I shall discuss in chapter 96, there is a fragment from book II, chapters 28, 29, and 30 of the *Etymologies*. In the inventory of the Vatican Library it is entitled *On Topics and Logical Definition*.

In Palatine Codex 216, which I shall discuss in chapter 102, Isidore’s books *On the Scourges of God*, *On the Despair of Sinners*, and *On the Day of Judgment* are cited—namely, fragments or certain chapters of the *Sentences* and the *Synonyms*.

20. Isidore’s letter *On the Names of Heretics* is found in certain Codices, as I reported in chapter 75. The catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris, Codex 1557, records it under a similar title.

Bandini says in vol. I of the *Latin Codices of the Laurentian Medicean Library*, pluteus 20, codex 48, where there are *Sentences from the Book of Prognostics*, as may be gathered from a specimen of Saint Julian of Toledo, p. 36, that there is a letter of Saint Isidore *On the Names of Heretics*:

> “Certain heretics,” etc.

He notes that Fabricius does not mention this letter.

But one might have observed that in this Codex the title of the letter is given to chapter 5 of book VIII of the *Etymologies*. In Vatican Codex 1346, fol. 15 verso, this chapter is inserted under the following rubric:

> “From book IX [another reading: VIII] of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop, to Braulio, bishop, on the heresies of Christians.”

From Fabricius I also showed in chapter 55 that this catalogue of heretics was often printed separately.

21. It may be asked here whether Isidore’s book *On Heresies* has been lost.

> “He published,” says Braulio, “one book *On Heresies*, in which, following the examples of his predecessors, he collected, as briefly as he could, what had been dispersed.”

This could be applied to the catalogue of heretics that he inserted into the *Etymologies*, unless Braulio had mentioned it as a different work.

I therefore believe that Isidore composed a book *On Heresies*, which he reduced to an epitome and incorporated into the work of the *Etymologies*.

But someone may say: Why should we not suppose that the book *On Heresies* found in certain Codices under the name of Saint Jerome, appended to Isidore’s shorter catalogue, is the very work praised by Braulio?

22. Yet this may be contradicted by the fact that Augustine, in the chapter on the Luciferians, already quoted certain words from this work:

> “Yet in the work of a certain person,” he says, “whose name I did not find in that same little work of his, I read that the Luciferians were placed among the heretics in these words: ‘The Luciferians,’ etc.”

Unless we say that Isidore, in his customary manner, drew from an earlier catalogue of heretics and transcribed much from it.

There are, however, many points on which Isidore’s catalogue differs from the other anonymous, or “Hieronymian,” one.

This short work was published at Paris in 1617 under the care of Claudius Menardus.

Near the end of Augustine’s *On Heresies* we read:

> “I have heard,” he says, “that Saint Jerome wrote on heresies, but we have not been able to find that very work of his in our library, nor do we know where it can be obtained. If you happen to know, gain access to it, and perhaps you will possess something better than this work of ours—although I do not think that even he, despite being a most learned man, was able to investigate all heresies.”

23. Critical scholars believe that the work on heresies published by Menardus is not Saint Jerome’s. Thus Gallandius, in a letter to Zaccaria dated September 23, 1758, expresses amazement that, amid such a mass of doubtful and spurious short works found in the latest Paris and Verona editions of Saint Jerome, this catalogue of heretics had been assigned no place, and had not even been mentioned by the authors of the *History of French Literature*, vol. II, where Gennadius is discussed—although many attribute the final part of the *Indiculus* to him.

In the Albanian Codex of the *Etymologies*, book X (in the edition, book VIII, chapter 4), after Isidore’s words “they leave errors,” the title is:

> “Here begins Jerome’s *Indiculus on the Heresies of the Jews*: ‘First, the Efnei say,’ etc.”

At the end:

> “Here ends Jerome’s *Indiculus*. Likewise, from the place above, Isidore’s.”

The same *Indiculus* exists in Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive. Compare what will be said in chapter 93 concerning Vatican Codex 623.

24. Mucciolus, in vol. I of the *Catalogue of the Manuscript Codices of the Malatesta Library*, p. 173, published among the unpublished works *Jerome’s Indiculus on the Heresies of the Jews*, which is found among the Isidorian works of Codex 1, pluteus 24.

What he did and what judgment he formed concerning this *Indiculus* are evident from the following three notes of his.

25. In this catalogue we have imitated the writing of the Codex itself exactly in every respect, even though the punctuation is placed improperly in it, producing an imperfect and confused sense of the language; even though it lacks the proper short lines that, as needed, clarify the reading; and even though it observes no rules of orthography.

Yet, so that we should not be excessive, we give from it only the history of the Jewish heresies; afterward, only the first and last chapters, together with the history of the Christian heresies and a concise indication of the other heretics.

26. I searched long and diligently for this short work in both the older and more recent editions of Jerome’s works, and especially in the edition recently prepared by the distinguished Vallarsius with immense labor and skill, but in vain.

This caused me not to dare to count it among Jerome’s works; nor do I think that anyone of sound mind could judge otherwise.

If, however, you demand what I myself think, listen.

Jerome says the following in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, vol. II, p. 197, § 23, of the aforementioned Vallarsian edition:

> “I say nothing of the heretics of Judaism, who before Christ’s coming scattered the law that had been handed down: that Dositheus, leader of the Samaritans, rejected the prophets; that the Sadducees, arising from his root, also denied the resurrection of the flesh; that the Pharisees, separated from the Jews on account of certain superfluous observances, received their name from this separation; that the Herodians accepted Herod the king in place of Christ.”

Now compare these words with what is read in the first part of our *Indiculus* concerning the Jewish heresies. You will find that, if not all, at least very many of the authors of those heresies are the same, and that the heresies themselves are entirely the same, described in nearly the same words in both places—namely, in the *Dialogue against the Luciferians* and in our *Indiculus*.

Therefore, since the matter stands thus, the work seems readily to flow toward this conclusion: if it is not to be attributed to Jerome, it must at least be assigned to someone who drank from Jerome’s fountain. And since, whoever the author may be, he appears to have attained Jerome’s familiar style to a considerable degree, perhaps for this reason the name of the greatest doctor was inscribed upon the little work.

Critical scholars know that this has happened more than once not only to Jerome but also to other holy Fathers, especially Augustine, to whom, among other works, the treatise *On the Spirit and the Letter* was attached—surely for no other reason, as the Benedictine Fathers clearly demonstrate in the Appendix to vol. VI of the Paris edition of the works of the holy Doctor.

## 78. 27.

What we have judged is also supported by the passages concerning Christian heresies, if we compare what is found in the Codex with what Jerome writes in the aforementioned *Dialogue against the Luciferians*. We shall find many passages in our *Indiculus* similar to his.

Let us consider, I beg you, what we have just published concerning Basilides’ second heresy. We shall find nearly the same things written by Jerome in the same place cited above. For he says:

> “Then Simon Magus and Manander (read: Menander), his disciple, asserted themselves to be divine powers. Then Basilides propounded the supreme God ABRAXAS together with three hundred and sixty-five *editiones* [‘emanations’ or ‘orders’].”

These *editiones* are the Powers, the Prince, and the Angels, which Basilides distributed among 365 [heavens], according to the number of the heavens. For he imagined there to be 365 heavens, and he preferred to call the spheres traversed by the sun in its daily motion by that name.

The supreme God and prince of these was Abraxas, a name which displays this very number in its letters.

Who does not see that these matters are clearly explained in the context of our *Indiculus* and excerpted from Jerome?

It contains certain barbarous names, and the *Indiculus* shows that from things found in the sacred Scriptures the enemies of the Christian and Catholic faith fantastically drew out their impious ravings.

The same holy Father also indicated this when, at the end of the same *Dialogue*, he writes:

> “If anywhere you hear those who are called Christians being named not from the Lord Jesus Christ but from someone else—for example, Marcionites, Valentinians, Montenses, or Campites—know that they are not the Church of Christ but the synagogue of Antichrist. For by the very fact that they were established later, they judge themselves to be those whom the Apostle foretold would come. Nor should they flatter themselves if they seem to affirm their doctrines from the names used in Scripture, since the devil too has spoken some things from the Scriptures, and the Scriptures do not consist in reading but in understanding.”

I shall not pursue this further. Read the same Saint Jerome’s book *On Illustrious Men*, and you will find that the author of this *Indiculus* used not only the same ideas but repeatedly the very same words as Jerome in listing the names of heretics and their errors.

Would that I had this little work’s edition by Claudius Menardus, published at Paris in 1617, or could find it in the libraries. Claudius had not known of another copy of the same work, preserved in our library.

I would certainly compare the edition with our Codex, so that any diversity of readings might be clearly discerned.

I am greatly surprised that the editors of the complete works of the holy Doctor, who collected both the genuine works of Saint Jerome and the apocryphal works published under his name, make no mention of this *Indiculus*.

These considerations also caused me to provide a concise indication of many of the heretics.

28. Menardus published the little work from worm-eaten and rotten parchment, after several chapters of Isidore’s book VIII.

The edition bears this title:

> *Saint Jerome of Stridon’s Indiculus on the Heresies of the Jews, Now Published for the First Time under the Care of Claudius Menard, propraetor of Juliomagus of the Andecavi, at Paris, by Sebastian Chappelet, 1617, in Octavo.*

Menardus’s preface is as follows.

## 79. 29.

Quodvultdeus consulted Augustine and requested catalogues of heresies. Since the old man was occupied with various labors of writing, Augustine delayed for a long time and wished to refer him to Jerome’s treatise on a similar subject, although he had been unable to find it in his papers.

Learned posterity has always lamented and complained of the loss testified to by this account.

When, therefore, amid worm-eaten and rotten parchment, after several chapters of Isidore’s book VIII *On the Philosophers of the Nations* and other matters extending to the end of that book, we read a short work under Jerome’s name, with the title:

> “Here begins Jerome’s *Indiculus on Heresies*,”

nothing seemed unworthy of so great a Father’s style and care; yet the *Catalogue of Writers* contains certain matters in almost precisely the same words. Some hesitation arose because, in the *Luciferians*, he writes:

> “Yet in the work of a certain person, whose name I did not find in that same little work of his, I read that the Luciferians were placed among the heretics in these words,”

which you have here in exactly as many syllables. It therefore seemed necessary to conclude that the title of Jerome’s book had remained unknown to the holy man.

Whatever the truth may be, it was of the greatest importance that this monument of venerable antiquity should not perish.

Farewell.

[Column 0636C] **[Note: We have transferred this catalogue here from Appendix X to the *Etymologies*. See the note prefixed to the aforementioned appendix, vol. LXXXII, col. 745. Editor.]**

## HERE BEGINS THE CATALOGUE

[Note: Whether this is a catalogue of heretics, namely the book *On Heretics* mentioned by Braulio, I discussed in *Isidorian Studies*, chap. 86, no. 21ff. I judge that it is different; but since this little work, whoever its author may ultimately be, has been preserved only in copies of the *Etymologies*, it is rightly placed here. I gave Maccioli’s judgment on this catalogue in the same work, no. 259. As for Hugo Menardus’s preface to it, see the same place, no. 29. I now present the exceedingly useful little work, corrected against the Albanian, Malatesta, Modena, Vatican 623, the first Vatican Archive manuscript, and Menardus’s edition.]

### OF SAINT JEROME: ON THE HERESIES OF THE JEWS

**1. The first.** The Essenes say that Christ taught them complete abstinence. The second, the Galileans, say that Christ came and taught them not to call Caesar “lord” and not to obey his commands. The third, the Masbotheans, say that he himself is the Christ who taught them to keep Sabbath in everything.

**2. The fourth.** The Pharisees deny that Christ came, nor do they share anything with the three groups mentioned above. The fifth, the Sadducees, deny the resurrection, saying: “It was said to Adam in Genesis: ‘You are earth, and into earth you shall go’” [Note: In the Vulgate: “You are dust, and into dust you shall return.”]. The sixth, the Genistae, presume that they are of the lineage of Abraham. The seventh, the Meristae, divide the Scriptures, refusing to believe all the prophets, saying that they prophesied through different spirits.

**3. The eighth,** the Samaritans, who, when Israel had been taken captive and brought to Babylon, were transferred and came into the land of the region of Samaria. From the Israelites they retain, in part, the practice which they learned from the priest who was brought back; in part, they retain the Gentile practice which they had in the land of their birth. For in their observances they are wholly separated from the Jews, whose superstition is undoubtedly known to everyone. **The ninth.** The Herodians. This heresy arose in the time of the Savior. They magnified Herod, saying that he was the Christ. **The tenth.** The Hemerobaptists, who wash every day both their bodies and their house and household goods.

[Column 0637A] **Other heresies of various doctrines, namely the first: the Simonites.**

**4. The first.** A certain magician named Simon introduced a new heresy, saying that he was a heavenly power, and that all creatures that exist were not made by God but by some power above. Therefore, he says, he descended in order to save the lost sheep; but Christ did not suffer among the Jews. This is the Simon to whom Peter pronounced a curse in the Acts of the Apostles. Menander and Saturninus said the same.

**Another heresy: the Basilidians.**

[Note: Cotelerius should be consulted, vol. I of the *Apostolic Fathers*, p. 336, concerning the heresy of Basilides.]

**5. The second.** Basilides taught that from the unbegotten God alone came Mind; from Mind, Word; from Word, Prudence; from Prudence, Virtue; from Virtue, Wisdom; and from Wisdom came Principalities, Beginnings, Powers, and Angels, who made 365 heavens. From the last heaven, he says, this entire creation was made, including the human being who is in it. The angels, moreover, were divided among all the nations. One of them is the God of the Jews, who received his portion through the Hebrew race and led them out of the land of Egypt from slavery.

**6.** This angel, through his arrogance, exalted himself above the other angels, and sought to usurp their portion for himself and to subject the other peoples to the Jews. Therefore the other angels, angered against them, stirred up wars, destroyed their cities, and scattered their entire people.

**7.** Next he says that it was not Jesus who suffered, but Simon of Cyrene, who, compelled to do so, carried his cross. Against him Agrippa, surnamed Castor, a very learned man, wrote, exposing all his mysteries and listing his prophets, Barcobbas and Barcopet; and, to terrify his hearers, he also mentioned other barbarous names, fabricated for religious purposes. He also named the greatest god, Abraxas, whose name, when calculated according to the Greek numerical system, seems to contain the number of a year.

## The Nicolaitans

[Column 0637C] **8. The third.** Nicolaus was a deacon of the church of Jerusalem. He was appointed by Peter, together with Stephen and the others, on behalf of the widows. Having departed from the truth, he began to teach and say: “There were darkness, the abyss, and water, and the Spirit, which separates itself from the darkness, the abyss, and the water. From these there emerged four other powers, which made God and the aeons.” He calls them the right and the left. He gave them the names Barbelo, Prunica, Ialdabaoth, and Caulacau. The Holy Spirit, calling this a heresy, says to the Church: “But this you have, that you hate the deeds of the Nicolaitans, which I also hate.” For they teach people to do many things without distinction, to eat things sacrificed to idols, to be in temples, and to carry on everything publicly and in common.

**9. The fourth.** The Gnostics say: There was one of the aeons called Ialdabaoth, emitted by a certain mother, Prunica. He made seven sons for himself, and they made seven heavens, above which Ialdabaoth himself had his feet. Without his knowledge, the seven sons made a human being, but he was not complete. For he was like a serpent and rolled about like a worm. Therefore the heavenly mother, wishing to empty Ialdabaoth of his power, caused a spark of power to descend into the human being, and immediately raised him up so that he stood on his feet. At once the human being, through his own intelligence, ascended above the seven heavens and bestowed honor upon three of them.

When Ialdabaoth learned of this, distressed that it had been done without his counsel, he looked upon the remaining substance and begot a serpent. The serpent deceived the woman and persuaded her to taste the tree of knowledge; for she obeyed it as though it were the Son of God. These are the Ophites, who worship and adore this serpent, saying that it brought the knowledge of power. It is he who consecrates the Eucharist for them. For after arranging loaves, they summon him from his cave; he coils himself around the loaves and, touching each offering with his tongue, consecrates for them the bread of destruction.

## The Marcionites

**10. The fifth.** The Marcionites deny God the Father, saying that one being is the creator of creatures and the maker of evils [Note: Menardus printed: “that he is the one … and the maker of evils.”]. There is another God, however, good and merciful, who receives only the souls of believers. They say that he sits in the highest part of heaven, as though in some upper room, either releasing living souls or awaiting those who return. They call the former just and the requiter of deeds, but the latter merciful and forgiving of sins. They deny the incarnation of the Son of God, wishing him to have been a phantom rather than flesh.

## On the Manichaeans

**11. The sixth.** The Manichaeans say that there are two natures and substances, one good and the other evil. From the latter, they say, five opposing powers emerged. They call these five evil gods. They assert that there are two good powers, of the sun and the moon, which they say are a heavenly substance. Moreover, they assert that souls flow from God, as though from some fountain; or at least that light proceeding from God, like a river, makes itself a channel and from there sends forth, as though in measured portions, a substance of souls.

**12.** In that upper fountain, or in the channel of the divine river, everything is universally mingled and shares a nature with God. They say that a particle of this light, once held captive by darkness, God wishes to free; they call it the Pearl. They reject the Old Testament. They accept the New and partly blaspheme the prophets, using according to their depravity the words: “All who came before me are thieves and robbers” (John 10:8).

## On Other Gnostics

**13. The seventh.** The heresy of the Gnostics arose from the heresies mentioned above—those of Nicolaus, Basilides, and Marcion—as though an exceedingly impure body had arisen from certain savage seeds of wickedness [Column 0638C]. The later Manichaean also, although later in time [Note: Others read: “the later Manichaeans.”], is found to have proceeded in the same impurity. For the impurity of all these people uses poisons united within itself. It also possesses some features native to its own wickedness. In its other assertions it agrees with those mentioned above; the rest are, as it were, its own peculiar doctrines.

**14.** These are the doctrines which Irenaeus explained in this way. He says that this heresy teaches that the soul does not sin, since it wishes the soul to be God’s substance; but that from an opposing and alien substance it assumes another airy soul and an earthly body, which they call evil and diabolical. As this body follows its own nature, it sins of itself. They ascribe the rest to the soul of divine substance, and by these means make room for their shameful and accursed mysteries. In them, through magical prayer, they employ the invocations of their angels, who, by creating through their coming, set fire to bodies formerly destined for Gehenna, turning them into the service of what they regard as religious destruction.

**15.** As for the rest, it is shameful to say what an accursed outrage they inflict upon themselves through their sacraments. Moreover, they pretend that the things which appear to be done by the power of another god—the sounds of thunder—are voices of demons. They also say that this evil god, when souls arrive through traps arranged as though they were principalities, prepares snares of destruction for them and offers them the gift of destruction in each of the places of heaven. He also assigns them decrees which they must fulfill. Thus his heaven, the pivots of the heavens, the signs and the circles of the signs are opposed to them, and in this way whatever belongs to the alien substance is opposed to the alien substance in every respect.

[Column 0639A] **16.** For some of them, as Irenaeus, the neighbor of the apostles, reports, say that twelve patriarchs have been set against the twelve signs. In the same way, the other things which, according to the wise, are said in the world to be single, double, triple, quadruple, fivefold, sixfold, or sevenfold are set in opposition, with an equal and corresponding arrangement, to the numbers of the saints. They also understand the Scriptures perversely, asserting that the sons of promise were born not through intercourse with a man but through the word of God, so that they do not call him the only-begotten Son of God.

Wishing to take away God’s omnipotence, they insist that God made everything not from nothing but from something, so that they may introduce two substances. These points have been stated in part for knowledge of the truth. But it would take too long to enumerate how many things we know them to assert concerning the interpretation of the signs in the Gospels and concerning the pagan mysteries of the Greek letters.

## On the Valentinians

**17. The eighth.** Valentinus says that the aeon was complete in a great, unnameable multitude, which is called Depth, or **βυθός** (*bythos*, “depth”). It contains itself in a great Silence, which in Greek is called **σιγή** (*sigē*, “silence”) [Note: “Which in Greek is called Silence.” I think this should be restored in place of “called silence for this reason.”].

This Depth, or **βυθός**, emitted Mind, which is called the Only-begotten, the Father, and the Beginning; Truth was joined to it. This is the fourfold root of the entire mystery: Depth, Silence, Mind, and Truth. Mind, understanding for what purpose it had been sent, itself also sent forth Word and Life.

**18.** From Word and Life, through their union, Human Being and Church were emitted. These constitute the first-born **ὀγδοάς** (*ogdoas*, “Octad”), the root and substance of the universe. The four unions are: Depth and Silence; Mind and Truth; Word and Life; Human Being and Church.

Word and Life, in honor of the Father, emitted these aeons: Bythius [Note: “Bythius,” etc. Such names are often corrupted in ancient copies.] and Myxin, Ageraton and Henosis, the one proceeding from them, and Ithedon, Acinetus and Syncrasis, Monogenes and Macaria.

Human Being also emitted twelve other aeons: Paraclete and Faith, Datrikus and Elpin, Matríkus and **ἀγάπη** (*agapē*, “love”), Ainus and **σύνεσις** (*synesis*, “understanding”), Ecclesiasticus and Blessedness, Theletus and Wisdom.

The Aeon Forefather is Mind, alone begotten; he is the first-born of Chaos and is invisible and incomprehensible to the others. Thus the thirtieth Aeon, which is Wisdom, desired to see the Father.

**19.** When she entered into him, she nearly perished, because she could not contain the Father’s glory; and since something imperfect had been brought forth, they call it the Mother. Because she became alienated, she was afraid, suffered grief, wept, and laughed. From these passions, therefore, this world was generated: from alienation, darkness; from fear, spiritual wickedness; from grief, the established earth; from tears, waters were poured forth; and from laughter, this light was made.

He says that Christ taught that he had been sent into this world, and that Christ himself, sent by the Father for the salvation of the world, did not derive from Mary the flesh in which he was born, but had a spiritual body and passed through Mary’s womb as water passes through a pipe. Therefore he does not believe that Christ rose again, because, as they blasphemously claim, he did not even die, since he did not possess mortal flesh [Column 0639D].

**20.** He also says that there are three kinds of human birth: **χοϊκόν** (*choikon*, “earthly”), animal, and spiritual. The earthly are unbelievers and must necessarily perish. The animal are intermediate; they will possess a portion wherever they incline themselves. The spiritual, which they say they are, have received by nature (**κατὰ φύσιν**) the seed of salvation; they will rest at the consummation of the ages.

The consummation of all things will come when all the spiritual beings have been taught the knowledge of God’s secrets. He moves the animal beings toward spiritual teaching. When these things have been done, fire will shine everywhere [Note: “Fire will shine.” Others, less well, read “light will shine”], and it will consume and burn up the entire worldly substance, to such an extent that even the fire itself will no longer appear.

## On the Cainites and Judaizers

**21. The ninth.** The Cainites and the Jews are those who sanctify Cain, saying that he proceeded from a heavenly substance, which is on the right, whereas Abel came from the left; and therefore they say that Abel was killed. They have been taught that Judas, the betrayer of Christ, was more learned than all the apostles. For since he knew God’s secret and understood that his passion would bring salvation to all human beings, while the earthly powers opposed it, he, by becoming Christ’s betrayer, saved the entire human race.

## On the Sethians

**22. The tenth.** The Sethians say that, from the two men Cain and Abel, the one unjustly killed although he was righteous, all the angels were divided. Therefore the heavenly female power, called the Threefold Power, caused Seth to be born [Column 0640B], and deposited in him every spark of righteousness, so that all the wickedness of the earthly substance might be laid aside. For this reason every birth of righteousness is traced back to Seth.

But since transgressing angels, through unlawful intercourse, produced under the sun the harmful birth of giants, by which it happened that through the flood the entire race of living beings was destroyed and passed away, and only the righteous race was saved—namely, eight souls: Noah and his wife, his three sons, and the wives of his sons in the ark—they say that the seed of wickedness had been hidden in the ark. After the flood, as time passed, wickedness again increased. They say that this Seth himself is the Christ.

## On Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion

**23. The eleventh.** Carpocrates, Cerinthus, and Ebion succeeded one another. They taught that everything required by the Law should be practiced: circumcision, observance of the Sabbath, and the Jewish feast days. For Christ observed all these things, and they say that it is sufficient to be as he was, the Lord and Teacher.

They deny that Christ was born from the Virgin Mary through the Holy Spirit, saying that he was conceived by Joseph through marital intercourse, as a human being. They say, however, that he possessed a prophetic spirit and would come to judge the living and the dead.

## On the Stoics

**24. The twelfth.** The Stoics say that every sin is equal; they are censors marked by harshness and severity. Nevertheless, they said that the soul perishes. They love the virtue of continence, although they deny that it exists [Note: Others omit “although they deny that it exists.” In Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, chap. 6: “They also love the virtue of continence and seek eternal glory, although they admit that they are not eternal.” The variant readings should be compared at that passage.]. They seek eternal glory, although they admit that they are not eternal.

## On the Peripatetics

**25. The thirteenth.** The Peripatetics, with Aristotle as their leader, say that some part of the soul is eternal, but that the greater part of the remainder is mortal.

## On the Adamites

**26. The fourteenth.** The Adamites, like the heresies mentioned above, say that there are two substances. They have this peculiar feature in their mysteries: they are said to pray naked in church, using as their testimony that Adam and Eve were naked in paradise, as it is written [Note: In the Vulgate: “Both were naked, Adam and his wife, and they were not ashamed.”]: “They were both naked and were not ashamed” (Genesis 2:25). They consider it supremely blessed perfection if, by doing these things, the shame which has been taken away from them is now seen.

## On the Platonists

**27. The fifteenth.** The Platonists say that God creates human souls, while angels create bodies. They assert that, after the passage of many years, souls return into different bodies.

[Column 0641A] ## On the Epicureans

**28. The sixteenth.** The Epicureans say that God does nothing, that everything consists of bodies, and that the soul is nothing other than a body.

## On the Sethians

**29. The seventeenth.** The Sethians say that Seth derived his substance from the heavenly and higher powers, whereas Cain derived his nature from the lower powers. They say that the higher nature can neither sin nor become mutable. They wish the lower nature to possess natural wickedness and natural sin, and they always assign the higher nature, like the seed of Seth, to the saints, and the lower nature, like the seed of Cain, to sinners.

## On the Apellites

[Note: Concerning the Apellites, Saint Augustine, no. 23: “Some say that this Apelles held such false opinions even about Christ that he said Christ had not indeed brought down flesh from heaven [others: ‘derived it’], but had received it from the elements of the world and returned it to the world when, rising without flesh, he ascended into heaven.”]

**30. The eighteenth.** The Apellites say that Christ was not truly God but a human being in appearance. Their founder was Apelles. He was reproved by Rhodon, a man of Asian origin, because he did not know the God whom he worshiped.

[Column 0641B] ## On the Severianists

**31. The nineteenth.** The Severianists. Severian, inflated by the spirit of eloquence, constructed their heresy. They observe three Lents in the year, and during them they practice *xerophagy*, that is, they use dry foods.

## On the Cataphrygians

**32. The twentieth.** The founders of the heresy of the Cataphrygians were Montanus, Prisca, and Maximilla. In them, the most futile delusion of deceived people venerates Montanus as the Paraclete and Prisca and Maximilla as prophets. This heresy—or rather, this destruction—has unspeakable mysteries.

For every year they offer a one-year-old infant [Note: “A one-year-old infant,” etc. Saint Augustine also relates this concerning the Cataphrygians, no. 26; but Saint Epiphanius attributes the crime specifically to the Pepuzians]. After pricking its little body with wounds, they receive its blood into flour; thus, making bread by mixing in this blood with the most wicked grain, they eat the diabolical sacrament of a most deadly Eucharist.

If the infant dies from the piercing of its wounds, it is honored as a martyr through the ritual of martyrdom; if it lives, it is regarded with reverence as the highest priest.

Against the prophets of those mentioned above, Apollonius, a most eloquent man, wrote a notable and lengthy volume, asserting that Montanus and his mad prophetesses perished by hanging, and reporting many other things about Prisca and Maximilla:

> “If they deny that they accepted gifts, let them admit that those who accept gifts are not prophets, and I shall prove this with a thousand witnesses. Prophets are also tested by other fruits. Tell me: Does a prophet dye his hair [Note: Others less correctly read “drive away” in place of “dye”]? Does a prophet paint his eyes with antimony? Does a prophet play at boards and dice? Does he accept interest? Let them answer whether these things may be done or not. It is my task to prove that they did them.”

## On the Artotyrites

**33. The twenty-first.** The Artotyrites use bread and cheese in their sacred mysteries in place of the Eucharist, saying that, from the first human beings onward, an offering had been made from the fruits of the earth and the produce of sheep.

[Column 0641D] ## On the Helvidians

**34. The twenty-second.** The Helvidians, deceived by the perversity of a new spirit, deny and confess various things concerning the glory of holy Mary, saying: “A virgin before childbirth, not a virgin after childbirth.”

## On Jovinian and Auxentius

**35. The twenty-third.** Jovinian and Auxentius introduced this new doctrine of their perversity at Rome, saying that there is no difference between married women and virgins and no distinction between those who abstain and those who simply feast. They also produced this example: In the Old Testament the saints had marriages and fathered children; virginity cannot be preferred, lest the union that generated the glory [perhaps: “glory”] of the prophets be void.

## On the Anthropomorphites

**36. The twenty-fourth.** The Anthropomorphites say that God is represented as composed of the same outlines of limbs as a human being, and they believe that, according to this image in which we walk, God is like a human being.

## On the Hieracites

**37. The twenty-fifth.** The Hieracites. Their founder, Hierax, said that the Son is from the Father as a lamp is from a lamp, or as a torch divided into two parts, so that he wishes the Son to be subordinate to the Father, not to be of the same substance.

## On the Luciferians

**38. The twenty-sixth.** Although the Luciferians hold the Catholic truth in all respects, they slip into this most foolish error: they say that the soul is generated through transfusion, and they say that it is both from the flesh and of the substance of the flesh [Note: Saint Augustine cites this passage in his *Book on Heresies*, as Menardus noted in his preface. Augustine doubts, however, whether the Luciferians truly held this opinion about the soul and whether they should be listed among heretics or only among schismatics.].

## On Sabellius

**39. The twenty-seventh.** Sabellius, who is also called Patripassian and likewise Unionite, says: “When the Father exists, he is neither Father nor Son; when the Son exists, he is not the Father; when the Holy Spirit exists, he is neither Father nor Son, and he is neither visible nor tangible. Yet he is mutable and passible” [Note: Others read: “nor is he the Son; he is visible and tangible,” intending that, just as there is one God, so there should be one person in the Godhead: “yet mutable,” etc.].

Before he assumed flesh from the Virgin, he was God alone. At his birth from the Virgin, he was called the Son by that very birth. After the Ascension, having been taken up into spiritual glory, and descending upon the apostles to give spiritual grace, he was called the Holy Spirit. Sabellius wished the Trinity to exist in the names of its functions, not in three forms of persons, but, just as there is one God, so there should be one person in the Godhead.

## On Apollinaris

**40. The twenty-eighth.** Apollinaris first said that the Savior had not assumed flesh. Convicted on this point, he said that he had assumed flesh but not a soul. Convicted again, he said that he had assumed both flesh and soul but not a mind. Yet he himself was the mind, subtly teaching the cunning of his fraud. He wished the mind to be a third substance distinct from soul and flesh, or to exist outside the soul. Therefore, when he refuses to say that it was assumed, he confesses that the soul was not assumed, since the mind is the function of the soul.

## On Paul of Samosata

**41. The twenty-ninth.** Paul, bishop of Mesopotamia, introduced the sect of Artemon against the faith of the Church, saying for this reason [Note: Others read “saying moreover.” The Modena manuscript numbers this heresy as the thirty-fourth] that Christ was a holy human being and one of the prophets.

## On the Pneumatomachi

**42. The thirtieth.** The Pneumatomachi are the Macedonians. They resemble the Homuncionites and say that the Holy Spirit is not God’s substance but a creature superior to the other creatures, and the servant of the Father and the Son. That is, he must be numbered with angels, archangels, and the other powers.

They say that he is nevertheless not circumscribed by place and boundaries in the way angels are. Although the angels, because of the swiftness of their nature, can easily pass from one place to another, when they are elsewhere, even though they then have the capacity to move, they cannot be present elsewhere at the same time; thus they are circumscribed. They assign locality to the Holy Spirit, although they call him a creature superior to the other creatures.

Even if he is superior to any creature and power is assigned to him above the others, he nevertheless has the same substance as they do. For a creature can be divided by power, but not by kind. Therefore, by calling the Holy Spirit a creature, they subtly circumscribe him by place and power; and by granting him only superiority over the others, they take away his omnipotence.

## On the Chiliasts

**43. The thirty-first.** The Chiliasts say that the kingdom of the saints will be fleshly in the flesh. They refuse to accept our flesh as renewed and spiritual, but assert that the carnal goods of the earth will be eaten carnally for a thousand years.

Dionysius, bishop of Alexandria and a disciple of Origen, wrote against the bishop Nepos, the founder of this heresy, who maintained in his writings that Christ’s bodily kingdom would last a thousand years. Dionysius also argued most diligently about the Apocalypse of John, saying that all the things to be seen there are spiritual, not to be understood carnally.

## On the Donatists

**44. The thirty-second.** Donatus, from whom the Donatists arose throughout Africa under the emperors Constans and Constantius, asserted that our people had handed the Scriptures over to the pagans during the persecution. By his persuasion he deceived nearly the whole of Africa, and especially Numidia. Many of his writings relating to his heresy still exist, as does a book on the Holy Spirit that agrees with the Arian doctrine.

## On the Circumcellions

**45. The thirty-third.** The Circumcellions, as they are called, hold the doctrine of the heresy mentioned above. The madmen follow their own well-known insanity. More desirous of the name and praise of martyrdom than of the love of Christ, they sometimes kill themselves after prayer, by leaping from a height or by fire; or they invite others to kill them and are slain by the sword, so that, departing violently from this life, they may be called martyrs.

## On Novatian

**46. The thirty-fourth.** Novatian, a presbyter of the city of Rome, attempted to seize the priestly see against Cornelius and established the doctrine of the Novatians. He refused to receive apostates who repented, and baptized those who had already been baptized. His leader was Novatus, a presbyter of Cyprian.

## On the Montenses

**47. The thirty-fifth.** The Montenses are heretics chiefly found in the city. During the persecution they hid in the mountains with the Scriptures. Those who were in the city first resisted the tortures of suffering; then, remaining steadfast in their purpose and despising the tortures of persecution, they were, through the cunning device of the pagan judges, granted security so that they might conduct themselves in the churches and serve God as they had been accustomed to do.

**48.** Afterwards, when the churches were suddenly invaded, the Scriptures were seized by the pagans, who thought that Christians would more easily be turned away from the faith if the defenses of the sacred Scriptures were taken from them. Those who lived in the mountains accuse them of this supposed handing over of the Scriptures and separated themselves from the body of the Catholic Church.

These people agree with the two heresies mentioned above. For in their doctrine they accept the doctrine of the Donatists. In rejecting penitents, and finally in rebaptizing those who have already been baptized, they follow the error of the Novatians.

## On the Arians

**49. The thirty-sixth.** Arius was the founder of the Arian heresy. Driven by the profane spirit of his eloquence, he asserted that the Son was not coeternal with the Father. Concerning this he says: “There was a time when he was not,” and that he was made from things that did not exist—that is, from nothing.

## On Photinus

**50. The thirty-seventh.** Photinus was from Galatia and was a disciple of Marcellus; he was bishop of Sirmium. He attempted to restore the heresy of Ebion, which says that Christ was conceived by Mary through Joseph by marital intercourse.

Berillus, formerly bishop of Arabia, was once similarly perverse, because he denied Christ before the incarnation; but he was later corrected by Origen. For letters of his to Origen still exist in which he congratulates himself on having been corrected by him.

## On Eunomius

**51. The thirty-eighth.** Eunomius, subtler than Arius through the devil’s craft, introduced not only the heresy of Arius’s unbelief but also a doctrine of another sort. He said that the Son’s substance was not from another, that he was not God’s perfect creature, but that the Son’s substance was from the very substance of the Father; that he was the radiance of light, not light itself, and the image of God, not God himself.

Through his impiety he fails to see that he himself is denying what he professes to believe. For when he confesses substance in the Son, by saying that it is from the very substance, he confesses something lesser which is nevertheless that substance itself. He condemns the very substance which he wishes to be a substance derived from his own lesser substance [Note: “Which he wishes to be a substance.” Many manuscripts end the catalogue here. Vatican Archive Codex 1 prefixes an index of thirty-eight heresies and ends with the Eunomians. It then adds: “Thus far Jerome.” Immediately follows: “ON THE PHILOSOPHERS OF THE GENTILES,” evidently from Isidore. In the copy of the Malatesta manuscript, where the ending is likewise “to be a substance,” this note is appended: “Francis Gualterius, priest of Cesena, copied all this on the first of September in the year of human restoration 1755. I thought it should be noted that I transcribed all these things so faithfully that I reproduced even the nearly innumerable errors concerning Latin construction exactly.” In Vatican Archive Codex 2, the chapters of Isidore dealing with heretics are omitted, and after the words “they wish to be a substance,” it adds: “Thus far Jerome.” Then, as though under Isidore’s name, it adds: “We believe in one God,” etc., which I judged should be published under the title of a profession of faith after the catalogue’s addition on heretics from Gennadius.].

> *(Thus far Jerome. The material that follows was set down by Saint Gennadius, presbyter of Massilia.)*

## On the Predestinarians

**52. The thirty-ninth.** The Predestinarians are those who say that God did not create all human beings for the purpose that all might be saved, but so that the world might be adorned by a multitude of human beings.

Although Scripture says in a general proclamation, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you,” they say that God does not call everyone with the intention that everyone should follow the one who calls. Nor, they say, do all who obey the call through his inspiration receive perseverance in carrying out good works. After many labors and fruits of righteousness, if they are not among the number of those who are to be saved, strength for action is withdrawn from them so that they do not continue in goodness.

Conversely, those who are predestined to eternal life, even if they wallow for a long time in unbelief or in every kind of sin, will receive an opportunity through which they will believe in God and live according to God’s commandment, so that they may possess fellowship with the righteous.

By this definition they strive to teach that God is a respecter of persons; that he draws some, even unwillingly, to salvation after many evil deeds; that he rejects others after good deeds and compels them toward evil, so that they may perish eternally.

## On the Nestorians

**53. The fortieth.** The Nestorians are named after Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who asserted that the blessed Virgin Mary was the mother not of God but only of a human being, making one person for the flesh and another for the divinity. He did not believe in one Christ in the Word of God and in the flesh, but separately and distinctly proclaimed one Son of God and another son of man.

**54.** The Nestorians say that the holy Virgin Mary gave birth to Christ, not to God. They wish Christ to be something other than God—that is, the temple of God, not God himself—and say that he was preserved free from all sin by a special grace of God, so that he was worthy never to be abandoned by God but always to have God dwelling in him and working through him.

Because of this confidence in holy conduct, he called God his Father, and he himself was accordingly called the Son. They decree that he should also be adored and worshiped as God, or together with God, but not as the true God—just as one may honor a king’s statue or an emperor’s ambassador. They use the Apostle’s saying according to their perverse understanding: “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself.”

**55.** Hence they do not believe that God was either born or suffered in a human being for the redemption of the human race. They say that it is impious to believe that a woman gave birth to one older than herself or to anything other than herself—that is, to anything other than a human being—or that God could have been killed by human beings.

Instead, they say that an innocent and most faithful human being was killed, at the Lord’s own handing over and permission, in order that he might testify to God and provide the human race with an example of martyrdom. Therefore, on account of the merit of his good life and good confession, he was the first to be raised from the dead and united with God; and he would also provide perpetual advocacy for those who faithfully believe in God through his teaching and serve God with a pure conscience.

## On the Eutychians
56. Forty-first. The Eutychians, named after Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who denied that Christ continued to exist from two natures after assuming humanity, asserting that there was in him only the divine nature. The Eutychites say that the Lord Jesus was indeed the true God, born from a virgin and in a true body, but not in the flesh of the human race—that is, that he did not derive flesh from the virgin’s flesh, but displayed a body as though from heaven, which, enclosed within the virgin’s womb, he fashioned into human form; and that in this body God was born in the likeness of a human being. In support of this they impiously produce the Apostle’s testimony, where, speaking of Christ’s Incarnation, he says: “Made in the likeness of a human being, and found in appearance as a human being.” And elsewhere: “The first man was from heaven, heavenly.”

57. “Behold,” they say, “the Apostle called the heavenly body a human being”; and they claim that he testified that Christ was therefore without sin because he did not assume flesh subject to original sin, but a body resembling sinful flesh. Hence, they say, human flesh, though freed from original sin in baptism, still retains within itself, as though by nature, the incitement to sin; Christ, however, did not assume in the dispensation of the Incarnation flesh of that kind; through fellowship with his flesh, human flesh could be wholly freed from the impulses of the vices acquired through Adam’s transgression. Eutyches, the author of this heresy, presumptuously undertaking this novelty out of ambition for the episcopate, caused Saint Flavian, bishop of the city of Constantinople, to die in exile, and gave the Alexandrians an occasion for separation from the Church.

### On the Timotheans

58. Forty-second. The Timotheans say that the Son of God was indeed born from the Virgin Mary as a true human being, but that he did not so constitute one person that he was not reduced to one nature. They wished the Virgin’s womb to have been a kind of furnace or melting-pot, through which the two natures—that is, God and man—were dissolved and compacted into one mass, producing one form of God and man, while the properties of the natures that effected the union were evidently changed.

59. To confirm this kind of impiety, which asserts that God was turned from his own nature, they force the evangelist’s testimony into their service: “And the Word became flesh.” They interpret this as meaning that the divine nature was changed into the human, thereby charging the inviolable substance with destruction. The beginning of this impiety was made by Timothy, who, then living in exile at the city of Biza in Bithynia, deceived many by the appearance of a temperate and religious life.

### On the Bonosians

60. Forty-third. The Bonosians are said to have originated with a certain bishop Bonosus, who asserted that Christ was the adoptive, not the proper, Son of God.

### On the Acephalites

61. Forty-fourth. The Acephalites—literally, “headless”—are so called because they follow heretics whose originator cannot be found. These opponents of the three chapters of Chalcedon deny the distinct property of the two substances in Christ and proclaim one nature in his person.

### On the Theodosians and Gaianites

62. Forty-fifth. The Theodosians and Gaianites were named after Theodosius and Gaianus, who, in the time of the emperor Justinian, were ordained bishops on the same day at Alexandria by the election of the perverse populace. Following the errors of Eutyches and Dioscorus, they reject the Council of Chalcedon and assert that the two natures in Christ are one. The Theodosians maintain that this one nature is corruptible; the Gaianites, incorruptible.

### On the Agnoites and Tritheites

63. Forty-sixth. The Agnoites and Tritheites arose from the Theodosians. The Agnoites are so called from “ignorance,” because they add to the perversity from which they arose the claim that Christ’s divinity is ignorant of future things, including what is written concerning the day and hour of the last judgment. They do not remember that Christ’s person is speaking in Isaiah: “The day of judgment is in my heart.”

64. Forty-seventh. The Tritheites are so called because, just as they assert three persons in the Trinity, so they also assert that there are three Gods, contrary to what is written: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God.”

65. There are also other heresies without authors and without names. Some of them think that God is threefold. Others say that Christ’s divinity is passible. Others assign a beginning in time to Christ’s birth from the Father.

### Notes

30. In the Zaccarian papers I found this conjecture recorded concerning the words *hoc usque apud quemdam tamen*: namely, that *Augustinus*, not *hoc usque*, should be read. Certainly those words, as they appear printed by Menard without any punctuation—*hoc usque apud quemdam tamen*—make no sense. Some meaning, however, can be extracted by applying the distinction I have supplied: when Augustine is understood, in the work *Against the Luciferians* he has *hoc usque: Apud quemdam*, and so forth. The sense will be that he has this passage as well.

31. From the Ambrosian Library at Milan Nicolas Antonius reports a work bearing the title *The Second Book of Wisdom*. I have no doubt that this is the second book of the *Sentences*, which is likewise recorded in the printed editions: “The Second Book of the Sentences. The First Chapter of Wisdom.” The work preserved in the same library, *Soliloquies on the Formation of a Good Life*, is either the *Synonyms*, or the little work *On the Rule of Life*, or another work on the formation of a good life, also called *Collected Sayings on Tears*, or some other similar fragment of the *Synonyms*. The *Book on the Rules of Canons*, cited from the same library, is either some fragment of the second book *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as Nicolas Antonius conjectures, or rather an ancient rule for canons composed for the most part from Isidore’s *Sentences*, as I demonstrated in chapters 31 and 71. It is not so easy to discover what the *Dialogue on the Conscience of One Receiving the Body of Christ*, which is listed from the same Milanese library, may be. I nevertheless think that it is a fragment from book I, chapter 18, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*: “Some say that, unless some sin intervenes, the Eucharist ought to be received daily,” and so on. “They speak well indeed,” and so on. This fragment was published separately, as I said in chapter 69, and perhaps acquired the name *Dialogue* because of the words “Some say”; “They speak well,” and so forth.

32.
