The *Little Book on the Practice of the Lenten Fast*, found somewhere by Zuerius Boxhorn under Isidore’s name, is either a sermon on this subject preserved in the Mozarabic Breviary, or a fragment from book I of the *Offices*, as I explained more fully in chapter 72. In the Codex Regio-Vaticanus, which contains certain works of Isidore, there is a little work on the observance of the four seasons. It begins: “The fast of the first month, therefore, is …” It ends: “he will possess joys.” These things are not contained in the books *On Offices*; rather, the little work is transmitted without its author’s name, and there is no other basis for attributing it to Isidore.

33. In the Vatican catalogue, page 244, Codex Vaticanus 1357 lists *Excerpts from Isidore’s Book on Kings Who Rule Well*. But this book *On Kings* is nothing other than chapters 48 and 49 of book III of the *Sentences*, *On Prelates* and *On the Justice of Rulers*. From these chapters the rubric is excerpted in book XVII of the *Decree* of Ivo, contained in that codex: “On kings who rule well, from the sayings of Isidore.” There is also another rubric: “On the same subject, from the sayings of the same author.”

Something similar appears in the codex of the *Sentences* belonging to the Roman College. After the second book and certain excerpts from the *Etymologies*, this title occurs: “On kings and leaders: Hear, therefore, O kings, and understand,” and so forth, from Solomon.

Montfaucon, in his *Library of Isidore’s Manuscripts*, lists *Sentences of Isidore on the High Priest and His Worship*, which indicates a fragment from the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. He also lists *Isidore’s Rhetoric*, *Grammar*, *On Figures*, and *On Wars*, as well as fragments from the books of the *Etymologies*. The same applies to what Trithemius reports as Isidore’s book I *On Grammar and Words*, and likewise to the *Book of the Arts* mentioned by Trithemius and Pastrengo. These works seem to have been taken from nowhere else than the books of the *Etymologies*, which treat grammar, rhetoric, poetry, philosophy, words arranged alphabetically, and other similar subjects. Nicolas Antonius nevertheless suspects that the book *On Grammar and Words* belongs either to the books of the *Differences* or to glossaries.

34. Among the excerpts I willingly include certain little works listed in the catalogue of the Royal Library of Paris as follows:

- Codex 2320, thirteenth-century parchment: “Questions of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the day of judgment and the lives of the saints.”
- Codex 3607, fifteenth-century parchment: “Commentary of blessed Isidore for discovering the blessed life.”
- Codex 2994 A: “Isidore’s *Art of the Formation of Discipline*, parchment, partly of the eighth and partly of the eleventh century.”
- Codex 2825: “*Physiologus* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on the nature of beasts.”
- Codex 5014: “On the Sibyls.”
- Codex 7369: “On Music.”
- Codex 2831: “Admonitions extracted from the sayings of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, for instructing a person how he may avoid vices, and so forth.”
- Codex 7530: “On the Parts of Speech.”

35. In Vatican Codex 2951, paper, sixteenth century, octavo, there is this title: “Isidore. Here begins the book *On the Structure of the World and Its Parts*.” The Vatican catalogue lists it as *On the Situation of the World*. It is book XIV of the *Etymologies*, abridged and with many omissions. It ends with “places scorched by the sun’s heat,” namely chapter 5 of book XIV.

In Vatican Codex 1348, *Isidore on the Interpretation of the Canon* is listed; this is a fragment from chapter 16 of book VI of the *Etymologies*. I discussed certain excerpts from the *Sentences*—such as the book *On Converts*, another *On Prelates*, and *Flowers of the Sentences*—in chapter 68; and others from the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, namely *On Various Forms of Monastic Life*, *On Receiving the Eucharist*, and so forth, in chapter 69. Excerpts have also been made from the books of the *Sentences* and from commentaries on the rule of monks, which Constantine Cajetanus falsely calls *Commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict*. I discussed these in chapter 71.

I also think that excerpts are involved in those mentioned by Tomasinus in *Bibliotheca Patavina Manuscripta*, page 71: “Certain sayings of Isidore on confession,” in small octavo, from the books of the *Sentences* or the *Etymologies*.

36. Some works have been wrongly attributed to Isidore. On medical works, see chapter 75; on the fourth book of the *Sentences*, chapter 67. In the catalogue of Montfaucon’s Manuscript Library, an *Martyrology of Isidore* is listed; but in the body of the catalogue a certain codex of Cardinal Ottoboni is described under this title: “Isidore and a Martyrology written in the tenth century.” It should not be attributed to Isidore.

In one catalogue, four books *On the Empire of the Church Militant* were attributed to our Isidore. This work is the varied and learned treatise of Isidore de Isolanis, of the Order of Preachers, published at Milan in 1517.

37. Eisengreinius added a *History of the Lombards* to Trithemius’s catalogue among Isidore’s works. Nicolas Antonius conjectures that he was misled because Lucius Marineus Siculus mistakenly called histories of the Goths or Vandals by that title.

Didacus Lopez de Almella, author of the *Histories of Valerius*, falsely attributes to Isidore a book *On the Purpose of the Perfection of Virginity*, addressed to his sister Florentina. It seems to be none other than the book *On the Institution of Virgins*, which Leander addressed to his sister Florentina.

Padilla also lists, in *Centuries* VII, chapter 22, among Isidore’s other books, *On the Perfection of Virginity*, two books dedicated to Saint Florentina, and in the margin, in Latin, “On the Perfection of Virginity,” book 2.

38. Fabricius, in *Bibliotheca media*, mentions writings missing from what he calls the most recent, namely the Breulian, edition of Isidore’s works; concerning most of them we have already spoken.

On the short *Chronicle of the Visigoths*, whose author some have called Wulsa, see chapter 79. The *Sentence on the Rule of the Devoted Women* is an added chapter of the *Rule of Monks*, according to Martène; see chapter 71.

The manuscript work *On the Parts of Speech* in the library of Charles de Montchal, codex 99, does not seem different from the chapters of book I of the *Etymologies* and from those fragments which, as I said in chapter 55, were also printed separately. Nicolas Antonius likewise mentions this little book, citing Labbe in *Specimen of Ancient Readings*, or *New Manuscript Library*, page 198.

Pseudo-Luitprand, page 486 of the *Adversaria*, reports that he saw a book of Isidore’s prophecies written in Latin, Gothic, vernacular Spanish, and Arabic. But the whole story is fabricated, as everyone now knows. Perhaps the architect of Luitprand’s *Adversaria* had in mind the prophecy concerning the future destruction of Spain, which is attributed to Isidore in his life by the Bollandists, chapter 9, and in other historical records of the thirteenth century.

39. Fabricius adds a synodal address delivered at the Council of Seville in 636, shortly before Isidore’s death, in which he condemned the Arian heresy and the superstition of the Acephalites. He says that Braulio and the author of the cited Life, chapter 9, mention it.

Braulio, however, merely records Isidore’s disputation against the Acephalites and Gregory, the leader of this heresy, which is preserved in the Second Council of Seville, held in 619. The author of the Life, in the cited chapter 9, describes and interpolates Isidore’s address shortly before his death, based on the account of Redemptus that I presented in chapter 6. This address is not synodal, nor does it refute the heresy of the Acephalites or Arians.

The same author had prefaced the cited chapter 9 with Isidore’s profession of faith at the Fourth Council of Toledo, which he himself presided over in 633; immediately afterward he adds that Isidore vigorously overthrew the Arian heresy and the superstition of the Acephalites.

Nicolas Antonius, book V, no. 193, also mentions the synodal address delivered at the Second Council of Seville, of which Braulio speaks. Bayerius notes that none of the little works mentioned by Nicolas Antonius from no. 182 onward exists in the Escurial Library under Isidore’s name, nor had he encountered them elsewhere. But, as I have already observed, this synodal address should not be sought outside the Second Council of Seville; Nicolas Antonius himself seems to acknowledge this.

The same is true of what is usually cited under Isidore’s name as the *Order of the Councils*: namely, the collection compiled by Isidore Mercator from the Fourth Council of Toledo, over which Isidore presided, and from other documents. On this, see Labbe’s *Councils*, volume I, column 7.

40. The matters concerning Papias’s *Alphabet of Judgments*, the alphabetical list of verbal and theological distinctions, the alphabetical list of books, and the alphabetical arrangement of prayer—which Fabricius says are missing—were discussed in chapter 81, when the penitential lament arranged alphabetically was treated.

In the interpolated preliminary notice by Braulio, certain works of Isidore unknown to others are listed. In addition to the two books *Against the Jews*, there is one book *On the Eternal Birth of Christ from the Father and His Temporal Birth from His Mother, According to the Testimonies of Isaiah*. He abridged the books of the *Morals* of blessed Pope Gregory at Gregory’s request. He also composed very extensive works in canon and civil law.

Elsewhere there is discussion of commentaries on the *Song of Songs*, the Psalter, and the Gospels, as well as of the compilation of the Bible and the translation of the Psalter.

After a catalogue of all the other works, this is added: “Finally, by writing, he made clear the names, kinds, offices, causes, and every obscure matter of seats, places, regions, and all divine and human things, matters now almost removed from human minds.”

By these words the interpolator seems to indicate some particular work. But since they are taken for the most part from the genuine preliminary notice, they should be understood as referring to Isidore’s learning, which shines through all his works.

41. Bayerius indicates certain works omitted by others in a note on no. 216 of the *Bibliotheca veterum Hispanorum*. “Whether,” he says, “these are in fact different from the preceding works, or differ only in title, and whether they are rightly or wrongly attributed to Isidore, let the readers judge.”

Among these is an address of Isidore which he delivered in the church of the blessed martyr Vincent, when he was about to receive the sacred Viaticum before his death, according to an Escurial codex. Bayerius rightly conjectures that this is the very same address which Redemptus expressed and inserted in his account of Isidore’s death, and which others likewise list under the title of an address.

42. A little work *On the Office of Baptism and the Order of Those Coming to the Faith*, attributed to Isidore in a ninth-century codex after an exposition of the Mass, discusses four classes: candidates for baptism, catechumens, the baptized, and those anointed with sacred chrism. It also discusses the order of penitents, among whom are counted the weeping, the hearers, the prostrate, and those standing.

Bayerius says that it appears to have been taken from Isidore’s books *On Offices*, especially book II, chapters 21 and following, unless, he adds, it was the separate little book *On Converts*, which Barthius attributes to Isidore in *Adversaria*, book XXVIII, chapter 1.

The former conjecture must certainly be retained. For the little book *On Converts* is a fragment of book II of the *Sentences*, as Nicolas Antonius had already noted in no. 186, where book I of the *Sentences* was mistakenly printed instead of book II. The material added about penitents may belong to another author.

43. In an old Escurial catalogue Bayerius found the following entry: “Isidore, *On Adverse Fortune*.” He remembered having read this title nowhere else. I too cannot determine what lies beneath it, unless perhaps someone chose to give this title to certain chapters of book III of the *Sentences*: *On Oppressors of the Poor*, *On the Tribulation of the Just*, and similar subjects.

44. Lucas of Tuy sometimes cites Isidore’s words in his books *Against the Albigensians*, although Mariana did not indicate their locations in the margin, as he usually does elsewhere.

In book I, chapter 7, Lucas quotes Isidore as follows: “Purgatorial fire is a place of burning where, after death, certain minor sins of the faithful are punished, or where those who, after detesting sin and making a legitimate confession, have not fully completed the fitting satisfaction of penance are punished.”

This doctrine appears in other words in chapter 14, *On the Order of Created Things*, and agrees with what Isidore teaches at the end of the books of the *Sentences* and *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. But the words were taken either from some lost work of Isidore or, as I more strongly believe, from a work falsely attributed to Isidore.

The same is my judgment concerning the other words which Lucas, in the same book I, chapter 8, produces as though from Isidore: “Indulgences of days, which are granted by the pastors of the Church on the feasts of the saints, or at other times on account of works of charity, benefit not only the living but also the faithful dead, and they receive the grace of the remission granted to them, if they are such as can be freed from the punishments of penalties through the benefits bestowed by the living.”

45. Vatican Codex Urbinas 585, concerning which see chapter 104, contains Isidore’s *Chronicle on the Ages of the World*. On page 6 it also contains a catalogue of the abbots of Monte Cassino, which the inventory designates with the letter E—that is, as belonging to the same Isidore whose *Chronicle* preceded it.

But, apart from the fact that Isidore’s name is not prefixed in the manuscript codex itself, the catalogue continues in the same hand from Saint Benedict down to the eleventh century. Nor is there any reason to think that Isidore, who nowhere in his genuine works mentioned either Saint Benedict or Benedictine monks, began a catalogue of the abbots of Monte Cassino and brought it down to his own age.

## CHAPTER LXXXVII  
### Whether Isidore had any part in arranging the Gothic Bibles or in preparing a new edition of the Psalter; and which version of the Bible he used

1. In a letter to the distinguished Peter de Castro, which I translated into Latin in chapter 40, and in a fragment of another letter to Father Rabagus, which I prefixed there, Burrielius thinks that the Gothic Bible, a copy of which is still preserved in the archive of the Church of Toledo, was arranged by Saint Isidore in such a way that he revised Saint Jerome’s version, added a preface to each book—out of which the *Book of Prefaces* was formed—described the deeds of the prophets, from which the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* arose, prefixed to the books of Kings a chronology of the kings of Judah and Israel corresponding to Isidore’s *Chronicle*, and inserted other embellishments, discussed more fully in the cited passage.

Burrielius also suspects that Isidore prepared a new edition of the Psalter, namely the very edition used by the Mozarabs in their breviary, which differs from Jerome’s edition preserved in the Gothic Bible of Toledo.

This opinion was already current in the thirteenth century. For in the preliminary notice of Braulio, interpolated in that century or rather earlier, this is reported of Isidore: “He compiled a library; he published a fourth translation of the Psalter.” Here “library” means the sacred books.

Burrielius composed a special dissertation in 1759 on the version of the sacred Bible that was in use among the Spaniards in Saint Isidore’s time. From it one might better see what he himself had devised concerning this subject. But it is uncertain where that dissertation may be found.

2. We must first provide a fuller account of the Bibles once used by the Gothic Church, some copies of which are preserved in Spain. We should hear the opinion of John Mariana, who often handled the Gothic Bible of Toledo, from his dissertation *For the Vulgate Edition*, chapter 18:

> “Yet, finally, against the points so far established, the Gothic Bible written more than six hundred years ago in Gothic letters and preserved in the church at Toledo has brought considerable uncertainty in recent times. Many features indicated that it contained Jerome’s complete version, differing from the old Vulgate edition. The Psalms had been translated from Hebrew, as they exist among his works—something perhaps found in only a few biblical codices. Baruch was omitted, as Jerome says that he omitted it; so too were the two books of Esdras, the third and fourth, which Jerome calls dreams. Moreover, the books of Kings were divided in the manner in which the Hebrews divide them into First and Second Samuel, and again into First and Second Kings, which we call Third and Fourth Kings.
>
> “In this Bible all the books appear except the Psalms, as in our Vulgate edition, with only a few words changed, evidently because of regional variation; but it is clear that there was no different translator. This consideration led me to think that, apart from the Psalms, all the books of our edition were Jerome’s. But since he certainly did not translate them all, it is likely that, close to his own time, those books were added from the old edition so that nothing would be lacking in Jerome’s Bible. A few others were also added, whose translation was not sufficiently accepted by the people.
>
> “Therefore this is our opinion: most of the books in our edition come from Jerome’s translation, while a few come from another edition, once called the Vulgate edition among the Latins. Neither group is entirely pure, but in certain places or words they have been changed from the other edition.”

3. From this I conclude that the Gothic Bible agrees for the most part with our Vulgate edition, whose author most people believe to be Jerome, except for the Psalter, which was taken from Jerome’s third edition, as Mariana explains more clearly in chapter 19.

After first stating that Jerome prepared three editions of the Psalter—first, a lightly corrected edition of the Septuagint, once used by the Roman Church and now by the Vatican Basilica and the Mozarabs; second, the same edition more carefully corrected and arranged, which was admitted into the Vulgate edition of the Bible and adopted by the Roman Church; and finally, the Psalms translated from the Hebrew truth—Mariana adds:

> “The Gothic Bible, although almost entirely Jerome’s and differing from the ancient books, has joined to the other divine books the Psalms which at this time are rejected among his other works. In those ancient times the practice had not yet arisen of substituting in books the Vulgate Psalms, whose use was retained in the churches.”

4. Another explanation may be offered for why the Bibles in Spain were arranged chiefly according to Jerome’s version. The Spaniards had earnestly requested them from Jerome and had received them carefully copied.

From his letters we learn of an exceptional example of Spanish devotion. In Vallarsius’s new edition, Jerome’s letter 71, formerly 28, written in 398, is addressed to Lucinius—also called Lucinianus or Licinius; Cassiodorus calls him Lucius. In some manuscripts *Baetican* is added.

After praising Lucinius at length, Jerome says:

> “Your abundance has supported the poverty of many, and so forth. I gave my little works, which you say you desire not because of their own merit but because of your goodness, to your people to copy, and I saw them copied in paper codices; I frequently urged them to compare and correct them more carefully. I gave the canon of the Hebrew truth, except for the Octateuch, which I now have in my hands, to your boys and scribes to transcribe. I do not doubt that you also possess the edition of the Seventy Interpreters, and many years ago I gave it to diligent scholars after correcting it with the greatest care,” and so forth.

Perhaps the adjuration in Jerome’s name to scribes, which I shall quote from Codex Urbinas 386 in chapter 104, refers to the care with which Jerome arranged for codices to be copied.

5. Jerome again treats the same subject in letter 75, formerly 29, written in 399 to Theodora, the widow of Lucinius:

> “Although many admire and praise this, I shall praise in him above all his zeal and devotion to the Scriptures. With what eagerness he demanded our little works, and, having sent six scribes because in this province there is a scarcity of writers in the Latin language, had everything that we had dictated from our youth to the present copied for himself.””

The subject is Lucinius of Baetica, Theodora’s deceased husband.

You therefore see the origin of the version of the Bible found in the Gothic Bible of Toledo. For that Bible, written in Baetica, seems to have been derived from no other source than the copies that Lucinius had arranged to have made for himself.

Incidentally, I note that we should disregard the slight suspicions with which Molkenbuhr attempts to persuade us that these two letters, like several other works of Jerome that everyone accepts as genuine, are spurious. See his *Critical Dissertation* 18, pages 58–59.

6. The time and place in which this Gothic Bible was copied can be inferred from the same Toledo copy. It is a parchment manuscript in large folio, written in three columns in a thick volume. It is extremely difficult to read because of the great similarity of the letters, the abbreviations of words, the joining of words, the rare division of sentences, and the almost complete absence of orthography and punctuation.

Florez, volume VII of *Sacred Spain*, page 93, gives the subscription divided into verses as follows:

> “In the name of the Lord our Savior Jesus Christ, the author and possessor of this book, in which the entire Old and New Sacred Testament is contained: Servandus, whose memory is blessed. For he was born and educated in the blessed see of Seville, and afterward deserved to hold the see of Bastigita. From this illustrious man this codex was granted to John, his intimate companion, who, after being nourished in this distinguished see of Seville and educated by his uncle Stephen, of blessed memory, most wise and most eloquent … [lacuna] … bishop, was ordained to the priesthood and sent as bishop to the see of Carthage; and from there he was transferred and elected bishop of Cordoba, that great and royal see.
>
> “From that see, sound in body and mind, he resolved to offer this codex, beautifully completed, to the Lord God in the aforementioned see of Seville, in the presence of the ever-holy Virgin Mary, on the tenth day before the Kalends of January, in the year 1026 of the era.”

7. John Baptist Perez wrote in the margin of the codex: “Perhaps *Astigitanae* should be read instead of *Bastigitanae*.” Salazar de Mendoza retains *Bastagitanae* and understands it as the see of Bastitania, the town now called Baza. He concludes that Servandus was bishop of Bastitania in the year 1026 of the era, or 988 of Christ.

But, as Florez notes, the Bible was given by John in that year, and chronological considerations suggest that Servandus died around the year 980. Florez thinks that the word *Bastigitanae* indicates the see of Astigi more likely than that of Bastitania.

He further observes that Salazar incorrectly inferred from this subscription that Felix was archbishop of Toledo and Stephen bishop of Seville at that time. Felix is not mentioned at all, while Stephen is called bishop of … [lacuna] …, that is, of Asidona, the town now called Medina Sidonia.

8. Florez believed this monument to be unpublished when he wrote, in 1751 or the following year. But it had already been published at Rome in 1740 by Blanchini in his *Canonical Vindications of the Sacred Scriptures*. There he inserted the preface of Christopher Palomares to the various readings collected from the same Gothic copy of Toledo, so that they might be useful for the correction of the Bible that Pope Sixtus was preparing. Palomares dated his preface at Toledo, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of November, 1588.

In this preface Palomares gave the subscription of the Gothic Bible, somewhat fuller than Florez’s version, perhaps because it was then more complete. There are minor differences in the wording: *Cum enim vero* instead of *Qui enim vero*, *magnaeque* instead of *magnae*, and *et mente* instead of *ac mente*.

A significant difference must be noted. Where Florez reads *luculentissimoque … onensis episcopo*, and from this, again in volume X, page 62, establishes Stephen as bishop of Asidona without any other evidence, Palomares reads *luculentissimoque Spalensis episcopo*. This supports Salazar’s opinion, rejected by Florez.

Those who carefully inspect the copy itself will be able to judge which reading is preferable—if, indeed, the letters have not by now faded.

Palomares also changes the era and adds the following:

> “In the year 1006 of the era, with such a provision that no cleric may [lacuna] this codex or dare to remove it from the aforementioned see. And if anyone should do so, which God forbid, let him be condemned by God and his angels.”

9. Palomares testifies that the Toledo copy was compared with and corrected against other copies. He argues that the corrector was John, the donor of the codex, on the basis of the words *compte perfectum*—“beautifully completed.” I would rather understand these words of the codex’s external ornamentation. It was customary for codices, especially those dedicated to a church, to be adorned and decorated with a precious or beautiful covering.

Palomares says that it is unknown in what period the codex was written. But since Servandus is called the author and possessor of the book, why should we deny that Servandus either copied the codex himself or at least arranged for it to be copied for him—and perhaps even had some part in the material that was introduced into the Bible from other sources?

Servandus was alive with his friend John toward the end of the tenth century. This accords with what Mariana says in his dissertation *For the Vulgate Edition*: that this Bible had been written more than six hundred years earlier, for Mariana published that dissertation in 1609.

Burrielius, however, in his letter to Francis Rabagus, discussed in chapter 40, quotes Mariana’s judgment from the dedicatory letters to his commentaries on the Old and New Testaments as though Mariana had thought that this Bible was copied before the Moors invaded Spain.

Indeed, in his dedicatory letter to Cardinal Bellarmine, Mariana says:

> “We have been assisted by the most ancient Gothic books of our people. In them a more genuine version of the sacred books, made by Jerome, is preserved. This is shown, among other things, by the fact that his interpretation of the Psalms is also contained in those books, for which our codices substituted the version of the Seventy Interpreters.”

More clearly, in his dedicatory letter to Andrew Schottus:

> “Among us there is a Gothic codex on parchment, of great authority and perhaps written more than eight hundred years ago, I believe by the Goths who held power before Spain was overthrown by the Moors. Certainly it was given to the Church of Seville six hundred and thirty years ago, as is written at its end.”

10. To gain a fuller knowledge of the order in which the Gothic Bibles were usually written, several surviving copies should be compared with one another and then with other ancient monuments.

Besides the catalogues of the books of Sacred Scripture found in Isidore’s works, there are others in verse composed by our ancient writers. These were usually attached to copies of the Bible, or, as they then called them, libraries.

Mariana, in chapter 4 of his dissertation *For the Vulgate Edition*, produced the verses of Eugenius, which begin as follows:

> “The books that the rule of faith commands us to know—  
> These our present library contains.”

Most of the remaining verses are hexameters. This is poem 59, part 2, page 68, in the edition of the Toledan Fathers, as I already noted in chapter 81. But Mariana has some variant readings that should not be disregarded.

Eugenius counts the prophets as twice eight, or sixteen. Accordingly, Baruch appears to have been omitted by him, as he is also omitted in the Gothic Bible of Toledo.

In these Bibles the books of Kings are divided so that the first two are called First and Second Samuel, and the remaining two First and Second Kings. But in Eugenius’s poem they are expressed as follows:

> “Twice two books of Kings are joined in order.”

11. I discussed similar verses in the cited chapter 81: those composed by Alvarus of Cordoba for the title of Leovigild’s Bible, and by Cyprian, archpriest of Cordoba, for the titles of the Bibles of Saturninus and Adulfus.

Cyprian explains nothing particular about the number and order of the sacred books. Alvarus agrees quite clearly with the Gothic Bible of Toledo. Concerning the books of Kings he writes:

> “Ruth likewise, whom Samuel and Malachim (Kings) follow.”

He omits the prophet Baruch and lists only two books of Maccabees. He also appears to list only two books of Esdras, for where he says:

I judge that the text should be restored as:

“[lacuna] and the two shining [books]  
follow Ezra and beautifully reform the Law.”

12. In the monastery of Saint Peter of Caradigna, or Cardeña, there is preserved a Psalter written in Gothic script. Yepes, volume I, folio 92; Berganza, volume I, page 222; and Flórez, volume XXVI, page 16, discuss it. At its end the copyist recorded:

“This book was completed by the notary Sebastian, deacon, in the era 987” (that is, in the year of Christ 949), “with the most serene [Col. 0656A] Ramiro reigning in León,” and so forth.

In the monastery of San Millán there is a Gothic Bible, which Flórez, volume XXVI, page 76, catalogues after Berganza. Its copying was completed in the year 825, but from an older exemplar dating from the year 662, as is inferred from the end of the Second Book of Maccabees:

“Here ends the Second Book of Maccabees. At last, having finished the books of the Old Testament which the Catholic Church receives into the canon of the divine Scriptures, with Christ’s help we have reached the Gospels and the New Testament.”

A.M. By Quisus, monk of San Millán, in the era 700, which is the year 662.

Some material here is repeated from Isidore’s prologue to the Book of Prologues, namely, “which the Church …,” and so forth.

13. A copy of a Gothic Bible from the tenth century, in which a short book on genealogies follows the Gospels, is preserved [Col. 0656B] in the archive of the Church of León, as I indicated in chapter 85. Concerning another copy at Complutum, in which there is the common prologue that was lacking in the Toledo Bibles, Burriel informed us in a letter to Father Francisco Rabago; I excerpted some passages from it in chapter 40. These and any other Gothic Bibles, or those deriving from Gothic sources, should be carefully examined and compared, so that we may gain a clear understanding of the form of the Bibles used by Isidore and the other Gothic Fathers.

92. 14. I stated in chapter 61 that I was entirely unpersuaded by Burriel’s opinion that Isidore’s book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* was composed from the eulogies of the prophets which Isidore inserted into the Gothic Bibles. [Col. 0656C] His other opinion—that the Book of Prologues was composed from the prologues which Isidore prefixed to the individual sacred books—is not so unreasonable, as I showed in chapter 62, and as the very title *Book of Prologues* indicates.

It must be held altogether that Isidore himself published both the Book of Prologues and the other work *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, for Braulio explicitly reports this. It is probable that Isidore had the sacred Scriptures copied for his own use. Some draw this conclusion from the words of the preface to the *Mystical Exposition of the Sacraments*: “And since long ago the entire discourse has already been composed by us according to the literal sense,” and so forth. Others, however, more appropriately refer these words to literal commentaries, as I demonstrated in chapter 65.

It is likewise probable that Isidore inserted certain prologues and eulogies of the prophets [Col. 0656D] into Bibles copied for himself. But it is by no means established that the Gothic Bibles as they now exist were arranged and ordered entirely by Isidore in this manner. It is more likely that someone selected from Isidore’s works various pieces to insert into his Bibles.

It is even less certain that Isidore revised the Vulgate, or Hieronymian, version. The variant readings observed in the Gothic Bibles could have arisen from the diversity of exemplars themselves, without any new revision. Mariana, in chapter 21 of his dissertation on the Vulgate edition, cites several passages from the Gothic Bibles that are read differently in the Vulgate, but in such a way that the Gothic Bible’s reading appears to have arisen from the first hand of the translator, whereas the Vulgate reading was introduced at a later time. Even if some reviser was involved, there is no sufficient reason to suppose that he was Isidore rather than any other reviser. [Col. 0657A]

15. There is, however, some authority for a fourth edition of the Psalter completed by Isidore. Although Braulio’s fuller notice, in which this is reported, has been interpolated—as indeed it has—nevertheless, by the thirteenth century, or even earlier, that notice was already circulating in an expanded form.

Our Mariana must again be heard, in chapter 19 of his dissertation on the Vulgate edition:

“Nor should we omit what Braulio of Zaragoza says in his Life of Isidore—or rather what Lucas of Tuy himself added to the material copied from Braulio for his Life of Isidore—namely, that he published a fourth translation of the Psalter. That edition was used in Gothic Spain, as the writings of Isidore, [Col. 0657B] Julian, and others of that period indicate. It is still retained wherever worship is conducted in the Gothic manner by those whom the common people call Mozarabs; for this reason it may properly be called the Gothic, or Hispanic, Psalter.

“It frequently agrees with the Roman Psalter, although it also differs from it in many places. It is worthwhile to give a few examples. Psalm 3, verse 5: ‘I lay down, slept, and arose, because the Lord received me.’ The Goths read: ‘I lay down, rested, and rose again, because the Lord raised me up’; and Isidore cites the passage in that form in Book I *Against the Jews*.

“Psalm 6, verse 10: ‘Let them turn back and be greatly ashamed very quickly.’ The Gothic codices have: ‘Let them turn back and be greatly confounded very quickly.’

“Psalm 7, verse 12: ‘The strong and patient one—does he become angry every day?’ They have: [Col. 0657C] ‘The strong and long-suffering one, who does not bring anger every day.’

“Psalm 9: ‘The enemies’ swords have failed utterly.’ The Goths: ‘The enemies’ sword has failed utterly.’

“Psalm 16, verse 11: ‘They have shut themselves in with their fat’; and verse 16: ‘They are filled with desires,’ where we read, ‘They are filled with sons,’ and the Roman Psalter, ‘They are filled with swine’s flesh.’

“I pass over countless other passages in which the Gothic Psalter differs from the Roman.”

16. Mariana treated these matters carefully and diligently, except that several errors occur in these works of Mariana, since they were published at Cologne without the author being present, and sometimes the sense can scarcely be understood. I would read or understand the final words as follows:

In Psalm 16, verse 10, the Gothic versions have, “They have shut themselves in with his fat,” whereas we and the Roman Psalter have, “They have shut in their fat”; and [Col. 0657D] in verse 14, “They are filled with desires,” whereas we have, “They are filled with sons,” and the Roman Psalter, “They are filled with swine’s flesh.”

In the new edition of the Gothic Breviary, published under the care and at the expense of the most eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, the Gothic Psalter was reprinted from a very ancient codex containing psalms, canticles, and hymns. In some places, however, it differs from the readings reported by Mariana. Where Mariana reads, “Let them turn back and be confounded,” the Gothic Psalter has, “Let them be turned back [avertantur retrorsum] and be confounded”; where Mariana has, “The strong and long-suffering one, who does not bring anger,” the Gothic Psalter has, “The strong and patient one—does he become angry?”

17. The Roman Psalter—that is, the Psalter once used by the Roman Church and still used by the Vatican Basilica—was published in volume II of the works of the venerable Cardinal [Col. 0658A] Thomasius, edited by Vezzosi at Rome in 1747, after several earlier editions, for which one may consult Vezzosi’s own preface.

The venerable Thomasius, in his preface to the Psalter according to the two editions called the Roman and the Gallican, reports approximately the following: both editions are according to the Septuagint translators; both were corrected by Saint Jerome; and the Roman edition, which perhaps belongs to that ancient version called the Itala, was formerly used at Rome, in Italy, Gaul, Spain, and elsewhere. The first to depart from it were the Gauls, who preferred Jerome’s other edition, distinguished by obeli, asterisks, and additions taken from Theodotion. That edition subsequently passed to others and became common.

The Roman edition remained among the Mozarabs and at Rome until, by order of Saint Pius V, [Col. 0658B] the Roman Breviary was restored for the common use of all churches. It was also adopted at Rome, except in the Vatican Basilica, which, out of reverence for venerable antiquity, retained the Roman edition of the Psalter.

18. This is the older edition of the Psalter which most of the ancients undertook to illuminate with their commentaries. Bruno of Asti referred to it in the preface to his commentary on the Psalms:

“When I was still a young man, I expounded the Psalter according to another translation—namely, a translation which differs in so many places from this translation used by the Roman Church that this translation cannot in any way be understood according to the exposition of that one. That one has many expositors; but whether anyone has expounded this one, I do not know.”

Bruno Brunus, [Col. 0658C] the learned editor, maintains in Book I, chapter 2, of his *Prolegomena* that Saint Bruno illuminated with his commentary the old edition still used by the Vatican Basilica. Yet although Saint Bruno’s words seem to suggest this, the facts oppose it, since he expounds the psalms as they are read in our Bibles. I think Saint Bruno wrote: “according to another translation used by the Roman Church, which translation, namely, …”

19. Most agree that the edition of the Psalter used in the Vatican Basilica is the same as that used in the Mozarabic office. Since it was corrected by Saint Jerome, there is no reason to believe Isidore the author of a fourth edition. Although certain variant readings are observed between the Vatican and Mozarabic copies, this variation cannot constitute a different edition; [Col. 0658D] otherwise nearly as many editions would have to be admitted as there are copies differing according to region and time.

Cardinal Bona, in Book II of *Liturgical Matters*, chapter 4, number 5, after explaining the version of the Psalter used by the Vatican Basilica, says:

“The Ambrosians also use this same version today according to ancient custom, although in some places it differs from the Roman. The same Psalter also appears in the old Hispanic Breviary according to the rule of Saint Isidore, which is called Mozarabic,” and so forth.

Compare Antonio Martinetti’s dissertation on the Roman Psalter, published at Rome in 1745.

20. Although the Roman Psalter—that is, Jerome’s first edition—is preserved in the Gothic office now extant, it nevertheless appears that formerly both editions, the first and the second—the Roman and the one now called [Col. 0659A] Gallican—were in use among the Goths in the divine offices. For Isidore, in chapter 41 of *On Illustrious Men*, adorns his brother Leander with this praise:

“He also labored with no small diligence in ecclesiastical offices; for throughout the whole Psalter he composed prayers according to a double edition.”

Isidore therefore recognized two editions of the Psalter whose use belonged to the ecclesiastical offices. What other editions could these have been than Jerome’s first and second? That no church accepted Jerome’s third translation according to the Hebrew text is testified by Mariana in chapter 19 of his dissertation on the Vulgate edition.

21. Even if one wishes to make an exception for the ancient Gothic Church, because in the Gothic Bibles of Toledo the psalms are given according to Jerome’s third edition, it must still remain certain that the Roman Psalter did not always prevail in the ecclesiastical offices of the Gothic Church [Col. 0659B], as is proved by Saint Leander’s prayers according to the double edition of the Psalter.

Sigebert, in chapter 83 of *On Illustrious Men*, writes concerning Einhard:

“He imitated Bede, who abbreviated the Hebrew Psalter by excerpting from it all the verses containing words of prayer. He likewise abbreviated the Gallican Psalter, which we Gauls use, excerpting from it all the verses containing words of prayer.”

But the venerable Thomasius, in the preface to the Psalter according to the two editions, says:

“Sigebert perhaps would have spoken more accurately if he had said that Bede compiled this little work from the ancient Roman edition, which we suppose was then used in Britain.”

[Col. 0659C] 22. It was customary among the ancients to append prayers to the psalms, generally using words from the psalms that had preceded them, as the same venerable Thomasius observes in the preface to the Psalter according to the two editions. There he less accurately quoted Isidore’s passage concerning Leander as: “Throughout the whole Psalter he composed editions according to a double prayer.” It should be written, as I gave it above: “He composed prayers according to a double edition.”

This varied practice, whereby the same Psalter was not recited in the Gothic churches, was finally abolished by the Fourth Council of Toledo in the year 633, canon 2:

“Therefore let one order of praying and singing be preserved for us throughout all Spain and Gaul.”

23. It can scarcely be determined with confidence which version of the Psalter and of the other books of sacred Scripture Isidore chiefly [Col. 0659D] used in his works. To pass over other matters common to the rest, Isidore often uses not so much his own words as those of other Fathers; thus he generally reproduces passages of Scripture as he had read them in earlier writers.

Nevertheless, he considered Saint Jerome’s version preferable—the version believed to be our Vulgate. “The presbyter Jerome,” he says in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 4, “skilled in three languages, translated these same Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin [Col. 0660A] and rendered them eloquently; his interpretation is rightly preferred to the others. For it is more faithful to the words, clearer in the precision of its meaning, and, being by a Christian translator, more truthful.”

Again, in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 12:

“Only the presbyter Jerome translated the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Latin; and all the churches everywhere generally use his edition because it is more truthful in meaning and clearer in wording.”

Isidore transferred this eulogy, which Augustine had applied to the old Itala version, to Jerome’s version. This is the Hieronymian version which, as we have noted, appears in the Gothic Bibles of Toledo.

24. Following the same principle, Saint Gregory preferred this new translation to the old one—that is, to the Itala—because the former is said to have rendered everything more truthfully. “Whatever is said in it must be believed,” he writes in Book XX of the *Moralia*, chapter 32.

Nevertheless, he himself produced testimonies from both the old and the new versions, as he acknowledges in the letter with which he sent the books of the *Moralia* to Leander: [Col. 0660B]

“I expound the new translation; but when the need for proof requires it, I draw testimonies now from the new, now from the old, so that, since the Apostolic See over which, by God’s authority, I preside uses both, the labor of my study may likewise be supported by both.”

25. Niccolò Antonio praises Mariana’s diligence. In his notes to the books *Against the Jews*, Mariana observed that Isidore, when citing passages from the psalms, drew certain readings from the Roman Psalter and from the Psalter proper to the Gothic office; and that in other books he had before his eyes a version other than that now in common use [Col. 0660C] in the Church.

He gives an example from Book I, chapter 19:

“Therefore another prophet also says of them: ‘They have become for me a returning arrow.’”

Mariana thinks these words belonged to one of the countless ancient versions that have perished, perhaps Hosea 7:16:

“They turned back so as to be without a yoke; they became like a deceitful bow.”

For “deceitful bow” corresponds to “returning arrow,” which turns back upon the one who shoots it.

Niccolò Antonio adds that something similar, almost proverbial, occurs in Psalm 77:57:

“Like their fathers, they turned back as a crooked bow.”

For this is the sense of the Hebrew and Greek words also, which Isidorus Clarius (incorrectly printed in Niccolò Antonio as *Isidorus clarius*, with *clarius* treated as an adverb) interprets as “a crooked,” or “deceitful,” bow: one that does not aim at the target but, being bent back, strikes the person who drew it.

26. The use of the Gothic Psalter continued in Spain even after the Gothic office had been abolished, as can be observed in Saint Martin of León in the twelfth century, who frequently uses the version [Col. 0660D] of the Mozarabic Psalter, as in volume I, pages 173, 322, 361, 368, and 375, and volume III, page 103, although he also uses hymns and much else from the Roman Breviary, as in volume I, page 408, and volume II, pages 56, 67, 160, and 163.

Rodrigo of Toledo, Book VI of *On the Deeds of Spain*, chapter 5:

“The translation of the Psalter, the Gothic one, is still recited today in very many cathedral churches and monasteries.”

## CHAPTER LXXXVIII

What part did Saint Isidore have in the Gothic Office, called Isidorian and Mozarabic? Summary of what the Bollandists have discussed on this subject. Observations of the Marquis Scipione Maffei on the Gothic *Orationale* preserved among the Veronese.

1. For many centuries throughout Spain there prevailed a definite manner of praying to God in the ecclesiastical offices, which was said to follow the rule of Blessed Isidore. [Col. 0661A] Among foreigners as well, the opinion became established that Saint Isidore was the author of the Gothic Office, especially after the Breviary and Missal of that rite had been committed to print at the command of Cardinal Ximénez.

The Lateran Canons wished to attest this in their own proper offices for 4 April, lesson 2 of the second nocturn:

“In that synod—the Fourth Council of Toledo—it was decreed that one sacred rite should be observed everywhere throughout all Spain in every ecclesiastical ministry. The Fathers therefore imposed upon that holy man, Saint Isidore, who surpassed the others in knowledge and understanding of such matters, the task of composing a volume of ecclesiastical offices, to be used both in the Masses and in the hours of singing. He carried this out; for a Missal and Breviary [Col. 0661B] still exist, redolent of sacred antiquity, which were committed to print under the title of that same Isidore.”

Anyone wishing to know the complete history of this rite, tracing it back to its origin, will find it in *Mozarabic Liturgy, or a Historical and Chronological Treatise on the Ancient Hispanic, Gothic, Isidorian, Mozarabic, Toledan, and Mixed Liturgy, collected, arranged, and illustrated from the councils of Spain, the deeds of the Roman pontiffs, the charters of the Spanish kings, and other documents discovered for the present purpose, by John Pinius, theologian of the Society of Jesus.*

This treatise appears in volume VI of the *Acta Sanctorum* for July, reprinted in the Bollandists’ *Collection of Prefaces, Treatises, Dissertations*, and so forth, at Antwerp and Venice. It was also published in volume I, part 1, [Col. 0661C] of the works of the venerable Cardinal Thomasius, through the study and care of Giuseppe Bianchini, at Rome in 1741.

From this source the author of the work entitled *Real Academia de buenas letras de Barcelona* was misled: on page 392 he believed the venerable Cardinal Thomasius to be the author of the treatise on Hispanic liturgy, and also attributed to Cajetan Cenni material that properly belongs to Bianchini.

2. Pinius therefore undertook to illustrate the ancient Hispanic liturgy after Francisco de Pisa, Eugenio Robles, the most eminent Bona and Aguirre, Jean Mabillon, Edmond Martène, Pietro Bruno, and others. We shall briefly summarize his opinions.

The sacred liturgy, propagated by Saint Peter and the other apostles, was everywhere the same in substance and remains unchanged in the Catholic Church. To that original substantial institution certain external rites were added in different places.

The first origin of the liturgy in Spain must be traced to Saint Peter, as Isidore traces it, [Col. 0661D] whether Saint Peter preached the faith in Spain, as Gaspar Sánchez maintains, or other apostolic men sent to Spain by Saint Peter introduced the Order of the Mass received from the prince of the apostles, as Innocent I and Gregory VII imply. Paul may also perhaps have contributed his efforts there.

The apostle James likewise established the sacred rites of the liturgy in Spain, insofar as the time of his residence permitted.

99. 3. What the Hispanic liturgy was like during the first four centuries is a very obscure and difficult question. Nothing certain can be extracted from the Fathers who wrote during that period; [Col. 0662A] indeed, nothing can be extracted if the opinion of some is correct that during the Church’s first four centuries no liturgy was committed to writing, but was handed down solely by word of mouth. Pinius defends this view at length.

Leaving aside the fabrications of the pseudo-chronicles, the first traces of the ancient Hispanic liturgy appear in the first council, held in the year 400. Yet many of its canons properly concern the ecclesiastical hierarchy rather than the liturgy; others presuppose a liturgy but do not state what kind it was.

4. At the beginning of the fifth century, barbarians occupied Spain: Vandals, Suevi, and Goths. The Goths had received their liturgy from the Churches of the East. There were therefore then two liturgies in Spain: one ancient Hispanic, the other Eastern, brought in by the Goths, which may perhaps [Col. 0662B] have contracted some stain from the Arian heresy.

In these turbulent times, knowledge of liturgical matters in Spain is obscure. Scarcely anything can be discerned from the general Hispanic council held at the urging of Pope Leo in 447; from Leo’s letter 95, or 109 in another numbering; from the letter of the bishops of Tarragona to Pope Hilary in 465; and from Pope Simplicius’s letter to Zeno, bishop of Seville.

For the Council of Braga of 411, which Aguirre considered genuine, is now generally rejected as apocryphal.

5. In the sixth century, monuments of the liturgical rites become clearer in the Council of Tarragona of 516 and that of Girona of 517. The latter prescribed that, just as it was done in the metropolitan church, so throughout the entire province of Tarragona both the order of the Mass itself and the custom of singing or ministering [Col. 0662C] should be preserved, together with other provisions concerning litanies and so forth.

There was therefore some variation among the churches of the province of Tarragona, which the Fathers of the Council of Girona wished to remove. It was also easy for churches within the same province to differ somewhat from one another in their ecclesiastical offices, since the authority to regulate them belonged to the bishops.

And since an Eastern liturgy had been introduced into Spain by the Goths, it may have pleased some Hispanics, or perhaps a third liturgy arose, mixed from the Hispanic and Eastern rites.

6. The same matter seems relevant to the fact that Profuturus, metropolitan of the province of Braga, consulted the Roman pontiff concerning the celebration of Easter, the order of prayers, and the solemnities of the Mass. Pinius conjectures that the liturgy [Col. 0662D] of Braga had diverged from the order of the Roman liturgy toward the Eastern liturgy.

The order of the liturgy in the province of Braga and in the Roman Church could nevertheless have differed for other reasons. From apostolic times, when each bishop freely arranged the sacred rites while retaining the substance of the liturgy, it could scarcely have happened that the same rites remained unchanged or became fixed in different regions—especially if during the first four centuries of the Church no liturgy had been transmitted in writing.

7. The Councils of Barcelona, about the year 540; Valencia, in 546; and Braga, in 561, issued further decrees concerning the order of prayers. They prescribed that one and the same order of singing, and the text of the canonical prayer which Profuturus had received in writing [Col. 0663A] from the authority of the Apostolic See itself, should be retained by everyone, since previously the divine offices had been maintained by each bishop according to varied and disordered custom.

Other practices adapted to the rites of the Eastern Church are also reported. It is therefore clear that the text of the canonical prayer sent by the Roman pontiff to Profuturus was not immediately accepted by all the bishops of the province of Braga.

It is likewise clear that in the sixth century the Hispanics willingly inserted several elements from the Eastern liturgy into their own liturgy, both because they understood that this was agreeable to the Goths and Suevi and because Martin of Dumio, bishop of Braga, though born in Pannonia and educated in Greek learning, transmitted to the Hispanics a collection of canons from the Eastern synods.

I add a verse from his epitaph, quoted by Sirmond:

[Col. 0663B]

“The bishop established the worship and the rite of sacred things.”

We should not understand this as referring to the original institution of worship and sacred rites, but to a certain elucidation, or rather restoration and supplementation, drawn from Greek custom.

Flórez, volume XV of *España Sagrada*, page 125, thinks the verse concerning Saint Martin should be referred to the rule of faith and holy religion mentioned by Saint Isidore in *On Illustrious Men*. But it will be better understood as referring to the worship of the ecclesiastical office, which Martin partly restored. I would also like to attribute to him the Mass of Saint Martin of Tours, together with the celebrated prayer known among liturgists.

8. John of Biclaro, a Goth by origin, is also believed to have mixed Greek rites with the Hispanic ones. When he was a young man, he went to Constantinople and returned to Spain [Col. 0663C] equipped with Greek and Latin learning.

The same must be thought of Saint Leander, who at Constantinople formed an especially close friendship with Saint Gregory the Great and therefore could easily have followed his example. Saint Gregory readily accepted new and useful Greek customs, as is demonstrated by his letter 63, Book VII, to the bishop of Syracuse.

Indeed, at the Third Council of Toledo, in which Leander played a major role, the Hispanics were the first among the Latins to adopt the custom of reciting the Creed at Mass according to the practice of the Eastern Churches.

Other decrees concerning ecclesiastical offices were issued in the sixth century at the Council of Narbonne in 589. At that time both Spain and Narbonese Gaul were subject to the Gothic king Reccared. [Col. 0663D]

9. In the seventh century Hispanic liturgical practice flourished above all and was in some manner stabilized by the decrees of the Fourth Council of Toledo, presided over by Isidore, at which sixty-two bishops of Spain and Gothic Gaul were assembled at Toledo.

It was prescribed above all that one order of praying and singing should be preserved throughout Spain and Gaul; one manner should be followed in the solemnities of the Mass; and one manner in the morning and evening offices.

There were therefore then different customs of sacred rites in Spain. The variation found in many particular rites is indicated and individually prohibited by the council itself: concerning the solemn day of Easter; the celebration of the office on the Friday of the Passion; the blessing of the Paschal candle; the daily recitation of the Lord’s Prayer; not singing the alleluia during [Col. 0664A] Lent; not singing the praises before the Gospel; retaining the use of hymns; the use of the hymn of the three young men; the conclusion of the psalms; the Gloria at the end of responsories; proclaiming the Book of Revelation during the time of Masses from Easter to Pentecost; and so forth.

The council’s chief purpose was that thereafter there should be no diversity in the sacred office, but that from the many and varied rites practiced throughout Spain and Narbonese Gaul the best should be selected, so that there might be one order of the liturgy, one manner, and one uniform custom.

As for Pinius’s incidental statement about the boundaries of Narbonese Gaul according to the division of dioceses in Wamba’s time, as reported by Aguirre, I believe it should be noted that learned men now regard such a division as spurious and attribute it to Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo. [Col. 0664B]

10. Since Saint Isidore presided over the Fourth Council of Toledo and is believed to have drawn up its canons, this is the place to discuss whether he was the author of the new Gothic Office. I shall therefore reproduce paragraph 3 and 4 of chapter 3 of Pinius, where he examines this question.

102. Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, greatly deserving of the Hispanic Gothic Office: was he its founder?

11. No one who knows the rare gifts of this most learned man, joined with an equal bond of learning and holiness, can doubt that Saint Isidore could have rendered the greatest service to liturgical matters.

His acts were celebrated among us on 4 April. On page 329, testimonies to his outstanding learning are presented. The following brief statement comes from the Eighth Council of Toledo, held in 653, seventeen years after the saint’s death:

“An outstanding teacher of our own age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those [Col. 0664C] who preceded him but not inferior in doctrine, and—what is greater—most learned at the end of the ages, Isidore, whose name must be spoken with reverence.”

He was therefore highly accomplished in the other sciences, as his books show, and supremely learned in ecclesiastical offices, as is clear from the erudite works he composed on this subject.

Everything in him was so well ordered that he, if anyone in the entire kingdom of Spain, could have shed the greatest light on the hidden and mysterious realities of the liturgy.

Whatever he could accomplish in this field, he actually accomplished at the Fourth Council of Toledo. Since he presided over it with such honor and favor, I shall scarcely depart from the truth if I say that from such a president—or rather from the living voice and oracle of that council—there proceeded all, or at least most, of the canons concerning the administration of the liturgy prescribed at that council and listed above by me. To whom could these canons be attributed more suitably or plausibly?

12. Whatever the truth may be, the holy doctor inspired such high esteem among authors for the work done there [Col. 0664D] concerning the ecclesiastical office that they believed and reported that he had founded a new office at that time.

Baronius, under the year 633, in which I stated that council was held, says:

“It was the opinion of many, to which I willingly and gladly subscribe, that at this council the Fathers entrusted Saint Isidore—who surpassed the others in knowledge and understanding of ecclesiastical matters—with the task of composing, according to the council’s prescription, volumes of ecclesiastical offices, which all the churches of Spain were to use both in the sacred Masses and in the canonical hours of singing, by night and by day. He carried this out most successfully, so that he also published a Missal and Breviary.”

I would be more expansive if I were to cite the Spanish authors and gather from their words what and how much they attribute to Saint Isidore in the matter under discussion. For they do not all speak in the same way, and some add Saint Leander to him; [Col. 0665A] others say that Leander was the author of the sacred office.

These works may be consulted in the authors I cite: our John Mariana, *On the Affairs of Spain*, Book VI, chapter 5; Francisco de Padilla, *Ecclesiastical History of Spain*, century I, chapter 10, and century VII, chapter 20; Vaseus under the year 717; Ambrosio de Morales, Book XII, chapter 19; Álvaro Gómez, *On the Deeds of Cardinal Ximénez*, Book II, page 969; the Marquis of Mondéjar, folio 136. One may also add the observation on the councils held in Hither Spain in Labbe, volume IX, column 1198.

I shall quote their words below on another suitable occasion. For now it will be useful to hear the matter explained elsewhere.

13. Nicolás Antonio, in the *Old Hispanic Library*, Book V, chapter 4, page 269, while listing Isidore’s works, says:

“A Missal and Breviary are also attributed to him, which the churches of Spain used, according to that decree of the Fourth Council of Toledo—which, it is believed, is contained in its second canon—‘Concerning one order,’ and so forth.

“Since the Arian heresy could not fail to disturb the entire right order [Col. 0665B] that was to be observed in ecclesiastical discipline, and to introduce variation everywhere as a consequence of error, nothing was more necessary for the Catholic bishops than to prescribe that the entire sacred rite and ceremonies, both conformable to the true faith and uniformly observed by all the provinces under Gothic rule, in Spain as well as in Gaul, should be established.

“In this matter there can scarcely be any doubt that Leander, while he lived, fulfilled his office as the expeller of Arianism. But since this Gothic Missal and Breviary Office is commonly called Isidorian, we cannot deny our Isidore some principal honor and praise for this construction and for this learned, serious, and at the same time pious composition.”

The author cited confirms this from Guitmund and Elipandus, whom I shall discuss shortly. He then continues:

14. “Although, to speak frankly, I would not wish to admit that this was accomplished by that decree of the council, lest we compress a work of no slight labor [Col. 0665C] and exertion into so brief a period—the time necessarily extending from the council that was held to the death of the holy bishop.

“For it seems much more probable to me that he had already undertaken the completion of this work long before, after the earlier efforts of others, by the time the council was held; or that this Isidorian rite had already come into use at the time of the council, and that the Toledan Fathers directed their decree toward it, prescribing that throughout the entire territory of the Gothic name the same order of praying and singing—the Breviary is indicated—and the same manner in the solemnities of the Mass—the book of the Missal is signified—should be observed.

“For unless some rite had already been promulgated or approved for the clergy to use, it would have been pointless to legislate against diversity and the scandal arising from it.”

After inserting several points that create difficulty for attributing the work under discussion to Saint Isidore as its author, he adjusts his view to the present question by adopting a middle position: he neither assigns the entire undertaking to Isidore nor wholly removes it from him [Col. 0665D], but partly grants and partly denies it. He expresses this in the following words:

### 15 [Col. 0666A]

“All these things, certainly devised with judgment, however much they deny our Isidore the praise of having begun and completed the Office, ought nevertheless to establish this much among all who reason rightly: that, among others devoted to this undertaking, Isidore should not be regarded as having the least distinction, since these books are commonly called Isidorian and bear a name derived from the remotest antiquity.”

But apart from the fact that this is not properly at issue, it also agrees sufficiently with what I said at the beginning of this paragraph, where I set out without obscurity what I thought should be attributed to Saint Isidore in this matter. Yet several writers demand more—not only those who can claim no authority from antiquity, but also others of considerable age.

Guitmundus, bishop of Aversa in Italy, who flourished in the eleventh century and concerning whom Ughellus writes among the bishops of that see in volume I of *Italia sacra*, column 488 of the latest edition—I mean Guitmundus, in book III of *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist* (found in the Cologne edition of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, 1618, volume XI), page 369, says:

> “In a certain Spanish Missal, which they say Saint Isidore dictated, during the week before Easter, I found the following in a certain Mass,” etc.

Among the works of Alcuin, or Albinus, who was the teacher of Charlemagne and became famous toward the end of the eighth century, there is a letter of Elipandus, bishop of Toledo, addressed to Alcuin. In it he says the following, on column 917 of the Paris edition of those works, said to have been printed in 1617:

> “For we too sing at the Easter Vigil, Saint Isidore saying: ‘He put on flesh, but did not lay aside his majesty; seeking our substance, but not abandoning his own.’”

### 16 [Col. 0666B]

You have heard what can be said in the present controversy on behalf of Saint Isidore. Now understand what arguments count against him, from the most eminent Cardinal Bona, book I, chapter 11. After he had cited Baronius, as well as the title of the books containing these Offices—a title that confirms Baronius’s assertion and is usually as follows:

> “The Gothic, or Mixed, Office, according to the Rule of Saint Isidore, called Mozarabic,”

he immediately presents the following difficulties, using these words:

> “For my part,” he says, “there are certain considerations that present a serious difficulty and prevent me from immediately embracing this opinion. First, in the Mass of Saint Martin, in the prayer after the names, these words are read: ‘May you command this man, whom the times of our age have brought forth, to bring help to our times.’ But Martin died in the year of the Lord 402, and he was the first of the confessors to begin receiving public veneration shortly after his death. Therefore this Mass was written long before Isidore. Moreover, if Isidore was the author of this Office, why do neither Braulio of Zaragoza nor Ildefonsus of Toledo—holy men and associates of Isidore, the former in his eulogy of Isidore, the latter in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*—make any mention of a work so outstanding?”

### 17 [Cols. 0666C–0666D]

“To this may be added that the Fourth Council of Toledo mentions several rites of this Office in canon 11 and the following canons as already customary. Likewise, the Third Council of Toledo, forty-four years before the Fourth, in canon 2, decreed that the Creed should be recited in every church before the Lord’s Prayer was said—a practice peculiar to the Mozarabic Mass.

“Isidore himself, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, while reviewing the writings of his brother Leander, his predecessor in the see of Seville, testifies that Leander devoted no small effort to the ecclesiastical Offices and composed many things in praise of the sacrifice and in psalms, with a sweet style. Joannes Mariana, book VI, chapter 5 of *On the Affairs of Spain*, says that the practice arose of attributing the Mozarabic rite to Isidore, although Leander had discovered certain parts of it.

“If Leander merely discovered it, I would believe that this Office was older than the Third Council of Toledo, which Leander attended, and that it was already in use in the fifth century, as we have just shown from the Mass of Saint Martin; but that its first author is unknown. Nevertheless, it was illuminated by Leander, enlarged by Isidore, and expanded by others as time passed—specifically by Ildefonsus, whose works Julian of Toledo divided into four parts in the Appendix to his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, saying that the third part consisted of Masses, hymns, and sermons.”

### 18 [Cols. 0666D–0667A]

“It is likewise said that Julian himself, who ended his final day in the Spanish Era 728—that is, in the year of Christ 690—wrote, as Bishop Felix reports in the same appendix, a book of Masses divided into four parts according to the entire annual cycle. In it he corrected and completed some Masses that had been corrupted and left incomplete through the negligence of antiquity, while he composed others entirely.

“Likewise, he gathered together and left for the use of the Church of God, out of love for holy religion, a book of prayers for the festivals that the Church of Toledo was accustomed to celebrate throughout the annual cycle—partly drawn from the resources of his own style, and partly carefully corrected from material corrupted by long antiquity.

“Peter, bishop of Lérida, also published prayers and Masses in elegant language, appropriate to different solemnities. Salvo, abbot of the monastery of Abla, is likewise said to have composed Masses, prayers, and hymns, imparting the greatest compunction of heart to those who read and hear them.”

### 19 [Cols. 0667A–0667B]

These, then, are the arguments that this cardinal, highly learned in liturgical matters, assembles concerning the present controversy. They seemed so vigorous and solid to the celebrated Nicolás Antonio that he not only candidly and openly acknowledged them, as we have seen, to have been devised with judgment, but also offered nothing to weaken their force.

For this reason he added the clause mentioned above, tacitly admitting that a new liturgy had not been composed by Isidore, as is clear from the words quoted earlier.

To the argument that Cardinal Bona draws from the additions made to the sacred liturgy by men who followed Saint Isidore, Antonio responds appropriately as follows:

> “That, after the Council’s decree had once prescribed an order for the sacraments, for prayer and psalmody, and also for the Masses and the daily prayers recited at the canonical hours, holy and learned bishops nevertheless continued to compose prayers and Masses … may be interpreted as meaning that precisely what commonly happens today occurred at that time. For the present Roman Church, without disturbing the order established in its substantial rules and finally stabilized by the blessed—now saint—Pius V, most holy pontiff, frequently permits or commands the recitation of entire Masses and Offices, or parts of them, for different churches or for the whole body of the faithful, after they have been approved.”

Thus Antonio answers the argument of the most eminent cardinal, which is drawn from the men who enlarged the Spanish liturgy; but he does not answer the others. For that reason, the opinion that denies to Saint Isidore the composition of a new liturgical order appears to me closer to the truth.

### 20 [Cols. 0667C–0668A]

The most eminent Aguirre likewise held this opinion. In volume I, page 143, while discussing the decrees of the Fourth Council of Toledo, he writes:

> “From these decrees is believed to have arisen the arrangement of that most ancient Missal and Breviary according to the Gothic rite, which is commonly called Isidorian—the designation being taken from Saint Isidore, who presided over that synod and arranged it in a better form—although the same rite had already been received and disseminated, with some variation, in various churches of Spain from the time of the disciples of Saint James, or thereabouts, as the Marquis of Mondéjar proves at length in chapter 24.”

Nevertheless, he admits that he cannot determine precisely what form this Mass had in its beginnings, since the monuments that would establish it are lacking.

This is highly consonant with the opinion I set out earlier concerning the obscurity of the Spanish liturgy in its earliest centuries. The argument drawn above from Elipandus proves little or nothing. It may be answered that he spoke in that way in order to lend greater authority to his words by adding the name of Saint Isidore. He knew that, for Alcuin, to whom he was writing, that name ought to be more venerable than those of the other Fathers gathered at Toledo with him. Yet in the same letter Elipandus had shortly before prefaced his statement as follows:

> “Again, the testimonies of the holy and venerable Fathers serving Toledo, set forth in the prayers of the Masses, say the following,” etc.

Here he attributes the Masses to the Fathers of Toledo; there he attributes something to Saint Isidore that was sung at the Easter Vigil, though he did not speak in the same manner.

But suppose that the saint truly prescribed those words to be sung at that time. Does it follow that he composed a new liturgy? As for what was objected above from Guitmundus, I reply that scarcely anything can be established from it against Cardinal Bona’s opinion. For the word *dicunt*—“they say”—certainly indicates that at that time there was a report that Saint Isidore had dictated a Missal; but the arguments proposed to the contrary seem to suggest that what was then said had not in fact occurred earlier.

Moreover, Guitmundus was too far removed from the time of Saint Isidore for his “they say” to establish certainty. See the celebrated Count of Mondéjar, folio 136 verso, where he observes that no testimony has yet been found preceding the Moorish invasion of Spain by which this common opinion—that Saint Isidore was the author of the Office—could safely be established. He himself rejects that opinion on folio 138.

Now, since the argument drawn from the Mass of Saint Martin of Tours is especially troublesome to the contrary opinion, something might be added here concerning the time when that Mass was composed, as well as concerning certain other circumstances. But since an opportunity to discuss those matters will present itself elsewhere, I refer the reader there. Meanwhile, I shall offer a few specimens from Saint Isidore, so that it may become clear what order of the sacred mysteries flourished in this seventh century, at least as far as their prayers are concerned, and so that the opinion may be confirmed which attributes the composition of a new liturgy for Spain to this saint.

### Prayers in the Sacrifice of the Mass in the Time of Saint Isidore; Some Matters Concerning the Sacred Liturgy Drawn from Various Councils of Spain

### 22 [Cols. 0668B–0668C]

Saint Isidore discusses the Mass and its prayers in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 15, and defines how many prayers were then used, what kind they were, and for what purpose. He says:

> “The first is a prayer of admonition directed toward the people, so that they may be stirred to entreat God. The second is an invocation, by which God is asked mercifully to receive the prayers of the faithful and their offering. The third is poured out for those who offer, or for the faithful departed, so that through the same sacrifice they may obtain forgiveness. The fourth is introduced after these for the kiss of peace, so that all, reconciled to one another in charity, may be joined together as worthy participants in the sacrament of the body and blood of Christ. For the indivisible body of Christ does not admit anyone’s dissension. The fifth is the *Illation* in the sanctification of the offering. In it, the whole assembly of earthly creatures and heavenly powers is summoned to the praise of God, and ‘Hosanna in the highest’ is sung, because, with the Savior born from the line of David, the salvation of the world has reached even to the heights. Thereafter the sixth follows, the confirmation of the sacrament, so that the offering made to the Lord, sanctified by the Holy Spirit, may be confirmed as the body and blood of Christ. The last of these is the prayer that our Lord taught his disciples to pray, saying: ‘Our Father, who art in heaven.’”

### 23 [Cols. 0668C–0668D]

After briefly commenting on the petitions of this prayer, Saint Isidore concludes as follows:

> “These, therefore, are the seven prayers of the sacrifice, commended by apostolic and evangelical teaching. The reason for this number appears to have been established either because of the sevenfold universality of the holy Church or because of the sevenfold Spirit of grace, by whose gift the things offered are sanctified.”

The same holy bishop of Seville discusses the Nicene Creed in chapter 16:

> “The Creed,” he says, “which is proclaimed to the people during the sacrifice, was issued through the deliberation of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers at the synod of Nicaea. Its rule of true faith excels in so many mysteries of doctrine that it speaks concerning every part of the faith, and there is scarcely any heresy to which it does not respond through its individual words or statements. For it tramples upon all the impieties of error and the blasphemies of unbelief, and for this reason it is proclaimed by the people in every Church with a common confession.”

### 24 [Cols. 0668D–0669A]

In chapter 17 he discusses blessings among the people, but I extract nothing from it, since it contains only an analogy with the blessing given by Moses under the ancient Law.

Nicolás Antonio says, on page 269:

> “The order of the Mixtarabic Missal—which is commonly believed to be the same as the Isidorian Missal—is different from the order that Isidore, in book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15, reports to have been observed in his time throughout the whole world.”

This was noted both by Jacobus Pamelius, who indicated the parts in which they differed in his Latin Liturgies, volume I, page 642, and by Joannes Grialius in his notes on this testimony of Isidore.
