But the discussion of the Mozarabic Mass will return in its proper place. For now, the time warns us to bring to an end the controversy sufficiently and more than sufficiently treated here, and to examine what occurred in liturgical matters during the course of this seventh century.

### 25 [Cols. 0669A–0669B]

In the Fifth Council of Toledo, recorded by Aguirre as having been held in the year of Christ 636, canon 1 decrees that, beginning on the Ides of December, litanies should be celebrated for three days each year in succession; but if a Sunday should intervene, they should be celebrated in the following week.

In the Sixth Council of Toledo, recorded by Aguirre on page 512 as having been convened in the year of Christ 638, canon 2 decrees that these days of litanies, which had been established in the preceding synod, should be observed with every distinction at the same time each year at which they had been ordered to be celebrated.

So that I may not interrupt the order continued through this and the following periods of the century, I shall proceed through the councils themselves and afterward review the men who deserved well of liturgical matters in this age.

In the Seventh Council of Toledo, held in 646, as indicated by Aguirre on page 523, canon 2, the Fathers say:

> “We judge it fitting that, when the sacred mysteries are consecrated by priests during the time of Mass, if any event of illness occurs by which the ministry of the consecration begun cannot be completed, it should be permitted for a bishop or another priest to carry out the consecration of the Office already begun … Yet, lest what is provided because of the weakness of nature be turned into a ruinous presumption, no one may celebrate Mass after taking even the smallest amount of food or drink; and no minister or priest, once he has begun, may presume entirely to abandon unfinished Offices without an evident cause of distress. Whoever presumes to attempt these things shall endure the sentence of excommunication.”

Concerning the priest’s fasting before offering the sacrifice, one may consult Loaisa’s note in Aguirre, page 526.

### 26 [Cols. 0669B–0669D]

The Eighth Council of Toledo, held in 653 and found in the repeatedly cited synodical collection, page 540, states:

> “In the sacred solemnities of the Masses, with one accord we profess and say: We believe in one God, the Father almighty,” etc.

The notes on this Creed may be seen in Aguirre, page 563.

On page 545, canon 8, the following provision is made:

> “With the concern prompted by our eighth deliberation, we have discovered that certain men devoted to the divine Offices are filled with such extreme ignorance and negligence that they are not found adequately instructed even in those orders which are used daily. Therefore it is carefully established and decreed that no one of whatever ecclesiastical dignity shall henceforth receive a rank unless he thoroughly knows the entire Psalter, or the supplement of the customary canticles and hymns, or that of baptism,” etc.

In the Ninth Synod of Toledo, held in the year of Christ 655, I find nothing relevant to our purpose, so far as I have been able to observe from the titles prefixed to it.

The Tenth Council of Toledo, held in the year of Christ 656 and recorded by Aguirre beginning on page 579, discusses in title 1 the celebration of the festival of the Lord’s mother [another reading: “the Annunciation”]. Then, in chapter 1, the Fathers make clear their singular affection for and devotion and veneration toward the Virgin Mother, an affection that has continued with the greatest constancy among that most devout people down to the present day.

The chapter therefore decrees as follows.

### 27 [Cols. 0669D–0670A]

> “If the day of the birth and death of the incarnate Word is held to be so fixed and certain that it is celebrated without variation throughout the whole world by the entire Church in common, why should not the festival of his glorious mother likewise be observed everywhere on one and the same day and with similar honor?
>
> “For in many parts of Spain the feast of this holy Virgin is not celebrated on one and the same day throughout the entire annual cycle … Since, therefore, the day on which the angel is found to have announced to the Virgin the conception of the Word in words and to have bestowed it through miracles cannot suitably be celebrated when at times the days of Lent or the Paschal festival appear to intervene … it is decreed by special constitution that, before the eighth day on which the Lord was born, the day of his Mother also be held with the greatest distinction and splendor.
>
> “For an equal honor is established: just as the dignity of the days following the Son’s birth follows upon his nativity, so the sacred solemnity of as many days should follow the festival of the Mother. For what is the festival of the Mother other than the incarnation of the Word? Its solemnity ought therefore to be as great as that of the same Word’s nativity [another reading: ‘of the Word’s Nativity’].
>
> “Yet this does not appear to have been instituted without the example of an established custom, which is known to be observed in various parts of the world. In many churches, distant from us both in space and in lands, this custom is known to be maintained. Therefore, so that every doubt may henceforth be removed, the solemnity of the Lord’s Mother shall be celebrated without exception on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January.”

### 28 [Cols. 0670A–0670C]

The Synod of Mérida in Lusitania, held in the year of Christ 666, decrees in canon 2 that, just as in other churches, in the evening, after the light has been offered, the *Vespertinum* is said before the *Sonus* on feast days, so this practice should also be observed by us in our churches, say the bishops of that synod.

In the Eleventh Council of Toledo, held in 675 and recorded by Aguirre on page 664, chapter 3 contains the following:

> “It has pleased this holy council that, compelled by the authority of the metropolitan see, the bishops and rectors of the churches of every province should maintain one and the same manner of psalmody, the manner they have learned to be established in the metropolitan see; nor should they allow themselves to be separated from the metropolitan see by any variation in any order or Office … To abbots, Offices are indeed granted which they are to fulfill regularly according to the will of their bishop; but the other public Offices—that is, Vespers [another reading: ‘Vesper’], Matins, or the Mass—may not be celebrated otherwise than in the principal church. Whoever proves to be a violator of these decrees shall be deprived of communion for six months and shall remain with the metropolitan under the discipline of penance, until corrected,” etc.

Canon 14 establishes that wherever the availability of time, place, or clergy permits it, every person who sings to God and offers sacrifice should always have behind him the assistance of a nearby helper, so that if, by some accident, the person who approaches to fulfill the Offices should become disturbed or fall to the ground, he may always have behind him someone who can carry out his role without fear.

### 29 [Cols. 0670C–0670D]

In the year of Christ 675, a council was held in the aforementioned Lusitania, at Braga. Aguirre discusses it on page 675 and records that it was the third council of that name; elsewhere, however, it is called the fourth, as is gathered from a marginal note in the cited Aguirre.

In this council, chapter 1 confronts errors committed concerning the most holy Eucharist in the following words:

> “A manifest and varied error among all our people has been reported in our assembly … For some have been reported to offer milk in the Lord’s sacrifices, and a bunch of grapes instead of wine; they also believe that the Eucharist soaked in wine ought to be presented to the people as the completion of communion. And, worse than all these things, some priests place food for themselves in the Lord’s vessels and presume to eat from them. Some priests have also been reported to dare to celebrate Mass without the stoles, omitting the order of ecclesiastical custom; and on the solemnities of martyrs they place relics around their necks for display,” etc.

The following chapters oppose these errors. For the sake of brevity, it is enough to transcribe their titles here:

2. That, after all superstitious opinions have been rejected, only bread and wine mixed with water be offered in the sacrifice.

3. That vessels consecrated to God not serve human uses.

4. That a priest should not dare to celebrate Mass without a stole.

6. Concerning the condemned presumption of certain persons, etc.

### 30 [Cols. 0670D–0671A]

Two councils of Toledo remain from this seventh century under discussion that are relevant to our purpose, namely the Twelfth and the Seventeenth.

The first, assembled in 681, deals in canon 5, in Aguirre on page 685, with priests who do not communicate as often as they offer sacrifice. This is clear from the title of the canon on page 681, which reads:

> “Concerning the most shameful custom of certain priests who do not communicate after offering sacrifices to God themselves.”

For, as the text of the canon says, if on one day they offer several sacrifices to God themselves, they abstain from communicating at all the offerings, and receive the grace of holy communion only at the offering of the final sacrifice.

The matter is illustrated by the notes in Aguirre, page 692.

### 31 [Cols. 0671A–0671B]

The other council I mentioned was the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, held in 694. Its canon 4, as is clear from its title, concerns sacred ministries or the ornaments of churches.

The title of canon 5 reads:

> “Concerning those who maliciously dare to celebrate a Mass for the dead on behalf of the living.”

The title of canon 6 concerns the celebration of the Days of the Litanies throughout all twelve months.

Aguirre presents the canons themselves beginning on page 755. I refer any reader interested in examining them to that work.

Now let us recall the men distinguished by their liturgical writings in this seventh century, whom we postponed to this point. They will add some new light to what I have so far attempted to gather from the councils held in this age. For, besides the information about such men supplied above when an opportunity arose, there are several further matters of this kind that cannot be omitted.

### 32 [Cols. 0671B–0671C]

From what Pinius has so far collected and discussed, it may be argued that the ancient Spanish liturgy was brought into a new splendor from the time of the Fourth Council of Toledo, with many provisions established for observance throughout Spain.

Since, therefore, the liturgical canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo are attributed to Isidore, and since Isidore wrote much else concerning ecclesiastical Offices, the Spanish liturgy could reasonably have been called Isidorian after that time—that is, arranged according to the canons and teaching of Isidore—even though it retained much from antiquity, as the canons of the Fourth Council itself required, and even though much was later added and brought to greater distinction.

For although the Fourth Council of Toledo ordered that there should be one manner and order of sacred worship, the Fathers seem to have understood this in such a way that, while the same order was retained in certain principal matters, they nevertheless considered it permissible for bishops to add new Masses, prayers, hymns, and similar material, and to differ from others in certain matters of lesser importance.

### 33 [Cols. 0671C–0671D]

I believe that this gave rise to the diversity of the liturgy which the canons of the subsequent synods, reported by Pinius, endeavored to abolish. From this also arose the corruptions that remained in some places in the performance of the sacred Office, which other canons proscribed.

Yet it is certain that, even after Isidore, distinguished men usefully devoted their efforts to enlarging and illuminating the Spanish liturgy: Conantius of Palencia, who lived until 639; Eugenius the Younger, bishop of Toledo; Ildefonsus; and Julian, likewise bishops of Toledo.

From these and other Gothic Fathers, the Spanish liturgy—which was also called Isidorian—received the name Gothic.

But it seems to me that the following question must be asked: are there in the Gothic Breviary and Missal certain parts composed by Isidore, just as we know that many were composed individually by Leander, Ildefonsus, and Julian?

### 34 [Cols. 0671D–0672A]

We may reasonably conjecture that Saint Isidore was the author of several things in the Gothic Office, but it is not so easy to demonstrate this.

The ancients were silent about this labor of Isidore. They were occupied in recounting his many and very important works and disdained to pursue these lesser matters: whether he had composed Masses, certain prayers, hymns, or other such pieces inserted into the Gothic Offices.

Recent writers, on the contrary, are excessively generous. Since it is certain that many other Fathers had a considerable role in the Gothic liturgy, they praise Isidore as the author of whatever they read in the Gothic Missal or Breviary, deceived by the name of the Isidorian Office.

Nevertheless, some appear to attribute certain parts of the Gothic Office to Isidore for particular reasons. Tamayus, in the *Hispanic Martyrology*, who does not attribute everything contained in the Gothic Office to Isidore, reports that the prayer of Saint Vincent the Martyr in that Office was composed by Saint Isidore.

### 35 [Cols. 0672A–0672C]

In the proper Offices of the Spanish saints, on July 17, in the third lesson of the second nocturn, the following is handed down:

> “Rufina too, surviving her most holy sister for further contests, was brought into the arena at the governor’s command and, as Saint Isidore reports, was exposed to a most savage lion.”

This appears to have been taken from nowhere other than a chapter of the Gothic Breviary.

Something similar is reported in the feast of Saints Servandus and Germanus, on October 23, in the third lesson of the second nocturn:

> “The body of Germanus, as Saint Isidore reports, was buried at Cádiz and afterward transported to Mérida.”

That too is evidently taken from the Gothic Office.

I said in chapter 81 that certain hymns of the Gothic Breviary are attributed to Isidore in the *Proper Offices of the Spanish Saints*, although other hymns of that same Gothic Office are presented without an author’s name.

What, then, accounts for this difference? These are recent testimonies; and since the authors of the proper Offices of Spain were different, one person attributed to Isidore what he found in the Isidorian liturgy, while another, weighing the matter with more mature judgment, presented it as anonymous.

### 36 [Cols. 0672C–0672D]

Yet in the Breviary itself there is a sermon explicitly inscribed with Isidore’s name, as I explained in chapter 72.

This is also relevant: Elipandus says in his letter to Alcuin:

> “For we too sing at the Easter Vigil, Saint Isidore saying: ‘He put on flesh,’” etc.

Pinius replies that Elipandus said this in order to lend those words greater authority. But since Elipandus cites other testimonies in the names of Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julian, or of the venerable Fathers serving Toledo, he seems to have found something peculiar in the Office of the Easter Vigil. Why, then, would he name Isidore as its author?

Florezius, volume III of *Hispania sacra*, page 266, thinks that Elipandus corrupted the Missal of his church and therefore sometimes cited only his predecessors Eugenius, Ildefonsus, and Julian without naming Isidore.

Certainly Elipandus may have corrupted the liturgical books. But, as I think, at that time either the names of the authors to whom the individual parts belonged were written in the ecclesiastical books themselves, or the matter was known from other documents, although perhaps the authors of certain more ancient prayers were unknown.

### 37 [Cols. 0672D–0673C]

Receive a not insignificant argument for this point.

Samson, abbot of Córdoba, who composed his *Apologeticus* in the ninth century, published by Florezius in volume XI of *Hispania sacra*, says in book II, chapter 13:

> “What the venerable doctor Julian says in the daily Mass that follows: ‘About to receive, dearest brothers, the heavenly sacrifice within mortal bowels,’” etc.

These words come from the Gothic Missal, in the prayer found before the Lord’s Prayer in the Sunday Mass before the fast of the Kalends of November.

Again, the same Samson says in book II, chapter 23:

> “Saint Julian also intimates this to us in these words in the daily Mass, when he says: ‘It is worthy and just that we give thanks to you, almighty God, whose divinity is immeasurable,’” etc.

These words occur in the same Mass of the Gothic Missal, in the *Illation*, which corresponds to the preface of our Missal.

What Samson means by the name “daily Mass” is discussed in the Notice prefixed to these prayers in volume II of the *Fathers of Toledo*, page 325, though no sufficiently satisfactory explanation is found, as the author of the Notice candidly admits.

Perhaps the following conjecture will prove more attractive: these prayers may once have been contained in a Mass common to many weekdays and may have been called “daily” in that sense. This conjecture is supported by the Gothic, or Old Gallican, Missal edited by V. Thomasius. After several Masses common to martyrs and confessors, and a proper Mass of Saint Martin the bishop, it contains six Sunday Masses, followed by the beginning of the daily Mass under this title:

> “Daily Roman Mass: O God, who are offended by sin,” etc.

Vezzorius notes that this same daily Roman Mass exists in the Sacramentary of the Bobbio Codex, although it does not begin with the same prayer. From that codex it is clear that the Mass had been adapted to the Gallican rite, although, in Mabillon’s opinion, it was taken from the Roman, or Gregorian, order.

In the ancient Gallican Sacramentary of the aforementioned Bobbio Codex, besides the daily Roman Mass, there are other daily Masses and daily Sunday Masses.

Why should it be otherwise, when, as I shall say below, daily Masses also exist in the ancient codices still preserved at Toledo?

Nor do I doubt that these daily Masses correspond to the daily hymns described after the Psalter in the recent edition of the Mozarabic Breviary.

### 38 [Cols. 0673D–0674A]

In the meantime, this much is established: Samson did not fail to know who had been the author of the prayers recited in that Mass, whether the author’s name had been written in certain Masses or whether the fact had then been established from other documents.

The same Samson, however, did not know who had been the author of a certain antiphon for the feast of the Annunciation of the Mother of God, and suspected that it had been composed at the time when the Arian heresy was raging in Spain.

Hostegesis, bishop of Málaga, had taught that, when God became incarnate, he had been enclosed in the Virgin’s heart. Later, partly refuted by Samson, he conceded that the Word had become flesh in the Virgin’s womb, but in such a way that it should be said to have been enclosed in the Virgin’s womb.

The badly Latinized words of Hostegesis are these, in book II, chapter 11 of Samson’s *Apologeticus*:

> “They have rashly and prematurely condemned the psalmody that earlier Fathers have sung until now among the ecclesiastical rules. Nor should I pass over the text of this antiphon, so that the doctrine of faith rightly expressed in it against Nestorius may immediately be shown:
>
> “‘O what a great and unheard-of miracle! Power looked forth from heaven and overshadowed the Virgin’s womb. Majesty is able to be enclosed within the chamber of the heart, the doors being closed. We believe, we believe that the Word of almighty God entered the Virgin’s womb and, according to the union of person, was there with the doors closed. And, so that the doctrine of Nestorius may yield, we do not doubt that he was enclosed,’” etc.

### 39 [Cols. 0674A–0674C]

Samson rightly mocked the solecisms of Hostegesis and looked forward to better times for Spain. In book II, chapter 7, he says:

> “For believe me: these shadows of ignorance will one day be dispelled, and knowledge of the art of grammar will again be restored to Spain. Then it will become clear to everyone how many errors you yourself are subject to—you who today are thought by brutish men to possess literary knowledge.”

In the first edition of *Hispania sacra*, *abolebuntur* was correctly printed; in the second it was incorrectly changed to *adolebuntur*.

Concerning the antiphon, Samson replies in book II, chapter 12:

> “Tell me, my friend: since today you say with me that Christ, the Son of God and man, was incarnate in the Virgin’s womb, and consequently was also enclosed there according to the union of person, why do you not sing what you say you believe? And why do you correct the others in imitation of those copies that read ‘within the chamber of the kingdom’ or ‘of the womb’?”

In the first edition of *Hispania sacra*, the correct reading is *id canis*—“why do you sing this”; afterward it was most corruptly printed *id carnis*—“of the flesh.”

The copies of the Cordoban Gothic Missal therefore differed in this antiphon.

Samson adds that he had long ago noted the antiphon as bad in a copy in which the reading was “within the chamber of the heart”:

> “For several years ago, after hearing this antiphon, I questioned a certain priest who seemed somewhat learned … Having reasonably defeated him, I marked this antiphon and wrote above it: ‘BAD.’”

And indeed, according to this sense, it is very bad.

### 40.

Samson speaks more clearly in chapter 15 about the disagreement among the manuscripts and about the meaning of the antiphon:

> “It is therefore just that my friends should agree not with me but with those manuscripts in which it is written, ‘within the chamber of the kingdom,’ or at least with those in which it reads, ‘within the chamber of the womb’ . . . I certainly did not write this in their copies, but perhaps the author or corrector of the antiphon itself did. But if the author published it in such a way as to put either ‘the chamber of the kingdom’ or ‘of the womb’—both of which designate the same thing—the copyist must be blamed, since it is clear that the text was corrupted by him. Or if perhaps it was published by the ancients, who, placed under the Arian error and long occupying Spain, asserted that the divinity of the Son of God was created and consequently local and circumscribed, and therefore judged it capable of being enclosed, and said that it had been enclosed in the heart of the Virgin mother: after peace had been granted to the Church by God, etc., it is sung there in sanctification when it says, ‘Can majesty be enclosed within the chamber of the womb or of the kingdom?’ But since others attached little importance to it, as it had been issued by the Arians, they have continued to use it in its corrupted form without any correction . . . But if (which I do not think) the Latin expression permits either *includi* [‘to be enclosed’] or permits the womb to be called the heart, then perhaps the antiphon itself may be considered irreproachable.”

### 41.

115 From this manner of responding I infer that copies of the Gothic liturgy underwent the corrections of certain people under the rule of the Moors, who nevertheless perhaps corrupted the true and genuine reading. At that time some Spaniards were persuaded that certain parts of the Gothic office had been composed during the period of the Arian heresy, and perhaps by Arians, although they had been retained by Catholic teachers, either corrected or left without correction because they could be understood in a Catholic sense.

The antiphon that Samson criticized so severely still remains in the Isidorian, or Mozarabic, Breviary, on the feast of the Annunciation of the holy Virgin Mary, 18 December, in the closing Vespers, p. CCCLV of the recent edition:

> “O what a great, unheard-of miracle! Power looked forth from heaven; it overshadowed the Virgin’s womb. Majesty is able to be enclosed beneath the chamber of the heart, with its doors closed.”

Here *infra* stands for *intra* either as a typographical error or as the correction of some copyist who, agreeing with Samson, thought that *intra cubiculum cordis*—“within the chamber of the heart”—ought to be rejected.

### 42.

I do not, however, approve Samson’s conjecture that the antiphon was composed by Arian heretics. Samson objected to two things in it: first, that it might be inferred that the Virgin conceived in her heart; second, that God, who is uncircumscribed, is said to have been enclosed.

The first error—that the Virgin conceived in her heart and not in her womb—could be shared by Arians and non-Arians alike. The second error—that the Son of God was believed to be created and consequently local and circumscribed—is properly Arian. How, then, does Samson say that the antiphon was sanctified in the manuscripts in which it is sung:

> “Majesty is able to be enclosed within the chamber of the womb or of the kingdom”?

For the word *includi*—“to be enclosed”—still remains there, and that word alone could suggest the Arian heresy. If majesty can be enclosed, it makes no difference to the matter whether it is enclosed within the chamber of the heart, the womb, or the kingdom. In place of this last word Samson may perhaps have written *ventris*—“of the belly”—or *renum*—“of the kidneys”—or, in the singular, *renis*; for he had previously mentioned the words *uteri* and *regni*, either of which can easily be understood as referring to the womb. But “the chamber of the kingdom” cannot easily be drawn into this meaning.

### 43.

Since, then, even by Samson’s own admission, the manuscripts agree in the word *includi*, the antiphon must on this point be judged Catholic and not attributed to the Arians. God is indeed uncircumscribed and immeasurable and cannot be confined by place; but, because of the communication of properties, he is said to have been enclosed in the Virgin’s womb as capable of suffering, mortal, and so forth.

Thus, too, in the hymn of Venantius Fortunatus for the Matins office of Saint Mary on Saturday, we sing:

> **Blessed mother, through whose gift**  
> **the heavenly Artisan,**  
> **who holds the world within his handful,**  
> **was shut beneath the vault of the womb.**

I pass over countless other examples from our ecclesiastical offices and from the Fathers, which Petavius lists in book X, chapters 8 and 9, *On the Incarnation*. Nor does Samson disagree, for he continues in book II, chapter 15:

> “There is no unheard-of miracle in the whole antiphon unless the Word of God is said to have been made human in the Virgin’s womb and, because of the union of person, to have been enclosed.”

### 44.

[Col. 0676A] Although there would be less danger of error if the antiphon read *infra cubiculum*—“beneath the chamber”—instead of *intra cubiculum cordis*—“within the chamber of the heart”—I believe that the genuine reading of a Catholic author, and one to be received in a sound sense, is *intra cubiculum cordis*. For it is evident that some of the ancients spoke similarly. In the fifth responsory of the Circumcision of the Lord we find:

> “The heart of the Virgin was confirmed; in it, when the angel announced it, she conceived the divine mysteries. Then, beautiful in form above the sons of men, he was received in chaste inward parts.”

Compare Benedict XIV, book II, *On the Beatification*, chapter 32, no. 8, and what I noted in my commentary on Prudentius’s *Apotheosis*, verse 583, against the error of Peter of Lucca, who, deceived by a woman’s revelation, asserted that the Blessed Virgin conceived not in her womb but in her heart:

[Col. 0676B]

> “Virginity and ready faith drank Christ in the womb  
> of the heart, and, about to give birth, hid him in inviolate recesses.”

Perhaps the author of the antiphon in the Gothic Breviary was Saint Ildefonsus, whose is the Mass of the Gothic Missal for the same feast of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There certain similar expressions are found:

> “In the recess of her breast faith disclosed the Word,” etc.

In connection with the prayer called the Mass, Lesleus quotes these words about the Virgin from Saint Peter Chrysologus, homily 42:

> “Blessed is she who received and preserved the divine pledge in her breast in such a way that the whole exterior of her body was unaware of it.”

### 45.

Among the Gothic Fathers who, after Isidore, illuminated and enlarged the liturgy, or ecclesiastical offices, we may rightly include Quiricus, bishop of Barcelona, who lived before the year 656 and until approximately the year 666. His is the hymn in honor of Saint Eulalia of Barcelona, fol. CCXXVII of the Isidorian Breviary, as I infer from these words:

> “Among these, may Quiricus himself too seek [a place], having been admitted,” etc.

Or, as Florez reads it in volume XXIX of *Hispania sacra*, p. 138:

> “Among these things, having been admitted,  
> may Quiricus himself rest.”

These are words of Quiricus the author, who imitated Prudentius, accustomed to pray in this manner in his hymns.

### 46.

Nor should Braulio be passed over. In his letters, first published in volume XXX of *Hispania sacra*, he discusses certain matters concerning ecclesiastical offices—namely, in Letter 14 to Fruminianus, to whom he sends a commentary on the Apostle:

> “Read it carefully first,” he says, “and arrange it in order; and since it also has written in the margin the opinions of various people, weave each point into the body of the work as you see it to accord with the Catholic faith and as the order presents it.”

Here *conscriptas*—“written”—should plainly be read *ad oram*, “in the margin”; and perhaps *se offeret* should be read instead of *se afferet*.

Braulio adds the following relevant passage:

> “For you ask whether on Good Friday, after each of the readings, Amen ought to be answered, or GLORIA sung in the customary manner. This is done neither among us nor anywhere that we have seen it done, nor among my lord Isidore, of outstanding memory, and finally not even at Toledo or Gerona. At Rome, as they say, no office is celebrated on that day. I believe, indeed, that the only reason is that the memory of the Lord’s Passion may always be renewed,” etc. . .

“But for this reason also it seems to me that mourning was instituted for that night, so that, by the Church—which is still visibly present in this world—those things that were bodily accomplished in Christ might be visibly fulfilled.”

Compare Lesleus, p. 516, in the note to the *Mozarabic Missal*.

### 47.

After other material on the same subject he continues:

> “As for clothing the altar, or hanging curtains—perhaps *velo mittendo*, ‘the curtain that is to be hung’—the practice of the churches is that, when the day is already declining toward evening, the church is adorned and the true light, rising from the dead, is received with ceremony, because those virgins who prepared their lamps also awaited the bridegroom’s arrival in the glory of the resurrection. Therefore festivals are celebrated during that night until the night has passed its midpoint, at which hour we too believe that we shall rise and that the Lord will judge the living and the dead,” etc.

### 48.

Braulio shows that the dead were customarily commemorated in the sacrifice of the Gothic Mass, in Letter 20 to Hoio and Eutrocia, whom he consoles on the death of Hugnanis:

> “For already,” he says, “we too have made mention of his name in the offering”—perhaps *in oblatione*, “in the offering”—at the altar of the Lord, and we have commended his soul to Christ almighty.”

### 49.

After Pinius had reviewed the ancient Gothic Fathers who enlarged the Gothic-Hispanic liturgy, he thoroughly demolishes Mabillon’s arguments. Mabillon had maintained that the Gallican liturgy was older than the Hispanic liturgy and had in some way supplied its form and origin.

Pinius then explains the history of the Hispanic liturgy in the eighth century and the following centuries under the Saracens, at which time it began to be called Mozarabic. We assign the following event to the eighth century: Alfonso, called the Chaste, built at Oviedo a splendid church of Saint Saviour for the twelve Apostles, made of stone and mortar, “and established the entire order of the Goths at Oviedo, both in the church and in the palace, just as it had been at Toledo.” The matter is related in the ancient Albeldensian Chronicle, p. 452, volume XIII of *Hispania sacra*. The author of the Chronicle flourished in the ninth century.

Some derive the etymology of the name “Mozarabic” with Roderic of Toledo, a thirteenth-century writer, from the fact that the Christians who used this liturgy were mixed with Arabs. Others derive it from Muza, a famous Arab commander. Others, more probably, agree with Pagi and derive it—not from a marquis rather than a count, as Pinius calls him—from the Arabic word *Mustarabes*, by which people were called “Arabs by assimilation”: not Arabs by origin and nature, but living among Arabs.

The opinion of others is less credible: that the Mozarabs were so called from Muza because this word signifies “Christian” among the Arabs, as though “Arab Christians.” Those skilled in Arabic, however, do not find this meaning in the word *muza*, although Florez, volume III, p. 191, cites from the *Vocabulista* of Father Alcalá the Arabic word *Macih* for Christ.

The etymology proposed by some others must also be rejected: namely, that Mozarabs were so called because they retained, in certain rites, the practices of Christians living in Arabia.

### 50.

The reason why the same office is called Toletan can be explained either by the Fourth Council of Toledo, through which it received great splendor; or because it was frequently practiced at Toledo among the Arabs for nearly four centuries; or because that rite was observed and cultivated with special dignity in the Church of Toledo above all others. This is sufficiently demonstrated by the example of Alfonso the Chaste that I mentioned in the preceding section.

After the Mozarabic liturgy survived only at Toledo, it could with greater right be called Toletan.

Pinius, together with Cardinal Bona, reports that it was called “mixed” because Cardinal Ximénez added and intermingled certain elements from the Roman office. Many others generally adopt this opinion, but Lesleus rightly opposes it. He teaches that a *Missale mixtum* is the same as a complete missal. Since the parts of the missal were accustomed to be written and bound separately, when all the parts coalesced into a single body and each part was inserted in its proper place, it was called a complete, or mixed, missal.

As I shall say later, Pinius reports from Camino that five Gothic missals were preserved at Toledo, each containing certain parts of the Mass. When these parts were mixed together in their proper order, a complete, or mixed, Missal was produced—and perhaps this occurred even before the time of Ximénez.

Ducange, under the entry *Missale mixtum*, cites from the will of the Count of Rouergue in the year 1291:

> “We give to the Friars Minor one MIXED MISSAL for the use of the said chapel.”

But he conjectures that this was a missal in which, besides matters pertaining to the Mass, other material also occurred.

More correctly, under *Mixtum* 3, Ducange says:

> “A book, if I am not mistaken, an ecclesiastical one.”

From the *History of the Abbey of Condom*, p. 507:

> “He wrote with his own hand ecclesiastical books, namely two missals, two graduals or *Jornaria*, two prosaries, and one MIXED [book].”

He adds the explanation “that is, assembled from others.” The copyist was Brother Andreas de Chica, a good and useful cloistered monk of the fourteenth century, who wrote, among other things, two missals of Saint Peter and of Our Lady, as well as an Evangelistary and an Epistolary, two graduals, etc., as reported by Cangius.

### 51.

Whether in the eighth century the Mozarabic liturgy was corrupted by the errors of Felix of Urgel and Elipandus of Toledo concerning Christ the adoptive Son of God is a matter of major controversy. But since most Spaniards vigorously resisted the heresy of the Adoptionists, it must be established as certain that the liturgical books of Spain were free from that error—unless Felix and Elipandus perhaps corrupted some copies.

Otherwise, these heretics could have cited certain words from uncorrupted Mozarabic ecclesiastical books in support of their error, either by twisting words expressed in a Catholic sense toward their own heresy or by expounding passages of the Mozarabic liturgy in their writings with insufficient fidelity, without laying hands upon the ancient parchments.

When Alcuin responds to Elipandus, he implies that he had not seen the ecclesiastical books of the Spaniards. But since elsewhere he describes prayers under the name of Isidore—of which I spoke in chapter 81—that appear to have been drawn from ecclesiastical offices, we must believe either that he encountered those prayers as separately published pieces or that he composed the work *On the Offices* according to the ferial days after the controversy against Elipandus.

As for Pinius’s view that the origin of the corrupted copies can be traced to Theodiscus, the successor of Saint Isidore, that fable had long since been exploded in the notes to the Life of Saint Isidore on 4 April.

### 52.

[Col. 0679A] For the ninth century Pinius reports no other monuments of the Mozarabic rite except that, in the presence of Charles the Bald, priests from Toledo celebrated the divine offices according to that rite, which had already been abolished in Gaul; and that Ambrosius Morales wrote about the condition of the Christians of Córdoba in his notes to the Life and Works of Saint Eulogius of Córdoba.

Morales seems, however, to have taken the word *bibliotheca*, which writers from Córdoba in that period used for the sacred Scriptures, to mean a book-chest or library.

One may add the controversy that I recently recounted between Samson and Hostegesis concerning the antiphon for the feast of the Annunciation of Saint Mary the Virgin, as well as the Council of Córdoba held in the year 839. Florez first published it at the beginning of volume XV of *Hispania sacra* and reprinted it in the second edition of volume X. It proceeds against the Acephali and asserts in explicit terms that it was instituted by the Holy Fathers that no cleric should be ordained without a fixed title. No one should be considered a bishop whom neither the clergy nor the people of his own city had sought.

Certain people are rebuked who claimed that they had been sent from Rome but nevertheless taught many errors.

### 53.

At the beginning of the ninth century the Mass read in the old Missal of Barcelona on 6 November, the feast of Saint Severus, bishop and martyr, is believed to have been composed by Bishop John, as the title states. On this matter see Florez, *Hispania sacra*, volume XXIX, p. 76. On p. 54 he also presents, from a parchment ritual book of the tenth or eleventh century, a prayer for the feast of Saint Severus:

> “Be favorable, we ask,” etc.

He also presents a hymn from the old Breviary of Barcelona, published in 1540. But the office of this Breviary already belongs to the Roman rite. The Mass of the ninth century, however, belongs to the Mozarabic office, although it does not appear to have been received by the Mozarabs of Toledo, since it is not found in their ancient manuscripts.

### 54.

In the same century there lived a learned man named Vincent, whose authority, while he was still alive, Alvarus of Córdoba invoked in Letter 1, apparently from an ecclesiastical office composed by Vincent for some feast of Our Lord Jesus Christ. Alvarus’s words are:

> “Therefore our teacher Vincent now says, while making such an appeal: ‘May the very Word of the Father, through whom the Father founded the ages, who afterward was silent before the judge for our sake, raise you up to be crowned for eternal reward among the company of the saints’”—perhaps *coronandos*, “those to be crowned.”
>
> “May that right hand which made heaven and earth, and which afterward, unjustly judged by Pilate, was bound in chains, command that you be joined to the saints by its own embrace at the time of judgment.
>
> “May that face which, unable to bear the sight of the gardener of paradise after midday, fled”—perhaps *fugit*, “flees”—“and which, after the transgression of him and his offspring, was stained by the spittle of unbelievers, command that it display itself to you in the appearance of tranquility and peace when it comes to judge the world in fire.”

Florez observes in volume XI of *Hispania sacra*, p. 6, that these words bear the appearance of the prayer called the blessing in the Mozarabic Breviary and Missal, which consists of three similar parts.

### 55.

The following also belongs to the history of the Mozarabic office in the ninth century. Saint Eulogius of Córdoba, in book I of the *Memorial of the Saints*, no. 21, quotes these words from Tobit, which are absent from the Vulgate but occur in the Mozarabic Breviary:

> “Cursed are all who despise you, Jerusalem, and all who blaspheme you; cursed are all who hate you and all who have spoken a harsh word against you,” etc.

No one doubts that this was said of the Church.

The eminent editor Lorenzana observes in the notes to volume II of the *Toletan Fathers*, pp. 442 and 561, that these words from Tobit 13:16 are read in the Mozarabic Breviary at the vigil of Epiphany, among the Canticles at Lauds, and on p. 82 of the latest edition, Canticle 52.

He adds that Alvarus cites these same curses in the *Indiculus luminosus*, no. 7, where he continues:

> “Is there still anyone who does not declare worthy of a curse those whom he has sung as accursed for so long with the Church as his teacher? For every year the Church cries out this curse openly and luminously, not secretly, against those who hate her.”

From this the learned Cardinal believes that the usage of the Roman Church in the annual publication of the bull *In Coena Domini* against heretics and other enemies of the Church may be traced—a usage that ceased after the year 1770. Zaccaria left a manuscript history of that bull, perhaps never to be published.

### 56.

The integrity of the Mozarabic office in the tenth century is confirmed by an ancient document, first published by Aguirre and later more correctly by Florez in volume III of *Hispania sacra*. By comparing the manuscripts with one another, Florez determines that the era in which the office of the Hispanic Church was praised and approved at Rome was 962, that is, the year of Christ 924.

[Col. 0680B]

> “At this time Zanellus the priest, a papal legate, visiting Spain, diligently examined and investigated the entire order of the ecclesiastical office and the rule for consecrating the body and blood of Our Lord Jesus Christ. He read through the canons and sacramentary books. Finding all these things fortified by the Catholic faith, he rejoiced and reported to the lord Pope John and to the entire assembly of the Roman Church what he had found. When the lord Pope and the whole Roman Church heard this, they gave thanks to God, and it pleased them only to add this: that they should celebrate the SECRETS OF THE MASS according to the custom of the Apostolic Church.””

### 57.

Baronius, Pinius, Florez, and others explain this “secret of the Mass” as referring to the words of consecration, following, as I suppose, Ambrosius Morales as their sole guide.

The basis of this interpretation seems to be that the following form of consecration is presented in Ximénez’s Mozarabic Missal:

> “This is my body, which will be given for you. This is the cup of the New Testament in my blood, which will be poured out for you and for many for the remission of sins.”

In the margin, however, it is noted:

> “This form of consecration is included so that antiquity may not be unknown; but today the tradition of the Church is to be observed. See below.”

That is, below it is placed the form of consecration in the same words now used by the Roman Church.

But can we assert with certainty that this change had already taken place by the year 924? Is there any ancient testimony establishing that the words of consecration were called “the secret of the Mass” among the Spaniards or others?

The term is ordinarily used either for everything said in a low voice during the Mass, or for the entire canon of the Mass, or, according to more recent usage, for the prayers that precede the preface, which are commonly called *secretae* and formerly *secretellae*. But, as I believe, no one designated the form of consecration by the expression “secrets of the Mass.”

This would have happened even less readily at the beginning of the tenth century. For, as Cardinal Bona proves in book II, chapter 13 of *Liturgical Matters*, in ancient times the words of consecration were pronounced aloud even in the Western Church; Florus the Master mentions this custom as still prevailing at the end of the ninth century.

We therefore cannot easily understand what “secret of the Mass” signifies in the document mentioned unless we compare the manuscript copies that preceded that period with more recent ones.

### 58.

In his copy of the *Missal of the Offerers*, which contains the canon of the Mozarabic Mass, Pinius found only the words used by the Roman Church. Roblesius observed the following:

> “Although it is true that the Mozarabic priests could have attached themselves to the words found among the Evangelists and consecrated with them, because they are proper words of the Gothic office, even though they differ in part from those used by the Roman Church, nevertheless they amount to the same thing and have the same meaning. But today a sheet of paper is attached to the margin of the missal, containing the words of the Roman office, which the Mozarabs now always use. These indicate a very recent practice, not a law established by apostolic authority in the tenth century.”

### 59.

In this tenth century, around the year 930, the Mass of Saint Pelagius was composed. He suffered martyrdom at Córdoba while the Saracens ruled. The Mass was published by Sandoval, bishop of Tuy, in his book *On the Antiquities of the City and Church of Tuy*, from an ancient manuscript of his church, and was annotated by Lesleus in the appendix to the *Mozarabic Missal*.

### 60.

Salvo, abbot of Albelda, who died in the year 962, is said by many to have enlarged the Mozarabic offices. Florez, in volume III of *Hispania sacra*, argues against Cennius, who assigned to this Salvo the greater part of the Mozarabic liturgy.

Indeed, since so many distinguished men had previously been engaged in this same work, why should we attribute what now survives to Salvo rather than to those ancient Fathers?

An ancient author of his Life praises Salvo in these words:

> “His prayer—that is, in the hymns, prayers, verses, and Masses that he composed in distinguished language—bestows abundant compunction of heart and great sweetness of speech upon those who read and hear them.”

These words clearly imply that Salvo’s offices were not only composed by him but also brought into ecclesiastical use. For this is what the compunction of those who read and hear them concerns.

Nor is it clear that they were numerous, and perhaps they were admitted only in certain churches, through the efforts of some bishop who was his friend or disciple. For the final words of the Life are:

> “At whose feet the disciple, Bishop Velasco, rests in peace.”

The example of Salvo and of Vincent of Córdoba, whom I mentioned shortly before, sufficiently proves that Spaniards living under Arab rule nevertheless considered it permissible to add new offices or new parts of an office while preserving the ancient rite.

### 61.

Pinius follows at length the various changes of the Mozarabic office in the eleventh century. A certain privilege in liturgical matters was granted to the monastery of Ripoll. The Council of Coyanza, held in the diocese of Oviedo in the year 1050, established several regulations intended to preserve the order of the liturgical apparatus. The Council of Compostela in 1056 issued several decrees very well suited to the dignity and order of the sacred liturgy.

It is known that the ecclesiastical order was restored at the Council of Jaca. Pinius, however, doubts whether this proves that the Mozarabic liturgy was abolished.

Zurita thinks that Ramiro I, then king of Aragon, admitted the Roman rite and abandoned the Gothic office. Pinius translates Zurita’s Spanish words and renders *dejar* as “to leave,” “dismiss,” or “abandon.” Because the word has an ambiguous meaning and can sometimes mean “not to remove,” Pinius, misled by Zurita’s opinion, judged that the Roman custom had indeed been admitted for the celebration of Masses but that the use of the Gothic Breviary had merely been left—that is, not removed. Yet, says Pinius, Zurita elsewhere indicates that it too was abolished.

But, as I have said, Zurita does not assert that the use of the Gothic Breviary continued; he asserts that it was removed.

### 62.

Florez, for his part, entirely rejects Zurita’s opinion and maintains that nothing was decreed against the Mozarabic rites at the Council of Jaca held in 1063.

Regarding the abolition of the Mozarabic office, which took place during that century, he arranges the chronology as follows.

Cardinal Hugo Candidus, a papal legate, came to Spain in 1064. Finding that the Mozarabic office had been confirmed by the Roman pontiffs, he judged that nothing should be changed.

In 1066 or the following year, certain Spanish bishops attended the Council of Mantua. After the books of the Spanish Gothic rite had been presented, they again obtained approval from the Roman pontiff.

Florez produces the document already cited by the Bollandists, which proves that the Gothic office had been approved by Alexander II. He observes that it appears to have been written before the year 1078, when the same office was abolished, because it makes no mention of the abolition.

In 1067 Cardinal Hugo returned to Spain but stopped in Aragon. In 1068 an assembly of the kingdom was held at Barcelona, where the abolition of the Gothic laws was discussed. But this was neither a council of bishops nor was the abolition of the Gothic office attempted at that time.

Some assert that a council concerning the same matter was held at Lérida in that year, but they do not demonstrate it.

### 63.

Finally, in the year 1071 the Roman office was introduced into Aragon; the same occurred at Barcelona in that year. In 1072 the papal legates Gerald and Rembald attempted to change the Mozarabic rite but achieved nothing.

In 1074 certain Spanish bishops attended a Roman council and promised their assistance so that the Gothic liturgy would be abandoned in Spain.

In the same year Saint Gregory VII wrote to the kings of Castile and Navarre concerning the abolition of the Toletan office. In 1076 he also wrote to Simon, bishop of Auch—that is, Burgos, not Huesca, as is incorrectly printed in the editions—so that he might arrange for the Roman office to be introduced into Spain.

In 1077 the controversy was submitted to a duel but not settled. In 1078, through the efforts of the papal legate Richard, the Roman office was introduced into the kingdom of Alfonso VI, king of Castile and León.

In 1085 the abolition of the Gothic office was confirmed at the Council of Burgos. At that time the Roman office was also admitted at Toledo, while the ancient Gothic office was retained simultaneously in certain churches of the city of Toledo, after the ordeal by fire had taken place, of which Pinius gives a fuller account.

Mabillon reports another similar ordeal concerning the Ambrosian office in volume I, part II of *The Italian Museum*. It is also reported by Landulf the Elder in book II, chapters 4 and 10 of his *History*, in Muratori, volume IV, *Writers on Italian Affairs*.

In 1090, at the Council of León, the Gothic characters with which ecclesiastical offices had customarily been written according to the ancient usage were abolished.

Florez, volume III, p. 188, observes that the Roman office was also called Gallican in Spain because it had first been received in Gaul. The queens and wives of the kings of Spain who had come from Gaul—Almodis, Ermessenda, Agnes, and Constance—had insisted that it be received in Spain.

### 64.

As I have said, the Mozarabic office was retained in certain churches of the city of Toledo. The Mozarabs who lived according to their ancient rite received numerous privileges and concessions in the twelfth, thirteenth, fourteenth, and fifteenth centuries, which Pinius reviews at length, although in the twelfth century Pope Eugenius III unsuccessfully attempted to draw the Mozarabs over to the Roman office.

As time passed, however, the ecclesiastical rite of the Mozarabs began to decline even in those churches where it had been preserved. It was used only on a few appointed feast days, while the Roman rite, which had gradually crept in, was practiced on the remaining days.

The first to attempt to stabilize the Gothic office was John of Tordesillas, bishop of Segovia, in 1436, as Florez reports. He established a college in the church of Saint Mary of Aniago where the sacred rites of the Mozarabic tradition could be restored and celebrated. But this plan did not last long, since the college was transferred to the Carthusians in 1441.

The entire glory for restoring the Mozarabic liturgy, which had already almost collapsed, belongs, as is well known, to Cardinal Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros. Some later imitated his example at Salamanca and Valladolid, with the strong support of the supreme pontiffs and the kings of Spain.

Pinius lists the distinguished persons who honored the Mozarabic Mass at Toledo by their presence up to the year 1723, as well as the men distinguished for virtue and learning who belonged to the Toletan congregation of Mozarabic pastors and beneficiaries up to the year 1706.

### 65.

Pinius then presents information about the Mozarabic office and its individual parts from Eugenio Roblesius in Cardinal Aguirre.

I have Roblesius’s Spanish book at hand. Its title is:

> *Compendio de la Vida, y hazañas del cardenal Don Fray Francisco Ximenez de Cisneros; y del oficio y misa muzarabe.*

That is:

> *Compendium of the Life and Deeds of Cardinal Don Fray Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros, and of the Mozarabic Office and Mass.*

It was written by Master Eugenio de Robles, parish priest of Saint Mark and chaplain in the chapel of the Mozarabs in the holy Church of Toledo. 1604.

At the end it reads:

> *En Toledo por Pedro Rodriguez, impressor del rey.*

“That is, printed at Toledo by Pedro Rodriguez, printer to the king.”

It is a quarto volume dedicated to Don Bernardo de Sandoval y Rojas, cardinal and archbishop of Toledo.

It is preceded by an elegy by Father Jerome Roman Higuera, sufficiently elegant, in which a man certainly not unlearned, but greatly devoted to fabrications destined for eternal disgrace, expressed his opinion of the Mozarabic office in these words:

> “Through you, the book of the Mozarabs, like another phoenix,  
> lays aside the losses of old age in the world.  
> This work, Isidore, is yours; only your golden hand  
> accomplished this work, destined to live through the ages.”

What Roblesius discussed concerning the Mozarabic office appears excerpted and translated into Latin in the supplement to Bigne’s *Library of the Fathers*, and was reprinted from there by Blanchini after Pinius’s historical and chronological treatise on liturgical matters.

### 66.

Pinius reexamines the fragment of an ancient calendar that Francisco de Pisa printed at Toledo in 1593. He concludes that, except for the so-called Bucherian calendar, it is the oldest of all the others that survive—or at least yields to none of them in antiquity.

He conjectures that it was written at the end of the fifth century or the beginning of the sixth.

I must nevertheless point out that learned men now doubt whether the fragment of such a calendar published by Pisa is a genuine monument. I am certain that such a calendar could not have been written before the seventh century, since the feast of the Circumcision is not listed in the books of the Offices of Saint Isidore, who died in 636. Nor did it begin to be celebrated in Spain until after Isidore’s death, or only shortly before his death, as I observe in chapter 71.

On Pisa’s calendar, compare the preface of the eminent Lord Cardinal Lorenzana to the Mozarabic Breviary.

### 67.

Pinius adds much other material concerning the calendar used by the modern Mozarabs, the immediate preparation of the priest before Mass, the structure of the Mass, and a description of its ceremonies. He also discusses the *Missal of the Offerers*, which is in a manner the Ordinary of this sacred liturgy.

Finally, after comparing an example of the hours and the Mozarabic Mass from the feast of Saint James, taken from the Mozarabic Missal published by order of Cardinal Ximénez, with the Gallican rite, he explains the agreements and disagreements between the Mozarabic liturgy and the ancient Gallican liturgy. He rejects Bruni’s opinion that the Mozarabic liturgy received its model or form from the Gallican liturgy.

He also provides information about and descriptions of the manuscript volumes of Mozarabic books preserved at Toledo, drawn from Pedro Camino Velasco, rector of the parish church of Saint Sebastian of the Mozarabs in that city, together with various observations.

### 68.

Camino lists eight Mozarabic volumes:

1. **Mozarabic Missal, part 1, Gothic**—perhaps “in Gothic characters”—containing Masses from Easter to Pentecost.

2. **Mozarabic Missal, second Gothic part**, containing Masses for the temporal cycle and for the saints.

3. **Mozarabic Missal, second Gothic part**, containing various Masses of the saints and daily Masses.

4. **Mozarabic Missal, second Gothic part**, containing Masses of the saints and offices.

5. **Mozarabic Missal, second Gothic part**, containing Masses of the Blessed Virgin Mary composed by Saint Ildefonsus.

6. **Mozarabic Breviary, first Gothic part**, containing portions of the Psalter, Canticles, and Hymns.

7. **Mozarabic Breviary, second Gothic part**, containing portions of the Psalter, proper offices of the saints, and hymns.

8. **Mozarabic Breviary, second Gothic part: Lent.**
### 69

In the second Codex there is a Mass of the Chair of Saint Peter at Antioch. In the first prayer of that same Mass, which is called the *Missa* and begins, “The day on which, to the most blessed Peter, etc.”, the initial letter *D* is written in an unusual form. In its upper circle this inscription appears in Gothic characters: “Elenus, abbot, though unworthy, wrote.” Nothing certain is known about this abbot Elenus. I myself wondered whether it ought instead to be read, “Telenus, abbot, though unworthy, wrote,” since, as all the letters are enclosed within the circle, the beginning may be taken either from a *T* or from an *E*. The name Telenus is no less obscure than Elenus.

A specimen of the characters is taken from this same Codex and from the celebrated Mass of Saint Martin, which Benedict XIV also discusses, book I, *On Beatification*, chapter 5, no. 5:

> In the Mozarabic Missal, he says, published by Cardinal Ximenes, whose use—if the later additions are removed—flourished not only in Spain but also in other kingdoms even before the age of Saint Isidore of Seville, there is an extremely ancient Mass of Saint Martin of Tours, from which Cardinal Bona copied a large part, etc.

Codex 5 contains Masses of the Blessed Virgin, composed by Saint Ildefonsus; Nicholas Antonius and others discuss them. Caminus observes that the Masses of the Annunciation, Nativity, and Assumption of the Mother of God found in this Codex have been inserted into the Mozarabic Missal of Ximenes, but not in the order or form in which they appear in the Gothic Codex, nor with equal fullness.

The characters of the Codex are large and formed in a rather rough manner, so that they cannot be read without considerable effort. The writing is continuous in its ductus, and certain pen-flourishes observed in other copied Gothic Codices do not occur here. Caminus considers this exemplar to have been copied very shortly after the time of Saint Ildefonsus himself.

Codex 8 belongs to a later period. It is written in black and red ink, in a more finished script, on polished parchment. The following rubric is added without a date:

> Here ends this book. Thanks be to God. In the reign of Lord Alfonso, by the hand of Ferrand Joanniz, priest of the church of Saints Justa and Rufina in the city of Toledo, in the month of April.

I suspect that the Codex was written during the reign of Alfonso VI, after he recovered Toledo from the Moors—that is, toward the end of the eleventh century, certainly not before the conquest of Toledo.

### 70

How desirable it would be for all Codices of this kind to be printed in the order in which they were written, with nothing, however small, omitted! In *Prudentiana*, no. 104, I noted that the prefect of the library of Saint Geneviève in Paris, the abbot of Saint-Léger, relying on Burriel’s insufficiently understood letters, asserted that the Gothic Office published by Cardinal Ximenes differed in reality and substance from the Gothic manuscript Codices at Toledo.

This seems to imply that Cardinal Ximenes had compiled some new office and passed it off as the Gothic one. Yet it is certain that the form and substance of the most ancient Gothic Office have been preserved in the Ximenian Breviary, and that the Ximenian Breviary differs no more from the ancient Gothic one than the present Roman Breviary differs from the old one.

Nevertheless, since in offices of this kind certain new elements were introduced from time to time, others omitted, and some recast into a better form, and since Cardinal Ximenes did not intend to represent the whole antiquity of the Gothic Office as though in chronological order, but selected from the various volumes available—some extremely ancient, others more recent—those portions that seemed best suited to arranging the Mozarabic Office and joining it into a single body, he achieved what he had attempted: Mozarabic priests could perform their rite with less labor than before.

But for critical scholars, who like not only to distinguish ancient material from recent but also to compare the more ancient with the less ancient, and to leave no part of ecclesiastical antiquity entirely unknown, it remains desirable that all such Codices should be brought into public view, just as the Gothic Orationale was published by Blanchini and several other missals, antiphonaries, and hymnaries by Mabillon, Cardinal Thomasius, Muratori, and others.

### 71

Why, then, have the Masses of the Blessed Virgin, composed by Saint Ildefonsus, remained hidden for so long? Although a large part of them appears in the Ximenian Breviary, they occur there, as we learn from Caminus, in a different order and form, and are shorter than in the most ancient Codex of the eighth or ninth century.

It would also be useful to know with certainty which words are actually Saint Ildefonsus’s among those inserted into the Missal. Gothic Codex 2 contains, as Caminus stated, various Masses of saints and daily Masses. There is no daily Mass in the Ximenian Missal, at least not one expressed under that name. From this arose the difficulty mentioned above: what did Samson, abbot of Córdoba, understand by the name “daily Mass”?

The Most Eminent Cardinal Lorenzana, in the new edition of the Mozarabic Breviary, insofar as the purpose of his undertaking permitted—and since he was chiefly concerned with the convenience of the Mozarabic priests who recite the divine praises—shed greater light upon antiquity. For he published the Gothic Psalter with its canticles and hymns as it is found in the ancient parchments, from the Codex which Caminus identified by the number 6, and perhaps also from the following Codex, number 7.

### 72

The inscription of the Psalter is as follows:

> In the name of the Lord begins the Book of Psalms according to the prophet David: prophecy concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, or concerning the fruit of the righteous and the destruction of the wicked. The first Psalm begins. Antiphon: “His will was in the law of the Lord day and night; he will meditate upon his law.” “Blessed is the man who has not walked in the counsel of the ungodly,” etc.

When Psalm 40 is finished:

> The first book ends. The second book begins.

Likewise, the third book follows Psalm 71; the fourth book follows Psalm 88; and the fifth book follows Psalm 105. After Psalm 151:

> The Book of Psalms ends. The canticles begin.

Canticle 51, Solomon’s, is “At the Consecration of a Basilica.” The Canticle of Tobit is “On the Restoration of a Basilica.” At number 55:

> The canticles for the Daily Office begin.

The Canticle of Moses, etc. The final canticle is number 77: the angels’ canticle on the birth of Christ:

> Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace to people of good will, etc.

The canticles end. The prologue of the hymns begins. There are thirty verses, poorly Latin, incorrectly written, unmetrical like hexameters and acrostic in form. From their first syllables one obtains: “Mauricus, at the request of Veranianus, published [this]” (*Mauricus obtante Veraniano edidyt*). Their substance is drawn from canon 13 of the Fourth Council of Toledo and from Saint Isidore. It runs as follows:

> The first miracles of hymns, with clear melody,  
> The angels proclaimed when the Lord was born—now,  
> Namely, gifts poured down from heaven in small number,  
> Which the earthly ranks of shepherds, having seen, would take up again.  
>
> Already in the old time the order of hymns had shone forth  
> When the three mouths of the young men, having overcome the furnace-fire,  
> Together with the ancient Father, the Son, then already joined to them,  
> Took up a hymn of praise for the life of all, which in the lofty  
> Circuit of the Olympiad and in the circle of the earthly course  
> Was offered to the blessed company and to every created element.  
>
> So many sacred places, so many country places [*Toth sacra toth rura*],  
> Had hymns through the art of the singing Muse.  
> Now the Church, spread throughout the whole world,  
> Celebrates this, established in the divine sacrament;  
> And when the Redeemer, fulfilling the sacred time of the supper,  
> Pays to the eternal Father a hymn in apostolic concord,  
> Turning his blessed footsteps for the sake of prayer,  
> He went out upon the neighboring mountain to entreat the Father.  
>
> The Ruler of faith and Master of all throughout the ages,  
> Paul also admonishes us to speak in psalms and hymns.  
> From this the sacred doctrine of hymns arose,  
> Through Hilary, [a] pope, Ambrose, and the others, after their manner:  
> To compose such melodies of hymns for divine praise,  
> Now to recount the praises of the Lord, now the triumphs of the martyrs,  
> And to pour forth every celibate [or “heavenly”?] sound in voices,  
> Making sweet melody for the Maker of all.  
>
> The supreme glory of God consists in praise and joy;  
> In these both the Trinity is praised and the Church burns brightly.  
> When we speak a hymn, we give honor and glory;  
> When we sing a hymn, we display the Church’s vows.  
> At last we also seek the end of all wrongdoing.

### 73

The title of the Hymnary is:

> The hymns for the whole circle of the year begin. A hymn for the Advent of the Lord and for the feast of the saints, thrice mixed, to be sung at Matins when the Advent of the Lord begins: “Rejoice, flowers of the martyrs”—“Hail, peoples of the nations,” etc.

Perhaps *Adventus* should be read instead of *Adventu*. *Ter mistus* also appears to be an error.

After the hymns come the hours. “Aurora” begins; it is recited before Prime on weekdays throughout the year. Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline follow. After Compline there are certain prayers, acts of mercy, blessings, the sprinkling of holy water, and so forth.

That all these items, together with the hymns, are contained in the same Codex may be gathered clearly enough from the preface of the Most Eminent Cardinal Lorenzana to the Isidorian Breviary, p. 18.

### 74

It is not known at what time this Codex was written. The names of Mauricus, who wrote it, and Veranianus, who ordered it to be written, are otherwise unknown. The script suggests approximately the eleventh century, and the verses placed before the hymnary are not inconsistent with that period.

It may still be questioned, however, whether the Codex was copied from another, more ancient Codex of the Gothic kingdom. As regards the Psalter, there is no definite reason for denying this. But the hymnary and the other material appended to it belong to a later period.

The learned editor observes that in the hymn of Saint Thyrsus four verses are missing which were admitted into the Ximenian Breviary, namely:

> This temple, Lord, Cixila founded;  
> May he have a worthy lot here in heaven;  
> With the highest citizens may he sing songs,  
> Rejoicing throughout all perpetual ages.

Florez, who believed that these verses were found in the most ancient manuscripts at Toledo, and who maintained that no other proper offices had been admitted into the Gothic Breviary after the arrival of the Arabs in Spain, devotes considerable attention in volume V, p. 345, to explaining these verses, lest the Cixila mentioned here be understood as the bishop of Toledo who wrote the Life of Saint Ildefonsus in the eighth century.

### 75

Perhaps these verses were received into the Ximenian Breviary from Gothic Codex 7, in which, as we learn from Caminus, hymns are also found. Yet even if we suppose that in other Codices these verses were written by the hand of some interpolator, there are nevertheless many things in the hymnary copied by Mauricus that seem more recent than the Gothic period.

For, to omit those hymns in which the Saracen yoke is mentioned quite clearly—a point which Florez struggles to deny—it is worth observing that on page 105 the first hymn concerning the saints is “*Sanctorum meritis inclyte gaudia*,” where one should read *inclyta gaudia*, “illustrious joys.” This is the hymn which Hincmar, in his book *On the Non-Trine Deity*, calls recent, and whose conclusion, “*Te trina deitas, unaque poscimus*”—“You, triune Godhead, we ask as one”—also found in the Mozarabic Breviary, he made the subject of his dispute with Gottschalk.

Hincmar was writing in the advancing ninth century. I have discussed more of this entire controversy in *Hymnodia Hispanica*, no. 234, dissertation, p. 205. It should now be added that Hincmar was deceived in believing the hymn “*Sanctorum meritis*” to be recent—not because it is found in the Mozarabic hymnary, but because its first verse is quoted by Julian of Toledo in a work *On the Art of Grammar* that has not yet been published. I shall discuss this when I describe Codex Palatinus 1746 in chapter 103.

### 76

After Compline the following rubric appears:

> On Saturdays or on the principal feast days, when the psalms of Compline have been completed in order according to the modern usage, as has been said, this responsory and the other things that follow are said.

You see that this Codex already mentions the “usage of the moderns.” But who are these moderns? Perhaps certain Mozarabes were the authors of such a usage. I believe it more likely that the reference is to those who followed the Roman rite.

For, as I conjecture, this Codex was written after the city of Toledo had been recovered by the Christians. To this period belong the hymns for the king’s ordination, for the king’s birthday, and the hymn for the departure of the army, which is to be sung until the army returns, on the days of the litanies. Among its stanzas is this one:

> So that, like calves moving onward, your people,  
> From the flock of faith, with free boldness,  
> May toss the barbarian nations with their horns  
> And trample the wicked beneath their feet.

These verses certainly could not have been sung at Toledo unless Christian kings were already ruling there and were sending weapons and armies against the Moors of other provinces.

### 77

Just as this Codex contains many things which appear not yet to have been introduced into ecclesiastical offices while the Goths ruled Spain, so it contains other things that are absent from the Ximenian Breviary.

There are daily hymns, Sunday hymns, daily evening hymns, “For the Twelfth Hour,” “Before Compline,” “For the First Watch,” “For Rest,” “At Midnight,” “At Nocturns,” “At Cockcrow,” “At the Crowing of the Chicks,” daily Matins hymns, “For the Fourth Hour,” “For the Fifth,” “For the Seventh,” “For the Eighth,” “For the Tenth,” “For the Eleventh,” again “For the Twelfth”; and the final hymn is “For Vespers.”

Most of these hymns are omitted from the Ximenian Breviary.

Florez, volume III of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 247, observes that the sixth prayer in the Mass *Post pridie* presupposes that *Pridie* preceded it. Yet he had found no old copy of the Missal of the Offerers, or ordinary, at Toledo from which he could determine whether *Pridie* had once preceded it. In the title *Post pridie*, however, all the manuscript Codices he had seen agreed.

He asserts that the Ximenian Breviary and Missal abound in errors, partly through the printer’s carelessness and partly through corruption in the Codices. Nevertheless, Ximenes did not intend to deceive anyone by representing the Gothic Office in precisely the order in which it had been observed by the ancients.

### 78

The first rubric of the Breviary is perfectly clear:

> **Rule.** The hours to be sung or recited begin, according to the rule of the greatest doctor of Spain, the most blessed Isidore, and of the distinguished confessor Ildefonsus, prelate and teacher of Toledo—not simply as the ancients formerly enjoyed that rule, but in a qualified manner. For formerly there were twelve customary hours in the day, as is shown in the ancient books, besides certain other things which those ancients used at night: namely, at the beginning of the night and before going to bed, at the equinox, or in the middle of the night and at rising from bed. These things have been discarded and removed by the moderns. But [the hours are observed] in the manner in which the moderns continue and practice them, as will become clear in what follows.
>
> And because there are few who know how to preserve and arrange the order of these hours, through the negligence and carelessness of many, since they care only about receiving the revenues of the Church; and because many fine buildings easily collapse after a long passage of time unless a remedy is applied; therefore a certain unskilled and unworthy cleric, considering this holy and thoroughly devout work, produced by so great a prelate through divine inspiration, lest it perish but return to human memory, moved by an impulse and prompting of piety, for the praise and glory of the Trinity, of Jesus, and of Mary his mother, and for the honor of the aforesaid supreme confessor, and for the enlightenment of the present and future clergy, according to the poverty of his knowledge and the weakness of his understanding, having invoked divine assistance and its shining aid, endeavored to compose this rule as follows, and translated and transferred this Codex from Gothic letters.

### 79

From this we learn that the cleric who wrote the Mozarabic Breviary in Latin characters and prefaced it with the order of recitation presented the Office in the form then used by the Mozarabes, while nevertheless recognizing another, more ancient form preserved in the old books.

We may also conclude that this cleric translated the Breviary from Gothic characters into Latin characters on his own initiative, not at the command of Cardinal Ximenes, in order to serve the convenience of the Mozarabic priests. Perhaps such an exemplar provided Ortizius, who arranged for the Missal and Breviary to be printed, with a kind of model, enabling him to make the work more exact by collating ancient parchments.

### 80

Since it is clear that in the Mozarabic Office as we now possess it the ancient order is not fully preserved, with much omitted from the old manuscripts and other material added, it would be extremely useful to produce, as Burriel desired, a collection of all the existing Codices of the older Gothic liturgy, illustrated with critical notes.

For, as he observes, besides the eight Codices described by Caminus, there are three others in the church at Toledo, together with certain fragments of others. Further Codices exist in the monastery of Caradigna, or Cardeña, from which Berganza selected and excerpted several pieces. Who would doubt that others are preserved in other monasteries?

Burriel also thinks that everything hitherto published under the title of the old Gallican rite belongs here, for the Gothic-Hispanic Orationale published by Blanchini is certainly ours. Montfaucon, in *Bibliotheca Manuscriptorum*, records from the Coislinian-San-German library Codex 1297, “The Breviary of Saint Isidore of Seville, called Mozarabic.”

Florez, in volume X, includes among his appendices a Gothic hymn of Saint Crispin, more accurately corrected than in the Mozarabic Breviary because, as he says on page 85, Father Martín de Roa collated it with manuscript Codices from Córdoba. I am convinced that some further monuments of this Mozarabic Office are still preserved at Córdoba.

Would that the four Codices which were presented and approved at the Council of Mantua could be found somewhere! These books are listed in the *Vetus Instrumentum* as follows:

> One was the book of the offices of the greater monastery of Albaida, containing baptism and burial; another was a book of prayers from the monastery of Iraze; a missal book belonged to Santa Gemma; and an antiphonary book belonged to Iraze.

### 81

Moreover, any other external monuments by which the Mozarabic Office might in some way be illuminated should be compared. I shall present here some items not commonly encountered in authors who discuss the Isidorian liturgy.

The first is drawn from the history of the monastery of Saint John of Réomay, illustrated by Peter Roverius of the Society of Jesus. On page 177 a vision is related from which it may be inferred that by the year 1018 some practice already existed in Spain of celebrating the feast of the Most Holy Trinity on the first Sunday after Pentecost—a practice later approved by the universal Church.

Roverius adds on page 587:

> This circumstance greatly commends the judgment of the holy priests of Spain, who so wonderfully approved it long beforehand.

The vision was as follows:
