> Suddenly the whole enclosure of that same church was filled with men clothed in white garments and distinguished by purple stoles, etc. It was the octave Sunday of Pentecost, etc. Meanwhile the bishop who presided began to celebrate the solemn Masses over the altar of Saint Maurice the martyr, intoning the antiphon of that same Trinity.
>
> In the meantime he asked the aforesaid brother—Wulferius the monk, to whom the vision was being shown—who they were, or where they came from, or for what reason they had arrived there. They gave him this gentle answer:
>
> “We bear the profession of Christianity, but, in defending our homeland and the Catholic people, the sword separated us in the war against the Saracens from the habitation of human bodies,” etc.
>
> Moreover, the one who was performing the office of the Mass, after the Lord’s Prayer had ended and after giving peace to all, sent one who would give the kiss of peace to that brother.

Nevertheless, in the Missal and Breviary of the Mozarabes the Mass of the Most Holy Trinity has no place, as Lesleus notes on page 554. Nor is the rite of giving the kiss of peace after the Lord’s Prayer proper to the Mozarabes, who made peace before the consecration of the gifts, as the same Lesleus teaches on page 540.

### 82

The second item is this: around 1787 the abbot of Saint-Léger published a sheet entitled “Literary Particulars concerning the Mozarabic Liturgy,” etc. It consisted of material taken from Burriel’s already published letters, which he himself did not know: one addressed to Father Francisco Rabago and another to Don Pedro de Castro.

At the end he added some material from a Latin work, *The Ten Divisions of All the Nations of Christendom*, printed at Rome by Johannes Besicken and Sigismund Mayer on 16 June 1494, in octavo. This work had been unknown to Father Audiffredi, author of the *Catalogue of Roman Editions of the Fifteenth Century*. It contains the following about the Mozarabes, who constitute the tenth nation:

> These Mozarabes were formerly numerous in the regions of Africa and Spain, but now they are few. They are called Mozarabes because in many things they retained the ways of the Christians of Arabia. They use the Latin language in divine offices and obey the Roman Church and the Latin prelates. They consecrate in unleavened bread, like the Latins, but differ from the Latins in many respects:
>
> their divine offices contain very long hours; when the natural day is divided into twenty-four hours of day and night, they have that many offices, or hours, and psalms and hymns and certain prayers, excessively long, which they do not recite in the manner of the Latins, for what the Latins say at the beginning they say at the end or in the middle.
>
> Some divide the sacrament of the Eucharist into seven parts, others into ten. They are a very devout nation. In marriage they are joined only to persons of their own people or nation. Among them, when a woman has lost her first husband, she never marries another but remains in perpetual chastity.

### 83

Other authors also speak of the Mozarabes of Africa as though they observed the same rites as the Mozarabes of Spain.

Jacobus de Vitriaco, in *Historia Orientalis*, chapter 81, Douai edition, 1597, writes:

> **Concerning the Mozarabes.** Those Christians who live in Africa and Spain among the western Saracens, called Mozarabes, use the Latin script and the Latin language in their writings, and obey the holy Roman Church, like the other Latins, with complete humility and devotion, deviating in nothing from the articles of faith or the sacraments.
>
> They make the sacrament of the altar from unleavened bread, as do the Latins. Some of them divide the sacred form of the Eucharist into seven parts; others into nine, whereas the Roman Church and others subject to it divide the Eucharist into only three portions. Since this division does not belong to the substance of the sacrament, it neither changes nor impedes the sacrament’s power.

### 84

Sanutus puts the matter more briefly, book III, part VIII, chapter 4:

> There are also other Christians who live in Africa and Spain among the western Saracens, called Mozarabes. They use Latin script and language in the divine writings, and obey the holy Roman Church, like the other Latins, with complete devotion and humility, deviating in no respect from the articles of faith or the sacraments of the Church. Nevertheless, they divide the Eucharist into seven parts, and some into nine. Since this concerns the sacrament accidentally, it does not impede the sacrament’s truth and power.

### 85

The Spaniards themselves, who were free from the yoke of the Saracens, regarded the Mozarabes as a separate nation.

A contemporary author of the *Life of Saint Theotonius*, prior of the monastery of Santa Cruz at Coimbra, writing in the twelfth century and cited by the Bollandists under 18 February, chapter 2, part II, relates:

> When Alfonso, the noble Infante of Portugal, had led an army toward the more distant part of Spain called Seville and had ravaged almost the whole province of the Saracens, his fighting men, among the immeasurable booty, also captured and subjected by the law of war a certain people of Christians whom the common people call Mozarabes. They had been held there under pagan rule, but nevertheless observed, in whatever way they could, the practice of the Christian God.

### 86

Another document concerning the Gothic liturgy is found in the epitome of universal history by John Laziardus Coelestinus, extending to the death of Pius III and published at Paris in folio. Fabricius mentions its author in the *Bibliotheca medica*. Vossius observes on page 666 that a large part of this work was copied word for word from the *Historical Breviary*, which an anonymous Gaul, around the year 1428, professed to have abridged from Landulfus Sagax and others; it was printed at Poitiers in 1479.

Laziardus therefore writes in chapter 53:

> In the time of this pontiff (*Deusdedit*), two doctors of the Church flourished in the province of Spain: one was Braulio of Zaragoza, the other Isidore, bishop of Seville. Concerning him, certain histories relate that he composed the office of the Mass in the said church of Seville, in which the deacons and priests say and read many things; and there are two remarkable features in the office of that Mass.
>
> The first is that when the Eucharist is raised, the deacon sings aloud toward the people, saying: “See in whom you believe.”
>
> The second is that when the Lord’s Prayer is sung at Mass, however many clauses it contains, so many responses are made by the clergy. Thus, when the Lord’s Prayer is sung—“Our Father, who art in heaven, hallowed be thy name”—the entire choir responds, “Amen.”
>
> When “Thy kingdom come, thy will be done, on earth as it is in heaven” is added, the choir likewise responds, “Amen.”
>
> But when “Give us this day our daily bread” follows, the choir responds with a brief chant, “Who is God.”
>
> In all the clauses that follow, the choir responds, “Amen.”
>
> There are many other things in that office unlike our usage.

### 87

Zaccaria, volume I of *Bibliotheca Liturgica*, chapter 2, book I, discusses two collections of liturgical materials. One of them had begun to be published by Joseph Aloysius Assemani but remained interrupted and incomplete; the other was merely announced by Father Emmanuel de Azevedo.

In his prefatory letter to Clement Argenvilliers, later a cardinal, Assemani says:

> The Western Churches whose liturgies we present are the Roman Church, mother, head, and teacher of them all; the old Gallican Church; the Hispanic or Mozarabic Church; the Milanese or Ambrosian Church; and certain others.

Azevedo published an outline of his collection under the title:

> *Synopsis of a Liturgical Treasury Containing the More Ancient Monuments Pertaining to the Sacred Rites.*

He intended to insert in the third volume the principal liturgies distinct from the Roman, including:

> “The Hispanic, Gothic, Isidorian, and Mozarabic.”

He adds:

> The Mozarabic Missal itself, in order to satisfy the wishes of many, is extremely rare and contains a most ancient liturgy; we shall publish it complete. Taking this opportunity, we shall display the piety, learning, and devotion to divine worship of the Spanish people.
>
> We shall append the psalmody and Breviary of the Mozarabic Liturgy as it was formerly published by Cardinal Ximenes. We shall nevertheless indicate in the margin of the book those prayers which approach the age of Saint Isidore or are perhaps even older.
>
> We also profess our care and diligence in correcting errors—not those caused by the printer, but those found in the exemplars of the Ximenian edition. For this task we have the greatest assistance from the Veronese Gothic-Hispanic Orationale, published by the learned Blanchini in volume I, at the end of part I, in the commentary on the works of the Venerable Cardinal Thomasius.
>
> There will also be added whatever we hope the most learned men will bring to us from Spain.

Azevedo signed this from the Roman College, on the Kalends of January 1748. What Azevedo had planned concerning the publication of the Mozarabic Missal was completed by Lesleus at Rome in 1755.

### 88

Blanchini illustrated with his notes the Orationale of the Hispanic Gothic rite, which Azevedo likewise mentions. Hernandez, in his observations on the prospectus of the Isidorian manuscript edition promised by Zaccaria, warned that Blanchini’s notes needed correction in certain places.

Blanchini prefixed not only Pinius’s treatise on the ancient Hispanic liturgy, but also the order of the divine Gothic-Mozarabic Office from Robles’s book on the life of Cardinal Ximenes, a specimen of the characters of the most ancient Veronese Codex containing the Gothic prayers, and the judgment of Cajetan Cennius concerning this book of prayers, taken from volume I of *Hispania Ecclesiastica Antiqua*, pages 28 and following.

Florez rightly criticized and corrected that judgment in volume III of *Hispania Sacra*, where he states that the hymn of the Mozarabic Office in praise of Saint James is older than the invasion of the Moors.

### 89

Among Zaccaria’s papers I have found the manuscript judgment of the Marquis Maffei concerning this same Veronese Codex of the prayers of the Gothic Office, which I am pleased to share with others. When Maffei was about to describe Codex 184 of the Chapter Library at Verona, he made the following notes.

### 90

The religious testimony and worship of Christian priests toward almighty God consist chiefly of two things: the liturgy and the Office. From the most ancient times these have been administered by means of two principal books, which we now call the Missal and the Breviary.

We have seen how remote in age the book of the Missal preserved in this library is. Let us now see whether a Breviary of equal or greater antiquity survives there as well.

The former is conspicuous for its uncial letters; the latter, except for its headings, consists of almost square writing in cursive characters, with a few minuscule forms mixed in. Nevertheless, all the evidence proves that it was produced in the sixth or seventh century.

I remember that when I once went through this Codex and copied out a large part of it, I was training myself to understand rapid writing. It presents the ecclesiastical Office, not one composed for the use of Verona or Italy, but a Hispanic one. It is precisely the Office to which the name Mozarabic became attached.

In 1732 I communicated an account of this previously unknown Codex in part III of *Verona Illustrata*, p. 250, where, among other things, I wrote:

> It contains the Mozarabic Breviary, which, according to the information available, is not seen elsewhere in its ancient purity, although learned men have repeatedly sought exemplars of it in vain in every region. The one printed by order of Cardinal Ximenes is full of additions and adapted to later divine offices.

I subsequently published what follows among the short ecclesiastical pieces appended to the *Theological History*. I do not hesitate to reproduce it here. In this book, etc.

### 91

In the same volume I reproduced a specimen of the script in plate 4, no. 18. In this manuscript *B* is used for consonantal *V* almost everywhere, as in other manuscripts originating in Spain.

Several years after I had published the account of the Codex, a copy of it was sent to the learned Father Blanchini at Rome. He carefully published the whole Codex, attaching it to the works of Cardinal Thomasius, and reprinting there Pinius’s extensive treatise on the Hispanic Liturgy. In that treatise, however, he discusses the Mass, not the Breviary.

The publisher calls this collection a small book, although it contains more than a thousand prayers, approximately three hundred of which are absent from the published Mozarabic Breviary. I had decided to publish only these, but I approve still more of Father Blanchini’s having published them all, especially because books printed at the command of Cardinal Ximenes are so few and so rarely encountered.

In the printed edition the diphthong *ae* is consistently represented, but it is absent from the Codex, where *e* is always written.

Who can guess how these parchments came from Spain to Verona so many centuries ago? The reference to the church of Saint Fructuosus seems to suggest that they belonged to the people of Tarragona; but a prayer to Saint Leocadia, which is transmitted along with thirty others, points to Toledo. It says, although incorrectly:

> The honor of her tomb is presented to human eyes; the honor that ought to be rendered is opened honorably.

The whole Office was performed more briefly. The conclusion of prayers, *through our Lord*, never occurs. Rogations are not mentioned, nor are the fasts of the four seasons. The Sunday before Lent is called *In carnes tollendas*, “for taking away meat.”

At the end of each Matins there is a prayer called Compline, together with a blessing over the people. The rubric is:

> Likewise Compline, after the praises have been completed, which they continue by singing as far as the holy Jerusalem; it is to be said at Saint Fructuosus.

Singing is mentioned several times.

### 92

Moreover, as has happened in other regions and with respect to other matters, so too in Spain the liturgy and ecclesiastical offices acquired their name from the peoples who invaded and ruled the country. They were therefore called Gothic, and later Arabic, although neither the Goths nor the Saracens composed them; they were the product of the piety and learning of the ancient Spaniards.

The Goths and Arabs agreed in this same sense only when, softened by the blending of religion, customs, and blood, they had become Spaniards and already excelled in holiness.

In the year 561 the Synod of Braga decreed:

> It has pleased all by common consent that one and the same order of psalmody be observed at the morning and evening offices.

In the year 633 the famous Fourth Council of Toledo decreed:

> Therefore let one order of praying and psalmody be preserved by us throughout all Spain and Gaul; one manner in the solemnities of the Mass; one in the morning and evening offices.

The Missal and Breviary used by the Churches of Spain are consequently attributed to Saint Isidore, who presided over this council, as Nicholas Antonius notes (*Bibliotheca Hispana*, book V, chapter 4).

Much shows that, before that council was convened in 633, these prayers—containing the morning and evening Office—had already been collected and prescribed. I noted this both long ago and recently.

Add also that no Office for Good Friday is listed here, although that custom was in use in certain Spanish Churches before that celebrated council; it was rejected and abolished by the council in its sixth canon.

### 93

But in order that complete information about so ancient and distinguished a codex may finally be brought forth, it is fitting to add certain details. Before the Breviary begins, there are three leaves covered in the same kind of script, and likewise a seventh page that follows. Although the type of lettering is the same in these portions, the writing is nevertheless darker and more difficult. You have a specimen of it in plate 4, no. 18. These leaves appear to have been placed at the beginning; and, since they were blank, they were subsequently filled by another hand, disorderly and without any formal dignity of headings. There are many prayers here also, but they pertain to the liturgy, not to the Office. Among them are twelve prayers arranged around the names of the winds of the compass, in Latin and Greek. [Col. 0695C] The Greek, however, is written in Latin letters. There are also poems beginning in this way for each of the winds:

> The four winds rise from the four-sided boundary.

### 94

I formerly transcribed the rest, but since I have lost my copy, I now spare my failing eyes. On the lower part of the preceding page, in another though still ancient hand, is written: “Sergius, the vicedominus, sanctcel . . .” [The reading is uncertain.] Other letters are visible before and after “141,” whose exact meaning cannot be determined. On the sixth page is found the hymn *Pange lingua gloriosi praelium certaminis* [“Sing, tongue, the battle of the glorious struggle”]. Beneath it, in a different and later hand, are the words:

> Maurizio Canevarius, and fidilocor de amphoravino.  
> De bonello in XX anno Liuprandi regis.

I think it should be read:

> De anfor Avino de Bonello.

The twentieth year of King Liutprand falls in 732. These additions were made to the book when it was already worn through use, and after it had been transferred from Spain to the Veronese canons; for Liutprand’s year would not have been recorded outside Italy. Of the prayers written on these leaves, I shall not hesitate to present the earlier ones, unchanged by any correction.

[Col. 0695D] **Mass for the Wednesday of Easter. Those who will approach on the morrow.**

### 95

“Most beloved brothers, let us go beforehand to the Lord’s Supper, before the presence of Jesus our Lord and Redeemer, in confession with complete confidence; and let us ask him with tears to make us, purified from all our sins, approach tomorrow the chalice of his most sacred Passion.

“And likewise:

‘Do not cast us away, good Jesus, tomorrow from the banquet of your table [the preceding words are uncertain: *inbeteratae bestis abfectionem*]. Today [Note: [Col. 0695] It is written thus repeatedly. I had taken it to mean *Dominica die* (“on the Lord’s Day”); but it is a scribal error, not found elsewhere, for it must be read *Hodie dona* (“Today grant”).] grant us the vestibule of nuptial dignity, so that tomorrow we may joyfully approach the banquet prepared for your Passion. Today let there be true confession in us, and tomorrow let the swiftest remission of sins follow. Today receive vows; tomorrow grant the rewards of vows. Today offer us a taste of your love; and tomorrow grant us the fullness [Col. 0696A] of charity, Creator and Redeemer of the human race, Christ, Son of God the Father. Grant your servants that today remission of sins may be given both to those who drink and to the departed, so that tomorrow there may be in common the complete fullness of every kind of rejoicing.’

**For Peace.** Prepare us for yourself, Lord; save our heart through the good of peace, a pure offering, so that we who are to receive the Lord’s Supper tomorrow may not be at war with one another through any discord, but, full of the fruit of your love, may tomorrow receive the rivers of charity that flow forth from your entrails.

**Preface.** It is worthy and just that we should always give you thanks, holy Lord, almighty Father, God, through Jesus Christ, your Son, our Lord, who willed to suffer for the ungodly and to be unjustly condemned for the wicked.

“Here is the final prayer of all:

‘Almighty God, who led your martyr, after the blood of his passion had been shed, to the palm of victory, grant us that we may be protected by the shade of his stature, lest we be tormented by the fires of human desire.’”

[Col. 0696B] ### 96

What Maffeius observes in no. 91—that the Gothic prayer-book of the Veronese Codex belonged to the people of Tarragona, because in the prayer for the Sunday before Lent, or for the putting away of meat, mention is made of the church of Saint Fructuosus—appears to be true. Nor is it an obstacle that he adds that the people of Toledo are indicated in the prayer of Saint Leocadia. For when the proper Offices of the saints were celebrated, the Goths, as is also clear in the case of other saints, used those prayers or petitions that had been composed by those who were present to honor the saints’ tombs.

Thus, in the Office of the Seven Apostles, which was also recited at Toledo [142], one reads “in the neighborhood of this city,” which must be understood of the city of Acci, not of Toledo. But the mention of the church of Saint Fructuosus on the Sunday before Lent unquestionably indicates [Col. 0696C] that the Veronese Codex was once written for the use of the people of Tarragona.

Florez, in volume VIII of *España Sagrada*, p. 184, and in Appendix I, no. 4, discusses a sermon of Saint Leander, as it is now believed, in honor of Saint Vincent, which is found among the sermons of Saint Leo; he says that much of it was taken from the Gothic Office of Saint Vincent. Florez observes that such an Office of Saint Vincent appears to have been composed by Saint Leander for the principal church of Seville, which was dedicated to Saint Vincent. For at the end of the prayer *Post sanctus* it says:

> “Therefore we pray that there, where a portion of his relics has been deposited for us, the fullness of protection may be established.”

Certainly this prayer was composed for one particular church; for it cannot be believed that a portion of Saint Vincent’s relics was preserved in every Gothic church. [Col. 0696D] But as time went on, as I have said, Offices that had been arranged for a particular church were adopted by others without any change being made in the wording. I think this happened especially when the Spaniards were already being oppressed under the yoke of the Moors.

# CHAPTER LXXXIX  
## On the Preface of Alexander Lesleus to the New Edition of the *Missale Mixtum* According to the Rule of Blessed Isidore

### 1

The Mozarabic Missal and Breviary, formerly printed at the command of Cardinal Ximénez, were counted among the rarer books. In our own time a new edition of each has been prepared: that of the Missal by Alexander Lesleus, and afterward that of the Breviary by His Eminence Cardinal Lorenzana. Each prefixed a learned preface, which not only illuminates the Gothic liturgy but also casts a distinguished light upon the works of Isidore themselves. This is why I shall insert into my work on Isidore certain passages from these two most learned prefaces.

Lesleus committed the Missal to the press under this title:

> *Missale Mixtum secundum Regulam beati Isidori dictum MOZARABES, praefatione, notis et appendice ab Alexandro Lesleo S. J. sacerdote ornatum.*

“Mixed Missal according to the Rule of Blessed Isidore, called MOZARABIC, furnished with a preface, notes, and appendix by Alexander Lesleus, priest of the Society of Jesus.”

Rome, 1755, at the expense of Venantius Monaldini, printed by Giovanni Generoso Salomoni; large quarto, 143 [pages]. After the dedicatory letter to Pope Benedict XIV comes a long preface by Lesleus, in which he discusses the [Col. 0697B] Gothic liturgy learnedly.

### 2

Lesleus first sets forth praises of the ancient Spanish liturgy and asserts that it is contained in the Ximenian, or Mozarabic, Missal published by Ximénez. He then describes the Missal and the order of the Masses. He discusses whether the Mozarabic Missal is an ancient sacramentary, and proves that it is an ancient sacramentary because it contains a liturgy entirely different from the Roman and Ambrosian Mass, as well as from the anaphoras of the Greeks and other Eastern peoples, while being precisely that liturgy which formerly prevailed among the Goth-Spaniards and the earlier Mozarabs, and which resembles the ancient Gallican liturgy.

He maintains that the things added in later centuries do not make it possible to call the liturgy of the Ximenian Missal corrupted. He demonstrates that the Mozarabic Missal was always free from the errors of Felix and Elipandus.

[Col. 0697C] ### 3

To demonstrate the antiquity of the Gothic liturgy, Lesleus maintains that the Goth-Spanish liturgy must be distinguished from the Goth-Spanish Missal and Breviary. First the liturgy was established; then the Missal was arranged, and in a similar manner the Breviary was compiled. The liturgy, namely, is a fixed form and method of prayers observed in the Mass and in the ecclesiastical Office. The Missal is a collection of all the Masses, and the Breviary a collection of all the Offices of that same liturgy.

He denies that Saint Leander should be regarded as the author of the Goth-Spanish liturgy. Then, in section 12, he asks: “Was Saint Isidore the author of the Goth-Spanish liturgy?”—and answers in the following sense.

### 4

Another opinion, which recognizes Saint Isidore as the author of the Goth-Spanish liturgy, is more accepted and widespread among recent writers.

[Note: Cardinal Baronius, *Annales*, under the year 633; Mabillon, *De Liturgia Gallicana*, book I, chapter 4, no. 8; Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, part I, p. 269, no. 194; Juan de Mariana, *De rebus Hispaniae*, book VI, chapter 5; and many other Spanish authors, whom it would be too lengthy to enumerate individually. Most of them do not distinguish the author of the liturgy from the author of the Mozarabic Missal.]

This opinion rests upon two arguments. The first is the generally received belief, confirmed by the designation “Isidorian,” by which the liturgy is called. The other is that the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo assigned Saint Isidore the task of composing the form of the liturgy, which all the churches of Gothic Spain and Gaul were thereafter to observe once the variety of rites had been removed.

But this opinion too lacks the authority of the ancients and rests upon mere conjectures. Until now they have been unable to cite a single ancient writer who called the Goth-Spanish liturgy “Isidorian.” Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, who is said to have died in the year 1080 of the Christian era, is cited as the earliest writer to have said that Saint Isidore wrote some Spanish Missal.

[Col. 0698A] [Note: Guitmund, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*, where he speaks of a Spanish Missal, not of the liturgy.]

It is therefore surprising that Nicolás Antonio, a learned and careful man, should have written:

[Note: *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, book V, chapter 4, no. 195, p. 269.]

that the name “Isidorian” had been attributed from the most remote antiquity to the Mozarabic Breviary and Missal.

Nor is the other argument they use any more substantial. It is commonly asserted that the Fourth Council of Toledo imposed upon Saint Isidore the task of composing a new liturgy. But this assertion is in no way supported by ancient authority. The Fourth Council of Toledo says nothing about it; and if it had assigned Saint Isidore this responsibility, it would certainly have established a canon concerning it, as is customary. No such canon exists. Braulio and Hildefonsus also, who wrote about the works of Saint Isidore, ought to have mentioned the task imposed upon him of composing the liturgy, and the liturgy composed by him; yet they were completely silent about both.

### 5

Nor was there any reason for the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo [Col. 0698B] to entrust Saint Isidore, or anyone else, with the task of composing a new form of the liturgy. Their chief concern was certainly that one and the same form for celebrating the mysteries and performing the ecclesiastical Offices should be observed uniformly throughout the entire Visigothic kingdom. They introduced the form that the Goth-Spanish Church afterward consistently retained.

But this liturgical form was not new, nor was it unknown to the churches of Spain and Gaul. It was the very form to which they had become accustomed through immemorial usage. Since, therefore, the Fathers of Toledo wished only to ensure that all the churches of the Visigothic kingdom retain the ancient Spanish order, after innovations had been removed, they had no reason to impose upon Saint Isidore the task of composing some new order of rites and ceremonies.

Moreover, it is perfectly clear that the liturgy which Saint Isidore illuminates and explains in his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* is none other than the Goth-Spanish liturgy—namely, the liturgy that the Fourth Council of Toledo confirmed and established by its authority. It is also sufficiently certain that Saint Isidore wrote his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* before the Fourth Council of Toledo was held. For he had dedicated those books to Fulgentius, bishop of Écija, his brother, who had died piously and yielded his see to Aventius before that council assembled, as appears from the subscriptions of the bishops.

### 6

It is now clear that the Fathers of this council did not assign Saint Isidore the task of composing a liturgy which they knew perfectly well had already been composed long before and was in frequent use. Nor is it credible, as Cassander observed in writing to Pamelius, that Saint Isidore explained and illuminated in those books *On Ecclesiastical Offices* a liturgy that he himself had composed.

[145] Finally, in the brief prologue that he prefixed to his books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Saint Isidore declared that he would explain from which authorities the things celebrated in the ecclesiastical Offices had originated. He acknowledges neither himself, nor Leander, nor any others as authors of the Goth-Spanish liturgy, but rather Sacred Scripture, the tradition of the apostles—namely, of those who established the churches in Spain—and the custom of the Church.

Nothing, therefore, should be attributed to the opinions that proclaim Saint Leander or Saint Isidore the authors and founders of the Goth-Spanish liturgy. They are merely inventions of later writers, arising after the tenth and eleventh centuries without any certain author, and subsequently propagated by those who sought to protect and defend the native rites against their opponents under the shield, as it were, of the celebrated names of Saints Leander and Isidore.

“But,” they say, “at least it must be granted that Saint Isidore was charged with purging the ancient liturgy of the innovations that had crept into it through the negligence of the bishops, and that for this reason the Goth-Spanish liturgy was rightly called Isidorian.”

For my part, I think that Saint Isidore played the leading role not only in matters pertaining to the liturgy but also in framing the other canons of this council. He presided over the synod and enjoyed a great reputation for learning and holiness. Nevertheless, since the Goth-Spanish liturgy is not called Isidorian by ancient writers, and since all the canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo were published in the common name of the Fathers, the correction of the liturgy ought rather to be attributed to the whole council than to Saint Isidore.

### 7

Lesleus raises other questions. Did the Goth-Spanish liturgy remain continuously in use in Spain from the age of the apostles until the destruction of the Visigothic kingdom? He argues that it did. Among other observations, he notes that the Goth-Spanish liturgy contains several prayers composed at the time when idols were worshiped. Among them is the following, which is read in the Mozarabic Breviary at Terce—incorrectly, in Lesleus, at Prime—on the first day of the fast of the Kalends of January:

> “Lord . . . grant . . . that your mercy may exclude idols from the assembly of the Church, and that truth may turn doubtful hearts toward knowledge of your worship.”

These words call to mind the interpretation of the celebrated canon 30 of the Council of Elvira offered by Balthasar de Bastero, bishop of Gerona, in *Ephemerides Trivultinae* in 1750, article 43, and in Zaccaria’s collection, *Dissertationes Italicae*, volume X, p. 107.

The canon reads:

> “It has been decided that there should be no paintings in the church, lest what is worshiped and adored be depicted on the walls.”

Bastero says [Col. 0699C] that the first part of the canon names paintings generally and prohibits them from being in the church. The second part—“lest what is worshiped and adored”—is to be understood of idols, which the pagans commonly depicted even on the walls of their houses.

[146] The mind of the council, therefore, was that the places in which the faithful assembled should be entirely without paintings, so that every precaution might be taken to prevent the images that were worshiped and adored by the pagans from being depicted on the walls of the church—that is, of the place in which the faithful gathered.

To this interpretation, as I said, the words of the Mozarabic Breviary may be referred:

> “that your mercy may exclude idols from the assembly of the Church.”

The attempt recently made by someone to prove that the Council of Elvira was spurious certainly tends toward this result: that nothing in antiquity is so sacred that it cannot be called into question.

### 8

Some believe that the Roman liturgy was adopted by the churches of the province of Braga at the First Council of Braga. Lesleus explains the text of the canonical prayer that Pope Vigilius sent to Profuturus, bishop of Braga, and that was afterward received at the First Council of Braga. He discusses the canon of the Mass, not the other parts of the liturgy.

Whether the liturgy spread from Spain into Gaul, or from Gaul into Spain, is a famous controversy. Lesleus establishes this as certain: the ancient liturgy was not propagated from Gaul into Spain. He adds that the Goth-Spanish and ancient Gallican liturgies—which are the same, if credit is given to the Anonymous cited by Spelman—began in Asia, from where they reached Gaul through the work of Irenaeus and, as is credible, were brought somewhat earlier into Spain by those bishops whom Peter and Paul, after ordaining them at Rome, sent to preach in Spain.

Having established these points, Lesleus asks in section 16 whether Saint Leander, Saint Isidore, or Saint Julian was the author of the Mozarabic Missal, and answers in the following words.

### 9

Among the Spaniards and other peoples there is a commonly admitted and widespread opinion that the Mozarabic Missal—that is, the Goth-Spanish Missal—was edited either by Saint Leander, or by Saint Isidore, or by both. Some assign the leading role in this distinguished work to Saint Leander and the secondary role to Saint Isidore; others, on the contrary, hold that Leander began the work and Isidore completed it.

But these opinions were unknown to the ancients, for no author who wrote before the destruction of the Visigothic kingdom is cited in their support. By this single consideration all the arguments and conjectures of later writers are proved false. For how could it have become known, without the testimony of the ancients, to writers of a later age that the holy Leander and Isidore had been the authors of the Goth-Spanish Missal?

Saint Isidore, in his book *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 41, lists the works of Saint Leander without mentioning the Missal [147]:

> “He labored with no small zeal on the ecclesiastical Offices. For throughout the entire Psalter, in a twofold edition, he composed prayers; and in the Sacrifice also, with praises and psalms, he composed many things in a sweet melody.”

Saint Leander, therefore, wrote an *Orationale*, which he published in two editions; and he also composed a book of *Sacrifices*—namely, the antiphons that were sung while the people offered. He composed a book of *Praises*, which were sung after the Gospel had been read, and a book of *Psalms*—namely, those that were sung at Mass.

[Col. 0700C] [Note: Saint Isidore discussed the Sacrifice, or Offertories, the Praises, and the Psalms in *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapters 14, 13, and 5.]

Among these there is no book of the Missal, which Saint Isidore certainly would not have omitted.

### 10

By the same argument it is established that Saint Isidore was not the author of the Goth-Spanish or Mozarabic Missal. Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza [Note: In the eulogy prefixed to the works of Saint Isidore.], who lived nearly ten years after Saint Isidore, and Saint Hildefonsus [Note: *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9.], bishop of Toledo, compiled catalogues of his works. Neither mentions any liturgical book of his except the two books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

Since these men did not recognize a Missal written by Saint Isidore, we should not listen to later writers, who lived after the eleventh century, when they attempt to persuade us that the Mozarabic Missal was composed by the holy doctor.

One of the first of these was Guitmund, bishop of Aversa, who, in the work he wrote against Berengarius [Col. 0700D], citing the Mozarabic Missal, attributes it to Saint Isidore.

[Note: Guitmund, book III, *On the Truth of the Body and Blood of Christ in the Eucharist*, says: “In a certain Spanish Missal which they say Saint Isidore dictated.” These words are indeed spoken of the Mozarabic Missal, but they are not asserted as a fact; rather, they report an opinion, commonly circulated without any certain author.]

Guitmund is said to have died in 1080. But this opinion appears to have arisen in Spain in the eleventh century and to have been propagated into neighboring Gaul and also into Italy by those who sought to defend the Mozarabic rites against their opponents by the authority of Saint Isidore.

For when the Goth-Spanish liturgy used by the Mozarabs had been accused before the Roman pontiff, the Spaniards sent several bishops to Italy to plead the cause of the Mozarabic rites and to demonstrate the legitimacy of their manner of consecrating the Eucharist. In the year 1060, before Pope Alexander II and the bishops assembled at the Council of Mantua, they presented their liturgical books for examination and conducted the entire case in such a way that the Mozarabic liturgy was approved by the pontiff and the whole council.

[Note: Baronius, *Annales*, under the year 1064; Aguirre, *Councils of Spain*, volume III, p. 174 onward.]

From that time, in Italy also, the composition of the Mozarabic Missal began to be attributed to Saint Isidore.

### 11

Some have thought that the Fourth Council of Toledo commanded that throughout the entire Visigothic kingdom there should be one Missal and one Breviary, and that the task of composing these books was entrusted to Saint Isidore.

[Note: Mariana, *On the Affairs of Spain*, book VI, chapter 5, includes this among the decrees of the Fourth Council of Toledo: “Let there be one Missal and one Breviary in Spain. Since Isidore is believed to have been entrusted with completing this task, usage has prevailed that the Mozarabic Breviary and Missal should be attributed to him. But no such canon was ever issued by the Fourth Council of Toledo.”]

[148] But this opinion is in no way supported by the testimony of the ancients, who made no mention of a Breviary or Missal composed by Saint Isidore.

Moreover, those who hold this opinion think that the variety of Missals and Breviaries cannot be separated from a difference in liturgy, and that when the Fathers of Toledo decreed that one manner should be maintained in the solemn celebrations of Masses and one in the Morning and Evening Offices, they consequently abolished every variety of Missals, lectionaries, prayer-books, antiphonaries, and other liturgical books.

But it is perfectly clear that liturgical agreement can coexist with a variety of liturgical books.

[Note: Something was said about this matter in no. 88.]

The Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo knew this from experience. Although all the Spaniards used one and the same liturgy, they did not use the same liturgical books everywhere. Indeed, each province appears to have had its own lectionaries and Missals.

[Note: This concerns canon 20—or, as others have it, chapter 2—of the First Council of Braga, cited in book IV, title 15, of the *Code of Canons of the Goth-Spanish Church*, concerning the prohibition of different readings on the Masses and vigils of solemn days. It follows that on nonsolemn days different readings were permitted, and consequently that different lectionaries existed not only in different provinces but sometimes even within the same province. And if it was permissible to have different lectionaries, why not also different Missals and antiphonaries, and so forth?]

The Fourth Council of Toledo did not remove this difference, whatever its extent, among the liturgical books; rather, it permitted each province to retain its own customs in this matter untouched.

From this another argument is derived to prove that neither Saint Leander nor Saint Isidore was the author of the Mozarabic Missal. For this Missal was not common to the whole of Spain, nor was it proper to the province of Baetica; it was peculiar to the province of Toledo, that is, to the province of Carthaginensis.

[Col. 0701C] There was no reason, however, for the metropolitan of Baetica to assume responsibility for writing a Missal intended specifically for the uses of the province of Toledo.

Finally, when Elipandus cited this Missal, he did not name Leander or Isidore as its authors, but rather his predecessors, the bishops of Toledo, Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julian.

[Note: Elipandus, in his letter to Albinus, writes: “The testimonies of the holy and venerable Fathers serving at Toledo, published in the prayers of the Mass, say thus”; and the Council of Frankfurt reports Elipandus’s words from his little book: “Likewise our predecessors Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julian, bishops of the see of Toledo, said in their doctrines,” and so forth.]

The composition of the Mozarabic Breviary and Missal should therefore be attributed to these men rather than to Saint Isidore.

### 12

Nevertheless, if by the author of this Missal we mean the person who composed the Masses contained in it, neither Saint Isidore, nor Saint Hildefonsus, nor Saint Julian, nor any one individual should be called its author.

For whoever examines the Mozarabic Missal with a little attention will find that it is the work neither of one writer nor of one age. Apart from the variety of style that is sometimes detected within the same Mass, there are many Masses that were composed before the age of Saint Isidore. There are also many that were written after the death of the holy doctor. No one would say that the same man was the author of all these Masses.

But if by the author of the Mozarabic Missal we mean the person who corrected the Toledan Missal, or who enlarged it with one or another Mass composed by himself, several such authors are found among the bishops of Toledo. Elipandus named Eugenius, Hildefonsus, and Julian; and Julian, while listing the works of Saint Hildefonsus, says that a third part of them consists of Masses, hymns, and sermons.

[Note: At the end of Saint Hildefonsus’s work *On Illustrious Men*, published among the works of Saint Isidore.]

Nevertheless, no one, in my opinion, can be named with better right as the author of the Mozarabic Missal and Breviary than Saint Julian. Felix himself, also a bishop of Toledo, wrote the following while listing the works of his predecessor:

[Note: In the same place.]

> “Likewise, a book of Masses for the entire cycle of the year, divided into four parts, in which he corrected some portions that had been corrupted through the negligence of antiquity and completed those that were incomplete; likewise, a book of prayers for the festivals of the year that the Church of Toledo was accustomed to celebrate throughout the entire cycle of the year—partly drawn from the resources of his own skill in composition, partly corrected—he gathered together into one volume and left it for the use of the Church of God, out of love for holy religion.”

### 13

From this it is clear that Saint Julian carefully revised and corrected the liturgical books of his own church. Felix mentions two works. The first was a book of Masses, or Missal, which he divided into four parts. In some Masses he corrected what had been corrupted through the negligence of copyists; in others, which were incomplete, he supplied what was lacking by adding the prayers that had been omitted. Felix does not at all report that Julian added complete new Masses.

[Col. 0702C] The other work was a book of prayers for the festivals of the year, or the sanctoral section of the Toledan Breviary. This book he not only corrected but also enlarged by adding prayers for certain saints that had been lacking.

[Note: Concerning this volume, and whether it still survives in the library [Col. 0702D] of the Church of Toledo, consult Nicolás Antonio, *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, book V, chapter 7, no. 415, p. 309.]

I do not dare assert that this Missal of Saint Julian was the same as the one afterward called the Mozarabic Missal. For the Mozarabic Missal is a fully mixed, or plenary, Missal, whereas Saint Julian’s book of Masses, I think, was not of this kind.

[Note: That mixed, or plenary, Missals were in use before the eighth century is proved by the Bobbio Sacramentary, which is of that type. Such Missals were not merely convenient and useful but almost necessary for priests who celebrated privately, without the assistance of ministers. Since it was customary among the Goth-Spaniards to celebrate privately, it is credible that mixed Missals were in use among them. Nevertheless, I do not think that the book of Masses corrected by Saint Julian was mixed, both because Felix would not have omitted this qualification and because Saint Julian had corrected the book of Masses for the use of the Church of Toledo. In the more splendid churches, however, where there was an abundance of sacred books and ministers, it was considered dishonorable and shabby to bring a mixed Missal to the altar while Mass was being sung solemnly.]

Furthermore, the Mozarabic Missal contains some Masses composed after the destruction of the Gothic kingdom. [Col. 0703A] Nevertheless, I think that the earlier Mozarabs used Saint Julian’s book of Masses [150] in the solemn celebration of the Masses, and that this mixed Missal later called Mozarabic was composed from it.

[Note: It seems certain that the Mozarabs of the province of Toledo used Saint Julian’s book of Masses and other liturgical books of the same church. That the Mozarabs—or Spaniards who were subject to Christian princes—used the liturgical books of the Church of Toledo in the sacred Offices is shown by Lucas of Tuy. In the year 828 of the era, that is, in the year 790 of Christ, he writes:

> “Alfonso the Chaste . . . ordered that the entire order of the Goths, as it had been at Toledo, should be carried out at Oviedo, both in the church and in the palace.”

“And again, speaking of the death of Ferdinand, surnamed the Great, king of Castile and León, who died around 1065, he writes:

> “On that celebrated night of the Nativity of the Lord, while the clerics were singing the Christmas Matins in the festal manner, the lord king was present among them . . . a verse came to us, which at that time they sang IN THE TOLEDAN MANNER, with the succentors responding: ‘Receive instruction, all you who judge the earth.’”

In the Mozarabic Breviary, at the Matins praises on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, the same verse is still sung in the chant after the canticle *Benedictus*. These things show that the Spaniards, living both under the rule of the Saracens and under Christian princes, used the Toledan liturgical books at Mass and in the ecclesiastical Offices.]

### 14

Who its composers were, however, I cannot say with certainty. Whoever they were, they appear to have contributed only their own labor and industry, arranging Masses previously composed by others in such a way that priests celebrating privately, and those serving in rural and very poor churches where there was a lack of books and ministers, might have in this one book a lectionary, antiphonary, benedictional, and books of rites, prayers, and petitions, all suitably and orderly arranged within each Mass, so that nothing necessary for the efficient celebration of the mysteries would be lacking.

It is credible that the Mozarabic Missal was enlarged more than once by the reception of certain new Masses. It also appears that later Mozarabs added some rubrics, so that it cannot be denied that several people had a hand in its composition.

### 15

If we are speaking of the Breviary and Missal in the form in which Cardinal Ximénez arranged for them to be printed, I think that the person who reduced and combined all the parts into the form we now see lived at the very time of the edition, or shortly before it, as is gathered from the first rubric of the Mozarabic Breviary, described in the preceding chapter, no. 78.

Nor do I approve Lesleus’s interpretation of Isidore’s words concerning Leander:

> “For throughout the entire Psalter, in a twofold edition, he composed prayers.”

Lesleus explains this as:

> “He wrote an *Orationale*, which he published twice.”

But Isidore plainly speaks of a twofold edition of the Psalter, as I explained in chapter 87, nos. 20 and 21.

### 16

Finally, after comparing the Mozarabic Missal with the Gallican liturgical books, Lesleus offers this judgment:

> “Therefore, whether the integrity of the ancient rite is considered, or usage—which is given principal importance in books of this kind—it must be admitted that the Ximenian Missal far surpasses all the Gallican books published to date. For so much is still lacking in those books that is necessary for the efficient celebration of Masses that no one, however well equipped with those books, could recite even a single Gallican Mass without the assistance of the Ximenian Missal. A Mozarabic priest who possesses only the Ximenian Missal, however, can celebrate Mozarabic—and therefore Goth-Spanish and Gallican—Masses every day, if he wishes, with ease. Thus what I said at the beginning is fully established: by having the Mozarabic Missal printed, the excellent Cardinal Ximénez splendidly provided not only for the ancient sacrificial rite of the Spaniards but also for that of the Gauls.”

# CHAPTER XC  
## Excerpts from the Preface of His Eminence the Most Reverend Lord Don Francisco Antonio Lorenzana to the Gothic Breviary According to the Rule of Blessed Isidore

[Col. 0703D]

### 1

His Eminence Lorenzana, who had already rendered outstanding service to the Mozarabic liturgy when, as archbishop of Mexico, he published an authoritative edition and explanation of the Gothic Mass from the Angelopolitan press, was afterward appointed archbishop of Toledo and successor to that great hero, Cardinal Ximénez de Cisneros. He prepared a most magnificent edition of the Gothic Breviary, which surpassed the Ximenian edition not only in splendor but also by its correction, for the lasting glory of his own name no less than of the Isidorian rite.

Its title is:

> *Breviarium Gothicum secundum Regulam beatissimi Isidori archiepiscopi Hispalensis, jussu cardinalis Francisci Ximenii de Cisneros prius editum, nunc opera excellentissimi D. Francisci Antonii Lorenzana sanctae Ecclesiae Toletanae Hispaniarum primatis archiepiscopi recognitum ad usum sacelli Mozarabum.*

“Gothic Breviary according to the Rule of the most blessed Isidore, archbishop of Seville, first published by order of Cardinal Francisco Ximénez de Cisneros, now revised through the work of the most excellent Lord Francisco Antonio Lorenzana, archbishop of the holy Church of Toledo and primate of the Spains, for the use of the Mozarabic chapel.”

Madrid, 1775, at the press of Joaquín Ibarra, printer to His Catholic Royal Majesty and to the archbishop’s dignity; folio.

### 2

The preface of His Eminence the Cardinal is filled with varied learning, through which the entire Gothic liturgy can be greatly illuminated. I shall extract certain passages that particularly concern Isidore and our subject. After praising Cardinal Ximénez and explaining the etymology of the Gothic rite, he continues as follows:

152

### 3.

When Leander and his brother Isidore discovered that many things in the sacred liturgy and the divine office had been distorted, corrupted, and subverted by the perfidy of the Arians—for it is indeed incredible that, from the time of Athulf until Reccared, while Arian errors prevailed and Catholic bishops were in exile, very many faults did not creep into the sacred originals—they resolved to purge them of errors, restore them to greater purity, and arrange them in a better order. For this reason Leander and Isidore wrote on the divine offices, and nearly the entire purpose of the Fourth Council of Toledo, presided over by Saint Isidore, was to establish the order of the Mass sacrifice and the divine offices throughout Spain and Gaul, and to restore their disfigured appearance to its former condition. [Col. 0704C]

### 4.

On account of such great labors and prolonged scholarly exertions, the rite deservedly began to be called Isidorian: “Breviary and Office according to the Rule of the most blessed Isidore,” that is, according to the canons of the Fourth Council of Toledo, which he himself had chiefly prepared, being president of the council, vicar of the Apostolic See, moderator of ecclesiastical rite and discipline, and the most brilliant star of the whole world.

### 5.

After Spain had been subdued by the arms of the Moors, the Gothic rite nevertheless remained, and began to be called Mozarabic and Toledan. Much is said concerning the version of the Bible, which is used in the Mozarabic Breviary and especially in the Psalter. A description of the Gothic codices preserved in the Toledan library is appended.

### 6.

In that library there are eight Gothic manuscript codices. In one of them, besides seven Masses—believed to have been composed by Saint Ildephonsus, with musical notation—they contain the offices of the Nativity, Circumcision, and Manifestation of the Lord, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and the office of John the Apostle and Evangelist; in another, the complete office of Lent through Palm Sunday, exclusive; in a third, besides several Masses, the office of Holy Week through Easter inclusive, together with certain offices of the saints; in another, the offices of the saints throughout the year; in another, the Epistles and Gospels throughout the year; in another, the Masses of the saints throughout the year; and, finally, in another, the complete Psalter with canticles and hymns.

Besides these codices, the aforesaid library preserves a Gothic Bible that belonged during the time of the Muslim captivity to Servandus, bishop of Astigi, and later to John, bishop of Carthage and Córdoba, who donated it to the church of Seville in the Spanish era 1026, that is, in the year of Christ 988. [Col. 0705A]

### 7.

It is further shown that Cardinal Ximenes did indeed add certain things to the Isidorian Breviary, but nevertheless did not thereby alter the Gothic rite. That the ancient Gothic rite continues in the Mozarabic Breviary is confirmed by the following particular considerations. [Col. 0705B]

### 8.

Since, therefore, in the Psalter we possess a highly esteemed ancient Italian version, and since at the end of every psalm it says, “Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,” in accordance with article 14 of the Third Council of Toledo in its profession of faith, and canon 15 of the Fourth Council, presided over by Saint Isidore, there is no room for doubt that the rite remained entire and without any substantial alteration until the time of Cardinal Ximenes. Nor could this be changed by the festivals taken by Cardinal Ximenes from the ancient Toledan Rite, whose Missal was later printed by Cardinals John de Tavera and Martínez Silíceo, before the revision of Pius V.

### 9.

That the use of the psalms with chant at the beginning, and, when they were longer, with a pause made several times around the middle—a practice they called the diapsalma, as has been said—existed in the age of Saint Isidore, as will appear in the Psalter in the form in which it survives in the manuscript original published by us, Saint Isidore himself demonstrates in *On the Divine Offices*, book I, chapter 1, paragraph 1, concerning the Psalms, in these words:

> “For the carnal in the church, not for the spiritual, the custom of singing was instituted, so that, since they are not pierced by words, they may be moved by the sweetness of melody . . . For in the sacred words themselves—according to Augustine—our minds are moved more religiously and fervently toward the flame of piety when they are sung than when they are not sung. For all our affections—again, Isidore says—are aroused more by the diversity or novelty of sounds, through some hidden familiarity, when something is sung with a sweet and skillful voice.”

### 10.

The holy doctor mentions hymns in the following paragraph, listing their earliest composers: namely, Hilary, bishop of Poitiers, distinguished for eloquence, and Ambrose of Milan, whom he calls a man of great glory in Christ, a most illustrious teacher in the Church, and prolific in the composition of such poems. Hence hymns are called Ambrosian after his name, and devotion to his renown was first observed in the Church of Milan and afterward throughout the Churches of the West. We therefore now ask the reader to turn his eyes to the hymns of the present Isidorian Rite; he will find that the same hymns which Saint Isidore records were recited. If others are found, they were composed by the Spaniard Prudentius, who flourished in the fourth century. [Col. 0705D]

### 11.

Those who have devoted themselves to reading the works of Saint Isidore will find there testimony to his wisdom, and every doubt concerning our Rite and his universal learning will vanish. In the liberal arts he proceeded as a more learned modern scholar might; and, concerning ecclesiastical offices according to the golden beginnings of the Roman centuries, he himself, as apostolic vicar, presided over the national Fourth Council of Toledo. In view of these outstanding achievements, it is incredible that the stream of his eloquence did not pour forth upon everyone, especially in the ordering of the sacred liturgy and divine offices.

[Col. 0706A]

### 12.

In the manuscript original that we have before our eyes for the edition of this Breviary, unmistakable signs of this matter appear. We shall point out several, so that the similarity of the others with the Rite truly and deservedly called Isidorian may be recognized.

First, to mark a paragraph, so that one matter may be separated from matters that occur in connection with it, Saint Isidore uses this sign: Γ, in chapter 10—elsewhere chapter 21—of book I of the *Etymologies*. For it denotes a difference of discourse, and you will find the very same sign in our manuscript original marking the division of a treatise, or before the beginning of the numbering of the Psalms.

### 13.

Another sign appears in the form of [the figure is absent or illegible in the supplied text], which he calls *phietro*; it is placed to indicate a difficulty where there is some obscurity. The very same sign, with a slight alteration, is sometimes used in our manuscript original. [154]

### 14.

The chant without clef and lines, now unfamiliar, appears in our manuscript as consisting solely of musical points. According to Isidore, these were distinguished clearly and openly in the three parts of music: harmonic, rhythmic, and metric. As regards the harmonic, it produces movement in all who sing with their own voice, from the mind and ardor, and from movement it produces sound.

According to Isidore, *Etymologies*, book III, chapter 22, a tone is an acute utterance of the voice, a difference of harmony, and a quantity consisting in the accent or sustained quality of the voice. Musicians divided its kinds into fifteen parts, of which the Hyperlydian is the last and highest, while the Hypodorian is the lowest of all. Chant, therefore, is an inflection of the voice according to the rules laid down by Saint Isidore, for direct sound is distinct, and sound precedes chant. [Col. 0706B]

### 15.

The holy doctor was not unaware of the difference between sweet and full voices. He defines with remarkable precision the acute, thin, high, harsh, rough, blind, *vinnolata* [the term is uncertain], and perfect voice. The perfect voice is high, sweet, and clear: high, so that it may rise upward; clear, so that it may fill the ears; and sweet, so that it may delight the minds of those who hear.

### 16.

To distinguish musical numbers, Saint Isidore supplies certain arithmetical rules that will please those most skilled in the art of music today.

> “You shall seek numbers according to music in this way,” he says in the cited book, chapter 23. “Taking the extremes, for example 6 and 12, you see by how many units 12 exceeds 6, and it is by 6 units. You multiply by the square: six times six makes 36. You join those first extremes: 6 and 12 together make 18. You divide 36 by 18. The result is a double ratio [*dipondius*]. You join these with the smaller sum, namely 6. They will be 8, and 8 will be the mean between 6 and 12, because 8 exceeds 6 by two units, that is, one-third of six, and 8 is exceeded by 12 by four units, one-third of the whole. By the proportion in which one exceeds, it is exceeded.”

Why should we hesitate any longer, if the way is open for readers to probe Isidore’s statements?

### 17.

The agreement between the works of Saint Isidore and this Breviary shines forth especially in the heading of the reading from Ecclesiasticus. In the Breviary it bears this title: “Reading from the book of Ecclesiasticus of Solomon.” Since it is universally established that the book of Ecclesiasticus was composed by Jesus, son of Sirach of Jerusalem, and not by Solomon, a difficulty immediately arises. Why, then, is it identified in this way in the Breviary?

Saint Isidore answers this in his book *Prologues to the Old Testament*, under the paragraph “On Ecclesiasticus”: “Because of the great similarity of its meaning and the equality of its eloquence, it is prefaced with Solomon’s name.” [Col. 0706D]

### 18.

Having brought forward these and many other considerations, the eminent editor concludes that the Mozarabic Breviary, published by Cardinal Ximenes, is rightly entitled Isidorian, or “according to the Rule of Blessed Isidore.” For although he was not the author of the rite, he nevertheless arranged and corrected it, just as Gregorian chant is called Saint Gregory the Great’s, although Saint Gregory was not its author.

To the preface is appended an explanation of the melodic Eugenian chant, by Don Jerónimo Romero, prebendary of the Holy Church of Toledo and master of melodic chant. This Eugenian chant, instituted or arranged by Saint Eugenius III, continued uninterruptedly in the Church of Toledo from the time of the Goths and continues even now.

# CHAPTER XCI

## What is the genuine Hispana collection of canons? Was Isidore its author? The spurious collection of canons under the name of Isidore Peccator, or Mercator, was neither fabricated in Spain nor by a Spaniard. Learned studies by the Ballerini brothers on these collections.

### 1.

There are many learned dissertations on the ancient collections of canons, and the Spanish collection of canons occupies no small place among them, both the old genuine collection and the spurious Isidorian one.

Peter de Marca, in his dissertation on the ancient collections of canons, discusses the most ancient collection, as he believes, of the Roman Church before the Council of Chalcedon; the collection of canons after the Council of Chalcedon; and the difference between that collection and the Dionysian collection.

Cajetan Cennius, however, published a dissertation entitled *On the First Collection of the Canons of the Holy Roman Church, and on Its Archive and Library under Saint Leo the Great*, inserted in volume XIV of Zaccaria’s collection of *Italian Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*. In it he maintains that, before the eighth century, the Roman pontiffs used no collection of canons of their own. He also left a manuscript volume on this subject.

De Marca had judged that the collection which alone prevailed in the East before the Dionysian collection was the very one used by the Gauls until the time of Pope Hadrian and by the Spaniards until the Saracen rule. He explains it from two manuscript codices of the monastery of Ripoll in Catalonia, having transcribed the preface. This is certainly the old genuine Hispana collection, found also in many other manuscripts, both in Spain and outside Spain. [Col. 0707B]

### 2.

The same De Marca discusses the spurious Isidorian collection in book II, chapter 5, of *On the Harmony of Imperial and Priestly Power*. Natalis Alexander treats it in dissertation 21 of the first century, as do innumerable others after the earlier Turrianus, Blondel, and others.

Learned men rightly wonder—and even stand amazed—at Cardinal Aguirre’s attempt to prove that this collection was the genuine offspring of our Isidore of Seville, after the unanimous agreement of scholars in rejecting as apocryphal many of the decretal letters in the collection.

Bonaventure Malvasia of Bologna, of the Order of Saint Francis, undertook to defend the same cause against Blondel, publishing at Rome in 1635 an octavo work entitled *A Messenger of Truth Sent to David Blondel*.

With better judgment, the distinguished Zaccaria, in volume II, chapter 1 and following of his *Antifebronius*, acknowledges that the Isidorian decretals are indeed forged, but demonstrates against Dupin, Fleury, and Febronius that ecclesiastical discipline was in no way disturbed by such decretals.

Fabricius is therefore seriously mistaken when, in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under the entry “Isidore Mercator,” he asserts that Catholics are compelled to prove that papal usurpations were supported by false decretals. For, as Mansi observes there, Blancus the Minorite, who sharpened his pen against Giannone, and the learned Dominicans Ursius and Mamachi obtained their weapons for defending papal rights from a source quite different from the Isidorian workshop. [Col. 0707D]

A judgment on this subject, written in Italian by the distinguished Marchetti against Fleury’s *Ecclesiastical History*, deserves to be read.

Fabricius discusses this and other ancient collections of canons at greater length in volume XI of his *Bibliotheca Graeca*, page 17 and following, and in volume II of his *Bibliotheca veterum Latinorum*, chapter 10, book IV, no. 4. [Col. 0708A]

### 3.

The Ballerini brothers far surpassed all the others in industry in their treatise on the ancient collections and collectors of canons, which they prefixed to volume III of the works of Saint Leo.

The distinguished Zaccaria entitled the fourth dissertation of volume II of his *Italian Dissertations on Ecclesiastical History*: “On Two Ancient Unpublished Collections of Canons.” He began as follows:

> “It may seem strange that, after the famous treatise on the ancient collections of canons prefixed by the Ballerini to the third volume of the works of Saint Leo the Great, it should still be possible to speak of such collections without repeating what they said. Nevertheless, the two collections about which I am going to speak in this dissertation will show that this subject is not so easily exhausted. It is true that this will be a gathering of gleanings after the abundant harvest reaped by those able men; but it will not therefore be useless either to publish one collection or to bring the other into a clearer light than has hitherto been done.”

This is what Zaccaria says concerning the collection of canons in the seventh- or eighth-century Mutina Codex, which he published, and concerning the collection of canons of Cardinal Deusdedit in Vatican Codex 3833, which he treated more briefly and less accurately than the Ballerini had done. [Col. 0708B]

### 4.

What the Ballerini wrote about the Spanish collections of canons is certainly excellent and must not be omitted by us, especially since men both highly learned and most free from partisan bias greatly support our cause.

Since, however, some matters have also occurred to me by which their opinions may be clarified, and since I have examined ancient codices in which certain monuments cited by them can be found in more correct form, I shall do what lies within my power so that their labors may receive some additional light from my observations.

[Col. 0708D]

### 5.

First, it should be noted that, even after the Ballerini, a learned work on the collection of canons of Isidore Mercator came into public circulation. Its author was Carlo Blasco, who nevertheless does not appear to have had old exemplars of this collection before him and scarcely mentions the Ballerini’s work except in the additions.

Blasco’s peculiar theory is that the supposed collection of Isidore Mercator gave rise to the opportunity for inventing the story of Pope Joan. He supposes that someone aware of the fraud devised a sort of riddle, as though some pope—or rather some female pope—had produced a spurious offspring.

And since the name of the female pope Joan is said to have been John the Englishman, he conjectures that the author of the spurious collection of canons of Isidore Mercator was a certain John, an Englishman by nationality, who was a contemporary of Alcuin and had contrived the fraud at Mainz.

What else Blasco did throughout his work can be sufficiently understood from the title itself and the list of chapters, which I append. [Col. 0709A]

### 6.

**Commentary on the Collection of Canons of Isidore Mercator.** In it the origin and fortunes of the collection are discussed, and inquiry is made into the person and principal purpose of the collector. The impostor’s frauds are likewise exposed, and it is argued, on solid evidence, that from them arose the opportunity for inventing the story of Pope Joan; from this the impostor’s true name also becomes clear. At the end of the work there is appended an appendix on the pseudo-pope Cyriacus, companion of Saint Ursula, and so forth; also a disputation on the chapters attributed to Pope Hadrian I.

### 7.

**CHAPTER I.** Synopsis of the collections that preceded Mercator.

**CHAPTER II.** The appearance of Mercator’s collection.

[Col. 0709B]

**CHAPTER III.** How Mercator’s collection emerged, and its development.

**CHAPTER IV.** The Roman pontiffs used Mercator’s documents without fraud, and therefore without fault, and indeed with moderation.

**CHAPTER V.** The detection of the falsity of Mercator’s documents.

**CHAPTER VI.** Who Isidore Mercator was, and at what time and place he flourished.

**CHAPTER VII.** Mercator’s purpose.

158 **CHAPTER VIII.** That Mercator’s purpose of securing the protection of bishops is demonstrated in numerous chapters by the false decretals themselves:

1. From the condemned usurpation of Church property.

2. From the restriction of the power of chorepiscopi.

3. From the exaggerated spiritual marriage between the bishop and the church.

4. From the honor to be shown to priests, especially bishops.

5. From the restoration, before all else, of bishops who had been dispossessed, and from granting them a respite.

6. From the restriction of the license to accuse clerics, especially bishops.

7. From the rule that no accusation should be made unless correction had first been attempted.

8. From the rule that an accusation likewise should not be made without a prior written indictment.

9. From the rule that absent persons should not be condemned or accused.

10. From the qualifications of witnesses and the number required for the condemnation of bishops.

11. From the invalidation of an extorted confession.

12. From the procedure imposed upon trials.

13. From restoring penitents to their honors.

14. From the free right of appeal, and from the rule that bishops should not be judged without consulting the Holy See. [Col. 0709C]

**CHAPTER IX.** On the rights that Mercator attributes to the Roman pontiff.  
§ I. On the criminal cases of bishops.  
§ II. On the authority of the Roman pontiff in synods of bishops.

**CHAPTER X.** It is demonstrated by many arguments that Mercator took no account of the rights of the Roman pontiff that do not pertain to criminal cases, especially those of bishops:

1. From the fact that he did not reserve the power of transferring bishops.

2. From the fact that he did not reserve the power of accepting their resignations.

3. From the fact that he did not grant the power of ordaining them throughout the world.

4. From the fact that he did not grant the authority to ordain clerics of other churches.

5. From the fact that he did not mention the power of ordaining anyone, at least in cases of devolution.

6. From the fact that he did not reserve the power of ordaining bishops of his patriarchate, nor even of his province.

7. From the fact that he did not mention the oath of obedience and submission.

8. From the fact that he did not grant permission for the ordination of bishops by a single bishop.

9. From the fact that he did not grant the power of delegating to a presbyter the administration of confirmation.

10. From the fact that he did not reserve church dedications.

11. From the fact that he neglected the commemoration of the pope’s name in the Masses.

12. From the fact that he did not reserve absolution and the imposition of penance for more serious crimes.

13. From the fact that he did not grant the power to confer privileges.

14. From the fact that he did not mention the power of dispensing. [Col. 0709D]

159 **CHAPTER XI.** Objections are answered, and it is shown that Mercator at times granted so much to bishops that he appears injurious to the Roman pontiff.

[Col. 0710A]

**CHAPTER XII.** Mercator’s other purpose, namely, establishing primates whom he equates with patriarchs, is exposed.

**CHAPTER XIII.** The place in which Mercator chiefly wished to establish a primate; various indications prove that it was Mainz.

**CHAPTER XIV.** The conjecture that Mercator intended a primacy at Mainz is confirmed by what subsequently occurred, and objections are refuted.

**CHAPTER XV.** What Mercator includes beyond his purpose, he presents from genuine documents under the appearance of truth, especially from the *Book of the Pontiffs*.

**Final Chapter.** The story of Pope Joan arose from Mercator’s collection of canons, or, at least, the opportunity for inventing it was supplied by that collection.  
§ I.—The opinions of others are reported and rejected.  
§ II.—The conjecture derived from Mercator’s collection of canons is explained and proved.  
§ III.—On John the Englishman concealed under the mask of Isidore Mercator.

**Appendix.** On the pseudo-pope Cyriacus, companion of Saint Ursula and the eleven thousand virgins, who suffered martyrdom with them. [Col. 0710B]

**Disputation.** On the chapters attributed to Pope Hadrian I and addressed to Angilramnus.

### 8.

There exists a *Sylloge of Dissertations on Ancient Collections of Canons*, edited by the distinguished Andrea Gallandi, Venice, 1778, in folio; namely:

1. A dissertation on the ancient collections of canons and on the various editions of the letters of the Roman pontiffs, by Pietro Costant.

2. Peter de Marca’s dissertation on the ancient collections of canons.

3. A treatise in four parts on ancient collections, both published and unpublished, and on the collectors of canons down to Gratian, by the brothers Peter and Jerome Ballerini.

4. Carlo Sebastiano Berardi’s dissertation on the various collections of sacred canons before Gratian.

5. Three dissertations by Paschasius Quesnellus: the first on the Codex of the canons of the Roman Church; the second on the various creedal documents contained in the ancient Codex of the Roman Church; the third on the first use of the Codex of the canons of Dionysius Exiguus in the Gallican regions, together with the Ballerini’s annotations on these dissertations of Quesnellus.

8. Blasco’s *Commentary on the Collection of Canons of Isidore Mercator*, mentioned above.

9. A dissertation on the method and authority of Gratian’s collection and of all the other collections of decretals after Gratian. There is also a discourse on the proper method of studying canon law, by Francesco Florente.

10. Two books of dialogues by Antonio Agostino, *On the Correction of Gratian*. [Col. 0710C]

### 9.

From all these works we must obtain, as I said, those matters that touch the Spanish collection more closely and illuminate it more clearly, especially from the Ballerini’s treatise. I shall therefore describe several chapters of the second part, beginning with chapter 4, and shall add my own notes wherever it seems appropriate.

## On the Spanish Collection

### § I.—The principal authors who have treated this collection. How it was compiled. Its codices.

### 10.

It will become clear from what follows in part IV, chapter 4, where there will be discussion of the most ancient abbreviation of the canons contained in manuscript 59 of the Veronese chapter, that several very ancient collections, now lost and different from the one usually called the Spanish collection, once existed among the Spaniards.

[Note: [Col. 0711D] The title of the most ancient abbreviation of the canons in the Veronese Codex is: “Here begin the chapters of all the holy councils established by the blessed Fathers, or of the decretal letters decreed by pontiffs or apostolic men, briefly collected and written down.”

It presents certain councils absent from the old Spanish collection, namely the Fifth Council of Orléans, which was later added to the Spanish collection, and four synods edited from the Aemilian Codex: the Second Council of Zaragoza, and the councils of Narbonne, Huesca, and Barcelona.

Among the synods presented by the abbreviator, the most recent is that of Huesca in the year 598. These and other facts show that the abbreviator did not have before him the collection called the original Spanish collection, but worked from older books. He cites the Bracarensian, Complutensian, and Agabrensian books.

A similar abbreviation of the canons exists in the Lucense Codex, concerning which I dealt above, from Mansi, in chapter 44 of volume I. Concerning the city of Agabra, or, as it is read in the Lucense Codex, Gabra—with the first letter omitted—Mansi’s conjectures are found in volume II of the *Supplement to the Councils*, in the preface to the appendix.]

This is also confirmed by two synods older than the Spanish collection, in which codices of canons are reported as having been produced and read.
