In the First Council of Braga of the year 563 it is stated: “The canons both of general synods and of local synods were reread from the Codex before the council.” And in the Second Council of Seville of the year 619, chapter 2: “The synodal decrees were read aloud after the canons had been produced.”

We must now speak of the Spanish collection, of which several manuscript copies survive. After the Dionysian collection, it is the most orderly and complete of the others.

The first person to provide a brief but sufficiently distinct account of this collection was Antonio Agustín, archbishop of Tarragona, in his little work on certain ancient collectors of canons, chapter 17. Peter de Marca published not a little about it in his *Opuscula*, although he had a less accurate knowledge of its origin and use.

Stephen Baluzius and others after him used copies of the same collection; but they indicated so little about them that scarcely anything distinct can be extracted from their accounts.

Since Antonio Agustín’s works were extremely rare and had been overlooked by most people, this distinguished collection remained little known until P. Coustant discussed it more extensively in section X of the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, from no. 132 through no. 152.

Although he gave an accurate description of it, since we have been able to discover and compare several codices, we are confident that we can offer something further by which this collection may be more fully illuminated. [Col. 0711B]

### 11.

Like the Dionysian collection, this one is divided into two parts, one of which presents the canons of councils and the other the letters of the Roman pontiffs.

In the second part, the collector drew from Dionysius. For all the letters that he found in Dionysius, he copied from that work with the same titles and inserted them into his own collection. Other papal letters that he found elsewhere he added in their proper places, following the same arrangement as Dionysius, with titles composed by himself.

As for the canons contained in the first part, however, he received nothing from Dionysius. Since, with regard to the Greek canons, another older version prevailed in Spain—the version taken from this collection by Isidore Mercator and published from Isidore’s codices, and therefore usually called Isidorian—he did not wish to adopt the new Dionysian translation, although it was better and more carefully corrected, fearing that this novelty would offend Spaniards accustomed to the ancient version.

The widespread use of that old version in the Spanish churches is sufficiently confirmed by the Third Council of Toledo in the year 589, in which three passages of that same version are cited.

For a similar reason, it must be said that he did not wish to borrow from Dionysius the African canons, although they were more accurately written there, because another peculiar collection of African canons was so firmly established in the Spanish regions that it appears to have passed from Spain into Gaul. For this reason it is praised in the Second Council of Tours of the year 567, as we proved in part II, chapter 3, section 2, no. 4. From this we also concluded that certain errors which we carefully noted in the recension of the African canons of this collection in the same paragraph are to be attributed not to the Spanish collector, but to the earlier author of that African collection.

The Spanish collector did, however, provide at least this benefit with regard to the Greek canons: following Dionysius’ method, he added titles to the individual decrees. From manuscript 58 of the Veronese chapter it is clear that these titles were absent from the beginning in the ancient version.

Nor did the Spanish collector present only the Greek and African councils, which alone are read in Dionysius; he also added Gallican and Spanish councils.

The authority of the Gallican synods was great among the Spaniards. Hence synods of this kind were widely known among them, and they often fashioned their own canons from their words and judgments, even where they do not name them. Often, too, they openly and expressly proposed their example and authority for imitation, as Sirmond observed in his preface to the *Councils of Gaul* and confirmed by citing the evidence.

The Spanish collector therefore enriched his Codex with these widely circulated copies of the Gallican synods.

We detected two errors in the same collector in the First Council of Toledo, volume II, columns 1379 and 1380, note 5. One of them, insofar as it slipped into the collector’s work, we shall explain more appropriately in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation XIV, section 2, no. 3.

We pointed out another error in the catalogue of bishops incorrectly attributed to the Second Council of Arles, although it belongs to the First Council of Arles, in the Observations on Quesnellus’s Dissertation V, volume II, columns 1018 and 1019, note 14.

It was very easy to collect the Spanish councils from the codices of the churches of Spain. [Col. 0712A]

### 12.

Before describing the collection itself, a brief account must be prefixed of the codices on which its description depends.

[Note: [Col. 0712D] Burrielius lists very many manuscript copies of the Gothic collection of canons above, chapter 40, no. 19.

Flórez, in volume VII of *Sacred Spain*, page 163, gives the following subscription from the Toledan Codex in a more correct form than that found in Nicolás Antonio, Morales, and the Count of Mora:

“Here happily ends the book of the canons of the councils of the holy Fathers, or the decrees of the Roman pontiffs. Thanks be to God. Julian, an unworthy presbyter, wrote it. With God’s help, he resides at Alkalaga, which is situated above the laudable plain, on Wednesday, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of June, in the Spanish era 1133.”

That is, in the year 1095. The Codex of Cardinal Passionei is now preserved in the Angelica Library.]

Copies of this collection are rare in Italy. We found one in the Vatican Library, marked no. 1341. Its transfer from the Gallican church of Autun, or Augustodunum, is demonstrated by the following profession of Theotard, abbot of Saint Martin, written shortly after the beginning in a more recent hand:

> “I, Theotard, now about to be ordained abbot of the monastery of Saint Martin, promise that I shall perpetually render to the Holy Church of Autun, in the presence of Lord Bishop Agano, the submission and reverence established by the holy Fathers and the obedience prescribed by Saint Benedict; and I ratify this promise with my own hand.”—

who flourished around the middle of the eleventh century—

> “And then: Let him read this over the altar.”

We were able to see two other codices: one, Vatican Palatine 575, confused and mutilated, which once belonged to the monastery of Saint Martin at Mainz; the other in the library of the eminent Cardinal Passionei, likewise mutilated, and apparently written in the tenth and perhaps even the ninth century.

By far the finest and oldest copy, which we arranged to have collated with the letters of Leo, is the Caesarean Vindobonense, marked no. 41. Lambecius, in book II, chapter 8, page 932, no. 281, calls it “a parchment volume of astonishing antiquity, in folio, entirely in ancient Gothic or Toledan letters,” written in the year 736.

There are many manuscripts of this kind in Gaul and Spain. Among numerous Spanish ones, John Baptist Perez chiefly describes four: the Lucense, Hispalense, Alveldense, and Saint Aemilianus codices, about which more will be said below.

García Loaysa praises two other Toledan codices in the preface to the *Councils of Spain*. He calls the one which Perez names Alveldense “Vigilanus,” because it was written by the presbyter Vigila.

We have learned from the notation of the year 962 and from the documents contained in it that the codex he calls Hispalense is the same as the one Perez called the Codex of Saint Aemilianus.

Peter de Marca and Stephen Baluzius mention two manuscript books from Ripoll and one from Urgell, as well as Colbertine and Lyonese codices, which agree with those same Spanish copies.

P. Coustant praises the Spanish Gerundense copy and four Gallican ones: Laon, Noyon, Beauvais, and Soissons. He also mentions a Coislinian and a Colbertine copy, which seem to approach the Spanish rather than the Gallican origin of the codices of this collection. Their difference will be discussed in section 5. [Col. 0713B]

## § II.—The original edition of this collection. Table of its contents. The letter of Innocent I to Aurelius is exempted from the suspicion of Isidorian forgery.

### 13.

Although among so many codices some are richer in contents than others, no copy represents the original collection free from later additions.

The original collection is ordinarily determined from the index, or table, of chapters, so that if any chapters are found written in the body in addition to those in the same table, they are recognized as having been added later.

If, among the tables of different codices of the same collection, some present fewer chapters and others more, the table consisting of fewer chapters provides an indication of the original collection.

Among the codices of the Spanish collection mentioned above, fewer chapters are read in the tables of the Vindobonense Codex, Perez’s Hispalense Codex, the Ripoll codices, Vatican 1341, and certain other Gallican codices. Although these copies have some chapters inserted into their bodies, they did not receive any additions in the previously given table of chapters, as happened with certain other Spanish copies.

For this reason, their untouched indices or tables are rightly believed to belong to the original edition of this collection. In describing the first edition of the collection itself, therefore, we shall use the evidence of these shorter tables; the additions introduced later will be discussed in due course.

14. [Note: [Col. 0713D] In Vatican Codex 1341, mentioned by the Ballerini, the table lists six general councils and forty-four non-general synods. Title 45 is added: “Sentences not found in the old copies,” etc.; title 46: “Decrees of the Roman prelates”; and title 47: “The Toledo Synod of sixty-eight bishops.” After the table comes “The Sites of the Various Provinces.” Then, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, begins “The order for celebrating a council”: “At the first hour of the day,” etc., “may we be able to speak the word with complete confidence.” It ends: “Immediately, without a title”; then “The Canons of the General Councils,” etc., which is the preface transcribed by the Ballerini, with these various readings: *facultas* (“permission”). Then, “. . . the Church holds . . . which [Col. 0714D] the aforesaid . . . asserted.” “Consubstantial . . . . . the third synod is the First of Ephesus, two hundred . . . . . so that the divine and human natures may be confessed in one substance.” Perhaps: “so that the nature, both divine and human, may be confessed in one substance” (that is, subsistence) . . . “the synods completing the Catholic faith” . . . “on account of authority.” I shall present the various readings of the final part of the preface in Book VI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 16, no. 12. After the words “The preface ends,” there is again a table: “Here begin the chapters,” etc. Then comes a table of the Roman pontiffs: 102 decrees are indicated, followed by the fifty Canons of the Apostles, then the Council of Nicaea, etc.] The table of the first part is divided into forty-five chapters. We place the complete preface to this part first.

164. “The canons of the general councils began in the time of Constantine. For in the preceding years, while persecution was raging, no opportunity at all was given for instructing the peoples. Consequently, Christianity was split into various heresies, because the bishops had no permission to assemble in one place except in the time of the emperor mentioned above. He himself gave Christians permission to assemble freely. Under this emperor also the holy Fathers, assembling at the Council of Nicaea from the whole world, handed down, in accordance with the evangelical and apostolic faith, the creed that follows the Apostles.

“There are four principal councils from which the Church possesses the fullest doctrine of the faith, both concerning the divinity of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, and concerning the incarnation of the aforesaid Son and our Savior. The first of these is the Council of Nicaea, held under Constantine Augustus by 318 bishops. There the blasphemy of Arius’s impiety was condemned—Arius had asserted the inequality [another reading: *concerning the inequality*] of the Holy Trinity. Thus, through the creed, that holy synod defined the Son as God, consubstantial with God the Father.

“The second is the council of 150 Fathers assembled at Constantinople under Theodosius the Elder. It condemned Macedonius, who denied that the Holy Spirit was God, and demonstrated that the same Paraclete was consubstantial with the Father and the Son. All Greece and the Latin world proclaim this in the churches.

“The third is the First Council of Ephesus, held under Theodosius Augustus the Younger by 200 bishops. It condemned with a just anathema Nestorius, who asserted two persons in Christ, showing that the one person of the Lord Jesus Christ remains in two natures.

“The fourth is the Council of Chalcedon, held under the emperor Marcian by 630 priests. There the same judgment of the Fathers condemned Eutyches, abbot of Constantinople, who proclaimed one nature of the Word of God and the flesh; Dioscorus, formerly bishop of Alexandria, his defender; and Nestorius himself again, together with the other heretics. The same synod proclaimed that Christ God was born of the Virgin in such a way that we confess one person of both the divine and human nature.

“These, as we have said, are the four principal and venerable synods embracing the whole Catholic faith. Yet whatever other councils the holy Fathers, filled with the Spirit of God, enacted remain firmly established after the authority of these four; their acts too are contained in this volume.

“At the beginning of this volume we have placed the Council of Nicaea because of the authority of that great council. Thereafter, we have arranged within this volume the various Greek and Latin councils—both those held earlier and those held later—in chapters distinguished according to their order and dates. We have also appended the decrees of the Roman prelates, in which there is an authority equal to that of the councils because of the eminence of the apostolic see. Thus the discipline of ecclesiastical order, gathered and arranged by us into one body, may constrain the holy prelates by ancestral rules [another reading: ‘instruct them’], and obedient ministers or peoples of the Church may be imbued with spiritual examples.

“But the canons called those of the Apostles—or rather, because neither the apostolic see receives them nor the holy Fathers have given them their assent—are excluded from canonical and apostolic authority, since they are recognized as having been composed by heretics under the name of the Apostles and are assigned among the apocrypha, although some useful things are found in them.”

[Col. 0714D] After this is added:

“But *canon* in Greek, in Latin is called *regula* [‘rule’]. Now *regula* is so called,” etc., as in Gratian, *Decretum*, distinction 3, chapters 1 and 2. After those words, at the end of the second chapter, “and may correct what is wrong” follows: “Now *synod* is translated from Greek,” etc., as in the same Gratian, distinction 15, chapter 1, at the end. After the final words, “from the association of many into one,” there follows: “The preface ends.”

The table of chapters of this first part is as follows.

## HERE BEGIN THE CHAPTERS OF THE COUNCILS OF GREECE

### I.

[Note: [Col. 0715D] In the aforementioned Vatican Codex 1341, a certain epigram is placed before the Council of Nicaea under this title: “Here begins the preface of the holy council.” Similarly, in Vatican Codex 1342, p. 18, and again on p. 21, the same epigram is found with the heading: “Here begins the preface of the same council” (the Council of Nicaea). Mansi produced this metrical prologue from the Lucan Codex mentioned earlier, believing it not yet to have been published; but Labbe had already published it at the beginning of volume I of the *Councils*, p. 15. From the title in the manuscript codices, Labbe believed the preface to belong to the Council of Nicaea. I nevertheless think that the scribes were misled: seeing the epigram placed before the Council of Nicaea, they took it as the prologue of that council, whereas it is rather a preface to the collection of councils and decretals. The verses run as follows:

> The sacred Council founded the heights of venerable law  
> and gave us fitting reins.  
>   
> So that, well established under just governance,  
> the clerical order may be ruled while remaining undefiled.  
>   
> The supreme pontiffs, following the precepts of the ancients,  
> explained these things more plainly in their admonitions.  
>   
> Hence the path of our faith opens before us,  
> and the holy doctrines condemn all the ways of error.  
>   
> Whoever is a servant of God and a priest of Christ,  
> seasoned with this salt, will pour forth sweet honey.

For *sacrum* (“sacred”), another copy has *sacri*; for *gerens* (“bearing” or “maintaining”), another has *regens* (“ruling”); for *clericus ordo* (“the clerical order”), another has *clerus et ordo* (“the clergy and the order”); for *planius* (“more plainly”), another has *plenius* (“more fully”); for *fluet* (“will flow”), another has *fluit* (“flows”). All printed copies and manuscripts have *pontificis summi* (“of the supreme pontiff”); I restore *pontifices summi* (“the supreme pontiffs”), since the sense requires it, and nothing is more common in manuscripts than the interchange of *e* and *i*. What is said in the first verse, “the sacred Council,” is to be understood of all the councils, not of Nicaea alone.]

The Faith of Saint Gregory the Great was also added, beginning, “One God, the principle.” This is an ancient interpretation of the written creed by Saint Gregory of Neocaesarea, published after the Greek text in volume I of the *Councils*, col. 863.

In the body of the collection, under this title, two celebrated letters of Saint Cyril written to Nestorius before the Council of Ephesus are presented—letters read and inserted at that council. One of them concludes with twelve anathemas. The note of the Spanish compiler placed before these letters is reproduced in Father Labbe’s observations, volume III of the *Councils*, col. 959; the first letter appears in col. 960. Since this is the version separately published by Dionysius Exiguus, it is clear that it was taken from him.

The second letter—or rather, a fragment of a letter—begins with the words, “Accordingly, the holy and great synod says: He who is naturally born from God the Father,” etc. It was taken from an older translation, from which Saint Leo appended a lengthy testimony beginning with the same words in Letter 165, volume I of our edition, col. 1397, and in this volume, col. 291.

This is the older collection in which these two letters of Cyril are inscribed under the name of the Council of Ephesus. That it is older than the Spanish collection is clear from manuscript Codex 59 of the Verona Chapter, which contains excerpts from older Spanish copies; in these, the letters were written among the Councils of Greece under the same title of the Council of Ephesus. See what we shall note in Part IV, chapter 4.

The subscriptions of the Fathers are also appended, together with three imperial laws:

1. “To All Peoples,” beginning, “At long last,” and also found in the collection published in this volume, chapter 26.

2. “To Palladius, Praetorian Prefect,” beginning, “The divine power always,” etc. See volume IV of the *Councils*, col. 1811, note e.

3. “To the same Palladius,” beginning, “Although now the most sacred constitution,” [Col. 0716A] etc., as it will be found in our collection, chapter 28.

[Note: [Col. 0717D] Dominic López de Barrera attempted, in a special dissertation published at Rome in 1757, to demonstrate that the ancient codex of canons which he produced was the true codex of the ancient Spanish Church, arranged according to the reform of Saint Martin of Braga. Flórez discusses the collection of canons of Saint Martin of Braga at length in volume IV of *España Sagrada*, pp. 151 ff.

In the Gothic codices the title was: “Chapters collected from the synods of the Eastern Fathers by Martin, bishop of Braga, for [another reading: at] the Lucan council.” “Chapters” is correct, or, as our ancient Fathers called them, “Excerpts of Martin”; the name “collection of canons” ought not to be considered appropriate.

That there had been another collection of canons in Spain before this very collection of chapters is suggested by the First Council of Braga: “The canons both of the general synods and of the local synods were read again from the codex before the council.” This old collection was later enlarged by the addition of various materials, including the chapters or excerpts of Saint Martin of Braga.

Sentences not found in the old copies of the Councils, but inserted by some people.

These sentences are the twenty-three canons appended in the commonly printed editions to the Council of Agde, from canon 48 through canon 70.

Here it must be noted that these sentences are omitted from the body of the Vindobonensis Codex, Vatican Codex 1341, and other similar codices, although they are recorded in the preceding table of chapters under number 45. Because of this omission, the chapters of this first part ought to number only forty-four.

Since, however, the same sentences are appended in those manuscripts to the forty-seven canons of Agde—perhaps so that they would not be repeated unnecessarily under chapter 45—they were omitted from the body of the text. But since, in the table, the index of the original collection, these sentences are attached to chapter 45, we have no doubt that in the original copies they were written here in the same form in which we find them written separately in the manuscript of the more extensive Spanish collection belonging to Cardinal Passionei, and also in Vatican manuscript 4587 of Juan Bautista Pérez. The latter notes that they are read at the end of all the councils in the Lucan Codex.

García Loaysa likewise printed them from other Spanish codices after the Seventeenth Council of Toledo, and they were reprinted from him in volume VIII of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, col. 91. Compare what we shall say concerning the number of the canons of Agde in Part IV, chapter 4, no. 21.

After the table of the first part given above, the documents themselves follow. [Col. 0717C]

Then the table of the second part is presented, with 102 chapters, preceded by this shorter preface:

> “The councils of the holy Fathers having thus been arranged, the decrees of the Roman prelates will follow. The constitutions of the prelates of the aforesaid apostolic see, which pertain either to the rule of faith or to ecclesiastical discipline, have been collected in this book with diligent care. Thus, whatever decrees we have found belonging to each pontiff have been prefixed with their proper titles in the sequence of each pontiff’s letters, in the same manner in which, above, the canons of the ancient Fathers were arranged through our efforts, so that the diligence of the reader may more easily understand them when he attends to their division into their proper chapters.”

It must be noted that this table of chapters of the second part, in the manuscripts from which Father Coustant published it, as also in another similar codex, Vatican 1341, suffers from two defects.

At number 17, after the two letters of Innocent to Aurelius, it skips over another letter of the same pontiff to the same bishop, which is found in the body of those codices. The aforementioned Father Coustant, in his account of the letters of Innocent, no. 41, col. 932, lists this letter—which is Letter 12 in the edition of the *Councils*—among those forged by Pseudo-Isidore.

But we are absolutely certain that it is found in the genuine Spanish collection, which is earlier than Isidore and contains no spurious document. It exists not only in codices of Gallican origin belonging to that collection, which we shall note at no. 26 to have received a few spurious items from Isidore, but also in copies of Spanish origin that represent this collection without any spurious Isidorian addition. Such are the Vindobonensis manuscript and the other manuscripts used by Juan Bautista Pérez. From these, indeed, Pérez recorded it in the table of the same collection under number 17, as we have learned from Vatican Codex 4587.

This is confirmed above all by the ancient abridgment of the Spanish collection [Note: [Col. 0721B] Concerning the ancient abridgment of the Spanish collection indicated here by the Ballerini, it is worth noting that it is the very one also published by Cennius under the title *Codex of the Ancient Canons of the Spanish Church*. See Burriel above, chapter 40, nos. 16 and 20.

It is a canonical work divided into common titles. Cennius foolishly believed our Isidore to be its author; Juan Bautista Pérez more probably attributed it to Saint Julian of Toledo. The Ballerini show by suitable arguments that it was compiled shortly after the death of Saint Julian.

It prefaced the collection of the Lucan Codex, from which Juan Bautista Pérez transcribed it. It is also found in other Gothic codices of the Spanish collection of canons. Two such codices are inferred to be preserved in the Church of Toledo from *Palaeographia Hispana*, volume XIII of *Spectaculum Naturae*, p. 316. The older of these is marked at the beginning with this note: “This book was begun on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of February, in the era 986,” that is, in the year 948.

Hernández, as he himself had stated above, chapter 42, no. 39, had resolved to reprint such excerpts of the canons, or the more corrected canonical work, in volume II of the *Toledan Fathers*; but for some reason he did not carry out this highly useful plan.

In a document of Ferdinand I from the year 1046, volume XVI of *España Sagrada*, p. 458, mention is made of a Book of Canons in these words: “We have also selected from them whatever is found in the most holy canon and Gothic law concerning rebels or opponents of the king, or concerning their possessions, as it is established or written in the second book and its titles, or is determined to have been written by the holy Fathers of old.”

Perhaps “in the seventh book” should be read, since the index of the ancient canons of the Spanish Church contains a book “On the Honor and Affairs of Princes”; or perhaps it should rather be understood as referring to the second book of the *Forum of the Judges* and Gothic, or Visigothic, law.]

of the Spanish collection [Note: [Col. 0721D] See Part IV, chapter 5.] published by Cardinal de Aguirre, which was excerpted from genuine copies of Spanish origin.

In it the same letter is cited in Book I, title 34, in these words: “So that no one may be made a bishop contrary to the order of the canons.” The letter of Innocent is numbered 16 in full, but this must be corrected to 17, since the letter to Juliana, a noblewoman, which follows the letter to Aurelius, is marked in the same abridgment as number 18 in Book X, title 6. This is precisely the title of Letter 12 to Aurelius.

Add that it is similarly cited in another, older abridgment contained in manuscript 59 of the Verona Chapter, which we shall see in Part IV, chapter 4, to have been excerpted from Spanish codices older than the collection. For there we read:

“Also, of Innocent to Bishop Aurelius: Let hands not easily be laid on anyone. Let no one be ordained bishop from the laity.”

These sentences are contained only in that one Letter 12 to Aurelius.

Nor should the suspicion of forgery be raised by the corrupt consular notation expressed in the commonly printed copies as follows: “With Julius the Fourth and Palladius, most illustrious men, as consuls.” It must instead be corrected to: “With Junius Quartus Palladius, *vir clarissimus*, as consul,” who was the western consul of the year 416.

On the other hand, Father Coustant in his table adds among Leo’s letters to Marcian one that is absent from the collection. For from numbers 58 to 61 he lists four letters of the same pontiff to Marcian, whereas the body contains only three, and he omits one to Anatolius, which should be assigned number 58.

Correcting these errors in the table given above, we have brought the numbers of the chapters back into conformity with the sequence of the letters that are found in the collection [Col. 0722A]. These documents, meanwhile, were neither more nor fewer in the original collection than those that have been described.

## § III. On the Date, Place, and Author of This Collection
16. [Note: [Col. 0721D] I have explained in chapter 51, no. 16, how Isidore could use in the *Etymologies* the words of the preface to the collection, whose proceedings are contained in this work. For I believe that both here and elsewhere Isidore indicated, either in the margin or in the text, by abbreviations of letters, the writings from which he was drawing; copyists, through carelessness or ignorance, disregarded these abbreviations. I also suspect that the ancient preface to the collection of canons, which existed before the *Etymologies* had been completed, contained only the words quoted above by the Ballerinii: “The canons of general councils … assigned to the apocrypha.” The remaining words found in the manuscripts—“A *canon* [*canon* in Greek means “from the association of many into one”]”—I believe were added from the *Etymologies* themselves by someone who enlarged the collection after Isidore. Nor do I agree with the Ballerinii, who claim that the date of the preface and collection can clearly be placed between the year 633, when the Fourth Council of Toledo was held, and the year 636, when Isidore died. For, as I demonstrated in chapters 21 and 27, Isidore sent the book of the *Etymologies* to Braulio around the year 630; consequently, the preface to the collection already existed before that time, and Isidore inserted it into the *Etymologies*. Indeed, even if we are willing to grant—which is not clearly established—that Isidore had some part in the collection of canons, since it is otherwise evident that a certain collection existed before Isidore, there is no reason to deny that the preface we now possess in the manuscripts belonged to that earlier collection. In commenting on the words of the preface—“also adding the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, in which, as the summit of the apostolic see, there exists an authority not inferior to that of the councils”—the Ballerinii say that one should note here testimony from the Spaniards concerning the authority of the Roman pontiff. But already at the Third Council of Toledo in 589 this same authority was proclaimed, chapter 1: “Let the constitutions of all the councils remain in force, together also with the synodal letters of the Roman pontiffs.” These words perhaps refer to the preface of the Spanish collection. Before that time, Saint Martin of Dumium, in his letter to Boniface *On Triple Immersion*, wrote: “For here too I have learned more clearly that, some years ago, the metropolitan of this province requested from the very chair of the most blessed Peter a formula of absolutely certain authority concerning the institution of baptism. When I read its copy with particular care, I found it written as follows,” and so forth. He also wrote: “The priests of this province, retaining the writings received from the authority of the Roman bishop,” and toward the end: “Let them confidently hold from us what has also been handed down through the authority of the Roman see,” and so forth. I therefore believe that, after the collection of Dionysius Exiguus’s canons had reached the Spaniards, they did not delay long before enlarging and revising their ancient collection with a similar preface and certain additions.]

Since the most recent document of the original Spanish collection is the Fourth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the year 633, this collection is evidently arranged after that year. Furthermore, since almost the entire preface to its first part is found in book VI of the *Origins* of Saint Isidore of Seville, chapter 16, it may be doubtful whether the author of the preface took it from Saint Isidore, or whether Saint Isidore instead drew from the preface, just as he was accustomed to derive various materials from other authors while repeatedly suppressing their names. The latter conclusion is strongly suggested by these words, which occur both in the preface and in Isidore’s excerpt: [Col. 0722B] “The proceedings of these councils are also contained in this work.” For, as Father Coustantius correctly observed after Antonius Augustinus, these words fit a preface placed before a collection of the proceedings of councils, but not the books of the *Origins*, which reproduce no proceedings of synods. It must therefore be certain that Saint Isidore transferred that fragment of the preface into his books of the *Origins* and, when copying it, inadvertently included the words that ought to have been omitted from the work of the *Origins*.

This preface, then, together with the collection attached to it, was composed some time before Saint Isidore wrote the books of the *Origins*. Moreover, that the books of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*, were Saint Isidore’s final work, which he left unfinished at his death, is attested by Saint Braulio in his preliminary notice to those same books. Isidore died in the year 636. Thus the date of the collection can be clearly established: namely, between the year 633, when the Fourth Council of Toledo was held, and the year 636.

17. [Note: [Col. 0723C] The letter of Saint Gregory the Great to Claudius, duke of Hispania, is omitted from the old Spanish collection. The words of the preface—“which all Greece and the Latin world proclaim in the churches”—do not necessarily prove that the preface was composed after the Third Council of Toledo. They may be understood not of the creed, which, by order of this council, was sung or proclaimed aloud by the people in the churches of Spain before the Lord’s Prayer was recited, but of the Council of Constantinople itself, which the whole Church venerated, as is expressed by canon 11 of the same Third Council of Toledo: “Whoever believes that there is another faith and Catholic communion besides that of the universal Church—which we call the Church that equally holds and honors the decrees of the Councils of Nicaea, Constantinople, the First Council of Ephesus, and Chalcedon—let him be anathema.”]

It is beyond doubt that this collection, from whose preface Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, extracted the fragment mentioned above, was composed in Spain, no. 175. The older manuscripts of this collection, which come closer to its origin, are Spanish and written in the ancient Gothic script proper to the Spaniards. The distinctive Spanish notation of the era, which is appended even in several non-Spanish documents after the consular dates, openly declares its Spanish origin. What should be said of the Spanish synods with which this collection abounds? What of the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs presented in it, which were addressed to Spaniards? Here one must not omit the excellent observation of Father Coustantius in the preface to volume I of the *Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 147:

> “That he omitted none of these ancient letters which we know to have been addressed to Spaniards proves, even without his saying so, that he himself was a Spaniard. He was the first of all to publish the letters of Hilary to Ascanius of Tarragona; those of Simplicius and Felix to Zeno of Seville; two of Hormisdas to John of Ilici; one of the same pope to Salustius of Seville, another to the bishops of Baetica; two others likewise to the bishops of Spain, sent together with John of Constantinople’s little book; and finally those of Vigilius to Profuturus of Braga. Does he not also reveal himself as a Spaniard when, from Gregory’s letters—which we possess in almost innumerable numbers—he presents only four: namely, three to Leander of Seville and one to Reccared, king of the Goths, while leaving aside the others because they were not addressed to Spaniards?”

Finally, that passage of the preface which states that the faith of the Constantinopolitan creed is proclaimed by all Greece and the Latin world [Col. 0723C] “in the churches” openly shows that the author of the preface and attached collection was a Spaniard. Seeing that what the Third Council of Toledo had ordered to be done throughout all the churches of Spain by its first canon had already been adopted there in his own time, he believed it to be equally customary in all Latin churches. Certainly, since such a practice was accepted by the other Westerners only later, as Father Coustantius demonstrated in no. 139, no one but a Spaniard could have inserted that statement into the preface. From this falls the opinion of Peter de Marca, who in his *Opuscula*, p. 201, considered this collection to have been edited after Chalcedon through Leo’s authority and to have been common to the Western churches.

18. [Note: [Col. 0723D] There is certainly no difficulty in the fact that Saint Isidore inserted the preface of the book of canons into his *Etymologies*, even though he himself is believed to have been the author of the preface. But, from another consideration, there is no argument by which we can conclude that he composed the preface himself or had it composed by someone else at his command. Since the book of canons already existed, it could have been furnished with this very preface. The fact that the final documents of this collection are the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo does indeed show that a copy of the ancient collection, enlarged after the year 633—whether by Isidore or by someone else—was circulated, and that the table of chapters consequently passed into other, still more expanded copies. Pseudo-Isidore, however, assumed the name of Isidore of Seville either because this name was especially famous among the Spaniards, or because, having established the old Spanish collection as the supposed soil and foundation of his fiction, he found in it that the last synod was the Second Council of Seville, over which Isidore presided and subscribed first. Once that synod was completed, there immediately follows a brief preface to the decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs: “The councils of the holy Fathers having thus been arranged, the decrees of the Roman pontiffs will follow [*Al.*, “followed”] … as many decrees as we have found should be prefixed, under the sequence of each letter, with their proper titles, in the same way in which the canons of the ancient Fathers were arranged earlier through our labor.” Nothing was more natural than that the architect of the Pseudo-Isidorian collection, living in the Franco-Gallic realm, should believe that the Fathers of the Second Council of Seville, and especially Isidore, who presided over it, had organized the old Spanish collection which he himself had decided to interpolate. But whether there was formerly a tradition, before the Pseudo-Isidorian collection was fabricated, that Isidore had devoted his efforts to arranging the canons cannot be gathered from any ancient documents.]

It is now permissible to conjecture about the Spanish author. Antonius Augustinus, in his *Judgment and Censure concerning Certain Ancient Collectors of Ecclesiastical Canons*, testifies that some people in Spain attributed this book of canons to Saint Isidore of Seville. Two matters, however, may create difficulty here.

1. Saint Braulio, in his preliminary notice to the books of the *Origins*, and Saint Ildefonsus, *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 9, who both compile catalogues of Saint Isidore’s works, make no mention of this collection.

2. Since a considerable part of the preface attached to this collection was transferred into the books of the *Origins*, it seems incredible that Saint Isidore, who excerpted no small amount from other writers, should also have copied something from his own preface.

Nevertheless, since the more recent documents of this collection correspond especially closely to Saint Isidore’s lifetime—namely, the Second Council of Seville of 619 and the Fourth Council of Toledo of 633, over which he presided—it is not unreasonable that its author was long believed to be Saint Isidore himself. This is also inferred from Gratian, who attributes a fragment of the preface, in the first part of the collection, to Isidore, *Distinction* 16, chapter 1. Certainly, if it was not Isidore himself, at least someone appears to have compiled the collection at his command. For this reason Pseudo-Isidore, who incorporated this collection into his own, appropriated Isidore’s name and attached to his preface the title “of Saint Isidore, bishop,” because tradition had represented the collection as having been arranged either by Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, or under his direction.

That there were older books of canons, and that they were read at earlier Spanish councils, is clear from § 1, no. 10. Since some things were lacking in them, and perhaps what they did contain was not entirely organized but confused, the idea occurred to Saint Isidore of reviewing, enlarging, and reducing the old books to a better form. The fourth canon of the Fourth Council of Toledo may have provided him with both the occasion and the stimulus, for that canon prescribed the following general rule for the celebration of councils: while all sat silently in their proper places, a deacon dressed in a white garment was to bring the book of canons into the midst and announce the chapters concerning the business of the councils.

177 § IV. — Concerning the additions that were subsequently made to the original Spanish collection. The documents attached to the more extensive Spanish collection after the Second Council of Constantinople, otherwise called the Sixth General Council, are vindicated. [Col. 0725A]

19. [Note: [Col. 0725D] I believe that additions of this kind were made in the ancient copies themselves, and sometimes through the private efforts of particular individuals. Hence the old table always remained, while later copyists copied the old books as they found them; consequently, some copies are more extensive than others and present a different order.]

Having thus written about the original Spanish collection, we must now explain the additions that were subsequently inserted into it. The older additions are found in the very ancient Vindobonensis manuscript 41 and others like it. After the beginning of the First Council of Braga, which is listed as no. 40 in the table given above, these manuscripts insert, without any number and outside their proper place, nine Councils of Toledo—namely, the Fifth and the subsequent councils through the Thirteenth, held in the year 683. They then repeat the First Council of Braga and give it in full. After the chapters of Martin of Braga they add another Council of Braga, from the year 675, and append the remaining materials listed in the cited table of the original collection.

Since such manuscripts, which contain the Councils of Toledo collected with greater care, include the later Thirteenth Council of Toledo of 683 but lack the Fourteenth Council of Toledo, celebrated in the following year, 684, it appears certain that these additions entered the first example of this type shortly after the Thirteenth Council of Toledo itself and before the Fourteenth was held.

20. [Note: [Col. 0725D] Copies of the old Spanish collection were enlarged not only by the addition of councils held after Saint Isidore, but also by the insertion of other, older documents that had been overlooked by ancient collectors or had escaped their diligence—much as now happens when collections of councils published in print become more extensive over time. The example of the Spanish collection of canons that once belonged to Cardinal Passionei, as I have already indicated, is now preserved in Rome, together with his other manuscript books, in the Angelica Library.]

This collection subsequently received new additions, which appear in the manuscripts consulted by Antonius Augustinus, in the Lucense copy praised by Perezius, in the book of the Church of Urgell, and in several others. In these, however, all the synods of each city are described together, in sequence, with a continuous series of numbers.

Among the Greek councils, after the First Council of Constantinople, the Second Council of Constantinople is added, dated to the Spanish era 720, together with five letters relating to it: one by Leo II to the Spanish bishops; another by the same pope to Quiricus; a third by him to Simplicius the count; a fourth by Benedict, the presbyter elected after Leo, to Peter the regional notary; and a fifth by the aforementioned Leo II to King Ervig.

Among the Gallican councils, the Second Council of Vaison, held in 529, is appended to the First Council of Vaison. After the First Council of Orléans, another, held in 533, is described, together with five further Gallican documents: the Council of Epaon of 517, the Council of Carpentras of 527, the First Council of Clermont of 535, a letter from the same Council of Clermont to King Theudebert, and the Second Council of Clermont of 549. Since the latter, however, has the same preface and the same canons as the Fifth Council of Orléans, Perezius rightly observed that it should instead be called the Fifth Council of Orléans.

Among the Spanish councils, after the Fourth Council of Toledo, thirteen further councils of the same city are appended in order, likewise distinguished by their own numbers, from the Fifth through the Seventeenth, which was convened in the year 694. After the two Councils of Seville, the Council of Mérida of 666 is added. Nor are the *Sentences* omitted, although they are absent from the older copies of the councils. Thus the chapters of this part in these manuscripts number 68; see their sequence in part IV, chapter 5, no. 3.

The Vatican Palatine manuscript 575 agrees with these manuscripts, although it is incomplete and its order is confused. So does Cardinal Passionei’s manuscript copy, which, because it is mutilated, lacks the councils of Greece and Africa and, among the Gallican councils, breaks off after the two Councils of Vaison and that of Agde.

These manuscripts also append to the Second Council of Toledo [Col. 0725D] two letters of Montanus, bishop of Toledo: one to the brothers and sons of the territory of Palencia, the other to Turribius. To the Third Council of Toledo they add a homily of Saint Leander, bishop, delivered after the canons had been established, on account of the conversion of the people, along with several other items.

In the second part, after the letters of Saint Gregory, which close the original collection, they add at no. 103 the *Decrees of the Roman See concerning the books to be received and not received*, issued by Pope Hormisdas. It is the decree concerning the apocrypha, which in published editions of the councils is attributed to Gelasius; see part II, chapter 11, § 5.

21. This more extensive collection, whose latest document is the Seventeenth Council of Toledo of 694, was used by the author of the *Breviary*, or index, of the Spanish collection of canons; we shall say more about him in part IV, chapter 5. For the numbers of the chapters under which the documents of that collection are cited there correspond exactly to the numbers found in this more extensive collection.

This is the *Corpus of Canons* that Alexander III called authentic, as is evident from these words of Innocent III in letter 121 to Peter of Compostela, book II:

> “He established by many arguments that the Council of Mérida was authentic: first, because it is contained together with the other councils in the book called the *Corpus of Canons*, which Pope Alexander, by an interlocutory judgment, called authentic; and then because …”

The Council of Mérida is described only in the aforementioned more extensive collection. All its documents are genuine, and the collection is free of every spurious document.

Someone might raise a difficulty concerning the Second Council of Constantinople, which, as it is presented there, led some people—especially after the great Baronius—to suspect it, particularly because of the letters appended to it. The Constantinopolitan synod that is called the Second in this collection is the Sixth General Council, held at Constantinople against the Monothelites. It is called the Second Council of Constantinople because of the order of the collection, in which it immediately follows the First Council of Constantinople; or because the Fifth Synod was unknown to the Spaniards. For this reason, at the Fourteenth Council of Toledo it was decreed that this Constantinopolitan synod—the Sixth General Council—should be accepted after Chalcedon and inserted into the book in its proper order.

Not all the proceedings of that synod were sent to the Spaniards, but only the definition of faith, the acclamations of the bishops—also called the *prosphoneticus*—and the imperial edict concerning the faith. For at the beginning the entire proceedings were not translated, but only the principal sections, just as we have seen happen with the Council of Chalcedon as well, volume II, col. 1218; these were rendered into Latin and sent to Spain, as Leo II states in his letter to the Spanish bishops. The bishops declare in the aforementioned Council of Toledo that they learned the entire order of the proceedings and the proceedings in their proper sequence from this letter, not from a translation of the whole synod.

Only the definition belonging to session 17 of the Sixth General Council was inserted into the enlarged book of canons. If the Constantinopolitan Council held in the years 680 and 681 is assigned in the same book the Spanish era 720, which corresponds to the year 682, this must be attributed to an error by the collector, who, from the chronological notes transmitted with the definition of the council, was entirely unable to determine the true year.

It is objected that Leo II’s letters state that the council was held in the ninth indiction, whereas the acts of the final sessions, 17 and 18, bear the tenth indiction. But although among the Greeks the tenth indiction began in September of the year 681, Leo chose to use the tenth indiction that was still running among the Romans.

Nor should one be troubled by the fact that, in the letter of the same pontiff to King Ervig—a letter appended in the manuscripts to Benedict’s letter, which Loaisa wrongly attributed to Benedict, contrary to the evidence of our manuscripts—it is written that the emperor sent letters to Agatho concerning the convening of the synod, whereas he had sent them to Domnus. Since those same letters, written to Domnus, were brought to Rome after his death and handed over to Agatho, his successor, Leo could write that they had been addressed to Agatho.

There is therefore no serious objection to believing that these documents, belonging to the seventh century, were sent to the Spaniards and were added by the Spaniards to this most ancient Spanish collection toward the end of that century or at the beginning of the eighth, and that they are genuine. Thus Alexander III was right to declare this body of canons, enlarged by these and other additions, authentic.

22. [Note: [Col. 0727D] The reason why certain documents appear in some copies and are absent from others must be sought in the fact that, as I said, additions to the collection were ordinarily made by private individuals in their own books, and one person could obtain more councils than another. For the proceedings of councils were not sent to all bishops. Braulio asks Isidore in a letter: “O pious lord, I beg you to have the proceedings of the synod in which Sintharius, though not purified by the fire of your examination, is nevertheless found to have been melted down, sent to us quickly through your influence by your son, our lord the king. For our petition also sought his glory in this matter, since much is needed in the council for the investigation of the truth.” We know, of course, that many councils were formerly held whose proceedings did not reach us. Why, then, should we be surprised that the proceedings of some are found in certain books but not in others?]

The manuscript of Saint Aemilianus, mentioned by Perezius, supplied other particular documents concerning the Spanish councils: namely, the Second Council of Zaragoza of 592 and the Third of 691; two Councils of Barcelona, one around the year 540 and the other in 599; the Council of Huesca of 598; the Council of Egara of 614; two Councils of Toledo distinct from the seventeen already mentioned—one held in the twelfth year of King Reccared, that is, in the year 597, and the other under Gundemar in 610; the law of King Chintila, which confirmed the Fifth Council of Toledo; and the Council of Narbonne of 589.

The Council of Narbonne was inserted among the Spanish councils because at that time the province of Narbonne was subject to the Gothic rulers reigning in Spain, was one of the six provinces of Spain, and the metropolitan of Narbonne with his suffragans attended and subscribed the Spanish councils.

Stephen Baluzius, in the preface to his new collection of councils, no. 13, writes: “John Baptist Perezius raises suspicion about the falsity of two Councils of Toledo, namely the one said to have been held under King Gundemar and the other under Reccared, as is clear from his second preface to the Councils sent to Rome.” But Perezius’s words raise no suspicion of falsity. He merely expresses surprise that these councils were not listed with their proper numbers and in their proper places together with the others, and he tries to conjecture why this happened:

> “Moreover, it is more doubtful to me why this council held under Gundemar and the other Council of Toledo in the twelfth year of Reccared, also described here by us, were not included in the number of the Councils of Toledo, since by chronological order they ought to have been called the fourth and fifth. That number is regularly assigned to the councils that follow. Nor can anyone claim that the numbers were added to the Councils of Toledo in our own time, since we learn from chapter 9 of the Thirteenth Council of Toledo that the Goths used the same numbering: what we call the twelfth is there plainly also called the twelfth. Nor is it plausible that these two councils were unknown to later Goths, given how recent they were. Thus the reason is not yet clear to me, unless perhaps their brevity and small size prevented them from being included in the numbering of the greater councils.”

The testimony of the cited manuscript of Saint Aemilianus is reinforced by another much older collection, or abbreviation of an earlier collection, contained in the manuscript of Verona, about which we shall speak in part IV, chapter 4. Four of the councils mentioned are listed there: the Second Council of Zaragoza, the First Council of Barcelona, the Council of Huesca, and the Council of Narbonne.

Likewise, the Second Council of Zaragoza was found in another manuscript, the Alveldense, written by the priest Vigila. The Council of Toledo under King Gundemar was also found both in that same Alveldense manuscript and in another from Soria, as Perezius testifies in his second preface.

Finally, in that same manuscript of Saint Aemilianus one finds a letter of Turribius, later bishop of Astorga, to Idacius and Ceponius; the renunciation of the Priscillianist heresy made by the bishops Dictinius and Symphosius; and the judgment of the First Council of Toledo concerning whether communion should be restored to or withheld from certain bishops.

We defended these documents, which Ambrosius Morales had published from the same manuscript of Saint Aemilianus and which Baluzius and others had called into question, in volume I, col. 1475, and more fully in volume II, col. 1376 and following.

181 § V. — A notable distinction between manuscripts of Spanish origin and those of Gallican origin.

23. It is of the greatest importance to distinguish two classes of manuscripts of this collection: some are of Spanish origin, others of Gallican origin. We call those manuscripts of Spanish origin which are more common in Spain, or which were carried from Spain to other regions, and which represent the pure Spanish collection.

There are, however, other manuscripts which, although they contain the same collection, differ considerably from that exhibited by the pure manuscripts in two respects: first, because of quite a few readings corrected by conjecture, which are very far from the true reading; and second, because of certain added chapters, or even entire documents, not found in the pure copies of the same collection.

We call these manuscripts of Gallican origin because all those that we have found to belong to this class are more common in Gaul, while those existing elsewhere came from Gaul; consequently, their origin appears to be attributable to Gaul.

Such are Vatican manuscript 1341, which we have seen belonged to the Church of Autun, and the three Gallican manuscripts mentioned by Father Coustantius—the Laon, Beauvais, and Noyon manuscripts—which, as is perfectly clear from the observations of Coustantius himself, agree entirely with the aforementioned Vatican manuscript.

These manuscripts contain neither the original shorter collection nor the enlarged Spanish collection that we explained in no. 20. Rather, they contain the collection with the additions listed in no. 19, such as we find in the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin.

[Note: [Col. 0728D] From this one can see the great benefit that would result if the Spanish collection preserved in the Gothic manuscripts of Spain were published in print. For the arbitrary corrections in the collection of Gallican origin could, by comparing the manuscripts with one another, be restored to the true reading. The Spanish councils themselves, which Loaisa corrected, could still be greatly assisted even by the variant readings alone that John Baptist Perezius sent to Rome and which seem also to have been neglected by Aguirre.]

24. As regards the arbitrary corrections by which the manuscripts of Gallican origin differ chiefly from those of Spanish origin, when preparing the edition of Saint Leo’s letters we took care to collate both the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin and Vatican manuscript 1341 of Gallican origin. We discovered that the Vindobonensis contained several erroneous and corrupt readings which, in the cited Vatican manuscript, had been corrected so as to yield an appropriate sense.

If nothing else had been available to us, we would have believed these corrected readings to be the genuine readings of Saint Leo. But since we had other copies of the same letters from different and even older collections, which had preserved the true Leonine readings consistently, we learned that the erroneous readings of the Vindobonensis manuscript of Spanish origin more often approached those true readings, whereas the corrections presented in the Vatican copy departed from them considerably.

It is therefore clear that some ancient Gallican scholar, who had undertaken to copy the Spanish collection from a manuscript of Spanish origin as faulty as the Vindobonensis, corrected those erroneous readings with excessive freedom and according to his own judgment, introducing new readings that differ from all the other manuscripts.

We could provide many such examples from Leo’s letters. But since we have noted them in their proper places in volume I, and they are indicated together in the index to that volume, col. 1539, under the heading “Spanish Collection,” we refer readers there.

There is no doubt that the freedom used by that scholar in the letters of Leo was also used in the other documents, which in the manuscripts of Spanish origin, such as the Vindobonensis and similar copies, contain many frequent errors.

This is evident from the edition of the councils by Severinus Binius, in which the Spanish councils are presented in two editions: one from the previously published edition and the other from the edition of García Loaisa. The published edition derives from Isidore, who transferred the Spanish collection into his own work from manuscripts of Gallican origin. Loaisa’s edition, however, was prepared according to manuscripts of Spanish origin.

The notable variety of readings visible in that published edition must be attributed to the arbitrary corrections of an ancient copyist who, while transcribing a faulty Spanish exemplar, believed that he ought to correct it on his own authority. Loaisa, however, happened to find purer and more accurate Spanish copies, from which his edition is free of the errors found in the Vindobonensis and similar manuscripts.

The exemplar used by that first Gallican copyist who corrected the Spanish collection was either the Vindobonensis itself [Note: [Col. 0729D] Thus, in the Vindobonensis and likewise in the aforementioned manuscripts of Gallican origin, once the First Council of Braga has scarcely begun and is immediately broken off, nine Councils of Toledo, from the Fifth through the Thirteenth, are inserted; then the First Council of Braga is again appended, this time in full.] or another manuscript similar to the Vindobonensis, whose frequent errors provided the occasion for so many arbitrary corrections.

Two indications show us that these freer corrections were introduced by the learned man into some manuscript before the publication of the Isidorian collection:

1. We find the same corrections already received in the Herovallian collection, which we shall see in part IV, chapter 7, to be earlier than the Isidorian collection.

2. When Isidore transferred the Spanish collection into his own, he copied its documents with the same corrections.

25. In this matter I should also point out that Isidore Mercator is credited with corrupting the heading of Pope Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus. In his collection and in the aforementioned Gallican copies of the Spanish collection, the letter is addressed to Eutherius, although in the table of those same manuscripts given above it is said to have been addressed to Profuturus.

In fact, the reading “to Eutherius” was introduced by that earlier copyist who corrected the erroneous readings of the Spanish manuscript. In the Vindobonensis the faulty title reads in the body of the text: *Epistula Vigilii papae ad Futurum episcopum* (“The letter of Pope Vigilius to Futurus, bishop”); and in the heading: *Dilectissimo fratri Futuro Vigilius* (“Vigilius to his most beloved brother Futurus”).

Since the form *Futuro* referred to an unfamiliar name, it was easy to read it as *Euturo* and correct it to *Eutherius*. Thus, when Isidore copied the manuscript of Gallican origin, he did not change the name Profuturus, but transferred into his own collection the reading that he found corrected in that manuscript.

[Col. 0729D] **26.** Again, after Isidore, hands were laid upon this same Hispanic collection of Gallican origin. For, besides the readings emended arbitrarily—which we have seen to be earlier than the Isidorian collection—the Codices mentioned received certain additions, partly genuine and partly apocryphal, which are recognizable as having been taken from Isidore’s collection.

> **[Note: [Col. 0729D]]** It is by no means necessary that we settle upon one particular pseudo-Isidore as the author of all the apocryphal documents found in the pseudo-Isidorian collection. Just as some Gallican added arbitrary emendations to the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin, so this man or another could have appended false documents, whether fabricated by himself or taken from elsewhere. Pseudo-Isidore, as I think, found the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin already enlarged in the form in which it is now found in manuscripts; he himself undertook further to enlarge and interpolate it, and to arrange it in some fashion by means of a preface and suitable indexes.

First, before the preface, there are placed not only the annotations concerning synods, the booklet on the provinces, and the description of Gaul, which likewise precede Isidore’s collection, but also an *Order for Celebrating a Council*, which Isidore testifies in his preface that he inserted into his Codex. Then, after the table of the first part, the Apostolic Canons were intruded—canons which the author of the Hispanic collection rejected in his preface as apocryphal. In Vatican Codex 1341 these same canons are indicated at the beginning of the prefixed table, but without a number—for the numbering of the chapters begins with the Nicene canons—which confirms that these canons are additions in these Codices.

They seem, however, to have been added from the manuscripts of Isidore Mercator, who first joined these canons with the other documents of the Hispanic collection. In the second part, which begins with two letters of Damasus, three letters drawn from Isidore’s spurious wares were intermingled with another letter of this pontiff: one from Archbishop Stephen and three councils to Pope Damasus; another from Damasus to the same Stephen and to the councils of Africa; and a third from the same Damasus to the bishops of Numidia. These letters have been interwoven with the same genuine letters of Damasus, divided into sections, in such a way that we shall discuss the matter more distinctly in the Isidorian collection, chapter 6, § V.

It is surprising that the person who added these three spurious letters under Damasus abstained from several others supplied from the same Isidorian source under the following pontiffs. Only in the letters of Vigilius to Profuturus did he append from Isidore two chapters, the sixth and seventh, which are absent from the pure Hispanic Codices. Finally, from the genuine documents he added at the end, contrary to the evidence of the table and of all the Codices of Hispanic origin, the decree—or Roman council—of Gregory the Younger, together with seventeen anathemas and the subscriptions of the bishops, which seems to have been taken from the same Isidore.

Except for these few additions, partly supposititious and partly genuine, the Codices of Gallican origin mentioned present, in the rest of the collection, the enlarged form of the Hispanic collection that receives, in the Vindobonensis manuscript of Hispanic origin, nine councils of Toledo and the Council of Braga of the year 675, added to the primitive collection.

Hence the scribe of the first exemplar from which the four Codices of Gallican origin mentioned—that is, Vatican 1341, the Laon, Beauvais, and Noyon Codices—derive, had two exemplars before his eyes: one of the Hispanic collection, more freely emended, from which he copied it likewise emended; and one of Isidore, from which he selected those additions.

If, of the three letters of Saint Gregory the Great to Leander indicated in the preceding table, the Codices of Gallican origin mentioned exhibit only two—for they omit the second—this must either be attributed to an omission by the first scribe from whom such Codices derive, or at least to the fact that this scribe used a Codex of Hispanic origin in which a similar scribal omission had occurred through the copyist’s negligence. This defect of the Codices of Gallican origin must be kept in mind because of what we shall say about Isidore in chapter 6.

**27.** We believe that one point must be noted here. If all the Codices of the Hispanic collection of Gallican origin were of the same character as Vatican 1341 and the other three reviewed and cited by Father Coustant, so that they all exhibited, besides the freer emendations, the indicated additions excerpted from Isidore, and if it were impossible to find even one free from these additions and distinguished only by the freer emendations—which we leave to those who are able to discover and collate more such exemplars in Gaul—then a strong suspicion would arise that Isidore Mercator himself, whom we shall see to have been a Gaul, was perhaps the author of these exemplars of Gallican origin. In copying a Codex of Hispanic origin, he would have emended it according to his own judgment and enlarged it with the additions indicated, both genuine and supposititious, before arranging his collection, filled with numerous impostures, into which he inserted the Hispanic collection after he had already emended it himself.

Nevertheless, caution will be necessary in deciding this matter, especially if certain earlier Isidorian collections, such as the Herovallian, received from some Codices of Hispanic origin and Gallican provenance only a number of arbitrary emendations and none of the additions just reviewed.

## § VI.—On those who edited or emended documents from the Codices of the Hispanic collection, and especially on John Baptist Perez

**28.** The first edition of the documents of the Hispanic collection is that of Merlin, which, since it derives from a Codex of Isidore, presents the same documents received by Isidore, together with the readings of the Codices of Gallican origin that Isidore used. Consequently, the readings of this edition that were repeated in the commonly used editions of the Councils ought to be regarded with suspicion, because they contain the freer emendations indicated in § 24.

To distinguish and restore the genuine readings of the Hispanic collection, it would be necessary to collate the Codices that preserve Hispanic origin. The first person to undertake highly useful work in this matter was John Baptist Perez. When Gregory XIII was searching everywhere for ancient exemplars of the canons and decretals, either to copy or to collate them for the edition and emendation of Gratian’s books, and learned that the finest Codices of this kind were to be found in Spain, he entrusted the task to Gaspar Quiroga, then bishop of Cuenca, later archbishop of Toledo and cardinal: he was to arrange for those Codices to be collated with the printed texts, especially as regards the Hispanic councils, and for unpublished material to be transcribed from them.

Quiroga entrusted this work to his very learned associate, John Baptist Perez, who later became a canon and head of the library of the Church of Toledo, and subsequently bishop of Segorbe. Because of the shortness of time, Perez used one Lucensis manuscript—which seemed the oldest and richest of all—and occasionally two others.

> **[Note: [Col. 0731D]]** This celebrated Lucensis Codex, transferred to the Escorial library, is believed to have been burned in 1671. Various readings from it concerning the councils of Spain, collected by Perez, remain in the Vatican Library, as does an accurate description of the same Codex with an index, prepared by Juan Vázquez del Mármol. See Flórez, vol. IV of *España Sagrada*, p. 152. He emended five hundred significant passages in the councils mentioned, transcribed six unpublished synods and many fragments from others, and also copied an abridgment or index of the canons of the Hispanic collection, of which we shall speak in Part IV, chapter 5.

All this was written and sent to the pontiff in 1575 in the book preserved among the Vatican manuscripts under number 4887. From this manuscript we shall append at the end of this chapter Quiroga’s letter to Gregory XIII, Perez’s preface, and another special note by Perez, all of which will be useful for several matters.

When this first work pleased the Roman pontiff, and Perez, having been most generously rewarded for this excellent labor, was encouraged to undertake the other tasks he had promised, in the following year, 1576, he transcribed other Hispanic synods not yet printed, chiefly from the Codex of Saint Aemilianus. He also arranged with the greatest accuracy the chronology of the councils of Spain, later printed by Cardinal de Aguirre, in another book. From this book there will be found both another letter of Quiroga to the pontiff and Perez’s preface to the reader, after Stephen Baluzius’s preface to the *New Edition of the Councils*, and thereafter in Apparatus I to Labbe’s Venetian edition of the Councils, columns 48 and 49.

Perez had also sent a copy of one of these two books to Antonio Agustín, then bishop of Lérida and designated archbishop of Tarragona, as we learn from two letters of Agustín to Perez, published by Cardinal de Aguirre in volume IV of the *Councils of Spain*, pages 650 and 651 of the Roman edition of 1692. These books subsequently passed into the library of the distinguished Gaspar Mendoza Ibáñez, Marquis of Mondéjar and Count of Tendilla, who later communicated them to Stephen Baluzius and eventually presented them as a gift to the aforementioned Cardinal de Aguirre.

**29.** The Roman correctors of Gratian made use of these distinguished labors of Perez when they emended several passages on the authority of the Lucensis Codex. Cardinal Baronius, and Binius following him, published the Council of Narbonne of the year 589 as it had been copied in the second volume of Perez from the Codex of Saint Aemilianus.

In 1593, Garcia Loaisa, of the Order of Preachers, tutor of Philip III, king of Spain, and later archbishop of Toledo, used in his edition of the Councils of Spain nearly the same Codices that Perez had used.

> **[Note: [Col. 0732D]]** The learned Ballerini brothers mistakenly called Garcia Loaisa a member of the Order of Preachers. That Loaisa did not profit from Perez’s books is shown above all by the fact that he seems wholly to have ignored many variant readings noted by Perez—readings by no means contemptible, and in some cases necessarily to be introduced into the text.

[Col. 0732B] Some suspect that Loaisa benefited from Perez’s books. But several indications clearly show us that he had not seen them. If he had examined them, he would hardly have asserted in his preface that the Lucensis Codex had been copied and sent to Rome, since Perez did not copy the whole Codex in the books he sent to Rome, but only the variants and the unpublished material from the councils of Spain.

Moreover, of the four principal Codices praised by Perez, Loaisa recognized only three; among them he called one the Hispalensis, although he would more correctly have called it Saint Aemilianus had he read Perez. We pass over other observations, since these two points sufficiently clear Loaisa of the charge of plagiarism.

If his edition agrees in many respects with Perez’s books, this is not surprising, since both used the same Hispanic Codices. Thus only the councils of Spain can be said to have been emended or edited from Codices of Hispanic origin. The rest are councils of Greece, Africa, and Gaul, which, having been published from Isidore—or from Codices of Gallican origin—lack the readings of exemplars of Hispanic origin. In addition, most of the decretal letters of the pontiffs, contained in the second part of the Hispanic collection, still await the same assistance. We have applied this diligence to the letters of Leo. Others have published genuine readings, both in the remaining councils and in the letters of the pontiffs, from other collections and exemplars of the best quality. But the readings of the Codices of Hispanic origin, from which the genuine text of this collection might be established, are still lacking in most cases.

**30.** We must now append from Vatican manuscript 4887 the materials that we previously received.

### Letter of Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca, to Gregory XIII

> “To our most holy lord Gregory XIII, supreme pontiff: Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca, after most humbly kissing his feet, offers greeting.
>
> “Since the Catholic Church daily receives many benefits from the solicitude of Your Holiness—benefits that will consecrate the name of Your Beatitude to immortality—I think that nothing will be more illustrious in the eyes of all posterity than your undertaking to purify the sources of canon law, that is, the collection of Gratian and the letters of the Roman pontiffs.
>
> “For since almost the entire discipline of ecclesiastical government rests upon the authority of these books; since no books are more constantly in everyone’s hands or more frequently cited in the schools, we heard with no small embarrassment that they were filled with innumerable errors, contracted either through the faults of an unlearned age or through the negligence of printers.
>
> “The great solicitude with which Your Holiness is arranging for the correction of these books is sufficiently attested by the fact that you have established in Rome a congregation of highly learned men for this very purpose, and that you search everywhere for ancient exemplars or order copies made from them to be brought to you.
>
> “When Your Holiness heard that several ancient Codices of the councils existed in Spain in the library of Saint Laurence, which the Catholic King Philip is day by day furnishing with books of every kind with no less zeal than that Ptolemy called Philadelphus, Your Holiness immediately instructed me, by an Apostolic Brief sent concerning the matter, to arrange for a certain book of canons to be copied from those Codices, for the councils to be collated with the printed texts, and for the result to be sent to Your Beatitude.
>
> “I immediately began this work, out of my devotion to Your Holiness and to the Apostolic See, and at last, with God’s help, I have brought it to completion. Because of my very numerous occupations, I made considerable use of the assistance of my household servant, the learned young man John Baptist Perez, who was highly practiced in this branch of letters; and, unless I am mistaken, he has displayed outstanding faithfulness and diligence in this work.
>
> “I now humbly ask Your Holiness graciously to accept this evidence of my devotion and my supreme eagerness to obey, and frequently, in accordance with your right, to command me to perform whatever you see that I am able to undertake. May Almighty God preserve Your Beatitude safe and sound for His Church for as long as possible.
>
> “Madrid, 18 March 1575.”

### Preface of John Baptist Perez to Volume I of the Collations, which he sent to Rome after copying them in the aforementioned Vatican manuscript 4887

> **“The Copyist of These Collations to the Reader**
>
> “My most reverend lord Gaspar Quiroga, bishop of Cuenca and general inquisitor throughout Spain, having been ordered by our most holy lord Gregory XIII to arrange for the collation of the councils of Spain, selected me from among his other servants to entrust this work to me.
>
> “Although I know that I have not fulfilled this duty adequately to its dignity, whoever you are who reads these pages will nevertheless not entirely disapprove of my faithfulness and diligence in it.
