But in order that you may know what this volume contains and what has been done by me, it is necessary that I first say a few words here.
>
> “I shall not now labor to explain how much usefulness ancient manuscript Codices bring to preserving the pure sources of every discipline, since so many books of corrections published by learned men of our own age have already demonstrated this, with great benefit to scholarship.
>
> “Nor will anyone deny the immense advantages of this labor unless he is so blind that he cannot see that all later copies, when repeatedly made from a single exemplar, continually deteriorate, or so witless that he loves daylight no more than darkness and thinks it makes no difference whether something is affirmed or denied.
>
> “If such diligence is praised in restoring Cicero, Galen, or Aristotle, it ought to be praised much more highly when applied to ecclesiastical books and to the canonical decrees of councils and Roman pontiffs, whose authority is surpassed only by that of the books of Holy Scripture.
>
> “There are indeed throughout Spain many very ancient Codices of the councils, all written in Gothic letters, which could provide especially great assistance in correcting these councils. For besides the four ancient Codices preserved in the royal library of Saint Laurence, built by the zeal of the Catholic King Philip—and of which I shall speak before the Council of Elvira—and two in the Church of Toledo, many others still exist in ancient churches, such as those at Oviedo and Urgell, and in the monasteries of Saint Facundus, Saint Zoilus, Saint Peter of Montes, Oña, and perhaps others unknown to me.
>
> “If someone were to consult all these Codices, it is astonishing how much light they would bring to the councils. For my part, in these collations of the councils I used almost exclusively one Lucensis Codex, both because I was pressed by haste and because this Codex seemed to my lord bishop the oldest and most complete. I did occasionally use two others, but only in a few passages, as I attest in the corrections themselves.
>
> “If I emended five hundred significant passages in the Hispanic councils from a single book, what, one might ask, would have been the result if I had used the remaining Codices, and had collated not only the Hispanic councils but also the Greek, African, and Gallican councils?
>
> “Moreover, if from this Codex I added six councils not yet printed—namely, the five later Councils of Toledo and one of Mérida—and many fragments from others, how great an addition would there have been if I had added from the Codex of Saint Aemilianus what it contains: three Councils of Toledo, one under Gundemar, another in the twelfth year of Reccared, and another in the first year of Chintila; also the second and third Councils of Zaragoza, two of Barcelona, and the Councils of Huesca and Egara, all of them Hispanic?
>
> “I omit those later than the devastation of Spain, though ancient nevertheless: the Compostellan, Leonese, Valladolid, Coyanza, and many others of this kind that we possess. But reserving all these matters for another time and volume, let us now discuss this volume of ours, which is in hand and in which the following materials have been copied by us.
>
> “First, we transcribed from the Lucensis Codex a book entitled *Excerpts of the Canons*—for this title appeared on each page—although the same work is also found in other ancient Codices of the councils, such as the Vigilian and Ovetan Codices.
>
> “This work is a collection, or index, of all the canons contained in councils or in letters of the Roman pontiffs up to that time. It is arranged not alphabetically but by common topics, with the several classes of subject matter distributed among them. As far as I know, nothing has yet been established concerning its author.
>
> “It is certainly older than Burchard, Ivo, and Gratian, who arranged canon law by common topics. That it is not by Isidore is shown by the fact that the Councils of Toledo are repeatedly cited in it down to the twelfth, whereas it is certain that Isidore died before the Sixth Council of Toledo.
>
> “But if I may speak conjecturally, I would rather attribute it to Julian, archbishop of Toledo, who flourished at that time and presided over four Councils of Toledo with great renown for learning. This is indicated by his three works already printed, namely the *Prognostics*, *Against the Jews*, and *Antikimena*, besides the others enumerated by his successor Felix. Felix also reveals that Julian played with verse, so that one may even suspect that the poems prefixed to some books of this work were composed by him.
>
> “As for the fact that these poems are empty and composed only of bombast, that defect may reasonably be forgiven in so crude an age.
>
> “The reader should be warned that where it is repeatedly written there, from chapter 20 or 30, this means that the council from which some passage is then cited is the twentieth or thirtieth from the beginning of the councils contained in the Lucensis Codex. The same applies to the letters of the pontiffs, which it likewise enumerates in order. You will understand this from the index of the councils and pontifical letters, which we shall place before the work itself.
>
> “The Hispanic councils follow. We collated them from the Lucensis Codex with the printed edition of 1567. For the sake of brevity we used certain sigla in them, namely L, H, A, and Ae, concerning which we shall speak shortly before the Council of Elvira.
>
> “Although we noted all the passages in which the printed texts differed from the manuscripts, we marked in the margin with an asterisk only those that we judged clearly and altogether in need of correction in the printed texts, so that the hurried reader might pass over the rest if he wished.
>
> “No one should be surprised that we copied not only passages that were better in the manuscripts but also those that we saw to be plainly corrupt in them. Who would deny that manuscripts too are faulty in many places, and that the true reading must be extracted by collating many of them with one another?
>
> “Nevertheless, we preferred to apply the greatest possible faithfulness and to err on the safer side. Taught by experience, we hope that there will not be lacking those who, by investigating, will often discover traces of some true reading even in corrupt writing.
>
> “Accordingly, in the other Councils of Toledo and in the Council of Mérida, which we have copied here in full, we have often left the corrupted writing in the text itself—as it stood in the Codex—and, having supplied only the labor of true punctuation, for there was none at all in the Codex, we have added our conjectures in the margin. In many of the most hopeless passages we may perhaps have provided a remedy.
>
> “It remains only to say that if we have erred anywhere in setting forth our judgment, we submit the whole matter to the correction of the Catholic Roman Church, which we do with the most obedient mind.”

### Note by the same Perez before the variants of the Council of Elvira, in which he discusses the four most important Codices of the Hispanic collection

[Col. 0735B] Among the several excellent notes that Perez wrote in the aforementioned Vatican Codex, we append here especially the one in which he promised in his preceding preface to explain the marks L, H, A, and Ae of the Codices. Since the mark L indicates the Lucensis Codex, H the Hispalensis, A the Alveldensis, and Ae the exemplar of Saint Aemilianus, he writes as follows concerning each:

> “These four Codices are manuscript parchment books written in Gothic letters. They are preserved in the Monastery of Saint Laurence Royal at the Escorial, recently built by Philip II, Catholic King of Spain.
>
> “The Lucensis was brought from the Church of Lugo. It does not state the year in which it was written, but it is certainly six or seven hundred years old. Besides the councils in print, it contains the following councils not yet published: the Council of Mérida and five Councils of Toledo, from the thirteenth through the seventeenth.”

> **[Note: [Col. 0735D]]** The thirteenth Council of Toledo was so mutilated in Perez’s time in Merlin’s edition that it could not yet be said to have been published.

> “The Hispalensis began to be called by our people by this name because it is conjectured to have been written at Seville.

> **[Note: [Col. 0736D]]** He means Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville.

> “It belonged to Martin de Ayala, archbishop of Valencia, and was written in the era 949, as it states—that is, in the year of Christ 911. It contains the councils commonly found also in the older printed editions, according to that division adopted in all the manuscripts and, as I think, first used by Isidore: namely, into Eastern, African, Gallican, and Hispanic councils. In this Codex, however, the only council not extant [in the editions] is the thirteenth Council of Toledo.

> “The Alveldensis was written by the priest Vigila in the monastery of Saint Martin of Albelda in the era 1014, as it states—that is, in the year of Christ 976. Besides the printed councils, it contains the fifteenth and sixteenth Councils of Toledo and the second Council of Zaragoza.

> “The Codex of Saint Aemilianus was brought from the monastery of Saint Aemilianus of La Cogolla near Nájera and was written in the year of the Lord 962, as it states there. It is by far the most complete of all. For besides the common material, it contains the following unpublished councils: the second and third Councils of Zaragoza, two Councils of Barcelona, the Council of Huesca, the Council of Egara, the Council of Toledo under Gundemar, another Council of Toledo in the twelfth year of Reccared, and yet another Council of Toledo in the first year of Chintila.”

Other material that was read in this same manuscript and had not yet been printed, relating to the case of the Priscillianists, Perez not only indicates in another note, from which we gave an excerpt in volume II, column 1376, but also transcribed in that same volume.

## On the Hadriano-Hispanic collection, which exists in Vatican manuscript 1338

**31.** Since the author of the ancient collection edited by Luc d’Achery, and Rabanus Maurus—of whom there will be discussion in Part IV—cite the canons of the Greek synods, the African canons, and the Apostolic Constitutions with the same titles and numbers as the Hadrianic collection; and since, moreover, among the canons of the councils they cite a considerable number of African, Gallican, and Hispanic canons that are contained not in the Hadrianic but in the Hispanic collection, it is clear either that they used both collections or at least another collection that contained the aforementioned canons of the Hispanic collection together with the Hadrianic collection.

The latter seems more probable to us. For if they had used the complete and separate Hispanic collection, they would at least sometimes have cited not only the canons of the councils found in it but also its decretal letters, which are absent from the Hadrianic collection. Yet lest this seem like a dream, we have obtained Vatican Codex 1338, in which a Hadriano-Hispanic collection of this kind is presented.

**32.** It is a parchment Codex in folio, written in the eleventh or twelfth century, whose individual pages are arranged in two columns. A table of the first part, concerning the canons of the councils, precedes it. The fourfold division of the councils is taken from the Hispanic collection. First are listed the chapters of the councils of Greece, then of Africa, afterward of Gaul, and finally of Spain.

The table is followed by this note:

> “This Codex was written from that authentic one which the lord Hadrian the Apostolic gave to the most glorious Charles, king of the Franks and Lombards and patrician of the Romans.”

In the first series, which concerns the councils of Greece, there are presented not only the canons of the Greek synods in the translation of Dionysius, but also the Latin African canons produced by Dionysius. Thus this first series contains the whole first part of the Hadrianic collection, with a few insertions chiefly from the Hispanic collection, as will become clear from the order that follows. This first series is divided into twelve chapters.

**1.** The Apostolic Canons, number 50.

**2.** The Nicene Canons, number 20, preceded by a chronological note and a creed and followed by a catalogue of bishops, as we saw in the Hadrianic collection. A particular feature, however, is that after the Nicene Creed and before the canons, without any title, the following is added:

> “After the Council of Nicaea, a council was assembled in the city of Rome by Catholic bishops, and they added concerning the Holy Spirit,” etc.

We likewise saw this inserted in another Vatican manuscript, 1337, of the Hadrianic collection, chapter 2, number 6.

**3.** The Canons of Ancyra, number 24.

**4.** Under the name of the Council of Ephesus, two letters of Saint Cyril to Nestorius inserted from the Hispanic collection.

**5.** The Canons of Neocaesarea, number 14.

**6.** The Canons of Gangra, number 20, together with the letter to the bishops of Armenia and a catalogue of bishops, as in the Hadrianic collection.

**7.** The Canons of Antioch, number 25, with the names of the bishops copied from the Hadrianic collection.

**8.** The Canons of Laodicea, number 59.

**9.** The Canons of Constantinople, number 3, with the creed and subscriptions.

**10.** The Canons of Chalcedon, number 27, with the definition of faith and the catalogue of bishops.

**11.** The Canons of Sardica, number 21, with the same clause that we noted in the Hadrianic manuscripts.

**12.** Finally, the Carthaginian canons are divided into two parts, which we observed to be characteristic of the Hadrianic collection. First, thirty-three canons are presented, preceded by the Dionysian materials likewise received in the Hadrianic collection; then the subscriptions follow the thirty-third and final canon. Next, from the Hispanic collection, the *Formata* of Atticus of Constantinople is inserted. Afterward the remaining 105 canons from various councils of Africa are added; these conclude the first part of the Hadrianic collection.

**33.** The materials presented under the titles of the councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain were entirely excerpted from that Hispanic collection which received the Councils of Toledo down to the thirteenth and the Council of Braga of the year 675.

Although the African canons had previously been copied under the title of the councils of Greece from the Hadrianic collection, since in the Hispanic collection they are presented with a different division and numbering, they are here likewise exhibited under the title of the councils of Africa from that same Hispanic collection. See what we noted in the preceding chapter, number 19; from it you will learn the sequence of all the synods—African, Gallican, and Hispanic—received here.

The fact that these synods were copied not from the Isidorian but from the Hispanic collection is clearly demonstrated by the readings. One principal and evident example will suffice. All the Isidorian Codices that we have carefully examined present an interpolated seventh canon in the second Council of Seville. They contain the word *chorepiscopos* twice, inserted into the text, and at the end of the same canon they exhibit an additional passage; all these additions are known to have been prohibited by the Apostolic See. This refers to the spurious pseudo-Isidorian letter of Damasus to the bishops of Numidia.

These interpolations are absent from the manuscript books of the Hispanic collection, as is evident from Loaisa’s edition, which was taken from pure Hispanic exemplars. On this matter see volume II of this edition, column 1270, and our note 5 there.

Since these interpolations are not found in the present Vatican 1338 collection, it is manifest that this collection received the canons of the councils of Africa, Gaul, and Spain from Hispanic, not Isidorian, Codices.

**34.** In the second part, which contains the Apostolic Constitutions, these were transcribed solely from the Hadrianic collection. Since the Codex is mutilated at the end, it ends with Leo’s letter to Anastasius of Thessalonica.

# THE COLLECTION OF ISIDORE MERCATOR

## § I.—On the spurious documents of this collection; how late the imposture was detected; whether Nicholas I approved such a collection; the stronger arguments for its supposititious character

**35.** The collection of Isidore Mercator is distinguished from the preceding collections chiefly by this feature: it is filled with a greater number of supposititious documents. It presents several letters of the most ancient Roman pontiffs, from Saint Clement down to Saint Sylvester, although no decrees of theirs survive; and it attributes other letters to pontiffs down to Gregory the Great, inserting them among the genuine documents.

It is astonishing that so conspicuous an imposture—which did not emerge gradually or in parts, but appeared all at once in its entirety in a single book—was not detected immediately.

> **[Note: [Col. 0737D]]** It should be observed, as I have already mentioned, that before pseudo-Isidore there were others who forged ancient documents and inserted them into collections of canons. It is therefore not very surprising that his fraud was not immediately apparent, since his collection consisted of many documents which, even if supposititious, had already been found in other collections before him.

It is believed that Hincmar of Reims and other Gallican bishops sensed something suspicious, for they wrote to Nicholas I. Yet they do not seem to have admitted any doubt of their falsity into their minds; rather, they thought that the letters should be deprived of authority only for this reason, as they said: they were not entered in the Codex of Canons (Nicholas I, Letter 42, to the bishops of Gaul). They meant, of course, that the letters were not in the Hadrianic collection, which at that time, because it had been adopted for the use of the Churches, they called the Codex of Canons.

When Nicholas wrote back to those same bishops, he rightly considered this sole reason worthless, since that collection contains not all the otherwise most genuine constitutions of the Roman pontiffs, but only a very small number; and those same Gallican bishops, whenever they see that these decretals—the decretals of the earlier pontiffs—support their purpose, use them without distinction.

Since they transmitted those decretal letters, although they were not copied in the Codex of Canons and were less accepted, not as spurious but as genuine, so that they used them whenever they wished, the same pontiff, who knew them only from the Gallicans’ report and suspected no fraud so long as no contrary evidence appeared from elsewhere, could not reject them. Nor can his words, by which he seems in some way to have approved them, be taken as a true and legitimate approval resting upon the presumption advanced by the Gallican bishops. Such approval could not be given without reading the letters themselves, and Nicholas did not possess them.

This is evident from the fact that in his own letters, when he had many opportunities to cite them, he more carefully praises other documents not found in the Codex of Canons. He also praises certain apocryphal documents that, having once been fabricated and circulated, had entered the older collections, such as the synod of Saint Sylvester, the other Synod of Sinuessa, the proceedings concerning the purgation of Sixtus III, and those concerning Polychronius. Yet he never used the pseudo-Isidorian decretals.

That these decretals were not known to Leo IV, his immediate predecessor, is clear from his letter to the Britons. In it, when reviewing the decretals contained in the Codex of Canons, he begins with Sylvester and recalls the other contents of the Hadrianic collection in such a way that, if some matter should arise that could not be settled by those documents, he directs them to have recourse to the writings of the holy Fathers Jerome, Augustine, and others. He gives no indication of the other decretal letters then in circulation.

[Col. 0738B] 36. There are indeed many marks of forgery contained in these decretals and in the other Isidorian materials—marks that would easily have led attentive and competent men to detect their falsity at the very beginning. But the circumstances of those times and of the periods that followed were such that few possessed a clear knowledge of the more remote past or were willing or able to exercise sound criticism. The first to suspect and point out their spurious character was Cardinal Nicholas of Cusa, in his work *Catholic Concordance*, book III, chapter 2. Wycliffe, who had blurted out the following before him—“The decretal letters are apocryphal and lead people away from the faith of Christ, and the clerics who study them are foolish”—was attempting not merely to cast suspicion on the decretals forged by Isidore, but to overthrow the authority of all decretals. After Cusa, however, many others gradually became alert to the matter, and they brought forward so many substantial arguments in proof of the forgery that no one can now reasonably doubt such impostures.

[Col. 0738C] 37. It will be enough here to touch upon some of the arguments for the forgery. The evidence disclosed by the preface itself is not insignificant. Its title reads: “To Saint Isidore, bishop.” That he was indeed a bishop is also made clear by the very formula inserted in the preface, in which the author calls bishops “our brothers.” His Spanish origin is suggested by these words of the same preface: “At the beginning of this volume we have set forth how a council is celebrated among us.” After the preface there follows an order for celebrating a council, taken from canon 4 of the Fourth Council of Toledo. What other Isidore could there be—Spanish, a bishop, and a saint—except the celebrated Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville? It is sufficiently well known from the same preface, as Hincmar of Rheims states in letter 7, chapter 12, that this collection, scarcely after it had been published—that is, in the ninth century—was commonly attributed to that saint.

What greater fraud could there be than to attribute to Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, a collection containing eight Councils of Toledo, from the Fifth through the Thirteenth, and one Council of Braga, all of which were held after his death? And what greater anachronism than that the preface itself should mention the Sixth Ecumenical Council, which had not yet been held while Saint Isidore was alive? [Col. 0738D] Moreover, in the letters attached to the ancient pontiffs of the first three centuries, many testimonies from Sacred Scripture are read in the version of Saint Jerome, which was published later. Moreover, most of the consular notes appended to those same letters either mention consuls who never existed in the consular fasti, or, if the names do occur in the fasti, they do not at all agree chronologically with the period of the pontiff who supposedly wrote the letter. Add the invented names of officials—*archiflamini*, *primi flamines*, and so forth—and the terms “primates,” “archbishops,” and “apocrisarii,” which anyone even slightly acquainted with ancient history and ecclesiastical discipline will readily recognize as wholly foreign to the age and usage of those ancient pontiffs. Add also that the same letters contain no indication of ancient customs, but very many features of later discipline. Others have noted numerous additional arguments at greater length; it is neither possible nor necessary to recount them here.

38. We do not think two points should be omitted. Although each might separately receive some answer, when joined together they provide an evident demonstration of the forgery. First, some of these letters are said to have been addressed to all bishops, others to all the orthodox, to all the Churches, to the bishops of Italy, Gaul, Spain, Africa, Germany, and so forth. Many copies of them, therefore, ought to have been disseminated throughout the world. How, then, could it have happened that, out of so many letters circulated throughout the world, not one was discovered and praised by anyone before the ninth century?

Second, those same letters repeatedly display not merely the opinions of authors from the later fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth centuries, but also their words and entire, often quite lengthy, sentences copied from them. Father Philip Labbe, following Blondel, carefully noted this in the margins of those same letters. To the first argument it may be answered that the letters remained hidden until the ninth century and therefore were praised by no one. To the second, someone has replied that the later authors who present the indicated opinions in the same words copied them verbatim from the letters themselves.

Neither answer is probable; indeed, one contradicts the other. For if the letters remained so hidden immediately after their origin and until the ninth century that no one could cite them, then they were not available to later writers either, so that they could copy sentences from them. But if entire sentences were excerpted from them by several authors separated by considerable distances of both time and place, then they cannot be said to have remained buried in darkness for so long. Whichever alternative one chooses, the forgery is established; and the conflict between the answers makes this much clearer.

If several ancient writers had taken from the letters their opinions, words, and sentences, then the letters must have been known and made familiar through frequent use, and they must have been useful for many purposes, so that they could be praised by many—especially by those who had learned from them. Among these, surely, the supreme pontiffs, councils, and Fathers who present the same words and sentences would have cited these letters of the most ancient pontiffs just as they are found citing the genuine letters of others.

But if, among so many men who lived before the ninth century—men both most holy and renowned for their learning—although they present the same opinions in the same words in their works, not one is found to have mentioned those letters, then it follows that they in fact took nothing from them. The matching opinions and sentences found in the letters, therefore, were undoubtedly derived by the author of the letters from those same writers. This clearly demonstrates that the letters have a spurious origin. [Col. 0739D] For the same reason, they were praised by no other author before the ninth century—not because they remained hidden, or because there was no material or opportunity for citing them, but because the one who would forge them had not yet been born. Otherwise, just as after the time when they were fabricated and published we find them widely praised and not a few passages from them transferred into collections, so we would also discover the same thing happening in earlier times if they had truly been written and published by the ancient pontiffs to whom they are attributed.

§ II.—Other genuine documents inserted into the same collection, and the sources from which they were drawn. The importance of identifying these sources for distinguishing what Pseudo-Isidore fabricated. Certain genuine documents interpolated by him. The two last synods attributed to Symmachus, and the Capitula ascribed to Hadrian I, which many believe to be genuine, shown to have been fabricated by the same Pseudo-Isidore.

39. Pseudo-Isidore did not construct his collection solely from the spurious documents he himself pieced together. He intermingled many wholly genuine and independently known records with the false ones. The sources from which he derived these genuine documents must be identified, for this will be of no little help in separating those which he invented from his own imagination.

The principal source is the Hispanic Collection, which he inserted in its entirety into his own collection. Since it was commonly believed that Saint Isidore of Seville had been the author of the Hispanic Collection, he gladly seized upon the name of Isidore, which was venerated by everyone, and placed it in the preface. He took the Hispanic Collection not in its earliest form, which extended no further than the Fourth Council of Toledo, but in the somewhat enlarged form that included nine Councils of Toledo and the Council of Braga of the year 675. Nor did he use copies of this collection that were of Hispanic origin, but those of Gallican origin, as we shall establish at greater length in section 48.

The second source is the Hadriana Collection, from which Pseudo-Isidore excerpted certain materials absent from the Hispanic Collection. The third source is the old collection published by Quesnell and reprinted by us in this volume. For quite a few documents found in the Isidorian Collection, but read neither in the Hadriana nor in the Hispanic Collection, were derived from that source, sometimes in the same order. The author drew a few other items from the *Tripartite History* and from other sources, which we shall indicate in the catalogue below, each in its proper place.

40. It is so useful to have identified these sources that anything not found in them must with certainty be declared to have been fabricated by Pseudo-Isidore. If documents that are genuine in themselves are shorter in those sources but longer in Pseudo-Isidore, whatever addition has been made that is not found in those sources may be affirmed to have been fabricated by the same impostor.

Thus the two final chapters—the sixth and seventh—of Vigilius’s letter to Profuturus are spurious. They are absent from the genuine manuscripts of the Hispanic Collection, but are read in the Isidorian Collection. Indeed, since certain ancient documents that are otherwise apocryphal are likewise fuller in this collection, although they were received into some older collections in a shorter form, their additions too must be attributed to the impostor.

Thus no one can now doubt that several more extensive chapters of the two letters of Saint Clement to James were fabricated by him. Those letters were once forged among the Greeks and translated into Latin by Rufinus; they found their way into some old collections, but are much shorter in those collections, whereas in Pseudo-Isidore they are found only in an expanded form containing those additions.

Nor should we omit here the brief interpolation inserted into canon 7 of the genuine Second Council of Seville, concerning which we spoke in the preceding chapter, section 33. Here, moreover, please observe the character of the impostor: he was so inclined to fabricate that he spared neither genuine nor apocryphal documents, even though comparison with older manuscripts could readily expose his inventions. How much more boldly, then, would he fabricate entire letters that did not have to fear comparison with any older copies by which the fraud might be detected!

41. By the general rule we have proposed, the two apocryphal synods—the so-called Fifth and Sixth under Symmachus—as well as the Capitula attributed to Pope Hadrian in printed editions and in most manuscripts are exposed as forgeries, since they are found only in the Isidorian Collection. It is astonishing to us that many otherwise extremely acute critics, who carefully examined each individual document in that collection, raised no doubt about the two synods just mentioned or about the Capitula. Indeed, Blondel, who attacked Isidorian fabrications more than anyone, was so far from doubting them that he repeatedly lists the aforesaid synods and the Capitula of Hadrian among the more ancient records from which Pseudo-Isidore composed his apocryphal letters, as though these materials were genuine and ancient and Pseudo-Isidore were not their author.

First, as regards the two synods under Symmachus, not only is the Hadriana Collection unaware of them, but so is the oldest of all the collections, contained in Vatican Manuscript Regina 1997. This manuscript, produced shortly after the age of that pontiff, presents with the greatest care all his genuine synods and all the other documents pertaining to them. If only three synods are presented there, rather than four, no one should suspect that the fourth genuine synod was omitted from that manuscript. The opinion that there were four synods arises from a certain note that is absent from the older and superior manuscripts, as we observed in part II, chapter 4, section 5.

Furthermore, if the three genuine synods that alone have been published are compared with the two described only in Isidore, everyone will detect an obvious difference in their introduction, style, and entire mode of expression; this sufficiently demonstrates that they have different authors. Add that in the so-called Sixth Synod the Gangrian canons are said to have been enacted by apostolic authority, which is entirely false. Two such canons are cited from Dionysius’s interpretation, although at that time the Roman pontiffs had received no canons of Greek synods other than those of Nicaea and Sardica. See part II, chapter 1.

Finally, in the so-called Fifth Synod certain decrees are read that Symmachus declares to have been established by his predecessors: “For,” he says, “it has been decreed and confirmed synodally by many of our predecessors.” The decrees are then produced and recited in exactly the same words in the pseudo-letters of Zephyrinus, Stephen, Eusebius, and Julius. The same person, therefore, is recognized as the fabricator both of those letters and of that synod. Symmachus could not have praised letters forged so much later.

Nor should anyone find it incredible that Pseudo-Isidore, when assembling that synod, copied words from letters he himself had fabricated and invoked the authority of the pontiffs to whom he had attached them. This was his customary practice: in letters he attributed to later pontiffs, he sometimes repeated decrees in exactly the same words from fictitious letters inscribed with the names of their predecessors, and introduced the authority of those predecessors.

Once the fabrication of such synods has been exposed by these arguments, there can be no doubt that the subscriptions attached to the pseudo-synods—taken partly from genuine councils of Symmachus and partly from the Council of Chalcedon, which especially reveals the fraud—also came from the same impostor.

42. We now turn to the Capitula that are attributed to Pope Hadrian I in printed editions (vol. VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, col. 537). We saw in the Vatican Library a manuscript numbered 631 in which these Capitula are attributed not to Pope Hadrian but to Ingelram, or Angilramn, bishop of Metz. It begins:

“Capitula collected from various councils, or from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, by Angilramn, bishop of Metz, and presented to Pope Hadrian.”

Another manuscript of the Library of Saint Victor in Paris bears precisely the same inscription, as Baluze testifies in his preface to the books of Antonius Augustinus *On the Correction of Gratian*. In his notes to those same books, p. 492, he then cites another manuscript from the monastery of Laetus, where a similar title is expressed in these words:

“Book of Capitula collected from various councils, or from the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, by Anilramn, bishop of Metz.”

But most of the older and better manuscripts—Vatican 630, 1340, 1344, 3791, and others—preserve the commonly printed reading:

“From Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, these Capitula were collected here and there and delivered at Rome by Blessed Pope Hadrian to Agilramn, bishop of the city of Metz, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his case.”

That this title should be preferred above all others is demonstrated by Hincmar of Rheims, a contemporary of Pseudo-Isidore, who likewise read it in his manuscript. For in his treatise against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, he writes: [Col. 0742A]

“As for the decisions said to have been collected from Greek and Latin canons and from the decrees of Roman prelates and rulers by Pope Hadrian and delivered by him to Engelramn, bishop of Metz, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his case, and so forth.”

The fuller inscription, which records the time and occasion of the Capitula and states that they were collected not only from the decrees of pontiffs and the canons of councils but also from the laws of princes and of the Romans, is recognized as the more truthful. [Col. 0742B] Therefore there can be no doubt that this collection of Capitula was attributed to Hadrian.

Pope Hadrian, moreover, gave his name to no other collection than the one he himself delivered to Charlemagne, which is called the Hadriana. Hence Leo IV, in his letter to the bishops of Britain, when citing ecclesiastical canons—especially those by which bishops both judge and are judged—lists the canons contained in the Hadriana. But concerning these Capitula attributed to Hadrian, which, since they contain almost nothing other than material relating to the judgments of bishops, ought especially to have been mentioned, he says not a word.

Moreover, the Capitula themselves contain certain provisions that the Roman pontiff would certainly never have proposed, such as chapter 6, which directs that cases of appeal be referred to Constantinople rather than to the apostolic see; and chapter 49, taken from book X, title 10, number 2, of the Theodosian Code, or from the *Breviary of Anianus*: “Let the informer’s tongue be cut out, or, once convicted, let his head be severed.” Everyone can see how foreign this is to ecclesiastical gentleness.

Angilramn, bishop of Metz, who is called by his contemporary, Paul the Deacon, a most gentle man and outstanding in piety, in book IV, chapter 6, of *The Deeds of the Lombards*, would likewise have recoiled most strongly from inserting such a sanction into a collection of canons.

We shall add, for a fuller proof of the forgery, that the pontifical decrees from which these Capitula are said chiefly to have been collected are almost nothing other than the Isidorian apocryphal decretals. In them the same opinions and the same words are repeatedly recited, as can be gathered from the notes of Antonius Augustinus on these same Capitula. Anyone who considers the agreement between those letters and the Capitula will readily perceive that they had the same architect.

Most people have hitherto failed to grasp the force of this argument because they believed that the author of the pseudo-letters had drawn from the Capitula, which seemed to be genuine. But we can demonstrate, on the contrary, that the Capitula were composed after the pseudo-letters and, wherever they agree with those pseudo-letters in exactly the same opinions or words, were derived from them. Many arguments can be brought forward for this. For the sake of brevity, one especially clear example will suffice.

The same lengthy decree of the Roman synod that is read in chapter 5 of the Capitula is also contained, in exactly the same words, in the spurious letter of Felix I to the bishops of Gaul. That this decree was transferred from this letter into the Capitula, rather than from the Capitula into the letter, is clear from the fact that the Roman synod to which the decree is attributed in the Capitula is none other than the spurious synod under that same Felix I, described in the same letter, which contains the account of the synod.

This is made clear by the following words of that letter (vol. II of the Councils, col. 924):

“But we,” says Pseudo-Felix, “summoned for your assistance more than seventy of our brothers and fellow bishops, with whom we decided that the matters inserted below should be considered according to the rule. For, after your letters—which, as you know, contained many complaints and oppressions of your own—had been read aloud before everyone, and the decrees concerning accusations against bishops, the holy synod said: ‘These are the measures that henceforth, because of the snares of evil men, etc.’”

After reporting this decree, Pseudo-Felix concludes his account of the synod as follows:

“These things, brothers, were decreed unanimously in the synod for your assistance and that of all your fellow bishops, so that, if perhaps some foolish men should accuse you, etc.”

Therefore this Roman synod and its decree, which are recited in the Capitula, could have been taken nowhere else than from this pseudo-letter of Felix I, through which alone they first came to light. If the author of the Capitula drew the same decree from this pseudo-letter, then the Capitula are later than that letter and likewise later than the other apocryphal decretals from which many other passages were similarly extracted.

The Capitula therefore cannot be attributed either to Hadrian I or to Angilramn, bishop of Metz. In their time those pseudo-decretals had not yet appeared, and consequently neither had the Capitula derived from them. Hence no one can agree with Stephen Baluze, who, in the preface mentioned above to the books of Antonius Augustinus *On the Correction of Gratian*, attributed those Capitula to Angilramn of Metz and wrote:

“He collected them for the most part from the newly discovered letters of the ancient pontiffs and presented them to Hadrian, seeking protection for his case.”

Their author is that same Pseudo-Isidore who fabricated the letters themselves; and therefore they are found only in his collection. Indeed, in Vatican Manuscript 630, the oldest of all, they are found in an appendix to the Isidorian Collection, because they were composed later by Pseudo-Isidore from the apocryphal documents contained in the first formation of the collection and were added as an appendix to the earlier copies, as will become clear from the notes in section 5.

In the first formation of the collection, which the same impostor testifies in the preface to have extended as far as Saint Gregory, these Capitula attributed to Hadrian I could not have had a place. It is therefore confirmed that they were fabricated and added only later.

43. For a clearer recognition of the impostor’s character, we think the following should be noted here: when copying from the pseudo-letter of Felix the decree of the Roman synod mentioned shortly before, he altered some of the words of that decree rather freely. For whereas the pseudo-letter reads:

“At the appropriate time—that is, in autumn or summer—they shall regularly summon a council,”

the Capitula read in chapter 5:

“At the time prescribed by the canons of Nicaea they shall canonically summon a council.” [Col. 0743C]

The impostor saw that the Council of Nicaea could not be mentioned in the letter and synod of Felix I, who preceded the Council of Nicaea. But since he had in fact taken this decree—at least the clause prescribing the convocation of councils—from the Council of Nicaea, he did not hesitate to mention that council in the Capitula attributed to Hadrian, who lived later.

Thus he exposed a double fraud: one, when he attached to the Roman synod what properly belonged to Nicaea; the other, when he interpolated the decree taken from that Roman pseudo-synod by altering some of its wording.

200 § III. The purpose for which Pseudo-Isidore fabricated so many spurious documents. Whether ecclesiastical discipline was altered by these fabricated documents.

44. We must not omit the question of what spirit and purpose led Pseudo-Isidore to fabricate so many documents. Some believe that he was moved and prompted to produce them by a desire to enlarge or defend the authority of the Roman pontiffs. But they are plainly mistaken. For although the greatness and authority of the apostolic see are commended in many passages of these documents, that was not the impostor’s purpose. Nor did that see—which rests its privileges and rights upon very many genuine and ancient documents—need those apocrypha, as Cardinal Baronius noted under the year 865, number 8.

Pseudo-Isidore’s purpose was quite different, as can be sufficiently discerned from the preface to the collection itself. After indicating the documents that were to be inserted into his collection, he gives the following reason for gathering them:

“So that the discipline of the ecclesiastical order, collected and arranged by us into one body, may instruct the holy prelates by the rules of the Fathers, and obedient ministers of the Church—or the peoples—may be imbued with spiritual examples and not deceived by the wickedness of evil men. For many, brought low by depravity and greed, have oppressed priests by accusing them.”

He then continues with a vehement attack on those who dare to accuse bishops in order to excuse themselves through them or enrich themselves from their goods. Referring to several such abuses of judicial procedure, he insists that bishops cannot be compelled to answer a charge if they have been accused and stripped of their possessions, deprived of their rank, or expelled from their sees, unless they have first been restored. He adds various provisions concerning the rejection of accusers and accusations. By all this he openly signifies that he composed the collection chiefly to protect bishops who were being accused.

This is even clearer in the apocryphal documents he fabricated. He consistently displays the same care and concern for accused bishops. Whenever he praises the authority of the apostolic see, he invariably directs everything toward this end: that bishops attacked and condemned through accusations may flee to that see if they consider themselves oppressed, since it can reconsider the judgments of synods and, if it deems it just, annul them.

The same purpose is especially evident in the Capitula attributed to Hadrian. Since they were taken chiefly from the apocryphal letters, they may be called a kind of abridgment and compilation of the apocryphal documents. Most of their provisions aim to ensure that bishops cannot be accused by just anyone and that, even if they are accused, the accusers are not readily believed. They also provide various grounds for rejecting accusers and for allowing judges to be challenged, for judgments of synods to be reconsidered, and for other measures of the same sort that were likewise inserted into the apocrypha. If all these provisions are understood as having been collected and fabricated to provide protection, defense, and support for bishops who were accused, stripped of their possessions, or deposed, no one can justly deny it.

201 45. Quite a few people complain more harshly about Pseudo-Isidore, as though his fabrications had abolished the ancient discipline and introduced a new one, so that the ancient canons were abandoned, the sinews of discipline broken, the rights of bishops and provincial councils thrown into confusion, the laws of judicial procedure removed, and other injuries inflicted upon ecclesiastical affairs. [Note: Many recent writers—Zaccaria, Marchetti, and others—have argued this case in order to show that the ancient ecclesiastical discipline was not disturbed by the Pseudo-Isidorian collection.]

Everyone will readily understand how unfair this criticism of a new and altered discipline is if he observes two things. First, most of the excerpts in Isidore’s pseudo-letters are taken from the opinions of the holy Fathers, from the genuine constitutions of Roman pontiffs after Siricius, from the canons of councils, and from Roman laws. These are certainly not a new law or a new discipline. Second, the remainder for the most part presents a discipline that had either long been established or had begun to be introduced somewhat earlier.

The forgery consists in this: Pseudo-Isidore attributed those opinions to authors to whom they do not belong, and attached the discipline of a later age to earlier pontiffs, as though it had flourished equally during the earlier centuries of the Church.

In any case, as for the claim that a new discipline was introduced, the impostor would have been utterly foolish if he had hoped that his collection would be accepted by people while containing a wholly new discipline opposed even to the customs and practices of his own age. If anything introduced contrary to custom—even if good and useful—tends to cause disturbance merely by its novelty, then this must be feared all the more in the case of someone attempting to overthrow and alter a discipline that was in itself excellent, supported by more sacred laws, and accepted by everyone through long usage.

No disturbances or outcries were heard over the introduction of the apocryphal decretals except in the area concerning the cases and judgments of bishops. Some material on these matters is found in Hincmar and in the letters of Nicholas I. But even in these very cases and judgments, what is conveyed in the pseudo-letters and Isidorian synods was not entirely new.

Were not the more serious cases, which concern accusations against bishops, reserved to the apostolic see by definite decrees of ancient pontiffs and incapable of being settled without its consent? See, among others, the letters of Leo 6, 13, and 14, and the first letter of Gregory IV to all the bishops.

Have we not proved that episcopal appeals to the same see were grounded in ancient canons and custom, and also in the law of primacy, in our Observations on Quesnell’s dissertation V, part I, chapters 5, 6, and 7?

To prevent everyone indiscriminately from being admitted to accuse a bishop, provision had been made in canons 128, 129, 130, and 131 of the Code of Africa, as well as in canon 6 of the Council of Constantinople, which Nicholas I cites from the Greek Code in his eighth letter.

That bishops who had been expelled and stripped of their possessions were not to be compelled to trial unless they had first been restored to their rank and everything taken from them had been returned can be gathered from chapter 87 of the Code of the African Church.

These and other provisions of the same kind, which are said to have introduced a new discipline through the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals, may be read in letters 8, 9, and 38 of Nicholas I. Yet he confirms them not from the apocrypha, which he did not possess, but from older documents. Gregory IV had done the same before him in his first letter to all the bishops, in which he reserved to himself the judgment of Bishop Wenilo.

It may indeed be that this discipline, although established by ancient rights and decrees, was not widely observed, or was observed only rarely, in certain places that followed other customs and canons. It may also be that the same discipline, established in favor of upright men to guard against fraud, was perverted by some into an abuse and served the impunity of the wicked.

But we have learned from Pseudo-Isidore’s preface that his purpose was remote from such wickedness: he sought only to assist bishops who were unjustly oppressed.

It may also be that in that part of Gaul where Mainz is situated—where, as we shall soon say, these Pseudo-Isidorian materials were fabricated—the discipline set forth in them had already long prevailed through the work of Saint Boniface, bishop of Mainz. That he held the authority of the apostolic see in high regard and sought to introduce the same observance in those regions is clear from his letters. See, among others, his letter 105 to Cuthbert, archbishop of Canterbury, in which several principal elements of discipline established in those regions by that holy martyr and apostle of Germany, and later repeated in the Pseudo-Isidorian letters, are presented.

The same spirit also passed to his successors, Lullus, Riculf, and Autgar, as is clear from other records.

If, therefore, the Pseudo-Isidorian decretals present a discipline that was supported both by earlier decrees and canons and had already long prevailed, at least in the regions where Pseudo-Isidore composed them, everyone will understand whether it is fair to attribute the introduction of a new discipline to those decretals.

Nevertheless, it seems impossible to deny that this same discipline spread more widely and took much deeper root after the decretals had been published and disseminated, and soon praised in certain councils and subsequently inserted into the collections of Regino, Burchard, and others. Their brevity and method made them highly useful.

§ IV.—On the author and date of the same collection.

### 46. The name of Isidore was inscribed in the preface by the impostor in order that the work might be attributed to St. Isidore, bishop of Seville

We indicated this in no. 37, where we also proved that this collection cannot be attributed to that saint.

[Note: Since the pseudo-Isidorian collection was produced in the German-Frankish empire and fabricated for that empire, it is certainly absurd to think of a Spanish author, whether called Isidore or by some other name. The architect of the fraud, in order to deceive more easily, published the collection under the name of Isidore of Seville. For those who spread fables commonly prefix to their fabrications some already familiar name and generally boast of a work composed in foreign regions.]

Most people assign it to Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, who, as was thought, published at Mainz and disseminated in the neighboring regions of Gaul the collection brought from Spain and regarded as that of Isidore of Seville. Hincmar of Reims reports this in his work against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24:

> “But if you collected such material,” he says, “by mutilating, transposing, and disarranging the statements previously mentioned—those of Angilramnus—and the often-mentioned letters, because perhaps you thought that no one besides yourself possessed those same statements or letters, and therefore believed that you could freely gather such things, this is astonishing, since this land is full of those very statements, just as it is full of the book of collected letters by Isidore, which Riculfus, bishop of Mainz, brought from Spain, obtained—for he was diligent in such matters as well as in royal capitularies—and caused these regions to be filled with them.”

But Riculfus of Mainz, who succeeded Lullus in 786 or 787, died in 814; and since the Isidorian collection contains certain letters—for example, those of Urban I and John III—in which the impostor inserted verbatim several statements from the Council of Paris held in 829, it is clear that these fabrications cannot be attributed to Riculfus.

[Note: Blondel concludes that Riculfus introduced something new from book VII of the Capitularies, chapter 205, now 281, where he is said to have brought forward at the assembly of Worms a letter of Pope Gregory, of which no memory existed either before or afterward. Yet this is not a spurious but a genuine letter of Gregory II to Boniface, bishop of Mainz, which is printed in volume VIII of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 178.]

Hincmar, however, should be excused, since we believe that he took this material in good faith from Benedict the Levite. In the preface to books V, VI, and VII of the Capitularies, which he himself compiled and published about the year 845, Benedict had written:

> “These Capitularies, which we have endeavored to gather together in the following three little books, we found scattered in various places and on various sheets, just as they had been issued in various synods and general assemblies; and especially we found them stored in the archive of the holy metropolitan church of Mainz by Riculfus, metropolitan of that holy see, and afterward discovered by Autcarius, his second successor and kinsman. We have preferred to insert them in this little work in the form written above.”

Among the capitularies inserted by him in the books mentioned, however, there occur several taken from the apocryphal letters of the ancient pontiffs, some from the pseudo-synods of Symmachus, and nearly all the capitularies falsely attributed to Pope Hadrian by Angilramnus; yet they are cited without any author’s name.

Nor should you suppose that Benedict the Levite took these from some collection of the Frankish kings’ Capitularies, from which pseudo-Isidore likewise excerpted them and attributed them to those ancient pontiffs, to the synods of Symmachus, and to Hadrian I. For if those decrees had been included in genuine Capitularies, some such capitularies would surely have been found—if not all, at least several—in which they were read.

Thus, when Ansegisus compiled his four books from genuine Capitularies, diligent scholars found those same Capitularies, containing nearly all of Ansegisus’s chapters, as well as the chapters omitted by Ansegisus but added by Benedict the Levite from genuine Capitularies in his own books.

Why, then, is not even a single chapter from those apocryphal documents found in any older Capitularies, unless Benedict derived them not from genuine Capitularies but from the pseudo-Isidorian wares, in which alone they are found?

These chapters of the pseudo-Isidorian collection, therefore, seem to be among those which Benedict reported as having been stored in the archive of the church of Mainz by Riculfus. Since Benedict thus attributes this collection—or at least places it within the period of Riculfus, whom we have already seen died before the collection was composed and published, he appears to have done so for no other reason than to create authority for the same documents and to remove suspicion from a fraud of which he himself was not unaware.

Since Benedict himself was the first, or nearly the first, to use such fabrications, and since he was a Levite of the church of Mainz, from which the collection emerged, some, together with Blondel, suspect that he may himself have been the architect of these same fabrications.

### 47.

It is certain that the collection was composed at this time and in Germany—not in Spain—namely, in Germany, which under the ancient administrative arrangement was reckoned among the Gallic provinces and subject to the Frankish kings. It therefore had a German-Frankish author.

Since the most recent document from which the impostor extracted entire statements when fabricating the apocrypha is the Council of Paris of 829, the publication of this collection cannot be placed before that year.

Moreover, the Council of Aachen of 836, chapter 2, no. 8, decrees that holy oil should be prepared by the bishops each year on Maundy Thursday, according to apostolic tradition and the provisions of the decretal letters, in which the same matter is prescribed. This is generally thought to indicate the second pseudo-letter of Fabian. Hence the publication of the collection seems to have to be placed after 829 and before 836.

It is remarkable, however, that Rabanus, who shortly after the year 841 dedicated a Penitential to Otgarius, or Autcarius, bishop of Mainz, produced nothing from the Isidorian apocrypha. Whether he did so because he placed no trust in them, or because they had not yet appeared, so that the decree of the Council of Aachen is incorrectly referred to the pseudo-letter of Fabian, others may judge.

If the latter view is considered more probable—and still more if, with Blondel, one believes that the impostor extracted certain formulas and phrases from the letter of Jonas of Orléans to Charles the Bald, who obtained the kingdom in 839—the Isidorian collection ought to be regarded as having been published around the time when Benedict the Levite issued his books of Capitularies, namely about 845. The first explicit mention of the apocrypha would then be found in the letter written by Charles the Bald to the bishops assembled at Quierzy in 857.

Nor should one be disturbed by the collection attributed to Remedius of Chur and published by Goldastus (*Rerum Alamannicarum*, vol. II, part II, p. 134, edition of 1730), with this title:

> “Ancient canons of the Alamannic Church, excerpted from the letters of the pontiffs by Remedius, bishop of Chur, at the command of Charles the Great, king of the Franks and Alamanni.”

Since this king died in 814, Goldastus thinks that the collection was composed about 813.

This collection was more extensive, and additions were made to it by Notingus, bishop of Constance, who died in 934. Yet Goldastus reports that these additions of Notingus, together with a considerable portion of the canons collected by Remedius, were cut out and removed from his manuscript.

Only forty-nine chapters published by him survive. They present, in order, excerpts solely from the pseudo-letters of the ancient pontiffs, from St. Clement down to St. Urban.

These excerpts themselves, however, which the author derived from the pseudo-Isidorian collection—compiled, as we have seen, after Charlemagne—plainly show that there is an error in the title or in the explanation of the title concerning Charlemagne, and that Remedius, who is reported to have been the author of these excerpts, must be assigned to a later period.

Perhaps Charles the Fat should be understood instead of Charlemagne; he may have been called “Charles the Great” in the same way that the emperor Louis II is found called “Louis the Great.” Charles the Fat was, in fact, already king of the Alamanni when the pseudo-Isidorian collection had become widespread, and afterward obtained the empire.

### 48.

Many things prove that pseudo-Isidore was not a Spaniard but a German-Frank.

We have learned from Hincmar that the collection came from Mainz and was disseminated throughout Gaul. Although Hincmar is mistaken in assuming that the author was St. Isidore of Seville and reporting that the collection had been brought from Spain, his statement that the collection was published from Mainz is strongly confirmed by the testimony of Benedict the Levite.

For this reason, those who first praised those apocrypha in the ninth century were German Gauls; no Spanish or other regional writers did so.

[Note: No copy of the pseudo-Isidorian collection has ever been found in Spain. What confidence, I ask, could it have deserved among the Spaniards, since it contradicted their genuine collection in many places? Among other things, the forger begins as follows: “You ought to know that eighty bishops, who compelled me to begin and complete this work, and all the remaining priests of the Lord, …” What Spaniard, I ask, would have dared to address Spaniards in this way in the ninth century, or even to attribute such a preface and collection to Isidore of Seville?]

That the Spaniards remained ignorant of this collection for a longer time, or did not accept it, may be inferred from book II of Innocent III’s letter 121. From it we learn that, in a certain case, they presented to Alexander III their own book of canons, in which the Council of Mérida was described along with other councils.

But since that council is described with the others not in the Isidorian collection but in the more extensive Spanish collection, it follows that at that time the accepted corpus of canons among the Spaniards was still the Spanish collection.

The oldest Isidorian manuscripts are German-Frankish, so much so that those which were carried into other regions and reach the ninth century also came from Gaul, as will be shown in the following section concerning two Vatican manuscripts written in the ninth century.

Moreover, the pseudo-letters contain several German-Frankish idioms and the same barbarous style detected in other Gallic and German writers of the same period. Yet none of the idioms peculiar to the Spaniards—such as may be observed in Etherius and Eulogius—is present.

The matter is even clearer because the impostor transcribed a number of passages from the letters of St. Boniface, bishop of Mainz, and from the letter of Cangith, an abbess, to that same Boniface. These could have been found not in Spain but at Mainz and in Germany, where those persons lived.

Finally, there is an argument which seems to us the strongest of all. When the impostor incorporated the Spanish collection into his own, he did not use manuscripts of Spanish origin but those of Gallic origin.

We learned this by comparing the letters of St. Leo. We used two manuscripts of the Spanish collection: the Vienna manuscript 41, of Spanish origin, and Vatican manuscript 1341, of Gallic origin.

We have already noted the remarkable diversity of these manuscripts in their readings in chapter 4, no. 23. In the Vienna manuscript the readings are certainly corrupt, but even its errors approach the true reading; in the Vatican manuscript there are manifest arbitrary emendations that depart from the genuine text.

We recognized that this Vatican manuscript, which came from Gaul to the Vatican Library, is entirely similar in its readings or emendations to three other Gallic manuscripts cited by P. Coustant. No one can doubt that such manuscripts, found and disseminated in Gaul, derived from some diligent Gallic antiquarian who once copied and corrected a corrupt Spanish manuscript.

See what we noted on this subject in the place cited.

Furthermore, we compared the same letters of Leo with Merlin’s edition, which was derived from an Isidorian manuscript, and also with other Isidorian manuscripts, especially Vatican manuscript 630. Among the Isidorian manuscripts this is by far the oldest and contemporary with pseudo-Isidore; it contains a purer form of his collection.

The readings of these manuscripts not only differ greatly from those of the Vienna exemplar of Spanish origin; they reproduce precisely the same readings and emendations found in Vatican manuscript 1341 of Gallic origin.

This became so evident that, when we compared the Isidorian manuscript Vatican 630 with the Spanish Vatican 1341 in those same Leonine letters, one appeared to have been copied word for word from the other.

There can therefore be no doubt that, when inserting documents from the Spanish collection into his own, pseudo-Isidore used a manuscript not of Spanish but of Gallic origin.

Why was this so, unless he compiled his collection in Gaul, where such manuscripts existed, and not in Spain?

Who, then, after so many and such clear indications, could still doubt that the author was Gallic, or German-Frank?

## § V. On the Isidorian Manuscripts

### The order and catalogue of the documents in this collection taken from the oldest manuscript of all, Vatican 630. The spurious, genuine, and interpolated documents are carefully distinguished.

### 49.

Although manuscript copies of the Isidorian collection are common in libraries, most of them differ from one another so greatly that many people doubt what the primitive collection contained.

Many manuscripts contain only the decretal letters and lack the canons of the councils, although it is clear from pseudo-Isidore’s preface that he inserted those canons into his collection.

Among these manuscripts, some contain more letters and others fewer; some also occasionally differ in the order of the letters.

Those that present the canons together with the letters do not always agree either. Some are more extensive in their letters, which they either insert among the Isidorian material or add at the end.

We were able to find thirteen copies. Five of them, lacking the canons of the councils, differ generally both in the number and in the order of the letters. These are Vatican manuscripts 629, 3788, 3791, 3873, and Vallicellian manuscript D. 38.

Eight manuscripts containing both letters and canons—of which P. Coustant was unable to find even one (*Preface*, vol. I of *The Letters of the Roman Pontiffs*, no. 155)—were available to us: Vatican manuscripts 630, 931, and 1340; Vatican Ottobonianus 93; Casanatensis A 11, 14; Florentine, Library of the Dominicans of San Marco, 182; Patavinus 100; the manuscript of the Lateran Canons of St. John in the Green Garden; and the Venetian manuscript of the Ducal Library of San Marco, divided into two volumes, one marked no. 168 and the other no. 169.

Some of these, however, are mutilated and lack certain letters at the beginning or end.

### 50.

In order that, amid such great manuscript diversity, one may safely determine what the genuine pseudo-Isidorian collection was, or which documents were inserted into its original form, the following words of its preface provide the necessary light. In them the author expresses the outline, summary, and order of the documents in his collection:

[Note: Among the ecclesiastical disputations published by Michael Thomasius Taxaquet in Rome, in his own house, in 1565, there is a disputation on the manner of holding provincial and diocesan councils and on the matters principally to be treated in them. To it is appended Isidore’s order for celebrating a council. This is precisely the order discussed by the Ballerini.

In Vatican manuscript 630 of the pseudo-Isidorian collection, regarded as the oldest of all, the following inscription is written in a more recent hand: “A very useful book of Isidore of Seville on synods and decrees.” At the end is this note: “Peter de Pareja, household officer of the cardinal of Santa Croce, restored this book in the name of the cardinal to Lorenzo Parmenius, custodian of the Palatine Library; and the latter returned the silver cup on 8 January 1521.”]

> “At the beginning of this volume,” he says, “we have placed an account of how a council is to be celebrated among us, so that those who wish to follow our order may know how they ought to conduct it. Those, however, who choose to conduct it better should do what they judge by a just, canonical, and most prudent deliberation.
>
> “Finally, because of their authority, we have placed before the other councils the canons called apostolic, although some call them apocryphal, because many receive them, and the holy Fathers confirmed their statements by synodal authority and placed them among the canonical constitutions.
>
> “Next we inserted the decrees of certain letters of apostolic men—that is, of Clement, Anacletus, Evaristus, and the other apostolic men—such letters as we have so far been able to find, down to Pope Sylvester.
>
> “Afterward we placed the Nicene synod because of the authority of that great council. Then we placed within this volume the various councils of the Greeks and Latins, whether held earlier or later, distinguished by their own chapters according to the order of their numbers and dates. We also added the remaining decrees of the Roman bishops down to St. Gregory, together with certain of his letters, in which, because of the eminence of the apostolic see, there is an authority equal to that of the councils.”

Those manuscripts, therefore, which first present, after the preface, the order for celebrating a council; then give the canons of the apostles; afterward the letters of the apostles, or ancient pontiffs, from St. Clement to St. Sylvester; then Nicaea together with the other Greek and Latin councils; and finally the remaining letters of the pontiffs down to St. Gregory—these manuscripts must be regarded as containing the true and complete Isidorian collection.

We found precisely two such manuscripts: Vatican 630 and Vatican 631, both entirely complete.

Three others—Vatican Ottobonianus 93, the Florentine manuscript of San Marco, and the Casanatensis—contain both decretal letters and council canons; but since they are mutilated, they cannot provide knowledge of the complete collection.

Another manuscript, Vatican 1340, and the two Venetian manuscripts of San Marco add several documents after St. Gregory. Since these cannot be attributed to pseudo-Isidore, they must be assigned to additions, which will be discussed in the following chapter.

We did not have sufficient time to examine carefully Patavinus 100, of St. John in the Green Garden, although it is complete but of a later period.

Accordingly, from the two complete and pure Isidorian manuscripts, Vatican 630 and 631, which we examined more carefully, we shall provide a description of the entire Isidorian collection; some further remarks on the others will be added later.

Between these two complete Vatican manuscripts, however, we shall chiefly follow manuscript 630 in its series and order.

It must unquestionably be preferred to all the others, since it is not only Gallic—that is, from the region in which this collection was composed—but is also praised as the oldest of all by Montfaucon and Cardinal de Aguirre.

Two things prove that it is Gallic:

1. A note written at the beginning in a more recent hand: “This book belongs to the use of John, bishop of Arras.”
2. The letter of Luitard, bishop of Vence, to Wenilo of Rouen.

Its extreme antiquity and near-contemporaneity with pseudo-Isidore are shown by the catalogue of Roman pontiffs, which ends with Leo IV, Benedict III, and Nicholas I. From this it is recognized that the manuscript was written under Nicholas I, that is, between 858 and 867, at the time when the documents of this collection began to be cited by Hincmar and other Gallic bishops.

Hence this manuscript must be regarded as one of the earliest copies of the collection. This is repeatedly confirmed by two appendices containing certain documents which pseudo-Isidore had added in later revisions: in this original form of the collection they are appended at the end, whereas in other manuscripts they are inserted in their proper places.

Everyone can therefore see how much greater weight must be given to this manuscript than to the others in establishing and describing the collection.

### 51.

Before the collection, besides the catalogue of Roman pontiffs—which, as we noted, ends with Nicholas I—there is a note on the four general councils.

This is found in Gratian, distinction 15, chapter 1, and was taken from St. Isidore of Seville, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 16.

Then follows a note on six councils, as in Gratian, distinction 16, chapter 10; then another note on twenty-one other councils. The first eight of these are Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, Laodicea, Carthage, and Africa, which reflect the order of the Hadrianic collection.

The remaining thirteen are Gallic; none is Spanish. This indicates that the note was composed in Gaul.

The same note appears in Gratian, distinction 16, chapter 11, although three other Gallic councils are added there, thereby bringing the number to twenty-four.

Then, in the manuscript, after the mention of the Council of Mâcon proposed under number 21, eight further numbers, from 22 through 29, are supplied but left blank.

There follow another eighteen numbers, from 30 to 47, under which the Spanish councils and the remaining councils are indicated. These are later recalled in the table of councils under the same numbers.

A *Notice of the Provinces* is appended, which Andreas Scotus, Petrus Bertius, and Emmanuel Schelestratius published; afterward comes a *Notice of Gaul*, which has been published by several authors.

All these notes and notices occur not only in Vatican manuscript 631 and in other copies containing the complete Isidorian collection, but also in Vatican manuscript 1341, a Gallic manuscript containing a collection of Spanish origin. It is therefore beyond doubt that they were transferred either from some such copy of the Spanish collection into the Isidorian manuscripts or from Isidorian manuscripts into those copies of the Spanish collection.

All the material preceding the collection of Isidore and not belonging to it is concluded by the aforementioned letter of Luitard, bishop of Vence, to Wenilo of Rouen, written in 868. It is peculiar to Vatican manuscript 630 and was published from it in volume X of the Venetian edition of the Councils, column 1403.

### 52.

After this, the Isidorian collection begins with a preface bearing this title:

[Note: The old inscription of Vatican manuscript 630 is: “Here begins the preface of Isidore, bishop, to this book. This is Isidore Mercator.” In old Vatican manuscript 4160, folio 48 verso, there is an abridgment of the pseudo-Isidorian preface with this title: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the preface of St. Isidore, bishop. Isidore, servant of Christ, to Hector, his fellow servant and kinsman in the Lord, greeting. I am compelled by many,” etc. It ends: “the laws of the world prescribe.”

Perhaps this brief preface preceded another, fuller one, which is now found in the already published pseudo-Isidorian collection.

Then follows: “From the sayings of St. Boniface, chapter 1: Concerning the fact that a layman or an adulterer,” etc.

Instead of *Hector*, the other manuscripts give *reader*, but perhaps the author intended *Hector*. For it is not sufficiently appropriate for Isidore the bishop to call any reader a kinsman in the Lord.

Hector, bishop of Carthage, did sign the Council of Tarragona in 516; but this bishop is too early for us to suppose that the architect of the collection had him in mind as the person to whom he dedicated the work under the name of Isidore of Seville.

In Vatican manuscript 631 the title is: “Here begins Isidore’s preface to the following work. The servant of Christ sends greeting to his fellow servant, reader, and faithful kinsman in the Lord.”

In Vatican manuscript 629, discussed below in chapter 94, the title of the preface begins: “Isidore Mercator, servant,” or, if one prefers to understand it thus, “Isidore Mercator, servant of Christ.”

In one manuscript I found the name *peccator* (“sinner”) or *mercator* (“merchant”) written ambiguously.

There is some controversy as to whether the true reading is *Isidore peccator* or *Isidore Mercator*. The latter may be supported by manuscript copies that have it; also by the fact that in the ninth century Isidore Mercator, brother of St. Eulogius of Córdoba, lived, and some attribute the spurious collection to him.

The manuscripts, however, oppose this, and say that the author was a bishop. He could nevertheless have been called Mercator, as was Marius Mercator.

It is more probable, however, that the forger of the collection, observing that bishops and other pious men commonly called themselves sinners, attached this title to his Isidore.

Elipandus, in his letter to Migetius, volume V of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 550, refutes the quibble of this heretic:

> “Concerning priests, why do you assert that they call themselves sinners if they are truly holy? Or if they certainly confess themselves to be sinners, why do they presume to approach the ministry?” etc.

This sufficiently shows that it was in some sense a common practice for priests to call themselves sinners.

There is no time to collect examples. Some were indicated by Nicolás Antonio, who discusses the pseudo-Isidorian collection, and in a note by Bayer.]

> “Here begins the preface of St. Isidore, bishop. Isidore Mercator, servant of Christ, sends a greeting of faith to the reader, his fellow servant and kinsman in the Lord.”

“I am compelled by many,” etc.

This was published from Vatican manuscript 630 by Cardinal de Aguirre. See volume I of the *Councils*, p. 4.

Merlin omits *Mercator* and reads *fideli* (“faithful”) instead of *fidei* (“of faith”). The printed editions of the Councils substitute *peccator* for *Mercator*, but none of our manuscripts has that reading.
