*Mercator* is also read in the Paris manuscript seen by Harduin, as well as in Ivo’s *Decree*; only in the margin of the latter does *peccator* appear.

The preface is followed by the spurious letter of Aurelius to Damasus, beginning: “The glory of the apostolic see,” together with the apocryphal reply of Damasus, beginning: “The writings of your holiness.” See volume II of the *Councils*, columns 1011 and 1012.

In Vatican manuscript 631 these letters are written before the preface, but incorrectly; for Hincmar of Reims, in his work against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24, praises Damasus’s reply to Aurelius and says that Isidore placed it beneath his preface and set it before his collection.

Afterward follows the *Order for Celebrating a Council*: “At the first hour of the day,” etc., as in volume I of the *Councils*, from column 8 through column 12.

The author had accepted this order, taken from the beginning of the Fourth Council of Toledo, as something to be placed before the collection in the preface.

Next comes a table of councils with forty-seven titles. The first forty-five are those which we presented in the Spanish collection, chapter 4, no. 14. The other two are:

46. Decrees established by certain Roman prelates concerning the rule of faith and ecclesiastical discipline.

47. The Synod of Toledo of forty-eight bishops.

This same table, with the same forty-seven titles, is also found in the Casanatensis manuscript A 11 and in Vatican manuscript 1341, which contains the Spanish collection of Gallic origin. It therefore passed from one source into the other.

Certainly titles 46 and 47, which agree with neither the body of the Spanish collection nor that of the Isidorian collection, are recognized as additions.

There is indeed an error in title 46: it does not designate any council but is the very title prefixed in the Spanish collection to its second part, which contains the decretal letters of the apostolic see.

Two other spurious letters follow: one of St. Jerome to Damasus, beginning “The glory of your holiness,” etc.; and the other of Damasus to Jerome, beginning “The Church rejoices in your fountain,” etc.

They were published by Henschenius, Schelestratius, and others, and most recently were inserted into the appendix to the works of St. Jerome, volume XI of the Veronese edition, p. 275.

Since these letters are also found in certain manuscripts of the *Roman Pontifical* attributed to Damasus, which pseudo-Isidore used, it is impossible to determine whether their forgery originated with pseudo-Isidore himself or with another earlier author from whom he received them.

Next, fifty Apostolic Canons in the Dionysian version are described from the Hadrianic collection.

Then follow the letters of the ancient pontiffs, from St. Clement to Melchiades, all spurious and all fabricated by pseudo-Isidore, with the sole exception of two letters of St. Clement, which he nevertheless interpolated.

Here is their sequence, as they can be found in the published editions of the Councils.

Five letters of St. Clement: two to James; the third to all bishops and priests, etc.; the fourth to Julius and Julian; and the fifth to the inhabitants of Jerusalem with James their bishop.

The first two had already been fabricated by some Greek author and translated into Latin by Rufinus; they had passed into the older Italian and Gallic collections.

Only the second letter is entitled in the Italian collections “The Precepts of St. Peter.” Under that title we shall publish it from those same collections in this volume among the documents of the ancient canon law.

In the Gallic manuscripts cited by Harduin and Coustant, however, it is entitled “The Letter of the Precepts of Pope Clement, sent to James, the Lord’s brother,” or “The Letter of St. Clement of Rome to James concerning the mysteries of the Church.”

Pseudo-Isidore excerpted these two letters from the Gallic collections, and therefore retained the inscription of the second letter.

He himself fabricated the other three letters.

To the two spurious letters that he received from elsewhere, he added new fabrications by expanding them with lengthy interpolations.

Anyone will recognize these interpolations by comparing the same letters, as published from the Isidorian collection in the Councils, with the much shorter versions presented in this volume from the Rufinian translation and from the older collections: the first in the collection to be presented in chapter 64, column 454; the second among the documents mentioned shortly before, no. 5, column 674.

Three letters of St. Anacletus: the first to all the Easterners, the second to the bishops of Italy, and the third to all bishops.

Two of St. Evaristus: one to the African bishops and the other to the Egyptian bishops.

Three letters of St. Alexander I: the first to all orthodox Christians and the other two to all bishops.

Two letters of St. Xystus I: the first to all Christians and the other to all bishops.

One of St. Telesphorus, to all Christians.

Two letters of St. Hyginus: one to all Christians and the other to the Athenians.

Likewise two of St. Pius I: the first to all Christians and the second to the Italians.

One of St. Anicetus—printed as Anitius—to the bishops of Gaul.

Two of St. Soter: the first to the bishops of Campania and the second to the bishops of Italy.

One of St. Eleutherius, to the provinces of Gaul.

Two letters of St. Victor I: one to Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria, and the other to the Africans.

Two of St. Zephyrinus: the first to the bishops of Sicily and the second to the bishops of Egypt.

Two of St. Callistus I: one to Bishop Benedict and the other to the Gallic bishops.

One of St. Urban I, to all Christians.

Two of St. Pontian: the first to Felix of Succribo and the second to all Christians.

One of St. Anterus, to the bishops of the provinces of Baetica and Toledo.

Three of St. Fabian: the first to all bishops, the second to the Easterners, and the third to Bishop Hilary.

Two of St. Cornelius: one to all bishops and the other to Bishop Rusticus.

One of St. Lucius I, to the bishops of Gaul and Spain.

Two of St. Stephen I: the first to Bishop Hilary and the second to all bishops.

Two of St. Xystus II: the first to Bishop Gratus and the second to the bishops of Spain.

Two of St. Dionysius: one to the prefect Urban and the other to Bishop Severus.

Three letters of St. Felix I: the first to Bishop Paternus, the second to the bishops of Gaul, and the third to Bishop Benignus.

Two of St. Eutychian: the first to the bishops of Baetica and the second to the bishops of Sicily.

One of St. Gaius, to Bishop Felix.

Two of St. Marcellinus: one to Bishop Solomon and the other to the bishops of the East.

Two of St. Marcellus: the first to the bishops of the province of Antioch and the second to the tyrant Maxentius.

Three of St. Eusebius: the first to the bishops of Gaul, the second to those of Egypt, and the third to the bishops of Tuscia and Campania.

One of St. Melchiades, to the bishops of Spain.

In this first part, which concerns the ancient pontiffs from St. Clement through Melchiades inclusively—or, exclusively, up to St. Sylvester—pseudo-Isidore fabricated fifty-nine letters and reproduced and interpolated two letters formerly attributed to St. Clement.

### 53.

The part containing the councils follows.

It is prefaced by a work entitled *On the Primitive Church and the Nicene Synod*. Since this work is placed beneath the letters of Melchiades, it is cited by Gratian and others under the name of that pontiff. In the manuscripts, however, it bears no name.

It is, as it were, pseudo-Isidore’s prologue to the constitution that follows. It begins: “No one who reads the divine Scriptures,” etc., as in volume I of the Venetian edition of the *Councils*, column 1562.

The *Constitution of Constantine to Sylvester* follows: “In the name,” etc.; “Those things which our Savior and Redeemer,” etc. It is printed in the same place, column 1564.

This document is apocryphal. Some attribute it to pseudo-Isidore.

Balsamon quotes certain Greek fragments of it. P. Possinus, however, found the complete document written in Greek in the Greek Vatican manuscripts 614, folio 76; 789, folio 185; 973, folio 39; and 1416, folio 127, as P. Labbe noted.

For this reason, Baronius and Binius not implausibly suspected that this constitution was fabricated by the Greeks, later rendered into Latin, and then excerpted by pseudo-Isidore.

It is indeed read in Latin in the Gallic collection presented first by the ancient Colbertine manuscript 3368. See what we said in part II, chapter 8, no. 3.

Although this document appears to be an addition in that collection, since the Colbertine collection is older than pseudo-Isidore and received nothing Isidorian, it is sufficiently credible that pseudo-Isidore drew this document from that collection—or perhaps from another older Gallic collection.

It continues: “At what time the Council of Nicaea was held. The canons of the general councils began from the time of Constantine,” etc., and ends with the words “they handed down the second creed after that of the Apostles.” This is the beginning of the preface to the Spanish collection, which we gave in full in chapter 4, no. 14.

**213.** Here begins the letter, or preface, of the Council of Nicaea, to the most blessed Silvester, bishop of the apostolic see in the city of Rome, etc. This is a preface taken by Pseudo-Isidore from the collection published in this volume. See col. 22.

Next are transcribed the canons of the councils of Greece: Nicaea, Ancyra, Neocaesarea, Gangra, Sardica, Antioch, Laodicea, Constantinople, Ephesus, and Chalcedon, together with Atticus’s letters of communion (*formatae*). There are also the canons of eight councils of Africa, namely seven of Carthage and that of Milevis. Then follow the canons of the councils of Gaul: the three councils of Arles, and those of Valence, Tauriana, Riez, Orange, Vaison, Agde, and Orléans. Finally come the canons of the councils of Spain: Elvira, Tarragona, Gerona, Zaragoza, Lérida, Valencia, and Toledo I, II, III, and IV; then the beginning of Braga I, which is interrupted by the insertion of nine other synods of Toledo, from VII through XIII. The last of these is mutilated at the end in Merlin’s edition, but is read in full in Vaticanus 630 and other Isidorian manuscripts. Braga I is then supplied again, this time complete, followed shortly by Braga II. Next come the Chapters (*Capitula*) of Martin of Braga, the Council of Braga of the year 675, and finally two councils of Seville.

All these materials Pseudo-Isidore took from a fuller Spanish collection of Gallican origin, such as that found in manuscript Vaticanus 1341, with the same repetition of Braga I and the same readings, more freely corrected, as we noted earlier. Only in the Nicene material, after the creed, is the catalogue of bishops omitted—a catalogue that is found in the same manuscript of the Spanish collection.

**54.** The third part follows, presenting the letters of the remaining Roman pontiffs, from Saint Silvester to Saint Gregory. The same preface is placed before them: “The councils having thus far been arranged,” etc.; we cited it from the Spanish collection in chapter 4, no. 15.

The first document presented, however, is spurious. “Here begin certain excerpts from the synodal acts of Saint Silvester the pope. In the time of Saint Silvester the pope and Constantine the most devout Augustus, a great council was held at Nicaea,” etc., as in volume I of the Councils, from col. 1575 through the words at col. 1578, “the document was signed.” Since, however, in the edition of the councils the actual synodal acts of Saint Silvester are placed after these excerpts under the title “Canon, or Constitution of Silvester,” and since Pseudo-Isidore extracted these excerpts from them, these acts too, which are equally spurious, are transmitted as incorporated into the Isidorian collection. Yet although they are found in one Isidorian manuscript, they are absent from our manuscript and from the others we have consulted. He would have undertaken pointless labor in composing excerpts from those same acts if he had thought the acts themselves should be inserted into his collection. Hincmar of Reims mentions only these excerpts as found in his own manuscript, in his often-cited work against Hincmar of Laon, chapter 24; there too he rejects such acts as apocryphal.

Since, moreover, these materials were compiled under the age of Symmachus together with other apocryphal documents and inserted into certain Italian collections, and since they also passed into Gaul—as they are read in the ancient Colbertine manuscript 784, concerning which see part II, chapter 6, nos. 4 and 5—Pseudo-Isidore must be said to have derived these excerpts from some such Gallican exemplar. It is also beyond doubt that he had before his eyes the Roman *Pontifical*, attributed to Damasus, whose author presents the same synodal acts of Saint Silvester in abbreviated form. For certain portions of Pseudo-Isidore’s excerpts agree more closely with the abbreviation of the *Pontifical* than with the acts themselves.

The spurious letter of Athanasius and the other Egyptians to Pope Mark, in which they ask for a copy of the Nicene canons, and Mark’s equally spurious reply to them. See volume II of the Councils, cols. 488 and 490.

“Faith treated in the sacred Roman council by the most blessed Pope Julius and the other bishops of the true faith. In the name of the Lord God and Savior,” etc. Ibid., col. 549. This too is a Pseudo-Isidorian fabrication.

Pope Julius’s letter to the Orientals on behalf of Saint Athanasius: “You ought, brothers, to instruct others in ecclesiastical disciplines,” etc. Ibid., col. 497. It is apocryphal.

The reply of the Orientals is likewise apocryphal: “Although concerning all,” etc. Ibid., col. 502.

Julius’s reply to the same Orientals: “You ought, against the holy Roman and apostolic Church,” etc. Ibid., col. 506. It is apocryphal.

The synodical letter of Athanasius and the Egyptians to Pope Liberius is apocryphal: “The rights of your most blessed fatherhood,” etc. In the same volume II of the Councils, col. 817.

Liberius’s reply to the same persons is likewise spurious: “Formerly and from the beginning,” etc. Ibid., col. 819.

The apocryphal letter of Athanasius and the Egyptians to Pope Felix: “We bring word to your holy apostolate,” etc. Ibid., col. 993.

Felix’s reply: “Your sacred synodical letter,” etc. Ibid., col. 999. Another letter of the same pope to the same persons begins, “Grace to you,” etc., col. 1005. Both are spurious.

Liberius’s letter to all the bishops: “There is nothing that can stand,” etc. Ibid., col. 815. It is apocryphal.

Damasus to Paulinus: “Through my son Vitalis,” etc. Ibid., col. 1014. This genuine letter of Damasus was taken from the Spanish collection.

Afterward Pseudo-Isidore divided another genuine letter of the same Damasus to the same Paulinus, taken from the Spanish collection and otherwise entitled “Confession of Faith to the Same Paulinus,” into three parts, inserting three apocryphal letters among them. A table of six chapters is placed first; the three genuine portions of the letter and the three spurious letters that follow the table correspond to it as follows:

1. **Damasus to Paulinus.** “After the Council of Nicaea, another council was later assembled in the city of Rome,” etc., as in volume II of the Councils, col. 1061, through the words: “If anyone thinks rightly concerning the Father and the Son but does not hold rightly concerning the Holy Spirit, he is a heretic.” This is the first part of the aforementioned letter, or confession of faith, to Paulinus, except that here the decree against those who migrate from their own churches to others is omitted; it is supplied below under title 6.

2. **The letter of Stephen and the three councils of Africa to Damasus.** “We make known to your blessedness,” etc. Ibid., col. 1018. It is spurious.

3. **That all heretics who think wrongly concerning the Son of God and the Holy Spirit are found in the unbelief of the Jews and Gentiles.** “But if anyone allows God the Father, God the Son, and the Holy Spirit to be called gods,” etc. This is the final part of the aforementioned genuine letter to Paulinus. Ibid., col. 1063B. After the final words, “let us believe without doubt,” the Isidorian manuscript adds several further sentences that are not found in the pure copies of the Spanish collection.

4. **The letter of Damasus to Prosper of Numidia and the other Africans.** “Although, dearest brothers, these things are known to us,” etc. Ibid., col. 1025. It is apocryphal.

5. **On priests who migrate from their own churches to others.** “Those priests, however, who move from churches to churches,” etc. Ibid., col. 1062C, through the words “let him rest in the Lord.” This is a decree from the aforementioned genuine letter of Damasus to Paulinus, which had previously been omitted.

The synodical letter of Damasus to the bishops of Illyricum, “We believe your holy faith,” etc., was taken from Epiphanius’s version in the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 29. Pseudo-Isidore added to it the spurious chronological note: “Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November, in the consulship of the illustrious men Siricius and Ardabur.” See volume II of the Councils, col. 1031.

The apocryphal letter of Damasus to the bishops of Italy: “I had wished, beloved,” etc. Ibid., col. 1033.

The three letters of Siricius are all genuine and were taken from the Spanish collection: one to Himerius, another to various persons against Jovinian, and a third to the orthodox throughout the various provinces. Ibid., cols. 1212, 1218, and 1223.

The two spurious letters of Anastasius: the first to the bishops of Germany and Burgundy, the second to the most noble man Nerianus. Ibid., cols. 1428 and 1430.

The twenty-three letters of Innocent are all genuine and were excerpted from the Spanish collection. They are read in volume III of the Councils, from letter 1 of that pontiff through letter 23, col. 13 and following.

The letter of the Council of Carthage to Innocent and Innocent’s reply; then the letter of the Council of Milevis to the same pontiff, together with his reply; likewise the private letter of five African bishops to Innocent himself and his response; finally, Innocent’s private letter to Aurelius. These seven letters are read in the Gallican collection printed in this volume, from which Pseudo-Isidore drew them. See below, col. 128 through col. 164.

The two letters of Zosimus, excerpted from the Spanish collection: one to Hesychius and the other to the clergy of Ravenna. They appear among the letters of Zosimus in volume III of the Councils, letters 1 and 2.

The letter of Pope Boniface to the Emperor Honorius, together with Honorius’s reply, and another letter of the same pontiff to the bishops of Gaul. They are genuine and were taken from the Spanish collection. They appear in the same volume III of the Councils among the letters of Boniface.

The three letters of Celestine, likewise from the Spanish collection: one to Venerius and the other Gallic bishops; another to the bishops established throughout the provinces of Vienne and Narbonne; and a third to the bishops of Apulia. In the Councils they are letters 1, 2, and 3 of this pontiff.

One apocryphal letter of Sixtus III to the Oriental bishops. It is in volume IV of the Councils, letter 3.

Afterward, from the Spanish collection and in precisely the same order, there follow thirty-nine letters of Saint Leo and others, which we listed in the description of the Spanish collection in chapter 4, no. 15.

Three documents of Pope Hilary from the same Spanish collection: namely, a synodal decree and two letters to Ascanus of Tarragona. In the Councils they are letters 1, 2, and 3.

The letter of Pope Simplicius to Zeno of Spalatum, and the letter of Acacius to Simplicius, from the same collection. The former is letter 1 of that pontiff in the Councils; the latter follows letter 8.

The three letters of Felix II—called Felix III by Pseudo-Isidore—from the same Spanish collection: one to the Sicilians, another to Acacius, and a third to Zeno of Spalatum. In the Councils they are letters 6, 7, and 8.

The decree of Pope Gelasius concerning books to be received or not received, beginning “After the prophetic and evangelical Scriptures,” etc., as in volume V of the Councils, col. 386. This genuine decree was copied from some older collection or Gallican manuscript, such as Colbertine 784, discussed in part II, chapter 6, and Colbertine 3368, discussed in chapter 8 there.

Another general decree of the same pope, elsewhere entitled “Letter to the bishops of Lucania and Sicily.” Also another letter of the same pope to the Sicilians. These two were excerpted from the Spanish collection and are read in volume V of the Councils, letters 7 and 10.

Four letters of the same Gelasius: the first to the master Faustus, the second to the emperor Anastasius, the third to the bishops of Dardania, and the fourth to the Orientals. These were taken from the Gallican collection printed in this volume, chapters 48, 49, 50, and 51.

The letter of Pope Anastasius to Anastasius Augustus, from the Spanish collection. It appears in volume V of the Councils, letter 1, among the letters of that pontiff.

The letter of Pope Symmachus to Caesarius of Arles, likewise from the Spanish collection. Ibid., letter 5 among the letters of Symmachus.

Three genuine councils under the same Symmachus are appended from the Hadrianic collection; in volume V of the Councils they are entitled Synods I, III, and IV. In most Isidorian manuscripts two other synods under the same pontiff are inserted here; we have proved the two former fictitious, while the other is genuine and taken from Ennodius. In Vaticanus 630, however, these are relegated to the end of the collection; they will be discussed below.

Eight letters of Hormisdas and two to Hormisdas, in the same order in which we listed them in the Spanish collection, from which Pseudo-Isidore derived them.

Two letters of Pope John I: one to Zacharias the archbishop and another to the Italian bishops. They are spurious.

Two further spurious letters of Felix III—called Felix IV by Pseudo-Isidore: the first to all the bishops and the second to Sabina.

The apocryphal letter of Boniface II to Eulalius.

The apocryphal letter of John II to Bishop Valerius.

The equally apocryphal letter of Agapetus I to Anthemius, bishop of Constantinople.

The letter of Bishop Amator to Pope Silverius and Silverius’s reply: both are spurious.

The genuine letter of Vigilius to Profuturus, taken from the Spanish collection; but in Pseudo-Isidore it is addressed to Eutherius because of a corrupt reading, concerning which see chapter 4, no. 25. To this letter he added two chapters of his own, the sixth and seventh.

The spurious letter of Pelagius I to Bishop Vigilius; in Vaticanus 631 it is addressed to Julius.

The equally spurious decrees of Pope John III to the Germans and Gauls.

The apocryphal letter of Pope Benedict to Bishop David.

The three letters of Pelagius II: one to the bishops of the Council of Constantinople, a second to Archbishop Benignus, and a third to all the bishops, especially those of Campania and Italy. All are apocryphal.

Six letters of Saint Gregory the Great. The first three are genuine and were taken from the Spanish collection: the first and second to Leander, bishop of Seville, and the third to King Reccared. They are read in book I, letter 43, and book IX, letters 121 and 122, of the Maurist edition of the *Register*. After these are placed three other letters of Gregory, which could have been taken either from his *Register* or from other Gallican collections: one to Secundinus, found in book IX, letter 52, but interpolated in Pseudo-Isidore with a long addition, which we shall see in part IV, chapter 8, was fabricated by another earlier impostor; another to the patrician Theoctista, found in book XI, letter 45; and a third to Augustine, which presents Augustine’s questions and Gregory’s answers, as they are read in the same book XI, letter 64.

A synod under the same Gregory the Great, with six canons, through the words “seeks to undergo servitude,” as found in volume VI of the Councils, col. 1310.

The decrees of Pope Gregory the Younger. This is the Roman synod printed in volume VIII of the Councils, col. 185. With this synod the original Pseudo-Isidorian collection ends. In manuscript Vaticanus 630, from which we have reproduced the description of this collection, a blank leaf follows. This confirms that the collection ended with the synod just mentioned, so that the materials appended after that leaf in the same manuscript must be counted as a later addition.

The following documents, written in the same hand as the entire manuscript, are appended; they concern the case of Pope Symmachus.

The apologetic booklet of Ennodius on behalf of the Roman Palmary Synod and Symmachus. See volume V of the Councils, col. 479.

Synods V and VI under the same Symmachus, which we proved spurious in no. 42. They appear there at cols. 501 and 509.

Two letters of Ennodius attributed to Symmachus: one to Laurentius of Milan, beginning “The movement of a religious conscience has emerged.” It is found among the works of Ennodius, but under the title “Ennodius’s Third Speech, given to Stephen, the most venerable vicar, to be delivered to Bishop Maximus”; the other to the patrician Liberius, which in the same Ennodius is letter 1 of book V.

Since these documents—especially the two spurious synods—are attributed to Pseudo-Isidore, and since they are found inserted in other copies of the Isidorian collection after the three genuine synods of Symmachus, they seem to have been added through the later efforts of Pseudo-Isidore. For that reason they are copied at the end of the aforementioned Vaticanus 630, which in its preceding leaves contains the original collection without these documents.

**218.** After these additions, another blank and empty page is left in the same manuscript; afterward the following materials are added in the same hand.

The chapters attributed to Pope Hadrian and delivered to Angilram, bishop of Metz. There are fifty-two chapters, to the last of which another nineteen chapters are immediately attached. These, published in volume VIII of the Councils, col. 599, are spurious; we demonstrated in no. 42 that they were arranged by the impostor after his first production.

The disputation of the emperor Constantius and Liberius, Roman pontiff: “The emperor Constantius said,” etc., as in the *Tripartite History*, book V, chapter 17.

Certain sanctions collected piecemeal from the proceedings of the Council of Chalcedon, which we have also found in other collections.

On the transfer of bishops, from book XII of the *Tripartite History*, chapters 8 and 11.

Also from a letter of Pope Pelagius: “That a bishop ought not to pass from city to city.”

Here the manuscript ends. The chapters falsely attributed to Hadrian I are appended, in other Isidorian manuscripts that insert the pseudo-synods of Symmachus in their proper place, after the decrees of Gregory the Younger. They are believed to belong to the Isidorian collection—since they are found only there, together with materials deriving from the Isidorian collection. Certainly their spurious character reflects the character of Pseudo-Isidore; we have observed that they were excerpted from spurious letters composed by him, so that the same author of all these materials is discernible.

Since Pseudo-Isidore wrote in his preface that he would append the decrees of the Roman pontiffs not through Hadrian but through Saint Gregory, these chapters must be said not to have belonged to his original production, but to have been fabricated afterward by the same person. They are therefore rightly listed separately among the additions in our manuscript.

[**Note:** Thus far I have taken from the Ballerini brothers what should suffice to distinguish the ancient Spanish collection of canons from the spurious Pseudo-Isidorian collection. These highly learned men add further material concerning certain manuscript codices that do not contain the Pseudo-Isidorian collection either wholly pure or complete; concerning certain apocryphal letters wrongly attributed to Pseudo-Isidore; concerning additions to the Pseudo-Isidorian collection published by Merlin; and concerning the various codices in which the same collection is presented in different orders.

The substance of all this is that the genuine ancient Spanish collection, in whose enlargement and arrangement Saint Isidore of Seville probably had some part, is preserved among the Gothic manuscripts of Spain free from every fraud; that the same collection, somewhat adulterated and interpolated, is found in Gallican manuscripts; and that from these manuscripts, already corrupted to some extent, either Benedict the Levite or someone else in the Germanic-Frankish empire took the opportunity to construct a spurious collection under the assumed name of Isidore of Seville. Many genuine documents were added, many spurious ones that had already been circulated before him, and many others fabricated by himself.

This very spurious collection was then exposed to the frauds of other falsifiers, who sought to enlarge it with new fabrications. I intend, at the appropriate place among the appendices, to include the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo, which Isidore presided over and to which most of the material is generally attributed. I shall also add from the ancient Vatican manuscript 4160 the brief preface mentioned shortly before at no. 52, written in the name of Saint Isidore to Hector, which has not yet been committed to print and perhaps provided Pseudo-Isidore with a model for composing a fuller preface of his own.]

Manuscript Vaticanus 631, formerly belonging to Cardinal Peter, bishop of Rouen, and written in the twelfth century, contains everything found in Vaticanus 630 except the two final additions concerning the transfer of bishops and the letter of Pope Pelagius. The order is altered in certain places; and although the additions concerning Symmachus are copied in their proper place after the three genuine synods of that pontiff, the Chapters of Hadrian are appended after the decrees of Gregory the Younger without any indication that they are an addition. A distinctive feature of this manuscript is that, after the Isidorian collection, it adds the entire Hadrianic collection and the version of the Sixth Council under Pope Agatho.

## CHAPTER XCII. Was Isidore the author of the Visigothic law code?

1. Some attribute the code of Visigothic laws—or Gothic law, or Gothic right—to Isidore, as though such a code had been arranged and promulgated at the command of Sisenand in the Fourth Council of Toledo, of which Isidore was president and played a major part. Niccolò Antonio says that this error was drawn from the titles of ancient codices, which attribute the work to Sisenand.

But, as the same author observes, since the twelve books comprising the Gothic Code consist for the most part of the laws of Chindaswinth and his son Recceswinth, who lived after Sisenand and Isidore, the volume was either compiled in the time of Egica, as Ambrosio de Morales thinks in book XII, chapter 16, or in that of his son Wittiza, to whom belongs law 3, title 1, book VI. The opinion of those who refer it to the time of Alfonso the Chaste, at the end of the eighth or beginning of the ninth century, must be rejected altogether.

In the Emilian Codex of the Councils, concerning which Flórez writes in volume III of *España sagrada*, p. 390, images of the kings Chindaswinth, Recceswinth, and Egica are shown with the caption: “These are the kings who arranged the Book of Judgments.” Images of other kings are added. The codex is from the tenth century.

2. The code of Gothic laws was called by the Spaniards the *Book of Judgments*; it was also often called the *Forum of Judgments*, as though meaning a tribunal, or the laws of the judges, whence the Spanish expression *Fuero Judgo*, or *Fuero Juzgo*. At the Council of Coyanza near Oviedo, held in 1050 under Ferdinand I, king of Castile, the *Book of Judgments* and Gothic law are mentioned. Thus chapter 7 says: “Let them receive the punishment that is established in the Book of Judgments concerning false witnesses.” Chapter 9 says: “Let every church, as the canons prescribe and as Gothic law commands, recover and possess its rights at all times.” Again, chapter 12 says: “Let him do what Gothic law commands.”

Bayer, in his note to no. 181 of book V of the *Bibliotheca Hispana*, lists an Escorial codex written in 1014, entitled *Forum Judicum*, or *Laws of the Visigoths*.

3. A code of the ancient laws of the northern peoples was published at Frankfurt in 1613, and included in this system of laws was the code of Visigothic laws, which was also published in the third volume of *Hispania illustrata*, p. 841.

Alfonso de Villadiego Vascuñana, a Toledan jurist, published in Spanish at Madrid in 1600, in folio, *The Ancient Forum of the Gothic Kings of Spain, Formerly Called the Book of Judgments, Today Called the Fuero Juzgo*, in twelve books. He added a brief catalogue and history of those and the other kings of Spain.

This edition of the Spanish version of the *Fuero Juzgo* is not very highly regarded by our learned men. Aldrete was considering the preparation of a fuller edition, as the Madrid *Literary Journals* report in volume V, article 2. Indeed, Burriel, in a letter to Don Pedro de Castro, rightly desired that a new edition of the Latin text and the Spanish version be prepared from old exemplars, many of which are preserved in the archives of Spain. The Madrid public news announced on 31 May 1796 a second, corrected edition, with a preface, by Don Juan Antonio Llorente.

4. Whether Isidore prescribed any of the laws found in the *Fuero Juzgo* may reasonably be questioned. Although ancient historians are silent concerning this labor of his, it is nevertheless established that Isidore was held in great honor by the kings of his time. As Braulio says in his preface, Isidore “explained domestic and public discipline, the names, kinds, duties, and causes of all divine and human things.”

Moreover, how well versed Isidore was in civil law is demonstrated most clearly by book V of the *Etymologies*. “Isidore,” says Niccolò Antonio, “could certainly have been the author of some of the laws in that Code which kings contemporary with him had promulgated publicly. Hence Lucas of Tuy may have called him the legislator of Spain in book III of his *Chronicle* at the beginning. And perhaps these are the laws that appear scattered everywhere throughout the work under the heading ‘ancient,’ without any mention of their promulgator.”

**221.** 5. The authority of Lucas of Tuy must not be passed over casually. In his chronicles, when he discusses Ervig, he records the following:

“This man held a great synod with the bishops at Toledo; he partly corrupted and partly corrected the laws that had been issued by his predecessors, and commanded that those handed down by Isidore of Seville, bishop and primate of Spain, be marked with his own name, or called ‘ANCIENT,’ so that it would not appear that judicial proceedings were being conducted in the name of the Church.”

If this account is true, the laws that in the Gothic Code are called “ancient,” or are prefaced with Ervig’s name, were handed down by Isidore—at least some of them. For it cannot be believed either that Ervig enacted no laws of his own, or that before Isidore there were no laws called ancient. Indeed, I think that no laws ever stood in the Code under Isidore’s name; rather, some ancient laws were arranged by him into an orderly form, while others were newly enacted but marked with the names of contemporary kings.

6. It was an old conviction among the Spaniards that Isidore was the legislator of Spain, as may be gathered from the same Lucas of Tuy, who says in his chronicle concerning Ferdinand I, king of Castile:

“Because the blessed confessor Isidore had been the teacher and legislator of Spain, King Ferdinand decreed that the Gothic laws should be learned by all the people of León in his church.”

A variant reading is noted: “should be preserved”; but perhaps it is preferable to read “should be learned.” To this I refer what Saint Martin of León, older than Lucas, also included among Isidore’s praises in his sermon on Isidore’s death, above, chapter 10, no. 7:

“He explained to priests the ecclesiastical offices and the ranks of all orders; he established laws for kings and princes; he forbade greed to judges.”

Some think that the Gothic laws were arranged by Isidore at some council of bishops, either the Fourth Council of Toledo or another. Perhaps this is what the author of a certain account found in the tomb of Saint Severus, bishop of Barcelona, in 1405, had in mind; Flórez discusses it in volume XXIX of *España sagrada*, p. 57.

The parchment, written after the year 1226 and found in the tomb of Saint Severus, reported among other things:

“This Severus, bishop of Barcelona and most holy martyr, was crowned with martyrdom on the eighth day before the Ides of November in the year of our Lord 608. His body rests eight miles from the city of Barcelona, in a place called OCTAVIANI, in the monastery of Saint Cucuphas. He was one of those seventy bishops who established the Gothic law in Spain.”

Some copies give 638; others say that the date is absent; and some even read: “who established the Gothic laws in Spain.”

7. Flórez argues that the parchment was written in a later age by someone ignorant of the condition of the Gothic kingdom, and that there was no other bishop and martyr of Barcelona named Severus apart from the one who, under the emperor Diocletian, received the crown of martyrdom.

Yet certainly the author of the account, when he mentions seventy bishops, seems to allude to the Fourth Council of Toledo, which Isidore presided over and at which sixty-two bishops, besides the representatives of seven bishops, subscribed. This shows that the Spaniards were then influenced by the belief that the Gothic law had been established at that council.

But since the council’s acts say nothing at all about Gothic laws, we can assert nothing with certainty. On the other hand, it is well established that the Goths used their own laws before that time. Isidore, in his *History of the Goths*, era 504, says of Euric:

“Under this king the Goths began to have established laws; previously they had been bound only by customs and usage.”

Again, era 606, concerning Leovigild:

“In the laws too he corrected what seemed to have been incoherently established by Euric, adding many laws that had been omitted and removing many that were superfluous.”

8. Two questions still remain. First, whether before Euric the Goths had no written laws at all; second, whether, even if Euric was the first to gather the laws into a single body and others later enlarged and shaped the same collection, Sisenand nevertheless produced some new system of laws that could in large part be attributed to Isidore.

When the Royal Academy of Madrid proposed the completion of a vast work entitled *Universal Critical Dictionary of Spain*, Antonio Fernández Priego, an advocate in the Madrid court, was assigned the task of investigating Spanish laws. From these beginnings arose the work *History of the Royal Law of Spain, Containing an Account of Some of the Primitive Laws and Most Ancient Customs of the Spaniards; Those of the Ancient Fuero of the Goths; and Those Established Later, from the Beginning of the Restoration of This Monarchy until the Time of King Alfonso the Wise, under Whom the Fuero Real and the Seven Partidas Were Instituted*. Madrid, 1738, Antonio Sanz, quarto.

He promised a second part on the laws of the *Ordinance*, the *Style*, Toro, the *New Compilation*, and the *Pragmatic Sanctions*.

**223.** 9. The learned authors of the literary periodicals, who at that time reviewed the works of recent writers in Madrid, set out Fernández’s opinions in volume V and sometimes reject them. From the words of Isidore cited above, Fernández had concluded that Euric was the first of all to give laws to the Goths.

But the periodical writers, following Sirmond on Sidonius, letter 1 of book II, conjecture that some Gothic laws existed before Euric, although Euric was the first to gather them, together with others, into one body. They cite these words from an old manuscript codex, published in the collection of the Writers of Gaul, volume I, p. 818:

“First, Athanaric ruled among the Goths for fourteen years,” etc. “Under him the Goths began to have law and letters.”

10. Fernández had denied that a new collection of Gothic laws was made by Sisenand. Against this, the *Literary Journals* appeal to the Escorial manuscript codices, whose titles are as follows:

*The Fuero Juzgo arranged by Sisenand, Gothic king of Spain, and its bishops*, in ancient script and on original parchment.

Another: *The Fuero called Juzgo, arranged by Sisenand.*

Another: *The communal or Juzgo Fuero, composed and arranged by Sisenand and the bishops of Spain at Toledo, which Don Alfonso the Wise ordered to be copied. It speaks of insults and the penalties imposed for them; they are as follows,* etc.

These three codices agree in attributing the arrangement of the legal system to Sisenand. Two of them also seem to allude to the Fourth Council of Toledo, which Isidore presided over, since many believe that the Book or *Fuero Juzgo* was arranged at that council.

11. Although the authority of these three codices should not be rashly dismissed, no entirely certain argument can be drawn from it, since it is clear that they were written long after the Gothic kingdom and certainly at a time when the opinion had already become widespread that Isidore was the legislator of Spain.

Nor can it be conjectured that such codices were copied from older ones dating from the Gothic period. Since the laws are presented in the Spanish language, the first exemplar of codices of this kind cannot predate the age of Saint Ferdinand. Pellizerius is therefore rightly ridiculed for thinking that the collection of Gothic laws, whose formation began under King Euric, was written in the language in which it is now read, and for using this to argue for the antiquity of the Spanish idiom, which he supposed the Spaniards had used from their earliest origins.

The Gothic Code of law was therefore written in Latin. The *Literary Journals* assert that its oldest exemplar exists in the Escorial library and describe it as follows:

“The most ancient and most carefully corrected Gothic codex of the Judgments of the Goths in Spain, with exorcisms and blessings used by them, written in Gothic script on parchment.”

There is no mention there either of Sisenand, or of Isidore, or of the bishops of Spain, although the blessings and exorcisms could have been arranged only according to the prescriptions of bishops. Perhaps this is the codex that Bayer, as I said earlier, reports as entitled *Forum Judicum*, or *Laws of the Visigoths*. After the third book it contains a little poem on the degrees of kinship under this heading: “Verses of Lord Isidore on affinity,” etc.

Fernández asserts in chapter 6 of book II that other manuscript codices of the *Fuero Juzgo* exist in the archive of the Church of Toledo. Burriel lists three in his letter to Don Pedro de Castro: one is written in Gothic script with Arabic annotations; besides these, there are two others, one in the convent of Saint John of the Kings and the other in the college of Saint J.

[Col. 0763C] **12.** Therefore it is not in the Latin copies, but in the inscriptions and prologue of the Spanish version of the *Fuero Juzgo*, that it is asserted that such a collection of laws was compiled by Sisenand at the Fourth Council of Toledo, under Isidore’s presidency. Fernandez, indeed, asserted that the Gothic laws were translated into the Spanish language between the years 900 and 1000, when the counts governed Castile. Laurentius Hervás, a most prolific writer, affirms in his *Catalogue of Languages*, chapter 4, article 5, no. 326, that the law code *Fuero Juzgo* is believed to have been composed in the ninth century—at the time, namely, when the poem of Cidi was composed, whose beginning is: “From their eyes, weeping very bitterly.” In truth, the Spanish version of the *Fuero Juzgo*, which must be the subject here (for the Latin text was the work of the Gothic kings), must be assigned to the thirteenth century. The Madrid diarists rightly attribute the translation to Saint Ferdinand on the basis of the words of that same *Fuero*, granted to the people of Córdoba in 1241, after Saint Ferdinand had captured their city: “I further establish and command that the *Juzgo* book, which I shall give to the people of Córdoba, be translated into the vernacular,” etc. The letter of Burriel mentioned above should also be consulted.

**13.** Moreover, from the same Madrid *Diaries*, volume VI, article 5, it should be added that Joseph Bermúdez, an eminent judge of criminal cases in the royal court, published a notable work entitled *Regalia del aposentamiento de corte, su origen, y progreso, leyes, ordenanzas, y reales decretos*, etc. [*The royal prerogative concerning court lodging, its origin and development, laws, ordinances, and royal decrees*], Madrid, Antonio Sanz, 1738, quarto. [Col. 0764B] Bermúdez thinks that Sisenand collected 225 laws in the *Fuero Juzgo*, which were observed in Spain until the tyranny of the Arabs. After Spain was recovered, observance of the same laws continued, and those laws were granted by name to certain cities. Among these, Saint Ferdinand gave the people of Córdoba the *Fuero Juzgo*, ordering that it be written in the Spanish language, as appears from the autograph *Fuero* itself preserved in the Cordobese convent of Saint Paul. Bermúdez possessed a copy of it, and the diarists had seen another.

**14.** Just as Burriel had decided to publish for the general public a Spanish collection of the canons, furnished with commentaries and dissertations, so too he had prepared the *Fuero Juzgo*, embellished with notes and variant readings, so that it might be printed. This is recorded in the manuscript catalogue of his works [Col. 0764C], which I possess in the hand of his brother Antonio. In this connection, Burriel’s learned Spanish letter, together with others of his printed at Madrid in earlier years, was published under the title *Ad D. Joannem de Amaia: De legibus Hispaniae* [*To Don Juan de Amaia: On the Laws of Spain*]. How capable he was in this field is also shown by his excellent Spanish work, *Informe de Toledo sobre igualacion de pesos, y medidas en todos los reynos, y señorios de su mag., segun las leyes* [*Report of Toledo on the equalization of weights and measures in all the kingdoms and lordships of His Majesty, according to the laws*], which appeared in quarto in 1758 without the author’s name. But, apart from the fact that the matter can be established from other sources, Burriel himself, in the copy he gave to Zaccaria and which I preserve, as I noted elsewhere, wrote in his own hand that he was the author.

## Part Four. DESCRIPTION OF ROMAN MANUSCRIPT CODICES THAT CONTAIN ISIDORE’S WORKS

[Col. 0763]

## CHAPTER XCIII. Manuscript Codices of the Vatican Library Containing Isidore’s Genuine, Doubtful, or Spurious Works

Six such codices from the old Vatican Library are described. A fragment of Isidore’s commentary on Genesis, perhaps the literal commentary, which has perished. On the juridical and musical notations found in some manuscripts of the *Etymologies*. Isidore’s *Etymologies* interpolated in many copies. A notable example of interpolation.

[Col. 0763D]

The Vatican Library is so rich in manuscript codices containing several works of Isidore [Col. 0764D] that I do not know whether such a quantity of copies can be found in any other region. One might reasonably wonder whether this redounds more to the praise of Isidore, whose copies are so numerous in a single Vatican Library, or to the commendation of the Vatican Library, which presents us with so many handwritten books of one Isidore. I am undertaking to examine all these codices carefully, insofar as I am able, following the method I have maintained in publishing other ancient Fathers, and also so that I may offer some specimen of the wealth of this kind that fills the Vatican Library. It is fair, however, first to acknowledge that in this part of my work I owe much to the singular courtesy of the most distinguished prelate Joseph Reggio, prefect of the Vatican Library. Besides greatly assisting my efforts by the wide-ranging learning in which he excels, he most kindly granted me permission to examine all the Isidorian codices and collate them at leisure.

**2.** The manuscript books of the Vatican Library are divided into five classes. The first is that called the old Vatican Library and sometimes designated simply by the name “Vatican Library.” The second is the Royal-Vatican Library, or that of Queen Christina of Sweden, also called the Alexandrian Library; into it were brought, for the most part, those manuscript books that once belonged to Christina, queen of Sweden. The third is the Palatine Library [Col. 0765B], containing the manuscript books of the Heidelberg Library, given to the Vatican Library by Duke Maximilian of Bavaria after he had conquered Heidelberg. The fourth is the Urbino Library, formerly belonging to the dukes of Urbino; its printed books are kept in the Roman Library of the Sapienza, and its manuscripts in the Vatican. The fifth is the Ottobonian Library, formed from the codices once belonging to Alexander VIII Ottoboni, among which are also some that once belonged to Queen Christina’s library. I shall therefore first review the Isidorian codices of the old Vatican Library, or simply of the Vatican Library.

**3.** Vatican Codex 202, parchment, small folio, with rubricated titles. The inventory indicates on page 156: *Excerpts from Isidore’s book on Genesis*. Also certain sayings of his on virginity. At the beginning of the codex, in a more recent hand, are some moral monostichs. Then the rubric:

“In this codex are the following letters of Caecilius Cyprian, seventeen in number, and three books to Quirinus on the sacrament of Christ. The first letter is to Donatus,” etc.

Among other works there is also Cyprian’s treatise *On the Lord’s Prayer*, which was recently printed at Florence through misguided labor as though it were an unpublished work of Saint Augustine. On page 139 is Saint Augustine’s letter to Macedonius, beginning, “Your business is exceedingly pressing,” etc. On page 146 is Saint Augustine’s sermon *On Penance*: “Penitents, penitents, penitents—if indeed you are penitents.” After other sermons of the same Augustine comes Pope Leo’s letter to Theodore of Fréjus, beginning, “Your concern indeed,” and on page 154 Saint Augustine’s letter *On the Tree of Knowledge*.

[Col. 0765D] **228 4.** Immediately, on page 156:

> “Also, sayings of Lord Isidore from the book of Genesis according to the literal sense. On the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This tree was truly visible and corporeal, harmful as food [Perhaps: harmless], because God, who made all things good, could not have established something—or some thing—evil in paradise. But it was called the tree of the knowledge of good and evil for this reason: through experience, man learned from it what was the good of obedience and the evil of disobedience.”

Nothing else is added. But since these words are not found in the commentary on Genesis by Isidore that we now possess, they perhaps belong to the literal commentary that Isidore composed on all the books of Sacred Scripture, as I demonstrated in chapter 65. The word *Domini* [“of the Lord”] is marked as ancient in the manuscripts; in them *Ysidorus* is also written instead of *Isidorus*.

[Col. 0766A] **5.** On the same page, page 165:

> “Of Isidore the Younger, *On Virginity*. But now, what the sacred integrity of virginity is,” etc., “let her display at the crown of her head.”

This is the whole of chapter 18 of Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*; in Breulius it is chapter 17, where it ends with “let her display at the crown of her head.” The Grialian edition agrees with this codex even in Solomon’s words, “Let time be made distant from an embrace,” whereas Breulius gives “from embraces.” It should be noted that Isidore, the author of the books *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, is called “the Younger” in this codex, which is sufficiently ancient; yet he is not called by this title when his sayings from the book of Genesis according to the literal sense are cited. The script of the codex is clear and Gallic, as some call it—of the kind that began to be used in Gaul, especially around the ninth century. There are points between the letters, easily joined letter forms, and sometimes a period and comma; diphthongs are joined, namely, with a comma placed beneath the letter *e*. The codex seems to have been written in Gaul in the tenth or following century, at the time, namely, when the Gauls were already calling our Isidore of Seville “the Younger.” But which other Isidore did they understand to have been “the Elder”? I explained this in chapter 16.

**6.** In the same codex follow certain sentences of Ambrose and Augustine. At the end of page 157 verso there is the rubric:

> “This book was acquired by Lord Damianus of Santa Croce.”

Again, on page 158, in darker script but of the same form:

> “Cyprian the priest sends greetings to the brethren: Although I know,” etc.

Afterward:

> “Cyprian the priest sends greetings to the priests, deacons, and people residing at Furni. Seriously,” etc.

**7.** Vatican Codex 287, parchment, folio, of approximately the fifteenth century [Col. 0766C], elegantly written. It contains several works of Saint Ambrose:

1. *On the Incarnation*: “Brothers, I desire to discharge the debt,” etc.
2. *On the Mysteries and on Initiation*: “We have held a daily discourse on moral matters.”
3. Six books *On the Sacraments*: “Concerning the sacraments that you received.”
4. Two books *On Penance*: “If that is the end of virtues.”
5. *On the Trinity*: “No one who thinks soundly.”
6. Three books *On Virgins*: “If according to the judgment of heavenly truth.”
7. *On the Place of Paradise*: “And he planted.”

**8.** On page 84 verso follows the rubric:

> “Here begins the book on the Life, Origin, and Death of the Fathers who went before us in the Lord: Of certain saints,” etc.

It ends with Judith, but in such a way that the work appears mutilated, since its final word is *Machabaei* [“of the Maccabees”], which belongs to the final chapter of the first part concerning the Fathers of the Old Testament. [Col. 0766D] Just as certain other little works of Isidore are found inscribed under the name of Ambrose, so this work too is falsely attributed to Ambrose in the following rubric:

> “Here ends the book of blessed Ambrose on the Life, Origin, or Death of the holy Fathers who went before us in the Lord. Here begins the book of the same author on the figures of the Old Testament: Adam bore the figure of Christ,” etc.

These are the *Allegories of the Old Testament*, likewise a work of Isidore. It ends, “received the crown of heavenly glory.” A false rubric is added:

> “Here ends the book of blessed Ambrose, archbishop of Milan, on the figures of the Old Testament.”

These two works agree with Isidore’s printed editions, apart from certain variations of wording of the kind usually found in manuscripts. In the *Allegories* Isidore’s customary prologue to Orosius is absent.

**9.** After the *Allegories*, on page 94, there is the following rubric [Col. 0767A]:

> “Here begins the preface of Isidore, bishop, on the Old Testament: Genesis according to the reliability of history,” etc.

It ends with the Roman commanders and the deeds of embassies. This is Isidore’s book of *Prefaces to the Old Testament*, without the prologue. In the Vatican Library inventory, written in Holstenius’s hand, it is noted that these two books—*On the Figures of the Old and New Testaments* and *Prefaces to the Individual Books of the Old Testament*—are present in this manuscript under the title of Saint Ambrose. The note adds that this is false, since they are by Saint Isidore. In truth, the note ought to have been attached to the first two books, *On the Birth*, etc., and *On the Figures*, since the third, *Prefaces*, is clearly attributed to Isidore. Nor do the allegories in this manuscript extend to the New Testament; they end with the Old Testament.

**10.** In the same codex follow other works of Augustine on the Psalms, Jerome’s prologues to the Psalms, [Col. 0767B] and several sermons of Ambrose. At the end it is noted that the codex was copied at the request of Cardinal Philip, bishop of Albano, by Laurentius Spreuwe, a cleric of the Morinensis church of Mont-Saint-Winoc in Flanders, in the year 1487, at Saint Lawrence in Lucina, in the palace of the aforementioned cardinal, during the reign of Paul II. An inept little verse is added:

> “And thus is the end: let praise and glory be to the Three.”

**11.** Vatican Codex 351, parchment, small folio, approximately of the fourteenth century, in Gothic-German script of the kind seen in some early printed editions. The book is entitled *Letters of Jerome*, whose image is displayed in the initial letter. It is preceded by an index, or table, under the rubric:

> “Table of the letters written in this codex.”

The letters of Damasus, Jerome, Augustine, Theophilus, Pope Leo, Cyprian, and, on page 217, the *Synonyms of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville*, are indicated. But in the book itself the title is absent, and the work begins:

> “Dear son, love tears,” etc.

It ends:

> “For love proceeds from reverence.”

In the Vatican Library inventory it is entered as “Certain excerpts from Isidore’s book of *Synonyms*,” with Holstenius’s note: “That it belongs to Isidore is apparent from the table of the book itself at the beginning.” This is Isidore’s work entitled *Collected Sayings on Tears and Instruction in the Good Life*, as I noted in chapter 82. The codex appears to have been copied at Venice, since certain notes concerning that city are entered in it—for example, that the church of Saint Mark was built in the year 1351.

**12.** Vatican Codex 473, parchment, folio, of the fourteenth century or later. The sermons of Saint Augustine are marked with rubricated titles. [Col. 0767D] In the initial letter, an image of Saint Augustine speaking to the people from a pulpit is represented, painted in gold and various colors. There are ninety-three sermons: on the words of the Lord, on the words of the Apostle, and others.

**13.** Then, on page 109, the rubric:

> “Here begins the prologue of the *Soliloquies* of Isidore, bishop: Recently there came into my hands a certain note—or rather, a little sheet—of Cicero,” etc.

The first book begins:

> “Chapter one. Man says: My soul,” etc.

It ends:

> “Here he will be safe. Here ends Book I.”

Book II begins:

> “Reason: I ask you, soul.”

It ends:

> “You please me concerning my life, forever and ever. Amen.”

> “Here ends the book of the *Soliloquies* of Isidore, bishop. Thanks be to God.”

There follows an anonymous homily on the apostolic reading:

> “The natural person does not perceive the things that belong to the Spirit of God.”

[Col. 0768A] **14.** On page 116 is the rubric:

> “Here begin the chapters in the book of blessed Augustine, bishop, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*,” etc.

> “The chapters end. Here begins the book of blessed Augustine, bishop, *On Ecclesiastical Dogmas*: We believe that there is one God the Father,” etc.

This is the book that Bignaeus added to Isidore’s other works, as I said in chapter 83. It agrees for the most part with Bignaeus’s edition. Chapter 2: “But the eternal God is man,” etc. Chapter 11: “From this, however, we believe that they are corporeal,” etc. It ends, like Bignaeus’s edition, with “to be found in morals.” The following rubric then appears:

> “Sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, the eminent doctor [Perhaps: excellent]. There is a great question concerning the recent Gospel reading.”

**15.** Codex 511, Vatican, parchment, very large folio, written in two columns in the tenth or following century. The rubric reads:

> “In the name of the Holy Trinity, here begins the book of Saint Augustine [Col. 0768B] *On the Unity of the Trinity*, from the disputation held with Felician the heretic: You have compelled me,” etc.

In the initial letter Augustine is depicted disputing with Felician and refuting him. Folio 2 verso: Augustine’s letter to Dardanus. Folio 3: *The Debate of Athanasius against the Arians*. Folio 5: Augustine’s *Book on Christian Doctrine*. Folio 14: Augustine’s *On True Religion*, with his image in the initial letter. Folio 18 verso: Saint Augustine’s *Soliloquies*, likewise with his portrait: “Many and varied things for me,” etc. Folio 32, without a title: “That I may know you, my Knower,” with Augustine’s portrait represented in the initial letter. Folio 32: an image of Alcuin at the beginning of his letter to the emperor, which is the dedication of his book *On the Trinity*. After the letter are three couplets:

> “O king august,” etc.

Again there is an image of Alcuin at the beginning of the book. Folio 37: letters of Albinus, [Col. 0768C] or Alcuin. In the letter to Eulalia there are several verses in various meters. Folio 38 verso: the letter of the deacon Quodvultdeus to Augustine, and Augustine’s little work to him *On Ninety Heresies*. It ends:

> “May you assist me with your prayers. The end.”

Other material is added concerning the Nestorian, Eutychian, and Timothian heretics.

**16.** On the verso of folio 42, this note is added in the margin:

> “Sayings of Saint Isidore on heresy and schism.”

The text begins:

> “Heresy, in Greek *hairesis* [αἵρεσις],” etc.

It continues from chapter 3 of Book VIII of the *Etymologies* to the end of chapter 5 of that same book:

> “Nevertheless, he can be called a heretic.”

Thus the catalogue of heretics is completed; on this subject see chapter 55 above. No particular textual discrepancy is observed.

**17.** There follow Saint Augustine’s books *On the Trinity*, in which his image frequently appears. Folio 72 [Col. 0768D] contains a work without a title or author’s name, which is by Gezo, abbot of Dertona. At the beginning of the letter, or preface, to the brethren is a painted image of a bishop, which may indicate that Gezo was eventually ordained bishop somewhere. It begins:

> “To the most beloved brethren, to whom, by divine dispensation, insofar as personal weakness permits, I offer paternal care, Gezo, servant of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

Mention is made of Gisemundus, bishop of Dertona, who had founded the monastery of Saint Marcianus and placed Gezo in charge of it. Gezo says that he is writing about the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, a honeyed and flower-laden cup drawn from the writings of the Catholic Fathers:

> “Following,” he says, “the authors—namely, the most blessed priests of the Lord, Cyprian, Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, John, ISIDORE, Isitius, [Col. 0769A] Jerome, and Bede.”

After the list of titles are hexameter verses:

> “It is fitting that those who feast at the heavenly banquet be pure,” etc.

There is perhaps a portrait of Gezo in the initial letter *C*. Then come other verses:

> “Whoever wishes to approach the solemn rites of the sacred King’s table.”

I would prefer:

> “Whoever wishes to approach the solemn rites of the sacred King.”

**18.** Muratori published a large part of this work of Gezo from a manuscript of the Ambrosian Library in volume III of his *Anecdota*, pages 239 ff. Mabillon, as is clear from his *Museum Italicum*, pages 164 and 207, had encountered two manuscript codices of the same work, and published the preface and list of chapters in Part II of the *Museum Italicum*, page 89. Muratori omitted much of what Gezo had taken from the books of Cyprian and others, as well as the little book of Paschasius Radbertus, which Gezo had copied almost in its entirety. From his Milanese manuscript, however, he published the verses beginning “It is fitting that those who feast,” etc., inscribed under the name of Lord Odo, in which the first verse reads *Deus esse* [“to be God”] instead of *decet esse* [“it is fitting to be”]. He also published the verses beginning “Whoever wishes to approach the solemn rites,” etc., which are by Paschasius Radbertus and addressed to his disciple Placidus. The first fifteen had already been printed in volume XIV of the Lyon *Library of the Fathers*, page 720. Muratori thought that the remaining sixty-seven, beginning “He arranges the matter,” etc., and ending “He receives judgment who does not judge,” had not yet been brought into the public light.

The verses of Odo, abbot of Cluny, are also found in volume XVII of the *Library of the Fathers*, page 313. In our manuscript the bishop and founder of the monastery of Saint Marcianus at Dertona is called Gisemundus; Muratori calls him Giseprandus or Giselprandus. He flourished in the tenth century, around the year 950.

**19.** Vatican Codex 623, parchment, folio, containing the *Etymologies*, approximately of the eleventh century. Small strokes sometimes appear above *i*, especially at the beginning, but these were added by a second hand, as is seen in other older manuscripts. It is clear that the first scribe did not employ this practice. The first rubric is:

> “Book I, on Grammar and its Parts. Chapters.”

After the table of chapters comes the rubric:

> “Here begins Isidore’s book of the *Etymologies*.”

In manuscripts it is usually written *Ethimologiarum* instead of *Etymologiarum*. There follow eight exchanged letters of Isidore and Braulio: two from Isidore to Braulio the archdeacon, the first beginning *Dum a me litteras* [“While letters from me”], whereas the printed editions have *Dum amici litteras* [“While letters from a friend”]; the second, *Quia non valeo* [“Because I am unable”], [Col. 0769D] etc. Then follow six other familiar letters. But the letter beginning *Tuae sanctitatis* [“Of your holiness”] is repeated, and in the Vatican Library inventory it is said at the end, following its example, to be longer. In fact, nothing is added, for what immediately follows, *En tibi sicut pollicitus sum* [“Here you have it, just as I promised”], etc., belongs to that brief letter which serves as a preface.

**20.** This copy of the *Etymologies* contains many interpolations absent from most other copies. Another similar one is found in Ottobonian Codex 477. In Book I, after chapter 23, on juridical notations, there is a catalogue of those notations:

> “*Aus.* Augustine [I shall read: Augustus], *Aa*, Augusta.”

Bayer, in his note on no. 103 of Book V of the *Bibliotheca vetus Hispana*, after stating that he had seen more than forty codices of the *Etymologies*, including some Escorial and Toledan codices more than a thousand years old [Col. 0770A], added:

> “The ancient, more-than-millennium-old codices of the *Etymologies*, under the title of Book I, chapter 23, present a list of juridical notations which, as Isidore says there, the new emperors decreed should be abolished from the law books because through them many ignorant people of crafty intelligence were deceived. They are very similar to the compendia of Valerius Probus that commonly circulate.”

I think Bayer means Escorial or Toledan codices, since in our ancient codices it is scarcely possible to find such juridical notations, which clearly were added after Isidore.

**21.** Although Bayer does not provide a specimen of them, I nevertheless think they do not differ from those read in this Vatican codex and in Ottobonian 477. [Col. 0770B] These notations are not so much like the compendia of Valerius Probus as like the legal notations collected by Magnon. Valerius Probus’s little book *On Interpreting the Notations of the Romans*, after its prologue, begins:

> “A. Augustus, or Aulus, or *Aut*, or *Aliquando*, or *Ager*, or *Agrum*, or *Aiunt*. AA. *Augusti*, or *Augusta*.”

Magnon’s juridical notations were published in Dionysius Gothofredus’s *Auctores linguae Latinae*, page 1481, and in Putsch’s *Grammarians*, pages 1544 and 1676, where an explanation of juridical notations by another author appears on pages 1666 and 1683. In Gothofredus the title is:

> “Legal notations collected by Magnon: Willingly accept these legal signs, O king, Charles; your devoted Magnon offers them to you.”

> “Aug. Augustus; AA. Augusti,” etc.

It is uncertain to which King Charles the author dedicated this collection, Charles the Bald or Charles the Great. I suspected that the reading should be:

> “Your devoted servant offers these to you, O great one,”

from which someone may have made *Magno* [“to the Great One”] into *Magno*, thinking it was the author’s name. On this same subject Peter the Deacon’s book *On Letter-Forms According to Roman Usage*, addressed to Emperor Conrad, should be consulted.

In the same Vatican Codex 623, after chapter 21, at the end of *Synaeresis*—“to say” [Grialius printed *Synchoresis*]—three chapters are added: *On the Figure of Dianoia*; *On Transposition, or Transformation, of the Parts* (in the connection of the letters of the parts); and *On Reading*. In Book III, chapter 12, geometric figures are displayed. After chapter 13, at the end of “they do just as much,” another chapter is added, *On the Explanation of Certain Figures*: “Another method,” etc. Several geometric figures are drawn there, and perhaps some concern ancient music, since the words *tonus*, *diapason*, etc., appear inside. Burriel asserts that ancient musical notations are copied in a certain Toledan codex, but perhaps these are the notations that were in use before Guido of Arezzo and that are still preserved in many codices. The more recent Guidonian musical system is compared with the ancient system in a table in Meibomius’s notes on Euclid’s *Introduction to Harmonics*, page 51.

**22.** A rubric concerning the prologues follows; it is more accurately placed in the table of books and chapters as “Prologue.” It begins:

> “I thought that two little books, already composed in concise language for those learning, on the nature of things and the reckoning of times, were necessary,” etc.

This little work, written in another hand, has been mixed into the *Etymologies*. Its author says that, at the request of the brethren, he would publish a fuller book on the reckoning of times. Then follows another rubric, *On Computing by the Fingers and Hands*:

> “With the Lord’s help, we shall speak about the reckoning of times,” etc.

This little book, which belongs wholly or largely to Bede, concerns times, indictions, numbers, and so forth; they make *neuma*. Hence perhaps arose the attribution to Isidore of a book on computation. See chapter 86.

Nor is it only in this codex that one can observe that Isidore’s *Etymologies* were notably interpolated; the same is true of many others. Many people freely inserted into this volume material omitted by Isidore and material that might be useful to themselves or others—not, I think, with malicious intent, but certainly as a bad example. At the very least, they ought to have distinguished what was added to Isidore’s original work [Col. 0771B], as I have noticed was done by some people in certain other works.

**23.** The chapters on music are presented as in the printed editions; some chapters on astronomy are also included. In chapter 53 different forms of the moon are represented, as I have observed in other manuscripts as well. After this chapter, other material is inserted concerning the sun’s axis, the moon, lunar eclipse, and so forth. After chapter 69, on the state of the stars, follows another chapter on the signs, their domiciles, and their properties, which are explained in a manner different from that of the printed editions, with a representation of the sphere, or circle, placed before it. It begins:

> “Aries, therefore, is the domicile of Mars, but the kingdom of the sun.”

**24.** Book IV, *On Medicine*, is as in the editions. But after the final chapter, “the body is cured,” other material is added *On the Cause and Origin of Medicine and from whom it received its beginning and name*:

> “Finally, in those days,” etc.

It ends, “and becomes healthy,” and contains much explanation of medical matters and of the principal inventors of medicine. In Book V, chapter 27, on the punishments established in the laws, much extraneous material has been inserted. After chapter 5 of Book VII, following “they demonstrate the mystery,” other material is added concerning the actual construction and mass, and concerning the power of the angels:

> “What the first form was,” etc.

The same sophist relates this.

**25.** After chapter 4 of Book VIII, “let them wash their bodies,” comes the rubric:

> “Here begins Jerome’s little book on the heresies of the Jews: Among the Hebrews they are called *transitores* [‘passers-over’],” etc.

It ends:

> “They wish to be the substance.”

Another rubric follows:

> “Thus far Jerome. On the heresies of Christians according to Isidore: Certain heretics also,” etc.

I said in chapter 86 that in certain codices of the *Etymologies* a little book of Jerome on heretics is found inserted. But it should be observed that the little book in this codex differs from the printed one, and that its opening words—“Among the Hebrews” (read: “The Hebrews are called *transitores* [‘passers-over’]”), etc.—belong to chapter 4 of Book VIII of the *Etymologies*, which concerns the heresies of the Jews.

**26.** At the end of Book VIII, chapter “Walk gently,” another chapter is added *On the Names of the Fates*. It nevertheless explains many names of minor gods of various nations and even of other things. It ends:

> “*Torridum* is called dry, or roasted.”

Book IX, *On the Languages of Nations*: its tables of consanguinity and affinity differ from those in the printed editions. On page 80 there is a table with the rubric:

> “Here begins the horologium.”

The end of the book is as in the printed editions:

> “To consist under protection.”

On page 84 is the rubric:

> “Here begin names interpreted in Greek and Latin.”

> “*Poeta*, a prophet-seer. *Poeticus*, a book. *Poema*, a work of one book,” etc.

It ends:

> “*Tetracolon*, four-membered.”

Certain Greek words are explained by Latin vocabulary.

**27.** This is followed by the rubric *Prose on Certain Properties*. It begins:

> “All you who desire to see me dancing the *oannus*, now attend as listeners to one who is singing and placing [the words].”

Perhaps the readings should be *cantantes* and *jocantem* rather than *cantantis* and *locantem*. At the beginning of this prose the author praises the emperor Charles, of whom he says:

> “Rejoicing in miracles, lavish in garments—  
> When, victorious and crowned, he triumphs among the nations.”

The work entitled *The Supper*, falsely attributed to Cyprian and habitually placed among Cyprian’s spurious works, consists of similar rhythmic verses. The author of this prose also attributes it to Cyprian.

**28.** Another rubric reads:

> “Verses of blessed Benedict, abbot: I shall begin from where, holy Benedict, your triumphs,” etc.

It ends:

> “O father Benedict, may they, I pray, be fitting for you.”

These are the elegiac, echoing, or recurrent verses of Paul the Deacon, already published. An explanation of certain words follows:

> “*Tramites*,” etc.

It is taken from the final chapter of Book V of the *Etymologies*.

**29.** For Book X the rubric reads:

> “Here begins Book X, *The Origin of Certain Names*, etc. Amos, a strong and wise man.”

The manuscript reads *Aeros*, “a strong man,” etc. Yet the reading *Amos* should not be rejected. As Calmet notes in his literal translation of Hebrew names, following the biblical dictionary, *Amos*, with aleph, the father of the prophet Isaiah, means “strong, robust,” from *amats*. Nor should *heros* be written *aeros*. See, however, the note on the cited Book X, no. 2.

Book X ends with *alatores* and *pressores*, with the rubric [Col. 0772C]:

> “Here ends Book X, the first part of Isidore’s *Etymologies*. The second part begins.”

Summaries of the following ten books are added. In Ottobonian Codex 477, which, as I said, is very similar to this Vatican codex, this division into two parts is not found. Perhaps because the *Etymologies* were at some point divided into two volumes, their two parts were distinguished. The numbering of the books nevertheless continues in the same sequence.

**30.** Books XI and XII are nearly as in the printed editions. In Books XIII and XIV circles, wheels, or spheres are drawn, as in the book *On the Nature of Things*; these are absent from Ottobonian 477. In chapter 5 of Book XIV, after the words “they thought it was paradise,” the names of the Fortunate Islands are written at the bottom of the page in a different hand; they are entirely absent from Ottobonian 477. Likewise, in chapter 6, after the words “to bloom twice with flowers in spring,” some material is added about the inhabitants of Taprobane, which we now call Ceylon.

**31.** After chapter 11 of Book XVIII, almost as a little wall, other chapters are appended [Col. 0772D]:

> “On the *baster­na* and the *trucurra*: They make *trucurras* and *basternas,” etc.

In Ottobonian 477, *bastarina* is written. Then:

> “On the craft of the *trucurri*: Of the craftsmen of the *trucurri*,” etc.
>
> “On those who dig the earth: From the seed of Japheth there is a land between the Ocean and the Birtenian Mountains, a foolish people,” etc.

Afterward:

> “On shields,” etc.

The word *basterna* is sufficiently well known in Latin. But I also miss the word *trucurrus* in Ducange’s *Glossary of Medieval and Late Latin*.

**32.** In the same Book XVIII, after chapter 15, “they cover in silence” (*silentio tegunt*; Grialius has *obtegunt*), the following rubric appears in the margin in the first hand:

> “Here begins Book XX according to some.”

In Ottobonian 477 these and the following divisions are not indicated in any way. After chapter 26, “the contests of punishments,” there is a marginal rubric:

> “Here begins Book XXI according to others, who place twenty-eight books in this volume.”

Likewise, after chapter 41:

> “Here begins Book XXII according to some.”

After chapter 52, “having the form of a semicircle” (*semicirculi habens figuram*; Grialius: *semicirculi figuram habens*), the rubric reads:

> “Here begins Book XXIII according to some.”

After chapter 59:

> “Here begins Book XXIV according to some.”

**33.** At the beginning of Book XIX, *On Ships*, etc., there is a similar rubric:

> “Here begins Book XXV according to others.”

After chapter 1 of Book XIX, other material is added:

> “On dove-shaped ships: *Pempe* ships, which they call *colibas*,” etc.

Ottobonian 477 reads:

> “*Penipe* ships,” etc.

Then:

> “On ships, the philosopher of inquiry: For with great perplexity the same philosopher,” etc.
