Perhaps the *Cosmography of Aethicus* or another work of the same author is meant.

After chapter 7:

> “On *murina*, where there is an abyss: *Murinus* was therefore the first to mention,” etc.
>
> “On the underworld and the sooty water: For he says to the underworld,” etc.
>
> “On the heat of the sea: For the same Wise Man reports in his riddles that the sea will be turbulent in so great a heat.”
>
> “On the disposition of Etna: For when it is boiling.”
>
> “On the interpretation of Vulcan: Concerning these matters the Philosopher says, ‘For vain sorrow I am compelled to seethe.’”
>
> “On Vulcan: And the sea, sulfurous.”
>
> “On Sardinia. On Corsica.”

There, concerning the islands:

> “which they commonly call Majorca and Minorca.”

Then:

> “On Mount Caucasus. On the entrance of the river Ganges, or on the heat of the sun. On India and King Feresim.”

There:

> “And we bade farewell to the gods and goddesses of India, and to the court of King Ferezis,” etc.

**34.** Chapter 8 of Book XIX follows, *On the Construction of Walls*, together with the rubric:

> “Here begins Book XXVI according to some.”

Chapter 17 ends, as in Breulius, in the margin:

> “*Calcanthum* is so called because it is the *thymum* of lime—that is, a flower; hence among the Latins it is also called the flower of bronze.”

Grialius passes over the word *chalcantum* without interpretation. Chapter 19 ends with:

> “*Canterium*. *Gubia*.”

Immediately follows:

> “Here begins Book XXVII according to some.”

After chapter 21, other material is added:

> “Also, on priestly garments: let us pursue what the modern priestly garment, compared with the ancient dress, signifies mystically.”
>
> “On the *superhumerale*.”
>
> “On the *podere*.”
>
> “On the girdle.”
>
> “On the *mapula*, or napkin.”
>
> “On the *orarium*: The fifth is called the *orarium*, which by some is called the STOLE, and is granted only to preachers,” etc.
>
> “On the *dalmatica*.”
>
> “On the *casula*.”
>
> “On sandals.”
>
> “On the pallium. In addition to all these, the honor of the pallium is granted to the supreme pontiff and archbishops by apostolic privilege.”
>
> “On the variety and names of different garments: The variety of garments,” etc.

At the beginning of chapter 23, the manuscript has *Gallis lineae*, whereas Grialius has *lenae* and others *linnae*. Shortly afterward the manuscript has *Hispanis stringens*, while Grialius has *stringes*. In chapter 25, the manuscript has *Regillum est praelautum*, with Grialius; Breulius has *praelatum*.

**35.** At the beginning of Book XX, *On Tables*, etc., there is the rubric:

> “Here begins Book XXVIII according to those who place twenty-eight books in this volume.”

The final chapter is as in the printed editions. There the manuscript has *ferrum caloratum*, with Grialius, instead of the reading *coloratum* found in some copies. It ends, as in the printed editions:

> “so that the force of the disease may be dried up by the heat of the fire.”

I have wished to present this specimen of a codex of the *Etymologies* interpolated outside Spain, and, as I believe, in the Frankish-German Empire. Another quite similar codex, Ottobonian 477, will be described in chapter 105.

## CHAPTER XCIV. Review of Eleven Manuscript Codices of the Old Vatican Library

What is the summary of the alphabet according to Isidore? A copy of the *Exposition on the Old Testament* somewhat fuller than the printed editions. A fragment of a chronology concerning the year of the Savior’s birth. Certain writers and works not commonly known are identified.

1. Vatican Codex 624, a parchment manuscript in folio, written in two columns, of the tenth or eleventh century. The headings are written in Roman capitals; the remaining script is Gallic, clear, and of medium size. Points occur for the most part [Col. 0774B] between letters; summaries of the contents have been added in the margins; diphthongs are almost entirely absent. At the beginning: “Which books it is appropriate to read in church: But now we must discuss the divine Scriptures,” etc., continuing to “we believe must be included,” from the decree of Gelasius concerning books to be received and not received, which I published and reviewed among the appendices to the works of Sedulius. It continues: “Concerning the Book of the Apocalypse”; but after a few lines it ends, and perhaps these first two folios belonged to another codex. In a later hand there is a full alphabetical index of the subjects and words of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, with the books and chapters indicated. The following verses occur in an older hand:

> Give voice, reader; the painted voice will speak with you;  
> and while you speak, you will be a hearer, when he brings forth such things.  
> The bishop Baptist, with twice four royal gold pieces,  
> [Col. 0774C] bought me from Hilary Anselm and dedicated me to himself.

The word *loquetur* (“will speak”) is obscure and might be rendered *loquatur* (“may he speak”).

2. An inscription in large Roman letters, partly red: “Here begins Book XX of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, Spanish bishop.” Letter to Bishop Braulio: “To the Lord,” etc. The first *D* in *Domino* is ornamented with flowers and the figure of a dog or another animal, as in other codices of that period. *Hispaniensis* has been written by mistake for *His​palensis*, unless one prefers to understand it as indicating Isidore’s nationality rather than the see of his bishopric. The five customary letters of Isidore and Braulio are present; the brief letter, or preface, “Behold for you,” etc., is omitted.

In the chronicle, Book V, mention is made of King Reccesuinth of Spain, as in other manuscripts; various readings may be consulted concerning them. [Col. 0774D] All these materials appear to have been taken from some exemplar which Saint Ildefonsus, or someone else of his time, caused to be copied during the reign of Reccesuinth. The tenth book is arranged alphabetically: “Origin,” etc. It omits “Aeros, a brave man,” etc., and begins with “Auctor,” etc.

3. At the end of the *Etymologies*, in the same script: “It ends. Here begin the Differences of nouns or words: Between *metus*,” etc. In a later hand Roman numerals have been added in the margin: there are 300 differences. The last is “Between *mĕrĕo* and *mĕrĕor*,” etc., “I ruminate,” and similar items. Here the codex ends. On the last page a few passages from Eusebius’s *Chronicle* are read. From this single Vatican codex I found several variant readings of the *Differences* in the Zaccarian papers, copied in another hand, as I said at the end of chapter 45.

[Col. 0775A]

4. Vatican Codex 625, parchment, in octavo, apparently of the twelfth century. Rubric: “Here begins the Alphabetical Summary according to Isidore’s *Etymologies*.” It begins: “*Abba*, father, a Syriac word.” At the end: “The great labor has ended happily; therefore, farewell.” On the first folio the letters are already fading. It is a very full glossary, containing many words that are absent even from Isidore’s *Etymologies* and other works, or from Isidorian glossaries. Here is a specimen from the letter M:

> *Maceria*, a hedge, or a wall without mortar.  
> *Macta*, increased.  
> *Machinatur*, he thinks evil, he lies in wait, etc.  
> *Meatim*, in my manner.  
> *Meapte*, of my own accord.  
> *Micto*, I urinate.  
> *Migina*, small or crushed straw.  
> *Mycenae*, a city of Greece, etc.

The alphabetical order is arranged with reasonable accuracy. It consists of 73 folios, in small script. Dots appear above *i*, but were added by a later hand. [Col. 0775B] For *migina*, *migma* seems to be the correct reading; this word occurs for “small straw” in Cange’s glossary, from other more ancient sources. Concerning this alphabetical Isidorian Summary, compare chapter 55. At the beginning one should note the explanation of the word *Abaso*: “*Abaso*, the lowest part of a house, the apse.” See Isidore’s Glossary.

5. Vatican Codex 626, parchment, in folio, of the thirteenth or fourteenth century, with many letters in various colors, some in gold; dots above *i* have been added by a later hand. Rubric: “Here begins the preface of the book of blessed Isidore, bishop of Hispala: ‘The history of the sacred law,’” etc. Near the end of this preface to the commentaries on Genesis one reads: “by the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and the outstandingly eloquent Gregory of our own time.” [Col. 0775C]

The commentary on Genesis has an index of 31 chapters. The commentary begins: “The creature of heaven,” etc. At the end: “The exposition of Genesis ends. Here begin the chapters of Book II.” There are 59 chapters. It begins with the preface on Exodus: “Certain mysteries,” etc.

The index of the 17 chapters of the book on Leviticus differs slightly in chapter 16 from the Madrid edition. In the manuscript chapter 16 ends with the words “you shall not accept them,” and chapter 17 begins with “First it is rejected” and ends “by the Catholic Church.” “The book on Leviticus ends.”

The index has 29 chapters on Numbers. The preface to the book of Numbers begins: “Therefore this book,” etc. There is likewise an index of 22 chapters on Deuteronomy, 17 on the book of Joshua, and 9 on the book of Judges. Chapter 5 concerns Ruth the Moabite, but that chapter is omitted at this point in the text. At the end: “he will triumph.” [Col. 0775D] “The exposition of Judges ends. Let us now consider Ruth. For this book has,” etc., “for ever and ever. Amen.”

6. A certain chapter relating to Exodus follows, namely, on Exodus chapter 20, which is absent from the printed editions:

> There are some who say that what is written in Exodus—“You will repay” (or “repaying”) “the iniquities of the fathers,” etc.—

This will have a place among the appendices. The index of the chapters of the First Book of Kings follows, and likewise those of the other books, including Ezra and Maccabees, as in the editions. It ends:

> “And all these things were figures of us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come; and all things have been completed in mysteries through our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom are honor and glory, kingdom and power, with the Father and the Holy Spirit, for ages of ages. Amen.”

7. Thus far it is almost as in the editions; but in this manuscript the following unrelated material is added:

> “After the death of Simon Maccabaeus, 128 years are reckoned up to the birth of Christ, since his son John, who was also called Hyrcanus, held the high priesthood for 26 years after his father. Then Aristobulus, the son of John, in the first year after Alexander Jannaeus—read *Jannaeus* for *Janecis*—had been king and high priest for 26 years. Then Alexandra, the wife of Alexander, who is otherwise called *Saussa*, ruled the Jews for nine years. After her, her son Hyrcanus ruled for 34 years. After him, the foreigner Herod succeeded to the kingdom; in the thirty-second year of his reign Christ was born. Praise be to you, Christ, because this book has been created.  
> “All worldly things are like empty dreams.  
> “He has achieved the whole point who has mingled the useful with the pleasant.”

These statements should be compared with the various opinions of authors concerning the year [Col. 0776B] of Christ’s birth, which many, with Labbe, place in the thirty-seventh year of Herod’s reign.

8. The same codex presents the *Etymologies* without a title. Six customary letters precede it. In the letter beginning “It is accustomed to be filled,” a few variant readings are indicated in the same old hand: “with small loaves,” or “with few”; “the multitude of loaves,” or “the greatness.” After the letters there is a rubric: “Here begin the chapters, twenty in number, of the books of the *Etymologies*.” Nothing unusual occurs.

At the final chapter of Book VI, as in the editions: “Sacrifice is so called,” etc., “and by the blood of Christ,” etc. “The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood, which for that reason,” etc.

At the beginning of Book X, a later hand has written: “The ninth book ends. Here begins the tenth book: concerning certain names arranged alphabetically. The origin of certain names,” [Col. 0776C] etc. In Book XIX, the divisions of titles and chapters are more numerous, as in many other codices. Chapter 33 of Book X, the disputed passage concerning rings, is corrupt, as in most manuscripts: “*Lugente*,” etc. “I seek a very white pearl,” etc.

The final Book XX ends with “is dried by heat.” “It ends.” The codex was written in Spain, or at least appears to have existed there, since the note *ojo*—that is, “eye”—has often been added, where others have *nota bene*. There are many ligatures.

242

9. Vatican Codex 627, parchment, in quarto, of the thirteenth or fourteenth century. Rubric: “Here begins Isidore’s preface to the explanation of the history of the divine law: ‘The history of the sacred law,’” etc. The preface ends: “Here begin the chapters.” They are numbered 32, because the first chapter is called the second. It ends: “over all flesh.”

Here begin the chapters of Exodus. There are 60 in this manuscript, 59 in Grialius, and 51 in Breulius, owing evidently to a different method of division. The titles generally differ from those in the editions. It ends: “in those who believe in him.”

Here begin the chapters of the book of Leviticus. Only 14 are indicated in the table of chapters, but 17 appear in the text, though somewhat confused. Chapter 17 in Grialius, “But neither is the bread of a foreigner,” etc., continues in this codex, as in the Bologna Codex:

> “But neither is the bread of a foreigner offered to the Lord . . . and foreign things are reckoned . . . For such sacrifices are rejected by the Lord . . . by the Catholic Church. Yet even in these things there were figures of us, because our cleansing and God’s propitiation for us are impossible without the blood of Christ. But the truth of those figures,” etc.,

as in the Bologna Codex and in the new Madrid edition, among the appendices [Col. 0777A] of volume III, through the words “may possess them forever,” but with some difference, as I shall soon say.

10. The chapters of the book of Numbers—or, as it is written here, *Numeri*—are indicated as 30, but several are divided further in the text. Deuteronomy has 22 chapters; Judges, 9, including the chapter on Ruth. The First Book of Kings has 21 chapters; the Second, 7; the Third, 8; and the Fourth, likewise 8. The book of Ezra has 4 chapters, including the chapter “On the Maccabees.” It ends:

> “They were figures of us, upon whom the ends of the ages have come, and all things have been completed in mysteries through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, God, for all ages of ages. Amen.
>
> “Pen, stop your course, for this book is complete.
>
> “May the writer not be eager to die quickly.”

[Col. 0777B] In the same codex, but apparently in another script, follows a commentary said to be on Job, about which I have said more than enough in chapter 65.

11. Although this codex agrees in Leviticus, as I said, with the Albornozian Bologna manuscript, a certain transposition of sentences must nevertheless be noted. After the words cited, “But the truth of those figures,” the Vatican manuscript continues:

> “It is Christ, by whose blood we have been redeemed.”

When the question is asked why a Christian does not observe unleavened bread, like the Jews, etc., it follows the Albornozian manuscript through “is preached to the peoples.” Immediately the Vatican manuscript has:

> “When it is asked why a Christian celebrates Passover from the blood of the lamb,” etc.,

then “thus he already celebrates Passover,” etc., continuing through “now it is not sin.” It immediately adds:

> “But now concerning certain ceremonies,” etc.,

as at the beginning of chapter 17 in the Albornozian manuscript, through “offered eagerly.” [Col. 0777C] It then adds:

> “But to fail to be joined continually to the tabernacle of God, which is the Church, is always a sin,” etc.,

through the end, “they may possess them forever.” Here begin the chapters of the book of Numbers.

12. Codex 628, Vatican, paper, in quarto, of the fourteenth century or later. Rubric: “Here begins the book of Saint Isidore called *Synonyms*, that is, many words.” Prologue:

> “A short document recently came into my hands which they call *Synonyms,” etc.

“The prologue ends. Here begins the argument: ‘In the following book, which is called *Synonyms*, that is, joined together in one meaning,’” etc. Grialius has: “converging into one meaning.”

After the argument there is a rubric: “Here the human being speaks to Reason: ‘My soul,’” etc. Other similar rubrics follow. “The human being speaks. Reason responds.”

After Book I: “The first book ends. Here begins the second. Counsel: ‘I ask you,’” etc. The titles are more frequent than in Breulius. The end is: “you take pleasure in my life.” “The book of blessed Isidore called *Synonyms* ends.” Some words are inserted that appear to belong to a later letter: “Your letter has made us exceedingly glad at your excellence.”

13. The letters of Clement to James follow: “I make known to you”; again to James: “Since, just as from blessed Peter”; “To all the bishops,” etc.; “It presses us”; “To Julius and Julian: ‘It is fitting, brothers.’” Learned men agree that all these letters are spurious.

There may be doubt concerning the letter that follows in this codex, namely, the letter of blessed Dionysius to Timothy concerning the death of Saint Paul the Apostle, as there may concerning the other works and letters bearing the name of Saint Dionysius the Areopagite, which are debated among learned men who disagree with one another. An anonymous work without a title follows, treating, in scholastic fashion, of the veneration of the Mother of God and of sacred images: “First, the negative position is argued,” etc. Some other material concerning religion is appended.

14. Next comes a letter of James Lulineus to John Barocius, bishop. I presently have nothing to say about Lulineus. By Barocius I understand that John Barrocius of whom Fabricius says a little in the *Bibliotheca media*. A narrative follows of a conversation between Philip the Christian and Theodosius the Jew, in the time of the Emperor Justinian. It is an apocryphal work.

The Jew asserts that in a certain commentary of the Hebrews one finds Jesus, son of God and of the Virgin Mary, listed among the priests. [Col. 0778B] Against this disgusting little tale there is a work in volume XIX of the Lyon *Bibliotheca Patrum*, p. 728: “Refutation of a certain Jewish imposture concerning the legal priesthood of Jesus Christ, taken from Suidas, by John Henten of Mechelen, a Hieronymite.” Fabricius gathers further material on this subject in volume I of his *Codices Apocryphi Novi Testamenti*, p. 371.

15. Afterwards come hymns for requesting rain:

> “The fields of the soil lie parched.”

For requesting fair weather:

> “They have covered the sky.”

For a time of war:

> “Now the peoples are sad.”

Another:

> “The savage man sows wars.”

These hymns occur in the Mozarabic Breviary and are attributed to Saint Ambrose in the Hymnary of Venerable Thomas. But in our Vatican codex they are not written in the same hand as the *Synonyms*.

Also written in a later hand is the prayer of Leodrisius Cribellus before Pius II. Two Leodrisius Cribelli are mentioned in Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca media*, with notes by Mansi; but their works have been confused, and this prayer is not mentioned.

Other works are added: an anonymous little work on Latin diphthongs, beginning “Diphthongs, which the ancients.” At the end:

> “May you preserve these diphthongs, which I desire, for a thousand years,  
> so that you may always remember our love.”

There is a brief treatise on indulgences by De Mayronis of the Order of Preachers; but I think “Order of Minors” should be restored. For Francis de Mayronis was an eminent Minorite theologian, of whom Wadding, among other works, records a treatise on indulgences:

> “I possess this manuscript, in which he treats this subject excellently and clearly.”

There are many other miscellaneous pieces, [Col. 0778D] including elegiac verses about a monkey representing or imitating a dead matron, and others about an ironsmith as a companion in death.

16. Codex 629, Vatican, parchment, in folio, of the twelfth century. The inscription bears no author’s name: “Here begin the Lives, Origins, or Deaths of the saints who have gone before us in the Lord.” Preface: “Of certain saints,” etc.

There is an index of 63 chapters of the Old Testament. Grialius has 54, but in the manuscript Haggai is omitted from chapter 50. The order is nearly the same as in Grialius, but in the text the manuscript, without explanation of the history, passes over Micah, Nahum, Habakkuk, Zechariah, Addo, Azariah, again Zechariah, and the Maccabees.

17. There are 22 chapters in the New Testament, the first concerning Zechariah and the last Titus, as in Grialius. Chapter 70—chapter 71 in Grialius, since the numbering continues—concerns James son of Zebedee; it says: “He wrote, and of Spain,” etc., [Col. 0779A] “and at the western end of the world . . . and he was buried in Achaia Marmarica.”

At the end of the Old Testament: “Here ends the account of those who lived under the Old Testament. Here begins the account of those saints who are in the New.” At the end of the work: “The Deaths, or Lives, of the Saints end.”

Since in this manuscript the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is presented without Isidore’s name, someone wished to record the following in the inventory:

> “Take note that this treatise circulates under the name of Isidore; but in this manuscript the author’s name is absent. Therefore know that some doubt whether it is Isidore’s.”

Yet from the omission of Isidore’s name—although it is clearly expressed in six hundred other manuscripts—a weak argument is drawn against our view that Isidore is the author of the book, especially since other works by the same Isidore follow in this codex. The *Allegories*, in particular, which follow, have no inscription at all, although Isidore’s name is customarily placed before the dedicatory letter.

18. Thus, after the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, the *Allegories* begin without any title:

> “To the holy and most reverend” (I very frequently find *reverentissimo* in manuscripts instead of *reverendissimo*) “brother Horosius, Isidore: ‘Certain well-known things,’” etc.

They are allegories of the Old and New Testaments. At the end:

> “will be healed by the resurrection of eternal blessedness.”

“It ends.” Breulius has “will be filled by refreshment”; Grialius has “will be filled by the refreshment of eternal blessedness, to which refreshment may Christ lead us. Amen.”

After the *Allegories* comes Bede’s work *On Sacred Places*: “I have briefly described the boundaries and locations of the places.”

19. Page 14, rubric: “Here begins the Book of Prefaces of Isidore, bishop, to the New and Old Testament: ‘Genesis according to the faith,’” etc. The prologue, “The fullness,” etc., is omitted. The work is mutilated at the end: it ends, “John wrote three . . . but the third.”

20. Page 17 verso, rubric: “Here begins the letter of Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo, to Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, in the book of the *Prognostics*: ‘To the most holy,’ etc., ‘that day,’ etc., ‘to ask for the judgment.’” “It ends.”

The index has 22 chapters in Book I, 37 in Book II, and 62 in Book III. It ends: “whose end there is none.” “The third book ends. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

Concerning this work, which was reprinted in the elegant Madrid edition of the Toledan Fathers, following the editions of Douai and Leipzig because manuscripts were lacking in Spain, I remember writing several things in the notes to Dracontius, Book III, verse 52. In the Vatican manuscript the response of Idalius, bishop of Barcelona, and Julian’s prayer to God are absent; in the editions these precede Book I. Otherwise this codex deserves to be compared with the edition. Julian’s work is followed in the manuscript by Eusebius’s ecclesiastical history, translated by Rufinus.

21. Page 110 verso, rubric: “Here begins Isidore’s *Chronicle*: ‘A brief exposition of times,’” etc. The preface says “Victor, bishop of the church of Toron,” for which Grialius correctly has “of Tunnis.” Likewise, “a brief sequence of times” should replace “for the generation.” The manuscript chronicle ends in the fifth year of Heraclius and the fourth of Sisebut: “then its completion is his.” The text should read “in the fourth year of Heraclius” [Col. 0780A] and “the fifth of Sisebut”; the numbers of the years are often transposed in this manuscript.

A chronology of the Lombard kings and of the emperors of the West is appended, from Aldoald to Henry, who reigned eighteen years after Conrad; and of the emperors of the East, from Heraclonas to Alexius Comnenus, that is, toward the end of the eleventh century. This codex was perhaps copied in Germany somewhat after that time.

22. Page 115 contains the pseudo-Isidorian collection of canons. A catalogue of the Roman pontiffs is placed first; by the first hand it continues to Honorius II, successor of Callistus II, who was raised to the papacy in 1128. A second hand adds concerning Honorius: “He sat five years, two months, three days.”

In the inventory of the Vatican library, page 212, Damasus is indicated as “Roman by nationality”; but in the codex one plainly reads: “Damasus, Spanish by nationality.”

After the catalogue of the Roman pontiffs there is a rubric:

> “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the preface of Saint Isidore to this book, whose chapters are as follows: ‘Isidore Mercator, servant of Christ,’” etc.

The last item copied is the synod held at Piacenza by Urban II in 1095. The Ballerini discuss this codex in *On the Antiquity of the Canonical Collection*, p. 235. From the same codex I shall present a few variant readings of the *Allegories*, *Prologues*, *Chronicle*, and preface to the pseudo-Isidorian collection of canons among the appendices.

23. There are other Vatican codices of the collection of canons, councils, and decretal letters under Isidore’s name, although they differ greatly among themselves in arrangement, fullness, and selection of material, such as Codices 630, 631, 1340, and 1349.

In the inventory for Codex 630 this note is attached:

> “That Isidore completed the collection of canons, Gesner says in his *Bibliotheca*; it is nevertheless reported by John Gerson.”

You should add that the same thing is reported by Hincmar, bishop of Reims, whom you will find below among the councils, old number 1891, under chapter 32, “On the Spanish Councils,” at the end.

24. Vatican Codex 632, parchment, in folio, of the thirteenth or fourteenth century, in large and clear script, with few and unobscure abbreviations, and no dots above *i*. Rubric: “Letter of Isidore to Mason, bishop: ‘To the holy and meritoriously blessed brother Mason, bishop, Isidore, bishop: “When,”’” etc., “to Nicetius.” It ends: “or the stronger authority exists.” [Col. 0780D]

“Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our most glorious lord, King Witteric.”

In the same script is appended:

> “If any man or woman has committed adultery, he or she must attain perfection in seven years according to the former stages.”

Then a rubric: “Here begins Book I of Saint Isidore, called the *Sentences*.” The index has 31 chapters in Book I, 43 in Book II, and 68 in Book III. It ends: “not those whom the heavenly court encloses to be made glad.” “The third book of Saint Isidore ends.”

Smaragdus’s *Diadem of Monks* follows:

> “May we deserve to have this little work,” etc., “joy. Amen.”

Smaragdus collected this little book from various virtues and gave it the name *Diadem of Monks*, because just as a diadem shines with gems, so this little book shines with virtues. Nothing else is added in this codex.

[Col. 0781A]

25. Vatican Codex 633, parchment, in quarto, of the tenth century, with clear letters of medium size, joined diphthongs—though they are lacking in some places—and few ligatures, which are easily understood.

Rubric: “Here begins the first book of Saint Isidore”; other words followed, but have now been erased. At the top of the page, in a later hand: “Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*.”

There is no index of chapters, but the rubric of the final chapter of Book I gives the number 31. Then: “Here begins the second book of the *Sentences* of Saint Isidore.” The final chapter is 44. “Here begins the third book of Saint Isidore.” The final chapter, 66, ends: “he encloses to be made glad.” “The third book, called the *Sentences* of Saint Isidore, ends.”

26. Vatican Codex 641, parchment, in folio, of the ninth or tenth century. On the first pages is a mutilated work [Col. 0781B] by Albinus the teacher, *On the Life of Saint Martin*. It ends: “the pieties of those rejoicing, by the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ,” etc.

Page 3: “Here begins the preface of the lord Bede on the Apocalypse.” Thus the name *Beda* sometimes occurs in manuscripts; but perhaps, according to the custom of those times, it would more properly be *Bedanis*, just as among the Spaniards there were many names of this kind: *Cixila, Cixilae*, or *Cixilanis*; *Suintila, Suintilae*, or *Suintilanis*, etc.

27. Some little works of Fulgentius, Augustine, Ferrandus the deacon, Victor, and Fastidiosus the Arian follow; the sermon of Fastidiosus occurs among the published works of Fulgentius. After Fulgentius’s letter or book *On the Rule of True Faith to Peter*, which others wrongly attribute to Augustine, page 93 contains verses by someone concerning blessed Fulgentius:

> “When you shine forth with sacred studies, when you grow ardent in sacred things,” etc.

These verses appear to be by Immo the copyist, from the verse “Immo, who delivered [this book] into the hands of the servant Bermundus.” But who is this Immo? It would be useful if someone compiled a catalogue of ancient scribes or copyists whose names have come down to us, so that the age of many codices could be determined. Perhaps I shall publish many such names, which I have noted incidentally, at a later time.

For now I observe that mention is made of Immo the librarian in Pez’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, preface to volume I, no. 64. There a nine-hundred-year-old codex containing homilies of Origen is described, at the end of which the following is written:

> “I, therefore, in the name of God, IMMO, wrote this book—not by my own merit, but by the grace of God; nevertheless, a priest. Brothers, you who read in these volumes and find places that need correction, do not assail me with curses [perhaps *maledicatis*, ‘curse’], but correct it with every diligence, and deign to pray for me, an unworthy sinner. Farewell in the Lord for ages [perhaps *aevi*, or *aeviternis*, ‘everlasting’]. May Christ, your merciful one, long greet you.”

From this a plausible conjecture may be drawn: that this same Immo was the copyist of our Vatican codex, in the ninth century or the following one. Mabillon, in the Benedictine *Annals*, mentions several Immos; but it cannot be determined from this whether any one of them worked at copying books.

28. Page 98, in the same script: “In the name of the Lord begins the book of the *Offices* of Saint Isidore, bishop: ‘To my lord,’” etc. “You ask me.” The index of Book I has 44 chapters. “The capitulation ends.”

“Here begins the first book of Isidore’s *Offices*: ‘Those things which belong to the offices.’” The final chapter, 44, is entitled “On the eating of meat or fish”; in Grialius and Breulius, “On the use of meat or fish.” It ends: “nor did the apostles forbid,” as Grialius has; Breulius has “prohibited.”

Book II follows without any title: “Since the origins.” The table of chapters has 26. The last, which is chapter 27 in Grialius, “On the laying on of hands” (others: “of the hands”), or “confirmation,” ends as in Grialius:

> “These are small things out of many . . . to have received instruction . . . to be strengthened by sentences.”

Grialius adds “Pray for me”; for *parva* he has *pauca* (“a few things”); and for *percepisse doctrinis* he has *praecepisse doctrinas* (“to have taught doctrines”). Nevertheless, the manuscript reading seems preferable. I shall note other matters among the variant readings.

29. Immediately follows a rubric: “Book II ends. In the name of Christ begins the book of Isidore the Elder—read *Prologues* for *Primorum*—concerning the books of the New and Old Testament. ‘The fullness of the New Testament’ . . . ‘let us append brief prologues to the narratives.’ The preface ends.”

“Here begins the text of the third book: ‘Genesis according to the faith,’” etc. It ends: “and the river of baptism, and the wood of the life of our Lord Jesus Christ.” “The third book of the *Prologues* ends.”

“Here begins Book IV, *On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Fathers*: ‘Adam, the first-created man and settler’;” it continues only to the chapter on Joseph: “because of envy he is sold, having been made humble, up to” [the text ends].

Here the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is defective, although it is unquestionably attributed to Isidore, since after the two books of the *Offices*, Book III of the *Prologues* is attributed to Isidore, and in the same sequence the work *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers* is Book IV.

From the book of the *Prologues* I excerpted several variant readings and copied an entire chapter on Esther, which is absent from the editions. But why are the *Prologues*, and consequently the books of the *Offices* and *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, attributed to Isidore the Elder?

The following note is found in the inventory of the Vatican library:

> “In this manuscript *Senioris* occurs; see whether it should be *Junioris*.”

This refers to the controversy explained in chapter 16 concerning the different Isidores. The name “Elder” suits our Isidore of Hispala better than “Younger,” if he is compared with the other Spanish Isidore. The ancient Spaniards recognized no Spanish Isidore older than Isidore of Hispala. Therefore, after Isidore of Pacensis began to flourish in the eighth century, they called him “Younger” and the former “Elder.” For this reason [Col. 0782D] I judge that this Vatican codex was copied from some Spanish exemplar in which Isidore of Hispala was called “the Elder,” in comparison with Pacensis.

30. After a few pieces, as I said, from the book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, the following little works follow in the same script: “A remarkable miracle concerning the image of our Savior: ‘At Caesarea of Cappadocia.’” Then a miracle in the *Life of Saint Jerome*. The *Life of Saint Jerome*. Sermons of Saint John Chrysostom, said to number 45, though only eleven are copied in the codex.

31. Codex 650, Vatican, parchment, in small folio, of the twelfth century, defective at the beginning. After certain Masses for weekdays according to the Roman rite, there is a rubric:

> “The Masses of Saint Augustine, bishop, for all weekdays now follow; because we did not find them among the others, we have placed them separately.”

“First weekday. A. ‘Give me, Lord, a sign for good’ . . . P. ‘Incline, Lord,’” etc.

These Masses too are incomplete.

32. The table of works indicates Alcuin’s *On the Trinity*, certain works of Augustine and Jerome, etc., and at no. 19: “Here begins a single book *On the Conflict of Vices and Virtues*,” which perhaps was the book listed under this title among Isidore’s works; but it is now absent from the codex, as is noted in its proper place by an old hand.

Other works are added: “The Conference of Abbot Serapion on the Eight Principal Vices.” Excerpts from Gregory the Great. Also “An exposition of the active and contemplative life,” Gregory’s work on Job, which differs from a work of nearly the same subject attributed to Isidore, discussed in chapter 85.

33. Folio 108, title: “On the Song of Songs: ‘After the paradise,’” [Col. 0783B] etc. After the prologue: “Let him kiss me with the kiss of his mouth. ‘Angels to her.’” It ends: “that is, I considered you like my chosen ones.”

The author’s name is absent from the text, but it is indicated in the table of works at the beginning as follows: “Two homilies of Gregory on the Song of Songs.” In fact, the Maurists vindicate this commentary for Gregory the Great, as I said in chapter 65.

After the commentary are verses beginning “These I ask,” etc., which in the new Madrid edition are appended to the verses of Isidore’s library; but here they are found more complete and corrected, as I observed in chapter 81.

34. The letter of Jerome to Damasus follows; then Origen’s work, etc., “A translation of Origen’s treatise in the nuptial songs: ‘How we have learned.’”

Folio 121: a sermon of Saint Augustine to all, especially monks and widows: “We have often always said.”

Folio 139: an acephalous book *On Contrition of Heart*. It ends: “your insatiable beauty. Glory to the Father, who saved us,” etc.

The catalogue indicates 59 admonitions of Basil; in the text the title is: “Here begins Basil’s work to the monks: ‘Hear, son, the admonition of your father.’”

Folio 98 verso, in another and more recent script: “Here begins the Life of Saint Giles the Confessor: ‘Indeed, the saints,’” etc.

35. In this part the codex has been overwritten: namely, the *Life of Saint Giles* was written over an earlier text, which was erased. Thus the works listed in the table at the beginning of the volume after Saint Basil’s admonitions are missing, because someone erased the letters from the parchment in order to write something else over them.

No. 74 in the index had read:

> “In the name of Christ begins the first book of the *Synonyms* of Saint Isidore of Hispala, [Col. 0783D] bishop, and two sermons” (thus).

It is regrettable that not only the *Synonyms* but also these two sermons, which appear to have been attributed to Isidore, perished through the ignorance or greed of the copyist, who, having been ordered—or having undertaken on his own—to write the *Life of Saint Giles*, was unwilling to purchase clean parchment.

36. Codex 657, Vatican, parchment, in folio, in scholastic script, that is, the kind used in schools, with rubrics and letters in various colors, approximately of the fifteenth century.

Works of Anselm: *On Truth*, *On Free Will*, *On the Virginal Conception*. Homilies of Bede. Anselm’s *Menologium*. *The Book for the Fool*. *On the Incarnation*. Anselm’s book *On the Procession of the Holy Spirit*. His work *On the Sacrifice*. Other works of the same Anselm: *Why God Became Man*, *Enchiridion*, etc.

Augustine’s fifteen books *On the Trinity*; four books *On Christian Doctrine*: “The books on Christian doctrine,” etc., by the same Augustine, but without the author’s name. The four books of John of Damascus *On the Orthodox Faith*. At the end: “Damascus ends.”

37. Isidore’s work *Sentences* follows in this manner: “Here begin the chapters of Books I, II, or III,” with “and III” incorrectly corrected by a later hand. In the margin: “Here begin Isidore’s chapters *On the Supreme Good*.”

Book I has 31 chapters; Book II, 44; Book III, 65. It ends: “encloses those to be made glad.” Although the work is attributed to Isidore only in the margin, the same name occurs, as in all the other editions, in chapter 1 of Book III: “Have mercy, Lord, on wretched Isidore.”

The title *On the Supreme Good* is plainly of a later period. Nothing else worthy of particular notice occurs, except perhaps that the passage in the editions is nearly corrupt in Book II, chapter 6, “that they may delight in lowly and outward things”; in the manuscript it reads: “that they may delight in what is lowly and outward.”

38. The work *On the Spirit and the Letter* follows, beginning “Since it was said to me.” Another work *On Grace and Free Will* begins:

> “D. G. to Abbot Theodicus, Brother S.” (perhaps the *S.* is actually *B.*).

At the end are Saint Augustine’s *Retractions*. The entire codex is miscellaneous, as is evident in itself.

252

## CHAPTER XCV

Five other manuscript codices of the old Vatican library are described. Roderick Sanchez de Arévalo and Alfonso of Saint Mary, bishop of Burgos, are praised. Ancient expositions of the Mass. Some curious material concerning Leucius, the author of the apocrypha. Ancient homiliaries and lectionaries are described.

[Col. 0784C]

1. Vatican Codex 939, on paper, in folio, of the sixteenth century, ornamented with rubricated headings and a first letter in variegated gold. Some works by Augustine of Ancona. By the same author, *On the Affair of the Templars: Whether It Is Permissible for Secular Persons to Attack Them*. Books by Jerome and Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*. A book attached to Pliny in many manuscripts, *On Illustrious Men*: “King Proca.” Rabanus’s treatise *Allegory on the Commendation of Numbers*, etc. “The Nature of Numbers.” It ends: “One hundred and forty-four thousand . . . a lie has not been discovered.” Isidore’s book *On Numbers* deals with this same subject, as I explained in chapter 63.

The following works succeed these in the Codex. *The Book on the Wisdom of the Saints*, without the author’s name; at the beginning, in the table of contents, it is attributed to Bonaventure, but a later hand notes in the margin that it was published by Wading in Rome in 1655 under the name of John of Wales. Petrarch’s work, *How Many Hercules There Were*. A sermon for Good Friday, which the index attributes to Saint Bernard: it begins, “Who will give to my head,” etc.

2. Page 146, title: “Certain Beautiful Sayings of Saint Isidore against the Jews, and on the Passion of Christ.” These are certain sentences excerpted here and there from Isidore’s book addressed to Florentina, *On the Passion of the Lord*.

3. After these excerpts from Isidore come other works: Bernard’s *On Contempt of the World*, against wicked ecclesiastics; Jerome’s *Mirror of Virginity* and brief rule of apostolic life; Bernard’s *On the New Knighthood*, addressed to Hugh; the *Life of Saint Sylvester, Pope*, by Eusebius of Caesarea, translated by Rufinus; and other spiritual little works, including a letter of Saint Catherine of Siena to a certain friar: “I write to you,” etc.

4. Page 125: *A Dialogue on the Excellence and Dignity of the Roman Curia above all others*, etc., against those who defame it: “I know that there are many.” A panegyric delivered by Latinus Pacatus to Theodosius: “If anyone ever.” Poggio’s *Book of Facetiae*. Rufus Sextus: *Deeds*.

253. 5. The speech of the bishop of Burgos at the Council of Basel: “When in public,” which, as I think, has been corrected by the author’s own hand. A letter from Francesco of Anguillara, count of Aversa, detained in the Castle of Sant’Angelo, sent to the bishop of Oviedo, the castellan: “Although from this your greatest kindness.” He gives thanks to the castellan. The castellan’s reply begins: “Your letters have been delivered to me”; it is a beautiful and learned letter. The castellan consoles the count.

It would be lengthy and contrary to my purpose to explain individually all the writings that occur and to identify their authors, although I would sometimes find that agreeable and perhaps others would not find it unwelcome. With regard to Spanish writers, however, who present themselves to me, I shall not hesitate to offer a few indications, since otherwise they are not so generally known to foreigners; nor, as I think, will others resent my doing this in a somewhat particular manner.

This bishop of Oviedo is Roderic Sánchez de Arévalo, prefect of the Castle of Sant’Angelo. Cardinal Quirini discusses him learnedly, among others, in the appendix to the *Life of Paul II*, p. 169. Marchantius, too, compiled a long catalogue of Roderic’s works in his *Dictionary*. If anyone should undertake to publish a collection of all his works—which might perhaps be useful—he ought above all to consult the Vatican Library, which contains many distinguished manuscripts of his books.

The bishop of Burgos, whose speech was praised shortly before, is also an illustrious fourteenth-century writer: Alfonso de Santa María, or of Cartagena, son of Paul, likewise bishop of Burgos. Both are celebrated with due praise in *Hispania Sacra* and in Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, who identifies his speech at the Council of Basel from Vatican manuscript 232.

6. Vatican Codex 1146, on parchment, in folio, approximately of the tenth century. Rubric: “Here begins the book of Offices, how the Roman Mass is celebrated.” It is noted that this work was published in Ferrarius’s *Roman Order* of 1591, but differs in certain respects. It begins: “First of all it must be observed that there are seven regions of the ecclesiastical order of the city of Rome.” It ends: “and they enter the sacristy.” A recent note states: “Up to this point in the printed editions.”

Rubric: “Here begins the ecclesiastical order of the Roman Church, how the Mass is celebrated. Here begin extracts from the Roman Order and from the four prayers of bishops, or of the people, at Mass.” The words “at Mass” are in black ink, but by the same old hand appears: “Here begin the chapters of the following little work: We preface.”

254. 7. There is a certain *Exposition of the Mass*. Among other questions it asks: “Why do the males stand on the southern side and the females on the northern?” The answer is that the weaker sex ought to be placed in the more suitable position, just as the angel of the Apocalypse placed his right foot upon the sea and his left upon the earth. For stronger limbs are stationed in greater dangers, and the other ones in suitable situations.

Later it asks: “Why is the deacon in the ambo facing south?” In the margin there is a note by another, though ancient, hand: “Among us, toward the north; because he speaks against him who said, ‘I shall place my seat toward the north.’” These observations may be useful for illustrating ancient rites.

8. The canon of the Mass is reported almost as it is now used; I discussed it in chapter 84. There is also another *Exposition of the Mass*: “First, in the order of the Mass,” etc., as I said there. In this Mass the following words of the Canon deserve notice:

“Together with your servant, our pope, because he is the head of the Church in the apostolic capacity; therefore he is named first in this prayer. And with our bishop,” etc.

It ends: “the Apostle commended.” This is followed by *On the Sacraments of the Church*:

“The sacraments of the Church are baptism and chrism, the body and blood; they are called sacraments from *secretis*—‘secret powers’—or from *sacris*—‘sacred things.’”

These passages are taken from Isidore, Book VI, chapter 19. I discussed their interpretation against Bingham in chapter 30.

9. Page 19, another brief *Exposition of the Mass*:

“On the order of the Mass: First, in the celebration of the Mass,”

and it ends:

“permission to depart, the Mass having been completed.”

Rubric: “In the name of the Lord (or of God), a few excerpts from the volumes of learned men” [the manuscript reads *auditorum*, apparently incorrectly]. “Here begin the chapters on the Catholic Church and its ministers, and on the office of baptism. These chapters came from the Palace of Aachen. *Ecclesia* is Greek.”

A note by a recent hand says: “These excerpts are taken from the published *Institution of Clerics* of Rabanus Maurus.” But why not from Isidore, *Etymologies*, Book VIII, chapter 1, which begins in exactly this way: “*Ecclesia* is Greek”? It is established that Rabanus himself compiled Isidore’s writings.

10. Page 20, verso, another *Exposition of the Mass*: “The Lord be with you. He greets,” etc. This is the exposition of the Mass attributed to Isidore in certain manuscripts, as I explained in chapter 84.

11. The chapters of Bishop Theodulf follow, published by Sirmond in volume II of the *Councils of Gaul*. Some works by Walafrid. An anonymous exposition of the Lord’s Prayer: “What is this prayer called?” Another work on the sacraments, various rites, and the Mass; Bede is cited.

255. 12. Page 62, rubric: “Here begins the work on baptism and its entire order according to the investigation of the Catholics”:

“If I unfold the sacrament of baptism by recounting it from its first origin, Moses baptized,” etc.

Chapter 2: “John also baptized, but not completely.”

Chapter 3: “Jesus first baptized in the Holy Spirit.”

The other chapters proceed similarly.

Chapter 10, rubric: “On catechumens: Isidore.”

Chapter 12: “On the reception of salt: Isidore.”

Chapter 20: “On renunciation: Isidore.”

These last three chapters are taken from Book II of *The Offices*, chapter 21; the preceding material on baptism is taken from chapter 25 of the same second book.

13. Page 66, rubric:

“On the order of those coming to the faith, whose first degree is that of catechumens, the second that of the competent, and the third that of the baptized. On catechumens: Isidore.”

Likewise:

“On exorcisms: Isidore. On the reception of salt: Isidore.”

All these passages are excerpted from the same book of Isidore.

[Col. 0787A] 14. Amalarius’s work *On the Order and Causes of Ecclesiastical Offices* follows; Fabricius discusses it at greater length in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, after Mabillon. This copy ends: “by drinking we may be redeemed. The Book of Offices is complete. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

Amalarius, to note this incidentally, cites our Isidore in Book III, chapter 2:

“It”—the Church—“is called *Kyrica*, because it is of the Lord . . . it is called a basilica, or royal building,” etc.

Hence Isidore says: “Basilicas were formerly called the dwellings of kings.”

15. Vatican Codex 1267, on parchment, in large folio, approximately from the end of the eleventh or beginning of the twelfth century. The titles are rubricated; the majuscule letters are variegated and ornamented with various figures. This Codex was donated to the Vatican Library by Gregory XII in 1577.

Homilies and sermons. A homily of Remigius, bishop, *In the Name of the East*. Others by Augustine and Leo, very many by Bede, and some by Fulgentius and Hilary.

Folio 89, verso, rubric: “Sermon of the blessed Isidore, bishop, on the Nativity of the Lord.” Another title, in black ink and also ancient: “Sermon of the blessed Isidore, bishop, on the Nativity.” It begins: “The day of the Lord’s Nativity, for this reason,” etc. This is chapter 26 of Book I of *The Offices*; it ends, “Christ was born.” In Breulius it is chapter 25, where we read “of whose assumed incarnation,” whereas the manuscript and Grialius read “of whose assumed flesh.”

16. Page 117, sermon of Saint John Chrysostom: “The prophets,” etc.

Page 121:

“Here begins the prologue on the Life and Assumption of the blessed John, apostle and evangelist. Melito, servant of Christ and bishop of Laodicea, to all the Catholic bishops: eternal salvation in the Lord. I wish your fraternity to be concerned about a certain Leucius, who wrote the Acts of the apostles—of the apostle and evangelist John, and of the apostles Andrew and Thomas—who spoke truthfully about the miracles that the Lord performed through them (the manuscript reads *quae*, ‘which’), but lied greatly about their teaching. For he said that they taught two principles,” etc.

Here begins the History: “The second persecution after Nero,” etc.

In the margin: “Reading I.” This Leucius, who is discussed here, or, as others call him, Seleucus, is that writer of apocryphal works who is called a disciple of the devil in the Gelasian decree on books to be received and not to be received. I examined and annotated that decree in Appendix 5 to my edition of Sedulius based on manuscript codices.

Gerhard John Vossius seems to be speaking of this Codex in *On the Genealogy of Christ*, p. 34:

“This Seleucus is also mentioned by Melito, bishop of Laodicea, in the preface to the *Life of Saint John the Evangelist*, which has not yet been published but exists in the Vatican and other libraries; or by Melito, bishop of Sardis (for no other person should be understood), in the book *On the Passing of the Blessed Virgin*, volume VII of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*.”

17. Folio 132, verso, rubric: “Here begins the sermon of Saint Severian, bishop, on the Innocents” [the manuscript reads *Innocentum*, “of the Innocents”]: “With the zeal toward which he tends,” etc.

In Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi* I read the following: “Cangius mentions the sermons of Severinus the abbot on the feast of the Holy Innocents in the library of Saint-Germain.” In our manuscript Severian, bishop, is named; but he appears to be the same author, to whom perhaps also belongs the frequently published little work entitled *The Teaching of Severinus, Bishop*, of uncertain see and age.

[Col. 0788A] 18. Page 139: “Here begins the Life of Saint Sylvester: Sylvester, therefore, bishop of the city of Rome, when he was still a little child,” etc.

Page 193: accompanying the text of the Gospel of John is an image of Saint John the Baptist holding a lamb in his hand.

Page 258, verso: the end of Saint Gregory the Great’s homily on the Gospel, *The Lord Designated*, in these words:

“What you have received, prepare. But these things that we say we obtain better from you by praying than by speaking. O God, who wished to call us shepherds among your people, grant, we ask, that we may be able in your sight to be what we are called by the human mouth. Through our Lord.”

19. Vatican Codex 1268, on parchment, in large folio, apparently written in the same script as the preceding Codex. It is a homiliary and lectionary, as in the preceding volume. In some words a sign indicating that the penultimate syllable is to be shortened or lengthened is added, just as in our breviaries, but by a more recent hand. The dots indicating questions, however, belong to the first hand.

It begins with Septuagesima Sunday: “Do you not know that those who run in the stadium,” etc. “The distinguished preacher, willing and desirous,” etc., without the author’s name. The sermons of John of Constantinople, Jerome, Bede, and others follow.

Folio 37, rubric: “A sermon on the same fast, by the blessed Ambrose, as it is thought: The meaning of Holy Lent, whose beginning we celebrate today.”

20. Folio 44: sermon of Saint Faustus, bishop, on fasting: “I beg and admonish you, dearest brothers.”

Folio 79, verso: beside the Gospel of Matthew, “Behold, a Canaanite woman,” images are painted of the Savior, two apostles, the Canaanite woman, and her daughter, tormented by a demon.

Page 122, verso: sermon of Saint Severian: “The page was now speaking of our most magnificent prince.” Perhaps “Severinus” should be read, concerning whom I spoke earlier; compare Mansi’s notes to Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

Folio 123, verso: from the commentary of Remigius: “It is written that Abraham had two sons. Not without reason.”

Folio 131: above it, a sermon of Saint Severian, bishop: “Today the blessed evangelist [spoke of] the widow’s son.”

Folio 167: a sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, at the vigil of Hosanna: “After the Lord had [raised him after] four days.”

21. Folio 185, verso, rubric:

“Here begins the preface of Saint Isidore, bishop, to the Testimonies of Scripture on the Passion of Christ: To the holy lady, sister Florentina, Isidore [corrected from *Hysodorus*],” etc.

In the manuscript is *praenunciata* (“announced beforehand”), where Breulius reads *pronunciata* (“pronounced”). The prologue ends, “reject ignorance”; the rest is omitted.

Rubric: “Here begin the testimonies of Scripture”:

“Thus Jeremiah had foretold in the person of the Lord: ‘She has transgressed by transgression.’”

Thus begins chapter 19 of Book I *Against the Jews*. These are the testimonies contained in this and the following chapters, up to the end of chapter 50 of Book I:

“They build around me so that I may not go out.”

But certain words of Isidore are omitted.

22. Folio 225, on Good Friday, rubric: “A sermon of Saint Severian, bishop, apparently continuing the preceding one: Coming together at the station of the Mother Church.”

Folio 235, rubric: “Here begins a sermon of the blessed Roman, on the Sabbath evening: How, according to Matthew,” etc. I do not know whether this Roman—if “Roman” is indeed the correct reading—is one of those Romans mentioned by Fabricius in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

After this homily, on folio 233, verso, rubric: “Here begins the Life of the blessed Pope Gregory: Gregory, Roman by birth and a philosopher by profession.”

The following passage occurs there:

“For he had been earnestly entreated by the same brothers, and especially by Leander of Hispalis [perhaps *Hispalensis*, ‘of Seville’], bishop, who had come to Constantinople at that same time as an envoy on behalf of the affairs of the Visigoths, and he was compelled to unravel the Book of Job, which was wrapped in many mysteries.”

The author of the *Life* is Paul the Deacon. It is published in volume IV of Saint Gregory’s works in the Maurist edition, where the reading is “by Leander of Hispalis” and “on behalf of the affairs of the Goths.”

23. Folio 241, rubric:

“Here begin the chapters on the Life and Miracles of the blessed Benedict, abbot: Benedict was a man venerable by the grace of his life,” etc.

The *Dialogue of Saint Gregory*, etc.

At the end is a homily of Saint Ambrose on the Annunciation: “The angel Gabriel was sent,” etc.

24. Vatican Codex 1269, on parchment, in larger folio. A homiliary and lectionary, like the two preceding ones, in the same or a similar script.

Rubric: “A sermon of the blessed Ambrose on the feast of the martyrs after Easter.”

Other sermons follow: on the feast of the holy Cantians, by Saint Ambrose; on the feast of Saint George; of Saint Andrew; of Saint Barbara; and of Saint Nicholas of Patara, in larger letters. This last sermon, however, is incomplete. Homilies of Saint Augustine follow, in the first script.

25. Folio 19, rubric: “The Finding of the Holy Cross: Helena proceeded to Jerusalem.”

Folio 31: “On the feast of Saint John the Baptist,” with a painting of the Virgin Mary’s visitation to Elizabeth and another of the birth of Saint John the Baptist.

Folio 47: sermon of Saint Leo, pope, on the celebration of his elevation: “This day, dearest ones, is honorable to me.”

Folio 53: another sermon by the same author on the feast of the apostles Peter and Paul: “The most blessed apostles Peter and Paul.” In the initial letter are images of Peter above and Paul below.

Folio 75: “On Saint James” [the feast or nativity]: “He approached.” A homily of the Venerable Bede, priest: “Our Lord, creator and redeemer.”

Folio 77: “On Saint Peter in Chains.” An exposition by Bede the priest of the Epistle, from his commentary on the Acts of the Apostles.

Folio 84: on the feast of Saint Lawrence, a martyrdom graphically depicted in colors.

Folio 91: a sermon of Saint Ambrose, as above: “O truly blessed humility of Mary, who gave birth to the Lord for human beings.”

In a more recent hand: “Of Ambrose Autpert.” The feast is entitled “On Our Lady Mary, Mother of God.” I reported more about this sermon in chapter 61, where I noted that our Isidore is praised by its author.

26. Folio 106: a sermon on the beheading of Saint John the Baptist; at the beginning is a painting of the beheaded Saint John.

Folio 112: on the Nativity of Saint Mary, a sermon of Peter Damian. Saint Peter Damian died in 1072, and I think that the Codex was written not long afterward.

Folio 117: on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross:

“At that time, after the sign of the Holy Cross had been shown to Constantine Augustus as he hastened to war against Maxentius.”

There is a painting of this apparition.

27. Folio 127: on Saint Michael the Archangel, a sermon of the blessed Pope Gregory: “The nature both of angels and of human beings.”

Folio 129, rubric: “A sermon of Isidore, bishop: The name ‘angels’ is a name of office, not of nature.” This is from Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 5:

“The designation ‘angels’ is a name of office, not of nature,”

and in the same words from Book I of the *Sentences*, chapter 12.

The manuscript lacks the words “we say” after *gratia*. It ends, “and restored to the angels,” which is the conclusion of the cited chapter 12.

Immediately afterward, on page 900, after *redditam*, there is a rubric: “Of Saint Gregory, pope, as above: Sometimes,” etc.

On this matter compare what I said in chapter 72; I shall discuss it again when I describe the very ancient and extremely valuable Vatican Codex 3836, of the seventh or eighth century.

28. Folio 137, the Kalends of November, the Feast of All Saints:

“We read in ecclesiastical histories that Saint Boniface, who held the episcopate of the city of Rome as the fourth after the blessed Gregory, obtained by his prayers from the Emperor Phocas that it be given to the Church . . . the Pantheon,” etc.

Compare Baronius, year 1 of Boniface IV, with Pagi’s note on the year 607. The commemoration of the dead is absent.

At the end are sermons for the common feasts of saints. Saint John Chrysostom, whose sermons are included in part, is usually called “Osaureus” in this Codex. The apparition of Saint Michael the Archangel on Mount Garganus is also inserted in it.

## CHAPTER XCVI

Review of sixteen Codices of the old Vatican Library. Miscellaneous works from the Fathers. Curtius’s History of Alexander. Collections of canons. Several works of ancient grammarians, glossaries, vocabularies, synonyms, and differences of words in manuscripts of remarkable antiquity.

1. Vatican Codex 1290, on parchment, in large quarto, approximately of the fifteenth century; it contains many and various works.

Genealogical tables of consanguinity. Verses indicating the subjects of the biblical books: “The law forbids,” etc. Excerpts from the *Scholastic Histories*: “There are four modes.” Excerpts from Peter Lombard’s *Books of Sentences*: “Book I, on the Trinity,” etc. The four books of the *Sentences* have been reduced to a summary.

A *Summa of Cases*: “Simony is.” At the end: “The *Summa of Cases* in prose is complete.”

A metrical *Summa of Master Raymond*: “At the principal feasts, one is said at Mass—only one collect,” etc.

A compendium of Gratian’s *Decretum*: “The human race.” The index attributes it to Brother Raymond. Also a *Summa of Vices and Virtues*. Also *Biblical Difficulties*: that is, certain biblical words explained alphabetically. There Jubilee is interpreted as “the year of remission,” etc., according to Isidore, namely from Book V of the *Etymologies*, chapter 37.

2. Folios 151 and following: Sayings of the saints concerning the Blessed Virgin. Sayings of the saints on various subjects. Sayings of Bernard from the *Soliloquies*: “I shall know you, Lord, my knower.”

Also a book of the blessed Bernard, *Many Know Many Things*. Anselm’s *Proslogion*: “Come now, little man, flee.” Fulgentius’s letter to Reginus: “Having received your letter.” Certain works from Saint Dionysius. A book of the blessed Jerome, *On the Names of the Lord*: “Almighty God.” Certain works by Saint Ambrose.

3. Folio 184, rubric:

“Here begins the book of the *Soliloquies* of the blessed Isidore: Know, O man,” etc.

It is taken from Book II of the *Synonyms*, from the chapter on humility through the words “remove from your heart an offense against your brother,” near the end of the chapter on patience. The author of this excerpt omits, adds, and alters certain passages, as usually happens in similar cases.

4. Other little works, or excerpts, by Hilary, Hugh of Saint Victor, and Ferrandus follow.

A book under Seneca’s name, *On the Cardinal Virtues*: “Every sin is an action.” It is preceded by: “Lucius Annaeus Seneca was from Getica, and his residence was in the district of Nero,” etc.

Other works of this sort concerning Seneca, to whom the book of Martin of Braga, or of Dumium, *On the Differences of the Four Cardinal Virtues*, is also falsely attributed in other manuscript Codices.

There are also other works: a homily of Origen, “Mary stood outside at the tomb, weeping: At the present solemnity,” etc. Certain medicinal herbs are depicted in various colors.

5. Vatican Codex 1344, on parchment, in large folio, written in an elegant French script, approximately of the tenth century. Several leaves have been bound outside their proper place and order.

Rubric:

“Here begins the order of the *Ordination* concerning the wickedness of Dioscorus of Alexandria: After Dioscorus,” etc.

Letters of Simplicius and Felix.

Folio 6, verso:

“Here begin the decrees concerning books to be received or not to be received, written by Pope Gelasius with seventy highly learned bishops at the apostolic see of the city of Rome: After the prophetic and evangelical books,” etc.

It ends: “we confess them to be condemned.”

I discussed this celebrated decree of Gelasius at greater length in the appendix to Sedulius.

The following works succeed it: “Concerning Faustus, mentioned above,” etc. Other letters of Gelasius, Anastasius, Symmachus—under whom there are subscriptions by several bishops—Hormisdas, Pope John, Felix, Boniface, John, Agapitus, Silverius, Vigilius, Pelagius, John, Benedict, Pelagius, Gregory the Great—under whom there are subscriptions by bishops—and Martin.

6. Page 90, verso, rubric:

“Here begin the chapters that have been collected piecemeal from Greek and Latin canons, Roman synods, and the decrees of Roman prelates and princes, and were delivered by the blessed Pope Hadrian to Engilramnus, bishop of the city of Metz, on the thirteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the ninth indiction, when proceedings were being conducted on account of his own business [perhaps ‘on account of his business’]: ‘He accuses God’s ordinance,’ etc.”

Writers who discuss collections of canons speak at length about these Chapters. In certain Codices Engilramnus, or Angilramnus, is said to have delivered the chapters to Hadrian, not Hadrian to Engilramnus, as is asserted in this Vatican manuscript. In either form, the work is considered spurious.

7. [Col. 0791D] After the letter of Vitalian to George, bishop of Syracuse, which ends “we might see,” the following rubric appears:

“Here begins a letter of Isidore, bishop of the city of Hispalis, sent to Laudefredus, bishop of Córdoba. To the holy and meritoriously blessed brother Laudefredus, bishop, Isidore, bishop: Having read through,” etc.

It ends: “the preparation of the sacrifice.” *Landefredus* is written twice instead of *Laudefredus*.

Another rubric follows:

“Here begins another letter of the same Isidore, bishop, on restoring honors and clerical ranks after penance to clerics who have fallen into a bodily crime [perhaps ‘the ranks of honor’]. To the holy and meritoriously blessed brother Masona, bishop, Isidore, bishop: When Nicetius came to us,” etc.

It ends: “authority. Given on the second day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of our most glorious lord, King Witeric. The letter of Isidore, bishop, is complete.”

These two letters are also found in the old collection of canons, Vatican Codex 3791, and in others.

8. Vatican Codex 1346, on parchment, in small folio. It contains a collection of canons divided into seven books, from the beginning of the twelfth century. Ballerini discusses it in *On the Ancient Collection of Canons*, Part IV, chapter 18.

A catalogue of Roman pontiffs precedes it, where we read: “Damasus, born a Spaniard,” etc.

Page 15, verso, contains a catalogue of heresies from Isidore’s *Etymologies*, as already stated in chapter 86.

262. 9. Vatican Codex 1348, on parchment, in octavo, of the eleventh century or the following one. It presents a collection of canons divided into five books, which, unless I am mistaken, the Ballerini brothers do not mention in *On the Ancient Collection of Canons*.

Preceding it is a treatise *On the Faith of the Holy and Undivided Trinity*: “We believe that there is one God,” etc. It ends, “and to join the account together.” This is a little work compiled from the beginning of the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogma* and other sources, as I said in chapter 83.

After another little work *On the Chamber of Christ*, written in a more recent hand, the following is added:

“This book belongs to the monastery of Saint Mary of the Angels at Florence.”

10. The following rubric succeeds:

“Here begins the book *Excerpt from the Sentences of the Canons of the Holy Fathers*, which is divided into five parts.

1. Book on the Primacy of the Roman Church, etc.
2. On the Common Life of Clerics, etc.
3. On Baptism, etc.
4. On Marriage, etc.
5. On the Admonition of Priests, etc.”

Many passages are excerpts from the apocryphal decretal letters. The seventh and final title of Book V is “On the Essence of the Soul and how it varies because of different acts,” where many passages occur from an unnamed book of Isidore, *On the Differences of Things*.

11. After the collection of canons the following rubric deserves notice:

“Chronicle of Isidore—or, more truly, of Saints Augustine and Jerome—begins: A brief exposition of times,” etc.

It ends in the fourth year of Sisebut: “its completion,” where other copies read “the completion of the age.” Some material is added, some is missing, and some is intermixed.

When the subject is Adam, the following is added in the margin in the same script:

“There were, then, all the days of Adam’s life nine hundred and thirty years.”

There are other similar additions elsewhere.

Concerning Constantine the Great it says:

“Constantine the Great, emperor, reigned thirty-one years. He was the first Christian emperor and gave Christians permission to assemble freely,” etc.

I do not know where the scribe obtained the idea that this chronicle belonged rather to Augustine and Jerome than to Isidore. In chapter 77 and following we vindicated this kind of chronicle for its proper author; but in this Codex, as in most others, it appears interpolated.

12. When the Chronicle is complete, the following rubric appears:

“Here follows a calculation for finding the indiction according to the periods of the kings: In the first year of King Alboin, this was the indiction in Italy.”

It ends in the year 1027.

A Chronicle of the Roman pontiffs follows, the last of whom is Paschal II. This chronology likewise says: “Damasus, born a Spaniard.”

At the end of the Codex is this note:

“Isidore. But *canon* in Greek, *regula* in Latin, means a rule, etc., made into one by a group of many.”

This is a fragment from chapter 16 of Book VI of the *Etymologies*, which in the Vatican catalogue is called “A Fragment of Isidore on the Interpretation of *Canon*.”

13. Vatican Codex 1357, on parchment, in folio; see chapter 86. It contains excerpts from Isidore’s *Books of Sentences* on kings, etc.

14. Vatican Codex 1471, on parchment, in folio, of the eighth or ninth century. Its letters are majuscule, either red, yellow, blue, or variegated.

An alphabetical glossary, mutilated at the beginning. It begins:

“*Licenter*, lawfully. *Lingurrit*, he licks.”

It ends:

“*Zephyri*, winds. *Zona*, a belt.”

Another glossary follows, with this title:

“Here begins the ancient *Hermeneumata*, which the most ancient peoples of Italy used under Latinus and Saturnus: *Alieno more*, in a foreign manner; *alieno genere vitae*, with a foreign way of life,” etc.

It ends:

“*Vidubium*, those [perhaps ‘those women’] who love two husbands. *Vulsum*, what is pulled out. *Vurat* [perhaps *vorat*], he consumes. *Vestibulum*, a threshold. *Vollo, luit, fovet* [uncertain readings].”

The Codex is full of errors. Among other entries it explains *brudus* and *gurdus*.

15. Page 16: “Here begins the Book of Etymologies, that is, on the property of speech, or Glossary, that is, *Hermeneumata*, from A.”

“Ah is the sound of one who is suffering,” etc.

It ends:

“*Virgultum*, a small forest, or a little branch.”

Something appears to be missing.

This glossary is extremely extensive. It contains many entries that seem to have been taken from Isidore’s *Etymologies*, and perhaps for that reason the name *Book of Etymologies* was given to it.

Another headless glossary of words from Sacred Scripture follows. It begins:

“*Encaenia*, a new building, or dedication.”

It ends:

“*Zozamin*, preparation in battle array.”

16. Page 98, rubric:

“Here begins the distinction of words: Between *absconditum* and *absconsum*: *absconditum* belongs to reason, whereas *absconsum* belongs to custom.”

This is the ninth difference in Isidore’s *Book of Differences*, in the royal edition of Madrid. In this manuscript the work proceeds alphabetically, but is mutilated at the end.

It ends:

“Between *profugum*, *exsulem*, *extorrem*, *relegatum*, and *transfugam*—a fugitive, exile, outcast, banished person, and deserter, respectively: a *profugus* is,” etc.

Some synonyms are added without a beginning:

“*Ductus aquae*, a watercourse, a path, a current. *Dubium pendens*, a hanging doubt,” etc.

End:

“*Vultuosus*, sad. *Ypotheca*, the whole estate.”

17. Page 127: “Here begins the *Etymologies of the Common Language* used by poets.”

“*Ambages*, circumlocutions or doubts. *Ala*, a part of an army,” etc.

It ends:

“*Vocis praeconio*, by proclamation of the voice, by praise.”

Page 130: “Interpretation of the sons of Jacob from Hebrew into Latin.”

“*Amen*, truly. *Ruben*, the spirit of God.”

There are many other entries translated in the same manner from the Hebrew language into Latin.

Page 137: “Here begins the interpretation of scholarly expressions, that is, the glossary of Jerome the priest.”

“*Ab origine*, from the beginning, from the origin. *Abstrusa*, hidden, concealed.”

It ends:

“*Zorobabel*, master of Babylon.”

18. Page 191:

“Here begin names interpreted from Hebrew into Latin speech, as the blessed Jerome explained them: *Adonai*, Lord,” etc.

This, too, follows an alphabetical method. It ends:

“*Zizania*, *arseius*, or ‘while the Lord listens.’”

Also: “Preface. I had earlier painted this little gloss of brilliant interpretation by writing it rapidly,” etc.

Also a glossary:

“*Abgrego*, I separate,” etc.,

continuing through:

“*Zizania*, darnel.”

Also a glossary beginning “*Auxiliari*,” etc., which becomes defective shortly after the beginning.

This Codex contains much material shared with Isidore’s *Differences of Words* and glossaries, which I discussed in chapters 56 and 57.

[Col. 0794A] 19. Vatican Codex 1491: at the beginning, on parchment, there is a chain of the Fathers on the *Magnificat*. The remainder is on paper, apparently from the fifteenth century.

The grammatical work of Capri: “Where this road leads, we shall say—not ‘where.’ Cato descended, not ‘discended.’”

It ends:

“Call it *stellionem* from its resemblance to the stars.”

Rubric: “Agraetius.”

“*Agraetius*, even when you write in Latin, must be written with a diphthong, not, as some think, with *y*, *Agritius*. You will say *triceni* for three hundred,” etc.

It ends:

“We use *supplicia* for torments and for prayers.”

20. Rubric: “Q. Remmius Palaemon: All the nouns,” etc., “fully explained.”

Rubric: “Donatus: A barbarism is,” etc., “he carried to the cities.”

Rubric: “Servius of Nicomedia: Speech is called,” etc., “He sowed seed.”

Aemilius Aper follows: “Art is a comprehension,” etc., “vicious and most shameful.”

Sergius Maurus, *Centimeter*: “To illustrious Albinus,” etc. “Apply yourself to the labor.”

Pompeius: “A barbarism is,” etc., “barbarolexis.”

Metrorius: “Although concerning letters,” etc. “Or is it Melibaeus?”

Maximus Victorinus [perhaps *Victorinus*]: “But the liquid letters,” etc., “one beyond.”

Sergius, *On the Elements*: “A letter is so called,” etc., “I sing of Troy.”

21. Donatus the Younger: “The voice is air,” etc., “cola and commas.”

Albinus: “The principal parts,” etc., “these clever men,” and similar passages.

Phocas the Grammarian: R. R. R. [as written].

“My art belongs to many whom the ancient ages brought forth,

or the new brevity asserts that you are mine,” etc.

“I believe that some will attain,” etc., “simplicity.”

Quintus Terentius Scaurus’s *On Orthography*, addressed to Theseus: “The method of writing, however.”

The work is mutilated at the end.

[Col. 0794C] 22. I reviewed this Codex in order to identify the work of Agroetius, since the book entitled *On the Difference of Words*, under Isidore’s name, begins with the same words and treats the same subject. I discussed it in chapter 56.

23. Vatican Codex 1558, on paper, in quarto, of the fourteenth century or the following one.

Rubric: “Here begins the book *On the Property of Speech*, from Nonius Marcellus, arranged alphabetically.”

“*Avernus lacus*, the Avernian lake,” etc.

It ends:

“*Vulpinari* is said,” etc.

Another anonymous glossary:

“*Apud*, near; Sisenna, historian, Book III: ‘While they removed their former fault by sweat from their bodies at the fire.’”

It is a glossary consisting of rarer words and their meanings, with passages from authors, especially ancient ones, cited as evidence. But it proceeds only as far as the word *ineptitudo*, from Caecilius.

[Col. 0794D] 24. Page 160, rubric:

“Here begins the book *On Differences of Words*: Between *abducit*, *producit*, and *deducit* there is this difference: someone is led away (*abducitur*) toward a dishonorable matter,” etc.

The alphabetical order is not maintained.

It ends:

“Between *deforme* and *turpe*: *deforme* pertains to the body, *turpe* to crime or to the mind.”

25. Page 177, rubric:

“Some further material on differences of expressions or words: Between *polliceri*, to promise, and *promittere*.”

These are Isidore’s differences, as they appear in the Bignaean edition. They proceed only as far as difference 140.

“Between *commodare*,” etc.

In difference 8 Bignaeus has *nivibusque completur*, “and is filled with snow”; the manuscript adds *aestate torret*, “in summer it is scorched,” that is, “dried.” Compare chapter 56 above.

26. Page 199: “Here begins Paul’s epitome from Festus.”

“*Augustus locus*, a sacred place,” etc.

It ends:

“*Ungulatros*: ‘large and *aspersos* [read *asperos*, ‘rough’] claws,’ as Cato said.”

The author of the epitome is Paul Warnefrid, whom Fabricius discusses in his *Bibliotheca medii aevi* and in *Veteres Latinae*, Book IV, chapter 6.

Page 263: a letter of the same Paul:

“By the gift of divine generosity, resplendent in wisdom and power, to D. Charles, most exalted of kings, Paul, the least little servant, desiring to add something to the libraries, since I can accomplish very little from my own resources, necessarily borrowed from another. Festus Pompeius, finally,” etc.

It ends:

“will rouse him to better things.”

By this letter Paul dedicated his book. Concerning it the anonymous writer of Melk, *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 67, says:

“Paul, a learned man, wrote among other works a very useful book entitled *On the Meaning of Words*.”

27. Vatican Codex 1869, in folio, on parchment, apparently of the twelfth century.
