At the beginning there are some extracts from the *History of Alexander the Great* by Quintus Curtius Rufus: “Now when Philip had died,” etc. On page 5 begins the preface to the book of Freculphus, the most noble historian: “To the most longed-for master.” The initial D is skillfully painted in various colors and decorated with gold. The other initial letters are likewise executed. After the preface come verses by the same Freculphus:

“Under your leadership, Christ, it is easy to travel every road—  
those which nature denies,” etc.

After Book VII of Freculphus there are some excerpts from historians, including from the book of Isidore, bishop of Seville: “Tiberius reigned,” etc. Fraculfus, or Freculphus, flourished in the ninth century.

28. Page 91, *On the Description of Times*: “The first age at its beginning contains the creation of the world,” etc. This is an abridgment of the Isidorian chronicle, which appears in the *Etymologies*. It ends: “Heraclius, year 27. In his fifth year, and in the fourth year of the most devout emperor Sisebutus,” etc. “Here ends the brief annotation on the division of times.” See chapter 77.

29. Some poems of Ausonius follow, without the author’s name being given, as well as the *Definitions of Philosophers on All Matters for Conversing with the Querulous*, where there is the following definition by Cicero: “There are no more hidden ambushes,” etc.; I published it from Palatine Codex 930, chapter 81, no. 17.

On page 95:

“An angelic vision which God showed to His servant Guerinus. The vision of Guerinus, first a canon and afterward a monk, which God showed him through an angel; and we, his brothers, servants of Saint Vincent at Metz, wrote it down as he narrated it.”

It ends: “he closed the hour of life.” I do not know whether this vision has been printed.

30. Heading: “The Miracle of the Lion and the Ass: For one day, as evening was falling, when blessed Jerome,” etc.

A sermon on the beheading of Saint John the Baptist: “Josephus relates that he was bound.”

On page 101 the heading reads: “The verses begin: ‘So many choice apples I have plucked for you with my hands— / With this pen I traverse the forests with the eyes of the wise.’” The last verse is: “Whoever forgives his brother, Christ also forgives him.”

The author is Alcuin or Columbanus. Certainly among the poems of both is found a poem consisting of a single line, as it is called, beginning: “Let him read these precepts”; and among the other verses of this poem there is the same sentiment: “Whoever forgives his brother,” etc., as there are also other verses of the poem beginning, “So many evils for you,” etc.

Then begin verses of Bishop Fortunatus on the consolation of the dead: “Harsh is the condition, and irrevocable the lot of the hour.”

31. Books III and the following books of Quintus Curtius Rufus succeed. Book X ends successfully. Then begins the account of the birth of the same Alexander, and of how he killed Nectanabus and his father Philip: “The sages of Egypt,” etc.

These passages should be compared with what Fabricius discusses in *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, Book II, chapter 17, concerning the antiquity of the history of Alexander the Great written by Curtius.

There follow a letter of Alexander to Aristotle on the location of India, and alternating letters of Alexander and Didymus, king of the Brahmans. In the Roman edition of Quintus Curtius of 1590, after the ten books *On the Deeds of Alexander the Great*, there is added a *Life of Alexander the Great*, abridged from the books of the Histories, written by John the monk and translated by Angelo Cospo of Bologna. But its beginning differs from the work *On the Birth of Alexander*, etc., which follows Quintus Curtius in the Vatican Codex.

John the monk’s book begins: “Philip, king of Macedonia,” etc. In the same edition there follows a letter of Alexander the Great to Aristotle on the location of India, said there to have been translated into Latin by Cornelius Nepos.

32. Page 199. The history of King Apollonius begins: “In the city of Antioch there was once a king named Antiochus,” etc.; “he placed the second in his library.” Here ends the history of King Apollonius.

This history is fictitious. In it, Apollonius is said to have drawn his own daughter into an incestuous relationship, and astonishing complications of events are invented from this.

At the end of the Codex, in a more recent script, are excerpts from the deeds of Alexander, from Claudian, Valerius Maximus, Trogus Pompeius, and Juvenal.

33. Vatican Codex 1974, on parchment, in folio, of the twelfth century: one book of the *Histories* of Paulus Orosius.

At the end: “Here ends Book VII of Orosius the presbyter, addressed to Augustine the bishop, concerning the histories against the accusers of Christian times.”

34. Isidore’s chronicle follows, with this title added by a more recent hand: “Here begins the Book of the Chronicles of Isidore of Seville: A Brief Explanation of Times”; others have “series.”

It concludes in the fourth year of Sisebutus: “then for him is the consummation of the age.” It agrees for the most part with the edition of Grialius; it omits some things, such as the passage on Julius Caesar: “Gaius Julius Caesar, five years. He first obtained the singular rule of the Romans; from him the Caesars also received their name.”

Of Constantine it reports as follows: “Constantine reigned for thirty years. He was the first among the emperors to become a Christian emperor,” etc.

The *Deeds of Alexander the Great* follow—“The sages of Egypt,” which is the beginning of the work in Vatican Codex 1869, described above. Then comes the letter of Alexander to Aristotle on the location of India.

There is also a letter of G. [I suppose Gregory VII] to the bishops of Gaul, inviting them to a council to be held in the middle of November, so that an end might be put to the disagreements between the Apostolic See and the kingdom: “How great tribulations,” etc., “to recall them by walking along the royal road.” Mention is made of King Henry, whom I suppose to have been emperor.

This letter is not found among the other letters of Saint Gregory VII reported by Labbe. At the end of the Codex is the beginning of the *History of Sozomen*.

35. At the beginning of the volume, before Orosius’s *History*, is placed a brief preface on the life of Orosius: “Here begins the brief preface on Orosius.”

In the inventory of the Vatican Library it is described as follows: “Some material on the life of Orosius from Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*.” But in fact the author’s name is not given in the Codex, nor is that life found in Isidore’s *On Illustrious Men*. This chapter, therefore, should be assigned among Isidore’s doubtful or spurious works.

36. Vatican Codex 2439, containing the fictitious commentary of blessed Isidore on the *Aphorisms* of John Damascene, which has already been described in chapter 75.

37. Vatican Codex 2902, on paper, of the fifteenth century, in quarto. The little book of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *Topics* addressed to Trebatius begins: “We have undertaken to write about greater matters.”

On page 25 the heading reads: “Isidore: The Topics is the discipline of discovering arguments.” This is from chapter 30 of Book II of the *Etymologies*, with a few words altered or written in another form. It ends: “so that the intellect may fall” (*ut ingenium cadat*); others have the reversed word order, *ut cadat ingenium*.

Another heading reads: “Likewise Isidore: From here to the dialectical species.” This is the end of chapter 28 and the whole of chapter 29 of the same book.

Boethius’s work on Cicero’s *Topics* follows: “At your exhortation,” etc.

In the Vatican inventory, Isidore’s fragments are entitled *On the Topics and the Definition of Logic*.

38. Vatican Codex 2930, on paper, in quarto, of the fifteenth or early sixteenth century.

Fragments of Palæphatus: “I have written these things concerning the incredible.” It ends: “the end of life. Here ends Palæphatus’s work on incredible histories.”

Excerpts of Constantine Lascaris from Suidas.

Cornelius Severus, *On the Death of Cicero*.

Pedo, *On Germanicus*: “Long ago, after it had been placed behind his back,” etc.

Mark Antony’s funeral oration for Caesar, from Dio.

*Kinds of Poets*: “Some poets are dithyrambic,” etc.

Miscellaneous material concerning myths.

39. Page 62. An untitled ode, *On the Power of Fortune*, by an uncertain author: “Fortune is powerful and envious toward the brave.”

A short work of Victorinus *On Orthography*: “Now the matter has reminded us,” etc. “The consonant letters did not double,” etc.

Some material from the letters of Cassiodorus.

A life of Virgil from M. Valerius Probus.

Notes on Virgil’s *Bucolics* and *Georgics*. They end in Book IV at the passage on the Po: “winding banks, as horns are,” with a heading noting that the work is incomplete and mutilated.

40. Page 113. A work printed without a title.

“Cicero sends greetings to his Vetturius: I have collected those words,” etc.; “therefore let us begin alphabetically.”

“Hidden, covered,” etc.

In the margin it is noted that the words are arranged according to the order of the letters instead of alphabetically. These are the *Synonyms*, concerning which see more in chapter 56.

There follow the *Differences* under Cicero’s name, as I stated there. Other material is added concerning the Psalms; and near the end: “The laws established by Romulus,” from Pomponius: “Let them do nothing except after taking the auspices,” etc.

At the end, in red letters: “Francis Petrarch died in the village of Arguada in the year of Christ 1379.” These things were written in the year 1506.

41. Vatican Codex 2951, on paper, containing Isidore’s book *On the Structure of the World and Its Parts*, that is, fragments from Book XIV of the *Etymologies*, as I explained in chapter 86.

In the same Codex follows a book *On the Origin of Law and of All Magistracies*: “I am about to interpret the ancient laws,” etc.

Then, on page 15, a brief chronicle from the beginning of the world to the eighth century: “In the beginning God created from nothing,” etc. It ends: “Berengar was the last Italian emperor,” etc.

42. Page 37: Xenophon’s book *On Tyrannical and Private Life*.

Pages 49 and following: various materials from Cicero and others.

Page 79: several letters under the names of Plato, Lepidus, Virgil, Alexander the Great, and others. Others are by Francesco Filelfo and Francesco Petrarch.

Page 83: a letter of the Blessed Virgin Mary to her beloved and fellow student Gynasius. Among the apocryphal letters of the Mother of God, I do not see this one mentioned—not even by Fabricius, volume II of the *Codex Apocryphus of the New Testament*, pages 833 and following.

43. Page 135: sayings of various kinds collected from different authors, among whom Isidore is frequently cited.

Page 265: poems of the poet Vegius: “Praise, and all pour forth joyful voices.” Other poems by other authors.

Page 272: verses of Sedulius from an elegy, *Let Us Sing*, under this title: “The Hellespontine Sibyl concerning Christ: Great joys of God,” etc., up to “Believe now, wretched ones; the Lord will come.”

The reading should be “the Hellespontine,” or “of the Hellespont,” Sibyl.

44. Vatican Codex 3320, on parchment, in large folio, in Gothic script, which they call cordellato, pale or only slightly black, with letters sometimes in red.

At the beginning, in a more recent script: “An ancient lexicon written in Lombard letters, on parchment, in folio. Fulvius Ursinus.” This perhaps indicates that the Codex once belonged to Fulvius Ursinus.

The title is: “In the name of the Lord begins the Book of the *Etymologies*, that is, On the Properties of Words, or Glossary—that is, *hermineumata*—from A to Z.”

“A is the voice of one who grieves,” etc.

This is a very extensive vocabulary, fuller than that of Codex 1471, which begins in the same way. Much of it is clearly drawn from Isidore’s *Etymologies* and other works, for example:

“The philosophers said that atoms fly here and there throughout the whole world, just as the finest particles of dust appear in the rays of the sun; and from these, they say, all crops, grasses, and trees arise, as well as fire and water, and all things are generated and composed,” etc.

More is added concerning atoms from Book XIII, chapter 2, of the *Etymologies*. Nevertheless, I would read: “the particles of dust appearing in the rays of the sun. From these, they say,” etc.

In both dictionaries it reads: “Blessed, wise, or immortal.”

In this Codex it ends:

“Zema, a pot.  
Zizania, darnel.  
Zona, a belt, that is, a girdle.  
Zepher, wind,” etc.

It is suggested that this is a singular form for *favonius*, the west wind.

45. Another fragment of a vocabulary follows, without alphabetical order, from *Vayeka*, that is, Leviticus, to “zeal, rivalry, envy.” End.

Immediately afterward is an epigraph: “Here begins Cicero’s *Synonyms*, arranged in alphabetical order: Love, ardor, heat,” etc., collected by some incompetent compiler, as is evident from the many errors.

46. Vatican Codex 3321, in quarto, in two columns.

A note by a recent hand reads: “Lexicon of sacred and profane words, with some short works of Isidore of Seville and others, written in majuscule letters in quarto on parchment, touched by Panormita. Fulvius Ursinus.”

At the beginning are some fragments of a homily on fasting, in very ancient majuscule letters, which wrap around the Codex. In an ancient script, but in more recent majuscule letters between two columns, one reads: “Stephen the archpresbyter”—“should drink” for “should live.”

Page 1: a vocabulary, formerly copied for the most part by the distinguished Cajetan Marini. A seated monk holding a book presents the appearance of a teacher from his chair.

It ends: “rich, satisfied. Commonly: peoples, everywhere, or all.”

Some letters in the headings are red. Marini shared his copy with me.

47. Page 164. “The *Synonyms* begin,” in red letters, as are also the opening words under which other synonyms are placed, in three columns:

“Sharp, intent, vehement, fierce, excited, burning.”

It ends: “time, opportunity.”

Page 176. “The *Differences of Words of Isidore the Younger* begin,” etc., copied by Marini as far as “between faithful and trustworthy.”

This work too is written in majuscule letters, but in only one column or line. It ends: “between zeal and envy … and torments the mind.”

The letter F begins with Grialius, but after no. 202: “between scissors,” etc.; again: “What difference is there between faithful and trustworthy? Answer: A faithful man is a friend; a trustworthy man is a servant. Between fornication,” etc.

The order of the *Differences* is alphabetical, although somewhat rearranged.

48. There follows: “Here begins the chapter on Hebrew names.” There are fourteen chapters.

Chapter 1, *On Hebrew Names*: “Adonai,” etc.

Chapter 2, *On Various Vocabulary*: “Alleluia,” etc.

Chapter 3, *On the Explanation of Various Things*: “Mandrake,” etc.

Then follows the title:

“All the names or terms that follow are found in the books of Exodus or Kings. Those that are obscure occur in the old translation, while those that appear clearer are contained in the text of the new translation.

“Calamisus, reed.  
Anconiscos, notches.  
Aspidicas, hooks of a fringe, or little chains [a recent hand: ‘small chains’].  
Degrapide, engraving.  
Petalis, plates.  
Perimetrum, a line.  
Spiras, the capitals of columns, or their workmanship.  
Elami, porticoes, but it is better interpreted as ‘before the doors,’ or ‘vestibule,’ in the vision of the City; in the old translation it has ‘sheepfolds’ or ‘treasuries.’  
Trociscos, formed almost in the shape of a ship.  
Thee, a bridal chamber.  
Aileu, forehead.  
Elaumoth, vestibule.  
Pultandrion, multitude.  
Spitames, a palm’s breadth.  
Manaa, sacrifice in Kings.  
Caenotama, images, which in Greek are called *opia*.”

49. Chapter 4, *On Gentile Names*, follows: “Gomor,” etc.

Chapter 5, *On Places*: “Jebus; it is Jerusalem itself,” etc.

Chapter 6, *On Rivers*: “Gihon,” etc.

Chapter 7, *On Months*: “Nisan,” etc.

Chapter 8, *On Feasts*: “Year,” etc.

Chapter 9, *On Idols*: “Idols,” etc.

Chapter 10, *On Clothing*: “Caracallae,” etc.

Chapter 11, *On Birds or Winged Creatures*: “Pelican, a small bird,” etc.

Chapter 12, *On Beasts or Reptiles*: “Rhinoceros,” etc.

Chapter 13, *On Weights*: “Obol,” etc.

Chapter 14, *On Measures*: “Chorus,” etc.; read “Corus.”

Chapter 15, *On Greek Names*: “Receive now,” etc. “Theos.”

50. Page 220. *Orthography* begins.

“Aper is written with a single a” [perhaps it was *asper*]. “Arena is written with h and a,” etc., in alphabetical order.

It ends: “Zoticus, Zenon, and so forth, or similar names.” For it must be written with z, the double Greek letter, because it is short.

Heading: “Likewise another orthography: Religion is so called because it binds souls back to divine worship. I wrote *propterea* with p because among the Greeks there is the letter *psi*, which they call psi.”

51. On the reverse of page 223 the following heading follows: “Likewise on orthography.”

“Orthography: grave,” etc., is chapter 26 or 27 of Book I of the *Etymologies*. It ends: “to be a letter.”

There, *Xps*, because it is Greek, ought to be written with X; likewise *Xrisma*.

52. A description of the fourteen regions of Rome follows, along with other material on weights, measures, days, months, hours, years, seasons, and leap years. These are for the most part taken from Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Book V, chapter 29, etc.

At the end: “Of Antonius Panormita,” perhaps in his own hand.

## CHAPTER XCVII

Nineteen other manuscript copies of the old Vatican Library are described. A collection of ancient canons. Extensive collections of homilies. The Pseudo-Isidorian collection of canons. Several copies of the *Differences of Words*, arranged alphabetically and not alphabetically, with Isidore’s name omitted.

1. Vatican Codex 3788, on parchment, in folio, of the eleventh century, as the Ballerini believe.

The work is mutilated at the beginning, and perhaps also at the end. It concerns the lives of the Roman pontiffs, arranged in the form of readings for ecclesiastical office. For it is preceded by the heading: “On the feast of Saint Callistus, Roman pontiff and martyr,” and similarly in the other cases.

After Callistus come Urban, pontiff and martyr; Pontian, pontiff and martyr; Anterus, pontiff and martyr; Fabian, pontiff and martyr; Cornelius, pontiff and martyr; Lucius, pontiff and martyr; Stephen, pontiff and martyr; Xystus, pontiff and martyr; Dionysius, pontiff and martyr; Felix, pontiff; then, in a later hand, “under Claudius and Aurelian”; Eutychian, Caius, Marcellinus, Marcellus, Eusebius, and Melchiades. All these are pontiffs and martyrs.

Of Silvester it says: “He baptized Constantine Augustus, whom the Lord healed of leprosy through baptism.”

Saint Mark follows. Then:

“On the feast of Saint Felix, pope and martyr: Since much is disputed about him, I shall add part of his eulogy:

‘Felix, a Roman by nation, born of his father Anastasius,’ etc. ‘He too was beheaded, together with many faithful clergy, secretly beside the walls of the City, at the side of Trajan’s aqueduct, on the third day before the Ides of November. Afterward Christians, together with the presbyter Damasus, carried away his body and buried it in the aforesaid basilica on the Via Aurelia, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in peace; and his episcopate ceased for thirty-eight days.’”

2. The catalogue of the Roman pontiffs follows to its end:

“107. Nicholas, in office nine years, six months, and twenty days.  
108. Adrian, in office …”

Therefore this catalogue was compiled under him, that is, in the ninth century.

Immediately afterward is another catalogue: “Pontiffs of the Church of Constantinople.”

1. Alexander the Confessor.  
2. Paul the Martyr.  
3. Macedonius the heretic, etc.

The last is number 52, Ignatius the Orthodox, who was first deposed and afterward restored.

The Pseudo-Isidorian collection of Decretals follows, in the order described by the Ballerini in *On the Collection of Canons*, Part III, chapter 6.

3. Page XI: “From the sayings of blessed Peter the Apostle to Clement the bishop,” etc.

There it reads: “From the sayings of blessed Isidore to Lanfred, the bishop.” It is a fragment of a letter to Leudefred, but interpolated, as I observed in chapter 73.

Before the letters of Saint Silvester, on page 153, are the *Acts of the Great Emperor Constantine*, concerning the primitive Church and the Council of Nicaea:

“No one who reads the divine Scriptures is ignorant,” etc.

There follow excerpts from the synodal acts of Pope Saint Silvester: “In the time of Saint Silvester,” etc.

A letter of Athanasius to Pope Mark, and the latter’s letter to Athanasius.

Decrees of Popes Julius, Liberius, Felix, and Damasus.

Page 198. “The canons of Pope Silvester, bishop, begin”:

“In the time of the lord Constantine Augustus, when many nobles rejoiced that Constantine had been baptized by Silvester,” etc.

Page 200. “The six ecclesiastical orders of blessed Jerome to Rusticus, bishop of Narbonne, begin.”

In another ancient script, addressed to Patroclus the bishop: “Indeed, it is sufficient for your faith,” etc.

Page 207. “The decree [of the synod] of blessed Gregory, pope of the City of Rome, begins: ‘While reigning,’ etc., in the thirteenth year of Maurice.”

A letter of Gregory to his most reverend brother Augustine, together with Augustine’s questions and Gregory’s answers concerning the Church of Britain.

Page 214, heading:

“Letter of the same Gregory, pope, to Alexander [Leander], bishop of Spalatum: on single immersion in baptism: ‘By triple … the period of three days is expressed’” [the reading was *exprimitur*, “is expressed,” not *exprimatur*, “let it be expressed”].

It is only a fragment.

A Roman council in the sixth year of the emperor Leo follows, under Gregory.

Chapters of Pope Gregory VII: “Whoever among the soldiers,” etc. It ends: “must undergo danger.”

Nothing else is found in this beautiful Codex.

4. Vatican Codex 3836, in a small folio approaching a square format, written in uncial letters in two columns.

The diphthongs are sometimes joined and sometimes separated. The letters are generally joined without division between words. Periods are sometimes separated by a point placed between letters, sometimes by a point and comma; but a more recent hand occasionally added these punctuation marks.

In the inventory the Codex is described as being in square folio, in large Lombard characters. It is believed to belong to the seventh or eighth century. I think no one later than Isidore is named in this Codex.

The first heading is: “Here begins Saint Augustine’s sermon on the Kalends of August, the feast of the holy Maccabean martyrs: ‘Thanks be to our Lord God, beloved,’” etc.

5. Folio 12. Likewise, a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of the martyrs.

The ninth reading from the Gospel is found on folio 18 verso and the following pages. It is in a single column occupying the whole page.

Folio 21 again has two columns.

Folio 23: “The sermon of Saint Laurence begins.” VIII—that is, the eighth sermon of the Codex—“of the most blessed martyr Laurence, whose feast we celebrate today; I believe you know his passion,” etc., without the author’s name.

Likewise, from the passage above: “Ninth reading, first,” etc. “The Lord says in the Gospel: ‘To what is the kingdom of God like?’” etc.

“On the feast” of the saint mentioned above, X: “When all the blessed martyrs.”

Likewise another sermon, XI: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of heaven, and to what shall I liken it?” etc.

The sermon of Pope Saint Leo on the feast of Saint Laurence begins, XII: “Since, beloved, the sum of all virtues and the fullness of all righteousness,” etc.

Other headings are similar.

Likewise a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Laurence the martyr, XIII: “The triumphant day of blessed Laurence.”

Likewise a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Laurence, XIV: “The solemn day of the blessed martyr Laurence,” etc.

Reading XII, without a title: “Your faith recognizes the grain,” etc.

Likewise a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Laurence the martyr, XVI: “Among the laurel-crowned confessors.”

Likewise a sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Xystus, XVII: “Of all honors,” etc.

This sermon is reading XIV for the feast of Saint Laurence.

6. Some sermons are divided into several readings.

Page 55 and following, in another, more recent script: “The sermon of Saint John Chrysostom begins: ‘The solemnity of all the martyrs.’” A recent hand indicates that it is found in volume VII of the works.

Folio 61: the sermon of Saint Antipater begins: “Again the holy and ever-praiseworthy Mother of God calls us to a spiritual banquet.”

Folio 64, in reading 3 of the Assumption: the initial letter displays an image of a woman, apparently the Mother of God.

Folio 70 verso: a homily of Proclus, bishop of Constantinople, which begins: “Today is the virginal solemnity.”

7. From this point the original script of the Codex returns.

Page 80 verso: “Likewise, a homily of Saint Gregory on the holy archangel: ‘For the nature of angels and of human beings,’” etc.

Folio 87, for reading 2, the heading in the same original script:

“Here begins the sermon of Saint Isidore on the Holy Archangel: ‘The name of angel is an office,’ etc. … and ‘restored to the angels.’”

Heading: “Likewise, from the passage above, III.”

Sometimes, however, God also speaks to human hearts through an angel. These passages are not Isidore’s.

8. Folio 95: “The homilies for the feast of Saint Andrew the Apostle begin.”

Folio 174 verso, heading: “The homily on the feast of the holy confessors begins. For it is written in the Gospel reading that a certain man, going abroad,” etc.

Folio 183: “Likewise, a sermon on the feast of virgins: ‘You have heard, dearest brothers, while the Gospel reading was being read, where the Lord speaks in parables about the ten virgins,’” etc.

Folio 190, on the dedication of a church.

Folio 198 verso, heading: “The great instrument of good works for the building up of the soul begins. First, love the Lord your God,” etc. This is from chapter 4 of the Rule of Benedict.

Several other sermons for the building up of the soul follow.

Folio 233: “A sermon of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Vincent: ‘Dearest brothers, we have witnessed a great spectacle of Saint Vincent.’”

9. Folio 248, apparently in the original script: “The homily of Saint John Chrysostom begins, when he returned from Asia to Constantinople: ‘That great servant of God, Moses,’” etc.

Folio 176, after a sermon of Saint Augustine: “Here end one hundred sermons of Saint Augustine on the feasts of various saints.”

Homilies for the stations of Lent follow, in a script also in majuscule letters but more recent:

“Saturday of the second week. At Saint Peter and Marcellinus: ‘A certain man had two sons,’ etc. ‘Today the Lord presents us with a father and his sons,’ etc.

“Third week, Friday, at Saint Laurence in Lucina [sic]: ‘It is not unfamiliar to your ears,’ etc.

“Fourth week, Wednesday in Lent, a homily of the same author in the Basilica of Saint Paul at the Middle: ‘A lengthy reading has been recited.’”

In the sermon on the angels attributed to Isidore by Constans Cajetanus, the second part is anonymous in this Codex and presents the passage of Daniel that is missing from Saint Gregory the Great.

Before the homily under Isidore’s name there is another by Gregory the Great on the angels.

Compare what has already been said about this Codex in chapter 72.

10. Codex 4088, Vatican, on paper, in ordinary folio, of the sixteenth century, in German script; see chapter 86.

*On Meteorological Impressions*: “As Aristotle says at the beginning of the *Metaphysics*.”

Page 8, *On the Form of the World according to Isidore*: “To the student of wisdom who diligently investigates hidden things in the depth of knowledge,” etc.

In the margin: “Image of the world.”

At the end: “Here ends the map of the world composed by Saint Isidore.”

This is the *Image of the World* of Honorius of Autun, whose prologue ends: “But I place nothing in it except what the tradition of our ancestors commends.”

The work begins: “The world is called *mundus* because it is moved everywhere. For it is always in motion,” etc.

Much is taken from Book III of the *Etymologies*, chapters 28 and following, especially from Book XIII, chapter 1 and following, and Book XIV, chapter 1 and following.

11. Page 24, *On the Elections and Aspects of the Moon according to Albumasar*.

Albumasar said: “It pleased me,” etc.

“Arrendadores,” a Spanish word, are mentioned. In one place there is the note *ojo*, that is, “eye,” to arouse attention.

Other astrological works of judicial and astronomical character follow.

12. Vatican Codex 4160, on parchment, in octavo, of the tenth or eleventh century.

“Here begin the ecclesiastical rules, sentences of the holy Fathers, excerpted by legates of the Apostolic See itself in Gaul for the regulation of ecclesiastical cases.”

Page 48 verso:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the preface of Saint Isidore the bishop. Isidore, servant of Christ, sends greetings in the Lord to Hector, his fellow servant and relative.”

In the Codex the reading is clearly “Hector,” and this is also how it appears in the inventory of the Vatican Library.

I had wondered whether it should be read “Lector,” as in the preface to the book *Differences of Words*, or *On the Properties of Speech*: “Isidore sends greetings to Lector.” But what follows, “his relative in the Lord,” may suggest that the author has expressed the proper name of someone.

This Codex contains an epitome, arranged by classes, of the Isidorian collection of the supposedly forged Decretals, comprising 317 chapters.

The first is from Deuteronomy, chapter 14: “If you perceive that a judgment among you is difficult and ambiguous,” etc.

There follows a section on the seventy canons of the Council of Nicaea, which are not found in the canonical books commonly used.

There is also a letter of Athanasius to Pope Mark.

After Isidore’s letter, which ends “the laws of the age command,” there is the heading: “From the sayings of Saint Boniface.”

Chapter 1: “Concerning the layman.”

It ends: “who agree with those who do it.”

Aguirre, volume I of the *Hispanic Councils*, page 27, published the preface attributed to Isidore, which he himself believes to be genuine. We shall reproduce the same preface among the appendices with variant readings.

13. Vatican Codex 4250, on parchment, in duodecimo, approximately of the twelfth century.

Isidore’s collection from books *On the Trinity*, namely excerpts from the *Etymologies*, as I explained in chapter 86.

The book of Boethius *On the Trinity* follows, and on page 57: “A statement on the Trinity begins: ‘God, the cause of all things,’” etc.

These are sayings collected from the Fathers—Augustine, Ambrose, Jerome, and Isidore.

14. Vatican Codex 4327, on paper, in folio, of the fifteenth century.

Heading:

“Here begins the book of Saint Isidore *On Christ against the Jews*. To the holy lady Florentina, his sister, Isidore. Certain things,” etc. “Here ends the prologue. Here begins the first book of Saint Isidore the Younger *On Christ against the Jews*. Here ends the first book. Here begins the text of the second book.”

“Vincentius Navarra, writer of the library of Our Most Holy Lord the Pope, was writing in the year of the Lord 1561.”

This Codex appears to have been copied from the older Vatican Codex 4918, which will soon be described.

15. Vatican Codex 4411, on parchment, in duodecimo, approximately of the fourteenth century.

The inventory describes it as: “Rabbi Moses’s exposition of various passages of Sacred Scripture, divided into various chapters to which the names of the holy Fathers have been attached.”

In the Vatican index it is called “R. Moses Maimonides the Spaniard.” It may perhaps be Peter Alfonsi.

The first title in the Codex is: “Dionysius. Rabbi Moses: ‘May the Lord open your heart,’” etc.

There appear to be excerpts from Dionysius, Hilary, and Bede, whose names are customarily written at the beginnings of the pages.

On page 13, Isidore is cited in the margin, and in the text: “Isidore, in the treatise *On the Supreme Good*: ‘He ought not to rebuke the faults of others,’” etc. Chrysostom is cited at the beginning of this page.

At the beginning of page 36 verso there is “Hysidorus,” and thereafter either “Hisidorus” or “Ysidorus,” continuing through page 42.

There are, as it were, ten chapters, chiefly concerned with the resurrection. At the beginnings of other pages Symmachus, Haymo, Augustine, Rabanus, and Rabbi Moses are also cited.

Page 79 contains an index of subjects, together with the names of the authors whose authority is cited concerning those subjects.

16. On page 81 the following work begins: “Grace has been poured upon your lips: There is a twofold state,” etc.

Damascene, Ambrose, Origen, Gregory, Bernard, Jerome, Adamantius, and Hesychius are cited.

On page 159 it ends: “and sits at the right hand of God.”

Sermons and various other materials follow. Finally there is an index of notable subjects.

In the first work, various passages of Sacred Scripture appear to be expounded from the holy Fathers, especially passages concerning Christ.

17. Vatican Codex 4418, on parchment, of the twelfth century, in quarto or small oblong folio, containing much by Galen and Hippocrates.

After Galen’s book *On Gout*, on page 108, there is the heading:

“Here begins a letter of Isidore the Spaniard [sic]: ‘There are four winds,’” etc.

I discussed this letter, fabricated from Isidore’s works, in chapter 75, and intend to place it among the doubtful or spurious works.

After this supposed letter there is another medical work, beginning:

“Vindicianus sends greetings to his nephew Pentadius. You should know,” etc.

In the same chapter 75 I noted that in the Angelica Library there is another work under Isidore’s name addressed to his nephew, but its beginning is different.

Page 143 contains a medical vocabulary explaining words, especially Greek words, relating to medicine. Many other materials on this same medical subject occur in the Codex.

18. Vatican Codex 4498, on parchment, in quarto, approximately of the fourteenth century.

A work *On Aqueducts*, without a title, by order of the emperor Nerva:

“When every matter delegated by the emperor,” etc.

The author is Sextus Julius Frontinus.

Rufus *On the Provinces* follows: “Since your request, worthy of me, frequently moves me.”

Another short work without a title: “Your Clemency orders that a brief little book be made.” It ends: “Valentinian Augustus.”

Then Suetonius *On Grammarians*, and the same author *On Rhetoricians*.

Under Pliny’s name, a book *On Illustrious Men*: “Concerning Proca,” etc.

Tacitus *On the Life of Julius Agricola*.

A mutilated dialogue of Gaius Cornelius Tacitus *On Orators*.

Tacitus *On the Origin of the Germans*.

Page 109 verso, heading: “Marcus Junius Nipsus *On Measures*.”

“It is known to all, Celsus, that the entire sum of our studies rests with you.” The work is incomplete; it ends: “For before Jupiter the boundaries did not …”

On page 3, in a recent hand, this title appears: “By an unknown author, though he appears to be some Christian.”

The short work begins: “The smallest part of weights is the *calculus*, which consists of two chickpea grains.”

19. Page 112, in a recent hand: “Isidore.”

After this title: “The signs of weights,” etc., the beginning of chapter 26 of Book XVI of the *Etymologies*.

Then Seneca’s *Apocolocyntosis* against Claudius.

Censorinus *On the Birthday*.

Other material on years, days, months, the position of the heavens, music, geometry, meters, and rhythms. The following should be noted:

“Rhythm is believed to have been named from Rhythmon, son of Orpheus, and the nymph Marica of Iduomea, as Nicrotates reports in the book he composed about Museus, brother of Rythion.”

It ends: “Likewise the Priapean, if you remove a syllable, becomes heroic.”

The nymph Iduomea is perhaps confused with Timothoe, or Cymothoe, in Isidore, Book I of the *Etymologies*, chapter 39.

20. Vatican Codex 4712, on paper, in folio, of the sixteenth century.

The inventory describes it as: “A translation of the *Apologeticus* of Gregory Nazianzen, translated by Isidore,” for which reason this translation has been attributed by some person to our Isidore.

But in the Codex the words “translated by Isidore” are absent, and only the following title now appears:

“Apologeticus of blessed Gregory Nazianzen, the theologian, concerning his flight to Pontus and his return from there, after he had been chosen priest; in it he discusses what the priestly profession is and what a bishop ought to be: ‘I have been overcome, and I openly confess it,’” etc.

If the author of the inventory established, as he seems to have done, that the translator was Isidore, this must be understood of Isidore Clarius, who is known to have excelled in this kind of study and translation.

In the same Codex are added some materials relating to Aristotelian philosophy, with the author’s name omitted.

### 21. Codex 4877

Vatican, paper, in folio, approximately of the sixteenth century. Some material concerning the Greek Christian emperors. Ancient inscriptions of Ancyra in the suburbs. Series 1: Latin poems addressed to Bonetto and others on various subjects [Col. 0805D]. There is a discussion of Cremona, Milan, and Ferrara. On the reform of the calendar: the brief of Leo X, “To all and each of the colleges, doctors, etc.,” dated 24 July 1514, is signed by Jacopo Sadoleto. Pagan Calendar: January—Agon, Agonalia, etc. On folio 51 begins the book of James, cardinal deacon of Saint George at the Golden Veil, *On the Hundredth Year, or Jubilee Year*: “Something of the future, etc.” Transcribed from the library of the Basilica of Saint Peter. A poem by the same author on the Jubilee: “Golden centuries rise with Phoebus at the hundredth year.” Other material on the Jubilee. Observations on the observance of Lent, excerpted from the Fathers.

### 22.

In the same manuscript, page 73: Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, *On Illustrious Men*. “Of men, etc.” The variant readings agree with the Albanian Codex, about which elsewhere. There follows the *History of Countess Matilda* [Col. 0806A]. A translation of the First Council of Ephesus. Some other material in Italian concerning the war against the Turks.

### 23. Codex 4918

Vatican, parchment, in octavo, approximately of the eleventh century, acquired from the books of Cardinal Sirlet. Rubric: “Here begins the book of Saint Isidore on Christ, etc.,” as above in Codex 4411, which was copied from this one. “The prologue ends, etc.” The first book ends. The text of the second book begins. At the end, however, the following is written entirely in large red letters:

> The book of Saint Isidore the Younger, against the Jews, ends. Thanks be to God.

> Pour forth prayers to Christ for the book you see here:
>
> May its scribe be just, chaste, and handsome,
>
> Placidus, who truly seeks to have Christ for himself.

Another version:

> You who see this book written by Placidus:
>
> By a gentle prayer, gently make Christ gracious toward Placidus.

[Col. 0806B] Page 280. A question concerning the spirit of blasphemy follows, taken from Augustine, together with another work from the same Augustine and from Ambrose. On the verso of page 127, a later hand has written the title: “Seneca’s Book on the Formula of Life”; another title reads: “Seneca’s Book on the Four Virtues.” It begins: “To commit no sin belongs to God alone.” This is a work falsely attributed to Seneca, as is well known.

### 24. Codex 4948

Vatican, very old parchment, oblong in folio, from the books of Cardinal Sirlet. A later hand records at the beginning that this codex contains a fragment of ecclesiastical history, translated by Rufinus, and the complete book of Saint Isidore, which is said not to have been printed—although in fact it had already been printed. The annotator adds that the book is written in Lombard characters and approximately seven hundred years earlier, and that it was given by Fulvius Ursinus to Cardinal Ascanio Colonna in 1588. Thus, at that time, it was believed to have been written in the eighth century. Some fragments are taken from Theodoret, Socrates, and Sozomen.

Folio 23: “The first book of Sozomen’s *Ecclesiastical History* ends. The second book of the same *History* begins. The chapter titles of Book I begin: ‘On the bishops of the Churches.’”

Folio 43 verso: “The second book of the *Ecclesiastical History* ends; the third book begins. The titles begin: 1. ‘On the conversion of the Indian people,’ etc.”

Page 75, chapter 31 of Book III: Constantine’s letter on behalf of Athanasius, etc. It begins: “The most reverend bishop Athanasius, etc.” On folio 99, after Book IV, in a contemporary hand: “I have collated P., which is lacking in the earlier copies.” At the end of Book V: “I have collated P.” The same occurs at the end of Book VI [Col. 0806D], and a transverse line is always placed in the lower part of the letter P. The titles of Book VII number forty, but the book ends at chapter 24.

### 25.

On the verso of page 171 begins the prologue of the book called *Synonyma*, that is, of “Lord Isidore, bishop of Seville.” “In what follows, etc.” The prologue ends. “My soul, etc.” It ends: “he will be saved here.” The first book ends. The second book begins: “I ask you, soul.” It ends: “you please me above my life.” Other copies read: “above my life.” Immediately follows: “Here begins the order of all the months. January, etc.,” namely, for finding the Kalends. There are no titles, except occasionally in the margin, written in Lombard characters but by a later hand.

### 26. Codex 4951

Vatican, parchment, in folio, approximately of the twelfth century, from the books of Sirlet. In this codex one may observe question marks and other punctuation, joined diphthongs, and a few clear abbreviations of letters. It contains homilies of ancient Fathers. There is an index at the beginning. The authors are Leo, Fulgentius, Maximus the bishop, Isidore, Augustine, Eusebius the bishop, John the bishop, Faustinus the bishop, and Laurentius the bishop.

At the end of the index there is a note in the same hand:

> It should be noted that sermons read at night in church are not usually read in the refectory, namely, on the Nativity of the Lord, etc.

The book appears to have been prepared for some dining hall or refectory. On folio 1, in a later hand, at the bottom of the page:

> The book of the Roffes monastery—[the abbreviation or letter R is unclear]—whoever removes it, conceals it after its removal, or fraudulently erases this title, let him be anathema. Amen.

Similar anathemas occur frequently in manuscripts.

[Col. 0807B] ### 27.

Among other material are eight sermons for the Rogation Days: 1. On the Holy Trinity; 2. On the fast of the seventh month; 3. On Saint Vincent; one sermon of Saint Augustine on rendering tithes and avoiding the evil practices committed at the festival of Saint John the Baptist; three sermons on the feast of Saint Lawrence; one on the Assumption of the Mother of God; one on the ordination of a bishop; one on the anniversary of a bishop’s ordination; one on the character of good and bad Christians; one on seeking the health of the soul rather than that of the body and avoiding diviners; one addressed to those who, through drunkenness, commit many shameful acts at the festivals of the saints; one addressed to those who observe omens and consult *caragii* and diviners on any matter; one sermon of Saint Augustine addressed to those who try to assist the eclipse of the moon with their shouting; one on maintaining chastity even with one’s wife on Sundays and the other festivals, and on women who take potions not to conceive or to kill what they have conceived; and one on martyrdom in a time of peace and improper familiarity with unrelated women.

Many of these sermons are anonymous. There follow excerpts from the Decrees of blessed Pope Gregory, stating that monks may everywhere minister together with the priestly office.

[Col. 0807C] ### 28.

Folio 7, rubric: “Sermon of blessed Isidore, bishop, on the Nativity of the Lord.” “The day of the Lord’s birth, for this reason, etc.” This is chapter 25 of Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. The codex reads: “worse than all the practices of idol worship.” Breulius omits “all.” It ends: “that Christ was born, who with God the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God throughout all ages of ages. Amen.”

In some places the letter *o* is marked in the margin, with a transverse line through the middle, perhaps standing for *ojo*, or “eye.”

### 29.

On the verso of folio 31, rubric: “Sermon of blessed Augustine, bishop, on the Kalends of January and on avoiding the sacrileges committed on the Kalends themselves.”

A recent marginal note reads: “To be investigated. Compare the notes on chapter 40 of Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.”

The sermon begins:

> The day of these Kalends, dearest brothers, which they call the January Kalends, received its name from a certain lost and sacrilegious man named Janus. This Janus was once the leader and prince of pagan men; ignorant people and peasants, while fearing him as though he were a king, or while beginning to worship him as a god, etc.

See Isidore at the place cited above, where he constructed that chapter from this sermon and the following one. For the rubric then reads: “The preceding sermon on the same subject.” A recent note says: “To be investigated.” [Col. 0808A] It begins: “Although I do not doubt, etc.” It concerns not calling the days Monday, Friday, etc., but rather the second feria, etc.

### 30.

Folio 58: “From the preceding: a sermon during Lent.” A recent note says: “To be investigated.” It begins: “The solemn season has arrived, etc.” It concerns fasting and almsgiving. The following beautiful sentence occurs there:

> When the body is chastised and subjected to servitude, pleasures must be restrained, not exchanged.

Folio 66, rubric: “Sermon of Bishop Laurentius on the Canaanite woman.”

> Indeed, many winds are in conflict and storms rage; but temptation has not dissolved your assembly, nor has zeal violated it.

A recent note says: “To be examined.” In the meantime, Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Laurentius, Mellifluus,” may be consulted. The prologue ends:

> For it is not right to continue any longer mocking the enemies [of Laurentius himself] and to despise wise sons.

Thus, yesterday the apostle Paul prepared a banquet for us; today Matthew does so, etc.

### 31.

On the verso of folio 100, rubric: “Also, a sermon of blessed Faustinus, bishop, on Easter.”

> Although the benefits of our God are great and wondrous, etc.

A recent note says: “To be investigated.” Concerning this Faustinus, the same Fabricius and Martène, volume V of the *Anecdota*, should also be consulted.

On the verso of folio 148, rubric: “A sermon on the Rogation Days and on who instituted this observance.”

> Behold, dearest brothers, these days are sanctified and venerable, etc. We read, however, that this custom was first begun by Saint Mamertus, bishop of the city of Vienne [the wording is unclear], etc.

This was done to avert the plague. The author continues by reproving those who on the Rogation Days put on expensive clothes [Col. 0808C] and prepared sumptuous banquets for themselves, etc. A similar custom of the people of Bologna could be noted here; perhaps it derives from so ancient an origin.

Folio 169: Sermon on the Holy Trinity:

> We confess and believe in the holy and ineffable Trinity, etc.

It ends:

> Through this faith, by which we have adhered to it, may we reign with him without end. Amen.

There follow sermons of Pope Leo on the fast of the seventh month. See chapter 38, or alternatively 39, of Book I, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. Three sermons of Saint Augustine on the feast of Saint Vincent occur; beside the third is written:

> It is found in Augustine, but is so corrupt and mutilated that it must necessarily be transcribed here.

### 32.

Folio 187: Sermon of blessed Jerome the presbyter on the Assumption of the Blessed Mother of God, Mary:

> You compel me, O Paula and Eustochium, etc.

Page 210: On avoiding divination. There:

> They hang up demonic amulets and magical characters, etc.

Much more is said on these matters. Even if it is said to you that the amulets themselves truly contain the Scriptures and divine readings, do not trust that health will come to you from them, etc. I discussed such amulets on page 438, in connection with Appendix 5 to Sedulius.

There, in the Church of God, occurs *verbosantur*. This word should be noted as one frequently used by Augustine, meaning “they speak at length” or “they talk excessively.”

Folio 211: Against *caragii*, or diviners, etc. There: “My admonition achieves little among some people.” Also there: against the worship of trees, etc. For what is the meaning of this: when that tree, at which vows are fulfilled, falls, no one brings wood from that tree to his hearth? He is speaking against Christians who at that time were devoted to these forms of worship and divination.

On folio 213 and the following pages is a sermon on chastity:

> Finally, when women take husbands, they do not dare enter the church for thirty days. Men ought likewise to do the same.

Also:

> I ask you, brothers, to pardon me, because for the salvation of your souls I seem often to admonish you about such matters with great fear, or trembling, and also with shame, because it is useful for me to do this, and you ought to listen.

Those who treat a similar subject in moral theology commonly employ the same line of apology.

Folio 217: Decrees of Pope Gregory:

> The bishop ought to celebrate Mass at the ordination of a presbyter, and the abbot at the ordination of a monk, etc.

In this codex there are question marks and other punctuation, joined diphthongs, and a few simple and easily understood ligatures of letters.

[Col. 0809B] ### 33. Codex 5002

Vatican, parchment, small in folio, approximately of the fourteenth century. The *Panormia* of Ivo of Chartres. Rubric: “Here begins the book of sacred Canons.” The first part contains material on faith, etc. Isidore is cited, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, the *Book of Sentences*, etc.

Folio 84, rubric:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity begins the little book which Isidore, bishop of Seville, compiled from various works of the Fathers: On the exposition of History; the history of the sacred law, etc.

The authors cited there are Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and, outstanding in our own times, the eloquent Gregory.

A table of thirty-one chapters follows. At chapter 23, on Genesis, it is noted:

> Rabbi Moses punctuates this text as follows: “I am: your firstborn, Esau.” But our teachers explain it otherwise.

Rabbi Moses attempts by that punctuation to remove the difficulty of Jacob’s lie. The work ends: “over all flesh.”

The table of Exodus contains fifty-nine chapters. It ends: “in those who believe in him.” Leviticus contains seventeen chapters. The end of chapter 16 and the whole of chapter 17 agree entirely with Breulius. Numbers contains thirty-five chapters. It ends: “and let us extinguish vices.” Deuteronomy contains twenty-two chapters. It ends: “we are found without sin.” Joshua contains eighteen chapters. It ends: “he does not impose greater things.” Judges contains nine chapters; the last concerns Ruth. It ends: “he promised through his son, etc.”

The First Book of Kings has twenty-one chapters. At the end of Judges, however, there is the rubric:

> The book of Judges ends; the chapters in the Book of Kings begin. Up to this point are excerpts from Isidore the bishop; what follows is excerpted by Bede the presbyter.

These are Isidore’s own commentaries on the four Books of Kings, Ezra, and Maccabees. The manuscript ends with:

> and all things have been completed in mysteries through Our Lord Jesus Christ, etc.

This agrees with Breulius, and nothing is added.

### 34. Codex 5077

Vatican, parchment, in octavo, approximately of the fifteenth century. A moral compendium on penance, marriage, etc. Page 41, rubric: “Here begins the book of Saint Bernard: Many know many things.” Page 60: “Here begins *philum* (sic) on holy Charity,” just as the bride pleases the bridegroom’s carnal eyes more, etc. It ends: “May Jesus Christ, the bridegroom of faithful souls, lead us, etc.”

### 35.

Page 65, rubric:

> Here begins the little book of blessed Pope Leo on the Conflict of Virtues and Vices: The apostolic voice cries throughout the world, etc.

Where Breulius has *simulatio* (“pretence”), the manuscript reads *hypocrisis* (“hypocrisy”). Thus some titles differ in wording from Breulius [Col. 0810A], while some are omitted. At the end:

> The book of blessed Pope Leo on the Conflict of Virtues and Vices ends.

It concludes:

> Pay attention to what I say, and bravely resist the ambushes of so deceitful an enemy.

I discussed this work in chapter 84.

### 36.

Page 65, rubric:

> Here begins Book II of the *Soliloquies* of Bishop Isidore. “Man: I ask you, soul, etc.” Later: “Reason replies: Know, man, etc.”

There are more titles than in Breulius. Some passages are omitted or abridged. For example, the final chapter ends as follows:

> You are the guide of life, the teacher of morals and virtues; you are the discoverer of good things, without whom human life can be nothing. Through you the rule of living is given to all; by your precepts souls are formed. If anything is distorted, you correct it; if anything needs correction, you amend it. For nothing is dearer than you; you please me above my life. Thanks be always to God and to the Lord Jesus Christ. This reading is more splendid than gold, brighter than gems, more radiant than light, sweeter than honeycombs, and sweeter than honey. Amen. The book of the *Soliloquies* of blessed Isidore the bishop ends.

### 37. Codex 5120

Vatican, papyrus, in quarto, of the fifteenth century. Some of Cicero’s *Philippics*, together with certain works on the art of oratory and on grammar.

Page 64, without a title: Isidore’s preface to the *Differences of Words*:

> Most of the ancients, etc.

The preface continues: “and I append it for you, reader, for your enjoyment.” Breulius: “[p. d.] I have noted [this] below.”

The *Differences* begin immediately:

> The distinction between *caelum* and *aether*, and between *aether* and *aer*, is this: not only is that place the region bearing the stars, but this air too is called *caelum*.

It ends:

> Between *flere* and *plorare*: *flere* is to shed abundant tears [“abundantly” is unclear]; *plorare* is to weep with the voice; but *plangere* is to strike the breast or face with tears.

Nothing appears to be new that is not found in our copies, except that no order of differences is preserved in this manuscript.

### 38.

Some examples of letters follow, for practice; then several odes of Horace with notes. Next comes Omnibono of Vicenza’s *Art of Meter*. It ends:

> It is called that which performs the function of a foot, etc.

It was written at Ravenna by Antonius Perusinus. The author is Omnibonus Leonicenus, about whom see Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii aevi*.

There follows Leonardo Bruni of Arezzo’s work *On Warfare*, addressed to Rinaldo Albizzi of Florence:

> I confess, most illustrious man, etc.

### 39. Codex 5134

Vatican, paper, of the fifteenth century. Materials prepared for acquiring fluency in speaking and writing Latin.

Page 64, without any title:

> The distinction between *polliceri* and *promittere* is that we promise when asked, but offer voluntarily.

The work proceeds as in Book I of Breulius, but later varies. It ends:

> Between *atramentale* and *atramentarium*: an *atramentale* is a vessel; an *atramentarius* is a man who sells ink.

Immediately follows:

> Here begin the alphabetical *Differences of Marcus Tullius Cicero*: the distinction between *abundare* and *superfluere* is that a wave abounds, while every liquid overflows.

It ends:

> The distinction between *vesper*, *vespera*, *vespere*, and *vesperum* is that *vesper* and *vespere* are nouns of the third declension; *vespera* is feminine and of the first declension; *vesperum* is neuter and likewise of the second declension.

These are the differences found under Isidore’s name in another codex.

[Col. 0811A] ### 40.

A work without a title follows, *On the Proper Meaning of Words*:

> *Sandapila* is the place where the bodies of low-born people are buried, etc.

It ends:

> *Sordiscum*: raw hide.

The work differs from Fulgentius Placidus’s little book *On Ancient Speech*.

### 41.

There follow hexameter verses by Francesco Fiani, on despising wealth and loving poverty:

> Let whoever wishes ascend happily to the heights.

Then verses of Lactantius on the Phoenix:

> There is a place, etc.

Sappho’s elegy to Phaon. Book XIII of the *Aeneid*, with the argument:

> When Turnus poured out his life under the final battle of Mars.

The beginning of the book:

> When Turnus, defeated in the final battle, poured out his life.

[Col. 0811B] ### 42. Codex 5203

Vatican, papyrus, in quarto, of the fourteenth or following century. A glossary, or vocabulary arranged alphabetically, with quotations from authors supplied for most words.

It begins:

> To abjure is to deny under oath a thing entrusted.

It ends:

> They call houses *zephas*, etc.

Page 119, without a title: “The distinction between *polliceri* and *promittere*, etc.” It ends: “The distinction between *atramentale*, etc.,” as in Vatican Codex 5134, mentioned shortly before.

### 43.

On the verso of page 131, without a title: alphabetical *Differences*:

> The distinction between *abundare* and *superfluere*, etc.

It ends:

> The distinction between *vesper*, etc., as in the cited Vatican Codex 5134.

Other differences of words follow, without alphabetical order and in mutilated form.

### 44.

Page 164, rubric:

> Apuleius, *On the Mark of Aspiration*: Every mark of aspiration, etc.

A work on diphthongs follows without a title:

> The diphthongs which the ancients used, etc.

Some rules of prosody without an author’s name. On the verso of page 188, the *Art of Meter* begins:

> Having previously laid out the rules of prose composition and rhythm, in this book we shall explain the principles of meters.

Finally, an epigram beginning:

> Receive me, and look upon me.

## CHAPTER XCVIII

Ten other codices of the old Vatican library are described. Some works against the Jews. Ancient penitentials. Several very ancient codices formerly belonging to the monastery of Bobbio. A collection of ancient chronicles of Spain, by Luca of Tuy as author or compiler.

### 1. Codex 5420

Vatican, parchment, small in folio, approximately of the fourteenth century, in a clear script, from the books of Francesco Peña, dean of the Rota.

Rubric:

> These are some extremely devout things concerning the Passion of our Lord, Master Jesus Christ, taken from the Hebrew Bible, which are not written in our Latin Bible. The following little work was composed by a worthy doctor named Isaac, who was first a Jew and afterwards became a most Christian man. First begins the author’s prologue: “Considering that I, Isaac, am Hebrew by carnal descent and Christian by spiritual regeneration, etc.”

The work is filled with absurdities and fables and, in my opinion, is pseudonymous. On page 7 one reads:

> And all the things mentioned above are written in the Hebrew Bible, according to that master Isaac, and published to the people.

Revelations of a certain Saint Nudo are sometimes cited:

> Saint Nudo says, etc.

On the verso of page 3:

> As that master Isaac preached in the presence of the friars of Saint Francis.

### 2.

Page 14, rubric:

> Saint Isidore, doctor and bishop, refutes the Jews. To his most beloved sister F. [Florentina], Isidore the bishop sends greetings: Some things were foretold at different times among the books of the Old Testament, etc.

It ends:

> Let them all come into the valley of Jehoshaphat, where I shall judge them. Amen. Thanks be to God.

This is a compendium of Book I *Against the Jews*, in old Italian, which has much in common with Spanish.

There follows the *Disputation of Jerome of the Holy Faith against the Jews*, in the year of Christ 1412, the eighteenth year of the pontificate of Benedict XIII, the antipope, in Italian. It begins:

> These are the arguments presented in the presence of the most holy Father, etc.

There is also his treatise against the master of the Talmud:

> This, then, is the matter, etc.

It discusses at length the frauds and injuries committed by the Jews against Christians.

### 3. Codex 5751

Vatican, parchment, small in folio, damaged and mutilated. The inventory records that this codex contains the genuine Roman Penitential edited by Morinus. It bears the inscription: “Anastasius of the papal library.”

At the beginning is the Synod of Agde:

> In the name of God, and with the permission of our Lord, etc.

Page 2, at the beginning:

> The book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio,

in an old script, like that of the Turin Sedulius, about which I spoke in chapter 3 of the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*.

On the verso of page 3 are subscriptions:

> I, … in the name of Christ, etc., have subscribed … in the twenty-second year of the reign of our lord King Alaric.

It ends. A penitential follows:

> Whenever Christians approach penance, etc., not because luxury is in wine, but because it is in drunkenness. The prologue ends. If someone should perhaps be unable to fast, etc.

Page 8:

> Here begins the Synod of Arles: Those who gathered for the dedication of the basilica of Saint Mary … determine that this is to be observed among them.

### 4.

Page 9, rubric:

> Here begins a work on the usefulness of penance and on how one should believe in the remission of sins through penance: Apart from the gift of baptism, etc.

It ends:

> to judge the censure of the Canons.

This work is discussed again under number 7.

### 5.

On the verso of page 11:

> In the name of Christ begins the work on the penance of John Chrysostom: With a prudent mind and profound reflection they ought to understand, etc.

It ends:

> and you will find rest unto eternal life. Amen.

[Col. 0812D] ### 6.

On the verso of page 14:

> Here begins the work on the eight capital vices: There are eight principal vices that afflict the human race.

It ends:

> it must be understood.

Page 15:

> How Christians ought to give counsel: We make known to your charity that many, etc.

It ends:

> while entreating the Lord.

Page 16:

> Here begins the work on sacrifices and the remission of brothers: But perhaps the hearers of the Church will say, etc.

It ends:

> he must restrain himself from what is permitted.

### 7.

Page 18:

> An excerpt on the usefulness of penance by Bishop Alitparius [or Alitgarius]: Although original sins, etc., remission is promised in heaven.

A fragment follows that has already been included in the work on page 9, *On the Usefulness of Penance*, etc.

On the verso of page 19, rubric:

> Here begins the little book on the eight principal vices and their remedies, which we have excerpted from the books of Gregory, Augustine, and also Prosper: From the joys of paradise.

Book II, *On Virtues*. It ends:

> Now, how each vice must be cleansed by priestly judgment is briefly to be inserted in the little book of the work that follows.

Rubric: “The second book ends.”

This chapter is from a letter of Saint Gregory the pope to Secundinus the Recluse or Inclosed One:

> Most beloved, etc. The letter of your affection, etc., came to redeem …

### 8.

Rubric in the same script:

> Here begins Isidore’s letter to Mason, the bishop: To the holy and in merits blessed Mason, bishop, Isidore the bishop sends greetings in the Lord: When your religious servant, the man Nicetius, came to us, [he brought] a letter, etc.

It ends:

> either an older or a more authoritative authority exists. The letter ends.

These two letters of Gregory and Isidore [Col. 0813B] appear to constitute the third book of the work *On Vices and Virtues*. The script is a clear, small Gallican hand, approximately of the tenth century.

A rubric in a similar script follows:

> In the name of Our Lord Jesus Christ begins an excerpt from the Canons, consisting only of sentences [perhaps “of sententiae”], from the book of Martin, bishop of Braga in Galicia, on various councils.

It is found in collections of councils. Excerpts from the Canons of several councils follow, including the Council of Barcelona. Also from a letter of Pope Clement:

> Let a bishop be irreproachable.

There are also excerpts from Siricius, Innocent, Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius.

### 9.

On the verso of page 41, rubric:

> Excerpts of Theodore on the Canons: At the ordination of a bishop, he himself must sing Mass.

This is called Theodore’s Penitential. The rubric sometimes reads: “Also, the foregoing: the judgment of Theodore, archbishop.” [Col. 0813C] Also: “The foregoing: the judgment of Commeom.”

It ends:

> Let him carry the Gospel while reading it upon his shoulders.

There follows Pope Clement’s letter on the Sacraments of the Lord’s body:

> Since, just as from Peter …

Also, an order for administering penance:

> First you ask him …

The Roman Synod of Pope Boniface II follows:

> After the consulship of Lampadius, etc.

On the verso of page 62, a Sapphic ode to Bishop Adelard:

> Lord, protector of the stars and ruler of heaven, etc.

Perhaps it is by Alcuin.

### 10.

On the verso of page 71, in an old script but by another hand, an elegy:

> The lament of a certain R. … [perhaps a religious]; the letters have almost entirely faded.

It begins:

> Night and day I groan, because I am a pilgrim and needy [perhaps “sick”];
>
> Worn down by fevers, night and day I groan.

Distichs 3 and 4:

> Great Columba, pray to the Lord that I may not be rejected by him.
>
> Pray, great Columba, that I may be restored to himself.
>
> Saint Zeno, do not despise your wretched servant, I beg you.
>
> Restore your servant to Columbanus, Saint Zeno.

Some decretal letters of the Roman pontiffs and letters of emperors are interspersed in this codex.

### 11. Codex 5763

Vatican, parchment, in folio, in Lombard script, very similar to that observed in ancient papyri. At the beginning: “The book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio,” as in the Turin Sedulius.

A later title reads: “Six books of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.” Another reads: “Treatise of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.”

At the bottom of the page, in a Gallican script of approximately the eleventh century:

> Boniprandus offered this book with a willing mind
>
> To the distinguished Father Columbanus; therefore, whoever reads it,
>
> Say: “Grant forgiveness, God, and repay his merit.”

Letters of Isidore and Braulio:

1. “With every desire.”
2. “O pious one,” etc.

In the title: *Christique electo* (“and chosen for Christ”); Bignaeus reads *Christoque electo* (“and chosen for Christ”). There: “In which Sinthaurius”; Bignaeus reads: “in which Sintharius.”

3. “Because you are safe and sound.”
4. “It is usually filled again.”
5. “Of your holiness.”

There:

> And although it is uncorrected because of ill health, nevertheless I had lately intended to offer it to you for correction, if I had reached …

It ends:

> may the crimes be forgiven.

The letter of Isidore to Bishop Braulio ends.

Rubric:

> Here begin the books of Isidore,

in a later script above:

> Of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, or to his own lord and son Sesibutus: Behold, as I promised you, I have sent you the work on the Origin of certain things, from, etc.,

as in Bignaeus.

Rubric:

> These are the chapters of the first book.

There are twenty-four. The last is “On History.”

### 12.

On Military Terms, chapter 23, or alternatively 24:

> The letter T was used as a sign, etc. But when they wished to signify ignorance, they used the letter lambda.

The book ends:

> They are against nature.

The first book of the *Etymologies* ends. The chapters of the second book begin. Twenty-two chapters are numbered. It ends:

> It has nothing third.

The second book ends. The third book begins. A preface on the four disciplines that follow: “On Mathematics. Mathematics is called so in Latin, etc.” There are eleven chapters.

The fourth book, *On Music*, contains ten chapters. There are no musical notes.

Book V, *On Astronomy*, contains forty-four chapters. It ends:

> may lead him away and raise him to contemplation above.

Breulius reads “may lead away” and “may place.” Book V, *On Laws*, contains twenty-eight chapters. [Col. 0814C] It ends:

> it has been permitted,

as in chapter 27 of Book V of Breulius.

Rubric: “The fifth book ends. The sixth book begins. On Medicine, etc.” It contains thirteen chapters and ends: “the body may be treated.” The book on medicine, Book VI, ends.

Book VII, *On Times*, begins. The table contains twelve chapters, the last being “On the distinction of times”; but the codex is incomplete, with leaves torn away beginning at chapter 2 of this book.

The codex is a palimpsest. The first text was written in large square Roman script, in a single line or column. A few words can be understood, such as in chapter 38, *On Prose*, on the verso:

> She sent messengers to the king.

At the end of Book I:

> and the Lord delivered him into the hands …

Later:

> and he encounters [or “encamped”] … And they said to him … But he was unwilling to comply.

It appears to be something from sacred Scripture. The words of the first text are connected with one another.

### 13. Codex 5764

Vatican, parchment, in octavo, in Lombard script. On the first page an old hand has written:

> This book belongs to Saint Columbanus.

Later:

> The following are contained in this volume: three books of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, namely the eighth, ninth, and tenth.

Then, in an older script, perhaps of the ninth century:

> Here begin the chapters of the eighth book of Isidore’s *Etymologies*.

After the table of chapters, in an old script like that of the Turin Sedulius:

> The book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio.

The table contains fifty-six chapters. The first fifteen chapters, however, comprise not Book VIII but Book VI: “On the New and Old Testament,” etc., with some interpolations, such as chapter 2, on History [Col. 0815A], writers, and the names of the sacred books.

It begins:

> History is a narrative of an event, through which things done in the past are recognized. It is called *historia* in Greek, ΔΙϹΑΜωΗ ΙϹΤωΡΙΝ, that is, “to hear” or “to know.” Histories are therefore called *monumenta*, because they preserve the memory of things done. According to the Hebrews, these are the authors of the Old Testament, etc.

Chapter 7, at the end: “formerly of the letters”; Breulius reads: “formerly of the conversations of the letters.”

Chapter 11:

> Poems, which we know as fires of the air.

Chapter 14:

> whose deeds, begun in this body, are contained and preserved.

There:

> Hence also *concilium* and *consilium*, with the *c* passing into the letter *s*.

Chapter 15 of the codex ends:

> Amen signifies … resound in heaven,

which belongs to chapter 19 of Breulius.

### 14.

In the same codex chapter 16 follows: Cassiodorus, *On the Titles of the Psalms*:

> In the First Book of Chronicles, etc.

The discussion of the Psalms continues through chapter 27, apparently taken from Cassiodorus. Chapter 26 concerns Psalm 118.

> This Psalm is arranged by the letters of the Hebrew alphabet, etc.

### 15.

Chapter 27 follows:

> Also, on ecclesiastical offices: “Hosanna,” in the meaning of another language, cannot be transferred completely, etc.,

as in chapter 19 of Breulius.

There:

> Sacrifice is so called as though it were “made sacred,” because by mystical prayer, etc., and by the blood of Christ,

as in Breulius.

Also:

> The sacraments are baptism, the body and blood of the Lord, and for that reason they are called sacraments, etc.

Breulius reads: “baptism and chrism, the body and blood.”

Chapter 28 follows, on the Trinity:

> Trinity is so called because it is one whole composed from certain three things, etc.

This is chapter 4 of Book VII of Breulius, continuing through:

> I said: You are gods.

### 16.

Chapter 29, on angels, is chapter 5 of Book VII in Breulius. In it the passage “Uriel … it was commanded” is omitted. [Col. 0815C] See Codex 5813.

Chapter 36, on man:

> Man is so called because he was made from *humus*, earth.

These excerpts are taken from chapter 1 of Book XI in Breulius.

Chapter 31, on the apostles:

> *Apostoli* means “those who have been sent.”

This is excerpted from chapter 9 of Book VII. Other chapters that follow are similarly excerpted from the same Book VII.

### 17.

Chapter 37, “On the Church and Synagogue”:

> *Ecclesia* is a Greek word, etc.

This is taken from Book VIII, chapter 1. Other chapters likewise come from the same book.

Chapter 40 is an exposition of the Creed from Saint Augustine, Homily 23 on John.

### 18.

Chapter 41 contains the rubric:

> On the catechumens of Isidore in the Book of Ecclesiastical Offices.

Other chapters are likewise taken from various Fathers. Chapter 43, on pomp, is from Jerome and Isidore. In chapters 16, 47, and 66, the last chapter, “On the Imposition of the Bishop’s Hand,” Isidore is cited.

On page 71 there follows, without a title, a table of eighty-four chapters: “On Discipline and Art,” etc. The first six chapters are excerpted from Books I and II of the *Etymologies*. The next six chapters are excerpted from Books III, IV, and V of the *Etymologies*, with some explicitly attributed to Bede. The compendium of the *Etymologies* proceeds more or less in this manner, but without preserving the order of the books.

Chapter 83, on Triumphs:

> Every kingdom of this world is sought through wars and obtained through victories. Victory is so called because it is acquired through force, that is, through virtue, etc.

### 19.

The final chapter is 84, a description of the provinces of Italy:

> The first province of Italy, therefore, is Venetia, etc.

Other excerpts from Isidore follow, on man and his parts, on the ages of life, etc. Others, perhaps from different authors, concern vices and virtues.

Page 191: “On the seven rules of the Law,” attributed to Isidore:

> There are seven among the other rules, etc.

This is taken from Book I, chapter 19 of the *Sentences*.

### 20. Codex 5765

Vatican, parchment, small in folio, in square Roman script. Sometimes the title of a chapter is written in green as a rubric. At times two small strokes are attached to the margin, namely when words of other authors are being copied, as is done today. There are periods, commas, and colons. The spelling *obaedientia* is used.

The age of the codex may be assigned to the eighth or ninth century. At the beginning, as in other codices already described, there is this note:

> The book of Saint Columbanus of Bobbio.

Rubric:

> Here begins the second book of Saint Isidore,

in a later script:

> On ecclesiastical ministers: Since we pursue in order the causes of the origin of the offices that are celebrated in common by the Church [*caelebrantur*, so written] … of those who devote ministries of religion to divine worship.

The prologue of Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices* differs somewhat from the printed editions. A table of the twenty-six chapters of the same Book II follows; the last is “On the Imposition of Hands or Confirmation.” But the codex breaks off at chapter 19, at the words:

> while even pagan women serve their husbands according to the common law of nature.

Therefore: “the law of nature.”

### 21. Codex 5813 Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in octavo, approximately of the thirteenth century. The *Etymologies* are mutilated at the end; the last chapter is “On vessels for storage,” Book XX. Perhaps a folio bearing the title and table of contents is missing at the beginning. The first rubric is:

> Here begins Book I, On Discipline and Art: “Discipline” derives from *discere* [to learn], etc.

Some passages are abbreviated, [Col. 0816C] others enlarged and interpolated: Book IV is “On Music,” whereas in Breul it is “On Medicine.” In the same Book IV is “On Astronomy.” Book V is “On Laws.” Book VI is “On Medicine.” Book VII is “On the word *chronica*,” etc. There is a brief chronicle there:

> In the fourth year of the most religious prince Sisevotus [Sisebutus], 293 Jews in Spain become Christians. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone.

Book VII ends; Book VIII begins, “On the New and Old Testament,” etc., corresponding to Book VI in Breul. In the final chapter there: “A sacrifice is called,” etc.; as in Breul, “it becomes a sacrament.” The Greeks call a sacrament *eucharistia*, which is what we call the body and blood of Christ. The sacraments are baptism, the body and blood of the Lord, and for that reason they are called sacraments, etc. Other material is omitted.

### 22. Book IX

Book IX, “On God”; there, chapter 5, “On angels” [Col. 0816D]:

> Uriel is interpreted as “fire of God,” just as we read that fire appeared in the bush. Thrones, etc.

Book IX proceeds as far as chapter 5 of Book VII in Breul. Book X begins, “On the philosophers of the nations.” Philosophers are so called from a Greek designation. It contains everything that follows in Breul, including Book X, or the vocabulary, with its preface. There:

> *Aerus*: a brave and wise man. *Aegistus* is so called because he is nourished by the head. For *ega* in Greek means “head.” *Auctor*, etc.

Book XI is “On man,” etc. The remaining books proceed in the same order as in Breul. An example of an interpolation in Book XVIII, chapter 58 [Col. 0817A]:

> Not by crime but by madness. Martial. A certain young man named Carpophorus, in the time of Titus, killed twenty bears that had been released against him simultaneously in the arena. Likewise he fought at the same time against a lion, a leopard, a tiger, and a boar. For these spectacles, etc.

### 23. Codex 5992 Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in small folio, of the fifteenth century. At the beginning it is ascribed to the convent of the Holy Apostles in Rome. It contains certain notes, or biblical miscellanies, in a scholastic hand, with other material added in a different hand. On page 166: Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*. Its first title was: “A Certain Theology.” The beginning has been erased, and not long after the beginning of the second book the work breaks off. In another hand follows: “The Understanding of the Sentences in Verse,” that is, the *Sentences* of Peter Lombard bound into verse. The manuscript was of no use to me.

### 24. Codex 6265 Vaticanus

A paper manuscript in small quarto, of the fifteenth century: notes, or miscellanies, from letters and speeches.

Leonardo Aretino’s *Book Against Hypocrites*. [Col. 0817B]

> Elegy on the Death of Leonardo Aretino: “Now, holy Muses…”

Epitaph:

> “This tomb covers Leonardo Aretino,” etc.
