A poem beneath Leonardo Aretino’s portrait:

> “Here, Leonardo, for you,” etc.

An anonymous work *On Illustrious Men*. It begins:

> “Those men who excelled throughout Italy in my time,” etc.

Leonardo Aretino’s speech of Heliogabalus to prostitutes. At the end:

> “Leonardo Aretino dictated this while playing and laughing, for the refreshment of his wit. Hence he asks older men not to read it, and more urbane men not to offer thanks to God.”

Poggio, *On the Change of Fortune*, etc.

An epitaph, or verses, in a certain church near Santo Spirito in Rome:

> “You who proceed with a tranquil mind, pause for a moment,” etc.

Others in Santa Maria Maggiore in Rome, beneath an image of Christ crucified near the high altar [Col. 0817C]:

> “To ungrateful Venus I promised gifts as a suppliant,” etc.

Others in the palace of the Priors in Florence.

A speech of the archbishop of Crete delivered before Martin V on 6 December 1418.

### 25. Page 204

> “Cicero to his Victurius, greetings. I have collected these things, etc.; let us begin alphabetically. *Abditum*, hidden, covered, concealed, etc.”

It ends:

> “A great, full, large, rough, clear, melodious, bright, sweet, pleasant, delightful, agreeable, abundant, affable voice. To avoid, turn aside from, flee. Here ends what was found concerning Cicero’s synonyms by Sercolutius.”

The manuscript appears to have been written at Ancona around 1460. More about a work of this kind of *Synonyms* is found in chapter 56.

### 26. Codex 6878 Vaticanus

A manuscript in octavo, partly paper, [Col. 0817D] partly parchment, and partly cotton paper. It contains an anonymous book, elsewhere ascribed to Pliny, *On Illustrious Men*: “Procas, king of the Albans.”

On the verso of page 23 is Isidore’s treatise *On Astronomy*. It begins:

> “The moon is the first of the planets, the smallest of the stars.”

This treatise is found inserted into Honorius of Autun’s *Image of the World*, as I said in chapter 86, whether it truly belongs to Honorius or was taken from Isidore. But the script of this little work in this manuscript is so entangled that it can scarcely be read.

### 27.

There follow several parchment folios in an ancient hand, perhaps of the eleventh century. Jerome’s chapter on Joseph in the book *On Illustrious Men*. There he says of Christ in Book XIX, chapter 1:

> “For he was an accomplisher of wondrous works,” etc.

### 28.

In the same place, Pilate’s letter to Tiberius concerning Christ.

There also is Ignatius’s letter to John:

> “We grieve over your delay.” [Col. 0818A]

Another of the same writer to the same recipient:

> “If it is permitted me…”

Another of that same Ignatius to Mary, the bearer of Christ:

> “Me, a neophyte…”

Another:

> “To Ignatius, the beloved disciple, the humble handmaid of Christ: concerning Jesus, what was [said] by John,” etc.

The Letter of Lentulus:

> “He appeared in our times,” etc., concerning Christ.

On these matters, see Fabricius, *Codex Apocryphus of the New Testament*.

There follow paper folios: Peter Paul Vergerius the Elder’s book:

> “Francis, your elder grandfather,” etc.

### 29. Page 70

Parchment folios, like those described above. An epigram on Verona in the form of personification:

> “Now, kindly mother, you may scatter festive applause for yourself.”

That is, after the recovery of liberty. The verses are hexameters.

In the same place, a poem of Antonio Panormita, the Sicilian poet, to Cyriacus of Ancona [Col. 0818B]:

> “Cyriacus, eloquent in high style,” etc.

His epitaph for Cyriacus’s mother:

> “The splendor of Ancona lies in this tomb, Masiella,  
> The one parent of antiquity and of Cyriacus.”

These are written in a different hand.

There follow paper folios. Claudian, *On the Baths of the Aponus district*.

A letter of King Theodoric to Aloysius the architect:

> “If the wonders of ancient men, once heard, etc. … At Ravenna, on the third day before the Kalends of June, Aurelius Cassiodorus, superintendent of the palace, wrote this.”

These folios appear to be made of silk paper. Some material on herbs follows.

Peter Paul Vergerius’s comedy:

> “While this modest poet was composing this play for me,” etc.

The comedy concerns the education of young men.

### 30. Codex 7004 Vaticanus

A paper manuscript. An autograph letter of Francesco Penia—so he calls himself—or Pegna, to Cardinal Baronius, 26 March 1597, [Col. 0818C] in which he proves that this manuscript really contains the history written by Lucas of Tuy.

Penia had thought that the history of Tuy was a work of Julian Pomerius—he means Julian of Toledo, incorrectly called Pomerius—but he withdraws this opinion.

There follows an autograph letter of Alfonso de Spinosa, archdeacon of Tineo and canon of Oviedo, written at Madrid on 25 January 1597. Spinosa states that, because of the persecutions of the bishop of Oviedo, he was absent from Oviedo. He says that in the Church of Oviedo there remained only the division of the dioceses of Ithacius; that the histories of Sampirus, Sebastianus, and Pelagius had once existed in that church; but that they were thought to have been taken by Diego de Muros, bishop of Oviedo, to the college at Salamanca, which he founded.

A letter of the schoolmaster Salazar follows, dated 15 July 1595, by which he sent the history of Tuy, transcribed from an ancient manuscript [Col. 0818D]. In Penia’s letter he is called Doctor Gascha de Salazar, head of the school at Salamanca.

### 31.

Next, without a title, comes the *Chronicle of Tuy*:

> “The blessedness of temporal power,” etc.

After the prologue:

> “A brief annotation of the times,” etc.

The Chronicle of Isidore and the history of the Goths, which end with Sisenand, preserved the hidden knowledge of future events.

Without a title there follows Ildefonsus’s continuation:

> “Since the illustrious doctor Isidore…”

The continuation ends:

> “Under the emperor Constantine; thus far the blessed Ildefonsus, primate of the Spains,” etc.

### 32.

Immediately: “Era 704, after Receswinth,” etc.

The division of the bishoprics; the history of Wamba and Paul; the other Gothic kings; the incursion of the Moors. The kings of Spain down to [Col. 0819A] Saint Ferdinand.

It ends:

> “Alhamge, Montor, and certain other fortresses.”

### 33.

There is no division into books. Isidore’s Chronicle ends with Scintilla, or Suinthila:

> “The consummation of the age is…”

Then, without a title:

> “Although prudence has made men of virtue,” etc.

This is Luke’s prologue, in which he says:

> “We set forth the third book of Isidore, doctor of the Spains, in this work.”

Perhaps he numbers the sixth age as the second book.

After Luke’s prologue:

> “To Antoninus, son of Bonienfisuandus, king of the Goths, Isidore: concerning the origin,” etc.

After the prologue, Era 447: the Alans, Sueves, and Vandals. This is the *History of the Vandals*. It ends:

> “To the destruction of Gelimer.”

There follows, Era 446, under Ermeric, king of the Sueves: the *History of the Sueves*. It ends:

> “It is written that they remained for 177 years.”

There is appended:

> “The most ancient [Col. 0819B] origin of the Goths,” etc.

It ends, as I said, with Sisenand. These materials ought to be compared with the printed editions.

### 34.

After all of Luke’s Chronicles and the final words, “other fortresses,” there follows, without a title:

> “The Son of God, Jesus Christ, under Augustus,” etc.

A chronology of the Roman pontiffs down to Fabianus in the year of the Lord 238.

There follows:

> “Charles, a Roman by nation, began in the year of the Lord 252. He sat for three years and ten months,” etc.

Read “Cornelius,” who nevertheless held office for one year.

A narrative of Turpin is added, describing how Charlemagne liberated Spain and Galicia from the power of the Saracens, etc.

> “Here ends the Chronicle of the blessed Turpin, archbishop.”

The work is fictitious. French historians exaggerate Charlemagne’s deeds in Spain; the Spaniards disparage them.

# CHAPTER XCIX

## The library of Christina, queen of the Swedes, transferred to the Vatican; many manuscripts containing works of Isidore. Some of these manuscripts formerly belonged to the library of Fleury. Sixteen such Regio-Vatican manuscripts are listed. Several copies of the *Etymologies*. A specimen of the Isidorian glossary. What is Isidore’s book *Spermologon*?

[Col. 0819C]

### 1.

Among the famous libraries that, after various vicissitudes, eventually migrated to the Vatican, a special place is claimed by the library of Christina Alexandra, queen of the Swedes, distinguished less by the number of its books than by their selection. Nevertheless, it also abounds in a considerable number of manuscript codices, especially if we include those that were first brought to the Ottobonian Library and afterward came to the Vatican together with the whole Ottobonian Library. But there will be another occasion to speak of these Ottobonian manuscripts.

For now I will merely point out that Alexander VIII Ottoboni selected 1,900 manuscript codices from those Christina had gathered from everywhere, adding a few from his own household library, and assigned them to the Vatican in 1690, distinguishing them by the name “Alexandrine” and by a separate hall. This is the library also commonly called the Regio-Vatican Library, or the Library of the Queen of the Swedes.

When Queen Christina’s library was being adorned with so many precious monuments, various other resources were collected from all sides, including a large part of the books of the famous monastery of Fleury, rescued from fire and ruins, together with other books purchased by the queen from Alexander Petau.

[Col. 0819D]

### 2.

The monastery of Fleury was once renowned for its learned men and its abundance of books. John a Bosco Coelestinus, volume II, or part III, of the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, page 302, in a note on the *Life of Saint Abbo* by Aimoin of Fleury, reports the following:

> “The schools once maintained in the monastery of Fleury were so distinguished and celebrated that the number of students in them was reckoned at more than five thousand. In gratitude for the honor of their teaching office, they offered their teachers two manuscript volumes each.”

He adds that so abundant a library was plundered, scattered, and torn apart by the Calvinists in 1561–1562.

The same John a Bosco, on page 409, records a statute of the abbot of Fleury concerning the repair of old books and especially the acquisition of new choir books:

> “Seeing that the codices of our library, because of excessive age, are decayed and corrupted by the woodworm and the moth,” etc.

[Col. 0820B]

### 3.

This remarkable library was indeed scattered by the Calvinists; nevertheless, a large part of it was later rescued and collected again, after many years and various dangers, and, through a particular act of divine providence, brought into the Vatican.

The authors of *Gallia Christiana*, volume VIII, column 1540, report the following about the library of Fleury:

> “Yet it was not entirely scattered; for, having been collected somehow through the efforts of Peter Daniel, it passed into the Vatican.”

More explicitly, in column 1566, where they discuss the Calvinists and Odet de Coligny, the former cardinal and former abbot of Fleury, they assert that silver and gold codices of the Gospels and Epistles were plundered, etc.:

> “For, having plundered almost all the manuscripts, Peter Daniel, who was conducting business in the market at Orléans, and the magistrate of Fleury bought from them for a very small price whatever they had not torn apart; from there the material passed into the possession of Petau and Bongars, then of the Elector Palatine and Christina, queen of the Swedes, and finally into the Vatican.”

Just as the Petavian Library was united with Queen Christina’s library, so the Bongarsian Library was united with the Palatine Library. The latter, after Heidelberg was captured, was given as a gift to the Vatican.

Concerning this same library of Fleury, plundered by the Huguenots, and its many books, transferred to the Vatican by various turns of fortune, see Mabillon, in the preface to the *Gallican Liturgy*, section 12; Lesleus, in the preface to the *Mozarabic Missal*, section 16, page 77; and Claudius Estiennot’s letter to Mabillon, which is entirely devoted to this subject, among Mabillon’s posthumous works, volume I, page 461.

[Col. 0820D]

### 4.

The monks of Fleury could easily have obtained books from Spain. For, in the same volume VIII of *Gallia Christiana*, column 1541, the following is related about Mummo, or Mummolenus, abbot of Fleury in the middle of the seventh century:

> “While traveling to Spain to fulfill a vow, he is said to have died at Bordeaux in the monastery of the Holy Cross. Perhaps he had gone to that region to organize the nearby monastery of Régula, which, before the time of the Normans, had been subject to Fleury, as the document concerning its restoration shows.”

The monastery of Régula was in Gascony; it is mentioned in the *Life of Saint Abbo*.

But there is no time to dwell longer on these matters. Let us instead list the Regio-Vatican codices themselves.

### 5. Codex 61 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in octavo, formerly numbered 1890.

The first work is mutilated at the beginning. It concerns [Col. 0821A] the mystical interpretation of Noah’s ark; this is part of the second book, which ends:

> “Let us desire one thing, our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The third book begins:

> “In the first station, therefore, there is knowledge.”

There is much more about the book and the tree of life, etc. It ends:

> “For, to tell the truth, in this treatise we find more things that ought to be written than things we shall write [perhaps: ‘than things we have written’]. For I do not blush to confess my ignorance even in this matter. Explicit.”

A fairly long poem follows:

> “Angel, who are my guardian through heavenly devotion,  
> Keep, protect, and guide me, entrusted to you,” etc.

It ends:

> “And let all the people add: ‘Let it be so,’ and ‘Amen.’”

There follows:

> “In the deeds of the fathers of old I read something amusing, [Col. 0821B]  
> Yet useful as an example, which I tell you in verse:  
> Abbot John, small in stature but not in virtues,” etc.

It ends:

> “Since he could not be an angel, he learned to be a good man.”

I have seen this little work published, unless I am mistaken, by Theophilus Raynaudus. The script appears to belong to the eleventh or twelfth century.

### 6.

The following rubric comes next:

> “Here begins the book of Isidore, bishop, On God the Father.”

The script appears different, and perhaps belongs to the thirteenth century. This is Book VII of the *Etymologies*. It begins:

> “The most blessed Jerome,” etc.

It continues to the end of chapter 4, ending with “not by nature.”

Immediately there is the rubric:

> “On nature.”

It begins:

> “Nature is so called from the fact that,” etc.

This is chapter 1 of Book XI, continuing in part [Col. 0821C] to the end of chapter 1.

Another rubric:

> “On the world: The world is heaven,” etc.

This is chapter 1 of Book XIII, continuing to the end of chapter 18 of that book.

Then the rubric:

> “On the earth: The earth is in the middle,” etc.

This is chapter 1 of Book XIV, together with certain other chapters.

There follows “On cities,” chapter 1 of Book XV, and the whole of that book.

Likewise, “On dust and the globes of the earth,” which is Book XVI, to the end.

Then follow Books XVII, XVIII, XIX, and XX.

It ends:

> “Let it be dried by the heat of fire.”

### 7.

Immediately there is a rubric:

> “Here begins an exposition of ancient expressions, with testimonies of Fabius Planciades Fulgentius, called Vergilius.””

It begins:

> “Lest it be thought that, through disobedience, I had curtailed anything of your commands, most serene lord,” etc.

“What is a *sandapila*?” etc.

It ends:

> “Your words are so soothing.”

> “Here end the ancient expressions with their testimonies.”

The work of Fulgentius is entitled *On Ancient Speech*. [Col. 0821D]

A rubric follows:

> “Augustine, On the Exposition of the Alphabet.”

It begins:

> “From an appropriate sound we recall the spirit through the opening of the mouth.”

Next follows an imperfect Book XII of the *Etymologies*, beginning with the words “Spanish and Numidian,” near the end of chapter 1, and continuing to chapter 6, “On fish,” which is incomplete.

Nothing else in this manuscript is worthy of notice.

### 8. Codex 84 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in duodecimo, approximately of the eleventh century.

The rubric is:

> “Here begins Book V of Isidore’s *Etymologies*: Moses,” etc.

It continues to the end of chapter 27 of Book V:

> “It has been granted by nature.”

But certain passages have been abridged, as also those that follow.

Rubric:

> “From Book IX of Isidore’s *Etymologies*: Citizens are called,” etc.

This begins with chapter 4 and ends with “brothers and sisters,” chapter 6.

Several letters [Col. 0822A] without a title follow:

> “It is right that those who share in prosperity should share in adversity.”

Then there are other miscellanies.

### 9. Codex 112 Regio-Vaticanus

A folio manuscript of the eleventh century.

At the beginning is written:

> “Alexander Petau, son of Paul, senator of Paris.”

A distich is also added in a recent hand:

> “Care, labor, merit, honors gained in return for service—  
> Go far away; trouble other souls.”

This comes from Seneca’s epitaph, which appears in other manuscripts, as in Codex 112, item 11, where it will be reported.

The title is “Isidore,” and the rubric is:

> “Here begin little findings on feet, necessary for us: There are twenty-eight feet.”

It begins:

> “The composition of feet,” etc.

It ends:

> “They are contained in words of equal sound.”

This little work differs from chapter 17 of Book I of the *Etymologies*, “On feet,” although much is shared by both.

[Col. 0822B]

### 10.

There follows, without a title:

> “To my lord … with every desire,” etc.

Letter 1 to Braulio.

Then:

2. Braulio’s letter to Isidore:

> “To my lord … O pious lord and most distinguished of men, the inquiry is late,” etc.

3. Isidore to Braulio:

> “Because I know you to be safe and well.”

4. Braulio to Isidore:

> “Joy is accustomed to be filled,” etc.

5. Isidore to Braulio:

> “The letter of your holiness found me in the city of Toledo.”

6. The same writer to the same recipient:

> “Here you have it, just as I promised.”

The titles of twenty-three books are attached, although in the text there are twenty. A brief preface to Sisebut follows:

> “Here you have it,” etc.

It is written in the style of the ancients, as in the letter to Braulio.

Then follow the titles of the first book, etc., through the end of Book XX. Isidore’s books of the *Etymologies* end here.

Another index of twenty books is added.

At the end [Col. 0822C], in a different hand:

> “This book was written in the year 1012 from the Passion of Christ.”

The script is large; the lines are straight and formed with considerable skill. Diphthongs are sometimes separated and sometimes joined. There are frequent points, not beneath the letters but between them in the middle. The letters are clear and distinct, with few ligatures.

### 11. Codex 119 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment folio manuscript [Col. 0822D] of the thirteenth century.

Hugh of Saint-Laurent’s *Book on the Cloister of the Soul*. This is Hugh of Fouilloy, prior of Saint-Laurent in the diocese of Amiens, who also wrote *On the Twelve Abuses of the Cloister*. The *Book on the Cloister of the Soul* was printed among the works of Hugh of Saint-Victor, to whom it is wrongly attributed.

This manuscript contains four books. A letter and prologue precede them.

There follow the spurious letters of Seneca to Paul and of Paul to Seneca.

Then Seneca’s epitaph:

> “Care, labor…”

This is found among the poems of Philip, abbot of Bonneval, page 801.

Next come the *Sentences of Seneca*, as well as those of various philosophers and saints.

There follows the *Life of Saint John Chrysostom*, translated into Latin by Leo the Cleric, surnamed John. It has been expanded by countless words and corrected in many places, and is dedicated to Lupus the presbyter, once called Julian.

The prologue begins:

> “The sacred dignity of the supreme priesthood.”

This *Life* appears to have been unknown to the Bollandists, who discuss Saint John Chrysostom on 14 September.

At the end:

> “Here ends the Life of Saint John Chrysostom, bishop and confessor. In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the Life of blessed Fulgentius, bishop.”

This is Fulgentius the African; the author of the *Life* was one of his disciples.

At the end is the rubric:

> “Here ends the Life of Saint Fulgentius, bishop.” [Col. 0823A]

Isidore’s *On the Praise of the Same Man* is chapter 27, elsewhere chapter 14, of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

There follows the *Passion of Saint Quentin*.

Then *On the Assumption of Blessed Mary*:

> “After the Ascension,” etc.

It ends:

> “Her Assumption is celebrated, that of the Mother of God and Virgin Mary, on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of September, through the favor of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

At the end:

> “In the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1211.”

This appears to be the year in which the manuscript was written. Two small strokes are already visible above two *i*s. The hand is clear and large, with frequent but not difficult ligatures; joined diphthongs; points, double points, and a point with a comma above.

### 12. Codex 125 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment folio manuscript, [Col. 0823B] approximately of the fourteenth century. It is identified at the beginning as the *Legendary of the Church of Saint Marius of Forcalquier*.

The first sermon is for the feast of the Holy Eucharist:

> “The immense [thing] of the soul,” etc.

It is by Saint Thomas, together with the office of Corpus Christi.

There follows a work, or homily, *On the Trinity*:

> “All those whom I have been able to read,” etc.

Then come readings, or homilies, of the Fathers, including some by Saint Maximus the bishop.

### 13.

In the same manuscript, page 65, is a sermon of blessed Isidore, bishop, on the Nativity of the Lord:

> “The day of the Lord’s Nativity … may be recalled, because Christ was born.”

This is from Book I, chapter 25, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*.

In the same place, page 69, a sermon of Fulgentius, bishop, on the Nativity of the Lord:

> “Desiring something … may preserve it in charity.”

Another, page 82, is by Fulgentius, bishop of Carthage, on Saint Stephen.

In the same manuscript, page 76, is a sermon of Saint Augustine on the Nativity of the Lord.

Verses of the Sibyl on the final judgment:

> “The sign of judgment.”

### 14.

Page 88: on the Nativity of Saint John the Evangelist, on the sixth day before the Kalends of January [Col. 0823C], a sermon of blessed Isidore, bishop:

> “John the apostle and evangelist, son of Zebedee,” etc.

It ends:

> “Let the dust boil up.”

This is chapter 73, elsewhere chapter 72, *On the Death of the Fathers*.

In the same place, page 98, on the fifth day before the Kalends of January, at Bethlehem in Judea, is a sermon of blessed Severianus:

> “Where will zeal tend?” etc.

It ends:

> “It is a divine gift.”

Severianus was a bishop in Syria at the beginning of the fifth century.

In the same place, page 100, there is likewise a sermon of blessed John the bishop—I understand Chrysostom—on the same Innocents:

> “A new thing is dedicated,” etc.

It ends:

> “It is obtained through destruction.”

The manuscript is mutilated at the end; [Col. 0823D] it appears to belong to the fourteenth century. There are points, a point with a comma above, and clear, distinct letters. The ligatures are frequent but not obscure. There are points, or small strokes, above two *i*s; elsewhere the point above a single *i* is absent. The diphthongs are joined, so that the lower comma is attached to the lower part of the letter *e*, as appears in many printed books.

I have read somewhere that this manuscript belongs to the twelfth century, but it is clear that it was written after Saint Thomas Aquinas and the office of the Most Holy Body of Christ composed by him.

### 15. Codex 137 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment folio manuscript, formerly Petavian volume LXIII, of the fourteenth century or later.

At the beginning, in a more recent hand, is written the name Bourdelot, who may perhaps be Jean Bourdelot, mentioned in the supplement to Moreri’s *Dictionary*.

This beautiful manuscript contains the *Etymologies* in the same order of books as the printed editions. There are six letters of Isidore and Braulio.

A letter of blessed Isidore, archbishop of Hispalis, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.

An index of the chapters of the first book of the *Etymologies*, etc., through [Col. 0824A] the end of Book XX.

> “Here ends the book of the *Etymologies* of blessed Isidore, bishop.”

There follows a table, or alphabetical index, with the note:

> “The method of the following table is as follows,” etc.

The chapters are distinguished by Arabic numerals, although these differ considerably from modern forms.

### 16. Codex 191 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in octavo, of the ninth or tenth century.

If Adololdus, who appears to have been the manuscript’s copyist, as I shall soon say, is not distinct from Adalgaudus, or Adalcalus, or Adalcalcus, mentioned in volume VIII of *Gallia Christiana*, column 1542, then at least part of the manuscript was written at the beginning of the ninth century, since Adalgaudus was abbot of the monastery of Fleury in 818.

At the beginning of the manuscript is the following rubric:

> “In the threefold divine name of God [or Lord] of heaven I trust.”

There follows Isidore’s preface to Fulgentius, [Col. 0824B] *On Offices*:

> “To my lord,” etc., Isidore.

Then comes a table of the following forty-four chapters.

At the bottom of the first pages is written:

> “The book of Saint Remigius, through the labor of brothers Flotueus and Adololdus.”

The second book follows, with an index of twenty-six chapters. At the bottom of the page:

> “The book of Saint Remigius, through the labor of brother Adololdus.”

He appears to have been the copyist of this volume.

Twenty-six chapters are indicated; the last is “On the laying on of hands, or confirmation.”

The last two chapters of Breul’s edition are missing. But in chapter 26, after the words “But since, after they transmit the Spirit, the Paraclete,” certain additional material is added, almost as in the Madrid edition:

> “These are a few things from many that we have learned through the teachings of reputable men, and whose words we accordingly recognize as appearing in certain places in our own work, so that our discourse may be confirmed by the judgments of the Fathers.”

There follows [Col. 0824C] a brief exposition of the Creed, with a marginal note:

> “On Palm Sunday: I ask you, brothers … presume with an undoubting mind; through the gift of him who reigns,” etc.

### 17.

Next:

> “From the book of Saint Augustine: We believe in God the almighty Father. Of all visible things … the soul consists of a body.”

There is also:

> “On the ministers of the Church of Reims, whom Bishop Ebo found in disorder, and, at their entreaty, inspired by the Holy Spirit, dictated the following.” [Col. 0824D]

It appears to be noted in the margin that this was published by Sirmond.

It begins:

> “It is fitting for the one placed in authority…”

Ebo, or Ebbo, died toward the end of the ninth century.

There follow four chapters of Hincmar against the Predestinarians at Quierzy:

> “Almighty God,” etc.

A preface to the Mass, or Canon, is added, as I said in chapter 84.

There is also Albinus’s little book to Fredegisus the deacon:

> “It has pleased your prudence,” etc.

That is, a work on the Trinity.

Another work is on penance and confession.

There is also Homily 8 of Pope Gregory:

> “Since our discourse concerns the resurrection of the flesh…”

Likewise Prudentius of Troyes:

> “On the Old and New Testament.”

He died in the ninth century.

These last items are written in a different hand.

In Isidore’s book there are points, a point and comma arranged in this manner, and conversely a comma above and a point below. Diphthongs are both joined and separated. The script is small and clear, commonly called Gallic by many and Roman cursive by others.

### 18. Codex 199 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment manuscript in quarto. [Col. 0825A] It is suggested that this volume belonged to Petau.

A more recent title is:

> “The Book of the *Sentences* of the Divine Isidore of Hispalis.”

The chapters are indicated in the text by Roman numerals, with more recent Arabic numerals added.

Book I contains 31 chapters. Book II contains 84 chapters. Book III contains 66 chapters.

> “It ends. Thanks be to God.”

There is an addition from Saint Jerome:

> “Let the softness of feathers not warm youthful limbs. Let the heat of the baths not inflame the new blood of adolescence. The widow who lives in luxury is dead while alive.”

There follows, in another hand, an exhortation to virtue, in which certain Leonine verses on the punishments of hell are inserted:

> “Those who are enclosed there, unable to die, die.”

There are others of this kind.

### 19.

Added in the same hand, or one slightly more recent than that of the books of the *Sentences*, is a work *On Saint Abraham, who was the first way of believing*:

> “Abraham, son of Terah,” etc.

A brief *Life of Abraham* follows, and then the lives of other fathers of the Old and New Testament.

These lives differ greatly from Isidore’s book *On the Death of the Fathers*, but in many places they agree completely. I have already said something about this work in chapter 61; I intend to list it among the appendices.

The chapter on Saint James [Col. 0825B] reads:

> “James, whose name is interpreted as ‘supplanter,’ son of Zebedee and brother of the apostle John, by trade a fisherman like Peter, afterward became a follower of Christ. Leaving his net and boat, he followed the Savior; leaving his father Zebedee, he obeyed God. Leaving the sea and fish, he became in the sea—that is, in the world—a heavenly fisherman, a preacher to Spain and the western regions. Under Herod he was struck down by the sword and died, and he was buried in Achaia Marmarica on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.”

### 20.

The last is Stephen, who is absent from Isidore’s genuine book.

There follow various passages concerning our Lord [Col. 0825C] Jesus Christ: how he became man; on drunkenness; on peace and discord; on penance. This is the mystical work *On Numbers*, as I noted in chapter 63.

On page 84, without a title, there is a passage on the reading of books:

> “The whole of Scripture must undoubtedly be understood in two ways.”

A decree of Gelasius is inserted, somewhat altered; I listed it among the appendices of Sedulius.

This manuscript can be assigned to the eleventh century. There are points between the words; the script is clear; the diphthongs are joined; the orthography is approximately that now in use. In both works there are few, clear ligatures.

### 21. Codex 205 Regio-Vaticanus

A paper quarto manuscript in obscure Gothic-Germanic script, of the fourteenth century. Petavian volume LXV.

The twenty books of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, *On the Etymologies*.

The reciprocal letters of Isidore and Braulio; the index of books and chapters, as in the printed editions.

The *Etymologies* are followed by Cassiodorus’s book [Col. 0825D] *On the Soul*:

> “Here begins the book of the Soul: According to Isidore’s *Etymologies*, Book I,” etc.

> “Here ends Cassiodorus’s book *On the Soul*.”

Cassiodorus did indeed write a book *On the Soul*, which in the printed editions begins:

> “Since the work already undertaken…”

and, after the preface:

> “The human soul, therefore…”

But since Cassiodorus flourished in the sixth century, he could not have cited Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Accordingly, the beginning of the book *On the Soul* in this manuscript was added by a later hand.

### 22. Codex 215 Regio-Vaticanus

A parchment quarto manuscript, formerly marked with the number 1,87.

At the beginning of the book, in red letters:

> “Of Saint Mar…”

The rest has been erased, but it appears to indicate Saint Marius of Forcalquier.

The date of the manuscript can, at least in part, be assigned to the end of the eighth century.

The first work is presented under this title [Col. 0826A]:

> “Certain excerpts from the synodal acts of Pope Sylvester: In the time of Saint Sylvester.”

Later:

> “Here begins the letter of the Eastern bishops sent to Julius the Roman,” etc.

> “The letter of the most holy Julius, Roman archbishop, written in reply to Eusebius,” etc.

Page 12:

> “At the Council of Braga [sic], On the dignity of the good and on discipline: When the blessed Apostle rebukes … he will suffer the sentence.”

Prosper, *On the Active and Contemplative Life*.

This is Julian Pomerius.

Certain letters of Saint Jerome follow.

Augustine’s book to Jerome, *On the Origin of the Soul*.

Jerome’s treatise *On the Seraphim*.

Then Cicero’s *Synonyms*, as I said in chapter 56.

There follows a work *On Orthography and Prosody* [Col. 0826B]:

> “Greek names … these are Papiriarus [sic] and Cassiodorus.”

Next comes Jerome’s *Commentary on Genesis*.

Afterward begin glosses on the Old and New Testaments. For these glosses, see chapter 65.

Page 106: a hymn of Saint Peter is inserted in a hand that appears different:

> “Release the delays of the tongue” [read: “Release the delays of the tongue,” or “the tongue’s delays”], “and render praises to blessed Peter.”

### 23.

Page 122: certain verses on prosody, among which are these:

> “Cerellia says she is an old woman, although she is a girl;  
> Gallia says she is a girl [read: Gellia], although she is an old woman.  
> For a single *synthesis* produces great cold;  
> Finally, the Paraclete wields the Father’s scepter.”

These are examples for recognizing syllable quantity. The names of authors are usually attached to them. In the verses just quoted, “Catal” or “Call” is indicated; [Col. 0826C] from these letters I cannot reconstruct the poet’s name, especially since the first three verses are by Martial, while the fourth is by some Christian poet.

In other examples the author’s name is clear.

Among these examples, Isidore is cited on page 125:

> “Our library too brings you forth through your books.”

There follows, without a name:

> “Which my library does not contain in its entirety.”

There is much here from Prudentius and Paulinus.

### 24.

Page 127: names of the weekdays.

> “The first day belongs to Phoebus,” etc.

Verses on Palm Sunday:

> “Supreme King, to you … Christ the Redeemer,” etc. … “Creator of all things.”

On the verso of the same page [Col. 0826D], verses of Saint Augustine *On the Soul*:

> “All things are good, because you, who are good, create all things.”

The last verse:

> “If unhappy, then much more unhappy there.”

### 25.

Page 128, verso: verses of Plato on God:

> “Almighty, whom the age-old span of heaven looks up to…”

The final verse:

> “Whatever it is that is vigorous, by which [perhaps: ‘whereby’] living bodies are stirred.”

Page 129: certain verses from Alcimus Avitus for determining syllable quantity. Likewise verses of Juvencus and Fortunatus.

### 26.

Page 131:

> “Here begins the book of the Chronicle of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis: A brief account,” etc.

Certain additions are made concerning the kings of France down to Charles, Carloman, and Louis.

The manuscript is written in a small hand, [Col. 0827A] perhaps in the time of Charlemagne, of whom it is said:

> “The thirty-seventh year of whose reign is now being observed.”

The diphthongs are joined. There are points above. The first works appear to have been written by a different hand.

306 27. Codex 227, Regio-Vatican, paper, quarto, of the fifteenth century. A book of glosses collected from various glossaries. On the outside it is inscribed, “Glosses of Isidore.” Inside, nothing is stated. It begins:

“Anger, Spartharius, one who constricts—that is, tightens—a spartha. —Albanae, in the plural number, Praenestine nuts. —Astrosus, lunatic. —Aularius, courtly, palatine. —Agagola, procurer, pantomime actor. —Angaria, arianus, one who works the field so that he may receive angariae. —Anteritas, antiquity. —Antela, antilena, just as postela, postilena.”

Nearly the same words occur in the published Isidorian Glossary [Col. 0827B], but arranged differently and sometimes written incorrectly, as in *Spartharius* and *spartam*, which are given in place of *Spatharius* and *spatham*.

28. Codex 231, Regio-Vatican, parchment, quarto; formerly numbered 1351. Clear Gallic script. Rubric: “Here begin the chapters of the great book of Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator, concerning the Soul: there are sixteen chapters.” Page 18, rubric: “Here ends Cassiodorus’s book concerning the Soul. Peace to the reader, life to the believer, salvation to the writer, glory to God the giver, who reigns forever and ever: Amen. Here begins the book of Saint Prosper for the Preachers of the grace of God, against the book of the presbyter Cassian, entitled *On the Protection of God*: The grace of God, by which we are Christians, etc.” Page 40, verso: “Here ends the book of Saint Prosper against the book of Cassian, formerly abbot, entitled *On the Protection of God,* [Col. 0827C] or against the doctrine of Pelagius and Coelestius [perhaps formerly *Coelestinus*].” Some words have been erased, and what follows is “of the enemies of the grace of God, and of Our Lord Jesus Christ.”

29. There follow Alcuin’s three books on the Trinity, with the verses “O king august, etc.” On page 88, without a title: “We believe in the holy Trinity, that is, the Father, etc.” Then Albinus’s questions on the Trinity addressed to Fredegisus: “Your prudence has been pleased, etc.” Albinus’s letter to Eulalius: “To your holy solicitude, etc.”

30. Page 105, verso, rubric: “Here begins an exposition of the holy Gospel: Matthew, first in order, etc.” Page 109, rubric: “Here begins the account of the generation of Jesus Christ Our Lord according to the flesh: How, etc.”

31. Page 113, verso, rubric: “Also, on the New Testament: [Col. 0827D] The four evangelists of the Lord Jesus Christ figuratively express him under the forms of four animals, etc.” These are Isidore’s allegories on the New Testament. It ends: “they shall be satisfied with refreshment.” Immediately follows the rubric: “Also, prefaces to the books of the New Testament; The preaching of the Gospel, etc.” Isidore’s prologues; but they end at no. 1, “they published in speech.”

307 32. In the same place, page 123, rubric: “Here begins the book on the interpretation of certain names of the Old and New Testament: To the lord and servant of God, Bishop Orosius, Isidore: Certain very well-known names, etc.” It ends: “and received the crown of heavenly glory”; this is the ending of the *Allegories of the Old Testament*. There follows, without a title: “Our most merciful Lord and Savior, instructor of his own [Col. 0828A], wishing to teach his disciples what they should pray for, etc.” On prayer in general, and soon afterward on the Lord’s Prayer. It ends: “and by whose mercy we are set free. Amen.” No mention is made of “Isidore of Córdoba” or “the presbyter Orosius,” nor is the reverential epithet applied to Orosius. More concerning these matters is found in chapter 60. The *Allegories of the New Testament* are absent, perhaps because they had already been placed above.

33. After the exposition of the Lord’s Prayer, page 138, verso, rubric: “Here begin the interpretations of names from Hebrew into Latin. *Hel*, God; *Heli*, my God, etc.” Later come Greek names: “*O theus*, God.” It ends: “A repository of books.” Page 142, rubric: “Here begins an explanation of the Apostles’ Creed: When we read the blessed Paul, etc.” It ends: “I faithfully believe what is contained in the Creed. Amen.”

34. There follows, without a title, an exposition of the Creed: “*Quicunque*: You have entrusted to me that little work of faith which is recited everywhere in the churches, etc.” In the same place: “For it is handed down that it was composed by blessed Athanasius, bishop of the Alexandrian Church; for I have always seen it so entitled even in ancient codices.” It ends: “are returned by the Lord.” In connection with the celebrated controversy concerning the Athanasian Creed, it should be noted that it had already been observed around the tenth century that it was attributed to Athanasius in ancient codices.

35. Codex 239, Regio-Vatican, approximately of the thirteenth century, parchment, quarto, written in clear but small script, with many letter abbreviations, and divided into two columns. Petavian volume LXII. At the end it is called [Col. 0828C] “the book of Saint Andrew.” It contains the twenty books of the *Etymologies* in the order found in the printed editions. They are preceded by four letters, from among the six already published and known, and by an index of the books.

36. Codex 254, Regio-Vatican, parchment, quarto, formerly numbered 1488. Rubric: “Here begin the chapters of the first book of the *Sentences* of Isidore, archbishop.” Book I has 31 chapters; Book II, 44; Book III, 67. “Here ends the third book of the *Sentences* of Isidore, archbishop.” There follow Origen’s homilies on Psalms 36, 37, and 38. There are nine homilies, with the chapter titles in rubricated script. Then follows a letter of Pope Eugene 308 to the Cistercians, dated at Segni on the Nones of August: “I would wish, dearest sons, to be present in person at your holy college.” At the end: “The book of Saint Mary of …” Nothing else can be read. Thus far the codex is written in the same clear and even script, of the thirteenth century or the following one. There are two commas above two *i*’s, joined diphthongs, a point, and a point with a comma above it; frequent letter ligatures, but they are not obscure.

37. In the same volume, in a different script, a rubric follows: “Here begins the book of the *Soliloquies* of the same bishop Isidore: I ask you, O soul, I beseech you, etc.” In Breul’s work this is the second book of the *Synonyms*. The ending in both places is: “You please me above my life.” There is no division into chapters. These leaves appear to have been sewn in from another volume, in which other works of Isidore in the same script had preceded them.

38. There follows: “Here begin sentences excerpted from various books of the holy doctors.” “Isidore, Bede, Xystus, Gregory, Augustine, Seneca, [Col. 0829A] Jerome” are praised, as I stated in chapter 33. Later: “Excerpt from the letter of blessed Gregory to Secundinus, God’s recluse, concerning the snares of the crafty enemy: The ancient enemy, etc.” At the end:

“Finished: may the writer finish, and go play.”

In a more recent script: “This book is for the use of Brother Gerard of Fleury, of the Order of Friars Minor of Saint Francis, doctor of sacred theology.” The final words are not sufficiently clear. Nevertheless, the codex appears at some time to have belonged to a Spaniard: somewhere in the margin is written *ojo*, “eye,” by which word Spaniards indicate that something should be read with close attention, as I have already noted in other codices. The script of this final part of the codex is for the most part Gothic; a comma or short stroke is added above *i*, apparently by another hand [Col. 0829B]; above two *i*’s, and in the rubrics, the first hand seems to have added short strokes. There are many letter abbreviations, and diphthongs are generally absent.

39. Codex 255, Regio-Vatican, parchment, quarto, formerly numbered 1487, of the eighth or ninth century. A later title in the script reads: “Isidore, *On the Nature of Things*. Prologue to Sisebutus.” Index of 46 chapters. Chapter 27 is missing; Breul has it, while the Madrid edition omits it. The ending is: “which will never have an end.” Rubric: “Here ends Isidore’s first book.” There follows, without a title:

“You perhaps, sluggish in the grove [read *luco*], produce wandering songs,

and among clear streams and musical breezes, etc.

The moon travels on, pressing upon her brother with direct aspects.” [Col. 0829C]

In the recent Madrid edition, that poem is printed incorrectly; we shall publish it corrected. It is followed by an antiphon with ancient musical notation: “Kalends of October: O most unconquered athlete, Germanus the bishop.” And antiphons concerning the chains of Saint Peter: “Herod the king laid hands upon him.”

40. Then the rubric: “Here begins the book of *Prognostics* [sic], published by Julian, bishop of Toledo [read *Toletano*], for Didalius [read *Idalius*], bishop of Barcelona.” After the prologue and prayer, the rubric reads: “Here ends the prologue, or prayer, of Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo [apparently *Tolitana*]. Here begin the chapters of the first book.” Book I contains 22 chapters; Book II, 37; Book III, 62. After chapter 62, which has no ending [Col. 0829D], another previously unrecorded chapter follows, with an ancient black title, absent from the Madrid edition of the Toledan Fathers: “Treatise of Saint Ambrose on the Pride of the Flesh. To you I extend my hand, etc., fasting and prayer.” “Here ends the book of *Prognostics*.” The number 63 is placed in the margin of this chapter.

There follows a fairly long work or homily without its beginning. Its first words are: “You are adorned with arms! He receives from Christ the beauty of the ornaments of virtues for his soul; for always, etc. … and you grant that, together with your saints and elect, he may reign eternally in everlasting blessedness, because with the eternal Father and the Holy Spirit there is for you one Godhead, glory, power, dominion, and authority forever and ever. Amen.”

41. Attached is a “Confession for Prime” [sic]: “I confess [Col. 0830A] to the Lord and to you, father, that I have sinned in the worst thoughts … may he lead [me] to eternal life. Amen.” In addition, there is an index of the chapters of Book I of the *Sentences* and of Book III. The index of Book II is missing.

Afterward comes the title: “Here begins Isidore’s book of *Spermologon*.” That is, Book I of the *Sentences*, with 31 chapters. At the end: “The book ends. The book begins: Everyone who according to …” This is Book II, with 44 chapters: “The second book ends. The third begins,” with 67 chapters; its ending is: “it includes those who are to be gladdened.” I explained the title *Spermologon* in chapter 67.

The codex is ancient, approximately of the ninth century; its script is clear and Roman, with points sometimes below and sometimes above the letters, and few ligatures. The letters *i*, *d*, and *h* extend farther outside the line; there is a point with a comma above it, elsewhere a comma with two points above it; diphthongs are sometimes [Col. 0830B] joined and sometimes separated.

42. Codex 256, Regio-Vatican, parchment, apparently of the fourteenth century: “Here begins the summary of Master Beleth on ecclesiastical offices throughout the course of the year: In the primitive Church, etc.” Page 72, without a title: “The holy Roman Church, after those books of the Old and New Testament, etc.” This is Gelasius’s decree concerning books to be received and not received.

43. Page 92, verso, rubric: “Decretal letter of Pope Innocent for the correction of the universal Church: Certain priests have the custom that, every day, immediately after Mass has ended, the Gospel *In principio erat Verbum* is read; because it proceeded neither from the Roman Church nor rests upon any valid basis, we altogether prohibit it. Likewise, certain laypeople have the custom that, neglecting the office of the day, they ask to have private Masses sung for themselves—that is, Masses of the Holy Trinity, of Saint Mary, of Saint Nicholas, and the like. We also prohibit them from doing this any longer except at the appropriate time. But if anyone wishes to hear the sacred mysteries of the Mass out of pious devotion, let him hear the Mass of that day for the salvation of the living or the dead.”

Also another decretal letter of the same Innocent, in response to inquiries from a certain patriarch: “Our counsel, etc. Among us, on weekdays, when Mass is celebrated in honor of the blessed Virgin, neither the angelic hymn nor the Creed is sung, although the proper preface is chanted in the Mass, so that a distinction may be shown between commemoration and solemnity.” This concerns votive Masses. We now use other rubrics, following Saint Pius V. If you please, consult the curious work of Scortia on the most holy Sacrifice of the Mass, book IV, chapter 31, no. 6, and title 41, “On the Celebration of Masses,” chapters 2 and 4.

44. Page 102, letter of Jerome to Nepotianus, concerning the life of the clergy: “You ask me, Nepotianus.” Other letters of the same author. Page 110, rubric: “Isidore, *On Clerics*: When all ecclesiastical ministers are to be ordained, etc.” This is chapter 1 of Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, with some alterations.

Rubric: “Which precepts apply specifically to monks, and which are generally shared by Christians. On account of certain simple people who, when admonished and reproved by religious and learned men, often object that only monks ought to observe the precepts of the holy Scriptures, etc.” [Col. 0831A] It ends: “will receive his reward.” There follows Saint Gregory’s *Pastoral Care*, mutilated shortly after the beginning.

311 CHAPTER C. Thirteen additional manuscript copies in the Regio-Vatican Library are described. Several short works of various subjects. Our Isidore is more than once called “the Younger” in very ancient parchment manuscripts. An old history of the Goths, not yet published. Certain fragments of Isidore written in Tironian notes.

1. Codex 261, Regio-Vatican, paper, formerly numbered 1612, in semi-Gothic or German script. It contains several works. First appears a book on the consolation of human nature, published by Master John Jarsonius, professor of theology at the University of Paris, as a commentary on Boethius’s *Consolation*: [Col. 0831B] “Since, according to the Apostle …” It ends: “the heavenly court shall receive it; which …” Near the end, the following verses are quoted:

“Who does not become accustomed to virtue while he is young

does not know how to depart from vices when he grows old.”

2. Second, Anselm’s *Meditations*, but without a title; one has been added by another hand. It begins: “The devout soul desiring …” Third, an untitled work: “What is God, etc.” Fourth, a sermon on contempt of the world without the author’s name: “See how carefully you walk.” Fifth: “Here begins the treatise on the Psalms of blessed Augustine: The song of the Psalms.”

3. Sixth: “Here begins the book *On the Misery and Usefulness of the Human Condition*, published by Lord Lotharius, cardinal deacon of Saints Sergius and Bacchus, who was afterward [Col. 0831C] called Pope Innocent III.” This is also called “On Contempt of the World.”

Seventh: “Here begins the prologue to the most devout treatise on the mystical crown of the Virgin Mary: The golden crown, etc.” It ends: “Defender of orphans, who, seated on the imperial throne, etc.” (Among the doubtful works of Saint Ildefonsus, volume I of the Toledan Fathers, pp. 393 ff.)

Eighth: “Eight reasons why the Virgin Mary is called most blessed: The Virgin Mary is called most blessed for eight reasons. First, because she conceived by the Word. Second, without sin. Third, she gave birth without pain. Fourth, she carried God and her Creator in her womb. Fifth, because through her the sin of our first parent was erased. Sixth, whatever she asks of God is granted to her. Seventh, because she is in heaven in body and soul. Eighth, because she has been exalted above the choirs of angels.” [Col. 0831D]

Some works with a similar title were later published, such as Peter Ribadeneira’s book entitled *El porqué de la Compañía* (“The Why of the Society”). The following rubric comes next: “How many years the Virgin Mary lived.”

“The Virgin of God lived sixty-three years;

fourteen she was blessed in childbirth,

thirty-three she lived with her son,

and sixteen after her son had ascended to the stars.””

4. Ninth: “Here begins a treatise on the virtue of prayer, published by the Venerable Hugh of Saint Victor: With what diligence and with what affection, etc.” Tenth: “A treatise for converting the Jews from their error concerning the Messiah, whom they still await, and concerning observance of the Law.” Alfonso Bonihominis, a Spaniard, sent this book, long concealed, after translating it himself from Arabic into Latin [Col. 0832A], to Hugh, master of the Order of Preachers. Alfonso was writing in Paris. The author of the book is Samuel the catechumen, a native of the city of Feth, belonging to the king of the Morothitani [sic], who writes to Isaac, master of the synagogue at Subvilmeta in the same kingdom. At the end Alfonso adds a note concerning the book’s concealment for 236 years, arranged by the Jews. It was translated into Latin in the year 1339.

5. Eleventh: “Here begins a treatise, published by Lord Peter, cardinal of Cambrai, on four spiritual exercises. The devout soul desiring, etc.” Twelfth: “The following verses were composed by the venerable Lord Brother G. Eden, who was minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, patriarch of Antioch, and bishop of Catansis: Jesus, saving victim, saving sacrifice, Jesus, saving grace, [Col. 0832B] saving benefit, etc.” In my search, I have not encountered any mention of this G. Eden, minister general of the Order of Friars Minor, in Wadding.

6. Thirteenth: “Admonition of Saint Augustine to monks concerning Gospel reading and the fire of purgatory: In the apostolic reading that was recited to us a little earlier, dearest brothers, we heard the Apostle saying: ‘For no other foundation …’ Let us hasten to redeem [our sins] by generosity.”

Fourteenth: “Here begins a sermon of Saint John Chrysostom—the Golden Mouth—on the patience and thanksgiving written above, and that one ought not to mourn the dead so intensely, especially when the little ones of the world have been separated from this life. Come, especially today let us enter more diligently than in previous days into sermon and instruction … we have been numbered through Jesus Christ, etc.”

[Col. 0832C] Fifteenth: Other sermons of Saint John the Golden Mouth, or Chrysostom. Finally, on page 175, a sermon of Saint Isidore on the temptations of the devil. This is chapter 5 of Book III of the *Sentences*, as I stated in chapter 72.

313 7. Codex 281, Regio-Vatican, already described in chapter 85, perhaps of the ninth century. Diphthongs are both separated and joined; there is a stroke below and above a point, sometimes only a stroke and only a point. There are *Differentiae* concerning the active and contemplative life, attributed to Isidore. A rubric follows in large red letters, intermixed with smaller ones: “Here begin the chapters of the first book on the Contemplative Life.” The author’s name is not given; the work is usually attributed to Prosper, but it is by Julianus Pomerius. At the end: “You who read, pray for this [Col. 0832D] writer, if you have the Lord as your protector in all things. Agambaldus, an unworthy monk, wrote this. Thanks be to God.”

8. Codex 287, Regio-Vatican, quarto, parchment, of the twelfth century or later, Petavian volume LXI. The last ten books of the *Etymologies*. Some material from the second book, on rhetoric, is added. The following note is found: “The book of Saint Peter’s church of Ghent. Blessing to the one who preserves it, curse to the one who removes it; let anyone who removes or cuts a leaf be anathema.” Similar anathemas may be read in other manuscript books as well. This copy perhaps belongs to the division by which some maintained that the *Etymologies* were divided into two parts.

9. Codex 293, Regio-Vatican, quarto, parchment, formerly 1485, Petavian volume LVII, approximately of the tenth century [Col. 0833A]: “Here begins the preface of Bishop Isidore on the book of Genesis. Isidore sends greetings to the reader. The history of the sacred Law, etc.” Thirty-one chapters are numbered. At the end: “Here ends the treatise on the book of Genesis. Here begin the chapters on the book of Exodus.” There are 59 chapters. Some mystical material from the book. It ends: “in those who believe in him.”

Seventeen chapters of the book of Leviticus: “Here begins the treatise on the book of Leviticus: The varieties of sacrifices.” It ends: “Such a sacrifice is not approved by the Catholic Church.” But “it ends” is not stated, and one leaf appears to be missing; nevertheless, something may have been added to this page.

10. “Here begin the chapters of the book of Numbers.” There are 30. “Therefore this book is one, etc.” “Here ends the book of Numbers. Here begin the chapters of Deuteronomy”: there are 22. “Here begins the treatise on Deuteronomy: The book of Deuteronomy, etc.” “Here ends [Col. 0833B] the book of Deuteronomy. Here begin the chapters in the book of Joshua.” There are 18. “Here ends Joshua.” The chapters of Judges begin: “The history of Judges.” Chapter 9 concerns Ruth. “Here ends Ruth.” The chapters of Kings begin. After the book of Judges there are 21 chapters of Book I, 6 chapters of Book II, and 9 chapters of Book III. Breul has 8 chapters, for he joins the two final ones. There are 8 chapters of Book IV of Kings. The books of Ezra contain 3 chapters. Of Maccabees, one chapter. “Here ends Isidore, bishop of Seville’s little work on the books of the Old Testament.”

11. “Here begins Prosper’s first book, *On the Calling of All Nations*: Among the defenders of free will, etc.” “Here ends Prosper’s second book *On the Calling of All Nations*.” There follows Pope Leo’s letter to Juvenal, bishop, concerning the Eutychian heresy. Another of the same author to [Col. 0833C] Julian. Another to the empress Pulcheria. To the emperor Leo. A letter or decree of Pope Innocent to Bishop Decentius. Jerome’s letter to Magnus, the Roman orator. At the beginning of this codex is written: “The book of Saint Peter and Saint Rodobertus” (or Crodobertus, or rather Hrodobertus) “of the cell.” There are two points, a point with a comma above it, a single point, easy and not numerous ligatures, clear and even script, straight lines made with a ruling instrument; points above *i* are absent; diphthongs are partly joined and partly separated.

12. Codex 294, Regio-Vatican, parchment, folio, small format, in small but clear script. Petavian volume LX. [Col. 0833D] There are some ligatures, but they are easy to read; a point, a comma below and above a point, joined diphthongs, and lines ruled straight by means of a device. The codex was perhaps written in the eleventh century. The *Etymologies* are mutilated at the end. At the beginning: “Here begins the letter of Isidore the Younger of Seville”; other material has been erased. After the six familiar letters there is an index of the twenty books, followed by an index of the chapters of Book I. The order of the books is as in the printed editions.

13. Codex 309, Regio-Vatican, parchment, folio, apparently of the tenth century, in brilliant Gallic script. A work consisting of seven books, like that in the Veronese Codex, which contains an abridgment of the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, described in chapter 44. The codex formerly belonged to the monastery of Saint-Denis in Paris. A recent note at the beginning reads: “I believe that all the treatises contained in this codex belong either to the venerable Bede or to Isidore.”

[Col. 0834A] 14. It is preceded by the following: “How can it be recognized what number has been conceived by any mind?” Let any number be assumed. In the margin, a recent hand cites Bede, volume II, column 133. Page 4, verso, contains a table of all the works included in this volume.

Book I has 11 chapters. Chapter 1: “A note containing the birthdays of the saints, etc.” Chapter 2, concerning the course of the moon, etc. Chapter 3, a martyrology, with a few saints written by the first hand. Some others were added by an ancient hand, such as “5 Ides of December: in the monastery of Saint Medard, the reception of Saints Sebastian the martyr [315], Gregory the pope, and Saint Leocadia.” Compare Flórez, volume V of *Hispania Sacra*, p. 308, concerning the translation of the body of Saint Leocadia. The beginning of winter is on the seventh Ides of November.

Chapter 4, concerning cycles. Chapter 5, an abridgment of the chronicle. Thus, on page 59 [Col. 0834B], the rubric reads: “Abridgment of the chronicle, where it should be inserted. When Adam was 130 years old, etc.” A recent note reads: “See whether this work is by Isidore or Bede.” Another note: “Published in volume III of Duchesne’s *Historians of the Franks*, p. 125.” It ends: “The total number of years from the origin of the world to the present year is 4,771” (but perhaps it was 4,861), “namely, the ninth year of Charles, who reigned after Carloman.”

15. Chapter 6, folio 60, verso, rubric: “Here begins *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*: Adam, etc.,” as in the aforementioned Veronese Codex. In the margin, Greek letters appear in place of numbers: “I shall publish this little work among the appendices, after comparing various readings from other manuscripts.”

There follow other materials on the reckoning of time, and on folio 65, concerning the seventy prophetic weeks.

Book II contains 22 chapters, on cycles [Col. 0834C], finding the years, the day of Easter, etc. Book III has 14 chapters, on reckoning by joints or fingers, on years, the calculation of leap years, the Kalends, etc. Book IV has 27 chapters: on the moon, its days, its correspondence with the sea, etc. Book V has 12 chapters, excerpts on astrology, the stars, eclipses, and signs of storms. The signs of the zodiac are depicted with considerable elegance. Book VI has 7 chapters, on the calculation of ounces, the testing of gold and silver, and the measurement of wax and metal in cast works. A fragment of Macrobius, *On the Measurement of the Earth*, etc., and of the sun, etc. Of Capella, *On the Measurement of the Moon and the Earth*.

16. Book VII. There is also a book, with its chapters, by Bede the presbyter, containing material *On the Natures of Things*. On folio 107, verso, the rubric corresponds: “Verses of Bede the presbyter: The various natures [Col. 0834D] of things, etc.” An index of 51 chapters, folio 19: “Here ends the book on the natures of things” (that is, Bede’s). Immediately follows the rubric: “On Measures and Weights: A measure, according to Isidore, is whatever, etc.”

After this little work on measures and weights there is material on epacts, with questions: “If you wish to know, etc.,” as in other codices and in Muratori’s *Anecdota*, volume III, pp. 111 ff. On folio 125, verso, verses for finding the date of Septuagesima:

“The Februae proceed on the fifth under the lot of the Kalends, etc.”

There are carefully prepared tables of epacts, with verses.

17. In Book I, after chapter 4 on cycles, from folio 37 onward, a table and sequence of years is inserted, on more recent parchment, from the first year of Christ’s birth to the year 1566 [Col. 0835A]. Certain events are noted for some years, such as: “1: Our Lord Jesus Christ is born, after 5,700 years from the origin of the world have elapsed”; but 700 is not very clear.

The first hand that added the numbers of the years assigns events in this way to approximately the year 1175, noting especially matters concerning the Frankish kings and monasteries. Another hand follows, recording many more events, likewise concerning Gaul and monasteries. Then a third hand, and finally a fourth, which records under the year 1374: “Charles V of France reigns.” All subsequent years are free from such historical annotations.

18. In the first hand, under the year 775, it is written: “Charles proceeded into Spain.” Under the year 1154: “King Louis took as his wife the daughter of the king of Spain.” Under the year [Col. 0835B] 1160: “Queen Constance of Spain died.” In the same year King Louis married the daughter of the count of Blois. Under the year 1233 it is noted: “In the same year Alfonso of Spain married the countess of Boulogne.”

The authors of these notes appear to have been monks of the Parisian monastery of Saint-Denis, concerning which they insert several particular details.

19. Codex 310, Regio-Vatican, parchment, folio, approximately of the tenth century: “In the name of the holy Trinity, here begins the book of Prologues on the fullness of the books of the New and Old Testament [Col. 0835C], which the Catholic Church receives in the Canon [or: as the Canon], according to the ancient tradition of those who came before. It begins: In the beginning, namely, etc.” Also, prefaces to the books of the New Testament: “The preaching of the Gospel, etc.” Here ends the book of Prologues.

There follows: “Here begin annotations of the provinces of Gaul with their privileges. The province of Lyon, etc.” There are 17 provinces and 115 cities.

Then: “Here begins Isidore’s book of Wheels, to the lord and son Sisebutus, etc.” Index of chapters, etc. It ends: “which will never have an end.” Chapter 47, “On the Parts of the Earth,” is missing; it is present in some manuscripts and absent in others.

20. Afterward: “Here begin glosses from the New and Old Testament, or composed spiritually from the *Etymologies* [perhaps *Etymologiis*].” It begins: “*Avavus*, the father of a great-grandfather, that is, the grandfather of a great-grandfather. *Abba*, father; it is a Syriac word.” It ends: “*Zizania*, darnel.” It is a very extensive glossary, or index of the *Etymologies*.

In addition: “Here begin the chapters of the tenth book, that is, certain names [Col. 0835D] arranged alphabetically: ‘Concerning the remaining names according to the order of the elements of the letters.’” This is Book X of the *Etymologies*.

It is followed by: “Here begins *On the Properties of Words or Things*: Between *polliceri* and *promittere*, etc. Here begin the spiritual differences of Isidore, bishop of the Younger Spaniard: Between God and man, etc.” It ends: “of Christ’s humility: here end Isidore’s differences, whether spiritual or carnal.”

21. Next comes: “In the name of the Lord, to his dearest and most beloved brother Braulio, archdeacon, Isidore.” Breul published this letter from this very codex, which I appear to have before me: for he praises the Petavian Codex, and it is like this one. It is included among the other Isidorian works.

22. Added: “Here begins the *Soliloquies* of Isidore the Younger [Col. 0836A], bishop of Seville. Isidore sends greetings to the reader. Recently there came into my hands a certain note of Cicero, etc.” Breul refers this prologue to the preface of the book *On Contempt of the World*.

After this prologue: “My soul is in anguish, etc.” “Here ends the first book; the second book begins: I ask you, O soul, etc.” There is no division into chapters in the codex. It ends: “does not cleanse, but enlarges.” One leaf, however, appears to be missing.

There follow two sermons under the name of Saint Augustine. According to the note I find, the first was made from Sermon 13 *On Time*; the other is by some writer who lived around the year 500. The second begins: “Let your love, dearest brothers, hear in the present how, etc.” Compare the sermons of Caesarius.

23. The codex is mutilated at the end; the script is clear [Col. 0836B] and larger at the beginning. In the book *On Nature* there are points, sometimes below the letters and sometimes in the middle; there is no other punctuation. The diphthongs are separated, either always or for the most part. In the other works that follow, the writing is different: there is a point with a comma above it and a single point. The codex has been corrected very little.

24. Codex 349, Regio-Vatican, quarto, contains various miscellanies. First are a few verses placed before an image of the *Pietà*—the Crucified Christ:

“Look, sinner, whether I am not a true lover.”

And in chapter 2, prayers or commemorations of Saint Jerome and Augustine. Third, Saint Bernard’s jubilus: “Jesus, sweet remembrance,” and his rhythms:

[Col. 0836C] “Hail, salvation of the world.

Hail, hail, dear Jesus.”

Fourth: “A method for preserving us in the love of God,” from fourteen Fathers and also from four others: “I consider, etc. … in his love.”

Fifth: “Five rules for recognizing when a sin is mortal. The first rule … applying deliberation.”

25. Sixth: A rhythm in honor of Saint Jerome; a greeting of the Lord’s Holy Body; the virtues of the Lamb of God, etc. Seventh: Seneca’s *Book of Morals*: “Every sin is an act, etc.” Eighth: Saint Bernard’s *Instruction for Religious Life*: “For this let him strive, etc.” Ninth: Saint Bernard’s *Mirror of Monks*: “If anyone of more reformed life …” Tenth: Other verses and many other works of Saint Bernard, Peter Damian, Augustine, Gregory, etc. Eleventh: A confession arranged at the Grande Chartreuse [Col. 0836D]. Twelfth: The spurious letter of Lentulus to the Romans concerning the appearance of Jesus Christ, and Pilate’s letter concerning Jesus Christ. Thirteenth: On the three apparitions of Our Lord Jesus Christ that are not found in the Gospel; concerning these I spoke to Sedulius, Book V, verse 362. Fourteenth: Francesco Petrarch’s letter to Gerard the Carthusian, his brother.

26. Fifteenth: An excerpt from Book III of Prosper’s—or rather Pomerius’s—*On the Contemplative Life*. Sixteenth: From the Vatican Library: “Here begins the council of the city of Rome held under Pope Damasus: On the explanation of the Catholic faith”; I published it after Sedulius among the appendices.

There follows: “From the Roman council under Pope Martin I, in which the words of the Fifth Synod are reported,” namely from decree 18: [Col. 0837A] “But everything that does not agree, etc.,” “they proclaimed to the end.”

Seventeenth: Several Greek passages, including some from the holy Fathers. Eighteenth: Authorities for the claim that Constantine was baptized at Rome by Saint Sylvester. Isidore of Seville is also cited, without the location being indicated. See chapter 33. Nineteenth: Various other miscellanies.

Thus, in this volume of miscellanies, on page 107: “Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, *On Illustrious Men*.” It begins with Xystus, Macrobius, etc. The final chapter concerns Bishop Maximus. There follows a eulogy of Isidore composed by Braulio. At the end: “If it seems good to the Reverend Father, master of the sacred palace, let it be printed. M. Antonius, archbishop of Vuasin [unclear], vicegerent.”

There are 47 chapters, including two concerning Sedulius but excluding Braulio’s chapter on Isidore. Sedulius is mentioned twice, namely in chapters 11 and 21.

[Col. 0837B] 27. Codex 421, Regio-Vatican, parchment, quarto. A few leaves near the end have been added on paper. The parchment script is ancient, perhaps of the eleventh century. It is a miscellaneous book, in which the first item is an elegiac poem with the title: “Theology addresses the Synagogue, saying: Almighty in the beginning,” which is noted as being by Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans.

Second, verses of Israel on the art of meter concerning the noun and the verb:

“Let the praises of meter bid Robert be well, etc.”

We say nothing other than what Servius and Bede say. This Israel appears to be different from the other one discussed by Fabricius in the *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*.

Third, a choriambic meter:

“Christ, who are the head of the sacred …”

“And you, exceedingly dear to God, Hadeuviga, and beloved, etc.” [Col. 0837C]

This virgin, perhaps Hegelwitha, apparently ordered the poem to be written in the ninth century, in praise of the Strong Woman, which follows:

“King Solomon, who shone throughout the world with supreme wisdom, etc.”

It proceeds in such a way that the middle and final letters correspond somewhat in sound.

28. Fourth: A note concerning Cain’s punishment, and then a diagram representing the figure of Christ’s length, as I explained in Appendix 5 to Sedulius. Fifth: “How many languages are there in the world? There are seventy-two, etc.” Sixth: On the individual days of the week. There are seven. Verses of Eugenius of Toledo. “There creeping things and shrewd human beings”; and earlier, “the feathered birds.” The rest is as in another Codex, Regina 2078, which I discussed in the prolegomena to Dracontius.

Seventh: The Lord’s Prayer and the Catholic Creed in Greek and Latin. A brief Greek litany in which Christ, the Mother of God, Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Peter, and Paul are invoked by name.

In the same place, page 16: “Isidore to his sister.” A fragment of Book I *Against the Jews*. “Isaiah [perhaps, ‘but Isaiah’] more openly [said that] the Son was begotten by God, etc.,” through the end of chapter 1, “On the Nativity.” The script is approximately of the ninth century. In the manuscript it reads “so that he may choose between the two,” without *sibi*.

On the following leaf there is an acephalous work or excerpt: “A cleric is one who serves the Church of Christ.” On priestly vestments, the authority of baptism, and fasting. Page 21 contains certain ancient verses:

“We beseech you, almighty God, have mercy on us;

grant the wretched forgiveness, and a crown to those contrite in heart.”

Also:

[Col. 0838A] This is a beautiful house: may this hall of salvation, I pray, be so,

and may it, ever inhabited, gladden its occupants. Likewise:

A splendid hall, decorated with square windows,

A hospitable sheltering-place for the poor and the simple. Likewise, on the table of blessed Augustine:

Whoever loves to gnaw at the lives of the absent through his words,

Let him know that this table is unworthy of him (sic). Likewise:

If you wish to know, traveler, whether poets live after death,

What you read, behold, I speak: your voice, indeed, is mine.

29. Next, concerning the observance of the four seasons: “The fast of the first month,” etc. … “he shall possess joys”; this is a work different from the 320 chapters of Book I of Isidore’s *Offices*, in which fasting is discussed. Other sayings from Augustine and Jerome follow, together with a note concerning six bishops:

“These are those whom blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, sent together to Gaul to preach the Gospel: Dionysius, bishop of the city of Paris; Memmius, bishop of the city of Châlons; Xystus, bishop of Reims; Eutherius, bishop of the city of Trier; Sabianus (sic), bishop of Sens; Sinetius, bishop of Soissons, together with their other companions.”

A note is added: “Concerning the six general synods.” Page 27: an anonymous elegy, perhaps also acephalous:

“This the consecrated stream of your Jordan brought forth”; bearing the names of Charles and Hildigard, on the death of their son Alytarius. The elegy ends:

“To join them to their sacred voices.”

30. An enigma follows:

“The first sounds like the fourth; the fifth answers the second.” [Col. 0838C] It ends:

“I climb the warm pole; I run across the frozen ground.”

It is written *respondit*; for *i* in place of *e* is frequent in manuscript codices. A fable about a lion is appended:

“Once, it was reported, a lion lay sick,” etc. Here papyrus leaves are attached, on which the fable and other pieces continue. Verses by an uncertain author:

“Rustic, wanderer, goat-footed, horned, two-natured,” etc.

“Cast out in the crossroads, unburied, a smooth

Human skull lay there, bald and bare of hair.” (This is by Ausonius.) An eclogue by an uncertain author. In the margin of the piece concerning the cuckoo it is noted that it is by Bede: “Let us lament the cuckoo,” etc. Other epigrams follow, and Bede’s contest between spring and winter:

“All suddenly they meet, but on the lofty mountains.”

31. In the same place, page 31: eulogies of certain Fathers, by an uncertain [Col. 0838D] author—Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome (from the library of Isidore, as I said in chapter 81). In the same place:

“Our library also sets you forth through your books.”

Some other pieces by uncertain authors follow, and at the end are verses of Strabo, which appear in Canisius, *Ancient Readings*, vol. VI, p. 635. A parchment leaf of an old script, dating approximately from the eleventh century, follows. An acephalous alphabetical hymn begins with C: “The blast of the trumpet through the fourfold,” etc. There, in place of X, is the name of Christ: “Xpm, the King, now resplendent with his paternal glory.” It concerns the universal judgment.

32. Codex 551, Regio-Vaticanus, parchment, in folio, apparently of the fourteenth century. Petau’s volume 211. The name Bourdelot, a Parisian lawyer, is also present in a more recent script, as elsewhere I inferred from Moreri. It begins with [Col. 0839A] the prologue of Rufinus, a most eloquent man, to the book of Ecclesiastical History. After the prologue is a eulogy of Eusebius by Jerome and Gennadius. Folio 119:

“Here ends the eleventh book of Ecclesiastical History. The prologue to the Life of Saint Sylvester the pope begins. Our historian Eusebius, etc. The prologue ends. The acts of Saint Sylvester the pope begin. Sylvester, therefore, bishop of the city of Rome, when he was still a little child, etc., baptized at Easter; and from that time the name of Our Lord Jesus Christ began to be magnified by all the Roman people, etc. The acts of Saint Sylvester end. The miracle concerning Peter Igneus begins: To Alexander, most reverend and universal bishop of the principal see, the clergy and people of Florence offer the service of sincere devotion: ‘For a long time now weariness,’ etc., ‘that you may not hesitate graciously to bestow it.’”

Peter Igneus flourished in the eleventh century. Consult Baronius in the *Annals*.

33. Folio 127: the prologue of Saint Jerome the priest to the book *On Illustrious Men* begins:

“You urge me, Dexter,” etc. There are 135 chapters. The book of Saint Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*, ends. An anonymous work follows, sufficiently inept, by which the chapters are continued to 147:

“Do you now wish, my brother Desiderius, to see sharply,” etc.

The writers discussed are Augustine, Hilary, Origen, Eusebius, Heliodorus, Ambrose, Dardanus, Paulinus, Pelagius, Jovinian, Julius Africanus, and Fannonius. See Fabricius, *Ecclesiastical Library*, after Jerome’s book. That little work passes judgment on these writers, but for the most part unjustly.

34. Folio 141. The chapters in the book of Gennadius [Col. 0839C] the priest, *On Illustrious Men*, begin. There are 98 chapters; Sedulius is absent, as in most other copies. In the text there are only 97 chapters, Gennadius included. Folio 150: “Here ends the book of Gennadius, priest of Massilia, on Illustrious Men.” The chapters in the book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, *On Illustrious Men*, begin. There are 33 chapters, as in Breul, p. 526 and following, and in the same order.
