In chapter 20 Breul has: “Justinian, bishop of the Church of Valencia”; the manuscript has: “bishop of the Valentian Church.” At the end: “Here ends the book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, on Illustrious Men.” The preface of Cassiodorus Senator to the books *On the Institution of Divine Scripture* begins. At the end: “Here ends the second book of Cassiodorus Senator on the institution,” etc. Nothing else is found in this fine codex, which, as I said, may be assigned to the fourteenth century. Dots above a single *i* are absent, but commas or short strokes are correctly placed above two *i*’s.

35. Codex 571, Regio-Vaticanus, small-format parchment in folio, of the tenth century. On the first folio is the end of a homily or book concerning a woman caught in adultery; the ending is: “grace corrects what punishment could not.” The book ends. The names of the bishops of Paris begin: Dionysius, etc., Peter, Maurice, Odo. The latter is the last who flourished in the tenth century; in a more recent script are added Peter and William. It is also noted, in the same recent script, “E Mss. S. Mariani Antissiodorensis,” by which some things are likewise corrected in the catalogue.

36. A certain document of Geoffrey, abbot of Saint-Germain of Paris, follows in an old script similar to the first. [Col. 0840A] Then follows an untitled work:

“These are the causes which the ever-August Lord has always commanded to us for the benefit of the holy Church of God through his sacred letter.”

Chapter 1: “How, or in what manner,” etc. Besides others, Ephrem, Cassian, and Cassiodorus are praised. The work is incomplete. It should be noted that *causae* is used for “things,” as among Italians and Spaniards, *cose*, *cosas*. Another mutilated work follows: “You lay in the manger.” There are Sibylline verses:

“Hear what she said: ‘Of judgment,’” etc.

In the headings of the verses, both in Latin and Greek, one finds: “Jesus Christ, Son, God, Savior” (*Iēsous Christos Yios, Theos, Sōtēr*).

37. Page 6, in the same script: verses of Jerome to blessed Augustine:

“He lies,” etc.

Augustine to Jerome:

“Bethlehem celebrates you; the whole world resounds with you;

[Col. 0840B] Our library also sets you forth through your books.”

Consult chapter 81 on the verses of Isidore’s Library. A prophecy of the Sibyl concerning the end of the world follows:

“There shall arise a leader. On one side his name is Salic, and on the other side Lombard.”

There are several prophecies concerning the Saracens, etc. It ends:

“Then the Lord Jesus Christ will come to judge the world by fire.”

The Sibyl is said to have lived 362 years, from the time of David to the time of Darius, king of the Medes. She was born in Syria, of Manasseh as father and Papilia as mother, from the family of Alexander the Great. From there she came to Cumae. Thus the old book.

38. A description of a certain learned man, briefly excerpted from codices, addressed to Queen Gerberga, daughter of Henry, the most noble king of the Saxons, concerning the Antichrist, evil in every respect, etc.

“At the beginning we must set forth for ourselves,” etc. [Col. 0840C] In the same place:

“Certain of our teachers, however, say that one of the kings of the Franks will hold the Roman Empire in its entirety; he will exist at the end of time, and he will be the greatest and the last of all kings.”

It ends: “He determined [*praefinxit*], perhaps ‘preordained’ [*praefinivit], that he must be judged.” Lest I linger over these matters, see Baronius, year 939, no. 4, as well as Pagius and Saint Martin of León, vol. IV, p. 378 and following. An untitled piece follows:

“One must not think that the devil remained in heaven for any length of time,” etc.

Also, certain excerpts from the Fathers.

39. In the same place, page 13: “Isidore on the signs of storm or calm.” This is chapter 38 of *On the Nature of Things*, beginning with the words: “Signs of storms for sailors, etc.; there will be heat.” After this follows an untitled homily:

“Dearest brothers, on this day on which we celebrate the feast of our glorious Lady, namely, the mother of our Redeemer, etc., to recover and possess the perpetual grace of her Son, Our Lord Jesus Christ, who, etc.”

40. A *Method for Liberating Those Held in Chains with God’s Help* follows. Thirteen Masses are prescribed, to be sung by thirteen priests; while each is being sung, a deacon or another cleric is to sing the psalm “Praise the Lord, all nations,” etc., one hundred times, with genuflections. These practices have the odor of superstition. The script of this part of the codex is from the thirteenth century. Concerning the thirty Masses which are called Saint Gregory’s, and in what sense they were prohibited, the Bollandists provide instruction in the *Chronological-Historical Commentary*, where they discuss Saint Gregory. Incidentally, the *Dictionary* of Ducange should be corrected: there the words of Paul Maffei, “We began the Masses commonly called Saint Gregory’s …,” are explained as referring to Masses celebrated according to the Gregorian rite, whereas they should be understood as referring to the thirty Masses called Saint Gregory’s.

A homily for the feast of Saint Peter in Chains follows. A miracle and the discovery of the chains at Jerusalem in the time of Pope Alexander are recounted:

“It should be noted, dearest brothers, for what reason this feast is celebrated,” etc., “the giver of very many gifts of healing,” etc.

41. In another script, no older, is the *Life of Leufredus the Abbot*, with a prologue. It appears in the Bollandist *Acts*, 21 June. He lived under the kings Hildebert and Hilperic, etc.; he died on the eleventh day before the Kalends of July. The author wrote the Life from ancient records and the tradition of his forefathers. “In our times,” he says, “he was transferred by John, bishop of Bolensis [Col. 0841B] and abbot of that place,” etc.—that is, in the ninth century.

42. The *Life of Saint Theobald the Confessor*, with a prologue to Arnulf, Theobald’s father:

“He flourished in the times of Henry the Emperor, and of Henry, king of the Franks, and of his son Philip.”

The author says at the end:

“I call upon his indwelling Holy Spirit as witness that I have omitted many things known to me and have barely touched upon a few branches from a great forest.”

Theobald lived in the eleventh century. The *Life of Saint Anianus, Bishop of Orléans*, follows:

“At that time, when the shining new planting of the faith was spreading through the Gallic land on the wheel of the world,” etc.

43. In another, older script follows Sallust’s *Catilinarian War*, without a title: “All men,” etc., “were celebrating joys.” In the same place is the *Jugurthine War*, without a title:

“He falsely complains about his own nature.”

It is mutilated near the end: “he wished the peace to be ratified”—the final words of this work. On page 71 verso is an ancient geographical map, perhaps written in the ninth or tenth century, on which, as I said in chapter 61, among other things, the following peculiar statement is recorded in farther Spain near the river Minius:

“Here Saint James preached.”

44. The *Virtues, or Miracles, of Blessed Dionysius* follows. It begins: “Very many miracles”; it ends: “of this saint’s investigator.” The script belongs to the twelfth or thirteenth century and differs from the preceding one. Subsequently, in a more recent script of the same kind:

“Concerning the death of Gervasius, archbishop of Reims: ‘Of certain religious men,’ etc.; ‘he prepared what was necessary, by the favor of,’ etc.”

45. In addition, the *Life of Dagobert, the King’s Brother*:

“Fourth from Clovis,” etc., “he ended his life together with his kingdom.”

In the same script, with a more recent title: “Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis on the church built by him: ‘Of divine things,’ etc., ‘the choir of angels and the holy Cross.’” The work is mutilated. See Baronius with Pagi’s notes at the year 1140, no. 21.

46. Codex 667, Regio-Vaticanus, paper, in octavo. Another number, 1059, is given, and the codex is cited under that number in some places, as I said in chapter 79. It was Petau’s volume 288. Title: *Chronology and Order of the Gothic Kings*. Also, *The History of King Wamba of Toledo*, published by Julian, bishop of the see of Toledo. The notice of the person who later, in the age of printing, copied these little books from an old codex follows; he says that he copied them faithfully and in conformity with the original.

47. Page 2: *Chronology and Series of the Gothic Kings*. [Col. 0842A] “The first to reign among the Goths was Athanaric,” etc. It ends with Roderic and the invasion of the Moors. At the end:

“In the era DIX. LXV, Charles, king of the Franks and patrician of Rome, reigned.”

Perhaps one should read *era 765*. The little work seems to have been composed in the time of Charlemagne by some Gaul from chronicles of the genuine Goths that then existed; for that reason I judged it worthy of being copied.

Page 11 verso:

“Letter of Paul the traitor, who tyrannically rebelled against Wamba, the prince of Toledo. The history of Wamba, king of Toledo, published by Lord Julian, archbishop of the see of Toledo, concerning the expedition and victory by which he subdued, in a celebrated triumph, the province of Gaul rebelling against him:

‘It is customary for virtue to be a protection,’” etc.

It ends:

“let him recognize through proscriptions. End of the history.”

“Judgment pronounced against the treachery of tyrants, by the same Julian [Col. 0842B] as author:

‘The marked transgression of traitors ought to be struck all the more harshly,’” etc.

It ends:

“lest the ages to come refuse to imitate it” (read: “refuse,” plural).

These passages should be compared with those published in volume II of the *Toledan Fathers*. A subscription is added:

“In the year 1127 from the incarnation of the Lord, Peter William, armarius, wrote this book in honor of Saint Giles, under Peter the abbot and in the twentieth year of Louis, king of the Franks.”

This is the copyist of the book in the year 1127, from an older codex containing the chronology; the subscription was retained by a more recent copyist.

48. Codex 846, Regio-Vaticanus, parchment in folio, perhaps of the eighth century. At the beginning there is a note assigning it to Alexander, son of Paul, Petau, senator of Paris, in 1647, perhaps in his own hand; the index of contents in this volume was written in the same hand. The chapters of the Theodosian book begin. It is the Theodosian Code, abridged by Anianus at the command of King Alaric, together with the Novels of Valentinian, Marcian, Majorian, and Severus. Book I and the beginning of Book II are absent. Gaius’s Book I follows—that is, the *Institutes* of Gaius. The *Sentences* of Paul follow, and the Gregorian Code through chapter 7, exclusive. Several leaves have been torn out.

Page 68: “The chapters of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, from the book of the *Etymologies*, concerning laws, begin.” In the initial letters, smaller letters are mixed with capitals. It is Book V of the *Etymologies*, consisting of 27 chapters; some things are omitted. It begins:

“First of all,” etc., “has been granted through nature.”

On the verso, in the same script:

“These are the names of the Frankish kings: Chlothar,” etc. [Col. 0842D] “The last: Pippin reigned for sixteen and a half years” (sic). The codex therefore appears to have been written after the year 768, as can also be inferred from the script. Some leaves are missing. An index of the Salic Law follows, mutilated at the beginning, with 48 chapters.

49. The decree of King Childebert follows:

“The illustrious men, when in the name of the Lord … they had been preserved.”

At the end:

“In the eleventh year of the reign of the lord Charles, most glorious king, in the month of March.”

This appears to have been written by the copyist of the codex to indicate the date when the codex was written: the script is the same, but Roman capital letters are mixed with others of smaller form.

Page 39: a work mutilated at the beginning, copied in Tironian notes. The title of chapter 3, in red, is: “On Penance.” The title of chapter 4 cannot be understood in the notes; chapter 5: “On the Second Age,” though *second* is obscure; chapter 6: “On Virginity”; 7: “On Justice”; 8: “On Envy”; 9: “On Silence”; 10: “On Pride”; 11: “On Wisdom.” Leaves are missing. Chapter 22: “On Desire”; chapter 23: “On Discipline and Reproof”; chapter 25: “On Teachers, or Rulers”; chapter 26: “On Faith”; chapter 27: “On Hope”; chapter 28: “On Grace”; chapter 29: “On Discord”; chapter 30: “On Oaths”; chapter 31: “On Acceptance of Persons”; chapter 32: “On the Journey.” Leaves are missing. Chapter 40: “On the Old and the Young”; chapter 41: “On Disputes”; chapter 42: “On Curiosity”; chapter 43 has its final title written in the notes.

In the same Tironian notes:

“The consolatory letter to those going to war begins: ‘Men, brothers.’”

These words are explained in Latin letters; others remain enclosed in notes.

[Col. 0843B] 50. There is added:

“The extracted sayings on various matters begin.”

At the beginning, *Homo* (“man”) is clearly legible, and after several notes *humum* (“earth”), and after others *limo* (“clay”); thus certain words are written out in full. Page 103, in the same notes: “Prologue.” The following words can be read in this prologue:

“Since, frequently, I had promised, more celebrated.”

Afterward:

“The work on names begins” (perhaps “of the Hebrews,” for the note adds:) “Adonai, Sabaoth, Jesus, etc. Rachel.”

Then:

“The names of the Patriarchs begin: Reuben … Aaron … Pharaoh.”

Then:

“On leaders: Joshua … Simon … besieging …”

Then:

“The names of the apostles: Peter … guardians of the Samaritans.”

51. Page 1[…..]8 verso, in the same notes:

“The *Orthography* begins. Orthography …”

This is chapter 26, or alternatively 27, of Book I of the *Etymologies*, as is clearly inferred from the many words written out in full. The final word is written very clearly: *sicilicus*. The same notes are followed by *Antidotum Egias*, that is, certain medical remedies. For *Egias*, perhaps one should read *Hygias*, that is, “of Health.” The work certainly concerns health. The script of the codex is extremely ancient; diphthongs are written separately, and there is a single point, usually in the middle of the letter.

## CHAPTER CI

The remaining fourteen manuscript copies of the Library of Queen Christina of Sweden are reviewed. Certain old works on years, cycles, the computus, and so forth. The book of Ethicus, translated into Latin by Saint Jerome. Ancient writers on music. *Etymologies* in an order different from that of the printed editions.

[Col. 0843D] 1. Codex 982, Regio-Vaticanus, oblong quarto. At the beginning it is noted that several quires have been removed from this codex, containing the constitutions of Boniface VIII [327] and others. First is a dialogue, mutilated at the beginning, on biblical matters. The final question is:

“Why is Jesus called an infant boy, when infancy ends in the seventh year and boyhood closes in the fourteenth?”

Answer:

“This is certainly so because Jesus came to minister and to hunger” (read: “to serve”), “for the Son of Man did not come to be ministered to, but to minister,” etc. “Indeed, every minister and every servant is called a boy,” etc.

The first question encountered here is:

“In how many ways did John understand that he was to be baptized by Christ?”

It appears to be a dialogue between a teacher and a pupil. The following then begins:

“In the name of Our Lord Jesus Christ, the names of the cities situated in the three parts of this world begin, namely Asia, Africa, and Europe: ‘Let no one think me ignorant,’ etc. ‘Lugdunum comes first,’” etc.

In listing the Gallic cities, the author dwells especially at length. Jerome’s letter follows:

“How clerics ought to live, to Oceanus: ‘You have asked,’” etc.

In the same place, page 12 verso:

“The sayings from Saint Isidore’s exposition on Leviticus begin: ‘On the High Priest and his worship.’”

This is the end of chapter 12 of the commentary on Leviticus, beginning with the words:

“For he says of him: ‘He shall not uncover his head,’ etc. Likewise, a saying of Saint Isidore, bishop, on Leviticus.”

This is the whole of chapter 13.

Likewise:

“The work from Saint Isidore’s book *On Offices*, concerning clerics, begins: ‘Therefore all who are in the ranks of ecclesiastical ministry,’ etc.”

Chapters 1, 2, and 3 of Book II *On Offices*. The titles of the Theodosian Code follow. The script of this codex is thus far of the eighth or ninth century. There are points, a point and comma, and a comma and point. Some fragments of a document concerning Saint Anianus, a decree of the pontiffs, and so forth, have been added in a more recent script. At the end is a line measuring the length of Christ, which I set out in Appendix 5 to Sedulius.

2. Codex Regio-Vaticanus 1026, containing a collection of canons entitled *Polycarpus*, parchment quarto. At the beginning is a catalogue of the Roman pontiffs. The last are Calixtus and Honorius, who attained the pontificate in 1124. In this catalogue too, as in others, we find:

“Damasus, a Spaniard by birth, sat,” etc.

The following rubric is appended:

“The prologue of Gregory, cardinal priest of the title of Saint Chrysogonus, begins. To Didacus, bishop of the church of Saint James:

‘To the beloved Lord Deacon (read: Didacus), adorned with the pontifical insignia of the church of Saint James, the humblest of the presbyters [the printed text has “gr gr”] sends greetings. You asked long ago,’” etc.

After the prologue there is an index. The title of Book I is “On the Primacy of the Roman Church,” as is indicated in another Vatican codex cited by the Ballerini, part IV, chapter 17, concerning ancient collections of canons. Decrees of councils are also added; in the margin it is noted that, from the Roman council of 1124, certain items missing in Labbe are found in this codex.

3. After several other items there is the rubric:

“The letter of Isidore, bishop of Seville, directed to Ludefredus, bishop of Córdoba, begins: ‘Having read,’” etc.

It is mutilated at the end, as in Gratian and Breul, p. 413; it is also written incorrectly: shortly after the beginning, *affectu superno* appears instead of *affectu paterno*. At the end of the codex are certain collections of sayings in which Isidore’s *Etymologies* are cited:

“In the part of Syria which is called Phoenicia, and …”

4. Although this collection of canons still lies hidden in manuscript, it is frequently celebrated by those who have devoted themselves to the emendation of canon law. The Ballerini did not see this Regio-Vatican codex, nor another of the same Library of Queen Christina, numbered 987, parchment quarto, with the following title:

“Distinctions of the ancient Fathers divided into eight books and confirmed at the apostolic see of the city of Rome,” as is stated (in the abbreviation P) at the beginning and end of all the books.

“The titles of Book I, concerning the primacy of the Roman Church, begin,” etc.

Decrees of councils are also appended in this codex; [Col. 0845A] but, it seems, leaves are missing at the end. This codex is older than Regio-Vatican 1026; and I think it should be noted that the collection in Codex 987 is not attributed to Cardinal Gregory, nor dedicated to Didacus, bishop of Compostela—namely, the one called Gelmírez. The distinguished Bayer, in his note on chapter 6 of Book VII, no. 109, of the *Bibliotheca Veterum Hispanica*, plainly calls the author of this collection Gregory, a Spanish priest. This is by no means established. It seemed to me that he was some one of the Roman cardinals whom Didacus Gelmírez, who had formerly lived in Rome, had made his associates. My friend Menchaca had intended to discuss these matters, if his other occupations had allowed him to publish the collection itself, annotated as he was preparing it.

5. Codex 1048, Regio-Vaticanus, parchment in folio, of the eighth or ninth century. The first title fills the entire page in five lines, partly in red and partly in black letters of larger form, with some smaller letters mixed in; namely:

“Certain excerpts from the book of the *Etymologies* begin.”

On folio I verso is the title:

“From what causes words in Roman laws received their origin and names: On the authors of the laws,” etc.

There are certain chapters from Book V of the *Etymologies* and from Book IX, with genealogical tables of relationships, many things being omitted.

6.

“The chapters from the Book of Laws begin. The chapters from the first book of Theodosius.”

There are sixteen books.

“The chapters from the books of the Theodosian corpus end. The chapters of the title of the Novels begin. The chapters of Book I of the Novels of the divine Theodosius end. The chapters of Book II of the Novels of the divine Valentinian begin. Book III of the divine Marcian begins. The chapters of Book IV of the divine Majorian begin. The title of Book V of the divine Severian begins. The chapters of Book VI of Gaius (read: Gai, as at the end) from the Theodosian corpus begin.”

At the end:

“The chapters of the Book of Gaius, Book I, end. The chapters of Book I of Paul’s *Sentences* begin. Book II of the same author; Books III, IV, and V. The chapters from the Gregorian corpus begin. The work of Hermogenianus begins. The work of Hermogenianus ends. The work of Papianus begins (sic). The chapters of the Book of Laws end.”

After the title of Papianus is added:

“The *condictio* begins”—the word is obscure, perhaps *edictio*—“when, in the presence of that illustrious man, etc., he is not first heard by the judge.”

7. Immediately, in the same ancient script:

“King Theodoric reigned seventeen years. King Clovis reigned three years. King Childebert reigned seventeen years. King Dagobert reigned five years. King Hilperic reigned five years. Likewise King Theodoric reigned seventeen years. In the meantime no other king reigned for one year. King Hilperic reigned eight years. In all, there are seventy-nine years. King Pippin reigned eighteen years. The work ends happily.”

The codex seems to have been written shortly after Pippin. The following then appears:

“In the name of the immeasurable Holy Trinity, glosses of letters composed in three languages—Latin, Hebrew, and Greek—begin.”

It begins:

“Affectat, captat, temptat” (“He seeks, catches at, attempts”).

They are mutilated at the end. Almost all the words that remain visible are Latin. At the beginning of the glosses, written in a more recent but ancient hand, is:

“Robert the count, and Duke Manasses.”

The script of the codex is Roman, clear, and large; diphthongs are joined; points occur below, above, and in the middle; also a point and comma.

8. Codex 1260, Regio-Vaticanus, parchment quarto, apparently of the ninth century, written in a polished Gallic script. At the beginning is the name of Peter Daniel of Orléans. On the first page, in an old script, are two enigmas:

“There is a house upon the earth, but it always lives in the waves.

If you remove its head, a strong man in armor appears.

If you remove its middle, a blow with a sword becomes evident.

If you remove its end, a winged creature seeks the sky with its feathers.”

Another:

“Not sown in marriage, I am born a virgin from a virgin.

I am born through intercourse, yet I am not conscious of intercourse.”

Rubric:

“The book of Bede the priest, *On the Nature of Things*, begins: ‘The various natures of things,’” etc.

There are interlinear glosses. *On the Nature of Things* ends. Without a title:

“Times in moments, hours, months,” etc.

Much follows concerning Easter, etc. Page 10, without a title:

“Time is divided according to the six ages of the world,” etc.

A brief chronicle. There Tiberius is given nine years. Hermenegild, king of the Goths, is crowned with martyrdom. It ends: “Leo, three years. Tiberius then completes his fifth year,” etc.

9. A letter *On the Equinox*, which is by Bede. It ends:

“confirms that it was the equinox.”

A recent note says: “Up to this point it agrees with the printed editions” (of Bede). The following untitled work begins:

“For there is a method by which the date of Easter can be found.”

Much follows on this subject, as in other manuscripts. Page 17, without a title:

“To Lord and son Sisebutus, Isidore. Although I am not unaware that you excel in talent and eloquence and in the varied flower of letters, nevertheless you devote still greater care and demand from me certain things from the nature of things, [Col. 0846C] or from their causes, to be supplied to you.”

A recent note says:

“I found this book of Isidore cited in an old glossary or lexicon, to which he assigns the title *On the Natures of Things*.”

Then comes a table of contents. The final chapter is 46, “On Mount Etna.” There are notes and verses concerning the winds in a smaller old script; the chapter on the names of the sea and rivers is absent. At the end:

“he will never possess”; in the same hand, chapter 47 is noted in the margin, though it seems to have been partly erased again by the same hand. Namely, in the same script there follows:

“You perhaps, sluggish in the grove,” etc.,

a poem which someone entitled chapter 47. There are some recent marginal notes. I think that poem was formerly published from this codex; see chapter 76.

10. Page 44 verso:

“The book of Hyginus, an experienced teacher, on astronomy begins. Hyginus sends very many greetings to Marcus Fabius. Although I see that you, led by your study of grammatical art, excel not only in the regulation of verse (the same hand corrects this to ‘melody’), which few have perceived, but also in the variety of histories, through which knowledge of things is discerned,” etc.

Isidore seems to have imitated this opening in his book *On the Nature of Things*. The work ends:

“The sun returns from the summer circle.”

A recent note says: “Here Hyginus ends in the printed editions.”

11. Page 84, without a title:

“Each of the planets has its own circles,” etc.

Page 80 verso, verses:

“To the regions of Boreas the Bear and the Serpent turn.”

A recent note says: “They are attributed to Ausonius.”

Page 87, rubric:

“In the name of God, a few things concerning the method of computing according to the sun and moon begin:

‘Let him read me who wishes to know the cycles of the years,

Who wishes to know the changing seasons and the stars of the sky together.’”

“It must be known to us,” etc.

Isidore is frequently cited. A lengthy work on cycles, with tables, etc., as in Muratori’s *Anecdotes*. Page 118: “Arguments for investigating times,” etc., from Dionysius:

“If you wish to know how many years there are from the incarnation of the Lord,” etc.

The total is 788. The work was being written in that year. Page 119: other arguments from Victurius (Victorius) of Massilia:

“If you wish to know how many hours the moon shines on each night,” etc.

12. Page 125, rubric:

“The book of Ethicus, published from a philosophical oracle and translated into Latin by Jerome the priest, begins. From the cosmography—that is, the account of the world—published by the philosopher and cosmographer Ethicus:

‘Investigating the notebooks of philosophers through shrewd inquiry,’” etc.

It ends:

“he hastened to the holy mountain and the most famous altars of Jupiter.”

In other manuscripts too this translation is attributed to Jerome.

Page 165, rubric:

“The *Hermeneumata* begin. On ten kinds of medicines:

‘These are derived from terrestrial and marine animals; from herbs or seeds; from woods or stones; from flowers or tears; from juices’ (perhaps *succis*, “juices”), ‘and from metals. Translated from Greek into Latin. Asarum, that is, a berry or vulgagine,’” etc.

There are several lexica of words of this kind. The second begins:

“Aarsicon, that is, the berry of the juniper.”

The third concerns only the letter P. From the *Antebolumina*:

“Proaganta, that is, a line.”

It ends:

“Proxilocasia, brateus.”

“The *Antebolumina* of Galen end.”

The fourth, “On Weights,” etc., without alphabetical order:

“Calculus,” etc.

The fifth: “On Herbs or Pigments: Anefus, an herb,” etc.

The sixth:

“Antrix, that is, redness on the surface of the skin.”

The seventh is again Galen’s *Antebalumina*, alternatively *Antebolica* or *Antebolumina*, with a prologue. These differ from the preceding works.

13. Codex 1315, Regio-Vaticanus, large folio, written in an elegant fifteenth-century script, mutilated at the end: a collection of certain works on music.

1. Rubric:

“The first book of Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius on the art of music begins. Proemium: ‘Indeed, the mind,’ etc.”

Five books with diagrams. Page 72: a saying of Macrobius on music from his commentary on the *Dream of Scipio*. Page 78 verso: a saying of Fulgentius on music in the book *On the Fictions of the Poets*.

[Col. 0847D] 14. Page 81, rubric:

“The saying of Isidore on music in the book of the *Etymologies* begins.”

There are nine chapters from Book III, *On Music*, chapters 14 through 22. Page 84, rubric:

“On metrical feet according to Isidore. Feet are those which,” etc.

It ends:

“*Dasian* produces *psilen*.”

“The work on metrical feet according to Isidore ends.”

These are chapters 16 and following of Book I of the *Etymologies*.

15. Page 86 verso, rubric:

“Isidore’s treatise on harmony and celestial music, and on the seven consonances of the planets, begins; I discussed it in chapter 86.”

“The sayings of Isidore on music end. The *Enchiridion* of Odo, abbot, on the art of music begins:

‘Just as articulated voice,’” etc.,

with diagrams and scholia, which are mutilated at the end.

16. Codex 1573, Regio-Vaticanus, parchment quarto, from the beginning of the eleventh century. At the beginning, in a more recent script, it is noted:

“Choisnyn, herald of Castries,”

who was perhaps once the owner of the book. First is the Martyrology of Saint Peter of Ferrières, for the whole book seems formerly to have belonged to the monastery of Ferrières; on the sixth day before the Ides of October is celebrated the passing of Saint Aldricus, archbishop of Sens and abbot of this place.

Certain events from the Old Testament are noted, for example, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of April:

“A woman deceived Adam.”

On the eighth day before the Kalends of April:

“The forming of Adam, the Annunciation of the Lord, the sacrifice of Isaac, the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt, and the Crucifixion of the Lord.”

On the eighth day before the Kalends of March:

“The Chair of Saint Peter. Spring rises.”

On the tenth day before the Kalends of December:

“Of Cecilia the virgin. Winter rises.”

And likewise summer and autumn.

A table of the ecclesiastical computus follows: [Col. 0848B] verses concerning the week, “The first day of Phoebus,” and other verses concerning signs and months:

“You behold the April Kalends, Aries of Phrixus,” etc.

Many other tables and explanations concerning the ecclesiastical computus follow.

17. After this work is the rubric:

“The preface of Herericus on the method of the computus begins:

‘With certain of our brothers,’” etc.

Herericus also taught grammar; he cites Bede. He was writing in the year 978, as is clear from chapter 24. Here he is called Helpericus by Pez in *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, vol. II, col. 183; Pez observes that the manuscripts vary concerning the year in which he wrote, for some give 975, others 980, others 1005, others 1020, and others 1090. This variation should be attributed to the scribes, who calculated the year in which they themselves were writing. In our codex, a recent hand notes at the beginning that it was written in 981; but this is an error, because the author of the note did not pay sufficient attention to Herericus’s words.

It ends:

“that we may attain it more easily. It ends. May those who wrote and made it rejoice, recorded in the everlasting book.”

The letter of Abbo, abbot of the monastery of Fleury, follows:

“Abbo, lover of Christ, lover Abbo, rector of the people of Fleury, to brothers and sons G. and U. I [*epe*; perhaps *saepe*, ‘often’] remember wishing to benefit you more than I was able, whom I regard as men of longing. Therefore, desiring to unravel the nature of the great cycle and its most obscure question,” etc.

The names Goffridus and Umbertus are indicated in the margin. Abbo was writing in 1003. There are many tables and diagrams concerning the ecclesiastical computus, epacts, etc.

18. On folio 66 verso: “Here begins the Book of Astronomy. Astronomy is the law of the stars,” etc. Chapters 23 and following of Book III of the *Etymologies*: “that he might lead to contemplation” (*contemplatione perduceret*); Breulius reads “he might place in contemplation” (*contemplatione collocaret*). The codex is incorrectly written. Then: “On the preparation of the bissextile year. Therefore, in the first year of preparation for the bissextile year,” etc. Then: “Here begins the book on the Fourteen Divisions of Time. How many are the divisions of time? Fourteen, namely, atom, moment,” etc. Isidore is frequently cited: “Isidore defined,” “saying,” and similar expressions. This is a work of no small size, attributed to Bede in volume I of his works. On page 89: “Here begins the Book of the Stars of Heaven, edited by Isidore, Bishop of Seville. To the Lord Brother Sisebut, Isidore:” [Col. 0849A] “While you,” etc. Chapter 47, “On the Parts of the Earth,” is present: “Now the earth,” etc.; “they estimated [it at] one hundred and eighty thousand stades and five.” Breulius reads “they estimated” and omits “and five.”

19. A geographical map follows, with the east above and the west below; to the right of one looking at it is the south, and to the left the north, much as in another map in which, as I have already noted, the preaching of Saint James is related. Another work follows, on the moon and ecclesiastical computation, written in the year 826. “If you wish to know for how many hours the moon shines,” etc. Thereafter the year then current seems to be indicated as 834. Such material, or similar material, occurs among Muratori’s *Anecdota*, volume III. The following then appears: “Here begins an exposition of letters: how they are named and what sound they have among themselves. It is asked who first [formed] letters,” etc. The work is mutilated at the end: leaves seem to be missing.

20. Appended is the following: “Here begins, first, the book of numbers: Therefore one book out of five,” etc. This is a work of Saint Isidore abridged, namely, the *Commentary on Numbers*. Also present is *On Computation, or the Speech of the Fingers*: “On the Reckoning of Time, with God’s help,” etc. This work too is attributed to Bede, but in the printed edition, volume I, other material precedes it. [334] After some other miscellaneous material there is a rubric in elongated letters, partly Carolingian and partly Roman:

> Here ends this book of Saint Peter, which I, namely Gotifridus and Unbertus, had written in his honor, for the repose of our souls.

The book was therefore written at the beginning of the eleventh century. The names of the abbots of the same monastery of Saint Peter follow, in a different script:

> In the time of King Odo, Abbot Engelelmus. In the time of Charles [Martel] and Rudolf, kings of the Franks, Atto was abbot in this place. Hildemannus in the time of Lothair. The abbots Christian, Archemboldus, and Rudolf in the time of Louis. Walfaudus was abbot in the time of Chlothar. Guido and Wuitbaldus in the time of Lothair and Louis.

The first name, Engelelmus, is placed above as though outside the sequence. The script of the codex is clear and Roman; the diphthongs are generally joined in more than one way, sometimes separated; there are points above, few ligatures, and clear forms.

21. Codex 1823, Regio-Vaticanus, quarto, on parchment, in a Gothic Spanish script called Cordellate; I gave a specimen of it in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, p. 59. It may be assigned to the tenth century. It contains the *Books of Sentences* of Saint Isidore. Book I is mutilated at the beginning. It begins with chapter 10, “On Angels”:

> Whose creator is the Holy Spirit,

etc. The work ends:

> It encloses those who are to be made joyful. Here happily ends the third book. Thanks be to God. Amen. I, John, although an unworthy deacon, who wrote out this codex, ask all of you who are going to read this book to pray for me, a sinner, if you have God as your protector.

A similar subscription is read in *Palaeographia Hispana*, plate 14, no. 2, and in other manuscripts. John the deacon, the copyist, may perhaps be the very man who copied the Leonese Codex, described in chapter 85, no. 6. On the verso of the same page, p. 117, there is a note concerning Saint John the Baptist: “As the Easter feast was approaching, John was beheaded, and when the cycle of the year had turned, at the same feast the Lord suffered.”

[Col. 0850A]

22. Folio 118: *On More Difficult Questions of the Old and New Testament*, about which I spoke in chapter 64. It ends: “was being consumed after it had been handed over.” A recent hand notes that a few further items are present in the printed editions, but that the following work, *On the Figures of the Old and New Testament*, is missing.

23. On page 158, without any title or rubric now visible, the following begins: “Certain very well-known names are read [correct *Legis*, ‘of the Law’] and of the Gospels,” etc. This is the prologue to Isidore’s *Allegories of the Old and New Testament*. After the end of the prologue, with corrections according to judgment [335] and some division but without a rubric:

> Adam bore the figure of Christ,

etc. After the Old Testament, at the bottom of the page, in an old but different hand:

> The meanings, or figures, of the names and deeds recorded in the books of the New Testament follow. The four Evangelists,

[Col. 0850B] etc. It ends:

> They will be satisfied with resurrection. Amen. The end.

24. On the verso of the same folio, 175, there is the rubric:

> The difference between Christ’s birth and ours is this.

The text continues:

> That every human being,

etc., and similarly in the other differences. These are Isidore’s *Differences* from Difference 6 through 13. The manuscript reads *nunquam emolliat*, “may he never soften”; Breulius reads *emolliatur*, “may it be softened.” Then no. 15:

> Between infancy,

etc. “The first age of a human being.” Thus some material is taken up and ends with a number, or at chapter 31. “Faith is the confession of divinity.” There is nothing else in this codex except a brief note on the time for celebrating Advent.

25. Codex 1824, Regio-Vaticanus, quarto, on parchment, approximately of the fourteenth century, in German Gothic script. Isidore’s *Etymologies*, and, without a title, two of his letters: *Your Holiness* and *Behold for you*, which are the last two letters placed by Breulius before the *Etymologies*. Then comes an index of the chapters of Book I, beginning, “Discipline derives from learning,” etc., and continuing to the end of chapter 4. At this point a rubric is inserted:

> In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the treatise of the book of *Etymologies*, composed by blessed Bishop Isidore.

Book I, “On Grammar”:

> Grammar is the science,

etc. It proceeds in this way through the words, “It would be wicked for us to claim that we have helped against the Rutulians,” chapter 30 of Book II. “On Mathematics,” Book IV:

> Mathematics in Greek is called in Latin …

In the final chapter of Book VI, several additions concerning the solar year, epacts, and so forth are appended. This section begins, “The solar year, as the diligence of our ancestors establishes,” etc., and ends, “they may attain more easily thereafter.” These matters have been treated at length by Bede and others.

26. Thus many things have been added in this codex to Isidore’s genuine *Etymologies*; some others have been abridged, most have been confused and presented in a different order, and they are also found in the printed editions. On the verso of page 70 the copyist wrote in the margin:

> I am the one who wrote this, and I am a good man.

Could this be Alfonsus Bonihominus the Spaniard? At the end:

> Here end the twenty books of the *Etymologies* of the most blessed Isidore, Bishop of Seville. Thanks be to God. Amen.

In a more recent script it is added that prayers were ordered by the Roman pontiff on 15 July 1524 on account of a certain pestilence.

27. Codex 1838, Regio-Vaticanus, paper, octavo or small quarto, [336] of the fifteenth century. It contains several and varied works.

[Col. 0851A]

First, *Scholastic Life* by Bonvicinus of Ripa [otherwise, of Riva; see Tiraboschi, volume IV of the *History of Italian Literature*], which, as noted here, belonged to the library of Saint Sylvester. Bonvicinus’s work is an elegiac poem by which boys are instructed in virtue.

Second, *The Ten Consonants* of Master Sclavus of Barro, composed in verse by James of Benevento. This too is an elegiac poem, in which the way of virtue is taught. Tiraboschi, volume IV, also discusses James of Benevento.

Third, a short work on marriage, which begins in Latin but continues in old Italian:

> In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity: Place, Lord, etc. Venerable Lords, etc.

Fourth, indulgences granted for the feast of Corpus Christi.

Fifth, Saint Anselm, Bishop of Venice, *On the Nativity, Passion, and Resurrection of Christ*. It is leonine prose [Col. 0851B] with glosses.

Sixth, *On Orthography*:

> I ask what orthography is,

etc. Technical verses are interspersed:

> A certain John James of Ferrara, pupil of Posinus of Mombello, wrote this,

and therefore he appears to be the author. The work was written after 1470.

Seventh, *A Sermon on the Mass*:

> A great burden,

etc.

Eighth, Prudentius’s *Dittochaeum*, inscribed with glosses and a commentary, together with Prudentius’s *Book on the Dove*, about which I spoke in my *Prudentiana*.

Ninth, epitaphs of John Visconti, archbishop, and of Simon of Trent, the boy martyr.

Tenth:

> The summer, already burning, scorched the lands of the Ethiopians,

an eclogue and dialogue between Pseustis and Alethia. The author is Christian, but the work appears to have been copied from an old codex, for it is mutilated in places. Verses of Saint Cyprian are inserted:

> There is a place,

etc. The eclogue then continues. It ends on 26 October 1474.

28. Although in this codex the eclogue is anonymous, Goldast published it in the *Biblical Manual* under the name of Bishop Theodulus, prefacing it with the title *Pseutis, Alithia*. He nevertheless doubts whether this is the Theodulus mentioned by Gennadius, who flourished in 475, or Theodulus, Bishop of Sion, who lived around the year 500. In Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, Theodulus the Italian is asserted to have been the author of this eclogue in the tenth century. In it, the miracles of the Old Testament are compared with the inventions of the ancient poets. Yet in a certain manuscript it is said that Saint John Chrysostom composed this poem. Several editions are also listed.

I have found the same eclogue in many manuscript codices: in Vaticanus 5161, on parchment, where it is attributed to Theodulus; in Vaticani 1479 and 1663, under the name of Theodulus or Theodorus, with the title *Theodulus’s Eclogue, Paradise, or On Faith*, with a gloss; in Regio-Vaticanus 1386 [337], with this inscription:

> Poem on the Fathers of the Old Testament, by Matthew of Vendôme.

The codex is a parchment octavo. In Regio-Vaticanus 1556, according to the inventory:

> Poem by Matthew of Vendôme, or by Theodulus, on the Fathers of the Old Testament.

In Ottobonianus 279, on paper, according to the inventory:

> An exodal book [perhaps *eclogal* or *dialogal*], in verse, on the creation of the world, falsely attributed to Saint John Chrysostom.

In Ottoboniani 1502, 1961, and 3145, it is attributed to Theodulus or Theodorus. Eberhard of Béthune, a twelfth-century poet, in the third poem of his work *On Versification*, published by Polycarp Leyser in his *History of the Poets of the Middle Ages*, reports the following about this eclogue among the other poets whom he praises:

> Theodulus keeps truth and falsehood from contention;  
> In meter theology plays with itself.

29. Codex 1850, Regio-Vaticanus, large folio, on parchment, approximately of the fourteenth century, formerly belonging to the library of Saint Sylvester. At the beginning, in a recent hand:

> Manuscript books of the *Origins*, or *Etymologies*, of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, arranged in a different order from the printed editions.

The rubric begins:

> On victims, holocausts, and sacrifices, and what their individual kinds signify.

Chapter 10 appears to have been erased, for chapter 11 follows, “On the Divine Sacraments,” etc. The preceding material is missing. After chapter 15 comes Book VI, “On Man and His Parts.” In the printed editions this is Book XI. The final chapter of Book XX is chapter 43, “On the Furnace of Smiths” [Col. 0852B]. Then comes Book XXI, “On the Construction of Walls,” chapter 23, “On Ornament.” It ends:

> and with the silver of heavenly eloquence.

These are allegorical expositions, examples of which I shall present in the Appendices. Leaves appear to be missing. There are Arabic numerals.

30. Codex 1852, Regio-Vaticanus, quarto or small folio, on parchment. It is written in a more recent script:

> Chronicle of the Monastery of Saints Sergius and Bacchus near the city of Angers.

A note in another hand says that almost nothing in this chronicle concerns Angers. I think it is called the chronicle of that monastery because it had been written for its use, and because certain matters concerning its abbots and affairs of Angers have been inserted.

First, without a title, comes the *Chronicle of Saint Isidore*:

> A brief exposition of the ages.

On the verso of page 17:

> He suddenly converted the Jews of his kingdom to the faith of Christ.

Up to this point Isidore of Hispalis is the author of this chronicle: he flourished until the fifth year of Heraclius and produced many other books. The chronicle is continued in the same script by a certain Peter, as a recent hand notes. It begins:

> Heraclius, however, [recovered] the Lord’s cross from King Chosroes.

It continues in the same script to the year 1138. There, concerning King Louis:

> For after William, Count of Poitiers, had died at Saint James, he took his daughter in marriage; and while he was staying in Aquitaine to celebrate the wedding, her father died and was buried at Saint-Denis.

Here the first script ends. A short chronicle follows in another script, from the year 1138 to 1158; in yet another script, from 1158 to 1165; and in another different script, from 1165 to 1180.

> King Louis of the Franks died.

Thus it ends.

[Col. 0852D]

31. A catalogue of the abbots of the monastery of Saint Sergius is appended; it is mostly erased. On page 27, in another fairly old script, there is another chronicle in which events concerning Angers are recorded, beginning in 1067:

> A terrifying comet appeared,

etc., and continuing to 1157. It ends:

> with the decision that it should be celebrated.

Some additions in a more recent Gothic script concern the years 1180, 1181, and following. The script of the codex is a clear, recent Roman script: strokes appear above the two *i*s; the letters are closely joined together.

In the same codex, in an older Roman script of approximately the tenth century, there is also the following:

> In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. Here begins the episcopal letter of Saint Jerome the presbyter: “Glory to your holiness,” etc.

In the same place:

> Or who could be recognized as having transgressed against the Canons of the Apostles?

The context makes clear that he is speaking of the Roman pontiffs.

> The Letter of Damasus. “The Church rejoices,” etc.

Damasus sends Jerome the *Lives of the Pontiffs*. In the same place:

> Felix, a Roman, born of Anastasius, etc., is crowned with martyrdom and beheaded … He too, having been beheaded together with many clerics and faithful, was secretly brought near the walls of the city, at the Trajan site [*forma Trajana*, uncertain], on the third day before the Ides of November; thereafter the Christians took his body with the presbyter Damasus and buried him in the aforementioned basilica on the Aurelian Way, on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of December, in peace.

There:

> Damasus, a Spaniard by nation, born of Antonius,

etc. The last entries are 96, “Stephen”; 97, “Hadrian, born of Theodore,” etc., from the eighth century. It should be noted that from Leo the Younger onward some of the lives are longer. Some more extensive ones also appear earlier:

> On Gelasius the African, etc. In his time the Manichaeans were discovered in the city of Rome, and he ordered them to be deported into exile; their books he burned before the doors of the basilica of Saint Mary.

Labbe reads, “in exile … and their books also.” In no. 26, after Sixtus and before Felix, the author inserts Dionysius, formerly a monk, “whose parentage we were unable to discover,” etc. Note the care taken in investigating his homeland. The author of this catalogue appears to be earlier than Anastasius the Librarian, since it ends with Stephen and Hadrian. This further confirms that Damasus was genuinely a Spaniard.

[339] 32. Codex 1953, Regio-Vaticanus, large folio, from approximately the eighth or ninth century. “To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio, Isidore”: in large letters, among which some small letters are mixed. Six letters of Isidore and Braulio follow. After the letters, in another ancient script, are these verses:

> Virgin Mother of God, forever a virgin after childbirth—

There are thirty-two verses; the last is:

> You surpass a thousand worlds of light poured forth.

I have copied these verses for publication in Appendix I to the *Etymologies*. Then follows an index of the chapters of Book I, etc. All twenty books of the *Etymologies* are present. At the end:

> Here ends the *Etymologies*.

The book is elegantly written and divided into two columns. The script is Roman; there are points between the middle letters; diphthongs are both separated and joined. Occasionally there are a stroke and a point, but these seem to have been added by a more recent hand. On page 102, in a more recent hand, these verses are inserted:

> Every being draws to itself the terms of two things;  
> Of these, the first is a substance known by name,  
> by whose death its second being soon perishes.  
> But if it should happen to fall, the formula of the subject will stand.

It appears to be a riddle. There are twenty books, though they are not always divided in the customary order.

33. Codex 2034, Regio-Vaticanus, on paper, large folio, formerly belonging to the library of Saint Sylvester, I think on the Quirinal Hill.

> The book of Eusebius Pamphilus on the ages begins. The adjuration of Prosper. I adjure you, whoever you may be who has copied these books, by our Lord Jesus Christ and by his glorious coming, at which he will come to judge the living and the dead, that you compare what you have written and carefully correct it against the exemplars from which you copied it; and that you copy this form of adjuration in the same way and transfer it into the codex you copy.

Jerome’s preface, etc.:

> This ancient work of eloquent men,

etc. Eusebius’s preface:

> Moses of the nation,

etc. Eusebius’s *Chronicle*:

> The ages begin,

etc., through the twentieth anniversary of Constantine:

> Thus far Eusebius; from here onward, Jerome.

It continues to the death of Valens. Prosper follows through the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nonius. After these have been completed, on page 90 there is the rubric:

> Here begins the *Chronicle of Eusebius of Caesarea*,

about which see chapter 61.

Then follows the rubric:

> Chronicle of blessed Isidore: Adam lived 330 years and begot Seth, from whom came the sons of God,

etc., almost as in chapter 39 of Book V of the *Etymologies*. It ends:

> Heraclius, for twenty-seven years. In the fourth and fifth years of this most devout prince, the Jews in Spain, under Sisebut, are baptized. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone. The whole period from the beginning of the world to the present nineteenth year [but this appears to have been corrected to “tenth year”] of the glorious prince Reccesuinth is reckoned as era 616. Amen.

In the margin: “V 834.” The rubric reads:

> Here ends the *Chronicle of blessed Isidore*. Thanks be to God. Amen.

34. The following comes next: *Matthew Palmieri of Florence, On the Ages, to Pietro, son of Cosimo de’ Medici*:

> To our minds,

etc. This codex contains Palmieri’s complete chronicle. At the end of the preface:

> I therefore ask whoever may one day copy this book to write it out carefully, preserving the same order, and to compare and correct what he has copied against the exemplars.

It continues to the year 1448. For information about the author and editions of the work, Fabricius’s *Bibliotheca medii aevi* should be consulted.

[Col. 0854C]

35. Codex 2093, Regio-Vaticanus, large folio, approximately of the fourteenth century. At the beginning, in an ancient script:

> Book of the Holy Cross of the City, of the Carthusian Order;

and in another script:

> First book of the Roman Charterhouse.

The *Pastoral Care* of blessed Pope Gregory follows. After the *Pastoral Care*, on page 54, there is the rubric:

> In the name of the Lord. Here begin the chapters of the *Book of Sentences* of Lord Isidore, Bishop of Seville.

Books I and II of the *Sentences* are present, as well as Book III up to the chapter *On the Justice of Rulers*, including the words:

> Kings easily build up or destroy the lives of their subjects by their own examples.

Leaves are missing. The script is semi-Gothic, with many ligatures; the letters are closely joined together.

## CHAPTER CII

### Manuscripts 13 of the Palatine Library of the Vatican, containing works of Isidore

Homilies of the ancient Fathers. On Isidore’s literal commentaries. A book *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*, and questions on the Old and New Testament, not yet published, in a very ancient codex written in large Roman letters. Several copies of the *Etymologies*.

[Col. 0854D]

1. The Palatine Library, transferred to the Vatican, is filled with old and precious manuscript exemplars. It contains not only those which, as I said in chapter 99, no. 3, came from the monastery of Fleury to the Palatine through the hands of Bongarsius, but also many others formerly preserved in the most ancient monasteries of Fulda and Saint Nazarius at Lorsch. These passed to the Vatican Library together with the whole Palatine collection as a gift from Duke Maximilian of Bavaria in 1623, as Leo Allatius reports in his edition of Eustathius of Antioch’s *Hexaemeron*, p. [Col. 0855A] 151, and *On the Photian Synod*, p. 288. Allatius himself had been sent to bring them away. A catalogue of those libraries, compiled approximately in the eleventh century, still exists in Codex 1877; I have mentioned it elsewhere. Omitting Palatine Codices 59 and 60, about which enough has already been said in chapter 65, and 226 and 233, discussed in chapter 46, I proceed to review the others.

2. Codex 67, Palatine, small folio, on parchment, which Blanchinus describes in volume II of the *Evangeliorum Quadruplex*, p. 604, as follows:

> Description of the Palatine-Vatican Codex numbered 67, which appears to have been written at the beginning of the eleventh century. A specimen of its script is provided as no. 2 of plate VI, placed after page 60. It contains the following: a homily of Saint Isidore beginning, “Brief is the happiness of this world,” etc. Also a sermon on the false friend: “Protector and nourisher,” etc. Then there is this prayer to God, which was recited before the penitential psalms: “Have mercy, Lord, have mercy,” etc. After this there is an image of Erembert prostrating himself before Saint Martin the bishop, with this inscription: “Holy and pious pontiff Martin, grant indulgence to your humble servant Erembert, who begs you.” Immediately afterward follow the sixteen penitential psalms, the last of which is, “Lord, hear my prayer; give ear to my supplication,” etc. At the end of this psalm one reads: “Christ, hear us,” etc. Finally the codex ends with an incomplete commentary on the Psalter, whose beginning is this: “Lord, do not rebuke me in your anger, nor correct me in your wrath. This is the voice of penitents,” etc.

[Col. 0855C]

3. Thus far Blanchinus, who transcribes the entire prayer before the penitential psalms, as well as the prayers after those same psalms. Some believe that the codex is older and assign it to the ninth century. Anyone skilled in judging scripts can form an opinion from the specimen of the handwriting supplied by Blanchinus. The script of the pages preceding the psalms is smaller but equally ancient. I would believe that the author of the commentary was Erembert himself, who is depicted with Saint Martin, unless one prefers to regard him not as the author but as the copyist of the book. The commentary ends: “until he obtains his reward.” I discussed the homily or homilies of Saint Isidore in chapter 72.

4. Codex 216, Palatine, parchment, small oblong folio, approximately of the eleventh century.

> Here begins Saint Augustine’s exposition of Genesis against the Manichaeans: “If the Manichaeans were to choose whom they might deceive,”

etc. Only the beginning of the second book is present; after a few words it breaks off. There is also a homily of Saint Augustine on the Advent of the Lord:

> By the propitiousness of God,

etc. Another homily by the same author, addressed to Sancta, begins:

> A joyful, desirable, glorious, and singular solemnity—that is, the Nativity of the Lord.

5. The following rubric appears:

> Here begin homilies on the Nativity of the Lord: “We read that holy Moses was giving commandments to the people of God.”

The author’s name is not supplied. Nevertheless, the following is added:

> Also another homily by the same author: “Hear, sons of light, adopted into the kingdom of God.”

Here “by the same author” may perhaps mean “on the same feast.” Then come two anonymous homilies for the feast of Saint Stephen:

> Yesterday we celebrated the birthday. Blessed Stephen was the first.

[Col. 0856A] On the verso of page 39 the rubric reads:

> Here begins a homily on the Nativity of Saint James and Saint John the Evangelist: “At that time the mother came to Jesus,” etc.; “we can”; he said to them, “I will take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord.”

Immediately he adds:

> What this cup may be,

etc. Also another homily by the same author:

> After these things Jesus took Peter, James, and John,

etc.

> But it must be asked why Peter, James, and John are here, and in other passages of the Gospels, separated from the others,

etc. Near the end of this homily the discourse proceeds as follows:

> John the apostle and evangelist, the son of Zebedee,

etc. In the margin is added:

> This is John the apostle,

etc. It ends:

> Let the dust boil up; he who lives and reigns forever.

From Isidore’s *On the Origin and Death of the Fathers*. An anonymous homily on the Holy Innocents follows:

[Col. 0856B]

> Today, dearly beloved brothers, we celebrate the birthday of those infants whom Herod,

etc.

6. On the verso of page 52 the rubric follows:

> In the name of Christ begins the Life, or Death, of Saint Landibert, bishop, who suffered on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of October in the village … under the care of Leodium, where the lord Apostolicus himself also rests in peace. If the savage, impious, and prolonged pomp of pagan fictions is eager to commend many lies to its books, so that their empty glory may spread, why should we Christians remain silent about the saving miracles of Christ, when we can reveal to men, even in humble speech, edifying accounts from the history of the saints? Therefore, although the narrative of so great a matter—that of the holy man Landibert, the bishop—

etc.

Its beginning is taken from Sedulius, Book I, at the beginning. Below, Landibertus is said to have suffered in the village of Leodium [Col. 0856C]; but in the title, between “village” and “under the care of Leodium,” there are some letters which I cannot make out. This Life of Landebert, or Landibert, or Lambert, is attributed to Godescalcus the deacon by the Bollandists. See Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Godschalcus.” On page 76 there is a homily of Saint Augustine:

> Dearly beloved brothers, let us do good to all,

etc.

7. On the verso of page 79 the rubric reads:

> An excerpt from the book of Saint Isidore *On the Scourges of God*: “As the subtlety of divine wisdom examines consciences inwardly like a witness, so outwardly,”

etc. It ends:

> and when the day of judgment comes, may they not be punished with the impious and sinners, but may they deserve, with the just and merciful, to attain eternal rewards, with his help,

etc. From chapter 1 of Book III of the *Sentences*, with additions.

[Col. 0856D]

8. On page 83, a homily of Saint Augustine:

> The pious and merciful Lord, dearly beloved brothers, exhorts us through the prophet to contrition,

etc.

On the verso of page 85 the rubric reads:

> Here happily begins an excerpt of Saint Isidore: “Beloved [perhaps ‘most beloved’], keep death before your eyes at every hour; concerning your death,”

etc. From Saint Isidore’s *Synonyms* and other works. It ends:

> they drag them down more heavily, so that the last things of that man are worse than the first.

Immediately follows the rubric:

> Here begins the book of the saint on the despair of sinners [the saint’s name is not stated]: “It is not by distances of place, but by good or evil affection, that one goes away from or returns to the Lord.”

It ends:

> what we shall be toward the end of life.

These passages are from chapter 14 of Book II of the *Sentences*. Immediately follows the rubric:

> Here begins the book of Saint Isidore on the Day of Judgment and on the Despair of Sinners. “I ask you, dearly beloved brothers, and, with great humility, let none of you be angry at this for the sake of happiness.”

[Col. 0857A] It ends:

> may we acquire through merits.

I shall speak of this book below.

9. On the verso of page 96, the rubric reads:

> Here begins an admonition of Saint Faustus. “Now, dearly beloved brothers, when the divine reading was being read, we heard the Apostle admonishing us terribly and beneficially,”

etc.

On page 100:

> Here begins an excerpt from the letter of Saint Fratalus [so it seems] *On the Christian Life*: “I ask you, my son, and in fatherly affection I admonish you,”

etc.

On page 104:

> Here begins Saint Augustine’s letter *On Purifying Fire*: “In the apostolic reading that was recited to us a little earlier, dearly beloved brothers, we heard the Apostle saying: ‘No one can lay any other foundation,’”

[Col. 0857B] etc.

On page 109:

> Here begin the sayings of Saint Jerome; whoever reads them and fulfills them in deed will possess eternal life. “Dearly beloved brothers, we ought to have humility, to keep God’s commandment,” etc. Blessed Augustine says: “Truth cleanses; vanity defiles.” … Jerome says: “Do not seek glory,” etc.

These are not solely sayings of Jerome. On page 116 there is a homily on the Epiphany:

> As we have already suggested to your charity on some occasion.

On the verso of page 121, Saint Augustine’s homily on purifying fire is repeated, somewhat differently but in many respects the same. This is followed by the beginning of the life, or vision, of Saint Paul, who saw in the kingdom of God the works of the just and the punishments of the impious. On page 127 there is a homily of Saint Augustine to the people:

> Dearly beloved, we recall to our memory,

etc.

There is nothing else in this codex, which contains some Lombard letters and many ligatures in the titles, with the letters joined and interwoven. As concerns the works of Isidore mentioned above, the following observations should be made. On the verso of page 47 is chapter 73, elsewhere numbered 72, *On the Origin and Death*. There the text reads:

> Reclining, the streams of his Gospel.

Breulius reads:

> Reclining, and the streams of the Gospel.

Some additions occur in the manuscripts which are present in the fuller book *On the Origin*, about which I spoke in chapter 61, namely:

> The son was left behind. This apostle and evangelist was chosen and loved by our Lord in such great loving affection that at the supper he reclined upon his breast, and, standing alone beside the cross, he entrusted his own mother to him, so that the one whom he had summoned, while she wished to marry, to the embrace of virginity, he might also entrust with the care of the Virgin. While he was preaching the Gospel of Christ in Asia,

etc. The rest is almost as in Breulius. It omits:

> He rested at Ephesus on the sixth day before the Kalends of January.

10. On the verso of page 79, *On the Scourges of God*, etc., chapter 1 of Book III of the *Sentences*, in the form of a homily, as can be gathered from the conclusion. In the manuscripts:

> In this life God spares the impious, yet he does not spare the elect; in that life he spares the elect, yet he does not spare the wicked.

At the beginning:

> Have mercy, Lord, on wretched Isidore.

Thus it does not proceed beyond the words:

> For after death it is more unjust.

In the same context it continues:

> Splendid in charity, white through almsgiving,

etc., words which I have not found verbatim in Saint Isidore, but which seem to have been taken from his works, perhaps even from works that have perished. On the verso of page 85, from Book I of the *Synonyms*, after the middle of the chapter:

> Having resisted,

and from Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 13, *On Penance*, whose ending is:

> worse than the first,

there are passages slightly altered. Everything is badly written. Immediately afterward, partly in red and partly in black letters:

> Here begins the book of Saint Isidore on the despair of sinners,

corrected to:

> On the Day of Judgment.

The words “of Saint Isidore” are red and appear to be by the first hand. Perhaps the first title was:

> Here ends *On the Despair of Sinners*. Here begins *On the Day of Judgment* of Saint Isidore.

The sermon that follows is:

> On the Day of Judgment and on Penance.

There it says:

> For this reason I endeavor to make known to you so frequently, and to make you dread beneficially, the day of judgment,

etc. It is found among the appendices to Saint Augustine, as I said in chapter 82.

11. Codex 239, Palatine, on parchment, oblong folio, from the tenth or eleventh century [345], in a clear French, or cursive, script, with separated diphthongs, points, strokes, and few abbreviations of letters.

> Here begins Prosper’s exhortation to his wife: “Act, I beg, concerning my affairs,”

etc. It ends:

> Let it be one, and let one spirit nourish two. Here begin general sentences in individual verses: “With useful admonitions.”

It ends:

> Things harsh to endure become pleasant to tell.

These verses are found in Hildebert. Without a title there are other sentences arranged alphabetically:

> A woman either loves or hates; there is no third possibility.

It ends at the beginning of the letter L:

> Long is what desire demands.

12. On the verso of page 6 the rubric reads:

> Here begins the book of the *Chronicle* of Saint Isidore, the Younger, bishop: “A brief sequence of the ages,”

etc. In the prologue:

> up to the rule of Augustus, Heraclius, or Lothair, and of King Sisebut,

etc. The name Lothair has been inserted. “The first age of the world. In six days God formed the creation of all things.” Some material is omitted, some added or altered. In the account of Enos, after “the nature of God,” it omits “During the same period he fulfilled.” In the account of Cain, it adds:

> He begot Mahuhiahel, whose name is interpreted: “Who is the Lord God?” or “God from life.”

In the account of Enoch:

> They think so. It should be known that up to the Flood, wherever someone is said in our codices to have begotten at two hundred years and more, the Hebrew has one hundred years, followed by the remaining years.

Jerome is cited in the margin. Later there is inserted:

> It is a famous question,

etc., and in the margin:

> Jerome again.

A few things are then inserted, while more are omitted. At year 5621:

> At this time Pelagius the Briton opposed,

etc. The printed editions omit “the Briton.” At year 5801:

> They return to the Catholic faith. At this time Saint Gregory, the distinguished bishop of Rome, is celebrated. At the same time the Avars, fighting against the Romans, are driven back more by gold than by iron. Phocas,

etc. Other material is omitted. At year 3814:

> converted. Thus from the beginning of the world to the present era there are 5,813 years, that is, in the fifth year of the reign of Heraclius and the fourth year of the most devout prince Sisebut. Years were added according to the calculation that after Heraclius had reigned, Chlodovech, king of the Franks, reigned in his sixth year. Thirty-six years were added to the aforesaid era, which must be reckoned with them. The remaining time of the age,

etc., as in Loaisa:

> the consummation of the age is at hand.

The rubric reads:

> Here ends the book *A Brief Account of the Ages*, carefully collected by Saint Isidore, bishop, according to the truth of history. Amen. From the monastery of Saint Nazarius.

The first chronicle appears to have been interpolated after those thirty-six years, since this codex seems to have been copied in the tenth or eleventh century.

13. Codex 267, Palatine, on paper, folio. First, the *Pastoral Care* of Saint Gregory: “Pastoral care,” etc. Then Saint Bonaventure’s *Book of Meditations*, which is called *The Image of Eternal Life*: “I bend my knees,” etc.

14. On the verso of page 60: “Here begins the first book of blessed Bishop Isidore on Ecclesiastical Institution, and the rest, which is otherwise entitled *On the Highest Good*: Isidore *On the Highest Good*, the *Sentences* of Isidore: ‘The highest good,’” etc. Chapter 19 of Book I is “On the Seven Rules,” etc. The penultimate chapter is 30; the final chapter is numbered 32, but ought to be 31. Book II has 44 chapters. Book III has 39 chapters, the last “On Carnal Priests.” There follows “Book IV, chapter 1, On Angry Teachers.” The chapters continue to be numbered in this way; in the same hand “Book IV” is written in the margin. There are 17 chapters. It ends: “He enclosed those who are to be made joyful.”

15. On page 109: “Treatise on the Seven Advances of Religious: ‘The advances of religious persons are distinguished by seven stages.’” An anonymous work. Bernard is cited in it. It ends: “or we give thanks for benefits received, or for those promised, which may the Lord grant us. Amen.” Then: Meditation on *Miserere* by the venerable Anselm, Bishop of Canterbury: “Most mighty God.”

[Col. 0859C] **16.** Page 517. “Letter of blessed Eusebius to Damasus (sic), bishop of Porto, and to the Roman Senator, concerning the death of the glorious Jerome, cardinal and distinguished doctor.” The Senator is called “Theddonius.” Letter of St. Augustine to Cyril, bishop of Jerusalem, concerning the praise of St. Jerome. Letter of Cyril to Augustine concerning the miracles of St. Jerome. All these are spurious and have already been published. At the end there is a register of the books of the *Sentences*, or *On the Supreme Good*, in which chapters 19 and 20 of Book I are combined under one title, “On the Seven Rules.” After chapter 39 of Book III is added, “Register of Book IV of *On the Supreme Good*.”

**17.** Codex 275 Palatinus, parchment, quarto, apparently of the thirteenth century. At the beginning, in a fairly old hand: “This book belongs to the monastery of Blessed Mary Magdalene [Col. 0859D] at Frankenthal, between Speyer and Worms, of the Canons Regular of the Order of St. Augustine, bishop and doctor.” I discussed this monastery briefly in the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*, p. 37.

**18.** On page 1 there is a verse arranged in a square, in red Roman letters, 347, and within the square an old note: “This writing arranged in a square is a verse in which the final syllable, namely *RUS*, is excessive; it is as follows: ‘Bresit dictando patenter inhaesit Isidorus.’” The antiquarian is mistaken. It should in fact be read: “Isidorus Bresit dictando patenter inhaesit,” with the rhythm and the third short syllable in *Isidorus*, as in the continuation of the *Chronicle* under the name of Isidore by Ildephonsus, and in the verses of Isidore’s library from a Codex of the Vatican Archives. A title in a not very old hand reads: “Isidore [Col. 0860A] on the Old Testament from the beginning of Genesis up to the Migration.”

**19.** Before Isidore’s exposition, from the beginning to folio 33, there are certain biblical observations drawn from the Fathers, especially from Isidore, who is frequently cited. Augustine, Jerome, Victor, Gregory, and Philip are also cited. Page 11: “Concerning that other heaven, however, which is corporeal, Peter says: the water which was within the world, in the space between that first heaven and the earth, is stretched out as though congealed like frost and solidified into crystal.”

**20.** The beginning of this work is: “In the beginning God created heaven and earth, etc.,” up to “he rested from the work which he had performed. In Sacred Scripture four things are sought: the person of the writer, the time of writing, [Col. 0860B] the place of writing, and the character of the teaching.” Perhaps some of Isidore’s literal expositions have been inserted into this work. On page 2, after the words “God made,” is added: “Behold, you have the Father; ‘In the beginning,’ behold, you have the Son; ‘The Spirit of God was moving,’ behold, you have the Holy Spirit.” Rubric: “Isidore: Therefore the Father commands, the Son makes, and the Holy Spirit gives life: one cooperation always exists in the three. For what the Father said, the Son also says, and the Holy Spirit says—or say. What the Son does, the Father also does,” etc.

**21.** Page 3, rubric: “Isidore: Others have interpreted this passage improperly. For they say that it does not concern the Holy Spirit, but another spirit, namely the Spirit of God; among them is Victorinus. They should be asked about that spirit, whether it is a creature [Col. 0860C] or not,” etc.

**22.** Page 7, rubric: “Isidore: In the book *On the Nature of Things* it is said: ‘The Egyptians, however, derive the beginning of the following day from the beginning of the night’” (Breulius has *tradunt*, “say,” less well). In the same place: “Isidore says in the books of the *Sentences*: Before every creature, the angels were made, when it was said, ‘Let there be light.’” Page 32, rubric: “Isidore on the fact that Christ was king: Christ was a king, as the angel foretold when he said, ‘And he will reign over the house of Jacob,’ etc. And he was a priest, as the Psalmist says, ‘You are a priest forever.’” On the same page, rubric: “Isidore on the names of Mary: On the name of holy Mary and on the number of women called Mary in the Gospels. In the Hebrew language, *Maria* sounds like ‘Lady’ or ‘illuminated.’ She is called ‘Lady’ [Col. 0860D] because she carried the Lord of heaven and earth in her womb. Thus she deserved to be called Lady. Again, she is called ‘illuminated’ because, when the sun of righteousness arose from the Virgin’s womb, she was illuminated, and the whole world is illuminated.”

**23.** Isidore’s exposition of Genesis begins on page 33 after the rubric: “Isidore on the word ‘hallelujah.’ These materials were therefore taken from the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and, in our own times, from the notably eloquent Gregory. The chapters of the Book of Genesis begin,” etc. “The creation of heaven and earth,” etc. “Christ is the Beginning,” etc. Here there is a rubric: “Isidore on heaven,” etc. The division into chapters is frequent. On page 68, in the same context and without a rubric, an exposition of Exodus begins: “Certain mysteries . . . weariness.” [Col. 0861A] Rubric: “On the increase of the faithful: First of all,” etc. On page 82 verso: “Exodus is complete. The chapters in the Book of Leviticus begin.” The fragment of the Codex of the College of St. Clement at Bologna is not added. Then come Numbers, Deuteronomy, and the Book of Joshua. It ends: “does not subdue greater things”; Breulius has “does not subject greater things.” Then the Book of Judges, etc. “The exposition of the Book of Judges is complete. The Book of Ruth begins. Let us now consider Ruth, etc., who promised through his son,” etc. It is divided into three chapters:

1. “On the conversion of the nations.”
2. “On St. John the Baptist: First, etc.”
3. “Also on St. John and Christ: That he loosens his sandal.”

Then follow the Books of Kings. Page 128 verso: “The Third Book is complete.”

**24.** Page 129, rubric: “The First Book on Joshua [Col. 0861B] begins: God bestowed the name,” etc. (Rabanus’s work). Page 154 verso: “The Eleventh Book is complete. The Twelfth Book begins according to Bishop Rabanus.” Page 178, rubric: “The Twenty-Sixth Book begins, but it corresponds to the Sixteenth.” Much additional material outside the Book of Joshua is included here concerning Jephthah, Samson, and others. On page 182, rubric: “On the Maccabean brothers. What shall I say about the Maccabean brothers? . . . and all things were completed through Our Lord Jesus Christ.” This is Isidore’s chapter on the Maccabees. It is preceded by other material from Ezra. The Codex appears to have been badly assembled, with Isidore’s exposition mixed together with other material. The final rubric of the Codex is: “Also on kings and prophets.”

In the first biblical work, on page 6, Isidore is cited concerning the days of the month, thirty or thirty-one, etc. “The first day of the world is the Lord’s Day, etc. Whoever wishes to prove this should consider the exposition of St. Theophilus on the calculation of Easter. He was archbishop of Caesarea in Palestine. When he was asked by Pope Victorinus, bishop of the city of Rome, to establish the calculation of Easter, he summoned the bishops of Asia, etc. What else do we believe to be the first day of the world but the Lord’s Day? Theophilus replied: ‘Prove this.’ They answered: ‘And there was evening, and there was morning, one day.’”

This is taken from the acts found in the copy of the *Etymologies* in the Vatican Archives, concerning which see chapter 107. This Codex appears to have been written in the thirteenth century.

**25.** Codex 276 Palatinus, large nearly square quarto, parchment, in a clear cursive hand, of the tenth century or somewhat later. At the beginning, in an old hand, is written: “Book of the monastery of Lorsch. Whoever steals it, let him be cut down by the sword of the demon.” Rubric: “The chapters begin: 1.
