On the birth of Samuel,” etc. There are 21, as in Breulius. “The chapters are complete. The brief exposition of St. Isidore on the Book of Kings begins. After the Book of Judges comes Kings,” etc. Then: “The interpretation of the Second Book of Kings begins.” There are six chapters. Book III has nine chapters, but its final chapter is missing, although listed as follows: “On Elisha and his virtues, chapter VIII.” Book IV has eight chapters. After chapter 8, “pride, aspiring to lofty things . . . rests in fabrication” (Breulius has “in confessing”), there are fragments not yet published. Rubric: “On the unity of faith and charity, which is the fullness of the law. What is ‘one man,’ etc. On Eliana,” etc.

Page 33, another rubric: “On intercourse with a near relative or a deceased brother’s wife: From the law concerning the deceased near relative.” Correct this to [Col. 0862A] “of the near relative.”

Page 38: “The chapters from the Book of Ezra begin.” Four chapters are distinguished, whereas Breulius has three. “The interpretation of St. Isidore on the Book of Ezra begins. For that even after seventy years, according to the prophecy of that same Jeremiah.” Breulius has “of that same Ezra.” At the end of chapter 8 of Book IV of Kings, the prophet Jeremiah is cited. It ends: “we do not repeat.”

Rubric: “The Book of Maccabees begins: ‘What shall I say about the Maccabean brothers? . . . the whole mystery has been completed through Our Lord,’ etc. Amen. Happily complete. Thanks be to Christ God. These are the verses of Isidore, bishop of Seville,” namely the verses of the library, concerning which see chapter 81.

**26.** Page 41: “The Preface begins: To my most beloved brother Nothelm, Bede sends greetings. What concerns the Book of Kings,” etc. There are 30 chapters. “The Book of Questions on Kings itself begins. What the prophet said,” etc. “Enter into the joy of your Lord. The Book of Questions on Kings is complete.” There is nothing else in this handsome Codex.

350 **27.** Codex 277 Palatinus, parchment quarto, written in square Roman letters in the eighth or ninth century, with the words joined together and with every other indication and sign of great antiquity. “The Book of Prefaces—or ‘premiors’ (sic)—of the Old and New Testament begins.” In a more recent hand is added: “Of St. Isidore of Seville. The Prologue begins: The fullness of the New and Old Testament, which the Catholic Church receives in the canon according to the ancient tradition of earlier authorities, is as follows.” The prefaces to the Old Testament end: “and the embassy was completed. The Old History is complete”—for *historia*.

[Col. 0862C] **28.** Page 18, without any title: “Although it is fourfold, it is nevertheless one,” etc. “The preaching of the Gospels” is missing before “although.” These are the prefaces to the New Testament. At the end: “the tree of life, our Lord Jesus Christ. Complete.”

**29.** Immediately afterward, on page 22, without an inscription, is the prologue to the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*: “Of certain most holy and most noble men,” etc. The index lists 83 chapters, but the work contains 84, since Mark was omitted from the index.

**30.** After this book, on page 56: “The authority of the present work begins: Christ, favor good prayers. Now it is time for truth to have taken its seat in the chamber,” etc. “Complete.” This is the prologue. It is followed by the rubric: “The chronicle-history begins, which Clement, or Theophilus, the most beloved bishops of God and chroniclers, likewise explained, and also the beloved chronicler of God, Eusebius Pamphili.” The Chronicle begins: “In the forty-second year of Octavian Augustus Caesar, the Lord was born.” The evangelical history is narrated and expounded at length. A brief chronicle of the emperors from Augustus to Justinian is appended; Justinian reigned thirty-nine and a half years, and Justin, nine years. “The Chronicle is complete. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

**31.** Page 28, rubric: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, the questions of St. Isidore on both the New and Old Testament begin: Tell me. What is,” etc. It ends: “through the waters of the Flood.” This is an unpublished work of Isidore, as I said in chapter 64.

[Col. 0863A] **32.** Page 89, rubric: “The letter on the calculation of days begins: Years together with months, etc., the tradition of the leap year.” Page 90 verso: “Also the computation: Since all the apostles, etc., for celebrating Easter. Complete.” This belongs to the council on the celebration of Easter convened by Theophilus. It is found in a fuller and more correct form among the books of the *Etymologies* in the Vatican Archives Codex 351 than in the published collections of councils. Page 92: “The judgment of Pope Leo on apocryphal writings begins: For it must be taken care that, etc., they are read as the order requires.”

**33.** Page 94, rubric: “Isidore to Orosius, servant of God and most reverend brother: Certain very well-known names, etc., will be satisfied by restoration.”

**34.** Codex 278 Palatinus, parchment octavo, approximately of the eleventh century. The index of chapters of Book I of St. Isidore’s *On the Calling of the Nations* follows. After the title of chapter 60, “Because he will come to judge,” is added: “The superscription of the work. The chapters of this book are complete. Thanks be to God. Amen. In this volume are contained the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the nations. The preface of this book begins: To the holy lady, sister Florentina, Isidore. Certain things,” etc.

The first folios are torn and mutilated. In the table the penultimate chapter is called 60; in the rubric of the text it is 61. The following rubric reads: “The superscription of the work, a summary.” In black letters: “Chapter 62. Behold, new things,” etc. Breulius calls it the Epilogue.

Then follows the table of chapters of Book II, the last being 27. “Recapitulation of the work. The chapters are complete. The text begins. Summary of the preceding little book.” The words “of the preceding little book” should be joined to “the chapters are complete.” Instead of “summary,” perhaps “preface” should be read or understood. It begins: “In part,” etc. It ends: “in which he dwells forever. Amen.”

Rubric: “The Isidore whom he made for Florentina is complete.” This should be emended: “The work of Isidore which he made for Florentina is complete.” Breulius adds: “You say that the formulas of spiritual understanding are to be composed and sent to you,” etc., which is absent from the others and appears to be spurious.

**35.** The Book of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, on Baptism follows: “To the most reverend and dearest Bishop Magnus, Theodulf,” etc. Also his chapters for his clergy, which Baronius published under the year 835: “I beseech you, most beloved, that you strive for the improvement of the subject peoples,” etc. It ends at chapter 44; the work is incomplete. [Col. 0863D] There, chapter 8 reads: “An ancient custom existed in these regions of burying the dead in a church, etc.” The *Capitulare* likewise reports this; I saw the manuscript among the papers of the distinguished Peter Lazeri, under the name of an unidentified bishop. See Sirmond.

**36.** The Codex’s script is small cursive, or Gallic; the point and comma represent the joined diphthong *ae*, sometimes with a point above; two points, a point below, and a comma above; few and simple ligatures, or contractions of letters.

352 **37.** Codex 279 Palatinus, nearly square quarto, approximately of the eleventh century, in a clear Gallic or bookhand. Rubric: “The book of the holy and most blessed Isidore to his sister Florentina begins: Certain things which are different,” [Col. 0864A] etc. These are the two well-known books addressed to Florentina. Book I has 62 chapters, as in Breulius, without a table. At the end: “Summary: Behold, new things,” etc. Then follows the table of the 26 chapters of Book II, and after chapter 26: “Recapitulation of the work.”

This book is mutilated: it ends at chapter 14, “On the cessation of the Sabbath” (chapter 15 in Breulius). At the end, “Thus therefore all things whatsoever belong to them”; instead of “all things,” “for” seems to be intended. Book II begins: “In part,” etc. The chapter titles differ from those in the editions. In this Book II, after chapter XI, “he would be crucified,” comes immediately: “Chapter XII, On the perpetual ruin.” Chapter XI in Breulius’s edition, “Thus the Lord speaks through Isaiah: Who is this,” is chapter 9 in the Codex.

**38.** Codex 280 Palatinus, paper folio, in obscure semi-Gothic letters, of the fifteenth century. First inscription: “Isidore’s *On the Supreme Good* begins.” Again: “The title of this book: Isidore the Spaniard in the *Sentences*.” It is then suggested that people ignorant of the true title named the book from its opening words: “The supreme good begins,” etc.

Book I has 31 chapters; Book II, 44; Book III, 67. Chapter 1 of Book III begins: “Have mercy, Lord, on wretched Isidore, doing what is unworthy,” etc. Book III ends: “encloses those who are to be made joyful.” The book is said to have been written in 1444. Another hand adds: “This book needs correction.” A brief alphabetical index of subjects follows.

Then comes St. Bernard’s treatise *On the Body of Christ*: “Most holy Father Peter, hear,” etc. Several letters of St. Jerome follow, together with St. Augustine’s *Enchiridion*. Then comes the *Sophologium* of Jacob, of the Order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, to Michael, bishop of Auxerre. There are three books; each book is divided into several treatises. Isidore is often cited, for example, Book I, treatise 2, chapter 2: “According to Isidore, rhetoric is,” etc. Chapter 4: “On arithmetic according to Isidore. Arithmetic is a discipline,” etc.

**39.** In Book III, treatise 3, chapter 12, Orosius, Book II, *De Or m' esta mundi* [reading uncertain], is cited; concerning this title there is a very famous question. At the end is the rubric: “The *Sophologium* of Brother Jacob, of the Order of the Hermits of St. Augustine, is complete, written in the year 1444,” as I think. The author is Jacobus Magni of Toulouse, not of Toledo, as some have thought.

**40.** Codex 281, parchment folio, of the eighth or ninth century, written in two columns in a bright cursive or bookhand. The *Etymologies* bear this title: “In the name of the supreme God: To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio, Isidore: With every desire,” etc. Then: “To my lord and truly lord, Isidore, chosen of Christ and supreme among bishops, Braulio, an unworthy servant of the saints of God”—with *sanctorum* corrected to *servorum*, “servant of the servants of God”—“O pious lord.” Other letters follow: “Because I have you safe and well. It is accustomed to be filled. Of your holiness. Behold for you,” etc.

The table of the chapters of Book I follows. There are 29 chapters. It ends: “against nature.” Book II has 32 chapters. It ends: “has nothing third”; corrected to “does not have a third.” The preface of Book III ends: “may be displayed”; Breulius has “may be recognized.” There are 70 chapters. It ends: “to place in contemplation.” The musical figures said to occur in some manuscripts are absent, as in a certain Toledan manuscript. [Col. 0865A] Book IV has 15 chapters. It ends: “the body is healed.”

**41.** Book V has 39 chapters. Chapter 39: “On the description of times. The first age at its beginning contains the creation of the world.” At the end: “Heraclius, 23 years. In the fifth and fourth year of this most religious prince Sisebut, the Jews in Spain are baptized. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone. Book V is complete. The chapters of Book VI begin, namely on the order of the Scriptures, cycles and canons, festivals and offices.” There are 20 chapters.

In the same place, chapter 17: “whose deeds have been set down in this work,” etc. Chapter 22: “The sacrifice is so called . . . by the blood of Christ?” as in Breulius, but “he commanding this . . . by the blood and body of Christ?” Above *operante*, an old hand has written *cognominatione*. [Col. 0865B] In the same place: “The sacraments are baptism and chrism, the body and blood, which for that reason,” etc. There is a point between “baptism and chrism,” but none between “body and blood.”

Book VII has 14 chapters, as in Breulius. Book VIII has 11 chapters. Book XIX has 7 chapters; Breulius has 8. The manuscript alone has a single genealogical diagram in the form of a cross.

**42.** Book X: “On certain names arranged alphabetically. On the remaining names according to the order of the elements: The origin of certain things,” etc., as in Breulius. “We have inserted into this work. On certain terms of names by derivation. Although we have set down the origin,” etc. “Aeros, a strong man,” etc. At the end of the letter A the manuscript reads *utitur*; Breulius has *utatur*. Otherwise it is nearly as in Breulius.

Book XI has 4 chapters. Book XII has 8. Book XIII [Col. 0865C] has 22. Book XIV has 8; Breulius numbers 9, but adds nothing. The manuscript ends: “from here they are brought in”; Breulius has “from here and there they are carried,” less well. Book XV has 16 chapters. It ends: “that is, may they be recognized”; Breulius has “that is, may they be known.” Book XVI has 26 chapters. Book XVII has 11. Book XVIII has 71; Breulius has 69. In both, the last chapter is “On the ball.”

Book XIX has 33 chapters, Breulius 34. Chapter 31, or elsewhere 32, “On rings,” contains a passage which is corrupt in most copies and is given as follows:

> . . . . they called them.
>
> Flaccus, mourning my life, neither emerald  
> nor beryl for me, Flaccus, nor shining  
> pure-white pearl do I seek,  
> nor rings which the polishing file  
> has carefully smoothed, nor jasper stones.

Book XX has 15 chapters; Breulius has 16. It ends: “Let it be dried by the heat of fire. Book XX is complete. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

This is a handsome copy, with red titles and, at the beginning of the books, somewhat expansive titles for each book, as in Book XX: “The chapters of Book XX begin, namely on tables, foods, drinks [perhaps ‘drink’], and their vessels; on wine and oil vessels, cooks, bakers, river-workers, beds, chairs, rural vehicles, and gardens, or on the equipment of horses.”

The division of books and chapters is extremely similar to the editions, written by the first hand without any variation by a second hand. Some variant readings are written in the margin, but for the most part they are worthless.

**43.** Codex 282 Palatinus, parchment folio, approximately of the fourteenth century. Rubric: “The chapters in the Book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, begin.” At the beginning is an index of the twenty books. At the beginning of each book is an index of chapters.

Book I has 28 chapters. Book II has 20; the last is “On figures of words and sentences.” Then follows the rubric: “The chapters of the art of dialectic begin, and this is the second part.” There are 10 chapters.

Book III has 10 chapters. Then the rubric: “This is the second part of the third book. The chapters of the discipline of geometry begin.” There are 4 chapters.

Rubric: “The chapters of the art of music begin, and this is the third part of the third book.” There are 9 chapters.

“The chapters of the art of astronomy begin, and this is the fourth part of the third book.” There are 19 chapters.

Book IV has 12 chapters. Book V has 27. “The second part of the fifth book begins. On the word ‘chronicle,’” etc. There are 12 chapters. The Chronicle ends:

“Heraclius, 27 years. In the fifth and fourth year of this most religious prince Sisebut, the Jews in Spain are baptized. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone. The whole period from the beginning of the world up to the tenth year of the glorious prince Recceswinth is reckoned as era DCXCVI V DCCCLVI.”

[Col. 0866B] Book VI has 21 chapters. In the final chapter: “The sacrifice is so called,” as in the editions. At the end: “more rightly by the blood and body of Christ.” Immediately afterward: “The sacraments are baptism and chrism; the body and blood, which for that reason,” etc.

Book VII has 16 chapters. Book VIII, 11. Book IX, 8. Twenty-one verses on kinship are inserted into the text:

> “There are brothers first, and kindred second,” etc.

I shall present them in the Appendices. This book ends: “to stand in protection.”

Book X: “On certain terms: The origin of certain terms, that is, whence they come . . . into this work, etc. *Heros*, a strong man,” etc.

Book XI has 4 chapters. Book XII, 8. Book XIII [Col. 0866C], 2. Book XIV, 7. Book XV, 16. Book XVI, 21. Book XVII, 9. Book XVIII, 70. Book XIX, 37. There the difficult passage on rings mentioned above occurs, concerning Flaccus:

> Mourning my life, I seek neither emeralds  
> nor beryls for me, Flaccus, nor shining things,  
> nor pearls through pure whiteness,  
> nor those [rings], etc.

Book XX has 16 chapters. It ends: “let it be dried by the heat of fire. The Book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, is complete.”

There are certain notes in an old hand, and often verses expressing the text or adding something. I shall present examples separately in the Appendices.

**44.** Codex 282 Palatinus, parchment folio, approximately of the fourteenth century. Rubric: “The chapters in the Book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Seville, begin.” At the beginning is an index of the twenty books; at the beginning of each book, an index of its chapters. Book I has 28 chapters. Book II has 20, the last being “On figures of words and sentences.” The following rubric reads: “The chapters of the art of dialectic begin, and this is the second part.” There are 10 chapters. Book III has 10 chapters. Then follows the rubric: “This is the second part of the third book. The chapters of the discipline of geometry begin.” There are 4 chapters. Rubric: “The chapters of the art of music begin, and this is the third part of the third book.” There are 9 chapters. “The chapters of the art of astronomy begin, and this is the fourth part of the third book.” There are 19 chapters. Book IV has 12 chapters. Book V has 27. “The second part of the fifth book begins. 1. On the word *chronicle*,” etc. There are 12 chapters. Thus the *Chronicle* ends: “Heraclius, 27 years. In the fifth and fourth year of this most religious prince Sisebut, the Jews in Spain are baptized. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone. The whole period from the beginning of the world up to the tenth year of the glorious prince Recceswinth is reckoned as era DCXCVI V DCCCLVI.”

[Col. 0866B] Book VI has 21 chapters. In the final chapter: “The sacrifice is so called,” as in the editions. At the end: “more fittingly by the blood and body of Christ.” Immediately afterward: “The sacraments are baptism and chrism; body and blood, which for that reason,” etc. Book VII has 16 chapters; Book VIII, 11; Book IX, 8. Twenty-one verses on kinship are inserted in the text: “There are brothers in the first degree, and kinsmen in the second,” etc., which I shall print in the Appendices. This book ends: “to stand in protection.” Book X: “On certain terms: The origin of certain terms, that is, whence they come . . . into this work, etc. *Heros*, a strong man,” etc. Book XI has 4 chapters; Book XII, 8; Book XIII [Col. 0866C], 2; Book XIV, 7; Book XV, 16; Book XVI, 21; Book XVII, 9; Book XVIII, 70; Book XIX, 37. There occurs there the difficult passage on rings, mentioned above, Flaccus:

> Mourning my life, I seek neither emeralds  
> nor beryls for me, Flaccus, nor shining  
> pearls of pure whiteness,  
> nor those [rings], etc.

Book XX has 16 chapters. It ends: “let it be dried by the heat of fire. The Book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, is complete.” There are certain notes in an old hand, and often verses expressing the text or adding something. I shall present examples separately in the Appendices.

**45.** Codex 283 Palatinus, parchment quarto, approximately of the fourteenth century. First inscription: “The rubrics of Book I of Isidore’s *Etymologies*,” etc. It is a table of all the books, which number 22.

The first twelve books are as in Breulius. Book XIII, *On the World*, has 11 chapters. Book XIV, *On Waters*, ends with “On Floods.” Book XV, *On the Earth*, ends with “On Lower Places.” Book XVI, *On the Authors of Founded Cities*, etc., ends with “On Roads.” Book XVII, *On Dust and Clods*, ends with “On the Signs of Weights.” Book XVIII, *On the Authors of Rural Things*, ends with “On Fragrant Vegetables.” Book XIX, *On Wars*, etc., ends with “On the Ball.” Book XX, *On Ships*, ends with “On Building Tools”; in the text, “On Woodworkers.” Book XXI, *On the Invention of Woolworking*, ends with “On Footwear.” Book XXII, *On Tables*, etc.; its chapters continue to the end of the *Etymologies*.

**46.** After the table of chapters and books, placed at the beginning of the volume, there is a letter from Isidore to Braulio: “To my lord,” etc. “With every desire,” etc. Then Braulio’s prologue to Isidore: “To my lord,” etc. “O pious lord.” Isidore’s letter to Braulio: “Because I have you safe and well.” Braulio’s prologue to Isidore: “It is accustomed to be fulfilled”; the edition has “filled.” Isidore to Braulio: “Of your holiness . . . Isidore to Braulio: Behold for you,” etc., “in the style of our ancestors.”

A notice is added: “So that you may quickly find in this work what you seek, this page, reader, shows you the subjects on which the author of this Codex discussed matters in each book: on grammar,” etc. The subjects of the books are indicated.

Immediately afterward is the rubric: “Isidore to Sisebutus: To my lord and son Sisebutus, Isidore: Behold for you,” etc., “in the style of our ancestors. The chapters begin,” etc. It should be noted that Braulio’s name is sometimes indicated only by the initial letter B.

Formerly, together with Isidore’s *Etymologies*, certain other books had been bound in this volume, such as Boethius’s *On Scholastic Discipline* and some anonymous works, which are indicated at the beginning in an old hand. The volume now ends: “Let it be dried by the heat. Isidore’s *Etymologies*, wonderfully worked out in twenty-two books, is complete.”

The Greek alphabet follows. There is also another hand’s note on the cross: “The holy cross is worshiped for four reasons,” etc.

## CHAPTER CIII

Review of Codices 11 of the Vatican-Palatine Library. The most ancient Sacramentary. Old works on epacts, computation, and related subjects. An abridgment of the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*. Books on grammar and rhetoric by Dynamus and the unpublished works of St. Julian of Toledo.

[Col. 0867C] **1.** Codex 327 Palatinus, paper folio. Books III and IV of the *Master of the Sentences*, written by a certain Leonardo of Monaco in the suburb of Innsbruck in 1429. Page 135, rubric: “The formula of the honorable life of blessed Bernard the abbot to his brother Bernard begins: You ask me, my dearest brother, what never and nowhere,” etc. It ends: “may hinder diligence in good works.”

Then: “Another formula of an honorable and spiritual life begins: Give . . . your attention more carefully.” It ends: “let us sing alleluia,” etc. Perhaps this is a prologue, for several chapters follow: “On perfection: If you wish to be perfect,” etc. “On the hours to be recited,” etc.

**2.** Page 140 verso, letter of Peter of Cluny to someone: “For the narrowness of the cell, the breadth of paradise.” It is followed by: “On the various snares of demons by which they especially tempt solitaries: He has enemies,” etc. [Col. 0867D] “The letter of Peter of Cluny is complete; but excellent—perhaps obscure—passages on virtue begin,” etc. There are 22 passages. The little work ends: “to attain eternal joys.”

**3.** Page 148, rubric: “The flowers of blessed Isidore begin. Beloved son, love tears; do not delay them,” etc. It ends: “either is justified or is condemned. Certain excerpts, or flowers, of blessed Isidore are complete.”

Then there is a note: “I neither approve nor condemn receiving Communion of the Eucharist every day; nevertheless I urge Communion on every Sunday,” etc.

A work follows, *On the Return of the Lord from Egypt*, etc.: “When they had completed,” etc. Meditations of St. Bernard are appended: “Many know many things,” etc.

Page 187: “The prologue to the history of King Alexander begins: After the law of Abraham,” etc. [Col. 0868A] “The history begins: Of the stars,” etc. There are three books. Eusebius on the death of Jerome follows, together with Augustine, etc., and Cyril on the miracles of Jerome, etc., as in other manuscripts, which I have already discussed.

Page 251 verso: “The deeds of St. Silvanus with the heretics begin: In a pleasant and most delightful place.” Later there is more recent miscellaneous material. Lives of the philosophers. In the same place, no. 72: “Quintilian the poet came from Spain to Rome and maintained a public school there,” etc.

**4.** Codex 391 Palatinus, paper folio. “The *Manipulus florum* of Master Thomas of England.” It proceeds alphabetically, but by distinctions. At the end: “The Book of Distinctions is complete.” The prologue begins: “After he had spoken.”

Then: “The questions begin: There are six reasons for abstaining from food.” The first title, “*Manipulus*,” [Col. 0868B] etc., is in a later hand.

A certain collection arranged alphabetically follows in this volume, with a prologue in which Augustine and other Fathers are listed, as well as Isidore and various profane authors, including Pliny. It begins: “Abstinence is good,” etc.

Then follows a catalogue of books “with respect to their beginnings and endings and the number of chapters in individual books.” There: “Isidore, *On the Supreme Good*, etc. ‘It encloses those who are to be made joyful.’ *Etymologies*, twenty books, prologue: ‘To my lord,’” etc. It ends: “let it be dried by the heat. *On Ecclesiastical Offices*. End: ‘might be strengthened by ancestral judgments.’” There is nothing else by Isidore.

**5.** Codex 485 Palatinus, parchment quarto, approximately of the tenth century. At the beginning, in a more recent hand: “A good book: Sacramental Agenda, and a twofold exposition of the Mass.” [Col. 0868C] The first work is mutilated: certain prayers and readings from the Epistles and Gospels.

Page 2: “The confession of every wise person begins: Whenever you wish,” etc. “And the priest shall bless and pray and say to him: Almighty God, who says, ‘Whoever confesses me before human beings,’ etc., may he bless and protect you and grant you remission of all sins.”

Then comes “The common confession of sinners,” apparently in the German language.

A short work on epacts follows. Then a calendar: “January, etc. Thirteen days before the Kalends of February: the passion of St. Sebastian, martyr.” In a more recent hand: “King Louis the Younger died.” In the same place, eight days before the Kalends, in a recent hand: “The Conversion of St. Paul.” July, five days before the Ides: “The arrival of St. Nazarius at Lorsch, and the birthday of St. Benedict the abbot.” October, eight days before the Ides, in a more recent hand: “Wars between Charles [Col. 0868D] and Louis.” December, two days before the Ides—read four days before the Ides—“the birthday of St. Eulalia, virgin and martyr.”

Some observations on the moon, illnesses, secret writing, and related matters follow. Page 13 verso: “Mass at cockcrow: God, who has consecrated this most holy night,” etc. Secret prayer: “May it be acceptable to you, Lord,” etc. A Mass is also indicated: “At the feast of Sigismund, for a sick person.”

**6.** Page 16, rubric: “Blessed Jerome was the first to translate the interpretation of Hebrew names into the Latin language: ‘In the beginning, however.’” Page 17 verso, exposition of the Mass: first, the prayer, “Almighty God, have mercy,” etc., as I said in chapter 84.

“Again begins the exposition of the appropriate rite: To the sacred priests and to all who worthily serve throughout our diocese in Christ, the humble bishop sends greetings in the Lord: Since indeed,” etc. Augustine is cited. Catechumens, the Creed, and related matters are also discussed. This is a work different from the Isidorian one.

The final title is: “On the confirmation of the body and blood of Christ: Finally, the infant is confirmed by the body and blood of Christ.” It ends: “that he may be given life. Complete.”

Page 46 verso, title: “Isidore on the Church. Question: What language is ‘Church,’ and what does it mean? Answer: It is Greek, and it means ‘assembly.’” This is from Book VIII, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*, and from Book I, chapter 1 of *Ecclesiastical Offices*, but in different words. Other material on temples is added from Book XV, chapter 4 of the *Etymologies*. This little work should be assigned to the Appendices.

Another title: “Also on the ministry of the Church: It is permitted to place a church in another location,” etc. It is not said to be Isidore’s; nevertheless, it contains some distinctive material and will be placed among the Appendices. Other material on baptism and exorcisms follows, with Isidore cited in the margin.

**7.** Page 46 verso, title: “In the name of God, a few excerpts from volumes of learning. Materials begin on the Catholic Church and its ministers, and on the office of baptism: ‘Church’ is Greek, which is translated into Latin as ‘assembly,’” etc., from Book VIII, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*. Other material on clerics and ecclesiastical orders is drawn from Book VII, chapters 12 and 14 of the *Etymologies*.

Page 48, prayers for Holy Saturday: “Let the angelic throng now rejoice,” etc.

Page 49, rubric: “From the authentic book of the Sacramentary of St. Gregory, pope of the city of Rome, a prayer for making a catechumen: Almighty and eternal God, deign to look upon,” etc. Other prayers follow, including prayers for the sick.

[Col. 0869C] Several blessings follow: a prayer for a threshing floor, the blessing of a new well, “a prayer over vessels found in an ancient place, for cutting the hair, for cutting the beard, over a granary,” etc.

Page 55 verso, prayer at the entrance for visiting the sick: “God,” etc. Rubric: “Then let a more private place be provided for confession; thereafter, once they have received penance and made an explicit profession of faith, let the visitors return,” etc.

359 **8.** On the following page another rubric: “After these sacred acts, anointing is to be applied with the priest’s right hand, palm extended, first on the chest and the place of the heart; then between the shoulder blades; then in the form of a cross on the place of greatest pain. Saying this, he shall begin: ‘I anoint you with oil sanctified by God, bestowed upon us as a heavenly gift, in the name of the holy and undivided Trinity, so that it may itself give you life by healing you within and without—the Trinity which preserves its entire creation lest it perish.’”

A more recent hand has noted: “In this anointing it is not said that sins are forgiven through these things” [perhaps “through it” or “on account of it”]. But the word “within” should be noted as directed against the heretic, as I think, who wrote this note.

Other material on the Mass for the sick follows. Page 58 verso, rubric: “In the rite for the dying. As soon as he sees that the person is approaching death, he is to receive Communion from the holy sacrifice, even if he has eaten that very day” (that is, without fasting).

Other prayers for the deceased follow, etc., together with the rubric: “Afterward let the body be washed and placed in a coffin.” Exorcisms, blessings, and related material follow, including the blessing of palms and branches.

9. On page 64, rubric: “Here begins the preface of the holy council: [Col. 0870A] The sacred council, etc.” This is the epigram customarily prefixed to collections of councils. Then follow the twenty chapters of the Council of Nicaea. The fifty Canons of the Apostles. On page 73, rubric: “Here begins the penitential book taken from the canons of the catholic Fathers, for the healing of souls, belonging to Archbishop Egbert.” It has thirteen chapters. It begins: “That holy institution which was observed in the days of our fathers never abandoned the right paths.” It ends: “he acquires a good standing for himself before him who is God, blessed above all,” etc. Immediately follows the rubric: “Saint Boniface published it: How can we perform penance for seven years,” etc. On page 80, a title in a later hand: “The Capitular of Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, addressed to the priests of his parish: I beseech you,” etc. It ends, “to be contained within the cloisters of the monastery”; in a more recent hand: “Here ends Theodulf’s Capitular,” about which I have spoken elsewhere. On page 91, rubric: “A Sermon: Hear, brothers, and consider more attentively,” etc. It concerns baptism.

10. On page 92, rubric: “Here begin the chapters: Just as the holy synod of Nicaea forbids it, no priest shall ever permit women to live with him in his house.” There are twenty-seven chapters. It ends: “now, because, with the help of the Lord God and by the permission of our lord the emperor” [sic], “I present myself for correcting everything, both in the matters denounced in the aforementioned chapters and in the others which are brought before me” [the text has “before me” with the number 360 intervening]. There are also other chapters: “On the arrangement of the baptistery,” etc. There are eighteen of these, containing, as it were, an examination of priests. Rubric: “In the name of the threefold and simple [God]: From the earlier records we have excerpted the very few remedies for sins that follow. In all these matters, however, we have used not the authority of a censor but rather the counsel of one who sympathizes.” This is a certain penitential book. Page 101. Bede’s admonition: “If anyone wishes,” etc.

11. On the reverse of page 101: “Preface on the saving medicine of souls. On remedies for wounds, etc. Here begins the rule: The intoxicated,” etc. This is a certain penitential book. At the end, rubric: “Here ends this book, written by Comminianus. Here begins the preface of the little book which Father Theodore composed, in response to various questioners, as a remedy for penance. The disciple of the Umbrians, to all the catholic English, especially the physicians of souls, healing health in the Lord Jesus Christ: First of all, etc.” It ends: “may be preserved with all diligence. Here it ends.” It has often been edited. The codex seems to be of the same period as the collection of grammarians found in Codex Palatinus 1746, to be described below: in both, *enim* is written with the ligature H, and the letter-forms have similar strokes.

12. Codex Palatinus 602, paper, in folio. Some materials relating to the Council of Basel. Augustine, *On Catechizing the Uninstructed*: “You asked that I should write something to you.” On page 52, without a title: “Here begin the chapters of Book I: That God is the highest good,” etc. In a later hand: “The Three Books of Sentences of Isidore, which are, as it were, GENERAL CANONS, if they are examined perceptively.” In Book III, chapter 1: “Have mercy, Lord, on wretched Isidore, doing unworthy things,” etc. It ends: “the heavenly court encloses those who are to be made joyful. Here ends the third book.”

[Col. 0871A] 13. This is followed by Bernard on Psalm 90, “He who dwells: I trust your labor.” At the end the year 1433 is given. Then comes a treatise on the Sacraments of visible temples: “Since it concerns a dedication”; it ends: “he could not accomplish what he wished. Here it ends.” Next comes a work without a title: “The world corrupted by original and actual sins,” etc. It ends: “or comprehend by human thought.” After this: “A Sermon on the Lord’s Prayer, by the author mentioned above.” But above there is no author’s name. It begins: “There are two things, dearest ones, which are chiefly,” etc. “On penance, by William of Paris”: the name “William” is obscure. It begins: “The second plank after shipwreck,” etc. At the end: 1433, which seems to be the year in which the codex was written.

361 14. Codex Palatinus 834, parchment, in small folio, or quarto, approximately of the tenth century. At the beginning is the crucified Savior, covered with a loincloth or linen cloth, with four nails. Beneath it is the following couplet:

> Dear reader, remember to restore me to Nazarius,  
> for I do not wish to endure the claim of another master.

Rubric: “Here begins the Martyrology of Bede the priest.” In the same place, on 4 December: “The feast of Saint Eulalia the virgin in the city of Barcelona in Spain,” etc. This is really Eulalia of Mérida. In the same place, on 23 November, concerning Saint Clement: “and they found the body in a stone coffin in a marble temple.” The account of certain saints is longer; this does not seem to be Bede’s genuine Martyrology. At the end it says: “Here ends the Martyrology of Bede the priest.”

[Col. 0871C] 15. On the reverse of page 28 there are pictures of three saints. The one on the right holds a book in his hand; the other two hold a folded or rolled-up volume. Who they are is not stated. Their heads, however, are crowned with haloes, and above them are these verses:

> This picture remains in common worthy of the highest praise,  
> and likewise the remarkable hand, shining with distinguished praise.

On the following page: “Here begins the computation of Eusebius and Jerome,” etc. It ends in the year 814. Then these verses:

> You, Father and Son, and kindly Spirit, etc.

They are written in a later hand. Then follow tables of epacts, etc. On the computation or language of the fingers: “With the Lord’s help, we are going to speak about the reckoning of times,” etc. The work is attributed to Bede. Other material is added concerning signs, the moon, epacts, and so forth.

[Col. 0871D] 16. On the reverse of page 47, rubric: “Here begins the book *On the Stars of Heaven* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville. The prologue begins: To the lord and brother [corrected: son] Sisebutus, Isidore. Although I am not unaware that you are outstanding in talent and eloquence and in the varied flowering of letters, you nevertheless devote still greater care,” etc. There is a table of forty-eight chapters. Chapter 44 is “On the names of the sea and rivers,” not yet published. Chapter 48 is “On the regions of the earth.” It ends: “and they estimated [it at] five stadia.” On page 95: “Here begin the divisions of philosophy. Philosophy is first divided in three ways.” There are paradigms of the division and subdivision of the parts of philosophy, similar to those which I shall identify as coming from the grammarian Dynamus in Codex Palatinus 1746. It ends: “he died for our sins.”

17. Codex Palatinus 927, parchment, in folio, approximately of the thirteenth century, although some works appear to have been written in the eleventh century. On the first page the tomb of Peter Comestor is depicted, with this epitaph:

> I was Peter, whom the stone covers, and I was called Comestor, etc.

Below are these verses:

> Reader worthy of reverence, know that the codex in which you read these things  
> belongs, without deceit, to the Holy Trinity,  
> whose most beautiful sheepfold is situated  
> not far from Verona, worthy of great praise.

On the following page are images of Augustine and Orosius, seated and conversing, each holding a book in his hand. Beneath them are these verses:

> May God save the man who wrote this book,

and several other similar verses. Then follows the inscription: “A work excerpted from the second book of Orosius: I think that no human being now exists.”

18. On page 6 are two images: “Pompey Trogus and Justin, his abridger.” Rubric: “The Epitome of the Histories of Pompey Trogus. Book One begins: At the beginning of events,” etc. It ends: “they are added to the representations of the spear.” On page 18 are three images: Adam, Seth, and Enos. A chronicle from the beginning of the world to the year 842 follows. It ends with Theophilus, son of Michael, and Michael, son of Theophilus. In the same place, under Justin: “The abbot Benedict shone with the glory of virtues, which Gregory wrote about in the book of the *Dialogues*.” This differs from Isidore’s Chronicle, although I think that many things were taken from it.

[Col. 0872C] 19. On page 31 is a picture of three men, namely King Ninus and two soldiers. “The birth of Abraham.” On page 32, rubric: “Excerpt from the Chronicle of Eusebius. Ninus was the first to rule all Asia, except the Indians.” On page 57: “An epitome from the book of Orosius, etc. In the year 355 from the founding of the City,” etc. Some material concerning the persecutions of the Church is connected with this, along with other material extending to Theodosius and Leo: “Leo, twenty-four years, three months, fourteen days.” There, under Gallus and Volusianus: “Cornelius, bishop of Rome, at the request of a certain matron, Lucina, secretly raised the bodies of the apostles from the catacomb” [above the word is *catacumbas*, “catacombs”] “by night and placed them—Paul’s, indeed, on the Ostian Way where he was beheaded, but Peter’s beside the place where he was crucified, among the bodies of the holy bishops, in the temple of Apollo on the Golden Mount in the Vatican, at the palace of Nero, on the third day before the Kalends of July.” Some material is shared with the chronicle reported earlier in this codex, such as the mention of Saint Benedict.

[Col. 0872C] 20. On page 74 are images of Constantine, Cassiodorus, Theodoret, Sozomen, and Socrates. Rubric: “A work excerpted from the Ecclesiastical History of Cassiodorus Senator, etc., under the Caesars Crispus and Constantine,” etc. On page 122 are images of Alaric, Radagaisus, Theodoric, and Odoacer. “On the first arrival of the Goths,” etc. From Isidore’s *Chronicle of the Goths*. “In the reign of Honorius”: Isidore is not named. A number of variant readings occur. On the reverse of page 123 is another fragment from the same Chronicle. Other material is added from the book of Jordanes on Attila: “Attila of the Huns,” etc.

21. On page 134 and following, the arrival of the Lombards in Italy is depicted. The six books of Warnefrid. Warnefrid’s *History of the Lombards*, as printed by Grotius, ends in chapter 58 with “guarding the peace”; in this manuscript it continues: “Then Hildeprand, whom the aforementioned king had made his partner in the kingdom,” etc. It ends: “in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 773. He sent the aforementioned Desiderius and his wife to Francia. Thus ended the kingdom of the Lombards, which lasted for 206 years after they entered Italy.”

A continuation by years follows: “In the year 776, Rotgaud, duke of Friuli, was killed,” etc. There: “In the year 794, in Gaul, at a place called Frankfurt, a great synod was assembled against Elipandus, bishop of the Toledan see in Spain, and Felix, his associate.” This continuation ends in the year 825 [Col. 0873B], with Lothair, the oath which he exacted from the pope and the Roman clergy concerning fidelity to the emperor, and the canonical election of the pope. In Duchesne, volume II of the *Annales Francorum*, page 206, it ends in the year 814.

22. Another brief chronicle follows, beginning in the year 1117 and continuing in a different hand to 1223, apparently for the Veronese monastery of the Holy Trinity. It begins: “In the year 1117 from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, in the tenth indiction, on the second day before the Ides of January, this church was consecrated,” etc. On the reverse of page 216 is a cycle table, preceded by words from Isidore, Book VI, chapter 17: “Hippolytus [calculated] the Paschal cycle,” etc. In the same place, the manuscript has: “On what day of the Kalends, or under what moon.” The table begins: “The fourth day before the Ides of April, moon 21.” It ends: “The twelfth day before the Kalends of May, moon 17.”

[Col. 0873C] 23. Some material is added concerning the Lord’s tomb, together with rhythmic verses about the crime that occurred in the year 1187:

> In a voice of lament I am compelled to recount  
> the crime that recently occurred beyond the sea,  
> when Saladin was permitted to lay waste  
> the land which you, Christ, deigned to love so greatly, etc.

The subject is the war in which the king was captured with the Cross, many Templars were killed, and so forth. This material was added in a later hand, for the earlier works in the codex belong approximately to the eleventh century.

24. Codex Palatinus 973, parchment, in quarto, of the ninth or tenth century. Rubric: “On the six ages of the world: The first age, therefore, contains,” etc. A brief chronicle resembling that of Isidore’s *Etymologies*. In the same place: “Tiberius, nine years. Hermenegild, king of the Goths, is crowned with martyrdom.” It ends: “Charles, who is mentioned above, forty-five years, who in his thirtieth year is crowned emperor by Pope Leo.” Shortly before this: “Pepin, etc.; in his second year Boniface was made a martyr.” On page 5, rubric: “Here begins the Chronicle of Julius Caesar: When Julius Caesar and Marcus Antonius” [corrected to *Antonius*] “were consuls, the whole world was traversed,” etc. The work is incomplete. Added is “an arrangement or examination in the order of the venerable Fortunatus addressed to Gregory” [of Tours]. The letter of Hormisdas to all the provinces: “Behold, most clearly,” etc. On page 18: “Here begins the section on foods: Not without reason the race of mortals,” etc. That is, concerning healthful and harmful foods, and so on. On the reverse of page 19: “From the book of Prosper: How much remedy confession of sins possesses, and what punishment deceitful concealment deserves. To this is added that sins themselves,” etc. Gregory’s letter to Secundinus is included, beginning: “For your holiness.”

25. On page 22, rubric: “Here begins the letter of Isidore, bishop, to Massona on the resurrection of the priest: To the holy and meritoriously blessed brother Massona, bishop, Isidore, bishop. When the religious Nicenius arrived,” etc. [Some copies have *Nicetius*]. It ends: “whose authority rather stands firm. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our lord King Witteric.” Immediately follows the rubric: “A certain teacher’s opinion: ‘Uncleanness says,’ etc.” This is a fragment from near the end of the book *On the Conflict of the Vices and Virtues*, concerning which see chapter 84. Next, without a title: “Very many people, understanding the judgments of the Rule of our holy Father Benedict not at all fully,” etc. Rubric: “Here begins Saint Cyprian’s work *On the Twelve Abuses of the World*: There are twelve abuses of the world; that is, a wise man without works,” etc. This little work is attributed to Isidore in some sources, as I said in chapter 85. On page 39 are sentences, or excerpts from the Fathers Siricius, Augustine, and others: “On marriage,” etc. There, concerning the third conference of Abbot Theonas, chapter 21: “Yet for that reason we ought not to withdraw ourselves from the Lord’s communion because we acknowledge ourselves to be sinners,” etc. There is much material on frequent communion.

26. Page 43. The Capitular of Abbot Ansegisus. Preface: “When he was reigning,” etc. There is a table of 162 chapters. “Preface of Lord Charles: When he was reigning,” etc. Chapter 1: “For there are certain people,” etc. Preface to Book II: “Above”; a table of forty-six chapters. Book III: “Previously,” etc. Ninety chapters. Book IV: “As above.” Seventy-four chapters. Rubric: “The ecclesiastical chapters of Lord Charles [Col. 0874C], emperor: For this reason I have not joined them to the foregoing,” etc. After the chapter titles: “Also the secular chapters of Lord Charles, emperor,” etc.

On the reverse of page 125: “On the observance of the four seasons: The fast of the first month, therefore,” etc. There: “In the same month the first fruits of the earth are gathered, and this month is called by some the *hodea* month” [perhaps *hordeaceus*, “barley month”], “because our ancestors then already harvested barley,” etc. On page 125, a sermon of Saint Augustine, bishop, on conscience: “Brothers, be faithful in all things.” It ends: “will be on the shore, that is, at the end of the age.” Some miscellaneous material from the canons. On the same place, reverse of page 126: “In the Council of Toledo, chapter 31: A priest may not sit in that court where a man is handed over to death.” On page 129: “Here begins Saint Augustine’s sermon on tithes: It is written, brothers, ‘The earth is the Lord’s,’ etc.” It ends: “you did not wish to redeem. Here ends Saint Augustine’s sermon on tithes.” On page 131 a diagram of Noah’s ark is explained.

27. Codex Palatinus 1050, paper, in small quarto. Some letters. A scholastic work on the soul. At the end: “In the year 1455,” and in a different hand: “At Leipzig, by Johann Nitkel”; perhaps he is the author. On page 93: “On divine and human laws, from Book V, chapter 2 of Isidore of Seville’s *Etymologies*: All laws, however,” etc. It ends: “It is an instrument by which we construct something.” (Chapter 25.) Some philosophical material follows concerning the material and formal causes, etc. There is miscellaneous material, including several Latin poems by Germans from the beginning of the fifteenth century. Questions concerning heaven, generation, sensation and the sensible, and so forth. These appear to be works by Peter Nitkel, whose autograph letter, as I think, is read near the end, addressed to Wimpertus Liitinista: “I love you, my Wimpertus, more than usual,” etc.

28. Codex Palatinus 1357, parchment, in folio. *The Image of the World*. The codex, with rubricated titles, was carefully written, perhaps in the thirteenth century. At the beginning are two spheres. Preface: “For the instruction of many who lack an abundance of books, let this little book be published and let its name be *The Image of the World*.” Chapter 1: “The world is so called because it is moved in every direction.” On page 20: “Here begin the names of the eleven regions containing within themselves 113 provinces: Italy,” etc. In the margin, in a later hand: “A little book of the Roman provinces, somewhat fuller than the commonly known one.” The work ends: “the city: Gothia, Bosfoa.”

29. A mutilated work follows: “endurance. Hence beardless old men and unbeautiful youths are such because a face furrowed by the razor absorbs the timely grace of the hair through its scar,” etc. “In the following section we shall speak of this; now let us return to the history of the Visigoths. The Visigoths, therefore, after the death of Hermeric,” etc. It ends: “having abandoned Italy, he withdrew to Gaul.” Here the author takes much from Jordanes, whom he praises shortly before the end: “restored to his former liberty. This Jordanes, a certain grammarian descended from the same race of Goths, wrote an account of the origin of the Getae and the nobility of the Amuli” [perhaps *Alani*, “Alans”], “not embracing everything that is written and reported about them, as he himself says,” etc.

[Col. 0875C] On page 41, without a title: “This sensible world consists of four elements,” etc. It ends: “was deprived even of its parts.”

30. On page 53: “Here begins the prologue to the book of philosophy: Since, as Tullius says,” etc. After the table of chapters: “Philosophy is concerned with those things which exist and which are not seen.” This is an encyclopedic work by a Christian. It ends: “we have discussed the summaries in order that the reader’s mind might approach the learning of the remaining matters more eagerly. Here we bring the length of the fourth part to an end. Here ends the fourth book of philosophy. The commentaries of Julius Solinus, or the Grammarian, *Polyhistor*, edited and revised by him, on the situation of the world,” etc. Thus the work on philosophy appears to be incomplete, etc.

After Solinus: “An excerpt from the Ethical Cosmographer, *cata*, that is, according to Jerome: Hell in one part,” etc. It ends: “they could in no way live.” Alexander’s letter to Aristotle: “Always mindful,” and another to the same: “It is worthwhile, my teacher,” and another to his mother Olympias: “Concerning these matters, indeed,” etc. A work without a title follows: “Rumor reports that no one can greet the kings of the Parthians without a gift. But to you, my lord,” etc. Then: “The description of the provinces by Orosius the priest: Our ancestors [called] the world,” etc.

31. On page 137: “The Measurement of the Provinces by Jerome the priest. Further India ends in the east at the Ocean.” There, after Gaul: “Astodio” [perhaps *Asturia*] “and Galicia, Lusitania on the east, Cantabria and Aquitania [Col. 0876A] on the west at the Ocean; their extent is 580 miles in length and 585 miles in breadth. Further Spain is bounded on the east by Oretania, on the west by the Ocean, on the north by the river Ana, and on the south by the Iberian Sea; its extent stretches for 283 miles in length.” The little work ends: “at the British Ocean.”

32. On page 138, rubric: “Isidore the Younger, bishop, on the Earth. The earth is in the middle region of the world,” etc. This is Book XIV of the *Etymologies* and chapter 1 of Book XV, *On Cities*, where the manuscript omits “Caesaraugusta of Tarraconensis” through “it was reduced to desolation.” It later omits “Ceuta . . . lies by the strait.” Other chapters, “On the Ocean,” etc., from Book XIII, are added in intermixed form. It ends: “heated by movements,” [Col. 0876B] which is the end of chapter 13.

The following rubric succeeds: “In the name of the Lord begins the division of the whole globe made under the consuls Julius Caesar and Marcus Antonius” [sic]: “The whole world was traversed by the wisest and chosen men,” etc. It ends: “they brought them under their own dominion.”

33. On page 154: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the book of the blessed Methodius, bishop of the Church of Patara and martyr of Christ, which he took care to translate from Hebrew and Latin—that is, concerning the beginning of the age, the kingdoms of the nations, and the end of the ages. The blessed Jerome commended this illustrious man in his works: For we must know, dearest ones, how in the beginning God created heaven,” etc. It ends: “of virgins and of all the saints.” Saint Methodius flourished in the third century; this book should be compared with his works already published.

34. Codex Palatinus 1448, parchment, in folio, approximately of the tenth century, written in a bright French script, which some call typographical or Italian cursive. At the beginning:

> Let him read me who wishes to know the cycles of the years,  
> the changing seasons and at the same time the stars of heaven.

“In the name of God begin a few things concerning times and the various spans of time. Amen. Whence times are so called. They also received their name from tempering, as Isidore testifies in Book V of the *Etymologies*, saying as follows: ‘Times are so called from the tempering of things together,’ etc.” In a more recent script, on page 2, it says: “This book belongs to the library of Saint Martin’s Church of Mainz.” The work ends: “varied on account of the Lord’s Day.” It concludes: “Thanks be to God. Amen.” Much is taken from Isidore.

35. Next follows: “The course of the moon through the twelve signs.” After a table of letters or figures: “Every Paschal moon, whatever its age, is,” etc., which is a brief note. Rubric: “Here begins the solar order of the year with the letters placed above by Saint Jerome, for determining the day of the week and investigating the age of the moon on each day throughout nineteen years. Therefore, if anyone is less capable of calculating,” etc.

Then comes a calendar, with various feasts noted. Kalends of January: “The octave of Our Lord Jesus Christ” [sic]. February 2: “Blessed Mary offered our Lord in the temple.” The seventh day before the Ides of February: “The beginning of spring has ninety-one days.” The sixth day before the Ides: the beginning of Lent. The eighth day before the Kalends of March: “Spring rises”; the feast of Saint Peter the apostle. March: the fifteenth day. The seventeenth day before the Kalends of April: “The first day of the age.” The eighth day before the Kalends of April: “Our Lord Jesus Christ was crucified.”

May: the seventh day before the Ides: “The beginning of summer; it has ninety-one days.” The eighth day before the Kalends of June: “Summer rises.” The fifth day before the Kalends: “The dedication of the church of Saint Maximinus, bishop of Trier,” etc.

June: the eighth day before the Kalends of July: “The feast of Saint John the Baptist and the conception of John the Evangelist.” The third day before the Kalends of July: “The feast of the apostles Peter and Paul.”

July: the twelfth day before the Ides of July: “The division of the apostles for preaching.” The thirteenth day before the Kalends of August: “The feast of Saint Vulfmar.”

August: the seventh day before the Ides: “The beginning of autumn; it has ninety-two days.” The tenth day before the Kalends of September: “Autumn rises.”

September: the sixteenth day before the Kalends: “The feast of Saint Lambert.”

November: the seventh day before the Ides: “The beginning of winter; it has ninety-two days.” The seventh day before the Kalends of December: “Winter rises.”

Other material follows concerning cycles and epacts, extending to the year 835 [Col. 0877B] of the Lord. Then, from the beginning of the world to the year in which he was writing, the author reckons 6,822 years from the Incarnation of Christ, in the year 810.

36. On page 19, rubric: “In the name of the Most High God. Isidore to Sisibutus, lord and son: Although I know you to be outstanding,” etc. There is a table of forty-eight chapters. Title: “Here begins the book of the Wheels of Saint Isidore, bishop.” Chapter 1 concerns days. A blank space is left for the wheels or spheres. Chapter 46 concerns the names of the sea and rivers, which is absent from the printed editions: “On the names of the sea and rivers: In Prata, Tranquillus,” etc. The book ends: “they judged it to be stadia.” It concludes: “Amen. I give thanks to my God as far as I am able. Farewell.”

37. A work without a title follows: “A day has twenty-four hours,” etc., together with a method of counting on the fingers. Other material concerns the *as* and the *uncia*, etc. On the reverse of page 41 is the distribution of Volusius Maecianus, together with the terms and symbols for monetary matters according to weight, number, and measure: “I have often noticed, *Caesor*” [the printed editions read *Censor*], “that you are distressed because of the division of the *as*,” etc. It ends: “expenditure and measurement.”

Another title follows: “On measures: The *chorus*” [read *corus*] “is so called from its resemblance to a hill.” Concerning Volusius, see Fabricius, *Bibliotheca medii aevi*, under “Volusius,” and *Bibliotheca Latina vetus*, Book IV, chapter 9.

On page 45: “Here begins the computation: Times therefore receive their name from tempering, or because each thing,” etc. Something may be missing after “receive.” The author is English, as appears from the context. Other material is inserted, already described at the beginning of the volume, perhaps excerpted from this work. Compare Bede.

38. On page 62, verses on the months:

> The first [month] of the Romans.

On days:

> The first opens.

Other verses on the months:

> This is the month of Janus.

On the signs:

> The ram is the first to appear.

On page 64 is a calendar, with certain feasts added in a second but ancient hand during the first months. In the same place, in January: the seventh day before the Ides, “of Isidore the bishop and of Saints Fausta and Evilasius.” On the Ides, “of Hilary and Julian.” March, the seventh day before the Kalends of April: “The burial of Saint Luthgarius.” November, the Kalends: “The commemoration of all the saints.” The third day before the Ides: “At Tours, the burial of Saint Martin.”

After other material come verses mentioning Bede:

> Which the remarkable teacher Bede once wrote out in full.

The last is:

> I ask you, remembering your Flaccus: farewell forever.

[Col. 0878A] Thus Albinus appears to be the author of the work. At the end of page 74, after some further material on epacts:

> These arguments, beloved companion, I have written out for you  
> through labor of my own; now tell me with what gift  
> you would compete with me today, while I give you such things, weary.

39. On the reverse of page 74, without a title: “There are several segments of the world, which our people called circles and the Greeks called parallels. It begins with the part of India turned toward the south and extends as far as Arabia,” etc. In Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 10 begins: “In defining the world, philosophers say that there are five circles, which the Greeks call parallels, that is, zones,” etc. The manuscript’s little work ends: “they added to the circles.”

40. On page 76, rubric: “Here begins *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*. Adam, father of the human race, by the hands of God,” etc. In the same place: “James, son of Zebedee, while evangelizing in Spain, was struck down with the sword by King Herod and buried in Achaia Armarica.” It ends with Titus: “There he rests in peace.” The Old Testament is not distinguished from the New. Numbers are attached to the margin of each chapter in Greek letters; the last of these Greek letters are ξ and H.

41. After the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers*, on the reverse of page 82, there is a work *On Times, Hours, and Moments*: “Times, moments, hours, days,” etc. In this work, on page 89, under the title *On the Ages of the World*, a chronicle is inserted containing much from Isidore’s brief Chronicle. It begins: “The times of the world are divided into six ages,” etc. In the same place: “Concerning the sixth age: The sixth age contains 709 years that have passed. Octavianus, 56 years,” etc.

This is Bede’s Chronicle, whose sixth age Schelstratus published in volume I of the *Antiquitates*, page 609, under the title: “From the 900-year-old Codex 511 of the Library of Queen Christina of Sweden” [formerly, I think, of the Queen, since it is now Palatine], “containing Bede’s shorter book *On Times*.” But the printed edition says: “It contains 707 years that have passed.” Likewise the printed edition has: “Justin, nine years; the heresy of the Acephali is called.” Our manuscript reads: “Justin, eight years; the heresy of the Acephali is renounced.”

Later: “The Armenians receive the faith of Christ.” The manuscript adds: “Tiberius, seven years. Hermenegild, king of the Goths, is crowned with martyrdom. Maurice, twenty-one years. Gregory flourished as bishop at Rome. Phocas, eight years. The Saxons in Britain receive the faith of Christ. Heraclius, thirty-seven years,” etc.

Schelstratus omits “Tiberius . . . receive,” and published “Heraclius, thirty-six years,” followed shortly by *Eradonas* instead of *Eraclonas*, because in some manuscripts there is confusion between *cl* and *d*. It ends: “It is open to God alone. Here it ends.”

Rubric: “On the nineteen-year cycle.” Much in the Chronicle comes from Isidore, as I have said. What follows concerns cycles, epacts, and indictions. The preface discusses Eusebius and Proterius of Alexandria, who wrote on this subject under the Emperor Marcian and was praised by Pope Leo.

There, on the reverse of page 95: “For the holy Roman and apostolic Church itself testifies that it holds this faith in the very little records which it customarily writes annually on its candles, where, recalling the time of the Lord’s Passion to the people,” etc. “Finally, in the year 701 from his Incarnation according to Dionysius, in the fourteenth indiction, our brothers who were then at Rome reported that they had seen this written on the candles of Saint Mary on the Nativity of the Lord and had copied it from there: ‘From the Passion of Our Lord Jesus Christ there are 668 years.’”

The author was writing at the beginning of the eighth century, and the codex appears to have been copied not long afterward. The script of the book *On the Birth and Death of the Fathers* displays the same or greater antiquity than the rest of the script of this volume. The earliest works, however, appear to have been written in a less ancient script.

42. Codex Palatinus 1746, of the ninth or tenth century, parchment, in folio. At the beginning, in an ancient script: “The codex of Saint Nazarius at Lorsch.” An index was added in an old hand:

“First, the Arts of Saint Augustine. Augustine’s Rule on the noun and the other parts of speech. Donatus’s Art, which Paul the Deacon explains. Saint Isidore, bishop, on Grammar, its parts, and figures. Dynamus the grammarian to his disciple. The Grammar of Julian, bishop of Toledo. The Grammar and Art of Tacuinius. Another Art, or Grammar, of Julian of Toledo. Asper’s Art on the eight parts of speech. The Art of Lord Boniface, archbishop and martyr.”

The script of the codex is French. *Est* is written with the ligature H; diphthongs are separated and joined in various ways; there are a point, two points, a comma and point, a question mark, and a long *i*, almost like *l*, as is commonly found in Lombardic script.

43. The first work, the *Arts of Augustine*, is mutilated at the beginning. Immediately upon reading, one encounters mention of the comparative with the genitive, “as in *major horum charitas*,” etc. Then comes the rubric: “Here begins the section on the pronoun: A pronoun is a part of speech,” etc. It ends: “useful to citizens, suited to the stage.” Explicit: “The Arts of Saint Augustine, successfully completed.”

44. On page XI, rubric: “In the name of the Lord begins the rule of Augustine, bishop, on the noun: All nouns end in thirteen letters.” It ends: “*mille* is indeclinable”; I shall say more about this work shortly.

On page 27, rubric: “Here begins Donatus’s Art, which Paul the Deacon explained. D. How many parts of speech are there? M. Eight. D. Which? M. Noun,” etc. In the same place: “As Juvencus says: ‘The illustrious offspring of David.’” It ends: “such as *ac*, *at*, *et*, and any similar forms.”

On the reverse of page 40, rubric: “Here begins Saint Isidore, bishop, on Grammar and its parts: Discipline comes from learning,” etc. This is Book I of the *Etymologies*. In chapter 7 the manuscript reads: “Virgil wrote the *Bucolics*; we add the pronoun: ‘he himself wrote the *Georgics*.’” In chapter 16 the manuscript has: “The feet are . . . they stand upon”; Breulius reads “they consist.” In chapter 23: “but when he [comes to] boyhood . . . the letter lambda,” etc. In chapter 25: “*datatim* gives itself,” etc. “*A labris*” (“from lips”) instead of “*Et a libris*” (“and from books”). It ends: “because they are contrary to nature,” which is the end of the first book.

45. Page 59. Inscription: “Dynamus the grammarian said to his disciple: O how pitiable is the condition,” etc. The preface ends: “into eternal dwellings.” Question: “Who was first called by the name of philosopher?” Answer: “Pythagoras, out of humility,” etc. The ligatures used to express question and answer belong to a later hand.

The author is a Christian, as is clear also from the letter, or prologue, which appears to have been published already. The arts are explained through various diagrams, or paradigms and figures, by which the divisions of the parts are demonstrated.

On the reverse of page 62, concerning letters: “We read that among our ancestors there were first eleven, then sixteen, and afterward twenty-three letters invented, as they are found today. But after the *regionem*” [perhaps *religionem*, “religion”] “of the Christian faith, we used twenty-eight letters in the sacred writings, that is, in the name of Christ, Ξ and Π” [the note says “it seems to be *sembitur et p*”], “in IHS, H, and in the Apocalypse, Α and ω. *IHU* is written instead of *HIS*.”

46. On page 76 examples are given:

> Raise your eyebrow if you recognize yourself as a friend.  
> (Sedulius, in the preface.)

> He places torches bound around the tails and throws them into the crops.  
> (Prudentius, in the *Dittochaeon*.)

It should be noted that the leaves are not properly joined: this material no longer belongs to Dynamus. It ends there, on the reverse of page 71, with the section on the interjection: “joined now before, now after.” Then, apparently in another but equally ancient script, on page 72: “How many syllables does the arsis claim for itself, and how many the thesis,” etc. This is part of the work of Julian of Toledo, to be mentioned shortly.

On the reverse of page 76 is *On Punctuation*. In the same place: “What, for example, if I say:

> A harsh condition, and the irrevocable fate of the hour,  
> which a sorrowful origin gave to the human race.

In the same place: “For even the book which we call *commicum* we ought not to call *commicum*, but *commatum*, because obscure statements from many books have been set down there. Here ends the first treatise,” namely of Saint Julian of Toledo.

47. On the following page, 77: “On barbarism: Barbarism is one defective part of speech in ordinary language, that is, in prose.” On page 85 Augustine is cited in the books *On Christian Doctrine*. Rhetorical figures are discussed at greater length than in Isidore. It ends with an explanation of the parable: “Likewise, in the Gospel Christ said of Herod: ‘That fox.’” These materials also belong to Julian’s work.

Immediately afterward, on page 87, rubric: “Also Julian, bishop of Toledo, on the letter: How many parts does the art of grammar have? [perhaps something is missing here: ‘two.’] The first part is,” etc. This is the beginning of the first treatise of Julian’s work. Shortly afterward, at the beginning, it gives verses by Eugenius of Toledo, without naming him, concerning the inventors of letters:

> Moses was the first, etc.  
> Wulfila brought forth the final letters of the Goths which we see.

Then, on the reverse of the same page, it takes an example from the unnamed Dracontius:

> So that the vulture may know in what region the carcass lies.

48. On page 88, from Book IX, chapter 1 of the *Etymologies*, without naming the source: “The Greek language, among the languages of the other nations,” etc. “But the Latin languages are four,” etc. On the reverse of the same page are several verses from Prudentius’ *Dittochaeon*, again without naming him. There is also the following from Sedulius, unnamed:

> Christ was bread, Christ was rock, etc.

He repeats it more than once:

O mortal man, remember the circumstances of death: this is a verse of Eugenius of Toledo, Book I, Poem 2. On the verso of page 89, heading: “It begins with the syllable. What is a syllable? A combination of letters.”

49. Page 90: “Give an example where *au* occurs”:

> The fourth day had already sent Aurora forth over the waters,

from Dracontius. “Give an example where *eu* occurs”:

> Weep, poor Eugenius; grievous illness presses hard,

[Col. 0881A] from Eugenius, Book I, Poem 13. Page 91: “On the noun, on final syllables. *A* terminates…” and similarly other headings concerning the other parts of speech and meters. It ends on the verso of folio 98: “bearing arms, and rushing joyfully.” Many passages are from Eugenius, such as the verse “Woe is me,” etc., from Book I, Poem 11. On page 99 follows the heading: “The Art of Talvinus begins” [perhaps *Alcuinus*]. “There are eight parts of grammatical speech.” At the beginning of the volume one appears to read *Tacuini*, corrected to *Talvini* or *Tatuini*; in the old catalogue it is written *Tatuini*. The author is a Christian. He cites Donatus. On the verso of page 101: “Other ethnic names, such as Greek and Spanish: those who were the founders of the provinces of Greece and Spain.” It ends with the heading: “Common nouns: Among common nouns, etc., as they wished; given, thanks be to God.”

[Col. 0881B] 373

50. On the verso of page 126: “The Art of Julian, Bishop of Toledo” (so written). “How many are the parts of speech? Eight. Which? Noun, pronoun, verb, etc.” This is the beginning of the second treatise of Julian’s work. On the same page, 129: “There is a seventh case if I say: ‘Isidorus is more learned than Antonius.’” On page 134: “Why is it called less than the finite? Because I am speaking of a known and absent person; for example: ‘Do you know Lord Ervigio? He is the prince of Spain’” (above, *Hispaniae*). The name “Isidorus” is frequently introduced in examples, and more than once “King Ervigio,” as in no. 326: “Lord King Ervigio.” On the verso of page 150:

> And silently he grieves over the matter and searches his heart;

this verse of Dracontius is given in the Azagra Codex, according to Eugenius’ correction, as follows:

[Col. 0881C]

> For this reason he silently grieves and searches his heart.

Copies older than Eugenius had it differently, as I said in my note on Dracontius, Book I, verse 357. On the same page:

> But neither earth gives birth to man, nor the sea from its waters,

(Dracontius). It ends, “belong to this part,” which is the conclusion of Julian’s second treatise.

51. Page 157, heading: “The Art of Asper, concerning the eight parts of speech, begins: There are eight parts of speech, etc.” It ends, “at Augustodunum, and similar expressions.” Page 162: “The Art of Lord Boniface, bishop and martyr: Aristotle was the first concerning the parts of speech, etc.” It ends, “and on the other side.” There are paradigms of conjugations. Some passages cannot be read.

52. After Julian’s second work, on page 152, there is a hymn that can scarcely be read because the letters are fading. From them I reconstruct the following:

> God, life of the saints and of the angels,  
>   
> life likewise of all the devout,  
>   
> Christ, who by dying overcame  
>   
> the servant of death.
>
> 
> Now, in these peaceful days,  
>   
> preserve your chosen servants,  
>   
> when holy Easter is celebrated  
>   
> throughout the ages.
>
> 
> Easter—when, returning victorious from below  
>   
> and rising again with many others,  
>   
> you yourself lifted the flesh you had assumed  
>   
> above the lofty stars.
>
> 
> Now the Lord shines on high,  
>   
> and God is exalted above the heavens.  
>   
> From there he will come as man,  
>   
> again as judge.
>
> 
> Lift up our hearts now,  
>   
> to where they sit at the Father’s right hand on high,  
>   
> lest you cause those seated there  
>   
> to be hurled down into the depths.
>
> 
> May the Father, the same consecrated Spirit of them both,  
>   
> gracious Christ, grant this with you,  
>   
> with whom one God reigns  
>   
> forever throughout every age.

Perhaps one should read: “May the Father, the same consecrated one, grant this with you.” In place of *residentes* I would read *retinentes*, and *regnas* for *regnat*.

53. The Maurists, in the first work included in their edition of the works of Saint Augustine, entitled “The Arts of Saint Augustine,” do not mention it. They judged the second, “The Rule of Augustine, etc.,” to be spurious and relegated it to the appendices of volume 374, because it is not written in dialogue form and does not raise the soul toward incorporeal things—features that ought to agree with Augustine’s book on Grammar, mentioned in the *Retractations* [Col. 0882B]. Dupin subsequently maintained this opinion, and Tillemont inclines toward it in note 6 to the Life of Saint Augustine; but he did not understand the Maurists’ admonition. For he in some way reproaches them because they said that the beginning of this book on Grammar, which appears in printed editions, is absent from old and recent manuscripts, whereas elsewhere they assert that they had found no manuscript copy of this work. But the Maurists certainly do not say that “the beginning of the published work” is absent from manuscripts; rather, they are speaking of “the appended clause” in the book of the *Retractations*, in which that beginning is mentioned. Here are their words:

> “A difficulty was raised by the appended clause of chapter 7 (in their edition, chapter 6) of Book I of the *Retractations*, namely: ‘This work begins as follows: All nouns are thirteen.’ This is the beginning of the following book, On Grammar. But we exposed the deception from manuscripts—both old and recent ones—which do not contain it.”

54. The beginning of the work in our Codex is identical with that in the appended clause. At the end the Maurists printed, “*mille* is declinable”; the Palatine Codex has, “*mille* is indeclinable,” which is preferable, since *mille* is indeclinable in the singular, while *millia* is declinable in the plural. It should also be considered whether the first work, “The Arts of Saint Augustine,” might with greater right be attributed to the holy Doctor. In Spain, as I hear, certain learned men are preparing a Maurist edition of the works of Saint Augustine. It would be desirable that they not be content, as printers commonly are, merely to reprint what they find, since many additions could make the edition more distinguished. For this reason I will not omit mentioning that in two Vatican Codices, nos. 4991 and 4992, there are already preserved collections entitled “Various Readings in Saint Augustine from Ancient Vatican Manuscripts,” as is clear from the Inventory. In the Royal-Vatican Codex 299 there are other materials concerning the edition that was being prepared at Rome in the sixteenth century, from Stapleton, Jerome Torrensis, S.J., and Emmanuel Sa. More may be seen in Peter Morinus, letters 13 and following.

55. Dynamius, whose work is copied in this Codex, may perhaps be that Dynamius of Bordeaux whom Ausonius celebrates among the professors of Bordeaux in Poem 24, concerning whom, among other things, he says:

> Whom wounded reputation drove away on a charge of adultery,  
>   
> whom little Ilerda sheltered in its hidden places;
>
> 
> whom his Spanish wife enriched while he lay concealed;  
>   
> for there, under an assumed name, you were a rhetorician…
>
> 
> Although belated affection had restored you to your homeland,  
>   
> soon the house at Ilerda drew you back again in retirement.

[Col. 0883A] This conjecture may be confirmed by the fact that Dynamius’ work is joined in the same volume with the works of Isidore and Julian of Toledo on grammar.

56. But what should be thought about the work of Julian of Toledo? It is not mentioned by Felix in his Life, perhaps because it deals with secular disciplines. For when Felix was about to discuss the books of Saint Julian, he prefaced them as follows:

> “Reader, learn from there the sum of his books, which God brought forth through him for the benefit of His Church.”
