Moreover, the genuineness of the title in the very ancient Codex is confirmed by the mention [Col. 0883B] of “King Ervigio of the Goths, in whose time Julian flourished.” The same conclusion is suggested by the examples repeatedly drawn from “Eugenius of Toledo,” who was Julian’s teacher, and from “Dracontius,” corrected by that same “Eugenius”; by the cities of Spain—“Emerita, Toledo, Caesaraugusta”—not to mention the reference to Isidore and the many passages taken from him. Add the use of the Gothic Psalter in no. 189: “He sent among them a dog-fly,” from Psalm 77, verse 45.

57. The antiquity of the Codex is confirmed by an old catalogue of the Laurissana library, from the tenth century or the following one, in parchment quarto, which is still preserved in the Vatican-Palatine Library, no. 1877. Its title, in majuscule letters, is: “Summary of the Books of Saint Nazarius.” In this catalogue our Codex was already listed in the following words:

[Col. 0883C]

> “An abbreviated grammatical art of Saint Augustine. Also another work of his. Also Paul the Deacon to King Charles. Also Saint Isidore, bishop. Also a certain wise man (I think Dynamius is meant). Also Tatuinus (so written). Also Julian, Bishop of Toledo (so written). Also another work of his, on the letter, on barbarism, and on the other faults. His work on figures. The Art of Marius Victorinus the grammarian, and Althelmus on the Rule of Meters, and the riddles of Symphosius in one Codex.”

All these works seem once to have been contained in a single Codex. The beginning of Saint Julian’s work may then have been taken from the verso of page 126, where it now reads, “The Art of Julian, Bishop of Toledo,” beginning: “How many are the parts of speech, etc.” Thus the second part will be the work now found on page 87 under this title:

[Col. 0883D]

> “Also Julian, Bishop of Toledo, on the letter.”

The matter comes to the same conclusion.

## 376. CHAPTER CIV

Manuscript copies of thirteen works in the Vatican-Urbino Library described. French translation of the *Catena Patrum*. An unpublished little work of Isidore on Heaven. Interpolated *Soliloquies* and *Chronicles*. Various works on epacts, computation, calculation, etc. Ancient grammarians. Isidore’s *Chronicle* interpolated outside Spain.

1. Although the manuscript Codices that formerly belonged to the Dukes of Urbino and are now preserved in the Vatican Library were transferred there by Alexander VII in 1658, the ceded materials being compensated by a favor, and although they are more notable for elegance, scribal artistry, and pictorial decoration than for antiquity, nevertheless some among them are either extremely ancient or, though recent, are still to be held in high esteem [Col. 0884A], since they were copied with great care and diligence from older manuscripts of good quality, sometimes even rare ones. I will give first place to a French translation of a certain *Catena Patrum* drawn from Isidore and others. Although I had resolved to pass over such chains and collections, with which the Vatican Library is filled in all its departments, this one nevertheless seemed, because of its rarity, not to be omitted.

2. Urbino Codex 11, formerly numbered 42, parchment, large folio. It is described in the Inventory as follows:

> “Godfrey of Pinkegui’s chain from the Fathers on the four Gospels, the Acts of the Apostles, and the Apocalypse, compiled by him and translated into the French language.”

The Codex was issued by the author in 1321 and copied by Peter of Cambrai in 1322. The Fathers used by the compiler are identified as Augustine, etc., “Isidore, etc.” The copy is elegant and marked by a painter’s work, with images, an initial medallion, and decorations painted in red and gold, as Urbino Codices are customarily adorned. When the Magi offer their gifts, the Virgin is depicted holding the child in her hands, already dressed and not crying in a cradle. Hardouin speaks of a similar image in his commentary on the New Testament. The devil tempting the Lord is depicted with feet like those of roosters. Isidore’s name occurs rarely, for example on page 76, or on the verso of page 77, at Matthew chapter 14, in this sense:

> “If you had the wisdom of Solomon, the beauty of Absalom, the strength of Samson, the long life of Adam, etc.”

In the Gospel of Saint John the Crucifixion is depicted, and indeed [377] “with only three nails”; the right side is opened by a soldier. The Mother of God is represented lifeless. See Lazeri’s note on Bruno, volume II of the revised edition of the complete works, page 144. After the four Gospels come the Acts of the Apostles, but historically and without glosses by the Fathers. Then comes the Apocalypse without glosses by the Fathers. Godfrey of Pinkegui completed the work in 1321; Peter of Cambrai completed the copying of this volume in 1322.

3. Urbino Codex 60, formerly numbered 72, parchment folio, elegantly written in the fifteenth century in gold and various colors. It contains certain works of Saint Gregory Nazianzen and Saint John Chrysostom. In the initial letter an image of Saint Gregory is visible. On page 126 is Chrysostom’s treatise on Psalm 50. After the homilies in praise of Paul come verses by Basil, or Chrysostom, in praise of the same Saint Paul:

[Col. 0884D]

> Paul, pole of the earth, etc.

Then follows the inscription:

> “The distinguished verses in praise of the Apostle Paul by the most illustrious man Damasus, supreme pontiff of the Roman Church, begin.”

I have excerpted several variant readings from this Codex for the edition of Saint Damasus prepared through the work of Merenda, having collated it myself.

4. On the verso of page 178 is a eulogy of Saint John Chrysostom from Isidore, from chapter 21, as it is said there, of *On Illustrious Men*; but in Grialius it is chapter 19, and in others chapter 6. It ends, “they thrust him into exile.” Ambrose of Camaldoli’s translation against the detractors of the monastic life follows; from the prologue it is clear that this was the beginning of his studies. In this Codex, on page 175, in Homily 7 of Chrysostom on the Praise of Paul, we read:

> “With what freedom, too, does he close the mouths of the wicked? Yet not content to remain there, he even hastened onward into Spain.”

This is marked as absent, and the following is added:

> “Note that it is not commonly accepted that he went to Spain; rather, he had once said that he intended to go there, as is clear from Romans, chapter 15.”

5. Urbino Codex 100, formerly 141, parchment folio, with clean script, rubrics, and gold letters, dating approximately from the fifteenth century. Several works of Isidore are contained in this Codex. Heading:

> “The text of Isidore’s letters to Braulio, and of Braulio’s to Isidore, concerning the request for the book of the *Etymologies*, begins auspiciously.”

A table of the chapters of twenty-two books follows. Book I, on Grammar, etc.: there are 29 chapters. Book II, on Rhetoric: 21 chapters. Book III, on Dialectic: 6 chapters. [Col. 0885B] Book IV, on Mathematics: 69 chapters. Book V, on Medicine: 12 chapters. Book VI, on Laws, etc.: 28 chapters. Book VII, on the word “Chronicle”: 12 chapters. Book VIII, on the order of the Scriptures: 21 chapters. Book IX, on God and the angels: 14 chapters. Book X, on the Church: 11 chapters. Book XI, on the languages of the nations: 7 chapters. Book XII, on certain names in alphabetical order. The remaining ten books are as in the last ten books of the printed editions.

6. At the end of the *Etymologies*:

> “Book XXII of Isidore’s *Etymologies* ends auspiciously. Isidore’s letter begins auspiciously. Since I know you to excel in talent and eloquence, and in the varied flower of letters, yet you devote yourself, etc.”

After the letter is the heading:

> “Book XXIII of Isidore on Astronomy begins auspiciously. On days: first chapter. A day is of the sun, etc.”

In the table of books this work is represented as separate from the other books of the *Etymologies*. There are spheres, or circular diagrams, and others of various forms; the chapters number 49. Chapter 45 is “On the names of seas and rivers. In the annalistic books, Tranquillus of the Fathers, etc.” The last chapter is “On the parts of the earth: Now the position of the earth, etc.” After the final words of the printed editions, “they estimated [the distances in] stadia,” the following is added: “But three hundred in length and two hundred in breadth—this will be said in the Catholic histories.” A diagram of the earth with its three parts—Asia, Europe, and Africa—follows. Heading on Heaven:

> “It is asked whether there is one heaven or several, etc.”

Some questions about heaven follow. It ends, “the capacity of all human [Col. 0885D] intellect.” Heading:

> “The book of Isidore on Astronomy and Heaven ends auspiciously.”

That first question—whether there is one heaven, etc.—is discussed in this book on *The Nature of Things*, chapter 13, in different words. See above, chapter 86, no. 5.

7. Page 191, heading:

> “The Book of Prologues” (correct to *Prooemia*) “begins auspiciously. On the fullness of the books of the New and Old Testament, etc.”

It ends, “and the acts of embassies.” Heading:

> “Also, prefaces to the New Testament. The preaching of the Gospels, etc.”

It ends, “the tree of life, the Lord Jesus Christ.” On the verso of page 146, heading:

> “The Origins and Life, or Deaths, of the Saints who have gone before in the Lord; the preface begins auspiciously.”

At the beginning of the page is the heading:

> “Isidore on the Death of the Fathers. Preface: of certain saints, etc. Adam the first-formed, etc.”

All the chapters of the New and Old Testament number 84; the last is “On Titus.” Chapter 70, on James the Greater, reads as in the printed editions:

> “He wrote … poured out … and was buried in Achaia Marmarica, on the eighth day before the Kalends of August.”

On Peter: “toward the eastern region.” On Paul: “toward the eastern region.” On Matthew: “in the mountains of Persia.” On Thomas: “in Calaminia.” In chapter 79 [379], the division of the apostles is joined to the section on Simon:

> “James [went to] Spain … Philip [went to] Gaul.”

8. On the verso of page 204:

> “The book of Isidore to Orosius begins: To the holy and most reverend brother Orosius, Isidore. Certain very well-known matters, etc.”

It ends, “they will be filled with the refreshment of eternal blessedness.” These are the *Allegories*. At the end is the heading:

> “The Book of the First [correct to *Allegories*] of Saint Isidore to Orosius ends auspiciously. The Book of the *Soliloquies* of blessed Isidore to Father Orosius begins. The prologue of the *Soliloquies* begins: Isidore sends greetings to the reader. Recently a certain little sheet came into my hands, which they call the *Synonyma*, whose form persuaded my mind, etc.”

Perhaps instead of “to Father Orosius” one should read “to Orosius the presbyter”; but the entire passage seems to have been ineptly repeated by the scribe from the preceding work, since Isidore’s *Soliloquies* are not dedicated to Orosius.

9. In the dialogue the headings precede their respective sections: “The grieving man: the admonishing reason.” At the end again:

> “The Book of the *Soliloquies* to Father Orosius ends auspiciously, and so forth; the end.”

The first book continues directly into the second. Near the end of Book II in the printed editions one reads:

> “In heaven, not on earth, reward is promised to the saints”;

in the manuscripts, “to the just,” with the addition:

> “Among my other admonitions, you should also know that sin is committed in four ways, etc.”

This is nearly as in chapter 17 of Book II of the *Sentences*, but more fully. Other material is added that is absent from Isidore’s works, concerning the seven original sins of Adam, Christian discipline, etc. The *Soliloquies* end:

> “a good mind and a peaceful life,”

with the heading already reported. Much is omitted from the work. Books I and II continue as follows:

> “He who sins frequently and mourns scarcely deserves pardon. Then your work will be perfect if you persevere to the end” [perhaps: “if it has persevered to the end”]. “Always consider yourself, man, and know what you are and for what purpose you were brought forth into the world.”

[Col. 0886D] Other passages are likewise mutilated.

10. Page 217, heading:

> “The Book of the Differences of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, begins: What is the difference between God and Lord? Between God and Lord, some have defined it in this way, etc.”

It ends, “and an example of Christ’s humility.” These are *Differences of Things*, which agree sufficiently with the printed editions. Heading:

> “The Book of the Differences of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, ends auspiciously.”

Page 227, heading:

> “Preface, or Recapitulation of the Catholic Faith, or Superscription of the Work of Isidore, Bishop of Spain, addressed to his sister Florentina. To his holy sister Florentina, Isidore, Bishop of Toledo: Certain things which [are treated] variously, etc.”

In other manuscripts as well, Isidore is incorrectly titled “of Toledo.” Heading:

> “The Preface, or Recapitulation [Col. 0887A] of Isidore, ends. The First Book of Isidore Against the Jews begins auspiciously, etc.”

The final chapter is 63, etc.

> “The First Book of Isidore Against the Jews ends auspiciously. Prologue to the second book, or summary of the preceding book. In some respect, etc. The Second Book of Isidore on the Calling of the Nations begins auspiciously.”

The final chapter is 28:

> “Recapitulation of the work, etc. The Second Book of Isidore on the Calling of the Nations Against the Jews ends auspiciously.”

11. Page 253, heading:

> “The Book of Chronicles of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Seville, from the beginning of the world to the reign of Heraclius and the rule of Sisebut, King of the Goths, who reigned around the year of the Lord 600, beginning from the creation of the world in 4060, begins. The prologue of Isidore begins auspiciously. A brief sequence of times through the generations, etc.”

There it reads:

> “We have summarized these times from the beginning of the world to the reign of Augustus Heraclius and the rule of Sisebut, King of the Goths, etc.”

The prologue ends, “the first man, Adam.” But beside the words “it may be known. In six days God formed the creation of all things,” a marginal note has been added:

> “The first age of the world: on the creation of things.”

12. In the ancient history before the birth of Christ it agrees sufficiently with the published chronicle. Some things are abridged, as near the end of the fifth age:

> “Cicero is considered famous for his oratorical praise. Cleopatra, year 1, because in her third year [perhaps: year 11, in whose third year] Julius Caesar assumes power. The sixth age: Gaius Julius Caesar reigned five years. He first obtained sole rule among the Romans; from him the Caesars are so called, and from this point the emperors follow. Octavian Augustus reigned 61 years”—

above, in the same hand, or perhaps 51.

Thereafter, in the accounts of the first emperors, some things are added and some omitted. There is little about Nero. Galba, Otho, and Vitellius, omitted in the printed editions, are added:

> “After Nero, Galba reigned four months and was killed in the forum at Rome. Otho reigned 205 days, lived 34 years, and killed himself in Italy near Hebraicum. Vitellius reigned eight months, lived 54 years, and was killed by the commanders of Vespasian.”

Of Constantine:

> “It was discovered. And when he was preparing war against the Persians, in a public villa near Nicomedia, having arranged the state well and entrusted it to his sons, he died; he lived 66 years.”

Other material is omitted. Under Julian:

> “The sign of the cross appeared. While he was wandering incautiously through the vastness of the desert, he was struck and killed by a certain enemy horseman he encountered” [perhaps: by an opposing weapon or spear]. “He lived 30 years.”

13. There are many variations in these and the following emperors. Concerning Justinian:

> “At the same time Pompeyiopolis suffered from divine indignation” [perhaps: “the wretched city”; *misit* is uncertain]. “For the earth was split by an earthquake, and the middle of the city was buried together with its inhabitants; they were beneath the earth because of the earthquake, and their voices were heard crying out that mercy be shown them. The emperor gave much to bring out the young men” [perhaps: “the survivors”].

Spanish affairs are either omitted or abridged, as in:

> “Mauricius reigned 21 years. The Suebi are subjected by Leovigild, having been conquered by the Goths” [the text has *ab optentis*, so written]. “The Goths, under Reccared, return to the Catholic faith. Saint Gregory [Col. 0888A] is held in distinction. In the same year the Avars performed an embassy, etc.”

The compiler, or interpolator, chiefly follows the affairs of the emperors. Saint Hermenegild is not mentioned.

14. After much concerning Phocas, it ends:

> “When war had been undertaken, the grace of Christ conquers the tyrant. But the common people seized and killed him, and burned him by fire at Boi.”

Heading:

> “The Book of Chronicles, or of Times, of Saint Isidore, Archbishop of Seville, ends.”

The rest that follows was written by another hand up to the end of the book:

> “Heraclius reigned 31 years. Therefore, having entered upon the royal power, he was crowned, etc.”

The history of the emperors is woven together at length up to Michael:

> “Michael the most devout, etc., and he captured Adrianople, which had been besieged.”

After him the Lombard kings are briefly summarized, as I think, by another continuator:

> “Alboin, the tenth king of the Lombards, first reigned in Italy over the Lombards for three years and six months. When he died, it was the fourth indiction, in the year of the Lord 568, etc. Berengar, king, after the death of Charles, etc.”

Here and in what follows the account is somewhat fuller. The last entry is:

> “Afterward his son Henry reigned six years. Then, coming to Rome in the year 1046, and having held a council on account of the simoniacal heresy, he deposed Pope John, surnamed Gratian” [I read: “Gregory”]. “The venerable Pope Clement succeeded him and, granting the crown to the aforesaid king, reigned six years and died in the year 1055. The end.”

Heading:

> “Another Chronicle, from Heraclius to the end of the book, ends auspiciously.”

[Col. 0888C]

15. Page 273, heading:

> “The Book of Prosper on the Contemplative Life begins auspiciously.”

This Prosper is said to have been the notary of Saint Pope Leo. He flourished around the year 458. There is a preface and three books. At the end:

> “The Third Book of Prosper on the Contemplative Life ends auspiciously.”

It has often already been noted that these books are not by Prosper but by Julianus Pomerius. There is nothing else in this beautiful Codex, nor is it said by whom it was written. After the table at the beginning there is a large circle with ten smaller circles, in which the works contained are indicated. At the beginning of the *Etymologies*, among the other decorations, there is the papal coat of arms of the House of Urbino, but without the letters F.R. or F.D., which occur elsewhere. The scribe frequently uses Arabic numerals. Ten works are indicated in the circles, because the book of Astronomy, or *On the Nature of Things*, is treated as a work distinct from the *Etymologies*, although in the text itself it is called Book XXIII of the *Etymologies*, as I have already observed.

16. Urbino Codex 105, formerly 146, folio parchment, apparently from the fifteenth century, decorated with gold paintings outlined in red and with an initial medallion:

> “The Sermons of Aymo, a most learned and holy man.”

At the beginning is an image of Aymo with mitre and staff. The first is a homily on the Gospel: “There will be signs, etc.” The last is on the Gospel of Luke: “Let your loins be girded. The luxury of men is in the loins, but that of women is in the navel of the belly, etc.” The book of the Homilies of the Doctor Aymo ends.

17. Certain sayings from Gregory and Isidore follow. The first is without a title:

> “Just as bundles of wood are for burning,”

from chapter 32 of Book I of the *Sentences*, where Isidore takes several passages from Gregory. “Isidore” is named with this saying.

> “Isaac dug wells among a foreign people, etc.”

This is from the Commentary on Genesis, chapter 22, but not in exactly the same words. The Codex ends:

> “Jesus, thanks be to God, amen.”

It was copied after the time of Saint Bernardino. The coat of arms of the Dukes of Urbino is present, with papal insignia added on both sides and the letters F.D.; perhaps this indicates Duke Federico, as elsewhere in a similar coat of arms that appears in other Codices, showing two eagles, though sometimes without the symbol of papal dignity.

18. Urbino Codex 106, formerly 156 or 159, parchment folio with figures and paintings, and at the beginning a circular design [Col. 0889B] and the papal coat of arms of the Dukes of Urbino. In the circle is the inscription:

> “In this Codex are contained the three books of Hugh and Herianus on the Immortal God, and the three books of Isidore, Bishop of Hispalis, on the Highest Good.”

The prologue of Hugh and Herianus on the Immortal God begins auspiciously:

> “Once Moses, etc.”

On page 120, heading:

> “The book of Hugh on the holy and immortal God: The account of the memorable virtues of Pope Alexander III and the great emperor Manuel, published at Constantinople in Latin and Greek, ends.”

There follow letters from Hugh to Pope Alexander, from Alexander [383] to Hugh, from Hugh to Aimericus, Patriarch of Antioch, and from the latter to Hugh, in which he sends “one silver cup” from which he might drink. There is also a consolatory letter from Pope Lucius on the death of Master Hugh to his brother. [Col. 0889C] This book of Hugh was published—that is, written at Constantinople in Greek and Latin—as is clear from the note at the end.

19. Page 126, heading:

> “The preface of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Hispalis, in the book On the Highest Good begins: To the holy and meritoriously blessed brother Masona, bishop, Isidore, bishop, etc.”

In this letter one reads:

> “In Nicerius, etc., an authority either older or more authoritative exists. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our Lord, the most glorious King Witteric. The prologue ends. The chapters of the first book begin.”

The table displays only fifteen chapters of the first book. Several are included under one title, and some are omitted. Here Book I is defective: “and they will be purified in terror,” the penultimate chapter, near the end. Page 149, heading:

> “The Second Book of the *Sentences* of Saint Isidore begins.”

[Col. 0889D] A table of 41 chapters precedes it. The last concerns abstinence, which in Breul’s edition is numbered 44. Book II ends as in the printed editions:

> “but also presents danger.”

It adds some barbarous and faulty verses:

> “Receive, reader,” etc.

Book III lists 65 chapters. In the text the final chapter is 68. It ends:

> “not those whom the heavenly court encloses in joy. It ends.”

> “The Book of the *Sentences* of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Hispalis, ends. Thanks be to God. Amen.”

20. Urbino Codex 290, parchment folio, approximately from the eleventh century, in French or Roman cursive script. It contains various astronomical and astrological miscellanies, anonymous. Page 3:

> “Pet[osiris?] greets King Micipsa. Concerning those things that I discovered for the protection of human life, etc.”

On the verso:

> “Rem. Favius” [I read: “Fanius”]. “On weights and measures:
>
> 
> The weights commemorated in the ancient Paeonian books.”

In the table of epacts and indictions, which runs from the year 988 to the year 1234, certain events are recorded in a more recent hand.

21. Under the year 1095 mention is made of Aldebert, who was deposed; Wecelin, archbishop, succeeded him (I think the archbishop of Cologne). Under the year 1000: “The ordination of Archbishop Heribert.” Under the year 1049: “Here the foundations of our monastery were laid.” Under the year 1033: “The appointment of Abbot Tegeno.” The succession of abbots and monasteries is reported up to the year 1179, when the notes of the second hand end. The work may have been made in the year 988. Page 12:

> “Hermann’s computation according to nature: why the moon’s age so often does not agree with our calculation.”

384

22. Pages 30 and following:

> “On the number of the fingers, or on the method of counting by the fingers, with diagrams.”

Page 31: verses on the months in tetrastichs:

> “Now this month,” etc.

Monostichs on the months:

> “The first [month] of the Romans.”

Verses on the signs:

> “First appears the ram.”

Verses on the sphere:

> “Toward the regions of the North,”

attributed to Ausonius. Verses on the signs and months:

> “The beginning of January.”

Verses on the week:

> “The first day belongs to Phoebus.”

A work on divisions of time:

> “How many are the divisions of time?”

Page 44, heading:

> “The saying of Saint Augustine and Isidore in praise of computation begins: Isidore in praise of computation. The reasoning of numbers, etc.”

From chapter 4 of Book III of the *Etymologies*. On the verso of page 51 [Col. 0890C], without a title:

> “When I had begun to explain in ordinary speech certain rudiments of the art of calculation to our younger brothers, etc.”

After the prologue is the heading:

> “The little book of the art of calculation by Helpric begins: The solar year, as the skill of our ancestors establishes, etc.”

There are 38 chapters. In chapter 38, which is the epilogue:

> “Sometimes earthen vessels tend to be more useful the cheaper they are, etc. But whoever disdains these things should know that they were not said for him, but only for those who do not yet know how to penetrate greater matters.”

23. Page 64. A table of epacts with the names of the archbishops of Trier up to the year 1098. On the verso of page 64, a table of epacts with the names of the archbishops of Cologne.

[Col. 0890D]

24. Urbino Codex 307, also 529, parchment, fifteenth century, with figures and paintings in gold. It does not bear the coat of arms of the Dukes of Urbino. Among the boys painted on the first page, one is playing a musical instrument resembling our violin, or in Italian, a *violino*. Heading:

> “The concise doctrine of Nonius Marcellus the Peripatetic of Tuburgium, arranged by letters for his son, begins auspiciously.”

“*Serium* is weariness and hatred,” etc. The initial letter displays an image of Nonius Marcellus. It ends, “in Afranius and the very ancient writers.” The printed editions have, “and the very ancient writers of law.”

25. Page 146, heading:

> “The abridgment of Festus Pompeius, On the Meaning of Words, begins auspiciously. Augustus’ place, etc.”

An image of Festus appears in the initial letter. Page 209, heading:

> “Selected words from the grammarian Servius on the *Aeneid*, by Guarino of Verona: ‘To abjure is,’ etc.”

[Col. 0891A] The words are arranged alphabetically. Page 264, heading:

> “On the names of weights and instruments for weighing according to Isidore. A balance is a double pan of weights, etc.”

From Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 24. Other material on measures follows, from chapter 25.

26. Urbino Codex 308, also 530, a clean parchment manuscript, ornamented with paintings and images in gold and red, with the papal coat of arms of the family of the Dukes of Urbino. Within the first circle:

> “Nonius Marcellus, On Concise Doctrine”;

a more recent hand has noted:

> “It is not Nonius, but Diomedes, On Speech, etc.”

On the first page a schoolmaster is depicted; elsewhere he is teaching boys from a chair; elsewhere he is beating the buttocks of a boy who hangs from another boy’s shoulders. The feet of the one being punished are restrained by other boys. The schoolmaster raises a whip in his hand [Col. 0891B], with a wooden handle and three cords. The work begins:

> “The art of pure Latinity, etc.”

There are three books. It ends:

> “the grateful testimony of readers, if not for labor, certainly for simplicity, will be attained.”

27. On the verso of page 124, without a title:

> “To my lord Enchiesius” [others: “Eucherius”], “bishop, Agroetius sends greetings. We can preserve Caprus’s little book, etc. Farewell; remember me and my protector. *Agroetius*, when you write in Latin, should be written with a diphthong, not, as some think, *Agrytius* with a *y*. *Triceni* derives from *tricenti*, etc.”

It ends:

> “We call punishments *supplicia*, and divine prayers *preces*.”

The end. Read chapter 56.

28. On the verso of page 150, heading:

> “The school of Albinus the grammarian on grammar, etc. There were in Albinus’ school two pupils, one Abstemius from Macerata in the town of Flaminia [Col. 0891C], and the other Zolphus of Pergula, etc.”

There is a dialogue among these three. Page 192, heading:

> “The work of Nonius Marcellus the Peripatetic, On Undifferentiated Genera, arranged by the letters of the alphabet, begins auspiciously for his son: *Angiportus* is masculine in gender, and among many it is neuter.”

It ends:

> “arisen, painted, figure.”

Red verses:

> These things he willingly recorded, although they will perish with time,  
>   
> so that you might know, Duke Federico, that Golphus is yours.  
>   
> For he preserves monuments of you, greater in his heart,  
>   
> destined not to die through years or any decay, etc.

Perhaps this Golphus is the author of the dialogue among himself, Albinus, and Abstemius.

29. Urbino Codex 382, also 606, clean and adorned with paintings in gold, etc. The coat of arms does not appear to be that of the Dukes of Urbino. In the large circle and the other smaller ones [Col. 0891D] one reads:

> “In this highly ornamented Codex are contained the works noted in the circles: Eusebius on Times; Marcellinus on Times; Matthew on Times; Jerome on Illustrious Men; Gennadius on Illustrious Men; D. Alphonsus on Illustrious Men; Isidore on Illustrious Men; Isidore on the Death of the Saints.”

30. Page 1: “Here begins Eusebius’ Chronicle: Jerome’s, with additions by Prosper. Jerome’s adjuration: ‘I adjure you, whoever you may be who have copied these 386 books, by Our Lord Jesus Christ and his glorious coming, at which he will come to judge the living and the dead, to compare what you have written and correct it carefully against the exemplars from which you copied it. And you shall likewise copy and transfer this form of adjuration into the Codex that you copy.’” Compare Sedulius’s Prolegomena and what was said above in chapter 87 from Jerome’s letter to Lucinius of Baetica.

It ends in the year of the world 5646: “In the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nono [so]. Here ends the Chronicle of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper.”

Page 82, rubric: “Likewise, what we have culled from Marcellinus’ Chronicle: here begins the prologue of the same work: ‘After the remarkable work, etc. Theodosius the Spaniard, etc.’” It ends: “he received the office of teacher. A collection of all the years, etc.”

Page 90: “Likewise, Matteo Palmieri of Florence, On Times, etc.” It ends in the year 1448.

Page 142: “The book of the divine Jerome, On Illustrious Men: ‘You urge me.’ Of the same author, On the Ten Doctors, etc.” (Falsely attributed to Jerome.)

Page 158 verso, rubric: “The book of Gennadius, bishop of Marseille [so], On Illustrious Men.” The final chapter is on John, presbyter of the parish of Antioch.

31. Page 167 verso, rubric: “Here happily begins Isidore, archbishop of Seville, On Illustrious Men: ‘Although above, etc.,’” as in Grial. The order is the same, but after Victorinus the manuscript has: “Eucherius, bishop of Gaul, etc.” After Eusebius the manuscript has: “Sedulius, a presbyter skilled in grammar, etc.” Again, after John: “The presbyter Sedulius published, etc.” After Fulgentius: “On Rucerius, bishop. Rucerius, an elegant bishop, etc.” This is Eucherius in Grial’s printed edition. The final chapter is “On Isidore, bishop.” In the margin is the rubric: “Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, composed this life of Isidore.”

At the end of this Life: “The book of Isidore, On Illustrious Men, ends. The book of Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, On Illustrious Men, begins.” Preface: “An annotation of men, etc.” There are fourteen chapters, as in Grial: “Pope Gregory, etc.” The final three are Eugenius, Braulio, and a second Eugenius. Then follows the rubric: “On Ildefonsus, bishop: ‘Ildefonsus, memorable, etc.,’” without the author’s name, whether Julian’s or Felix’s. At the end of the Life of Ildefonsus: “The book of Ildefonsus, bishop, On Illustrious Men, ends.”

32. In the same place: “Here begins Isidore, bishop of Seville, On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Holy Fathers who excelled in virtue in the Old and New Testaments. Preface: ‘Certain men, etc.’” Then follows a table of chapters. The order is as in Breul. In the manuscript: “Dan, Issachar”; Breul has “Issachar, Dan.” The manuscript has: “Jonah, Micah, Nahum”; in Breul: “Azariah, Elijah, Elisha, Zechariah” (repeated), “Tobias.” The manuscript has: “Judith. Here ends the Lives of the 387 saints of the Old Testament. What follows concerns those who were in the New Testament: Zechariah, etc.” Breul has: “Judith, the Maccabees, Zechariah, etc.”

In this Codex: “James, whose name means ‘supplanter,’ son of Zebedee, brother of John, fourth in order, preached the Gospel in Spain and the western regions, and at the setting of the world shone forth with the light of his preaching. He was slain by the sword in Marmarica of Achaia by Herod the tetrarch, and was buried there.”

33. After the book On the Origin and Death of the Fathers, on page 186, the rubric reads: “Here begins Isidore, bishop of Seville, Book of Chronicles, etc.,” as stated in chapter 78. A table of titles follows, as in Codex 392, formerly 609, after the prologue, where one reads “Jerome’s Chronicle” without “presbyter.” After the table: “Here begins the first age, etc. In six days, etc., God first made Adam in his own likeness.” Rubric: “On Adam, etc.” Later: “Here begins the sixth age of the world, with which the seventh also runs, etc.,” as the same Chronicle begins in Schelstrat.

Under Valentinian: “they remained, although they had been neglected,” as in Schelstrat. Under Tiberius: “they are laid waste, and he himself is crowned with martyrdom” (concerning Saint Hermenegild).

It ends: “Eradius, etc.” (for Heraclius). “In the time of this emperor, up to the fourteenth year of his reign, and in the fortieth year of the reign of Lothair, the most glorious prince of the Franks, many losses were inflicted upon the state by various peoples, etc. Thus, from the beginning of the world to the fifth year of the emperor Eradius [read: Heraclius], and the fourth year of the reign of the religious prince Sisebutus, there are 5,820 years. Here ends the Book of Chronicles of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville.”

You can see that the interpolator was a Frank. The same words about Lothair are also found in Schelstrat.

34. Bede’s Chronicle follows in the same Codex: “Adam, being one hundred and thirty years old, begot Seth, etc.” Under Maurice there is an extensive account of the martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild and of Leander, bishop of “Hispalis,” who had taught him. It ends: “may deserve to receive the palm.”

Observe that the Chronicles of Isidore and Bede are not included in the circles on the first page, although they were written in the same script.

35. Codex 392 Urbinas, formerly 609, under which number Schelstrat published Isidore’s Chronicle. It is a small-format parchment manuscript, written in large, clear script, with golden paintings, multicolored figures, varied ornamentation, and the pontifical coat of arms of Federigo, duke of Urbino.[Col. 0893C] At the beginning is an index of the contents within an oblong rectangular frame 388.

The first work is Isidore’s Chronicle, as I have just described it from Codex 382, formerly 606.

36. Page 36, rubric: “Here begins Isidore, bishop of Seville, On the Origin, Life, and Death of the Holy Fathers who excelled in virtue in the Old and New Testament. Preface: ‘Certain holy men, etc.’” The table and order of chapters are as in Codex 382. The chapter on James is as in that same Codex 382. Concerning James the Younger, both Codices have: “the peoples eagerly desired to reach them. He writes a letter to the twelve tribes that are dispersed among the nations. While he was in Jerusalem, etc.” These two exemplars agree also in this work.

37. There follows a short work falsely attributed to Jerome in other manuscripts as well, On the Twelve Doctors: “Do you now wish, my brother Evagrius, etc.” Page 81: a calculation of years by eras: “In the year 5,194 from the creation of the world, Our Lord Jesus Christ was born.” The year of Christ 409 is mentioned.

Page 85 verso, rubric: “Extracts from Papias: ‘An age is properly called, etc.’” A brief Chronicle extending to the emperor Conrad and Henry the Younger.

Page 94: another Chronicle, or rather a history: “The kingdom of this age is acquired through wars, etc.” In the same place: “In whose time Alba was founded by the Latins; it has now been destroyed by the Romans, when the German emperor inflicted a great slaughter upon the Romans at Mount Porcus, on account of the pope’s heresy.” I think this was written by some schismatic in the twelfth century, during the time of Alexander III.

A history of various kingdoms and empires is woven together. It ends: “Titus succeeded for two years; he left the empire to his brother Domitian. Rufus sees: HE PRESIDES.” Then follows the rubric: “On the praises of Victorinus of Feltre: ‘I think it most truly worth reporting, etc.’”

38. Page 106 verso, rubric: “Here begins the Epitome of the divine Titus Livius of Padua: ‘The arrival of Aeneas in Italy, etc.’” It is an abridgment of 140 books, following continuously one after another. It ends: “He was praised by Caesar Augustus, his stepfather, and he bestowed many honors at his final funeral.”

39. Page 217: “The Augustal Book of Benvenuto of Imola, addressed to Marquis Alberto of Este.” In the same place: “Phocas, etc., who was the first to secure that the Roman Church should be head of the churches, whereas previously it called itself Constantinopolitan.”

A Catalogue of pontiffs and emperors follows: the pontiffs extend to Pius II, and the emperors to Frederick III. At the end: “By the hand of Matteo of Volterra.” He is the copyist of the book.

389

40. The book On the Origin and Death of the Fathers in the Old Testament agrees sufficiently with Breul in both of the Codices mentioned above, 382 and 392; but in both the final chapter on the Maccabees is missing. The chapters on Elijah, Elisha, Zechariah, and others, which are duplicated in Breul, are also absent.

In the New Testament, the section on the Blessed Virgin Mary ends in both manuscripts: “although a tomb is nevertheless found.” Perhaps “not” is missing.[Col. 0894C]

Concerning Peter, as in Breul: “toward the eastern region, etc.” Concerning Paul: “in the thirty-sixth year, etc.” Breul has “thirty-seventh.” Concerning John: “John, whose name means ‘grace,’ apostle and evangelist, etc.” Thus both manuscripts have it.

“Philip, whose name means ‘mouth of a lamp,’ from Bethsaida, etc.” Of the same: “His corpse rests there together with his daughters. Thomas, whose name means ‘abyss,’ etc. In the city of Calamina, etc.”

41. An interpretation is likewise added for some of the other apostles.

“James of Alphaeus, bishop of Jerusalem, etc., because of his death, etc. Matthias, one of the Seventy-Two, etc., to whom the preaching of the Gospel in Judea was assigned.”

In the division of the apostles: “James [was assigned] Spain, Philip Galilee.” Thus both manuscripts have it. But earlier it had been said of Philip: “He preaches Christ to the Gauls.”

Concerning Timothy: “of a Greek father, that is, an Athenian.” Breul has “that is, a pagan.”

Concerning Titus: “whom the apostle left in Crete to instruct the churches.” Breul has: “whom the aforesaid apostle left to establish the churches of Crete.”

Most other passages are the same in these manuscripts and in Breul. The place of Matthew’s burial is stated in both manuscripts: “He rests in one of the mountains of the Parthians.”

42. Codex 479 Urbinas, formerly 140, paper, quarto. The first title is: “Isidore’s Etymologies.” A table of the twenty books in red letters follows: “Here begins the letter of Isidore, bishop, to Braulio, bishop, etc. Commonly called the Letter.” Rubric: “Here begins the book of Isidore, bishop of Seville, addressed to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza.” Above is “Spanensis [Spanish], alternatively Spalensis [of Split],” and shortly afterward, alternatively, “Caesaraugustanum [of Zaragoza].” “Here you have, etc.”

Then follows the table of chapters of Book I, and so on. The order of the books is as in the printed editions. It is Book X. At the end: “may be dried by the heat of fire. Here ends Book XX of the Etymologies of Isidore the Younger, bishop of Split.” When the book is finished, let praise and glory be to Christ. It ends: ‘Do all this, Christ the King, make it known to me.’”

43. Codex 585 Urbinas, a large-octavo parchment Psalter, or Breviary. In one place I read that it is from the fourteenth century, but, as I think, it is from the eleventh century, written in Lombard or, as they call it, Beneventan script. It is ornamented with large golden initials, at times filling an entire page.[Col. 0895B]

At the beginning is the rubric: “Here begins Isidore’s Chronicle on the ages of the world: ‘The first age of this world is from Adam, etc.’” It ends: “Heraclius XVI, 5,775. In his fifth year and the fourth year of the most religious prince Sisebutus, the Jews in Spain become Christians. 5,824. The remaining time of the sixth age is known to God alone. Thus far Isidore.”

Some material in this brief Chronicle is inserted by the hand of a monastic interpolator, as it seems, in the original script; thus, under Justinian: “Saint Benedict flourished.” Under Maurice: “Gregory was distinguished at Rome.”

The Chronicle may have been taken from a fuller Chronicle of Isidore. At the beginning, certain matters concerning the ages of the world are prefixed which are absent from both Chronicles.

44. The Chronicle of this Breviary more clearly agrees with the Chronicle in the Etymologies, apart from certain interpolated passages. It is continued by the same hand with the rubric: “From here, from other histories,” up to the eleventh century and to Popes Urban and Paschal, whose years are not numbered.

Then follows the rubric: “Here begins the Catalogue of the abbots of the monastery of Monte Cassino.” In the Inventory it is rashly attributed to Saint Isidore; in the manuscript it is anonymous, and it extends to the eleventh century.

It begins: “Saint Benedict, first abbot and founder of the monastery of Monte Cassino. Abbot Constantine.” It ends: “Desiderius, abbot, who was also Pope Victor, sat for twenty-nine years, III, IV, and twenty-four days [as printed]. Abbot and cardinal Olerisius sat for … years.”

This Breviary, therefore, was written toward the end of the eleventh century. There is also a table of epacts from the year 1000 to 1244, with certain historical events noted, but only up to the year 1167.[Col. 0895D] A calendar follows.

45. Before the Psalter is painted an image of the Mother of God, holding a clothed child in her hand and lap; beneath her stands a praying monk.

After the canticles is the rubric: “Hymn of King Sisebutus: ‘We praise you, God, etc., I shall not be confounded forever.’” More will be said of this below.

After a few other items: “The Catholic Faith of Saint Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria: ‘Whoever, etc.’” A Hymnal follows.

For the Assumption of Saint Mary, without the author’s name: “Who could, with mighty speech, all-powerful, etc.,” which is attributed somewhere to Saint Ambrose.

Among the prayers for Saint James the Greater is a prayer from the Breviary, but it ends: “and may serve you in safety.” After the prayers is the rubric: “Here begins the BREVIARY, or order of the offices.”

This is clearly the order of recitation, as I observed in another similar Beneventan Breviary of the old Vatican library, Codex 4928, from which order, it is thought, the name “Breviary” was soon imposed upon the entire office.

After this Breviary are chapters from the Gospels with homilies of the saints and certain other matters pertaining to the office.

46. There follows an image of Christ fastened to the cross with four nails and covered with a loincloth.

Several hymns are added for the feast of “Saint Dominic the Confessor” (I think Dominic Loricatus). “For the praise of the Lord, Dominic whom we honor, etc.”

For the feast of Saint Nicholas, bishop: “Behold, the day has returned in jubilation.”

For the feast of Saint Sabina: “Grant, O Christ, to those who sing, etc.”

For the feast of the holy martyrs Rufinus and Caesidius:

> Eternal and most high King,  
> Give the gift of joy, etc.

47. Concerning the hymn “We praise you, God,” which is attributed to King Sisebutus in this Breviary, several attributions from manuscript Codices are cited in the notes to the Hymnal of the Venerable Cardinal Tommasi, volume III of Vezzosi’s edition, page 614 and following. Among them is this: “Hymn of Saint Sisebutus,” from Codex 11 of the Vatican Basilica.

Our bibliographers, when discussing King Sisebutus, do not mention this most celebrated hymn. Nor could I readily be persuaded, on the evidence of one or another Codex, to believe that this king was the author of the celebrated hymn which elsewhere is attributed to Saint Abundius and more commonly to Saints Ambrose and Augustine.

48. Otherwise, it would not be absurd to think that this hymn might have been composed by our Sisebutus. For, as Saint Isidore says in the dedicatory letter of his book On the Nature of Things, he “excelled in talent and eloquence, and in the varied flowering of literature.” His works themselves demonstrate this, having been published by Florez in volume VII of *Hispania Sacra*. In them one can also see the king’s piety and his mind devoted to ecclesiastical studies.

Some faults of Latin that appear in the work belong partly to that age and partly to the scribes; for it is clear that the text was incorrectly copied, as I observed in chapter 76.

49. Codex 1504 Urbinas, formerly 142, small quarto, on paper. Rubric: “Here begins Isidore’s book On the Supreme Good.”

At the end of the table of Book III: “Written by me, Brother Antonio of the town of Pinelio” (or Prinelio), “1432.”

After chapter 51, “On the end,” which is the final chapter in the table, and after the ending “the heavenly court encloses those destined for blessedness,” there is added the rubric: “The final chapter on hell: ‘The twofold punishment of the damned, etc.’” This is chapter 31 of Book I in the printed editions, and it is found in this Codex in that same place.

Then follows the rubric: “The examination of a certain bishop, living badly and very wickedly with God, and concerning his great ingratitude toward God, and concerning a certain grace obtained through the Blessed Virgin Mary, near the city of Merseburg, etc.”

This is the story of Udo, the condemned archbishop, to whom a heavenly voice sounded: “Udo, make an end of your playing, because you have played enough, Udo.” This story has already been printed.

Page 130, rubric: “Here begins Saint Isidore, bishop of Spain’s, Book of Differences: ‘Between God and Lord, etc.’” It ends: “an example of Christ’s humility.” The order is as in Breul, but many errors occur.

In the Inventory and Catalogue, page 62, a book On Ecclesiastical Dogmas is listed;[Col. 0897A] but there is only a table of chapters and the beginning of Book III of the *Sentences*, as I said in chapter 83.

## CHAPTER CV

Eighteen manuscript codices of the Vatican’s Ottobonian Library are described. A fragment of Isidore on numbers. A council concerning the celebration of Easter. Isidore’s *Differences of the Catholic Faith*. A tale of Charlemagne restoring the church of Saint James in Spain. The *Etymologies* attributed to Sisebutus in certain exemplars. Images of authors customarily painted in the initial letters of works.

1. That part of the Vatican Library called Ottoboniana is furnished both with very many books collected from every quarter and with many that once belonged to Pietro Bembo, others to Alberto Pio of Carpi, and later to Augustine Steuchus, Marcello Cervini, Guglielmo Sirleto, Ascanio Colonna, and finally to the Altemps Library; some also had belonged to Christina, queen of Sweden.

Benedict XIV added all these Codices, purchased with money from the Ottobonian patrimony, together with others selected from his own library, to the Vatican Library in 1749, as may be seen in volume I of the eminent Cardinal Borgia’s *Anecdota Romana*, page 65, and in Tiraboschi, volume VII of the *Italian Literature*, part I, book I, chapter 5.

Constantine Ruggieri composed a brief history of the Ottobonian Library from its first origin; the learned prelate Joseph Reggio preserves it in manuscript.

2. Codex 6 Ottobonianus, parchment, octavo, apparently from the tenth century. Miscellaneous contents.

First: “On the fact that Almighty God judges sin in four ways: ‘The beginning of every sin is pride, etc.’” There are likewise other titles on sins and other maxims. Jerome, Augustine, Isidore—also written Hesidorus or Esidorus—the *Origins*, the *Lives of the Fathers*, and Gregory are cited.

Second, on page 9 verso: “Here begins the order according to which a bishop or presbyter should prepare himself for the divine offices,” as I said in chapter 84.

Third, an exposition of the Mass, concerning which see the same chapter.

Fourth, a work on astronomy, mutilated at the beginning. There one reads: “Isidore on the air: Air is everything that resembles emptiness; it diffuses this vital spirit beneath the moon.” Other passages are likewise from Isidore.

At the end: “Here ends Bede’s book On the Nature of Things. Here begins his book On the Nature of Times: ‘Times are measured by moments, hours, days, etc.’” In the same place: “The course and order of times. The first age, therefore, etc. The sixth age contains 703 elapsed years.” In the same place: “Ermenegild, king of the Goths, is crowned with martyrdom.”

It ends: “Leo, three years. Tiberius then enters his fifth year, etc. Here ends Bede’s abridgment On Times.”

Fifth: various material on epacts. Verses on the signs, etc., and on the months; all of these are frequently found in manuscripts. In the same place, page 25, is chapter 66 of this work: “Verses on the winds: ‘Four from the square, etc.’” It ends: “by the mouth of the Muse,” as in chapter 37 of Isidore’s book On the Nature of Things. On these matters, see chapter 76.

3. Sixth, page 25 verso, rubric: “On numbers, by Bishop Isidore: ‘Arithmetic is the discipline of numbers.’” These passages consist of the first chapters of Book III of the *Etymologies*.

Seventh, page 26, rubric: “Likewise, on Isidore’s number: ‘Cardinal numbers are, etc., twice, three times.’” This may be classified among the fragments of the *Etymologies*.

Eighth, page 27: names of the Latin kings: “Janus, Saturn, etc.” Names of the emperors. Names of the Lombard kings. It ends: “the year 904.”

“On the abbots of Nonantola: Anselm, most holy abbot.” It ends: “in the year 933.”

Ninth, page 29, rubric: “Isidore’s statement on the body and blood of the Lord: ‘The sacrifice, moreover, which is offered to God by Christians …’” This is chapter 18 of Book I of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, and in substance it agrees with the printed editions.

Tenth: certain formal or commendatory letters.

Eleventh, page 31: maxims from the Fathers—Jerome, “Isidore,” Caesarius, Augustine, Gregory, Ambrose, Basil, and others—arranged under headings, with sayings first from Sacred Scripture and then from the Fathers.

Twelfth, page 70: “Here begin Isidore’s words. First, on charity: ‘Although some, etc.’” This is chapter 3 of Book II of the *Sentences*. Several other chapters from the books of the *Sentences* follow in the same way.

4. Codex 14 Ottobonianus, parchment, octavo, approximately from the twelfth century. It formerly belonged to Cardinal Jerome of Recanati and later to the Altemps Library.

At the beginning, in a script different from that of the rest of the Codex: “Here begins the letter of Peter the monk on Antichrist and the day of judgment: ‘To the most beloved brother Adam, Peter, a sinful monk, offers humble service in the Lord: What, dearest brother, what existed before the creation of the world, etc.’”

The *Enchiridion* of Saint Augustine to Laurence follows.

After the *Enchiridion*, on page 72 verso, is a sermon of Saint Augustine: “The worshipers of God, soldiers of Christ, ought not to be disturbed by any anxieties, etc.”

Then follows Pope Gregory’s letter to Secundinus, a recluse, concerning a fallen priest’s ability to rise again to his former rank: “I have received the letter of your affection, etc.”

Pope Hormisdas’s letter concerning clerics caught in adultery: “Behold, it is most clearly established, etc.”

Page 80, rubric: “The letter of Saint Isidore, bishop, to Bishop Manso, concerning a fallen priest’s ability, through penance, to rise again to his former rank: ‘When your servant, the religious man Nicetius, came to us, etc.’”

It ends: “whose authority is either older or more weighty. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of our Lord King Wittericus.” Some write “Witteric.”

Afterward: “From the sayings of Pope Gregory on the pastors of the Church: ‘As I consider …’”

At the end: “The second letter of Augustine to Serenus, bishop, on perjury: ‘Among other matters, as you had asked, I inquired of Father Ambrose, etc.’”

5. Codex 53 Ottobonianus, parchment, oblong quarto, apparently from the twelfth century. Rubric: “Here begins the preface of Isidore, bishop, on the Old Testament: ‘The history of the sacred law, etc., by the authors Origen, Victorinus, Ambrose, Jerome, Cassian, Augustine, Fulgentius, and the notably eloquent Gregory of our own time.’”

There is an index of twenty-two chapters.

“Here begins the exposition of the Book of Genesis: ‘In the beginning God made heaven and earth, etc.’” This follows as a kind of title after the indicated twenty-second chapter: “How the history, etc.” It ends: “over all flesh.”

There are fifty-eight chapters on Exodus. It ends: “in those who believe in him.”

There are fifteen chapters on Leviticus. It ends: “But neither are the bread offerings of foreigners offered to the Lord—that is, the superstitious doctrine of heretics, or the superstitious studies of secular literature, which are outside the faith and are regarded as foreign. For such sacrifices are rejected by the Lord, and this kind of offering is cast out by the Catholic Church.” Other manuscripts, such as the celebrated Bolognese Codex, add other material.

There are twenty-eight chapters on the Book of Numbers. It ends: “we extinguish vices.”

There are twenty-two chapters on Deuteronomy. It ends: “we are found without sin.”

There are seventeen chapters on Joshua. It ends: “He triumphed over the demons.”

Then, without a title: “Let us now consider Ruth, etc.; he promised through his son, etc.”

There are twenty-one chapters on Judges. It ends: “slippery mountains.”

There are seven chapters on Book I of Kings, nine on Book II, eight on Book III, and four on Book IV. It ends: “we do not enter baptism.”

Then, without any explicit title: “But what shall I say to the brothers about the Maccabees, etc.?”

6. Codex 122 Ottobonianus, formerly Altempsianus, small oblong quarto, approximately from the eleventh century, in small, slightly faded French script.

Rubric: “In the name of the Lord, here begins the book of the offices of the lord Isidore: ‘To my lord and servant of God, Fulgentius, bishop, Isidore. You ask me, etc.’”

There is an index of forty-four chapters. “Those things which, etc.” Chapters 11 and following are complete, as in Hittorp.

Chapter 43: “On the varied use of foods.”

There is an index of the chapters of Book II, numbering twenty-six. “Since the origins …” The final chapter is “On the laying on of hands, or confirmation.” It ends: “may be strengthened by the judgments of the Fathers. Here end the two books of the offices of the lord Isidore. Thanks be to God and to the holy Virgin Mary.”

Page 36, without a title, is a treatise on epacts, etc.: “The years of the Lord are marked, etc.” There is a passage concerning the moon: “For philosophers maintain that this created thing does not possess natural light, but receives it from the sun, as Isidore says.”

7. Page 46, rubric: “Here begins the account of how the first calculation of the Paschal cycle was discovered and confirmed by Christians: ‘After all the apostles had departed from this world, there were different fasts throughout the whole world. For all Gaul also kept one annual day of Easter on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, saying, etc.’”

A council is inserted, convened by Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in the province of Palestine, to establish the cycle. I compared it with the same council transcribed from the Albanian Codex, which I shall discuss below.

Page 47 verso, rubric: “Here begins the sermon of the venerable Ambrose, bishop of Milan, called *Pastoral*: ‘If anyone, brothers, remembers the oracle, etc.’”

8. Page 52 verso, rubric: “Here begins Book I of Blessed Ambrose of Milan, On the Mysteries: ‘We have held our daily discourse on moral matters, etc.’”

It ends: “may accomplish the truth of regeneration. Here ends *On Initiation*. Here begins Book I *On the Sacraments*.”

There are five books, but they are brief. It ends: “that we may be able to attain the rewards of virtue, through the Lord, etc.”

Immediately, on page 74: “Here begins the exposition of the Creed, written by Fortunatus the presbyter: ‘Reviewing the whole summary of the Catholic faith …’” It ends: “entering as victor, he reigns in heaven.”

Page 76 verso, rubric: “From Book I of the *Sentences* of the lord Isidore.” Chapter 10, on the angels: “The name of angels is a designation of office, etc.” It ends: “to have been given back to the angels.”

Three other chapters of the same book follow, chapters 11, 12, and 13.

Page 80 verso, rubric: “The exposition of Jerome the presbyter: ‘First, the time, place, person, and reason of all the books must be sought, and why twelve Gospels are not accepted, but only four.’”

Page 81 verso, rubric: “Exposition of the Creed: ‘Symbolon in Greek means sign, or knowledge, in Latin, etc.’” Soon afterward, in the form of questions and answers: “How many creeds are found in the canons, etc.?”

Page 83 verso, certain sayings from the Fathers begin, including from “Isidore, in the Book of Offices and in the Book of Etymologies.” They concern baptism, exorcism, the laying on of hands, and other matters.

9. Codex 128 Ottobonianus, parchment, quarto, apparently from the fourteenth century.

Rubric: “Here begins Isidore, On the Supreme Good: ‘The supreme good, etc.’”

Chapter 20: “On the seven rules of the law.” The final chapter is chapter 31, “On the glory of the saints.”

Book II has a rubric concerning wisdom; but in the margin chapter 32 is indicated as continuing the numbering of the preceding chapters.

Chapter 36: “Predestination is twofold, etc.; let the weak and external things take delight.”

Chapter 37 begins: “The reward is not promised to those who begin, but is given to those who persevere.”

Chapter 75 concerns the scourges of God; above the beginning of the page is written: “Book III.” The final chapters are not numbered.

It ends: “it encloses those who rejoice. Blessed be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and forever. Here ends Isidore, On the Supreme Good.” Most other manuscripts have “those destined to rejoice.”

Some passages from Augustine’s *Confessions* follow, together with the book *On the Misery of the Human Condition*, published by Lothair, later Innocent III.

A summary of the seven principal vices: “Pride is a vicious elevation, etc.”

Certain anonymous short works follow.

The first is mutilated at the beginning and concerns friendship. It ends: “unless the enormity of the offense removes it.”

The second is “On Confession: ‘You asked me to tell you something about the virtue of confession, etc.’” Isidore’s *On the Supreme Good* is cited there.

In the same place: “As we are taught in the Roman Penitential, the priest should receive the penitent with great gentleness and kindness, etc.” The author is Peter of Blois, whom I shall discuss shortly under Codex 159.

The third concerns the episcopal office: “You have most earnestly asked, most reverend Father, that I write about the episcopal office, etc. I, indeed, hiding in darkness and smoking beneath a bushel, etc.” It ends: “may smooth them with more diligent filing.”

10. Codex 139 Ottobonianus, parchment, octavo, approximately from the fourteenth century.

A theological work, mutilated at the beginning: “There follows the matter of restitution. First, therefore, the kind of restitution is sought, etc.” There are many such passages from moral and scholastic theology, as well as some sermons, for the use of a religious.

Page 37 verso, in the margin: “Isidore, On the Supreme Good.” These are certain sayings from Book II of the *Sentences*, chapter 31, concerning oaths and the failure to fulfill evil promises.

Page 50, rubric: “Bernard to Robert the Apostate: ‘I have endured enough, etc.’”

Fragments and sayings of the Fathers follow.

Page 51, rubric: “On Saint Francis: ‘But far be it from me to boast, etc.’”

After page 100 are notes for sermons on the feast days of Saint Bernard, Saint Lawrence, and others.

In some places the word “ojo” appears in red in the margin, by which the reader is instructed, in a Spanish word, to read attentively.

11. Codex 159 Ottobonianus, parchment quarto, apparently from the fourteenth century.

Homilies of Saint Caesarius to monks: “The divine word exhorts us, etc.” There are ten homilies to monks.

“Likewise, a homily of the same author on how the word of the Lord ought to be desired.” There are five others. Altogether there are fifteen.

Then, on page 30 verso, there is an index of the thirty-two chapters of Book I of the *Sentences*, followed by the rubric: “Here begins Book I of Saint Isidore, bishop, On the Supreme Good.”

Chapter 20: “On the seven rules of the law.”

Chapter 24: “He offers himself voluntarily for the defense of truth in the contest … A holy man ought not voluntarily to offer himself in the contest of justice for the sake of strife, but, etc.”

There is an index of the chapters of Book II, numbering forty-four.

In chapter 6: “let the weak and external things take delight.”

In chapter 18: “by small and very little drops … abundance.”

The chapters of Book III number sixty-six. It ends: “the heavenly court encloses those destined for blessedness. Amen. Here ends Book III of Blessed Isidore, bishop, On the Supreme Good.”

Page 121: “A short work of Peter of Blois, archdeacon of London, against the perfidy of the Jews: ‘The complaint in your letter, etc.’”

Then, by the same Peter of Blois, a treatise On Confession: “You asked me to tell you something about the virtue of confession, etc.”

“Here begins another treatise On Penance: ‘The excessive harshness of your severity, etc.’” This is continued from the preceding work in Codex 128.

It ends: “his mercy.”

A treatise by the same author On the Episcopal Office follows: “You ask most earnestly, most reverend Father, etc.” This treatise is mutilated at the end.

12. Codex 240 Ottobonianus, small parchment quarto, approximately from the twelfth century, formerly belonging to the library of the Queen of Sweden.

At the beginning are several pages from another Codex, containing various sayings and little verses, such as:

> What is the work of the prudent? When he can, to be unwilling to harm.  
> What belongs to the fool? To be unable, and yet to wish, to harm.

There are sayings of the Seven Sages, set out in verse.

Page 1 of the Codex: Didymus’s book On the Holy Spirit: “While I was staying in Babylon, etc.” This is Saint Jerome’s prologue.

Page 2: an image, as I believe, of the seated Didymus holding a book in his hand.

Page 52, rubric: “Here happily ends Didymus’s book On the Holy Spirit. Isidore, On the Differences of the Catholic Faith: ‘Between God and Lord.’” It ends: “an example of Christ’s humility. Here ends Isidore, bishop, Book of Differences.”

The differences are numbered in the margin. The last is number 41, “On the distinctions among the four vices.”

13. Codex 278 Ottobonianus, octavo parchment, apparently from the thirteenth century.

An exposition of Luke’s Gospel, mutilated at the beginning. Much is written in red, namely the expositor’s words; other material is in black.

The first page is chapter 11: “The Lord Jesus was casting out a demon, and it was mute.”

It appears to be an autograph, with additions.

Page 23: an exposition of John’s Gospel with a verse by Juvencus:

> Flying like an eagle, John seeks the stars through the Word.

It begins: “In the beginning, etc., that is, in whom all things are begun or brought to an end.”

Page 51: an exposition of the Acts of the Apostles. It begins: “The discourse, that is, the Gospel.”

Prologue: “Luke the evangelist writes to Theophilus that the Lord Jesus commanded, etc.”

Expositions of words occur at the beginning; afterward there is only the text.

Seven Catholic Epistles are appended.

Page 86: “Here begins the prologue of Blessed Remigius on the Epistle to the Romans: ‘From the region of Achaia, etc.’”

Page 87: the Inventory lists the Epistle to the Romans with a preface by Saint Isidore, bishop, on all the Epistles of Paul. Rubric: “Here begins the preface of Isidore, bishop: ‘The apostle Paul, in fourteen epistles … the style … neither exceeding, etc., and he recalls them to the grace of the Gospel.’”

These are taken from the prologues to the New Testament. In most of them there are expositions without the author’s name; neither in the Epistle to Philemon nor in the others is Isidore named.

After Paul’s Epistles, the text of the Apocalypse is mutilated at the end.

14. Codex 302 Ottobonianus, paper quarto.

First is a brief of Sixtus IV concerning the celebration of the feast of the Visitation of the Mother of God to Saint Elizabeth, with an octave.

Then follows the office of the Visitation with an octave.

Page 21, title: “The History of Blessed Eugenius,” with nothing else.

Page 22: “On the feast of Blessed Eugenius.” This is the office of Blessed Eugenius I, bishop of Toledo.

Hymn: “The renowned martyr Eugenius’ honor, etc.”

Hymn at Matins:

> Leader of the martyrs, grant pardon,  
> Jesus, life of mortals.

Lesson 1: “To the most reverend Father in Christ, Lord Pedro Mendoza, cardinal and archbishop of Toledo, the history of Blessed Eugenius begins.

‘The history of the most blessed martyr Eugenius, the first predecessor of Toledo, I have considered worthy of restoring at your command, most reverend Father and illustrious lord. Although it was pleasing to readers neither in expression nor in arrangement, when perfected under your authority, it will display dignity and splendor. “He was the first [concerning] Christ’s name, etc.”’

These are Acts and miracles.

15. Page 35: “The Office for the Nativity of Saint Leocadia.”

Hymn:

> We sing the triumph of the holy virgin,  
> Whose nativity and glorious merits, etc.

Hymn at Matins:

> Leocadia, worthy of praise.

Virgin, citizen of our city, etc. The Acts are divided into nine lessons. In Lesson 9, the vision of St. Ildefonsus. There: “Then the Virgin Leocadia . . . greets Ildefonsus with these words: ‘O Ildefonsus, through you my Lady lives.’ To her the most holy Ildefonsus replies: ‘O virgin, fellow-citizen of heaven, blessed are the ages that brought you forth. But more blessed is the Virgin who bore God, by whose merits we live for Christ.’” On page 43, without any heading: “Julian, disciple of Eugenius II” (for us, Eugenius III). This is the Life of Julian of Toledo by Felix, which is placed after Isidore’s book and Ildefonsus’ *On Illustrious Men* in editions of the works of St. Isidore. Page 45. Office of St. Ildefonsus: “God of the Lord’s glory, Ildefonsus, etc.” Hymn at Matins: “Christ, salvation of believers, etc.” Nine lessons concerning his life. Lesson 8: “‘Rising from the tomb, the virgin Leocadia . . . said, ‘Ildefonsus, through you my Lady lives.’” There are also lessons throughout the octave on the Life of Ildefonsus. Page 58, Office of St. Mary of Egypt, with hymns: “We sing, O Christ, the devout offerings of praise, etc.”

[Col. 0903A] 16. Codex 312 Ottobonianus, in folio, on parchment, handsome and elegantly written, apparently from about the tenth century. Heading: “Concerning the order of the Mass, etc.,” as I explained in chapter 84. Page 3 verso; heading: “The preface begins: Dionysius [Exiguus] to the venerable Father Stephen, bishop. Although most dear, etc.” Fifty-one Apostolic Canons; twenty Nicene Canons; those of Ancyra, etc. The decrees of Siricius, Innocent, etc. Titles of the decrees of Pope Gregory Junior. After this index, on page 14, the heading reads: “The letter of Isidore to Bishop Massona, given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of the reign of the most glorious lord Witteric,” the philosopher-king. Concerning the restoration of a priest. “To the holy and meritorious blessed bishop Massona, Isidore, bishop. When your servant, the religious man Nicetius, came to us, etc.” [Col. 0903B] It ends: “whose authority is either more ancient or more weighty. Given on the day before the Kalends of March, in the third year of King Witteric.”

17. Appended is: “The Ancyrite Canons, number 400 XIX” [that is, 419]. “If anyone, whether man or woman, commits adultery, that person ought to attain perfection over seven years through the former stages.” The Collection of Canons of Dionysius follows: after the council of Gregory “Junior” under Leo Augustus, the statutes of the emperor Justinian addressed to Peter and thence to Epiphanius, archbishop. It ends: “to make these things known. Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of the illustrious Velisarius.” Some material is added concerning *litterae formatae*, the procession of the Holy Spirit from the councils, etc. On page 137, in a more recent script, is a catalogue of the popes from Peter to Victor and [Col. 0903C] Urban. On the verso, in an old script: “The Ecclesiastical Order of the Roman Church begins, or how Mass is celebrated. First of all, it must be observed that there are seven regions, etc.” These matters should be compared with the Roman Orders of Hittorp, where they also occur.

18. Codex 336 Ottobonianus, in folio, membranaceous, apparently from the fourteenth century. *Etymologies*. Notable letters, up to “as it stands written in the style of our forefathers.” Heading: “The books of Isidore Junior, bishop of Seville, addressed to Braulion, bishop of Caesaraugusta, or to Sisebutus, namely, lord and son, begin.” The letters beginning “Behold for you, etc.” are not preceded by a title. In most manuscripts the letter is said to be addressed to Braulion; in some, also to Sisebutus. Index of the chapters of Book I: 31. Book II has 34 chapters, but 32 in the text. Book III has 70 chapters. Book IV, on Medicine, has 13 chapters. The other books are generally as in the printed editions. Book X is a vocabulary, etc. Book XVIII, on wars, etc., has 71 chapters without further subdivisions of titles. Book XX ends: “may be dried by the heat of fire. The end.”

19. Page 167, heading: “In the name of the Lord, the chapters of the Sentences of blessed Isidore from Book I begin. The first chapter of Saint Isidore on the Supreme Good: ‘The supreme good, etc.’ Chapter 20 of Book I: On the seven rules of the Law.” The chapters are numbered by a more recent hand. Book I has 31 chapters; in chapter 6 of the first book: “and let the weak and outward things take pleasure.” Book II has 44 chapters. Book III has 66. It ends: “encloses those destined to rejoice in the heavenly court. The book of Isidore is complete. The chapters of the Book of Sentences of Saint Isidore, doctor of the Church, begin.” [Col. 0904A] In this table, Book III has 65 chapters. “The chapters of the Book of Sentences of Saint Isidore are complete. Thanks be to God, amen.” Page 213: “The book of blessed Bernard to Pope Eugenius begins, etc.” There are five books. The Meditations of St. Bernard follow: “Pride is exaltation, etc. Many know many things, and do not know themselves.”

20. Codex 343 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in large folio, apparently from about the thirteenth century, written in a large script approaching the German. At the beginning, in a recent script, is written: “Bourdelot,” concerning which name I have already spoken. Heading: “That you may be able, etc.,” as in the other codices. There is also a table of the twenty books; but the final heading reads: “The letter of Isidore to Sisebutus, king: ‘Behold for you, etc., as it stands written in the style of our forefathers.’” Table [Col. 0904B] of the chapters of the first book, which number 26. “The chapters are complete. The first book of the *Etymologies* of blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, begins.” There are twenty books, as in the printed editions; but in many places there are subdivisions of titles, as in some other manuscripts. It ends: “may be dried by the heat of fire. The books of the *Etymologies* of blessed Isidore, bishop, are complete. The exposition of ancient expressions by Fabius Placiades Fulgentius, with testimonies, begins: ‘Lest [something] of yours, etc.’ What is a *sandapila*? The ancients called a *sandapila*, etc.” It ends: “so very soothing. The exposition of ancient expressions by Fabius Placiades Fulgentius, with testimonies, is complete.” This volume was Petavius’s no. 68; either from it or from another very similar manuscript, Vulcanius published Isidore’s *Etymologies* and the appended book of Fulgentius.

[Col. 0904C] 21. Codex 345 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in folio, written in a pale Roman cursive or French script, apparently from the eleventh century. On the first page, in a more recent script: “Memorable Chronicle”; that is, a brief chronicle from the year 755 to 1326. Mainly sacred matters are set forth. It begins: “In the year of the Lord 755, the body of Saint Sylvester, pope, was transferred from Rome to the monastery of Nonantula in the diocese of Modena.” This indicates that the codex was from Nonantula. In the same place: “In the year of the Lord 800, blessed James the Apostle appeared in a vision to the aforesaid Charles, commanding him to go to Spain and restore a church for him. For his body had lain hidden from the time when the Saracens invaded the land. Therefore he quickly entered Spain, subdued the whole country, and built the church of Saint James, endowed it, and increased its honors. In the year of the Lord 1313, in the month of August, on the day of Saint Bartholomew the Apostle, the aforesaid emperor [Henry of Luxembourg] died in Tuscany, in the diocese of Siena, at a place called Bonaneth [perhaps Bonconventum], and he was poisoned, etc.” [Col. 0904D] The Chronicle ends shortly afterward.

22. Raynaldus firmly rejects the story of the poison administered to Henry in the Eucharist, under the year 1313, no. 24. No less fabulous is the account of the church of St. James of Compostela being restored by Charlemagne. Our ancient writers do not acknowledge those famous merits of Charlemagne toward Spain which the French exaggerate. The author of the *Chronicle of Silos*, who was writing at the beginning of the twelfth century, after saying in volume XVII of *Hispania sacra*, no. 18, “apart from God, no foreign nation lifted up Spain,” added the following: “But neither did Charles, whom the Franks falsely assert to have wrested certain cities below the Pyrenees from the hands of the pagans. . . Then, when he had approached the city of Zaragoza, corrupted by gold according to the Frankish custom, without any exertion to rescue the holy Church from barbarian domination, he returned to his own lands. . . For Charles was eager to be washed more quickly in those baths which Grani had lavishly constructed for this arduous purpose.” I correct the text to read, “in those baths . . . which Grani [built].” The reference is to the Baths of Grani. Nevertheless, in the church of Compostela an anniversary is celebrated on 6 July for Charlemagne, its distinguished benefactor.

[Col. 0905B] 23. The following heading comes next: “The book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop of Seville, begins. So that you may quickly find in this volume what you seek [others: in this work], this page, reader, shows you the subjects about which the author of this codex discussed in each individual book. 1. On grammar, etc.” There are twenty books. “The chapters concerning all the books of the entire codex are complete. The letter of Isidore, bishop, addressed to Braulion, bishop.” The letters have already been published, including the final one to Braulion: “Behold for you, etc.” Book I has 29 chapters. The last concerns history. Previously there had been other numbering. Book II has 21 chapters, with subdivisions under various titles in this and the other books. Book IV concerns Medicine, etc. Book X is a vocabulary, etc. The books are twenty from the first hand, and this numbering is not altered; [Col. 0905C] but in many books there are subdivisions. It ends: “may be dried by the heat of fire. The book of the *Etymologies* is complete.”

24. The following verses are added in the same hand:

> I am called Otto, servant of the servants of the Lord.  
> My surname was Stampa: thus I am called Otto.  
> I wrote this work; those who read it again call me Otto.  
> After my death, I beg you, Otto, always to spare me.  
> And now say “Our Father” for me, Otto,  
> So that I may ascend to the Lord’s seat, I who am thus called Otto,  
> And climb with his saints, I wretched Otto.

25. At the beginning of Book VII of the *Etymologies*, chapter 10: “Mary, the illuminatrix, etc.” The Mother of God is depicted seated, with hands outstretched, holding a flowering staff in her right hand and marked with a cross on her forehead.
