Beside the name of Pilate in the same chapter, a recent hand adds or notes in the margin: “Washed hands do not cleanse a defiled soul, nor is that which is committed with an impious mind expiated by fingers sprinkled with water.” In Book II, chapter 21, a marginal note by the first hand reads: “Alternatively, there are also in the precepts of eloquence certain figures of words and thoughts by which speech is enlarged and adorned.” In the text the chapter begins: “There are also certain figures in the precepts of eloquence by which speech is enlarged and adorned, including figures of words and thoughts.” In the text this chapter ends: “they permit us to say.” The same hand adds in the margin: “By these figures of thought and word speech is both enlarged and polished through various forms.” In the same place, Book II, chapter 24, on the definition of philosophy: “they live in the likeness of the future homeland.” A recent hand [Col. 0906A] adds: “But what else is it to live in the likeness of the future homeland than to enjoy meditation on divine goodness, in order to know our Creator and Savior and therefore to love and venerate him? So that at last, once freed from the labyrinths of the prisons and snares of the present life, we may fully enjoy him. In whose life-giving vision may rest and the glory of everlasting happiness be ours.” Book IV, chapter 4: “the care of the art”; in the margin, by the same hand: “he investigated the causes of illnesses by applying reason.”

26. Codex 352 Ottobonianus, formerly 261, membranaceous, in folio, apparently from about the fourteenth century. Heading: “Preface to Isidore’s *Etymologies*.” Notable letters follow. Later the heading reads: “The chapters of the book of Isidore Junior, bishop of Seville, written to Braulion, bishop of Caesaraugusta, in Book I, begin: ‘Behold for you, etc., in the style of our forefathers. So that you may quickly find in this work what you seek, this page, reader, shows you the subjects about which the author of this codex discusses in each book. In the first book, etc.’” After the index of the books: “To Lord and Son Sisebutus, Isidore: ‘Behold for you, etc.,’” as in the letter to Braulion. It ends, “as it stands in the style of our forefathers,” without the final verb *conscriptum*. Index of the chapters of Book I: 26. Book II has 21 chapters. Book III, 49. Book IV, 11. Book V, 39. Book VI, 18. Book VII, 14. Book VIII, 10. According to Grialius, there are 11 chapters.

27. Book IX, chapter 8. Book X: “Concerning certain names in alphabetical order, etc.” The remaining ten books are generally as in Breul, but with a certain separation [Col. 0906C] of the titles in Books XIII and XVIII, as in other manuscripts. It ends: “may be dried by the heat of fire.” Immediately follows the heading: “The treatise of the Venerable Bede, priest, on the figures and tropes of Sacred Scripture begins: ‘It is customary at times in the Scriptures, etc.’” Then follow certain incomplete biblical concordances and a lexicon of words, especially of Sacred Scripture. The following verses precede it:

> I strive to unfold the difficult passages borne by the Bible,  
> But I cannot, unless someone reveals the hidden places, etc.

It begins: “With the letter A, as Isidore says in the first book of the *Etymologies*, etc.”

28. Codex 404 Ottobonianus, partly papyrus and partly membranaceous, in quarto, begins without a title: “To my lord and servant of God Ambrose, Isidore: ‘Your Holiness’s, etc.’” A letter to Braulion, who is erroneously called Ambrose. It is followed by: “Behold for you, as I promised, etc.,” and immediately by the heading: “On discipline and art,” chapter 1 of Book I. Chapter 38 concerns fables; then comes the final chapter, on history, without a title. For the titles of the chapters are sometimes absent. Book V concerns Medicine. Book VI, Laws. Book VII, Times. The second book concerns Rhetoric, the third Dialectic, etc. There are twenty-two books, and the book on words in alphabetical order, which is tenth in the printed editions, is absent. At the end is an index of the books and chapters.

29. Codex 427 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in folio, apparently from about the thirteenth century. Six notable letters of Isidore and Braulion. A prefatory notice: “So that you may be able to find what you seek, etc.,” with a table of the books—or rather of the titles—without numbering. [Col. 0907A] There are 56 titles distinguished from one another by initial capital letters; these may perhaps be the very divisions into which Isidore had divided the work. The following heading reads: “Isidore to Sisebutus: To Lord and Son Sisebutus, Isidore. Behold for you, etc.” He is written as *Sesibutus*, as often elsewhere. Index of 27 chapters of Book I. Subdivisions of titles in Book III. Book IV concerns Medicine, etc. Book X is an alphabet of words, etc. Book XVIII has 69 chapters without subdivision of titles. Book XX, the last, ends: “may be dried by the heat of fire.” Some corrections have been added by an old hand. In Book XIII there is a subdivision already noticed in some other ancient codices.

30. Codex 477 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in folio, apparently from the twelfth century. Heading: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen. The chapters of the first book of Isidore’s *Etymologies*, on grammar and its parts, etc., begin.” A table of all the books and chapters. There are twenty books, in the order in which they appear in the printed editions. The codex is magnificent, ornamented with many letters in gold and vermilion and decorated with various figures of animals. After the table the heading reads: “In Christ the Lord and most beloved son B., archdeacon, Isidore: ‘While I was reading the letters of a friend, etc.’” In the letter D there is painted an image of Isidore dressed in pontifical vestments and standing, holding a staff in his right hand and a book in his left.

31. The following heading comes next: “In Christ, most dear and beloved brother Braulion, archdeacon, Isidore. Because I am unable, etc.” Another letter: “To my lord, truly my lord, chosen bishop of Christ, highest of bishops, B., useless servant of the servants of God” (Isidore’s name is missing). “O pious lord.” Another: [Col. 0907C] “To my lord and servant of God, B., bishop: Because I have found you safe and sound. Isidore is missing.” Another: “To the lord, etc. To Isidore, etc. It is usually completed.” Another: “To my lord and servant of God, B., bishop, Isidore: ‘Your Holiness’s letter.’” Another: “Behold for you, etc.” Heading: “So that you may be able to find what you seek, etc.,” as in the other manuscripts, followed by a table of the books. “The first book begins, etc.” In the first letter of the first word, *Disciplina*, that is, in the D, an image is painted of a teacher instructing a boy. The teacher appears from the form of his clothing to be a monk, but the color is blue, with red sleeves. There are variant readings in the same hand. In Book I, juridical notes occur in alphabetical order, as in some other codices. At the end of Book IX are Greek words explained, verses on the Supper of Cyprian, and verses on St. Benedict: “I shall begin: ‘Whence your . . ., etc.’” At the end: “The Codex [Col. 0907D] of the *Etymologies* of Saint Isidore, bishop of Seville, is complete.” This codex proceeds in the same order and contains everything found in Vatican Codex 623, about which I said more in chapter 93.

32. The image of St. Isidore which, as I said, is visible in the first letter of the first epistle gives me occasion to compile a curious catalogue of codices in which I have incidentally observed painted images of authors. In the prolegomena to Prudentius, chapter 2, no. 58, I observed that in the Urbinate Codex of the Works of Prudentius there is an image of him painted in the first letter of the preface. In a note I added that it was the custom of ancient scribes to attach an image of the author to the first letter of a work, as Virginius Valsechi proves in his dissertation in support of John Gersen the Benedictine, author of the book *On the Imitation of Christ*. Philostratus testifies to this or a similar custom in the *Life of Apollonius*: “The propriety and necessity of placing images of writers at the threshold of books persuade us that, just as the age enjoys the books through which it is educated, so it should possess, drawn from life, the likenesses of those by whom it is taught.” I have seen these words quoted somewhere in this form, but when I searched, the passage did not present itself to me in Philostratus. Nevertheless, the following distich, among the verses of the library of St. Isidore, about which I spoke in chapter 81, no. 5, may perhaps belong here:

> Those renowned masters of medicine whom the world celebrates—  
> The present image marks these men, painted here.

33. I spoke of another image of St. Isidore in a certain Florentine Codex of the *Etymologies* in chapter 55, no. [Col. 0908B] 21. In another Florentine codex, about which I spoke in chapter 43, nos. 11 and 12, there appears an image either of Isidore, or of Taio, or of both; for Bandinius did not clearly express his opinion.

34. In Vatican Codex 351, about which see chapter 93, no. 11, there is an image of St. Jerome; in Vatican Codex 473, discussed in the same chapter, no. 12, one of St. Augustine; in Palatine 927, chapter 103, nos. 17 ff., images of Augustine, Orosius, Pompeius Trogus, Justin, Cassiodorus, and others; in Urbinate 60, chapter 104, no. 3, one of St. Gregory of Nazianzus; in Urbinate 105, chapter 104, no. 16, one of Aymo; in Urbinate 307, chapter 104, nos. 24 and 25, those of Nonius Marcellus and Pompeius Festus; in Ottobonianus 240, chapter 105, no. 12, one of Didymus.

35. An image of Cardinal John de Turrecremata [Col. 0908C] is shown in Vatican Codex 2267, membranaceous, in large folio, at the beginning of his book *On Causes*; that of Terence in his comedies, Vatican Codex 3868; that of St. Bernard in many places in his book *On Consideration to Eugenius*, Vatican Codex 658; that of Cardinal Marco Vigerio in Vatican Codex 1125, on parchment, containing his *Decachordum*; those of Petrarch and Dante in Codex 3198; and that of Lactantius Firmianus in Vatican Codex 6977.

36. Codex Palatine 882, membranaceous and in folio, displays an image of Julius Caesar; Palatine Codex 74, membranaceous and in folio, written apparently in the ninth century in the time of Emperor Henry, contains an image of St. John the Evangelist in his Gospel. Ottobonianus 222 is from the twelfth century. The Bible, etc., with images of the sacred writers.

37. In the Vatican Urbinate library many such images of authors occur, painted in the first letters of works or at the beginning of volumes. Codex 464 contains the *Florentine History* of Leonardo Aretino; on its first page are images of Leonardo himself, King Alfonso of Aragon, and others, artistically executed in gold. Codex 487 contains the *Hispanic History* of Roderic Sanchez de Arevalo, with his likeness painted in vermilion. Codex 539 contained a general history of Spain with an image of Alfonso the Wise, but the codex is no longer found. The inventory reports as follows: “Codex 539: An anonymous general history, which Alfonso the Wise, king of the Spaniards, commissioned to be compiled, Part IV, from the History of Nebuchadnezzar to Ptolemy Philopator, with an image of Alfonso himself at the beginning. It is the autograph itself, published in the year 1318 of the Spanish era, [Col. 0909A] that is, in the year of the Lord 1280, written by the hand of Martin Perez de Maqueda, the aforesaid Alfonso’s scribe, as is noted at the end of the book. In Spanish: *Aqui se comenza* [Here begins]. An ancient parchment codex in large folio. Written leaves, 277.” In the final Urbinate Codex, 1763, there is a panegyric of Guidobaldo, duke of Urbino, by Baldassare Castiglione; his likeness is elegantly painted at the beginning.

38. To these may be added the images of Belasius and Sisebutus, the scribes of the Aemilianensis Codex, about which see chapter 108, no. 8, and other images of scribes and illustrious men, chapter 103, nos. 17 ff.

## CHAPTER CVI. Description of Fifteen Other Ancient Exemplars of the Ottobonian Library

One hundred manuscript codices were formerly extracted by royal hand from the Altemps Library. Interpolated and continued Chronicle of Isidore. *Historia Miscella*. Genealogy of the Spanish kings. A short work on the seven degrees of consanguinity. Several copies of Cicero’s *Synonyms*. A book on heresies written in Greek and falsely attributed under Isidore’s name.

[Col. 0909B]

1. Codex 508 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in octavo, apparently from the fourteenth century. At the beginning, in a script different from that of the rest of the body, are certain sentences from Isidore: “In the book *On the Supreme Good*, by Bernard and Gregory.” Then the heading: “The moral treatise on the seven deadly sins begins. This treatise contains nine parts, etc.” It ends: “He sometimes regretted having spoken, but never having remained silent. The summary of the seven deadly sins is complete. May the one who wrote it write on, and always live with the Lord.” [Col. 0909C] The name of the author who wrote the moral treatise is absent. Nevertheless, in the Inventory it is attributed to Isidore; I consider this entirely incorrect, although he did write certain material on the vices toward the end of Book II of the *Differentiae*, and some material in the fourth, spurious or doubtful, book of the *Sentences* is inserted after chapter 39 concerning the eight principal vices, from St. Gregory the Great. The treatise in this codex is by some scholastic theologian.

2. Codex 604 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in folio, apparently from the fourteenth century: the Chronicle of Eusebius (and Jerome). An adjuration described elsewhere: “I adjure you, etc.” Prologue: “Eusebius and Jerome to Vincentius and Gallienus, their own, greetings. This ancient work, etc.” At the end: “In the consulship of Valentinian VI and Nono.” Prosper ends here after Jerome. “The Chronicle of Eusebius, Jerome, and Prosper is complete.” The name IHS is appended. The *Summary of the Roman Empire* by Rufus Festus follows: “Let it be made brief, etc.” On page 81, without a title: “I undertake to describe the situation of the world, a difficult task, etc.” This is Mela’s work. In the same place: “And the Phoenicians who crossed from Africa inhabit [there], and whence we ourselves are: with *kratum* bathing, Mellaria, Bella, and Besimo.” After *tingente*, *Kratum* is somewhat separated, and the first two letters, *Kr*, are obscure; perhaps it is *Katum*. The passage is corrupt in the manuscripts in various places. At the end: “The concise cosmography of Pomponius is happily complete.” Next comes “The Synonyms of Marcus Tullius Cicero. Cicero to his Lucius Vecturius, greetings: ‘I have collected, etc. Therefore let us begin in alphabetical order. Hidden, covered, concealed, etc.’” It ends: “A plain voice, a grand voice, etc.; pleasing, affable. [Col. 0910A] Thanks be to God.” I discussed this work of Cicero’s *Synonyms* in chapter 56.

3. Codex 849 Ottobonianus, paper, in octavo, from the Altemps Library. A book by the name of Pliny the Younger, *On Illustrious Men*. Jerome, *On Illustrious Men*: “You urge me, Dexter, etc.” There are 137 chapters. Gennadius, *On Illustrious Men*, has 90 chapters. On page 112 verso: “Isidore, bishop of Seville, on illustrious men, begins.” There are 33 chapters. The first: Osius, bishop of the city of Corduba. The final chapter: “Maximus, etc. The book of Illustrious Men according to Isidore, bishop of the Church of Seville, is complete. The Life of the aforesaid Isidore. ‘Isidore, an outstanding man, etc., in works of charity.’ The Life of St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, is finished.” This is Braulion’s prefatory notice without his name.

[Col. 0910B] 4. Codex 869 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in quarto, from the fourteenth century or later. At the beginning is an incomplete theological work. Some works of Anselm. On page 141, without a title: “In the following book, which is called *Synonyms*, etc.” It ends: “you please me above all things in my life. The book of the *Synonyms* of Saint Isidore is complete.” A letter of St. Bernard to a certain soldier concerning the care of household affairs. After the prologue comes another prologue: “Recently a certain little document came into my hands which they call *Synonyms*, whose form persuaded my mind, etc.” The books are not distinguished. Augustine’s book *On True Innocence* follows: “True innocence is, etc.” A treatise of the doctor Francis de Viardius on Indulgences. Near the end are certain Latin verses:

> Death seizes great and small by equal law;  
> Now these, now those it throws down and carries away.

Three books of Aesop’s fables in Latin prose.

[Col. 0910C]

5. Codex 945 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio. “Saint Isidore Junior, *Against the Jews Concerning Christ*. One of the hundred codices of the Altemps Library extracted by royal hand—or, as it is said elsewhere, excerpted—now, however, most faithfully taken from the originals at his own expense by John Angelo, duke of Altemps, etc.” *Desumptis* is written incorrectly for *desumptus*. The old codex that was extracted from the Altemps Library is now, I think, no. 4918 of the old Vatican Library, described in chapter 97.

6. Codex 975 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio. Various sermons of the holy Fathers, etc. This too is one [Col. 0910D] of the hundred codices of the Altemps Library, etc., as above in Codex 945. The letter of Pope Leo to Flavian, etc. Page 26: “The sermon of blessed Isidore, bishop, on the Nativity of the Lord: ‘The Lord’s Nativity, etc.’” The old codex from which this was copied is now in the old Vatican Library, no. 4951.

7. Codex 958 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio. At the beginning is this inscription: “One of the codices of the Altemps Library extracted by Paul V with royal hand, but now transcribed from the originals at his own expense by John Angelo, duke of Altemps, so that the aforesaid library might not lack one already adorned with so great an honor.” It is a fragment of ecclesiastical history translated into Latin by Rufinus, and the complete Book of Isidore’s *Synonyms*. The codex extracted or excerpted by Paul V is now [Col. 0911A] Codex no. 4948 of the old Vatican Library, described in chapter 97. The description is not, as stated, entirely faithful. For immediately at the beginning it reads *traditum a Rufino* [handed down by Rufinus] instead of *traductum a Rufino* [translated by Rufinus]. The book of Isidore is in a transcribed exemplar: “The prologue of the book called *Synonyms*, that is, of the Lord, etc., begins.” In the original: “The prologue of the book called *Synonyms*, that is, of the Lord, etc., begins.”

8. Codex 1261 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio. The *Life of Statius* and the *Achilleid*, with notes. The final verse:

> And she transfers the necklace from her beloved neck.

The *Polyhistory* of John Caballinus de Cerronibus: “On the virtues and endowments of the city of Rome, etc.” There are ten books. Page 69, without a title, is Proba Falconia’s *Cento*, and in the margin a panegyric of Proba from Isidore: “Proba, wife of Adelphus . . . inserted among the apocryphal Scriptures.” A certain vocabulary follows: “*Agra*, a road in the sea, etc.” Page 148: “The book of Marcus Tullius Cicero on the differences of words [so] begins: ‘Between *polliceri* and *promittere*, etc.’” It ends: “Between *vesper* and *vespera*, etc.” Consult chapter 56 concerning this work.

9. Codex 1720 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio. Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*, without a title: “Concerning Pope Xystus, etc.,” as in Breul’s first exemplar and in the earlier editions. After Victorinus, in the manuscript: “Concerning Eucherius, bishop; concerning Statius, etc.; concerning Sedulius; concerning Cerealis, etc.” Soon afterward, concerning John, bishop (Chrysostom); again concerning Sedulius, priest; concerning Possidonius; concerning Primasius, etc. Later, concerning Fulgentius, Eucherius, Hilary, etc. At the end, concerning Maximus. A chapter on Bishop Isidore is appended. “Isidore, an outstanding man, etc.” This is Braulion’s prefatory notice, with the name omitted. The following begins: “The book of Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, on illustrious men. Preface: ‘Of illustrious men, etc.’ Concerning Pope Gregory: ‘Pope Gregory of the Roman See, etc.’” Then: “The book on the origin, life, and death of the holy Fathers who excelled in virtue in the Old and New Testaments begins. Preface: ‘Of certain men, etc.’” There are 62 chapters on the Old Testament, the final chapter concerning Judith. There are 22 chapters on the New Testament, the last concerning Titus. Concerning James: “He preached the Gospel, etc. He died by the sword in Marmarica of Achaea, slain by Herod the tetrarch, and was buried there.”

10. Codex 1737 Ottobonianus, on parchment, in folio, apparently from the eleventh century. [Col. 0911D] Heading: “The chapters of the book of Saint Isidore, that God is supreme and incomparable, begin.” A recent title: “Isidore’s books on God.” Book I has 31 chapters. Book II has 46 chapters, or 44 in another count. Book III has 62 chapters. It ends: “The heavenly court encloses those who rejoice. The third book is complete.” The *Enchiridion* of St. Augustine follows, together with the Life of St. Antony by St. Athanasius. At the end, in a script not especially ancient: “The book of Saint Mary of Turponay for the second part of Ambrose Autpertus on the Apocalypse.” And immediately: “Do not omit it, because that final part is excellent.” Blanchinus, volume II of the *Evangelia quadrupla*, page 603, describes the Regio-Vatican Codex no. 96, which appears to be an autograph and begins: “In the name of the Holy Trinity. The exposition of the priest Autpertus on the second part of the exposition of the Apocalypse [Col. 0912A] begins.” At the end of the codex, in uncial letters: “Ambrose, also called Autpertus, born in the province of Gaul . . . completed this work, etc.” In a more recent hand at the beginning of the codex: “This is the book of blessed Dionysius, etc.” This second part is mentioned in our Ottobonian codex.

11. After this: “The book of the Chronicles of Isidore, bishop of Seville, from the beginning of the world to the empire of Heraclius Augustus and the reign of King Sisebutus, begins. Preface: ‘A brief exposition of times through generations, etc., so that the sum of past time may be known. The first age, etc. God formed the creation of all things in six days, etc. Adam, etc., which is the stock of the sons of God.’” Toward the end, concerning Hermenegild: “and he himself is crowned with martyrdom. Maurice, etc. The Goths, [Col. 0912B] with King Reccared supporting them, return to the Catholic faith. At this time St. Gregory is regarded as a distinguished bishop at Rome; at that time the Avars, etc.” It ends, as in Schelstrat: “Heraclius reigned for twenty-six years. In the fifth year of his reign, while he was engaged in, etc.” In this manuscript, as in certain others, Braulio’s name as author is not prefixed to the prefatory notice of Isidore’s books. Marcus Michael took this as an opportunity to add chapter 50 to chapter 49 of Book *On Illustrious Men* in the fifteenth-century paper manuscript of St. Mark’s in Florence, no. 542, where Braulion’s prefatory notice is contained. He added the following: “Because it is considered ambiguous by many who are not sufficiently discerning who added the final chapter at the end of the aforesaid work of Isidore, and because the author of that chapter cannot be fully determined from the declaration placed immediately above, I, Marcus Michael, priest of Cortona, have therefore appended the following words, so that the truth may become clearer to readers: namely, that the chapter noted above, whose beginning is ‘Isidore, an outstanding man,’ was added in his praise by Braulion, bishop of Caesaraugusta.” Thus according to the letters of Rochus Menchaca sent to me.

12. Codex 1758 Ottobonianus, membranaceous, in folio, from the fifteenth century, formerly belonging to the queen of Sweden and previously Petavius’s volume 270. Rufus Festus’ *Breviary of the Deeds of the Roman People*, without a title: “Let it be made brief, etc.” On page 5 verso, the heading: “The Chronicle from the beginning of the world to the time of the Eunuch [read: Heraclius] and Sisebutus begins: ‘A brief sequence of times through generations.’” At the beginning of the volume it is noted that it may be Isidore’s. It is indeed Isidore’s Chronicle, but apparently interpolated by some monk of St. Columbanus. In the same place, concerning the time of Justinian: “At this time Priscian the grammarian flourished; Arator, versifier and subdeacon of the Roman Church; Cassiodorus, senator at Ravenna, later made a monk, distinguished for learning and eloquence. During the same period such a great famine occurred throughout all Italy that mothers ate the flesh of their children.”

13. Under Maurice: “At this time Cleander [read: Leander], a Spanish bishop distinguished for learning and faith, was held in high regard. Gregory the teacher shines at Rome.” Under Heraclius and Sisebutus: “During the same period Muhammad, the false prophet, arose, advancing from a leader of robbers [Col. 0913A] to royal power. At these times Isidore, bishop of Seville, illustrious for learning and eloquence, flourished; holy Gallus likewise, at the abbey of St. Columbanus, shone as his disciple in life and miracles. The Chronicle from the beginning of the world to the time of the rulers Heraclius and Sisebutus is complete. Thanks be to our Lord Jesus Christ. Amen.” Pages 13 and following: an anonymous Chronicle from the beginning of the world to the year 1430, without a title. It begins: “It is fitting for virtuous men, etc.” It is marked in a recent script: this work should be compared with Vossius, *On Latin History*, pages 504–505. The author says that he is gathering excerpts from other works, especially from the *Breviary* of Landulfus de Columna, canon of Chartres, “who took care to abridge histories from the creation of the first man down to John, English by nationality, who, as is read, was a woman.” In the events after the birth of Christ, the heading “Addition” is often inserted, followed after the addition by “end of the addition.” In the same place: “Damasus I, Spanish by nationality, etc.”

14. Much is inserted concerning the Franks, some of which is refuted by marginal notes in a later hand. On page 111 the heading reads: “Genealogy of the Spaniards: and, so that I may not pass over the kingdom of Spain with a slow step, it must be known that its country derives from *YS* [read: *patria ab YS*], which means ‘one’ or ‘alone’; *PAN* means ‘all’; *YA* means ‘star’; thus Spain is said, as it were, to be ‘the whole solitary star.’” After the encomium of Spain comes a history of the Vandals, etc., of the Goths, etc., down to Ordoño, son of Froila. It ends: “If you desire to know further the deeds of the kings of Spain, see their chronicles, etc.” Much is taken from Isidore and from the continuators. In the same work, after Benedict III, there is a tale about Pope Joan:

“John the Englishman sat in the chair of Peter for two years, seven months, and four days. He, as is reported, was a woman, etc., and is not included in the catalogue of Roman pontiffs because of his female sex. Some historians place this John before Benedict III, while others place him after him.”

It ends with Martin V and the statutes of the Council of Constance against heretics, with certain enigmatic verses added against them:

“You see Orontes climbing the opposing mountain,”

together with the beginning of the explanation. There is also a *Summary of the Chronicle of the Roman Pontiffs*, extracted from the books of Celeydor (or Celeydob) on the true Roman Empire, in the year 1454 at Rome. It ends with “Caius, Marcellinus.” Some leaves are missing.

15. Landulfus de Columna, whose *Historical Breviary* is praised in this Codex, is also called by another name, “Landulfus Sagax.” He dedicated his *Historical Breviary* to Pope John XXII in the year 1320; it was published at Poitiers in 1479. Some believe that this same Landulfus was the author of the *Historia Miscella*. But that there was also another man who worked on compiling the *Historia Miscella* after Landulfus is clear from our Codex. On this subject one may consult Fabricius in both of his *Bibliothecae Latinae*, and Mansi’s note on the *Bibliotheca media*. It would not be useless to compare with our chronicles what is related in this Codex about the history of the Goths.

[Col. 0914A]

16. Codex 1968 Ottobonianus, parchment, in octavo, dating approximately from the twelfth century. A work on rhetoric by M. Andra Gesti, or rather by Fortunatianus, without an old title, begins: “What is rhetoric? The science of speaking well.” It ends: “he did not otherwise begin.” The following work begins: “The orator’s duty is”; its recent title is: “The minor art, or rather, more properly, the major art.” It ends: “To speak well in writing: happily the rhetorical art of C. Julius Victor is complete. Of Hermagoras, Cicero, Quintilian, Aquila [unclear], Marcomannus, and Tatianus.” Immediately thereafter: “On the Position of the Stars: There are two extreme vertices of the world.” Near the end of the book is the title: “Isidore on the Seven Degrees of Kinship. In the first, upper degree are contained the father and mother.” This is an explanation of Isidore’s genealogical diagram, about which I spoke in chapter 86.

[Col. 0914B]

17. Codex 2524 Ottobonianus, parchment, in folio, apparently from the fifteenth century. Its recent title is: “Cases of the Decretals by John of God, Master and Professor.” There are five books. At the end of the books the author is called “John, a Spanish priest.” His book *On Judgments* follows; at the beginning he is called “John of God, priest,” and in the title “John, a Spanish priest.” Our bibliographers discuss this author more fully. There are other anonymous commentaries on the Decretals. Aristotle’s *Ethics* with commentary. Page 141: *Flowers from the Holy Fathers*, lacking its beginning: “from Isidore,” Bernard, Chrysostom, Saint Maximus, Augustine, Gregory, Ambrose, Jerome, and Seneca. Isidore is cited “from *On the Supreme Good*, in the *Etymologies*.” Page 147: *Flowers of Repentance* begin: “Since those who sin, etc.,” from the Fathers, Augustine, etc., “Isidore, etc.”

18. Codex 2992 Ottobonianus, paper, in octavo. The so-called *Synonyms* of Cicero: “Cicero to his Lucius Vetturius, greetings: I have collected, etc. Hidden, covered, etc.” It ends: “is veiled, is covered, etc.” I discussed these *Synonyms* in chapter 56. There are many other works, such as Petrarch’s life written by Petrarch himself; a letter of Francesco da Fiano to Leonardo Aretino concerning the cause of Ovid’s exile; Poggio’s letter to Leonardo Aretino concerning the execution of Jerome of Prague, whom he praises, as he says, “beyond belief”;  and other works of this kind.

19. Codex 3136 Ottobonianus, paper, in folio, formerly belonging to the Passionaean Library, written entirely in Greek letters in the eighteenth century. In the Inventory it is described as follows: “Isidore’s work on heresies in Greek.” I had supposed that either Isidore’s *Book on Heresies*, mentioned by Braulio, or the chapter of his *Etymologies* in which he discusses heresies had been translated into Greek by someone. But I found something quite different. The Greek heading is:

“Τῷ δεσπότῃ μου τῷ μεγαλοπρεπεστάτῳ, καὶ ἐνδοξοτάτῳ, καὶ φιλοχρίστῳ υἱῷ Σπορακίῳ Ἰσειδόρῳ περὶ αἱρέσεων, καὶ λοιπῶν λόγων.”

That is: “To my lord, most magnificent, most glorious, and Christ-loving son Sporacius Isidore, concerning heresies and other discourses.”

The word Σπορακίῳ (*Sporakiō*) is obscure. The inscription is rendered in Latin as follows: “To my most magnificent and most glorious lord, and most Christ-loving son Sporacius Isidore, concerning heresies and other matters.” The work is not by Isidore but by another author, addressed “to Sporacius Isidore,” namely Theodoret. The dedicatory letter of Theodoret, in volume IV of the *Theological Institutes* of Thomas of Venice, where the work is published, bears this inscription:

“To the most magnificent and most glorious lord, and most Christ-loving son Sporacius, Theodoret, bishop of Cyrrhus in Augustoeuphratensis, sends greetings in the Lord.”

It begins: “Praise is worthy.”

20. In a note Vezzosius wonders whether Sporacius, to whom Theodoret writes, was the man appointed by the emperor as judge who attended the Council of Chalcedon, or the man who held the consulship in the year 452, or someone else. From the Ottobonian Codex it may be inferred that Sporacius was also called Isidore. After the five books of heretical fables, this same Codex contains other Greek treatises: Saint Maximus, *On the Tree of Life*; Gregory the Theologian; Cyril; and others.

# CHAPTER CVII

Other Roman Manuscript Codices Containing Isidore’s Works—Namely, Those of the Vatican Archives, the Library of the Roman College, the Angelica, the Casanatensis, the Albani, and the Borgia—On the Various Readings of the Toledo Codices Sent to Rome

[Col. 0915B]

1. It is worthwhile to add to the immense forest of manuscript Codices preserved in the various parts of the Vatican Library several others that I examined outside that library. There are two by no means negligible Codices in the more private Vatican Archive, which its prefect, the distinguished Cajetanus Marinius, a man of illustrious reputation in public literary affairs, graciously allowed me to collate, with his exceptional kindness.

2. The older Codex, which I therefore mention first, is Vatican Archive, *Miscellanea*, cupboard 6, no. 46: parchment, large folio, apparently from the tenth century, written in Roman cursive script, but with *z* written in the German manner. There are few and uncomplicated abbreviations. Diphthongs are joined, though they are often omitted. The ink of the first hand was not very black; a second hand, however, wrote over the letters in the same style with darker ink, except that it reduced some of the longer forms to shorter ones. On the first page this same second hand copied the following from some old book, as I believe:

“At the beginning of the book: a letter. To my lord and servant of God, Braulio, from Isidore. The letter of Your Holiness, etc.”

—as in the printed editions.

3. After this letter comes: “Here you have it, as I promised, etc.” Immediately thereafter: “The Book of Isidore’s *Etymologies* begins. Prologue. Here are many sacred things, etc.” Then follow the verses for Isidore’s library, about which I spoke in chapter 81. Next comes a title in uncial letters, red with vermilion:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ begins the first book of the *Etymologies* of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis. To my lord and servant of God, Bishop Braulio, from Isidore. The letter of Your Holiness found me in the city of Toledo.”

Nothing else is added from this letter. An index of the chapters of Book I follows, and immediately afterward chapter 1: “Discipline derives from learning.” The work is divided into twenty-five books.

4. After Book XI—which in Grialius is Book IX—the “Alphabet of Certain Words,” which is Grialius’s Book X, is omitted, and Book XII, “On Man, etc.,” is added. In this respect, as in many others, it agrees with the Albani Codex, described below. The work of the *Etymologies* is complete, but the final leaf has been supplied by a later hand. At the end: “The *Etymology* of the book of blessed Bishop Isidore is complete.”

5. In the same Codex there follow glosses on the Old Testament, lacking their beginning, written in the old hand used for the books of the *Etymologies*. Their first words are:

“The providence of God was borne along, by which he created all things. ‘Let there be light’ ... It is this same light that afterward was diffused into the vessels of heaven, that is, into the stars. ‘He said’ ... through his word, etc.”

These glosses differ from the Ordinary Gloss of Walafrid Strabo and from the glosses on the divine books by Robert of Sorbonne, who wrote in the time of Saint Louis—that is, in the thirteenth century. These glosses appear in the edition of Menochius’s *Commentaries on Sacred Scripture*, Venice, 1743, page 472 of the Appendices. Robert’s glosses are largely drawn from Isidore’s books and from these very glosses in the Vatican Archive Codex. They continue only as far as chapter 3 of the Second Book of Kings; the final words, however, can scarcely be read. One may readily suspect that this is a literal interpretation of the text, of the kind Isidore discusses in the prologue to his mystical expositions, as I explained more fully in chapter 65. On the verso of the final page of the Codex is a letter from Gottschalk to a certain Lupus, I do not know the bishop of which see, since the letters are already fading:

“On the tenth day of August the letter of Your Holiness was delivered to me.”

6. The work of the *Etymologies* appears to have been divided by the first hand into twenty-five books; but the second hand has often erased or confused the numbers. The order of the books also differs from that of the printed editions, and perhaps this Codex was copied from various exemplars. It also contains an inserted *Index of Heresies* under the name of Saint Jerome, as in the Albani Codex and others; on this see chapter 86. It also contains the Council of Caesarea concerning Easter.

7. The second Codex of the Vatican Archive is parchment, in folio, and dates approximately from the eleventh century. Ligatures are frequent but easy to read, and there is usually a small line written above them. Diphthongs are joined. From chapter 4 of Book XI—or elsewhere, Book XII—“On Serpents,” the script appears more recent and the ink lighter. At the beginning a recent hand has written: “From the books of the Congregation of Saint Maur in Rome.” There are two letters of Isidore to Braulio:

1. “The letter of Your Holiness.”
2. “Here you have it, etc.”

This is followed by the heading:

“The books written by Isidore the Younger, bishop of Hispalis, to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, or to his own lord and son Sisebutus, begin. These are the chapters of the first book.”

Twenty-nine chapters are listed.

8. Book II has thirty-two chapters. Book III has seventy. Book IV has thirteen. Book V, *On Laws*, etc., has thirty-nine. The end of this book reads: “God alone knows it. Book VI is complete. The chapters of Book VII begin”; but this has been made into Book VI. There are seventeen chapters, the last concerning offices. Then: “Book VII is complete. Book VIII begins.” It has been corrected so that it is understood not to be Book VIII but Book VII. There are fifty-two chapters, for Books VII and VIII, which are divided in the printed editions, continue uninterruptedly in this Codex and merge into one; and the chapter on heretics has been divided into several parts. Chapter XVIII, “On Heresies and Schism,” ends with: “they return to their former errors”; in the printed editions this is chapter 4. Immediately follows chapter 19, entitled: “On the Heresies of the Jews. First: The Efnei say.”

9. “Chapter XX. Likewise, another heresy of diverse doctrines: that is, first, the Simonites. A certain magician named Simon, etc. Chapter LVIII. On the Eunomians.” It ends: “they wish it to be a substance. Thus far Jerome.” That is, as in the more recent Malatesta Codex, the Albani Codex, and others. But in this Codex Isidore’s chapters have been omitted, and after the words “Thus far Jerome” the following is added as though it were Isidore’s:

“We believe in one God, the Father almighty, and in one Lord Jesus Christ, etc.”

This fragment will be placed among the appendices, as I said in chapter 83. The work ends: “and reward. Book VIII is complete. The chapters of Book IX begin.” There are fourteen chapters. The first is “On the Philosophers of the Nations,” and the last “On Married Persons.” It ends: “not those whom integrity of conduct commends. Book VIII is complete. The chapters of Book X begin.” There are twelve chapters.

10. In Book IX the genealogical diagrams, or trees of law, are missing. Book X in this Codex is “On Man, etc.,” which is Book XI in the printed editions. The book “On Certain Words, etc.,” which is Book X in the printed editions, is missing. After chapter 4, “On Things Transformed”: “Book X is complete. Book XI begins.” The chapters of this book are contained in the preceding book: “On Cattle and Pack Animals, chapter 1.” In fact, twelve chapters had been listed at the beginning of Book X.

11. The book *On the World*, etc., follows, with nineteen chapters. It is called Book XII by the first hand and Book XI by the second. But at the end there remains: “Book Thirteen is complete; the chapters of Book Fourteen begin. On the Earth, etc.” There are nine chapters. At the end: “Book Thirteen is complete”; but this was something else. The next book seems to be designated XV by the first hand: “On Cities, etc.” The same applies to the book *On Dusts*, etc., designated XVI by the first hand and XIV by the second. The sequence proceeds in such a way that the final book is called XX by the first hand and XVIII by the second. At the end:

“Upon completion, may the holy Virgin Mary be praised.  
May he who completed this book be placed in paradise.  
When his good hour of departure comes.”

12. In the Library of the Roman College there is a paper Codex in folio. At the beginning is an enumeration of years, sometimes with a brief account of events, ending in the year 1175. The Codex therefore appears to have been copied from another of the twelfth century. A chronicle follows, mutilated at the beginning. At the end:

“The Chronicle of Saint Jerome the priest is complete. The *Chronography* [so] of Isidore the Younger begins.”

But the chronicle called Jerome’s extends to the ninth year of the Emperor Phocas and to the death of Pope Gregory. It ends:

“Eraclius, the most glorious prince of the Goths, subjected the Jews of his kingdom and converted them to the faith of Christ ...”

For *Eraclius*, read *Sisebutus*. Isidore’s chronicle begins:

“Over six days God fashioned the creation of all things.”

It ends: “then the consummation of the age is for him. The chronicle is complete.” Some additions follow, especially concerning the kingdom of France, down to the year 1107. Then follows:

“The History of Paul Orosius, priest of the Catholic Church, to Augustine, bishop, against the accusers of the Christian times. The brief history of the first book of Saint Orosius begins.”

Thus Orosius is called “Saint” in some manuscripts, according to the old custom. It ends:

“They lived in villages and suburbs.

He himself, after two chronicles, restored Orosius  
to you and to his native land, filled with the light of learning,  
and brought to completion what he had sought through long labor.  
By me, Karolus Reguardatus, a soldier of Nursia,  
on the fifth day before the Ides of October, 1459.”

The Codex appears to have been written at precisely this time.

13. In the same Library of the Roman College there is another Codex, in folio, on parchment, apparently from the thirteenth century, as a recent hand notes at the beginning. It is elegantly written and without a title. There is an index of the fifteen chapters of Book I of the *Sentences*, followed by the heading:

“The chapters are complete. The first book of Saint Isidore, called the Book of the *Sentences*, begins.”

Book II has forty-four chapters. At the end of Book II are nine hexameter verses. There are also excerpts from the *Etymologies*:

“Those called cousins, etc. The father of my race is my father, etc. On Kings and Leaders: ‘Listen, therefore, O kings, and understand, etc.’”

—the latter from Solomon. Book III follows. Sixty-eight chapters are listed, but the last is numbered 56:

“On the End of Life.”

It ends: “it encloses those who are to be gladdened. With the Lord’s favor, Book III of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences* is complete.” The diphthongs are joined; there are some ligatures, but they are clear, and a small line is rarely placed above *i*.

14. In the same Library of the Roman College there is a large folio paper Codex from the fourteenth century, without a title. It contains Braulio’s letter: “O pious Lord”; and two letters of Isidore. An index of the twenty books of the *Etymologies* follows, along with the index of chapters of Book I, etc., through Book XV, chapter “On Mountains.” The remainder to the end is missing.

15. In the Angelica Library at Rome, among the Augustinian Fathers, the following manuscript Codices of Saint Isidore are preserved. There is a parchment Codex in quarto, approximately from the fourteenth century, entitled: “Isidore and Others on Medicine.” I have already discussed this Codex in chapter 75.

16. In the same Angelica Library there is a paper Codex in folio from the fourteenth or fifteenth century. Its heading reads: “The Book of the *Etymologies* of Saint Isidore, Bishop of Hispalis, begins.” Another heading reads: “The prologue of Saint Isidore, bishop, to Bishop Braulio in the Book of the *Etymologies* begins. The letter of Your Holiness, etc.” There is an index of the chapters of Book I. The work of the *Etymologies* is complete. At the end there is another letter of Isidore to Braulio:

“Here you have the work I promised and sent, etc.”

17. In the same Angelica Library there is a small quarto parchment Codex, approximately from the fourteenth century, especially if the Roman numerals—which appear in certain places—are by the first hand. At the beginning is the heading: “Selected Questions on Ecclesiastical Offices begin.” It begins:

“Why is Septuagesima celebrated? Solution [perhaps]. ‘So that, just as the people of God, who because of their sins were in Babylonia, etc.’”

The final question concerns an antiphon; its last words are:

“For example, one reads and another learns at school, while another sows in the field.”

It is not sufficiently clear whether the work ends at this point. The heading reads: “The chapters of Book I begin.” The numbers here are red Roman numerals. After the index:

“The first book of Saint Isidore, bishop, begins: That God is supreme and immutable.”

Book I has fifteen chapters and ends: “the terrified will be cleansed.” Book II has forty-two chapters, apparently numbered in Arabic numerals by the first hand. It ends: “he presents danger.” Book III has sixty-six chapters numbered with Roman numerals, which here appear rather to be by a second hand. Before this are seven incorrectly written verses:

“Receive, reader, etc.”

This third book of the *Sentences* is otherwise mutilated at the end; it continues only to the beginning of chapter 58. There are many ligatures. Sometimes *s* appears at the end in the form now in use. Certain Gothic letters in the first and last lines extend very far, in the manner of Carolingian letters.

18. In the same Angelica Library there is a small folio parchment Codex from the fifteenth century. It contains Isidore’s Books of the *Sentences* with the letter to Massona, as I explained in chapter 73. Then comes the heading: “That God is supreme and immutable.” Book I ends: “by which he himself ascended and we shall ascend.” Book II ends: “he presents danger.” Book III ends: “he encloses those who are to be gladdened.” At the end is an index of chapters.

19. The Casanatensis Library preserves several manuscript Codices of Saint Isidore. Codex D. IV. 23, from the eleventh century or earlier, is a small-octavo parchment miscellany. It contains an antiphonary and verses:

“An arbiter, that he might drive away all the darkness of the world.”

This is the metrical preface of Saint Benedict of Aniane in Menard’s *Concordia Regularum*. Page 13: *Sayings of Saint Isidore, On the Kinds of Monks*: “There are six kinds,” from Book II *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, as I said in chapter 69. Excerpts from councils and decrees of Roman pontiffs follow. Page 46: “The Council of the City of Rome under Pope Damasus on the Explanation of the Faith begins”:

“It has been said: First it must be undertaken, etc.; we confess that it has been condemned.”

This is the text I published among the appendices to Sedulius. Page 49: “The Book of Saint Augustine, bishop, on the Rules of the Church begins,” with fifty-five chapters:

“We believe that there is one God.”

This is the book *On Ecclesiastical Dogma*. Page 54: “The admonition of Lord Leo, archbishop of Ravenna”—from the eighth century—“to Durantus the monk, or to the other hermits who are with him”:

“Since yesterday, [something] to me, etc.”

Immediately afterward are “thirty ladders and steps by which one ascends to heaven, and an equal number of steps by which one descends to hell.” This is a work different from John Climacus’s *Ladder*. There are sayings of Bede. There is an exposition of the Catholic faith by Saint Athanasius, archbishop:

“What is faith according to substance?”

What this work is, and whether it belongs to Athanasius, is unclear. There is also “On God’s Fourfold Work,” from the works of Saint Augustine. A chapter of Saint Isidore *On the Elements* begins:

“The elements differ from one another, both in their nature and in their position.”

The Codex also contains Isidore’s discussions of the firmament, the celestial waters, the stars, and the twelve signs, excerpted from the *Etymologies* and *On the Nature of Things*.

20. Codex G. VI, 7 of the same Casanatensis Library, formerly Altempsianus, is a paper octavo Codex from the fifteenth century. It contains spiritual miscellanies. Near the end:

“An excerpt from Isidore’s book called *Synonyms* begins, concerning a man lamenting and Reason admonishing. Note well that it is brief and useful for expressing oneself in Latin, or literally: ‘My soul is in distress; I am surrounded by evils,’ etc. Whatever you do, do it for the future reward.”

Amen. The heading reads:

“What human beings do, every intention judges.”

“Isidore’s aforesaid Excerpt is complete. Thanks be to God.”

21. Codex G. III, 1 of the same Casanatensis Library is a parchment folio Codex from approximately the eleventh century, written in French script. It contains Bruno of Asti’s exposition of the *Song of Songs*. Verses precede it:

“This Solomon sang, etc.”

I discussed these in chapter 81. There is also the same author’s exposition of the Apocalypse, with a more recent title at the beginning: “Also, a Chronicle from Adam to Titus, the disciple of Paul, according to Isidore.” But on page 57 the title is: “The Book on the Life and Death of the Just by Jerome.” After the prologue and index is the heading: “The exposition of Saint Jerome the priest begins: Adam, etc.” There are eighty-six chapters, with some variant readings in an ancient hand.

In the same work, concerning Saint Peter: “He was buried toward the south.” Concerning Paul: “toward the eastern quarter.” Concerning Saint James:

“James, son of Zebedee and brother of John, fourth in order, wrote to the twelve tribes that are dispersed among the nations, preached the Gospel in Spain and the western regions, and poured the light of preaching into the setting of the world. He was killed by the sword of Herod the tetrarch and was buried in a marble coffin.”

The old hand gives variant readings: either *acha marita*, or *in Achaia Marmorica*, as I indicated in chapter 61. At the end:

“The Life or Death of the Saints who went before us in the Lord is complete.”

On the word *chronicle*: “In Greek, *chronica* is said, etc.,” from Book V of the *Etymologies* through the end, in the fourth year of Sisebutus, etc.

22. Codex Casanatensis D. IV, 30, written in the ninth century, in the year 812, mostly in Lombard script, in an almost square quarto format. Schelstratius discusses it in volume I of his *Ecclesiastical Antiquities*, page 623. It contains calendars and works of Bede and Alcuin: “The Six Ages of the World,” by Bede or another author. There are various short works and fragments. On page 135:

“Isidore on the Decalogue of the Law. Therefore God gave the law to Moses for our innocence and for knowledge of himself, etc. The first commandment of the Decalogue pertains to God the Father, etc.”

It ends: “to the fellowship of one’s neighbor.” These are chapters 29 and 30 of the *Exposition on Exodus*, with some variation in the scriptural text.

23. In the select library of the Most Illustrious Albani Family at Rome there is a small folio parchment Codex, written approximately in the tenth century. The diphthongs are joined; a single point is sometimes used as punctuation between letters, either in the upper part or below; the words are only slightly separated from one another; there are some ligatures, but they are clear. The script is Italian or old French and quite legible.

At the beginning is Isidore’s book *On the Nature of Things*, mutilated at the beginning through chapter 4, “On the Months.” The final chapter is chapter 50, “On the Regions of the Earth,” which is added by Braulio and appears in the appendix to the recent Madrid edition. Verses follow, apparently summarizing several chapters of the book *On the Nature of Things*, through the chapter “On the Names of the Winds.” The verses on the names of the winds are placed in the notes by Grialius, who considers them older than Isidore.

24. Next follows:

“In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ. The first book of Isidore, bishop of Hispalis, of the *Etymologies*, begins.”

Without any letter, there is an index of the chapters of Book I, and likewise an index of the chapters at the beginning of each book. The final book, which is Book XX in the printed editions, is numbered 29 here and is mutilated at chapter 3. The book that is Book X in the edition, “The Alphabet of Certain Words,” is entirely omitted; and where its place ought to have been after Book XI, the following is written after that book: “Book XI is complete. Book XIII begins.”

In the book *On the Nature of Things*, chapter 7, near the end, after the words “is adorned with assemblies,” the Codex has the heading: “Likewise, a recapitulation of the foregoing.” In chapter X, instead of the heading, it has: “On the Circle of the World.” In the diagram one reads:

“The fourth eximerine circle, temperate and habitable”;

in the printed edition: “chimerine.” Likewise:

“The middle ysimerine circle, torrid and uninhabitable because of the heat”;

in the edition: “The third circle, uninhabitable because of heat.”

Chapter XI, “On the Parts of the World,” begins: “The elements of the world are four, etc.” It ends: “the appended picture expresses it.” Nothing was written in the diagram.

25. Chapter XII, “On Heaven,” begins with the words: “Moreover, Saint Ambrose, etc.” It ends: “and they meet the divided pole with powerful movement” [the manuscript reads *diviso*]. In chapter 23 the diagram reads:

“Saturn is said to complete its circle in thirty years, etc.”

The printed edition has: “It completes its course, etc.” In chapter 26, after the words “may become known to the senses,” comes chapter 27, “On Arcturus”:

“That Arcturus is, etc.”

After the words “it quickly sets,” comes chapter 28, “On the Pleiades”:

“The Pleiades, etc.”

Chapter 29 of the Codex is chapter 27 in the printed edition, and so forth. Chapter 45, “On the River Nile,” is chapter 43 in the printed edition. It ends: “the river returns,” and immediately in the manuscript:

“Chapter 46. On the Names of the Sea and Rivers. In Parthia, Tranquillus says ... as great precipices as possible.”

Chapter 47, “On the Position of the Earth. How the earth, etc.,” is chapter 44 in the printed edition. Chapter 46, “On the Names of the Sea and Rivers,” which has not yet seen the light and is certainly Isidore’s, will be published by me in its proper place from this Codex and others collated with one another.

26. The verses written after the book *On the Nature of Things*, by which several chapters of that same book are brought to completion in verse, are preceded by a note in prose:

“In the very beginning of creation—for I mean the act of creation—heaven was made, etc.”

Then comes the heading: “Likewise, verses on the same subject: ‘The first day in the world, etc.’” On these see chapter 76. Other similar headings follow: “Likewise, verses on Bootes. Likewise, verses on the Pleiades, etc.” The final heading of the poem is: “Likewise, verses on the winds.”

27. In the *Etymologies* of the same Albani Codex, after the middle of chapter 34 of Book I, a fragment has been inserted under the heading “On the Indiction.” It begins:

“Indiction is so called, as though it were a farewell, etc.”

The script is either by the first hand or from the same period. In the same script follows the heading: “The second orthography begins. *Ara* with *a* alone, etc. Zoticus, Zeno, and the rest.” These will properly be included among the appendices, fragments, or additions to the *Etymologies*. Chapter 34 of Book I of the *Etymologies* then continues.

28. Another addition appears in Book VIII of the Albani Codex—Book VI, chapter 17, in Grialius—after the words “so that Sunday should not be omitted”: namely, a council concerning the method of finding Easter:

“After the resurrection, or ascension, etc.”

This council was held by order of Pope Victor by Theophilus, bishop of Caesarea in Palestine. Its acts, preserved in this Codex, differ greatly from those published elsewhere by Baronius and Labbeus from Bede’s work *On the Equinox*. I shall publish them again after comparing them with Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive, Ottobonian Codex 122, and the more recent Malatesta Codex, also examining the copy found in the anonymous work *On the Computus* in volume III of Muratori’s *Anecdota*.

29. The Albani Codex also contains in Book X, chapter 4—Book VIII in Grialius—an “Index of Heresies” attributed to Saint Jerome, with the headings:

“Jerome’s Index of the Heresies of the Jews begins. Jerome’s Index is complete. Likewise, the passage above from Isidore, etc.”

It is found in a similar form in Codex 1 of the Vatican Archive, in the more recent Malatesta Codex, and in other manuscripts, as I said in chapter 86.

30. If it is agreeable, I shall add to these manuscript Codices another paper quarto Codex from the fifteenth century, which I acquired and which formerly belonged to the distinguished Magnani, prefect of the library of the so-called Bolognese Institute. It will be of no small use to me. The heading reads:

“The chapters of the first book of Isidore, entitled *On the Supreme Good*, begin.”

Book I has thirty-one chapters. Book II has forty-three. Book III has sixty-five. The chapters are numbered with Arabic numerals. There are many letter ligatures, and the script is semi-Gothic or German. At the beginning of the Codex a red monogram of Jesus has been painted, indicating that the Codex was not copied before Saint Bernardino of Siena, who died in 1444. At the end:

“Isidore’s Book of the *Sentences* is complete.”

31. After these Codices, through the singular kindness of His Eminence Cardinal Borgia, I saw another paper octavo Codex from the fifteenth century, which he himself owns and which he graciously had brought to me. Near the end is the title:

“Certain Notable Sayings of Blessed Isidore, Bishop.”

The heading of the first chapter is: “On Avoiding Sin.” This little work, or collection of sayings, begins:

“Act, therefore, O soul, as is fitting.”

It ends: “so that you may not abandon the good that you know.” End. It begins and ends almost in this way with Isidore’s *Rule for Living*, published by Bignaeus; but the two little works differ from one another considerably, so that this Borgia work too seems properly to belong among the appendices.

This Codex is preceded by certain curious miscellanies from Leonardo Aretino, Francesco Filelfo, Francesco Aretino, Antonio Panormita, and others. There is a satirical letter in the name of the devil to John, a Dominican and archbishop of Ragusa; funeral and nuptial orations; an apocryphal little work about Jesus Christ being entered by the Hebrews into a catalogue of priests; and many other works on various subjects.

32. Various readings from the Toledo Codices were recently sent to me. They had formerly been collected by Burriel and Bayer and are preserved in the Royal Library at Madrid. The Most Catholic King Charles IV, a deeply religious monarch, graciously permitted them to be communicated to me, with the matter being especially advanced by the distinguished Pedro Luis Blanco, prefect of the Royal Library and a most eminent supporter and cultivator of all learning.

33. The volume sent to me from the Royal Library at Madrid contains several things. First are collations of Saint Isidore’s *Sentences* with Grialius’s edition and with two Toledo manuscripts: one Gothic, dated to the era 953, that is, the year 915; the other paper, in Catalan script. The Gothic Codex is mutilated at the beginning and begins with chapter 3 of Book I. The Catalan Codex begins with the index:

“The Book of Isidore *On the Supreme Good* begins.”

At the end of the Gothic Codex are the following words:

“It ends on the second day before the Kalends of April, at the seventh hour, in the era 953. Amen. Thanks be to God. Teodemirus, although unworthy, wrote this. Pray for me.”

In the same Codex there follows, in Gothic script but in different ink, a chapter entitled:

“How great the perfection of charity is in those founded upon it: Therefore, if charity, etc.”

This ought to be rejected into the appendices.

34. On page 8 follows an *Alphabet of Prayer* from folio 103 of volume I of the collection of Don Juan Bautista Pérez. Pérez noted in his own hand in the margin:

“It is together with Luca of Tuy.”

Burriel adds:

“It is indeed found in the Codex containing Luca of Tuy’s chronicle, together with other parchment works, preserved in shelf 21, no. 12. We collated it with the autograph, as it is a copy of Pérez’s autograph, and marked the variant readings in the margins.”

The title is:

“The *Alphabet of Prayer* for repelling the temptations of the adversary and meriting the grace of God, edited by Isidore of Hispalis, archbishop of the church, whose memory is holy, begins.”

35. On page 18 of the same volume:

“The Translation of the Most Blessed Ildephonsus, Archbishop of Toledo.”

It begins:

“Of the most illustrious man Ildephonsus, etc.”

It ends:

“We have omitted noting this in the work.”

This narrative was copied from a certain Codex of the church of Toledo, shelf 14, no. 23. That Codex contains the works of Beatus and Etherius, and of Samson the abbot; Isidore’s book *On Differences*; his *Rule for Monks*; and the book *On Illustrious Men* by Hosius, with Ildephonsus’s continuation. It also contains an apology on the psalm “Judge me, O God,” addressed to Ferdinand Pérez de Guzmán. The translator of Saint Isidore’s work was a certain Franciscan religious, as may be inferred from the translation itself. It requires correction in many places.

[Col. 0923D]

36. On the verso of page 24 there is a specimen of the script of the Gothic Codex of the *Sentences* mentioned in number 33. That is, a certain scribe, imitating the ancient hand, copied numerous epigrams or poems of Saint Eugenius of Toledo, which are now extant in the highly praised edition of the Toledo Fathers, part II, the poems of Saint Eugenius, from number 60, “On Love,” to number 84, “On Judges.”

37. On page 33 begins the collation of the *Etymologies* with two Gothic Codices of the church of Toledo and with Grialius’s edition. Franciscus Pérez Bayer signs it; he collated the Codices in 1750. The older of the two Gothic Codices is marked by many Arabic annotations and some Latin ones. A specimen of its script is presented on page 30 of this volume. At the end of the *Etymologies* a Virgilian verse is added:

“At last it fell silent, and, having made an end here, came to rest.”

38. On the same final page are listed the names of certain cities, which it will not be burdensome to set down here, if some benefit may perhaps be derived from them for a geographical description of Spain: Pace, Lisbon, Ossonuba, Egitania, Coimbra, Viseu, Lamego, Calabria, Salamanca, Ávila, Elbora, Coria, Barcelona, Egara, Gerona, Ampurias, Ausona, Urgell, Lérida, Tortosa, Zaragoza, Huesca, Pamplona, Oca, Calahorra, Tarazona, Dumio, Porto, Tui, Ourense, Lugo, Britonia, Astorga, Iria, Itálica, Medina Sidonia, Elepla, Málaga, Elvira, Écija, Córdoba, Cabra, Martos, [Col. 0924B] Oreto, Baeza, Mentesa, Guadix, Baza, Urci, Játiva, Elche, Valencia, Valeria, Segovia, Segóbriga, Arcavica, Alcalá, Sigüenza, Osma, Palencia, Béziers, Maguelonne, Nîmes, Narbonne, Carcassonne, and Elne.

39. Each of the two codices of the *Etymologies* is divided into twenty books. In the older one, an index of the chapters is prefixed to each book. In book III of that same Codex 426 there are certain unusual geometric figures and musical signs, which D. Francisco Xavier Palomares accurately drew. An explanation of these figures is added in the text, although it is entirely absent from the printed editions. The more recent codex also agrees with the old one in many additions of this kind.

40. The chronicle of the *Etymologies* was collated by Burriel, as I believe, with two other codices of the Church of Toledo, written in the Latin script of the twelfth century [Col. 0924C]. He observed that the two Gothic codices already described had been written with greater care and diligence. The principal difference, however, lies in the designation of the numbers of the years; and errors can easily creep in in this area.

## CHAPTER CVIII. On the Ancient Manuscript-Codex Scribes, Collators, and Correctors

Their names ought to be entered in a catalogue. A specimen of such a catalogue.

1. In ancient codices that have come down to us, one can often observe not only the hand of the scribe who copied them, but also those of others who collated the work with autographs or more correct exemplars, or corrected the copyist’s errors by their own judgment. How diligently St. Jerome took care that the translation of the Bible made by him, as well as his other works, should be accurately copied and corrected by comparison with autographs, is clear from what I cited in chapter 87, no. 4. Writing to Lucinius Baeticus, he says: “I gave my little works to your men to be copied . . . and I frequently admonished them to collate them more carefully and correct them.” I also added another admonition in Jerome’s name to scribes, urging them diligently to collate and correct codices; it survives in Codex Urbinate 382, discussed in chapter 104. On such admonitions and curses against those who add or remove anything from books, see Fabricius, *Bibliotheca Graeca*, book V, chapter I, p. 75; Michael Lilienthal, *Selecta litteraria*, p. 1; and Pipping, *De Imprecationibus libris ascriptis*, Leipzig, 1721.

[Col. 0925A] 2. I discussed this subject at greater length in the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*, chapter 7, where I demonstrated with the clearest arguments that it is a foul slander to say that Tellerius, a man as pious as he was learned, had corrupted Codex 427 of St. Hilary preserved in the archive of the Vatican basilica by deleting the letters *pt* in the word *adoptatur* and substituting the letter *r*, so that it now reads *adoratur*. I revive that controversy now for only one reason: to point out two matters. First, the authors of the Venetian *Literary Journal*, who in volume XXIII, article 13, had charged Tellerius quite explicitly with that crime, later, in volume XXVII, p. 401, to some extent retracted their opinion, asserting that they had never believed that the deed had been committed by Tellerius, nor wished others to believe so. But the slander had already struck deep roots, implanted in the minds even of very learned men through the efforts of his rivals. The words of the authors of the *Literary Journal of Italy* at the place cited are as follows:

> In that *Novella* it is indeed said that the Codex was examined by Father Tellier, and that it was afterward found to have been RECENTLY adulterated; but it was never said that this alteration had been made by Father Tellier himself; nor is there anything to prevent its having been made before his examination. Therefore, just as this was not written by us, it has never been our intention that anyone should infer it from our words, since that is not in fact our view.

I have already shown at the place cited, by producing eyewitnesses, that in the sixteenth century the Codex read *adoratur*, not *adoptatur*, and therefore that it is false that the RECENT correction was discovered after Tellerius had inspected the Codex.

[Col. 0925C] 3. The second point I wished to make is this: Constantius, at the end of his edition of the works of St. Hilary, cols. 1399 and following, compiled a list of the manuscript and printed codices from which St. Hilary’s works had been accurately and correctly edited. There, col. 1401, he says:

> The books *On the Trinity* were revised against a manuscript of the Vatican basilica, which is kept in the archive of the Basilica of St. Peter in Rome and was written at the beginning of the sixth century. The variant readings of this exemplar, first annotated by Latinius Latinius, then by Petrus Ciaconius, and finally by Giovanni Battista Bandini, were sent to us.

Why, then, did Constantius fail either to observe or to inform us what those learned men had read? I have demonstrated at the place cited that Latinius and Bandinus read *adoratur*; nor do I doubt [Col. 0925D] that Ciaconius indicated the same. Perhaps someone conjectured that the variant readings, which I think were written in Muretus’s hand and in which it is stated that the reading was then *adoratur*, formerly *adoptatur*, belonged to Petrus Ciaconius. The very learned Blasius Nasarre, in his prologue to Christopher Rodriguez’s *Spanish Polygraphy*, noted the history of the controversy between Germonius and Constantius written by Johann Peter Ludewig; and Pliny the Younger, book X, letter 71, and Galen, *On the Nature of Man*, book II, volume V, and in the commentary, book I, p. 16, discuss forgeries of profane codices.

4. Since, while examining manuscript codices and reading other books, I have incidentally noted many names of those who formerly copied, collated, or corrected codices, it occurred to me that it might perhaps prove useful to compile, from catalogues of manuscript codices—many of which have already been committed to print—and from other monuments, a catalogue of Exscribers, Collators, and Correctors. The definite age of many codices, now unknown, could thereby be established. Moreover, once the status or learning of the scribes and correctors—known from histories elsewhere—had been examined, greater value would accrue to the codices. Some preliminary material could be taken from Christian Schoettgen’s history of the scribes and booksellers of antiquity and the Middle Ages, compiled from suitable records in volume III of Joannes Polenus’s *Thesaurus antiquitatum*, and from Joannes Andreas Eschenbach’s dissertation *On the Scribes of the Ancient Romans* in the same volume III. If the names of scribes and correctors can be of any use, I shall bring them forward—those names which, as I said, I have partly set down perfunctorily and while engaged in another task in these *Prolegomena*, and partly recorded on slips.

5. Pez, in the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, mentions Liutoldus, a graceful scribe of the twelfth century; Jacobus of Wrocław of the fifteenth century; Joannes de Spiz; Joannes Feybechk; Werinherus of the twelfth century; Bernardus; Baldo; Sigipoldus; Blessed Ellingerus; Pabon; Froumundus; Ludevicus; Conradus Reginbaldus; Monherus; Ysingrimus; Helphricus; and Nidkerus.

In the same work, volume III, part III, col. 515, the monk Werinherus—also called Veczil—of the eleventh century is praised in chapter 7 of the *Chronicle of Tegernsee* as “skilled in relief work in writings and paintings, and subtle in the ornamentation of books with gold and silver.” One should not therefore immediately judge a codex to be recent because ornaments of this kind in gold and silver appear in it, as some do. Three dissertations by Schwarzius on the ornamentation of books are extant.

The same Pez, in the preface to volume I, no. 29, also names Werinherus, but, as he says, in a twelfth-century codex bearing this subscription: “Werinherus, deacon and monk, prepared this book.” The codex contains the works of Gregory of Tours. In volume III, col. 609, the ancient notices of the Benedictine monastery celebrate, from the *Notices of the Benedictoburan Monastery*, the scribes of books: Queen Kisyla, later a nun, Engilhardus, Chadoldus, Tracholfus, bishop of the church of Freising, Rudpertus, and Racholfus.

A codex of forty homilies of St. Gregory is mentioned. After the twentieth homily it bore this subscription:

> Pray for the scribe, if you have God as your protector: Hengilhart.

At the end of the work:

> Here end the homilies of blessed Pope Gregory. Chaldold the priest wrote these homilies; he came with Queen Kysila to the monastery of St. Michael the Archangel at Quohchalun.

These scribes belong to the eighth century.

6. Next the epitaph of Gothelmus, or Gotaelmus, abbot of Benedictoburan in the eleventh century, is brought forward. He prepared many books, wrote many, acquired many, and had the *Moralia on Job* written by his monk Adolpertus. In the catalogue of that same Benedictoburan monastery from the thirteenth century, Augustine’s *City of God* was also listed, copied by Burchardus, a monk of the twelfth century. In his notes, Pez indicates Paul the Deacon’s *History of the Lombards*, copied by Ludevicus, and Conrad’s *Sunday Sermons*, copied by Wilkelmus in the fifteenth century.

7. In the same *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, part III of volume IV, the monk David is praised. He wrote books by learned authors for the brothers to read and meditate upon, according to chapter 8 of book I of Reinerus the monk’s *On the Famous Scribes of the Monastery of St. Lawrence at Liège*.

In Martène’s *New Thesaurus of Anecdotes*, volume III, cols. 507 and following, Gontherus, a most excellent ninth-century scribe, is said to have written three antiphonaries with his own hand. He gave one of them, more elegant and illuminated in golden letters, to blessed Bertinus. He also copied the *Computus*, and so forth.

That distinguished men in learning and rank sometimes copied books with their own hands so that they might have corrected copies is clear from Baluze’s notes on the *Capitularies*, volume II, pp. 1160 and following. The priest Harduinus, who died in 811, is described in the *Chronicle of Fontenelle*, as found in D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, volume III:

> “He instructed very many students in the discipline of arithmetic and trained them in the art of writing, for he was by no means unlearned in that art. Accordingly, he left behind many volumes written by his own labor for our church: namely, a volume of the four Gospels written in Roman letters, and so forth.”

8. Flórez, volume IX of *Sacred Spain*, pp. 241 and following, discusses John, bishop of Seville, who at the beginning of the tenth century explained the sacred Scriptures in Arabic commentaries, as Rodrigo of Toledo reports. From this some have wrongly inferred that he translated the Bible into Arabic. Flórez argues that John flourished in the year 911 from a Sevillian codex of the councils written by John the deacon at the command of the bishop of the same name. On John the Spanish antiquarian deacon, see chapter 85, no. 6. A *Homiliary*, or *Homiliarium*, dating approximately from the tenth century is described in volume X of *Sacred Spain*; its scribe is named Florentius.

9. The same Flórez, in volume III of *Sacred Spain*, p. 393, discusses the celebrated Aemilianensis Codex of the councils, which was begun in 962 and completed in 994. At its end are painted images of Belasco the scribe, Sisebutus the bishop, and Sisebutus the notary, with this inscription:

> “Sisebutus the bishop, together with Belasco the priest and scribe, and likewise with his disciple Sisebutus, produced this book. May their memory be remembered in blessing.”

Here the word *produce* (*edere*) is used for “to write” and “to arrange”; perhaps the bishop collated and corrected the Codex.

In Nicolás Antonio’s *Bibliotheca Hispana Vetus*, book V, no. 289, there is listed a Codex of St. Ildefonsus’s *On the Virginity of the Mother of God*, written by Atilanus, who held the bishopric of Zamora from 990 to 1009. Bayer, in his note there on no. 290, quotes the following subscription from another codex of the same work:

> “I, wretched Solomon, archpriest, an unworthy servant of God and sinner, wrote this little book on the virginity of holy Mary, virgin and Mother of the Lord, to the end. It was completed in the city of Toledo, in the church of the holy Virgin Mary, under Lord Paschalis, archbishop of the metropolitan see. Recorded on Friday, at the third hour, on the day of St. Cyprian the bishop, the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, in the year 1105 of the era.”

10. The names of those who copied codices have often been brought forward in these *Prolegomena*: Facundus of the eleventh century, in chapter 6, no. 5; Teodemirus of the tenth century, in chapter 40, no. 57; Bonihominus, or Homobonus, of the fourteenth century, in the same chapter, no. 38; Brother Joannes Gaius, a Dominican, in chapter 44, no. 27; Leonardus Ser Uberti of the fifteenth century, in chapter 45, no. 9; Petrus, in chapter 46, no. 8; Kerardus, a monk of the ninth century, in chapter 55, no. 3; Dominicus, a Spanish priest of the eleventh century, in chapter 61, no. 13; Dominicus, a Spanish priest of the eleventh century, who therefore seems to be the same as the preceding one, in chapter 63, no. 8; Benedictus the acolyte, in the same eleventh century, in chapter 65, no. 8; Petrus [Col. 0928B] Castrensis, a noble Spanish boy, in chapter 67, no. 18; and a certain Petrus, a Carthusian monk, “of the throne,” as it is said there, of the Blessed Virgin.

11. Likewise, in chapter 73, no. 7, the codex scribes Vigila and Sarracinus of the tenth century are mentioned; Christopher of Aquapendente of the fourteenth century, in chapter 78, no. 21; Petrus Willelmus Armarius of the twelfth century, in chapter 79, no. 11; Saturninus, a Spanish archdeacon of the ninth century, in chapter 81, no. 10; Sebastianus, a Spanish deacon and notary of the tenth century, in chapter 87, no. 12; Andreas Chica, a monk of the fourteenth century, in chapter 88, no. 50; Elenus, or Telenus, a Spanish abbot of uncertain but certainly ancient date, in the same chapter and number; Ferrandus Joanniz, a Toledo priest of approximately the eleventh century, in chapter 91, in the note, no. 12; and, among the Ballerini, Julianus the priest, in 1095.

12.
