Among the manuscript exemplars of the Vatican described above, the following scribes are praised: Laurentius Spreuwe of the fifteenth century, in chapter 93, no. 10; Placidus of approximately the eleventh century, in chapter 97, no. 23; Agambaldus, a monk of approximately the ninth century, in chapter 100, no. 7; Joannes, a deacon of approximately the tenth century, in chapter 101, no. 21; Leonardus de Monaco of the fifteenth century, in chapter 103, no. 1; Petrus Cameracensis, in chapter 104, no. 2; Brother Antonius de la Villa de Pinelio of the fifteenth century, in chapter 104, no. 49; and Otto Stampa of approximately the eleventh century.

13. The inventory of the Vatican Library lists several codex scribes. In Codex 3101 of the Old Vatican Library, the works of Hermannus Contractus were copied in 1077 by Benedictus the acolyte. Codex 6047: the five books of the *Decretals*, on parchment; Franciscus Florius wrote it on 1 September 1483. Codex 6840: *Legends*, and so forth; Veronius Branchus copied it in 1463.

14. In the Royal Vatican Library, Codex 128, Augustine’s work *On the City of God*, was written by Petrus Strozza in 1483, at the age of sixty-seven. Codex 1388: Xenophon’s *Prodigus*, and so forth; and three epigrams by Marius Philelphus addressed to Felix Felicianus of Verona, who elegantly wrote this Codex with his own hand: “You cannot be,” and so forth.

15. The inventory of the Palatine codices indicates several scribes. Codex 463, on paper: sermons of Petrus of England, in the hand of Joannes Meydeborg. Codex 815, on parchment: Josephus the historian’s *Jewish Antiquities*, written in 1439 by Thomas Tano, while Jannozzo was reading. In the same place [Col. 0929A], Josephus’s *Jewish War*, in the hand of Bartholomaeus Berti of San Miniato, in 1414.

Codex 895, on parchment: Florus’s epitome, written in 1396 by Nicolaus Carandulus, son of the late Petrus of Modena or Venice. Codex 971: *Various History of the House of Austria*, copied in 1508 by Nicolaus Numan of Frankfurt, a canon regular of the Order of St. Augustine. Codex 1622: Terence’s comedies, in the hand of the priest Hondideus Nihilinus of Rimini, in 1449. Codex 1637: Virgil, on parchment, in the hand of Augustinus of Treviso. Codex 1681: Lucan, on parchment, written in 1448 by Gaspar Rasina. Codex 1692: Statius’s *Thebaid*, in the hand of Gaspar Dominicus Guardi of Larciano. Codex 1708: Persius and Juvenal, on parchment, in the hand of Joannes de Pola, a notary of the Venetian duchy.

16. The following Urbinate codices have their scribes named in the inventory. Codex 30, on parchment, in folio, written in 1473 by Petrus of Utrecht, from Monte Massa; it contains certain works of Origen. Codex 112: the Roman Breviary that belonged to Matthias Corvinus, king of Hungary, written in 1487 by Martinus Antonius the priest and elegantly ornamented with distinguished paintings in gold and vermilion.

Codex 137: St. Thomas on the First Book of the *Sentences*, on parchment, in folio, written at Scarperia by Theodoricus Goch in 1437. Codex 173: Bartholus of Saxoferrato on the second part of the *Code*, written by Franciscus de Pantaleonis of Naples. Codex 196: Bessarion, and so forth, in 1472 by Petrus of Utrecht. Codex 220: Averroes on the eight books of Aristotle’s *Physics*, by Theodoricus of Erfurt, on parchment, in folio. Codex 227: Hieronymus Aretinus, and so forth, by Federicus Veteranus of Urbino, on parchment, in folio. Codex 245: Pliny’s *Natural History*, on vellum, in folio, by Antonius, son of Marcus, a Florentine, in 1440. Codex 305: Laurentius Valla, and so forth, in 1471 by Petrus of Utrecht, on parchment, in folio. Codex 329: poems of Federicus Veteranus in praise of Accursius Marchesinus: “The name from the deed,” and so forth. This is Federicus Veteranus, by whose hand many Urbinate codices were elegantly copied. Codex 348: commentaries of Domitius Calderinus, and so forth, in 1474, by Angelus of Cagli.

17. Urbinate Codex 349: Laurentius Valla’s Latin translation of Homer’s *Iliad*, written in 1480 by Federicus Veteranus. Codex 351, on parchment, in folio: Bernardinus Glicinius’s commentary on Petrarch. An Italian poem by Federicus Veteranus on the death of Federicus, duke of Urbino, for whom he copied this volume last, although he had written nearly sixty others. Codex 352: *Anticlaudianus*, and so forth, written in 1481 by Federicus Veteranus. This is the Codex from which I published Dracontius’s poem. Codex 368, on parchment, in folio: verses of Federicus Veteranus, librarian of the duke of Urbino: “Do not beware of tears.” Codex 383: Cassiodorus, and so forth, on parchment, in folio, in 1472, at Florence, by Petrus of Utrecht. Codex 402: Aeneas Silvius, and so forth; two epigrams of Federicus Veteranus, the scribe of this and many other codices.

Codex 427: Quintus Curtius, on parchment, in folio, by Matthaeus de Contusiis of Volterra. Codex 470: *Ceremonies of the Roman Curia*, on parchment, in folio, written in 1487 by Sigismundus de Sigismundis. Codex 542: letters for the whole liturgical year, on vellum, by Brother Simon Ferro, an Augustinian. Codex 548: *The Parables of Solomon*, by Matthaeus de Contugiis (also called de Contusiis), of Volterra. Codex 550, on parchment, in folio: the *Lectura* of Petrus of Candia, also called Alexander V, and so forth, by Gerardus Lamberti of Königsberg, a cleric of Cologne.

Codex 643: anonymous poems, on paper, in quarto, by Petrus Paulus de Coronata of Urbino. Codex 651: Terence, on parchment, in quarto, written in 1471 by Federicus Veteranus. Codex 736: poems of the same Federicus Veteranus of Urbino, on parchment, in octavo. Codex 984: the history of Paul the Deacon, on parchment, by Federicus Veteranus.

18. I shall now list the Ottobonian codices that indicate the names of their scribes, as appears from the inventory. Codex 66: the Pentateuch, written by Dominicus the priest in a large script very similar to the specimen Mabillon presents on p. 346 of *De re diplomatica*, from the letters of Paul. Codex 78: Cassianus, on paper, in 1469, by Marcellus de Plano. Codex 225, on paper: the *Lives of the Saints* by Petrus, bishop of Equilio, in 1408, by the priest Vaxilinus Hordanus. Codex 317: the *Register of Gregory VII*, by Joannes Dominicus Mamilianus. Codex 545: the *Breviary of the Friars Minor*, in 1464, by Brother Antonius of the same order.

Codex 746: an Old Testament and Gospel in verse, entitled *Aurora*, associated with Brother Raimundus Billond: “The frequent company of the brethren,” and so forth, on vellum, in folio. Since this poem belongs to Petrus of Riga, a cleric of Reims, whose name appears in Codex Ottobonianus 2873, Raimundus Billond may be believed to have been either the copyist or the possessor of the book. Codex 761: the chronicle of Martinus of Poland, on vellum, in folio, by Andreas de Nivicinno, son of the late Tomassinus, a citizen of Parma. Codex 800: canonical treatises by various authors, in 1469, by Galassius. Codex 1353, on vellum: miscellanies [Col. 0930C] copied in 1442 by Petrus Paulus of Ancona.

19. Codex Ottobonianus 1738, on paper: Petrus de Vineis, in 1386, by Lodoicus de Marcis. Codex 1752, on paper, in folio, in 1464, by Merchionne [perhaps Melchior] de Miccinellis. Codex 1771: Pliny the Elder’s cosmography, by Henricus de Becche, an Augustinian, at Florence in 1411. In the same place, Ptolemy’s cosmography, in the same year, by Simon de Grimmis, an Augustinian.

Codex 1954: Lucretius, on vellum, in octavo; Sulpicius Verulanus, having agreed upon payment, copied this work in 1466. Codex 1966: Suetonius, on vellum, in octavo, in 1438, by Joannes de Camenago. Codex 1975, on paper: Ovid’s *Fasti*, in 1480, by Lucas Sanctis. Codex 1985, on paper, from the fifteenth century, by Dominicus [Col. 0930D] de Fantis. Codex 1998: Terence, on vellum, in quarto, from the fifteenth century, apparently in the hand of Matthaeus Dominus Herculani of Volterra. Codex 2006: Eutropius, and so forth, most elegantly written at Naples in 1465 by Joannes Marcus, a disciple of the Florentine Petrus Strozza and originally from Parma.

Codex 2020: Aulus Gellius, on vellum, in folio, in 1465, by Michael Laurentius. Codex 2030: Seneca’s tragedies, on paper, in folio, at Padua in 1464, by Joannes Sobernheymer of Constance. Codex 2036, on paper, from the fifteenth century: Cicero’s *Tusculan Disputations*, by Matthaeus of Anglaria in the fortress of Gorzano. Codex 2126: Bernardinus of Verona on Tibullus, on paper, in 1487, by Franciscus Pagno. Codex 2182, on paper, from the fifteenth century: Guido delle Colonne’s *History of Troy*, at Lyons in 1455, by Joannes de Bosco, a cleric of Thérouanne.

[Col. 0931A] 20. Codex Ottobonianus 2353, on vellum, in octavo: Zacharias Chrysopolitanus’s *Harmony of the Evangelists*, written in 1420 by Andreas Bragadinus. Codex 2378: Diogenes Laertius in Latin, on paper, from the fifteenth century, by Clemens Dicius Ortinus. Codex 2837, on vellum: Virgil, in 1406, by Antonius. Codex 2839, on paper: Cicero’s *On Duties*, in 1466, by Angelus, son of Joannes Andreas Simonis of Tivoli. Codex 2863: Dante’s *Comedy*, on paper, in 1461, by Joannes Jacobi of Civita Castellana. Codex 2864, on paper: Dante’s *Comedy*, by Petrus Antonius, son of Bartholomaeus Guittoni of Arezzo. Codex 3293, on paper: sermons of St. Bernardino, in 1466, by Gozo of Michelangiolo Laguttiere. Codex 3321: a treatise on confession, and so forth, by St. Antoninus, in 1476, by Joannes Thomas, son of Raphael Rusfacanus.

[Col. 0931B] 21. Sometimes the copyists themselves corrected the codices they had written by collating them with autograph or corrected exemplars; at other times, other learned men corrected them. I have already noted some examples in the *Prolegomena to Dracontius*, no. 147.

In Martène’s *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, volume I, col. 445, there is reported a decree of Robert, abbot of Vendôme, from the year 1156, concerning the proper care of the library. It says: “The arrangement of the books was neglected; no new ones were being made, nor were the old ones being corrected as they ought to have been.”

Mabillon, book XII of the *Benedictine Annals*, under the year 721, p. 154, no. 56, mentions a commentary of St. Ambrose on Luke, written at the command of Leutcharius, or Leodegarius, abbot of Corbie, in the year 750, which Ratbertus later corrected with his own hand.

Pez, in the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, no. 65, reports that at the end of a Codex of Jerome on the Psalms one could read, after nine hundred years:

> Hiltigaen, I, Villirat, promise you correction:
>
> He who does not know how to write thinks there is no labor.
>
> For three fingers write, but all the limbs labor.

And in no. 66, from the *Life of St. Albert*:

> “He possessed nothing of earthly things except pens and ink for the correction and glossing of books . . . When asked why he corrected and glossed discarded books that no one cared for so diligently and laboriously, he replied: ‘The time will come when these and other little works of our Church will be embraced with care.’”

Braulio, in letter 38 of volume XXX of *Sacred Spain*, says the following about a Codex he corrected at the command of King Recceswinth:

> “It is so weighed down by the negligences of scribes that scarcely a sentence can be found that does not need correction; indeed, it would have been easier to write it anew than to correct it after it had been written.”

A poem of Venantius Fortunatus, book III, poem 19, is addressed to Abbot Paternus and concerns a corrected Codex. Among other things it says:

> I beg you, forgive me if something has perhaps escaped me,
>
> for this error habitually possesses my hands.

The bishops had a particular concern that the books containing ecclesiastical offices should be properly corrected. In Vatican Codex 3830 there is a manuscript capitulary of an unknown bishop, beginning *We do not believe it should be concealed*. In the chapter on books and sacred vestments, it prescribes the following:

> “The priests must also be admonished to take care that they possess a well-corrected missal, lectionary, psalter, or other books necessary to them, because often, while they wish to pray something properly to God, they pray wrongly through uncorrected books; and they must not allow their boys to corrupt them either by reading or by writing.”

Concerning Lanfranc, archbishop of Canterbury, in the eleventh century, Milo reports in his *Life*, chapter 6:

> “Because the writings had been exceedingly corrupted through the fault of scribes, he took care to correct all the books of both the Old and the New Testament, as well as the writings of the holy Fathers, according to the orthodox faith. He also corrected to the last detail many of the books that we use night and day in the service of the Church; and he did this not only through himself but also through his disciples.”

22. In Codex 3250 of the Old Vatican Library [Col. 0932B] are Cicero’s letters, collated and corrected by Salicetus of Bologna and Ludovicus, the royal Cornelian. In Palatine Codex 1711, Manilius’s *Astronomica* was read and corrected with Master Galeotto in 1469 by Joannes, archbishop of Esztergom.

In Ottobonian Codex 63, on vellum, in quarto, an ancient copy of Augustine’s fifteen books *On the Trinity*: at the end, “K. collated in the name of Christ.” Ottobonian Codex 98, on vellum, in folio: Augustine’s *City of God*. At the end: “I bought this book in the year 1452 from the birth of Christ for thirty-two gold chamber florins, and spent a year or thereabouts correcting it: Ja. of Vicenza.”

Ottobonian Codex 1740, on paper, in folio, from the fifteenth century: Caesar’s commentaries. At the beginning of each book one reads: “Julius Celsus Constantinus, a distinguished man, corrected it.” The same appears in a similar vellum codex, in octavo, no. 1963. I discussed other such inscriptions by the ancients who collated codices in my commentary on Prudentius, p. 844, and in the *Prolegomena to Sedulius*, chapter 7. Julius Celsus Constantinus’s autograph subscription was *emendavi* (“I corrected”), not *emendavit* (“he corrected”).

23. Ottobonian Codex 2047, on vellum, in folio, from the fourteenth century: Apuleius, and so forth. At the end: “I, G. Crispinus Salustius, corrected it at Rome.” Ottobonian Codex 2989: Sallust, from the fifteenth century, on very clean vellum, corrected by Pomponius Laetus.

24. Among the other reasons why codices emerged from the hands of scribes insufficiently correct and required correctors is the fact that young men or boys were sometimes employed for the task of writing, as is indicated by the title of the scriptorium among the verses of the library of St. Isidore:

> Whoever is a wandering scribe at midday,
>
> let his back be struck with two whips.

In the printed editions it is *Whoever is a wandering one*, or *Whoever may be wandering*, or, less incorrectly, *Whoever is wandering here*. At that time *quisque* was commonly used for *quisquis*.

The verses of Albinus, *For the Place Where the Scribes Sit*—“Let them sit here,” and so forth—edited by Brower after the poems of Fortunatus, should be compared with these. There were indeed monks among those entrusted with the task of writing. Thus, in Martène, volume V of the *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, col. 1629, in a dialogue between a Cluniac and a Cistercian, the Cistercian monk objects to the Cluniac that the Cluniac scribes, while writing in the monastery, did not attend the regular hours.

For carrying out this task, young men, and not always ones sufficiently educated in letters, were generally selected. Sometimes there were also intrusive visitors who, by their chatter, distracted the minds of the scribes elsewhere. Hence, in another title of the Isidorian library, *To the Intruder*—incorrectly printed in the editions as *to the interruption*—there is this couplet:

> A scribe does not tolerate anyone speaking in his presence:
>
> There is nothing for you to do here, chatterbox; go outside.

Nor were only boys scribes of codices [Col. 0933B]; sacred virgins devoted to God also were. Charles Meichelbeck, *History of Freising*, volume I, part I, book IV, says:

> “In the ninth century the emperor Louis the Pious ordered bishops, monks, priests . . . to teach boys to write books of every kind. He did not exempt even holy women from this labor. Books of every kind on parchment, written by holy virgins, are found throughout the libraries.”

Trotz, in his notes on Hermann Hugo’s little work *On the First Origin of Writing*, inserted his own treatise *On Scribes*. The following defect is also often observed in scribes: when the same word appeared before their eyes again after some interval, they would, deceived by it, omit the words that intervened; or, when the same word had to be written twice, they would copy it only once—sometimes deliberately and with an added sign indicating that the word was to be read twice. See Xavier Mattei, in his dissertation *On the Poetry of the Hebrews*, and volume XII of the Naples edition of the works of 1788, in the response to Canon Sicard, and again volume XIII, p. 399, as well as William Best’s treatise *On the Method of Correcting Laws*, chapter 1, § 4.

[Col. 0933C] 25. But since some who arrogated to themselves the authority to correct manuscript codices were occasionally inexperienced, it often happened that they corrupted the true reading. There is extant in Codex Urbinate 297 a little work by Nicolaus Perottus, bishop of Siponto, against those who rashly correct ancient writers: “I used to,” and so forth. Compare chapter I of these *Prolegomena*.

26. It will be especially worthwhile to record the names of those who excelled in ancient monasteries for their reputation for writing and correcting codices accurately. That Peregrinus, the scribe whom Pez discusses in the preface to volume I of the *Thesaurus*, no. 29, transmitted the following curious account of his method of writing:

> Eptaphonos, strophicus, punctus, porrectus, oriscus,
>
> Virgula, cephalius, olinis, quilisma, podacus,
>
> Scandicus and salicus, climacus, torulus, ancus,
>
> And the minor and major pressus: I use no more
>
> Neume signs; you are mistaken if you devise more.

Perhaps this Peregrinus should not be distinguished from Ysingrimus, concerning whom, in no. 5, Pez reports: “May almighty God spare Ysingrimus the pilgrim.”

27. The same Pez, in no. 32, produces an encomium of Diemudis, a nun of Wessobrunn, together with a catalogue of works written by her in beautiful letters; in no. 37 he says that she wrote very many books elegantly, ornamentally, and correctly.

Joannes Mezlerus, *On the Illustrious Men of St. Gall*, chapter 17, in Pez, volume I, part III, says of the monk Folchardus [Col. 0934A]:

> “Among the excellent scribes whom St. Gall has had at different times, Folchardus was distinguished. His hand, most beautifully ornamented, we can still see and admire in a very ancient Psalter Codex.”

And in chapter 28, concerning the monk Syntrammus, whom Eckerardus considered the finest of all scribes:

> “He wrote very much, and with perfect correctness; but the Gospels above all, with outstanding elegance.”

28. Pez also praises, in his *Introductory Dissertation*, volume II, Joannes of Spira, or Wiscler of Fresheim, who was born in 1383 and wrote with great polish and elegance. Several codices at Heidelberg were written by him. Among others, the following is listed: a determination by Master Gerardus Brant, professor at Heidelberg, in 1404, concerning the question whether, just as among the constitutions of the human body one constitution is better and more suitable than others for contemplation, so one region might be more suitable for philosophizing.

Pez observes that at the monastery of Melk certain hours had been assigned to copying books. In this art, the industry of this Joannes of Spira, Joannes of Weilheim, Joannes of Carniola, Antonius of Catalonia, Martinus of Senging, Wolfgangus Frischmannus of Ermerstoff, Christophorus Lieb of Isny, and many others was extraordinary.

29. Finally, I shall point out that one cannot always trust exemplars commended under the name and authority of some outstanding corrector. In the Roman *Ecclesiastical Journal* for the year 1795, no. 6, a work of Canon Dionysius De’ Blandimenti, *Funeral Orations*, and so forth, is announced. From it we learn that Boccaccio’s *Decameron*, as is commonly believed, was copied with the utmost care in 1384 from the autograph itself by Francesco de’ Amaretto [Col. 0934C] Mannelli.

The Mannellian exemplar was therefore held in Florence in great value and honor; and it was finally printed in 1761. Nevertheless, it has been demonstrated that the Mannellian text teems with errors, partly through the ignorance and carelessness of the copyist, and partly because Mannelli, sometimes supposing the autograph to be mutilated or incomplete, added certain words from his own resources. Many more examples could be added in the same sense; but these should suffice to make clear that great diligence is required in selecting the genuine reading, even when ancient and corrected exemplars are at hand.

439. ## CHAPTER CIX. The Method to Be Observed in the Present Edition of the Works of St. Isidore.

[Col. 0934D] 1. I have already explained in chapter 48, numbers 1 and 2, what order I had decided to follow in distributing and arranging Isidore’s Works. Namely, I shall give first place to those works that are universal and pertain, in some fashion, to all branches of learning. These will be followed in their proper order by the biblical, theological, physical, and historical works, with the provision that within each category those of broader scope shall likewise come first. As for Isidore’s genuine works, they will generally be arranged in the manner in which I have already mentioned each of them from chapter 48 onward. Certain fragments of genuine works found in some manuscripts will be appended to the works themselves.

2. Isidore’s other doubtful works will be printed after the authentic works, in the best order possible. [Col. 0935A] But I wish to warn readers beforehand that certain works are to be placed among the genuine ones concerning which some people doubt whether they are truly products of Isidore—either because the contrary opinion is much more probable, or because they were accepted as authentic in the royal Madrid edition, whose authority, no one will deny, deserves considerable weight. By a similar principle, we shall place among the appendices certain other works that most critical scholars maintain are spurious and falsely attributed—either because some consideration must be given to those who think otherwise, or because such works have already been included in other editions of Isidore, or finally because they are not found elsewhere although they bear only Isidore’s name.

3. Regarding annotations on Isidore, I have the following to say. I shall place the notes of Grial’s edition beneath the Isidorian text continuously. I shall likewise add my own notes, and I shall not allow them to be lacking even in those works that Grial did not know or passed over. I shall generally present the annotations of others after the conclusion of each work. I see that this has also been done by others, and it ought to please many readers who do not like to see the text of the ancient authors being elucidated apparently buried beneath frequent and lengthy observations placed below it.

4. This same consideration moves me to set out separately, after each work has been completed, the various readings which, even though many are rejected, must nevertheless in many cases be retained; some exceptions will be explained in the notes themselves for the easier understanding of the text. In reporting the variant readings, care must be taken that their abundance does not weary the reader by accumulating wholly useless variations in spelling, or readings that are plainly erroneous when no necessity requires their inclusion. At the same time, we must keep before our eyes the most wise warning of Juan Bautista Pérez in the preface to volume I of the *Collations*, discussed in chapter 91, number 30:

> No one should be surprised that we have transcribed not only passages that were better in the manuscripts, but also those that we plainly saw to be corrupted in them. For who would deny that manuscripts are erroneous in many places, and that the true reading must be extracted from many manuscripts collated with one another? Nevertheless, we preferred to employ the utmost fidelity in this matter and to err on the safer side; for, taught by experience, we hope that there will not be lacking those who, by diligently searching, may often find traces of some true reading even in corrupted writing.

Other critics have proceeded in much the same way.

5. In this arrangement of materials, and in the explanation of the matters themselves, I earnestly desire to be useful to most learned men more than I hope to be; for it is not even something to be wished that everyone should approve these efforts of mine, whatever their quality. Although the saying “as many heads, so many opinions” is not always true, no sane person would wish for what he sees to be impossible: that so many heads should hold one and the same opinion.

[Col. 0935]

# FIRST APPENDIX

## A PRELIMINARY COMMENTARY OF THE BOLLANDISTS ON SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP OF SEVILLE

[Col. 0935]

## 441 § I. Sacred Cult. The Life to Be Given Here. Was Lucas of Tuy the Author?

[Col. 0935C]

[Note: [Col. 0935D] No. 1. In the *Isidoriana*, chapter 13, number 1, I promised to place the Life of Saint Isidore published by the Bollandists, together with their—namely, Godefrid Henschenius’s—preliminary commentary, among the appendices. I am keeping my promise, and I shall not allow the appropriate annotations to be lacking wherever they are needed. For the learned Zaccaria had also promised in his prospectus of the Isidorian edition that he would do this; and, I think, he would have fulfilled his promise if he had undertaken the work. The readings of Saint Isidore from the Quignon Breviary indicated in this number were transcribed in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 15, whose title is: “Readings for the feast of Saint Isidore from ancient Breviaries; hymns; commemoration in other liturgical books.” The Bollandists rightly state that the Quignon Breviary was prepared in 1535; for it first appeared in that year, as I demonstrated in the dissertation which I entitled *The History of the Quignon Breviary* and appended to the *Hymnody of Spain*, where I listed several editions of that Breviary.]

1. Three distinguished cities of Spain rejoice in the magnificent and glorious display of the most holy doctor Isidore. The first is Cartagena, formerly New Carthage, in the kingdom of Murcia, on the Mediterranean gulf of Virgitania, adorned with a safe and very capacious harbor and an episcopal see. It was the homeland of Saint Isidore, his brothers Saints Leander and Fulgentius, bishops, and their sister Saint Florentina.

The second is Seville, the largest city of Baetica in Spain and a most famous commercial center. There, after being appointed bishop of that metropolitan see in succession to his brother Leander, he lived until his death under its most holy direction, and on this day, 4 April, departed to heavenly joy.

The third is León, which gave its name to the ancient kingdom of León, situated toward the Cantabrian Ocean. It was one of the seats of the ancient kings and, there also, of the bishops. To it the sacred body of Saint Isidore was transferred from the city of Seville under Ferdinand I, king of León and Castile. [Col. 0935D]

The latter two cities, Seville and León, together with their dioceses, venerate Saint Isidore solemnly as their patron. The rest of the churches of Spain celebrate his feast under the rite of a double feast, as that of a doctor of the Church; and his office, as it was formerly recited, is found throughout all the ancient Spanish Breviaries and Missals. Tamayo Salazar listed nineteen of these and adds that many others contain the same office.

There is likewise the Roman Breviary, prepared in 1535 by authority of Pope Paul III by Francisco Quignon, cardinal of the title of Santa Croce in Jerusalem, and afterward reprinted many times. In it the Office of this Saint Isidore is prescribed, together with a reading to be recited concerning his life and death.

On this same day, 4 April, his commemoration is entered in Usuard’s Martyrology in these words: “At Seville, the deposition of Saint Isidore, bishop.” In some manuscripts there is added “and doctor”; in others, “pre-eminent in faith and doctrine”; and in still others, “an illustrious man in life and doctrine.” Recent writers generally follow these versions, as do the Tables of the Roman Martyrology, with this wording:

> At Seville in Spain, Saint Isidore, bishop, distinguished for holiness and learning, who enlightened Spain by his zeal for the Catholic faith and his observance of ecclesiastical discipline.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] 2. The *New Spanish Library*, which Nicolás Antonio mentions, appeared at Rome in 1672.]

2. We give his Life and the history of his Translation, written long ago but hitherto unpublished, extracted from a manuscript codex of the Holy Church of Toledo, marked with the number 29. In 1565 Juan López de León and Francisco de Mendoza transcribed it with the greatest care. That copy is in the possession of the most illustrious Nicolás Antonio, knight of the Order of Saint James and agent for the affairs of His Catholic Majesty at the Roman Curia. We also knew him at Rome and experienced his exceptional kindness and comprehensive learning.

In a letter written at Rome on 16 April 1671, he wrote the following to us:

> After a long delay, I am at last fulfilling my promise by sending you, illustrious champions of the saints, the Life of the renowned Saint Isidore, archbishop of my own Church of Seville; and likewise a booklet distinct from this one, and perhaps by another author, concerning the Translation of his venerable body from my Seville to the city of León, together with some rather slight scholia or annotations. These are directed more toward somehow repairing certain *σφάλματα*—errors—of the exemplar than toward any intention of working carefully over these books in every respect. I could have supplied more substantial notes if I had had the time. But concern for royal affairs, stronger than my abilities and demanding the whole day as its special due, draws us away in the City from every better study. Thus, scarcely finding sufficient time to press forward the edition of the *Library of the Writers of Spain*, which is already panting near the finish line, I have only with difficulty been able to perform this brief office of our respect toward you. You will enrich it and perform work worthy of so great a doctor.

This was written by the aforementioned Nicolás Antonio shortly before the aforementioned *Library*, which we now hold in our hands and approve by our judgment, came to light. The *σφάλματα* he says require correction are either peculiarities of Spanish usage, or contractions of words not understood by the copyists, or the occasional omission of a small word. We have corrected them in our customary manner, complying with the wishes of that most learned man.

The notes that he had written in the margin, and which he wished to make more substantial, we collect under his name and insert throughout the Life, arranging it according to our custom into chapters and numbers and elucidating it with marginal summaries. Other matters requiring annotation follow.

[Note: [Col. 0937D] 3. I discussed the Life of Saint Isidore written in Spanish in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 13, number 18. In that entire chapter I showed that Lucas of Tuy does not appear to have been the author either of the Life or of the Translation of Saint Isidore’s body. I stated in the same place, number 21, on the authority of Florez, that Lucas of Tuy died in 1249. The Bollandists, with Sandoval, assign Lucas’s year of death to 1250. [Col. 0938D]]

3. Concerning the authors of this Life and Translation, the aforementioned Nicolás Antonio observes:

> This Life, or its abridgment—for I have no certain or verified information about this—is said once to have been printed in the vernacular. For Antonio [read: Ambrosio] Morales, book XII of the *History of Spain*, chapter 21, praises a Life of Saint Isidore published in Spanish at Salamanca, as well as a separate history of the Translation of his holy body and of the miracles then performed by God in his honor. He says that this history has great authority because it was written by Lucas of Tuy. Yet he dislikes several things in the Life and denies that the previously praised Lucas was their author.
>
> Nor do we possess any certain information about the author. For in that Toledo codex from which we transcribed the Life, no writer of that Life is named; and the name of Lucas the deacon—which refers to Lucas of Tuy—belongs to the Chronicle appended to the Life. Nevertheless, Alfonso Morgado believed both the Life and the history of the Translation to be by Lucas of Tuy, in book I, chapter 5, and book IV, chapter 4, of his *History of the City of Seville*; and in book V, chapter 14, he again calls it a Divine Book.
>
> But Francisco de Padilla, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, century 7, chapter 22, recognized Lucas of Tuy only as the author of the book describing the Translation and the miracles performed at that time. Aegidius González de Ávila did the same in his *Theatre of the Church of Seville*, where he discusses Saint Isidore, its archbishop.
>
> The author of the Spanish book mentioned by Morales is either anonymous or, as I am more inclined to believe—although we have never seen the book—Juan de Robles, canon of the collegiate church of Saint Isidore in the city of León. We know that he published a brief work on the Translation and miracles of that same holy doctor. Aegidius of Ávila likewise reports, in the same place, that Lucas, bishop of Tuy, did this.
>
> We have read somewhere that a book entitled *History of the Miracles of Saint Isidore, Archbishop of Seville* appeared in 1525. Certainly, in this work of ours, which we call the Life of Saint Isidore, everything is found that Morales considered less probable and that, in his view, detracted from the credibility of the other plausible elements. We shall point this out in the appropriate places.
>
> But if I am asked what I think about the writer of this Life—whether he was Lucas of Tuy or someone else—many considerations lead us to deny that Lucas was its author. The style is not entirely alike in this Life and in Lucas’s Chronicle and other writings. Lucas proceeds more historically and fluently, whereas in the author of the Life the discourse proceeds more awkwardly, through affectation.
>
> Moreover, the judgment or opinion of the two authors about matters is not the same. [The source text here is corrupt: “de rebus es . . Lucas.”] Lucas derives the name of Spain from a certain ridiculous etymology in the preface to his Chronicle, whereas the author of the Life prefers to derive it from the city of Seville. Lucas calls Isidore’s mother Theodora in the same preface; the author of the Life calls her Turtura. This author speaks more harshly than the Tudensian about the death of King Leovigild. Other differences also occur, which readers who examine both works carefully will easily observe.
>
> It is true that certain things are found similarly in both works, namely, the Life and the Chronicle; but they could have been transcribed from one into the other, even though the two books were not by the same author.

Thus far the most learned Nicolás Antonio, who, in his customary manner, being then wholly devoted—so far as royal affairs allowed—to adorning the aforementioned *Library of Spanish Writers*, deserves sufficient respect that we should wish to accept his judgment as that of a man highly experienced in such matters.

If, however, some should maintain that this Life and the History of the Translation were written by Lucas when he was younger, while he was a canon regular and still a deacon in the monastery of Saint Isidore at León, whereas the *Chronicle of the World* and his other works were composed by the same man when he was already elderly and bishop of Tuy and had polished them with more mature judgment, we would not reject their conjecture.

Certainly—as we shall say in the notes at the proper place—the keen-minded Mariana believes that the opinion, rejected by some, that these works were written by Lucas of Tuy ought to be retained in full force. Lucas was ordained bishop of Tuy in the Spanish era 1277, that is, in the year of Christ 1239, after the death of Saint Isidore in the year 603. He died in the Spanish era 1288, that is, in the year of Christ 1250, as Prudentius Sandoval explains at length; Sandoval himself was bishop of Tuy and wrote this in the *Antiquities of His Church*, folio 148 and following.

Some matters in the Life that are displeasing are the reports given in it and in the Tudensian Chronicle concerning Muhammad’s arrival in Spain. As we shall point out there, we have judged that these passages should be removed. In other matters, the annotations of the praised Nicolás Antonio, or our own, are appended.

## § II. The Testimony of Contemporaries concerning His Death and Translation; the Year and Place of His Death; the Saint’s Monastic Order

[Note: [Col. 0938D] 4. The ancient monuments indicated here by the Bollandists were all previously brought forward and elucidated by us in the *Isidoriana*. Numbers 4 and 5 had originally been included under a single number in the commentary; but in the additions and corrections the account was arranged differently and divided into two numbers, as I present it here. The Venetian edition throws everything into disorder and confusion.]

4. How familiar Isidore was with Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, was shown on 18 March in the historical synopsis of Braulio’s acts. The author of the Life likewise proves this, especially in chapter 7, where he reports that letters were exchanged and that in their titles Braulio is called a disciple of Saint Isidore.

Moved by this mutual affection and at the request of Braulio himself, Redemptus, a cleric of the Church of Seville, wrote something about the death of Saint Isidore. This work—or rather letter—appears before the saint’s works, printed at Paris in 1601. The author of the Life also inserted the same letter into his own work, chapters 9 and 10, but with considerable interpolation. We therefore found it necessary to append separately, among the annotations, both the beginning of the letter itself, which was omitted from the Life, and the interpolator’s words, separating them from the text by parentheses, and finally to note the differences in reading.

We did not think it advisable to reprint the whole letter separately, since we did not know whether the printed text preserved it sufficiently intact. Perhaps this will be done in a supplement to the work, once we have received a more genuine text from an ancient manuscript codex of Seville, which Don Juan Lucas Cortes, superintendent of royal works and forests, stated was in his possession. He was a man of extensive learning and great erudition, exceptionally well supplied with books, and by no means inexperienced in the study of ancient writings.

In his possession the aforementioned letter is found under this title:

> Here begins the book concerning the death of the most blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville, addressed to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza, by Redemptus, a cleric of that same Church of Seville.

The fuller conclusion found both in the manuscripts and in the printed editions is as follows:

> He completed his life in peace, namely Saint Isidore, on the day before the Kalends—or rather the Nones—of April, [after administering the pastoral care of a bishop irreproachably for nearly forty years], in the Spanish era 674, which was the year of Christ 636.

Since Saint Isidore succeeded his brother Leander toward the end of the sixth century, as was demonstrated in the account of Leander’s life on 13 March, it follows that the years of his episcopate, counted precisely, were only thirty-seven. When Redemptus said “nearly forty years,” he thereby showed that he was using a round number.

5. Tamayo Salazar lists many writers on Spanish affairs who dealt with Saint Isidore. Some of them we examined in order to elucidate the Life, especially Alfonso Morgado, Paulo Espinosa, and Rodrigo Caro in their works on the history and antiquities of Seville; Athanasius Lobera in his history of León; and Aegidius of Ávila in his *Theatre of the Churches of Seville and León*.

But since these writers are recent, we do not value having read them as highly as we value having received from the much-praised Juan Lucas Cortes the genuine Acts of the Translation of the body of the blessed Isidore, bishop of Seville. They were found in an ancient codex of more than five or six hundred years, written in letters now almost faded, and were sent to us.

Because the author wrote them as he remembered hearing them from those who had been present, and as he recalled having heard them from those who had heard them, and because they are free from the leaven of interpolation, we give them in the appendix. They are to be placed on page 333 before the history of the Translation and miracles composed by Lucas of Tuy—or by some other author—although for the greater part that work preserves the same words, scattered apart by many additions and especially altered at the end.

Retaining the ancient division into chapters, we have converted them into numbers.

On 30 April we shall give the Translation of Saint Indaletius, similarly made from the kingdom of Granada into Aragon, to the monastery of San Juan de la Peña, by the Cluniac monk Hebrelmus, certainly a Gaul. He was one of those who were repeatedly sent from Cluny to the monasteries of Cluniac observance established throughout Spain beginning in the eleventh century, in order to inspect and regulate them.

The fact that the author of this Translation too was the same Cluniac monk, or one like him, is suggested by the very similar style, and especially by the fact that in both works the years are counted from the Incarnation of the Lord—a practice hitherto unknown among Spanish writers and, as we conjecture, first introduced into Spain by these Gallic monks. It was not fully admitted into public records until long afterward, namely in the year 1383, when John I, king of Castile, abolished the use of the Spanish era even in these records.

That Translation was written in the year of Christ 1084. This one concerning Saint Isidore could not have been written much earlier, nor appreciably later than twenty or thirty years after the events occurred.

[Note: [Col. 0939D] 6. What can be said for or against Saint Isidore’s Benedictine monastic affiliation I explained in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 19. Zaccaria had promised in the prospectus of the Isidorian edition—chapter 41, number 7—that he would discuss Isidore’s Benedictine monasticism, but he had not even begun the discussion. [Col. 0940D]]

6. The proper rule prescribed by Saint Isidore for monks is discussed below.

> “His regulations are not in conformity with the rule of Saint Benedict, nor do they bind Benedictines,” teaches Benedictus Haftenus, book X of the *Monastic Inquiry*, treatise 6, inquiry 3.

Whether Saint Isidore ever professed the Rule of Saint Benedict in some monastery of the Benedictine order, let others debate. Since we have read nothing of the sort in the ancient sources, we prefer to remain silent on the question.

Antonius Yepes, a Spanish Benedictine, transmits the following concerning the monastic life of Saints Fulgentius and Isidore in his *General Chronicle of the Order of Saint Benedict*, under the year 599, chapter 1:

> There are those who make Saint Fulgentius a monk of the Order of Saint Benedict. We shall believe them when they produce for us an ancient and authoritative source . . . I also remove Saint Isidore from the order’s list, since both the life he led and the rule that the bishop of Seville wrote for monks suggest a different conclusion to me.

Meanwhile, Constantinus Cajetanus and Arnoldus Wion, book II of the *Tree of Life*, page 144, assign him to the Benedictine order, although Wion does so with hesitation, in these words:

> Saint Isidore . . . as they say, a monk of our Benedictine order . . . was made archbishop in the year of the Lord 603 and presided, as Saint Ildephonsus states in *On Illustrious Men*, for nearly forty years. He died in the year 642, or thereabouts, on the day before the Nones of April; his body rests at Bologna in the church of the Reverend Fathers Celestines.

Thus far Wion. Above we have calculated the years of his episcopate differently. It is entirely certain that his body was transferred from Seville to León and has been preserved there to this day with the highest veneration. [Col. 0940C]

[Note: [Col. 0940D] 7. I brought forward in the *Isidoriana*, chapters 8, 9, and 28, certain monuments that clearly establish both that Isidore departed from Seville to heaven and that his body rests at León. The Acts of the Translation will be presented below.]

7. The people of Bologna, through I know not what error, assert that Saint Isidore of Seville died in their city. Antonius Casalis Coelestinus, of Saint Stephen of Bologna, gives an extensive description of that basilica of his and calls it a new Jerusalem. Beginning on page 365, while explaining the Life of Saint Isidore from a manuscript Chronicle, page 370, he addresses the basilica as follows:

> Likewise, the body of the most blessed Isidore, confessor of Christ and illustrious doctor, rests in you. When he was returning from Rome, he lodged in this city and was detained there by a serious bodily illness, God so permitting; there he ended his life, and there he was buried by orthodox men amid the joy of the whole people.

Thus far Casalis. These words can and ought to be understood of another learned man named Isidore, and they may be examined more carefully on 16 September, when, he adds, the same abbot Casalis celebrates his feast on account of the translation of his body.

Leander Albertus, Donatus Pullienus, Cherubinus Ghirardacius, Carolus Sigonius, Celsus Falconus, Antonius Masinus, and others who understood these statements of Saint Isidore of Seville must therefore be corrected.

Constantinus Cajetanus, abbot, in his treatise on Saint Isidore, supposes that

> the people of Bologna, perhaps deceived by the similarity of the names, noted, believed, and called their own Isidore—the Sicilian bishop—in place of the Isidore of Seville.

Certainly Seville, also called *Sivilia* by some, which is *Hispalis*, and Sicily are not very far apart in name. But everything concerning Saint Isidore of Sicily is equally obscure; nor does Octavius Cajetanus, the brother of Constantinus, contribute much light. In his volume on the *Lives of the Sicilian Saints*, page 225, he assembles several details about the Isidore in question, principally from the Calendar of Constantius Felicius, under 15 January, as we stated at that point among the saints passed over, indicating others who followed Felicius without further examination.

[Note: [Col. 0941D] 8. I dealt briefly with this very question—whether Saint Isidore was a Carmelite—in the *Isidoriana*, chapter 19, at the end. It might perhaps be worthwhile to dwell longer on such controversies with Papebrochius and Henschenius; but since this is not necessary, I willingly refrain, also so that, if possible, I may avert the annoyance of those who despise these matters and raise other, supposedly more serious, matters to heaven.]

447 8. Whoever he may be who rests at Bologna, he is entirely different from the Isidore of Seville. While Benedictine writers assign him to their order with excessive hesitation and delay, the Carmelites thought it appropriate to lay hands upon him as though upon a derelict inheritance after Juan Bautista de Lezana, under the year 578, number 4, believed that he had drawn from the writings of Saint Isidore himself a solid argument for proving this assertion.

Discussing monks in book II, chapter 15, of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, Lezana asks:

> From whom did the practice of poverty flow down to monks? Or who was the author of this way of life, whose habit they imitate?

He answers:

> As far as the authority of the ancient Scriptures is concerned, the founders of this way of life were Elijah and his disciple Elisha, or the other prophets who lived in solitude. Leaving the cities, they made little huts for themselves near the streams of the Jordan. Then John became the founder of this way of life in the Gospel: he alone inhabited the wilderness, nourished only by locusts and wild honey. Afterward the most noble founders of this way of life arose: Paul, Antony, Hilarion, Macarius, and the other brothers.

Saint Isidore writes this. But how can it be concluded from these words that he himself belonged to the Carmelite order? We certainly do not see the inference. Those who regard it as clearer than the light of midday see it, since they believe that their order—which at the beginning of the thirteenth century, under the governance of its second prior Brocard, received its rule from Blessed Albert, patriarch of Jerusalem, as will be explained in the account of his Life on 8 April—was not newly founded under its first prior Berthold, but merely received a new form.

They believe that their order is the most ancient of all religious orders, indeed the source and beginning of the others, derived not only from the apostles and the apostles’ disciples but from Elijah himself, through an immediate succession on Carmel that was never interrupted at any time.

Since these claims rest on no solid authority from ancient monuments, and since they are defended as though they could not be subjected to examination without the greatest injury to the most holy order, we prefer to listen to them and accuse our own sluggishness of understanding rather than, by contradicting those who think this way, provoke their tongues and pens against us.

Let Saint Isidore therefore be a Carmelite according to them, just as according to the same people Saints Paul, Antony, Basil, Martin, Hilary, Patrick, and all the other holy monks anywhere who adorned the Church of God with their virtues before the propagation of the Benedictine Rule were Carmelites.

448 ## § III. Testimonies to His Excellent Learning; Benefits Conferred upon the Spaniards

[Note: [Col. 0941D] 9. I demonstrated in chapter 31 that Isidore’s learning was praised by the Roman pontiffs and in numerous councils. In chapter 29 I discussed whether the question had ever arisen of numbering him among the four Fathers of the Latin Church. [Col. 0942D]]

9. In addition to what has been reported above and what will be indicated below in the Acts, we touch here upon a few matters that greatly increase the posthumous glory of Saint Isidore.

First place among these should be given to the authority of the Eighth Council of Toledo, held in the Spanish era 691, that is, in the year 633, seventeen years after Saint Isidore’s death. At that council there were fifty-two bishops, twelve abbots, ten episcopal representatives, and sixteen illustrious officials of the palace. In their presence, chapter 2 dealt with rash oaths. After testimonies from Sacred Scripture and from Saints Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory the Great had been cited, various passages drawn from Saint Isidore’s books were added, together with this eulogy of him:

> Isidore, the distinguished doctor of our own age, the latest glory of the Catholic Church, last in age among those who preceded him but not inferior to them in learning, and—what is more—most learned at the end of the ages and to be named with reverence.

Similarly, Leo IV, supreme pontiff, numbers him among the other doctors of the Church in Gratian, distinction 20, *On Booklets*:

> If, he says, the sayings of those whom you have mentioned—Jerome, Augustine, Isidore, and the other similar holy doctors—are found, they must be retained or published with magnanimity, or referred to the Apostolic See.

Thus far the text.

Concerning this same Saint Isidore, counted among, or proposed for inclusion among, the other doctors of the Church, Juan Mariana transmits the following in book VI, chapter 7, of *On the Affairs of Spain*:

> Some writers report that, when Pope Boniface VIII was deliberating about those who were to be honored with the name and rank of Doctors of the Church, there were those who judged that Isidore ought to be preferred to Ambrose, or that a fifth should certainly be added to the other four. The learning of so great a man gives credibility to the opinion: he was easily outstanding in every branch of letters; and since two of the number are of Italian origin, no one is from the West.

[Note: [Col. 0942D] 10. It should be noted that in the manuscript codex of the book *On the Order of Created Things*, the words “after Rome,” namely “Zaragoza,” were not found by d’Achery; he added them conjecturally to indicate that the reference was to Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza. We discussed this controversy in chapter 23. In the Bollandists’ text I corrected *temone tuae auctoritatis*—“with the rudder of your authority”—in place of *timore*—“through fear”—and in the margin I corrected “to Pope Boniface V” in place of “to Pope Benedict V”; for the context concerns Boniface, and Benedict V does not belong to that period.]

10. The books written by Saint Isidore are named and praised in the Life, number 43, on the authority of Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza. Some others, later discovered or at least attributed to Saint Isidore, are inserted into Braulio’s list.

Besides these, Lucas d’Achery offers one recently brought to light in volume I of the *Spicilegium*, from a very ancient codex of the monastery of Saint Remigius, under this title:

> A book *On the Order of Created Things*, addressed to Braulio, bishop of the city of Rome.

Although ecclesiastical bibliographers, both ancient and modern, make no mention of it, d’Achery nevertheless says that its style and thought seemed so plainly Isidorian to him that no one could call into question his belief that it was Isidore’s genuine offspring.

In his preface to the reader, he conjectures that Zaragoza, once the chief of the Roman colonies in Spain, may have been called Rome by the Spaniards as a kind of prerogative, just as the emperors called Constantinople Rome, though for a different reason. For the sake of clarification, he therefore conjectures that after “Rome” the words “that is, Zaragoza” should be added.

I hold the judgment of a man practiced in distinguishing the styles of ancient authors in high regard. But the more weight we give it, the less plausible his conjecture appears to us. Although Braulio professes to enumerate only those books that had come to his knowledge, thereby implying that others had also been written, how could this book have failed to reach him when, according to its author’s own presentation, it was written in the form of a reply to him and directed to him under this epilogue?

> Behold, venerable Father: when you proposed to me the subject of the order of created things, I have answered you in summary form, in a brief discourse suited to the measure of my little intellect. I shall repay the gift of this small offering with your prayers. Not that the service of my insignificance can offer anything worthy in obedience to your reverence and authority, but the effort of obedience, and what it cannot attain, fulfills everything. Behold, in the treasury of the temple, the small gift of the poor widow’s coin is preferred to the abundant gold of many rich men . . . Therefore, do not disdain, in the same way, this obedience of my littleness in the gentle harbor of your heart; and across the unstable waves of babbling people, do not hesitate to steer the little boat of this present work with the rudder of your authority.

The author of this little book writes these and other words as to a Father, with an exceptionally humble profession of obedience—quite differently from the manner in which he usually writes to Braulio, his friend, who was not even his equal in episcopal rank.

Why, then, if we truly believe that the work was written for the bishop of the city of Rome, should we not understand it as addressed not to Braulio but to Boniface, the fifth of that name, who occupied the principal see of all Christianity from the year 616 to 625?

It is well known that ancient writers often indicated proper names by a single initial letter. When later writers wished to expand those letters in full, they frequently cast the history into darkness. Let Acherius believe that the same thing happened here through a copyist of Rheims, who found only the letter B and, observing that other works of Isidore were addressed to Braulio, conjectured that Braulio was also meant here. He will then extricate himself by a more straightforward path from these difficulties. For our part, we determine nothing here by our own conjecture, since we have not had the leisure to read the entire little work with sufficient attention.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] 11. Something has been set forth concerning the posthumous glory of Saint Isidore in *Isidoriana*, chapter 28.]

11. Moreover, what we have already said about the esteem in which his learning was held, together with what is to be related below in the *Acts* from Braulio and others, constitutes the first foundation of that great obligation by which Spain acknowledges itself bound to Saint Isidore. The second is that, through his favor, various cities were recovered from the hands of the Saracens. Concerning Toledo, which was recovered by the Christians at the urging and prompting of Saint Isidore, Mariana writes in book IX, chapter 16; Athanasius Lobera treats the matter more fully in chapter XXIX of his *History of León*. His words, translated into Latin by Tamaio Salazar, are these:

> Cyprian, bishop of León, was at that time a venerable, pious, and prudent man, instructed in every good work, who cherished the divine Isidore with the greatest love. When he desired to cast off the burden of his years and cling to Christ, he prostrated himself before the reliquary of the most holy prelate and, after pouring out a prayer, entreated Isidore to obtain from the Lord, by his merits, the release of his flesh. On the following night the holy confessor appeared to Cyprian and signified that his supplication had been accepted by God. As a sign of this, he said that on the next day one of his servants would come from Toledo to León and report how King Alfonso had decided to abandon the city, freed from the siege—a decision that would result in grave harm to the Catholic religion. He therefore commanded Cyprian, as soon as he heard the servant’s message, to write to the king and by no means to lift the siege, but rather to persist, since the Lord had determined to deliver the city to him within fifteen days, with Isidore himself fighting vigorously at the king’s side. After saying this, he disappeared, and on the following day the messenger arrived and disclosed the king’s plan. When Cyprian learned this, he wrote a letter to the king, revealing everything he had heard from the mouth of blessed Isidore, and sent it to Toledo with his archdeacon. The archdeacon reached the camp at the very moment when it was already being moved. Alfonso received the letter, and after reading it ordered the camp to halt; then, on the day designated by the holy doctor, he entered Toledo.

12. Thus far Athanasius Lobera. To this must be added the victory over the Moorish Saracens obtained through the aid of Saints James and Isidore, which Lucas of Tuy relates in his *Chronicle of the World*, under the era 1255, as follows:

> King Alfonso of León besieged the city of Mérida and captured it. At that time there was a certain distinguished barbarian named Abenenfuth, who expelled the Almohads from Spain and became king of the Berbers. His people called him the “king of valor.” Having gathered an innumerable army of Moors, he came to fight King Alfonso of León, who was at Mérida with only a few men. But King Alfonso, being brave and spirited, had his army cross the Guadiana by night against the Saracens. The Saracens had pitched their tents beside the fortress of Alange. At first light they saw our battle lines prepared for war, and they themselves drew up their ranks and hastened to battle. The Lord was with King Alfonso and the Christian people. In the engagement of that battle so many thousands of Saracens were struck down that many barbarian towns were left empty, all their inhabitants having perished in the battle. Abenenfuth, king of the barbarians, fled severely wounded. Indeed, Saint James visibly appeared in the battle with a multitude of soldiers dressed in white, and they were striking down the Saracens with a mighty hand. Blessed Isidore the confessor also appeared to certain people at Zamora, before Mérida was captured and before the battle took place, and told them that he was hastening with an army of saints to aid King Alfonso, and that he would deliver the said city to him and grant him a field-triumph over the Saracens.

This is Lucas of Tuy, whom Barnabas Moreno reproduces in book IV, chapter 11, of his *History of Mérida*.

[Note: [Col. 0943D] 13. The Bollandists published the life of Saint Ferdinand not only among the other acts of the saints but also separately, in quarto, at Antwerp in 1684. From that work I shall produce a monument that bears in some measure upon Saint Isidore, from the notes to chapter 18 of the longer *Acts*—namely, the inscription carved in marble on the celebrated tower of Seville, called the Giralda, in these words:

> SACRED TO ETERNITY.  
> To the Great Mother, the protecting Virgin; to the holy bishops Isidore and Leander; to Prince Hermenegild, pious and fortunate; and to the virgins Justa and Rufina, of unstained chastity and manly constancy, the tutelary divinities: the Fathers of the Church of Seville, at immense expense, undertook to restore this tower, of Punic construction and admirable mass, formerly raised to a height of 250 feet, into a more imposing form by careful and more splendid workmanship, adding above it an extraordinarily laborious summit of another 100 feet, under the auspices of Ferdinand Valdes, most pious bishop. In recognition of his excellent ordering of religious affairs, the reduction and overthrow of the rebels against the Roman Church, they commanded that upon it should be set the colossus of victorious faith, capable of turning toward every region of the heavens for the purpose of observing the coming storm. The work was completed in the year 1569 of restored salvation, under Pius V, Supreme Pontiff, and Philip II, august, Catholic, pious, fortunate, victorious, father of his country, and lord of the realm.]

13. Above all others, however, the capture of Seville itself is especially glorious, by which the Moors in Spain were defeated. We have a summary of the proceedings concerning the virtues, holiness, and miracles of the glorious, unconquered, and most holy Ferdinand III, king of Castile and León, printed at Rome in 1638. In number 8, and on page 81, it contains the following passage from the lessons to be recited in the office of the dedication of the Church of Seville:

> When Ferdinand, king of Castile and León, who acquired the title of Saint on account of the excellence of his virtues, had brought a large part of Baetica under his rule, he besieged Seville, the chief city of that province, with forces drawn from nearly all the Spanish nobility. He was reportedly urged to undertake this expedition by a vision of Saint Isidore, who wished to restore to Christ his own church, which had been profaned by unbelievers for so many centuries.

The city was captured on 23 November 1248. It is also said that, when the lands of Seville were subsequently divided, a portion was assigned and given to Saint Isidore.

[Note: [Col. 0944D] 14. The works of Saint Martin of León were published at Segovia from the year 1782 onward in four folio volumes, transcribed from an autograph exemplar by order of my most eminent lord, Cardinal Lorenzana. In the first volume, the life and illustrious deeds of Saint Martin are described and explained, especially from Lucas of Tuy’s work on the miracles of Saint Isidore. I touched upon some of these matters in *Isidoriana*, chapter 11. Saint Martin died on 12 January 1203, not in 1221, as Henschenius maintains, nor on 11 January or in February, as others have asserted.]

14. Under 11 February we published the life of blessed Martin, a regular canon in the city of León. Because a quarrel had arisen between the bishop of León and the monastery of Saint Martial, he had moved to the monastery of Saint Isidore, likewise belonging to regular canons; but, finding himself disliked there by his companions, he withdrew to the church of Saint Martial, where he had been educated.

> Only a few days had passed when Saint Isidore appeared to certain canons of the monastery dedicated to his name and addressed them: “Why have you expelled Martin, the servant of God? Bring him back into your fellowship. Do not seize upon a cause of offense, but rather an occasion of joy and holy delight, since you are permitted to see among yourselves a man who follows the path of perfection.”

When he had therefore been brought back to the monastery of Saint Isidore, he implored the saint’s patronage so that he might especially acquire knowledge of sacred letters:

> Saint Isidore stood before him in a splendid appearance, holding a book in his hand, and said: “Take, Martin, the book and eat it; through God’s generosity you will at the same time drink in knowledge of the sacred Scriptures.” Martin replied that it was not lawful for him to eat the book, since he was bound by the rule of fasting. “Eat without fear,” said the holy doctor, “for you will not on that account be deprived of the reward of fasting. I am Isidore, the patron of this monastery, sent by God to bestow this gift upon you.” While Martin remained astonished at these words, the saint came nearer, seized him by the chin, and forced him to swallow the book; then he suddenly disappeared from his sight.

Martin acquired knowledge, and his reputation for learning became renowned. At last, worn out by old age, he departed this life in the year 1221.

[Col. 0945]

## APPENDIX II. LIFE OF SAINT ISIDORE

By a regular canon of the monastery of Saint Isidore of León, perhaps Luke, later bishop of Tuy. From a Toledo manuscript sent by the most distinguished Nicolás Antonio.

(See this life at the beginning of volume LXXXII, together with our admonition prefixed to that volume.)

[Col. 0945]

## APPENDIX III. HISTORY OF THE TRANSLATION OF THE BODY OF SAINT ISIDORE

From the same Toledo manuscript.

492. PROLOGUE.

[Col. 0945B]

[Note: [Col. 0945C] 1. The older *Acts of the Translation* may be read in *Isidoriana*, chapters 8 and 9. This history was composed from those *Acts*, with many additions drawn either from tradition or from other records that have not come down to us. I would scarcely believe the author of this history to be earlier than the thirteenth century; for the following words in his Prologue do not indicate greater antiquity: “From these things the city of León, beloved from ancient times by the kings of the Spaniards because it was noble and famous in royal faith,” etc. In number 19 there is also mention of the relics of Blessed Thomas of Canterbury, who died in the year 1170. AREV.]

1. While many are not able to investigate the secrets of heavenly wisdom worthily, and no one is able fully to discover them, they narrow the mind’s power of understanding by failing to find what they investigate, even as they expand their hearts in the search for what they desire. For the reasoning of the heavenly counsel has wonderfully ordained that what is justly disposed from above by immortal Wisdom should rightly remain unknown to us, who are still mortal. Although divine providence, in the omnipotence of its sublimity, cannot be circumscribed by any prudence of the mind, nevertheless it presents all those whom it brought into being from nothing as subject to the laws of its justice: it humbles the reprobate through punishment and exalts the saints through glory.

Their patronage is indeed splendidly present to the Catholic Church, since the faithful, protected by their merits, also possess cities in which they dwell that are celebrated by frequent miracles. Among these, the city of León—beloved from ancient times by the kings of the Spaniards because it was noble and famous in royal faith—glories in venerating the distinguished confessor Isidore as its patron. The universal Church shines with the rays of his teaching; he, a mirror of holiness and uprightness, lives in fame and merits throughout the world.

Since León is both a priestly and a royal city, it is also worthy to receive, venerate, and possess, by a certain gift of right, the miraculous body of the most worthy confessor of Christ, Isidore, doctor of the Spains, with royal ceremony in a royal court. Seville itself, over which he presided while living in the body, and in which he lay hidden for many years after his death while the fury of the pagans had ceased, was unable to retain him concealed.

Therefore, the veneration owed to so great a confessor invites us to set down in faithful writing by what order, at what time, and through what persons this public gift, this protection of the fatherland, was transferred to the city of León from the aforesaid Seville. Through the teaching of that apostolic man, Seville had become prosperous and glorious, and it shone as the first metropolitan seat of the Spaniards—a city populated by King Hispanus, from whom Spain took its name.

## CHAPTER I. Most of Spain occupied by the Saracens; the principal parts gradually recovered

[Note: [Col. 0946C] 2. Saint Isidore’s prophecy concerning the devastation of Spain is reported in the same words in Life, number 32, Appendix II. Other material concerning the arrival of the Moors in Spain was taken from the chronicle of Isidore of Pacensis or from similar sources. There exists a learned dissertation by Joseph Perez, Benedictine, *On the Supreme Disaster Inflicted upon Spain by the Saracens*, appended as appendix 2 to his ecclesiastical dissertations. He endeavors to prove that the Spanish disaster occurred in the year 712 of Christ. AREV.]

2. While Saint Gregory the pope was happily governing the Church of God, and Reccared, the most Christian king, was nobly ruling the kingdom of the Goths in Spain, under the emperor Heraclius—who restored to Jerusalem the Lord’s cross that the impious King Chosroes had carried away—the madness of the Arians was growing powerful throughout almost the entire world. At that time Isidore, doctor of the Spains and archbishop of Seville, shone among the faithful as a most brilliant star amid darkness. He confirmed the Gothic people in the Catholic faith, completely removed from the Spaniards the heresy of the Arians and Acephalites, established Gothic laws for the kings, and handed on an ecclesiastical rule to the priests of the Church of Christ. With prophetic voice he proclaimed:

> “If you remain in these traditions with a pure heart, in the present life you will enjoy peace amid prosperity, and in eternal glory you will be crowned with perpetual praise. But if you abandon these precepts, terrible evils will seize you, and the Gothic people will fall through famine, the sword of their enemies, and plague. When, however, you have turned back to the Lord and sought him, your offspring will possess the gates of their enemies, and your glory will be greater than it has ever been.”

After his death, the kings and priests of Spain followed the footsteps of the holy shepherd and, insofar as they could, adhered to salutary institutions, happily governing the flock entrusted to them—until the infamous Witiza [Note: [Col. 0947C] King Witiza, after the death of his father Egica, reigned for nine years, from 701 to 710. BOLLAND.] unhappily acquired the kingdom of Spain.

Since he was disgraceful in character, he also compelled others to submit to his evil practices. For, setting aside all divine religion, despising the teachings of the holy doctor Isidore, and loosening the restraint of chastity, the lustful king commanded bishops, priests, deacons, and all ministers of the sacred altar to have carnal wives, so that the holy Church might not rise against him on account of such a great crime.

Bishops and the other prelates of the Church were also despised; the doors of the holy Church were closed; the sacraments were regarded as worthless; the synodal institutions of the holy Father Isidore were scorned; councils were dissolved; the sacred canons were set aside; and finally, whatever was sober and honorable was counted as nothing, while pleasures were introduced in its place.

Thus, when the tyrant Witiza had been separated from the Roman Church and had died, supported by such devices and other props of pride, Roderic, son of Theudofred, succeeded to the Gothic kingdom. He was not unlike Witiza in life and character. Instead of uprooting the wicked growth as he ought to have done, he increased it more and more through the dissolution of luxury.

By these things almighty God was provoked to anger. For divine Providence, which is always effective in its purposes and, in a just and ineffable manner, dispenses increase along with losses and restores losses through further losses, determined that in the seventy-fifth year after the death of the most holy Isidore, because the priests and kings had abandoned him, all the peoples of Spain should be corrected by the rod of indignation. In accordance with the holy doctor Isidore’s prophecy, they were delivered by a just judgment to be struck down by the sword of the pagans.

Through the sons of Witiza and Count Julian of Tingitania, the transmarine Saracens, together with Ulit [Note: [Col. 0947D] Ulit, called Taric by others. BOLLAND.], the most powerful king of Africa, crossed the sea that washes the city of Seville. They first captured that city [Note: [Col. 0947D] Seville was captured in the year 712. BOLLAND.], then occupied the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. King Roderic met them armed, having gathered an army of Goths. But because the aforesaid king, neglecting divine religion, had enslaved himself to the dominion of vices, he was immediately put to flight, and nearly the entire army was destroyed by the sword.

The Saracens then roamed far and wide, perpetrating countless and dreadful massacres. The extent of the slaughter and destruction they inflicted upon our people is attested by the ruined camps and the demolished walls of ancient cities. At that time all Spain mourned: monasteries were overthrown, bishoprics destroyed, books of sacred law burned, the treasures of the churches plundered, and all the inhabitants consumed by sword, fire, and famine.

[Note: [Col. 0947D] 3. The praises of Charlemagne inserted at this point may suggest that the author of the history was one of the monks who regularly moved from Gaul into Spain; for the Spaniards criticize rather than praise Charlemagne’s deeds in Spain. Yet in number 19 other evidence occurs from which one may infer that the author was a canon of León in the monastery of Saint Isidore: “In the aforesaid church there remain eight fairly large caskets filled with the most holy relics, as we have learned from our predecessors,” etc. I would believe that this entire work was compiled from fragments of various works by different authors; consequently, scarcely any conjecture about its author can be drawn. I discussed certain matters concerning Charlemagne in both directions in chapter 105. AREV.]

3. At last the mercy of God—which is not accustomed to destroy those whom it chastises utterly, but mercifully corrects them by scourging—strengthened the courage of a certain Pelagius, who was descended from royal stock. Against the Saracens, at a place called the Cave of Saint Mary, he rebelled and declared war upon them.

That the divine hand fought for our people in that conflict may be understood from the fact that the weapons hurled by the Saracens were turned back against the Saracens themselves; and a certain rock, severed by God’s command, collapsed and crushed and killed no small number of the Saracens. [Note: [Col. 0948C] The approach of the Saracens had driven Pelagius into the mountain of Anseva, to the cave called Cova of Saint Mary, now commonly called Cova donga. From there he went forth with the faithful to battle and killed 124,000 of the enemy, in the era 756, that is, in the year 720 of Christ, as Sebastian, bishop of Salamanca, writes. BOLLAND.]

If anyone wishes to know the matter fully, let him take care to read the mournful history of those times. From that time onward, as the Spaniards once more sought the divine precepts delivered to them through Blessed Isidore, the glory and kingdom of the Gothic people began gradually and little by little to sprout again, like a shoot from a renewed root. Through the industry of the kings, who were descended from royal stock and nobly governed the summit of the kingdom, it grew from moment to moment.

They were famous in resources and strength, outstanding in mercy and justice, and devoted to sacred religion. Pursuing the enemies of the cross of Christ courageously with the two-edged sword, they restored bishoprics, founded monasteries and enriched them with treasures, adorned them with gold, gems, and books, and did everything in their power to extend the glory of the Christian name.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The same Sebastian asserts that there were 63,000. BOLLAND.]

The famous Charles, king of France, also, warned in a vision by Blessed James the Apostle, exercised zeal for the law of God. Together with the noble stock of the Franks, he expelled the Saracens in triumphant vengeance from the borders of Poitiers and Gascony, and advanced through the Pyrenees as far as Zaragoza in the time of Alfonso, the great king of León.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] The remainder of this number is absent from Tamaio. We explained what Einhard related about Charlemagne’s expedition in his *Life*, under 28 January, chapter 3. Some passages here seem to have been inserted from Turpin and for that reason omitted by Tamaio; elsewhere he presents the whole of this history, with somewhat altered wording, under 2 December. BOLLAND.]

For the sake of affection, he gave that King Alfonso his most noble cousin in marriage.

[Note: [Col. 0948D] This is Alfonso III, son of King Ordoño, whom he succeeded—as Sampiro, bishop of Astorga, testifies—in the era 896, that is, in the year 860; some assign it to the year 862. BOLLAND.]

When the most Christian king Charles visited the threshold of the Apostle Saint James to pray, King Alfonso, following his sounder counsel, adorned the church of the Apostle Saint James with metropolitan dignity, with the consent of the Roman pope.
