He also decreed that both the king himself and all the clergy of Spain should live according to the rule of the holy Father Isidore, so that this might be the restoration of Spain, whose neglect had been the cause of its downfall.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] 4. When the Bollandists say that Saint Facundus suffered martyrdom at Sahagún, do not understand this as though the town had been called Sahagún before Saint Facundus; for the word *Sahagún*, or *Sagun*, is Spanish and derives from Saint Facundus. AREV.]

4. King Alfonso, moreover, slaughtering the Ishmaelite people in a dreadful massacre, gloriously extended the honor of the Church of Christ, and died in peace. From his illustrious lineage arose the distinguished Ferdinand [Note: [Col. 0949C] Sampiro calls her Xemena, and says that she was of Gallic lineage. BOLLAND.], son of the holy king. He took as his wife and consort in the royal power the most serene Queen Sancha, daughter of King Alfonso.

She possessed a particular prudence of mind, was not inferior to the Queen of the South, and, devoted to the administration of the kingdom, sometimes supplied the place of the king and her husband. Thus she was subject to her husband while sharing the labor of the kingdom.

When King Ferdinand [Note: [Col. 0949C] Ferdinand was first king of Castile from 1035 and king of León from 1038; he was crowned on 22 June. As for the ancient and true meaning of the name, signifying “peaceful hand” or “the hand that makes peace,” the usage of the preceding century, in which the name is written *Fredenandus*, comes closer to it. BOLLAND.] had taken possession of the royal scepters and received the insignia of the royal diadem, he adorned the scepter with honorable conduct. With drawn sword against the enemies of Christ, knowing neither how to be defeated but only how to conquer, he extended the boundaries of his realm and gained frequent triumphs.

To crown his happiness, Queen Sancha approached him with gentle words, asking that he prepare for himself and his descendants a fitting burial place in the city of León, and that he adorn it with the relics of the saints for the protection of himself and his people in both the present and the future life.

This city is powerful in the nobility of its situation: pleasant in its lands, healthy in its air, watered by rivers, fertile in meadows and gardens, delightful with mountains and springs, wooded with trees, and especially suitable for the habitation of religious men.

King Ferdinand had decided to have his body buried at Saint Facundus, whom he had always held dear, or in the church of Saint Peter of Arlanza.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] From this point onward, much the same material is read in the *Chronicle of Tuy*, after the era 1075. BOLLAND.]

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Facundus the martyr is venerated with Saint Primitivus on 27 November. He suffered martyrdom at Sahagún, in the diocese of León, where Alfonso III built a monastery in 905; after it had been destroyed by the Saracens, Alfonso VI, son of the aforementioned Ferdinand, restored it. Sandoval illustrated the monastery. BOLLAND.]

After Queen Sancha, therefore, had observed that in the cemetery of the kings of León, in the church of Saint John the Baptist, her grandfather King Vermudo [Note: [Col. 0949D] It is now Saint Isidore’s, and is a monastery of regular canons. BOLLAND.], Ordoño, her father King Alfonso of worthy memory, and her most serene brother King Vermudo were resting, she labored with all her strength so that she and her husband might also rest with them after death.

[Note: [Col. 0949D] Saint Peter of Arlanza was a town of Old Castile on the river Arlanza, above the duchy of Lerma, where there is a celebrated monastery. BOLLAND.]

King Ferdinand, therefore, consenting to the request of his most faithful wife, assigned masons to devote themselves continually to this most worthy undertaking.

## CHAPTER II. The body of Saint Justa sought and that of Saint Isidore obtained; his preceding apparitions

5. Meanwhile the king and his venerable wife, sharing the same supreme desire, considered how they might obtain at least one of the bodies of the holy martyrs who had been slaughtered in the city of Seville for the name of Christ.

After arranging affairs along the frontier, as soon as the opportunity arose, he gathered an innumerable army and set out hostilely into the provinces of Baetica and Lusitania. Having devastated the fields of the barbarians and burned many villages, King Benabet of Seville came to meet him with great gifts, begging him for the sake of friendship and the dignity of the kingdom not to persecute him and his realm, but to deign to hold him, like the other kings of Spain, as a subject tributary.

[Note: [Col. 0949C] Sandoval, in §38 of his *History of the Monastery of Sahagún*, says that this king of Seville was called Almun Camuz Aben Amet, so that *Benabet* may be a contraction of the final part of *Aben Amet*. BOLLAND.]

King Ferdinand, as was his custom, took pity on human distress. When the aged barbarian’s entreaties moved him, he ordered all capable men to be summoned from their winter quarters, so that, with their counsel, he might determine how to put an end to the Moorish king’s supplications.

Wise men accordingly advised him, through the dispensation of heavenly counsel, to receive the barbarian with his gifts and ask for the body of Blessed Justa [Note: [Col. 0949C] Saints Justa and Rufina, virgins and martyrs of Seville, are celebrated on 19 July. Yet Roderic of Toledo, book VI, chapter 11, says that the body of Saint Isidore was requested first. BOLLAND.], a martyr who had once gone from Seville to Christ with the crown of virginity and martyrdom, as he had conceived in his mind, in order to transfer it to the city of León.

This was done. As the Catholic Ferdinand desired, Benabet granted his petition and promised to give him the body of Saint Justa.

After this agreement had been accepted, and after the expedition had been gloriously concluded and they had returned to León, the court nobles were present, each using his own ingenuity to determine who was worthy to be sent on so holy a mission and could satisfy the royal will by prudent counsel.

At last the aforesaid king—whose hidden wisdom, under God’s authority, administered laws and rights to the peoples—summoned to himself a man of reverend holiness who had been appointed, by divine providence, bishop of the city of León. His name was Albitus; he had governed with vigor according to heavenly discipline the monastery of Amanus [Note: [Col. 0949D] The cited Sandoval §36, González de Ávila, and others say that Albitus, or Alvitu, had been taken from the monastery of Sahagún of the Order of Saint Benedict. BOLLAND.].

The king also summoned Ordoño, bishop of Astorga, a man of incomparable prudence, faith, and generosity [Note: [Col. 0949D] We discussed Ordoño among the *Praetermissi* under 23 February, where we stated that some venerate him among the saints on that day. BOLLAND.], as well as Count Munio [Note: [Col. 0949D] The cited Sandoval §37 calls him Munia Muñoz, the first of this embassy, whom the king rewarded with an inheritance at Campo de Salinas. He adds that others call him Nuño, and that he was descended from the blood of the kings of León and from the families of Osorio and Guzmán. BOLLAND.], together with Ferdinand and Gundisalvus, nobles of his palace. With a military escort—for they thought that rebels against the Catholic faith regarded Christ’s faithful as enemies—the shrewd and provident king sent them to Seville to bring back the body of the aforesaid virgin, lest some band of conspirators should harm them. When they arrived, they explained the purpose of their embassy to King Benabet.

498. 6. The pagan king [Note: [Col. 0949D] Lucas of Tuy and others likewise call the Muslims pagans and gentiles, and their religion a gentile religion. BOLLAND.] received them with the highest honor. He summoned the leading men of his kingdom, explained what the Catholic prince was requesting, and asked them to declare their opinion on the matter.

“For reason itself,” he said, “does not permit such majesty to be despised, since it stands above and distinguished from the other kings of the fatherland.”

The gentile men, although they had not been reborn in the sacred font and therefore spoke, as it were, from the judgment of their own understanding, answered their king:

> “Venerable king, although we are held by a gentile religion, we are protected by the merits of this virgin and the other martyrs; while they assist us, no hostile attack troubles this city. Therefore do not allow this light of the fatherland, this safeguard of your kingdom, to be transferred elsewhere. For this will be a humiliation to all who are subject to your rule.”

The gentile ruler, recognizing the counsel of his nobles as useful, told the envoys that he could not comply with King Ferdinand’s request concerning the martyr’s body, saying:

> “I know perfectly well that I promised your lord what you say, but neither I nor any of my people can show you the body you seek. Search for it yourselves—for you have permission—and when you have found it, take it away and depart.”

7. Having received this answer, the venerable Bishop Albitus secretly addressed his companions in these words:

> “As you see, fellow travelers, unless divine mercy comes to our aid, we shall depart frustrated by our labor. It therefore seems necessary, beloved brothers, that we seek help from God, for whom nothing is impossible, and devote these three days to fasting and prayer, so that the divine majesty may deign to reveal to us the hidden treasure of the holy body.”

All approved the exhortation of the holy bishop, and they completed three three-day periods in fasting and prayer. The day of the third three-day period had already come to an end and the fourth night had arrived when the holy Bishop Albitus continued in unbroken vigil and prayer.

Meanwhile, while he sat in his cell, meditating on the psalms and briefly supporting his weary limbs, he was overcome by sleep because of his excessive labor in keeping vigil. A certain man appeared to him, adorned with venerable gray hair and clothed in a bishop’s mitre, and addressed him in these words:

> “I know that you have come with your companions to transfer the body of the most blessed virgin Justa from here and carry it away. Although it is not the will of God that this city be left desolate by the departure of this virgin, divine goodness will not send you away empty-handed. My body has been given to you. Take it away, and return home without fear.”

When the reverend Albitus asked him who he was to impose such commands upon him, he replied:

> “I am Isidore, doctor of the Spains and bishop of this city.”

After saying this, he vanished from the eyes of the man who had seen him.

The bishop awoke, rejoiced in the vision, and began to pray to the Lord more intently, imploring him that, if the vision were from God, it might be made known more fully a second and a third time; but that, if it were not, it might depart.

Praying in this manner, he again fell asleep. Behold, the very same man appeared and delivered words not unlike those he had spoken before; then he vanished again.

The bishop awoke and more eagerly begged the Lord for a threefold confirmation of the vision. While he prayed to the Lord with still greater earnestness, he was seized by sleep a third time. The aforesaid man appeared to him, just as he had appeared once and then twice before, and repeated a third time what he had already said.

Then, striking the ground three times with the pastoral staff he held in his hand, he pointed out the place where the treasure of the holy body lay hidden, saying:

> “Here, here, here you will find my body. And lest you think that you are being deceived by a phantom vision, this will be the sign of the truth of my words: as soon as you have brought my body forth above the earth, you will be seized by bodily illness. You will come to us with the crown of righteousness, and the heavenly court will receive you in happiness; while I am your patron, the city of León will rejoice.”

After he had finished speaking, the vision disappeared.

[Col. 0952A] **8.** Therefore the bishop rose from sleep, certain of so great a vision but happier at his summons, and reported the sequence of this revelation to Bishop Ordonio. He rendered praises to the heavenly King for the visitation of the most glorious confessor, yet was sorrowful at the imminent death of his companion.

When morning came, the venerable Albitus exhorted his companions, saying:

> “It is fitting, dearly beloved, that you adore the omnipotence of the supreme Father with bowed minds and lowered faces. He has deigned to go before us by his grace and has not allowed the labor of our journey to be wasted. For by divine will we are forbidden to remove from here the members of the blessed virgin Justa, dedicated to God; but we shall carry away no lesser gifts, since we are to convey the body of the most blessed Isidore, who held the episcopal dignity in this city and adorned all Spain by his deeds and his word.”

Having said this, he disclosed the order of the vision in detail. When they heard it, they gave immense thanks to God, then approached the Saracen king and laid everything before him in order. Having heard this, the barbarian, although an unbeliever, was terrified as he recognized the power of God, [Col. 0952B] and replied to them:

> “And if I give Isidore to you, with whom shall I remain here?”

When his counselors saw this, they summoned the elders of the city and the adherents of the Catholic faith, carefully inquiring who that Isidore had been about whom such talk was circulating among the Christians. **Note:** Nicholas Antonius notes that the author is speaking of the Mixtarabs, who, as this passage shows, had inhabited that very great city among the Moors from the time of its capture. These Mixtarabs are called Muzarabs by others. **Bolland.**

Those Christian faithful themselves—for the city’s exceedingly renowned fame had made them natives there through successive generations—believed that the confessor of Christ was present with them as a mighty protector. They could not console themselves over his translation; indeed, if they had been free to leave with him, they would have preferred to migrate with him.

Nevertheless, anxious about the Saracens’ command, they also indicated what was their own—namely, their grief—by their clouded faces. They explained that this was Isidore, the greatest teacher of the Church, formerly metropolitan bishop of this city, honored by Pope Gregory with the archiepiscopal pallium, and in every respect an enemy of their Muhammad, who, even during the time of his preaching, was shamefully expelled from Spain by him [Col. 0951D].

**Note:** Above we said that this story about Muhammad being expelled from Spain by Saint Isidore must be counted among the fables, though it may have been true of some herald of Muhammad’s impiety. **Bolland.**

When the Hagarenes heard this, judging Christ’s confessor to have been their adversary from his earliest beginnings and wishing to drive away their enemy, they suggested to their king that, since it was not lawful for them to disregard a man of such authority, he should grant permission for the confessor’s remains to be sought, although this greatly disturbed him.

**Note:** **9.** I freely correct certain errors that plainly appear typographical, such as *almi itaque praesules* in place of *almi praesulis*, and *nectareique balsami* in place of *nectareque balsami*. It would not be useful to indicate them all. **Arev.**

**9.** I shall speak of wonders, almost unheard-of from the earliest times. For when the holy bishops, having arrived at the church in which the sacred body rested through a heavenly revelation, were seeking its tomb, the marks of the staff with which the holy confessor had indicated the site of the grave by striking three times were found in the very surface of the ground.

Finally, because human minds are considered doubtful or impatient, they dug in another part of the pavement, seeking their most precious treasure. While the bishops alone were praying beside the tomb, the force of sleep overcame them upon the very stone of the grave. The confessor of Christ, wearing his episcopal headgear, appeared to them and declared that the result of their petition was at hand.

> “Behold,” he said, “in accordance with the desire of your hearts, you shall find my body in this monument; and Spain, but especially the city of León, shall rejoice in me as its patron. And you, Albitus, when you return, shall put off the human being; but take comfort, because the heavenly court shall receive you happily.”

Thus the holy bishops, rejoicing at so great a revelation, summoned their companions. They urged them to rejoice over this announcement and without delay to open the holy tomb. When it had been uncovered, so great a fragrance of the sweetest odor poured forth that it covered the hair of the head, the beards, and the clothing of all who were present as though with a mist and dew of nectar and balsam.

A great crowd was present then, both Christians and [Col. 0953A] Saracens. With the utmost devotion they raised their voices to the stars in praise of God and his confessor Isidore. Among them were two blind men, as well as many mute and lame persons and others suffering from various illnesses; all of them were immediately restored to health.

The blessed body, however, was enclosed in a wooden vessel made of juniper.

**10.** As soon as it was opened, illness seized the revered bishop Albitus. Nevertheless, wrapping the most holy members in clean linens, he placed them in a sealed cypress chest and entrusted them to the reverend Bishop Ordonio. Sensing that his final day had arrived, he fell onto his bed.

Nor could any reasoning of the mind persuade him that the most blessed Isidore, who reigned with Christ and over whom no falsehood could prevail, had falsely foretold this to him. Therefore the mind of Bishop Albitus, which was already wholly directed toward heavenly things, considered that corruption of the flesh had been the mother of vice and sin; and because penitence alone is the sole hope of pardon, he ran with eager desire to the bath of repentance.

Accordingly, before the present most reverend Bishop Ordonio—whose heart, because of the imminent absence of the holy bishop, was overwhelmed by immeasurable grief—he faithfully disclosed whatever he had committed, whether deceived by the enemy of the human race or through his own guilt. Drawing sighs from the depths of his heart, he also begged Ordonio to obtain for him, through his continual intercession, the favor of the heavenly Majesty.

Then, having received the provision for his soul—the very price of our redemption, which the Christian faith sets forth as its defense and unconquerable protection against the enemy’s deceits—he surrendered his spirit to Christ on the seventh day, in the presence of a great gathering of the faithful.

**501. CHAPTER III. The body of Saint Isidore is brought from Seville to León. Benefits received.**

**Note:** **11.** In the older Acts of the translation the wording is more correct: “Behold, you are departing from here, venerable Isidore”; for these are three hexameter verses, as I observed in those Acts. **Arev.**

**11.** Bishop Ordonio of Astorga and the whole army, having received the body of Blessed Isidore and the body of Albitus, bishop of León, joyfully hastened to return.

When the body of the most blessed Isidore was placed in a wooden bier, the aforementioned Saracen king Benabet threw over it a silk curtain woven with marvelous workmanship. Drawing deep sighs from the innermost part of his breast, he said:

> “Behold, venerable Isidore, you are departing from here; yet you yourself know how your affairs and mine stand. Therefore I beg you always to remember me.”

I ask, brothers, with how great a reverence the King of glory and King of saints, Christ, embraces Isidore, since he inclined the heart of an ethnic and barbarian ruler

**Note:** That is, Christ, truly the supreme king of all the saints. **Bolland.**

to such solemn and extraordinary veneration of his relics to such solemn and extraordinary veneration of his relics that a blasphemer of Christ burst forth in praise of Christ’s worshiper; a persecutor of the saints grieved at the saint’s departure; and a plunderer of Christians honored the funeral rites of Christ’s confessor with royal gifts.

Yet many judge otherwise: namely, that the saint of God appeared to him and taught him the Catholic faith in a vision.

With this glorification of the holy confessor accomplished, the reverend Bishop Ordonio and the aforementioned nobles took leave of the king, whose gifts had honorably enriched them, and directed their steps homeward, rejoicing in the patron bestowed upon them from heaven.

**12.** On their return, the envoys truthfully reported what had happened to the serene King Ferdinand. At the arrival of the holy body, the illustrious king displayed indescribable splendor. Our simplicity cannot explain the immensity of the joy that filled the king, who, rejoicing that he possessed the protection of so great a confessor, burst forth entirely in praises of Christ.

Although the renowned king gloried in enjoying the assistance of the illustrious teacher Isidore, the death of Bishop Albitus wounded his mind indirectly, for he had always revered him with extraordinary affection. That death, indeed, was precious in the sight of the Lord.

With a crown of nobles and a very large military force, the king went as far as the river Douro [Col. 0953D] to meet them, accompanied by his sons, the very glory of the kingdom—Sancho, [Col. 0953D] Alfonso, and García.

**Note:** The river Douro divides the kingdom of León into Transdouro and Cisdouro. **Bolland.**

**Note:** After the death of their father Ferdinand, these became kings: Sancho of Castile, Alfonso of León, and García of Galicia. Consult Mariana, book IX, chapters 7, 8, and the following chapters, where he describes the boundaries of the individual kingdoms and the fortune by which Sancho occupied his brothers’ territories by force of arms; after Sancho was killed, Alfonso succeeded him. **Bolland.**

There the royal majesty, shedding tears from joy, gave countless thanks to the Creator of all things. The immense crowd present performed a three-step dance; the earth resounded with the voices of those glorifying God.

**502.** Who can explain how many caresses of heavenly mercy and how frequent the signs that followed the sacred body throughout the whole journey, as far as the city of León? And how great and magnificent was the procession of the religious princes, with the utmost devotion; how great the applause of the clergy, while the people rejoiced in spiritual gladness; and, finally, how great the gathering of both sexes?

The illustrious King Ferdinand’s greatness must also be mentioned. As though renouncing temporal privilege, he rejoiced, barefoot together with his illustrious sons, in carrying the body of the most holy confessor upon his shoulders, like David dancing with his servants before the Ark of the Covenant. Thus, the more humble he appeared before the people, the more glorious he might be considered before God; and divine mercy might prepare both kingdoms perpetually for him and his descendants.

Queen Sancha, his wife, accompanied by her daughters Urraca [Col. 0953D] and Geloyra [Col. 0954C], the beauty of the kingdom and the supreme dignity of a mother, was present on the bank of the river Douro before the illustrious confessor.

**Note:** Urraca and Elvira are named by the same Mariana: the former was given Zamora, the latter Toro, as their inheritance for the support of their lives. **Bolland.**

Archbishops, bishops, and abbots were also present, together with the clerical and monastic orders, all dressed in sacred vestments, with candles going before them and the other insignia of the Church. They magnificently praised God for the patron bestowed upon them.

And so that the jubilation might increase and praise be enlarged, a certain blind man named Eusebius, as he touched the bier, suddenly received light in his eyes.

**Note:** **13.** At first, the day of the translation was distinguished from the day of the church’s dedication. The dedication feast was celebrated on December 21, and the translation on December 22, as I showed in chapter 28, number 12. **Arev.**

**13.** When they reached the city gate called the Arch, a seditious dispute arose among the crowd. Many objected that the body of Bishop Albitus ought to be buried in the church of Saint John the Baptist.

At that time the venerable man Dominic, abbot of the monastery of Silos, was present at this most celebrated solemnity. Everyone extolled his holiness.

**Note:** Saint Dominic of Silos, or of Exile, is commemorated on December 20. In his Life, written by a contemporary monk and published by Tamayo, he is said to have died in the year 1073, on Friday, December 20, that is, with the Dominical Letter F. Tamayo adds that the same Life, together with 114 miracles, was preserved in Gothic script in the records of the monastery of Blessed Martin in Madrid. We greatly desire that both this work and the Life be transcribed for us in full, since Tamayo scarcely ever faithfully preserves the ancient style, and omitted the miracles because of their tedious length. **Bolland.**

He earnestly wished to bring the divided dispute to a peaceful conclusion, without prejudicing either side. When everyone’s wishes converged upon him, he poured out prayers to the Lord and invoked the most holy teacher Isidore. Then he ordered the bodies of the saints to be placed upon pack animals and decreed that the body of Bishop Albitus should be given burial wherever it went without human guidance.

At the entrance to the city he struck the horses once with a small blow of his staff. The irrational animals, carrying the sacred burden under angelic guidance—as we believe, since the pontifical church was not to be deprived of its bishop—proceeded by a straight route to the same church of the holy Mother of God, carrying the body of Saint Albitus.

But the horses carrying the holy body of Isidore came to the church of Saint John the Baptist and stopped in a certain pool highly damaging to the city. They could not draw them out by any means until they blocked the same pool with stones and earth. Once it had been blocked, they suddenly saw the horses, which they had thought were dying, safe and sound upon the ground.

Amazed at this, they glorified the confessor’s magnificence. All were astonished at the miracle; and, following the revelation of the same confessor, they carried him to the church of the perpetual Virgin Mary [Col. 0955B] until the body of Bishop Albitus had been honorably committed to burial.

**Note:** Gonzales de Ávila writes that the body of Saint Albitus was translated in 1527 and distinguished by many miracles. His feast day is assigned to December 27 in Tamayo Salazar’s Spanish Martyrology. **Bolland.**

After this, the illustrious King Ferdinand, having gathered all the archbishops, abbots, and nobles of his kingdom, carried the remains of the most holy teacher Isidore, with hymns and praises, to the church of Saint John the Baptist, where they are now venerated by the faithful. They decreed that it should be consecrated in honor of the holy bishop Isidore and that the day of the translation and dedication should be celebrated annually with festivity on the tenth day before the Kalends of January.

**Note:** Nicholas Antonius would prefer to read “the eleventh day before the Kalends,” asserting that the day of the translation was December 22. Tamayo Salazar printed “the twelfth day before the Kalends of January” from the same manuscript and from the manuscript Breviaries of León and Compostela, and referred everything to December 21. Marieta did the same in book V, chapter 26. Because the feast of Saint Thomas the Apostle, which impeded that day, may have caused some to transfer it to the following day, December 22, Wion, Dorganius, Menardus, Bucelinus in the *Benedictine Fasti*, and Ferrarius in the *General Catalogue* likewise give December 22. Sandoval, in the cited history of Sahagún, §36, reports the translation as having been recorded on the tenth day before the Kalends of January. **Bolland.**

The translation took place in the year 1101 of the era, in the year 1063 from the Incarnation of Our Lord Jesus Christ, in the first indiction, with the third concurrent [Col. 0956D].

**Note:** Rather, it should be the second: the solar cycle was VIII and the Dominical Letter E. Consult Petavius, *On the Doctrine of Times*, book VI, chapter 28. **Bolland.**

On that feast the illustrious king, with his entire household, displayed such devotion and humility out of reverence for the holy and blessed confessor that, when they came to the banquet, he set aside royal pride and personally placed delicate foods in the hands of the religious men, as a servant would. Queen Sancha likewise, as though she had seen her pious wishes receive a blessed fulfillment, humbly rendered every service to the rest of the multitude, in servant-like fashion, with joyful devotion together with her sons and daughters.

**14.** It also seems to belong to the praise of the holy bishop that, when the city of León was failing through drought and barrenness and the poisoned region was producing innumerable creatures, an abundance of rain poured forth and drove away every harmful thing. Fertility was granted to the earth, so that thereafter such creatures were scarcely seen in that region.

It is also worthy of veneration with what astonishment of wonder even the elements mourned the province deprived of so distinguished a patron and withheld their natural benefits from its growth. They prolonged the losses of grief so far that, contrary to the natural order of assistance, they rose violently against the land, imputing to its inhabitants the fact that they had been deprived of so great and distinguished a Father because of their wickedly rising merits.

For although heavenly mercy has bestowed upon the soil of Baetica, above the other provinces of Spain, a kindly climate, and the pleasing beauty of its places seems to smile upon the inborn fertility of all growing things like the irrigation of a fruitful paradise, the homeland mourned that it had been deprived of such a Father and showed the loss of so great a Father through such great disasters.

It was discolored and withered by the unusual severity of sudden rains. Although, because of the sea’s warm vapor, it had never been accustomed to endure the burning of frost, nevertheless, in the year when the blessed members were removed from it, it was so scorched by burning ice that no fruit remained in the vineyards, olive groves, or fig orchards.

Thus the city of Seville declared—or rather proclaimed by manifest signs—that it had been divinely provided with such a great patron through his merits, and that the greatness of the province and of so many benefits had been taken away solely through the absence of his relics.

**Note:** **15.** Some material has been inserted here from a sacred sermon delivered on the day of the translation, as the words suggest: “The holy intervention of this man” [perhaps “of the saint”] and “the sacred celebration of the translation of the present day,” and so forth. Unless one prefers to say that these words were taken from certain lessons of the church’s office. **Arev.**

**15.** In the place where the body of the holy teacher Isidore is venerated by the faithful people with fitting honor in a golden and gem-studded tomb, so many miracles occur that, if someone committed them to writing, he would produce no small volumes of books.

The constant signs that occur there reveal to the people how great is the merit of the glorious intercession of Christ’s confessor Isidore in the presence of the Creator of all things.

There, Blindness, you lose your strength. For the pious intervention of the most blessed Isidore gives light to the eyes that you hold deprived of light.

Whatever limbs the worst disease or a violent fever dissolves, you, holy confessor, restore to health through poured-out prayer, driving far away the danger of illness.

Those whom the dislocation of their limbs weakens and deprives of their accustomed strength stand at the saint’s tomb, supported by his prayers, rejoicing in firm steps.

A deaf or mute person who arrives there returns home rejoicing, restored to health through his merits.

The city rejoices that it has obtained protection, the region fertility, and the expulsion of serpents through the favor of the pious teacher.

These are indeed your works, Christ, who present on earth in distinguished miracles the illustrious confessor Isidore, whom you crowned in heaven with glory and honor.

May his holy intervention and the sacred celebration of the translation on this present day commend us continually to the heavenly King. May his confessor also confer upon us here the joys of salvation and peace through his patronage, by the favor of Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit reigns without time, for ever and ever. Amen.

**505. CHAPTER IV. The virtues and death of King Ferdinand the Great. The relics preserved in the church of Saint Isidore.**

**16.** After the arrival of the holy bishop Isidore’s body, the illustrious King Ferdinand, urged by Queen Sancha and himself burning with no lesser desire, diligently sought to adorn the same royal hall with various relics of the saints.

After a multitude of sacred pledges had been gathered there, he translated from Ávila to León the body of Saint Vincent the martyr [Col. 0956D], brother of the holy martyrs Sabina and Christeta, and joined the shrine of the most holy martyr Vincent to the body of Isidore, teacher of Spain, with the most fitting honor that his resources allowed.

**Note:** Saint Vincent and his sisters Sabina and Christeta, killed at Ávila under Diocletian, are commemorated on October 27 and are also included in the Roman Martyrology. **Bolland.**

**Note:** Lucas of Tuy gives the reason: the city of Ávila had formerly been reduced to desolation by the Saracens. Much of what follows is transmitted by him in the *Chronicle* in almost the same words. **Bolland.**

**Note:** Pelagius, bishop of Oviedo, after recounting the translation of Saint Isidore, adds the following: “This Ferdinand made a second translation of the holy martyrs Vincent, Sabina, and Christeta from Ávila: Vincent to León, Sabina to Palencia, and Christeta to Arlanza, to Saint Peter.” An inscription at the entrance to the cloister of the monastery of Saint Isidore records that this translation took place in the year 1103 of the era, that is, in 1065, on the sixth day before the Ides of May. Tamayo Salazar raises various disputed questions concerning that date, since the monks of Saint Peter at Arlanza claimed for themselves the bodies of all three. **Bolland.**

He also carefully observed the Christian religion, which he had devoutly embraced from childhood. The church he had newly built and caused to be dedicated with the greatest reverence in honor of the holy bishop Isidore, he adorned with gold and silver of the greatest beauty, precious stones, permanent privileges of security, and silk curtains.

He diligently attended the church morning and evening, during the night hours, and at the time of the sacred services. Sometimes he sang melodiously with the clergy; taking his turn as cantor, he exulted powerfully in the praise of God.

He loved the poor and pilgrims and took great care in receiving them. He showed the clerical order great reverence with incredible humility.

Moreover, wherever he discovered monks or women dedicated to God living, he was accustomed, out of compassion for their poverty, either to go there himself to console them or to send generous sums of money.

Indeed, he always provided with vigilant care that the better part of the spoils from his victories should be distributed among monasteries and the poor of Christ, to the praise of God, Saints Isidore and Vincent, and the most blessed apostle James, who made him victorious.

What more is there to say? Throughout his entire life, the pious and most excellent prince Ferdinand loved nothing more dearly than that the principal churches of his kingdom should flourish through his gifts with their ancient authority, and that all of them through him should not only become peaceful and protected but also be adorned and enriched through his labors.

**506. 17.** Strong in these virtues, he set out with a prepared army to devastate the villages of the Celtiberian province and plunder the settlements of the unbelievers. After remaining there for a long time and laying waste with sword and fire everything outside the fortifications, he approached the city of Valencia, which he would have conquered quickly had he not been confined by illness.

After receiving the surrender of all the cities and castles of the Celtiberian province, the holy teacher Isidore appeared to him and announced that the day of his death was near. Even while still physically ill, he came to León in the month of December.

He entered the city on the ninth day before the Kalends of January, a Saturday, and according to custom venerated on bended knees the bodies of Saints Isidore and Vincent. He asked that, since the terrible hour of death already threatened him, his soul—through the intervention of the angelic choirs—might be freed from the power of darkness and presented unharmed before the tribunal of Christ his Redeemer.

On the very celebrated night of the Lord’s Nativity [Col. 0957D]—the day before the Nativity of Christ in 1061, solar cycle X, Dominical Letter B. **Bolland.**—while the clergy were singing the Christmas matins according to the festive custom, the Catholic king was present among them. Joyfully, as far as he was able, he sang with them until the final verse of these matins, “It has come to us,” which at that time they sang according to the Toledan custom. The succentors responded: “Be instructed, all you who judge the earth.”

**Note:** The Chronicle of Tuy reads “the Psalm,” but it seems that the antiphon, or the following verse, *Advenit nobis*, is meant. **Bolland.**

This appropriately applied to the serene King Ferdinand.

**Note:** The Chronicle of Tuy adds: “For while he was permitted to live, he governed the kingdom according to Catholic principles; and, restraining himself with the bridle of chastity, he rendered himself thoroughly instructed.” **Bolland.**

When the bright day of the Nativity of the Son of God dawned upon the whole world, he perceived that his limbs were failing and asked for Mass to be sung. After receiving communion in the body and blood of Christ, he was led to his bed by the hands of soldiers.

**18.** On the following day, when the light had come, knowing what was to happen, he summoned the bishops, abbots, and every religious man to himself. To confirm his departure, he was carried with them to the church, dressed in royal attire and wearing a crown upon his head.

Then, kneeling before the altar and the bodies of the saints—the teacher Blessed Isidore and Saint Vincent, martyr of Christ—he said to the Lord in a clear voice:

> “Yours is the power; yours is the kingdom, Lord. You are above all kings. By your command all kingdoms, heavenly and earthly, are subjected. Therefore the kingdom that I received through your gift, and which I ruled for as long as your free will was pleased, behold, I return to you. I beg only that you receive in peace my soul, rescued from the abyss of this world.”

Having said this, he removed the royal cloak with which his body was clothed and set aside the jeweled crown that encircled his head. Then, lying prostrate on the church floor with tears, he earnestly begged the Lord for pardon for his sins.

The bishops then imposed a penitential discipline upon him. He was clothed in sackcloth instead of royal garments and sprinkled with ashes instead of wearing a golden diadem.

While he remained in such penitence before the altar of the saints, God granted him two days of life. On the following day, which was Tuesday, at the sixth hour of the day, when the feast of Saint John the Evangelist was celebrated, he surrendered his spirit to God and Blessed Isidore—who had appeared to him—into the hands of the bishops.

He was buried in that same church. Clergy and laity, monks and poor alike lamented him beyond consolation in the bitterness of their excessive grief, mourning not merely a king but a pious father.

Thus, in the year 1103 of the era, he went to the Lord in a good old age. He ruled the kingdom faithfully for forty years, six months, and twelve days.

Whoever seeks in prayer, with devout mind, the place where the bodies of Saint Isidore, teacher of Spain, and the most holy martyr Vincent rest, receives swift healing from his illnesses and the saving fulfillment of his petitions, through our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns for ever and ever. Amen.

**19.** The most serene and great King Ferdinand therefore placed the body of Isidore, the most holy teacher of Spain, in the church of Saint John the Baptist, which the same glorious king had newly built, as stated above.

With fitting honor he also placed beside it the body of the illustrious martyr Vincent and the greater part of his two sisters, namely Sabina and Christeta. Out of a desire to increase still further the honor of the pious confessor, the pious king ordered these relics to be brought from the city of Ávila to León.

He also added an almost innumerable multitude of relics of many saints, which together with the aforementioned Confessor make that place venerable and glorious. Their names are as follows:

- from the wood of the Lord;
- from the Lord’s sepulchre;
- from the column to which the Son of God was bound and scourged for the salvation of the human race;
- from the cloth with which he wiped the apostles’ feet on the day of the Supper;
- from the shroud in which his most holy body was wrapped in the tomb;
- from the milk of the blessed Virgin, Mother of Christ;
- from his garments;
- from the bones of blessed Anne, his mother;
- from the bones and garments of the apostles Peter, Paul, James of Compostela, Andrew, Bartholomew, and Matthew;
- from the bread of the Supper;
- the cutting instrument of that Supper;
- from the head of Blessed John the Baptist;
- from the bones of Blessed Lawrence;
- from the bones of Vincent, deacon and martyr of Christ, who was related in the second degree to that same blessed Lawrence;

**Note:** Nicholas Antonius remarks that concerning this relationship between the invincible martyrs, we trust the testimony of ancient Breviaries seen by John Francis Andreas Ustarrozius, a writer on the homeland of Saint Lawrence, chapter 5, page 83. These matters may be examined on August 10 in the Acts of Saint Lawrence. **Bolland.**

- from the bones of the Holy Innocents;
- from the myrrh that the Magi offered to the Lord;
- from the bones of Saints Claudius, Lupercius, and Victoricus, who were crowned with martyrdom in the city of León for the name of Christ and were brothers by both parents;

**Note:** Saints Claudius, Lupercius, and Victoricus, sons of Saint Marcellinus (or Marcellus), a centurion, suffered under Diocletian and are commemorated on October 30. **Bolland.**

- from the garments and bones of Blessed Martin, Blessed Nicholas, Saint Augustine, and Blessed Thomas, archbishop of Canterbury;

**Note:** Saint Thomas suffered in the year 1170, that is, 105 years after Ferdinand’s death. Nicholas Antonius therefore judges that the list of relics preserved in this church was copied by an author insufficiently concerned with the dates when the individual relics were brought there. **Bolland.**

- from the relics of Justus and Pastor;

**Note:** Justus and Pastor, martyrs of Complutum, are commemorated on August 6. **Bolland.**

- from the bones of the prophet Samuel;
- from the holm oak of Mamre, beneath which Abraham stood;
- from the oil that flowed through the merits of Blessed Catherine near Mount Sinai;
- from the bones of a certain cardinal who was burned at Constantinople in defense of the truth;
- from the bones of Malachy, bishop and confessor, who was a contemporary of Blessed Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux;

**Note:** Saint Malachy is commemorated on November 3 and Saint Bernard on August 20. Both also flourished in the twelfth century, the century after King Ferdinand. **Bolland.**

- from the bones and garments of Blessed Margaret, Speratus, the Virgin Marina, Blessed Agnes, Saint Dorothea, and Saint Engratia.

**Note:** Saint Speratus, leader of the Scillitan martyrs, suffered martyrdom with them at Carthage and is commemorated on July 17. Marina the virgin, a martyr in Galicia, is commemorated on July 18. **Bolland.**

**Note:** Saint Engratia, or Encratis, a martyr of Zaragoza, is commemorated on April 16. **Bolland.**

Apart from all the relics mentioned above, eight fairly large chests filled with the most holy relics remain in the aforementioned church, as we have learned from our predecessors. None of us, nor anyone else of the present age, has dared to open them.

Together with all these things, the sacred Isidore—holy, nourishing, and great in merits—adorns the same hall. May he stand continually before the Lord as intercessor for us all.

After the same king had bestowed many great gifts upon that place, he established for himself and his descendants a suitable place of burial, so that beneath the shelter of that dwelling he might rest after death with his successors. To him, already living immortally with so many blessed companions, he consecrated, as far as he was able, a worthy basilica.

There our Lord Jesus Christ continues to work, through Isidore, the nourishing teacher of his Church, and through the others whose names we have mentioned, very many miracles to the praise and glory of his name, even to the present day. Some have been buried in silence, partly through ignorance and partly through negligence; nevertheless, we have judged it fitting to commit a few of the many to writing with a faithful pen.

**CHAPTER V. The blind and mute healed; water and rain granted; victory given over the Saracens.**

[Col. 0959C]

20. A certain very wealthy Jew, out of fear of the good king Adefonsus, son of the great King Fredenandus, fled to the church of the aforesaid confessor, believing that there he would be safer. Meanwhile, behold, four men were carrying a certain sick man on a pallet, with his feet bound to his buttocks; he had never turned over in bed for many years. When the Jew saw him, he addressed those standing around and said: “If Isidore cures this sick man through his prayers, I will receive baptism and give very many gifts to this church.” Accordingly, all who were present, together with the sick man, poured forth tears and earnestly implored the mercy of the most glorious confessor.

[509] What more need be said? In the middle of the night, when everyone had surrendered to sleep, the sick man began to shout and emit loud cries, so that everyone arose and surrounded him. When they asked him why he was disturbing them so, he replied: “Do you not see my lord Isidore, drawing my legs and granting health to my infirmity?”

[Note: Nic. Antonius observes that *crura trahere* (“to draw the legs”) is a Hispanic expression, by which they say *traer las piernas*. BOLLAND.]

All were amazed and attentive, and they heard the sound of his veins, as when dry wood is broken. After several hours had passed, he rose healthy from his bed, immediately went on his own feet to the altar, embraced it with tears, and praised the confessor’s mercy. He promised to remain most devotedly in his service for all the days of his life. When the Jew saw all this and perceived that the sick man was healthy and walking on his own feet, he firmly believed; he immediately returned fearlessly to his house and, having been baptized with his entire household, devoted himself thereafter to serving God.

21. A certain man from the city of Asturica had raised a boy who had been mute and deaf from birth. When the man came to León, he brought the boy with him. While the man was passing through the city on his business, the aforesaid boy left the lodging-house and wandered through the city, which he had never before seen. By chance he came to the aforesaid church. Entering the church in childlike fashion and proceeding toward the altar, he encountered a most noble man dressed in episcopal vestments and carrying a bishop’s staff in his hand. The man drew out his tongue and said to him: “You have been freed from the bonds of your tongue and made healthy; give glory to God.”

Rejoicing and exulting, the boy returned. Going down through the town to the marketplace, he took off the new cloak his master had given him and attempted to give it to a merchant in exchange for wax. When the king’s steward’s servants saw this, they accused him of stealing the cloak and hastily sent him to prison.

[Note: Nic. Antonius wonders whether *aulici* should be read instead of *famuli*. BOLLAND.]

When his master searched for him throughout the city and passed through the marketplace inquiring about him, they told him that the aforesaid boy was in prison. He entered the prison, and when the boy saw him, he began to shout loudly: “Father, help!” Hearing the cries but not seeing the cloak, the man went out, saying: “I do not know this boy; for my boy was mute.” Unable to bear his father’s departure, the boy again began to cry out repeatedly, saying: “Father, father, have mercy!” The man returned, carefully examined his clothing, and asked how this had happened to him. The boy then related the whole event to his master. Astonished, the man freed him from his bonds and went throughout the city proclaiming the miracle.

When the bishop of León heard of the miracle that had been divinely accomplished, he came on foot with his canons to the church of the blessed confessor and, causing all the bells throughout the city to ring, praised the mercy of the Almighty. Likewise, citizens came from every quarter to the confessor’s basilica and offered innumerable praises to God. Jews who had come to the city for the sake of commerce also praised the miracle and extolled the confessor with their voices. Thus this miracle glorified the city and the region and, by God’s will, greatly exalted His confessor.

22. There is also a sufficiently noteworthy miracle concerning a certain soldier, which must not be passed over in silence. The king had decreed that he should be put to death unless, through the prompting of divine grace, he took refuge in the church of the aforesaid confessor Isidore. Nevertheless, the king ordered him to be guarded by armed men and, under threat of death, forbade anyone to give him food or drink.

What more need be said? After seven days had passed, the soldier reached the point of death. Yet divine grace did not abandon him: the stone beneath the feet of the celebrating priest miraculously emitted clear water. The soldier mentioned above drank it repeatedly and was sufficiently refreshed. What remained is preserved to the present in a glass vessel, for the honor of God and of Isidore, the most holy teacher of the Spaniards, and for the healing of the sick. It is so sweet and excellent that one would think it had just been drawn from a perfectly clear, perennial spring.

[Note: The Bollandists confuse Adefonsus, or Alfonso VII, with Alfonso X. Alfonso VII, son of Count Raimundus and Urraca, ruled at the beginning of the twelfth century and called himself emperor of Spain. Alfonso X, son of Saint Ferdinand and Beatrice, daughter of the German Emperor Philip, held the kingdom in the thirteenth century and was proclaimed German emperor. This work is speaking of Alfonso VII, not of Alfonso X, surnamed “the Wise.” Rodrigo of Toledo briefly relates the apparition of Saint Isidore in *On the Deeds of Spain*, book VI, chapter 11:

“And when the seed of dissension had already germinated in the purple of the diadem, the emperor, having gathered an army, besieged Beatia. When some of his men had withdrawn, the Saracens gathered from every direction and immediately came to raise the siege. Saint Isidore appeared at night, strengthening the emperor and promising to be his helper in the battle on the following day. Therefore, when dawn appeared the next day and battle had been joined, the emperor prevailed according to Saint Isidore’s promise,” and so forth.

Because of the miracle, he established the church of Saint Isidore with a community of Regular Canons and adorned it with many gifts. Beatia is the city in the kingdom of Granada commonly called Baeza. AREV.]

23. When the most serene emperor Adefonsus, in order to enlarge the boundaries of Holy Church and conquer the Ishmaelites, enemies of the Cross of Christ, had devastated many of their territories, he deliberately besieged Beatia, formerly a Christian city that had been invaded by the aforesaid Agarene forces, with a very small military contingent.

[Note: This is Adephonsus, son of Count Raimundus and Urraca, elected emperor during the imperial schism against Richard the Englishman in 1258, until he voluntarily resigned that dignity in 1274. BOLLAND.]

[Note: After capturing Almería, the maritime city of the kingdom of Granada, and Córdoba, he besieged Baeza. Thus Tudensis in his *Chronicle*: but here “Beatia” may perhaps be Baza, ancient Basti, in the same kingdom of Granada; or Baeza in New Castile, on the borders of that kingdom, as González de Ávila assigns it. BOLLAND.]

[Note: Tudensis adds in his *Chronicle* that the soldiers had melted away, and that for that reason he remained with few men. BOLLAND.]

When the Saracens learned of this from the surrounding cities, they gathered an innumerable multitude of their people and hastened to destroy the camp of the Catholic emperor. Considering the smallness of the Christian army and trusting in the strength and multitude of their own forces, the Saracens surrounded the Christian formations on every side as Thursday evening fell, prepared to kill the emperor and his men in a triumphant slaughter when Friday dawned and battle was joined.

[511] But when the illustrious emperor saw that he and his men could not withstand the enemy’s attack, they were dismayed in spirit and invoked merciful God for help. While these things were taking place, the emperor, sitting in his tent, was briefly overcome by sleep. A certain man appeared to him, adorned with venerable white hair and clothed in an episcopal mitre; his face shone like the brightest sun. He walked about, holding in his right hand a fiery, double-edged sword. He addressed the emperor kindly, saying:

“O Adefonsus, why do you doubt? For all things are possible for Christ, the great Emperor, our God.”

He added:

“Do you see this multitude of Ishmaelites? At first light they will vanish from your face like smoke. For I have been given by God as guardian to you and to those who will be born from your line, if you walk before Him in truth and with a perfect heart.”

The emperor said to him:

“Who are you, most holy Father, who speak such things to me?”

“I am,” he replied, “Isidore, teacher of the Spaniards, successor to the preaching of the blessed apostle James. This right hand belongs to that same apostle James, the defender of Spain.”

After he had said these things, the vision disappeared.

The emperor awoke, summoned the bishops and the counts who were with him, and related the vision to them in order. When they heard it, they poured out abundant tears from excessive joy and praised together the mercy of almighty God. Some of them said:

“Lord, if it pleases your majesty, let us establish a confraternity, commending ourselves to his protection both in life and in death.”

The proposal pleased everyone, and they confirmed it with the kiss of peace.

But because Queen Sancia, the lady, had earnestly urged the emperor to transfer the reverend Peter Arias, the prior who lived with his canons under the habit and rule of Saint Augustine in the monastery at Carvajal, to the church of Saint Isidore at León, certain knights, seeking to gain the favor of their lady queen, said in persuasion:

[Note: Sancia, the king’s sister, was ordered by him to be called queen. She remained a virgin, adorning Christ’s churches with many distinctions, building monasteries, and relieving Christ’s poor. Thus Todensis in his *Chronicle*. BOLLAND.]

“Lord, if it pleases your highness, what your sister, Queen Lady Sancia, requests would be exceedingly acceptable to God and to the most holy confessor, and, through the prayers of the canons, would bring salutary remedy to your whole empire.”

The emperor replied:

“And how do we know whether this pleases God and His confessor or not?”

The nobles answered him:

“Yes, lord; it has been revealed by heavenly disclosure to certain servants of God and to your sister, Queen Lady Sancia.”

The emperor gave thanks for this and blessed the Lord. The sacred bishops, together with the counts, also gave thanks and jointly decreed that, with acclamations of the names of Saint Isidore and Saint James, they should attack the enemy at first light.

After this the emperor, pressed by sleep, saw the blessed confessor appear to him with a joyful countenance, saying:

“The confraternity you have established I receive under my protection. To those who faithfully observe it, I shall be a helper in life and in death. As for what has been suggested to you concerning Prior Peter Arias and his canons, it is pleasing to almighty God, to His most glorious Mother, and to me. Therefore act, take courage, and be a man; for when dawn breaks, the Lord, through my intercession, will deliver this entire multitude to you. Moreover, all the Saracen kings beyond the sea will be subjected to your dominion.”

After saying these things, the saint disappeared.

Made bolder by the vision, the emperor ordered his men to advance to battle. They carried out his command manfully and devastated the Saracen army. When the Agarene forces saw the Christians’ boldness and saw their own men being slaughtered in mutual carnage, they turned their backs and fled, leaving a great quantity of spoils to our forces. The Saracens who were in the city came out to the emperor and surrendered themselves and the city to him.

The other kings of Spain, both Saracen and Christian princes, recognizing that heavenly victory had been granted to the Catholic emperor, made themselves his vassals and tributaries through the victory of the blessed Isidore.

After so many fortunate successes, the emperor returned to León. He summoned the venerable Peter Arias, the prior, and only with many entreaties could he obtain from him that he be transferred with his canons to the monastery of Saint Isidore. He gave them many gifts and privileges of perpetual freedom.

24. At a certain time—when, not without cause and justification, the Lord perhaps wished to correct the human race by withdrawing His benefits, or perhaps wished to display Himself as glorious in blessed Isidore—it happened that, because of the lack of rain, almost all the crops, together with the other things growing from the earth, perished for three years.

When Lord John, of blessed memory and at that time bishop of León, saw such a calamity,

[Note: John was made bishop about the year 1133, when his predecessor Arias, being ill, made his will. BOLLAND.]

religious men also saw it: namely, the abbot of Saint Claudius, and the priors of Saint Isidore and Saint Mark, who lived in that same city and its suburbs.

[Note: The Order of Saint Benedict. BOLLAND.]

They fled to the one and singular refuge, imploring almighty God. The aforesaid bishop therefore took the body of Saint Froilan, together with many other relics venerated in his church.

[Note: Saint Froilan, formerly a Benedictine abbot and later bishop of León, is commemorated on 3 October. BOLLAND.]

The abbot of Saint Claudius likewise took the bodies of Saints Claudius, Lupercius, and Victoricus, which rest in his monastery. The prior of Saint Isidore took the body of Saint Vincent and a substantial portion of the bodies of his two sisters, so that a procession might be arranged.

All prepared themselves in ecclesiastical vestments. Yet because they had already run, as it were, without the body of the most blessed confessor Isidore, and therefore without obtaining the prize,

[Note: This alludes to 1 Corinthians 9: “All indeed run, but one receives the prize.” BOLLAND.]

they believed that they could not attain it. Accordingly, the aforesaid bishop and the venerable virgin of Christ, Lady Sancia, the emperor’s sister, approached Lord Peter Arias, then prior of the monastery of Saint Isidore—for until his death they had no abbot—and asked that the body of the most holy confessor be carried in procession with the other bodies and relics of the saints. They believed that, through so great an advocate, everything they asked for would be obtained.

The prior was scarcely moved by their prayers. At length, having obtained the consent of his canons, who regarded the body as an incomparable treasure, he humbly agreed to have it carried.

They therefore carried with the greatest reverence a golden chest adorned with fresh and shining pearls, in which the relics of so great a Father were deposited.

[Note: Nic. Antonius, citing a manuscript of Ambrosius Morales, asserts that, according to its testimony, no relics in the world seemed to be preserved with such splendid and rich ornamentation; and that most of the chest was covered or gilded with gold plates, and so forth. BOLLAND.]

When the procession had been arranged, they reached a certain mountain not far from the city, beside the road leading to the threshold of Saint James. There a very great multitude of humble poor people gathered, shedding tears, groaning, and sighing. With still greater devotion, like the children of Israel once gathering before Moses at Elim,

[Note: Rather, at Marah, before they came to Elim, as Exodus 15:24 relates. There the people suffered from the lack of drinkable water, whereas at Elim there were twelve springs of water. BOLLAND.]

they humbly sought from the Lord the gift of rain.

There stood an extraordinary assembly of venerable priests and clerics; there were sacred communities of religious; there was a great crowd of all the people; and there was an almost innumerable multitude of both sexes.

The venerable bishop, the spouse of Christ’s Church, surrounded by so many children and adorned with episcopal vestments, urged them all in his honeyed speech to implore the Lord, asking that He graciously grant them a joyful return after they had obtained the mercies requested through the prayers of the saints.

But because the judgments of God are a great abyss, they were to some extent disappointed in their desire.

When, as was customary, the processional service had been completed—with almsgiving and the greatest devotion to prayer—they took up the bodies of the saints together with all the relics and approached the revered body with the greatest reverence in order to carry it back to its monastery.

But the Holy Spirit fixed it there with such weight that it remained immovable, like the blessed Lucia when she stood in the struggle of martyrdom.

[Note: Saint Lucia is commemorated on 13 December; on that day her Acts and Martyrologies celebrate her immobility. BOLLAND.]

When Prior Peter Arias and the flock entrusted to him saw that they had been deprived of so great a Father, they lamented bitterly and without restraint, displaying their pious affection of heart through tears and sighs. For they said:

“Who will console the afflicted in their tribulations?”

As they uttered these and similar words, they kissed the ground before his splendid chest.

Meanwhile Lady Sancia, the venerable virgin of Christ, who truly excelled in the holiness of her merits and loved him with the fervor of extraordinary devotion, came with a great crowd of nobles and ladies. With repeated sighs, great anguish of heart, and tears, she began to cry out in a most sweet voice, kneeling before the chest:

“O my spouse and lord,” she said, “you who, while you lived in the flesh, deigned to console the desolate—why do you leave me, your wretched bride, desolate? Where do you intend me to go without your consolation, as though cast off and rejected? Why do you not at least hear the company of the canons shedding tears, and the prelates together with the citizens who implore you beneath the shadow of your protection, our only consolation?”

Their individual grief became common to all, so that scarcely anyone could refrain from weeping.

At last the bishop, the abbot, and the aforesaid priors, together with all the clerics present, both religious and secular, seeing these things, made a vow confirmed by oath on behalf of themselves and their successors: henceforth, whatever danger might threaten and however great it might be, the sacred body would never again be moved from its church.

Meanwhile the whole multitude of people standing there, their faces wet with tears, promised to pay it a perpetual tribute if it would deign to return to its former place.

After three days had been completed in bitterness and lamentation, and after the vow had been made, they approached the chest of the most holy confessor. When they lifted it, they found it so light and portable that almost everyone, as was indeed the case, regarded the event as a miracle.

All who had previously seen and heard that the chest was immovable came running together. Filled with amazement, they began humbly to sing praises to God and to His blessed confessor Isidore.

The bells of the city were rung throughout all the churches. The air was filled with rejoicing, and the earth was made fertile by abundant rains. The entire city rushed out in crowds, and the whole region hastened to behold the mighty works of God, which the Lord of majesty had gloriously displayed in His saint. All glorified the omnipotence of the Savior for the fulfillment of their desire.

It is said that in that year there was such fertility of bread, wine, and the other fruits of the earth that the abundance seemed to exceed all measure.

At his return the entire region rejoiced, the city was filled with exultation, and the bright day shone with new lights. Everyone went out to meet him, and all celebrated solemn vigils.

They entered the monastery with hymns and praises, placed the most holy body in the sacred site, and strongly secured the chest with thick iron fittings, fastening it beneath the stones of the structure, so that, in accordance with the vow that had been made, it would never again be moved by anyone.

In memory of so great a miracle, on the mountain just mentioned—namely, where the Lord displayed the body of blessed Isidore as immovable—a church built in his name is still shown to this day.

## CHAPTER VI. Various Possessed Persons Delivered. Epilogue.

25. In the time of the emperor Adefonsus, a certain demoniac came to the aforesaid church and threw himself down before the presence of the blessed confessor. After remaining there for several days, one night, when the canons arose for the divine offices, the sick man—or, I know not who within him—began to cry out repeatedly, saying: “Isidore is driving me out.”

When everyone surrounded him, the demon departed with a great noise, leaving the sick man exhausted and grievously tormented. Everyone sounded all the trumpets with tears and gave praise to God and to His confessor Isidore.

26. At another time, a certain man brought his grown son, who was possessed by a demon, to the church of the aforesaid confessor and laid him before the altar. During the following night, when the father, exhausted by excessive labor and grief, had fallen asleep, around midnight—while we were performing the divine mysteries in the choir—the boy began to cry out, saying:

“Father, father, father.”

The father awoke, greatly disturbed, and carefully asked the boy why he had uttered so many cries. The boy related what had happened, saying:

“While you were sleeping, two noble men dressed in the most precious garments came to me. They announced that I had been healed, saying: ‘Our Lord Jesus Christ has saved you through us.’ When I asked them who they were, they said: ‘I am the apostle Peter, and this is blessed Isidore.’”

Thus restored to health, he gave praise to God together with his parents.

[Note: I have restored “from the regions of Saldania” in place of “from the regions of Sallavia.” For, as Florez observes in volume XXII of *España Sagrada*, p. 141, in the Spanish history of the miracles of Saint Isidore this miracle is said to have occurred “in the land of Saldana”; and our writers used *Saldania* for Saldana, which is a town in the open country of Old Castile. The Bollandists had also printed “at the church of Saint Bartholomew, which … is recognized as situated and begun to be built”—to which the note refers:

“It seems that the name of the place where that church was situated and begun to be built is missing.” BOLLAND.

I restored the reading “which is recognized as situated at Cepta,” since the same Spanish history reports “in the land of Cepeda.” Perhaps the author wrote *in Cepeda*. If the Spanish history of the miracles of Saint Isidore were available to me, I could restore more readings to their true form. AREV.]

27. In our own times, when not only bodies but merits also have failed, it happened that a certain man from the regions of Saldania, seeking the recovery of health for his little son—whom the most wicked demon was violently tormenting—went to the church of Saint Bartholomew, which is known to be situated at Cepta.

[Note: The name of the place where that church was situated and where its construction began seems to be missing. BOLLAND.]

After he had approached it with the appropriate and devout duty of supplication and had obtained nothing, as we believe, because of doubtful faith, he sorrowfully and mournfully prepared to return home.

When he had reached the outskirts of the city of León, and the cause of his labor became known, some people said to him:

“Come, hurry to the threshold of blessed Isidore, who is accustomed to grant unquestionable remedies of salvation to those suffering in this way, together with the saints whose relics are venerated there.”

When the boy’s father heard this, he flew swiftly on nimble wings, pouring forth tears and humbly asking the saint of God to deign to grant health to his son.

At once he lay down before the confessor’s shrine. A marvelous thing, rarely seen in our own times: as soon as the Lord’s wood,

[Note: A wooden cross, such as is customarily used in exorcisms, as is mentioned again below. BOLLAND.]

was placed upon the boy’s mouth and breast, the unclean spirit, driven out by divine judgment, was forced to depart through the unclean parts.

As a result, the boy, who could scarcely speak because of his age, suddenly burst forth by divine power with these words:

“Thanks be to God and to blessed Isidore; I am well.”

When an apple was offered to him—one that had been placed on the reliquary of the most blessed confessor Isidore and upon the altar as a remedy for health—the boy began to play with it. Or, more truly, the creature, in a childlike yet marvelous manner, rejoiced to our Creator.

[Note: “Nigrellos” may perhaps be what the Spaniards call “Negrillos.” AREV.]

28. A certain young girl from a village called Nigrellos was brought to the basilica of Saint Isidore when she was being grievously tormented by a demon. She did not depart from there until she had fully received the grace of health and had been freed from the most wicked spirit.

The sign of her healing—a thing that that malignant company is accustomed to do—was a coin, which the demon unwillingly expelled through the woman’s mouth and promised that he would never again return to her.

[516] The coin is carefully kept among us for his confusion, so that all who see it may glorify the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ with the Holy Spirit, who deigns to work wondrously through His saints.

Nor should we pass over what we learned from her account: the aforementioned demon had often thrown her into water or fire, unless blessed Isidore had mercifully and powerfully placed himself in opposition to him.

This can be clearly inferred from what happened when they came to the bridge of Rodrigo Justo. The demon who tormented her wanted to hurl her into the water and would have done so, unless blessed Isidore, as she herself said, had held her firmly by the hand. For the demon cried out that he could not be driven away from her except by blessed Isidore, as the outcome of the matter proved.

The evil spirit was also asked why he had dared to attack a woman devoted to the Christian religion. He replied:

“The occasion and cause of this matter was her neighbor, who, by reproaching her and falsely accusing her of having a lover, drove her soul into such bitterness that, her mind being more troubled than can be believed and her anxiety continually occupied with the charge brought against her, she opened a way for me to attack her. But in vain,” he said; “I leave unwillingly the one whom I entered, because my enemy Isidore is driving me out.”

[Note: I believe that the town Ollarios is called Olleros by the Spaniards. What is said below about a stone extracted from the “sea” of Salamanca I understand to mean the river of Salamanca. For medieval writers use *pelagus* for any body of water, including a river, as Cangius confirms with many examples in his dictionary. AREV.]

29. Not long afterward it happened that a certain woman, originally from a village called Ollarios, was violently and repeatedly agitated by demonic madness. Her relatives accompanied and restrained her, and she was brought to the church of Saint Vincent of la Gotera. There the demons repeatedly dashed her to the ground and said that they could be driven out only by Isidore, whom the woman had first invoked during the very moment of her possession.

Having received this response, they nevertheless did not trust the demon’s words but the power of the Lord, who heals the brokenhearted and binds up their wounds. They immediately brought her back to León, guarding her most carefully so that the evil spirits would not hurl her into the depths of the waters, something they had already attempted many times.

On Thursday, when she had entered the threshold of the church of blessed Isidore and wished to taste food blessed by the priest’s hand in order to restore the weakness of her body, the demons immediately seized her and dashed her down with terrifying cries.

When the priest attempted to drive them out by divine invocation, placing the Lord’s wood upon her, the demons said:

“You labor in vain, for we shall not leave the possession we have seized until the first Sunday. Then Isidore will come, who, together with Dominic of Silos, is engaged in freeing captives in Mauritania.”

[Note: Nic. Antonius observes that *Mauritania* here means the territory of the Moors in Spain. BOLLAND.]

They added:

“Because Isidore supports, against our side, the cause of a certain prostitute who has now died at Arévalo.”

[Note: Arévalo, commonly called Arévalo, is a municipality of Old Castile toward the city of Ávila. There is no doubt that the other places named above must likewise be sought within or near the boundaries of the kingdom of León, even if they are not explicitly found on geographical maps—namely Sallavia, Nigrellos, Ollarios, and so forth. BOLLAND.]

“Nevertheless,” they said, “Vincent, who is our enemy in every respect, has forestalled Dominic and Isidore.”

We should undoubtedly understand this as referring to blessed Vincent, the brother of the holy women Sabina and Christeta, whose body the most glorious King Fredenandus, not long after the translation of the most blessed Isidore, transferred from Ávila to León and placed beside Isidore’s body in the same church, in a reliquary made with marvelous workmanship, as we related above.

[Note: Nicolaus Antonius, citing Ambrosius Morales, reports that the reliquary was ivory covered with gold plates. BOLLAND.]

For it would be unworthy if the true fraternity of such great patrons, which lawfully claims the place in common, did not also claim the efficacy of miracles.

On the following Sunday, therefore, the treasurer, awakened by divine admonition, was told to hurry to the church and give the signal for matins. It happened that, at the first stroke of the bell, while the treasurer and very many other canons were present—those who had gathered to see the outcome—the woman was seized by the demons, just as the spirit of falsehood had predicted.

But when the spirit of truth pressed upon them, and the woman lay prostrate before the altar of blessed Isidore, the demons declared that they could no longer remain there. Miserably begging for the place through which they should depart, they were forced to leave through the part by which human excrement exits.

As a sign of the divine miracle, one of those demons expelled a coin through the woman’s mouth, and another expelled a small stone, which he claimed to have extracted at that very moment from the sea—or river—of Salamanca. A third had already given a piece of lead as a sign, which the same woman wore tied at the top of a ribbon.

When they saw this miracle, all of us who were present broke into a loud voice, singing the *Te Deum laudamus*, while all the bells were rung. We praised the author of the universe in a hymn of praise: He who, through the blessed Isidore and Vincent, never ceases to work miracles in order to display the magnificence of His power, “in the voice of exultation and jubilation, with strings and organ and melodious cymbals,” so that God might be praised from heaven.

30. When, contrary to the Church’s prohibition, a certain woman attempted to perform some servile work on the feast of the holy virgins Justa and Rufina, one of her hands was deprived of its function, so that she could not turn or move it at all [the reading *monere* is uncertain].

Believing that she would be freed through the merits of blessed Isidore, she was immediately carried, howling and crying out, to his church. When she touched the chest in which the ashes of his most holy body are kept, she recovered so suddenly that the many people present—both clerics and laypersons, men and women—were amazed.

31. Behold, that wondrous lawgiver Moses brings water from the rock for the thirsty people; and Isidore, truly the lawgiver of Christ, brings back a thirsty fugitive after giving him drink from the stone pavement of the altar.

Behold, Elisha raises the son of the Shunammite woman; and Isidore heals the deaf and mute boy from Asturica.

Behold, Peter restores Aeneas, the paralytic; and Isidore, after healing the paralytic, also converts the Jew who was astonished at the event.

Behold, James drives demons from possessed bodies; and from those bodies they openly cry out that Isidore frequently drives them out.
