Behold, Peter heals the lame man together with John; and the possessed boy declares that Isidore healed a sick man together with that same Peter.

Behold, Isidore, like Stephen full of the grace of God, performs great signs among the people in the city of León.

Behold, in almost the latest times, through his merits the dry earth is made fertile by rains, just as in the time of Elijah, who, standing on the summit of Carmel, prayed prostrate upon the earth until the sound of abundant rain was heard over the parched land.

It would be exceedingly fitting, but impossible, to recall and collect everything that the Lord works everywhere through him, especially in his church. For new wonders continually flash forth at his altar, and, through the multiplication of intercessors, glorious benefits for souls and bodies are obtained through our Lord Jesus Christ.

[Col. 0967]

## APPENDIX IV. THE SECOND SPANISH COUNCIL, OR SYNOD HELD IN THE CITY OF SPALIS ON THE IDES OF NOVEMBER, IN THE NINTH YEAR OF THE REIGN OF THE MOST GLORIOUS PRINCE SISEBUTUS, IN THE ERA 657, THAT IS, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 619, PRESIDED OVER BY SAINT ISIDORE, ARCHBISHOP OF HISPALIS.

(This council is found, among others, in volume 84 of the Collection attributed to Saint Isidore.)

[Col. 0967]

## APPENDIX V. THE FOURTH COUNCIL OF TOLEDO, OF SIXTY-TWO BISHOPS OF THE PROVINCES OF SPAIN AND GAUL, HELD IN THE ERA 671, IN THE YEAR OF CHRIST 633.

(This council also appears in volume 84.)

[Col. 0967]

## APPENDIX VI. PREFACE OF THE COLLECTION OF CANONS ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT ISIDORE IN A CERTAIN VATICAN CODE. IN THE NAME OF OUR LORD JESUS CHRIST, HERE BEGINS THE PREFACE OF SAINT ISIDORE, BISHOP.

[Col. 0967B]

Isidore, servant of Christ, to Hector, his fellow servant and kinsman in the Lord: greeting.

[Note: [Col. 0967B] 1. In the note at the end of chapter 91 of the *Isidorianorum*, I remarked that, after the two councils presided over by Isidore, this preface should be appended under Isidore’s name, addressed to Hector—or, as others read it, “to the reader”—as it is copied in Vatican Codex 4160. It may perhaps have given the Pseudo-Isidore an opportunity to fabricate another, fuller preface, which is found in the Pseudo-Isidorian collections; unless we prefer to say that this preface was first interpolated by Pseudo-Isidore himself and was later expanded either by him or by someone else. I nevertheless consider it more probable that this is a certain abridgment of the fuller preface to the canons, which has already been published in print.]

1. I am urged by many, both bishops and the other servants of God, to collect the provisions of the canons and reduce them to [Col. 0968B] a single volume, making one work out of many.

2. No one who has been stripped of his possessions or driven by force or fear from his own see may be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned according to canonical procedure.

[Col. 0969A] 3. No one who has been stripped of his possessions or driven by force or fear from his own see may be accused, summoned, judged, or condemned—according to canonical procedure—before everything taken from him has been restored to him by law, before he himself has long enjoyed his honors peacefully, and before, having been regularly restored to his own see, he has freely possessed its honor for a considerable time. Accordingly, the ecclesiastical history composed by Eusebius, bishop of Caesarea, says of a certain woman who was accused by her husband on account of her chastity:

“The emperor ordered, or it was decreed by an imperial law, that she should first be allowed to arrange her household affairs freely for a considerable time and only then answer the charges brought against her.”

[Note: [Col. 0969B] 4. In the editions of the fuller preface the reading is *concinnantiae*; in the margin, *concinnantia*. Perhaps *consonantiae* or *consonantia* should be read.]

4. All these laws—ecclesiastical as well as civil and public—give the same instruction. If all their agreement were set down, however, the day would end before the task was finished and the letter would become excessively long. Nevertheless, we have judged it appropriate to insert here some passages, for the sake of encouraging others.

5. For Saint Leo, bishop of the Roman [Col. 0969B] Church, says in the letter sent to the Council of Chalcedon:

“Because we are not unaware that the condition of many churches has been disturbed by wicked rivalries, and that very many of our [Col. 0970A] brothers have been unjustly driven from their sees, carried into exile, and replaced by others in the place of the survivor [perhaps: ‘of the survivors’], let the medicine of justice first be applied to these wounds, lest anyone be deprived of what belongs to him while another makes use of what belongs to someone else. Let everyone abandon such an error, so that no one’s honor should perish; rather, let the proper right of the former bishops be restored to them together with all their privileges.”

[Note: [Col. 0969B] 6. I do not think that *Apostolici* was customarily used simply for the Roman pontiffs until after the time of Saint Isidore.]

6. The ancient *Apostolici* [Apostolic bishops], who were before the Council of Nicaea, also enacted the same provisions. The council held at Lampsacus under Valentinian speaks in the same way. Many Roman synods bear witness to the same principle, as did Pope Symmachus and the other holy Fathers. To avoid prolixity, we have postponed inserting their statutes here.

[Note: [Col. 0969B] 7. Aguirre, volume I of the *Hispanic Councils*, page 25, placed the following title before his examination of the preface and of the collection of canons published under Isidore’s name:

“Joseph Saenz, Cardinal de Aguirre, *Apparatus to the Councils of Spain*, part one; or, a historical-critical-chronological examination or scrutiny of the Isidorian preface and collection of councils and decretal letters, especially those concerning Spain, for the honor and glory of Saint Isidore, archbishop of Seville, [Col. 0969C] most learned and celebrated teacher.”

Then, on page 27, he placed the *Preface of Isidore to his collection of canons and councils*, beginning:

“Isidore, a sinner, servant of Christ, to his fellow servant and companion in the faith: greetings in the Lord.”

This is the fuller preface that Labbe and others had already published, and which Aguirre, contrary to the opinion long accepted by nearly all learned men, attributed to Isidore together with the spurious collection of canons.

Among Zaccaria’s papers I find a collation of the fuller edition published by Aguirre and others with a certain parchment Vallicellian manuscript of the ninth or tenth century. It contains a collection of canons under Isidore’s name, compiled—I do not know by whom—and also appends a description of the collection. The variant readings are as follows:

Edition: *Preface … greetings*; manuscript: *Preface of Isidore the bishop*.

Edition: *Servants of Christ*; manuscript: *Servants of God*.

Edition: *One volume*; manuscript: *In one volume*.

Edition: *Some longer and others shorter*; manuscript: *Some short and others longer*.

[Col. 0969D] Edition: *From among many*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Editions*; manuscript: *Dictations*.

Edition: *As many codices as*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *They may have differed*; manuscript: *They may have disputed*.

Edition: *Are known*; manuscript: *Are recognized*.

Edition: *Nor does he ever draw it elsewhere*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *They say*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *The retinue*; manuscript: *We call it the retinue*.

Edition: *The gathering*; manuscript: *The assembly*.

Edition: *Of the council … passing through*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Or called a council*; manuscript: *But a council was held at Rome*.

Edition: *Let all direct*; manuscript: *Let him reduce all*.

Edition: *Of the eyes*; manuscript: *The protective defenses of the eyes’ winking*.

Edition: *For themselves*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Let them convene*; manuscript: *They convene*.

Edition: *And just as*; manuscript: *Just as*.

Edition: *And the assembly likewise*; manuscript: *The assembly or*.

Edition: *Said*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *At the beginning … of this*; manuscript: *But in this volume*.

Edition: *We have placed*; manuscript: *Let us place*.

Edition: *Who … judged*; manuscript: *Let those who have chosen to do this better do what they have judged according to the canons and the most learned council*.

Edition: *We have set before*; manuscript: *We set before*.

Edition: *Of men*; [Col. 0970B] manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Afterward … of this council*; manuscript: *Afterward, of the Nicene, Ancyrene, Neocaesarean, Laodicean, and Gangran councils; likewise of the bishops Siricius, Innocent, Blessed Zosimus, Celestine, Leo, and Gelasius*.

Edition: *Of the Greeks and Latins*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Distincta* (“distinguished”); manuscript: *Distinctae* (a change of inflection).

Edition: *We have placed*; manuscript: *We place*.

Edition: *For the summit*; manuscript: *Without doubt*.

Edition: *Convened*; manuscript: *Collected*.

Edition: *By the ministry*; manuscript: *Of the minister*.

Edition: *Many … oppressed*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *They established laws*; manuscript: *They composed laws*.

Edition: *Many, therefore … through the whole of number 20, inclusive*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Four*; manuscript: *Nevertheless, four*.

Edition: *The fullest Faith*; manuscript: *In full faith*.

Edition: *In which … defined*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Which … proclaims*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Which … Nestorius … person*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *In which … [Col. 0970C] nature*; manuscript omits this.

Edition: *Si quae sunt* (“if there are any”); manuscript: *Si qua sint* (“if there should be any”).

Edition: *The first, indeed … its proper order*; manuscript omits this.]

THE DESCRIPTION OF THE MANUSCRIPT FOLLOWS.

It begins with the grades and names, or with the ministries, merits, quality, and ordination of clerics. First, concerning the origin or order of clerics. Isidore: “The clergy, and clerics, are so called from this.”

Book I consists of 239 chapters, the last of which concerns the twelve abuses by which justice is suffocated.

Book II consists of 297 chapters, concerning the primates of the Church and the times of councils, the life and chastity of clerics, especially the prohibition of *consortia* (sic), “associations,” with women, and women discovered in fornication with clerics. It begins with the principle that no priest may be permitted to ignore the canons. The final chapter concerns monks, the tonsure, and religious clothing.

[Col. 0970D] The text begins. Book III concerns baptism and chrism, the Lord’s Day, and the festivals of the saints; first, that the bishop should travel through his diocese and first examine how the clergy observe the order of baptism. It contains 294 chapters, the last of which concerns the subjection of subjects to the authorities.

It begins with the usefulness of penance and holy communion, even for those placed at the point of death, and with other matters of Christian observance that have been obtained [text uncertain]. It contains 478 chapters, the last of which concerns *Caenodoxia*, “vain glory.”

It begins with lawful marriages, abductors, multiple marriages, and concubines. First, concerning the incomparable testimonies to Blessed Mary the Virgin and Joseph her husband. It contains 237 chapters, the last of which concerns those who have dared to violate the enactments of the decretals. The author appears to be an anonymous Greek-Italian, who reveals himself to be a monk in his prefaces, which precede each individual book.]

7. If anyone wishes to know and read these matters more fully, he will be able to find and read them completely in their own authors. For if these provisions have been established concerning secular women [perhaps: “secular women and men”], they have been granted much more to ecclesiastical men and priests. [Col. 0970B] These same provisions are commanded by ecclesiastical laws and prescribed by the laws of the world.

[Col. 0971]

APPENDIX VII.

(From Mai’s *Collection of Ancient Manuscripts*, volume III.) In the aforementioned Vatican codex of enormous size, containing the whole Bible, I read on page 260 this prologue as well. Since I did not find it in the distinguished edition of Isidore’s works by Arévalo, I judged that it should be published.

ISIDORE GREETS THE READER.

[Col. 0971A] Origen, that man who once labored among the Greeks with no small diligence on a work concerning the divine Scriptures, in order to show our people what reading was found in each edition of the Scriptures, set out the editions of the individual translations on separate pages or columns, so that whatever was lacking or considered superfluous in one could be distinguished by the various signs used in the others.

Delighted by this kind of undertaking, I too preferred to bring together the book of the Psalms in two translations: either as the Seventy Translators and the others translated it, or as it is read in Hebrew and is acknowledged to have been rendered into Latin speech by the most holy Jerome. Accordingly, we placed the two editions side by side, so that whatever is lacking—or rather, whatever is present in excess—in either one may be made clear by signs prefixed to the beginnings of the verses.

Therefore, wherever something is superfluous in the Septuagint translation, it is marked with the virgule sign ÷; but wherever something is lacking, so that this may be clear, it is marked with the figure of the asterisk +. When, however, the two translations differ from one another through disagreement [Note: [Col. 0971] Isidore agrees concerning the meaning of these signs in *Etymologies* I.21; Arévalo had the relevant material printed there on a copperplate table.], the siglum [Col. 0971B] V has been placed in both columns.

For without doubt in many passages they suggest a quite different [Col. 0972A] meaning; in many others, however, they proceed with such agreement of meaning that either may equally be used as an explanation of the other. The comparison of this twofold interpretation is of the greatest value to the reader: for the ambiguity of an obscure statement, difficult to understand through one version alone, is opened up by examining the other.

It should certainly be understood that nothing has been written in the same edition where blank verses have become apparent. They have not been omitted or removed through the fault of the ancient copyists; rather, they are said to be absent from the translation proper.

In the titles, however, where the Septuagint has “For the end, a psalm,” the Hebrew has *To the victor*. The two do not differ greatly from one another, since perseverance to the end is itself perfect victory, as it is written: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

The first and second psalms appear without inscriptions in the Septuagint. In Hebrew, however, these are the ones that lack superscriptions: I, II, XXXII, XL, XLII, XLIII, XLIV, XLV, XLVI, XLVII, XLVIII, LXX, CXV, CXVI, CXVII, CXXXVI, CXLVI, and CXLVII. The remaining psalms, apart from these, are either given titles [Col. 0972B] with proper names or are marked by their own headings without a name.

# FIRST PART OF THE ISIDORIAN MATERIAL

—Concerning the life, deeds, and teaching of Saint Isidore, and concerning the editions embracing all his works.

9. **CHAPTER I.**—The preparation of an accurate edition of Saint Isidore’s works is exceedingly difficult. The method adopted in these prolegomena. *Ibid.*

**CHAPTER II.**—The final chapter of Saint Leander’s *Rule* for his sister Florentina, collated with the printed copies and Gothic manuscripts. 14

**CHAPTER III.**—The preliminary catalogue of Saint Isidore’s books by Saint Braulio, bishop of Zaragoza. 15

**CHAPTER XI.**—A sermon of Saint Martin of León on the translation of Saint Isidore, with notes. Saint Martin of León’s learning was divinely infused through Isidore’s aid. Other Spaniards of the thirteenth century celebrate Isidore’s praises. 59

**CHAPTER XII.**—A continuation of the *Chronicles* of Blessed Isidore the archbishop, composed by Blessed Ildefonsus, archbishop of Toledo, as Lucas of Tuy asserts; in it certain fables about Saint Isidore have been mixed in. Notes on this continuation. A warning taken from the edition of the Toledan Fathers. 64

**CHAPTER XIII.**—Whether the life of Saint Isidore published by the Bollandists has Lucas of Tuy as its author. That life is relegated to the appendices. Lucas of Tuy is defended against certain persons who contend that he fabricated many things in his *Chronicles* and in matters concerning Isidore. The author of the book *On the Miracles of Saint Isidore*. 68

**CHAPTER XIV.**—The life of Saint Isidore, by Roderic of Cerrato. Notes on this life. 76

[Col. 0972]

**CHAPTER XVII.**—Isidore’s homeland, parents, and birth. 95

**CHAPTER XVIII.**—Isidore’s childhood; the omen concerning the swarm of bees; his education in virtues and letters. He was not a disciple of Gregory the Great. Isidore’s Roman journey on the very night of the Lord’s Nativity is fictitious. Whether Isidore acted in Leander’s place while the latter was in exile. The embassy and exile of Leander, and the martyrdom of Hermenegild, are discussed. 103

**CHAPTER XIX.**—Whether Isidore professed membership in some monastic institution, as a Canon Regular, or among the Carmelites. 111

Saint Ildefonsus as Isidore’s disciple; and whether Braulio and the cleric Redemptus were disciples as well. 116

**CHAPTER XXI.**—Isidore subscribed the decree of Gundemar in the year 610. Thereafter he presided over the Second Council of Seville and the Fourth Council of Toledo. Whether he also attended other councils. 119

**CHAPTER XXII.**—Whether a pallium was sent to Isidore by the Roman pontiff. Whether Isidore held the primacy of Spain. Whether he exercised the Roman pontiff’s authority in Spain. 125

**CHAPTER XXIII.**—Whether Isidore ever came to Rome, either to the pontiff or to a council. Whether the book *On the Order of Created Things* is Isidore’s. 128

**CHAPTER XXIV.**—The fiction concerning Isidore the exiled bishop and Gordianus intruded into his place. A catalogue of the ancient bishops of Seville. 131

**CHAPTER XXV.**—Fabulous accounts of Muhammad, allegedly expelled from Spain by Isidore; of two lamps burning perpetually; and of a prediction of Spain’s destruction. Other fictitious or doubtful deeds of Isidore. 136

**CHAPTER XXVI.**—It is shown that Saint Isidore died in the year 636. 139

**CHAPTER XXVII.**—The life of Saint Isidore with its chronological periods. 141

**CHAPTER XXVIII.**—The false report that the body of Saint Isidore of Seville is preserved at Bologna. Miracles at the altar of the Church of León, where his body rests. 147

[Col. 0973]

**CHAPTER XXIX.**—Isidore, a doctor of the Church. Whether formerly there was discussion of numbering him among the four Fathers of the Latin Church in place of Saint Ambrose. 147

**CHAPTER XXXI.**—Isidore praised by the Roman pontiffs and in many councils. 162

**CHAPTER XXXII.**—Isidore’s authority among the collectors of sacred canons. The canons of Gratian drawn from Isidore’s works, identified and corrected by Carlo Sebastiano Berardo. 166

**CHAPTER XXXIII.**—Isidore’s praises collected from certain ancient writers. 198

**CHAPTER XXXIV.**—Various judgments of some more recent scholars concerning Isidore’s writings are examined. 203

**CHAPTER XXXVI.**—The first Madrid edition of Isidore’s works, prepared by Juan Grial. His dedicatory letter to Philip III and his preface to the reader are described. 214

**CHAPTER XXXVIII.**—The more recent Madrid edition of Saint Isidore’s works. The learned preface that was being prepared to precede this edition, extracted from the papers of the distinguished author. 225

# SECOND PART OF THE ISIDORIAN MATERIAL

—Concerning the individual works of Saint Isidore and their particular editions.

305. **CHAPTER XLVI.**—The works of Saint Isidore are reviewed from ancient library catalogues. *Ibid.*

**CHAPTER XLVII.**—A catalogue of Saint Isidore’s works from ancient writers. 309

**CHAPTER XLVIII.**—In what order Isidore’s works should be arranged in this edition of ours. The books of the *Etymologies* are discussed first. 313

**CHAPTER XLIX.**—The judgments of learned men concerning Isidore’s *Etymologies*. Isidore’s special interest, in the *Etymologies*, in explaining matters peculiar above all to Spain. 320

**CHAPTER LII.**—Concerning the unfinished manuscript observations of Johann Salomo Semler on the books of the *Etymologies*: his preface. Observations on this preface. 334

**CHAPTER LIII.**—An index of the writers praised by Isidore in the *Etymologies* and in the books of the *Differences*. 337

**CHAPTER LIV.**—The editions of the *Etymologies* are reviewed. 341

**CHAPTER LV.**—Manuscript codices of the *Etymologies*. Excerpts, notes, and translations. 344

Whether the genuine book was corrupted by an interpolator after its publication. 382

The learned observations of Bayer on this fourth book. 433

**CHAPTER LXXVIII.**—An interpolated *Chronicle* of Isidore, which Lucas of Tuy included among his own chronicles. The *Chronicle of Mellitus*, identical with the Isidorian *Chronicle* but interpolated in another manner, and more often mutilated and abridged. Isidore’s words concerning Saint Hermenegild’s war against his father, explained. The remarkable silence of Isidore and the other Fathers of the Gothic Church concerning the glorious martyrdom of Saint Hermenegild. The obedience of the bishops of the Gothic Church in certain difficult actions of the kings. 543

**CHAPTER LXXX.**—Isidore’s book *On Illustrious Men*. Editions of this book; manuscript copies. Zaccaria’s preface. Hardouin’s ravings against many ancient writings. 561

—Concerning the doubtful works of Saint Isidore and other works falsely attributed to him.

The observations of Pedro Manuel Hernández concerning Brachario, bishop of Seville, as the author of the same book. 595

The spurious collection of canons under the name of Isidore the Sinner, or Merchant, fabricated neither in Spain nor by a Spaniard. —Description of the Roman manuscript codices containing Isidorian works.

Several copies of the *Etymologies*. 854

**CHAPTER CVIII.**—Concerning the scribes, collators, and correctors of the ancient manuscript codices. Their names ought to be entered in a catalogue. A specimen of such a catalogue. 924

**CHAPTER CIX.**—The method to be observed in the present edition of Saint Isidore’s works. 934

Appendices to the Isidorian material. 935
